--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page serves as a defensive preface or "Invective against the Critic," a common feature in early modern scientific and botanical texts to protect the author's reputation from unfair judgment.</meta>

### AGAINST ZOILUS.
<note>Zoilus was a Greek grammarian known as "Homeromastix" (scourge of Homer) for his harsh criticism; his name became a standard term for a spiteful or pedantic critic.</note>

> *Whoever you are, Zoilus, who comes to pluck at this work with a hostile pen,*
> *A work of the skillful Mind as weighty as it is brief.*
> *Your guts will burst, cracked by foul envy,*
> *And a dismal fate awaits your censorship.*
> *This Work does not only evade your jealousy and sharp pen,*
> *But indeed, it is greater than any praise.*
> *This Work throws open a vast, hidden treasure,*
> *Which conceals immense riches within a small volume.*
> *It does not flaunt vain wealth, nor useless weight,*
> *And absolutely everything it contains is useful to us.*
> *In this same way, spices are preserved in small jars,*
> *Which you could never match in value with any price.*
<note>original: "aromata" - refers here to fragrant spices or medicinal substances, emphasizing that the book's small size belies its high medicinal and intellectual value.</note>

<summary>A defiant prefatory poem addressed to spiteful critics, asserting that the book's compact size contains invaluable medicinal and scientific knowledge that transcends petty censure.</summary>
<keywords>Zoilus, literary defense, botanical treasure, medicinal value, envy, preface</keywords>

<meta>This page begins the formal dedication to George, Duke of Württemberg. The catchword "ME" from the previous page (not provided) likely leads into the opening address or the continuation of the author's name, though here it introduces the formal titles of the patron.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece depicting symmetrical foliate and floral motifs with scrolls, centered around two reclining figures flanking a central ornament.</image-desc>

### TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE
# GEORGE,
## DUKE OF WÜRTTEMBERG
## AND TECK:
## COUNT OF MONTBÉLIARD
### AND
### SUPREME LORD IN HÉRICOURT,
### BLAMONT, CLÉMONT, etc.
### MY MOST MERCIFUL LORD.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut decorative initial 'A' featuring architectural structures and scrolling vegetation within a square frame.</image-desc>

As it is made manifest by the hanging of the insignias of the most powerful men, Most Serene PRINCE, that villas and houses are under their protection, so are they defended from violence and impudence. And in hardly any other way—amidst the frequent encounters with the sinister-minded <note>original: "Theonum," referring to Theon of Alexandria, used here as a metaphor for harsh or envious critics</note>—can BOOKS enjoy free passage when they are sent out into the public Field of Fame. For the fastidious perversity of this age can hardly bear with a calm mind for anything to come forth under a name.

<margin>Festus, Pliny, etc.</margin>
The learned scrape at them, the unlearned gnaw at them, and the fools, dolts, and blockheads <note>The author uses three specific Latin terms for types of fools: Blenni (simpletons), Bardi (stupid people), and Buccones (babblers)</note> mock them; for each and every one, the descent is easier <term>toward finding fault than toward imitation</term> <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸ μωμᾶσθαι ἢ πρὸς τὸ μιμεῖσθαι. This was a common proverbial expression in the Renaissance to describe critics who can only criticize but not create.</note>. Thus did the Virgils <note>original: "Marones"</note> and Ovids <note>original: "Nasones"</note> once greet Maecenas <note>The famous Roman patron of the arts</note> by that name. Thus did Quadratus, the Bishop of Athens and disciple of the Apostles, address the Prince Hadrian. And thus from then on, in every age, the ranks of writers have continually done; nor is it our intention to make those accepted rituals void.

And so, since they are in readiness to traverse the various regions of the world one after another—the NYMPHS of the Gardens, Meadows, Mountains, Forests, and of the Rivers and Springs—they now present themselves before your Throne, MOST SERENE PRINCE—

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of the work to George, Duke of Württemberg, justifying the need for a powerful patron to protect the book from the "gnawing" of envious critics.</summary>
<keywords>George of Württemberg, patronage, dedication, literary criticism, Maecenas, nymphs, Montbéliard</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>The catchword "Te ita-" from the previous page suggests a formal address or dedication that continues into this opening appeal.</meta>

They present themselves as suppliants before me: your Most Serene Highness, they humbly entreat that you might be willing to allow them to be sheltered by your protection and illuminated by your splendor. We also present before your same Throne their principal World, which we here make a matter of public law <note>original: "publici facimus Iuris" - meaning to publish or release to the public</note>: desiring to inscribe and dedicate it, however great or small our work may be, to your Most Serene Highness.

It is certainly a deed of great audacity, bordering on temerity, to offer such a gift to a Prince whose lineage the world venerates, and whose character and virtues are beyond all that can be said. Yet we read that small birds once brought feathers to the most magnificent Temple of the Delphic Apollo when they had nothing wealthier to give, and bees brought their wax. Thus we bring to his altars what is within our power. And we know we approach a Prince who is Most Serene, Most Clement, Most Benign, and especially well-disposed toward Letters and the Learned. Furthermore, a client's loyalty drew the *Fate of Montbéliard* <note>referring to the County of Montbéliard, a sovereign enclave in France then ruled by the Dukes of Württemberg</note>, once conceived, toward the Prince of Montbéliard; nor was it finally promoted, arranged, and polished except through the Physicians of the Most Serene Princes of Montbéliard. Then, a client's loyalty drew the *Man* toward the same Most Serene Prince—one who, in that great critical year <term>Climacteric: a period of perceived great danger or turning point</term> of his domains, the year 1635, attained the office of Principal Physician to the people of Montbéliard. He sustained that office for several five-year periods, with affairs always balanced as if on a razor's edge, and to this day he still glories in that service. Finally, a client's loyalty drew this *Botanical Work* toward the Prince of Montbéliard, for on every page mention is made by name of plants, both those cultivated in his Princely Garden and those growing spontaneously in the ditches and walls of the cities of the whole region, in meadows, fields, mountains, hills, groves, rivers, watered places and shores, villas and villages.

<margin>Antoninus <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus</note></margin> It is indeed a *Paper* gift, but one which that Great Emperor would not have despised, who, speaking of his own and others' inclinations, is reported to have said: "Some love horses, others wild beasts, others birds; but to me <margin>Augustus</margin> belongs the passion for acquiring books." <note>original Greek: "Ἄλλοι μὲν ἵππων, ἄλλοι θηρίων, ἄλλοι ὀρνέων ἐρῶσιν: ἐμοὶ δὲ βιβλίων κτήσεως"</note> Nor would that other of the Caesars <note>Augustus</note> have rejected it, who, contrary to the modest request of the Mantuan Poet's <note>Virgil</note> will, forbade the burning of his poems by a Heroic Edict:

> *Let the venerable power of the Laws rather be broken,*
> *Than that one single day should consume*
> *So many labors gathered through nights and days.*

But again, why a *Herbal Gift* to so high a Prince? Here we would remain in suspense, if we did not have it from the Holy Scriptures that the wisest of Kings <note>Solomon</note> discoursed upon every plant; and if we did not know from others that Diocletian, having voluntarily left the Imperial fasces <note>symbols of power</note> at Nicomedia, grew old among the vegetables in his own fields; and if Archelaus, Masinissa, Gentius, the Illyrians, and other most powerful Monarchs had not transmitted their names through the centuries into the eternity of the ages by discovering, loving, and describing plants.

<summary>In this formal preface, the author dedicates a comprehensive botanical work to the Prince of Montbéliard, justifying the humble gift of a book by citing historical precedents of emperors and kings who loved scholarship and nature.</summary>
<keywords>Montbéliard, botanical work, dedication, Marcus Aurelius, Augustus, Virgil, Diocletian, medicinal plants, 1635, history of science</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication of the botanical work to the Duke of Württemberg, following the standard conventions of 17th-century scholarly prefaces.</meta>

And so, **Most Serene Prince**, we hope that you will not disdain this *Work* which so many Great Kings have judged worthy of their own study: like the island of Tacape <note>An ancient oasis in North Africa, modern Gabès, praised by Pliny for its incredible fertility</note> which displays such abundance, or the Trees of Shilo <note>original: "Silonis Arbores"; likely a reference to the legendary evergreen nature of certain biblical or classical groves</note> which are never stripped of their leaves. Here is a most complete History of Plants, so concisely arranged that—just as it was once said of the works of the painter Timanthes <note>A Greek painter of the 4th century BCE famous for suggesting more emotion or detail than he actually depicted</note>—more may be understood from it than is actually painted. Rather, may you graciously and kindly receive this monument of our most humble devotion, a dedicated offering <note>original: "anathema," used here in the classical sense of a votive gift hung in a temple</note> of our respect and submission, which we strive to hang within your sacred treasuries. Through this, let the whole World know that **We** wish to be eternally mindful of the Württembergian generosities in which we have shared; let Posterity know through this that this age, too, had its own Patrons of the arts. At the sight of such a venerable Name, let the critic Zoilus <note>A proverbially harsh and cynical critic from antiquity</note> burst with envy, let Malice be seized with a numbing chill, and let idle fault-finders silence their lips with their fingers. You, **Most Serene Prince**, which is the summit of our prayers: may you live most happily for a long time, until, late in life and full of years, you are received among the *blessed dead* <note>original: "μακαρίτας" (makaritas)</note> to enjoy eternal glory and bliss with them. <margin>Fragment <br/> <unclear>@@</unclear>, 7. Theogony <note>Likely a reference to Hesiod's Theogony</note></margin> May Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardum," a principality held by the Dukes of Württemberg</note> always flourish under such a renowned Prince. May the Pillars of his happy Reign flourish. Here I pull in the sails and make an end, **Most Serene Prince**; beginning and ending as,

->**Your Most Serene Highness’s**<-

At Yverdon-les-Bains <note>original: "Ebroduni Heluetiorum," a town in Switzerland</note>,
On the Calends of April <note>April 1st</note>, in the Year **1666.**

<margin>*Most subject, and most devoted in all service,*</margin>
**DOMINIQUE CHABRÉE** Doctor of Medicine,
Physician of the City of Yverdon.

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This is the preface to the "Sciagraphia Stirpium" (A Sketch of Plants) by Dominique Chabrée. It establishes the work as a condensed version of Jean Bauhin’s massive botanical history.</meta>

# A SKETCH OF PLANTS
## AN INSERTION.

->From the Author to<-
### THE SACRED MINISTERS OF APOLLO,
<note>original: "Sacros Mystas Apollineos" — a poetic reference to physicians and scholars of medicine, as Apollo was the god of healing.</note>
->And to Each and Every<-
### STUDENT OF BOTANY,
## PREFACE.

Three great lights of literature have composed and published histories arranged into forty books: first, in the time of Augustus, *Diodorus Siculus* wrote a Universal History; thereafter *Polybius* wrote a Roman History; and recently, the prince of botanists, *Jean Bauhin*, wrote a History of Plants. And if that first author dared to entitle his history his "Library," then by a much greater right, in the view of fair judges, we shall call this the "Library of Herbalists." For in this work, whatever the *Ancient Greeks, Arabs, and Latins*, as well as the writers of the more recent century, have produced concerning plants, is found collected in a clear and elegant order. One thing, however, was criticized in it: **THE BULK OF THE VOLUMES**, which was the cause of many inconveniences and various difficulties.

Desiring a compendium for the sake of many, we have contracted those works into **One**, and that one not so very large. But it is a volume in which you will find missing hardly anything of those matters treated at length in the others. For here are contained the images of every kind of plant, their sketches, birthplaces, seasons, qualities, and uses, and finally the opinions and errors of the Ancients and Moderns concerning them. Here, whatever the gardens, meadows, and fields produce, hide, and nourish; whatever the mountains, woods, and caves; whatever the snowy peaks, precipices, rugged places, stony ground, bare rocks, and the turf of hills; whatever the gravelly banks, shells, and quays; whatever the watered lands, streams, shores, and the Sea itself; and finally, whatever the ruined walls, rubble, waste heaps, thickets, and neglected places: all is depicted, explained, and weighed. Here the riches of this and the other world are uncovered. Here, with prepared feasts scattered everywhere, the "Table of the Sun" is spread. <note>A reference to a legendary bountiful table mentioned by Herodotus.</note>

However, one should by no means look here for a "Sybaritic" style of speech <note>luxurious or over-refined</note> composed of words chosen for beauty; by no means should one seek Attic wit. We proceed by crawling in the manner of the "Thong-foots" <note>original: "Imantopodum" — a reference to a mythical tribe who crawled rather than walked; here meaning a slow, humble, and methodical pace</note>, we pursue facts and strive for brevity. Let others delight in "little fruit from much chaff" <note>original: "ἐκ πολλῶν ἀχύρων ὀλίγος καρπός"</note>; we offer "much in little" <note>original: "ἐν ὀλίγοις πολλά"</note>. But, lest we seem too prolific in the preliminaries of a condensed writing, the poem of a grave man and highly learned Physician—who is rightly numbered among the primary Sons of Wisdom—which is to be subjoined immediately, will supply the place of all other things to be added.

---

## An Epic EXHORTATORY AND
## Laudatory Poem.

<image-desc>Below the title is a poem printed in two columns separated by a thin vertical line. The first line begins with an ornamental drop cap 'I'.</image-desc>

Whoever you are who desires famous sights in various forms | Here you will behold works gathered in a small volume,
---|---
Produced with the beautiful image of playful Nature | Which Chabrée, the glory of the Apolline race,
To enjoy with your eyes: whether in the springtime you survey | Presents to you and adorns: and with study and a wise mind
The ornamental gardens planted everywhere with flowering plants, | Embrace with diligent care the noble study of plants,
Or also the orchards planted with fruit-bearing apples: | Under such a learned leader and protector.
Turn your eyes here: most beautiful to see | That noble study which the Greatest of the wise once [pursued]...

<summary>This preface introduces a condensed botanical compendium, explaining that it summarizes Jean Bauhin's massive forty-volume work into a single, accessible book. The author, Dominique Chabrée, emphasizes utility and brevity over flowery language, framing botany as a divine and ancient pursuit.</summary>
<keywords>Dominique Chabrée, Jean Bauhin, botany, herbal, compendium, history of science, medical plants, Apollo, nature</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page serves as a laudatory preface or "encomium" for Dominique Chabrey’s botanical work, likely his 'Stirpium Icones et Sciagraphia' (1666). The tone is high-style academic praise common in 17th-century scientific texts.</meta>

Others have cultivated these matters, and others hold the governance,
Those Kings whom the Muses commend by this celebrated name.
Turn your eyes here, whoever is touched by diligent
Care to know the powers of herbs and the use of healing;
Chabrey <note>Dominique Chabrey (1610–1667), a Genevan physician and botanist.</note> will freely offer you welcome aid.
He will disclose the hidden fountain of the Medical Art:
From where you may seek assistance, medicines <term>Pharmaca: drugs or medicinal remedies</term> outstanding against foul diseases,
Cleansing the body of disease-causing juices,
Medicines driving out toxins with an antidote-like juice.
He will not feed your eyes and ears with empty pigment,
Nor his own mind with fiction: how the milky humor
Enters the deep recesses of the heart through winding paths;
By what wondrous gyre the red rivers <note>A reference to the circulation of the blood, a relatively new scientific certainty in the mid-1600s.</note> are rolled;
By what liquid the watered limbs of the body are moistened,
And which nutritious juice is more suited to those wings.
More useful teachings will bathe your mind with light,
By which the fountain and origin of the Medical Art will be unlocked
For you, and an ample storehouse will be opened:
From which you might weave delays for premature death,
And—all diseases having been driven from the body, with God’s help—
Prolong lives that were despaired of,
And lead a better life by the aid of the Art.
What thanks, Chabrey, for such a great gift
Will the triumphant, sacred crowd of Healers pour out to you,
To whom, with you as leader, the mysteries of things lie open,
And compendiums lay out an easy path for the history of plants,
And explain the way, and more deeply disclose the secrets
By which, performing near miracles, one may revive the sick,
Over whom premature death looms with its black claws?
All kinds of plants which the Indian has, which the scorched African,

And however many plants of America, the wandering inhabitant of the soil,
And however many the damp marsh, however many the green grasses of the field,
And the ornamental gardens with their cultivated mounds,
However many flowers they have, and however many stems the crags
Produce—this useful Book exhibits all the riches of the earth,
Published by your industry and care, Chabrey.
As long as the fat meadows are green with joyful grass,
As long as gardens are painted with beautiful-haired flowers,
As long as medicinal plants inhabit the inhospitable mountain places,
Your honor, name, and praises will always remain:
And you will always be celebrated by Physicians in ages to come,
Nor will long-lived antiquity be able to abolish your fame.
O our glory, use your happy fates:
And may God prolong your life for many years.
With the same foot you began, continue to cultivate the medical Art
Happily, and open the mysteries of deep things,
Which Mother Nature keeps hidden under a covering.
Thus may that great labor of yours bring back its rewards,
Thus may Posterity grant you deserved honors,
And may you engrave your name in the sacred temple of the Muses.
You also will always be celebrated in our songs,
Great Chabrey, as long as spirit rules these limbs of mine,
And breathes into my heart with its vital breath,
And my Muses are ready and elegant in Song.
Renowned glory, renewer of flower-bearing Pindus <note>A mountain in Greece sacred to the Muses; used here to signify poetic and scientific inspiration.</note>,
Live, Chabrey, for a long time, with the Fates applauding freely.
Live long, with great fame surviving after your passing.
And may this immortal Book live for eternal years,
Under whose guidance the equipped storehouse of Physicians will flourish,
And perform many miracles, once diseases are expelled.

---

->These things were sung in congratulation by<-
->I. P. D'APPLES.<-

->Let the learned judge, let the unlearned enjoy, and let all favor this:<-
->and consider our efforts with fairness and kindness.<-
->And, if anything has been omitted by us, supply it yourself:<-
->mindful of what the Roman Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Seneca or Pliny the Elder.</note> once said:<-

### One man can find more than another, but no one can find everything.

<meta>This page serves as an errata list (correction of printing errors) for a botanical or scientific treatise. The author addresses the reader regarding the inevitability of mistakes in first editions.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut horizontal band featuring scrolling floral and foliate motifs at the top of the page.</image-desc>

# TYPOGRAPHICAL ERRORS.
<note>original: "ΣΦΑΛΜΑΤΑ ΤΥΠΟΓΡΑΦΙΚΑ" (Greek)</note>

It is almost a matter of Fate that the first editions of books—especially if they are composed of very small type—should teem with errors. Nor should this be turned into a fault of the authors: for it happens mostly through the blame of the workers in the printing houses, who, while they busy themselves to fulfill the day's appointed labor, both hurry and hasten too much. Nor is this a vice only of our age: for Martial once complained about this very matter in his own time:

<margin>Book 2, Epigram 8.</margin>
> *If anything in these papers, Reader, shall seem to you*
> *either too obscure, or not Latin enough,*
> *the error is not mine: the copyist did them harm,*
> *while he hurried to count out the verses for you, etc.*

Therefore, we protest the same here as he did. In the meantime, however, we submit this list, from which the Reader will be able to restore the more serious slips observed by us during re-reading.

# OF IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## FIRST CLASS:
### WHICH CONTAINS APPLE-BEARING TREES AND PEARS: AND WHATEVER CAN BE REFERRED TO THESE IN ANY WAY,
->Both native and exotic.<-

---

**APPLE TREE: German *Apffelbaum*: Belgian *Appelboom*: French *Pommier*: Italian *Pommare*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an apple tree branch with leaves and several hanging apples.</image-desc>

Its two main divisions are the *Wild* and the *Domestic*. They vary greatly, however, in the shape, size, color, and flavor of the fruit.

The Apple tree loves almost any location (if you exclude the hottest and the coldest places,) but especially temperate or even somewhat humid ones.

Apple trees bloom in various ways, according to the variety of the species and the region: spring and early varieties bloom sooner, late-blooming ones later: a similar judgment should be made regarding the ripeness of the fruits, which they reveal by the blackness of the seeds.

Furthermore, all types of cultivated Apples are of a cold and humid nature: and are born for kitchens rather than for pharmacies <note>original: "officinis"; referring to the apothecary's shop where medicinal preparations were made</note>. In Wild apples, however, the juice is violently harsh and sour, and for that reason, they are strongly astringent <note>term: astringent (a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, often used to stop bleeding or secretions)</note>.

---

**PEAR TREE: German *Birbaum*: Belgian *Pereboom*: French *Poirier*. Italian *Pero*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pear tree branch with leaves and several hanging pears.</image-desc>

In the Pear, both in the tree and the fruit, the same differences are observed as in the Apple: thus some are called cultivated, others wild; some early-ripening, others late-ripening: and furthermore, they are variously distinguished by the author or cultivator, by the location, color, flavor, shape, and similar traits: and every region claims its own for itself.

In general, however, all Pears love a fertile soil, and bloom in the months of April and May: the fruit ripens in Summer and Autumn: and those which bloom late, bear fruit late.

According to Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> all types of Pears are astringent: but others speak differently and more distinctly. To these authors, the bitter ones are of an earthy nature, the sour ones are cold and watery, and the sweet ones hold a middle way: and whichever are not sweet are astringent: and indeed the wild ones more than the cultivated, the sour more than the sweet, and the dried more than the fresh.

<column-break/>

**THE SO-CALLED NON-FLOWERING APPLE, French *Pommier sans fleur*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an apple variety showing a branch with leaves and a single large fruit.</image-desc>

Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist</note> reports in his Appendix that an Apple is found which does not bloom, and yet bears fruit: Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist</note> mentions a certain Apple endowed with very small flowers, which bears fruits called *Poma nana*, that is, dwarf apples. We ourselves have also seen it in the garden of the Most Serene Prince of Montbéliard <note>original: "S. P. Montbelgardi"</note> ripening its fruit in July and August. This kind of Apple usually lacks seeds, and it is perhaps that which Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher known as the "father of botany"</note> mentions in the 3rd book of *On the Causes of Plants*, which he calls the *Spring Apple*, and says it produces fruit without that nut <note>meaning the core or seed</note>. But since the flower is the beginning of the fruit, and the seed the beginning of the tree: who does not see that the law of Nature is violated here once and then again? Let the most subtle minds exercise themselves in this matter: we attribute much to the internal principle.

---

**THE MANY-FLOWERED UMBEL-BEARING PEAR, Pear-leaf, and the monstrous Pear.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical curiosity: a pear branch where a leaf appears to be growing directly out of the center of a developing fruit.</image-desc>

This most beautiful kind of Pear is quite rare, nor have we seen it anywhere except at Bollwiller in Alsace, and at Montbéliard in the Prince's garden. It blooms, however, in April and May toward the fruit, which rivals the so-called Muscatel Pears, and ripens in June. Is it a type of Alpine Service-tree?

No less rare seems what Dalechamp <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist</note> writes, that not far from Lyon, in the village they call Fontaines, Pears are born from the middle of whose body a leaf arises, so that you might rightly call it *Pyrophyllon* <note>Greek: "Pear-leaf"</note>.

Nor should we pass over what Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a scholar and physician</note> writes, that in Gascony he saw a Pear representing a human face so beautifully that it was brought by shepherds to the local ruler as if it were a human head. *More on Apples and Pears in the Appendix.*

<summary>This page introduces the classification of pome fruits, specifically apples and pears, detailing their varieties, growing conditions, and medicinal properties. It also highlights botanical curiosities like non-flowering apples and "monstrous" pears with leaves growing from the fruit.</summary>
<keywords>botany, apple tree, pear tree, medicinal plants, astringent, botanical curiosities, Montbéliard, Gesner, Theophrastus, Pyrophyllon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of fruit-bearing trees, following the previous discussion on Apples and Pears. It focuses on the Quince, various species of Service trees, and the Medlar.</meta>

### THE QUINCE TREE. German: Quittenbaum. Belgian: Queappelboom. French: Coignier. Italian: Cotognaro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Quince branch with two large, rounded fruits and several leaves.</image-desc>

Of this tree, just as with the Apple and Pear, there are likewise two main kinds: the Wild and the Cultivated. And this latter kind, in turn, either bears larger fruits which the Ancients called *Struthea* <note>A large variety of quince mentioned by Pliny</note>, or smaller fruits which are the most common. We consider the "Mixed" varieties to be nothing other than fruits produced from the grafting of various shoots of the Apple or Pear kind, whether you call them Honey-apples <note>original: "Melimela"</note>, or New-wine apples <note>original: "Mustea"</note>, or by any other name.

It flowers in April and May, but ripens its fruit in September and October. The tree loves somewhat cool and damp locations.

The fruit, especially the Wild variety, cools and binds <note>term: "binds" (adstringit) refers to an astringent effect used to stop diarrhea or bleeding</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE SERVICE TREE. German: Sperverbaum, Speierlingbaum. French: Cormier, Sorbier. Italian: Sorbolero.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Service Tree (Sorbus domestica) showing a tall trunk with pinnate leaves and clusters of small, pear-shaped fruits.</image-desc>

Service trees differ by sex, wherefore some are Male and others Female; they also differ by fruit, which is either oblong, egg-shaped, or round, and more or less tart and fragrant; and by location, wherefore some are "insipid" <note>original: "fatua"</note> and others are wild. There are also other distinctions: the one called the Fowler’s Service tree <note>The Rowan</note>, the Torminal Service tree <note>The Wild Service tree</note>, and the Alpine Service tree, which we shall treat soon in order.

The Service tree loves mountainous, stony, cold, and moist soil. It grows abundantly in various regions of France; Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> writes that it is very commonly found in Italy in fields, vineyards, and orchards; Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, Swiss naturalist</note> finds it in the Swiss mountains. We have observed that it does not reject cultivation even in the Prince’s garden at Montbéliard.

It flowers in March and ripens its fruit in September, which is astringent and pleasant to eat.

---

### THE FOWLER’S SERVICE TREE: THE FOWLER’S ASH. German: Grosser Maelbaum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rowan or Mountain Ash branch with pinnate leaves and dense clusters of small berries.</image-desc>

It grows in marshy and shaded meadows, and especially along the banks of torrents, in which places it takes the greatest pleasure. It also grows on the highest mountains of Alsace, Burgundy, and elsewhere; and we have observed it being cultivated in the gardens of Montbéliard.

It flowers in May and June; the fruit is perfected in September, which is most pleasing to Blackbirds [wherefore this tree is called *Aucuparia* <note>From the Latin "aucupium," meaning bird-catching or fowling</note>], because it contributes to fowling.

The berries, according to Mattioli, are astringent, drying, and repellent, and are preserved through the winter for the purpose of catching birds.

<column-break/>

### PLINY’S TORMINAL SERVICE TREE. Theophrastus’s Crataegus. Perhaps the French "Poires d'angoisse"? <note>Literally "Pears of Anguish," likely referring to their extreme tartness</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Wild Service Tree branch with lobed leaves and clusters of small berries.</image-desc>

This kind of Service tree is the fourth in Pliny’s description and is called "Torminal" <note>term: "Torminal" refers to its use in treating "tormina," or griping pains of the bowels</note>. Whether it is the *Crataegus* of Theophrastus, as almost everyone seems to have decided, we have weighed in our *Universal History*; let the learned see and judge.

It is born in mountainous places in rich soil; it is frequent in Burgundy and the County of Montbéliard, where they call the tree *Anier* and *Aigretier*, and the fruit *Anotes*.

In September the fruit is ripe; it is strongly astringent and highly effective against the griping pains of dysentery, from which it takes its name.

The use of its wood is the same as that of the Alpine Service tree.

---

### THE ALPINE SERVICE TREE, PERHAPS THE ARIA OF THEOPHRASTUS? German: Maelbaum. French: Nantuat, Cirier. Burgundian: Anier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Whitebeam branch with simple, serrated leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

We contend in our *Great History* that this is not the *Aria* of Theophrastus, contrary to the opinions of Anguillara, Lobelius, Pena, Camerarius, and Tabernaemontanus <note>A list of prominent Renaissance botanists</note>.

It delights in very high, cold, and wooded mountains; it is not at all uncommon in Austria, Pannonia <note>Modern-day Hungary/Balkans</note>, Savoy, Switzerland, and Burgundy.

It flowers in May, but completes its fruit in October, which the peasants gather when ripe and store away. It is astringent, but less so than the Torminal variety; it is pleasant to eat and useful against chronic coughs.

Dalechamp <note>Jacques Daléchamps, French botanist</note> notes that firm and solid walking sticks are made from its wood. Also, the best charcoal is made from it, which retains fire for a long time, which is undoubtedly to be attributed to the hardness of the wood.

<column-break/>

### THE MEDLAR. German: Nespelbaum. Belgian: Mispelboom. French: Nesplier. Italian: Nespolaro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Medlar branch with large, simple leaves and the characteristic open-ended fruit.</image-desc>

The *Common Medlar* is generally distinguished into the Cultivated and the Wild, the latter being considered more fragrant; by some, it is divided into the thorny and the non-thorny. A difference is also observed in the leaves, which are sometimes serrated and other times not; and also in the size of the fruits, some of which equal the size of an Apple. Others maintain there is only one kind, but that they differ by cultivation.

It grows spontaneously in the forests between Strasbourg and the baths of Baden. However, it is cultivated everywhere in gardens.

It flowers in April and May. It completes its fruit in September and later.

Its quality is cold and dry, and it is useful for stopping the bowels <note>i.e., treating diarrhea</note>.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses of the Quince, various Service trees (including the Rowan and Whitebeam), and the Medlar. It emphasizes their astringent properties and provides local names across several European languages.</summary>
<keywords>Quince, Service Tree, Rowan, Medlar, astringent, Montbéliard, Mattioli, Theophrastus, medicinal botany, fruit trees</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE ARONIA MEDLAR OF THE ANCIENTS.
->German: *Italian Medlar*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mespilus Aronia plant showing a leafy branch with small flowers and separate details of the fruit and seeds.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> held that there were three kinds of Medlar: the Anthedon, the Setaneros, and the Anthenocides. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica."</note> listed two: the Aronia and the Setanium (also called the Epimelis). He does not mention the Anthenoides. However, we have demonstrated in our *Universal History* that the Aronia Medlar was the true Medlar of the Ancients.

In Italy, according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian botanist.</note>, it is planted abundantly in gardens, pleasure-grounds, and vineyards. It is found even more copiously in Sicily, though until now it has not been well known in Germany.

It ripens its fruit at the beginning of September. The fruit has an astringent quality <note>Causes body tissues to contract.</note> and strongly binds the belly; it is also most useful for pregnant women, as it relieves <term>Malacia</term> <note>A historical term for the cravings or "pica" experienced during pregnancy.</note>.

<column-break/>

### DWARF MEDLAR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamæmespilus branch with serrated leaves and small round fruits.</image-desc>

Among our wild plants, under the name of Dwarf Medlar, we have the branches of a certain shrub. These are thicker than those of either the Quince-leaved Medlar or the Date-plum, and are covered in a blackish, furrowed bark. Its leaves are oblong, smooth on both sides, and saw-toothed around the edges. The flowers are arranged in a rounded cluster, in the manner of the Alpine Mountain Ash. The fruits are similar to those of the Wild Service Tree. These branches were gathered on Mount Baldo and sent to us from there.

Gesner <note>Conrad Gesner, a Swiss naturalist.</note> was the first to mention this fruit and shrub in his *Letters to Fabricius*, attributing to them red, round berries marked with a five-parted "navel" <note>The depression at the top of the fruit.</note> and leaves saw-toothed at the edges—characteristics which match perfectly with the branch we depict here.

---

### COTONEASTER, GESNER’S DATE-PLUM, Bellonius’ WILD APPLE: French: *Amalanchier*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cotoneaster plant with oval leaves and clusters of small berries.</image-desc>

This is a branchy shrub, though it grows into a tree-like form with cultivation. It has leaves like those of a Quince tree; the flowers are concave, greenish, and joined together in groups. The fruit is similar in shape and taste to the fruit of the White-thorn or Hawthorn.

Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, a French physician and botanist.</note> considers this to be the "Epimelis" of Dioscorides and Theophrastus; others pass it off as the Dwarf Medlar, and some as the Lotus tree.

It grows frequently on the ridges of high mountains. We have seen it on Mount Salève near Geneva and on Mount Aquæceda near Basel. It flowers at the beginning of Spring and ripens its fruit in August.

<column-break/>

### TREE CORN-FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, broad leaf with prominent veining, characteristic of the Cyanus Arborea.</image-desc>

This plant claims its place here due to the similarity of its leaves to those of a certain tree, a branch of which we keep that was brought from Crete.

The color of the leaves is silvery underneath and green on top, with a white fringe; they have the width and proportion shown in the Illustration, which displays both sides of the leaf divided by the midrib. They surround a small stalk, at the top of which are seen flowers appearing like a wand <note>original: "thyrsi"</note>, arranged like those in the common Soapwort, but with the shape of a Corn-flower and a crimson color. These slowly dissolve into downy fluff. The seed is longer than that of Cumin.

It grows among rocks in the highest precipices.

---

### POMEGRANATE TREE: German: *Granatbaum*: Belgian: *Granaet appelboom*: French: *Grenadier*: Italian: *Granataro*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pomegranate branch with flowers, a whole fruit, and a cross-section showing the seeds.</image-desc>

The most general distinctions of this tree are the Mild (or cultivated), the Wild, and thirdly the <term>Balaustifera</term> <note>The flower-bearing pomegranate.</note>, which is likewise a wild variety.

The fruits are either large or small; sweet, sour, or sweet-and-sour. They received their name from Carthage, where the most celebrated ones grow <note>The Latin name "Malus Punica" means "Punic/Carthaginian Apple."</note>; they are also called "Granata" from the grains <note>seeds</note> contained within.

The tree loves chalky and lean soil; the climate best suited to it is a warm one. In Germany, it only graces the gardens of the Great Nobles. In Italy, it is cultivated in gardens. In Languedoc and Provence, it is grown in gardens and occurs everywhere in hedgerows; it flowers and perfects its fruit early, according to the nature of the place.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH BALAUSTIA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dense, multi-petaled flower head, representing the Balaustia (pomegranate flower).</note>

The flowers mostly imported as "Spanish" are the <term>Balaustia</term>, which are the large flowers of a certain Pomegranate, packed with a very dense cluster of purplish petals so that they look like hundred-petaled roses. Their taste is astringent.

These are said to be the flowers of the Wild Pomegranate, which bears only flowers. The flower of the cultivated variety is called the <term>Cytynus</term> <note>original: "Cytynus"</note>, which, like the Balaustia and the <term>Malicorium</term> <note>The pomegranate rind.</note>, is endowed with the power of binding and drying.

Furthermore, regarding the FRUIT OF THE POMEGRANATE: if they are sour, they are astringent and cooling; if sweet, they are less cooling and more beneficial to the stomach; if sweet-and-sour, they possess a middle nature.

<summary>This page describes various species of Medlars and Pomegranates, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical distribution, and medicinal properties such as their astringent effects. It reconciles classical botanical names from Dioscorides and Theophrastus with contemporary Renaissance findings.</summary>
<keywords>Medlar, Pomegranate, Aronia, Cotoneaster, Mount Baldo, medicinal botany, astringents, pregnancy cravings, Mattioli, Gesner</keywords>

--- Page 42 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of trees and shrubs, following the previous section on fruiting plants. The catchword "MALVS" (Apple/Fruit tree) indicates the broader category for the citrus species introduced here.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

## **STRAWBERRY TREE: <note>original: "Arbutus"</note> Comarus of Theophrastus. German: Hagappffelbaum. French: Arbouzier. Italian: Albatro.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Arbutus (strawberry tree) branch with serrated leaves and clusters of small, round, textured fruits.</image-desc>

Some call this a tree, others a shrub. Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> describes it under the name *Comarus*; however, by Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and herbalist</note> it is called indifferently *Comarus* or *Arbutus*.

A certain difference is observed in the fruit: for sometimes it does not exceed the size of a hazelnut; at other times it fills the breadth of a small apple.

It loves mountainous places and woods: and is also cultivated in gardens.

It flowers especially in the months of July and August, sometimes also in September, and finally ripens its fruit, commonly called *Memecilon*.

It is sweet and of a pleasant flavor, but it harms the stomach, and is food for swine rather than for men. According to Curtius, the tree and fruit are powerful in binding <term>astringendi: the ability to contract tissues or stop bleeding</term>. *Could this be the "Uniedo" of Galen?* <note>Galen was a prominent Roman physician; "Uniedo" or "Unedo" implies "I eat only one," suggesting the fruit is not tasty enough for a second bite.</note>

<column-break/>

## **THE ADRACHNE OF THEOPHRASTUS, closely approaching the Strawberry Tree or Comarus.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Adrachne plant, showing a central stalk with alternating leaves and clusters of berries, similar in appearance to the Arbutus but with distinct foliage.</image-desc>

It is well enough known that the herb *Andrachne* is that which is called Purslane, and it differs from the *Adrachne* tree which we depict here. This Adrachne is a wild tree, not growing in the plains, similar to the Strawberry Tree <note>original: "Unedoni"</note>, only with a smaller leaf that never falls. The fruit hangs in clusters, the size and color of a Raspberry <note>original: "Rubi Idaei"</note>, soft like the Strawberry Tree fruit: and it bears fruit twice a year, like the *Apharca*.

Bellonius writes that it grows frequently in Crete. We have observed it on the mountain by the Doubs river near *La Chaux-de-Fonds*.

The wood is useful to women for weaving work. Indeed, Thrushes and Blackbirds are delighted by the fruit: whereby it happens that by this lure in winter they are easily captured with birdlime, nets, or other snares.

---

## **THE CHARAMEI OF ACOSTA with the leaf of a Pear.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Charamei branch with oval leaves and small, ribbed, pumpkin-shaped fruits hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

This exotic tree, which is green with perpetual foliage, has leaves like a Pear; it is called *Charamei* in Canara and Deccan <note>Regions in India</note>, and *Ambela* by the Persians and Turks.

There are two kinds of this tree. One is the size of a Medlar, with leaves similar to a Pear, of a pale green, with fruit like hazelnuts and yellow, and of a pleasing acidity, which they commonly eat either ripe, or unripe, or preserved in salt. The other is of the same size, but the fruit is larger: the leaf is a little larger than an Apple leaf.

It grows in woods and mountains far removed from the sea. The root purges by the bowels and by vomiting. The fruit, which is like hazelnuts, preserved with salt and vinegar, stirs the appetite <term>orexin: the desire for food</term>.

<column-break/>

## **THE MEDIAN APPLE <note>The Citron</note>, German: Citronoepffelbaum. French: Citronnier. Italian: Cedri & Citroni. Spanish: Cidras.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Citrus Medica (Citron) branch with large, oblong, textured fruit and broad leaves.</image-desc>

It is also called *Citrus*: but it is called the Median, Assyrian, and Persian Apple, from the regions from whence it was first brought. Galen writes that the fruit is not called the "Median Apple," but the *Citrium*: having acquired the name, of course, from the color of the rind.

It varies in size and birthplace rather than in kind.

Indeed, all species of the Median Apple love a warm sky and are least subject to the injuries of winter.

The greatest harvest of them is in certain maritime tracts of the Kingdom of Naples, Spain, and Provence.

The flesh of the fruit is cold: the rind is moderately hot and dry in the second degree: the seed is dry and hot in the same degree: but the juice is cold and dry in the third degree. <note>These "degrees" refer to the Galenic system of humors used in Renaissance medicine.</note>

---

## **THE MONSTROUS CITRON OF THE LARGEST SIZE.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "monstrous" citron, showing a very large, elongated, and heavily wrinkled/warty fruit.</image-desc>

In Liguria and the islands of the Aegean Sea, according to the testimony of Matthiolus, Citron apples grow to such a great size that they equal melons. Cardanus writes that in Lombardy they sometimes reach a weight of ten pounds.

Indeed, that one of which we give the image, we saw at Montbéliard, but it by no means approached that weight: although it was of a monstrous size. It had a rare shape, resembling a Polish or Turkish shoe.

Perhaps Augerius Gallus mentions this or a similar variety in his book on Agriculture written in Italian.

<column-break/>

## **THE LEMON APPLE: THE FRUIT. German: Limonen. Belgian: Limoen. French: Limons. Italian: Limone.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lemon branch with oval fruit, including a cross-section showing the internal segments and seeds.</image-desc>

Most people refer this to the "Median Apple" of the Ancients, and not foolishly, as it approaches so closely to it. There are, however, many differences in the shape of the fruit, the rind, the flesh, and the juice.

Matthiolus makes them larger and smaller, and differing in the sweetness of the juice and the thickness of the rind. Amarus distinguishes Lemons into acid, sweet, and of a middle flavor, and those which are of a smoother or rougher rind. In Spain, there are Lemon trees taller than the rest, but whose fruit does not exceed the size of a nut.

This tree enjoys the same climate and cultivation as the Median Apple, and has not dissimilar virtues.

It focuses on their physical characteristics, medicinal properties according to the humoral system, and geographical origins.</summary>
<keywords>Arbutus, Strawberry Tree, Adrachne, Charamei, Citron, Lemon, Citrus Medica, Botany, Renaissance Medicine, Humors, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Galen</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<margin>Signature: A 3</margin>

**THE ORANGE TREE:** *German: Pomerantzenbaum.*
*French: Orangier. Italian: Arantio.*

**ADAM'S APPLES:** *German: ADAMSOEPFFEL. French:*
*Adam's Apples & Ponzires. Italian: Pomi d' Adamo.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a citrus branch with leaves and two oranges (Malus Arantia).</image-desc>

It enjoys the same locations and regions as the Citron tree <note>original: "Malus Medica"</note>, and it flowers in April and May, later or earlier depending on the condition of the place.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that the wild variety is found on the maritime coasts of Africa and Provence.

There are various names for the fruit: Orange Apples, Golden Apples, *Aurangia*, *Arangia*, *Amarantia*, Citrons, and Medic Apples: as well as the "Apples of the Hesperides" of the Poets. Fuchs, Manardus, Ryff, Joubert, Sarrazin, and many others classify them among the Citrons.

The virtues and qualities are the same as those of the Citron apples. However, from its flowers, a water of most fragrant scent is prepared for various uses, called *Naffa* <note>Orange flower water, from the Arabic 'naffat'</note>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a citrus branch with a large, textured fruit (Poma Adami).</image-desc>

These, like most others, are referred back to the "Medic Apples" of the Ancients, but the *Ponzirus* <note>likely a variety of pomelo or large citron</note> wavers between a Lemon and an Orange: for it is not oblong like a Lemon, nor entirely round like an Orange, but larger than both. The color of the rind is that of an Orange, but the juice is that of a Lemon. Indeed, they wish it to be called *Adam's Apple* because it seems to have marks like imprinted teeth on its surface, as if it had been bitten by Adam, the first man.

Furthermore, this apple is not found everywhere: but it is cultivated especially in Portugal, Spain, and Calabria, according to the authors Amato <note>Amato Lusitano</note> and Cordus. *Could it be the Citrangula of Cesalpino?*

---

### CARCAPVLI.
### A TREE WITH FRUIT SIMILAR TO AN ORANGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch with large, round, segmented fruits (Carcapuli).</image-desc>

The *Carcapuli* <note>likely the Garcinia cambogia or a related species</note>, according to Acosta, is a tree of vast size, bearing fruit similar in size and shape to a "Golden Apple" <note>Orange</note> from which the rind has been removed.

It grows on the Island of Funda: and there are various species and differences of the fruit: for some are white, some chestnut-colored, and some flesh-colored, commendable for their taste above the others.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, leafless succulent-like branch with small rounded fruits at the tips.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), an influential botanist</note> depicts and describes this leafless little branch brought from the region of the Black Africans <note>original: "Nigritarum"</note>: its fruit, because of its great similarity to Orange apples, claims this place for itself. *Could it be the "Aracynappil" of Paludanus?*

---

### INDIAN GUAVA, WITH FRUIT HAVING THE APPEARANCE OF AN APPLE.
### A TREE WITH LAUREL-LIKE LEAVES FROM GUINEA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Guava branch with leaves, flowers, and fruit, including a cross-section of the fruit showing seeds.</image-desc>

The Guava is a tree of middling size, with spreading branches, a leaf like Laurel, and a white, scented flower similar to the flowers of the Orange tree. The fruit is similar to our apples, of the size of those which are called *Camuesas* <note>a type of pippin apple</note> by the Spanish: green at first and golden through ripeness, crowned on the outside like a Medlar, white or reddish inside, containing stones like those of Medlars.

It is common throughout all India, and is usually eaten by both the Indians and the Spaniards. When green it is very astringent, but when overripe it loosens the bowels. *Could it be the Indian Medlar of Scaliger?*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch with laurel-like leaves and a large, round, gourd-like fruit.</image-desc>

Clusius attributes leaves similar to Laurel to it: the fruit is equal to a large Apple, and of an almost circular shape, and its rind is not very different from the rind of a Gourd. *Could it be a foreign kind of Gourd?*

# OF PLANTS

### THE FRUIT OF THE ABAVI OR BAOBAB.

<image-desc>A large, oval, textured fruit with a thick stem, marked with an asterisk at the top left.</image-desc>

This fruit is most elegant, approaching the size of a Citron <note>original: "Mali Citrij"</note>, covered in a gourd-like rind. It has a reddish pulp that is crumbly, acidic, and pleasant to the mouth; according to Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini (1553–1617), a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian flora</note>, it is especially useful for quenching thirst. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> and Honorius Bellus received specimens brought from Ethiopia to these regions; Bellus attributes to it a great affinity with the Baobab described by Alpinus.

<column-break/>

### A BRANCH OF THE BAOBAB-BEARING TREE.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with palmate leaves (five leaflets), marked with an asterisk at the bottom left.</image-desc>

The preceding plate shows the fruit of the Ethiopian Baobab-bearing plant; this one shows the branch. Descriptions of both, however, are to be sought from the books of Alpinus, Bellus, and Clusius.

<column-break/>

### THE GOURD-BEARING TREE, OR THE FIG OF THE BLACKS.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a tree with large, elongated fruits hanging from the branches, similar to cucumbers or gourds.</image-desc>

On a certain uninhabited island near the place called *Cape Verde*, a certain tree grows having leaves similar to our native Fig. It has a long fruit, two feet in length or thereabouts, and thick in proportion, so that it seems to approach the size of large, long gourds. Inside is a seed similar to a hare's kidney, the size of a bean. They eat this much like we eat melons.

In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586</note>, it is called the Fig of the Blacks <note>original: "Ficus Nigritarum"</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE HIGUERO OF OVIEDO AND THE MAMEI TREE.

<image-desc>Two large, broad, lanceolate leaves with prominent veining.</image-desc>

This is a very large tree, like the black Mulberry, bearing fruit similar to a round gourd, and sometimes even oblong. The rind has the color and shape of a gourd. The leaf is long, narrow, wider at the ends, and becomes narrower down to the little stalk.

It is common on the continent of the American Indies. In this plate, however, one leaf of the Mamei tree is also shown.

<column-break/>

### SAMACA.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a small tree with rounded leaves and small fruits, showing exposed roots.</image-desc>

The De Bry brothers <note>famous engravers and publishers known for their accounts of the New World</note> displayed a tree of India depicted under the name of Samaca; but besides the figure and the name, they have nothing else, nor have we observed anything else regarding that name in any other author. The fruit depicted on the tree seems to represent the shape of the Guanabana <note>Soursop</note>, but the leaves differ.

<column-break/>

### THE UREBEHA OF THEVET.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a tree with a thick trunk and dense foliage. A small quadruped animal (possibly a fox or dog) sits at the base of the trunk.</image-desc>

This tree is of marvelous height, whose branches grow one beneath the other. It has leaves like Cabbage, and the individual branches are burdened with fruits a foot long. It also produces a red gum. *Thus says Thevet.* <note>André Thevet (1516–1590), a French Franciscan priest and explorer</note>

<keywords>Baobab, Ethiopia, Cape Verde, West Indies, Prospero Alpini, Charles de l'Écluse, André Thevet, botany, exotic fruits, gourds</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of exotic fruits from the Americas and the East Indies, focusing on their physical descriptions, medicinal properties, and regional names.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE GUANABANUS OF OVIEDO, with scaly fruit.
<note>original: "Guanabanus Oviedi". Referring to Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, a 16th-century Spanish historian who described the Soursop.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Guanabanus (Soursop) fruit, showing a large, oval fruit with a scaly or prickly rind, hanging from a small branch with leaves.</image-desc>

It is a tall and beautiful tree, with leaves almost like those of the Citron tree <note>original: "Mali Medicae", the 'Median Apple' or Citron</note>, which they call Lemon-green. The fruit is very beautiful, the size of a medium melon. The rind of this fruit is green, marked with certain scales like a pine cone. The flesh is very white and of a most delicate flavor, through which black seeds are scattered. This fruit is cold <note>In Galenic medicine, "cold" foods were used to balance "hot" temperaments or fevers.</note>, and useful for that reason.

It grows throughout almost all of America, and in many ways corresponds with the Durians, of which we shall speak next.

<column-break/>

### THE DURIANS OF ACOSTA.
<note>original: "Duriones Acostae". Referring to Cristóbal Acosta, a pioneer in the study of East Indian plants.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Durian tree. The tree has a thick trunk and large, spiky fruits hanging directly from the branches. A single large, prickly fruit is shown in detail to the left of the tree.</image-desc>

Among the most celebrated fruits of India are these which are found only in Malacca. They say the tree is very large, in the manner of a walnut tree, with leaves like Laurel and flowers turning from white to yellow. The fruit equals the size of a cantaloupe, covered with a thick rind and many pointed bumps, greenish on the outside, but chambered within. It contains small, white or pale seeds the size of a chicken egg in each chamber, in which there is a stone very similar to the stones of a Peach. This fruit is hot and moist; it is of a most sweet taste, but at first offensive to those unaccustomed to it, on account of the intensity of the smell, which is like burnt or rotten onions. Is this the *Durian* of Scaliger? Or the *Doris rans bry* of the brothers?

---

<column-break/>

### THE INDIAN HEDGEHOG FRUIT.
<note>original: "Erinaceus Fructus Indicus". Likely referring to the Rambutan or a similar spiky fruit.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a fruit-bearing tree. The fruits are small and spiky, resembling hedgehogs (erinaceus). Some fruits are shown fallen on the ground.</image-desc>

This fruit grows in great abundance on the Island of Bali, the size of our local Apple, or rather a Pear, since it is round at the bottom and cone-shaped at the top, protected by a rough and prickly rind. It grows on high trees, hanging in clusters; when preserved, it is sweet, flavorful, and a convenient resource for Indian voyages.

<column-break/>

### THE INDIAN JACKFRUIT: called Panax by the Arabs; Funax by the Persians.
<note>original: "Iaca Indica". The Jackfruit.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Jackfruit tree (Iaca). Large, heavy, oblong fruits with a bumpy texture are growing directly from the main trunk and thickest branches. A cross-section of a fruit and its seeds are shown on the ground.</image-desc>

This is a very large tree in India, bearing very large fruit on the main trunk rather than on the branches, sometimes equaling the largest melons; it is green on the outside, but yellow within, covered with many small spines like a Hedgehog, but soft. It contains large nuts covered with a hard shell, which, once that is cast aside, are roasted or boiled and eaten just like Chestnuts, which they closely resemble. They excite <term>Venus</term> <note>They were considered aphrodisiacs.</note>, but they are hard to digest and harm the stomach. They establish two varieties of it: one called *Barca*, the other *Girafal*.

It grows only in coastal regions.

---

<column-break/>

### THE JAMBO OF ACOSTA.
<note>original: "Iambos". The Rose Apple.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Jambo (Rose Apple) tree. It features slender branches with elongated leaves and small, round fruits hanging in clusters.</image-desc>

It is a tree rising to the size of a Plum tree, with smooth, thick leaves a palm-length long, and a red, very fragrant flower. The fruit is the size of a goose egg, turning purple, and endowed with the sweetest scent of a rose. It is gathered throughout the whole year, with some just beginning to grow, others ripening, and others fully mature; thus the same branches are almost always loaded with flowers and both green and ripe fruit.

<column-break/>

### THE JAMBO OF LINSCHOTEN.
<note>original: "Iambos Linschottani". Referring to Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, a Dutch traveler.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of another variety of Jambo tree, similar in structure to the previous one but with slightly different leaf and fruit distribution.</image-desc>

Because the shape of this one differs not a little from that of Acosta, we present both. Furthermore, these fruits are usually eaten before other foods at the start of a meal, and during the day. Both the fruits and the flowers are also preserved and stored.

The people of Malabar and Canara call the Jambo fruit *Iamboli*. The Arabs call it *Tupha*. The Indians and Persians call it *Tuphat*. The Turks call it *Alma*.

It details their physical appearance, medicinal qualities (heat/cold), and the various names given to them by different cultures.</summary>
<keywords>Soursop, Durian, Jackfruit, Rose Apple, Botany, Malacca, Bali, India, America, Medicinal plants, Aphrodisiacs, Acosta, Linschoten</keywords>

# THE PLANTS: CARAMBOLAS OF ACOSTA. INDIAN AMBARE.

### CARAMBOLAS OF ACOSTA.
<note>original: "Carambolas Acosta"</note>

This tree is the size of a Quince tree, with leaves like an Apple tree and small flowers that turn from white to reddish, consisting of five small petals; they are odorless but elegant in appearance. The fruit itself equals the size of a large hen's egg, oblong, yellowish, and divided as if into four sections <note>The author is describing the distinct ridges of the Starfruit</note>, in the middle of which are tender seeds; the acidity of its flavor is pleasing to the palate.

In Malabar it is called *Carambolas*; in Canara and the Deccan *Camarix*; in Malay *Balimba*.

---

### MULBERRY: German *Maulbeerbaum*. French *Meurier*. Italian *Moro*.

<note>The Mulberry was vital to the European silk industry</note>

Camerarius, Pena, and Lobelius recognized three differences of Mulberry: the Black, the White, and the Ground-mulberry. However, almost all others make only two distinctions: the Black and the White. We depict the Black here; the White is more delicate in every respect. Whether it was known to the Ancients is debated, and not without reason, since Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Galen, Pliny, and the writers on agriculture <term>Geoponici: ancient Greek authors on husbandry</term> make very little mention of it.

The Mulberry loves warm, flat, sandy, and maritime locations. It is the "latest of the city-dwellers" to bud <note>A reference to its reputation for waiting until the frost has passed</note>, yet it ripens its fruit very quickly; for this reason, it is called the wisest of trees.

When ripe, it loosens the bowels, but when unripe, it is quite binding. To provide the history of Silkworms <term>Bombycum: silkworms</term> and the uses of the White Mulberry is not our purpose here.

---

### EGYPTIAN SYCAMORE, or the Sycamore of Alpinus.

The trunk, he says, the branches, the bark, the fruit, the milky sap, and the roughness and color of the leaves appear like those of a Fig tree, but the shape and size of the leaves correspond to the Mulberry. It is never without much fruit, which grows directly from the trunk <note>A botanical trait known as cauliflory</note> and not at all from the branches; these ripen slowly and imperfectly, nor do they have a watery or pleasant juice, which is why they are gathered and sold only for the use of the poor. The tree does not grow from seeds but is propagated from branches.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN AMBARE.
<note>Likely the Hog Plum or Ambarella (Spondias dulcis)</note>

This is a thick and large tree, having leaves like a Walnut and small white flowers. The fruit is the size of a Walnut but a paler green, with a heavy scent and a sharp taste. They excite the appetite for eating, and when preserved with salt and vinegar, they can be kept for a long time. Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine</note> describes it in a few words: It is, he says, a fruit the size of a Nut, fragrant and tawny when ripe; when unripe, it is covered with a certain greenish, cartilaginous rind. Ludovicus Romanus <note>The traveler Ludovico di Varthema</note> mistakenly confuses this with the *Amba* <note>The Mango</note>.

---

### SYCAMORE: German *Wilder Feigenbaum*, French *Sicomore*. Italian *Fico d'Egitto*.

It is also called Sycomorus, and by the Germans *Adam's Fig*, and the French *Figs of Adam*, because it is believed by some that Adam first sinned with this fruit. Among those things which grow in Egypt and nowhere else, Theophrastus and Pliny list the Sycamore. The *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> writes that many have tried to naturalize both the Spanish-European and the Indian varieties, but in vain. However, Amatus reports that it grows tall in India as well, and Anguillara says it abounds in Syria, which is why Zacchaeus climbed one when he wanted to see Christ. There is a figure by Matthiolus which differs not a little from the others.

---

### CYPRIAN SYCAMORE. French *Figuier de Cypre*.

Both the Cyprian and the Egyptian Wild Fig, or Sycamore, according to Rauwolf, equal the White Mulberry in height and thickness; it is also gifted with similar leaves, but less rounded and with no notches or serrations around the edge. It also bears fruit not unlike our Figs, yet sweeter, etc.

Furthermore, those who have become overheated either by travel or by the sun and have need of cooling and moistening eat these figs profitably; however, they loosen, weaken, and upset the stomach. Applied as a plaster, they heal hard and hot tumors. The juice is an antidote to plague and poisons. Wine is also made from Sycamores.

<summary>This page describes various exotic and Mediterranean trees, including the Starfruit (Carambolas), the Mulberry, and different species of Sycamore (Wild Fig), noting their medicinal properties and historical mentions.</summary>
<keywords>Carambola, Starfruit, Mulberry, Sycamore, Egyptian Fig, Garcia de Orta, Acosta, medicinal botany, tropical fruit</keywords>

It maintains the encyclopedic style of comparing classical authorities like Theophrastus with contemporary explorers like Oviedo and Acosta.</meta>

<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES.</header>

# FIG: German: Feygenbaum; French: Figuier; Italian: Fichi.
# GROUND-FIG.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing fig plant (Chamæficus) with broad, lobed leaves and several small figs attached to the stems and base.</image-desc>

The Ancients, both Greek and Latin, recorded a vast number of figs, categorized by their nature, shape, color, size, manner and time of growth, as well as by the variety of regions in which they grow and the authors who described them.

More recent writers distinguish them more concisely into the *Urban* <note>cultivated</note> and the *Wild* [the latter of which they say is similar to the Urban in all respects]. They assert that this wild state is due either to nature or to neglect; or at least insofar as it does not ripen its fruit, which is thus called <term>Caprificus</term> <note>literally "Goat-fig"</note>, an uncultivated fig, called "empty" by some, <gloss>an error of Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Aristotle and Theophrastus</note>.</gloss> The dried ones they call <term>Caricae</term> <note>Carian figs, named after Caria in Asia Minor</note>, about which we write more extensively elsewhere.

<column-break/>

They call one fig the *Mana*. It is grown in gardens and hanging gardens, and it seems to differ from the common variety in nothing but size.

Furthermore, the Fig was held in such high esteem among the Ancients that it held the second place of honor after the Vine, and all its parts were designated by unique names.

It is found throughout the more temperate or warmer regions of Europe; indeed, it grows abundantly in Spain, Italy, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and not without a pleasant rivalry with the vines, where you may see very elegant groves of "twice-bearing" figs producing both a Spring and Autumn crop.

Finally, Figs were so highly valued among the Ancients that Ananius <note>Ananius was a Greek iambic poet</note> said <unclear>they were cheaper and better than gold</unclear>. Whoever desires more details should seek them from our Universal History and the *Appendix to this work*.

---

# FOREIGN TREE, bearing FRUIT similar to a FIG.
# INDIAN FIG, THE ROOTING TREE OF INDIA, Or the Mangrove of Oviedo?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large tree with aerial roots descending from the branches to the ground, forming secondary trunks. Small round fruits are visible on the branches.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> mentions this in his *Exotics*: assigning to it a fruit similar to the fruit of a Fig, but not exceeding the size of a chickpea.

Is it the Indian Fig of Theophrastus that grows near the Acesines River?

Or is it truly the fruit of the Guagey tree, which Oviedo <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, chronicler of the New World</note> describes?

<column-break/>

It rises to a great height with a single, very thick trunk; it then spreads its branches out on all sides; when these have grown to several cubits, they turn their further growth downward, bending until they touch the earth. Then, having entered the ground, they take root like offshoots: soon they emerge again as a trunk, from which, after they have grown, they bend again, create another offshoot, and then another, and so on indefinitely: so that a single tree may occupy an entire Italian mile and create a very dense forest. Theophrastus attributes very large leaves to it, no smaller than a shield: the fruit is the size of a chickpea, similar to a fig, blood-red, sweet, and full of seeds.

---

# MUSA or AMUSA, called Darache Mou by the Arabs and Persians.
# THE MUSA WITH FRUIT. <note>The Banana or Plantain</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a banana plant (Musa) showing its large, broad leaves and a central stalk bearing a cluster of fruit and a large terminal bud.</image-desc>

This is a plant of Egypt, Cyprus, and the Indies, whose leaves are of portentous size, and which some refer to the Palm, others to the Plane tree, and others to the Indian Fig. It rises to a height of 18 or 20 spans, according to Acosta <note>José de Acosta, a Jesuit naturalist</note>; this is a beautiful and elegant tree, whose trunk consists of a connection of many rinds lying upon one another, and it reaches the thickness of a human leg: with a round and thick root. It is a pleasing fodder for elephants: the leaves are nine spans in length and two and a half in width, etc.

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that it is called *Muse* in Syria, and adds that among the Greeks and the Christian and Jewish inhabitants, it is considered the tree from which Adam ate, which had been forbidden to him by God.

<column-break/>

From the top of this tree, the same Acosta adds, there is born a kind of stalk of flowers crowded together, in the manner of a pine cone, of a rosy color: then it bears a single branch the thickness of a human arm, divided into many nodes, from each of which hang 10 or 14 Figs <note>bananas</note>: so that sometimes a branch is seen loaded with a hundred or two hundred Figs. The Portuguese distinguish these into different species, called *Cenorios*, *Chincapas*, and *Inninga*, etc. The trunk is certainly annual, and brings forth fruit only once in its life: but at the roots there swell up six or more shoots, which renew the parent and bring fruit to perfection the following year.

<summary>This page describes various types of figs, ranging from common European varieties to the exotic Banyan tree (Indian Fig) and the Banana (Musa), including their physical characteristics and historical lore.</summary>
<keywords>figs, Banyan tree, banana, Musa, botanical history, Theophrastus, Acosta, aerial roots, Garden of Eden, medicinal plants</keywords>

--- Page 48 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of exotic plants, focusing on species from the East and West Indies. It concludes the first class of the botanical collection.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### LINSCHOTEN’S INDIAN FIG.
<note>original: "Ficus Indica Linschottani"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a prickly pear cactus (Opuntia) with large oval pads and small fruits growing from the edges.</image-desc>

It grows to the height of a man, with leaves of an astonishing length. The fruits, resembling grapes in appearance but the size of a cucumber, cling to the stalks in great numbers. Each tree bears only one cluster, and when the tree is cut down, it grows back in a short time and bears new fruit. This is a common food for the Indians, and the finest come from Cannanore <note>A coastal city in Kerala, India</note>. A single cluster sometimes requires the strength of two men to carry; it is perhaps the same as that which the Holy Scripture records the Spies of the Promised Land brought back. *Linschoten.*

### PALM SHOOTS.
<note>original: "Palmites"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a palm tree with a tall, segmented trunk and a crown of long, radiating fronds.</image-desc>

This is a tree with a thick trunk, from which very long leaves grow without any stalks. It grows on the Island of Galopes, or Mauritius, across from Madagascar, and wine is made from it, just as it is from the Coconut tree. *The De Bry Brothers in the History of the East Indies & the Dutch Voyage.*

Linschoten mentions similar trees growing on the small island of Saint Mary.

### OPUNTIA, THE INDIAN FIG. German: Indianisch Feigen: French: Figue d'Inde.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mature Opuntia cactus with thick, branching pads and several fruits.</image-desc>

This plant is rightly counted among the miracles of Nature. Many suspect it to be the *Opuntia* mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny; others, however, have called it the Indian Fig due to a certain resemblance of the fruit, although it differs greatly and in a wonderful manner both from the Fig and from all other trees.

In the Peruvian Indies of America, and throughout the kingdom of New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico</note>, it grows abundantly in the countryside and in the wild. For many years now, it has begun to be cultivated in the gardens of noblemen in Italy, Spain, France, and even Germany. It is so full of life that it grows very easily either from a small seed or from a leaf buried halfway in the ground. The fruit ripens in Autumn.

<column-break/>

### AMERICAN PACOVERA.
<note>original: "Pacovera Americana"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a banana or plantain tree with large, broad leaves and a central stalk.</image-desc>

According to Thevet, the wild Americans call this tree *paquouere* in their own language. It grows neither in Europe, nor in Asia, nor in Africa, and perhaps more than others, one might not rashly call it the *Most Wonderful*. The inhabitants call the fruit *Pacona* in their language; when properly ripe, it is of exceptional sweetness and easy digestion.

Léry relates that the *Paco-aire* has leaves like Water Dock, ten feet long and two feet wide, or even wider. He does not believe leaves of such magnitude exist anywhere in Europe, Asia, or Africa; furthermore, they are thin, and when tossed by the wind, they split into parts, so that at first glance one might think they were ostrich feathers.

Is it perhaps a species of Musa <note>The banana genus</note>?

### AMERICAN LITTLE FLASKS.
<note>original: "Lagenulae Americae"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two dried gourds or calabashes, one larger and one smaller, connected by a cord.</image-desc>

These fruits were brought from the Southern Sea, which the Spaniards call the Pacific and commonly the *Mar del Sur*. They are pierced through the outer part by a small cord. They are very similar to those mentioned by Amerigo Vespucci in his second voyage when discussing the customs of the people where he had landed. He says that individual men carried two small, dry gourds hanging from their necks; one full of the herb they were chewing, the other full of a flour similar to white ground gypsum, which they sprinkled on the herb they chewed for the sake of quenching their thirst, etc.

### THE CEMENTING KIN OF THE OPUNTIA.
<note>original: "Opuntia Cognata Ferruminatrix"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller cactus variety with rounded pads and small flowers or fruits.</image-desc>

A small tree born spontaneously in the Indies and very closely related to the commonly named Indian Fig. The inhabitants call it the *Cementer* <note>original: "Ferruminatricem"</note>, as it is very beneficial for fractures and dislocations of the limbs. It is evergreen and reaches the size of a tree through a successive offspring of leaves. It has exactly the same leaves as the aforementioned Opuntia, but with smaller and thornier fruit that yields a purple, sticky juice, which is very tenacious for dyers to soak fabrics.
