# ON THE IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## SECOND CLASS,
### CONTAINING THOSE TREES WHOSE FRUITS ARE ALSO COMPREHENDED BY THE GENERAL TERM "POME" <note>original: "pomi"; here referring to fleshy fruits in general rather than just apples</note>: BUT WHICH HAVE AN EDIBLE OR NON-EDIBLE BONY NUT <note>the pit or stone</note> COVERED BY FLESH: AND THOSE WHICH HAVE SOME AFFINITY WITH THEM.

**THE PEACH TREE:** German: *Pfersingbaum:* French: *Pescheier:* Italian: *Persico.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Peach branch with leaves and fruit, including a cross-section of the fruit showing the pit.</image-desc>

It is called *Persica* <note>Persian</note> because it was first brought from Persia. In its fruit, various differences are observed, taken from the region, shape, size, sex, flavor, scent, color, smoothness or hairiness, the ease of removing the stone, and the flesh—both in its color and its hardness or softness. The first praise among these "Apples" goes to the *Duracina* <note>Clingstone or firm-fleshed peaches</note>, because they have a harder pulp and rarely stick stubbornly to the stone; and especially to those which, because of the brightness of their golden color and sweetness of scent, are called *Cotonea* <note>Quince-peaches</note>. The second rank is claimed by those which, when the skin is removed, pour out a blood-red juice. Next to these is the one called the *Nuci-Persica* <note>Nectarine</note>. The remaining very soft and watery ones are left to the men of the lowest common class.

Furthermore, this tree grows successfully in all sorts of places, but just as it matures quickly, it also grows old quickly. The fruits are cooling and moistening in the second degree <note>A reference to Galenic humoral medicine, where qualities were ranked 1–4</note>.

**ARMENIAN APPLES <note>Apricots</note>.** German: *Amarellenbaum:* French: *Abricottier.* Italian: *Albero Armelino.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Apricot branch with leaves and fruit, including a cross-section of the fruit and the stone.</image-desc>

Many have wished this fruit to be a species of Peach; others have reduced it to the genus of Plum. Galen called them *Praecocia* or *Praecoqua* <note>Early-ripening</note>; more recent authors call them *Baricocca, Bericocca,* and *Bericorca.* Lobelius and Pena say that in shape and leaf they resemble the Pear, but in the fruit itself, the Peach. Amatus wrongly distinguished the Armenian apple from the *Praecocia*.

However, this tree differs from the Peach in that its leaves are broader than those of the Peach, and the fruits ripen sooner. Also, the stones of Peaches are wrinkled and warty, while those of the early-ripening ones <note>apricots</note> are flat and smooth. And finally, the whole fruit of these is smaller than the Peach.

These fruits differ in size rather than in kind; and that is to be ascribed to the mercy of the sky <note>climate</note> and the "pimping" <note>term: mangonio; refers to the art of deceptive enhancement or intensive cultivation</note> of the gardener.

<column-break/>

**THE PERSEA TREE:** Arabic: *Allabuch.* Called by the Egyptians in their native tongue: *Amygdala* <note>Almond</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Persea tree branch with elongated, laurel-like leaves and pear-shaped fruit.</image-desc>

Agricola used to say that no one will wonder that we are ignorant of the *Persea* <note>A tree often identified as Mimusops laurifolia or sometimes confused with the avocado in later centuries</note>, for he had read of it in no one's work, and it was seen by him nowhere under the Roman Empire except in Alexandria.

Plutarch writes that it is greatly celebrated in Egypt, and that it bears fruit similar to a heart, and a leaf like a tongue.

Theophrastus says it is a tree of Egypt, beautiful and tall; in its leaves, flowers, and branches, and indeed in its whole shape, it is similar to the Pear; but it is evergreen, and produces mature fruit [of the appearance of an almond and of a grassy color] the size of a pear, etc. He adds that its flesh is sweet and easy to digest, which Dioscorides also holds. But in Persia, from where it was first transferred, it was said to be deadly.

**ARMENIAN APPLE <note>Apricot</note>:** German: *Marellen,* French: *Avant-pesches, Abricots:* Italian: *Armellini.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Apricot branch with fruit.</image-desc>

Armenian apples are commonly kept in the gardens and orchards of Italy and France; and also in Germany, but there the larger fruits are much rarer. We depict both species here with a double illustration.

The tree flowers in March and matures its fruit at the beginning of June, and sometimes, in warmer places, in May.

Dioscorides says it is more useful than the fruit of the Peach. Galen says it is moist and cold in the second excess. But that is to be understood regarding the flesh and juice; for the flowers, leaves, and kernels of this fruit, as well as the Peach, are of a hot and dry temperament.

Concerning both Peaches and Armenian apples, and also the Persea tree: more in the Appendix.

<summary>This page categorizes stone fruits (peaches and apricots) and the Egyptian Persea tree, discussing their nomenclature, physical characteristics, and medicinal temperaments according to classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>peach, apricot, Persea tree, pomology, Galen, Dioscorides, botany, stone fruit, humoral medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of exotic and domestic trees, focusing on fruits from the Indies and Europe.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### MANGO AND AMBA; ACCORDING TO ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mango tree branch with large leaves and several oval fruits hanging from it. Below the main branch are two detailed depictions of the fruit, one whole and one sliced open to show the large pit.</image-desc>

This is a tree with the appearance of a Pear tree, whose fruit is like a Peach, of a citron color, and yellow when ripe. The flesh has a honey-like flavor, with a stone inside similar to an Almond. The fruit is called <term>Amba</term> <note>The Sanskrit/Hindi term for mango</note>, and the trunk or tree is called <term>Manga</term>. It grows in Malabar, Goa, Gujarat, and other places in India, though those in Ormuz excel the rest. It is cold and moist <note>Referring to the Galenic humors</note>, and is the daily food of the servants.

### ALMOND: German: Mandelbaum: Belgian: Amandelboom. French: Amandier: Italian: Amandolano.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Almond tree branch with narrow, serrated leaves and several almond husks. Below the branch are three detailed views: a whole almond in its fuzzy husk, a hard shell, and the nut kernel itself.</image-desc>

The differences in this tree are found chiefly in the fruit: for some Almonds are common, others small, others very large; for the most part they are oblong, at other times round, and sometimes bent back at the top. Furthermore, they are either sweet or bitter: with a hard or brittle shell: and they have one or several kernels: and some even lack the downy fuzz.

The Almond loves a very hot climate and a dry, hard, and stony soil; it grows most successfully in Provence and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

They are heat-producing, according to Hippocrates: and they nourish well. However, the bitter ones are hotter than the sweet ones: and both serve the Physician as well as the Cook.

### MYXA, MYXA or MYXARIA to the Greeks: Sebesten to the Arabs. Domestic Myxa.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of the Myxa (Cordia myxa) tree with broad, rounded leaves and clusters of small, berry-like fruits. Below are two detailed views of the fruit and its internal seed.</image-desc>

This tree is rightly counted by Pliny among the Plums of Egypt and Syria; the ancient Greeks recorded nothing about it, but only the more recent ones such as Paulus, Aetius, Psellus, and Actuarius. The Arabs, who made it famous, called it <term>Sebesten</term>: and the Apothecary shops have retained the Arabic name, which was done in honor of Caesar, who was called <term>Sebastos</term>, that is, "venerable" or "honorable" <note>original: "Sebastos, id est honorabilis"</note>.

Alpinus identifies two kinds: one Wild, similar to a Plum; the other Domestic, differing from the former by its broader and thicker leaves and larger fruit.

In our age, it is also kept in the more cultivated gardens of Europe.

<column-break/>

### MANGO AND AMBA ACCORDING TO LINSCHOTEN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mango tree as described by Linschoten, showing a more complete tree structure with a thick trunk and numerous fruits hanging from the canopy. Several detached fruits and pits are shown to the right of the trunk.</image-desc>

To this illustration, which is Linschoten's, we shall add something concerning the wild kind of Mango. They call it <term>Mangas branas</term> <note>Wild mangoes</note>, and they say its fruit is so sharply poisonous that the natives use it to quickly kill one another; and it kills so swiftly that no Antidote has been found to this day to restrain its power.

### PLUM: German: Pflaumenbaum: Belgian: Pruimboom, French: Prunier: Italian: Sosmaro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Plum tree branch with oval, serrated leaves and several plums hanging from it. Below the branch are two detailed views of the plum fruit, one whole and one showing the pit.</image-desc>

There is a vast multitude of Plums, as Pliny writes, and the tree is too well known to be dealt with in a long series of words. Every region claims its own: and counts innumerable varieties. On these, let our *Universal History* be consulted, as well as its *Appendix*.

The Plum generally enjoys only a rich and moist soil, but a warm climate, and it is grown today in all the cultivated regions of the known world. It blooms for the most part with the Cherry, or even earlier; it ripens its fruit in various ways in the months of July, August, and September: and it is stubborn of life <note>hardy</note>.

Furthermore, all Plums are cold and moist, more or less, according to whether they have more or less sweetness or acid: and moreover they relax and soften [the bowels], are harmful to the stomach, and provide little nourishment.

### MYXA or MYXARIA, SEBESTEN, MYXA or Wild Mixa.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the wild variety of the Myxa tree, showing a branch with smaller, more pointed leaves and clusters of fruit. Below are detailed views of the fruit and its seed.</image-desc>

To those things which were said before concerning the Mixas, we shall only add the fruit, uses, and qualities.

And so <term>Sebesten</term> plums, according to Avicenna, are very nearly temperate [in humor]: and their use is most familiar for roughness of the throat and diseases of the chest; they quench thirst, loosen the belly by softening it, and drive out worms.

The birdlime, which is made from their pulp, is used in the manner of a plaster on hard tumors: and it is, as Matthiolus writes, most convenient for catching birds. Wine is also made from Myxas, according to Pliny.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal uses of the Mango, Almond, Myxa (Sebesten), and Plum trees, citing authorities like Pliny, Avicenna, and Linschoten.</summary>
<keywords>Mango, Almond, Sebesten, Plum, medicinal plants, Indian flora, Galenic humors, botany, Linschoten, Acosta</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on the various species of Myrobalans (astringent fruits often used in medicine) and their classification by Renaissance botanists.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>The title "Icones et Sciagraphia" refers to the visual representations and the structural descriptions of the plants.</note>

### THE PLUM CALLED MYROBALAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Prunus Myrobalanus branch with leaves and small plum-like fruits, with two detached fruits shown below.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> reports that this tree is cultivated in the Imperial garden of the Caesar <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note> at Vienna; he illustrates and describes it, noting that it was brought there from Constantinople. However, he confesses he does not know why the name "Myrobalan" was given to this type of Plum: for, he says, neither is the fruit similar, nor is the stone, which resembles those of other Plum varieties, though it is small.

### CITRINE MYROBALANS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several Citrine Myrobalans, showing their oblong, ribbed shape and a cross-section of the fruit.</image-desc>

Myrobalans are distinguished by size and color, primarily regarding their external features. They agree, however, in this: they possess a manifest quality for strengthening the internal organs and nature, and at the same time, they are powerful by their formal faculty for loosening the bowels and purging superfluities. Indeed, all types of Myrobalans are cold in the first degree and dry in the second degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of "humors" where medicines were classified by their temperature and moisture levels</note>.

Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a German physician and botanist</note> believes the Citrine variety is dried from India: having been left in India on its own tree until it grows large and begins to ripen.

### EMBLIC MYROBALANS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Emblic Myrobalans, showing small, rounded, segmented fruits and their internal seeds.</image-desc>

Cordus writes of them thus: The *Myrobalan*, he says, called *Emblica*, has its own peculiar and proper genus, distinct even from the Belleric; however, it is smaller than that one, and is almost never brought to us whole, but divided and fallen into fragments. We have observed it preserved with its kernels, just as the Figure represents, as well as the others quite elegantly.

Concerning these, as well as the remaining Myrobalans and all other types of Plums, we treat more extensively both in our *Great History* and in the *Appendix* to it.

<column-break/>

### CONCERNING MYROBALANS IN GENERAL AND INDIVIDUALLY: Indian Myrobalans, black, without stones.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Indian Myrobalans, showing small, dark, wrinkled fruits and a cross-section.</image-desc>

The Myrobalan is a discovery of the Arabs or Moors, from whom the more recent Greeks received them. Some have divided these into three types, others into four, others into six, but most into five. It has been observed, however, that different types are produced by different trees, although some have thought they spring from the same one. Because their origin is unknown to us until now, we have imitated Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, an influential Italian physician</note> and determined nothing certain about it.

The Indian ones are called *Asuar* by the Arabs: they are small and black, and have no bone <note>stone/pit</note>, perhaps because they were gathered before maturity.

### CHEBULIC MYROBALANS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chebulic Myrobalans, showing large, elongated, deeply ribbed fruits and a flowering sprig. <note>original: "Chebulæ Myrobalanæ"</note></image-desc>

In shape, flesh, flavor, and stone, these correspond in all respects to the Citrine ones: therefore Cordus thought that Chebulic ones are created when the Citrine ones have reached full maturity. Let the Readers weigh this. The artist neglected to paint the stone in our figure: and even the small branch, which we show here from Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a German herbalist</note>, by no means corresponds to the description by Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine in India</note>. The *Chebulic Myrobalans*, he says, are large and round, yet somewhat oblong and angular; with leaves similar to the Peach, etc.

### BELLERIC MYROBALANS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Belleric Myrobalans, showing rounded, slightly turbinate fruits and their internal structure.</image-desc>

These are flat on one side and cone-shaped on the other, ending in a small projection: the size is the same as the Citrine ones, and the flavor is also the same: but the Belleric are rounder, and their surface is smoother and less wrinkled.

Furthermore, whether those who believe Myrobalans to be the *fruit of the Palm*, or those who think they are the *Ben-nut* <note>original: "Nucem vnguentariam", the Moringa nut used for oils</note>, are correct or not, we have weighed in our *Universal History*. Likewise, whether the word *Myrobalanus* is of the feminine or masculine gender; and also, whether there are three or five types of Myrobalans. For us, the following verse holds:
> *There are five species of good Myrobalans,*
> *Citrine, Chebulic, Belleric, Emblic, and Indian.*

<summary>This page describes and illustrates various species of Myrobalans, medicinal fruits primarily from India and the Middle East, debating their classification and botanical origins. It cites major Renaissance authorities like Clusius, Cordus, and Garcia de Orta to compare the physical characteristics and medicinal properties of the five recognized types.</summary>
<keywords>Myrobalans, botany, pharmacology, Clusius, Valerius Cordus, Indian medicine, purgatives, plant classification, Renaissance science</keywords>

### A SPECIES OF MYROBALAN ACCORDING TO RAUWOLF.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing various parts of the Myrobalan fruit, including the whole fruit, cross-sections, and individual seeds/pits.</image-desc>

Leonhard Rauwolf <note>A 16th-century German physician and botanist famous for his travels in the Near East</note> described this fruit at length, and reports that it is found in Palestine, and that some consider it to be a species of Myrobalan <note>A plum-like fruit often used in tanning or medicine</note>. He was not able to see the tree itself.

In this small table, the reader also has an image of the *Fagara* <note>likely a species of prickly ash or Sichuan pepper</note>, which we shall discuss in the following Class.

### FEMALE CORNEL, OR THE BLOOD-RED ROD. German: *Spindelbaum* : French: *Cornellier sauvage*. Italian: *Sanguino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cornus foemina (Dogwood) shrub with leaves and clusters of small berries.</image-desc>

Pietro Andrea Mattioli <note>A famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note> says there is a plant not unlike the Cornel, which in Tuscany we call *sanguino* and *sanguinello* in the common tongue, because of the blood-red color of its twigs. There are those who wish it to be the "Female Cornel," but for what reason I do not see; I would not dare to affirm that it is the "Blood-red Rod" of Pliny <note>referring to Pliny the Elder's Natural History</note>.

The *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note>, Gessner, Belon, and others make the Female Cornel and Pliny’s Blood-red Rod one and the same. Some call it the Wild Cornel, but this is not the view of everyone: *let the learned judge*. <note>original: "iudicent docti"</note>

It flowers in April and May; the berries turn black as Autumn approaches. They are bitter, harsh, and astringent in taste, and are a favorite food for thrushes.

### SOUR BLACKISH CHERRIES, QUITE SHINY. German: *Amarellen, Wichseln* : French: *Griottier*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry branch laden with dark, shiny acidic cherries and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This tree does not reach the height of the wild varieties, nor do the branches spread out as in the others, but it somewhat resembles the Birch. The tree is commonly cultivated in gardens. The fruits, which ripen later, are dried for those suffering from parching fevers; and from them, mixed with good wine, a type of wine is made which is held as a delicacy during the Dog Days <note>The hottest days of summer, usually July and August</note>, under the name *Wichseln wein*. Could these be Pliny’s *Macedonian Cherries*?

<column-break/>

### CORNEL: German: *Cornelbaum*: Belgian: *Cornellenboom*: French: *Cornier, Cormier, Corneillier*: Italian: *Sorbo Albero*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cornel tree branch with oval leaves and hanging oblong fruits.</image-desc>

There are two main types: the Urban <note>cultivated</note> and the Wild. Others distinguish them into Male and Female: they say the latter is softer and pithy. The fruit also has its differences in color and size. This, however, is peculiar to this tree and the Service-tree: the fruits of the wild variety are riper and sweeter than those of the urban variety.

Thus, it rejects cultivation and grows in both damp and dry places. It flowers in February and March, sometimes before the leaves break forth. It ripens its fruit in September and October.

The leaves, fruit, and buds are powerfully drying and astringent. The wood, especially of the male, is a very hard material, almost like horn <note>Latin: *cornu*</note>, from which the tree takes its name.

### CHERRY: German: *Kirschenbaum*, Belgian: *kerseboom*: French: *Cerisier*: Italian: *Stregie*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry tree branch with large leaves and pairs of cherries.</image-desc>

The Cherry, a tree of common knowledge today, was once brought into Italy from the town of Cerasus in Pontus <note>Modern-day Giresun, Turkey</note> by Lucullus, the Roman General who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes. He named the fruit "Cherry" <note>Latin: *Cerasum*</note> after the name of his people's new territory.

There are many varieties, distinguished by taste, color, shape, size, location, and the authors or discoverers themselves.

The one we depict here is beautiful, producing a large, oblong fruit, approaching somewhat the shape of a heart, with hard and solid flesh, sweet, of a reddish-white color, and a large pit. Among the cultivated varieties, this one has great sweetness; we shall discuss the rest in what follows.

### COMMON DOUBLE-FLOWERED CHERRY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering cherry branch with dense, double blossoms.</image-desc>

This is a beautiful species of Cherry, even if you only look at the flowers, which are full like Roses or Pomegranate blossoms <note>original: "Balaufiorum"</note>. There are three species of it: 1. The Common, which we depict here. 2. One larger than the common, bearing fewer fruits. 3. The one called "Leafless": of which more soon.

<summary>This page describes various species of Myrobalan, Cornel (Dogwood), and Cherries, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for fevers, and historical origins involving the Roman General Lucullus.</summary>
<keywords>Myrobalan, Cornel, Dogwood, Cherry, Lucullus, medicinal wine, astringent plants, Cerasus, botanical history</keywords>

### CHERRY WITH LARGE DOUBLE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry branch with large, dense double blossoms and small developing fruits.</image-desc>

This variety is less fertile than the others and is rarely available; for a great deal of its strength is consumed by the flowers. <note>Double-flowered varieties often prioritize petals over fruit production.</note>

There are, furthermore, **SOUR REDDISH CHERRIES**, but of a paler red color, with flesh that is not particularly hard or firm. Their flavor, especially when properly ripe, is somewhat acidic, wine-like, and very pleasant. These are the ones specifically called *Zame Kirschen* <note>original: "Zame Kirschen"; likely "tame" or cultivated cherries</note> by the people of Basel and Alsace, and *Griottes* <note>A traditional French term for sour cherries, often used for brandy or preserves.</note> by the French.

<column-break/>

### LEAFLESS CHERRY WITH DOUBLE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry branch with blossoms that appear to lack petals or have very reduced foliage around the flower clusters.</image-desc>

We call it "leafless" <note>original: "Aphyllon"</note> because it has no leaves, or very few, as our Illustration shows. We cultivated this one and two other preceding types at Montbéliard in the Prince’s garden. <note>The author likely refers to the gardens of the Duke of Württemberg.</note>

<column-break/>

### CHERRY BEARING MULTIPLE FRUITS ON ONE STALK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry branch where multiple fruits hang from a single shared pedicel (stalk).</image-desc>

In the same place, two species of this Cherry are cultivated, namely a red and a black one; these produce sometimes two, sometimes three, and often even four or five fruits from a single stalk <term>pediculo: the stem of a fruit or flower</term>, and before the fruits appear, they have flowers similar to the common varieties.

<column-break/>

### CLUSTERED CHERRY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cherry tree branch with fruit growing in grape-like clusters (racemes).</image-desc>

In certain Cherries, the fruit grows in clusters <term>racematim: like a bunch of grapes</term>. These are called *Coregie grappelose* by the Tuscans, according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note>, while other Italians call them *Coregie del grasso*. They are kept specifically in gardens, vineyards, and pleasure-groves.

At this point, something should be added regarding the qualities and powers of Cherries. Simeon Seth <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note> reviews the facts according to the opinions of Dioscorides and Galen <note>The primary authorities on medicine in the ancient world</note> as follows: "Cherries," he says, "are cold and moist, and of poor juice; they loosen the belly, and are not at all suitable for a stomach that is moist, rather than hot and dry." But these remarks are to be understood as referring to "true" Cherries—that is, the sweet ones—and not at all to the sour and harsh ones. The gum of the tree, taken with wine, heals those suffering from stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

<column-break/>

### DWARF CHERRY, OR GROUND-CHERRY: German: *Wilde Kirschen*; Italian: *Ceregio nana*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing cherry shrub with upright branches and small fruits.</image-desc>

This little shrub is one or two cubits high <note>about 1.5 to 3 feet</note>, and it has all parts similar to the common Cherry, but four times smaller.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> writes that it grows spontaneously in Hungary, Lower Austria, and Moravia in elevated and dry places at the edges of vineyards. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> notes that it grows in thick bushes in Belgian gardens. The fruit is harsh.

This is the same "Ground-cherry" growing on the slopes of the noble mountains of Insubria <note>Modern-day Lombardy, Italy</note> mentioned by Gesner and in the *History of Plants of Lyon*.

<column-break/>

### WILD CHERRY, WITH RED AND BLACK FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild cherry tree with a distinct trunk and spreading branches laden with small fruit.</image-desc>

This tree, which we call "Wild," produces fruit differing in four varieties: Red and Black, and each of those either larger and fleshier, or smaller and leaner. The larger kind, both red and black, is sweeter than the others; we believe this is the result of cultivation. The smaller kind, which has never known any cultivation, is usually bitter—both the red and the black—but only to the extent that, with sweetness prevailing, it is not unpleasant, unless it grows in completely shaded places never reached by the Sun.

# OF PLANTS

### THE WILD, BITTER CHERRY: thought by the ARABS to be the MAHALEB.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mahaleb cherry branch with leaves, small flowers, and several individual fruits/seeds shown at the base.</image-desc>

Dalechamp <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist</note> writes that it is brought from Syria, although he himself reports—and others have observed—that it grows everywhere in hedges around Lyon. The tree is somewhat low, the fruit is less fleshy, the pit and seed are thinner and more slender, the leaf is rounder, and the flower is white, etc.

We have seen it between Valence and Lyon, and at Zurich.

The kernels are warming and softening; they soften and thin out coarse or stiff hairs through frequent rubbing. From these same kernels is prepared an oil of pleasant scent, which is used by those who scent gloves <note>A common practice in the 16th century to mask the smell of tanned leather</note>.

Could this be the *Lacathe* of Theophrastus? Or the *Vaccinia* of Pliny? Or the *Vaccinia* of Virgil? <note>The author is attempting to reconcile this plant with various unidentified plants mentioned by ancient Greek and Roman authorities</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE CLUSTERED CHERRY according to some: the PADUS of Theophrastus to others. German: *Vogelkirschen* <note>Bird cherry</note>; French: *Putier*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bird cherry branch featuring a long raceme of small fruits and broad, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This is a small Cherry, bearing small fruit in oblong clusters <note>original: "racemulis"</note>, which turns from green to yellowish when ripe; it is somewhat harsh to the taste, with a rough pit.

It appears in gravelly and sandy places around hedges and thickets, especially on riverbanks. We have seen it flowering in April and May at Geneva, Lyon, and between Basel and Solothurn; we have also cultivated it in the Prince’s garden at Montbéliard.

The fruit is pleasing to small birds, and children also delight in it; its seed is recommended for their epilepsy <note>A traditional folk remedy of the period</note>. Could this be the *Padus* of Theophrastus?

---

### THE LOTUS TREE WITH CHERRY-LIKE FRUIT: French: *Mirocoulier*; Italian: *Bagolaro, Perlaro*. <note>The European Nettle Tree, Celtis australis</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus Arbor (Nettle tree) branch with serrated leaves, small round fruits, and a cross-section of the fruit/seed at the bottom.</image-desc>

The meaning of "Lotus" is varied and manifold among Authors; our discussion here concerns the Lotus tree.

Writers, both Greek and Latin, also differ greatly in describing this. Dioscorides attributes a heavy scent to the berries, while Pliny attributes none.

They commonly identify three species of it: 1. The Lotus of Dioscorides, which is the *Celtis* of Pliny, and this again either with or without a pit; 2. The Lotus of Theophrastus, distinct from that of Dioscorides; and 3. what Theophrastus labels the "Greek Bean" <note>original: "Faba Graeca"</note> and *Diospyros*.

The first species, which was once known only in Africa and on the Island of the Lotus-Eaters <note>original: "Lotophagite"</note> visited by the companions of Ulysses, is now known to almost the entire European world. It flowers in March and ripens its fruit in Autumn, which is sweet, slightly acidic, and astringent.

<column-break/>

### GUAIACANA: according to some the THIRD species of LOTUS: the Greek Bean and Diospyros of Theophrastus. <note>Likely the Date-plum, Diospyros lotus</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Guaiacana branch with large oval leaves and several fruits, including a detailed view of the seeds.</image-desc>

In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Daléchamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is called the Third species of Lotus, which, even if it were not a Lotus, is nevertheless numbered among the Lotus kinds. To Mattioli, it is another African Lotus. A species of African Lotus, the "False Lotus" <note>original: "Pseudolotus"</note>.

It was once a stranger in Europe. Today, however, it is kept in the more cultivated gardens. Thus it is grown at Padua in the Physicians' garden, and is shown under the name of *Guajacum*. At Montbéliard, in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, it grew for us from seed sent from Padua; and we also saw it recently in the illustrious Wagnerian garden near Moudon, flowering in May.

Whether it possesses the same medicinal powers as the Lotus, as some believe, let the learned consider.

The reader will find more concerning the Lotus in the *Appendix*.

---

# OF PLANTS
## CLASS III.
### WHICH COMPRISES NUTS, AND THOSE TREES WHICH IN APPEARANCE, FRUIT,
### OR NAME, HAVE SOME AFFINITY WITH NUTS: WHETHER
### THEY BE NATIVE OR FOREIGN.

**The Walnut**: *German: Nußbaum*: *Belgian: Noteboom*:
*French: Noyer*: *Italian: Noce, Albero.*

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Walnut tree (Juglans regia) showing the full tree habit with a thick trunk and spreading canopy.</image-desc>

The definition of "Nut" is broad and multifaceted: we are not presently concerned with the various meanings of this word <note>The author notes that "Nux" was a general term for many hard-shelled fruits</note>. We are speaking here of the Walnut, which is called by some *Jovis glans* <note>Latin: "Jupiter's Acorn," from which the name *Juglans* is derived</note>, *Diuglans*, *Cayan*, Persian Nut, Royal Nut, Euboean Nut, and Greek Nut; it is not our current purpose to recount the origins of these names.

Various differences in this fruit are observed, taken from its size, its covering, its shells, and its place of origin; it is certain that nature has played with a wonderful luxury of shapes in this fruit.

Furthermore, the Walnut tree loves moist and cold mountainous places: it puts forth its catkins <note>original: "Iulos," referring to the cylindrical flower clusters</note> in March and April, and the fruit ripens in August and September. The fruit is judged to be dry in the first degree and warm in the second <note>These are "humors" or qualities in Galenic medicine</note>: the dry nut is warmer than the green one, which, when eaten, relaxes the bowels.

**The Macocqwer of the Virginians.**

<image-desc>Woodcut of a round, textured fruit or gourd, shown whole and in cross-section revealing seeds, with several loose seeds depicted below.</image-desc>

This fruit, which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> depicts and describes, was brought from the province of Wingandecaon, which the English (by whom it was first observed) have named Virginia: could it be the *Junipappeyva* of the Brazilians?

When the inhabitants of that region are delivered from some great danger or have finished a war, they sit by a constructed fire as a sign of joy; having removed the pulp and seeds, they fill this fruit with small stones and, fitting them to little sticks, they hold, shake, and move them by hand. These make a rattling noise, just like the Brazilians do with their *Tamarace* <note>A reference to a ceremonial rattle or maraca</note>.

<column-break/>

**Genipat, Junipappeeyva, and Xagua**
*Of America and the Brazilians.*

<image-desc>Woodcut of a botanical specimen showing a branch with leaves and several large, oval fruits, one of which is shown in cross-section. Below are smaller seed-like structures.</image-desc>

Thevet <note>André Thevet, a French explorer</note> and, following him, Léry <note>Jean de Léry, an explorer of Brazil</note>, make mention of an American tree which equals the size of a Peach tree and has leaves like a Walnut; they have given it the name *Genipat* <note>Likely the Genipapo tree</note>. It is handed down that the Americans, when setting out for some slaughter or to visit friends, stain their bodies a dark blue color with the juice of this tree's fruit.

Clusius writes that the *Junipappeeyva* is a tree with the leaf of a Walnut, and that the Brazilians use its fruit in the same manner and for the same purpose. Moreover, Oviedo <note>Spanish historian of the Caribbean</note> attributes these same qualities to his *Xagua*. Thus it has happened that we have joined them here, as they are perhaps the same, placing them under the figure of the *Junipappeeyva*.

**The Nutmeg**: *German: Muscat Nuß*: *Belgian: Note*
*Muscate*: *French: Noix muscade*: *Italian: Noce Moscada.*

<image-desc>Woodcut of Nutmeg (Myristica fragrans) showing the whole fruit, the fruit opening to reveal the mace-covered nut, the nut itself, and several dried nutmegs.</image-desc>

The Nutmeg, which is also called the Aromatic Nut and the Mystic Nut, is an Indian tree. Some report it to be related to the Pear in leaf and fruit; others say it has the leaf of a Walnut but the fruit of a Pear; and almost all others say it is related to the Peach.

It is distinguished by sex and size: for some are larger, which are believed to be Male, and others smaller, which are the Female.

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> describes the fruit in a few words: It has, he says, a thick green husk: then a small skin, which is the Mace, over a woody shell, in which is the Nut.

In an island of the Indian sea called Banda, it abounds wild in the woods. It is also found in the Moluccas and other places, but there it is not fruitful; however, it cannot become accustomed to our climate.

We shall describe its qualities and virtues later.

<summary>This page introduces the third class of plants, focusing on the common Walnut and exotic "nuts" from the Americas and the East Indies, including early descriptions of Nutmeg and American ritual fruits.</summary>
<keywords>Walnut, Nutmeg, Virginia, Brazil, ethnobotany, Clusius, Dodoens, medicinal qualities, New World exploration</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
## THE TREE
### The Female Aromatic Nut <note>The Nutmeg, *Myristica fragrans*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Nutmeg branch (female) with leaves, a whole fruit, and a cross-section showing the seed (nutmeg) and the surrounding aril (mace).</image-desc>

Therefore, Mattioli and others are completely mistaken <note>original: "toto cœlo errant," literally "err by the whole sky"</note> in imagining that Mace is the flower of the Nutmeg; likewise, Lonicer wrongly confuses Mace with Macer <note>Macer was a distinct medicinal bark from India, often confused with mace in early modern botany</note>.

The Nutmeg is hot and dry at the end of the second degree, and is styptic <note>astringent</note>: it strengthens the stomach and liver, and wastes away the spleen. It commends sweetness of the breath and, if chewed, abolishes the stench of a foul spirit; it clears freckles from the face, sharpens the sight, provokes urine, and stops a flowing belly <note>diarrhea</note>. It dispels wind <note>flatulence</note> and benefits cold afflictions of the womb: especially when fresh and preserved in sugar, as it is brought from India, taken in its entirety morning and evening before food. The virtues of the oil—which is expressed by a press from fresh nuts, crushed and heated in a pot—should be judged based on what was said above.

### The Macer of Dioscorides and the Greeks, called *Arbore de las Caneras* by the Portuguese, and the Holy Tree.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Macer plant, showing a branch with broad leaves and several pieces of dried bark or roots below.</image-desc>

It is a bark, says Dioscorides, usually brought from Barbary, yellowish, thick, and quite astringent. Galen calls it a bark also usually brought from India. Pliny indicates it is the bark of the root of a certain tree. Acosta states the Macer tree is of vast size, endowed with many branches, much larger than an Elm; and in the middle of its leaves is produced a seed the size of a denarius <note>a small Roman silver coin</note>, which stands in place of the flower and fruit. Its bark is said to be thick, rough, scabby, hard, and grayish.

Thus, how much Macer differs from Mace is not at all obscure: we settle this dispute in our *Universal History*.

It dries powerfully, and is drunk for the spitting of blood, dysentery, and fluxes of the belly.

### The Byzantine Hazel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Byzantine Hazel branch with leaves and clusters of nuts in their husks.</image-desc>

They report that the shrub of the Byzantine Hazel rarely grows above a cubit's height <note>about 18 inches</note>, and is always stunted.

Furthermore, Hazelnuts are hot and dry in the first order: they provide much nourishment, but are digested with difficulty:
-> hence the verse of Macer, <-
> From the smallest of Nuts, no healthful food is given.

However, they say they are more easily cooked if their inner skin is cast away. Regarding the use and abuse of the forked Hazel wand <note>a reference to dowsing or divining rods</note>, let the Reader, if he pleases, consult our *Universal History*.

<column-break/>

### The Male Aromatic Nut.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Nutmeg branch (male) with elongated leaves and fruit.</image-desc>

Here, as with the Female, we provide the illustration from Clusius, leaving the descriptions to be sought from his own Books.

But something must be said of Mace: there is very little agreement about it among Writers, both ancient and modern. Hermolaus, Cornarius, Baccanello, Amatus, and others thought the Mace of the Arabs and the Macer of the Greeks were one and the same. On the contrary stand Mattioli, Curtius, R. Constantius, Dodoens, Laguna, Garcia, Acosta, the *History of Lyon*, and many others—and not without reason, since the Mace of the Arabs is the outer membrane properly clothing the entire Nutmeg: whereas the Macer of the Greeks, of which we speak presently, is something else entirely.

Furthermore, it wonderfully strengthens the stomach, provokes urine, expels stones, and resolves wind.

### The Hazel or Filbert Nut: German *Haselbaum*: French *Coudrier*, *Noisettier*: Italian *Nucivolare*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common Hazel branch with leaves and nuts.</image-desc>

The Ancients called the Hazelnut, the fruit of this tree, the Pontic, Praenestine, or Heracleotic nut, after the places where it grew in abundance. Dioscorides called Pontic nuts *Leptocarya* <note>Greek: "small nuts"</note>.

It is either domestic or wild, and these produce nuts that are either larger or smaller, round or oblong. The domestic kind commonly has red and oblong nuts, and sometimes round ones an inch in width: those of Lyon are so called.

The Hazel loves mountains and also descends into the plains; it delights in damp and clayey places and becomes milder when transplanted. The leaves break forth at the very first season, even before winter has fully released its grip.

See the powers and qualities next to the following figure.

### Staphylodendron <note>Bladdernut</note>: German *Pimpernußbaum*: French *Baguenaudier*, *Arbre au raisin*: Italian *Pistachio salvatico*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bladdernut tree branch with pinnate leaves and drooping clusters of bladder-like seed pods.</image-desc>

Anguillara calls it the Vine Tree. In the judgment of Bock <note>Tragus</note> and Lonicer, it could be called the *Bladder Nut* or *Follicle Nut*: by others, it is called the Wild Pistachio.

It delights in wet and damp places, frequent around the town of Altdorf in Switzerland, and between Solothurn and Waldenburg. We have observed it cultivated in gardens at Geneva, Lyon, and Basel, and we kept it in the garden of the Serene Prince at Montbéliard. It flowers in March, but ripens its little nuts in September: it is very easily sown and propagated.

Planted in gardens, it is believed to ward off venomous animals. Poor people fashion prayer beads <note>rosaries</note> from the little nuts.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal uses of Nutmeg, Mace, and various Hazelnuts, while correcting common historical confusions between Mace and the medicinal bark known as Macer. It also details the Bladdernut tree, noting its geographical distribution in Switzerland and its use in making rosaries.</summary>
<keywords>Nutmeg, Mace, Macer, Hazelnut, Bladdernut, pharmacology, Renaissance botany, Dioscorides, Mattioli, Clusius, medicinal herbs, digestive health</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### PISTACHIO: German: Foreign Peppernut-tree; French: The Pistachio Tree; Italian: Pistachios.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pistacia branch with leaves and clusters of nuts.</image-desc>

Aside from the variety of leaves, with which nature sometimes plays, no differences are observed in this tree: for all the fruits are similar to one another. Palladius <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century Roman agricultural writer.</note> alone distinguishes between Male and Female, but erroneously, as is shown in our great History <note>original: "Hist. nostra magna," referring to the author's larger botanical encyclopedia.</note>.

It loves a warm and humid place and enjoys irrigation. They are kept in several places in Italy and Provence: but the fruits are not nearly as good as in Persia, Egypt, and Syria, from where they are imported to Venice.

We shall treat Pistachios further later on.

Furthermore, Pistachios are hot and dry at the end of the second degree <note>A reference to Galenic humoral medicine, which graded the "temperament" of substances from 1 to 4.</note>: they free the liver from obstructions, benefit the stomach, and provide much nourishment.

<column-break/>

### TEREBINTH: German: Turpentine-tree; French: Terebinthe; Italian: Terebintho.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Terebinthus branch with pinnate leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

The Terebinth <note>The Turpentine tree, *Pistacia terebinthus*.</note>, according to the author Theophrastus, is divided into Male and Female: some large, others small. By some, it is called the "green grain tree," and it takes its name from the similarity of its berries to Ebony or Chickpeas.

It grows in dry, stony places exposed to the sun, occurring spontaneously in many parts of Syria, Spain, Portugal, Italy, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France.</note>: it is also brought into gardens. It flowers in April; the fruit is gathered in September.

The leaves, fruit, and bark, according to Dioscorides, possess an astringent power, and they are suitable for the same purposes as the Lentisk <note>The Mastic tree.</note>, being prepared and taken in a similar manner. Regarding its Resin and its powers, let our great History be consulted.

---

### GREATER INDIAN TEREBINTH with round fruit.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick branch with large, broad leaves and clusters of round fruit.</image-desc>

The fruits of this tree are in no way inferior to Pistachios in quality, and they are similar to them, hanging from clusters just like those: but they are shorter and rounder. This affinity has caused them to be regarded as Pistachios by some: they are hot and dry, and they expel wind <note>i.e., they relieve flatulence.</note>.

Theophrastus says they report that the Terebinth is found in India; others say a tree similar to the Terebinth, whose leaves and branches and all other things are like the Terebinth, etc.

This similarity has led some to consider its fruit as Pistachios. They are hot and dry. Moreover, the tree grows abundantly not only in India, but also in Persia, Armenia, and Mesopotamia.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN TEREBINTH, WITH SMALL FRUIT approaching the shape of a little heart.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch with smaller, pointed leaves and clusters of small, heart-shaped fruits.</image-desc>

The little nuts of this tree, with their shells, are the size of a Pea, but in shape they resemble a little heart, not unlike Indian Millet; in other respects, they are similar to the preceding.

It grows in the same place as the preceding one.

Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a 16th-century German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant.</note> calls it the *Bel* of Serapion. Serapion writes that *Bel* is a medicine of India: and that it benefits the fluxes of the nerves and joints, as well as gout.

---

### EXOTIC LITTLE NUT OF THE PISTACHIO SPECIES, perhaps the BEL of Serapion and Avicenna?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several large, oblong nuts or seeds, shown both whole and in cross-section.</image-desc>

We keep these little nuts, which very closely approach the Pistachio, among our foreign fruits.

Is it the *Sel* of Serapion and Avicenna, of which Serapion relates: *Sel* of Isaac Eben Amram is the Indian Quince, a round fruit like a Hazelnut, without a shell. It has the virtue of Ginger. Rauwolf writes that it is found in places near the city of Jerusalem: and is also called *Seel*.

<column-break/>

### CACAO OF AMERICA, or Mexican Hazelnut, the Cacavate of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several cacao beans, showing their textured husks and internal structure.</image-desc>

The Cacao is a tree of moderate size, which withers as soon as it is touched by the Sun: it is not planted except in the woods in a shady and humid place. The fruit resembles the appearance of an Almond, and is reddish in both its shell and its kernel: it is famous throughout all America.

For from the Cacao kernel a certain cooling drink <note>original: "Sorbitiuncula," a small draught or drink.</note> is made, so greatly desired that they can exchange anything for them: it is the principal merchandise of those regions.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Pistacia genus (Pistachio and Terebinth) and their medicinal properties, concluding with an early European description of the Cacao tree from the Americas.</summary>
<keywords>Pistachio, Terebinth, Cacao, Turpentine, Humoral Medicine, India, Mexico, Rauwolf, Serapion, Botany</keywords>

### THE INDIAN HAZELNUT OF MEHEMBETENE.
#### Described by Cortusus. <note>Giacomo Antonio Cortuso (1513–1603) was an Italian botanist and director of the botanical garden in Padua.</note>

It is about a thumb's width long, triangular in shape, with a hard and woody shell. When cut open, it has three cells in which an oblong, white, and sweet kernel is found. There are some who relate it to the *Ointment Nut* <note>original: "Nucem Unguentariam," likely referring to the Ben Nut or Moringa, used in perfumery</note>, but we do not subscribe to their opinion in the least.

### THE MEHEMBETENE HAZELNUT OF CORTUSUS
#### another species, covered in shaggy hair.

This hazelnut also corresponds to the ones mentioned above. However, its triangular opening is covered with shaggy hairs; it is much like the *Areca nut* <note>original: "Feufel," an old term for the Areca or Betel nut</note>, being almost entirely covered in a certain hairy wrapping. It contains a sweet kernel enclosed in a thin, whitish membrane.

### THE SMALL INDIAN NUT OF LOBELIUS AND PENA. <note>Refers to botanists Matthias de l'Obel and Pierre Pena, authors of the "Stirpium Adversaria Nova" (1570).</note>

It is scarcely equal to a large olive in size, with a bark-like, oily, and flavorful kernel. We present it here both whole and broken open; the image of the whole nut bears a great resemblance to the fruit of the *Dwarf Fan Palm* <note>original: "Chamæryphes"</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE MEHEMBETENE HAZELNUT OF CORTUSUS
#### another species, smooth.

This fruit corresponds to the preceding one in size and shape, also having a triangular opening at the top. For its size, however, it is remarkably heavy, as if it were made of bone or stone. The color is dark brown or a blackish-grey, and it rattles when shaken—proof of the kernel contained within.

### CARAIRI, AN INDIAN FRUIT, THE SIZE
#### of a common walnut.

It is smooth and not at all heavy, even though it is very solid and endowed with a stony hardness; it sinks in water no less than a stone does. When broken open, it is found to consist of a thick and very hard shell, and it contains a white, succulent kernel of pleasing taste and delightful aroma. There is another of the same kind called *Camiri* <note>likely the Candlenut, Aleurites moluccanus</note> by the Indians.

### SMALL NUTS FROM GUINEA.

These are nearly the size of a Nutmeg, and the shape also very much approaches it; the flavor is almost the same. We received these as a gift from the Most Illustrious Prince of Württemberg, to whom Master Paludanus <note>Bernardus Paludanus (1550–1633), a famous Dutch physician and collector of rarities</note> had sent them. We present various figures showing the different faces of this small nut, depending on how much it has been stripped of its outer husk.

### IMAGES AND OUTLINE SKETCHES.

### INDIAN FRUIT resembling a WALNUT, tuberous.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a tuberous Indian fruit resembling a walnut. The top one shows the exterior texture with small bumps; the bottom one shows a smoother, slightly mottled surface.</image-desc>

It equals a Walnut still covered in its outer husk, roughened with continuous small bumps and longer ridges; it is a reddish-ash color. The lowest part has a flat navel <note>original: "umbilicum sessilem," referring to the point where the stem attaches</note>, while the opposite side tapers slightly into a cone. It is hard and heavy.

### INDIAN NUTS showing a MASK-LIKE appearance.

<image-desc>Three small, dark, oval nuts. The bottom-most nut has markings that resemble a face or mask (larva).</image-desc>

This fruit is also marvelous, representing in some way a certain mask of a long-tailed Monkey without a nose. It is depicted here at its actual size, showing first the back and then the front side. Another one follows that is very closely related to it.

### GROOVED TUBEROUS EXOTIC FRUIT

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a large, deeply grooved (sulcated) exotic fruit. The top view shows the longitudinal ridges; the bottom view is a cross-section or top-down view showing the radial pattern of the grooves.</image-desc>

The figure expresses its size. It is covered in an ash-colored bark, which is not hard, but spongy like Oak Galls <term>Galls: abnormal growths on trees often used for making ink</term>. It is beautifully grooved along its entire length, uneven and tuberous. At the bottom part where the grooves meet, there is a small pit; on the opposite side, however, there is a hump. If its substance is pierced with a needle, it is found to be quite hard.

<column-break/>

### SPINY INDIAN FRUIT.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a spiky or "hedgehog-like" (echinatus) Indian fruit. The top one is covered in small, sharp points; the bottom one is smoother but retains a similar shape.</image-desc>

It equals a Nutmeg in size; it is ash-colored and full of many blunt bumps. In taste, it is found to have a certain astringency. The little stalk is thick, and the fruit itself makes a sound when shaken; but we do not know what it contains inside, for we have not opened it at all.

### OBLONG INDIAN NUT, INTERNALLY resembling a Nutmeg.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of an oblong Indian nut. The top one shows the exterior with a veined or marbled pattern; the bottom one shows a similar texture, possibly the interior structure.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> labels this the *Indian Hazelnut* in Mattioli’s German History. Lobelius records it under the title of *Pine Palm*, but erroneously. Tabernaemontanus depicts it under the name *Areca* or *Faufel* <note>The Areca nut, often used in betel chewing</note>. In the History of Lyon, as well as by Camerarius, it is called the *Indian Hazelnut*.

### CHECKERED INDIAN NUT.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a "tessellated" or checkered Indian nut. The top view shows a circular cross-section with a central seed; the bottom view shows a complex, geometric, woven-like pattern on the surface.</image-desc>

Of no less—but rather more elaborate—natural display and particular elegance are the fruits depicted here, which we formerly received from the Serene Duke of Württemberg, and to which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note> has similar examples in his *Exotics*, brought from Guiana, a province of America.

# OF PLANTS

### LARGE INDIAN FILBERTS, CURCAS, Peruvian Petita, and Lery’s Manobi.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several large, oblong, textured seeds or nuts, some shown whole and others in cross-section or partially peeled.</image-desc>

The fruit which we show in this table is depicted and described by Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist.</note> in his latest Latin and Italian Commentaries.

However, we refer to this place various exotic fruits which have some affinity with Filberts <note>A type of hazelnut.</note>. Thus the **Curcas** <note>original: "Curcas"; likely Jatropha curcas, the purging nut.</note> comes to be mentioned here, which, according to Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine.</note>, grows in Malabar the size of a Filbert; likewise the **Peruvian Petita**; likewise the **Manobi** of Lery <note>Jean de Léry, a French explorer; "Manobi" refers to the peanut (Arachis hypogaea).</note>, which grows underground in the manner of Truffles, and which perhaps is a kind of **Trasi** <note>original: "Trasi"; likely Cyperus esculentus or tiger nut.</note> approaching very closely to the Filberts.

### MAD NUTS, or the MAD LITTLE PLUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a round fruit or nut with a textured, slightly patterned surface, shown attached to a small stem fragment.</image-desc>

It equals the size of walnuts, with a brown shell and a black membranous stone with a white spot.

The Belgians returning from the East Indies called this foreign fruit the **Mad Little Plum** <note>original: "Prunula insana"; likely the Datura or a similar narcotic seed.</note> from its effect: because all who had tasted or eaten it were seized by vertigo and alienation of the mind, and had wonderful imaginations, according to the temperament of each person's nature.

### MALUCCAN PINE KERNELS, or PURGING NUTS: French: Pignons d'Inde: Italian: Pignones de Maluco.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical sprig with leaves and several small, oval fruits or nuts hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

They are similar to our Pine kernels, but with a softer and blacker shell, white inside, fatty and sweet in taste. They grow in large cones. The tree is the size of a Pear tree. It grows spontaneously in the woods, and is also cultivated in gardens.

They are hot in the third degree and dry in the second <note>Refers to the Galenic system of humoral medicine used to classify the "potency" of drugs.</note>. Moreover, the Indians frequently use this fruit, both in curing certain diseases and also in their wickednesses. They purge bile, phlegm, and waters.

Furthermore, since Acosta <note>Cristóbal Acosta, a natural historian of the East Indies.</note> records that four grains may kill: while Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, who wrote on medicines from the New World.</note> offers five or six: it is rightly questioned whether they are writing about the same things.

<column-break/>

### SOAP SPHERES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several small, spherical seeds or berries, some shown with their outer husks and others as smooth, dark inner pits.</image-desc>

These are fruits equaling the size of a Cherry-Filbert, but not at all edible, containing a very hard and black round stone. The tree which produces these fruits has leaves similar to Fern leaves, but smaller: and it occurs frequently in the islands of Hispaniola <note>The island comprising modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note>.

Very elegant prayer beads <note>Rosaries.</note> are made from these stones when perforated. Indeed, with the whole fruit and hot water, clothes are cleaned, just as with soap. The pulp surrounding the stone is that which serves the purpose of soap.

### THE PURGING FILBERT OF THE NEW WORLD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of three large, smooth, oval-shaped nuts or seeds.</image-desc>

In color and form they are similar to ours, with a thin shell of a chestnut color, and the inner marrow white and sweet. With these the Indians commonly purge themselves. The dose is from half a drachm to one scruple <note>original: "3. ss. ad 1. i."; traditional apothecary measurements.</note>, but they must be roasted. Moreover, they are of a hot and dry temperament beyond the second degree.

### THE BERETINE FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several elongated, slightly curved seeds or pods, some shown in cross-section revealing the interior structure.</image-desc>

All the Molucca islands <note>The Spice Islands in Indonesia.</note> nourish this tree, which is larger than the Oak: the leaves are like Laurel, thick, shining, and not at all saw-toothed on the edge. The fruit is small, similar to Holm-oak acorns, and edible.

Moreover, Beretina Island especially abounds in that fruit: and the inhabitants there, by cooking it, or bruising it and cooking it in the manner of a pulp, relieve their hunger during a scarcity of other food.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### THE GEHVPH TREE or COBBAN.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small tree or shrub with slender branches and small, sparse leaves. To the right of the image is a descriptive text block.</image-desc>

It has small leaves, much like the tree that bears the Cathartic pod <note>likely Senna or a similar purgative</note>; the branches are shorter, with a yellowish bark. The fruit is somewhat thick and round, like a playing ball, in which a nut equal to a hazelnut is compressed, containing a bitter kernel.

In the Island of Taprobana <note>original: "Taprobana Insula", a historical name often used for Sri Lanka, though the text here identifies it as Sumatra</note>, today called Sumatra, it is found everywhere: for they diligently cultivate it near their houses and in gardens. The fruit is of great use for quenching thirst and various other purposes.

<column-break/>

### BARVCE, THE FRUIT OF THE HVRA TREE.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a fruit: the top shows a whole, ribbed, pumpkin-like fruit; the bottom shows a cross-section or a single segment of the fruit with a seed inside.</image-desc>

This fruit grows in Guyana on a fairly tall tree called the **Hura** <note>The Sandbox tree, *Hura crepitans*</note>. It equals the size of two fists and grows from several nuts joined together and, as it were, forced into one. It purges by vomiting and by loosening the bowels. *Clusius* <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>.

---

### ARARA, AN AMERICAN FRUIT.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a fruit: the top (marked I) is an oblong, pod-like fruit; the bottom (marked II) is a rounded seed or nut.</image-desc>

The two figures show the kernel both bare and covered by a shell or skin: its size is that of a wild Olive. From a decoction of it, they wash foul and malignant internal organs.

<column-break/>

### CVNANE, THE FRUIT OF THE MORREMOR TREE.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a fruit: the top (marked II) shows a long, textured pod; the bottom shows a smooth, oval seed.</image-desc>

It is long, says Clusius, oval, black, and marked with three small holes. It grows among the Americans <note>indigenous peoples of the Americas</note> on a tiny tree named **Morremor**. They eat it roasted against headaches. One of an ash-gray color, and not unlike the aforementioned, is depicted in the same plate.

---

### LENTISCVS: *German: Mastic tree; Belgian: Mastic tree; French: Lentisque; Italian: Lentisco.*

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of a Lentiscus (Mastic) branch with small leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

The commentaries claim the Lentiscus <note>The Mastic tree, *Pistacia lentiscus*</note> is named for the "lentor" <note>stickiness or flexibility</note> of its leaves; Ruellius says it is because it becomes sticky with a certain liquid. It is a tree, he says, the size of an Oak, with the leaf of a Service-tree, the scent of Turpentine, and berries like wild Millet: but he produces monsters instead of the Lentiscus. Nor is Matthiolus consistent with himself: assigning it leaves sometimes of the Myrtle, sometimes of the Pistachio; others better compare its leaves to those of the Olive.

Pliny, Ruellius, and Camerarius mention the Chian and Italian varieties: but the latter distinguishes again between the shrub-like and the tree-like, and between the cultivated and the wild.

Furthermore, the entire maritime coast of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> is very fertile in Lentiscus. It flowers in April; the fruit ripens in October.

Let the reader see the powers and qualities at the side of the following figure.

<column-break/>

### FRUIT OF THE PERUVIAN BALSAM.

<image-desc>An illustration of a curved, textured seed pod or fruit.</image-desc>

Clusius and the *History of Lyon* depict the fruit of the tree growing in the New World from which Balsam is extracted in this way. But if faith is to be placed in the description of Monardes, the fruit of the Balsam is much smaller.

In this vacant space, we add the virtues and qualities of the Lentiscus.

It is moderately warm, but dries in the second degree; it is equally astringent in all its parts: the tips of the branches, the shoots, the leaves, the roots, the fruit, and the bark. Regarding **Mastic**, the resin which this tree "weeps," it has been treated at length in our *Universal History*: and it will perhaps be dealt with in the Appendix to this work.

### THE NUT, OR SMALL STONE, CALLED CYPOTE, SIMILAR TO THE PERUVIAN BALSAM NUT.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations of seed pods or nuts, showing a textured, pitted surface similar to a peach pit or a dried nut casing.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> writes in his *Exotics* that this nut, called Cypote, is not at all unlike the fruit of the Peruvian Balsam; for that reason, we have used one of the illustrations of said fruit here.

<column-break/>

### A NEW BALSAM WITH CLUSTERED FRUIT.

<image-desc>A large, detailed botanical illustration of a single lanceolate leaf with prominent pinnate venation.</image-desc>

It grows wild in the Indies and on the island of Hispaniola <note>Modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note>, reaching the size of a tree, with ash-colored stems, green leaves, and fruit that grows in clusters and turns red when ripe. Its leaf is depicted here drawn from life.

When applied to ulcers and wounds, it restrains their bleeding, cleanses them, and heals them miraculously—even more effectively than true Balsam. From its tips, a distilled water is produced that is most useful for wounds and for diseases arising from cold humors.

---

<column-break/>

### TRUE BALSAM, OR WOOD-BALSAM: German: Balsam: French: Baume: Italian: Balsamo.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a small, gnarled shrub or tree with sparse foliage and small berries or seed pods hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

It is remarkable how much writers vary among themselves in the description of this small tree. According to Theophrastus, the tree is the size of a large pomegranate, with very many branches and a leaf similar to Rue, but somewhat white and evergreen. The fruit is similar to the fruit of the Turpentine tree in size, shape, and color, and is very fragrant, etc.

Pliny identifies three kinds of the tree: *Eucheryses* <note>meaning "easy to pour"</note>, *Trachy* <note>"rough"</note>, and *Eumetes* <note>"well-measured"</note>. Dioscorides records that it differs within its own species by its roughness, length, and slenderness.

He writes that it grows only in Judea and Egypt; Theophrastus says only in two gardens in Syria; Alpinus says in Arabia Felix <note>the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note>. More details can be found in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### THE OINTMENT NUT, ALSO CALLED THE OINTMENT ACORN and Myrepsica by Herbarists.

<image-desc>Botanical illustrations showing a cluster of long, thin seed pods (resembling vanilla beans or certain legumes) and several individual rounded nuts or seeds below them.</image-desc>

It grows in a pod which is depicted here alongside it. It seems that Martial alluded to this "acorn" when he said:

> What neither Virgil nor Homer said in verse,
> This consists of Ointment and the Nut <note>original: "Balanus," referring to the Ben-nut or a similar oily seed used in perfumes</note>.

There are those who identify two species: the *Greater*, the size of a hazelnut; and the *Lesser*, the size of a chickpea. This latter one is considered dangerous, and the larger leaf is more commonly used.

The juice is hot in quality, according to Galen, but the remains from which it is pressed have a dominant quality mixed with some astringency.

Medical practitioners are well-acquainted with the use of the Oil of Balanus <note>Ben oil</note> which is prepared from this nut.

---

<column-break/>

### THE OINTMENT NUT TREE.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a leafy plant with a thick, woody stem and visible root system, showing broad leaves and small clusters of fruit.</image-desc>

There is little agreement among authors regarding the Ointment Nut tree: some wish it to be the *Lilae* tree, others the *Ben*, *Been*, or *Behen* of the Arabs. Theophrastus seems to have known it best, describing it thus: *Balanos*, he says, takes its name from its fruit; it has a leaf like Myrtle, but longer. The tree itself is pure and quite large, not straight but twisted. The fruit is similar in size and appearance to the Caper (or the hazelnut, according to Dioscorides). It grows in Ethiopia, Egypt, Arabia, and the town of Petra near Judea, etc.

Whether it is found today in Italy, Spain, and India, we discuss in our universal history.

<column-break/>

### ANACARDIUM or ANACARDUS: German: Elephant-louse: French: Anacardes. AND THE CASHEW.

<image-desc>Illustrations of several heart-shaped or kidney-shaped nuts (Anacardium/Cashew), showing different angles and textures.</image-desc>

The name *Anacardium* <note>literally "like a heart"</note> is believed to have been given to the fruit because its shape rivals that of a small bird's heart. Ruellius, Matthiolus, and Rhegius write that it was unknown to the ancient Greeks; and we have not found the tree described even by more recent writers. Caesalpinus records that it is not unlike the *Perlea*.

The Anacardium is therefore the fruit of a tree, and is thus wrongly called "Elephant Louse" <term>Pediculus Elephantis: a common folk name for the cashew nut due to its shape</term> by the unlearned. There is a great yield of it in various provinces of the Indies, as well as in the volcanic mountains of Sicily.

Furthermore, Anacardiums are very hot in temperament, and are very suitable for cold ailments of the heart and brain.

The CASHEW <note>original: "Caious"</note>, a foreign fruit similar to a hare's kidney, we illustrate here together with the anacardiums.
