### AHOUAI, or HAOVVAI, a foreign poisonous fruit.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration showing a branch with three large, heart-shaped or triangular seed pods hanging from it.</image-desc>

Thevet and Lery have described this tree; Lery writes of it as follows: "In Brazil," he says, "there is a tree called *Ahouai* by the forest-dwelling people <note>The Tupinambá people of Brazil</note>, which is so foul-smelling and reeks so strongly of garlic that when it is cut or placed near a fire, the odor is unbearable." It has leaves like our Apple tree, with a fruit approaching the Water Caltrop <term>Tribulum aquaticum: a floating aquatic plant with spiny, nut-like fruit</term>, containing a highly poisonous and truly deadly kernel. However, once the kernel is removed, they use the dried shells as rattles in place of little bells.

<column-break/>

### THE NUX VOMICA OF THE APOTHECARIES, the Metella of the Arabs: German: *Kraenauglin* <note>Crow's eyes</note>: French: *Noix Vomique*.

<image-desc>Four circular cross-sections of seeds or nuts, showing internal structures and varying shapes from round to kidney-like.</image-desc>

Almost all writers assert that the "Vomiting Nuts" <note>original: "Nuces Vomicas"</note> sold by the dry-goods merchants are the *Metellas* of the Arabs; however, we have shown in our *Universal History* that they either come to kill <unclear>dogs</unclear> with them, or they contradict one another. Caesalpinus reports they are also called "Eastern Mushrooms." Fuchs and Ruellius call it *Tithymalus Myrsinites* <note>a type of spurge</note>; Dalechamps calls it the fruit of an Indian plant creeping on the ground, and further asserts that the true *Nux vomica* is actually *Datura* <note>Thorn-apple</note>.

The Monks say that the *Nux Vomica*, which is also called the "Vomiting Chestnut" or "Indian Chestnut," is understood to be that which is brought from Eastern regions; it is like a small cake, the size of a penny, whitish, flattened, and curved.

More on the nature and powers of the *Metella* nuts in the Appendix.

---

### THE FOREIGN "EYED" NUT: Is it the Mechil Nut of Serapion? Or the Heuden Nut of the Arabs?

<image-desc>Six botanical illustrations of seeds or nuts with distinct "eye" markings or lobed structures.</image-desc>

This is larger than the *Nux vomica* used in the shops, and not hairy like that one, nor is it entirely round, but somewhat curved around its circumference: it is marked with distinct "little eyes" <note>original: "ocellis"</note> corresponding to little compartments, in each of which is a seed similar to those of Apples or Pears.

Is it the *Metella* nut of the Arabs, as Lonicer believes?

Is it their *Heuden* nut?

Is it the *Mechil* nut of Serapion? <note>Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab physician</note>

<column-break/>

### A CERTAIN SMALL NUT FALSELY THOUGHT TO BE THE HIGUERO and Ahouai.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant stem bearing four oblong, segmented seed pods or fruits.</image-desc>

Lobelius and the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' botanical work</note> include these small nuts and label them as the *Higuero Fruit* from Clusius, yet Clusius never called this nut *Higuero*. Thus, Tabernaemontanus more rightly suspected it was the *Higuero*, but did not state so definitively.

Whether these are also the *Ahouai* of Thevet, as the 4th edition of Clusius's work on Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta</note> holds, must be examined: formerly the figure was placed here without a name or description.

---

### XYLON OR HERBACEOUS COTTON: German: *Baumwull*: Dutch: *Boomwull*: French: *Cotton*: Italian: *Cotone, Bombace*.

There is one *Xylon* <note>Greek for wood/tree</note> that is a tree, of which more shortly, and another that is an herb: both bear a nut, which is why they claim a place in this section. This plant was unknown to most of the ancient Greeks, just as the tree-type was to Theophrastus. In Latin it is also called *Bambax*, *Bombyx*, *Bombax*, *Bombacium*, *Babacium*, *Cottonis*, and various forms of *Cottonum*. But the downy fiber itself is properly called *Bombax*.

It delights in warm places; it is sown in March and April and harvested in September and October. Formerly it was planted only in Egypt, but now it is found almost throughout all of Europe. As for its use, there is no kind of linen that can be preferred to this down for whiteness and softness.

<column-break/>

### XYLON, or TREE COTTON.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of a cotton plant (Xylon), showing large lobed leaves and a cotton boll bursting open to reveal the fibers.</image-desc>

As Belon notes, Herodotus was the first to mention this wool-bearing tree, followed later by Theophrastus, Pliny, and many others; it is among the evergreens.

It differs from the Herbaceous kind in the height of its trunk and the smoothness of its leaves, which are hairy in the Herbaceous variety. However, it bears the same downy fiber as the Herbaceous one.

It grows in Egypt and Arabia, according to Alpinus and Belon; from it, the Arabs weave cloths thinner and finer than even silk.

We have cultivated both types of Cotton <note>original: "Gossypium"</note> in the garden of the Serene Prince at Montbéliard. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various exotic nuts and seeds, including the poisonous Ahouai from Brazil, the medicinal Nux Vomica, and the different varieties of the cotton plant (Xylon).</summary>
<keywords>Ahouai, Nux Vomica, Metella, cotton, botany, Brazil, Egypt, Arabia, medicinal plants, poisonous plants</keywords>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of exotic plants and fruits, focusing on specimens from the Americas and the East Indies. It maintains the botanical classification style established in previous sections.</meta>

### THE FOREIGN WOOL-BEARING TREE, AND THE Brazilian COTTON.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large, elongated seed pod or fruit with a textured, fibrous surface, hanging from a small stem. Below it are two smaller, circular seeds or cross-sections.</image-desc>

Trees bearing Cotton <note>original: "Bombacem"</note> are abundant in Brazil; they are of medium size and bear flowers similar to little bells, yellow, like those of Gourds. The mature fruit approaches the nature of the Beech, which splits into four parts.

The Cotton, called *Amenijou* by the Americans, hangs from these, the size of small balls: and in the middle are black grains, joined closely together, resembling a kidney. The forest-dwelling women gather this and prepare thread from it for their beds. *So says Jean de Léry.* <note>Jean de Léry (1534–1613) was a French explorer and author of an influential account of Brazil.</note>

Pierre Belon also mentions this Brazilian Cotton <note>original: "Gossypii"</note>, but he writes that it differs from the Asiatic variety especially in its millet-like seed. *The illustration is from Clusius.* <note>Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius) was one of the most influential botanists of the 16th century.</note>

### THE GREATER FAGARA.

<image-desc>Four small, dark, textured seeds or fruits shown from different angles, some appearing to have a split outer husk revealing a smooth inner seed.</image-desc>

Linschoten <note>Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, a Dutch voyager to the East Indies.</note> says that Fagara <note>likely a species of Zanthoxylum or Sichuan pepper</note> grows in Java, the size of a Cubeb or Pepper, covered with a thin husk (blackish-grey, according to Clusius) in which is a single grain covered with a very thin black skin. It dries and warms in the manner of Cubebs, and is beneficial for "cold" diseases. <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were classified by "humors" as hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>

Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina.</note> also mentions this. What is Fagara, he asks? A grain similar to a Chickpea, having the grains of Mahaleb: and in its cavity a black grain, like *Schebedenegi* <note>likely hemp seed</note>: and it is brought from Sofala.

### OREGIOELLA, AND THE QUADRANGULAR FRUIT, black with a vermilion membrane.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations labeled I and II. I is a large, ribbed, almond-shaped fruit. II is a smaller, rounded fruit with a textured surface.</image-desc>

Clusius depicts the Oregioella, yet he does not rightly know what it is. Its figure is in this plate under number I. Under the other number is depicted an exotic fruit; what plant it belongs to, in what region it was born, or by what name it should be called, could not be known to the same Clusius, even as he was illustrating and describing it.

<column-break/>

### ORIENTAL BERRIES: German: *Keckel Körner*: French: *Cocque de Levant*: Italian: *Cocca*, & *Coccole di Levante*.

<image-desc>Six small, kidney-shaped or heart-shaped seeds or nuts, shown in two rows of three.</image-desc>

The apothecary shops call these Oriental Berries <note>original: "Coccos Orientales"; likely Anamirta cocculus, used to stun fish</note>: others call them Elephantine Coconuts, because they are believed to be a very pleasing food for Elephants: some call them Grains of the Orient, others Fishermen's Grains.

It is not sufficiently clear from which plant they are produced. There are those who think it is the fruit of a Clematis. Ruellius suspects it is the fruit of a certain Birthwort. Amatus thinks it is the seed of a Spurge; however, how correctly he does so, we have weighed in our *Universal History*. By the testimony of Cardano and daily experience, nothing is more excellent than these berries for rendering fish stunned <note>original: "attonitos"</note>. They are hot and dry, but by what quality they drive fish into a stupor, we shall show in the Appendix.

### THE LESSER FAGARA.

<image-desc>Six small botanical specimens, similar to the Fagara Maior but smaller, showing husks and inner seeds.</image-desc>

Ferrante Imperato recognizes the Greater and Lesser Fagara as species. He relates that the Greater was diligently described by the Arabs: but that the Lesser is a different species, which is brought from Oriental regions. The <gloss>interlinear note: commentary</gloss> says the whole fruit of the Fagara is so similar to the Indian Cuckoo that at first sight it could be taken for it.

Furthermore, according to Avicenna, Fagara is a grain hot and dry in the third degree: having an astringency mixed with a resolving power.

### THE PALM: German: *Dattelbaum*: Belgian: *Dadelyboom*: French: *Dattier, Palmier*: Italian: *Palma*.

<image-desc>A collection of palm-related botanical parts, including a cluster of dates, a single date, a palm leaf fragment, and what appears to be a germinating seed or sprout.</image-desc>

The differences among Palms are many, taken from the wood, the fruit, the location, the size, and other forms: whence Cardano rightly said that there are so many kinds of Palms that they should not be considered a single tree. Commonly, however, they distinguish between Male and Female, Sterile and Fertile. André Thevet writes that seven species differing in fruit are found in the Indies.

The Palm is greedy for heat, and cannot bear the cold. It grows indeed in some of the warmer districts of the European World, such as Sicily, Spain, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, etc. But it is either sterile or bears harsh fruit. In Egypt and Syria it is best. Moreover, where the earth is salty <note>original: "falsa terra"</note> and said to be unfit for all other things, there it brings forth the best fruits.

Concerning its powers and properties, in the following pages.

It details their physical characteristics, geographic origins, and medicinal or practical uses, such as stunning fish or making thread.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

<sig>D 2</sig>

### DWARF PALM or GROUND-FAN, the non-spiny Spanish dwarf palm.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dwarf palm tree with fan-shaped fronds and a thick, fibrous trunk base, labeled with an asterisk.</image-desc>

The branches of this species, as well as the spiny variety, are carried throughout almost all of Italy during the season of Lent <note>The forty days preceding Easter</note> to decorate and cover with various woven patterns the Olive branches that are carried by everyone in the churches on the holy day of Palms <note>Palm Sunday</note>. These same branches are excellent (even today, just as in the century of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany," c. 371–287 BCE</note>) for preparing small baskets, mats, and brooms; for the branches along with the leaves are very suitable for making brooms, and they do not break except after a long time.

<column-break/>

### DWARF PALM or GROUND-FAN, the spiny dwarf palm.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dwarf palm tree similar to the first but with visible spines on the leaf stalks and small round fruits shown separately above the fronds.</image-desc>

Two differences are observed in the Dwarf Palm, called *Chamæriphes* <note>original: "Chamæriphes," from the Greek for "thrown to the ground," referring to its low growth</note> by Theophrastus: the spiny and the non-spiny.

Indeed, there is a rare and great abundance of it in Crete, Sicily, Portugal, and in many maritime coasts of Spain, Italy, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

Its berries are given for their astringent power against all fluxes of the body <note>such as diarrhea</note>; and the fatty, tuber-like growths that grow near the roots of some of these palms are of very pleasant taste and are delicacies for the palate.

---

### FOREIGN GROUND-FAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a palm with long, slender fronds and a textured trunk, labeled with an asterisk.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> depicts and describes this branch of a foreign Dwarf Palm bought from sailors; it was not at all known to him from where it was brought or in what place it grew.

Furthermore, the fruits of the palm are moist in the first degree and warm in the second <note>referring to the Galenic system of "humors" used in ancient medicine</note>. And the tree itself, in all its parts, shares in an admirable utility. We have shown in our *Universal History* that Bread, Honey, Wine, Vinegar, various Textiles, the best Charcoal, and many Medicines are made from palms, and even that Palms are put to unusual uses. The narrowness of this space does not permit us to record everything here. This one thing at least must be said: there was once a certain Persian Song in which 360 uses of the Palm were enumerated.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN NUT-BEARING PALM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coconut palm tree with a tall, ringed trunk and large pinnate fronds, bearing clusters of fruit (coconuts) at the crown.</image-desc>

It is a tree, says Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine who worked in India</note>, of vast size: with leaves similar to a Palm or a Reed, yet somewhat broader; with a flower like a Chestnut, and wood that is spongy and stalk-like.

Thevet <note>André Thevet, a 16th-century French explorer</note> also writes that the Indian Nut tree <note>The Coconut</note> is similar to the Egyptian or Arabian Palm in height and leaves; Massarus says that Indian Palms are far superior to the Jewish and African ones. It delights in sandy soil and proximity to the sea, so much so that it is not easily found in inland regions, according to the testimony of Garcia.

And he adds that this one tree provides absolutely all the instruments and material for nautical affairs <note>shipbuilding and rigging</note>.

Whether indeed Theophrastus, Pliny, and other ancient writers made mention of this or not, is not so easy to judge.

---

### THE PALM-PINE TREE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with scale-like bark and multiple cone-like structures emerging from the foliage.</image-desc>

Nature, in a playful mood, seems to have fused this tree together as if it were a certain hybrid of a Palm and a Pine.

Pena and Lobelius <note>Authors of the "Adversaria Stirpium," 1570</note> report that it grows in the region of Guinea: if at least it is the same as those which they call "Wild Palms," related to the common Palm, as it seems to be.

By Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus, a German botanist</note> it is called the Cone-bearing Palm: in German <term>Zapfenpalm</term> <note>literally "Cone-palm"</note>.

<column-break/>

### FRUIT OF THE PALM-PINE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, scaled fruit (resembling a pine cone or cycad cone) shown attached to a stem and also in a cross-section detail.</image-desc>

We depict here a fruit received from a friend most skilled in plants, which we believe to be the fruit of the Palm-pine tree. Let the experts judge.

Lobelius, in his *Observations*, thinks this fruit is the same as the <term>Indian Hazelnut</term> <note>original: "Avellana Indica"</note> of the oblong kind described by Clusius, which we have not yet granted to him.

# OF PLANTS

### THE INDIAN NUT: German: Indianische Nuß & Meer-Nuß; French: Noix des indes; Italian: Noce d’Inde.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coconut (Nux Indica) shown in three views: the whole fibrous husk, the inner hard shell with its three "eyes," and a cross-section showing the white meat and hollow center.</image-desc>

The fruit which is brought to us under the name of the <term>Indian Nut</term> <note>The coconut (Cocos nucifera)</note> sometimes equals the size of a human body, or even exceeds it; at other times it is the size of an Ostrich egg, and elsewhere scarcely larger than a Swan's egg. The shape is like a Gourd or a Melon: the color is for the most part a brownish ash-gray. Amatus <note>Amato Lusitano, a 16th-century physician</note> wrongly suspected this to be the *Elaten* or *Spatha* of Dioscorides. It is eaten fresh, with or without salt, and sometimes even with Sugar, or with Vinegar and Pepper; but when it begins to harden, it tastes like the head of a Thistle <note>Likely referring to the flavor of an artichoke heart</note>. We intentionally omit the remaining uses here for the sake of brevity.

### THE LEAF OF THE INDIAN NUT, ACCORDING TO SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, broad, tapered leaf with parallel venation, identified as a possible coconut leaf.</image-desc>

The leaf which we give pictured here seems to have been torn from some tree of the Palm family. It is arched in the manner of a roof tile, four or five cubits long, and two wide. Pena and Lobel <note>Famous 16th-century botanists</note> report it was brought from the West Indies, and they inserted it among the filaments of the Great Leaf in the palm section. The *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586</note> has the same image, but wrongly calls it the leaf of the Dragon Tree: for what similarity is there?

### THE COCO OF MALDIVA, or the INDIAN NUT celebrated against poisons.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double coconut (Coco de Mer), showing its characteristic bilobed shape resembling a heart or pelvis, with a fibrous exterior.</image-desc>

This Coco, or this Nut, is highly praised—and especially its marrow <note>the internal pulp</note>—against poisons. Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine</note> writes that he heard by common report that the Maldive Islands were once part of the mainland, but were submerged by an inundation of the Sea, creating these Islands in which Palms were buried; these palms then produced these Cocos. To this day, no one has been able to see the leaves or the trunk of the tree, but only the Cocos are cast up onto the shore, sometimes two joined together, and sometimes indeed single and separate. But no one is allowed to collect these except at the risk of their head <note>under penalty of death</note>, because they assert that whatever is cast from the Sea onto the shore belongs to the King; this circumstance has won greater authority <note>prestige or perceived value</note> for this fruit.

<column-break/>

### THE ELEPHANT PALM OF ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender palm tree with a tuft of fronds at the top and clusters of fruit hanging below the crown.</image-desc>

The tree is very tall and straight, and not particularly thick, especially at the top: for it gradually tapers from the bottom to the summit, and is of an ash color. Small steps, as it were, surround the trunk from the roots all the way to the top, which are formed where branches were cut off; the flower is similar to that of a Chestnut: the fruit indeed is larger than a human head, of a more oblong shape, and of a dilute green color. Thus says Acosta <note>Christóbal Acosta, a naturalist who studied Indian plants</note>.

We do not pursue the many uses of Palms here, because we are by no means sufficient to the task of describing them; for the constraints of this space, let the Reader consult our *Universal History* and its appendix. We shall say much here in a few words: namely, that the Tree is called the "Refuge of the Poor" because of its various uses. The fresh fruit is called the "Ambrosia of the Gods."

### THE SACK-BEARING PALM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a long, conical, sack-like structure (spathe) and two small round fruits or seeds below it.</image-desc>

In certain Islands of America, forests are found consisting of no other tree than a certain unusual kind of Palm, to which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary figure in 16th-century botany</note> gave the name "Sack-bearing" from its covering, which resembles a sack or a strainer in which the fruit is hidden. This is not without reason, since it is very similar to that sack or strainer with which pharmacists today are accustomed to filter aromatic wine, called "Hippocras."

### THE MANICONGO TREE, THE SAMBAUCAIE PALM, and certain other exotic Trees.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two exotic palm-like trees with thick trunks and broad, radiating leaves, possibly representing African or South American species.</image-desc>

There are Trees in the region of Manicongo <note>The Kingdom of Kongo in Africa</note> producing a fruit similar to a large Nut, which is green inside and out. From it, Oil, Wine, vinegar, Delicacies, and Bread are prepared. The Wine flows from the very top of the tree: and it is considered a specific remedy for stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>; from the marrow of the fruit, Oil and Delicacies are made, and from its husks, Bread.

The <term>Sambaucaie</term> tree of Brazil, and the <term>Ady Palm</term> of the Island of St. Thomas, are celebrated by these same names, and their uses are the same.

<summary>This page describes various exotic palms and their fruits, including the coconut, the rare Coco de Mer from the Maldives, and the "Sack-bearing" palm of the Americas, detailing their medicinal and dietary uses.</summary>
<keywords>coconut, Coco de Mer, Maldives, palm trees, medicinal plants, botany, Clusius, Acosta, Garcia de Orta, Manicongo, Brazil</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### THE DOUM PALM, HAVING THE APPEARANCE OF A PALM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations of the Cuciofera fruit (Doum palm), showing the whole fruit, a cross-section revealing the fibrous husk and central nut, and the isolated seed.</image-desc>

Theophrastus and Pliny <note>Ancient Greek and Roman naturalists</note> claim this tree is similar to the Palm in its trunk and leaves: and they say it differs only in this, that the Palm rises as a single trunk, while the Doum Palm <note>original: "Cuciofera"</note> is fork-shaped. The size of the fruit is such that it fills the hand, and the color is a commendable tawny yellow; the juice is sweet with a hint of tartness.

Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century botanist</note> calls this the *Smaller Indian Nut*. Others have supposed this Nut to be the fruit of the Bdellium <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum-resin</note>: but on what foundation?

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE DOUM PALM.

<image-desc>Additional woodcut views of the Cuciofera fruit, including a top-down cross-section and various angles of the inner nut showing its pitted surface.</image-desc>

The previous image represents the Nut opened: this one shows both the outer cushion <note>the fleshy part of the fruit</note> and the various sizes of the interior kernel.

Furthermore, Theophrastus records the Doum Palm among the trees of Egypt, and Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a renowned Renaissance scholar</note> has testified that it is peculiar to that region.

---

### FAUFEL OR ARECA, WITH PALM-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations of the Areca nut (Faufel) in its fibrous husk, including a longitudinal section showing the internal ruminate endosperm.</image-desc>

Among the Arabs, Isaac Eben Amram <note>A 10th-century Jewish physician in Tunisia</note> describes it thus: *Faufel*, he says, is the Indian Hazelnut: a fruit similar in size and color to the Nutmeg, wrinkled, with a somewhat warm taste and a little bitterness. It is brought from Sim <note>likely referring to China or the East Indies</note>.

Garcia de Orta and Clusius <note>Leading authorities on Eastern botany in the 1500s</note> describe the tree more accurately: to them, the Faufel Tree is straight and large, made of spongy material, with the leaves of a Palm. The fruit is similar to a Nutmeg or a small Walnut.

Some call the Tree *Faufel*, and the Fruit *Areca*. Others (Ludovico Romano and Varthema <note>Italian travelers</note>) make the Areca a specific tree whose fruit is called *Cossol*.

<column-break/>

### VARIETIES OF FAUFEL OR ARECA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations showing different varieties and shapes of Areca nuts, some smooth, some textured, and some in cross-section.</image-desc>

Of the Faufel nuts which we keep among our natural specimens, some are black, some reddish-brown, others ash-colored: the largest are the size of a Nutmeg, the smallest nearly equal to a Cherry, and there are others intermediate between these. And of the black ones, some are top-shaped <note>conical</note> and others are flat-bottomed.

Serapio <note>An influential Arabic medical writer</note> writes that they produce heat and possess a share of bitterness. Indeed, both the Indians and the Portuguese living in the Indies are so accustomed to this food that you may see them chewing it constantly: and they cannot live without Areca and Betel <note>A leaf often chewed with areca nut and lime</note>.

---

### OTHER VARIETIES OF FAUFEL OR ARECA.

<image-desc>Further woodcut illustrations of Areca nut varieties, including small, rounded seeds and those with distinct horizontal banding or ridges.</image-desc>

The Faufel grows mostly in Malabar, Gujarat, and the Deccan, as well as in Malacca and other regions of the Indies, and also in certain places in Arabia, but only those near the sea, for it rejects the inland areas. It is brought from the Indies to us in Europe, but very rarely, and its medical use has remained almost unknown until now.

<column-break/>

### A NUT RESEMBLING THE FAUFEL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations of an exotic nut related to the Faufel, labeled with Roman numerals I and II, showing a bristled or scaly exterior and a teardrop-shaped seed marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

Clusius describes exotic fruits very closely approaching the Faufel or Areca, sent under the name of Faufel, and he depicts them thus in his *Exoticorum libri* <note>Books of Exotic Things</note>.

# PLANTS

### EBONY: German: Ebenholtz: French: Eben noir. Italian: Ebeno.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an Ebony tree (Ebenus), showing a thick trunk with textured bark and a dense, rounded crown of foliage.</image-desc>

It is a tree of India and Ethiopia with a leaf like a Palm. This is the true or genuine and wild variety. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> mentions those of India and Ethiopia: and he preferred the latter because it is free of veins and "combs" <note>original: "pectinum"; referring to the grain or ridges in the wood</note>.

It is called *Ebenus* and *Ebenum* in the neuter gender, and both are also spelled with an aspiration as *Hebenus* and *Hebenum*. The word is common to almost all languages: Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, Chaldean, Latin, German, French, and Italian.

Various works are made from it: cases, small chests, counting boards <note>term: abaci (tables used for arithmetic or display)</note>, little boxes, and other things of this sort.

Our illustration, however, has the appearance of the *Hairi* Palm, which is considered by some to be Ebony, and which has the greatest similarity to Ebony. They differ most in this, however: that the *Hairi* tree is entirely thorny, while the Ebony is not at all.

<column-break/>

### THE LOW PAPER PALM, and concerning the Paper of the Ancients.

<image-desc>Two circular woodcuts showing the leaves or fruit of the low-growing paper palm, followed by a third circular woodcut showing a similar botanical detail.</image-desc>

Before the use of paper sheets, says Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author</note>, writing was first done on the leaves of Palms, and then on the bark <note>original: "libris"; the inner bark of trees</note> of certain trees. And even now in India, from the Palm called *Lantar*, they prepare their paper for writing and books, as Linschoten <note>Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, a Dutch traveler</note> writes. Lery <note>Jean de Léry, a French explorer</note> writes that in the Great Province there is a tree by the name of *Tal*, with a large leaf, which provides the use of paper in all of India. Peter Martyr <note>An Italian-born historian of Spain's explorations</note> says that the Chaldeans, the first discoverers of letters, first wrote on the leaves of the tree called *Ceiba*. M. Fumée <note>Martin Fumée, French translator of Spanish histories</note> says that besides the *Cepas* tree, there is also another called *Guaiabara*, on whose leaves the Indians write with a stylus or a small needle. We depict the leaves here, which although they have ribs and veins, these are nevertheless so thin that they hinder the hand of the writer little, or not at all.

For the small Papyrus tree, let the Reader consult the *Appendix*.

---

<column-break/>

### DRAGON TREE: German: Drackenbaum: French: l'Arbre du Dragon: Italian: Albero de Dragone.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a Dragon Tree (Dracaena draco), characterized by its thick, scaly trunk and a crown of sword-shaped leaves radiating from the branches.</image-desc>

This is a tall tree found in the islands of Madeira and the Canaries, formerly called the *Fortunate Isles*, and it also grows in Africa. It is hardly known in Europe: however, we have the testimony of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> that it once grew in Antwerp, in the garden of Coldemberg. Whether the ancient Greeks mentioned it is not so clear: but it is believed they were not ignorant of its gum and tears <note>resinous drops</note>, and that they labeled it Cinnabar <note>note: original "Cinnabarin"; here referring to the red resin, not the mineral ore of mercury</note>.

Among more recent authors, Thevet writes thus of this tree: In the island of Madeira, he says, certain trees at a fixed time of year exude a gum which they call Dragon's Blood.

Whether the Cinnabar of Dioscorides was the gum of this tree or some mineral; and whether the Dragon's Blood of the apothecaries <note>original: "Officinarum"</note> is genuine or manufactured, we have weighed in our Universal History and in the appendix of this work.

<column-break/>

### THE FRUIT OF THE DRAGON'S BLOOD, and the Scythian Lamb.

<image-desc>Four stacked circular woodcuts. The top three show the fruit of the Dragon Tree in various states of dissection, revealing a seed or "dragon" shape. The bottom circle depicts the "Scythian Lamb" (Agnus Scythicus), a mythical plant-animal hybrid resembling a small lamb on a stalk.</image-desc>

Concerning the Dragon tree and its "tear," Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, a Spanish physician and botanist</note> relates the following: It is a large tree, he says, with a very thin bark that can be easily cut. When it is wounded, that liquor flows out which they call "Dragon's Blood in tears," differing from that which is collected into masses, called "Dragon's Blood in cakes" <note>original: "in pane"; literally "in bread"</note>. Truly, the fruit of the same tree is most admirable: for when the skin that covers it is removed, a little dragon <note>original: "Dracunculus"</note> immediately appears, fashioned by nature with such skill that it would seem to be carved in marble by the most expert craftsman. And from this fruit the tree undoubtedly took its name, as did the "tear" which is gathered from it by incision. From this, the ignorance of the Ancients and Moderns is detected, who did not know what Dragon's Blood was, or why it was so called.

The *History of Lyon* and Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note> assert this is a fiction. But it seems to us far more strange what Scaliger and other distinguished men relate concerning the SCYTHIAN LAMB <note>note: A legendary "zoophyte" or plant-animal believed to grow lambs as fruit</note>.

---

# OF PLANTS
## CLASS IV.
### WHICH CONTAINS VARIOUS AROMATIC AND SWEET-SMELLING
-> TREES, AND ESPECIALLY EXOTIC ONES: AMONG WHICH VARIOUS KINDS <-
-> of Barks & Woods are interspersed. <-

---

**LAUREL: German *Lorbe-baum*: Belgian *Lorberboom*.**
**French *Laurier*: Italian *Lauro*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Laurel branch with leaves and berries (Laurus nobilis). To the left, individual botanical details are shown: a cluster of berries, a single leaf, and two seeds/fruits.</image-desc>

Of the Laurel (called "Plants of Good Spirit" by the Romans) various differences are recounted: Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist</note> lists thirteen; Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and botanist</note> two, the thin-leaved and the broad-leaved; Cato lists three: the Delphic, the Cyprian, and the Wild. Theophrastus <note>Greek philosopher, the "father of botany"</note> truly distinguishes them into male and female, and says the latter is fertile, while the former is sterile.

According to more recent authors, one kind grows like a tree, another is shrub-like: one is male, another female: one is fertile, another sterile: one is cultivated, another wild: one is thin-leaved, another oblong and narrow-leaved (which is the male), another broad-leaved (which is the female): and there is also some diversity in the Berries.

Concerning the Location, Time, Qualities, and Virtues, see later.

<column-break/>

**WILD LAUREL <note>original: "Laurus Tinus"</note>, WILD LAUREL.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering branch of Laurus Tinus (Viburnum tinus), showing clusters of small flowers and oval leaves.</image-desc>

Pliny reports that some understand the *Laurus Tinus* to be the Wild Laurel, while to others it is a tree of its own kind, and differs from the others in this: that its berry is blue.

No other of the Ancient authors mentions it, unless it be the Wild Laurel of Theophrastus, as Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, 16th-century French botanist</note> maintains, or the Wild Laurel of Cato, as Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> maintains. Among the more Recent authors, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse</note> has three illustrations, namely the two which we present here, and a third smaller one with hairy leaves. Thus Tabernaemontanus also has three illustrations. Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens</note> displays only one (certainly that which we place in the first position), under the title of *Tinus* or Wild Laurel.

The fields of Italy, Spain, and Portugal are fertile with it. Indeed, starlings greedily feed upon its berries.

<column-break/>

**THE SECOND WILD LAUREL.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second variety of Laurus Tinus, showing a branch with leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

The Laurel rejoices in warm places, yet it also endures colder ones: it is well enough known in France, England, Belgium, and Germany: but most of all in Italy and Spain, not only in gardens and vineyards, but also in the woods, especially those near the sea.

It is perpetually green. It flowers in March and April, but the Berries are ripened toward the end of autumn, and unless they are plucked, they cling to the tree throughout the whole Winter.

The leaves and fruit dry and heat intensely, and the fruit even more than the leaves. The remaining virtues and celebrations for which it was sung by the ancients (to say nothing of the modern Laureate Poets and the "offspring of Apollo" <note>A reference to physicians or scholars, as Apollo was the god of both healing and the arts</note>), the boundaries <note>original: "cancelli"</note> which we have set for ourselves here do not permit us to pursue.

<column-break/>

**CHERRY-LAUREL, LAUREL OF TREBIZOND.**
**Laurel of Trebizond: Gardens of Padua.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of Laurocerasus (Cherry Laurel), showing elongated serrated leaves and a spike of small fruits/flowers.</image-desc>

It is a very pleasant tree, with foliage that is eternal and equals the leaves of the Citron. The fruit is larger than a Cherry, somewhat long, turning from blue to reddish, arranged in clusters. Clusius writes that it was sent to him from Constantinople under the name *Trabison Carmasi*.

Moreover, it has the name Cherry-Laurel <note>original: "Laurocerasus"</note> from the similarity of its leaves with those of the Laurel, and its fruit being equal to Cherries. Dalechamps judged it to be the second *Lotos* of Theophrastus, or the "Palm of Trebizond," because it was first brought from Trebizond to Constantinople, and from there to us.

It flourishes in Genoa in the garden of Prince Doria.

<summary>This page describes various species of Laurel (Laurus nobilis, Viburnum tinus, and Prunus laurocerasus), citing classical authorities like Pliny and Theophrastus alongside contemporary Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Laurel, Laurus nobilis, Wild Laurel, Cherry Laurel, botanical classification, Pliny the Elder, Theophrastus, Clusius, medicinal properties, Trebizond</keywords>

--- Page 70 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of exotic plants, specifically focusing on the coffee plant and the clove tree. It maintains the encyclopedic style of comparing various historical and contemporary authorities.</meta>

### THE BON OR BAN TREE, ACCORDING TO ALPINUS: BUNA,
->The *Bannu* and *Bunchus* of the Arabs.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coffee branch (Bon vel Ban) with leaves and berries.</image-desc>

Prospero Alpini <note>Prospero Alpini (1553–1617) was a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian flora.</note> writes that he saw a tree in Cairo from which the very common seeds there, called *Bon* or *Ban*, are produced. He notes that from these seeds, all the Egyptians and Arabs prepare a very common decoction called *Caova* <note>Coffee; an early transliteration of the Arabic *qahwa*.</note>, which they drink in place of wine. It is sold in public wine-shops just as wine is sold among us, and it is furthermore useful for various medicinal effects.

Leonhard Rauwolf <note>A German physician and botanist famous for his travels through the Levant in the 1570s.</note> says that nothing is more frequent among the Turks than the drink made from *Bunnu*, which is called *Chaube*. When all these things are considered alongside the similarity of the names, it seems not at all absurd to establish that this *Bon* or *Ban* of Alpini is one and the same as the *Buna*, *Bannu*, and *Bunchus* of the Arabs.

### ILLUSTRATION BY CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of the clove tree (Caryophyllus) with leaves and flower buds.</image-desc>

According to the accounts of those who have surveyed the Indian coasts, this tree is very similar to the Laurel in height, thickness, and leaves (though these are somewhat larger and rounder). The fruits grow individually at the tips of the branches; they are reddish at first, then turn black in the sun. They follow a flower that is first white, then green, and finally reddish, which, when hardened, turns into the Clove <note>original: *Caryophyllum*</note>.

The harvest takes place from the 15th of September until January and February. The fruit is picked by hand into earthenware vessels, but the harvesters also beat the fruit down with reeds after the ground around the tree has been cleaned or spread with mats.

### ILLUSTRATION BY CAMERARIUS, in which the Flowers, Fruits, Husks, and their parts, and Leaves are skillfully depicted.

<image-desc>Detailed botanical woodcut showing various stages of clove development: flowers, seeds, and husks, labeled with numbers 1-4 and letters G, M.</image-desc>

The Clove tree grows in Eastern regions, on certain islands of the Indian Sea such as Ceylon <note>Sri Lanka</note>, Bantam, etc. However, it is not fruitful except in the Molucca Islands <note>The "Spice Islands" of Indonesia.</note>, which are five in number and bear nothing else besides Cloves that is distributed from there throughout the world.

Furthermore, Cloves are hot and dry in the third degree <note>A reference to Galenic humoral medicine, where "degrees" measured the intensity of a substance's qualities.</note>. They aid digestion, restrain fluxes of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, and assist the liver, stomach, and heart. They are also beneficial against all "cold" diseases of the brain and sharpen the eyesight; thus, they are useful both in kitchens and in apothecary shops. Regarding their Water, distilled Oil, and various other preparations, one should consult our *Universal History* and the Appendix to this work.

<column-break/>

### CLOVES: German: *Negelin*; Belgian: *Geroffle Naghel*; French: *Clou de Gerofle*; Italian: *Garofano*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of clove buds and a larger seed pod.</image-desc>

The Cloves themselves are better known to us than the tree, and they have obtained their name among almost all Europeans from their resemblance to a nail <note>The Latin *clavus* and French *clou* both mean nail, referring to the shape of the dried bud.</note>. They are called *Calafur* by the Arabs, Persians, Turks, and almost all Indians, and *Chanque* by the people of the Moluccas.

Neither Dioscorides nor Galen <note>Ancient Greek medical authorities.</note> made mention of the tree. Among other writers, some make the trunk and branches similar to the Boxwood tree, but the leaves similar to the Willow or Peach; however, those who liken it to the Apple, Pear, or Nutmeg tree are greatly mistaken. Others wrongly distinguish the *Anthophyllum* <note>The "mother clove" or the fully ripened fruit.</note> from the Clove; for they are not different things, but differ only in their degree of ripeness.

### ILLUSTRATION BY ACOSTA WHICH IS FALSE, regarding the placement of the Flowers and Fruits.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a whole clove tree, noted in the heading as having an incorrect depiction of flower and fruit placement.</image-desc>

Once beaten down, the Cloves are dried for two days, then stored and sent to various provinces, either with or without the "mother" <note>the mature fruit</note>. Those that remain on the tree become thicker and do not differ from the others except in age. Other trees grow spontaneously from fallen cloves, like Chestnuts, and they grow very quickly due to the abundance of rain.

The oblong stalks from which the fruits hang are called *Fusti*. Indeed, the leaves are fragrant with such sweetness of scent that they equal the cloves themselves; hence, explorers of those places can sense the scent of cloves over long distances at sea.

### FRUIT SIMILAR TO THE AROMATIC CLOVE.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a large, heart-shaped exotic fruit or seed pod resembling a clove.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist.</note> depicts and describes this exotic fruit brought from Java during the first Dutch voyage in the year 1597. It equals the size and closely resembles the appearance of the older aromatic clove fruit as it is forming, so that at first glance it could easily deceive someone.

But something must be added here regarding the Gum and Resin of Cloves. Garcia de Orta seems to deny its existence, but we have it, and among the more recent writers, Pena, Lobelius, Olivos, and Clusius write that it is found; as do the ancient writers Serapio and Avicenna, who say it corresponds to the properties of Turpentine and label it *Albotin*.

<summary>This page describes the coffee plant (Bon/Ban) and the clove tree (Caryophyllus), detailing their origins in Egypt and the Moluccas, their medicinal properties, and their physical appearance according to various botanical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>coffee, cloves, Moluccas, Cairo, herbal medicine, Prospero Alpini, Clusius, botany, spice trade, aromatics</keywords>

--- Page 71 ---
### MALABATHRUM, OR INDIAN LEAF. German: *Indianisch-Blatt*: French: *Feuille des Indes*: Italian: *Malabathro & Folio Indiano*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Malabathrum plant branch with several large, ribbed leaves and small clusters of berries or flowers at the nodes.</image-desc>

That which we depict here the Apothecaries call *Malabathrum* <note>original: "Malabathrū"</note> and *Indian Leaf*: and it is usually brought from *India*, sometimes still clinging to its branches, and often alone and torn away.

However, it is not the leaf of Nard, as Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> truly warns, nor is it that kind of leaf which the Arabs call *Betre*: nor does it float upon the waters, as Dioscorides and Pliny wrote: nor is it the Clove-leaf, as some assert: nor is it of such a strong scent as Saffron: nor of the taste of Nard, as Pliny wrote: nor does it grow in Syria or Egypt, as the same Pliny relates: But it is a Leaf of its own kind, plucked from a tree in India.

Furthermore, according to the author Dioscorides, it is assigned almost the same powers as Nard.

<column-break/>

### THE WOOD AND FRUIT OF THE INDIAN LEAF, AND CONCERNING The fruit of Cinnamon or Canella.

<image-desc>Two vertical wood-like sticks or bark segments, and a small cluster of acorn-like fruits or seeds.</image-desc>

These small sticks, which we received under the name of Cinnamon, we consider to be the Wood of the Indian Leaf of the Apothecaries.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist.</note> presents these under the *name of Cassia* in his History of Belgium; Clusius, Amatus, and Tabernamontanus present them under the name of Cinnamon. To the same category perhaps belongs that small piece of fragrant Cassia which Mattioli writes was given to him as a gift by Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria.

Indeed, the fruits representing the shape of acorns, which we have provided as illustrations in the preceding table, we received under the name of the fruit of Cinnamon or Canella, but we likewise judge them to be the fruit of the Wood of the Indian Leaf.

---

### BETRE OR BETELLE; CALLED TEMBUL BY THE ETHIOPIANS, Persians, and Arabs.

According to Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a Portuguese Renaissance physician and pioneer of tropical medicine.</note> the leaf is similar to the leaf of the Median Apple <note>The citron tree.</note>, but longer, and narrower at the ends. It bears a twisted fruit, similar to a lizard's tail, which is edible.

It creeps in the manner of a Vine, and stakes and props are added, by which it supports itself as it crawls, not otherwise than the manner of Ivy. It is therefore a climbing plant, and thus it differs greatly from that which produces the Apothecaries' Indian Leaf, which is an upright tree: let those who wrongly confuse Betre with the Indian Leaf take note of this.

Furthermore, it grows in all the maritime regions of the Indies known to the Spaniards. Indeed, it is held in such high esteem among the Indians that they chew Betre leaves and carry them in their hands in the morning, afternoon, evening, and even at night.

<column-break/>

### THE CINNAMON OR CANELLA TREE.

<image-desc>A large, leafy tree with a thick trunk. A small human figure is standing at the base of the tree, providing a sense of scale.</image-desc>

Cardanus writes that all parts of the Cinnamon are similar in every way to the Laurel: and for that reason, it is an Indian Laurel. Ludovicus Romanus relates that the Cinnamon tree is also similar to the Laurel in its leaves and berries.

Garcia, Linschoten, and Thevet say that Cinnamon, or Canella, is a tree the size of an Olive, provided with many straight branches: with leaves like Laurel in color, and like Citron in shape: with white flowers: and a black, round fruit the size of an Olive. Indeed, they say that Canella is nothing other than the second and inner bark of the tree.

Moreover, Cinnamon trees grow in Malabar, Java, and the Molucca Islands: but the more excellent ones are most frequently found in Ceylon <note>original: "Zeilan"</note>, and are inhabitants of the mountains.

---

### THE CANELLA TREE, ACCORDING TO ACOSTA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tree with a gnarled trunk and broad leaves, showing the root system and a small cross-section of a branch.</image-desc>

Acosta <note>Cristóbal Acosta, a Spanish doctor and natural historian.</note> certainly describes and thus depicts the tree: and he says there is a great abundance of these trees in the forests of the province of Malabar: but they are far inferior to those which grow on the Island of Ceylon. He seems to be depicting the Indian Leaf, as is evident from the branch depicted separately here and marked with a †.

Could this be the "Canella de Matte" of the de Bry brothers, or wild Cinnamon, endowed with no remarkable flavor, growing copiously in the forests of Java?

<column-break/>

### CASSIA, CANELLA, OR CINNAMON: German: *Zimmet*: French: *Canelle*: Italian: *Cassia, Canella*.

<image-desc>Three vertical segments of cinnamon bark, showing the characteristic curled or "quilled" shape of the dried spice.</image-desc>

What Canella is, we indicated a little earlier. It is surely the second and inner bark of the branches of the tree, which, having been taken off and cleaned of the outer bark, and cut into small quadrangular strips, is cast upon the ground: and thus it rolls up by itself so that it appears to be a single bark: although the parts are merely the bark rolled into tubes the thickness of a finger. Moreover, it acquires that rosy or ashy-wine color from the heat of the Sun: that which is not properly prepared becomes whitish or ash-colored: but that which is scorched too much by the heat of the Sun becomes black. Once the bark is removed, the tree is left alone for three years afterward. Sometimes, the thickness makes it manifest that the outer bark has been sent instead of the inner.

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical and pharmacological description of Indian Leaf (Malabathrum), Betel, and Cinnamon, distinguishing between these often-confused exotic spices and their trees. It cites various Renaissance authorities and explorers to clarify their origins in India, Ceylon, and Southeast Asia.</summary>
<keywords>Malabathrum, Indian Leaf, Cinnamon, Canella, Betel, Botany, Pharmacology, India, Ceylon, Garcia de Orta, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of exotic spices and barks, following the previous discussion of aromatic woods. The catchword "POLY-" suggests the following page may begin a discussion on Polium or a similar genus.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### COMMON CANELLA, OR CINNAMON,
### with a thicker bark.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, textured piece of cinnamon bark showing a rough exterior and fibrous interior.</image-desc>

This bark is three or four times thicker than that which is commonly available, possessing a woody and split texture, such that it might somewhat mimic the texture of Linden <note>original: Tilia</note>, especially on the inner part. On the outside it is wrinkled and tinged with a diluted rusty color; the flavor is sweet, aromatic, and quite sharp.

Is this the *Pseudocinamomum* <note>False Cinnamon</note> of Dioscorides? Or the *Xylocassia* <note>Woody Cassia</note> of Dioscorides?

### ANOTHER VARIETY OF COMMON CANELLA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two long, thin, rolled quills of cinnamon bark (cinnamon sticks).</image-desc>

Furthermore, many other varieties of this aromatic bark are held, whether you look at the flavor, the color, or the internal and external appearance of the bark itself.

These small tubes, however, are thick, brownish, and of a sticky flavor, which we received under the name of Cinnamon from Deccan <note>A region in India</note>.

It must by no means be ignored that those barks which are brought from Ceylon <note>original: Zeilan; modern Sri Lanka</note> are specifically gifted with the name of Cinnamon (which signifies "fragrant wood" and "Chinese Amomum"); but the inferior kinds, which are taken in Malabar and Java, are called Canella and Cassia. The narrowness of this space does not permit us to review the origins of the said names. Let the reader consult the Appendix.

### WINTER’S BARK OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, curved piece of Winter's Bark with a rough, spotted surface.</image-desc>

Is it White Canella? Or the aromatic wood of Monardes?

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> calls it "Winter’s" because it was brought from the Strait of Magellan by William Winter.

We shall conclude the history of this noble bark—I mean of Cinnamon, Cassia, and Canella—with an enumeration of its principal virtues.

According to Galen <note>An influential Roman physician</note>, it dries and heats in the third degree, and consists of thin parts. As Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> also dictates, it has the power of heating, provoking urine, drying, and gently binding; it is beneficial to women for the dilation of the womb, whether used in a sitz-bath or as a fumigant; and it is, finally, extremely useful for many other things. Apothecaries <note>original: Seplasia</note> and practitioners know how to prepare distilled water and oil from it.

<column-break/>

### A VARIETY OF CASSIA OR CANELLA,
### Perhaps the Cassia of the ancients?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two long, straight, relatively smooth pieces of bark.</image-desc>

The Ancients wrote so loosely and obscurely regarding Cassia and Cinnamon that you may not know what to conclude.

Among the more recent authors, Manardus, Amatus, and Cronemburgius, and almost all others, have been of the opinion that the Canella of the moderns, or the Cinnamon of the pharmacies, is the Cassia of the Greeks. And Gronemburgius thinks that if anyone investigates those great heaps of common Cinnamon which are brought to Antwerp, he will find all the types of Cassia mentioned by writers among them. In such a confused history, we consider it better to hesitate for a while than to think poorly of the Ancients or to disagree widely with learned posterity.

### WHITE CANELLA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two broad, somewhat flat and irregular pieces of white cinnamon bark.</image-desc>

Regarding the White Canella, of which we show an image, Clusius writes these things in *Exoticorum*: "A few years ago," he says, "a certain exotic bark began to be imported, to which—since it is mostly rolled into tubes like Canella, and also because of its whiteness—the name White Canella was given. I seemed to observe two kinds of it: one with smaller and longer tubes, and also thicker, which I considered of less value; the other thinner; but for both kinds, the outermost bark is rough," etc.

### THE LEAF OF CINNAMON ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single, elongated leaf with prominent longitudinal veins, identified as a cinnamon leaf.</image-desc>

That which Clusius (in his notes to Garcia), Lobelius (in his *Observations* and *Icons*), and also Tabernaemontanus exhibit as the Leaf of Cinnamon, we judge to be the Indian Leaf <note>original: Folium Indum; likely Malabathrum</note>; let the learned judge.

<summary>This page details the varieties of cinnamon and cassia, discussing their geographical origins in Ceylon and India, their medicinal properties according to classical authorities, and the botanical confusion surrounding their identification.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on aromatic woods, medicinal shrubs, and a legendary water-producing tree. It maintains the encyclopedic style of comparing ancient authorities like Dioscorides with contemporary Renaissance botanists.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### NARROW-LEAVED SEA KNOTGRASS
### According to Dalechamps. The WOOD CASSIA of some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a slender, upright plant with many small, narrow leaves arranged along the stem, resembling a species of Polygonum or Cassia.</image-desc>

The people of Montpellier call a shrub growing on the maritime coast of Narbonne Gaul <note>Modern-day Southern France</note> "Wood Cassia" <note>original: "Cassiam ligneam"</note>. It should be considered whether this is not rather a type of Knotgrass <note>original: "Polygoni"</note>, and specifically the one whose image we provide here.

### ASPALATHUS, ERYSISCEPTRUM: WOOD
### Rhodium, Wood or Bark of Bugia.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration showing thick, woody, knotted branches or roots, with a cross-section of a cut log at the base.</image-desc>

Matthioli and Cornarius, among others, confess that the Aspalathus of the Ancients is today unknown both to the Apothecary shops and to themselves. However, Lonicer, Ryff, and many others believe it to be the wood that is imported from the Islands of the Rhodians and is called Rhodium <note>Rosewood</note>.

According to Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician</note>, Aspalathus is a woody shrub, prickly with frequent thorns, growing in Istria, Syria, and Rhodes. He identifies two kinds: One is heavy, dense, fragrant, slightly bitter, and reddish or turning purple when the bark is removed—this is the best. The other is white, odorless, and woody, which is inferior.

The Arabs differ from Dioscorides in this: for them, Aspalathus is not a shrub, but a thick tree. Our illustration is of the first species.

### REDDISH RHODIAN ASPALATHUS
### highly fragrant.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large, curved piece of wood or root, showing the internal grain and texture, with a smaller fragment below.</image-desc>

Lobelius calls this Rhodian Aspalathus, both in his *Images* and in his *History of Belgium*. Caspar Bauhin, in his commentary on Matthioli, identifies it as the species of Aspalathus described by Pena and the *History of Lyon*, which is often sold in place of Agallochum <note>Agarwood</note>. It is also called Rhodium Wood by Cordus, and Rhodian Wild Olive.

Furthermore, the wood called Rhodium possesses a warming power with astringency: hence it is suitable for washing foul ulcers of the mouth; a decoction of it stops the bowels and restrains the spitting of blood.

<column-break/>

### THE WATER-DRIPPING TREE.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tree with a broad canopy, situated within a circular stone or brick enclosure that appears to be a well or cistern collecting water dripping from the leaves.</image-desc>

On the island of Ferro <note>El Hierro</note>, one of the Canaries, writers on Indian affairs report there is a tree that sweats and drips water from its leaves year-round. Indeed, it does so in such abundance that it can suffice not only for the inhabitants but for many more besides. This tree is of moderate size, with a leaf like a Walnut, though a little larger. It is surrounded by a stone wall like a fountain, and the water flowing from the basin is collected. It is truly a marvelous secret of nature that no water is found on the entire island except that which flows from this tree. Furthermore, a perpetual and dense mist clothes the tree, which nevertheless seems to gradually scatter and dissolve during the day when the heat of the Sun begins to burn.

### WOOD WITH THE SCENT OF ROSE, BY OTHERS WOOD
### of Incense: by others Aspalathus.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a gnarled, thick piece of wood or root, showing a distinct dark heartwood and lighter sapwood in the cross-section.</image-desc>

We have depicted the true and legitimate Aspalathus of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen, according to some. But the one we depict here is hard and solid, with a texture almost like Guaiacum <note>Lignum vitae</note>, with somewhat straight sections along which it is split; it is heavy, with an aromatic taste and a rose-like scent. It is two-colored like Guaiacum, yellow-brown in the middle and white on the edges. The bark is thick, rough, and brownish-gray.

Perhaps this is the wood of sweet scent mentioned by Lery and Palmarius, which is brought from America and breathes the scent of Roses.

### AGALLOCHUM, ALOES WOOD, XYLOALOES:
### German: Paradise wood; French: Wood of Aloes; Italian: Aloe wood.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large, heavy piece of wood, possibly a root or trunk section, with a smaller fragment showing the internal structure.</image-desc>

It is strange that Galen nowhere mentions Agallochum. Pliny also wrote little of it, under the name *Taru*. To Dioscorides, it is a wood imported from India and Arabia, similar to the wood of the Thyine tree, fragrant, marked with spots and dots, etc. But whether the Agallochum of the Ancients is the same wood that more recent authors call Aloes Wood <note>original: "Lignum aloës"</note> and Xyloaloes, we leave to the judgment of the learned. Ruellius, whom many have followed, says the Agallochum of the Ancients is unknown to the world. Sylvius says the Aloes Wood shown in the Apothecary shops is actually Aspalathus. Savonarola, deceived by ignorance of the Greek language, makes Aloes Wood different from Xyloaloes.

The whole tree, according to Garcia and Linschoten, has the form of an Olive and is a native of the Indies.

Concerning the differences and other matters of this place, see the Appendix.

<keywords>Aspalathus, Rhodium wood, Agallochum, Aloes wood, El Hierro water tree, botanical history, medicinal plants, Dioscorides</keywords>

### THE SASSAFRAS TREE.
### SASSAFRAS WOOD, or Pavan Wood: called *Pauamen* by the Indians: and Sassafras by almost all Europeans.

It reaches a great height, so that it sometimes equals a moderate Pine tree. The trunk is singular and not branched <note>meaning the main trunk rises significantly before branching</note>: the bark is thick and of a tawny color, covered by another thinner, ash-colored layer. The wood is white, merging into tawny. Green leaves cling to the branches, resembling those of Fig trees, and are fragrant. The root is flexible and, depending on the size of the tree, either thick or slender, wandering through the top of the earth. Whether it bears flowers and fruit is unknown.

It began to be brought into Europe not so long ago from Florida, a province of the New World. It grows in temperate maritime places, and the mountains abound with this tree, breathing out a most sweet scent to those sailing past. However, it does not grow throughout all of Florida, but only in the port of St. Helena and the port of St. Matthew.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sassafras tree trunk showing the texture of the bark and the interior wood grain.</image-desc>

It is of little weight and is covered with bark—the outermost being thin and ash-colored, the inner somewhat thick, reddish, and rather spongy and soft. The underlying wood is white, or turning from white to a darker hue, sometimes even verging toward ash-color in some parts; in softness and grain <term>pectinis: literally "combs," referring to the vertical wood fibers</term> it is like Linden wood, with a sweet aromatic smell and taste, somewhat sharp and slightly sweet, in some way like Anise.

This wood is hot and dry in the second degree <note>a classification from Galenic medicine regarding the intensity of a plant's qualities</note>: and the bark is a little hotter. However, the best part is the root; its decoction is more effective and fragrant than that of the rest of the tree and branches. It strengthens the liver and frees it from obstructions, comforts the stomach, and is very useful in dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> and chronic fevers.

---

### ZINGI, OR INDIAN ANISE.
### THE STAR-SHAPED ZINGI FRUIT or Indian Anise.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Zingi plant showing its leaves and star-shaped seed pods.</image-desc>

According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, it grows in the Philippine Islands, which are distant from the region of the Chinese by an interval of about two hundred miles. The proper name which it holds in its native place is *Damur*. Regarding the root, stalk, leaves, and even the flowers of this shrub or small tree, he says he can declare nothing, because he has seen only the parts of the seeds and the umbels <note>the umbrella-like clusters where the seeds form</note>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Detailed woodcut of the star-shaped fruit (star anise), a cross-section of a seed, and individual seeds.</image-desc>

It represents the figure of a star: and it consists of seven individual little nuts, meeting in the center in the manner of rays, triangular, long, lightly compressed, and covered with a double husk. In each of these hides a single and shining kernel, which has plainly the smell and taste of Anise: whence it is called *Indian Anise*. The illustration expresses the form and size very well.

---

### YELLOW SANDALWOOD.
### WHITE SANDALWOOD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two vertical planks of Sandalwood, showing the grain and structural characteristics of the timber.</image-desc>

Among the ancient Greeks, we find no mention of Sandalwoods: but among the Arabs who showed them to us, they made three kinds: *Yellow, White, and Red*.

Cæsalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino, an Italian physician and botanist</note> calls them "fragrant woods" and recognizes only two kinds: White and Red. He determines that the Yellow, which is had today, is the pith <note>the heartwood</note> of the White, much sweeter than the rest of the wood, which is white.

But of the more recent writers, almost all retain the three Arabic kinds, and write that they come from three distinct types of trees. Namely, in both the Indies, in very dense and vast forests.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two additional planks of Sandalwood, similar to the previous pair, illustrating the "White" variety.</image-desc>

It differs little in color from the Yellow, only it is more pale, and is quite similar in color to Pear wood, which is pale. Otherwise, it has the same substance, the same texture, and the same grain. But it is inferior in scent, which is so weak it is hardly perceived, as is the taste.

Moreover, both have a solid, heavy wood with straight grain; whereby it happens that it is split into straight shingles without difficulty. But the yellow has a bitterish aromatic taste and a fragrant scent rivaling Musk.

<summary>This page describes the physical characteristics and medicinal uses of Sassafras from Florida, Star Anise (Zingi) from the Philippines, and the different varieties of Sandalwood from the Indies.</summary>
<keywords>Sassafras, Star Anise, Sandalwood, Florida, Philippines, medicinal wood, botany, Clusius, aromatic plants</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of woods and trees, focusing on their physical properties, medicinal uses, and roles in dyeing. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern botanical texts.</meta>

### RED SANDALWOOD
<note>original: "Santalum Rubrum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, textured tree trunk or piece of sandalwood showing deep vertical grooves in the bark.</image-desc>

This has the same substance and texture as the others, and the same "combs" <note>likely referring to the grain or fibrous structure of the wood</note>; it differs from them in color and scent.

Matthioli, Amatus, Musa, Lacuna, Scaliger, Apollo, Caspar Bauhin, and others deny it has a scent. Curtius determines it to be sometimes odorless, sometimes scented. Caesalpinus makes some of it of slight scent, some of none, and some more scented than the yellow variety. I also find that Garcia, Acosta, and Caspar Bauhin deny it; however, Clusius and the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon</note> assert it. We leave this dispute to the judge <note>a Latin idiom meaning the matter is undecided</note>.

Furthermore, all Sandalwood cools in the third degree, but dries in the second: it cheers the heart, benefits a feverish liver, and opposes hot fevers; specifically, the Red variety restrains "fluxes" <note>excessive bodily discharges</note>.

---

### NEPHRITIC WOOD, staining blue and yellow:
->German: Gravel-wood.<- <note>original: "Griesholtz," used for kidney stones or "gravel"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a section of wood with a swirling, marbled grain pattern.</image-desc>

New Spain <note>Mexico</note> sends a certain kind of thick and knotless wood, with the material of a Pear tree: the medical use of which has long been accepted for diseases of the kidneys and sciatica, as well as for difficulties of urine.

Caesalpinus reports it to be of the Ash genus: and its shavings, soaked in water, after the space of half an hour, yield a most elegant blue color, even though the shavings themselves are white.

Monardes mentions another kind, staining saffron-yellow, with which the former is adulterated: Thevet mentions a "reed-wood" from which the Americans prepare their swords. Could it be the "Viri" of Serapion?

---

### BOXWOOD: German: Buxbaum: Belgian: Buexboom:
->French: Bouis: Italian: Bosso & Buxo.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Boxwood (Buxus) branch with small, oval leaves and clusters of flowers/seeds.</image-desc>

To some it is a shrub: to us a tree. It is a wonder that Dioscorides does not have a history of this most common tree.

Differences are observed in size: for in some places it is a tall tree, in others low; they call the latter *Ground-box* <note>original: "Chamæbuxum"</note>. However, the tree is called *Buxus*, and its material <term>Buxum</term>.

It flowers in April and March, and ripens its fruit in Autumn. It loves cold and sunny places and mountains; it is not uncommon on the hills of the Dauphiné, Switzerland, Savoy, and Burgundy. The town of Saint-Claude <note>original: "à D Claudio nomen"</note> is famous for various boxwood works; we observed a tall and thick tree nourished at the roots, curled and spotted, in the suburb of Embrun in Gallia Narbonensis, called *La plaine*. Concerning its powers, see later at the side of the following figure.

<column-break/>

### BRAZILWOOD: German: Bresilgen holtz: French:
->Bois de Bresil: Italian: Ligno Verzino.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender tree with a spreading canopy of small leaves.</image-desc>

This tree, about which the Ancients recorded nothing, grows to the height of an Oak, and is sometimes of such thickness that three men cannot embrace it. It has leaves similar to Boxwood, but produces no fruit. The color of the bark is ash-gray: the material beneath it is red, especially in the heartwood, which is of higher quality.

Caspar Bauhin, in his notes on Matthioli, makes two kinds of it: one reddish-brown, the other lemon-yellow: and he says the reddish-brown is either very red, or white within the red, and this is sought after by Dyers. The lemon-yellow kind is called *Bugia*.

It is carried from Brazil all the way to the islands of the Indies, sought after for dyeing fleeces and various other things. No medical power has become known so far.

---

### SMOKE TREE, called COTINUS CORIARIA by some.
->German: Yellow Brazilwood. French & Savoyard: du Fustet.<-
->To the inhabitants of the Apennines: Scotano.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of the Smoke Tree (Cotinus) with broad, rounded leaves and a feathery inflorescence.</image-desc>

If any other plant known today can be identified, certainly this one which we give pictured seems to be referable to the *Coccy-milea* of Theophrastus. Anguillara, Dodonaeus, Pena and Lobel, Dalechamps, Constantine, Tabernaemontanus, and Caspar Bauhin also judge it to be the same as the *Coccygria* of Pliny, but they seem to make *Coccygria* the same as *Cotinus* with too much carelessness. It is certainly the plant which we said a little before that Caspar Bauhin calls Yellow Brazilwood and *Bugia*. For it has a yellow or lemon color, and if its material is split into thin shingles with axes and boiled in water, it gives off a yellow or lemon color, which fullers use for dyeing wools and cloths.

It grows abundantly among the hedges of Lombardy in Italy: it flowers in May, and the fruit matures in July and August.

The roots and leaves have a drying and restraining power, useful for various things.

---

### TREE SIMILAR TO THE HOLY PALM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch with pinnate leaves, possibly Guaiacum or a similar species.</image-desc>

Thus the tree is depicted by Pena and Lobel, and also by the *History of Lyon*, from which we give an image: and in what things it agrees with the Holy Palm <note>likely Guaiacum/Lignum Vitae</note>, about which we shall soon speak, and in what things it differs, is clear from the consideration of both and their comparison with each other.

We will add here something about the use and powers of Boxwood. It is of a binding and drying nature, and there are those who say it is to the Italians what Guaiacum wood is to the Indians: but it is especially useful for topiary work, as it is easy to shape and pleasant with its perpetual greenness. In fire, it has a hardness like iron, and is useful neither for flame nor charcoal, if faith is to be given to Pliny: for they say its material does not feel age or antiquity; its hardness combined with bitterness prevents woodworms from being born in it: but it is most highly commended for the gift of making combs.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of exotic trees and plants, specifically focusing on those discovered in the Indies and described by early modern naturalists like Clusius and Acosta.</meta>

### GUAIACUM: GUAIACUM: Indian Wood: Holy Wood: Blessed Wood.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Guaiacum branch with oval leaves and small flowers/fruits.</image-desc>

Clusius depicts the branch of the Guaiacum with leaves and fruit in this manner in his *Exoticorum libri* <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational botanist</note>. The Guaiacum tree has leaves like those of the Ash; its wood is blackish on the inside, heavy and weighty, and does not float in water but sinks. It is resinous, and when set on fire, it breathes out a not unpleasant odor. Its taste is somewhat bitter, with a slight sharpness that pricks the tongue.

Oviedo <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, a Spanish historian of the Americas</note> identifies two kinds: namely, the common Guaiacum, and another which he calls *Palo santo* or Holy Wood; others maintain they are one and the same.

The title indicates that it is a gift from the Indies. Furthermore, it is hot and dry in the second degree <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors used in medicine at the time</note>; it thins [the humors], aids digestion, and induces sweating—the bark even more so than the wood.

### THE SORROWFUL TREE OF CLUSIUS. The Sleeping Indian Tree.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with opposite, serrated leaves and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius depicts the Sorrowful Tree in this way, and he also provides another illustration to which he adds thorns.

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> writes that a tree is found in India, leafy like a Rose, which closes its leaves at night and expands or opens them again at sunrise; by midday it is fully unfolded, and from then on it gradually composes itself again for the night. The inhabitants say that it sleeps.

<column-break/>

### THE SORROWFUL TREE OF ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering tree branch with pointed leaves and delicate blossoms.</image-desc>

It is the size of an Olive tree, with leaves like a Pomegranate and flowers like Jasmine, which are most fragrant at night. These flowers expand and unfold when the sun sets, but when it rises, they contract or fall off; such is their antipathy <note>natural opposition</note> toward the solar rays.

From this it also took its name, because it is "squalid with a sorrowful trunk when the golden-haired sun shines upon the ruddy world" <note>original Latin: "tristi quòd squalida trunco Auricomu rutilo cum nitet Orbi subar." This is a poetic description of the tree's withered appearance during daylight.</note>.

According to Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine in India</note>, this tree is peculiar to Goa and is not found elsewhere in India. Many have wished to transplant it to Portugal, but with failed effort.

They color food with the flowers in the manner of Saffron, and from them they extract a most fragrant water.

### TREES THAT SHUN THE TOUCH, THE LIVING TREE OF ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sensitive plant (Mimosa type) with pinnate leaves and a central stalk.</image-desc>

Acosta says that in some other places a certain plant is found, commonly called the *Living Herb* <note>original: "Herba viva"</note>, by some the *Love Herb* <note>original: "Herba amoria"</note>, by the Turks *Suluo*, by the Persians *Sulaque*, etc. It grows in hot and humid places. It is reported that if anyone desires to touch or grasp it, it immediately contracts its leaves, and if one grasps it, it becomes withered; but when the hand is removed, it immediately recovers its luster. It withers and revives as often as it is seized or the hand is withdrawn from it.

Theophrastus mentions a tree of this kind in Book 4, Chapter 3 of his *History of Plants*. Pliny also reports on the same, which he calls *Aeschinomene* <note>from the Greek "aischynomene," meaning "shamefaced" or "modest"</note>. The *History of Plants of Lyon* and other more recent authors also mention this tree. Acosta adds that it is of wonderful efficacy for restoring virginity and procuring love.

---
