# IMAGES AND DESCRIPTIONS
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS V.
### WHICH PRESENTS TREES AND SMALLER SHRUBS BEARING BERRIES.

**Myrtle:** *German: Myrtenbaum; Belgian: Mytenboom; French: Myrte & Meurte; Italian: Myrto.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrtle branch with small oval leaves and round berries.</image-desc>

Myrtle is either wild or cultivated: and both types are either white or black; broad-leaved or narrow-leaved; larger or smaller; and either native or an inhabitant of foreign regions.

Theophrastus and Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist and author of Natural History.</note> called the wild variety *Ruscus* <note>original: "Ruscum"; likely referring to Butcher's Broom, though the author notes the confusion here.</note>: although a true wild Myrtle is given, which is not distinct from the cultivated one in species, but only in size.

We depict the cultivated variety here, both the white and the black, as they differ in nothing but the color of the berries. It easily grows into a tree, with flexible and long branches and red bark: with somewhat long leaves that are evergreen, rivaling those of the Pomegranate, but paler in the white variety and darker in the black. The flowers are white and fragrant: the berries are oblong, somewhat resembling wild Olives.

It is cultivated in the gardens of Italy, Spain, France, and Germany.

**Broad-leaved Belgian Myrtle, perhaps the Roman Myrtle of Pliny.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrtle plant showing the root system, upright stems, and dense foliage.</image-desc>

This plant has a large leaf, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century Flemish botanist.</note>, green, arranged in a sparser order, and in a double row around the branches. The same Clusius thinks this could be called the Roman Myrtle of Pliny, and the "Conjugal" Myrtle of Cato <note>Cato the Elder, who associated this myrtle with marriage rites.</note>, and that it was brought from Italy and Rome into Belgium.

In the *Observations* of Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist.</note> it is called the first Myrtle, the largest of all, named *Laurea* <note>original: "Laurea"; meaning Laurel-like.</note> because of its Laurel-like leaf.

There are, furthermore, the smaller broad-leaved Belgian Myrtle, the broad-leaved Belgian Myrtle with denser leaves, the Belgian Myrtle with medium leaves, etc.

<column-break/>

**Broad-leaved Spanish Myrtle.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of Spanish Myrtle with broader leaves arranged in pairs.</image-desc>

According to Clusius, this is called *Araihan morisco* by the Spanish, that is, the Moorish Myrtle. It has quite thick branches: with leaves arranged somewhat sparsely in a double row, large and fragrant: however, it flowers or bears fruit more rarely, because they mostly use it for weaving hedges, which they are accustomed to shear.

Is this the *Exotic Myrtle of Pliny* mentioned by Lobel?

**Narrow-leaved Spanish Myrtle.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spanish Myrtle branch with narrower, more densely packed leaves.</image-desc>

This has the same density and arrangement of leaves as the broad-leaved Spanish Myrtle: but with a smaller and more deeply green leaf: and also with a smaller and spherical fruit, both white and black.

Is this the Exotic Myrtle of Pliny? Regarding this, Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, an Italian physician and botanist.</note> writes: The Exotic variety, he says, is now kept in the gardens and pleasure-grounds of Italy, with a leaf not unlike our native one, yet paler, with more abundant tapering: so dense that the branches are crowded with them everywhere. It bears oblong fruit, hanging from a long stalk, filled with seeds, not unlike the common Myrtle: the flowers are whitish, as in the other kinds: it is considered very suitable for topiary work <term>topiariis operibus: the art of clipping shrubs into ornamental shapes</term>.

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical classification of various Myrtle species, distinguishing between wild and cultivated varieties and describing regional types from Belgium and Spain. It cites classical authorities like Pliny and contemporary botanists like Clusius to establish nomenclature and horticultural uses.</summary>
<keywords>Myrtle, Myrtus, botany, Clusius, Pliny, Spanish Myrtle, Belgian Myrtle, topiary, medicinal plants, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of woody shrubs, specifically focusing on varieties of Myrtle and the "Vines of Mount Ida" (blueberries and their relatives). The catchword from the previous page was "CHA-", likely referring to a previous entry or a botanical characteristic.</meta>

### TARENTINE MYRTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrtus Tarentina plant, showing a woody stem with dense, small, pointed leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

It takes its name from Tarentum <note>modern Taranto</note>, a city of Apulia, where it grows in abundance. Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note> reports in his later *Commentaries* that the plant we illustrate here also goes by the name Tarentine Myrtle. He states its leaf is similar to our local variety but much smaller and sturdier; the fruit is smaller and crowned at the tip with several points. Its color is a purplish-black, containing small, crowded, whitish seeds inside. The flowers are similar to the common Myrtle, and finally, it is very well-suited for topiary <note>the art of clipping shrubs into ornamental shapes</note>.

Furthermore, the Tarentine Myrtle is cultivated especially in the gardens of Italy and France. It loves a warm climate, which is why it is rarer in Germany. Depending on the location, it flowers earlier or later, but usually in Summer, ripening its fruit in Autumn.

<column-break/>

### SMALL NARROW-LEAFED MYRTLE, MYRTIDANUM, and the powers of Myrtle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrtus Angustifolia Minor plant, featuring slender stems with narrow, lanceolate leaves and small round berries.</image-desc>

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> identifies this image as the previous Myrtle, while Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse</note> identifies it as the domestic Myrtle with white fruit.

Furthermore, almost everyone calls the fruit of the Myrtle a *Myrtillum* <note>little myrtle/bilberry</note>, though some, including Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock</note>, use the name *Myrtillum* to designate the entire shrub.

There is also *Myrtidanum* <note>original: "Myrtidanum"</note>, which according to Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note> is a warty growth that forms on the Myrtle; it is uneven, swollen, and the same color as the plant. It clasps the trunk of the Myrtle much like a hand. Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, a Renaissance scholar</note> calls it *Myrtadum*.

Regarding the powers of Myrtle: The entire Myrtle plant possesses an astringent <note>tissue-contracting</note> quality. The berries are cold and dry in the first degree and strongly halt the bowels <note>treat diarrhea</note>. The remaining uses, and how wine, syrup, and other medicines are prepared from them, the narrowness of space here does not permit.

---

### VINE OF MOUNT IDA: German: *Heidelbeer*; French: *Airelle* & *Cousines*; Italian: *Uva dell'orso*, *Myrtillo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Vitis Idaea (bilberry/blueberry) plant, showing a low shrub with oval leaves and drooping bell-shaped flowers or berries.</image-desc>

This plant is the same as the "Alexandrian Vine" in Pliny and the "Vine of Mount Ida" in Theophrastus. Specifically, as Pliny transcribed from Theophrastus, it is a vine growing around Phalacra (a part of Mount Ida), which is short, with branches a cubit long, a black berry the size of a bean, a soft and tiny pit, and very sweet drooping clusters. The leaf is small and round, without divisions. However, we do not yet dare to assert whether they meant this "Vine of Mount Ida," or the "Angular" one discussed next, or if, as Dodoens wishes, it is distinct from these plants. Some categorize it as a larger *Myrtillo*, others as black *Vaccinium* <note>blueberries</note>. Let the learned judge.

It grows in mountain alps and wooded, marshy wildernesses. Hunters report that the berries possess an intoxicating power.

<column-break/>

### ANGULAR VINE OF MOUNT IDA, with smooth, pointed leaves, serrated around the edges.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Vitis Idaea Angulosa, showing a plant with more angular stems and serrated, pointed leaves.</image-desc>

It grows in the Alps as well as in vast deserts, misty and dark valleys, and other damp places in France, England, Germany, Switzerland, Burgundy, and Savoy. It flowers in May and ripens its fruit in October.

By some it is called *Earth Myrtle* or *Dwarf Myrtle*, by others *Black Vaccinium*, and by some *Myrtillus* and *Bear-grape*. To Camerarius, if we are not mistaken, it is the *Black Vine of Mount Ida* found everywhere in the woods. Whether it is truly the "Vine of Mount Ida" of Theophrastus and the "Alexandrian Vine" of Pliny has already been noted above as a matter of doubt.

---

### EVERGREEN VINE OF MOUNT IDA, with red fruit.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Vitis Idaea Semper Virens (lingonberry), showing a low evergreen shrub with clusters of berries at the tips.</image-desc>

Some label this *Red Vaccinium*, *Red Vine of Mount Ida*, and even *Anguillara's Bear-grape*.

This also delights in wooded, stony, and shaded places, and commonly grows under Fir and Spruce trees. It flowers in May and June, finally ripening its fruit in September.

Furthermore, it is a matter of common agreement among all that the berries of the Vine of Mount Ida are generally of an earthy and cold substance. Therefore, both fresh and dried, they are usefully given to be eaten by those suffering from dysentery and celiac distress. Mattioli rightly established that they cool, dry out, strengthen, and restrain <note>the bowels</note>. Dyers use them specifically for dyeing linens and for staining paper a blue color.

<column-break/>

### THE SUPPOSED ROOT OF IDA; AND BEARBERRY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Radix Idaea (Uva Ursi/Bearberry) plant, showing trailing stems with small, thick, rounded leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

This plant is related to the Red Vine of Mount Ida; Clusius, if we are not mistaken, thinks it corresponds exactly to Galen's *Arctostaphylos* <note>Greek: "bear-grapes"</note> or *Uva Ursi*. It grows in the mountains around Geneva, as well as in the Vegamiis mountains of Narbonne. It flowers in March and April.

Is it perhaps the "Alpine Ground-tree" of Lobel, Pena, and Gerard? Or the "Broad-leafed berry-bearing Heather" of Tabernaemontanus?

<summary>This page describes various species of Myrtle and the "Vines of Mount Ida" (including blueberries, bilberries, and lingonberries), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations, and medicinal uses as astringents.</summary>
<keywords>Myrtle, Tarentine Myrtle, Myrtidanum, Vitis Idaea, Bilberry, Lingonberry, Vaccinium, Uva Ursi, Bearberry, Mattioli, Dodoens, Clusius, astringent, medicinal plants, botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on low-growing shrubs, berries, and resinous trees. It maintains the comparative style of the previous entries, citing authorities like Clusius and Dioscorides.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### GROUND-BOX OR DWARF-BOX.
<note>original: "CHAMÆBVXVS SIVE CHAMÆPIXOS"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small woody plant with oval leaves and small flowers, showing the root system and branching structure.</image-desc>

Is this the *Anonymos* with a Bladder-senna flower described by Clusius? <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational botanist.</note> Or the *Anonymos* with a Peach leaf described by Camerarius? Certainly the German name *Wintergrüen* <note>Wintergreen</note>, which it takes from its perpetual greenness, seems to point to that. Gesner used to call it Ground-box or Dwarf-box. By others, this undershrub is called Myrtle-Broom. It blooms in April and May; the seed is perfected in June. It is commonly found in many of the Pannonian or Austrian Alps. Thus far, however, it has been neglected and not called into medical use.

<column-break/>

### MANY-LEAVED MOUNTAIN PLANT RELATED TO THE VINE OF MOUNT IDA.
<note>original: "VITI IDEÆ AFFINIS POLYFOLIA MONTANA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with narrow, pointed leaves arranged in clusters, showing a woody stem and detailed leaf structure.</image-desc>

In its origin, leaves, and appearance, it resembles our Hullwort <note>Polium</note>, and is found in cold, marshy, and mossy mountain places. From the tips of the small branches hang little cups <note>calyculi</note> that are leafy and reddish; from these emerges an angular pyramid, promising the first form of some purple berry. Instead of roots, thin fibers like hair grow everywhere from the branches, gripping the earth with a "bite." We have taken care to depict the leaf as somewhat broad next to a narrow one, as both are observed in this plant.

Is this the *Thin-leaved Myrtle* of Thalius in his description of the Harz Forest? Or the *Red Bavarian Vine of Mount Ida* of Camerarius, with tasteless berries without juice?

---

### SOUR-BERRY, OR MARSH WHORTLEBERRY: Dutch *Veenbesien*: French *Cousines des marais*: *Moosbeeren* <note>Cranberries</note>.
<note>original: "OXYCOCCVS, SIVE VACCINIA PALVSTRIS"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a creeping vine with small, round leaves and large, dark berries (cranberries).</image-desc>

It creeps with very long, woody, dark-reddish vines that are stubborn against breaking, which the leaves of Wild Thyme clothe. The flowers are similar to the flowers of Bittersweet <note>Glycypicros</note>. The berries resemble the shape of a heart; they are whitish at the beginning, afterwards they are scarlet and sprinkled with purple spots, enclosing small seeds within. The root is hair-like.

Is this the *Vine of Mount Ida* growing in marshy places described by Clusius?

This also has its birthplace in damp, marshy, and shaded mountain places; it is frequent in Holland, and not far from the city of Nuremberg near the large fishponds. We truly observed it in abundance on the mountain *Bâlon* in Lorraine.

The berries ripen in the months of July and August and are astringent, as are the leaves.

<column-break/>

### PRIVET: German *Rheinvveiden*, *Mundholtz*, French *Troësne*, *Fresillon*: Italian *Ligustro*.
<note>original: "LIGVSTRVM"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a privet branch with clusters of small flowers and dark berries.</image-desc>

This is a tree-like shrub, which is rightly considered by some to be the *CYPRUS* of Dioscorides, and the *ALCANNA* and *HENNE* of the Arabs. Whether it could also be *PHYLYREA*, we have weighed in our great History by comparing the arguments and authorities of many learned men.

It grows for the most part in rough places, and especially among briars and thorns; it is very familiar to Germany, France, and Italy. It blooms in April and May, earlier or later depending on the region; in September the small clusters ripen, and they remain throughout the winter as a chief refuge for small birds.

The leaves, flowers, and berries have an astringent power, and are almost never used except externally.

---

### EGYPTIAN PRIVET: THE CYPRUS OF THE GREEKS, AND THE ALCANNA OF THE ARABS.
<note>original: "LIGVSTRVM ÆGYPTIVM: CYPRVS GRÆCORVM, & ALCANNA Arabum"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a henna plant with broad leaves and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

This has much in common with our native Privet, which is why many have thought them to be one and the same; however, we have shown them to be different things in our Universal History.

We judge this to be the true *Cyprus* of Dioscorides. According to his account, the Cyprus is a tree with leaves around the twigs similar to the Olive, but broader, softer, and greener; with white, mossy, fragrant flowers; and a black seed similar to the fruit of the Elder. The best grows in Ascalon and Canopus. It has an astringent quality.

Alpinus, following a corrupted version of the translators, says it is the *Ligustrum* of Dioscorides; and adds that it is the *Alkanna* of Avicenna, the *Cyprus* of Pliny, and the *Elhanne* of the Egyptians—names which Belon and Rauwolf also use.

<column-break/>

### MOLLE, AND THE RESIN GUM ELEMI.
<note>original: "MOLLE, & GVMMI ELEMI RESINA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with pinnate leaves and clusters of small berries (likely Schinus molle, the Peruvian Pepper Tree).</image-desc>

The *Molle* is a tall and spreading tree, with leaves much like the Mastic tree; with very numerous, tiny, star-shaped flowers; and berries like those of asparagus, fatty, bitter, containing a wrinkled and stony little pit.

Some assign Ash-tree leaves to it; Lobelius wishes it to be a species of Balsam; by others it is called the *Peruvian Mastic*. It grows abundantly in the region of Peru, and is also kept in the more cultivated gardens of Europe.

Wonderful things are told concerning its various uses. But whether the gum which it exudes is not that which is sold in the apothecary shops under the name *GUM ELEMI*, and is thought to be the tear of the Ethiopian Olive, we leave to the learned to weigh carefully.

<summary>This page describes various shrubs and trees, including the cranberry, privet, henna (Egyptian Privet), and the Peruvian pepper tree (Molle), focusing on their botanical identification and medicinal properties.</summary>
<keywords>Ground-box, Cranberry, Privet, Henna, Molle, Gum Elemi, Dioscorides, Clusius, Peru, botany, medicinal plants, astringents</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
### SAM

### PHILLYREA AND MAHALEB:
### Narrow-leafed Phillyrea.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Phillyrea angustifolia, showing a woody shrub with narrow, lanceolate leaves and small clusters of berries.</image-desc>

Just as those are completely mistaken <note>original: "toto errant cœlo," literally "err by the whole sky"</note> who confuse the Linden tree <note>Latin: Philyra</note> with the Phillyrea, so too is the error of those not slight who wish to claim that the Arabian Mahaleb and the Phillyrea do not differ; for the Mahaleb is the Bitter Cherry or Ground-cherry. Nor is the Phillyrea a species of Privet <note>Latin: Ligustrum</note>, as Amatus <note>Amatus Lusitanus, a famous 16th-century physician</note> maintains.

According to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacology</note>, the Phillyrea is a tree equal in size to the Cypress: with leaves similar to the Olive, but broader and darker: with fruit like the Mastick tree, black, somewhat sweet, and as if strained through a bag. It grows in rugged places.

We illustrate the Narrow-leafed variety here, intending to treat the remaining species afterward. This is the 5th Phillyrea of Clusius, the Flowering Phillyrea of Narbonne according to Lobel in his *Observations*. Others, according to Cesalpino, call it *Ilatrum* and *Linternum*.

### THE PHILLYREA TREE OF LOBEL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Phillyrea Arbor, depicting a small tree with broader, ovate leaves and visible root structure.</image-desc>

In its trunk and scattered shoots it equals the Plum or Cherry; the leaf is clearly that of a Phillyrea, only somewhat broader: the flower is like that of the Holm Oak, mossy: the berries are such as are available today in the Apothecary shops under the name of Mahaleb. It is found in Provence near Toulon, and is the Mahaleb of Serapion <note>An influential 9th-century Arab physician</note>. Thus says the *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note>.

Tabernaemontanus also classifies and illustrates it as the Mahaleb of Serapion, though with Lobel’s image slightly altered.

### HOLLY-LEAFED PHILLYREA, and on the virtues of Phillyreas in general.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Phillyrea Folio Ilicis, showing serrated leaves resembling holly and clusters of small fruit.</image-desc>

In the Florentine territory and also in the uncultivated lands of Portugal around Évora, it grows in great abundance. In the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is called the first Phillyrea of Clusius. Could it be the Crested Broad-leafed Phillyrea of Lobel’s *Observations*?

Regarding the medicinal Virtues of the Phillyrea: the leaves of the Phillyrea, as Dioscorides relates, are astringent just like those of the Wild Olive: chewed, they are beneficial for mouth ulcers: and a decoction of them is used as a rinse; the same decoction, when drunk, provokes urine and the menses. Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek medical writer</note> says the same regarding its Virtues, but the Arabs speak of them quite confusedly: the modern authors offer nothing more specific.

<column-break/>

### BROADISH-LEAFED PHILLYREA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Phillyrea Latiusculo Folio, showing a branch with broader leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

Is this the *Ilatrus* of Cesalpino, with a broader and shorter leaf? Or the Phillyrea of Bellonius mentioned by Gesner in his *On Gardens*, which grows wild in the rocky and mountainous parts of Italy? At the end of Cordus’s *History*, it is called the Mahaleb of Serapion. In the *History of Lyon* it is called *Philyca*, being the size of a Privet. In Dodoens’ *Latin History*, it is the Broad-leafed Cypress. According to Caspar Bauhin in his commentary on Mattioli, it is the Phillyrea of Dioscorides, which seems to have been called *Philyca* by Theophrastus.

### ALATERNUS-LEAFED PHILLYREA, and on the habitats of Phillyreas in general.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Phillyrea Folio Alaterni, showing an upright shrub with small, dense leaves.</image-desc>

This grows in various places in Portugal in hedges, but nowhere more abundantly than around the notable village of Tomar.

Furthermore, all species of Phillyrea, except for this one which we say has the leaf of the *Alaternus* <note>Buckthorn</note>, are seen not only in the most cultivated gardens of illustrious men: but also in various mountainous, rugged, and rocky places, and even by ditches in the embankments and hedges of fields. They flower in the Spring and ripen their berries in August or September.

### SPINABOURGI OF MONTPELLIER: French: *Bourgespine*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spinabourgi Monspeliensium, showing a branch with broad, slightly serrated leaves and berries.</image-desc>

This has the size of a Privet: the bark is black, the leaves oblong, somewhat round and slightly thorny: the flowers are like the Mastick tree: the berries are small, black, round, numerous, and three-seeded <note>Latin: tricoccæ</note>, not twin-seeded as Pena and Lobel say.

To the same Lobel in his *Observations* and *Icons*, it is called the *Alaternus* of Pliny; to Clusius and Anguillara, it is the *Spina cervina* <note>Buckthorn, literally "Stag's Thorn"</note> of certain authors.

Regarding this plant, the *History of Lyon* relates: some have thought it to be the *Apharca* of Theophrastus, others the Phillyrea of the Greeks: the Pharmacists of Montpellier call it *Bourgespine*, that is, Burgundian Thorn. It grows not far from the city of Montpellier, in the rugged and rocky places of the seacoast: it is of no great use, except for making dyes.

<summary>This page details various species of Phillyrea (mock privet), distinguishing them from the Linden tree and the Arabian Mahaleb cherry, while citing classical and contemporary botanical authorities. It describes their physical characteristics, habitats in Italy, Portugal, and France, and their medicinal uses as astringents.</summary>
<keywords>Phillyrea, Mahaleb, Privet, Dioscorides, Lobel, Clusius, Alaternus, Buckthorn, medicinal herbs, mouth ulcers, dyes, botany, Portugal, Montpellier</keywords>

### DWARF ELDER, OR HERBACEOUS ELDER: German *Niderer Holder*: Belgian *Haddick*: French *Hieble*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ebulus (Dwarf Elder), showing a herbaceous plant with pinnate leaves and terminal clusters of flowers/berries.</image-desc>

It wavers between the category of shrubs and the herbaceous genus; indeed, it so closely mimics the Elder <note>Sambucus nigra</note> that it earned its name by the addition of "dwarf." Thus it is called *Chamæacte* <note>Greek: "ground-elder"</note> by Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul of Aegina. To Pliny, it is another kind of Elder, more wild and much shorter, and called *Actæa* by the Greeks, or *Chamæacte*, which others call *Helion*.

It grows in shaded, damp, and watery places, and very often at the edges of plowed fields. It flowers in June and July; it ripens its berries in August and September; it is common in Germany, France, Switzerland, and Italy.

Its powers and uses are like those of the tree-like Elder. Platina writes that the flowers, when taken in food, benefit those suffering from liver, spleen, heart, and dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> ailments.

<column-break/>

### THE AZADARACH TREE: Called *Aftrigar*, or *Aftirgir* and *Azatadacht* by the Arabs.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Azadaracheni tree (Chinaberry), showing a woody stem with compound leaves and small clusters of fruit.</image-desc>

Gesner and Mattioli rightly rebuke those monks and others who identify this as the same as the Sycamore. By some it is called *White Ziziphus* and *False Sycamore*, by others *White Lotus*, and by Caesalpino *Tuber*.

The leaves and flowers burst forth together in the month of June; the berries are ripened in autumn and sometimes cling to the branches throughout the entire winter.

---

<column-break/>

### RHUS or SUMAC: German *Gerberbaum*: Belgian *Smak*: French *Roux*, *Rhon* & *Change*: Italian *Sumacho*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rhus (Sumac), showing a branch with serrated pinnate leaves and a dense, conical fruiting cluster.</image-desc>

It is a small tree exceeding the height of a man, which Theophrastus and Pliny distinguish into the *Male* or fruit-bearing type, and the *Female* or sterile type. Others make two kinds of Rhus: *Mageiricon* <note>Greek: "culinary"</note>, which is added to cooked dishes, and *Byrsodepsicum* <note>Greek: "tanner's"</note>, that is, for leather-working. Some hold there are Syrian, Pontic, Marine, Oriental, Red, and Black varieties, etc. However, one should not think for that reason that the Rhus trees differ from one another in species. For the Rhus of the cooks is nothing other than the leaves and small twigs of the bark. Red Rhus is the immature seed, which turns black upon maturity. Furthermore, regarding the Syrian and Pontic Rhus, they do not differ in kind from the Italian and Iberian.

<column-break/>

### THE SHRUB CONSIDERED TO BE PLINY’S RHUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Rhus, showing a woody shrub with smaller, rounded leaflets and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

In Spain, Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and especially in the hedges of the Montpellier region, in rich and dense soil, this small tree grows and rises to the height of a man; in size, leaves, flowers, and fruit, it is very similar to the common Rhus, and is held by Tabernaemontanus, Camerarius, Pena, and Lobel, and several others, to be the *Myrtle-leaved Rhus* of Pliny. It is used for strengthening leather, and its use can be the same as the other.

Furthermore, Rhus loves a warm climate, and in such it flowers and perfects its fruit. It dries in the third degree, cools in the second, and is greatly astringent. The kitchens use the fruit for seasonings. The perfumers <term>Seplasiæ</term> <note>named after the Seplasia, a famous street of perfume-sellers in ancient Capua</note> use the same and the leaves where there is a need for powerful drying and binding; the tanners use the dried shoots reduced to a powder.

---

<column-break/>

### LANTANA COMMONLY, by others VIBURNUM: German *Schlingbaum*: French *Viorne*: Italian *Lantana*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lantana (Viburnum), showing a shrub with broad, veined leaves and flat-topped flower umbels.</image-desc>

This shrub sometimes grows into a tree, with its root wandering in the top of the turf; it has leaves like the Alder: white flowers in an umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster</note>, and berries that are first green, then red, and black upon maturity, sweet, sticky, and of a less than pleasant taste.

It flowers in April and May; the berries turn red in July and August, but finally turn black in September. It grows mostly in uncultivated soil among other briars and hedges in thickets and fences, rejoicing in clayey and strong earth.

The leaves and berries have the power of cooling, drying, and binding: they are excellent for strengthening the teeth, for "rheumatisms" <note>inflammations</note> of the gums, and for the falling of the uvula <note>columella</note>, if they are boiled in harsh wine and the mouth is rinsed with the decoction. Boiled in lye, they turn the hair black and stop it from falling out.

<column-break/>

### PERHAPS THE SPIRAEA OF THEOPHRASTUS, ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spiraea, showing a shrub with elongated, serrated leaves and dense spikes of flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius describes and depicts it thus: and he thinks it can be referred to the *Spiraea* of Theophrastus: in our judgment it agrees well enough with *Lantana* or *Viburnum*, which the same Clusius writes is also thought by some to be the *Spiraea* of Theophrastus.

Furthermore, to add something regarding the use of Lantana and Viburnum: many eat its berries, and so that they may ripen more quickly, they are accustomed to store them upon straw or hay in alternating layers. Country folk conveniently use the twigs, which are almost unconquerable in their flexibility, for binding hedges and bundles of wood.

<summary>This page describes several shrubs and small trees, including the Dwarf Elder, Chinaberry, Sumac, and Wayfaring Tree (Viburnum), detailing their medicinal uses, culinary applications, and industrial roles in tanning and dyeing.</summary>
<keywords>Dwarf Elder, Chinaberry, Sumac, Viburnum, Spiraea, tanning, astringents, herbal medicine, botany, Pliny, Theophrastus, Clusius</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>F 3</sig>

### BLACK BERRY-BEARING ALDER; Germ. Faulbaum <note>Rotten tree</note>, Lausbaum <note>Louse tree</note>: French. Puierne, Black Alder, Pissefang.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of Alnus Nigra Baccifera (Alder Buckthorn) showing leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

This small tree which we depict here grows for the most part in woody and mountainous damp places, such as in the mountains of Muttenz and the Waterfall [Wasserfall] near Basel: in the forests neighboring Montbéliard, on the way to the watering place of Vaniencourt: at Geneva on Mount Salève and elsewhere. It flowers in May and ripens its fruit in October.

It is called *Alnus nigra* <note>Black Alder</note> by Dodoens, Pena, Lobel, the *History of Lyon*, Thalius, and many others. To some it is the berry-bearing Alder: to Gesner the Water Privet: to Crescenzi the *Avornus*. Lonicer and Schwenckfeld call it the "Stinking Tree," and Mattioli and Camerarius call it *Frangula* <note>Brittle-wood</note>, because its branches, especially when fresh, are easily broken. To others it is the *Siler* of Pliny. Regarding its powers, see below.

<column-break/>

### BLACK BERRY-BEARING ALDER with more WRINKLED leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of Alnus Nigra Baccifera with more wrinkled/textured leaves.</image-desc>

Some refer this and the preceding plant to the Buckthorns (*Rhamnos*), if only they were bristling with thorns. However, those we depict here we have observed in mountainous, rugged places exposed to the midday sun, in the County of Burgundy near Mesbe and St. Hippolyte: where they diligently collect the wood to prepare gunpowder from the cooked charcoal.

The outermost bark of these small trees has an astringent quality, but the innermost has a loosening effect: it opens obstructions of the internal organs and vessels, and when soaked in wine or beer, it induces vomiting and purges phlegm and other "sinning humors" <note>An early medical term for bodily fluids out of balance</note> through the bowels: it is an excellent remedy for country folk. The dose is double that of Rhubarb: but it must be taken dry, not green. When ground and smeared on the itch <note>scabies</note> with vinegar, it heals it immediately.

---

### DAPHNOIDES AND SPURGE-LAUREL: Germ. Zeiland: French. Laureoles: Ital. Olivella.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Daphnoides plant with long, slender leaves and berries along the stem.</image-desc>

Pena and Lobel say of the *Daphnoides* or *Laureola*, that just as its name suggests, so its nature entirely imitates a very small Laurel: so much so that even common people can scarcely distinguish it from Laurel at first sight. It is more than well known to horse-doctors and bedside women <note>midwives or folk healers</note> almost everywhere in Germany, France, and England. It grows for the most part in forests and shady, uncultivated, and somewhat cold mountains.

It stays green all winter: but in the month of February it is seen crowded with small yellowish flowers. The fruits are perfected at the end of summer.

It is hot and dry at the end of the third degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine indicating high potency</note>. The leaves, whether dry or fresh, purge the bowels, provoke vomiting and menstruation, and induce sneezing: but they sting and inflame the mouth, tongue, and throat, and upset the stomach.

<column-break/>

### DECIDUOUS-LEAFED SPURGE-LAUREL, or German MEZEREON.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mezereon plant with clusters of flowers/berries and leaves at the crown.</image-desc>

Those who distinguish the *Chamædaphne* <note>Ground-laurel</note> by sex call that one the Male and this one the Female. Some call it *Olivella*, to others it is the *Chamælæa* or *Thymelæa* of Dioscorides: but wrongly, for *Thymelæa* and *Chamælæa* are different plants, and this is neither of them. To others it is commonly *Mezereon*, and the *Mezereon* of Serapion, from which Tragus—based on the meaning of the word—labels it "Life-snatcher" and "Widow-maker."

It loves the same locations as the preceding plant, and flowers and ripens its fruit at the same time. Indeed, the leaves, bark, root, and fruit are hot and dry almost to the third degree. It is endowed with the same powers as the *Thymelæa*.

---

### HYPOGLOSSUM, DOUBLE-TONGUE, BONIFACIA: Germ. Zapflein: French. by some called Herb of the Crow.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Hypoglossum showing leaves with smaller leaf-like structures (tongues) growing from the center.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, it is a small shrub with leaves similar to the wild and slender Myrtle. It has a thorny head, and at the top or along the leaves it has "little tongues."

It is called *Hippoglossum* by some, as if "Large Tongue," but by others *Hypoglossum* <note>Under-tongue</note>, because near the top clusters, little tongues grow out as if attached. The Italian commoners call it *Bonifacia*: many call it "Country Tongue," some *Uvularia*: others Alexandrian Laurel and *Epiphyllocarpon* <note>Fruit-on-leaf</note>.

Two kinds are established: One, which consists of a double leaf: and the other, which has a single leaf and is considered sterile: a manifest proof that the upper leaf grows for the sake of the fruit.

It delights in shady and mountainous places, and, although it rejects cultivation, it is also grown in gardens.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER Image of DOUBLE-TONGUE or BONIFACIA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Bislingua with broader leaves and visible root system.</image-desc>

According to Marcello Virgilio, it possesses a sharp and heating power: and therefore it was used by the Ancients to dry out excessive moisture of the tongue in children: and from this it was called *Hyppoglotton*. Thus some tribes of the Insubres <note>People of Northern Italy/Milan</note>, according to the same author, use it for stuttering children. Tragus and Cornarius proclaim its use for a moist and collapsed uvula. Cesalpino praises it for childhood hernias (*enterocelas*), if a dose of a drachm and a half of its powder is taken for a long time at dawn in a decoction of Great Comfrey. Some write that it is given with great benefit in "suffocation of the womb" <note>hysteria</note>; others hang it around the necks of children <margin>they hang it</margin> so that their excessive moisture may be dried out.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal applications of the Alder Buckthorn, Spurge-laurel, and Horse-tongue (Hypoglossum). It details their use as purgatives, emetics, and treatments for childhood ailments like stuttering and hernias.</summary>
<keywords>Alder Buckthorn, Mezereon, Spurge-laurel, Hypoglossum, Bonifacia, herbal medicine, purgatives, botanical woodcuts, Dioscorides, Mattioli</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### ALEXANDRIAN LAUREL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Alexandrian Laurel plant, showing broad, oval leaves with prominent veins, arranged in a cluster on a short stem.</image-desc>

Valerius Cordus <note>A 16th-century German botanist</note> maintained that the plant called *Bislingua* <note>literally "Two-tongue"</note>, or *Bonifacia*, *Hypoglossum*, and *Vullatia*, is one and the same as the Alexandrian Laurel. To Mattioli and Cornarius, they are different plants. Dalechamps holds that *Bislingua* or *Bonifacia* is the *Laurus Taxa* of Pliny, but that the *Hypoglossum* of Dioscorides and Galen is the true Alexandrian Laurel. Others believe the Alexandrian Laurel of the ancients is unknown today. Amidst such a variety of opinions, we decide nothing on this matter; we merely display the image proposed by Lobel as the true Alexandrian Laurel.

<column-break/>

### BUTCHER'S BROOM: German: *Brusch* & *Bruscken*; French: *Brusco*; Italian: *Brusco*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Ruscus plant, showing a bushy shrub with small, sharp, leaf-like structures (cladodes) and small berries attached to them.</image-desc>

Dioscorides describes this under the names *Oxymyrsine* <note>Sharp-myrtle</note> and Wild Myrtle. However, this plant was overlooked by Galen, Paulus, and Aetius in their lists of simple medicines. The Arabs used to confuse its fruit with Cubebs, as has been skillfully noted by Mattioli, Laguna, and Camerarius. Marcellus named it *Myacantha* <note>Mouse-thorn</note> because of its use against mice.

Dioscorides recorded that it grows in rough and steep places; we have observed it growing everywhere in the hedgerows and rocky areas of Italy, and between Lyon and Vienne in France. In Germany, it is sown in gardens. It flowers in early Spring and perfects its seed in Autumn.

The root and berries are of great use for the stone <note>kidney stones</note>, trickling of urine, retained menstruation, dropsy <note>edema</note>, and Jaundice. More details are in the Appendix.

---

### SPURGE OLIVE, THREE-BERRIED SPURGE OLIVE.
#### German: Foreign *Seidelpast*; French of Narbonne: *Garoupe*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Chamelæa Tricoccos, showing a woody stem with narrow leaves and clusters of three-lobed fruits (tricoccos).</image-desc>

The history of the *Chamelæa* <note>Ground-olive</note> is quite obscure and intricate, as many other plants are improperly referred to it. In our Universal History, the views of the Ancients and Moderns on this matter are weighed, and many are retained. Here we shall deal only with certain plants known to us more specifically by the name *Chamelæa*.

They call this *Olivella* and *Oleastellus* <note>Little Olive</note> from the similarity of the leaves, though these are smaller.

It is a lover of hot, rocky, and rough coastal soil: growing spontaneously with abundant yield in various places in Spain, Provence, and Narbonne; it is also cultivated in some gardens in Germany and Belgium.

<column-break/>

### HOARY AND WOOLLY SPURGE OLIVE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Chamelæa Incana, showing a more slender, upright plant with small leaves and flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

Here we shall deal with the powers of the *Chamelæa* in general.

It is hot and dry in the third degree, approaching the fourth. The leaves bite the tongue and abrade the windpipe; they purge phlegm, bile, and serous humors from below, especially when swallowed in pills. And although their violence is great, they are nevertheless believed to be useful for those with dropsy, if administered with judgment. Dioscorides writes that these same leaves, crushed and taken with honey, cleanse foul and crusty sores; he also describes a "Chamelaitic Wine" made from them.

---

### HAIRY SPURGE OLIVE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Chamelæa Hirsuta, showing a plant with many branching stems and very narrow, hairy-looking leaves.</image-desc>

This plant, which we keep in our dry herbarium, we received under the name of Hairy *Chamelæa*, and in French *Bois Gentil*. It has a woody trunk, branches the length of a palm, and leaves similar to the deciduous Spurge Laurel, though shorter and much narrower, ending in a point and somewhat hairy.

<column-break/>

### SPURGE FLAX, CNIDIAN BERRY: German: *Seidelbast*; French: Wild Flax; Italian: Mountain Pepper. *Thymelæa* of Montpellier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Thymelæa plant, showing a woody base with upright branches covered in small leaves and berries (Grana Cnidia).</image-desc>

We said before that the history of the *Chamelæa* was intricate; so too is that of the *Thymelæa*, which is very closely related to it in form and nature; thus writers confuse these with each other and with others. Pena and Lobel wish it to be called *Thymelæa* as if it were *Tithymelæa*, because of its appearance being a mix of Spurge <note>Tithymalus</note> and Olive. They describe it as being clothed in a tough, ashen bark that peels from top to bottom, flexible like the bark of the Spurge Laurel. The grains, called *Cnidia* by the ancients, are nine or ten in number, green at first, then turning from yellow to red, with a delicate skin swollen with watery juice, enclosing a single seed.

Thus they aptly assert that the *Coccus* or Cnidian Berry—under which name the fruits of various plants are sold—is actually the fruit of the *Thymelæa*.

<summary>This page describes several low-growing shrubs including Alexandrian Laurel, Butcher's Broom, and various species of Spurge Olive (Chamelæa) and Spurge Flax (Thymelæa). It focuses on resolving botanical confusion between ancient Greek sources and contemporary 16th-century observations, noting their medicinal uses as purgatives and diuretics.</summary>
<keywords>Alexandrian Laurel, Butcher's Broom, Ruscus, Chamelæa, Thymelæa, Cnidian Berry, purgatives, Dioscorides, Lobel, Mattioli, Renaissance botany, medicinal herbs</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### SMALL SPURGE OLIVE OF CORDUS
<note>original: "Thymelæa Minor Cordi"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flowering shrub with slender stems and small, pointed leaves, showing the root system.</image-desc>

The plant we illustrated previously grows in rocky places in Italy, Spain, Provence, and Narbonne Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. However, Valerius Cordus <note>A famous 16th-century German botanist</note> reports that this specific variety grows in brushy and mossy areas, both in plains and highlands, around Augsburg and Regensburg. There are also other species of Spurge Olive which we shall discuss shortly.

Furthermore, the Spurge Olive is intensely hot in temperament and purges violently through the bowels; it possesses nearly the same nature as the Widow-Wail <note>original: "Chamelaea"</note>.

<column-break/>

### CNEORUM IN GENERAL.
### MATTHIOLI’S CNEORUM, A LOW SHRUB.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with thick, woody roots and clusters of small leaves and flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

In the judgment of all the most learned men, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note>, the *Cneorum* of Theophrastus does not differ from the *Thymelaea* and *Chamelaea* of Dioscorides: but, as Marantha notes, the latter names were more common to one author, and the former to the other. For *Cneorum*, Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, famous herbalist</note> presents this plant. It grows in mountainous places among the heather, whence Clusius writes that it grows in such abundance on the mountains near Vienna that country women, when it is in full bloom, bring many bundles of it to the market for sale to decorate dining rooms.

It flowers in April and May, and the fruit is ripe in June; it is of such fertility that it often flowers three times in the same year. Nor is it ever touched or nibbled upon by any living creatures <note>likely due to its toxicity</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPIUS’S WHITE CNEORUM, called by others Dorycnium.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems, densely covered in narrow leaves, and small flower clusters at the apex.</image-desc>

The branches of the White Cneorum which we illustrate here are downy and whitish: the leaves are somewhat larger than those of the Widow-Wail or Spurge Olive, approaching the size of the leaves of the German Mezereon <note>Daphne mezereum</note>, shining with a silvery down on both sides, with a velvet-like softness, and blunt at the tips. The root is large, going deep into the ground: the tips of the branches break forth thinned out into clusters. The seed is seen to be black and thick, hidden in a little husk like a grain chaff.

Cesalpino calls it *Dorycnium*, and writes that it is obtained from Sicily, where it is commonly called *Argentina* <note>Silver-weed</note>. The *History of Plants of Lyon* states it grows in stony and rocky maritime places.

<column-break/>

### IMPERATO’S DORYCNIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a central stalk, trifoliate or small grouped leaves, and delicate flowers, showing a taproot.</image-desc>

The leaf is similar to that of an Olive, but the flower is like a Bellflower, Bindweed, or Thorn-apple: it is evergreen and does not shed its leaves in Winter. Ferrante Imperato <note>An apothecary and naturalist from Naples</note> thought this was the *Dorycnium* of Dioscorides, as Clusius notes: we leave it to the judgment of the readers whether it is so; we shall treat *Dorycniums* more extensively in the eleventh Class. We once had it grown from seed in the garden of the Most Serene Prince at Montbéliard.

---

<column-break/>

### SANAMUNDA, CALLED "BLESSED" BY SOME, Smooth Sanamunda.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with dense foliage along the stems and a thick, branching root.</image-desc>

One variety of Sanamunda is smooth, another is woolly: we shall deal with the latter later. We give the name of "Smooth" to the shrub depicted here, once collected in the coastal region of Narbonne near the town of Agde.

If we are not mistaken, this is the plant to which the *History of Plants of Lyon* attributes leaves like Myrtle: a yellow flower, and a thick, bitter root that scrapes the throat. It adds that the odor of the whole shrub is heavy and the taste unpleasant. Micon wrote from Spain that he had sent it, and he believed it to be a species of Spurge Olive. Furthermore, it possesses a violent purgative power, even stronger than in the Widow-Wail: and by this remedy the Spanish farmers are purged.

<column-break/>

### THE TARTONRAIRE OF THE MARSEILLAIS, Sanamunda I of CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with small, oval leaves densely packed on the stems, showing a woody root system.</image-desc>

There are those who have thought this the same as the preceding [Smooth Sanamunda]: but many things argue against it, and among others the leaves, which in this one are hairy.

It is called *Tartonraire* by the people of Marseille and the inhabitants of Provence, because of the exceeding power of purging which it possesses: for which reason Clusius is the authority that it is called *Mierdacruz* <note>A vulgar Spanish name referring to its laxative effect</note> by the Spaniards.

It grows in great numbers around Marseille and in various places in Spain sloping toward the sea. It flowers in springtime and perfects its fruit in Summer; and with the silvery brilliance with which the hills clothed in these flowers shine, there is scarcely anything more pleasant to the sight.

The leaves are highly valued for their ability to purge: but they bring on dysentery and immoderate flux. Therefore, one must deal with them cautiously.

<summary>This page describes several species of small shrubs related to the Spurge Olive (Thymelaea) and Cneorum, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe, and their potent, often dangerous, use as laxatives.</summary>
<keywords>Thymelaea, Cneorum, Dorycnium, Sanamunda, Tartonraire, Valerius Cordus, Mattioli, Clusius, medicinal plants, purgatives, botany, 16th-century herbals</keywords>

# PLANTS
## CLUSIUS’S SECOND SANAMUNDA. CLUSIUS’S THIRD SANAMUNDA.
## DALECHAMP’S SMALLER SESAMOIDES.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of the Sanamunda II plant, showing a woody stem with small, narrow leaves and clusters of small flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

Charles de l'Écluse <note>original: "Clusius," a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> considers this plant a relative of the Sanamunda. He illustrated and described it as being found on the maritime coasts of Andalusia <note>original: "Baeticae"</note> and in the mountains of the Kingdom of Granada. He discovered it in February, when it was decorating the landscape with a numerous offspring of yellowish flowers.

He says that the Moors of Granada call it "Sanamunda," and among them, it is frequently used for the sake of purging the body. Indeed, a weight of one drachm <note>a classical unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> taken with a decoction of chickpeas purges the bowels wonderfully.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of the Sanamunda III plant (Sesamoides minus), featuring a central stalk with elongated leaves and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

Clusius labels this plant the "Third Sanamunda" and, like the previous two, considers it a relative of the <term>Thymelaea</term> <note>Spurge Olive or related species</note>. Myconus writes that it matches perfectly the description of "Cneorum" handed down by Theophrastus. However, the *History of Plants of Lyon* labels Clusius’s Third Sanamunda as the "Smaller Sesamoides of Dalechamp." It states that this plant has a great affinity in terms of kinship, origin, taste, and purgative power with the "Greater Sesamoides," and identifies it as Clusius's Third Sanamunda. For us, it is the third. That same *History* adds that it is named <term>Sesamoides</term> not in reference to the account by Dioscorides, but rather to the "Greater Sesamoides of Dalechamp," which many call <term>Tartontaire</term> in Marseille and Clusius’s First Sanamunda.

It flowers at the same time as those mentioned above and grows in the same locations.

---

### THE TERRIBLE SHRUB, EMPETRUM, or ALYPUM of Montpellier.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of the Frutex Terribilis, showing a leafy shrub with serrated leaves and globular flower heads. A separate detail of a flower head is shown at the bottom left.</image-desc>

This shrub has chosen its birthplace in various locations in Narbonne and Provence, on slopes facing the sea and the South, and especially in steep, rugged places. However, it is also found in several parts of Spain and is cultivated in the more well-equipped gardens of Italy. Matthias de l'Obel <note>original: "Lobelius"</note> writes that the entire plant is bitter and has the unpleasant taste of <term>Thymelaea</term> and <term>Chamaelaea</term> <note>Spurge-laurel</note>. Its purgative power is violent; hence, because of that violent ability to purge the body, it is called <term>Herba terribilis</term> <note>Terrible Herb</note> by the common people of Narbonne.

Some wish it to be the "Sneezewort" or the "Third Conyza" of certain authors; others call it the "Calcifraga" of Dioscorides, but many points contradict this. Nor is it the genuine <term>Alypum</term>, for the characteristics of the leaves are inconsistent—indeed, they are entirely lacking.

As for which plant can be called the legitimate <term>EMPETRUM</term> <note>literally "on the rock"</note> of the Ancients, even a diviner as wise as Oedipus could scarcely guess, since no herb currently exists under that name. We do not entirely reject the opinion of those who determine it to be the "Alypum of Montpellier," also called the "Terrible Herb."

<column-break/>

### THE INDIAN LEAFLESS PLANT AND THE ANGELINA, Trees for Canoes, or Indian Little Ships.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of the Aphyllon Indicum, depicting a thick, succulent-like trunk with scale-like markings, emerging from a base with two smaller rounded growths.</image-desc>

The Indians navigate in vessels hollowed out from single trees, which they call <term>Canoas</term> <note>Canoes</note>. Indeed, there are trees of such great thickness that ships can be fashioned from them without the defects of joined planks; indeed, they are of such great capacity that they sometimes carry fifty men.

Jerónimo Osório <note>original: "Osorius," a Portuguese historian</note> writes that from the bark of such great trees, little ships are made so spacious that they easily hold thirty men.

This illustration properly belonged to the class immediately preceding this one, but it was omitted. In its lower part is depicted the <term>Aphyllon Indicum</term> <note>Indian Leafless Plant</note>, about which more is written elsewhere.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS VI.
### PRESENTING THORNY BERRY-BEARING PLANTS, BOTH TREES AND SHRUBS.

**OLIVE:** German: *Oliuenbaum*: Belgian: *Olijuenboom*: French: *Oliuier domestique*: Italian: *Oliuo domestico*.

**WILD OLIVE, OR OLEA SYLVESTRIS:** German: *Wilder Oelbaum*: French: *Oliuier sauuage*: Italian: *Oliuastro*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of an Olive branch (Olea) with leaves and several oval fruits (olives) hanging from the stem.</image-desc>

There are two main kinds of Olives: the Cultivated, which we depict here, and the Wild, of which we shall speak soon. Of the Cultivated Olive there are again many varieties <note>original: "Differentiæ"</note>, but these are taken not so much from the tree itself as from the fruit: namely from its shape, color, juice, size, flavor, and quality. To review them all—including those named after their discoverers, those named for their various locations, or those handed down by the Ancients—would be a task of immense labor. Therefore, omitting all of those, as well as the "Aquatic" and "Emerald" olives of Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger, an influential medieval Arabic botanist</note> which are unknown today, we shall describe only those known to the European world in this century. First, then, we have the very large ones usually brought from Spain, which are deservedly graced with the title of *The Proud Ones* <note>original: "Superbarum"</note>; second, those of medium size from Narbonne <note>A region in Southern France</note>; and the smallest of all from Italy, among which are found some scarcely exceeding the size of capers, though of no small reputation in food. The narrowness of this space does not allow for more; the reader will find the rest in the Appendix, where Oil, Olive-lees <note>term: Amurca (the watery, bitter liquid that settles from olive oil)</note>, and Olive-glue <note>term: Visco (a sticky resinous substance)</note> will also be discussed.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A woodcut of a Wild Olive branch (Oleaster) showing narrower leaves and smaller, more numerous fruits compared to the cultivated variety.</image-desc>

In the size of its trunk and branches, it does not yield to the cultivated Olive; however, it is surpassed by the density of these branches. Furthermore, it possesses thorns along the branches. The leaves are smaller, though of a similar shape. The flowers, also packed together in clusters, precede the fruit, which is similar to an Olive but smaller, more astringent, and endowed with a biting, purple juice.

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> attributes a longer life to this tree because, like other wild plants, it is hardier and denser, and less fertile in fruit. It rarely becomes mild through cultivation, although a neglected Olive tree may revert into a Wild Olive.

Otherwise, it loves clay and pebbles just as much as the Olive does; it grows in such places with a fertile yield in the territory of Narbonne, and in very many places in Dalmatia, Italy, and Spain. It possesses the same medicinal power as the Olive, but is somewhat more effective.

---

**ON THE NIMBO, WITH THE LEAF AND FRUIT OF THE OLIVE.**

<image-desc>A woodcut of a botanical specimen labeled Nimbo, showing a branch with serrated leaves and small clusters of berries.</image-desc>

This is an exotic tree of the size of an Ash; it has the leaf of an Olive, though sharper, saw-toothed around the edge, and it grows very luxuriantly. The flower is white and similar to tiny Olives. The Indians commonly call it *Nimbo* <note>The Neem tree (Azadirachta indica)</note>, and some among them call it *pepolo*.

They frequently use the leaves and flowers to kill and expel all kinds of intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos"</note>, to which they are especially susceptible. There is also great use for them in pains of the joints, swellings, and weakness of the limbs. With the oil expressed from the fruit of this tree, the people of Malabar <note>The southwestern coast of India</note> cure wounds, punctures of the nerves, pains, and contractions.

<column-break/>

**CAPPADOCIAN JUJUBE, ACCORDING TO SOME.**
**Bohemian Olive: French: *Iunubier blanc*: Italian: *Zeingole*.**

<image-desc>A woodcut of the Ziziphus Cappadocica (Bohemian Olive) showing long, narrow leaves and small fruits, with a distinct root system at the bottom.</image-desc>

By the consensus of many, this is called the White Jujube <note>original: "Ziziphon albam"</note>; others have thought it to be the "Jupiter’s Beard" of Pliny; some the *Eleagnus* of Theophrastus; the common people in most places call it the Wild Olive.

It is a tree of fair size in the forests and gardens of Bohemia, growing spontaneously around houses; it is nourished in almost all pleasure-gardens not only throughout Spain, but also through France and Germany; it is also frequent in Ethiopia and Syria.

It blooms at the beginning of Summer, and the fruit ripens in Autumn; but it is very rarely fruitful in cold regions.

The *History of Lyon* <note>A reference to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586</note> has two images: one under the title of Cappadocian Jujube, and another by the name of Bohemian Olive, as if they were different plants; but this is in error.

<summary>This page describes the varieties of Olive trees (cultivated and wild), the Indian Neem tree (Nimbo), and the Bohemian Olive (Oleaster/Jujube), detailing their physical characteristics, geographic origins, and medicinal uses.</summary>
<keywords>Olive, Wild Olive, Neem tree, Bohemian Olive, botany, medicinal plants, Theophrastus, Pliny, Spain, India, Bohemia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Rhamnus genus (Buckthorn), following the previous discussions on thorny shrubs. The catchword "Rhamni" links to the plural classification of these species.</meta>

->OF PLANTS<-

**BUCKTHORN: German: Stechdorn. French: Rhamne. Italian: Rhamno. THE SECOND VARIETY OF THE FIRST BUCKTHORN ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.**

### WHITE-BARKED BUCKTHORN OF MONTPELLIER

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rhamnus branch with small, pointed leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

The history of the Buckthorn <note>original: "Rhamni"</note> has been rendered very intricate by the obscure and corrupted readings of ancient writers. According to Theophrastus, Buckthorn is of two kinds, the Black and the White. Pliny likewise made the same two kinds, but he wrongly assigned them to the genus of Oaks. Dioscorides has three; but Galen mentions only one. The more recent authors also have their own distinctions, which are soon to be listed in order.

The one we depict here grows in many places in Spain, Portugal, and Narbonnese Gaul: it grows abundantly outside the city of Montpellier. It flowers in March and ripens its berries in Autumn; it is the first species of Buckthorn, the leaves and shoots of which are eaten with oil and vinegar at the start of a meal.

<column-break/>

We present a second variety of the first Buckthorn observed by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, which is indeed similar to that first one, but lower and growing as a shrub with more frequent branches: with smaller and more fleshy leaves, having a salty taste, and with the upper part being whiter. Finally, the flowers are of the same shape as the former, but of a distinctly purple color.

Perhaps Belon writes of this in Book 2, Observation chapter 59, when he says: "We found a small tree similar to the other Buckthorn along the shore of the Red Sea: with very dense, salty, whitish leaves: with thorny branches, but with blunt thorns, as in the European Buckthorn."

---

### BUCKTHORN OR GERMAN WILD OLIVE

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch with long, narrow leaves and round berries, identified as Oleaster Germanicus.</image-desc>

It grows around rivers and springs in sandy and stony soil: as well as on the maritime shores of Holland and Flanders, and it is also found elsewhere in valleys and near flowing streams. It is very common at Geneva near the Arar and the Rhône in a very gravelly place, as it is also along many stretches of the Rhine, and especially near Basel and Chur.

It flowers in June: the berries finally ripen after Autumn, and thereafter they cling throughout the whole Winter. In Belgium, dining rooms and parlors are decorated with the shoots of this shrub, providing a pleasing sight in Winter with their many yellowish berries.

By Cordus and the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Lugdunensis</note> it is called the Wild Olive <note>Oleaster</note>. Is it perhaps Belon's European Buckthorn, mentioned before?

<column-break/>

### THE THIRD BUCKTHORN OF CLUSIUS

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thorny shrub with small leaves and dark berries.</image-desc>

It is shrubby, with frequent branches the size of a Blackthorn, covered in black bark and armed with long thorns. Many leaves sprout together from certain small swellings, as in the former kind; they are oblong and narrow, fleshy, green, with an astringent taste, and are evergreen. At the beginning of spring the flower is small, appearing in great numbers next to the leaves and growing in clusters, of a grassy color. In Summer it bears a black fruit, similar to the Wild Plum <note>the sloe</note>, round and sour.

Clusius writes that it is common in the kingdoms of Granada and Murcia, in uncultivated places among other shrubs. Is it perhaps Belon's Buckthorn with black fruit that grows in Crete?

---

### THE BAVARIAN BUCKTHORN OF DALECHAMPS

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy branch with clusters of small berries.</image-desc>

Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, French physician and botanist</note> inscribed this Buckthorn as "Bavarian" because he received it from a Bavarian from Ingolstadt. Because of its color, some call the Buckthorn *Leucacantha*, that is, "White Thorn." There are those who also call it the *Ceruna* Thorn.

To briefly touch upon the qualities and virtues of the Buckthorn simply so-called: Buckthorn leaves dry in the first degree. When the first degree is complete, they cool, they digest <note>disperse morbid matter</note>, and they heal herpes and also Erysipelas <note>a skin infection known as St. Anthony's Fire</note>, provided they are not immoderately hot. So Dioscorides and Galen determine concerning them. The former adds that branches placed at doors or windows drive away the evil spells of sorcerers.

<column-break/>

### PURGING BUCKTHORN, DYER'S THORN: German: Wegdorn. French: Neprun. Italian: Spino cervino.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody shrub with broad leaves and dark berries, identified as Rhamnus Catharticus.</image-desc>

Golius, Roëslin, Helsticus, and others call this small tree *Rhamnus* simply and absolutely. But they do so with a great lapse in judgment, as Amatus and Dodonaeus rightly note: since it cannot be the Buckthorn of Theophrastus and Dioscorides, nor does it truly correspond to any ancient genus of Buckthorn. However, nothing prevents it from being called *Purging Buckthorn* <note>Rhamnus catharticus</note> with that addition, because it approaches the Buckthorns in its thorns, berries, and certain other features.

It loves uncultivated places, and rivulets and ditches containing water: it grows in the vast thorny places and hedges of Germany, at the boundaries of fields, and in thickets located next to roads. We have observed it growing copiously between Montbéliard and Belfort around *Bermont*, as well as at Yverdon above the Mill. It flowers in May; the berries ripen in Autumn.

<summary>This page details several varieties of Buckthorn (Rhamnus), discussing their geographical distribution across Europe, their botanical characteristics, and their medicinal uses as described by both ancient and contemporary authorities.</summary>

-># IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
<margin>G 2</margin>

### PANNONIAN PURGING BUCKTHORN.
<note>original: "RHAMNVS SOLVTIVVS PANNONICVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rhamnus (Buckthorn) branch with serrated leaves and small clusters of berries.</image-desc>

Matthioli and Camerarius <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli and Joachim Camerarius the Younger, famous 16th-century botanists</note> have provided beautiful illustrations of the Purging Buckthorn, as has our own work, which is even more pleasing. However, the one we show here is what Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse</note> proposes as the second type of Pannonian Purging Buckthorn; he provided no figure for the first type.

But something must be said regarding the Use and Virtues of the Purging Buckthorn. Some maintain that the berries are cold and dry, and are usefully applied to creeping ulcers of the mouth. Others, on account of the bitterness which they report in the taste along with an astringency, determine them to be hot and dry in the second degree. However, no one denies that they are purgative, and draw out thick phlegm and bilious humors through the bowels. Regarding the methods and the reasoning by which saffron, green, and crimson colors are made from these berries collected in Summer or Autumn, we teach this in our *Universal History*.

### OENOPLIA or NABCA, THE AFRICAN CHRIST'S THORN.
<note>original: "OENOPLIA siue NABCA, PALIVRVS AFRICANA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small tree or shrub with a thick trunk, oval leaves, and small round fruits.</image-desc>

Theophrastus mentions the Libyan Christ's Thorn <note>Paliurus</note>, which grows in great abundance in Africa, and which the inhabitants of the Hesperides use for making hedges; Pliny calls it the *Zura* of the Africans. However, it is entirely different from the Greek variety, which Dioscorides confuses with his own Buckthorn. It is perhaps rather the *Oenoplia* of the Greeks, and the tree called *Nabca*. That tree has the size of a Lotus and is thorny like an Acacia; it has leaves similar to the Jujube, and small, white, clustered flowers, also very much approaching those of the Insubrian regions: the fruit is indeed so similar to a Wild Apple that one might take one for the other.

It is cold and dry in the first degree, extremely pleasant to eat and astringent: a delicacy among the Turks and Egyptians.

### ZIZIPHUS, JUJUBES: Germ. Brustbeelinbaum: Belg. Iujuben: Gall. Iujubes: Ital. Giaggiole.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ziziphus (Jujube) branch with alternate leaves and small oval fruits hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

The *Ziziphus* or *Zizipha* of Asia is cultivated and domestic, and is a fairly large tree; there is another wild variety which is a shrub, similar in its leaves, branches, and thorns to the first Christ's Thorn mentioned before. It is not yet clearly evident whether the older Greeks recorded anything about Jujubes, unless we admit that Galen designated them by the term *Serica*. Whether Jujubes are also the *Tuberes* of Pliny has been debated by the most learned men; we, the later generation, leave it to be decided by the judge, along with Mattioli, Tragus, Camerarius, and Dodonaeus.

Furthermore, the Jujube enjoys a warmer soil and sky, having been brought long ago from the East into Europe; but today it is commonly cultivated in the gardens of Italy, Spain, and Narbonnese Gaul. It flowers in May and June: the fruits are gathered in autumn. More on the following side. Figure.

<column-break/>

### CHRIST'S THORN: Germ: Meelbeyren, Gall. Paliure.
<note>original: "PALIVRVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Paliurus (Christ's Thorn) branch featuring zigzag stems, small leaves, and distinctive disk-shaped winged fruits.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides, it is called a well-known thorny shrub: and, as is the opinion of many, it is his third species of Buckthorn, as he is accustomed to treat the same plants in different places and under different names. We might also easily believe it to be the *Paliurus* of Theophrastus.

From the same Theophrastus, we gather that it grows in Greece, because he calls it "ours." Otherwise, it enjoys maritime, flat, and uncultivated places: growing spontaneously among hedges in various parts of Italy and Narbonnese Gaul. It flowers in May and June, and ripens its fruit in Autumn, which remains on the tree all Winter. In Belgium and Germany, it is cultivated in gardens.

Living hedges are prepared from it. The fruit and leaves are astringent, digestive, incisive <note>cutting through thick humors</note>, and crush stones in the bladder.

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF OENOPLIA or NABCA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen showing a branch with leaves and large, heart-shaped or ribbed seed pods/fruits.</image-desc>

We depict here a branch sent from Crete under the name of *Nabca* or *Napeca*. Since the *Nabca* with a Buckthorn leaf mentioned by Athenaeus is considered to be the Christ's Thorn, something must still be added concerning the Christ's Thorn by way of a conclusion.

Namely, writers disagree most greatly in the history of this plant: for the description of this species handed down by Dioscorides differs entirely from that which Theophrastus produced. And this hardly agrees with what Agathocles recorded; nor does that correspond to the one of which Plutarch is the author, which seems to dissent from all the others mentioned. Therefore, since so many diverse opinions are held and histories recorded concerning the Christ's Thorn, we might easily believe with Mattioli that *Paliurus* is a name imposed on various and different thorny plants according to the preferences of different nations.

### INDIAN BER WITH JUJUBE-LIKE FRUIT.
<note>original: "BER INDICA FRVCTV IVIVBINO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Indian Ber (Ziziphus mauritiana) branch with large oval leaves and clusters of small round fruits.</image-desc>

This fruit is called *Ber* in Canara, *Ber* in Deccan, and *Vidaras* in Malaya. The *History of Lyon* calls them Indian Apples, *Aieba*: for since the people of those islands and provinces lack other cooling apples, they commonly use these.

The Arabs by no means agree in recording the properties of the Jujube: Serapio and Rhazes say they are hot and moist; Averrhoes says they are cold and moist. This is certain: Jujubes prepared in various ways, as the perfumers <note>original: "Seplasię"</note> are accustomed to do, are effective against a cough and roughness of the windpipe, and are beneficial to the chest, kidneys, and bladder.

Wild varieties occur frequently <note>meta: catchword "quentes" completed as "frequentes"</note> around Montpellier and in some fields of Italy.

# OF PLANTS

### LACCA: German: *Legnuss*: French: *Lacque*: Italian: *Lacca*. & diminutively *Lachetta*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of three textured, cylindrical sticks or branches of Lacca (lac resin), showing a rough, encrusted surface.</image-desc>

On the tree already mentioned, it is produced as if in its native place, or indeed gathered by ants as if in a garden, as the writers of Indian matters <note>Historians of the East Indies</note> relate. Adhering stubbornly to small sticks of two or three ounces, it is transported into Europe from the Provinces of Pegu <note>Modern-day Myanmar</note> and Balaguate.

By the Persians, Turks, and Arabs it is called *Lac*, *Luc*, or *Loc Sumatri*, as if it were Lacca from Sumatra, because they believe it is produced there. It is red, translucent, and without flavor, serving chiefly for dyes. The apothecary shops prepare a remedy called *Dialacca* <note>A compound medicine made with lac</note> from it. We describe the manner of its generation and preparation, and its adulterations, in our Universal History: and we shall deliver even more concerning Lacca in the *Appendix* of this work.

### HAWTHORN (OXYACANTHA): German: *Hagendorn*: Belgian: *Hagendoren*: French: *Aube Espine*: Italian: *Amperlo*, *Spino bianco*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hawthorn branch with serrated leaves and small clusters of berries.</image-desc>

It is a shrub rather than a tree, although it sometimes grows out into large trees. There are those among the more recent authors who think it is the *Palinurus* of Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist</note>, but they err by the whole heaven <note>They are completely mistaken</note>: nor with any less a slip do others label it *Cynobatos* <note>Dog-rose</note>. By some, it is called *White Plum*, and *Wild Azarole*.

It grows spontaneously everywhere in the forests of Germany and France, on the margins of fields, in the hedges of gardens, and in places both mountainous and level, in dry as well as wet spots. In the month of May, it is remarkable for the beauty of its flowers and the fragrance of its scent; the fruits ripen in September.

From this plant, living as well as trimmed hedges are constructed: and its wood is the most excellent after Boxwood for handles and other things of that kind which are made on a lathe.

### BARBERRY (BERBERIS): German: *Erbesel*: Belgian: *Sauselboom*: French: *Espine vinette*: Italian: *Crespino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Barberry branch with oval leaves and hanging clusters of elongated berries.</image-desc>

Most herbalists confuse the name *Oxyacantha* <note>Greek for "sharp thorn"</note> with the Hawthorn: others wish for *Oxyacantha* in the masculine gender to be understood specifically as Barberry, and claim it was designated thus by Galen. Avicenna <note>The Persian polymath</note> seems to have embraced both the Hawthorn and the Barberry under the single name *Amyrberis*. If there be any other opinion, to us the *thorn depicted here* seems to represent the Appendix thorn of Linus excellently.

It loves cold places, and grows spontaneously in uncultivated spots, thickets, plains, and mountains, in dry and watery areas. It buds at the beginning of Spring, flowers in April and May: through September and October, the berries adorn the hedges with their ruddy beauty.

The leaves and fruit are of a cold and dry temperament in the 2nd degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine</note>. In what manner a wine may be made from the berries and for what it may be useful, we teach in our Universal History.

<column-break/>

### GOOSEBERRY (UVA CRISPA): German: *Krausselbeer*: Belgian: *Steckelbesien*: French: *Groseillier*: Italian: *Crispino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gooseberry branch with lobed leaves and large, round, ribbed berries.</image-desc>

One kind is entirely wild, the other cultivated in gardens, being less thorny and bearing larger fruit. Almost all the more recent authors believe it was overlooked by the Ancients, both Greek and Latin: Cornarius thought it was the second *Palinurus* of Theophrastus. However, Tragus, Lonicer, and Apollo, and others, make it the *Rhamnus* of Dioscorides. In the History of Lyon it is called the *Idos* of Theophrastus, but on what foundation? Gesner calls it *Acanthus*, Fuchs calls it *Vua interta*.

It loves cold regions, and is quite rare in warmer ones: it grows, however, in woody places, and is used everywhere in the construction of living hedges where it abounds. It turns green in March, flowers in April, and bears fruit in May. The berries are cold, and more suitable for food than for medicine.

### FIRETHORN (PYRACANTHA) OR HAWTHORN to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pyracantha branch with small, lanceolate leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

It is well known that *Pyracantha* and *Oxyacantha* are one and the same. Yet there are those who make the plant pictured here—whose flowers and fruit are similar to the common variety, but which has leaves like the Wild Pear—a lower species of Hawthorn. Others wish it to be the legitimate Hawthorn and the *Pyrina* or *Pyrianthe* of Dioscorides. Clusius, who with Anguillara is of that opinion, writes that it is cultivated in Belgian gardens. We have also seen it at Padua.

We shall treat of Pyracantha later. Otherwise, the chief gift of Pyracantha is in the sweetness of the scent of its flowers. There are those who attribute an astringent power to the fruit and leaves, and with Dioscorides, others say they stop the excessive flows of women: and that the seeds, indeed, break down stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones</note>, etc.

### EGYPTIAN AGIAHALID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Agiahalid (Egyptian Balsam) plant, depicted as a small tree with a thick trunk and sparse, thorny branches.</image-desc>

It is a tree, according to the author Alpinus, of the size of a Wild Pear, with rare and not many branches, rising equally straight up, covered in order with many very sharp thorns: bearing *leaves* very close to Boxwood, yet broader, few, rare, growing singly or in pairs at equal intervals. It has a few white flowers, similar to the flowers of the Oriental Hyacinth, but smaller: from which come black fruits similar to Dwarf Elder, with a somewhat bitter and astringent taste. He writes that the Egyptians use its leaves for children troubled by worms. He doubts, however, whether it could be the true *Lycium* of Dioscorides, concerning which we shall speak presently.
