<keywords>Lacca, Hawthorn, Barberry, Gooseberry, Pyracantha, Agiahalid, botany, medicinal plants, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Clusius, herbal medicine</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
<margin>G 3</margin>

# LYCIUM, called by some BOX-THORN: Arabic Hadad, Hadhuadh.
<note>original: "LYCIVM, quibusdam PYXACANTHA"</note>

Lycium, which some call Box-thorn, *says Dioscorides*, is a thorny tree with branches three cubits long <note>about 4.5 feet</note> or even longer, around which are leaves similar to Boxwood, growing densely. It bears fruit like black pepper, bitter, dense, and smooth; the bark is pale and resembles diluted Lycium juice; and it has many slanted, woody roots. It grows mostly in Cappadocia, Lycia, and many other places. It loves rugged locations. The juice is extracted from the roots and the shrub itself, crushed and soaked for many days, then boiled; then the wood is discarded, and the liquid is boiled again until it reaches the thickness of honey. It is often adulterated with oil dregs <note>original: "Amurca"</note>, etc. It is said that Indian Lycium is also made from a shrub called Lonchitis. *Pliny* says that this thorn from which Lycium is made in Greece is called Chironian Box-thorn, and has a root (Dioscorides says leaves) the color of Boxwood. *Galen* touches on the matter briefly: Lycium, or Box-thorn, he says, is the tree from which the medicine they call Lycium is prepared. This is clearly that liquid medicine which they use for arrow wounds, and for foul inflammations of the mouth; it possesses a drying quality, etc. Lycium used to be imported, as mentioned, from Lycia and Cappadocia, and was called Lycium because its use was first discovered among the Greeks in Lycia, or because the best is believed to be made in Lycia. Where that which is kept in pharmacies today is brought from is almost unknown; however, that there are local versions of Lycium in France, Italy, the island of Crete, and India will be clear from what follows.

<columns>2</columns>

### FRENCH LYCIUM.
<note>original: "LYCIVM GALLICVM"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Lycium Gallicum branch, showing small oval leaves and clusters of berries along thorny stems.</image-desc>

It bristles with very rigid thorns, around which are many small flowers together, clinging to the branch by short stalks: these are succeeded by berries which, when ripe, contain oblong, polished, and streaked seeds under the skin. The leaves somewhat resemble the Wild Plum, but are smaller, more tender, slightly serrated around the edges, veined, and deciduous. The berries are brought to Lyon under the name of "Dyer's Grains" <note>original: "Graines de teindre, Graines iaunes, Graines d'Avignon"</note>. It grows in the rugged places of Narbonnese Gaul. Even if it is not the genuine Lycium of the Ancients, it nevertheless possesses the same medicinal powers.

<column-break/>

### ITALIAN LYCIUM.
<note>original: "LYCIVM ITALICVM"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Lycium Italicum branch, featuring denser foliage and small berries on a woody, thorny stem.</image-desc>

Just as the French celebrate theirs, so the Italians celebrate their own Lycium, and even judge it to be better. Thus Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, 16th-century botanist</note> writes of it: The Lycium medicine of the pharmacies is not free from adulterations; in this age, it is not imported to us from Lycia; nevertheless, the Lycium tree also grows in Italy, and is frequently seen in Dalmatia and the Alps of Liguria. Therefore, where legitimate Lycium is not at hand, Mattioli adds, nothing prevents this from taking its place. For it binds, restrains, strengthens, dries, and represses.

<column-break/>

### CRETAN LYCIUM, CRETAN BARBERRY.
<note>original: "LYCIVM CRETENSE, BERBERIS CRETICA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Lycium Cretense, showing a branch with small, clustered leaves and elongated berries.</image-desc>

The berries of Cretan Lycium differ from the berries of French Lycium: for when dry they do not show angles, nor are they bitter. They also differ from the berries of Italian Lycium: for they resemble Corinthian raisins <note>currants</note> with their wrinkled skin, proof that when fresh they were full of juice. When moistened, they dye paper an elegant purple and violet. The seeds are smaller than in Italian Lycium: and the leaves also differ from French Lycium: for they are narrower and more pointed. Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, German physician and botanist</note> considers the Lycium of Lebanon to be "Zareat," a foreign shrub found between Ramla and Jaffa.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN LYCIUM, AND CATECHU.
<note>original: "LYCIVM INDICVM, ET CATÈ"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Lycium Indicum, showing a branch with pinnate leaves and small round fruits.</image-desc>

The tree from which the juice "Cate" <note>Catechu</note> is extracted, according to Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, pioneer of tropical medicine</note>, is the size of an Ash tree, with a tiny leaf very similar to Heather or Tamarisk, and is evergreen. They say it flowers, but deny it bears fruit: it bristles with many thorns: the wood is robust, hard, dense, heavy, and not at all liable to rot. It grows in almost all parts of India, but mostly in Cambay. Garcia believes that this "Cate" is nothing other than the Lycium of the Greeks and Latins: let the learned judge.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS VII.
### CONCERNING MAST-BEARING TREES, AND THOSE RELATED TO THEM IN SOME WAY. <note>The term "mast-bearing" refers to trees that produce nuts like acorns or beechmast, traditionally used as forage for livestock.</note>

->The **OAK** or **HARD-OAK**: German: *Eichbaum*: Belgian: *Eikenboom*: French: *Chesne*: Italian: *Quercus*.<--

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a mature oak tree with a thick trunk, spreading branches, and visible acorns. To the left of the trunk is a small separate detail of an oak leaf and a cluster of three acorns.</image-desc>

Pliny says that "mast" <note>original: "Glandem"</note>, properly understood, is produced by the Hard-oak, the Oak, the Winter-oak, the Turkey-oak, the Holm-oak, and the Salt-oak <note>original: "Robur, Quercus, Esculus, Cerrus, Ilex, & Haliphloeus"</note>. Thus he lists the Oak and the Hard-oak among the mast-bearing trees as if they were different species. Others call the hard kind of Oak "Robur" (called *Rouvre* in French and *Steineich* in German). Yet by almost everyone, "Robur" is used for "Oak," and vice versa.

These Oaks differ among themselves in location, sex, size, leaf, trunk, wood, fruit, excretions, and parasitic growths. For the Hard-oak, as the same Pliny also notes, produces many other things besides fruit: both kinds of Galls, Little Pellets, Grapes <note>likely oak-apple galls</note>, Mistletoe, and Fungi: about all of which we shall speak later, and more extensively in the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

->Another Image of the **OAK** or **COMMON HARD-OAK**.<--

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an oak branch featuring several lobed leaves and two large acorns in their cups.</image-desc>

The other image, which is from Fuchs's work <note>referring to Leonhart Fuchs, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, is not very pleasing; therefore we give a better one here and depict the one which has acorns hanging from long stalks (called *flants* acorns). Another common variety bears acorns attached by short stalks. And this is again twofold: for it either produces larger ones, and only in twos or threes: or smaller ones, in fours, fives, or more, which is perhaps the female, as the other is the male. We have observed the one depicted here to be very frequent in various forests of the County of Montbéliard.

Furthermore, the Oak loves mountains, but it also descends into the plains, and it delights more in Northern locations. The people of Bourges <note>original: "Bituriges"</note> praise their tall and thick Frontenac oak; the people of Basel praise theirs, famous for its antiquity and size. But in no place are there held to be more beautiful, taller, and straighter Oaks than on Mount Chérimont, in the jurisdiction of Montbéliard, where, being entirely devoid of lower branches, they equal the Firs in height.

---

->The **HARD-OAK** or **OAK WITH GALLS**.<--

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an oak branch with lobed leaves and several round, bumpy oak galls (oak apples) attached to the stems.</image-desc>

This is Clusius's <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> Third Hard-oak, which he says is low-growing and does not exceed a man's height: but it bears a very large Gall, the size of a small Apple, and so abundantly that a small branch scarcely longer than a palm sometimes contains nine, ten, or more Galls.

Otherwise, the Oak indeed buds in Spring, but later than many other trees. It produces new leaves in May; the acorns are ripe in August, and begin to fall in September, as do the Galls. Theophrastus, Varro, and Pliny write that the Sybaritic oak was evergreen. They report that such an evergreen is still found today in the Apennines and the fields of Anjou <note>original: "Andium agro"</note>.

<column-break/>

->**ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE HARD-OAK WITH GALLS**.<--

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of an oak branch showing leaves and several smaller, smoother galls compared to the previous image.</image-desc>

This one has shorter, twisted branches and rougher bark: the Galls, however, are born on the ends of the twigs, smaller than the others, smooth and without bumps, very similar to those found in the Apothecaries' shops: Clusius makes this the fifth kind of Hard-oak.

The settlers of Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunenses Coloni"</note>, as Du Chesne relates, call the Oak growing in a flat place *Chesne*: but that which has taken root in very high mountains, being of smaller and harder wood, they call *Reule* or *Rouvre*, as if it were "Robur" <note>meaning "strength" or "hardwood" in Latin</note>.

Now, to say something of the qualities and powers of the Oak: every Oak dries and constricts <note><term>adstringit</term>: astringent properties, often used to stop bleeding or diarrhea</note> in all its parts: and it has some degree of heat. When cut, it grows back in the third year; it easily tolerates being stripped of its bark, and when submerged in water, it lasts and becomes similar to Ebony.

<summary>This page describes various species of oak trees, distinguishing between the common oak and the "robur" (hard-oak), while detailing their growth habits, geographical distribution, and the production of acorns and galls.</summary>
<keywords>Oak, Hard-oak, acorns, oak galls, Pliny the Elder, Clusius, Montbéliard, botany, medicinal properties, astringent</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

# THE PHEGUS OR ESCULUS: French: *Escuil*: Italian: *Ischio*: Perhaps not yet known to those in the North.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with lobed leaves and acorns, identified as Phegus or Esculus.</image-desc>

Gaza and others err by the width of heaven <note>original: "Toto cœlo errant" — a Latin idiom meaning to be completely mistaken</note> who claim that this is the *Phegus* of the Greeks and the *Fagus* <note>Beech</note> of the Latins, which the Greeks call *Oxya*. Some, including Belon and Curtius, believe it to be the *Platyphyllon* <note>Broad-leaf</note> of the Greeks and the *Latifolium* of Pliny.

Pliny maintained that it was called *Phegus* from the Greek verb *Phagein* <note>to eat</note>, because it is edible: just as the etymology of *Esculus* is derived from eating and food <note>original: "esu & esca"</note>. Indeed, it is more delicate than any Chestnut, and in Pliny's time, it not only took the place of bread during grain shortages but was even served at the second course <note>dessert</note> throughout Spain. However, when eaten, it affects the head and intoxicates just like *Lolium* <note>Darnel or cockle-weed</note>.

The *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> has two figures: We have taken only the Male; we omitted the female because there is no notable difference that can be expressed in a drawing.

# THE CERRUS, CERRIS, THE AEGYLOPS OF THE IDAEANS, THE ASPRIS of the Macedonians, and the Farnia of the Italians.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with deeply lobed, pointed leaves and acorns in prickly husks.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes that he saw the *Cerrus* <note>Turkey Oak</note>, a tree not very well known to Europeans, on a journey along the road from Pesaro to Rome. Dalechamps makes two types, Male and Female. We depict the Female here from the very branch from which he drew his, which we possess in our dried Herbarium.

It has leaves like the common Oak, but as they are longer, so they are divided into thinner and deeper segments, though it is a tree where the leaves may vary in shape. The acorns adhere closely to the wood, sitting in rough and silky cups, clearly similar to those of the Burgundian Oak with the hairy cup, which was illustrated and shown previously.

Is this the *Aegylops* of the Idaeans, called *Aspris* by the Macedonians?

The leaves, bark, and acorn of the *Cerrus* stop fluxes <note>digestive or fluid discharges</note>. The root is effective against Scorpions.

# THE GALL: German: *Gallapffel*: *Eychoapffel*: Belgian: *Galnote*: French: *Noix de gale*: Italian: *Galla*.

Whether it be a fruit of the Oak or an excrement <note>an outgrowth or tumor</note>, we explain in our *Universal History*. Dioscorides makes two kinds: One is his *Omphacitis*, which is small, tuberous, heavy, and has no hole through it; the other is smooth, light, and perforated, being less effective than the *omphacitis*. Galen, Paulus, and Aetius hold the same distinctions. Pliny recounts more: solid and perforated; white and black; larger and smaller. Tabernaemontanus expressed eleven varieties of Galls in illustration: and perhaps no fewer have been observed by us, differing among themselves in region, hardness, color, shape, or other marks, as will be evident from what follows.

Furthermore, Galls are astringent, binding, and used for dyeing: their properties are the same as those of the Oak; and, as Pliny says, the same for all of them.

<column-break/>

# THE BURGUNDIAN OAK with the hairy cup.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with acorns featuring very hairy or "hirsute" caps (calyces).</image-desc>

This Oak is much like the one thought to be the *Haliphloeos*, and Dalechamps' "female *Cerrus*," as well as Clusius's *Cerrus*; we give its image here under the name of the *Burgundian Oak*. We label it thus because we received its branches and acorns, slightly larger than the common ones, from Burgundy.

Is it the *Cerris* of Pliny, or the *Cerrus*, a type of Oak with a rough cup? Is it the *Broad-leaved Pannonian Oak*, or more rightly the *Cerris* of Camerarius? Is it the species of Oak called *Farnia* in Tuscany and other parts of Italy, of which more soon? Is it the *Aegylops* of Theophrastus, called *Aspris* by the Macedonians?

# LARGE PRICKLY ACORN CUPS.

<image-desc>Two large, highly textured acorn caps (calyces) with prickly, sea-urchin-like (echinate) exteriors.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes that the *Cerrus* found on the journey from Pesaro to Rome has acorns whose cup is prickly, bristling with very hard overlapping scales, almost the size of a sea urchin <note>original: "Echini marini"</note>, and very thick. The acorn cups we show here seem exactly like those; nor is it unlike the one Clusius describes and paints, received from Virginia <note>original: "Wingandecaouu," an early name for the Virginia colony</note>: we keep even much larger ones among our treasures <note>original: "Keimilia" — prized possessions or museum specimens</note>.

These cups, both these and those of other acorns, are used for dyeing cloths a black color in place of Galls, but the dye from them is thinner, more fleeting, and cheaper.

# ORIENTAL GALLS, AND VARIOUS OTHERS.

<image-desc>A collection of various oak galls of different shapes: some spherical, some spiked, some irregular or tuberous.</image-desc>

Here you see various shapes of Galls: round, tuberous, many-angled, angular, stalkless, prickly, radiated, horned: so that one may observe eight or nine differences in this single plate. Those that are prickly, radiated, horned, and angular are harder than the common ones; the lower ones are white and approach the nature of some spongy wood. That single one seen in the middle of the bottom part of the plate expresses the "Bull's Head" mentioned by Theophrastus so beautifully that nothing could surpass it, and it is harder than the rest. Those two dotted, oblong, stalkless figures which you see in the middle of the aforementioned plate among the others represent the "pumice-like stones" of the Oaks. Finally, the ones at the top are the Oriental types. The common one is depicted in the preceding plate.

<summary>This page describes various oak species and their products, specifically distinguishing between edible acorns (Esculus) and the Turkey Oak (Cerrus), while providing a detailed classification of oak galls used in dyeing and medicine.</summary>

# OF PLANTS

### OTHER VARIOUS SPECIES OF GALLS, Illyrian, Istrian, and those resembling Fungi.

### NAVEL-SHAPED GALL, OR THE Navel-shaped viscous growth of the Oak.

### INDIAN GALLS.

<image-desc>A collection of botanical illustrations showing various types of oak galls. On the left, six small, rounded or conical galls are shown in two rows. In the center, a larger illustration depicts a leafy oak twig with a prominent, textured gall (Galla Umbilicata) attached to the stem. On the right, four more irregular, brain-like or clustered galls (Gallae Indicae) are numbered 1 through 4.</image-desc>

The galls which are depicted in the upper part of the first of these tables, we have received as *Illyrian* <note>original: "Illyricis"</note>: the *History of Lyon* calls them "Provincial." The middle part contains the *Istrian* galls. In the lowest part, their appearance shows that they are those which represent a *Mushroom* <note>original: "Fungum"</note>.

### THE CATKINS AND NUT-GROWTHS OF OAKS, AND THE PILLS of Oak leaves.

<image-desc>Illustration of an oak branch featuring catkins (iuli) hanging down and small spherical galls (pilulae) attached to the undersides of the leaves.</image-desc>

The upper part of the table displays the Catkins <note>term: "Iuli" - the drooping, tassel-like flower clusters of the oak</note> of the Oaks, crowning the quarter-foot long little ribbons to which they adhere at certain intervals in a whorled pattern. The lower part has the "Pills" <note>term: "Pilulae" - small, round leaf galls caused by insects</note>. These, for the most part, grow on the back of the leaves—that is, the part facing the ground—sometimes with several clinging to a single leaf, very closely and immediately; they are smooth, spongy, pale, and have a somewhat acidic and astringent taste. They are round, soft, and rarely equal a small Gall-nut in size, and they become wrinkled with age. They usually grow after the first rains of Autumn.

Dodoens says they are frequent in Belgium; Turner says in East Frisia; we ourselves have observed them at Montbéliard and in Burgundy in August. *More is noted at the side of the following figure.*

### THE OAK-GRAPE.

<image-desc>Illustration of a cluster of grape-like growths (Vva Quercina) attached to the root system of an oak tree.</image-desc>

This grows attached to and entwined around the fibers of the Oak roots beneath the earth, the size of a Walnut, compacted of many berry-like parts clinging together in a cluster (whence it takes the name *Grape* <note>original: "Vva"</note>). The substance is hard, of a reddish or rusty color inside, with a somewhat white center, and a remarkably bitter and cooling taste. During the Spring, at which time it is vigorous, its color is purple on the outside and white on the inside, almost milky; it ought to be gathered at that time, dried in the shade, and reduced to powder. For in Summer it perishes and becomes as if made of wood.

It helps and cures those desperate with Dysentery: and its juice is smeared on as a great comfort for those suffering from Gout <note>original: "Podagricis"</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE PERFORATED BUDS OF THE OAK LEAF, and Scaly Little Heads.

<image-desc>Illustration of an oak leaf with numerous small, cup-shaped or scale-like galls (Gemmae Foraminulatae) densely covering the surface.</image-desc>

Nothing is more beautiful to behold; these are very minute and almost innumerable, adhering to the back of the leaves (you would say they were glued on) like very tiny little crowned spheres, compressed, and perforated in the middle, but not entirely through. Their color varies from a fine linen-white to a shining tawny, elegantly glittering. We observed more than 130 on a single leaf of a common Oak in Autumn at Befford. We have also seen the little scales <note>original: "Squāmulas"</note> depicted here, which the peasants say are a sign of a very rich harvest of acorns when they occur frequently; we saw them on the common Oak at the same time and place.

Furthermore, the *Oak pills* mentioned before are called "Related Galls" by Lonicer; Mattioli and Tabernaemontanus call them simply "Galls": yet how much they differ from true Galls! Could they be the *Pills of the Donkey-killer* <note>original: "Pilula Onocicidæ"</note> mentioned by Galen?

### MOSS of Oaks, and of other Trees: In the Apothecary shops, *Usnea*: German, *Mooss*: French, *Mousse*: Italian, *Mosco*.

<image-desc>Illustration of a thick, branching lichen or moss (Muscus Quercuum) typically found growing on the bark of oak trees.</image-desc>

By the name of "Moss" are signified the gray tufts of the Oak and other trees, adhering to the trees on the outside, or hanging from them; nevertheless, they are born from them or grow upon them without a root, without a flower, and without a seed.

However, Mosses differ among themselves in their place of birth, the tree producing them, their scent, the density or thinness of their "hair," and their shape and division. According to Dioscorides, Moss is found on the Cedar tree, the White Poplar, and the Oak. The best is from the Cedar, the next from the Poplar: and in general, that which is whitening and fragrant is more approved. Pliny, contrary to the opinion of almost everyone, commends the Oak-moss above the others.

It has an astringent power, being moderate in heat and cold: taken in a drink, it helps dysentery; used in a sitz-bath <note>original: "insessu"</note>, it helps ailments of the womb.

### MISTLETOE: German: Mistel: Belgian: Marenten: French: Guy: Italian: Vischio. INDIAN MISTLETOE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mistletoe plant (Viscum) showing its characteristic paired leaves and berries, growing as a parasite on a branch.</image-desc>

Pliny writes that Mistletoe is of that genus which, since they have no habitation of their own, live upon others; and since they cannot be produced in the earth, they are born in trees. You might call it a "parasite" <note>original: "Catillonem," literally a plate-licker or scrounger</note>, a snatcher of another's nourishment. We have it from Virgil that it stays green in winter, who sings thus in *Aeneid* Book 6:
> —As Mistletoe is wont in the woods
> in the winter cold
> To flourish with new leafage.

But we shall deal with this "parasite" in the Appendix. Here we only present the Mistletoe which Pena and Lobelius <note>Pierre Pena and Matthias de l'Obel, famous 16th-century botanists</note> depict and describe, noting it was brought from Indian regions. The circles of the leaves certainly move one to admiration, appearing as if pressed by a carving tool, smooth on both sides.

<column-break/>

### HOLM OAK TREE: German: Stecheichen. French: Ieuse & Iouse: Italian: Lecino, Elice.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Holm Oak (Ilex) branch with serrated, prickly leaves and small acorns.</image-desc>

The Holm Oak <term>Ilex: the evergreen or holly oak</term> is of the Oak family, an inhabitant of warm regions. From the monuments of the Ancients, we have it that one is fruit-bearing, another sterile; one Male, another Female; one tree-like, another low and shrubby; one larger, another smaller. The difference is observed most especially in the leaves, whether they are prickly or not prickly, broad or narrow.
The Holm Oak loves mountains and valleys, although Theophrastus writes that it does not grow in the plains. It is very frequent in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and the forests around Montpellier abound with it. Throughout all of Spain, the prickly variety grows most abundantly, while the non-prickly variety grows in Tuscany. We depict the Male here, intending to deal with the Female shortly.

---

### CORK-OAK, ARIA, WILD OAK, Female Holm Oak, Oak-Cork.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Phellodrys or Suberiquercus branch with lobed leaves and acorns.</image-desc>

*Phellodrys*, if you look at the meaning of the name <note>Greek: phellos (cork) + drys (oak)</note>, is a tree intermediate between the Cork and the Oak; therefore, since it shares the nature of both, you might not foolishly call it the *Oak-Cork*. Modern authors have observed five kinds of *Phellodrys*: two with falling leaves, three with dark green leaves. But these are varieties upon which we shall not labor to paint or describe. It suffices to have designated the nature of the tree from Theophrastus and Pliny.
That which the Arcadians call *Phellodrys*, says Theophrastus, is intermediate in nature between the Holm Oak and the Oak: and thus some have thought it to be the Female Holm Oak. It is softer than the Holm Oak, but harder and denser than the Oak: similar in leaf to both, but larger than the Holm Oak and smaller than the Oak: with fruit smaller than the Holm Oak, larger than the Oak, etc.

<column-break/>

### ACORN-BEARING SMILAX TREE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Smilax Glandifera (likely a type of oak) with dense foliage and acorns.</image-desc>

We shall deal with various types of *Smilax* <note>here referring to an oak-like tree, likely Quercus coccifera, rather than the modern vine genus</note> in this Book of Plants: but here only with the acorn-bearing kind. Theophrastus says it is a tree similar to the Holm Oak, yet with a prickly leaf, but softer and more deeply cut; its wood is not solid and dense like the Holm Oak, but soft for working; it keeps its leaves forever.
Dalechamps observed two kinds of *Smilax*: one which is tree-like, called the *Smilax* of the Arcadians by Theophrastus; the other low and shrubby, which grows in the territory of Montpellier and is wrongly called *Robur* <note>Hard Oak</note>. This grows on the hills looking toward the Rhone from Vienne of the Allobroges down to Arles. By a great error, as Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, 15th-century scholar</note> skillfully notes, some of the Moderns make *Smilax* the same as *Phellodrys*.

---

### CORK: German: Korkbaum: Belgian: Korckboom: French: Liege: Italian: Subro. [the tree & the bark]

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cork Oak (Suber) showing its thick, textured bark and acorns.</image-desc>

One Cork tree has a sharp leaf, another a round one: one is narrow-leaved, another broad-leaved, which we depict here. Clusius writes that these are only varieties, establishing only a single genus of Cork. The tree is a species of Holm Oak, with a larger and inferior acorn, a huge trunk, and a crown that stays green forever. Three layers of bark clothe it: the first is very thick, which is chosen for the stoppers of jars and almost all vessels, and it lifts the nets of fishermen against the weight of the lead. The second strengthens sandals and winter footwear. From the third, which is fine, shallow bowls are made, from which whatever is given to those with hectic fever is drunk with great benefit. It grows abundantly in France, Italy, and Spain. More on *Phellodrys* and Cork in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### BEECH: German: Buchbaum: Belgian: Boeckboom: French: Fau & Foueau, the fruit: Fayne: Italian: Fagio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Beech tree (Fagus) branch with oval leaves and its distinct triangular nuts (mast).</image-desc>

It has been noted before that this tree, called *Fagus* by the Latins, is confused by some with the *Phegos* or *Phagos* of the Greeks. A "properly called" acorn is not attributed to it, except by the Poets, to whom all things are permitted; some recognize it as an acorn-bearing tree, but with a triangular nut inside.
It loves mountains, and also descends into the plains, being frequent throughout all Germany. It flowers in March; the fruit ripens in September. Since the fertility of all trees alternates, that of the Beech alternates most of all.
Furthermore, the Beech-nut <note>original: "Fagea Glans"</note> is somewhat warm, and is a most welcome winter food for pigs, mice, and thrushes. From the wood, various vessels and instruments are made: and it lasts uncorrupted in water, for which reason it is fit for aquatic buildings. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several species of trees, including the parasitic mistletoe, various evergreen oaks such as the Holm Oak and Cork Oak, and the Beech tree, detailing their physical characteristics and practical uses.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS VIII.
### CONTAINING WILD TREES.

<margin>LINDEN: German: Linden; Belgian: Lindenboom; French: Til, Tillet, Tilleu; Italian: Tiglia.</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tilia (Linden) tree showing its full form with a thick trunk and rounded canopy.</image-desc>

It is called *Philyra* by the Greeks <note>original: "Philyra"</note>, but it is not the same as the *Phillyrea* <note>a type of evergreen shrub</note>, although some have confused the Linden with the Phillyrea, being deceived by the similarity of the names. Theophrastus and Pliny <note>ancient Greek and Roman naturalists</note> distinguish one as Male and another as Female. To the Male they attribute hard, yellow, knotty, and thicker wood; and indeed a thicker bark that is not at all flexible. To the Female they attribute a whiter and more flexible wood, as well as a whiter and more flexible bark. Furthermore, according to the same authors, the male is sterile and without flowers; the Female, however, both possesses flowers and produces fruit. We depict here the common Female variety, and we shall review several of its variations. The learned maintain that it is not so easy to guess which might be the "Male Linden" of the Ancients. More on this in the following sections.

### LINDEN WITH THE LARGEST LEAF.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tilia branch with large heart-shaped leaves and clusters of flowers/seeds attached to a leafy bract.</image-desc>

Theophrastus called the Linden "very hot," while Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German botanist</note> called it "hot." In our judgment, Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> says more accurately that it is temperate in heat, but somewhat drying and astringent, and in temperament almost similar to the Elm. The leaves, crushed and sprinkled with water, disperse swellings of the feet. The berries are highly praised for dysentery and other flows of the bowels. From the flowers, a water is distilled that is very useful for epilepsy, tremors of the heart, pains of the womb, kidney stones, and various other ailments. The membrane that lies between the bark and the wood <note>the inner bark or bast</note>, when soaked in water, is beneficial for burns. The charcoal is used for preparing gunpowder. The timber also has the greatest uses: for it is tough, easily cut, light and smooth, and is made even smoother by craft.

<column-break/>

<margin>ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE LINDEN, better expressing the bracts, flowers, and fruit.</margin>

<image-desc>Detailed woodcut of a Linden branch showing the characteristic long bracts (ligulas) from which the flower clusters emerge.</image-desc>

The Linden loves mountains and valleys, and rejoices most in watery mountains. It desires a rich and fertile soil; it prospers most in manured ground, while in dry and rocky places it grows with difficulty. Throughout the whole region of Germany, in the courtyards of cities and walls, it is held in high esteem because of the shade which—either by itself or arranged into arbors <note>original: "attegias"</note>—it provides to those walking or reclining in the summer time. And indeed, you would hardly see another tree in Germany, or perhaps even in all of Europe, which can compete with the Linden in topiary work <note>the art of clipping trees into shapes</note> and in that ample and wide-spreading vastness.
Furthermore, it buds a little before the Equinox; it flowers in May and June; but it ripens its fruit in August.

---

<margin>ELM: German: Ulme-baum; Belgian: Olmenboom; French: Orme; Italian: Olmo.</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ulmus (Elm) tree showing its tall, upright growth habit.</image-desc>

Theophrastus makes the Elm two-fold: that which is simply so called, and the Mountain Elm, which is larger and broader. Pliny has four differences, but these can be reduced to those two in the judgment of the learned. Thus, one is the Mountain Elm, which is taller and sterile; the other is the Field Elm, which is more shrub-like and bears fruit.
It grows in forests, mountains, and rocky places, as well as in rich and fertile fields; it is of easy growth near waters, and is well known to the French, Italians, and Germans. It buds among the first trees, ripens its seed in May, and turns its leaves soon after the summer solstice.
The leaves, branches, and bark have an astringent power, according to Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note>, and they have many things in common with the Linden family.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics, medicinal uses, and cultural significance of the Linden (Tilia) and Elm (Ulmus) trees in Europe. It highlights the Linden's use in ornamental gardening and the medicinal properties of its flowers and bark, while distinguishing between ancient classifications of "male" and "female" specimens.</summary>
<keywords>Linden, Elm, Tilia, Ulmus, botany, medicinal plants, topiary, Theophrastus, Pliny, forestry, 16th-century science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of trees, focusing on the Elm, Birch, Alder, Beech, and Poplar, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal virtues, and practical uses in carpentry.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### A FOREIGN FRUIT RESEMBLING THE EXCREMENT OF THE ELM.

<image-desc>Three botanical illustrations of seed pods or galls, showing various cross-sections and external textures, resembling the "excrement" or galls of an Elm tree.</image-desc>

We keep this in our treasury of natural things. It equals the size of a Chestnut and in some way resembles the little bladders or excrements <note>original: "excrementa" – here referring to galls or abnormal growths caused by insects</note> of the Elm.

To those things which were said previously regarding the powers of the Elm in general, we shall add that in the leaves, bark, and branches, there exists a power not only of thickening, but also of contracting and knitting together wounds. The moisture of the small sacs <note>the liquid found inside elm galls</note>, if lint-compresses soaked in it are applied, heals the intestinal hernias <note>original: "enterocelis"</note> of boys, and is also very useful in gouty conditions while the fluids are flowing. Finally, the wood of the Elm easily surpasses other trees in strength, after the Cornel tree; it is very useful for doors, presses, wine-presses, and wagons. Its shavings, when applied to ulcers, cleanse and fill them.

### BIRCH: Germ. Birckenbaum: Belg. Berckenboom: French. Boule, Bouleau: Ital. Biola, Bedula.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Birch tree branch (Betula) showing serrated leaves and hanging catkins.</image-desc>

They wish the Birch <note>Latin: "Betula"</note> to be named from "beating" <note>Latin: "Batuendo"</note>, as if it were "Batula," because children are beaten with it. It rejoices most in cold and watery places, and also in sandy ones, as well as on shady mountains; it is very frequent in Germany. The catkins <note>original: "Iuli"</note> come forth at the beginning of Spring; the leaves in April and May; the chaff-like seed in the catkins is dispersed by the wind in July.

The leaves warm, dissolve, thin, and wipe away. The water or juice flowing out in the spring when the bark is wounded or the trunk is bored, is very beneficial for those with dropsy, stones, and jaundice; it heals poorly affected internal organs, removes spots from the face, and renders cheeses safe from worms if the stomachs of cattle (from which the milk rennet is prepared) are first soaked in it. Finally, it can be used as a drink to quench thirst. From the branches are made baskets and hoops most approved for binding the largest vats. The trunks provide convenient wood for Carpenters and Saddlers. But the rods have always been terrible: formerly in the hands of the Lictors <note>Roman officers who carried bundles of rods as a symbol of power</note>, now in the common Schools.

### HOARY AND HAIRY ALDER.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a branch of Hoary Alder (Alnus incana) with broad, serrated leaves and small cone-like fruits.</image-desc>

It bears catkins and little nuts just like the common variety: but the color of the catkins is whiter, and the leaves are less round, more deeply serrated, and hairy and hoary underneath. We have observed it in various places: Geneva, Montbéliard by the Doubs; at Basel below the village of Huningue, by the Rhine, and elsewhere; but it is mostly low-growing.

Furthermore, the Alder, according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist</note>, manifestly dries; but in coldness and heat it is not far from the middle. However, the bark excels in its astringent power, and in place of a Gall-nut, it dyes with a black color. The leaves reduce tumors and extinguish inflammations; and they are conveniently placed under the feet by weary couriers. Its wood is greatly commended for the foundations of buildings.

<column-break/>

### HEDGE BEECH: Germ. Hagenbusch: Belg. Heester: French. Hestre: and by some, Charme.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Beech tree branch (Fagus) with oval leaves and bristly husks containing nuts.</image-desc>

It is for the most part taller than can be confined by the lowliness of common hedges. By some it is called Mountain Ash, by others Wild Elm, by some the Ash-tree, the <term>oxya</term> <note>Greek: ὀξύη – the ancient name for Beech</note>, and "bird's tongue." Pena and Lobel called it the male Linden; Schwenkfeld called it the Ash of Tragus; many call it the <term>Ostrys</term> or <term>Orya</term> of Theophrastus. Cesalpino, Mattioli, Tabernaemontanus and others call it the Hornbeam <note>French: "Charme"</note>. Gesner called it the Hedge Beech, and said it was more related to the Elm than the Beech: such is the wandering confusion of Writers regarding this tree.

It grows everywhere in woods and various hedges. It produces catkins in early Spring, and the female fruit in a leafy catkin in Summer. You would hardly find a harder wood.

### ALDER: Germ. Erlenbaum: Belg. Elsenboom. French. Aulne: Ital. Alno, Alano.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Common Alder (Alnus) branch showing leaves, male catkins, and female cone-like fruits.</image-desc>

Called *Alnus* either because it is nourished by the river <note>Latin: "ab amne alatur"</note>, or because it nourishes the things <note>Latin: "sara alat"</note> which grow more succulent under its cover. Neither Dioscorides nor Galen made mention of it; however, Theophrastus described it and said it was of one kind.

It rejoices in water, and is born almost nowhere else than in moist and marshy places, especially in cold and shady valleys at the banks of rivers, whence the Poet <note>Virgil, in the Georgics</note> says:
> By rivers the Willows, and in thick marshes the Alders,
> Are born.

It occurs everywhere in Germany and the surrounding Provinces; in France it is rarer; and in Italy rarer still. Regarding its powers, see the side of the following Table.

### POPLAR: Germ. Aspen, Aspenbaum: Belg. Popelaer: French. Peuplier: Ital. Popolo.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Poplar branch (Populus) with rounded, slightly lobed leaves.</image-desc>

According to Theophrastus and Pliny, the Poplar is threefold: Black, White, and Libyan, which is the *Cercis*, similar to the white poplar. The ancient Latins call both the Black and White poplar *Farfarum*. But Tragus, Solerius, Lonicer, and Harchius unskillfully confuse the Black with the White; and with no less a slip, Theophrastus writes that the Black can be converted into the White spontaneously and without art, and vice versa. For how could we allow that in trees which are distinct from each other not only in fruit, leaves, and scent, but also different in form and species? When, however, "Poplar" is said or written absolutely, the Black, which we depict here, is commonly understood.

It rejoices in water and well-watered meadows; it is well known in Germany, Spain, Italy, France, and England.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics, medicinal uses, and cultural lore of several common European trees, including the Elm, Birch, Alder, Beech, and Poplar. It highlights the confusion among ancient and contemporary authors regarding tree classification and notes the practical utility of their wood and extracts.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
->H 3<-
<note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in order.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Populus Alba branch with broad, lobed leaves and hanging catkins.</image-desc>

**WHITE POPLAR: German: *Vveiss Popel, Alberbaum*: French: *Aubeau, Aubel*: Italian: *Popolo bianco, Albero*.**

The leaves of the White Poplar differ greatly from those of the Black Poplar, and its whole appearance reveals it to be a different tree. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous 16th-century scholar</note> writes that it is called *Albara* in Italy because of its color. Indeed, whatever Antiquity has recorded regarding the Poplar seems to pertain to this species. Yet Pliny and Lonicerus <note>Adam Lonicer, a German botanist</note> certainly seem to have needed spectacles; while they correctly described the leaf as being two-colored, they claim it is white on the upper side and green underneath, whereas the opposite is clearly visible <note>The White Poplar is famous for having dark green tops and silvery-white, felt-like undersides</note>. With no less error, they attribute trembling leaves to this tree, which actually belong to the *Cercis* <note>The Aspen</note> to be discussed shortly. Nor do we see how Alciatus can be excused, who in his *Emblems* depicts the Black Poplar but calls it the White.

It shares the same native habitats as the preceding species and puts forth its buds and catkins <note>original: "iulos"</note> at the same time.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Populus Lybica branch with rounded, serrated leaves and catkins.</image-desc>

**LIBYAN POPLAR, THE *CERCIS* OF THEOPHRASTUS. German: *Aspen, Zitterpappel*: French: *Tremble*: Italian: *Popolo montano*.**

Theophrastus places the *Cercis* <note>A Greek name for a poplar-like tree</note> below both types of Poplar; we, along with Anguillara, Solerius, Mattioli, the *History of Lyon*, and others, consider this to be the Libyan Poplar of Pliny.

It delights in growing in marshy woods among Birches and loves the mountains; it is very familiar throughout all of Germany. It possesses the same medicinal properties as the others, but they are weaker.

The wood of all these, which is white, light, curled, and wavy, is fashioned by turners into tables, counting-boards, spoons, wooden shoes <note>term: "colopodia" - clogs or lasts for shoemaking</note>, and other items of that kind. The branches with leaves, harvested in October, serve as winter fodder for goats and sheep. The moisture that flows from the "gray hairs" <note>likely referring to the catkins or sap</note> of the Black Poplar removes warts, pimples, and skin growths, according to Pliny. From the drop which the Poplars bear on their leaves, bees make Propolis <note>term: "Propolis" - bee glue used to seal hives</note>.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Acer (Maple) branch with characteristic lobed leaves and winged seeds (samaras).</image-desc>

**MAPLE: German: *Ahorn*. Belgian: *Maeshoutenboom*: French: *Erable, Opier*: Italian: *Acero, Arefo*.**

Theophrastus identifies three kinds of Maple: *Sphendamnos, Carpinus, and Stagirita*. He says that *Sphendamnos* <note>Greek for Maple</note> differs from the Hornbeam <note>original: "Carpino"</note> in that the former has white and fibrous wood, while the latter is yellow and curled. Thus, even today, Maple is distinguished into the *White* and the *Yellow* or *Curled* varieties; some call the former the Male and the latter the Female.

The Maple delights in steep, wooded hills and mossy places, but it is also found on the plains, among hedges and thickets. It flowers in April and May, and ripens its fruit in Autumn.

The trunk rarely rises above the height of a man; the rest consists only of shoots and small branches, or certainly limbs that are neither large nor widely spread.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Populus Alba Folio Minore branch with smaller, deeply lobed leaves.</image-desc>

**WHITE POPLAR WITH SMALLER LEAVES.**

This illustration is from Lobelius, as the preceding ones were from Gesner and Camerarius. Furthermore, various authors hold various opinions on the "temperament" <note>The Galenic balance of hot/cold/moist/dry</note> of the Poplar. Amatus made it cold, but by a great error. To others it is hot in the third degree, to others only in the first. We agree with the latter, though we establish that the "eyes" <note>buds</note>, being fragrant, are hotter than the other parts. The flowers, buds, resin, and leaves are drying and consist of subtle parts; however, the leaves are less effective than the rest. We have shown in our *Universal History* that the "Poplar Ointment" <note>original: "Unguentum Populeum"</note> ought to be made from the buds of the Black Poplar. It is effective against all "hot" ailments when smeared on; applied to the nostrils or the temples, it induces sleep. The uses of the wood and the moisture flowing from its catkins will be explained on the side of the following table.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Populus Novi Orbis branch with large, heart-shaped leaves.</image-desc>

**POPLAR OF THE NEW WORLD.**

The shoots of this tree are somewhat flexible; from their knotted joints, a single leaf emerges from each stalk: round, thick, rigid, and broad. From these same joints also emerge very long thongs <note>catkins</note> crowded with many tiny berries, clearly in the manner of a Poplar, which is why our people gave this exotic tree its name. The *History of Lyon* displays the same under the name *Poplar of America*.

We shall add here only from Pliny that the Poplar is pleasing to vines, as it provides no shade due to its "playing" <note>quivering</note> leaves. And for those holding a Poplar twig in their hand, chafing <note>original: "intertriginem"</note> is least to be feared.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Acer Monspessulanum branch with small, three-lobed leaves and winged seeds.</image-desc>

**MONTPELIER MAPLE.**

This is a tree of moderate height with fairly spread branches; the bark is somewhat purplish, the leaf similar to the common Maple but divided into only three points or angles, thick, veined, hanging from a long stalk, and situated at equal intervals on both sides. The fruit is twin; two membranes clinging together, similar to the wings of flies. Pena and Lobelius call it a relative of the Maple, though it is less known in the North.

The common Maple is frequent in Switzerland, Silesia, Lorraine, Lombardy, and Savoy; and especially around Geneva, where it is pruned for the vines called *Hutins*, and contributes greatly to supporting them, which is its chief use. The wood is of lasting duration and becomes more curled with age; it is then dedicated to the making of more elegant furniture.

It includes corrections of classical authors like Pliny and notes on the "Poplar of the New World" (America).</summary>

# OF PLANTS

### THE GREATER MAPLE: Called by some the Plane Tree: German: *Teutsch Ahorn*; French: *Plasne*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Maple tree branch with broad, lobed leaves and winged seeds (samaras).</image-desc>

We recognize three species of Maple, as do Gesner, the *History of Lyon*, and Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a famous German physician and botanist</note>; they say this Greater Maple is the most common. It delights in moist and very high mountains: it grows among Ash trees in rich, thick soil. It is found in Burgundy, near Blamont (the fortress of the Duke of Württemberg), at Geneva on Mount Salève, at Basel near the marksmen’s field, and in various other places.

It flowers and ripens its fruit at the same time as the common variety mentioned before. The wood is sought after by cabinetmakers and table-makers for various utensils; it is established from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 2, that the Trojan Horse was constructed from it.

> When now, he says, with maple beams joined together
> The Horse stood; etc. <note>original Latin: "Cùm iam, ait, trabibus contexit acernis Staret Equus"</note>

### THE ASH TREE: German: *Asch, Aschbaum*; Belgian: *Eschenboom*; French: *Fresne*; Italian: *Frassino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ash tree branch with pinnate leaves and clusters of seeds.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher, the "Father of Botany"</note> makes two kinds of it: one tall and stately; the other lower, which is rougher, harder, and more yellow. Thus the more recent authors distinguish them into the Greater and Lesser; Male and Female; sterile and fruitful (which would be the female); and finally into the Mountain and Field varieties. However, Ruellius, Lonicer, and Ryff mistakenly provide the illustration of the Rowan <note>The "Bird-catcher's Service Tree"</note> in place of the Ash.

It delights in moist places, equally in mountains and plains, and in cold as well as warmer regions: it is quite frequent in Montpellier, Geneva, Basel, and Zurich. It is easy to work with, sprouts quite rapidly, and yields its seed at harvest time; yet not all trees bear fruit everywhere. Concerning its use and powers, see what follows.

### THE ROUND-LEAFED ASH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ash variety with more rounded leaflets.</image-desc>

"Bird’s Tongue"—the fruit or seed of the Ash—is greatly celebrated by the Arabs and recent authors for stimulating Venus <note>Used as an aphrodisiac</note>. Indeed, the use of Ash wood is so extensive that Pliny did not hesitate to write that nature created the Ash above others for the sake of its most abundant material; for it is not only very tough and hard, but also most obedient in every kind of work. Thus it is most convenient for pikes, saddles, counting-boards, tables, wagons, spoons, cups, and other furniture and instruments of every kind. This applies to all its species and varieties. In some places, the foliage is used in winter to sustain sheep and goats. Finally, we have shown at length in our *Great History* that "aerial honey" (rightly called Manna) settles like pitch upon the leaves and is collected from them.

<column-break/>

### THE PLANE TREE: German: *Fræmbd Ahorn*; French: *Plane*; Italian & Spanish: *Platano*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Plane tree branch with large, deeply lobed leaves and spherical seed heads.</image-desc>

The Plane is a large, ample tree, similar in its broad spread to a Walnut tree; it was formerly held in great delight by kings and the wealthy. Whence we read in Herodotus that Xerxes <note>The Persian King</note> presented one—under which he had spent an entire day without necessity—with a golden necklace, and entrusted it to be guarded by one of the "Immortals" <note>The elite guard of the Persian Empire</note>.

It delights in well-watered and marshy places and the banks of waters, being an inhabitant of various provinces of Asia. But in our world <note>Europe</note> it is quite rare; it is found only in the gardens of the wealthy among the Italians, Spanish, Sicilians, and those of Constantinople. Thus the orchards of Florence have beautiful specimens, as do the gardens of Rome, Bologna, Padua, and the city of Naples. Truly, by a foul error, it is confused by some with the Maple, the Lime tree, and other trees. More on this in the Appendix.

### THE NARROWER AND SMALLER-LEAFED ASH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ash variety with narrower and smaller leaflets.</image-desc>

The painter has expressed this variety of Ash—from a branch which we keep among our natural specimens—with less skill. Might it be the *Ornus* <note>Manna Ash</note> of Columella, whose leaves he says are rather long, narrower, and a darker green?

Furthermore, the leaves and bark of the Ash are moderately warm and composed of fine parts; the seed, however, heats and dries in the third degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of humors</note>. The leaves and bark boiled in wine, if drunk, clear the liver and spleen of obstructions and strengthen those organs; it is effective for dropsy and cures pains in the side. Water distilled from the bark of the Ash is uniquely helpful for stones and the "royal disease" <note>Jaundice</note>. Many also prepare cups from Ash wood, from which, if one drinks constantly, they assert the spleen is thinned. More in the following.

### THE SPINDLE TREE: German: *Spindelbaum*; Belgian: *Papenhout*; French: *Fusain, Fusillon, Bonnet de prebstre*; Italian: *Fusano, Fusaro*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spindle tree branch with small oval leaves and characteristic four-lobed fruits.</image-desc>

*Euonymus*—that is, "of good omen"—is so named by antiphrasis <note>Naming something by its opposite; the plant was considered unlucky or poisonous</note>, and by some called *Anonymos*. By others it is called *Tetragonia* and *Quadratoria*, both because the seeds are contained in a four-angled pod, and because the branches, adorned with reddish lines stretching through the green bark, appear four-angled, which is peculiar to this tree.

It is absent from no region, whether hot or cold, growing along roads and the edges of fields: in living hedges, thickets, and woods among thorny plants, occurring everywhere in both flat and elevated places.

It flowers in April, and sometimes in May; it ripens its fruit in September, from which a triple color is made: yellow, green, and tawny. Let the reader seek the rest from what follows.

<keywords>Maple, Ash tree, Plane tree, Spindle tree, Manna, medicinal wood, Trojan Horse, Xerxes, botanical classification, European flora</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
## BROAD-LEAVED SPINDLE. SPINDLE WITH DEEP-RED FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branch of Evonymus latifolia with broad leaves and small flowers/fruits.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note>, who describes it at length, calls it the *First broad-leaved Pannonian Spindle*. We ourselves observed this variety in the Medical Garden at Padua.

The common Spindle, however, grows among the French and Italians in mountains, woods, and hedgerows; it is also very familiar in Germany, so much so that, if we believe Lobelius, it is absent from no region, whether hot or cold, appearing along hedges, roads, and the edges of fields. It flowers in April and May. As Autumn approaches, the four-cornered pods are tinged with a purple color until they turn completely red; later, they break open of their own accord into four parts in a cross-shape, and hang gaping in this way, displaying their little berries—a not unpleasant sight—well into Winter.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Evonymus flore phoeniceo, showing a branch with serrated leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

This is a small tree taller than a man, whose trunk and branches are rough with small bumps; the leaves are saw-toothed. The flowers are like the other common Spindle, but the *Coptos* <note>A specific variety or local name</note> grows in the wooded mountains of both Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note> and also in Moravia; elsewhere it is quite rare.

Whether it is harmful to livestock, as Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" from Ancient Greece</note> wrote of his own variety, is not yet agreed upon among writers. However, if three or four fruits are given to a human to be swallowed, they purge through the lower and upper parts <note>i.e., they act as both a laxative and an emetic</note>. They also soften and dissolve swellings when applied externally. Boiled in lye, they kill nits and lice, and dye the hair a yellow color. Finally, various vessels and instruments, women's spindles, fly-swatters, and larder tools are commonly made from its wood.

---

### SYRINGA: German: *Siringbaum*: French: *Syringue*: The "Philadelphus" flower of Apollodorus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Syringa (Lilac) branch with large, broad leaves and a cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

Two types are established: namely the one with the white flower, which is depicted here, and the one with the blue flower, of which more shortly. Some have thought this white one to be the "Philadelphus" flower of Apollodorus mentioned in Athenaeus; in the judgment of others, it is the *Ostrys* of Theophrastus. Nor is it lacking that notable mark of the fruit, which is similar to Barley; yet this opinion does not please everyone, nor does it please us.

It is cultivated in many gardens of Italy—at Padua, Bologna, Ferrara—and especially in the garden of the Duke of Florence. We also cultivated it in the garden of the Most Serene Prince at Montbéliard, having had it brought from Besançon. It flowers in April and May. Nothing regarding its use or qualities has become known up to this point.

<column-break/>

### BLUE-FLOWERED SYRINGA, or LILAC.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering Lilac branch with heart-shaped leaves and dense flower panicles.</image-desc>

Matthiolus says that the most distinguished man Ogier de Busbecq <note>A 16th-century Flemish diplomat</note> brought this plant with him from Constantinople, where he served as Ambassador for the Emperor Ferdinand I to Suleiman, the Emperor of the Turks, for seven continuous years, under this name *Lilac*. But Clusius, Pena, Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, and the *History of Lyon* have noted that he made a great error in thinking it was the "Ben-nut" <note>original: "Glande unguentariam"</note>.

Cesalpino labels it the *Oriental Privet* and the *Blue Jasmine of the Arabs*. Could it be the tree called by some *Fox-tail*? It was formerly brought from Africa, where it is very frequent, and is called "Syringa" in the local language. Today, however, many of the more refined gardens of Belgium and Germany nurture it. It flowers at the same time as the other.

---

### AGNUS CASTUS: German: *Keuschbaum*: French: *Agnus castus*: Italian: *Agno casto*, *Vitice*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Agnus Castus (Vitex) showing upright flower spikes and palmate leaves.</image-desc>

It is a wonder that not only pharmacists but also physicians have called this shrub *Agnus castus* <note>Chaste-Lamb</note>, since *Castus* in Latin means the same thing as *Agnos* in Greek, and vice versa <note>The name is a linguistic redundancy: both words mean "chaste"</note>. There are two kinds: one with a leaf that is not saw-toothed, which we depict here, and one with a saw-toothed leaf, of which more follows. Statius labeled it the "Chaste Tree." It was called "Chaste" because in the *Thesmophoria* <note>An ancient Greek festival in honor of Demeter</note>, matrons vowing chastity would use it for their bedding. It was also called *Lygos*, as if it were a wicker-twig, because of the toughness of its shoots.

It delights in marshy places and is cultivated in the more famous gardens of Germany, Belgium, France, and Italy; just as, by our care, it is also kept in the garden of the Most Serene Prince at Montbéliard. It flowers in June; the seed ripens in September.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE CHASTE TREE, with saw-toothed leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Agnus Castus with serrated (folio ferrato) palmate leaves.</image-desc>

It is hot and dry in the third degree, according to Galen, and possesses much astringency. According to the dictates of Dioscorides, the fruit, when drunk, helps those bitten by serpents, as well as those with spleen complaints or dropsy. It creates an abundance of milk, encourages menstruation, and <term>dissipates the seed</term> <note>original: "genituram exsoluit" — believed to reduce sexual desire</note>. A decoction of the herb and seed, used in a sitz-bath, helps with afflictions of the womb. The seed drunk with pennyroyal, or used as a fumigant or suppository, moves the monthly cleansings; and when smeared on, it dissolves headaches. With vinegar and oil, it is dripped onto the heads of those suffering from lethargy or frenzy. Furthermore, the leaves, both as a fumigant and when strewn on the floor, put venomous creatures to flight, and are used as an aid against the bites of venomous beasts, etc. From what has been said before, it is held to extinguish sexual desire in women.

It highlights the Chaste tree's historical use in maintaining vows of virginity and its various applications in treating snakebites and reproductive ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Spindle tree, Evonymus, Lilac, Syringa, Agnus Castus, Vitex, Busbecq, medicinal herbs, chastity, botany, 16th-century medicine</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

<margin>
**Willow** : German *Weiden* : *Weidenbaum* : Belgian *Wilge*.
French *Saule* & *Saulce* : Italian *Salice*.
</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall willow tree with slender, pointed leaves and a thick trunk.</image-desc>

### The Willow

According to Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note>, one Willow is Black and the other is White. Pliny identifies three kinds: the Black, the White, and the Helix <note>likely a reference to a twisting or "spiral" variety</note>. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of 'De Materia Medica'</note> writes of the Willow as if there were only one species. More recent authors list various differences: Tragus and Matthiolus identify four, while others list more or fewer. These distinctions are drawn from the place where they grow, their use, the color of the bark, their size, the appearance of the flower, the leaves, the brittleness or flexibility of the twigs, the fruit, or the pith.

We depict here the Greatest and tree-like Willow, which is white and hairy, and has brittle twigs. In our judgment, this is the White Willow of Theophrastus. It grows in damp places and well-watered meadows; from it are made long poles for gardens and vineyards.

---

### The Slenderer Willow, with smaller leaves smooth on both sides and brittle twigs.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a willow branch with smaller, more delicate leaves and catkins.</image-desc>

This Willow is sufficiently known from its Title and Image. Here, therefore, we shall treat the Habitat, Season, planting, and use of Willows in general.

Willows love water, but they also grow on mountains. They bud among the first of the trees; they grow quickly and die quickly. Among their kind are those which are most conveniently planted by any method of sowing, and once transplanted, they can endure very well. They are also of such a nature that they are not planted for their own sake, but for the sake of other things, especially vineyards <note>Willow twigs were commonly used as ties for grapevines</note>.

Furthermore, the fruit, leaves, bark, and juice of the Willow, on the authority of Dioscorides, have an astringent power. The leaves with the branches, spread out in bedrooms, cool the air; and when boiled in water, they are beneficial in footbaths for those suffering from fevers.

---

### The Dwarf Narrow-leafed Willow, ash-colored on the underside.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, shrub-like willow with narrow leaves.</image-desc>

In this kind, as noted by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note>, the twigs are more slender, usually a foot long, sometimes only nine inches, straight, flexible, and covered in a yellowish bark. The leaves are an inch long, narrow in the manner of cultivated Flax leaves: green on the upper side, but ash-colored on the underside, and when they are still young, they are entirely hoary <note>covered in white, downy hairs</note>. The flower, as in the common variety, is yellowish, born in a small, short, and soft spike <note>a catkin</note> before the leaves, and later dissolves into a white down. The root is the thickness of a finger, slanted, black, and provided with thin fibers.

It grows in wet, harvested woods below Frankfurt am Main.

<column-break/>

### The Willow with narrow and very long leaves, curled, whitish underneath, and green above.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a willow branch with very long, narrow, and slightly curled leaves.</image-desc>

A greenish or ash-colored bark covers the twigs; these are very long and simple, provided with no side-shoots, and are very compliant <note>flexible</note>. The leaves, such as are described above, crowd the branches in a dense line. Is this the 6th kind of Willow in the *History of Lyon*, which Dalechampius thinks is the *Eleagnus*? Or is it the Amerina of Pliny?

This also delights in damp places and well-watered meadows; and because it produces very long twigs without side-shoots, if they are flexible, they are woven into baskets, small hampers, winnowing fans, chairs, and reclining couches. The Artist neglected to depict the curliness of the leaves.

---

### The Willow Clusters or Catkins, Roses, and Scaly Heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing various reproductive parts of the willow, including catkins and rose-like galls.</image-desc>

This kind of Willow produces catkins <note>original: "nucamenta"</note> that are long and clustered, made of many little vessels like needles, which, gaping open into two little hulls, display a downy fluff. However, mossy little flowers precede these; as they begin to fall away, a certain cottony excrement <note>This refers to a "willow rose" gall caused by insects</note> grows at the tip of the catkin, more than an inch long, smooth, oblong, and resembling wool in every way. In the center of this, a very small, whitish kind of insect is found, etc. Concerning all these things individually, we write more fully in our *Universal History* and in the *Appendix*.

It occurs everywhere in the meadows and watered ditches of Basel, Breisach, Geneva, Montbéliard, and Yverdon.

---

### The Low Creeping Narrow-leafed Willow of Lobelius and Dodonæus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping willow variety with small leaves and visible root system.</image-desc>

In the heaths of the Antwerp region, it creeps with stems a hand-breadth or a hand-and-a-half long, with the leaf of the first *Rhamnus* <note>Buckthorn</note>, mossy flowers, and the bitter taste of the Willow. Thus Lobelius describes it in few words; Dodonæus, however, provides the Figure without a description.

To those things said above regarding the Medical use of the Willow, we shall add: not only are the dining rooms of those suffering from accidents or burning fevers strewn with Willow branches for the sake of cooling, but sticks are also made from the wood for scraping, with which the roughness of the tongue may be scraped and cleaned—though they labor in vain who do not extinguish the internal fire <note>A metaphorical warning that external hygiene cannot cure internal illness</note>.

<summary>This page details several varieties of Willow (Salix), discussing their physical characteristics, habitats near European cities like Frankfurt and Basel, and their practical and medicinal uses, including basket-weaving and fever reduction.</summary>
<keywords>Willow, Salix, botany, medicinal plants, basketry, catkins, Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, Clusius, Frankfurt, Basel</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA" — A common Renaissance title for botanical works providing both illustrations and descriptive sketches.</note>

### THE THINNER YELLOW WILLOW, CULTIVATED, For Wicker-work.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender willow tree (Salix lutea) with long, narrow leaves and visible root structure.</image-desc>

This genus of Willow grows into beautiful trees, whose shoots <note>vimen: a flexible twig or osier</note> are better for tying vines and similar tasks than any other known to us: for such is the flexible toughness of the cut branches that it rightly deserves to be called the "wicker-willow" <note>vimines</note> by way of excellence. It is covered in a bark the color of egg-yolk <note>vitellini coloris</note> and is bitter to the taste. The leaves are spaced out, sharp-pointed, about a span long and half an inch wide, shining with a gloss on the upper side, smooth, and hoary; on the underside they are somewhat hairy, with small teeth notched around the edges.

This tree, if any other, is cultivated everywhere for weaving vines and garden hedges. Is it the "White Willow" of Theophrastus, the "Yolk-colored" of Pliny, or the "Greek Willow" of Columella? A variety of this is found that is similar in all respects, but with a much paler bark.

<column-break/>

### THE WILD FRAGILE WILLOW, with Almond-like leaves: with and without ear-shaped appendages.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a willow branch with broader, almond-shaped leaves and small catkins.</image-desc>

This wild Willow is covered with a dark red bark, more rarely white, endowed with a powerful astringency and a slight bitterness. The leaves are long, moderately wide, and pointed: green and smooth both above and below; at their short stalk, two notched "ears" <note>auriculae: stipules or small leaf-like appendages at the base of the leaf</note> are attached. The thinner twigs can hardly bear being bent unless they are twisted; the smaller ones snap.

This grows on the sandy banks of rivers that rush with a headlong, swirling course: such as by the Rhine at Basel in more than one place, and everywhere around Montbéliard.

---

<column-break/>

### THE RED WILLOW, LEAST FRAGILE, with long narrow leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a red willow (Salix rubra) with very narrow, elongated leaves and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

The bark of this tree is intensely red: the leaves are oblong and sharp, smooth on both sides but somewhat whitening underneath, notched with small teeth on both sides. The shoot is long and, like inner bark <note>liber</note>, compliant. It varies occasionally, with a less red bark and a somewhat broader leaf.

It is cultivated everywhere at the edges of meadows and gardens, and is sometimes found wild. It is of great use wherever something must be tied.

It is the "Black Willow" of Theophrastus, and the "Reddish Greek Willow": and the same as the "Purple Wicker-willow" of Pliny; the "Sabine" and "Amerian" of Columella. The "Red Wicker Willow" of Tragus. The "Red Willow" of Mattioli. The "Phoenician" of the History of Lyon. The "Crimson Sabine" of Tabernaemontanus. Is it perhaps the "French Willow" of Cordus?

<column-break/>

### THE BROAD-LEAVED WILLOW, HAIRY UNDERNEATH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved willow (Salix latifolia) with oval leaves and prominent catkins.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are a span, or a span and a half long, a quarter-foot or even a span in width, and veined: the underside is hoary and hairy, the upper side green, with an astringent taste without bite or bitterness: the stalk is half an inch long, to which ear-shaped appendages <note>stipules</note> embracing the stem are often attached. It produces "kittens" <note>catulos: catkins</note> full of saffron-colored stamens; which we have painted separately with skill: these are followed in clusters of receptacles by a certain white woolly down. The shoots are quite thick, covered in a hoary, hairy, bitter bark, knotty and fragile: sometimes covered as if with soot.

It is produced in thin, sandy, and stony soil, but wet, at the edges of torrents and in shady woods; frequent at Basel and Geneva, as well as in the "Labyrinth" garden at Montbéliard.

---

<column-break/>

### THE BROAD-LEAVED WILLOW, NOT HAIRY, with Galls.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved willow branch featuring several spherical galls (Galla) on the leaves.</image-desc>

There is also another kind of broad-leaved Willow, whose leaves do not reach the great size of the previous one, but are equal only to the medium ones of that kind, and saw-toothed: but they are not hairy above or below, nor are they whitening, but green with a light smoothness: the bark covering the shoot is black, and for that reason, if the leaves were not broad, it could be referred to the "Black Willow" of Theophrastus. We observed it at Lyon with "pills" <note>pilulis: galls caused by insects</note> on the leaves.

<column-break/>

### THE DWARF BROAD-LEAVED WILLOW OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dwarf broad-leaved willow (Salix pumila) with a thick, woody root and small, upright branches.</image-desc>

The grassy and open ridges of mountains, he <note>referring to the botanist Carolus Clusius</note> says, nourish dwarf Willows, which have twigs the thickness of the little finger, spread on the ground, a foot long, sometimes even larger, provided with frequent small branches that rise upward and emerge among the grasses: they are beset with leaves nearly an inch long, green and shining above, grayish underneath. They bear on their tender branches soft spikes of little flowers, which are followed by small heads, as in the larger and broad-leaved Willow. The root is remarkably thick considering the thinness of the plant, etc.

It covers varieties ranging from the tall yellow willow used in viticulture to the dwarf species found in mountainous regions.</summary>

<keywords>Willow, Salix, wicker-work, viticulture, Basel, Montbéliard, Geneva, Theophrastus, Pliny, Columella, Clusius, catkins, galls, botany</keywords>
