# OF PLANTS

<column-break/>

### DWARF WILLOW WITH LEAVES SMOOTH ON BOTH SIDES; and Reddish Bark.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small willow plant with slender branches and pointed leaves, showing roots at the base.</image-desc>

This plant has twigs about a span or a span and a half long <note>A "span" is roughly 9 inches</note>, covered in a reddish bark: from which thin fibers sometimes emerge, by which it takes root again. The leaves along the branches are half an inch to an inch long, about a third of an inch wide, ending in a slight point, and smooth on both sides. The little heads <note>catkins</note> are large in proportion to the plant, clinging together like clusters of grapes; opening into two curved husks, they display a snowy white down.

<column-break/>

### ROUND-LEAVED DWARF WILLOW.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a willow with rounded, oval leaves and small catkins at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

This Willow hardly raises itself a span from the ground, provided with reddish branches which are for the most part bare; however, many very elegant leaves crown their tips, somewhat resembling the leaves of the Cotoneaster <note>a flowering shrub in the rose family</note>, being somewhat thick, stiff, wrinkled, turning greyish underneath and dark green on the upper part, with hidden heads at the base of the stalks, and a catkin sitting in its own private woolly furrow.

To those things which were said before regarding the use and virtues of the Willow, we shall add here: that the catkins and fruit of the Willow, when mixed into the fodder of cattle, fatten them. And some, as <term>Theophrastus Paracelsus</term> <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> notes, have held the juice of Willow leaves (for that longed-for metamorphosis of metals into gold), but with no success.

---

<column-break/>

### THE SAFSAF OF THE SYRIANS: ARNABO: ZARNABUM: Zerumbeth: Eleagnus: A species of Willow.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a woody shrub or small tree with serrated leaves and clusters of small flowers or fruit.</image-desc>

A certain peculiar species of Willow grows in Aleppo <note>in modern-day Syria</note>, called *Safsaf* by the inhabitants, which is similar to the Birch in its trunk, foliage, and branches. <term>Rauwolf</term> <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant</note>, who describes it at length, says it not only approaches the *Eleagnus* of Theophrastus, but can even be considered an *Eleagnus*. In his judgment, it is the *Arnabo* of <term>Aegineta</term> <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Greek medical writer</note>, and the *Zarnab* and *Zarnabum* of the Arabs, and even their *Zurumbeth*. Now, *Arnabo* is among the aromatics, and is of a hot and dry faculty in the third degree, similar to Cassia and Carpesium. But the unwary must be warned that *Safsaf* and *Saffas* <note>likely referring to Sassafras</note> are very different things.

<column-break/>

### THE CALAF OR BAN OF ALPINO.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with upright stems and elongated, lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

If <term>Alpino</term> <note>Prospero Alpini, a Venetian physician and botanist</note> is to be believed, this is a kind of Willow; and <term>Belon</term> <note>Pierre Belon, a French explorer and naturalist</note> also writes that the *Chalef* is a species of Willow growing in damp places. In its leaves it is somewhat similar to the Willow, but much larger, being both longer and wider. Its flowers are certain oblong white globules, growing on the stem near the roots of the leaves: it puts forth as many flowers as there are leaves on the tree. It grows to the size of the Chaste Tree, with many straight branches or shoots.

It is found in Egypt and grows in damp places. <margin>According to Alpino, who attributes remarkable powers to it.</margin>

---

<column-break/>

### THE GARB OF THE MOORS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small tree with a thick trunk and dense foliage of lobed leaves.</image-desc>

This tree is quite spreading, yet does not rise very high: the bark is a pale yellowish color, as are the leaves, which are about a span long and two fingers wide, indented around the edges like the leaves of Orach.

Rauwolf, the author of the description, denies having seen the fruit or flower, though he classifies it as a kind of Willow; he says, however, that the outer twigs are too tender and brittle to be used for wickerwork.

It is called *Garb* by the Arabs and Ethiopians, and *Far* by the Persians. Indeed, the *Gatab* of <term>Avicenna</term> <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> is the Willow: whence Avicenna attributes the same powers to his *Garab* as he does to the Willow.

<column-break/>

### GALE, THE FRAGRANT SHRUB OF THE NORTHERNERS; The Eleagnus of Cordus; The Chamaeleagnus of Dodoens.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a shrub with small, narrow leaves and clusters of catkins or cones at the branch tips.</image-desc>

This is a woody shrub, full of twigs, rarely reaching a cubit in height <note>about 18 inches</note>, divided into many branches, with bark that is reddish, inclining to a chestnut color, and smooth: the leaves somewhat approach the small Willow, and are smooth, hoary, and some of them are serrated. On the ends of the branches sit little heads like catkins, of a chestnut color. The bark is bitter, not without astringency; the wood is white, etc. Thus <term>Dodoens</term> <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> describes it. <margin>In Belgian: *Gale*. In Pliny: *Wild Rhus*.</margin>

It grows on shady heaths and in woody groves, being not uncommon among the Brabanters and Flemings. It flowers in May and June, and perfects its seed in August. By the French it is called *Royal Piment*; by the Flemings *Gagel*; and by the Scots, among whom it also grows in wet places: *Gale* <note>Sweet Gale or Bog Myrtle</note>. Its use will be handed down alongside the following table.

<keywords>Willow, Salix, Safsaf, Arnabo, Calaf, Garb, Sweet Gale, Rauwolf, Avicenna, Paracelsus, botany, medicinal plants</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.
# THE MAMBU TREE, GARCIA’S TABAXIR. THE MAMBU TREE, ACOSTA’S TABAXIR.

<note>The header refers to Garcia de Orta and Cristóbal Acosta, two pioneering 16th-century physicians who studied Indian medicine.</note>

*Tabaxir* <note>original: "Tabasheer"</note> is a Persian word, taken from the Persian language by Avicenna and other Arabs, and it designates nothing other than a milky juice, liquid, or moisture hardened in some place. By that name, the Arabs, Turks, and Persians understand a hardened juice which they hold in great value, and buy for an equal weight of silver, using it for wounds of the penis and testicles, and also against dysentery and cholera-like afflictions.

*We shall soon treat the tree from which it is collected: however, let it be permitted here to add something regarding the Gale shrub <note>Sweet Gale or Bog Myrtle</note>, of which we spoke before.* The whole shrub is exceedingly hot and dry: it drenches dining rooms with a sweet scent: it is boiled into beer in the absence of Hops: and placed between garments, it protects them from moths and worms.

The tree in which *Tabaxir* is produced, according to Garcia, is sometimes large and tall like a Poplar, sometimes smaller: having branches that are for the most part upright and marked by frequent nodes, with a leaf longer than that of an Olive. Between the individual internodes <note>the space between joints</note> a liquid, called *Tabaxir*, is generated: yet not all branches contain that moisture, but only those produced in *Bisnager*, *Baticala*, and part of the Province of *Malabar* <note>Regions in Southern India</note>. The inhabitants call the branches of the tree having that juice **Mambo** <note>Bamboo</note>: and the liquid itself **Sacar Mambu**, as if "Sugar of Mambo." The illustrations of Garcia and Acosta differ greatly from one another; therefore, since we do not know which is better, we present both.

---

### HALIMUS: French *Blanche putain*: Italian *Bidone*: CLUSIUS’S HALIMUS.

<note>Halimus refers to Atriplex halimus, or Sea Purslane.</note>

Some think the *Halimus* of the Ancients is entirely unknown to us: but Cordus writes more correctly that it is found, not by chance, on the German coast. Clusius proposes three kinds of Halimus: the first of which is depicted here and is, in the judgment of the more learned, the *Halimus* or *Halimum* of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny. We consider the second to be the same as Sea Purslane. For the third, let his own *History* be consulted.

Here it must be noted that both Pliny and some of the more recent writers have confused *Halimus* with *Alimus*: but wrongly, since *Halimus* is believed to be so named because it is a maritime vegetable, whence some have called it *Halmurida* <note>from the Greek 'halmuros', meaning salty</note>: whereas *Alimus* without the aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note> is the Asphodel, and in the opinion of some, a herb so named because it keeps away hunger <note>from the Greek 'a-limos', meaning 'without hunger'</note>.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPIUS’S HALIMUS: COLIC HERB: *l'Herbe du masclou* in Toulouse.

The ancient Halimus of Dalechampius, or *Herba du Masclou*, according to the *History of Lyon*, is cultivated in the gardens of Toulouse: and also grows spontaneously in hedges: especially near a village three miles distant from the city, which they call *Saint Agne* <note>original: "Sainct Heurens"</note>: in a lean, rough, high place. Thus Dalechampius says in his notes on Pliny, that both kinds of Halimus, the wild and the mild, grow in Toulouse. The people of Toulouse grind a handful of the Halimus leaves and administer them in white wine, with the greatest relief for colic pain and griping of the bowels, from which the name was given to the plant. The Portuguese receive the tender tops of the former Halimus into their food, just as they do with Buckthorn.

*The powers and properties of Halimus, and other things pertaining to it, will be handed down in the Appendix.*

---

# ON THE IMAGES AND OUTLINE
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS IX.
### CONTAINING CONIFEROUS AND RESIN-BEARING TREES.

**FEMALE FIR: German: *Thannenbaum*; Belgian: *Danneboom*; French: *Auet, Sapin*; Italian: *Abeto*.**

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a tall, slender coniferous tree (Abies foemina) showing its characteristic upright growth habit.</image-desc>

Neither Dioscorides nor Galen <note>Two of the most influential physicians and botanists of antiquity.</note> made mention of the Fir anywhere in their census of trees; Pliny, in the judgment of Jean Ruel, confuses it with the Palm. To Theophrastus, however, one Fir is "Male" and another "Female," and they differ greatly from one another. For in the Male, the leaves are sharper, more stinging, and more curved; the wood is tougher, harder, and fuller of marrow <note>pith or heartwood</note>, and the whole tree appears to the writer to be of a meaner aspect. Furthermore, in the Male, a few kernels are found in the forepart, while in the Female, there are none at all.

It is almost exclusively a tree of the mountains, and it grows successfully in both their shaded and sunny spots. Various provinces of Germany possess very beautiful ones; Virginia <note>likely referring to the New World colonies</note> has the tallest; and the Harz Forest has those most excellent for the firmness of their wood. More on this in the *Appendix*.

**THE SPRUCE OF THE LATINS: German: *Schvvarz Thannenbaum*; French: *Pesse, Pin, Garipole*; Italian: *Pezzo*.**

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a spruce tree (Picea), similar in form to the Abies but with denser foliage.</image-desc>

It is agreed among the learned that the "Spruce of the Latins" is the "Male Fir" of Theophrastus. However, it is also sufficiently well known that the Spruce of the Latins is not the *Peuce* <note>Greek: πεύκη, usually referring to the Pine</note> of the Greeks, of which we shall speak soon. Hieronymus Bock <note>original: "Tragus"</note>, who distinguished the Fir into White and Red (or Black), makes the Female the White, and this one the Red or Black.

It loves mountains and cold, as Pliny says; this is a funereal tree, which in former times was placed at doors as a sign of mourning. Nevertheless, it sometimes descends into the plains. Carolus Clusius writes that it is very frequent in the Vienna woods, and Conrad Gessner notes that the Zurich forests abound with it. We ourselves have observed it in the greatest abundance in the Burgundian mountains called the *Franche-Montagne*. It is, if any other tree be so, especially subject to the most venomous caterpillars.

<column-break/>

**THE FEMALE FIR WITH BRANCHES, CATKINS, Flowers, Julus-cones, Cones, Scales, and Seeds.**

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut showing a branch of the Abies foemina with needles, along with separate illustrations of its cones, scales, and seeds.</image-desc>

The limits we have set for ourselves do not permit us to describe the appearance and mode of generation of all these parts in graphic detail here; let it suffice to have painted them, and the rest may be sought from our *Great History*. We shall say only a little regarding their *use* and *powers*.

The Fir is best for buildings, and indeed the oldest wood is best, provided it is not decayed. It is also very useful for painters' tablets. But it is most fit for ships on account of its lightness; and from those very long trees which are transported from Switzerland and Rhaetia <note>The Alps</note> through the Aare and Rhine rivers to the seas, the taller masts are made. Johann Strupp is the authority for the fact that in times of desperate hunger, flour can be increased <note>stretched</note> with the cones. Its resin is hot and dry in the third degree; and whether taken internally or applied externally, it comes very close to the properties of Turpentine.

**DWARF SPRUCE.**

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a dwarf spruce (Picea pumila), showing a shorter, more shrub-like growth habit compared to the standard Picea.</image-desc>

The common Spruce is a very tall tree; but we have it from Clusius that some of its kind are found which do not rise very high, but remain dwarf. This is the *Pinus Tubulus* or *Tibulus* of Dalechamps.

Furthermore, the leaves of the Spruce are useful for the liver when a <term>drachm</term> <note>a small unit of weight, roughly 1/8 of an ounce</note> by weight is drunk with honey-water. Forests filled with these scents are most useful for those with <term>phthisis</term> <note>tuberculosis or wasting lung disease</note> and those recovering from great illnesses; today they provide the same benefits that voyages to Egypt once did. But the wood of the Spruce tree is thin and loose; and for that reason, it is not as suitable for making pipes for water conduits or other things and instruments as the Larch and the Fir. The Spruce also produces resin, but it is usually thick and hardened, rarely liquid, and its virtues are the same as those of the Fir.

**YEW**

It highlights the industrial use of these trees for shipbuilding and construction, as well as the health benefits of their resins and forest air.</summary>
<keywords>Fir, Spruce, Conifers, Resin, Forestry, Shipbuilding, Medicinal Plants, Theophrastus, Pliny, Clusius, Gessner</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE YEW: German: *Eibenbaum*: Belgian: *Ibenboom*: French: *If*: Italian: *Tasso*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Yew (Taxus) branch with needles and berries.</image-desc>

This is a tree with evergreen foliage and a tall trunk, similar to the Fir and the Spruce, but distinguished from both by certain characteristics. Pliny identifies two types, the *Male* and the *Female*: he says the male has harmful fruit and lethal berries, but it was discovered that it becomes harmless if a copper nail is driven into the tree itself. <note>This refers to an ancient folk belief that copper could "fix" or neutralize the toxins of the Yew.</note> Dioscorides calls it *Smilax*, but the meaning of *Smilax* is very broad, and the *Smilax* of Theophrastus—which is an acorn-bearing tree—differs greatly from this *Smilax* of Dioscorides.

It is native to the mountains and cannot grow in the plains. To speak generally, it is found in Italy, France, Germany, England, Switzerland, and Spain, and it delights in shady places. It buds very slowly, but the fruit matures in September.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE YEW, specifically showing the flowers, fruit, and other parts.

<image-desc>Detailed woodcut of Yew components: I. A branch with berries; II. A small sprig; III. A cluster of male flowers; IIII. A single berry; V. A seed.</image-desc>

Whether the Yew is of a hot or cold temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, plants were classified by "temperaments" (hot, cold, moist, dry) to determine their medicinal use.</note> is not yet sufficiently agreed upon among writers. Dioscorides and his followers determine it to be cold, because they say its poison must be countered with the same remedies as Hemlock; among these are Camerarius, Pena, and Lobel. Wierus also agrees. However, almost all others maintain that it is harmful everywhere, a side supported by daily experience. For those who eat the berries are afflicted with fevers and diarrhea; birds are rendered stunned and are easily captured. Because the wood is reddish with many intersecting veins and is resistant to decay, it is highly sought after by woodworkers, especially for fashioning spears, arrows, tables, and even heated rooms <term>hypocausts: rooms heated from below, often paneled in wood</term>.

---

### THE PINE: German: *Fichtenbaum*: Belgian: *Pinappelboom*: French: *Pin*. Italian & Spanish: *Pino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Pine tree branch with long needles and a large cone.</image-desc>

The Pine, which is the *Peuce* of the Greeks (not the *Pitys*, as some have wrongly thought), is divided by Theophrastus into the Urban and the Wild varieties. He further classifies these as Female, Male, or sterile, assigning specific characteristics to each. Modern authors have distinguished them differently, as will be clear from what follows. We depict here the most common Pine, called the *Cultivated* or *Domestic* Pine, which has hard seeds but long leaves.

It loves thin soil and maritime locations; in the mountains and among rocks, it is found to be larger and taller. It is characteristic of this tree to spread very widely in loose soil, as is apparent from the most pleasant Pine grove near Ravenna. It is cultivated in France, Belgium, and Italy, but is not very frequent in Germany. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### THE PINE WITH FRAGILE-SHELLED SEEDS, or the Swiss Pine.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Stone Pine (Pinus cembra) branch with a dense cone and shorter needles.</image-desc>

Simler and Gesner confuse this with the Pine properly so-called and the common variety. By Matthiolus it is called the wild pine *Cembro*: commonly called *Cembri* and *Cirmoli*. Munster, Belon, and others also call it the *Pinaster* and wild pine; some Germans call it *Fichtenbaum*; the French *Pin sauvage*. However, its leaves are shorter than those of the common Pine, and the cones are also smaller than those of the Pine. It also shares this trait with the cones of the fir: the scales are easily torn from the little stalk. Two or one seeds <note>original: "Pityides"</note> are hidden in each scale, half the size of the domestic pine; the seeds are three-sided, with a reddish, thin, and fragile shell, etc.

It is an Alpine tree, not uncommon among the people of Trento and the Savoyards.

---

### THE COMMON WILD PINE, Pinaster and Torch-wood.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Scots Pine (Pinus sylvestris) branch with small cones and paired needles.</image-desc>

The *Pinaster* or Wild Pine grows spontaneously in various places, especially in the Alps; we have observed it most frequently near Florence, and around Belfort and Raupach. Those who, following Pliny, make *Teda* <note>Torch-pine or resinous wood</note> a particular species of cone-bearing tree and a tree of its own genus are led by a great error. For *Teda* is properly the name for a specific disease of the Spruce, the Larch, and particularly the Wild Pine, by which those trees are said to be "turned into torch-wood" when not only the heartwood but the rest of the substance is changed into fatness <note>resinous saturation</note>. Furthermore, torches are made from *Teda*, and the soot serves for the making of book-ink; boiled in vinegar, it soothes toothaches when used as a mouthwash. Added to plasters, it is very useful for pestilential carbuncles.

<column-break/>

### WILD PINE, MUGO, or Crein, the Creeping Pinaster.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Mountain Pine (Pinus mugo) showing its low, spreading growth habit.</image-desc>

The tree which they call *le Crein* in Burgundy grows in the mountains they call the *Franche-Montagne*; it is a small and stunted tree compared to other resin-bearing trees, and occupies the lower parts of the mountains. They use it for torches in place of *teda*, though more rarely, because it is less fatty.

Is this the *Mughus*, *Mughi*, or *Mugho* pine of Matthiolus, growing in the mountains of Trento and Val di Non? Anguillara, the French Dodoens, Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, and Camerarius also mention the wild pine, both the creeping and the humble pinaster, and label it *Pinus Mughus*—could it be the *Tubulus* of Pliny?

It discusses their physical characteristics, geographic distribution, and medicinal or practical uses, such as the production of torches and ink.</summary>

<keywords>Yew (Taxus), Pine (Pinus), Pinaster, Teda (torch-wood), Swiss Pine (Cembro), Mountain Pine (Mugo), botany, Renaissance medicine, resin, classical authorities</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Pine family, specifically focusing on wild varieties (Pinaster) and maritime pines, following the previous descriptions of the domestic Pine.</meta>

### THE GREATER AUSTRIAN WILD PINE, WHITE & BLACK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pine branch with long needles and a single cone at the tip.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> depicts and describes this tree, and says there are two kinds, so similar to each other that few, except for experienced woodcutters, can tell them apart. One, however, has a broader and more upright trunk, smoother bark, and a larger cone; it is called *white fir* <note>original: "vveisse Fereur"</note> by the Austrians. The other has smaller cones, a twisted trunk, and a darker appearance; they call it *black fir* <note>original: "Schvvartze Fereur"</note>. Both grow in the mountainous regions of Pannonia <note>an ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note> and Austria. It must be considered how much it differs from our wild Pine described previously, or whether it is the same. From it, both the black and white varieties, are made planks, shingles, and vineyard stakes.

<column-break/>

### THE THIN-LEAVED AUSTRIAN WILD PINE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pine branch with very thin, dense needles and a small cone.</image-desc>

According to the same author Clusius, this grows at the roots of several Austrian mountains, among the rocks.

In this empty space, I am pleased to add the *uses and powers of the Pine and Wild Pine* in general. The bark, according to Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacology</note>, has an astringent power; a third part of it sprinkled on skin chafing or burns [is effective], and a fumigation of the inner bark on wool drives out the fetus and the afterbirth. When drunk, it stops the bowels and promotes urine. The *leaves*, crushed and applied, soothe inflammations and protect wounds from becoming inflamed. Crushed and boiled in vinegar, they ease toothaches if the mouth is rinsed while the liquid is warm. *Torch-wood* <note>term: Teda (resinous pine wood used for torches)</note> cut into small pieces and boiled in vinegar—as was just said above—soothes toothaches when used as a mouthwash. *More on this in the following sections.*

---

### THE DWARF WILD PINE, THE SMALLEST OF ALL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, shrub-like pine with several cones and short needles.</image-desc>

This Wild Pine hardly exceeds the height of a man; Clusius writes that he found it in the territory of the March <note>likely the March of Styria or a similar border region</note>. Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note>, however, says it differs very little from the Low Wild Pine of French Provence.

Furthermore, to continue recounting the *virtues of the Pine and Wild Pine*, pine nuts are most suitable for those with consumption <note>tuberculosis</note> and those wasting away. Indeed, from them is made a highly nutritious "Pine-milk" <note>a restorative drink made from ground pine nuts</note>, very pleasing for long-standing chest ailments, those with chronic coughs, the emaciated, and it is very useful for ulcerations of the bladder and kidney stones. Water distilled from Pine cones <note>term: Strobili (pine cones)</note> removes wrinkles from the face, prevents the growth of the breasts, and tightens the neck of the womb. A wine is also made from them, as Dioscorides teaches. The bark, leaves, and nuts of the Wild Pine provide the same benefits, and even more powerfully; however, the nuts of the Wild Pine are not for eating.

<column-break/>

### THE MARITIME WILD PINE, WITH CONES FIRMLY adhering to the branches.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pine branch with two large, heavy cones pointing downwards.</image-desc>

The cones on this tree are in pairs opposite each other, nodding downwards, and adhering firmly by a thick, woody stalk; by this name it differs from other species of Pine and Wild Pine.

Theophrastus <note>the ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> greatly praises the wood of the Pine and says its use in building is remarkable because of the openness and straightness of its grain, and because it can in no way be split if it is protected with glue. Moreover, round ships are made from it because they do not rot, the wood being very firm against decay and woodworms.

The resin, like all others, dries and warms. Since pitch <note>term: Pix (pitch/tar)</note> is drawn out by the force of fire from the fattest and most resinous wood of trees that has been turned into torch-wood, it is made especially from the Pitch-tree and the Pine.

---

### THE MARITIME PINE OF THEOPHRASTUS ACCORDING TO LOBEL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender pine tree with a distinct trunk and several cones.</image-desc>

The Maritime Pine of Theophrastus, says Lobel, seems in its trunk and the appearance of its branches and leaves to be entirely similar to the Mountain Wild Pine; but the cone is reddish-purple, shorter, and broader at the top. The branches and trunk are darker and smoother.

<column-break/>

### THE IDA PINE OF THEOPHRASTUS, ACCORDING TO THE SAME LOBEL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy pine with numerous small cones clustered among the needles.</image-desc>

This one, says Lobel, is easily distinguished from the other by the rough bark of the trunk and branches, by the abundance of leaves around the branches, and by the larger, longer, and more numerous, beautiful cones. To Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous Italian physician and botanist</note>, this is the *second kind of Maritime Pine*.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### AN EXOTIC FRUIT WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A PINE CONE.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of an exotic fruit resembling a pine cone, showing thick, overlapping woody scales and a short stem.</image-desc>

With a stalk nearly the thickness of the little finger, stiff, hard, and woody, the leaves <note>The author is describing the individual scales of the cone as "leaves."</note> grow by resting upon one another; they are nearly a finger long, firm, of a woody substance, and three-sided. They are narrower at the base, broader in the remaining part, and curved back toward the tip, covered with numerous small, leaf-like scales that are whitish and black. The leaves that lie hidden inside are shorter than the outermost ones and are enclosed by a denser crowding of their ranks. Having examined all these features, especially the shape, color, and the mutual overlapping of the leaves, we have given this fruit—brought from distant regions—the name "Fruit with the appearance of a Pine cone."

### LARCH or LAREX: German: Larch-tree; Belgian: Larch-tree; French: Mélèze; Italian & Spanish: Larice.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Larch tree branch with needle-like leaves and small cones.</image-desc>

It is considered unknown to Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and all the Greeks; nor does Homer mention it anywhere, although Pliny asserts that he does. Whether it was properly known even to the ancient Latins—Palladio, Vitruvius, and Pliny—is rightly doubted, since they write that the Larch does not burn, and Pliny specifically claims it has evergreen leaves, both of which are false. <note>The Larch is a rare example of a deciduous conifer; it drops its needles in winter.</note>

Today, various regions cultivate it in abundance: the territory of Embrun; the forests and mountains near Vienna (Austria); the Rhaetian Alps and the region of the Seduni among the Valaisans; and other places.

<margin>*</margin> We depict here the Agaric <note>original: "Agaricum"</note>, which grows upon it as a spongy concretion; however, we shall provide its uses and virtues, as well as the rest of the Larch's history, in the Appendix.

### CEDAR: German: Cedar-tree; Belgian: Cedar-tree; French: Cèdre, Cedar of Lebanon; Italian: Cedro.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Cedar of Lebanon branch with dense needles and a large, upright cone.</image-desc>

The Cedar is a large tree, not unlike the fir, whose fruits are called "cedrides," and from which the pitch called "Cedria" is collected. According to Theophrastus, Pliny, Galen, and almost all modern authors, there are two types: the Greater and the Lesser. Mattioli falsely established with Dioscorides that the Great Cedar is berry-bearing; for it is certain that it bears a cone. It should be known that the Great Cedar, also called the Cedar of Lebanon (which we depict here), differs greatly from the tree simply called Cedar, which is properly named *Oxycedros* <note>Prickly Cedar</note>, of which we shall speak shortly.

It is properly an inhabitant of Lebanon, growing there upon rocks—which is marvelous, since it turns out to be so tall and of such thickness that six or seven men can scarcely encircle the trunks with their arms. Furthermore, its wood is incorruptible.

<column-break/>

### THE TREE WITH THE LEAF OF LAVENDER.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a woody stem branching into three parts, each topped with a cluster of small, bud-like structures.</image-desc>

This branch was brought from the East Indies, and it is very little known to which tree it belonged. It equaled three feet in length, and the diameter of its thickness was about two inches. Its tip ended in a somewhat swelling, knotty head, from which five smaller branches, a foot and a half long, sprang forth, arranged in a very elegant series and order. On their leafy tips hung leaves resembling the leaves of Lavender in shape, color, and size. Because they were full of a juice somewhat resembling the resin of the Elemi tree, they claimed a place for this branch among the resinous trees.

### CYPRESS: German: Cypress-tree; Belgian: Cypress-tree; French: Cyprès; Italian: Cipresso & Curesso.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Cypress tree branch with scale-like leaves and round, woody cones (galbuli).</image-desc>

The Ancients did not bestow great praise upon the Cypress. Cato said it was difficult to rear, useless in fruit, grim in its berries, bitter of leaf, violent in scent, thin in its wood, and not even pleasing in its shade; and finally, it was sacred to Dis <note>The god of the Underworld</note>. They even called it "funereal," because it grows slowly and, once cut down, does not sprout back; for which reason they used to place it before the houses of the deceased as a sign of mourning.

It is distinguished into the Male, which is always unfruitful, and the Female, which remains sterile for a long time. It is quite common in Italy, but it is a source of profit especially for the Cretans. We ourselves have seen it in abundance at Paris and Montpellier, where it bears nuts in Autumn which last through the whole Winter and Summer. It is astringent and cooling, but the nuts are more effective than the leaves. More in the Appendix.

### PRICKLY CEDAR, BELLONIUS’S PHOENICIAN CEDAR, or Greater Juniper.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Prickly Cedar (Oxycedrus) branch with sharp, needle-like leaves and berry-like cones, including cross-sections of the fruit.</image-desc>

The Lesser Cedar is similar and related to the Juniper; but its leaves are twice as long and also broader, stiff, and stinging with a sharp point. The berries are twice or thrice larger than those of the Juniper, and in color they are not blue like those, but reddish-brown; yet they are similar in taste and smell. Those who call it the "Greater Juniper" are in error, for the similar size and color (as has been said) argue against it. Pliny labeled it the Phoenician Cedar; to almost all modern authors, it is called *Oxycedrus*.

It grows in some parts of Italy, most of Spain, and in certain rugged places of Gallia Narbonensis <note>Southern France</note>. From its wood, cut into small pieces and heated, the shepherds and peasants in the territory of Marseille extract a black and foul-smelling oily liquid, which they name *Huile de Cade* <note>Cade oil</note>, and which is called *Miera* by the Spaniards.

<summary>This page describes various resinous trees and exotic fruits, including the Larch, Cedar of Lebanon, and Cypress, noting their physical characteristics, geographical origins, and historical associations with death or medicine.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Larch, Cedar of Lebanon, Cypress, Cade oil, resin, medicinal plants, classical antiquity, exotic flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of coniferous trees and shrubs, specifically focusing on various species of Cedar and Juniper, following the previous descriptions of pines and firs.</meta>

### CEDAR, OR LYCIAN SHARP-CEDAR, Called *Morusine* by the people of Marseille, and *De cade serbin* by those of Avignon.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cedar branch with small needle-like leaves and round berries. Below the main branch are three detailed sketches of the berries/cones.</image-desc>

It is sometimes thorny, at other times not: because the leaves are blunt, Bellonius <note>Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French naturalist</note> described it as the Lycian blunt-leaved Cedar. Some call it the berry-bearing Savin, but incorrectly, as it differs greatly from the Savin in both scent and form; others think it is the *Thuia* of the people of Marseille. It grows in the same places as the preceding species, being very common around Marseille and Avignon.

In Spain, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> observed Mistletoe on the branches of the Sharp-Cedar. From the Phoenician Cedar, the Sharp-Cedar, and also from the Juniper, a certain gum exudes which they call Varnish, and is the *Sandaracha* of the Arabs. It heats and dries in the first degree; it halts catarrhs <note>original: "destillationes", referring to runny noses or mucus</note>, stops menstrual flow, and, applied in various ways, soothes toothaches.

### GREAT ILLYRIAN JUNIPER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Juniper branch with large, prominent oval berries and sharp, needle-like leaves.</image-desc>

Pena and Lobel <note>Authors of the "Adversaria Stirpium", 1570</note> describe it thus, both in their *Adversaria* and in their *Observations and Icons of Plants*. For Tabernaemontanus, it is the Greater Illyrian Juniper. In the *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum"</note>, it is simply the Greater Juniper.

As for what Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> says—that the fruit of the Greater Juniper sometimes equals the size of a Hazelnut <note>original: "Nucem Ponticam"</note>, and indeed sometimes grows to the size of a Walnut—this has not yet been observed in our European world.

### SAVIN: German: *Seuenbaum*; Belgian: *Seuenboom*; French: *Sauignier*; Italian: *Sabina*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Savin Juniper branch with scale-like leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

The Savin is a plant of evergreen foliage, which is always lower to the ground, growing more in width than in height; for this reason, some have not hesitated to call it an Herb, others a Shrub; although it is neither an herb nor a shrub, but a tree of almost fair size.

Dioscorides and Pliny make two species of it: One with leaves like the Cypress, but more thorny, foul-smelling, sharp, and burning. The other with leaves like the Tamarisk <note>original: "Myricæ"</note>. More recent authors have observed other differences: they call one Male and the other Female; they say one is sterile and the other berry-bearing or fruitful; and finally, they say one has leaves that are not at all thorny, while they attribute thorns to all the others. We depict here the berry-bearing one with non-thorny leaves.

<column-break/>

### COMMON JUNIPER: German: *Weckholder*; Belgian: *Genever*; French: *Geneure*; Italian: *Ginepro*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common Juniper branch with small berries and sharp needles.</image-desc>

The common Juniper is divided into the Greater and the Lesser, differing only in size. It is also distinguished in another way: namely, that one bears berries and the other only flowers; the latter is commonly called the Female, and the former the Male. However, the one that bears fruit does not flower: it has a thorn in place of a leaf.

It abounds everywhere in various places. It flowers in the month of May; after the flower, small green berries break forth, which only in the second year, as Autumn approaches (which is their time of maturity), are tinged with blue; and if they are kept into the third year, they are called three-year fruits.

The berries are hot in the third degree and dry in the first: the fruits, twigs, and branches of the Juniper are in use, as well as the whole wood; its many benefits can hardly be fully explained.

### ALPINE JUNIPER, SELAGO.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alpine Juniper or Selago plant with dense, upward-reaching foliage.</image-desc>

We depict here a branch of the Alpine Juniper which we received from Dauphiné. Clusius has a similar one in his *Plants of Pannonia* and his *History*; perhaps it is the *Selago* of Pliny?

Since we said above that it is not easy to review all the virtues of the Juniper, we shall also note something of its harms. One thing in this little tree is to be avoided and detested: namely, its shade, whence Virgil says:

> Let us rise; the shade is wont to be heavy for those who sing.
> The shade of the Juniper is heavy, and the shade is harmful to the crops.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SAVIN, STERILE SAVIN: with thorny leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sterile Savin branch with more prickly, needle-like foliage.</image-desc>

Ruellius writes that the name Savin is retained everywhere; some wish it to be named after the region of the Sabines, where it once abounded. Today it is kept everywhere in the more cultivated gardens. At Verona, we saw two large Savin trees, and others shaped into the figures of various animals <note>an early reference to topiary</note>, nor have we seen more beautiful ones anywhere else. You <unclear>also</unclear> find it growing wild with many berries, and leaves partly thorny, partly not.

Furthermore, Savin is of the third order of both heating and drying substances, being among those things which consist of the most subtle parts. It provokes the menses, extracts the fetus <note>referring to its use as an abortifacient</note>, stops spreading ulcers, etc. Is it the *Selago* of Pliny? Or the *Bruta* of Ruellius, known only from the East?

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

# TREE OF LIFE, or PARADISE TREE: German *Baum des lebens*: French *Arbre de vit*.
# ABHEL, THUJA OF THEOPHRASTUS, Atlantic Cedar, Pliny’s Bruta.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch from the Arbor Vitae (Thuja), showing scale-like leaves and small cones.</image-desc>

This is a very fragrant small tree, closely resembling the Savin <note>Juniperus sabina</note> and, like it, is evergreen. It bears flowers like the Cypress and carries oblong cones, not berries, as Gesner incorrectly wrote. Its wood is resistant to decay, wood-boring insects, and worms, and is not subject to corruption in any age—which is perhaps where it gets its name <note>Arbor Vitae means "Tree of Life"</note>. This was recently brought into our world from the province of Canada in Northern America, and today it is kept in several of the more cultivated gardens, such as those under our care in Montbéliard <note>original: "Möbelgardēsi"</note>. Is it the *Thuja* of Theophrastus? Is it the *Bruta* of Pliny? Is it an exotic species of Savin? Or is it a tree of the Peruvian region, whose resin, when smeared or dripped upon the deceased, protects the corpses from rot?

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Two detailed illustrations of the fruit/cones of the Abhel or Thuja, one showing the exterior and one a cross-section.</image-desc>

We depict here the fruit, known by the name *Abhel*, which is very well known throughout the entire Orient. It equals the size of Cypress pills <note>small cones</note> and has a color inclining from reddish to black. It is harvested from a tree of that same genus, very similar to the Cypress. Since the *Thuja* of Theophrastus is hardly known today except from his own history, Guillandinus, Clusius, and Camerarius have perhaps judged it to be this tree bearing the *Abhel* fruit. On the other hand, Anguillara and Mattioli believe that the *Thuja* of Theophrastus and the Atlantic Cedar of the Ancients are one and the same. Could it be Pliny’s *Bruta*, of which he says: "So great is the satiety of mortals for their own things, and their greed for foreign ones, that they seek the Bruta tree in the land of the Hazmaeans, which is similar to the Cypress," etc.

---

# FRANKINCENSE, OLIBANUM: German *Weyrauch*: Belgian *Wyerook*: French *Encens*: Italian *Incenso*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch of the Frankincense tree (Boswellia), showing pinnate leaves and small clusters of flowers/fruit.</image-desc>

*Thus* <note>Frankincense</note> signifies both the tree and the tear <note>the resin drop</note>; it is sometimes written without the 'h' <note>as 'tus'</note>, as if the name were given from the "tufa-like" clumps <note>original: "tofis glebis"</note>. According to Galen, the tree is called *Libanos* and the tear *Libanotos*, but according to Euripides, the tear is *Libanos* and the tree *Libanotos*.

It is clear from Pliny that the tree was not sufficiently known to the Ancients: some attributed to it the leaves of a Pear, others the Mastick tree, and others the Turpentine tree. Even today, writers do not entirely agree on its origin and appearance. Caesalpinus stubbornly asserts that no one among us has seen the *Frankincense tree*, and that only Theophrastus among the Ancients described it. Guillandinus maintains that Firs in Arabia drip with Frankincense. However, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, and the Moderns declare it to be a tree of its own distinct genus.

<column-break/>

# THE HOODED LEAF OF FRANKINCENSE.

<image-desc>An illustration of a singular, hood-shaped or tubular leaf, described as "cucullatum" (hooded).</image-desc>

The *Adversaria* <note>a botanical work by Lobel and Pena</note> also depicts this beautiful, hooded, and channeled leaf, which is usually brought from Florida, and they label it "the leaf of clear Frankincense." Thevet, from whom our illustration is taken, writes that not only Arabia (as the Ancients held) but many other regions are fertile with Frankincense. He claims that in certain places the trees are as common as Orange trees are in the French province of Provence; some of these yield 60 pounds of Frankincense, though the most excellent is held to be from Arabia. But why does he liken the tree to a Pine and depict it differently? Garcia <note>da Orta</note> describes it as low-growing and attributes leaves to it similar to the Mastick tree, stating there is one mountain variety that bears the best Frankincense, and another growing in the plains that bears a black and inferior kind.

---

# BDELLIUM: German, Belgian, French & Italian *Bdellium*: To the Arabs *Mochol, Mochel, Molochil, & Molochal*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a thorny branch of the Bdellium tree (Commiphora), showing small leaves and sharp spines.</image-desc>

Bdellium, according to Dioscorides, is the "tear" of a Saracen tree. According to Galen, it grows in Arabia, India, Media, and Babylon. Our figure is from Lobel. However, what Bdellium actually is, and whether the true and genuine kind is available today, is sharply disputed among writers. Some think it is legitimate Myrrh, others true Animé resin, and others something else. Whatever it may be, if Mattioli is to be believed, it is quite rare and is kept in apothecary shops only for show or as a standard for rejected goods. In Cornarius's judgment, the shops retain the name and the substance of Bdellium, but the names of the "Saracen" kind in Dioscorides, the "Babrian" in Pliny, and the "Arabic and Scythian" in Galen have fallen out of use. More on the following page.

<column-break/>

# STYRAX TREE AND TEAR: German, Belgian & French *Storax*: Italian *Storace*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Styrax tree branch, showing broad oval leaves and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

The Styrax tree is very similar in trunk and leaf to the Quince tree. It has whitish, bright flowers and fruit the size of a hazelnut, uniform and hoary, with a woody pit the color of boxwood. It is properly a tree of Syria and Palestine, yet it is also reported to be frequent on the Indian island of Zena. It is kept in Venice, Rome, and various other places in Italy, but it does not bear the "tear" <note>resin</note>, or only very little. We have had small trees grown from seeds in the princely garden at Montbéliard, and we have also seen them in Basel.

From the Styrax tree flows the Styrax Tear; regarding this, as well as the history of Bdellium, consult both our "Great History" and the following page.

# OF PLANTS

### EXOTIC WOOD: ETTALCHE.
### SMALLEST CONE-BEARING NUT.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration showing two specimens: on the left, a piece of dark, textured wood or bark (Ettalche); on the right, a small coniferous branch with needles and a tiny cone (Conifera Nux Minima). Both are marked with asterisks.</image-desc>

The wood we depict here is held and described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>: he says it was hard, heavy, firm, and smelled of Mastic <note>a resin from the lentisk tree</note>, and was taken from an American tree from which a resin is drawn out in the manner of pitch, and used for the same purposes, by which name it has claimed this place for itself.

Is it perhaps the *Ettalche*, a large tree with Juniper-like leaves, thorny, and emitting a gum similar to Mastic, with which the Africans—on account of the similarity of scent and color—adulterate true Mastic? Its wood is reported to be white in Numidia, violet in Libya, and very black in Ethiopia.

Or is it the *Capida* mentioned by Cato?

<column-break/>

We keep these small cones among our natural specimens; they closely resemble the cones of the Larch, but are much smaller, having stalks that are empty and curved. At their base, very short leaves of the Pitch-pine adhere. It is apparent that they consist of Larch-like scales—thin, broad, and furrowed—and that a leafy seed grows between the scales, as in the Pitch-pine or Fir. Whether these are the cones of the Larch or of another tree is not entirely clear to us.

Thus, as far as our intended brevity allowed, we have reviewed the trees specifically called "Resin-bearing." But since not all of them, or at least not sufficiently, have had their fragrant juices described, we shall fill this empty space with a selection of several accounts.

---

->There are two kinds of RESIN:<-

**Liquid & Dry.** The liquid flows from various trees, especially Pine and Pitch-pine, both spontaneously and when the branches or trunk are wounded. If it is found mixed with woody or stony debris due to careless collection, it is called *Confusanea* <note>mixed or jumbled</note>. The dry kind comes forth from cracks in the bark of the same trees or from cut branches; it lacks fatness and dries out quickly. Some make *Strobolina* a third kind, but incorrectly, as it only has that name because it is found hardened around the cones, or *strobili*.

**PITCH** <note>Latin: *Pix*</note> is drawn out by the force of fire from the fattest and most resinous woods, especially Pine and Pitch-pine, which have been turned into torches. It is either liquid or dry: the liquid is called *Crude* when it has experienced no fire other than the heat by which it flowed, or *Brutian*, which is dark, fatter, and thicker. *Dry* pitch is made from liquid pitch that has been boiled again: this is either boiled only to the thickness of birdlime, or, by a longer and stronger fire, is rendered dry, brittle, and scrapable.

**CEDRIA** is the "Tear of the Cedar," a pitch or resin which, because it destroys living things and preserves dead bodies (according to Dioscorides), is commonly called the *Life of the Dead*. Corresponding to it is the oil which the people of Provence are accustomed to make from Juniper, Ash, Cedar, and other such woods, which they call *Huile de Cade* <note>Cade oil</note>; it is especially useful for mange of the head, and for the mange and ulcers of cattle.

**FRANKINCENSE** <note>Latin: *Thus*</note>: where and how it is produced was said before. It is held in highest favor when it is *Mammosum* <note>breast-like</note>, specifically when one tear follows another and joins to it. This they call *Male* frankincense, though it is not called male elsewhere unless there is a female. Frankincense is distinguished into *Manna* and *Bark*. Pliny interpreted *Manna* as the crumbs struck off by shaking; Plautus called it a *Grain of Frankincense*, and Hermolaus called it *Hypofisma*. Frankincense warms and binds significantly; the bark possesses the same power, and even more effectively.

**MASTIC** is the resin of the Lentisk tree: the best comes from the island of Chios, concerning which we speak elsewhere.

**SARCOCOLLA** <note>literally "flesh-glue"</note>, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of a tree growing in Persia, similar to thin frankincense, somewhat yellowish and bitter. It has the power of gluing wounds together and checking discharges.

**MYRRH** is the tear of the tree of the same name, found mostly in Arabia; when cut in any place, it emits this very tear. Seven varieties are described, named after the places where they are obtained.

**STACTE** is not Balsam, as some wish, nor liquid Styrax, as others prefer, but the fatness of fresh Myrrh crushed with a little water and pressed out through an instrument. (*Dioscorides*)

**BENZOIN** <note>Latin: *Beniouinum*</note> is a gum or resin flowing from the wounded Benzoin tree. There are various kinds, but the one called *Amygdaloides* <note>almond-like</note> is preferred over the others. It is a large and tall tree, having leaves like a Citron tree, and growing in Sumatra, an island of the East Indies. Furthermore, it is clear that Benzoin was unknown to the Ancients because neither the Greeks nor the Arabs describe it; for it is not the *Balenzan* of Averrhoes.

**LIQUIDAMBAR** is the resin flowing from incisions in trees of vast size, beautiful and branchy, which have Ivy-like leaves and grow in New Spain <note>Mexico</note>. It is named by the inhabitants for its scent. It warms, dissolves, and settles pains: it is of the greatest use in Medicine.

**CANCAMUM**, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of an Arabian wood, somewhat similar to Myrrh but with a poisonous taste.

**ANIME** AND **COPAL** are synonyms. *Anime* is collected from wounded trees of moderate size, no differently than **Frankincense or Mastic**: and it takes its name from the place in Arabia where it is found, if we believe Hermolaus. There are two kinds, soft and harder. Why it is called *Anima* <note>Soul</note>, we do not know.

**TOCOTGEBIT** is a tree of the East Indies, similar to a Poplar, under whose bark is a resin similar to our Frankincense but whiter, which they use there as Frankincense.

**CARANNA**, so called by the Indians and Spaniards, is a resin also collected from wounded trees, the color of Tacamahaca but a little clearer, with a similar but heavier scent.

**AMBER** <note>Latin: *Electrum* or *Succinum*</note>, called *Carabe* by the Arabs, is the gum of a poplar tree according to Dioscorides; but according to Pliny and some more recent followers, it is a resin flowing from a tree similar to a pitch-pine. Yet by the reckoning of almost all others, it is born from Bitumen, which, flowing from the shores into the sea, hardens in the way we see. It is either *Yellow* or *White*: and it is found in the coastal regions of Germany, rolled onto the shore by storms.

**BDELLIUM AND STYRAX**, both the trees and the tears, were dealt with previously.

**CAMPHOR** is numbered among the gifts of the East Indies; it is a gum flowing from a tree similar to a poplar, growing in mountains near the sea. Four species are commonly reviewed: however, it differs greatly from the *Capura* of Qualcebeni.

**USUB**, a gum-bearing tree with which the Indians anoint the body, is mentioned by Thevet in *Antarctic France* <note>Brazil</note>.

**TACAMAHACA** is obtained from the East Indies and flows from a wounded large tree equal to a poplar: it is of great use for almost innumerable ailments.

**ACACIA, GUM ARABIC**, and all other Juices, Gums, and Tears will be discussed in their own place.

---

# END OF THE NINTH CLASS.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS X.
### CONCERNING BROOM-LIKE TREES AND SHRUBS.

**MYRICA or TAMARISK: German: *Tamarischenbaum*:**
**French: *Tamarisque*: Italian: *Tamarice*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrica (Tamarix) plant, showing its slender, feathery branches and small leaves.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> calls this a well-known tree that grows near sluggish waters. However, Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a successor to Aristotle</note> calls it "amphibious," because it is not only to be counted among aquatic plants but is also abundant in deserts. Pliny, being inconsistent, distinguishes between a Cultivated and a Wild variety; in one place he says it bears a fruit similar to a gall-nut, yet elsewhere he says its wood is called "unlucky" because it bears neither fruit nor seed.

More recent authors establish one as Cultivated, which is tall and tree-like, and another as Wild, which is low and shrubby, and is called by the diminutive name *Tamariscus*. This latter type they subdivide again, as will be discussed shortly. This tree-like Tamarisk is found frequently in Gallia Narbonensis <note>Southern France</note>, both near rivers and far from them. We have seen it in gardens in Paris, Montpellier, and in Belgium.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER TAMARISK, or SHRUBBY, called the GERMAN Tamarix.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Tamarix Minor, showing a more shrub-like growth pattern with upright, spiked flowering or leaf structures.</image-desc>

Two kinds of this are found: *one* with more solid wood and thinner leaves, the *other* with somewhat broad leaves and less solid wood. Thus Theophrastus established two kinds of Tamarisk: one with strong wood, the other weak. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German botanist</note> writes that the former grows abundantly by the Rhine at Strasbourg, and the latter on the banks of the Danube.

It loves damp and stony regions, and does not easily take to garden cultivation unless placed near water. We ourselves have seen both kinds in various places near flowing rivers and marshes: at Geneva, Zurich, Lyon, and Padua. It flowers in May and June.

Some distinguish this from the tree-like variety because it has downy <note>original: "papposos," referring to seeds with tufts of hair for wind dispersal</note> flowers, whereas the tree-like one does not, but rather has round, tiny, reddish flowers.

---

**EGYPTIAN TAMARISK, DOMESTIC OR CULTIVATED, Gall-bearing.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Egyptian Tamarix, showing a more robust trunk and distinct branching structure.</image-desc>

Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, a physician who studied Egyptian plants</note> writes that this grows to the height of a large Olive tree, and its fruit equals a walnut in size. Dioscorides names it the cultivated or urban variety, and says it produces fruit similar to galls.

Furthermore, the Tamarisk has a cleansing and cutting <note>term: "incidentis" - a medical term for breaking up thick humors or fluids</note> quality, and possesses some astringency. It frees the internal organs from obstructions, and a decoction of the leaves used as a rinse soothes toothaches. All parts of this tree—fruit, leaves, flowers, bark, wood, and wood-ash—are beneficial for those with spleen ailments. Such people find it useful to drink continuously from vessels made of its wood; hence Pliny wrote that pigs accustomed to eating their food from troughs made of it were found to lack a spleen. Dio <note>likely referring to Cassius Dio</note> testifies that the Ancients prophesied by the power of its branches.

<column-break/>

**ERICA or HEATH: German: *Heyden*: Belgian: *Heyde*: French: *Bruyere*: Italian: *Erica*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Erica (Heath) plant, showing its characteristic dense, needle-like foliage and small flowers.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides, the Erica is a shrubby tree with leaves like the Myrica, but much smaller. Many differences are observed in it, taken from its size, leaves, flowers, and fruit. Thus, one is low-growing, another tree-like; one has thin leaves, another has them in fours; in some they are hairy and downy, in others not; some have white flowers, others purple, grass-green, etc.; and finally, some bear berries, others do not. We depict here the one which is low-growing and has evergreen leaves, with flowers that are either purple or white.

It flowers in June, July, and August, and loves uncultivated places and wildernesses. It is very common in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, and between Montbéliard and Belfort, and again between Montbéliard and Porrentruy.

<summary>This page describes various species of Tamarisk and Heath (Erica), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical distribution across Europe and Egypt, and their medicinal uses, particularly for spleen ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Tamarisk, Heath, Erica, medicinal plants, spleen treatments, European geography, classical botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Theophrastus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of various species of heather (Erica), focusing on their physical characteristics, geographic locations, and medicinal properties.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### HEATHER WITH CORIS-LIKE LEAVES AND WHITE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heather plant (Erica) with thin, upright stems and small needle-like leaves, showing the root system at the base.</image-desc>

This kind of Heather does not resemble the leaves of the Tamarisk <note>original: "Myricæ"</note> as some others do; rather, it greatly rivals the *Coris* <note>likely *Coris monspeliensis*, or Montpellier Coris</note> in the shape and arrangement of its leaves. Of this genus, however, there are many species, differing greatly in size and in the shape and color of the leaves and flowers.

According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, it grows in the wildernesses of Portugal <note>original: "Lusitaniæ"</note>; it blooms in November, December, and January.

### TREE-LIKE HEATHER, WITH PALE YELLOW OR GRASS-GREEN TINY FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller, tree-like heather (Erica arborescens) with a thicker central woody stem branching out into dense foliage.</image-desc>

It is shrub-like, reaching a height of two cubits <note>about 3 feet or 90 cm</note> and sometimes more, with brittle wood and thin, minute leaves. The *flower* is smaller than the others and of a grass-green color; sometimes the tips of the branches bear small heads made of many leaves. We observed this in the *Aigremont* forest near Montpellier, and also in the Apennine mountains of Italy, between Florence and Bologna.

Among the uses of Heather, it is rightly numbered that "Briceta" <note>heather-moors</note> in vast wildernesses provide pasture for flocks of sheep. In some places, it serves in place of firewood for tending fires, and from it are made brooms for cleaning houses. Furthermore, even when dry, Heather nourishes flocks of sheep with very healthy fodder and preserves them from obstructions of the lungs, spleen, and liver.

### BRABANT HEATHER, WITH LEAVES IN FOURS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing heather with leaves arranged in whorls of four along the stems.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub only a foot high with thin, blackish twigs. Frequent leaves surround these, arranged in ranks of four. On the highest twigs hang the *flowers*, of a pale purplish color, similar to the flowers of the Lily of the Valley, but more oblong and not so bellied <note>swollen or rounded</note>.

It grows in many places in Brabant and Guelders <note>regions in the modern-day Netherlands and Belgium</note>. It blooms in Spring and Autumn. Is this the "Second Dwarf Heather of the Belgians" in Lobel's *Observations*? Or the "Low Heather from which brooms are made" in the *History of Lyon*?

<column-break/>

### MANY-FLOWERED HEATHER WITH CORIS-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heather plant with dense, multi-flowered clusters at the ends of the branches.</image-desc>

Is this Camerarius's "Greater and Taller Italian Heather"? Or the "Greater Heather of Narbonne with Ground-Pine leaves" mentioned by Pena and Lobel in their *Adversaria*? Or the "Densely Shrubbing Narbonne Heather with Juniper leaves" in their *Observations*?

Furthermore, the uses of Heather are not to be despised. A decoction of the flowers eases pains of the belly and loins. The juice of the leaves and flowers, rubbed onto weak eyes, benefits them. Water distilled from the flowers settles colic and removes redness of the eyes. Drunk warm every morning and evening for 30 days, it is effective for breaking down and expelling stones of the bladder <note>term: <term>calculos</term> refers to kidney or bladder stones</note>. There are also those who prepare a sweating bath from the fresh flowers for gout and paralysis. *More in the following [page].*

### TREE-LIKE HEATHER OF MONTPELLIER, with purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mediterranean tree-heather with elongated branches and small flowers.</image-desc>

The branches are covered in a thin, ash-colored bark; they are slender and often arranged around larger ones. They are not provided with leaves everywhere, yet those they have are almost like Wild Asparagus <note>original: "Corrudę"</note>, somewhat long, thin, and falling off. At the ends of the twigs are fairly large flowers of a purplish-blue.

It is very common in the mountains of Narbonne Gaul <note>Southern France</note> around *Ganges* and *Espérou*, and it blooms in October. Clusius found it frequently in the uncultivated places of Portugal around Lisbon, blooming in December.

### SMALL HEATHER, WITH GRASS-GREEN FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, prostrate heather species with dense foliage and small flower heads.</image-desc>

It rarely exceeds a foot in height and for the most part lies flat on the ground. The leaves are crowded, somewhat broad, and smooth. The *flowers* are tiny, endowed with a grass-green color. The root is hard and woody. On the twigs grow green heads, compacted from broader leaves, in the manner of Thyme heads.

We observed this in the Alps of Switzerland and Raetia, and we took care to have it painted from specimens brought from there. It blooms in May and June, at which time it is most pleasant to behold.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of heath species (Erica), concluding the tenth class of plants. It maintains the format of woodcut illustrations followed by descriptive Latin text, now translated into English.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALL ENGLISH HEATH, with hairy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, branching heath plant with dense, needle-like foliage and small clusters at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

We received this dried plant from England under the name of Heath <note>original: "Erica"</note>. It is entirely beautiful, scarcely nine inches <term>dodrantalis: a span or about nine inches</term> tall: the branches are thin and numerous: the leaves are very short, crowded, and hairy around the edges: they grow in groups of three or four at small intervals, as if at joints: at the tips are small, hairy heads.

<column-break/>

### LOBEL’S FOREIGN HEATH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender heath plant with upward-reaching branches and fine, feathery foliage.</image-desc>

Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that this species of Heath is cultivated in the hanging gardens of Belgium: it is shrubby in the manner of the others, with somewhat long leaves, and purple flowers around the branches consisting of four small petals. He did not know from where it was brought, and for that reason, he called it "foreign."

<column-break/>

### MATTHIOLI’S BERRY-BEARING HEATH,

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heath plant with small berries shown both on the branches and separately at the base of the stem.</image-desc>

Regarding his Berry-bearing Heath, Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Italian doctor and naturalist</note> relates these things. It is a plant, he says, growing in the mountains that separate Bohemia from Silesia, and from whose springs the river Elbe takes its origin. It spreads across the ground and occupies wide areas, with a leaf almost like the common Heath: it was not possible to see the flowers: but it bears berries that are blackish-purple, similar to Juniper berries, but smaller, etc.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note> in his *History of Rare Plants of Pannonia* labels this the first "Heath with a Coris leaf": and says it grows on the ridges of the highest Alps of Austria and Styria: and flowers in June. However, Pena, Lobel, and even Schwenckfeld wrongly confuse this berry-bearing Heath of Matthiolus with the marsh Whortleberries <note>likely referring to cranberries or bilberries</note>.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S PORTUGUESE BERRY-BEARING HEATH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust, upright heath plant with thick foliage and small berries along the stems.</image-desc>

It rises up with branches about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, which are brittle, with a bark darker than the others: the leaves are also similar to those, but darker and thicker, arranged in a triple row around the twigs. The fruit resembles dark pearls <note>original: "vniones"</note> in both shape and color, but it is juicy and slightly tart. Whether it flowers is not sufficiently certain; the inhabitants of the places where it grows say it does not, and they say the fruit swells gradually until it ripens. *Thus says Clusius.*

It is found only in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, and ripens its fruit in September and October, which is sought after by children and women, being very pleasant and useful to those suffering from thirsty fevers.

They call the tree *Camarinha*, and the fruit *Camarinhas*. In Amatus’s commentary on Dioscorides, the tree is called *Acacalis*.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS IX.
### CONTAINING CONIFEROUS AND RESIN-BEARING TREES.

**Female Fir** : German: *Thannenbaum* : Belgian: *Dannenboom* : French: *Auet, Sapin* : Italian: *Abeto*. <note>original: "Abies foemina". This is likely the Silver Fir (Abies alba).</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a young fir tree (Abies foemina) showing its root system, trunk, and needle-covered branches.</image-desc>

Neither Dioscorides nor Galen <note>Famous ancient Greek physicians and botanists.</note> made mention of the Fir anywhere in their census of trees; Pliny, in the judgment of Ruellius, confuses it with the Palm. According to Theophrastus, however, one Fir is "Male" and another is "Female," and they differ greatly from one another. For in the Male, the leaves are sharper, more stinging, and more curved; the wood is more supple, harder, and fuller of marrow <note>pith or heartwood</note>, and the whole tree appears more rugged and inferior in aspect. Furthermore, in the Male, a few kernels are found in the front part, while in the Female there are none at all.

It is almost exclusively a tree of the mountains, and it grows successfully in both their shaded and sunny parts. Various provinces of Germany have very beautiful ones; Virginia <note>likely referring to the American colonies</note> has very tall ones; and the Harz Forest has those most excellent for the firmness of their wood. *More in the Appendix.*

---

**The Spruce of the Latins** : German: *Schvvarz Thannenbaum* <note>Black Fir</note> : French: *Pesse, Piz*, Garipole : Italian: *Pezzo*. <note>original: "Picea Latinorum". Likely the Norway Spruce (Picea abies).</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a spruce tree (Picea) with a straight trunk and dense, downward-sloping branches.</image-desc>

It is agreed among the learned that the "Spruce of the Latins" is the "Male Fir" of Theophrastus. It is also sufficiently well known that the Spruce of the Latins is not the *Peuce* <note>Greek for Pine</note> of the Greeks, about which we shall speak soon. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note>, who distinguished the Fir into White and Red (or Black), makes the Female the "White" and this one the "Red" or "Black."

It loves mountains and cold, as Pliny says; this is a funereal tree, which in ancient times was placed at doors as a sign of mourning. However, it sometimes descends into the plains. Clusius writes that it is very frequent in the Vienna woods, and Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist</note> notes that the Zurich forests abound with it. We ourselves have observed it in the greatest abundance in the Burgundian mountains called the *Franche montagne*. It is, if any other tree be so, especially subject to very poisonous caterpillars.

<column-break/>

**The Female Fir with branches, nutlets, flowers, catkins, cones, scales, and seeds.**

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of a fir branch featuring needles and a large upright cone.</image-desc>

The limits we have set for ourselves do not permit us to describe the appearance and manner of generation of all these parts graphically here; let it suffice to have painted them, and the rest may be sought from our *Great History*. Here we shall say only something of their use and powers.

The Fir is best for buildings, and indeed the oldest wood is best, provided it is not decayed. It is also very useful for painters' panels, but it is most suitable for ships especially because of its lightness; and from those very long trees which are transported from Switzerland and Rhaetia <note>The Alps</note> via the Aare and the Rhine to the seas, the taller masts are made. Struppius is the authority that in desperate hunger, one may be satisfied by eating the cones. The resin is hot and dry in the third degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine</note>; and whether taken in a broth or applied externally, it comes very close to the properties of Turpentine.

---

**Dwarf Spruce.** <note>original: "Picea pumila"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a dwarf spruce (Picea pumila) showing a smaller, more shrub-like habit with cones.</image-desc>

The common Spruce is a very tall tree; but we have from Clusius that some of this genus are found which do not rise very high, but remain dwarf-like. In Dalechamps, it is called the *Pinus Tubulus* or *Tibulus*.

Furthermore, the leaves of the Spruce are useful for the liver when a drachm's weight is drunk with honey-water. Forests planted with these trees are very useful for those with consumption <note>tuberculosis</note> and those recovering from great illnesses; today they provide the same benefits that voyages to Egypt once did <note>Ancient doctors often prescribed sea air or Egyptian climates for lung ailments</note>. But the wood of the Spruce tree is thin and loose; and for that reason, it is not as suitable for making pipes for water conduits and other things and instruments as the Larch and the Fir. The Spruce also produces resin, but it is usually thick and hardened, rarely liquid, and its virtues are the same as those of the Fir.

<sig>YEW</sig> <note>original: "TAXVS". This is the catchword for the next page.</note>
