<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of coniferous and evergreen trees, moving from the general classification of "Images and Outlines" to specific species of Yew and Pine.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>I 3</sig>

### YEW: German: Eibenbaum: Belgian: Ibenboom: French: If: Italian: Taffo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Yew (Taxus) branch with needles and berries.</image-desc>

It is a tree of everlasting foliage, with a tall trunk, similar to the Fir and the Pitch-pine, but distinguished from both by certain marks. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> makes it twofold, Male and Female: and he says the male has harmful fruit and bears lethal berries: but it has been found to become harmless if a bronze nail is driven into the tree itself. Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> calls it *Smilax*, but the meaning of *Smilax* is very broad, and the *Smilax* of Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany"</note>—which is an acorn-bearing tree—differs greatly from this *Smilax* of Dioscorides.

It is native to the mountains and cannot grow in the plains. It is found, to speak generally, in Italy, France, Germany, England, Switzerland, and Spain, and it delights in shady places. It buds very slowly, but ripens its fruit in September.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE YEW, showing the flowers, fruit, and other parts in detail.

<image-desc>Detailed woodcut showing Yew flowers, berries (arils), and seeds, labeled with Roman numerals I through V.</image-desc>

Whether the Yew is of a hot or cold temperament <note>Referring to the "humoral" theory of medicine</note> is not yet sufficiently agreed upon among writers: Dioscorides and his followers determine it to be cold, because they say its poison must be countered with the same remedies as Hemlock; among these are Camerarius, Pena, and Lobel: and Wier. But almost all others maintain it is harmful everywhere, a side on which daily experience also stands. For those who eat the berries are seized by fevers and flows of the bowels <note>diarrhea</note>: birds are rendered stunned and are easily captured. Because the wood is reddish with many veins running through it and is resistant to decay, it is greatly sought after by woodworkers, especially for fashioning spears, arrows, tables, and even heated rooms <note>term: hypocausts; rooms heated from below, often paneled in fine wood</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### PINE: German: Fichtenbaum: Belgian: Pinappelboom: French: Pin. Italian & Spanish: Pino.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Pine branch with long needles and a large cone.</image-desc>

The Pine, which is the *Peuke* of the Greeks—not the *Pitys*, as some have wrongly thought—Theophrastus distinguishes into the Urban and the Wild: and this again he makes either Female, or Male, or finally sterile, assigning to each its own marks. More recent authors have distinguished them differently, as will be clear from what follows. We depict here the most common Pine, called the Cultivated and Domestic Pine, which has hard pits <note>seeds</note> and long leaves.

It loves a lean and maritime location: yet in the mountains and among rocks, it is found vaster and taller. It is characteristic of it, however, to spread its branches widest in "false" <note>loose or sandy</note> soil, as appears from the most pleasant Pine-grove near Ravenna. It is cultivated in France, Belgium, and Italy; in Germany it is not very frequent. More in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### PINE WITH FRAGILE-SHELLED SEEDS, or the Stone Pine.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Stone Pine or Swiss Pine branch with a cone and seeds.</image-desc>

Simler and Gesner confuse this with the Pine properly so-called and the common variety. By Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, famous 16th-century botanist</note> it is called the Wild Pine *Cembro*, commonly called *Cembri* and *Cirmoli*. Munster, Belon, and others also call it the *Pinaster* and Wild Pine; the Germans commonly call it *Fichtenbaum*: the French *Pin sauvage*. However, the leaves of this tree are shorter than those of the common Pine: and the cones are also smaller than those of the Pine: and it also has this in common with the cones of the fir, that the scales are easily plucked from the stalk. Two *Pityides* <note>pine nuts</note> or one are hidden in each scale, half the size of the domestic Pine: the pits are three-cornered, with a reddish, thin, and fragile shell, etc.

It is a tree born of the Alps, not infrequent among the people of Trento and the Savoyards.

---

<column-break/>

### COMMON WILD PINE, Pinaster and Torch-pine.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Scots Pine or similar wild pine with cones and seeds shown separately below.</image-desc>

The *Pinaster* or Wild Pine grows spontaneously in various places, and especially in the Alps: we have observed it most frequently near Florimont, and around Belfort and Raupach. Those who, along with Pliny, make the *Teda* <note>Torch-pine</note> a particular species of conifer and a tree of its own kind are led by a great error. For *Teda* is properly called a specific disease of the Pitch-pine, the Larch, and particularly the Wild Pine, by which those trees are turned into "torch-wood," when not only the heart but the rest of the substance is changed into fatness <note>resin</note>. Furthermore, torches are made from *Teda*, and the soot serves for the making of book-writer's ink. Boiled in vinegar, it soothes the pains of the teeth when used as a rinse. Added to plasters, it is very useful for pestilential carbuncles <note>sores associated with the plague</note>.

<column-break/>

### WILD PINE, MUGHO, or Crein, the Creeping Pinaster.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a Mountain Pine (Pinus mugo) showing its characteristic low, spreading growth habit.</image-desc>

The tree which they call *le Crein* in Burgundy grows in the mountains which they call *Franche montagne*; it is a small and stunted tree compared to other resin-bearing trees, and occupies the lower parts of the mountains. They use it for torches in place of *teda*, though more rarely, because it is less fatty.

Could this be Mattioli's *Mugho* Pine, growing in the mountains of Trento and Anaunia? Anguillara, the French Dodoens, Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, and Camerarius also mention the wild pine, both the creeping and the humble pine-shrub, and they label it *Pinus Mughus*—perhaps from Pliny's *Tubulus*?

<summary>This page describes various species of Yew and Pine, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses, and the historical debates regarding their classification by ancient and contemporary botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Yew (Taxus), Pine (Pinus), Stone Pine (Cembro), Mountain Pine (Mugho), resin, medicinal botany, Pliny, Dioscorides, Mattioli, forestry</keywords>

--- Page 117 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of various pine species, following the previous descriptions of the common forest pine.</meta>

### THE GREATER AUSTRIAN WILD PINE, WHITE & BLACK.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a pine branch with long needles and a large, textured cone pointing downwards.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> depicts and describes this tree, and says there are two kinds, so similar to one another that few, except for timber cutters, can tell them apart. One, however, has a more lush and upright trunk, smoother bark, and a larger cone; the Austrians call it the *Foreur* <note>original: "unisse Foreur"</note>. The other has smaller cones, a twisted trunk, and a more somber appearance; they call it the *Black Foreur* <note>original: "Schwartz Foreur"</note>. Both grow in the mountainous regions of Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and Slovenia</note> and Austria. It must be considered how much it differs from our Wild Pine described previously, or whether it is the same. From it, both the black and white varieties, are made planks, shingles, and vineyard stakes.

<column-break/>

### THE THIN-LEAVED AUSTRIAN WILD PINE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a pine branch with thinner, more delicate needles and a smaller cone.</image-desc>

According to the same author Clusius, it grows at the roots of several Austrian mountains, among the rocks.

In this vacant space, I am pleased to add the uses and powers of the Pine and Wild Pine in general. The bark, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacology (c. 40–90 AD)</note>, has an astringent power; when crushed and sprinkled on, it heals chafing, burns, and sores on the surface of the skin. Used as a fumigant, it expels the fetus and the afterbirth. When drunk, it stops the bowels and promotes urine. The crushed leaves, when applied, soothe inflammations and preserve wounds from becoming inflamed. Crushed and boiled in vinegar, they ease toothaches if used as a warm rinse. Pine wood <note><term>Tæda</term>: resinous pinewood used for torches</note> cut into small pieces and boiled in vinegar—as mentioned above—soothes toothaches when used as a rinse. More on this in the following sections.

---

### THE DWARF WILD PINE, THE SMALLEST OF ALL.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a dwarf pine branch with short, dense needles and a small, rounded cone.</image-desc>

This Wild Pine hardly exceeds a man's height; Clusius writes that he found it in the soil of the Kingdom of Murcia <note>In southeastern Spain</note>. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note>, however, says it differs very little from the low Wild Pine of the French province.

Furthermore, to continue describing the virtues of the Pine and Wild Pine: pine nuts are most suitable for those with consumption <note>tuberculosis</note> and those wasting away. Indeed, a highly nutritious "Pine-milk" <note>original: "Pineolatum polytrophon"</note> is made from them, which is very pleasing for long-standing chest ailments, for those with a cough or who are thin, and it is very useful for erosions of the bladder and kidney stones. Water distilled from Pine cones <note>original: "Strobilorum Pini"</note> erases wrinkles from the face, prevents the growth of the breasts, and tightens the neck of the womb. A wine is also made from them, as Dioscorides teaches. The bark, leaves, and nuts of the Wild Pine provide the same benefits, and even more powerfully—though the nuts are not for eating.

<column-break/>

### THE MARITIME WILD PINE, WITH CONES FIRMLY CLINGING TO THE BRANCHES.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a pine branch with thick needles and a large, sturdy cone attached closely to the stem.</image-desc>

The cones on this tree grow in pairs opposite each other, nodding downwards, and clinging firmly by a thick, woody stalk; by this name it differs from other species of Pine and Wild Pine.

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "Father of Botany" (c. 371–287 BC)</note> greatly commends the wood of the Pine, saying its use in building is remarkable because of the openness and straightness of its grain, and because it can in no way be split if it is protected with glue. Moreover, round ships are made from it because they do not rot, the wood being very firm against decay and woodworms.

The resin, like all others, dries and warms. Since pitch <note>original: "Pix"</note> is extracted by the force of fire from the fattest and most resinous liquids of trees turned into torch-wood, it is made especially from the Pitch-tree and the Pine.

---

### THE MARITIME PINE OF THEOPHRASTUS, ACCORDING TO LOBELIUS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a small, young pine tree with a straight trunk and radiating branches.</image-desc>

The Maritime Pine of Theophrastus, says Lobelius, seems in its trunk and the appearance of its branches and leaves to be entirely similar to the Mountain Wild Pine; but the cone is reddish-purple, shorter, and wider at the top. The branches and trunk are darker and smooth.

<column-break/>

### THE IDA PINE OF THEOPHRASTUS, ACCORDING TO THE SAME LOBELIUS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a dense, bushy pine shrub with numerous small cones visible among the needles.</image-desc>

This one, says Lobelius, is easily distinguished from the other by the rough bark of the trunk and branches, by being crowded with leaves around the branches, and by its larger, longer, and more beautiful numerous cones. To Matthiolo <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an Italian physician and botanist</note>, it is another kind of Maritime Pine.

It highlights the use of pine components for treating everything from toothaches and skin burns to respiratory consumption and wrinkles.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Austrian Pine, Maritime Pine, Clusius, Lobelius, Dioscorides, medicinal plants, resin, timber, pine nuts, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of exotic and coniferous trees, following the previous botanical descriptions. The focus here is on identifying species from both the New World/Indies and classical Mediterranean regions.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### EXOTIC FRUIT WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A PINE CONE.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of an exotic fruit resembling a pine cone, shown attached to a short, thick, woody stem with small scale-like leaves.</image-desc>

From a stalk nearly the thickness of the little finger—reddish, hard, and woody—leaves grow by resting upon one another. They are nearly a finger long, firm, of a woody substance, and three-sided: narrower at the base, broader in the remaining part, and curved back toward the tip, clothed with numerous leaf-like scales that are shining and black. The leaves that hide inside are shorter than the outermost ones and are enclosed by the crowding of their flowers. Having weighed all these features, especially the shape, color, and the way the leaves rest upon each other, we have given this fruit, brought from distant regions, the name "Fruit with the appearance of a Pine Cone."

<column-break/>

### TREE WITH THE LEAF OF LAVENDER.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a woody branch with three main upright stems, covered in small, narrow leaves similar to lavender, ending in tufted flower heads.</image-desc>

This branch was brought from the East Indies, though it is very little known from what tree it came. It was equal to three feet in length, and the diameter of its thickness was about two inches. Its tip ended in a somewhat swelling, knotty head, from which five smaller branches, a foot and a half long, sprang forth, arranged in a very elegant series and order. On their leafy tips clung leaves resembling the leaves of Lavender in shape, color, and size. Because these were full of a juice that tasted somewhat like <term>Gum Elemi</term> <note>A fragrant resin used in ointments and lacquers</note>, they claimed a place for this branch among the resin-bearing trees.

---

### LARCH: German: *Lerchbaum*; Belgian: *Lorkenboom*; French: *Meleze*; Italian & Spanish: *Larice*.

<image-desc>A tall, slender coniferous tree (Larch) with a straight trunk and drooping branches, showing small cones.</image-desc>

It is thought to have been unknown to Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and all of Greece; nor does Homer mention it anywhere, although Pliny asserts that he does. Whether it was properly known even to the ancient Latins—Palladius, Vitruvius, and Pliny—is deservedly doubted, since they write that the Larch does not burn, and specifically here, that it has evergreen leaves, both of which are false <note>Larch is unique among conifers for dropping its needles in winter</note>.

Today, various regions report it as common: the territory of Ambrun; the forests and mountains near Vienna (Austria); the Rhaetian Alps; the region of Sion among the Valais; and other places.

<margin>We depict here the <term>Agaric</term> <note>A medicinal fungus, *Laricifomes officinalis*</note>, which grows upon it in a thick mass; however, we will provide its use and virtues, as well as the rest of the history of the Larch, in the Appendix.</margin>

<column-break/>

### CYPRESS: German: *Cypressenbaum*; Belgian: *Cypressenboom*; French: *Cypres*; Italian: *Cypresso* & *Cusresso*.

<image-desc>A tall, conical Cypress tree with dense, dark foliage and small round cones.</image-desc>

The Ancients did not bestow great praise upon the Cypress. Cato said it was difficult to grow, useless in its fruit, grim in its berries, bitter of leaf, violent in scent, thin in its wood, and not even pleasing in its shade; it was also sacred to Dis <note>The god of the Underworld</note>. They even called it the "funeral tree," because it grows slowly and does not sprout back once cut down; for which reason they used to place it as a sign of mourning before the houses of the deceased.

It is distinguished into the Male, which is always unfruitful, and the Female, which remains sterile for a long time. It is quite common in Italy, but it is a source of profit especially for the Cretans. We ourselves have seen it in abundance at Paris and Montpellier, where it bears nuts in Autumn which last through the whole Winter and Summer. It binds and cools <note>referring to its medicinal astringent properties</note>, but the nuts are more effective than the leaves.

More in the Appendix.

---

### CEDAR: German: *Cederbaum*; Belgian: *Cederboom*; French: *Cedre*, *Cedre du Liban*; Italian: *Cedro*.

<image-desc>A large, spreading Cedar tree with a thick trunk and horizontal branching structure.</image-desc>

The Cedar is a large tree, not unlike the fir, whose fruits are called *Cedrides*, and from which the pitch called *Cedria* is collected. According to Theophrastus, Pliny, Galen, and almost all the moderns, there are two types: the Greater and the Lesser. Mattioli falsely established with Dioscorides that the Great Cedar is berry-bearing; for it is certain that it bears a cone. It should be known that the Great Cedar, also called the Cedar of Lebanon, which we depict here, differs greatly from the Cedar simply so-called, and that which is properly called *Oxycedros* <note>Prickly Cedar</note>, of which we speak next.

It is properly an inhabitant of Lebanon, growing there upon the rocks—which is a marvel, since it turns out so tall and of such thickness that six or seven men can scarcely embrace the trunks. Furthermore, its wood is incorruptible.

<column-break/>

### PRICKLY CEDAR, THE PHOENICIAN CEDAR OF BELON, Greater Juniper.

<image-desc>A smaller, shrub-like coniferous tree (Prickly Cedar/Juniper) with sharp needles and small berries.</image-desc>

The Lesser Cedar is similar and related to the Juniper: but its leaves are twice as long, and also broader, rigid, and stinging with a hostile point. The berries are twice or thrice larger than those of the Juniper, and in color not blue like those, but reddish; yet the taste and smell are similar. Those who call it the "Greater Juniper" are in error; for as has been said, the great size and the Phoenician color <note>original: "color Phoeniceas," referring to a deep red or purple</note> cry out against it. By almost all moderns it is called *Oxycedros*. It grows in some rugged places of Italy, most of Spain, and some parts of Narbonnese Gaul. From its wood, cut into pieces and burned, the shepherds and peasants in the territory of Marseille extract a black and foul-smelling oily liquid, which they name *Huile de Cade* <note>Cade oil, still used for skin conditions</note>, called *Miera* by the Spaniards.

<summary>This page describes various coniferous and exotic trees, including the Larch, Cypress, and Cedar of Lebanon, correcting ancient misconceptions about their growth and properties. It also details the production of medicinal oils like Cade oil from the Prickly Cedar.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Larch, Cypress, Cedar of Lebanon, Juniper, Cade oil, medicinal resins, Mediterranean flora, East Indies</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### CEDAR, OR LYCIAN OXYCEDRUS, called *Morusine* by the people of Marseille, and *De cade serbin* by those of Avignon.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cedar/Oxycedrus branch with needle-like leaves and small round berries. Below the branch are two detached berries, one shown in cross-section.</image-desc>

It is sometimes thorny, at other times not; because the leaves are blunt, Pierre Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564) was a French naturalist who traveled extensively in the Levant.</note> recorded it as the "blunt-leaved Lycian Cedar." By some it is called the berry-bearing Savin, but incorrectly, as it differs greatly from the Savin in both scent and form; others think it is the *Thuya* of the people of Marseille. It grows in the same places as the preceding species, being very common around Marseille and Avignon.

In Spain, Carolus Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a Flemish botanist and one of the most influential of the 16th century.</note> observed mistletoe growing on the branches of the Oxycedrus. From the Phoenician Cedar, the Oxycedrus, and also from the Juniper, a certain gum exudes which they call Varnish, and is the *Sandaracha* <term>Sandaracha: a resin, likely sandarac, used in varnishes and medicine</term> of the Arabs. It heats and dries in the first degree; it checks catarrhs <note>original: "destillationes" - the downward flow of humors, often meaning a cold or sinus drip</note>, stops excessive menstrual flow, and applied in various ways, it soothes toothaches.

<column-break/>

### COMMON JUNIPER: German *Weckholder*: Belgian *Genever*: French *Geneure*: Italian *Ginepro*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common Juniper branch with sharp, needle-like leaves and numerous small berries.</image-desc>

Of the common Juniper, one type is Greater and the other Lesser; they differ only in size. It is also distinguished in another way: namely, that one bears berries and the other only flowers; the latter is commonly called the Female, and the former the Male. However, the one that bears fruit does not flower. In some, a thorn stands in place of a leaf.

It abounds everywhere in various places. It flowers in the month of May; after the flower, small green berries break forth, which only in the second year, as Autumn approaches (which is their time for ripening), are tinged with blue. If they are kept into the third year, they are called "three-year fruit."

The berries are hot in the third degree and dry in the first. The fruit, twigs, and branches of the Juniper are in use, as well as the whole wood; its many benefits can hardly be fully explained.

---

### GREAT ILLYRIAN JUNIPER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-fruited Juniper branch with broader, scale-like leaves and large, prominent berries.</image-desc>

Pena and Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel and Pierre Pena, authors of the "Stirpium Adversaria Nova" (1570).</note> record it thus, both in their *Adversaria* and in their *Observations and Icons of Plants*. To Tabernaemontanus it is the *Greater Illyrian Juniper*. In the *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published by Rouillé in Lyon.</note> it is simply the *Greater Juniper*.

As for what Dioscorides says—that the fruit of the Greater Juniper sometimes equals the Pontic Nut <note>likely a hazelnut</note> in size, or even sometimes grows to the size of a Walnut—this has not yet been observed in our European world.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE JUNIPER, SELAGO.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alpine Juniper or Selago branch with dense, overlapping scale-like leaves.</image-desc>

We depict here a branch of the Alpine Juniper which we received from the Dauphiné region. Clusius has a similar one in his *Plants of Pannonia*; and in his *History*, he asks: is this the *Selago* of Pliny?

Since we said above that it is not easy to list all the virtues of the Juniper, we shall also note something of its harms. One thing in this little tree is to be avoided and detested: namely its shade, whence Virgil says:
> Let us rise; the shade is often heavy for those who sing.
> The shade of the Juniper is heavy, and a shade harmful to the crops.

---

### SAVIN: German *Seuenbaum*: Belgian *Seuenboom*: French *Sauignier*: Italian *Sabina*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Savin Juniper branch with fine, scale-like foliage and small berries.</image-desc>

The Savin is always green in its foliage; it is quite low and always grows more in width than in height. For this reason, some have not hesitated to call it an Herb, others a Shrub; although it is neither an herb nor a shrub, but a tree of almost fair size.

Dioscorides and Pliny make two species of it: one with leaves like the Cypress, but more thorny, foul-smelling, pungent, and burning; the other with leaves like the Tamarisk. More recent authors have observed other differences: they call one Male and the other Female; some say one is sterile and the other berry-bearing or fruitful; and finally, they say one has leaves that are not at all thorny, while they attribute thorns to all the others. We depict here the berry-bearing one with non-thorny leaves.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SAVIN, STERILE SAVIN: with thorny leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sterile Savin branch with more prickly, needle-like foliage.</image-desc>

Jean Ruel <note>French physician and botanist (1474–1537).</note> writes that the name "Sabina" is retained everywhere; some wish it to be named after the region of the Sabines, where it once abounded. Today it is kept everywhere in cultivated gardens. At Verona, we saw two large Savin trees, and others shaped into the figures of various animals <note>an early reference to topiary</note>, nor have we seen more beautiful ones anywhere else. It grows most safely wild with many others, its leaves being partly thorny and partly not.

Furthermore, Savin is of the third order of both heating and drying substances, being among those composed of the most subtle parts. It provokes the menses, expels the fetus <note>Savin was historically used as a dangerous abortifacient</note>, stops spreading ulcers, etc. Is it the *Selago* of Pliny? Or the *Brutes* of Ruel, a goddess known only to the East?

<summary>This page describes various species of Juniper and Savin, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations, and medicinal properties. It highlights the distinction between berry-bearing and sterile varieties and notes the historical use of Savin in medicine and topiary.</summary>

<keywords>Cedar, Oxycedrus, Juniper, Savin, Sandaracha, Dioscorides, Pliny, Clusius, Lobelius, Selago, medicinal plants, botany, topiary, abortifacients</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### TREE OF LIFE, or PARADISE TREE: German: *Baum des lebens*: French: *Arbre de vit.*
### ABHEL, THUJA OF THEOPHRASTUS, Atlantic Cedar, Pliny’s Bruta.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a small, bushy evergreen tree with dense, scale-like foliage, resembling a Thuja or Cedar.</image-desc>

It is a very fragrant small tree, closely resembling the Savin <note>a species of juniper</note>, and is evergreen like those; it bears flowers like the Cypress and oblong cones, not berries, as Gesner incorrectly wrote. Its wood is resistant to decay, wood-boring beetles, and worms, and is not subject to corruption in any age, which is perhaps where it gets its name <note>Tree of Life</note>. This was brought to our world not long ago from Canada, a province of Northern America, and today it is kept in several of the more cultivated gardens, such as the one under our care in Montbéliard. Is it the *Thuja* of Theophrastus? Is it the *Bruta* of Pliny? Is it an exotic type of Savin? Or is it a tree of the Peruvian region, whose resin, when smeared on or dripped into the deceased, protects corpses from putrefaction?

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Two small, rounded botanical specimens; the top one appears to be a seed or small fruit, and the bottom one is a cross-section or a different view of a similar seed.</image-desc>

We depict here the fruit known to the entire Orient by the name *Abhel*, which equals the size of Cypress pills <note>small cones</note> and has a color declining from reddish to black; it is gathered from a tree of that kind, very similar to the Cypress. Since the *Thuja* of Theophrastus is not known today except from his own history, Guilandini, Clusius, and Camerarius have perhaps thought that the tree bearing the *Abhel* fruit is that very one. And again, Anguillara and Mattioli have supposed that the *Thuja* of Theophrastus and the Atlantic Cedar of the Ancients are one and the same. Or is it Pliny’s *Bruta*, of which he says: "So great is the satiety of mortals for their own things, and their greed for foreign ones, that they seek the Bruta tree in the Haemus mountains, which is similar to the Cypress," etc.

---

### FRANKINCENSE, OLIBANUM: German: *Weyrauch*: Dutch: *Wierooch*: French: *Encens*: Italian: *Incenso*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a tall, slender tree with a textured trunk and sparse, leafy branches, representing the Frankincense tree.</image-desc>

*Thus* <note>Frankincense</note> signifies both the tree and the tear <note>the resin droplet</note>, and it is sometimes written without the 'h', as if the name were given from the melting of whole clumps. To Galen, the tree is called *Libanos* and the tear *Libanotos*, but to Euripides the tear is *Libanos* and the tree *Libanotos*.

It is clear from Pliny that the tree was not sufficiently known to the Ancients: some attributed to it the leaves of a Pear, others the Mastic tree, and others the Turpentine tree. Even today, writers do not entirely agree on its origin and appearance. Cesalpino stubbornly asserts that no one among us has seen the Frankincense tree, and that only Theophrastus among the Ancients described it; Guilandini maintains that Firs in Arabia drip with Frankincense; while Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, and modern authors declare it to be a tree of its own kind.

---

### BDELLIUM: German, Dutch, French & Italian: *Bdellium*: To the Arabs: *Mochol, Mochel, Molochil, & Molochal*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a gnarled, thorny tree with small leaves, representing the Bdellium-producing plant.</image-desc>

Bdellium, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of a Saracen tree. According to Galen, it grows in Arabia, India, Media, and Babylon. Our figure is from Lobelius. However, what Bdellium actually is, and whether the true and genuine kind is held today, is sharply disputed among writers. Some think it is legitimate Myrrh, others true *Anime* <note>a type of resin</note>, and others something else. Whatever it may be, if Mattioli is to be believed, it is very rare and is kept in apothecary shops only for show or as a standard for rejection. In Cornarius's judgment, however, the shops retain Bdellium in both thing and name, but the names "Saracenic" in Dioscorides, "Barbarian" in Pliny, and "Arabic and Scythian" in Galen have fallen out of use. More on the following page.

<column-break/>

### THE HOODED LEAF OF FRANKINCENSE.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of a large, hooded or pitcher-shaped leaf with prominent veining.</image-desc>

The *Adversaria* <note>a botanical work by Lobel and Pena</note> also depict this beautiful, hooded, and channeled leaf, which is usually brought from Florida, and they label it the "leaf of clear Frankincense." Thevet, from whom our image is taken, writes that not only Arabia (as the Ancients wished) but many other regions are fertile with Frankincense, and in some places the trees are already as common as Orange trees are in the French province <note>Provence</note>. He claims some of them bear sixty pounds of Frankincense, though the most excellent is held to be from Arabia. But why does he liken the tree to a Pine and depict it differently? Garcia makes it low-growing and attributes to it leaves like the Mastic tree, establishing another mountain variety which bears the best Frankincense, and another growing in the plains which bears a black and inferior kind.

---

### STORAX TREE AND TEAR: German, Dutch & French: *Storax*: Italian: *Storace*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a leafy branch with small flowers and round fruits, representing the Storax tree.</image-desc>

The Storax tree is very similar in trunk and leaf to the Quince; it has white flowers like the orange, and fruit the size of a hazelnut, uniform and hollow, with a woody pit the color of a berry. It is properly a tree of Syria and Palestine, which is nevertheless said to be frequent on the Indian island of Zena. It is kept in Venice, Rome, and various other places in Italy, but it does not bear the "tear" <note>resin</note>, or only very little. We have had small trees grown from seeds in the Saint-Fort garden at Montbéliard, and we have also seen them in Basel.

From the Storax tree flows the Storax tear; regarding this, as well as the history of Bdellium, consult both our Great History and the following page.

<summary>This page describes several aromatic and resin-producing trees, including the American "Tree of Life" (Thuja), Frankincense, Bdellium, and Storax, debating their botanical identities based on ancient and contemporary sources.</summary>

# PLANTS
### EXOTIC WOOD: ETTALCHE. SMALLEST CONIFEROUS NUT.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations of botanical specimens. On the left, a cross-section of a dark, dense piece of wood labeled with an asterisk. On the right, a small, detailed pine cone or coniferous nut, also labeled with an asterisk.</image-desc>

The wood we depict here is held and described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist</note>: he says it was hard, heavy, firm, and smelled of Mastic <note>a resin from the Mediterranean lentisk tree</note>, and was taken from an American tree from which a resin is drawn out in the manner of pitch, and used for the same purpose, for which reason it has claimed this place for itself.

Could it be the **Ettalche**, a large tree with juniper-like leaves, thorny, and emitting a gum similar to Mastic, with which—due to the similarity of scent and color—the Africans adulterate true Mastic? Its wood is reported to be white in Numidia <note>North Africa</note>, violet in Libya, and deepest black in Ethiopia.

Or is it Cato’s **Capida**? <note>A reference to an obscure vessel or wood type mentioned by Cato the Elder</note>

<column-break/>

We keep these small cones among our natural specimens; they closely resemble the cones of the Larch, but are much smaller, having stalks that are empty and curved. At their base, very short leaves of the Pitch-pine adhere. It is apparent that they consist of Larch-like scales—thin, broad, and furrowed—and that a leafy seed grows between the scales, as in the Pitch-pine or Fir. Whether these are the cones of the Larch or of another tree is not entirely certain to us.

Thus, as far as the brevity we proposed has allowed, we have reviewed the trees specifically called "Resin-bearing." But since not all—or at least not sufficiently—of the fragrant juices of each and every one have been described, we shall fill this empty space with a "gleaning" <note>original: *spicilegio*, a gathering of leftover grain</note> of several types.

---

->There are two types of **RESIN**:<-

**Liquid** and **Dry**. **Liquid** flows from various trees, especially Pine and Pitch-pine, either spontaneously or when the branches or trunk are wounded. If it is found mixed with woody or stony bits due to careless gathering, it is called *Confusanea* <note>mixed or jumbled</note>. **Dry** resin comes from the cracks in the bark of the same trees or from cut branches; it lacks fatness and dries out quickly. Some make a third type called *Strobolina*, but incorrectly, as it only has that name because it is found hardened around the cones, or *strobili*.

**PITCH** <note>original: *Pix*</note> is extracted by the force of fire from the fattest and most resinous woods, especially Pine and Pitch-pine, which have been turned into torches. It is either liquid or dry: the liquid is called *Crude* if it has experienced no fire other than the heat by which it flowed, or *Brutian* <note>from Calabria, Italy</note>, which is dark, fatter, and thicker. **Dry** pitch is made from liquid pitch that has been boiled again; this is either boiled only to the thickness of birdlime, or, by a longer and stronger fire, is rendered dry, brittle, and scrapable.

**CEDRIA** is the "Tear of the Cedar," a pitch or resin which, according to Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note>, destroys living things but preserves dead bodies; thus it is often called the *Life of the Dead*. Corresponding to it is the oil which provincials usually make from Juniper, Ash, Cedar, and other such woods, which they call *Huile de Cade* <note>Cade oil</note>; it is primarily useful for mange of the head, and for the mange and ulcers of livestock.

**FRANKINCENSE** <note>original: *Thus*</note>: where and how it is marked was said before. The "Breast-shaped" <note>original: *Mammosa*</note> variety is especially prized, namely when a second drop follows and joins itself to a previous clinging tear. This they call *Male* frankincense, though it is not otherwise called "Male" unless there is a "Female." Frankincense is further distinguished into *Manna* and *Bark*. Pliny interpreted *Manna* as the crumbs shaken off by jostling; Plautus called it a *Grain of Frankincense*, and Hermolaus called it *Hypofisma*. Frankincense warms and binds significantly; the Bark possesses the same power, and even more effectively.

**MASTIC** is the resin of the Lentisk tree; the best comes from the Island of Chios, *about which we speak elsewhere*.

**SARCOCOLLA** <note>literally "flesh-glue"</note>, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of a tree growing in Persia, similar to thin Frankincense, somewhat yellowish and bitter. It has the power of gluing together ulcers and restraining fluxes.

**MYRRH** is the tear of the tree of the same name, found mostly in Arabia; when cut in any place, it emits this very tear. Seven varieties are described, named after the places where they are obtained.

**STACTE** is not Balsam, as some wish, nor liquid Styrax, as others prefer, but the fatness of fresh Myrrh crushed with a little water and pressed out through a tool. *Dioscorides.*

**BENZOIN** <note>original: *Beniouinum*</note> is a gum or resin flowing from the wounded *Beninus* tree. There are various kinds, but the one called *Amygdaloides* <note>almond-like</note> is preferred over the others. It is a large and tall tree with leaves like a Citron, growing in Sumatra, an island of the East Indies. It is clear that Benzoin was unknown to the Ancients because neither the Greeks nor the Arabs describe it; for it is not the *Balenzan* of Averrhoes.

**LIQUIDAMBAR** is a resin flowing from incisions in vast, beautiful, and branchy trees with ivy-like leaves, which grow in New Spain <note>Mexico</note>. They are called *Ocofol* <note>Ocozotl</note> by the inhabitants. It warms, dissolves, and soothes pains; it is of the greatest use in Medicine.

**CANCAMUM**, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of an Arabian wood, somewhat similar to Myrrh but with a foul taste.

**ANIME** and **COFAL** <note>Copal</note> are synonyms. *Anime* is collected from wounded trees of medium size, no differently than Frankincense or Mastic; if we believe Hermolaus, it takes its name from the Arabian *lotus* in which it is found. There are two kinds: soft and harder. Why Amatus <note>Amatus Lusitanus, a 16th-century physician</note> calls it *Anima* <note>Soul</note>, we do not know.

**TOCOTGEBIT** is an East Indian tree similar to a poplar, under whose bark grows a resin similar to our Frankincense but whiter, which they use there as Frankincense.

**CARANNA**, so named by the Indians and Spaniards, is a resin also collected from wounded trees, the color of Tacamahaca but a little clearer, with a similar but heavier scent.

**ELECTRUM** or **AMBER** <note>original: *Succinum*</note>, called *Carabe* by the Arabs, is the gum of a poplar tree according to Dioscorides; but according to Pliny and some more recent followers, it is a resin flowing from a tree similar to a pitch-pine. However, by the account of almost all others, it is born from Bitumen, which, flowing from the shores into the sea, hardens in the way we see. It is either *Yellow* or *White*; it is found in the coastal regions of Germany, rolled onto the shore by storms.

**BDELLIUM** and **STYRAX**, both the trees and the tears, were discussed previously.

**CAMPHOR** is numbered among the gifts of the East Indies; it is a gum flowing from a tree similar to a poplar, growing in mountains near the sea. Four species are commonly reviewed; it differs greatly from the *Viua Capura* of Qualcebeni.

**USYB**, a gum-bearing tree with which the Indians anoint the body, is mentioned by Thevet in *Antarctic France* <note>André Thevet's 1557 account of Brazil</note>.

**TACAMAHACA** is obtained from the East Indies and flows from a wounded large tree equal to a poplar; it is of great use for innumerable ailments.

Concerning **ACACIA**, **GUM ARABIC**, and all other Juices, Gums, and Tears, they shall be in their own place.

# OF PLANTS
## CLASS X.
### CONCERNING TREES AND BROOM-LIKE SHRUBS.

**MYRICA** or **TAMARISK**: German *Tamarischenbaum*:
French *Tamarisque*: Italian *Tamarice*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tamarix plant, showing its feathery foliage and upright growth habit.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> calls this a well-known tree that grows near sluggish waters. However, Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> calls it "amphibious," because it is not only to be counted among aquatic plants but is also abundant in deserts. Pliny, being inconsistent, distinguishes between a Cultivated and a Wild variety; in one place he says it bears fruit similar to a gall-nut, and in another he says its wood is called "unlucky" because it bears neither fruit nor seed.

More recent authors create one category for the *Cultivated* type, which is tall and tree-like, and another for the *Wild* type, which is low and shrubby, and is called by the diminutive name *Tamariscus*. This latter type they subdivide again, as will be mentioned shortly. This tree-like Tamarisk is found frequently in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France.</note>, both near rivers and far from them. We have seen it in gardens in Paris, Montpellier, and in Belgium.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER TAMARISK**, or **SHRUBBY TAMARISK**, called **GERMAN Tamarix**.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the German Tamarix, showing a more shrub-like form with dense, needle-like foliage.</image-desc>

Two kinds of this are found: *one* with more solid wood and thinner leaves, the *other* with somewhat broad leaves and less solid wood. Thus Theophrastus established two kinds of Tamarisks: one with strong wood, the other weak. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German botanist.</note> writes that the former grows abundantly by the Rhine at Strasbourg, and the latter on the banks of the Danube.

It loves damp and stony regions, and does not easily take to garden cultivation unless placed near water. We have seen both kinds in various places near flowing rivers and marshes: at Geneva, Zurich, Lyon, and Padua. It flowers in May and June.

Some distinguish this from the tree-like variety because it has downy <note>original: "papposos" - referring to seeds with tufts of hair for wind dispersal.</note> flowers, whereas the tree-like one does not, but rather has round, tiny, reddish flowers.

---

**EGYPTIAN TAMARISK, DOMESTIC OR CULTIVATED, Gall-bearing.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Egyptian Tamarix, including a detailed view of its root system and branching structure.</image-desc>

Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, an Italian physician who studied Egyptian flora.</note> writes that this grows to the height of a large Olive tree, and its fruit equals a walnut in size. Dioscorides names it the cultivated or urban variety, and says it produces fruit similar to galls.

Furthermore, the Tamarisk has a cleansing and cutting <note>term: "incidentis" - a medical term for breaking up thick humors or fluids in the body.</note> quality, and possesses some astringency. It frees the internal organs from obstructions, and a decoction of the leaves, used as a rinse, soothes toothaches. All parts of this tree—fruit, leaves, flowers, bark, wood, and wood-ash—are beneficial for those with spleen ailments. Such people benefit from drinking continuously out of vessels made from its wood; hence Pliny wrote that pigs accustomed to eating their food from troughs made of it were found to have no spleen. Dio <note>Likely referring to Cassius Dio.</note> testifies that the Ancients prophesied by the power of its twigs.

<column-break/>

**ERICA** or **HEATH**: German *Heyden*; Belgian *Heyde*:
French *Bruyere*: Italian *Erica*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Erica (heather) plant, showing its woody stems and small, scale-like leaves.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides, Erica is a shrubby tree with leaves like the Myrica, but much smaller. Many differences are observed in it, taken from its size, leaves, flowers, and fruit. Thus, some are low-growing, others become tree-like; some have leaves in threes, others in fours; some are hairy and downy, others not; some have white flowers, others purple, or grass-green, etc. Finally, some bear berries, others do not. We depict here the one that is low-growing and has evergreen leaves, with flowers that are either purple or white.

It flowers in June, July, and August, and loves uncultivated places and wildernesses. It is very common in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, and between Montbéliard and Belfort, and again between Montbéliard and Porrentruy.

<summary>This page describes the varieties and medicinal properties of the Tamarisk and Heath plants, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny. It highlights the Tamarisk's use in treating spleen disorders and its geographic distribution across Europe and Egypt.</summary>
<keywords>Tamarisk, Myrica, Erica, Heath, medicinal plants, spleen treatments, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, European flora, Egyptian flora</keywords>

# OF HEATHERS

### HEATHER WITH CORIS-LIKE LEAVES AND WHITE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heather plant (Erica) with thin, needle-like leaves and small bell-shaped flowers clustered at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

This kind of Heather does not resemble the leaves of the Tamarisk <note>original: "Myricæ"</note> as some other kinds do; rather, it greatly rivals the *Coris* <note>A Mediterranean sub-shrub, likely *Coris monspeliensis*</note> in the shape and arrangement of its leaves. Furthermore, there are many species of this genus, differing greatly in size and in the shape and color of the leaves and flowers.

According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note>, it grows in the wildernesses of Portugal <note>original: "Lusitaniæ"</note>: and it blooms in November, December, and January.

<column-break/>

### MANY-FLOWERED HEATHER WITH CORIS-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a more robust heather plant with denser foliage and numerous flower clusters along the upper branches.</image-desc>

Is this the "Greater and Taller Italian Heather" of Camerarius? Or the "Greater Heather of Narbonne with Ground-Pine Leaves" of Pena and Lobel <note>referring to the botanists Pierre Pena and Matthias de l'Obel</note> in their *Adversaria*? Or is it the same as the "Juniper-leaved Densely Shrubbing Heather of Narbonne" in their *Observations*?

Furthermore, the uses of Heather are not to be despised. A decoction of the flowers eases pains of the belly and loins. The juice of the leaves and flowers, rubbed on weak eyes, is beneficial to them. Water distilled from the flowers settles the colic and removes redness from the eyes. Drunk warm in the morning and evening for 30 days, it is effective for breaking down and expelling stones of the bladder <note>term: calculi (kidney or bladder stones)</note>. And there are those who prepare a sweat-bath from the fresh flowers for gout <note>original: "podagram"</note> and paralysis. More in the following.

---

### TREE-LIKE HEATHER, WITH PALE YELLOW OR HERBACEOUS TINY FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, woody heather species with a central stalk and lateral flowering branches.</image-desc>

It is shrubby, reaching a height of two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> and sometimes more, with brittle wood, thin and minute leaves, and a flower smaller than the others, of a grass-green color: and sometimes at the ends of the branches there are little heads made of many leaves. We observed it in the *Aigremont* forest near Montpellier, and also in the Apennine mountains of Italy, between Florence and Bologna.

Among the uses of Heather, it is rightly numbered that: Heathlands in vast wildernesses provide fodder for flocks of sheep: and in some places, for tending fires, it takes the place of wood: and from it brooms are made for cleaning houses: Indeed, even dry Heather nourishes flocks of sheep with very healthy fodder, and preserves them from obstructions of the lungs, spleen, and liver.

<column-break/>

### TREE-LIKE HEATHER OF MONTPELLIER, with purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering shrub with dense, upward-reaching branches covered in small blossoms.</image-desc>

The branches are covered in a thin, ash-colored skin, appearing in threes and often surrounding larger branches: they are not provided with leaves everywhere, yet those they have are almost like Wild Asparagus <note>original: "Corrudę"</note>, somewhat long, thin, and deciduous: at the ends of the branches are flowers of a bluish-purple, which are quite large.

It is very common in the mountains of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> around Ganges and *Esperon*, and it blooms in October. Clusius found it frequently in the cultivated places of Portugal around Lisbon, blooming in December.

---

### BRABANT HEATHER, WITH LEAVES IN FOURS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing heather with leaves arranged in whorls of four and larger, drooping bell flowers.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub only a foot high with thin, blackish twigs: frequent leaves surround them, arranged in a four-fold order: the flowers cling to the highest twigs, of a pale purple color, similar to the flowers of the Lily of the Valley, but more oblong and not so bellied out.

It grows in many places in Brabant and Guelders <note>Regions in the Low Countries/Netherlands</note>, and blooms in Spring and Autumn. Is it the "Other Dwarf Heather of the Belgians" of Lobel in his *Observations*? Or the "Low Heather from which Brooms are made" in the *History of Lyon*?

<column-break/>

### SMALL HEATHER, WITH HERBACEOUS FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, prostrate heather plant with thick foliage and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

It rarely exceeds a foot in height, and for the most part lies prostrate on the ground: the leaves are crowded, somewhat broad, and smooth: the flowers are tiny, endowed with a grass-green color: the root is hard and woody: but on the branches grow green little heads, compacted from broader leaves, in the manner of the heads of Thyme.

We observed this in the Alps of Switzerland <note>original: "Heluetię"</note> and Rhaetia, and we took care to have it painted from the specimen brought from there. It blooms in May and June, at which time it is most pleasant to behold.

<summary>This page catalogs several species of heather (Erica), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and medicinal uses, including treatments for eye ailments and bladder stones.</summary>
<keywords>heather, Erica, botany, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Montpellier, Portugal, Switzerland, Brabant, eye health, bladder stones, fodder</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### Small English Heather, with hairy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, branched heather plant with needle-like leaves and small clusters of flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

We received this dried plant from England under the name of Heather. It is entirely beautiful, scarcely nine inches <note>original: "dodrantalis" — a Roman measurement of about 9 inches or 3/4 of a foot</note> tall: the branches are thin and numerous: the leaves are quite short, crowded together, and hairy around the edges: they grow in threes or fours at small intervals, as if at joints: at the tips are small hairy heads.

### Matthiolus’s Berry-bearing Heather.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heather plant with small berries shown both on the branches and in a detailed cluster at the base of the stem.</image-desc>

Regarding his own Berry-bearing Heather, Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist</note> relates the following. It is a plant, he says, growing in the mountains that divide Bohemia from Silesia, and from whose springs the river Elbe takes its origin. It spreads across the ground and occupies wide areas, with a leaf almost like common Heather: it was not possible to see the flowers: but it bears berries that are blackish-purple, similar to Juniper berries, but smaller, etc.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> labels this in his *Pannonian Flora* as the first Heather with a Coris-leaf; and he says it grows on the ridges of the highest Alps of Austria and Styria, and flowers in June. However, Pena and Lobelius, and even Schwenckfeld, wrongly confuse this Berry-bearing Heather of Matthiolus with the Marsh Whortleberries <note>likely referring to cranberries or bog bilberries</note>.

<column-break/>

### Lobelius’s Foreign Heather.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, upright heather specimen with dense, whorled foliage and small flowers along the upper stems.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), Flemish botanist and physician to James I</note> planted this species of Heather in the hanging gardens of Belgium: it is shrubby in the manner of a privet, with somewhat long leaves, and purple flowers around the branches consisting of four petals. He did not know where it was brought from, and therefore he called it "foreign."

### Clusius’s Portuguese Berry-bearing Heather.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust heather shrub with thick stems and clusters of berries at the branch tips.</image-desc>

It rises with branches about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, which are brittle, with a bark darker than the others: the leaves are also similar to those, but darker and thicker, arranged in a triple row around the twigs. The fruit resembles pearls <note>original: "uniones" — large pearls</note> in both shape and color, though darker, and it is juicy and slightly tart. Whether it flowers is not sufficiently clear; the inhabitants of the places where it grows say it does not, and they say the fruit swells gradually until it ripens. These are the words of Clusius.

It is found only in Portugal, and the fruit ripens in September and October; it is sought after by children and women, and is very pleasant and useful for those who are thirsty, especially those suffering from fevers.

They call the tree *Camarinhara*, and the fruit *Camarinhas* <note>The Portuguese Crowberry (Corema album)</note>. In Amato’s commentary on Dioscorides, the tree is called *Acacalis*.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES OF PLANTS
## CLASS XI.
### TREES, SHRUBS, AND UNDER-SHRUBS THAT BEAR PODS AND
### legume-like flowers: both those lacking thorns and those with thorns: and others similar to these.

**LABURNUM:** *German:* Tree-bean <note>original: Baumbonen</note>: *French:* Laburnum: *Italian:* Eghelo, Eghano, Auornello.

It is a shrubby tree, branched with boughs, having green bark and white, hard wood. The flower is like that of the Little Broom <note>Genistella</note>, the pod like that of Peas, and the seed is varied, hard, smooth, and shining, shaped like a kidney and the size of a Lentil.

Gessner, Dalechamps, and several other more recent authors agree with us that this is the *Laburnum* of Pliny. Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> wishes it to be the *Anagyris* of Dioscorides, but in great error: for the scent, leaves, pods, flowers, and seeds all argue against it. By Castore Durante it is called the *Lesser Anagyris*. By Pena and L'Obel it is called the *Less-stinking Anagyris*.

It flowers in the months of May and June, providing a pleasing sight in the mountains; we have also observed it being cultivated in the gardens of Padua and Lyon. Its scent kills mice; and Camerarius writes that the ashes of the whole plant are recommended for kidney stones. Mattioli claims it can perform all the same medicinal functions as *Anagyris*.

**CYTISUS <note>Broom</note>:** *German:* Goat-clover <note>original: Geicklee</note>: *French:* Cytise: *Italian:* Cytiso.
**CYTISUS WITH CURVED PODS.**

The description of *Cytisus* by Dioscorides is not so accurate that the *Cytisus* of the Ancients is sufficiently known from it. Because of this, different authors have presented different plants as *Cytisus*, and various other plants have been given the name. Pliny and Galen, following Dioscorides, called it a shrub; but Strabo makes it similar to the Balsam, a fragrant tree. We, along with Amato Lusitano, determine that it can be ranked among both trees and shrubs; and with the more experienced scholars, we believe the "legitimate" *Cytisus* of the Ancients is the one we depict here, which Maranta describes at length.

He collected it on a hill near Naples; but according to Belon, it abounds on the island of Rhodes and the high places near it. From its wood, sword-hilts and prayer beads <note>rosary beads</note> are made. Writers call it *Horned Cytisus* and *Maranta’s Cytisus*.

<column-break/>

**ANAGYRIS <note>Stinking Bean Trefoil</note>:** *German:* Stinking-tree, Tree-beans, Genani-beans: *French:* Stinking wood: *Italian:* Anagyri.

Mattioli and Tabernaemontanus confuse Laburnum with this plant. Gessner not only calls it *Anagyris*, but also *Anagyrum* and *Onogyrum*, and states it was unknown to Mattioli. However, it is the legitimate *Anagyris* of Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, and Paul of Aegina. Some of the moderns, chief among them Mattioli, have posited two kinds of *Anagyris*, observing a difference especially in the leaves. But who does not know the playfulness of nature in leaves? Therefore, we, along with Clusius, establish only one legitimate kind, such as was described by the Ancients.

It grows wild in several places, as Clusius observed a mile from Arles and around Seville; but it is kept especially in more cultivated gardens in Rome, Paris, and Padua, where it flowers in a joyful spectacle in February and March. It is a foul-smelling shrub, possessing the power to digest <note>disperse fluids</note> and to draw heat.

**CLUSIUS’S PANNONIAN CYTISUS,**
with entirely hoary <note>grey-white/fuzzy</note> leaves.

The twigs are a cubit long, thin, flexible, and osier-like; the leaves are in threes, narrow, hoary, thick, and bitter to the taste. The flowers at the top of the clusters are five or six in number, similar to the flowers of the Meadow Lotus, golden in color, and not lacking in scent. The pods are flat, somewhat oblong, and entirely hairy; and within them is the seed, reddish, flat, somewhat round, and hard. The root is hard and woody, blackish, and spread out in the topsoil.

It flowers in July, and thereafter until Autumn. The seed ripens toward the end of August and in September. According to Clusius, it is common throughout the Viennese countryside, especially above the pheasant-farm and in many other arid places of Austria and Pannonia <note>an ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note>.

<summary>This page describes and distinguishes between three similar pod-bearing plants: Laburnum, Cytisus (Broom), and Anagyris (Stinking Bean Trefoil), citing classical authorities and contemporary botanists. It provides physical descriptions, geographical locations, and medicinal or practical uses for each.</summary>
<keywords>Laburnum, Cytisus, Anagyris, botany, Mattioli, Clusius, medicinal plants, Pannonian flora, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Cytisus (Medick-tree or Broom) varieties, specifically focusing on species found in Hungary (Pannonia) and Spain (Hispania), as documented by the botanists Carolus Clusius and Matthias de L’Obel.</meta>

### THE SECOND SPECIES OF HUNGARIAN CYTISUS
#### very hairy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus plant with a thick central woody stem, numerous branches, and trifoliate leaves, showing a detailed root system.</image-desc>

This species of Hungarian <term>Cytisus</term><note>A genus of flowering plants in the legume family, often called Brooms</note> is much larger, and it has thicker twigs that are very hairy: the leaves are also twice as large, and the flowers and pods are bigger as well; the flowers also shine with a more golden color. It grows near hedges, and is rarer and less commonly encountered than the other species previously mentioned.

### THE FIRST SPANISH CYTISUS OF CLUSIUS,
#### with greening leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender, upright flowering shrub with small trifoliate leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

This grows sometimes to the size of a small tree; numerous leaves surround the tender little branches, which are covered in soft hair; the leaves are a pale green. The flowers are yellow and somewhat fragrant. The pods are equal to the pods of the <term>Genista</term><note>Common Broom</note>, being oblong, rough, and hairy. The seed is small and blackish; the root is woody and spreads in different directions.

According to <term>Clusius</term><note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note>, it grows in various places in both Castiles <note>The historical regions of Old and New Castile in Spain</note> along the roadsides. It flowers in June, and produces seed in July and August. We consider this to be the same as the Cytisus of Mount Galcaris mentioned by <term>Lobelius</term><note>Matthias de L'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note>.

### THE THIRD SPANISH CYTISUS OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen with long, thin branches, small leaves, and distinct flower clusters along the upper stems.</image-desc>

It rises with branches a foot high, and rarely a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</note> high; these are thin and entirely gray-white. Three leaves adorn these, attached by a short stalk, and the middle leaf is twice as long as the others. Golden flowers shimmer along the branches from bottom to top, possessing a pleasant scent. The small pods are similar to the pods of the species above, but smaller. Clusius did not observe the seed; he writes that he saw it in various places in Baetica <note>A Roman province in southern Spain, modern Andalusia</note>, and that it is very useful for the labor of silkworms.

<column-break/>

### THE THIRD SPECIES OF HUNGARIAN CYTISUS,
#### with spreading branches.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing or spreading plant with multiple stems emerging from a single root, featuring trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

It is provided with several branches that are spread out and cast upon the ground; they are thin and flexible, yet stubborn against breaking. These are covered with no leaves, or certainly very few; however, they produce many tender, hairy shoots from the sides, on which the leaves rest upon long stalks. They are always three in number, shorter than those mentioned above, green on the upper side, and growing white downy hair on the underside. The root is similar to the root of the first species. The flowers are similar in shape and color to the flowers of the others; the pods are flat and hairy, containing a tiny, brownish seed.

It grows of its own accord around Vienna, and in the forests of Austria and <term>Pannonia</term><note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>. It flowers in April and May.

### THE SECOND SPANISH CYTISUS OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy shrub with dense foliage and small flower clusters, showing a thick, branching root.</image-desc>

It is very similar to the first; but the twigs are entirely whitish and shorter, and the leaves are also smaller. The color of the flowers is more intense, and the seed is larger and blacker. Finally, the pods are somewhat long, rough, and turning black from purple, with the tip curved downward.

According to Clusius, it grows in the same places and flowers at the same time as the previous Spanish species.

### THE FOURTH SPANISH CYTISUS OF CLUSIUS.
### HAIRY CYTISUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust plant with large, hairy trifoliate leaves and dense clusters of flowers at the branch terminals.</image-desc>

It is endowed with blackish, hairy twigs three or four cubits high. The leaves are in threes, somewhat oblong, and hairy on both sides. Many flowers are crowded together at the tips and sides of the small branches; they are large, yellow, and emerge from long, woolly calyxes. The pods are covered with long hairs and are an inch and a half long.

This is the Fourth Spanish Cytisus of Clusius, who writes that it is found in the coastal regions of Baetica. However, We have found it in the Euganean Hills near <term>Patavium</term><note>Modern-day Padua, Italy</note>, and also near Baulme, a town in Burgundy.

It references the work of famous botanists Clusius and Lobelius to categorize these plants by their hairiness, leaf shape, and geographic distribution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Cytisus (Broom/Medick) genus, following the previous discussions on woody legumes. The catchword "TRIFOLIUM" links to the final entry on this page.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SMOOTH BROOM WITH NARROW PODS
<note>original: *Cytisus glaber, siliqua angusta*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus plant with slender leaves and narrow seed pods (siliqua), showing the root system, stems, and detached seed pods.</image-desc>

The appearance of this and the following plant are sufficiently expressed by the small illustrations; for that reason, we shall labor very little in describing them, deeming it enough that their margins are filled with the virtues and powers of the Brooms.

The leaves, according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist</note>, have a cooling power, and a decoction of them, when drunk, stirs the urine. Galen <note>The influential Roman physician of Greek origin</note> attributes to them a power of digestion <note>meaning to disperse or dissolve humors</note>, mixed with a watery, lukewarm quality. Marcellus Empiricus <note>A 4th-century medical writer</note> recommends Broom not as fodder for beasts of burden, nor for increasing the abundance of milk, but says it is a wonderful remedy against sciatica and arthritis; hence we agree with Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish botanist</note> that the Broom was not well known to him.

### GESNER’S BROOM, WITH FLOWERS ALMOST SPIKED
<note>original: *Cytisus Gesneri, cui flores fere spicati*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with trifoliate leaves and dense, spike-like flower clusters.</image-desc>

The twigs of this plant are longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, flexible, winged, and hairy at the top; the leaves are always in threes, clinging to a single stalk, and are hairy on the underside. The ends of the branches go off into long spikes of yellow flowers, similar to the flowers of the Pea, but smaller, and clinging to short stalks, with a pleasant scent. The pods are an inch or an inch and a half long, as wide as a stalk, compressed, hairy, and containing small, chestnut-colored seeds.

It grows in various places, in Austria, Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Balkans</note>, Switzerland, and elsewhere, in woods and by the roadsides, and is also cultivated in gardens. It flowers in the months of May and June.

### SHRUBBY ALYSSON WITH THE APPEARANCE OF BROOM, according to some, and Lobelius.
<note>original: *Cytissi facie Alysson fruticans quorundam, Lobelij*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrubby plant with small leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

This very elegant and uncommon exotic shrub is very little known, except in the green spaces of Belgium, where it shines in Summer with the yellow flowers of the smaller Stock-gilliflower, rising from numerous scattered, winding, and striated small stalks. The leaves are like Broom, but fuller, whitish, and bristly, stiff with spreading hairs. The root is hard and woody, and the seed is in small husks.

By Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History*, and also by Gerard, it is called *False Broom* <note>original: *Cytisus adulterinus*</note>.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH BROOM WITH BROAD PODS
<note>original: *Cytisus glaber, siliqua lata*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus plant similar to the first but with noticeably broader seed pods (siliqua lata).</image-desc>

To continue in relating the virtues of the legitimate Broom: it is praised with wonderful honors by Varro, Columella, and Pliny <note>Roman agricultural and natural history writers</note> as fodder for sheep, and when dried, even for pigs. Its utility, says Pliny, is like that of Bitter Vetch, but it satisfies more quickly; the quadruped grows fat on a very small amount, so much so that the beasts of burden despise barley. Nor is there a greater abundance or better quality of milk from any other fodder. He orders a decoction of it in water to be given as a drink to nurses in a deficiency of milk; and also given green to hens, or, if it has dried, soaked in water. He adds that bees will never be lacking where the fodder of Broom is available. We also have evidence of the richness of milk from Virgil’s *Eclogue 10*, where he sings: *So may your cows, fed on Broom, distend their udders.* <note>original: *Sic Cytiso pasta distentent vbera vaccæ*</note>

### A KIND OF BROOM, WITH PURPLE FLOWERS arranged in a spike.
<note>original: *Cytisigenus, floribus purpureis in spicam digestis*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with woody stems and upright spikes of flowers.</image-desc>

This grew for us at Montbéliard in the princely garden, from seed sent from Florence under the name *Ebony of Crete* <note>original: *Ebano Candia*</note>. This Broom was called the second Ebony, and perhaps not at all improperly, since the trunk of the Broom genus has a black and hard heartwood, very similar to Ebony; whence Theophrastus <note>The Greek "Father of Botany"</note> used to say its pith was so hard and thick that it seemed to come very close to Ebony.

Theophrastus adds, however, that Broom is so hostile to other plants that, by stealing their nourishment, it kills almost all of them.

### SHRUBBY TREFOIL: by some called Yellow-flowered Polemonium.
<note>original: *Trifolium fruticans: Polemonium flore luteo quibusdam*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with small flowers and a creeping root system.</image-desc>

From a white creeping root, green angular branches three cubits high arise, on which shoots rise alternately, producing shining leaves, usually in threes as in the Trefoils, and of a sharp and unpleasant taste. At the tops of the branches arise yellow flowers divided into five parts; these are succeeded by berries that are quite large, round, and red, containing a white seed similar to the common Pea.

It is called *Goat’s Rue* by some, *Yellow Jasmine* by others, but by most the *Polemonium of Montpellier*. It grows in the hedges at Montpellier; but it is cultivated in many gardens of Belgium, France, and Italy for its beauty; otherwise, it is of no use.

<summary>This page describes various species of Broom (Cytisus) and related shrubs, detailing their physical characteristics, their use as high-quality livestock fodder, and their medicinal applications according to classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Broom, Cytisus, fodder, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, botany, livestock nutrition, Ebony of Crete, Montpellier</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SHRUBBY TREFOIL, WITH BROOM-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Shrubby Trefoil plant, showing slender stems with trifoliate leaves and small clusters of flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

We preserve a branch of this plant, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in length, straight, rounded, with the appearance of Broom, striated, spongy, and divided into wings in an alternating arrangement. Four leaves cling to the joints; on one part they are trifoliate <note>three-leaved</note>, and at the ends they are single, very similar to Broom. The tops of the branches are occupied by yellow spiked heads of small flowers, but in this edition they are shown with <unclear>small</unclear> leaves. Master Schwezius, the primary physician to the Duke of Württemberg, brought this from Italy.

### SENNA: Germ. & Belg. *Sene*: Gall. *Sené*: It. *Sena*: Arab. *Sene*: Persis *Abatzeine*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Senna plant (Sena) with pinnate leaves and seed pods.</image-desc>

This was unknown to the ancient Greeks; for it is not the *Colutea* of Theophrastus <note>a 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note>, as some have wrongly thought, since *Colutea* is a herb and Senna is a tree. It was first discovered by Mesue <note>an 8th-century Persian or Arab physician</note>, from whose writings Mesue distinguishes one as *Cultivated* and another as *Wild*. Some make another variety round-leaved, and another with sharper leaves; others distinguish them by the seed, which is either white or black. However, the differences are chiefly drawn from their place of birth: hence one is called *Alexandrian* and *Oriental*, and another *Italian*. The Oriental is again established as two-fold: namely *Mechina*, which is brought from Mecca and is the most excellent, with a narrow, sharp, somewhat long and thick leaf; and the other named *Saette* from the place where it grows, which has a broader and rounder leaf, is of low value, and though better than the Italian, is inferior to the Mecca variety.

### COLUTEA ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colutea plant with small leaflets and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

This is called *Colutea* because it is "mutilated in its fruit" <note>original: "mutilata fructu"</note>; its shoots do not particularly stand out, and neither Dioscorides nor Pliny made mention of *Colutea*, or *Colytea*, or *Coloutea*, or *Coluïex*. Theophrastus describes three: one with a Laurel leaf, another with a Fenugreek leaf, and yet another whose leaf is similar to the leaf of a Willow (or Elm), which he says is a large tree and bears fruit in pods like legumes, which is rare among trees. We depict here the one that was first to him, and we shall soon describe various other species of *Colutea*.

<column-break/>

### SECOND TRIFOLIATE ASPALATHUS, The "Second Acacia" of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aspalathus secunda, showing a woody, thorny shrub with trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is firm and woody; the branches are a foot long, rigid, firm, woody, <unclear>unbending</unclear>, and striated. From these emerge fierce two-pronged or three-pronged thorns, which are themselves striated and the same color as the rest of the branch. The leaves of those thorns cling to longish stalks, not only at the joints but even in the middle; they are trifoliate, similar to Rue, and covered with a barely visible downy hair. The flowers are yellow, rivaling those of the Broom; these are followed by small pods containing three or four seeds. Almost all skilled herbalists would label this the "Second Acacia."

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SENNA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Senna, showing a more robust shrub-like structure with larger pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

We present here another image of this small tree from our purchased collection of Fuchs's works <note>referring to Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German botanist</note>. Furthermore, it grows not only in Italy but also in Provence and Narbonnese Gaul; however, it grows with difficulty among the Germans and Belgians because it is most impatient of the cold. Yet we saw an elegant plant in Switzerland, specifically in the illustrious Wagnetian garden in the village of *Luffans*.

It warms and dries to a moderate degree, and kindly evacuates all humors <note>in pre-modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids that governed health</note>. It is a medicine entirely suitable for the elderly, children, pregnant women, the delicate, the weak, and almost every age; it is familiar and domestic to nature, and free from any unpleasant quality. It is not our purpose here to declare the particular uses and methods of using it; let the practitioners and our *Great History* be consulted.

### BLADDER COLUTEA: Germ. *Linsenbaum*, Belg. *Lombaertschelinsen*: Gall. *Baguenaudier*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Colutea vesicaria (Bladder Senna), featuring its characteristic inflated, bladder-like seed pods.</image-desc>

Of the three *Coluteas* described by Theophrastus, none, in the judgment of Solenius, is this Bladder Colutea, as Ruellius, Fuchs, and Matthiolus wished. It is, however, a tree of common knowledge, which many cultivate in gardens for its beauty. It flowers in April, May, and June; it has its pods in August and September, and sometimes flowers and pods at the same time.

We have observed it in various places: Padua, Lyon, Geneva, and elsewhere. But nowhere have we seen one more elegant or longer-lived than that which the Reverend and Most Distinguished Mr. Chabræus, Senior Minister of the Church of Geneva, has cultivated for nearly fifty years in that garden of his which lies adjacent to the Court and the very pleasant promenade called *la Treille*.

<summary>This page describes various woody leguminous plants, including Shrubby Trefoil, several varieties of Senna, and the Bladder Colutea, noting their physical characteristics, geographical origins, and medicinal suitability.</summary>
<keywords>Senna, Colutea, Aspalathus, medicinal herbs, botanical gardens, Theophrastus, Mesue, Geneva, botany</keywords>
