<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Colutea genus, specifically focusing on the "scorpion-like" varieties and their medicinal substitutes.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SCORPION SENNA.
<note>original: "Colutea scorpioides"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scorpion Senna plant, showing a woody stem with pinnate leaves and curved, segmented seed pods resembling a scorpion's tail.</image-desc>

It is a sub-shrub <term>subfrutex; a plant that is woody at the base but has herbaceous stems</term> whose branches are covered in an ash-gray color. The leaves approach the form of Lentil leaves. The flowers are similar to those of the Broom plant <note>original: "Genista"</note> and are somewhat fragrant. The pods are also similar to the pods of the Orpine <note>original: "Telephium"</note>. The seeds, which are enclosed individually in each segment of the pods, are oblong, smooth, brownish, and of an unpleasant taste.

In Montpellier, it breaks forth in many wooded places among the Boxwood trees in June and July. In Narbonne, it is abundant in the Valena forest and near the riverbanks. In Geneva, it grows where one goes toward Collognium, and on Mount Salève. We have also observed it cultivated in the gardens of Lyon, Padua, Bologna, Parma, and Montpellier.

### CORTUSUS’S SCORPION SENNA, resembling Milkwort.
<note>original: "Colutea scorpioides Cortusi, Polygala similis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Scorpion Senna with denser, rounded leaflets and clusters of flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, this is the second Scorpion Senna; to Tabernaemontanus, it is the third Scorpion Senna. Clusius says it grows at the roots of the mountains that extend from the Danube and the overhanging Kahlenberg toward the Alps, among brambles and at the edges of vineyards. It flowers in May and June, though the following winter often destroys the young shoots.

### SENNA WITH THE SPONGY STEM OF BROOM.
<note>original: "Colutea caule Genistae fungoso"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with slender, upright stems, small pinnate leaves, and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

Could this be the third Milkwort <note>original: "Polygala"</note> of Clusius? Regarding it, he writes: The third Milkwort is found in the maritime regions of Valencia, a city in Spain, endowed with branches that are oblong, flexible, spongy or pithy, and entirely green. These are hedged by sparse leaves, which are even softer and thicker than the upper ones. The flower is like that of the second variety; I have not been able to observe the seed.

<column-break/>

### DWARF SCORPION SENNA.
<note>original: "Colutea scorpioides humilis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, spreading variety of Scorpion Senna with smaller leaves and curved seed pods.</image-desc>

In the form, number, and position of the leaves and flowers, it differs very little from the preceding one. The root and pods are also similar, but this one is lower to the ground and spread out across the earth.

It grows spontaneously in several places in Austria and Pannonia <note>An ancient province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, but when cultivated in gardens, it becomes a little larger. It flowers in May.

Furthermore, let us say something regarding the powers and properties of the *Colutea*. The leaves and seeds are temperate in heat. It is effective against all ailments arising from black bile <note>In the theory of the four humors, black bile was associated with melancholy and various physical obstructions</note>. It is of such great efficacy that it can be substituted for true Senna by the poor. However, we have shown in the Appendix that those who claim Senna and *Colutea* have the same powers are in error; *Colutea* is more closely related to the Broom plant.

### SMALL SPECIES OF SENNA, the Milkwort of Valencia of Clusius.
<note>original: "Coluteae parva species, Polygala Valentina Clus."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, shrubby plant with numerous small leaflets and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

According to Clusius, it is called *Coronilla del Rey* <note>Spanish: "The King's Little Crown"</note> by the people of Salamanca, which is to say, the Royal Crownlet. In that place, the apothecaries use it in place of Melilot <note>Sweet clover</note>.

It grows spontaneously in the fields of Salamanca, Murcia, and the Kingdom of Valencia, in sandy places and on sloping hills. It remains green perpetually and flowers for a very long time; it is believed that bees collect a great deal of honey from its flowers. It is also nurtured in Belgian gardens.

### SENNA WITH INDIGO-LIKE LEAVES.
<note>original: "Coluteae foliis Anil"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with larger, oval leaflets and long, straight seed pods.</image-desc>

Two branches were sent to us under the name *Anil* <note>Indigo</note>, about a foot long, almost similar to the branches of the Laburnum <note>original: "Cytisus"</note> with broad pods. They are somewhat stiff, hoary, and almost silvery. They are divided into leaves like the common *Colutea*, oval, blue-green, usually with five leaflets, more rarely three, on a hoary common rib. Nothing certain is known to us regarding the flower or seed. However, the appearance of the plant suggests enough that it can be referred to the *Colutea* family.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Scorpion Senna (Colutea scorpioides) and related species, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and their medicinal use as a cheaper substitute for true Senna.</summary>
<keywords>Scorpion Senna, Colutea, medicinal herbs, black bile, Clusius, Spanish flora, botanical geography, Senna substitute</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
L 2
<meta>Catchword: trifoliate</meta>

### ALPINI’S SOPHERA.
<note>Likely *Cassia sophera* or a related senna species described by the botanist Prospero Alpini.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sophera Alpini plant, showing a central stalk with pinnate leaves and several long, curved seed pods hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

The branches, which we keep among our natural specimens under the name *Sophera*, are depicted here, with the leaves, pod, and seeds also added in detail. Alpini describes his Sophera as follows: Sophera, he says, is a shrubby plant, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height. It is very close to the Goat’s Rue <note>original: "Galegæ"</note>: with hard branches and leaves like the Myrtle, but thinner and more numerous, arranged in order along the wing <note>the leaf stalk</note>. It bears saffron-colored flowers, rivaling the flower of the Cassia, without scent; from which small pods emerge, containing four or five seeds, clearly similar to the Sesban <note>Egyptian riverhemp</note>, which they say is poisonous to humans.

### JUPITER’S BEARD, SHINING BEAUTIFULLY.
<note>Commonly known as *Anthyllis barba-jovis*.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Barba Iovis plant, featuring a woody stem with clusters of small, narrow leaves and small flower heads at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

The name *Jupiter’s Beard* <note>original: "Barba Iovis"</note> is indeed of vague meaning; but the one we depict here is of a hard and almost woody material, covered in a hoary and downy bark. The branches are frequent and thick; the leaves are equal to the leaves of Lentils, hairy, shining with a silvery color, woven in five, six, or seven pairs. From the axil of the leaf stalk, unique downy appendages arise, at the ends of which cling yellow florets crowded together in heaps. It grows in stony and rocky maritime places, and especially on mountains situated by the shores.

The figure is not pleasing, and perhaps it would be better placed as the Persea tree.

### THE DORYCNIUM OF THE ANCIENTS, CALLED THAT OF CRATEVAS:
->*Montpellier Dorycnium.*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Dorycnium plant, showing a leafy stalk with small, clustered flowers at the apex and a detailed root system.</image-desc>

None of the Ancients, whether Greek or Latin, according to the testimony of Cordus, described the Dorycnium, except for Dioscorides, who took its history from Cratevas. Pliny reports on the Dorycnium in such a way that he seems hardly to distinguish it from the "Mad Nightshade" <note>original: "Solano manico"</note>.

But what we depict here is called the Dorycnium of Cratevas by some, but by most the Montpellier Dorycnium, and by some the Spanish Dorycnium of Clusius. It grows abundantly in various uncultivated places in Spain and along the roads, as well as in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> near the sea and elsewhere. It flowers in May and June, and the seed ripens in July.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN TAXOCOQUAMOCLIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Taxocoquamoclit plant, showing a climbing or upright stem with finely divided, needle-like foliage and long, slender seed pods.</image-desc>

From the similarity of the name, one might think this is Camerarius’s *Hoxocoquamoclit*, under which name he describes at length a plant sent to Florence and Nuremberg. However, to his *Hoxocoquamoclit* he attributes a cylindrical and oblong pod; but for this one of ours, it is compressed and very long. Therefore, we do not dare to assert that they are one and the same.

### A PLANT RELATED TO DORYCNIUM, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant related to Dorycnium, showing upright stems with trifoliate leaves and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

This plant, related to the Spanish Dorycnium of Clusius, grows in the Kingdom of Valencia and certain places in Andalusia <note>original: "Bæticæ"</note>. It has stalks a cubit high and flexible like Osier <note>willow</note>, more slender than the following species; the leaves are shorter and wider, joined three or five together on a short stalk and embracing the small branches. The oblong branches support three, four, or five flowers, smaller than Medick <note>original: "Medicæ"</note>, and of a green color. Otherwise, the whole plant is whiter than the following one—indeed, it is entirely hoary.

Botanists commonly label this a species of Dorycnium and a plant related to Dorycnium; and Tabernaemontanus and Gerard wrongly call it **Montpellier Dorycnium**, which Cactum considers the same.

### BROOM: German *Pfrimmen, Ginst*: French *Genestet*
### Italian *Ginestra*. SPARTIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Genista (Broom) plant, showing a woody base with many slender, upright, leafless-looking branches and small flowers.</image-desc>

Such a great similarity exists between Spanish Broom <note>original: "Spartium"</note> and Common Broom <note>original: "Genistam"</note>, both in appearance and properties, that some, deceived by their affinity, have decided these plants should by no means be separated. And indeed, since Pliny is found to have also doubted it, they thought that Broom was described by Dioscorides under the heading of Spanish Broom. But since the Spanish Broom of Dioscorides is a shrub devoid of leaves, and it is certain that it has flowers similar to the white Violet; while Common Broom brings forth rather long leaves, almost in the manner of Flax, and crescent-shaped flowers; the opinion of those who teach that Spanish Broom differs from Common Broom seems altogether preferable, even though they are related plants and one shares a very great kinship with the other. Here, however, is depicted the **three-leaved angular Broom**.

<summary>This page provides botanical descriptions and woodcut illustrations for several Mediterranean and "Indian" plants, including Sophera, Jupiter's Beard, and various types of Broom. The author compares contemporary findings with the classical accounts of Dioscorides and Pliny, noting discrepancies in classification.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Sophera, Jupiter's Beard, Dorycnium, Broom, Prospero Alpini, Carolus Clusius, Dioscorides, medicinal plants, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical classification of resinous plants and their products, following the previous discussions on coniferous trees.</meta>

# PLANTS
## EXOTIC WOOD: ETTALCHE. SMALLEST CONE-BEARING NUT.

<image-desc>Two woodcut illustrations of botanical specimens. On the left, a piece of exotic wood with a rough, textured bark and a cross-section showing growth rings. On the right, a small coniferous branch with several tiny cones attached to the needles.</image-desc>

The wood we depict here is held and described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist</note>: he says it was hard, heavy, firm, and smelled of Mastic <note>a resin from the pistachio tree</note>, and was taken from an American tree from which a resin is drawn out in the manner of pitch, and used for the same purposes, by which name it has claimed this place for itself.

Could it be the *Ettalche*, a large tree with Juniper-like leaves, thorny, and emitting a gum similar to Mastic, with which—on account of the similarity of scent and color—the Africans adulterate true Mastic? Its wood is said to be white in Numidia, violet in Libya, and deepest black in Ethiopia.

Or is it Cato’s *Cupida*?

<column-break/>

We keep these small cones among our natural specimens; they closely resemble Larch cones, but are much smaller, having stalks that are empty and curved. At their base, very short Spruce leaves adhere. It appears they consist of Larch-like scales—thin, broad, and furrowed—and that a leafy seed grows between the scales, as in the Spruce or Fir. Whether these are the cones of the Larch or another tree is not entirely certain to us.

*Thus, as far as the brevity we proposed allowed, we have reviewed the trees specifically called "Resin-bearing." But since the fragrant juices of each and every one have either not all been described, or at least not sufficiently, we shall fill this empty space with a census of several, having gathered them like gleanings after a harvest.*

---

->There are two types of RESIN:<-

*Liquid and Dry.* **Liquid** flows from various trees, especially Pine and Spruce, both spontaneously and when the branches or trunk are wounded. If it is found mixed with woody or stony debris due to careless collection, it is called *Confusanea* <note>mixed or jumbled</note>. **Dry** resin comes forth from cracks in the bark of the same trees or from cut branches; it lacks oiliness and dries quickly. Some make a third type called *Strobolina*, but erroneously, as it only has that name because it is found hardened around the cones, or *strobili*.

**PITCH** <note>original: "Pix"</note> is extracted by the force of fire from the oiliest and most resinous woods—especially Pine and Spruce—that have been turned into torches. It is either liquid or dry. The liquid is called *Crude* if it has experienced no fire other than the heat by which it flowed, or *Brutian* <note>from Calabria, ancient Bruttium</note>, which is dark, oilier, and thicker. *Dry* pitch is made from liquid pitch that has been boiled again; this is either boiled only to the thickness of birdlime, or, by a longer and stronger fire, is rendered dry, brittle, and able to be scraped.

**CEDRIA** is the "Tear of the Cedar," a pitch or resin which, according to Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician and botanist</note>, destroys living things but preserves dead bodies. It is often called *Life of the Dead*. To this corresponds the oil which the people of Provence are accustomed to make from Juniper, Ash, Cedar, and other such woods, which they call *Huile de Cade*; it is especially useful for mange of the head, and for the mange and ulcers of livestock.

**FRANKINCENSE** <note>original: "Thus"</note>: where and how it grows was said before. It is especially prized when it is *Mammose* <note>breast-shaped</note>, namely when a second tear follows and joins itself to a previous one. This they call *Male* frankincense, though it is not otherwise called "Male" unless there is a "Female." Frankincense is distinguished into *Manna* and *Bark*. Pliny interpreted *Manna* as the crumbs shaken off by jostling, which he called *Grain of Frankincense*; Hermolaus called it *Hypofisma*. Frankincense warms and binds significantly; the bark possesses the same power, and even more effectively.

**MASTIC** is the resin of the Lentisk tree; the best comes from the Island of Chios, which is discussed elsewhere.

**SARCOCOLLA** <note>literally "flesh-glue"</note>, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of a tree growing in Persia, similar to thin frankincense, somewhat yellowish and bitter. It has the power of gluing ulcers together and checking fluid discharges.

**MYRRH** is the tear of the tree of the same name, found mostly in Arabia; when cut in any place, it emits this very tear. Seven differences are described, taken from the places where it is obtained.

**STACTE** is not Balsam, as some wish, nor liquid Styrax, as others prefer, but the oiliness of fresh Myrrh crushed with a little water and pressed out through an instrument. (*Dioscorides*)

**BENZOIN** <note>original: "Benioinum"</note> is a gum or resin flowing from the wounded Benzoin tree. There are various kinds, but the one called *Amygdaloides* <note>almond-like</note> is preferred over the others. It is a large and tall tree with Citron-like leaves, growing in Sumatra, an island of the East Indies. Furthermore, it is clear that Benzoin was unknown to the Ancients because neither the Greeks nor the Arabs describe it; for it is not Averrhoes' *Balenzan*.

**LIQUIDAMBAR** is the resin flowing from incisions in vast, beautiful, and branchy trees which have Ivy-like leaves and grow in New Spain <note>Mexico</note>. They are called *Ocosol* by the inhabitants. It warms, dissolves, and soothes pains; it is of the greatest use in Medicine.

**CANCAMUM**, according to Dioscorides, is the tear of an Arabian wood, somewhat similar to Myrrh but with a poisonous taste.

**ANIME** and **COPAL** are synonyms. Anime is collected from wounded trees of medium size, no differently than Frankincense or Mastic; if we believe Hermolaus, it takes its name from the place in Arabia where it is found. There are two kinds: soft and harder. Why it is called *Anima* <note>soul/spirit</note>, we do not know.

**TOCOTGEBIT** is an East Indian tree, similar to a poplar, under whose bark grows a resin similar to our Frankincense but whiter, which they use there as Frankincense.

**AMBER** <note>original: "Electrum" or "Succinum"</note>, called *Carabe* by the Arabs, is the gum of a poplar tree according to Dioscorides; but according to Pliny and some more recent followers, it is a resin flowing from a tree similar to a spruce. However, by the calculation of almost all others, it is born from Bitumen, which, flowing from the shores into the sea, hardens in the way we see. It is either Yellow or White, and is found in the maritime regions of Germany, rolled onto the shore by storms.

**BDELLIUM and STYRAX**, both the trees and the tears, were treated previously.

**CAMPHOR** is numbered among the gifts of the East Indies; it is a gum flowing from a tree similar to a poplar, growing in mountains near the sea. Four species are commonly reviewed; it differs greatly from the *Living Capura* of Qualcebeni.

**USUB**, a gum-bearing tree with which the Indians anoint the body, is mentioned by Thevet in *Antarctic France* <note>André Thevet's 1557 account of Brazil</note>.

**TACAMAHACA** is obtained from the East Indies and flows from a wounded large tree equal to a poplar; it is of great use for almost innumerable ailments.

**ACACIA, GUM ARABIC**, and all other Juices, Gums, and Tears will be treated in their own place.

---

### END OF THE NINTH CLASS.

# ILLUSTRATIONS AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS X.
### CONCERNING BROOM-LIKE TREES AND SHRUBS.

**MYRICA** or **TAMARIX**: German: *Tamarischenbaum*:
French: *Tamarisque*: Italian: *Tamarice*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tamarix plant with feathery leaves and slender branches.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> calls this a well-known tree that grows near sluggish waters. Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> indeed calls it "amphibious," because it is not only to be counted among aquatic plants, but is also abundant in deserts. Pliny, being inconsistent, distinguishes between a Cultivated and a Wild variety; in one place he says it bears a fruit similar to a gall-nut, yet elsewhere he says its wood is called "unlucky" because it bears neither fruit nor seed.

More recent authors establish one as the Cultivated type, which becomes tall and tree-like, and another as the Wild type, which is low and shrubby, and is called by the diminutive name <term>Tamariscus</term> <note>Little Tamarisk</note>; this latter type they subdivide again, as will be mentioned shortly. This tall, tree-like Tamarisk is considered common in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, both near rivers and far from them; we have seen it in gardens in Paris, Montpellier, and in Belgium.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER TAMARIX**, or **SHRUBBY**, called GERMAN **TAMARISCVS**.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, more shrub-like variety of Tamarix.</image-desc>

Two kinds of this are found: one with firmer wood and thinner leaves, the other with somewhat broader leaves and less firm wood. Thus Theophrastus established two kinds of Tamarisk, one with strong wood, the other weak. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German botanist.</note> writes that the former grows abundantly by the Rhine at Strasbourg, and the latter on the banks of the Danube.

It loves wetter and stony regions, and does not easily take to garden cultivation unless placed near water. We have seen both kinds in various places near flowing rivers and marshes: at Geneva, Zurich, Lyon, and Padua. It flowers in May and June.

Some distinguish this from the tree-like variety because it has "pappose" <note>downy or tufted</note> flowers, whereas the tree-like one does not; rather, it has round, tiny, reddish flowers.

---

**EGYPTIAN TAMARIX, DOMESTIC OR** cultivated, Gall-bearing.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tamarix tree with distinct seed pods or galls hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, an Italian physician who studied Egyptian flora.</note> writes that this grows to the height of a large Olive tree, and its fruit equals a walnut in size. Dioscorides names it the cultivated or urban variety, and says it produces fruit similar to galls.

Furthermore, the Tamarisk has a cleansing and "cutting" <note>referring to the ability to break up thick humors in the body</note> quality, and possesses some astringency. It frees the internal organs from obstructions, and a decoction of the leaves used as a rinse soothes toothaches. All parts of this tree—fruit, leaves, flowers, bark, wood, and wood-ash—are beneficial for those with spleen disorders <note>original: "Lienosis"</note>; they even benefit from drinking continuously out of vessels made from its wood. Hence Pliny wrote that pigs accustomed to taking their food from troughs made of it were found to lack a spleen. Dio <note>Cassius Dio, the historian.</note> testifies that the Ancients prophesied by the power of its branches.

<column-break/>

**ERICA** or **ERICE**: German: *Heyden*: Belgian: *Heyde*:
French: *Bruyere*: Italian: *Erica*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Heather (Erica) plant with small needle-like leaves and clusters of tiny flowers.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides, Erica is a shrubby tree with leaves like the Myrica, but much smaller. Various differences are observed in it, taken from its size, leaves, flowers, and fruit. Thus one is low-growing, another tree-like; one has leaves in threes, another in fours; some are hairy and downy, others not; some have white flowers, others purple, grass-colored, etc.; and finally, some bear berries, others do not. We depict here the one which is low-growing and has evergreen leaves, with flowers that are either purple or white.

It flowers in June, July, and August, and loves uncultivated places and solitudes: it is very frequent in Pannonia <note>Eastern Europe/Hungary</note>, and between Montbéliard and Belfort, and again between Montbéliard and Porrentruy.

<summary>This page describes the varieties and medicinal properties of the Tamarisk (Tamarix) and Heather (Erica) plants, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny. It highlights the Tamarisk's specific use in treating spleen ailments and its geographical distribution across Europe and Egypt.</summary>
<keywords>Tamarisk, Heather, Erica, Myrica, medicinal plants, spleen treatments, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, European flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of various heath species (Erica), following the systematic classification of plants by their physical characteristics.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALL ENGLISH HEATH, with hairy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, bushy heath plant with numerous fine branches and small leaves.</image-desc>

We received this dried plant from England under the name of *Erica* <note>The Latin genus name for Heath</note>. It is entirely beautiful and scarcely nine inches tall: the branches are thin and many: the leaves are very short, crowded, and appear split or notched at the edges: they grow in groups of three or four at small intervals, as if at joints: at the tips are small, hairy heads.

<column-break/>

### LOBEL'S FOREIGN HEATH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender heath branch with needle-like leaves and small flower clusters along the stem.</image-desc>

Lobel <note>Matthias de Lobel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that this species of Heath is cultivated in the hanging gardens of Belgium: otherwise, it is shrub-like in habit, with somewhat long leaves, and purple flowers around the branches consisting of four petals. He did not know from where it was brought, and for that reason, he called it "foreign."

<column-break/>

### MATTHIOLI'S BERRY-BEARING HEATH,

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a heath plant with small berries shown both on the branches and separately in detail at the base.</image-desc>

Regarding his own Berry-bearing Heath, Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an influential Italian physician and botanist</note> relates these things. It is a plant, he says, growing in the mountains that separate Bohemia from Silesia, and from whose springs the river Elbe takes its origin. It spreads across the ground and occupies wide areas, with a leaf almost like the common Heath: I have not been able to see the flowers: but it bears berries that are blackish-purple, similar to Juniper berries, but smaller, etc.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note> in his *Pannonia* labels this the first Heath with a *Coris* <note>original: "Coris folio" - referring to leaves like the St. John's Wort relative, Coris monspeliensis</note> leaf: and he says it grows on the ridges of the highest Alps of Austria and Styria: and flowers in June. However, Pena and Lobel, and even Schwenckfeld, wrongly confuse this berry-bearing Heath of Mattioli with the marsh Whortleberries <note>Cranberries or Bilberries</note>.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS'S PORTUGUESE BERRY-BEARING HEATH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a more robust, upright heath shrub with dense foliage and small berries.</image-desc>

It rises with branches eighteen inches high, which are brittle, with a bark darker than the others: the leaves are also similar to those, but darker and thicker, arranged in a triple order around the twigs. The fruit resembles dark pearls <note>original: "vniones" - large pearls</note> in both shape and color, but it is juicy and slightly acidic. It is not well established whether it flowers; the inhabitants of the places where it grows deny it, and say the fruit gradually swells until it ripens. *Thus says Clusius.*

It is found only in Portugal <note>original: "Lusitania"</note>, and the fruit matures in September and October; it is sought after by children and women, and is very pleasant and useful for those suffering from fevers, especially those who are thirsty.

They call the tree *Camarinhas*, and the fruit indeed *Camarinhas* <note>The Portuguese Crowberry, Corema album</note>. In Amatus's <note>Amato Lusitano, a 16th-century Portuguese physician</note> commentary on Dioscorides, the tree is called *Azacalin*.

---

-> # END OF THE TENTH CLASS. <-

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut tailpiece featuring a central mask or face surrounded by elaborate floral scrolls and cornucopias.</image-desc>

<summary>This page describes four distinct varieties of heath (Erica), detailing their physical characteristics, geographic origins in England, Central Europe, and Portugal, and correcting previous botanical misidentifications.</summary>
<keywords>Heath, Erica, Botany, Mattioli, Clusius, Lobel, Portugal, Bohemia, medicinal plants, berries</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the classification of woody plants, specifically focusing on the leguminous or pod-bearing trees and shrubs. The catchword from the previous page, CYTISUS, is addressed here alongside Laburnum and Anagyris.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XI.
### POD-BEARING TREES, SHRUBS, AND UNDER-SHRUBS, AND
->those with pea-like flowers: both those lacking thorns and the thorny ones: and others similar to these.<-

**LABURNUM:** *German* Tree-beans (Baumbonen) : *French* Aubours : *Italian* Eghelo, Eghano, Auornello. <note>Commonly known today as Golden Chain tree.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Laburnum branch with trifoliate leaves and long, drooping racemes of pea-like flowers. To the right, a detail of the seed pod (siliqua) and individual seeds.</image-desc>

It is a shrubby tree, branched with limbs, with green bark, white and hard wood, flowers like the Little Broom <note>original: "Genistellae"</note>, pods like Peas, and varied seeds that are hard, smooth, shining, shaped like a kidney, and the size of a Lentil.

Gesner, Dalechamps, and several other more recent authors agree with us that this is the *Laburnum* of Pliny. Matthiolus maintains that the *Ebony* is actually *Anagyris*, but this is a great error; for the scent, leaves, pods, flowers, and seeds all argue against it. Castore Durante calls it the *Lesser Anagyris*. To Pena and Lobel, it is the *Less-stinking Anagyris*.

It blooms in the months of May and June, providing a pleasing sight in the mountains; we have also observed it being cultivated in the gardens of Padua and Lyon. Its scent kills mice; and Camerarius writes that the ashes of the whole plant are recommended for kidney stones <note>original: "calculum"</note>; Matthiolus claims it can perform all the same functions as Anagyris.

**CYTISUS:** *German* Goat-clover (Geisklee) : *French* Cytise : *Italian* Cytiso.
->**CYTISUS WITH CURVED PODS.**<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus plant showing a woody stem, trifoliate leaves, and curved seed pods (siliquae incurvae).</image-desc>

The description of *Cytisus* by Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> is not so accurate that the *Cytisus* of the Ancients can be sufficiently identified from it. Because of this, different authors have presented different plants as *Cytisus*, and various other plants have been given the name. Pliny and Galen, following Dioscorides, called it a shrub; but Strabo makes it similar to the Balsam, a fragrant tree. We, along with Amatus, determine that it can be ranked among both trees and shrubs; and with the more experienced scholars, we believe the legitimate *Cytisus* of the Ancients is the one we depict here, which Marantha describes at length.

He collected it on a hill near Naples; but according to Bellonius, it abounds on the island of Rhodes and others nearby. From its wood, sword handles and prayer beads <note>original: "sphaerulae precariae," likely rosary beads</note> are made. Writers call it the *Horned Cytisus* and *Marantha's Cytisus*.

<column-break/>

**ANAGYRIS:** *German* Stinking-tree, Tree-beans, Genani-beans : *French* Stinking wood (Bois puant) : *Italian* Anagyri. <note>Commonly known as Stinking Bean Trefoil.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Anagyris foetida, showing trifoliate leaves and large, curved legume pods. Detail of a single seed is shown to the left.</image-desc>

Matthiolus and Tabernaemontanus confuse Laburnum with this plant. Gesner not only calls it *Anagyris*, but also *Anagyrum* and *Onogyrum*, and asserts it was unknown to Matthiolus. However, this is the legitimate *Anagyris* of Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, and Paul of Aegina. Some of the more recent authors, chief among them Matthiolus, have posited two kinds of *Anagyris*, observing a difference especially in the leaves. But who does not know the playful variations of nature in leaves? Therefore, we, along with Clusius, establish only one legitimate kind, specifically that which was described by the Ancients.

It grows wild in several places, as Clusius observed at the first milestone from Atelas and around Seville; but it is especially kept in cultivated gardens in Rome, Paris, and Padua, where it blooms in a joyful spectacle in February and March. It is a heavy-smelling shrub, possessing the power to digest and to heat.

->**CLUSIUS'S PANNONIAN CYTISUS,**<-
->with leaves entirely hoary.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Cytisus variety (Pannonicus) with upright stems and clusters of flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

The shoots are a cubit long, thin, flexible, and willow-like; the leaves are in threes, narrow, hoary <note>grayish-white</note>, thick, and bitter to the taste. The flowers at the top of the clusters are five or six in number, similar to the flowers of the Meadow Lotus, golden in color, and not lacking in scent. The pods are flat, somewhat oblong, and entirely hairy; within them is the seed, which is dark, flat, somewhat round, and hard. The root is hard and woody, blackish, and spreads across the surface of the earth.

It blooms in July, and occasionally until Autumn. The seeds ripen toward the end of August and in September. According to Clusius, it is common throughout the Viennese territory, especially above the pheasant-breeding grounds, and in many other acidic locations in Austria and Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria.</note>.

<summary>This page describes several pod-bearing (leguminous) woody plants, specifically Laburnum, Cytisus, and Anagyris, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses, and the historical debates regarding their identification by ancient authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Laburnum, Cytisus, Anagyris, Dioscorides, Pliny, Matthiolus, Clusius, botany, seed pods, trifoliate leaves, medicinal plants, Renaissance botany</keywords>

--- Page 135 ---
### IMAGES AND OUTLINE

### A SECOND SPECIES OF PANNONIAN BROOM
->very hairy.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus Pannonici plant with thick, hairy stems and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

This species of Pannonian Broom <note>original: "Cytisi Pannonici"; likely a species of Chamaecytisus or Laburnum found in the Pannonian Basin of Central Europe</note> is much larger, and has thicker and very hairy twigs: the leaves are also twice as large, and the flowers and pods are broader; the flowers also shine with a more golden color. It grows near hedges, and is rarer and less commonly encountered than the other one previously mentioned.

---

### THE FIRST SPANISH BROOM OF CLUSIUS,
->with greenish leaves.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the first Spanish Cytisus described by Clusius, showing upright flowering stalks. Clusius was a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist.</image-desc>

It sometimes grows to the size of a small tree; numerous leaves, pale green in color, surround the tender little branches which are covered in soft hair: the flowers are yellow and somewhat fragrant: the pods <note>original: "Lobi"; here referring to the seed pods</note> are equal to the pods of the Common Broom <note>original: "Genistæ"</note>, oblong, rough, and hairy: the seed is small and blackish: the root is woody and spreads in different directions.

It grows, according to Clusius, in various places in both Castilles <note>regions of central Spain</note>, along the roadsides. It flowers in June, and produces seed in July and August. We consider this to be the same as the Broom of Mount Galcar mentioned by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, another prominent botanist</note>.

---

### THE THIRD SPANISH BROOM OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the third Spanish Cytisus, featuring slender stems and small leaves.</image-desc>

It rises with branches a foot long, and rarely a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, which are thin and entirely hoary-white: three leaves adorn these, attached by a short stalk, and the middle leaf is twice as long as the others: golden flowers shimmer along the branches from bottom to top, having a pleasant scent: the little pods are similar to the pods of those mentioned above, but smaller. Clusius did not observe the seed; he writes that he saw it in various places in Baetica <note>modern-day Andalusia, Spain</note>, and that it is very useful for the labor of silkworms.

<column-break/>

### A THIRD SPECIES OF PANNONIAN BROOM,
->with spreading branches.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the third Pannonian Cytisus species with spreading branches and roots visible.</image-desc>

It is provided with several branches, scattered and spread upon the ground, thin, flexible, yet stubborn against breaking: these are covered with no leaves, or certainly very few: however, they produce many tender, hairy branches from the sides, on which the leaves rest upon long stalks, always in groups of three, shorter than the ones above, green on top, and growing a hoary down underneath: the root is similar to the root of the first kind. The flowers are similar in shape and color to the flowers of the others: the pods are flat and hairy, containing a tiny, brownish seed.

It grows wild around Vienna, and in the forests of Austria and Pannonia <note>an ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and Serbia</note>. It flowers in April and May.

---

### THE SECOND SPANISH BROOM OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the second Spanish Cytisus, showing a dense, shrub-like growth.</image-desc>

It is very similar to the first: but the twigs are entirely white and shorter, and the leaves are also smaller. The color of the flowers is also more intense, and the seed is larger and blacker: and finally, the pods are somewhat long, rough, and turning black from purple, with the tip bent downwards.

It grows in the same places, according to Clusius, and flowers at the same time as the previous Spanish variety.

---

### THE FOURTH SPANISH BROOM OF CLUSIUS.
### THE HAIRY BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the fourth Spanish Cytisus, also called the hairy Cytisus, with prominent flowers and pods.</image-desc>

It is endowed with blackish, hairy twigs three or four cubits high: the leaves are in threes, somewhat oblong, and hairy on both sides: many flowers are clustered together at the tips and sides of the small branches; they are large, yellow, and emerge from long, downy calyxes <note>the outer protective part of a flower</note>: the pods are covered in long hairs and are an inch and a half long.

This is the Fourth Spanish Broom of Clusius, which he writes is found in the coastal areas of Baetica. However, we have found it in the Euganean Hills near Padua <note>original: "Patauium"</note>, and also near Baume, a town in Burgundy.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of Broom (Cytisus) found in Central Europe and Spain, detailing their physical characteristics, flowering times, and geographical locations. It relies heavily on the observations of the botanist Carolus Clusius and compares regional variations from Austria to Andalusia.</summary>

# OF PLANTS
## TREFOIL

### SMOOTH CYTISUS WITH NARROW PODS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cytisus plant with slender leaves and narrow seed pods (siliqua), showing the root system, stems, and detached seed pods.</image-desc>

The appearance of this and the following plant are sufficiently expressed by the small illustrations; for that reason, we shall labor very little in describing them, deeming it better to fill their margins with the virtues and powers of the *Cytisus* <note>The genus *Cytisus* includes various brooms and medicks</note>.

The leaves, according to the author Dioscorides, have a cooling power, and a decoction of them, when drunk, provokes urine. Galen attributes to them a power of digestion <note>In the sense of "digesting" or dispersing humors</note>, mixed with a watery, lukewarm quality. Marcellus Empiricus does not recommend *Cytisus* as fodder for beasts of burden, nor for increasing the abundance of milk, but says it is a wonderful remedy against sciatica and arthritis; hence we agree with Dodoens that *Cytisus* was not well known to him.

### GESNER’S CYTISUS, WHOSE FLOWERS ARE ALMOST SPIKED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Gesner's Cytisus, featuring trifoliate leaves and elongated flower spikes at the ends of the branches.</image-desc>

The twigs of this plant are longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, flexible, winged, and hairy at the top; the leaves are always three together <note>trifoliate</note> attached to a single stalk, hairy on the underside. The ends of the branches go off into long spikes of yellow flowers, similar to the flowers of the Pea, but smaller, and hanging from short stalks, with a pleasant scent. The pods are an inch or an inch and a half long, as wide as a stalk, compressed, hairy, containing small, chestnut-colored seeds.

It grows in various places, in Austria, Hungary, Switzerland, and elsewhere, in woods and by the roadsides, and is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms in the months of May and June.

### SHRUBBY ALYSSON OF SOME, ACCORDING TO LOBELIUS, WITH THE APPEARANCE OF CYTISUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrubby Alysson with small, dense leaves and clusters of flowers, showing a woody root. Alysson was historically used for its supposed ability to cure "madness" or rabies.</image-desc>

This very elegant and uncommon exotic shrub is very little known, except in the green spaces of Belgium, where it shines in summer with the yellow flowers of the smaller Stock-gilliflower, growing from numerous scattered, winding, and grooved stalks. The leaves are like those of *Cytisus*, but fuller, whitish, and bristly, stiff with thick hairs. The root is hard and woody, and the seed is in small husks.

In the *Icons* and *History* of Tabernaemontanus, and also in Gerard, it is called the "Bastard Cytisus."

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH CYTISUS WITH BROAD PODS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smooth Cytisus with broad seed pods (siliqua lata), showing the flowering branches and broad pods.</image-desc>

To proceed in relating the virtues of the legitimate *Cytisus*: It is praised with wonderful commendations by Varro, Columella, and Pliny as fodder for sheep, and when dried, even for swine. Its utility, says Pliny, is like that of Bitter Vetch, but it satisfies more quickly; a quadruped grows fat on a very small amount, so much so that beasts of burden will then scorn barley. Nor is there a greater abundance or better quality of milk from any other fodder. He orders a decoction in water to be given to nurses as a drink when there is a lack of milk; and also given green to hens, or, if it has dried, soaked in water. He adds that bees will never be lacking where *Cytisus* fodder is available. We also have the abundance of milk described wittily from Virgil’s 10th Eclogue, where he sings: *“So may the cows, having fed on Cytisus, distend their udders.”* <note>original: "Sic Cytiso pasta distentent ubera vaccæ."</note>

### A KIND OF CYTISUS, WITH PURPLE FLOWERS ARRANGED IN A SPIKE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a species of Cytisus with dark stems and flowers arranged in a spike.</image-desc>

This grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Prince, from seed sent from Florence under the name of "Ebony of Crete." This *Cytisus* was called the second Ebony, and perhaps not entirely improperly, since the trunk of the *Cytisus* genus has a black and hard heartwood, very similar to Ebony. Whence Theophrastus used to say its pith was so hard and thick that it seemed to come very close to Ebony.

The same Theophrastus adds that *Cytisus* is so hostile to other plants that, by stealing their nourishment, it kills almost all of them.

### SHRUBBY TREFOIL: CALLED POLEMONIUM WITH A YELLOW FLOWER BY SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrubby trefoil (Trifolium fruticans) with pinnate leaves and clusters of flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

From a white, creeping root, green angular branches rise three cubits high, on which shoots rise alternately, producing shining leaves, usually three together as in the Trefoils, and of a sharp and unpleasant taste. At the tops of the branches, yellow five-parted flowers arise, which are followed by berries that are quite large, round, and black, containing a white seed similar to the common Pea.

It is called *Ruta capraria* <note>Goat's Rue</note> by some, Yellow Jasmine by others, but by most the *Polemonium* of Montpellier. It grows in the hedges of Montpellier; but it is cultivated in many gardens of Belgium, France, and Italy for its beauty; otherwise, it is of no use.

<summary>This page describes various species of Cytisus (Broom/Medick) and shrubby trefoils, detailing their physical characteristics, their high value as livestock fodder, and their medicinal uses for nursing mothers and joint pain.</summary>
<keywords>Cytisus, Trefoil, Ebony of Crete, livestock fodder, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, botanical illustration, Montpellier, horticulture</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SHRUBBY TREFOIL, WITH BROOM-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Shrubby Trefoil plant with slender stems and small leaves.</image-desc>

We have preserved a branch of this plant, a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note>, straight, rounded, with the appearance of Broom, striated, spongy, and divided into alternate wings: at the joints of these the leaves are attached, in one part three-leaved <note>trifoliate</note>, and at the ends solitary, very much resembling Broom: the tops of the branches are occupied by spiked yellow heads of small flowers, but in a sparse arrangement and with small leaves interspersed. Dr. Schevvezius, the primary Physician to the Duke of Württemberg, brought this from Italy.

<column-break/>

### THE SECOND THREE-LEAVED ASPALATHUS, The second Acacia of some authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody shrub with trifoliate leaves and seed pods.</image-desc>

This plant has a firm and woody root: the branches are a foot long, rigid, upturned, woody, dark inside, and striated: from these emerge forked and rigid, fierce thorns, which are also striated and the same color as the rest of the branch: the leaves of those thorns are attached by somewhat long stalks, not only at the joints but even in the middle; they are three-leaved, similar to Rue, and pubescent with a barely visible hairiness: the flowers are yellow, emulating Broom: these are followed by small pods containing three or four seeds. Most all skilled Herbalists have labeled this the "Second Acacia."

---

### SENNA: Germ. & Belg. Sene: Gall. Sené: It. Sena: Arab. Sene: In Veii <note>an ancient region</note> Abazeine.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Senna plant with pinnate leaves and curved seed pods.</image-desc>

This was unknown to the ancient Greeks: for it is not the *Colutea* of Theophrastus <note>a famous Greek botanist</note>, as some have wrongly thought, since *Colutea* is a herb, while Senna is a tree. It is a discovery of the Moors, from whom Mesue <note>an Arabic medical scholar</note> distinguishes one as Cultivated and another as Wild. Some identify one as round-leaved and another with sharper leaves: others distinguish them by the seed, which is either white or black. However, the differences are chiefly drawn from the place of birth: hence one is called Alexandrian & Oriental, another Italian: and the Oriental is again established as two-fold: namely <term>Mechina</term> <note>Mecca Senna</note>, which is brought from Mecca and is the most excellent, with a narrow, sharp, somewhat long and thick leaf: and the other named <term>Saitica</term> <note>from Sais, Egypt</note> from the place where it grows, which has a broader and rounder leaf, and is of less value than the Mecca variety, but better than the Italian.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SENNA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Senna with broader leaves and distinct pods.</image-desc>

We present here another image of this small tree from our purchased collection of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous herbalist</note>. Furthermore, it grows not only in Italy but also in Provence and Narbonnese Gaul: however, it grows with difficulty among the Germans and Belgians because it is most impatient of the cold. Yet we have seen an elegant specimen of the plant in Switzerland, specifically in the illustrious Wagnerian garden of the district of <term>Luffans</term>.

It heats and dries moderately, and kindly evacuates all humors <note>bodily fluids in ancient medicine</note>: and it is a medicine entirely suitable for the elderly, children, pregnant women, the delicate, the weak, and almost every age, being familiar and domestic to nature, and entirely free of any offensive quality. It is not our purpose here to declare the particular uses and methods of using it; let the Practitioners and our "Great History" be consulted.

---

### COLUTEA ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colutea shrub with small leaflets and flowers.</image-desc>

Dr. Capitant [notes] that the *Colutea* is so named because its shoots are mutilated <note>original: "mutilata"</note>, and do not grow out before being pruned. However, neither Dioscorides nor Pliny made mention of *Colutea*, or *Colyita*, or *Coloutea*, or *Colotea*. Theophrastus describes three: One with a Laurel leaf, Another with a Fenugreek leaf, and yet another whose leaf is similar to the leaf of a Willow (or Elm), and which he says is a large tree and bears fruit in pods, like legumes, which is rare in trees. We depict here this one, which is his first, and we shall soon describe various other species of *Colutea*.

<column-break/>

### BLADDER SENNA: Germ. Linsenbaum, Belg. Lombaertschelensen: Gall. Baguenaudier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bladder Senna (Colutea vesicaria) with inflated seed pods.</image-desc>

Of the three *Coluteas* which Theophrastus describes, none, in the judgment of Solenius, is this Bladder *Colutea*, as Ruellius, Fuchs, and Matthiolus have maintained. It is, however, a tree of common knowledge, which many cultivate in gardens on account of its beauty. It flowers in April, May, and June: but it has pods in August and September, and sometimes flowers and pods at the same time.

We have observed it in various places: Padua, Lyon, Geneva, and elsewhere. But nowhere have we seen a more elegant or longer-lived specimen than that which the Reverend and most Distinguished Mr. Chabræus, Senior Minister of the Genevans, has cultivated for nearly fifty years in that garden of his which lies adjacent to the Court and the very pleasant promenade called *la Treille*.

<summary>This page describes various species of Trefoil, Senna, and Bladder Senna, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins, and medicinal suitability for all ages. It references several historical botanists including Theophrastus, Fuchs, and Matthiolus to clarify species identification.</summary>
<keywords>Shrubby Trefoil, Aspalathus, Senna, Mecca Senna, Bladder Senna, Colutea, medicinal herbs, botanical history, Geneva gardens, Leonhart Fuchs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Colutea genus, focusing on varieties with scorpion-like seed pods and their medicinal substitutes for Senna.</meta>

### SCORPION SENNA (Colutea scorpioides)

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scorpion Senna plant, showing a woody stem with pinnate leaves and curved, segmented seed pods resembling a scorpion's tail.</image-desc>

This is a <term>subshrub</term> <note>a small, woody plant, shorter than a tree</note> whose branches are covered in an ash-gray color. The leaves approach the form of Lentil leaves. The flowers are similar to those of the Broom plant and are somewhat fragrant. The pods are also similar to the pods of the <term>Telephium</term> <note>likely referring to Orpine or a similar succulent-leaved plant</note>. The seeds, which are enclosed individually within the segments of those pods, are oblong, smooth, brownish, and have an unpleasant taste.

It bursts forth in June and July in many wooded areas of Montpellier among the Boxwood trees. It is also abundant in Narbonne in the Valena forest and near the banks of the river. In Geneva, it grows on the road to Collogny and on Mount Salève. We have also observed it cultivated in the gardens of Lyon, Padua, Bologna, Parma, and Montpellier.

### CORTUSUS’S SCORPION SENNA, similar to Milkwort.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded leaflets and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note>, this is the second Scorpion Senna; to Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a German herbalist</note>, it is the third Scorpion Senna. Clusius says it grows at the base of the mountains that extend from the Danube and the overlooking Kahlenberg toward the Alps, among brambles and at the edges of vineyards. It flowers in May and June, though the following winter often destroys the young shoots.

### SENNA WITH A SPONGY BROOM-LIKE STEM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with small, narrow leaves and clusters of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Could this be the third Milkwort of Clusius? Regarding this plant, he writes: The third Milkwort is found in the coastal regions of Valencia, a city in Spain. It is endowed with oblong, flexible, spongy or pithy branches that are entirely green. These are hedged with sparse leaves, which are even softer and thicker than those mentioned previously. The flower is equal to the second variety, but I have not been able to observe the seed.

<column-break/>

### DWARF SCORPION SENNA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing variety of Colutea with similar pinnate leaves and curved seed pods.</image-desc>

In the shape, number, and position of the leaves and flowers, it differs very little from the preceding variety. The root and pods are also similar, but this plant is lower and spreads out along the ground.

It grows spontaneously in several places in Austria and Pannonia <note>an ancient Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria</note>, but when cultivated in gardens, it becomes a little larger. It flowers in May.

Furthermore, let us say something regarding the powers and properties of the *Colutea*. The leaves and seeds are temperate in heat. It is effective against all ailments arising from <term>black bile</term> <note>one of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and digestive issues</note>. It is of such efficacy that it can be substituted for **Senna** by the poor. However, those who maintain that *Colutea* and Senna have the exact same properties are in error; we have shown in the Appendix that *Colutea* is more closely related to the Broom plant.

### SMALL SPECIES OF SENNA, the Valencia Milkwort of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, bushy plant with numerous small leaves and flower clusters.</image-desc>

According to Clusius, it is called **Coronilla del Rey** <note>Spanish: "The King's Little Crown"</note> by the people of Salamanca, which means "Royal Garland," and in that region, the apothecaries use it in place of Melilot <note>Sweet Clover</note>.

It grows spontaneously in the countryside of Salamanca, Murcia, and the Kingdom of Valencia in sandy places and on sloping hills. It remains green perpetually and flowers for a very long time. It is believed that bees collect a great deal of honey from its flowers. It is also nurtured in Belgian gardens.

### SENNA WITH INDIGO-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with larger, oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem.</image-desc>

Two branches were sent to us under the name **Anil** <note>Indigo</note>. They are a foot long, almost similar to the branches of the Tree Medick with broad pods, somewhat stiff, grayish-white, and almost silvery. They are divided into leaves like the common *Colutea*, oval and blue-green; usually five leaves per stem, more rarely three, emerging from a common grayish-white stalk. We have no certain knowledge regarding the flower or the seed. However, the appearance of the plant suggests strongly enough that it can be classified among the *Coluteas*.

<summary>This page describes various species of Scorpion Senna (Colutea), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and their medicinal use as a substitute for Senna in treating black bile.</summary>
<keywords>Scorpion Senna, Colutea scorpioides, botany, medicinal herbs, Clusius, black bile, Spain, Austria, Coronilla del Rey, Indigo leaves</keywords>

--- Page 139 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on leguminous plants and shrubs, maintaining the descriptive style of the previous entries.</meta>

### ALPINUS’S SOPHERA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Sophera Alpini plant, showing a central stalk with pinnate leaves and several elongated seed pods hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

We depict here a branch which we keep among our natural specimens under the name *Sophera*, adding also the individual leaves, pods, and seeds. Prospero Alpini <note>Prospero Alpini (1553–1617) was a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian flora.</note> describes his Sophera thus: Sophera, he says, is a shrubby plant, a cubit <note>About 18 inches</note> in height, very close to the Goat’s Rue; with hard branches and leaves like the Myrtle, but thinner, many in number, and arranged in order along the ribs. It bears saffron-colored flowers, rivaling the flowers of the Cassia, without scent: from which small pods emerge, having four or five seeds, clearly similar to the Sesban <note>Egyptian Riverhemp</note>, which they say is poisonous to men.

### JUPITER’S BEARD, BEAUTIFULLY SHINING.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Barba Iovis plant, featuring a woody stem with small, clustered leaves and small flower heads at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

The name *Jupiter’s Beard* <note>Latin: Barba Iovis; likely Silver Bush (Anthyllis barba-jovis)</note> is indeed of vague significance: but this one which we depict here is of a hard and almost woody material, covered in a hoary and downy bark. The branches are quite frequent; the leaves are like those of the Lentil, hairy, shining with a silvery color, woven in five, six, or seven pairs. From the wing of the leaf-stalk, unique downy appendages arise, at the ends of which cling yellow florets crowded together in heaps. It grows in stony and rocky maritime places, and especially on mountains situated by the shores.

The figure is not pleasing, and perhaps it would be better placed as the Peisea tree.

### THE DORYCNIUM OF THE ANCIENTS, CALLED THAT OF CRATEVAS.
<margin>Montpellier Dorycnium.</margin>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Dorycnium Veterum, showing a leafy plant with multiple stems arising from a single root base, with small flowers at the terminals.</image-desc>

None of the Ancients, whether Greek or Latin, according to the testimony of Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), a German physician and botanist.</note>, described the Dorycnium, except for Dioscorides, who took its history from Cratevas. Pliny reports on the Dorycnium in such a way that he seems hardly to distinguish it from the "Mad Nightshade" <note>Latin: Solanum manicum</note>.

But that which we depict here is called the Dorycnium of Cratevas by some, but by most the Montpellier Dorycnium, and by some the Spanish Dorycnium of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a Flemish botanist.</note>. It comes out copiously in various uncultivated places in Spain and along the roads, as well as in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> near the sea and elsewhere. It flowers in May and June, and the seed ripens in July.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN TAXOCOQUAMOCLIT.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Taxocoquamoclit Indicum, showing a plant with long, slender seed pods and pinnate leaves similar to a legume.</image-desc>

From the similarity of the name, one might think this to be the *Hoxocoquamoclit* of Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist.</note>, under which name he describes at length a plant sent to Florence and Nuremberg: but to his Hoxocoquamoclit he attributes a cylindrical and oblong pod, whereas to this of ours it is compressed and very long; therefore we do not dare to assert that they are one and the same.

### A PLANT RELATED TO DORYCNIUM, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant related to Dorycnium, showing upright stems with whorled or clustered leaves and small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

A plant related to the Spanish Dorycnium of Clusius grows in the kingdom of Valencia and certain places in Andalusia. It has twigs a cubit high and flexible in the manner of Osier, more slender than the following: with shorter and broader leaves, joined together by threes or fives on a short stalk and embracing the small branches. The oblong branches sustain three, four, or five *flowers*, smaller than those of Medick, and of a green color: otherwise the whole plant is whiter than the following, indeed entirely hoary.

Botanists commonly label this a species of Dorycnium and a plant related to Dorycnium: and wrongly Tabernaemontanus and Gerard <note>John Gerard (1545–1612), author of a famous English herbal.</note> consider it to be the Montpellier Dorycnium, or *Cacum*.

### BROOM: German *Pfrimmen, Ginst*: French *Genestet* Italian *Ginestra*. SPARTIUM.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Genista (Broom) plant, showing thin, switch-like branches with small leaves and pea-like flowers.</image-desc>

Such a similarity exists between Spanish Broom <note>Spartium</note> and Common Broom <note>Genista</note>, both in appearance and in properties, that some, deceived by their affinity, have decided these plants should by no means be separated. And, since Pliny is found to have also doubted it, they thought that Genista was described by Dioscorides under the name Spartium. But since the Spartium of Dioscorides is a shrub devoid of leaves, and it is certain that it has flowers like the white Violet; whereas Genista produces rather long leaves, almost in the manner of Flax, and crescent-shaped flowers: the opinion of those who teach that Spartium and Genista differ seems altogether preferable, even though they are related plants and one has the greatest kinship with the other. Here, however, is depicted the angular three-leaved Broom.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and illustrations of various shrubs and legumes, including Sophera, Jupiter's Beard, and different species of Broom, while citing classical and contemporary authorities like Dioscorides and Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Sophera, Jupiter's Beard, Dorycnium, Broom, Genista, Spartium, Prospero Alpini, Charles de l'Écluse, Dioscorides, medicinal plants</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### BROOM WITH BROOM-RAPE: BY SOME CALLED Rapum Genistæ: French: Nanteau de Genestre.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Genista plant with a parasitic Orobanche (Rapum Genistæ) attached to its root system.</image-desc>

To the Broom and Small-Broom, say the *Adversaria* <note>Referring to the *Stirpium Adversaria Nova* (1570) by Pena and L'Obel</note>, there grows a kind of spurious offspring, though of a rarity seldom seen: an excrement, so to speak, in its origin, substance, growth, stalk, and appearance similar to *Hypocistis* or *Orobanche* <note>Parasitic plants that grow on the roots of others</note>. Some call it Broom-Rape <note>original: "Rapum Genistæ"</note> from its likeness to a turnip; others call it *Hypogenista* <note>Under-broom</note>, and others *Hypospartium*. A type of *Orobanche*, says Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous German physician and botanist</note>, accustomed to growing upon Broom, which the common people call Broom-Rape, and Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> calls the Greater *Orobanche*.

It is found in sterile, lean, and sandy soil, at the roots of the small Broom which does not reach full perfection, and which bears no flowers, or very few. It is found in June and July. Concerning its medicinal powers, see later.

<column-break/>

### DWARF BROOM, OR DYER’S WEED: German: Farbblumen: French: petit Genest.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing flowering plant with slender leaves and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

From a thick and woody root, you may gather many slender, twig-like shoots, a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note> and rounded, upon which grow leaves arranged alternately, like those of Hyssop or Flax, dark green above and below. The flowers are yellow in clusters, smaller than those of the narrow Broom: the pods are an inch long, somewhat broad, smooth, and contain the seeds.

Clusius writes that it is very frequent in the margins of woody meadows in Austria, Hungary <note>original: "Pannonia"</note>, and also in the fields of Frankfurt. We have observed it at Tübingen, Geneva, and Yverdon: and also at Montbéliard in the deer park. It blooms in the months of May, June, and July.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH DYER’S SMALL-BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branched shrubby plant with small leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Herbalists also label this the Dyer’s or Painter’s Small-Broom, and Clusius’s Dyer’s Broom. Clusius writes that he found this shrub in the soil of the Kingdom of Murcia: where it is called *Scopa* <note>Broom or brush</note> by the inhabitants; it is believed that if cows eat of it, they are stirred to lust and seek the bull.

Perhaps it is the herb of Thevet <note>André Thevet, a French explorer</note> growing in the stony and mountainous places of the Canary Islands, with which they dye leather elegantly, and which they call *Oricelle* <note>Orchil, a lichen used for purple dye, though here associated with this plant</note>.

In temperament and powers, as in form, these Small-Brooms are similar to the common Broom: because they serve for dyeing various things a yellow color, they have been given the name Dyer’s Flower <note>original: "Flos tinctorius"</note>.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED DYER’S BROOM of Lucca.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader, ovate leaves arranged alternately on the stem.</image-desc>

It differs from the other two chiefly by its leaves, which are broader, softer, shorter, and placed alternately; they are slightly hairy around the edges, green on one side, but a grayish-ash color on the other. Master Aggerius collected it in the mountains of Lucca, from whom we received it.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY SMALL-BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low, spreading plant with small, hairy leaves.</image-desc>

In the *History of Lyon* <note>The *Historia Generalis Plantarum* by Dalechamps</note> it is called the Least Broom: in Camerarius’s *Hortus* it is the Dwarf Broom. To Tabernaemontanus and Gerard, it is the Hungarian Small-Broom. It grows in various places among briars at the edges of woods, and in high, dry fields. We saw it in the forest of Aigremont near Montpellier, and in Soultz, Alsace: Clusius saw it in various places in Hungary. It blooms in May.

<column-break/>

### HERBACEOUS SMALL-BROOM, OR GROUND-BROOM: German: Erdpfrimmen: French: de la Spargelle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low herbaceous plant with winged stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

It is an herb rather than a shrub, rarely exceeding a cubit in height: the branches are soft, hairy, adorned with two wide soft fringes <note>referring to "winged" stems</note>, and divided as if by joints; at each joint is one oblong, blunt, hairy leaf, without a stalk, larger than in the angled variety, yet not triple as in that one. At the tops of the twigs are small yellow flowers, gaping open and almost forming a spike: the pod is very hairy: the root is woody, divided into several parts. We have observed it in various places: Frankfurt, Alsace, Basel, Montpellier, Geneva, Lyon, and Montbéliard.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Genista (Broom) and Genistella (Small-Broom), focusing on their physical characteristics, geographic distribution across Europe, and their use as yellow dyes.</summary>
<keywords>Broom-rape, Dyer's Weed, Genista, Genistella, Clusius, botanical dyeing, European flora, parasitic plants, medicinal herbs</keywords>

--- Page 141 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Genista (Broom) family, focusing on low-growing, radiating, and thorny varieties. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, citing contemporary botanists like Clusius and Dodonaeus.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES;
L 3

### BROAD-LEAVED HERBACEOUS GROUND-BROOM.
<note>original: "Chamægenista Herbacea Platyphyllos"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, flat leaves and clusters of bell-shaped flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

The branches consist of wide fringes, separated by intervals of thick leaves, as if you would say leaves are born from leaves, as is commonly said of the Indian Fig <note>The Prickly Pear cactus, Opuntia ficus-indica</note>: at every gap there are three points, between which, or in which, other leaves arise, and also other branch-like parts (unless you prefer to call the whole plant leafy), at the tops of which are gaping yellow flowers, similar to the flowers of the Broom. It is found in rough and uncultivated places, and it blooms in May.

### RADIATING OR STARRY BROOM.
<note>original: "Genista Radiata sive Stellaris"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with thin, radiating, needle-like leaves arranged in whorls around the stem, resembling stars.</image-desc>

The stem of this plant is divided into three branches, and these again into others, twice, three, or four times, always in threes: the spaces between nodes are two inches long: six leaves are placed around the stem in a whorl at every joint, as in Bedstraw or Goosegrass, hoary and hairy: the flowers at the ends of the tender twigs are dense and yellow.

In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is called *Broom of Elba*; by others *Alpine Broom*: and by some *Pliny’s Broom*.

### HEDGEHOG BROOM.
<note>original: "Genista Erinacea"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low, dense, mounded plant covered in sharp spines, resembling a hedgehog.</image-desc>

This plant is entirely new and elegant, nine inches high, spread in a circle along the ground, bristling with many green spines or prickles; the *flowers* are like Broom but a purplish-blue, always joined two or three together; the *leaves* are few, similar to Lentils, which, since they wither and fall off in a short time, the whole plant is seen for the most part without leaves, and with its manifold rampart of spines it represents a *Hedgehog* rolled up in itself: the *root* is woody and large in proportion to the plant. It grows, according to Clusius, in the Kingdom of Valencia, in rough places and along roadsides. It blooms in April.

<column-break/>

### SILVER BROOM.
<note>original: "Genista Argentea"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with small, trifoliate leaves and clusters of flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

This grows from a woody shoot, manifold, divided into many wings, rounded, and silvery. At the emergence of the small branches, single leaves cling, oblong, narrow, and covered with a silvery hairiness. It has *fruit* at the joints and ends of the small pods, similar to the fruit of the Balsam-tree <note>term: Carpobalsamum; the dried fruit of the Commiphora opobalsamum</note>, in which is a black, wrinkled, and somewhat round seed. We obtained this from the Pisan garden.

### LEAFY THORNY BROOM.
<note>original: "Genista Aculeata Foliosa"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrubby plant with small leaves and prominent thorns or spines along the stems.</image-desc>

This shrub grows with dense branches, armed with long and very frequent spines: the leaves are like common Broom, hairy and pointed: the *flowers* are yellow and spiked: the *pods* are small: the *root* is flexible and yellowish. It does not grow everywhere, but only in sandy, neglected, uncultivated, and rocky places; it is frequent along roadsides throughout Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Austria</note>, Brabant, and around Frankfurt. We have also observed it at Basel, Geneva, and Montbéliard. It blooms in May and June. Indeed, those who use it in place of common Broom are mistaken: for the powers of each are very different, and this plant has the same effect as Horsetail <note>term: Hippuris; used in ancient medicine to stop bleeding</note>.

### SMALL THORNY BROOM, and by some called NEPA or Scorpius.
<note>original: "Genistella Spinosae Affinis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very dense, prickly plant with small, scale-like leaves and numerous sharp spines.</image-desc>

This plant is as yet known to few, and described by none of the more recent authors, as the *Adversaria* <note>referring to the botanical work by Pena and L'Obel</note> says; the *roots* are woody, manifold, entangled, and thin; from which soon rise stiff, dense little spines; very similar to Wild Asparagus <note>original: "Corrudae"</note> but somewhat larger, they clothe the entire twigs to the very top, and thus the whole plant bristles with dense prickles instead of leaves, and presents the appearance of Wild Asparagus. It is the same as the Thorny Broom, or very similar to it; thus Dodonæus (in French) and Gerard call it *Thorny Broom*; by Camerarius and Tabernæmontanus it is called *Nepa*: by Cæsalpinus *Christ's Thorn*. Among the more learned, it is generally agreed that this is the *Nepa* of Gaza, or the *Scorpius* of Theophrastus. It grows everywhere, namely in uncultivated, dry, and rocky places: and it blooms in May and June, and sometimes throughout the whole summer.

<summary>This page describes six varieties of Broom (Genista), detailing their physical characteristics, such as "hedgehog-like" spines and "starry" leaf patterns, while citing major 16th-century botanists. It provides geographical locations for the species, ranging from Spain to Central Europe, and notes their medicinal distinctions.</summary>
<keywords>Genista, Broom, Botany, Clusius, Herbology, Thorny plants, Taxonomy, Medicinal plants, European flora</keywords>
