# OF PLANTS

### THORNY BROOM or PRICKLY SPANISH BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Genista plant with thin, leafless, thorny branches and small flower clusters at the tips.</image-desc>

Lobel and Pena in their *Adversaria*, *Observations*, and *Images of Plants* record this as the *Shrubby leafless Spanish broom, with rush-like thorns and woolly heads*, etc. Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History* calls it *Thorny leafless Spanish broom*. Lobel writes that it is found repeatedly on the rougher and steep slopes of the Alps of Sainte-Baume <note>original: "Alpium Magdalenae"</note> in the province of Gaul <note>France</note>. We keep the branches we have depicted here among our own natural specimens.

### SMALLER ASPALATHUS-LIKE BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Genista variety with more dense, needle-like foliage and visible roots.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves like those of Duckweed <note>original: "Lenticulae palustris"</note>; the branches bristle with thorns arranged alternately, and among them, throughout almost the entire length of the branches, are many golden flowers. To continue describing the use of Brooms: the water of Broom flowers is considered beneficial for those suffering from stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>. Bees love Broom flowers, but the honey made from them is not very good. The buds of the flowers, while still green and before they turn yellow, are picked and preserved in brine or salt like Capers—a great stimulant for the palate—and then eaten. Many people also put freshly picked flowers into salads and eat them in great quantities; this weakens the opinion of those who believe that Spanish Broom <term>Spartium: a specific genus of broom often confused with Genista</term> and Common Broom <term>Genista</term> possess the same properties. Regarding the ointments and lyes made from Broom, let the reader consult our *Great History*.

### SPANISH BROOM with Roundish Pods and yellow flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spanish Broom with larger, rounded seed pods (lobes) and sparse leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant fall off as soon as it begins to bloom, so that the whole plant then appears leafless. To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> it is the *Second Spanish Broom*; it grows in various places in Castile on sandy soil and flowers in May.

As for the agreement and similarity between Spanish Broom and Common Broom, as was said before regarding Brooms, those who believe they are the same in power and properties—just because they look alike—are greatly mistaken. For although Spanish Broom has the same temperament as Common Broom, it nevertheless disturbs, provokes, cuts, and thins more forcefully in all its parts: it evacuates humors from the joints, powerfully moves the urine, and purges violently through vomiting and stool. *More on this in the following sections.*

<column-break/>

### THORNY BROOM OF MONT VENTOUX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy, thorny plant variety from Mont Ventoux.</image-desc>

This plant has hairy and somewhat broad leaves; the branches are armed with thorns like those of Juniper, and at their tips are the golden flowers of the Broom.

Furthermore, Broom is hot and dry in the second degree: it is endowed with "thinning" parts which have the power of cleansing and cutting <note>referring to the Galenic medical theory of breaking up thick fluids in the body</note>. It moves the urine, is believed to break the stone, and purges phlegm, which is why it is of great use to women against gout <note>original: "podagram"</note>. The leaves, small branches, and tips, boiled in wine or water, are useful for those with dropsy <note>edema</note> and in obstructions of all the internal organs; it evacuates watery humors through the bowels and urine. The seed performs the same function and disperses goiters <note>original: "Bronchocelen"</note> and every kind of tumor. *More at the side of the following figure.*

### SPANISH BROOM, RUSH BROOM, Spanish Genista.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, reed-like Spanish Broom with elongated flowers.</image-desc>

It has the same name among the Germans, Belgians, French, and Italians as the Common Broom. And this is the shrub that Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note> calls *Spartium*: producing long, firm twigs without leaves that are resistant to breaking, providing a use as ties for binding vines. It has pods in which the seeds are like Lentils, and a honey-colored flower like a Stock-gilliflower <note>original: "Leucoii"</note>.

It grows spontaneously in all the warmer regions of the European world: especially in Tuscany <note>original: "Hetruria"</note>, where, according to Mattioli, it is very frequent; in the months of May and June, it offers a great and pleasant sight to travelers.

Our illustration is from our purchased Fuchsian prints <note>referring to the botanical woodcuts of Leonhart Fuchs</note>, and it does not please us in all respects. *More in the following.*

### WHITE-FLOWERED SPANISH BROOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spanish Broom variety with white flowers and more prominent foliage.</image-desc>

This is much larger than the aforementioned and rises to the height of a man. In its flower, pod, and seed it agrees with the one above, but all parts are smaller. It grows in sandy places facing the sea breeze.

Furthermore, to continue describing the properties of Spanish Broom, it breaks the stone in the kidneys and bladder, and does not allow impurities to settle in them and harden into a stone. The flowers and seed resolve scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and tumors of the spleen. Common Broom and Spanish Broom take the place of Willow for binding vines; they are even soaked in the manner of Hemp, and from the fiber, ropes and linens suitable for sacks are made. And finally, the wood is sought after by the Potters in Italy who make that kind of earthenware vessel which they call *Maiolica*.

<summary>This page details various species of Broom (Genista and Spartium), distinguishing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for stones and gout, and industrial applications in rope-making and Italian Maiolica pottery.</summary>
<keywords>Broom, Spanish Broom, Genista, Spartium, kidney stones, gout, herbal medicine, Maiolica pottery, botany, Dioscorides, Lobel, Clusius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of thorny and coastal shrubs, focusing on species known for their medicinal resins or unique structures, such as the Manna-bearing Agul and the sea-grapes.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### AGUL AND ARABIAN ALHAGI, a thorny plant yielding Manna.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small, thorny shrub with thin, branching stems and small leaves, showing the root system at the base.</image-desc>

Serapio, Avicenna, and Clusius (in his *Epitome of Indian Plants*) testify that Manna <note>A sweet, medicinal resin secreted by certain plants</note> originates upon thorny shrubs. These shrubs, upon which Manna most especially falls, are called *Agul* and *Algul*; the Persians name this Manna *Transchibin*, while the Arabs call it *Teneriabin* and *Trangibin*.

The *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> mentions these in these words: "A certain thorny plant," it says, "the *Alhagi, Agul, and Algul* of the Moors," etc.

The Agul grows in Persia, around Aleppo, and near the city of Kaeka in Mesopotamia. The leaves are of a hot and dry nature, and the inhabitants purge themselves with a handful of them.

<column-break/>

### THEOPHRASTUS’S SCORPIUS, NEPA: The second Aspalathus of Montpellier: The second Acacia of Anguillara:

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a woody, upright shrub with dense, needle-like foliage or thorns and small clusters of flowers or seed pods.</image-desc>

Regarding the *Scorpius* of Theophrastus, which Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Aristotle and Theophrastus</note> calls *Nepa*, various authors hold various opinions: those who judge it to be either *Asparagus* or Pliny’s *Tragus* are greatly mistaken. Theophrastus writes of it thus: "The Scorpius," he says, "is simply a thorn: for it has no leaf at all: it has a simple, deep, and short root." But how can it be both short and deep?

The shrub pictured here is called the "second Aspalathus" by those in Montpellier; to others, it is the "second Acacia" of Anguillara: but to most, it is the *Scorpius* of Theophrastus. We saw it in a stony place in Montpellier, on Mount Castelnauf; Clusius observed it in various places in Spain.

---

### RELATED TO THE ASPALATHUS OF MONTPELLIER, the second Scorpius of Clusius. Perhaps ECHINOPODA?

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a low-growing, very thorny plant with thick, tangled branches and small round seed heads or flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius believes this plant comes very close to the *Scorpius* or *Nepa*. It rarely exceeds a foot in height and bristles all over with very dense thorns, which do not grow in a confused order but maintain a certain sequence, always arising in pairs opposite one another. The **flowers** at the tips of the branches are solitary, in pairs, or in threes, and are yellow; the pods are the size of a vetch, etc.

Clusius observed it on the hills near Granada, specifically on the road to Córdoba and nowhere else; he says it is called *Melino* by the people of Granada, and he judges it to be very close to the *Echinopoda* <note>literally "hedgehog-foot"</note> mentioned by Bellus.

In the Latin edition of Dodonaeus, it is the *second thorny Broom*; in Lobelius’s *Observations* and *Images*, it is the *second thorny Spanish Broom*.

<column-break/>

### THE TRAGUS OF THE ANCIENTS: SEA GRAPE. German: *Meertrauben*: French: *Raisin de Mer*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a coastal plant with jointed, leafless stems resembling horsetail, featuring small berry-like fruits along the stalks.</image-desc>

It is not at all surprising that the name *Tragus* <note>original: "Tragum"</note> is today applied to *Scorpius*, the jointed *Cali*, *Fraxinella*, and species of *Inuci* and *Sedum*, as well as the *Sea Grape*; for even according to its first author, Dioscorides, some called the *Tragus* "Scorpius" and others "Traganum."

The *Tragus*, or Sea Grape, grows abundantly at Montpellier by the sea, where we saw it flowering in Spring and bearing fruit in August and Autumn. It grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Prince. Ten berries from the clusters, drunk in wine—on the authority of Dioscorides—help those suffering from abdominal pains and women with "the flux" <note>excessive discharge</note>. Pliny holds the same and adds that they are useful for dysentery and those spitting blood, but he attributes this to the tips of the branches, whereas Dioscorides more correctly attributes it to the berries.

---

### TRAGUS, OR THE GREATER SEA GRAPE.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a larger variety of the "Vua Marina" with thicker, more robust jointed stems and larger clusters of berries.</image-desc>

The other variety barely exceeds a palm’s width, but this one sometimes grows to the height of a man; like the former, it has rods divided by many joints, in which neither leaves nor traces of leaves appear. However, the **flowers** which are carried in crowded clusters at the top of the branches in the former variety, arise along the joints in this one—also in clusters—small and mossy, not unlike the flowers of the Cornel tree. Both have **fruit** similar to small Mulberries, reddish, succulent, and tart: and within them are several grains like Millet, black on the outside. The root is hard and woody.

It flowers and ripens its fruit at the same time as the preceding one; it is commonly labeled *Sea Grape* by authors.

<column-break/>

### TRAGACANTH, TRAGACANTH OF MARSEILLE: German: *Bockshorn*: French: *Espine de bouc*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a low, spreading, extremely thorny shrub with small pinnate leaves and a thick, woody root system.</image-desc>

Dioscorides records the following about Tragacanth: "The root of the Tragacanth," he says, "is broad and woody, and even stands out above the ground. From it come low, robust shoots spread very widely: and on these are thin little leaves among which thorns put themselves forward, which the leaves themselves hide—white, firm, and straight." There is also the "Tear of Tragacanth" <note>Gum Tragacanth</note>, which hardens upon the cut root and flows from the wound of the plant. It has the power to close the pores of the skin. Its use has become frequent for eye medicines, coughs, rough voices, and catarrh.

Theophrastus once wrote that it grew abundantly in Arcadia, Achaia, Media, and Crete; today, however, it grows plentifully on the coastal hills of Provence facing the South, and especially near the outskirts of Marseille.

<summary>This page describes various thorny and coastal shrubs, including the Manna-producing Agul, the Scorpius (Nepa), and the medicinal Tragacanth. It focuses on their botanical identification, geographical locations (such as Montpellier and Marseille), and their historical uses in medicine as recorded by Dioscorides and Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Agul, Alhagi, Manna, Scorpius, Sea Grape, Tragacanth, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Clusius, medicinal plants, botany, Montpellier, Marseille</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of thorny shrubs and "spiny" plants, concluding the eleventh class of the herbal. It references several contemporary 16th-century botanists including Carolus Clusius and Pierre Belon.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### ANOTHER TRAGACANTH, perhaps the Poterium of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, thorny shrub with intricate branching and small leaves, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This second variety is very similar to the **Tragacanth** <note>Goat's Thorn or Astragalus</note> already depicted, which seems to match the description handed down by Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> well enough. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> writes that it grows on the hills of the Kingdom of Granada in dry and useless soil, and has been seen nowhere else. It is quite shrubby, having many foot-long whitening branches, bristling with many long, graying spines. The leaves are many "wings" <note>pinnate leaflets</note> joined together, very close to those of the Lentil or the Tragacanth. These fall off in winter, unlike the other Tragacanth, which retains its leaves and does not cast them off until it has acquired new ones the following year. Clusius did not see the flower, nor the seed.

Is this the second kind of Tragacanth from the mountain peaks of Crete mentioned by Belon? <note>Pierre Belon, a French naturalist</note> To Clusius, it is the *Poterium* <note>Burnet-bloodroot</note>.

### THE ECHINOPUS OF PLUTARCH: ECHINOPODA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dense, upright spiny plant with needle-like foliage and a thick root.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub with many-cleft, reddish branches. In place of leaves, there are spines of the same color, an inch long, approaching the stiffness of Juniper leaves to some extent and of equal width with them, flat, slightly bent outward, and planted in such a dense formation that you would not know where to touch the little plant without being pricked.

**ECHINOPODA** <note>literally "Hedgehog-foot"</note> is not a type of Thistle, as Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, a French physician and botanist</note> established, but belongs to the genus of Shrubs. It comes very close to the *Genista Erinacea* <note>Thorny Broom</note>, except that it lacks leaves. However, it produces abundant yellow flowers and is seen spread out in a circle, entirely green in color; because of the multitude of its spines, it represents a Hedgehog <note>Latin: *Erinaceum*</note> most perfectly. It is very common in Crete, the island of Chios, and all of Greece. Could it be the *Chenopus* <note>Goose-foot</note> of Pliny?

<column-break/>

### THE HIPPOPHAES OF ANGUILLARA AND DODONÆUS, or the Purging Thorn.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy shrub with thorns and small clusters of berries or flowers, showing the root.</image-desc>

**Hippophaes**, says Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, an Italian botanist</note>, arises in the sandy coastal areas of the Peloponnese. It is a small shrub armed with very hard spines, spreading itself into a white, rounded head. The leaves are longer, narrower, and more tender than those of the Olive. The root is longer than a palm's breadth. If broken, it pours out a milky, bitter juice with a heavy odor. I have seen neither flower nor fruit. However, the root has a most violent power for purging, whence the plant gets the name **Purging Thorn**.

In Latin, it is called by Dodonæus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician</note> the *Hippophaes* of Anguillara, and the *Hippophaes* of Dioscorides and Pliny.

### GALASTIVIDA, A SPINY PLANT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, jagged, thistle-like leaves and a central stalk.</image-desc>

Regarding this shrub, Belon writes these things in a letter to Clusius: **Galastivida**, he says, was so named because of the similarity it has with *Stivida* (or the Spiny Pimpinella) in its multitude of spines. It arises in the southern part of the island of Crete; I do not rightly remember its form, etc. The peasants use it for building fires and heating ovens. Indeed, because of the similarity of the spines which it has with the *Stoebe* <note>Knapweed or Burnet</note>, and its white color, they call it *Gala-Stivida* <note>Milk-Stivida</note>, not because it emits milk.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## TWELFTH CLASS.
### WHICH CONCERNS THE RARER POD-BEARING TREES
### and those similar to them.

| | |
|---|---|
| **CAROB** <note>original: *Siliqua*</note>: German & Belgian: *St. John’s Bread*; French: *Carouger*, the fruit *Carouge*; Italian: *Caroba, Carobolo*. | **ANOTHER CAROB OR HORN-POD** <note>original: *Ceratia*</note> Illustration. |

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Carob branch (Ceratonia siliqua) showing pinnate leaves and long, curved seed pods (siliquae).</image-desc>

The fruit, twisted in the manner of a horn, gave the name "Siliqua" <note>Pod</note> to the Latins and "Ceratia" <note>Little Horn</note> to the Greeks. This tree has a thick and tall trunk; the branches are long and firm, the leaves are arranged in this manner: somewhat round, more or less three inches wide, thick, rigid, and veined, appearing individually and attached to the rib by a short stalk. The *flowers* are a reddish-purple; the *pods* are equal in length to an index finger, twisted and compressed; and within them are *seeds* separated by membranes, almost equal to the seeds of the laxative Cassia.

Matthioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, 16th-century physician and botanist</note> separates this tree from the "Siliqua" of Theophrastus and Pliny (called "Ceronia" by the Ionians and by some the *Egyptian Fig*) by a great error. Even those who wish it to be the *Judas Tree* stumble, in the judgment of Dalechamps; nor are those less deceived who think it is the Cassia Fistula. *More on this in the margin of the following figure.*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a single, large, curved seed pod, likely a variety of Carob or related legume.</image-desc>

The illustration now placed here was made while we were absent; it is the illustration of Alpini, and it pleases us little, wherefore we provide another from Camerarius in the German edition of Matthioli. Furthermore, we have it from the authors Theophrastus and Pliny that the Carob does not grow in Egypt, but in Syria and Ionia, around Cnidus and Rhodes. Today, however, it is found not only among the Eastern peoples and Indians, but also in various places in Spain and the Kingdom of Naples. It flowers as soon as winter is released <note>early spring</note> and ripens its fruit in Autumn. Galen writes that the tree and fruit possess an astringent and drying quality; Dioscorides writes that the green fruit, when eaten, is unpleasant for the stomach and loosens the bowels, but when dry, it stops the same <note>acts as an anti-diarrheal</note> and is more beneficial to the stomach.

---

| | |
|---|---|
| **PURGATIVE CASSIA** : French: *Casse*. German, Belgian, Italian & English: *Cassia*. | **INDIAN SINGLE-SEEDED HORN-POD.** |

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Cassia fistula branch with large oval leaflets and a long, cylindrical seed pod.</image-desc>

We have it from the authors Hermolaus and Ruellius that this was unknown in the ages of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen. Indeed, Cornarius marvels that Theophrastus, who spoke of other plants produced in Egypt, made no mention of this one, which is found there in great abundance.

The more recent Greeks called it *Cassia Syringodes*, that is, "pipe-like" <note>referring to the long, tube-like pods</note>; Actuarius called it *Black Cassia*; others call it *fistula, fistular, Indian, Egyptian, and purgative Cassia*.

The tree is said to be the size of a Pear tree, with leaves like a Peach but narrower and greener. It has yellow flowers like Broom, with the scent of Clove; when these fall, long pods grow beneath them. *We shall speak of its native location and properties shortly.*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a thick, curved, bean-like pod, identified as Ceratium Monococoon Indicum.</image-desc>

This fruit, which we keep among our natural specimens, we formerly received from Robin, the Royal Gardener.

To proceed in recounting the history of Cassia: it has now become common to Asia, but it grows without sowing in great quantities in Egypt and various provinces of both the East and West Indies. However, that which is brought from the East, and especially from places turning toward the North, is preferred. Its frequency in Cambay <note>a region in India</note> is so great (from whence they bring the most excellent kind) that one *Candil* [which is a weight of 512 pounds] is sold for only one gold coin. In heat and cold it is almost temperate, and moist in the first degree; by its softening nature, it purges gently. The Physicians <note>Practici</note> and Apothecaries <note>Seplasii</note> know the manner of using it.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal uses of the Carob tree and the Cassia fistula, correcting historical misidentifications by earlier scholars. It details their physical appearance, geographical origins in the Mediterranean and Indies, and their roles as laxatives or astringents.</summary>
<keywords>Carob, Cassia fistula, Ceratonia siliqua, medicinal plants, purgatives, botany, Theophrastus, Pliny, Matthioli, Egypt, India, pharmacology</keywords>

--- Page 146 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of exotic plants, focusing on species from the Indies, Arabia, and the Americas. It maintains the botanical descriptions established in previous sections.</meta>

### THE TAMARIND, OR TAMARIND TREE:
->German: *Saur dattel* <note>Sour date</note>; French: *Tamarinds*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tamarind tree with a thick trunk and spreading leafy canopy.</image-desc>

According to Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a Portuguese physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note>, this is a tree of the same size as an Ash, a Walnut, or a Chestnut. The wood is firm and not at all prone to rot. The branches are adorned with many leaves that are finely divided. The flowers are white, very similar to the flowers of the Orange tree. The fruit is formed in the shape of a bow or a curved finger, containing seeds <note>original: "nucleos"</note> with the shape and size of yellow Lupine beans, but of a tawny color and smooth. Once these seeds are cast aside, the pulp is used, which is tough and sticky. It is altogether marvelous that while this fruit is still hanging on the tree, it wraps itself in leaves for the sake of avoiding the cold; at other times, however, it frees itself and emerges from the middle of the leaves. Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, a Venetian physician and botanist</note> writes that the leaves close in on themselves at night, but open again when the Sun rises, and for this reason, they are called *Sun-followers* <note>original: "Solis Sequia"</note>.

### MATES, AN INDIAN FRUIT: BUNA,
->The *Bunnu* and *Bunchos* of the Arabs.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut showing various seeds and pods of the Mates or Buna plant, including several oval beans and a larger pod with leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note> writes that he received this fruit under the name *Mates*, and that it equals the seed of the purging Cassia or the Carob in size. He notes that it also resembles them in shape, but is more swollen and different in color, as it turns red as it ripens, like the fruit of the Hawthorn.

The same illustration is also presented for the *Buna*, *Bunnu*, and *Buncho* of the Arabs, and perhaps more appropriately so.

### PLANT SIMILAR TO THE CORAL TREE.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a plant with large, rounded, heart-shaped leaves on a branched stem.</image-desc>

This grew for us from a seed in the Princely garden at Montbéliard. In June, it produced a stem a palm's length long, thorny, and quite thick for the size of the plant. The leaves varied: sometimes they were single, large, and somewhat round; at other times they grew in threes, somewhat approaching the leaves of the Cyclamen. Whether it truly climbs or is a clinging plant could not be observed, for it perished in the cold.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE TAMARIND TREE
->with the Pod, seeds, and a single leaf.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut showing botanical details of the Tamarind: a long curved seed pod (siliqua), individual seeds, and a single compound leaf.</image-desc>

The Tamarind tree grows most abundantly in Arabia Felix <note>the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note> and Ethiopia; we depict a young one here. It is not very common in Egypt, although it is imported from there into our regions. We have seen several plants in Sprenger's garden at Heidelberg.

However, Matthiolus, Lonicerus, and others have been of the opinion that Tamarinds are the fruit of the Wild Palm, perhaps based on the fact that *Tamar Indus* and *Indian Date* <note>original: "Dactylus Indus"</note> are one and the same. By many of the Greeks, it is called *Oxyphoenicia* <note>literally "sour date"</note>. By almost everyone else, these fruits are called Tamarinds. Their pulp is brought to us in a black color and with a very sour taste. It is an excellent medicine, cold and dry in the second degree <note>a classification in Galenic medicine</note>, purging bile, calming the heat of the blood, and restraining the sharpness of the humors.

### BUNA OR BUNNU FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut of two coffee-like beans, one showing the flat side with a central groove.</image-desc>

We have a plate marked with this name among our collection; the experts will judge whether it is the fruit of the legitimate *Buna* <note>Coffee</note>. One may consult the History by Alpinus in Class V regarding *Bon* or *Ban*. Furthermore, a drink by the name of *Chaube* <note>Coffee/Kahve</note> is most familiar to the Turks, which they prepare from the *Buna* fruit. In the morning hours, they drink it publicly in the streets, sipping it from earthenware or porcelain cups, and they hold it in the same regard as we do wormwood wine or spiced wines.

### THE POD-BEARING CORAL TREE.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a small plant in a ceramic pot, featuring trifoliate leaves and a central upright stem.</image-desc>

This is an Indian tree called *Corall* because of the resemblance its flowers have to Coral. Its leaves are very similar to the leaves of the Judas Tree, but that tree has thorns, while this one has none. We saw a small tree at Stuttgart, born from a seed received from America; it was very thorny and had pods full of very large beans <note>original: "phaseolis"</note>.

<keywords>Tamarind, Coffee, Buna, Coral Tree, Arabian medicine, Garcia de Orta, Prospero Alpini, botanical gardens, 16th-century botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### EXOTIC FRUIT FROM BENGAL.
<note>original: "Bencala"</note>

It is nearly five inches long and encompasses the same in circumference; it is hunched on one side, consisting of a wrinkled and uneven rind that is wide, thick, hard, and woody, with a grayish-brown color. This rind contains two kernels, each an inch long, which can be divided into four parts; they are hard, reddish-brown in color, and have an astringent taste that is not unpleasant, etc. Thus Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist</note> describes it, and he believes this fruit has a great affinity with the *Cola* fruit, as it approaches it in substance, color, and taste.

### JUDAS TREE. German: *Iudæbaum*: French: *Guainier*: Italian: *Caribaria*: Spanish: *Arbol d'amor*. Is it the *Cercis* of Theophrastus and the Ancients?

By what name this tree was called by the Ancients is not easily said. Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a renowned physician and botanist</note> considers it a species of *Laburnum*, others the *Colutea* of Theophrastus: but it differs greatly from both, even in the judgment of Gesner. Those who believe it to be the *Siliqua* <note>Carob</note> of Pliny are also mistaken; nor did the Sienese <note>referring to Mattioli</note> show it any better when he presented the Judas Tree in a picture as the *True Acacia*. Clusius labeled it the *Wild Siliqua*, while Belon called it the *Siliquastrum*: most refer it to the *Cercis* of Theophrastus, some to the first type, others to the second.

It grows spontaneously in various places in Spain, Italy, and France, and especially in Tuscany, from where Mattioli rightly obtained it <note>original: "accersiuit"</note> from Constantinople. We have also observed it kept in various cultivated gardens, and we ourselves have cultivated it in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard.

### LARGE FOUR-SIDED POD.

Clusius, who illustrates and describes it, could not learn from where this pod was brought, nor what name it had been given, or what medicinal properties it possessed. However, he says it was of a quadrangular shape, seven inches long, nearly two inches wide, with the "back" and "belly" protruding and bulging in a certain way, and a long furrow on both sides from the head to the bottom of the pod, extending beyond the lateral wings. Its color is dark and shining. This pod contained several seeds in the central spine, as could be detected by shaking it, etc.

<column-break/>

### POD-BEARING FRUIT OF ORYCORIA.

Clusius describes it thus: It is the fruit, he says, of a tree growing in *Witapock* <note>likely a region in South America</note>, called *Iurruua* by the locals, which they use to treat wounds inflicted by the weapons and darts of enemies. For when the fruits are crushed or broken, they allow the juice to drip into the wounds to heal them. The fruit is flat and almost as wide as it is long (two inches), but twisted like the *True Cytisus*, though much larger, very wrinkled, and grayish in color, containing a flat seed. It was purchased from sailors returning from America in the year 1599.

### MORINGA: Called *Moria* by the Arabs and Turks: *Tamē* by the Persians: *Turiaa* by the people of Gujarat.

The Moringa is the size of a Mastic tree and has very similar leaves. It is endowed with few branches and abounds with many knots, and it is extremely fragile. The leaves are a deep green. It bears an edible fruit the thickness of a radish, marked by narrow ridges, with a paler green color on the outside but white on the inside; it is pithy and divided into certain compartments in which round, green, and tender seeds are contained. This fruit is eaten with meat or prepared in other ways. The root of the tree, however, serves as a substitute for Unicorn horn or the Bezoar stone <note>a "stone" found in the stomachs of goats, prized as an antidote</note> against all poisons. It grows abundantly in various parts of India, but especially throughout the Province of Malabar.

### YELLOWISH FRUIT ENCLOSED IN A TOUGH POD.

Clusius labels this thus in his *Exotics*, where he also writes of a fruit enclosed in a pod that is blackish with white veins, and of the "thorny pod" of the Indians called *Sampavatra*, and other such fruits enclosed in pods.

It highlights the era's reliance on botanists like Clusius and the global trade in medicinal plants.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Judas Tree, Moringa, Clusius, Bengal, Malabar, medicinal plants, New World flora, exotic fruits</keywords>

# OF PLANTS.

### ACACIA: German: *Egyptian Blackthorn*: French & Italian: *Acacia*: Spanish: *Tree of Gum Arabic*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Acacia tree with a thorny trunk and delicate, pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

According to all Greek, Latin, and Arabic writers, says Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), a German physician and botanist</note> in his commentary on Dioscorides, the Acacia is a small tree growing in Egypt. Near Aleppo, says Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a physician and traveler who explored the Levant</note>, a thorny shrub of the Acacia is seen, which is called *Schack* by the locals and *Schamu* by the Arabs: it is small and low-growing, mostly in the fields, and not surprisingly as hated by farmers as Ferns and Rest-harrow <term>Anonis: a tough-rooted weed</term> are by ours. The branches are ash-colored and curved; they have many thorns similar to those of Roses. The leaves are like those of Tragacanth, arranged like feathers as in the female Fern, and so many cling to a single rib that, as Bellonius <note>Pierre Belon, a French naturalist</note> reports, you could cover them with your thumb. The pods are dark on the outside, thicker and rounder than a Bean, spongy inside, and contain two or three reddish seeds. I have not seen the flowers, etc. More follows.

### AN INDIAN HAZELNUT PECULIAR TO SOME. Perhaps a type of the Hazelnut called *Mehembetene*?

<image-desc>Woodcut of a small, ribbed nut or seed, shown from two angles (marked 1 and 11) and a cross-section (marked with an asterisk).</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German botanist</note> depicts this in his revised editions of Mattioli, both in the German History and the Epitome, but he does not describe it. If, however, it is permitted to guess from the image alone, we suspect it is a certain variety of the Hazelnut called *Mehembetene*, which was discussed previously in Class III.

### ANOTHER EXOTIC FRUIT. Perhaps some species of Myrobalan?

<image-desc>Woodcut of an exotic fruit or seed pod, shown whole and in cross-section, revealing a fibrous interior.</image-desc>

It is unknown to us what tree produced this fruit, which I received in a dried state; therefore, we shall refer it for the time being to the Myrobalans <term>A dried plum-like fruit used in medicine and tanning</term>, which it seems most closely to resemble.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE ACACIA.

<image-desc>Woodcut showing a detailed branch of an Acacia with seed pods and thorns.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> recounts two kinds of Acacia: the *Acantha* and the *Egyptian Acantha*. Dioscorides also has two: the Egyptian and the Cappadocian. Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, who studied Egyptian flora</note> writes that a Male and Female of this tree are found in Egypt: the Male is bristling with thorns and bears no fruit, while the Female is filled with fewer and softer thorns. It flowers in November and March, bearing fruit twice a year; and finally, it grows most abundantly in the mountains of Sinai, located near the Red Sea. According to Bellonius, in the sterile deserts of Arabia by the Red Sea, no plant grows except the Acacia trees, which abound there, and from which the Arabs diligently collect the gum, which is called Gum Arabic, of which more follows.

### ANOTHER EXOTIC FRUIT: Juice of the Acacia: and Gum Arabic.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a rounded, ribbed fruit or seed pod and a smaller, darker seed or piece of resin (marked with an asterisk).</image-desc>

Let us tentatively add this fruit here, and also add something to the side of this table regarding the juice of the Acacia. We quite often find the thorns and seeds of the Acacia—such as we showed a little earlier in the table—along with what is called Gum Arabic <gloss>Gum of Acacia, Gum of the Egyptian Thorn, Babylonian Gum</gloss>, from which we conclude that it is collected from the Acacia. Ryffius <note>Walther Hermann Ryff, a medical writer</note> records it thus: From a certain Egyptian Thorn (the Acacia), from whose seed or fruit and leaves the juice is pressed, there also flows a Gum contracted into the shape of little worms, and transparent like glass. It cools, thickens, etc. The practitioners and druggists <term>Seplasia: ancient term for perfume or drug sellers</term> know its remaining uses.

### ANOTHER HAIRY EXOTIC POD, with a hard ash-colored Pea:

<image-desc>Woodcut of a long, hairy seed pod (lobe) on a stem, with two small, round seeds shown below (marked with an asterisk).</image-desc>

This pod, as Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note> recounts in his *Exotics*, consisted of a thin, skin-like shell, dark reddish in color and hairy with frequent small scales; it was three inches long and two wide. Inside were two fruits, the size, shape, and hardness of a Pea. He writes that he has also seen smaller pods with a single fruit, and it is easy to guess that such Peas are found in various places in Africa and America, because they are frequently found among the spices brought from Tripoli in Syria. Could it be the Indian Wild Chestnut?

### POD FROM WINGANDECAOW <note>original: "Vvingandecaovv"; an early name for the region of Virginia used by English explorers like Raleigh.</note>

This specimen is of remarkable thickness: it is six inches long and three inches wide. Externally, it is somewhat rough and uneven with small bumps, possessing a dark, shining brownish color.

### POD FROM WINGAND. or VIRGINIA, Illustration by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius) was a foundational 16th-century botanist famous for describing New World plants.</note>

Regarding this, Clusius reports the following: "Two pods of this kind," he says, "were sent to me. One was six inches long and two and a half inches wide; the other was only five inches long and two inches wide. Both, however, were an inch thick, covered with a thick, strong, hard, and firm rind. Two nerves or ribs extend from the stalk—which is thick and firm—to the very end of the pod along the length of the back. The exterior is brown in color, the interior ash-gray, and it is rough on both the inside and the outside."

### THICK SWOLLEN BRAZILIAN POD, with Citron-like seeds.

This is eight inches long and four and a half inches wide. It is flat, with a hunched back and a belly that is thicker and more swollen than the center itself. Within it are ten cavities, each two inches long, containing a quadrangular seed an inch in length, positioned obliquely. The color of the pod is brownish-gray on the outside.

<column-break/>

### POD FROM WINGANDECAOW, WITH branch and leaves.

From a small stone <note>original: "officulo"; referring to a hard seed or pit.</note> planted in the ground in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi"; the site of a famous botanical garden under the House of Württemberg.</note>, the plant which we depict here grew forth.

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION BY THE SAME CLUSIUS.

"The said pods," he continues, "contained a spongy pulp of an ash-gray color, in which were hidden five or six small stones, each an inch long, the size of a hazelnut or a cultivated Pontic nut. They were hard and black, containing a white kernel with the flavor of an almond or a hazelnut."

### ANOTHER SMALLER BRAZILIAN POD, with seeds.

This is of the same kind as the previous one, but smaller, and provided with only eight cavities, in which the seed is not very different from the seed of a Citron apple. Those who brought this and the preceding specimen from Brazil assert that both grow on very tall trees.

# OF PLANTS

### THE AMERICAN POD OF DABURI.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with two large, textured, pod-like fruits or follicles hanging from it.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist and director of the Leiden Botanical Garden.</note> received this fruit from London in the year 1585, having been purchased from sailors returning from America; he describes it at length. Whether it came from a tree or a shrub, Clusius does not know: for he received it still attached to its branch, which was quite smooth, and which seemed to have supported several pods.

*Is it the fruit of the tree of the "boundaries to be regulated" <note>original: "finium regundorum"</note> of Scaliger? Or the Bixa of Oviedo?*

---

### THE BIXA OF OVIEDO.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a branch with several spiky or bristly seed pods, similar to the Bixa orellana (Achiote).</image-desc>

This is a shrub rising to the height of a man, and sometimes even taller, producing leaves similar to those of the Cotton plant <note>original: "Xyli"</note>: the Brazilians use its fruit—elegantly depicted here—as well as the whole shrub, to dye their bodies with a red color: *with which the Indians anoint themselves. Appendix.* <note>original: "con que se untan los Indios."</note>

---

### THE EXOTIC FRUIT OF COLES.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a single, oval-shaped fruit or seed with a textured, ribbed surface.</image-desc>

Clusius, who describes it at length, says it does not exceed an inch in size, and that the outer part is wrinkled and black, and in some way similar to Cacao. Roelsius <note>Tobias Roels, a 16th-century physician and botanist.</note> maintains it is the fruit of a tree which has leaves like the Pine <note>original: "Pyti"</note>, but longer. He reports that the region of Africa which is near Cape Verde is fertile with it, and that the inhabitants, by chewing one or two in the morning, can easily endure fasting for the whole day; and by chewing that same fruit, any drink becomes more flavorful.

---

### THE STONE OF A FRUIT FROM THE PALM GENUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a single seed or stone (ossiculum), showing internal structure or markings.</image-desc>

Clusius includes this among his Exotics, and says it was two inches long, and three and a half inches in circumference: it was smooth and polished, and marked with many black veins from top to bottom, especially those which took their origin from several "navels" <note>umbilicus: a botanical term for the attachment point of a seed</note>, separated from each other by almost equal spaces, which brought great beauty to it.

*Is it the stone of a fruit from the Palm genus?*

---

### THE ACACALIS OF THE ANCIENTS; OR ACACALIS
#### Or the Kesmesen of some, with leaves of the Carob.

Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy.</note> writes that **Acacalis** is the fruit of a shrub growing in Egypt. To Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist.</note> it is a thorny shrub, to some a species of *Tamarix* or *Tamarisk*, to others the *Belleric Myrobalan*, to others the *Berry-bearing Heath*, to some the *Coris of Montpellier*, and to others the flower of the *Narcissus*. Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius, a German humanist and translator of Greek medical texts.</note> says he has found no one who has written about the Acacalis except Dioscorides and Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note>, who transcribed the words of Dioscorides. And in our age, they determine this little tree to be entirely unknown, along with the same Cornarius, Brunfels, Ryff, Mattioli and others. Belon <note>Pierre Belon, a French explorer and naturalist.</note> thought it was called *Kesmesen* by the Turks in Constantinople, and writes that it is brought there from Egypt; it is also of such great efficacy for eye diseases that there is a common proverb: *If your eyes ache, you have Kesmesen.*

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## THIRTEENTH CLASS.
### CONTAINING SHRUBS AND UNDER-SHRUBS,
### with rose-like flowers: and those related to them.

**Rockrose: German *Cisten roselin* : French *Rose canine* <note>Literally "Dog Rose," though here referring to the Rockrose family</note> : Italian *Cisto* : Spanish *Estepa*.**

Galen calls it *Cistus* or *Cisthanus*: Theophrastus calls it *Cissus* [Ivy], and Pliny, Gaza, Ruellius, and even Clusius followed him, though Clusius later noticed the corrupted reading in Theophrastus's text. According to Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist from the 1st century AD</note>, it is a shrub growing in rocky places, provided with many branches, leafy, and not tall. The leaves are round, bitter, and hairy: the flowers are like those of the Pomegranate, but in the Female variety, they are white.

Thus, he recognizes two main kinds of Rockrose, the *Male* and the *Female*: Theophrastus and Pliny hold just as many and the same types. But Dioscorides adds a third to them, which he says is called *Ledon* <note>The Gum Cistus</note>. We, following in the footsteps of Dioscorides, will also establish three main headings for the Rockrose, and we will describe the various species of each one individually.

**Male Rockrose III. With pale green leaves, Male Rockrose IV. of Montpellier with oblong whitish leaves.**

To the third Male Rockrose, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a vital 16th-century botanist</note> attributes smaller and shorter parts in all respects, and leaves of a paler green: he observed it growing wild in Portugal. Because he provides no illustration of it, we also do not depict it.

He depicts and describes the fourth Male Rockrose at length: and he reports that *Hypocistis* <note>A parasitic plant that grows on the roots of Rockroses</note> grows abundantly at its roots, which spread out and cling to the surface of the turf. This occurs specifically in early spring when the Rockrose prepares itself to bloom. It is quite common in Spain [especially Andalusia], Portugal, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. Our illustration elegantly shows the roots, the *Hypocistis*, and the remaining form of the plant.

<column-break/>

**Male Rockrose II. with longer leaves.**

Theophrastus attributes flowers to both the Male and Female Rockrose that are very close to Wild Roses: only smaller and without scent. He says the leaf of the Male is larger, harder, and more leathery, and the flowers tend toward purple, whereas in the Female they are white. Following his lead, and along with Clusius, we call that one the "Male" Rockrose which indeed rivals the Wild Rose in its flower, like the other kinds of Rockrose, but possesses a red color, sometimes deeper and sometimes paler. Clusius enumerates five species of it, differing among themselves in shape or color: of which he says the first (already mentioned as the Greater Male Rockrose with rounder leaves) and this one are frequent in Spain, but this one blooms longer than the others.

**Male Rockrose V. with curled and somewhat wavy leaves.**

Clusius observed this one only in Portugal, in very sandy soil: and he records that it is called *Rosella* <note>Little Rose</note> specifically by the Portuguese. Furthermore, the Rockroses bloom in the month of April: and sometimes even earlier, though occasionally later, according to the nature and temperament of the regions and places. The seed ripens in August, September, and October.

<summary>This page describes the classification and physical characteristics of various species of Rockrose (Cistus), drawing on classical authorities like Dioscorides and contemporary botanists like Clusius. It details the distinctions between "Male" and "Female" varieties and notes the presence of the parasitic Hypocistis plant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Cistus (Rockrose) family, specifically focusing on the "female" varieties and their medicinal parasites, following the previous descriptions of the "male" varieties.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### THE MONTPELLIER FEMALE ROCKROSE,
### with white flowers, and the Spanish with yellow.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with small, rounded leaves and several five-petaled flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

The Female Rockrose <note>original: *Cistus Foemina*</note> is also divided into various species: for it is either taller and shrubby with straight twigs, like the Male; or low-lying and spread upon the ground, like common Heather. Furthermore, both kinds vary in color, which is for the most part white, and sometimes yellow.

The Female Rockrose, however—both the Montpellier variety with white flowers and the Spanish with yellow flowers—has leaves of an almost circular roundness, softer and greener than in the Montpellier Male: the flowers are on long stalks, like Roses, but white: no smaller than those of the male, much larger than those of the *Ledum* <note>a resinous species of Rockrose</note>, scentless, but like the flowers of the *Ledum*, pleasant to the taste.

That which has a yellow flower is found only in Spain; the white, however, in France, and also Italy and Portugal; they bloom in April.

### ROCKROSE WITH SEA-PURSLANE LEAVES AND YELLOW FLOWERS.
### HYPOCISTIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with elongated, slightly wavy leaves and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> says this Rockrose is frequent in Portugal, in sandy soil or blown by the sea air, and was never seen by him anywhere else. In Lobel’s *Observations and Icons of Plants*, it is called the *Female Rockrose with leaves of Sea-Purslane*.

Because he writes that he saw *Hypocistis* <note>a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of Rockroses</note> at its roots, it seems something should be said of it here. At the roots of the Rockrose, says Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note>, there grows a certain thing similar to the flower of a Pomegranate, which is called *Hypocistis*, and by some *Robthrum*. There is a yellowish kind, a green kind, and a white kind: and the juice is pressed from it, just as from Acacia. Some, however, dry and crush it, then soak and cook it, and do the rest as is done with *Lycium* <note>a medicinal fruit extract</note>. *More on this in the margin of the following figure.*

### CLUSIUS’S LAVENDER-LEAVED ROCKROSE,
### perhaps the same as the upright Sun-rose.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with narrow, lanceolate leaves resembling lavender and small flowers.</image-desc>

This shrub, according to Clusius, is so similar to Lavender that unless the smell and taste prevented it, it could be taken for Lavender. He found it only in the Kingdom of Valencia, in dry and stony places, four miles from Valencia. However, Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, botanist and traveler</note> saw it in the mountains of Provence, blooming in May.

Furthermore, something must be added concerning the powers and properties of the Rockrose. It has, says Dioscorides, a binding <note>astringent</note> power, wherefore the flowers, crushed and drunk in harsh wine twice a day, are helpful for dysentery: applied by themselves, they restrain spreading sores. With a wax salve <note>cerate</note>, they heal burns and old ulcers. Pliny and Galen attribute the same properties to it; Galen further says this shrub is cold, yet partakes of some heat.

<column-break/>

### A CERTAIN SPANISH SPECIES OF ROCKROSE,
### with white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with broad, textured leaves and a single large flower at the top.</image-desc>

Several other kinds of Rockrose are observed, which are referred to the Female as the primary type, rather than to the Male or the *Ledon*: since they are not covered with any fatty or sticky liquid, nor do they have a rose-colored or purple flower. The one we give pictured here, we received at Lyon, brought from the Spanish lands. It has many small leaves, long and hairy. The flowers do not come out singly, but several together from the branches, as in the Montpellier *Ledum*, whitish: which are succeeded by pointed seed-pods, hairy with white down: and in them is a tiny, reddish seed.

### ROCKROSE WITH LONGER SEA-PURSLANE LEAVES,
### hoary and pointed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with pointed, grayish leaves and several flower buds.</image-desc>

This is taller than the preceding one and has firmer branches. It grows in the same places as that one; Clusius could not observe the flowers and seed, whose plant is labeled *The Second Rockrose with Sea-Purslane leaves* by Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, and the *History of Lyon*.

Furthermore, to proceed with the history of the *Hypocistis*: it grows on various kinds of Rockrose, as we shall note for each one. Nor are there lacking those who believe that the *Hypocistis* commonly used in the Apothecary shops grows on Goat's-beard <note>Tragopogon</note>: but this is a great error, the cause of which is rightly attributed to the Arabs, who called the Rockrose "Goat's-beard" <note>original: *Hirci barbula*</note>. Whether the juice boiled out of *Hypocistis*, such as is brought to us today, is the *Hypocistis* of the Ancients or not, we leave to the judgment of the learned.

### CLUSIUS’S MARJORAM-LEAVED ROCKROSE,
### which has a spot in the flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with small, rounded leaves and flowers showing a distinct dark spot at the base of the petals.</image-desc>

This is a shrubby plant producing many slender branches: on which grow small leaves, almost circular, hoary, similar to Marjoram <note>Sampsucus</note>, a little smaller and with a prominent back: they grow with stalks opposite one another, as in the other kinds of Rockrose. The flower is abundant at the tops of the branches, consisting of five white petals, the center of which is marked by a blackish-purple spot, with yellow hairs and stamens occupying the middle of the flower.

### CISTUS WITH THYME-LIKE LEAVES, DESCRIBED BY CLUSIUS.
<note>original: "CISTVS FOLIO THYMI CLVSII"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with small, narrow leaves resembling thyme, showing upright stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub to the height of a foot, with branches turning blackish-purple, hard and woody, and for the most part without leaves except at the tips where they grow in clusters. These leaves are very slender, green, mimicking Thyme, with an astringent taste. It bears a flower similar to the preceding variety, but smaller and marked with no spots. It has only been seen in the furthest part of Baetica <note>An ancient Roman province in southern Spain, roughly modern Andalusia</note>, where it faces Castile and Portugal.

### CISTUS LEDON WITH BLACK POPLAR LEAVES, THE LARGER VARIETY, DESCRIBED BY CLUSIUS.
<note>original: "CISTVS LEDON POPVLI NIGRAE FOLIIS Clusij, Maior"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger Cistus plant with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large flowers with dark spots at the base of the petals.</image-desc>

It rises only to two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> with branched shoots; the branches are brittle. The leaves are the largest of all the Cistus kinds observed by Clusius, green on the upper side and somewhat whitish underneath. They sometimes mimic the shape of Ivy leaves, but more often those of the Black Poplar, being quite coarse and fleshy. The seed heads are five-sided, pointed, and filled with small, blackish seeds. The young plants are neither oily nor fragrant, but only the year-old ones are, especially in Autumn, at which time all the oily Cistus plants are observed to be pregnant with more abundant juice.

### BROAD-LEAVED CRETAN CISTUS LEDON.
<note>original: "CISTVS LEDON LATIFOLIVS CRETICVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Cistus variety with prominent veining on the leaves and large, open flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has long, pointed leaves, whitish underneath and darker on top, with three veins running along their length as in Plantains. At the ends of the small branches are whitish flowers, hanging from stems an inch long; the calyxes <note>the green outer part of the flower</note> are hairy with short bristles. The seed heads or vessels are about the size of a Chickpea, oblong, hairy, and divided by membranes into five angles, containing tiny, poppy-like, dark, and angular seeds.

<column-break/>

### LEDON AND LADANUM: CISTUS LEDON, WITH FLOWERS MARKED BY A BLACKISH SPOT.
<note>original: "LEDON ET LADANVM: CISTVS LEDON, flore maculâ nigricante notato"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with lanceolate leaves and flowers featuring a distinct dark spot on each petal.</image-desc>

There is a certain kind of Cistus, says Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, which is called *Ledon* by some: a shrub growing in the same manner as the Cistus, but having longer and darker leaves, which in Spring collect a certain oiliness, etc.

From this plant is made that which is called *Ladanum* <note>A sticky resin used in perfumes and medicine</note>. For she-goats and he-goats, grazing upon its leaves, catch the oiliness on their beards, which also sticks to the flowers because it is viscous; having removed this, they refine it and store it formed into masses. Some also drag cords through the shrubs and scrape off the oiliness adhering to them to form it. More on this in the following section.

The shrub which we depict here from Clusius, he reports to grow in various places in Spain and Portugal.

### SMALLER SPANISH CISTUS LEDON WITH BLACK POPLAR LEAVES, DESCRIBED BY CLUSIUS.
<note>original: "CISTVS LEDON POPVLI NIGRAE foliis Minor, Hispanicus Clusij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of the Poplar-leaved Cistus, showing the root structure and smaller foliage.</image-desc>

Of this kind, says Clusius, another species is found, similar in almost every way but lower, not exceeding a cubit in height, whose leaves are also smaller; otherwise, it is not dissimilar in appearance, flower, seed, or taste.

Furthermore, to proceed with the history of Ladanum begun before: According to the dictates of Dioscorides, the best Ladanum is greenish, easily softening, oily, free of sand, and not crumbly, but resinous. Such is that which grows in Cyprus; for both the Arabian and Libyan kinds are of less value. It has an astringent, warming, softening, and opening use. It stops falling hair. It makes scars more decent. It cures earaches, etc.

### THE FOURTH CISTUS LEDON OF CLUSIUS, WITH WHITE FLOWERS.
<note>original: "CISTVS LEDON IV. CLVSII, flore candido"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the fourth Cistus variety described by Clusius, featuring white flowers and elongated leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius observed this kind only in Old Castile, in places neighboring the village of San Martín del Castañar, where it is called *Ardinicia* by the inhabitants. It is so common there that it is a local proverb: *He who goes to the mountain and can do no more, should at least gather Ardinicia*; that is, whoever goes to the mountain, rather than returning empty-handed, should at least collect *Ardinicia* (the lowliest plant). Among the Belgians, it has grown successfully.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Cistus (Rock Rose) found in Spain and Portugal, detailing their physical characteristics and the traditional harvesting of Ladanum resin. It cites the works of the botanist Clusius and the ancient authority Dioscorides for both botanical identification and medicinal uses.</summary>

# OF PLANTS

### GUM-BEARING CISTUS, OR THE LEDUM of Montpellier, with narrow, blackish leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with long, narrow leaves and a large flower at the top, showing the root system and branching structure.</image-desc>

This is a shrub reaching two cubits <note>about three feet</note> in height, fragrant, branching out into many arms, and covered in a black bark. The leaves are an inch and a half long, narrow, black, wrinkled, and grow opposite one another at short intervals. The flowers are white, resembling small wild roses, with yellow tips <note>stamens</note> in the center. These are followed by bristly seed pods, and seeds smaller than those found in the Male Cistus of Montpellier. At the roots of this plant grows the *Hypocistis* <note>original: "Hypocistis"; a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of Cistus</note>, or rather the *Hypoledon*: it clings to the root like a mushroom or Larch Fungus <term>Agaricus: a medicinal fungus used in early pharmacy</term>, and is not properly part of the substance of the shrub itself.

Nothing is more common than this kind of *Ledum* in most parts of Spain and Portugal, as well as in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. It blooms in April and May.

### CISTUS LEDON, WITH ASH-COLORED branches and leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus variety with more numerous, smaller leaves and a prominent flower, showing a woody stem.</image-desc>

This shrub is a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, branching out with many frequent limbs of an ash-gray color, and clothed in very dense, bristly, and entirely whitening leaves. Nevertheless, these leaves are oily, like the others. The flowers are abundant at the tips of the twigs, white, and similar to the preceding variety, just as the seed is also not unlike it. It also grows in the Kingdom of Valencia, and is called *Xaguarzo* <note>a local Spanish name for rockrose</note> by the inhabitants.

### CISTUS LEDON IX. ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Cistus plant with thinner branches and smaller leaves.</image-desc>

This is smaller than the one above, with leaves a little larger, but not white-haired underneath like the preceding one (which is Clusius’s eighth variety). Instead, the leaves are sparser and more sticky. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> observed that it supports thin, sapless, and withered twigs, with several empty seed heads that gape open once the seed has been shaken out. He reports that it grows in the furthest part of Baetica <note>Southern Spain/Andalusia</note> where it faces New Castile, and is also called *Xaguarzo* by the inhabitants.

<column-break/>

### CISTUS LEDON WITH SMALLER AND NARROWER leaves, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with very narrow leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

This is similar to the aforementioned Montpellier variety, but the leaves are smaller and narrower. The flowers, however, are larger and white, consisting of five petals. Like the previous variety, the leaves of this one are sprinkled with a sticky moisture. Clusius, who calls it *Cistus Ledon*, observed it in the Kingdom of Valencia and says it is named *Xaguarzo* by the locals.

### CISTUS LEDON, WITH THE LEAVES OF GARLAND Rosemary according to Clusius, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cistus plant with needle-like leaves resembling rosemary and a flower at the apex.</image-desc>

This one is also a cubit high, but the branches are very spread out. The leaves are thin, brownish-green on the upper side, but whitening on the underside, and smeared with a certain smooth and oily moisture. The flowers are numerous along the length of the branches, consisting of five petals, small and yellow. The seed is blackish-gray in small heads. Clusius says it is common in several places in Baetica, and is called *Romero* <note>Spanish for Rosemary</note> by the inhabitants.

### CISTUS LEDON WITH THYME LEAVES ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, shrubby Cistus with tiny leaves similar to thyme.</image-desc>

This reaches only a foot in height, with slender, woody branches that are nonetheless quite brittle, blackish, oily, and wet with a certain sticky moisture. The leaves are much smaller than in the ninth variety. Clusius, to whom this description belongs, did not observe the flowers. It grows in the same places and is called by the same names as the preceding ones.

It relies heavily on the observations of the botanist Carolus Clusius and notes local Spanish names like Xaguarzo.</summary>

### TUBERARIA: THE GREATER TUBERARIA of Myconus.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Tuberaria major, showing a plant with broad, ribbed basal leaves and a flowering stalk with five-petaled flowers and small buds.</image-desc>

This plant was called *Tuberaria* because Truffles <note>Latin: *Tubera*; the author notes a folk belief that these plants indicate where truffles grow</note> are very frequently found where it grows. It is thought to have been unknown to the ancients; Myconus suspects that if they did happen to know it, it was called the *Hydnoticum* <note>A "truffle-herb"</note> mentioned by Pamphilus in the writings of Athenaeus. Caspar Bauhin classifies it among the Female Rock Roses. The whole plant is somewhat hairy. The leaves are similar to the leaves of Plantain, some lying on the ground, others clasping the stem. At the top of the stems are yellow flowers; the seed is enclosed in a small pod. The root is woody, spread through the upper layer of the turf. It grows in dry places.

### OUR LOCAL TUBERARIA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Tuberaria nostras, showing a similar habit to the previous plant but with more elongated leaves and a branching flower stalk.</image-desc>

This was sent to us under this name from Pisa, collected on the nearby mountain called St. John’s. We suspect it is the same as the Greater Tuberaria of Myconus. However, we have observed this peculiarity: the very top of the stem is divided into two rather long stalks, one of which splits into three other shorter ones. On each of these sits a cone-shaped head, composed of many layers of leaves, the base of which is supported by tiny leaflets. Sometimes there are many flowers.

### CLUSIUS’S SECOND ANNUAL ROCK ROSE, with a pale flower marked with a crimson spot.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cistus annuus II, showing an upright plant with opposite, narrow leaves and flowers with dark spots at the base of the petals.</image-desc>

It is a foot in height, with slender, straight, delicate stems that are not very branched. The leaves are oblong, narrow, hairy, and greenish; during the heat of the Dog Days <note>The hottest part of summer, late July to August</note> they are covered in a sticky moisture. The flower is tiny, consisting of five petals, pale like the Sun-rose <note>Helianthemum</note>, and marked with a crimson spot. The seed heads are very delicate and three-sided, containing tiny, ash-colored seeds. It blooms in May and June and varies; sometimes the flower is not spotted, but most often it is spotted with either a reddish or crimson color.

<column-break/>

### THE LESSER TUBERARIA of Myconus.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Tuberaria minor, showing a smaller plant with a dense rosette of hairy leaves and a single flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant, like the Greater one already mentioned, is related in form and medicinal power to Mouse-ear Hawkweed. It mimics the Greater one in every way, but everything is smaller. It is found here and there in meadows, in rich and earthy places. Myconus sent both varieties from Spain, where they are called <term>yerua Turmiera</term> <note>Spanish: *hierba turmera*, meaning "truffle herb"</note>, that is, the Tuberaria Herb.

### CLUSIUS’S FIRST ANNUAL ROCK ROSE, with a rounder leaf.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cistus annuus I, showing a plant with rounded leaves and small flowers arranged along the upper stem.</image-desc>

It has somewhat long, hairy, straight, and sparse twigs. The leaves are green and somewhat round, with an astringent taste. The flower is pale or whitish; the seed is small and reddish, contained in three-cornered heads. Clusius observed it in the Kingdom of Granada and near Salamanca at the edges of vineyards.

### ANNUAL ROCK ROSE WITH GUM-CISTUS LEAVES, and a yellow flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cistus annuus folio ledi, showing a plant with narrow, lanceolate leaves and flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

It grows as a small shrub around Montpellier among the Yellow Rattle herbs. In the illustration by Lobelius which we have placed here, the stems are thicker than they ought to be in proportion. The stem of the plant is a foot or a foot and a half high; the leaves are hairy, similar to the leaves of the narrow-leaved Gum-Cistus. The flower is yellow, and the seed is angular and red.

# OF PLANTS

### THE SMALLEST ROCK ROSE WITH ROUNDISH LEAVES.
<note>original: "Cistus minimus folio subrotundo"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small Cistus plant with a single stem, small rounded leaves in pairs, and a cluster of seed pods at the top. The roots are shown at the bottom.</image-desc>

It is about half a span high <note>approx. 4 inches</note>: with a thin and woody root, which is longer than the rest of the plant: the leaves are small, somewhat round and broad, appearing in opposite pairs, ash-colored, on a single, smooth little stalk: the top of which is occupied by the seed capsules of the Sun-rose <note>Helianthemum</note>, which are covered in a white, downy fuzz. We observed this in a clay pot at Heidelberg at the house of Sprenger.

### SUN-ROSE: FLOWER OF THE SUN: German: Sonnenblum: French: Herbe d'or: Italian: Fior di Sole.
### COMMON YELLOW-FLOWERED SUN-ROSE.
<note>original: "Helianthemum vulgare flore luteo"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Helianthemum plant with multiple stems, narrow leaves, and several five-petaled flowers and buds. Detailed root system at the base.</image-desc>

The Sun-rose also belongs to the family of the Rock Roses <note>Cistus</note>, of which various species are recorded, which we shall discuss shortly. The one we depict here rests upon a woody, white, and flexible root: sending out small woody branches that are reddish and hairy; upon which are opposite leaves, like Hyssop but much broader, an inch long, ending in a moderate point, and hairy: the flowers are arranged in a long cluster <term>thyrse<note>a type of branched flower cluster</note></term>, and are yellow with their inner tips <note>stamens</note>, consisting of five petals, arranged like a Rock Rose, surrounded by hairy, three-parted husks, which are followed by the seed vessels, appearing in pairs, somewhat long and three-cleft, containing the seed. It grows abundantly in various places, such as Lyon, Montpellier, Geneva, Zurich, Basel, etc., and it blooms in May.

### ENTIRELY WHITE SUN-ROSE, with flowers sometimes white, sometimes pale.
<note>original: "Helianthemum omnino candicans"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a low-growing Helianthemum with spreading branches, small leaves, and flowers. The roots are thick and woody.</image-desc>

This is a tiny plant, provided with thin, woody twigs that spread across the ground: the leaves are similar to other Sun-roses but smaller, entirely white-ish, and astringent to the taste: the flowers sit at the ends of the branches, consisting of five petals, sometimes white in color, but most often pale. The root is woody and fibrous; the seed vessels and seed are as in the common variety. We saw it growing wild at Montpellier on the mountain near Castelnau, as well as on the banks of the Rhone between Lyon and Montluel. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, for whom this is the "First Low Rock Rose," says it is frequent in the fields of Salamanca.

<column-break/>

### ANNUAL SPECIES OF NARROW-LEAVED ROCK ROSE.
<note>original: "Cisti species annua angustifolia"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of an upright annual Cistus with long, narrow leaves and small flower buds along the upper stem.</image-desc>

It is three-quarters of a foot tall, or even larger, reaching a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>: the root is single, lightly fibrous and quite thin, growing straight: the stem is single, smooth, hairy, and slender, divided by four or five joints: at each of which are two leaves, longer than two inches, narrow, hairy, resembling the Gum Cistus of Montpellier: at the top of the stem are many small, three-cornered heads, leaning from stalks nearly an inch long toward one side, like a mane. We have not observed the flower.

### SUN-ROSE WITH LARGER LEAVES and white flowers.
<note>original: "Helianthemum foliis maioribus, flore albo"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Helianthemum with larger, broader leaves and several open flowers.</image-desc>

We saw this at Speyer and Strasbourg in basement gardens, blooming in October. It is called "Sun-rose with white flowers" by most herbalists, such as Camerarius in his garden catalog. It is the "White-flowered Sun-rose of Pliny," and the "Flower of the Sun of Mattioli." Tabernaemontanus, who calls it the "German White Sun-rose," says it differs from the yellow variety only in color.

The preceding plate shows the common yellow-flowered Sun-rose.

### WHITE-FLOWERED SUN-ROSE, with narrow hairy leaves.
<note>original: "Helianthemum flore albo, folio angusto hirsuto"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Helianthemum with narrow, hairy leaves and flowers, showing a spreading growth habit.</image-desc>

This little plant is gifted with branches a span and a half or three-quarters of a foot long, some of them upright and some spreading; the leaves are moderately large, half an inch long, narrow, hairy, and hoary like Lavender, tasteless and sticky. The rest can be gathered from the illustration and the title. To Clusius (in his Spanish flora) it is the "15th Low Rock Rose." To Lobelius it is the "Narrow-leaved Low Rock Rose." To Tabernaemontanus, the "Foreign Narrow-leaved Sun-rose." It grows frequently at Montpellier.

### SLENDER-LEAVED SUN-ROSE, smooth with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Helianthemum plant with thin, winding stems, small leaves, and a single open flower with five petals shown separately at the bottom left.</image-desc>

Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a famous French physician and botanist.</note>, in the *History of Lyon*, and Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish botanist.</note> called this the *Golden-flowered* Heather: Robert Constantinus <note>A 16th-century lexicographer and physician.</note> identified it as *Chrysocome* <note>original: "Chrysocomen"; likely referring to Goldilocks or a similar yellow-tufted plant.</note>.

Dalechamps observed that it grows in sandy, sunny, and wind-swept places on high hills, and blooms in July. It is abundant at Montpellier near the gallows of the New Castle, and in the sandy maritime areas of Venice.

### SUN-ROSE WITH HOARY THYME LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branched plant with small, oval leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

The twigs are numerous, thin, and hoary <note>covered in grayish-white fine hairs</note>, which soon divide into other spreading branchlets: the leaflets are like those of the harder Thyme, tiny, short, hairy, ash-colored, growing three, four, or sometimes more from a single stalk. The flower and the seed capsule—which gapes open into three chambers—possess hairy coverings, as in the common Sun-rose. The root is somewhat thick, twisted, woody, and many-forked. It is abundant in the mountains near Montpellier, and blooms in April and May.

### SUN-ROSE approaching the MONEYWORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping plant with rounded, opposite leaves resembling Numularia, with small flowers along the stem.</image-desc>

The branches of this plant are hairy with large bristles: the leaves are arranged in pairs, approaching the appearance of Moneywort <note>term: Numularia; a creeping plant with coin-shaped leaves.</note>, yet smaller, and with somewhat long stalks like those found in common Chickweed: at the "armpits" <note>axils</note> of the leaves, there are thin leaflets. We received this plant in a dried state, and it was not possible to observe more features in it.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE SUN-ROSE, with the leaf of Fuchs’s Lesser Mouse-ear.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine plant with a thick rootstock, basal leaves, and a flowering stalk with several blooms.</image-desc>

This is a shrubby herb with oblong leaves, similar to the Lesser Mouse-ear <note>term: Pilosella; named after Leonhart Fuchs, a founding father of botany.</note> of Fuchs, whiter on the lower part, green and hairy on the upper part, though less so than on the lower. The flower is yellow, like the common Sun-rose. We label it "Alpine" because we collected it in the dry places of the mountains around Geneva.

### SUN-ROSE WITH MARJORAM LEAVES, and very hairy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems, opposite leaves, and very hairy flower heads at the apex.</image-desc>

From a somewhat thick and long woody root, it sends out stems about nine inches high <note>original: "Dodrantales"</note>, and sometimes very crowded, which are stiff and extremely hairy. Along these, as if at nodes, grow opposite leaves, equal to the leaves of Marjoram <note>original: "Sampsuchi" or "Majoranae"</note>: some are oblong and somewhat broad, others narrower. The flowers at the ends of the branchlets are many, resting on extremely hairy stalks about half an inch long, yellow, and fortified by a streaked, shaggy calyx <note>the outer protective part of the flower</note>. It also finds its native home at Montpellier.

### RARE SPECIES OF SUN-ROSE, with a curved tuft, as in the Heliotrope.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a curved, scorpioid inflorescence similar to a heliotrope, with small leaves and a woody base.</image-desc>

Some have called this the *Telephium* of Dioscorides and the *Helenium* of Crateuas; let the learned judge how well they decide. It is found in many places in Provence, but especially on the arid ridges near Aix-en-Provence <note>original: "Aquis Sextijs"</note>. We have seen it in gardens at Paris and Basel, and we ourselves have cultivated it at Montbéliard, where it flowers in June and July.

<summary>This page describes six varieties of Sun-roses (Helianthemum), detailing their physical characteristics, hairy textures, and specific geographic locations across France and Switzerland.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Sun-rose, Helianthemum, Montpellier, Geneva, Provence, medicinal herbs, plant morphology, 16th-century botany</keywords>
