# OF PLANTS

### GROUND-ROSE WITH THYME-LIKE LEAVES, BLACK-
### ish and hairy: with a fragrant golden flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with small, rounded leaves and five-petaled flowers, showing a detailed root system.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> writes that this is found in the highest Alps of Austria and Styria, and that he has observed it growing wild nowhere else; however, in his own garden, it bloomed in May.

Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, Caspar Bauhin, and others also record this as the low or creeping Rock-rose, with Thyme-like leaves and yellow flowers.

### GROUND-ROSE WITH LEAVES OF TARENTINE MYRTLE,
### hoary or ash-colored.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody shrub with pointed, opposite leaves and clusters of flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

Clusius says it is found in greatest abundance in all those mountains which run in a continuous chain from Kahlenberg, overlooking the Danube, to the Austrian Alps; also on Mount Haimburg in Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and Slovenia</note>, and in other places of the same province, especially the higher elevations. To Clusius, this is the *Second Ground-rose*.

### TINY ROCK-ROSE, WITH WHITE LEAVES;
### and a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with narrow leaves and a single large flower at the apex.</image-desc>

This differs very little from the preceding plant and the Alpine Sun-rose <note>Helianthemum</note> mentioned before; perhaps Nature, merely due to the variety of its native soil, seems to play with these forms. Students of botany should examine them.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED GROUND-ROSE
### with a yellow flower, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, narrow leaves and several flowers, showing a thick, branched root.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus and Gerard record this as the low, narrow-leaved Rock-rose. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era</note>, this is the *Fifth Ground-rose*, or the narrow-leaved variety.

It is quite rare, so much so that Clusius found it in only two places: namely, on the mountain overlooking the Austrian baths at Baden, and on another in Hungary near the city of Bratislava <note>original: "Posonio"</note>. It blooms in June.

### SUN-ROSE ROCK-ROSE, WITH THE LEAF
### of Mountain Poley.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with clusters of small flowers and a prominent taproot.</image-desc>

This has whitish stems, four or five inches long <note>original: "unctatum," likely a typo for "uncialum" or "unciale"</note>, and branched: these end in thin stalks bearing small yellow flowers, three or four in number. The leaves are the whitish color of the common Mountain Poley <note>Teucrium polium</note>. We found it in rocky places near Agde in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

### DWARF ROCK-ROSE OF MOUNT BALDO;
### perhaps the Austrian Myrtle-leaved variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, dense shrub with thick leaves and large, open flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius says this shrub is extremely rare, as he has only observed it growing on the cliffs of Schneeberg <note>original: "Schnealben"</note>. It was blooming in June, and by August it was heavy with seed. By Tabernaemontanus and Gerard it is called the *Low Austrian Rock-rose*. To Caspar Bauhin, it is the *Tenth Ground-rose, or the hairy variety*.

<summary>This page describes several species of Ground-rose (Chamaecistus) and Rock-rose (Cistus), detailing their physical characteristics and specific alpine and European locations where they were discovered by botanists like Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>Rock-rose, Ground-rose, botany, Alps, Austria, Hungary, Clusius, Bauhin, medicinal plants, herbals</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### EXOTIC ROCK-ROSE WITH LEAVES LIKE A TREE, with woolly heads like a Plane Tree.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody plant with oval, rugose leaves and spherical, woolly flower heads or seed pods at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

The twigs of this plant are woody, similar in color and family to the Rock-rose <note>original: "Cisto"</note>: the leaves are likewise wrinkled, oblong, resembling Sage or Mint: But at the tips of the small branches, they display shaggy, perfectly spherical tufts, or rather, the woolly heads of a Plane tree.

By Lobelius in his *Adversaria* and *Icons* it is called the *Exotic tree with Rock-rose leaves*; by Tabernaemontanus, the *Exotic tree with Rock-rose leaves*; by Gerard, the *Exotic Rock-rose*; and in the *History of Lyon* by Lobelius, it is called *The foreign tree of Rock-rose or Ladanum by Penny.*

<column-break/>

### PENNY’S MYRTLE-ROCK-ROSE, WITH yellow, oblong FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrub with small, pointed leaves arranged in pairs and elongated, bell-shaped flowers at the ends of the stems.</image-desc>

This is a shrub sometimes reaching three cubits <note>about 4.5 feet</note> in height, with rough bark: the leaves are almost like Myrtle, smooth on the upper side but rough on the back, growing in pairs around the twigs as in other kinds of Rock-rose: the flowers sit at the ends of the branches, consisting of five yellow oblong petals, and provided with many rather long stamens inside: these are followed by a somewhat oblong and five-sided head, full of seed. The whole plant is fragrant, and it appears to pour forth a Gum or Resin, just like the varieties of Ladanum <note>original: "Ledi"</note>.

---

### ALPINE OLEANDER TO SOME, TO OTHERS LADANUM: German: Mountain-rose, Alpine-rose.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering alpine shrub (Rhododendron) with thick, lanceolate leaves and clusters of bell-shaped flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

This is considered to be of two types: the smooth and the hairy. Both their appearance and their places of birth join them together: the chief difference lies in the hairiness or smoothness. The smooth one, which we depict here, is a shrub a cubit high, with twisted and woody branches the thickness of a finger, covered in bark—the outer being ash-colored, the inner blackish: through these, the leaves are crowded around the top, smooth, clinging to short stalks, very much approaching the leaves of the Laurel. And among those, at the ends of the twigs, are many flowers, scarlet—though paler than the following kind—oblong, divided into five parts at the top, and sprinkled with tiny silver dots, in which small stamens surround a central pistil with a head: The root is oblong, woody, hard, and covered with a blackish bark.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ALPINE OLEANDER, THE HAIRY KIND.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a similar alpine shrub, characterized by smaller, more rounded leaves and hairy stems/pedicels.</image-desc>

This does not differ much from the preceding one. Only the leaves are shorter, more blunt, and hairy, and the stalks of the flowers are hairy, whereas in the former they are remarkably smooth. It has been observed that on the tips of the shoots of both kinds, certain oblong heads grow, composed of leafy scales: and also that on the branches and leaves, Tubers <note>galls</note> are sometimes found, the size of a hazelnut or a pea, reddish, spongy, astringent, and which are able to serve in place of Oak Galls.

Both are found in rocky and rugged mountains: they flower in June and July, and the seed ripens at the end of August. Indeed, the Alpine Ladanum that is less hairy, denoted by the letter A in the first table, grows in the mountains of Geneva, Saleve, and Thuiri.

---

### WILD ROSEMARY OF SOME: Rock-rose Ladanum with Rosemary leaves, to others.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with narrow, rosemary-like leaves and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

This is not the Heather <note>original: "Erica"</note> of Dioscorides, as some have wished. Those who believe it to be *Ground-pine* <note>original: "Chamæpytin"</note> are also in error; in Cordus’s commentary on Dioscorides it is called *Ground-pine-fir* <note>original: "Chamæpeuce"</note>, and by Camerarius *Cordus’s Ground-pine-fir*, as well as *Wild Rosemary*. However, it seems rightly to Clusius that it can be numbered among the kinds of Ladanum, whence some call it *Rock-rose Ladanum with Rosemary leaves*. To Schwenckfeld it is *Sucker-bearing Balm*.

It is found in many damp and deserted mountain places: it flowers toward the end of June: and in August it matures its fruit: It warms, thins [humors], opens, strengthens, aids digestion, resolves, cuts through [phlegm], and digests. Indeed, it is effective for almost all the same things as *Garden Rosemary*.

<column-break/>

### SCENTLESS WILD ROSEMARY according to Clusius: The False Rock-rose of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small shrub with very narrow, needle-like leaves and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

It is a shrub a foot in height, provided with thin, reddish twigs: the leaves clothe the branches in a confused order, narrow, oblong, green above, turning white below, with a very drying taste and no pleasant scent: on the highest branches also sit small heads, compacted from many short scales, in the manner of a winter-bud <note>original: "Cachryos"</note>: from which unfold thin little flowers, clinging to long stalks, consisting of five petals, of a grey color: and when these are cast off, five-sided heads are seen, short and with a blunt point, full of small and pale seed. Thus Clusius describes it: to Tabernaemontanus and Gerard it is the *False Rock-rose*. To the same Tabernaemontanus and Caspar Bauhin it is the *Narrow-leaved Alpine Dwarf-rhododendron*.

<summary>This page describes various species of Cistus (Rock-rose), Rhododendron (referred to as Alpine Oleander), and Wild Rosemary, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal properties, and the differing names assigned to them by Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Rock-rose, Rhododendron, Wild Rosemary, botanical classification, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Lobelius, Gerard, alpine flora, 17th-century botany</keywords>

# LESSER WILD ROSEMARY OF CAMERARIUS.
### Lesser Silesian Ledum of Schwenckfeld.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a small, woody shrub with narrow, needle-like leaves and a prominent root system. To the right, a second woodcut shows a similar but more upright flowering plant with clusters of small blossoms at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

<columns>2</columns>

This is perhaps the same as the previously mentioned scentless Wild Rosemary of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>: so we believe; for this plant is so similar to the one cultivated and depicted by Clusius in all respects, though everything is somewhat smaller and thinner. Or, if they are distinct plants, one might rightly call this a smaller species of Wild Rosemary. They also enjoy the same birthplaces, namely the swampy soil of shady forests. Both this and that variety have been observed in Silesia and Prussia, and they flower in May and June; however, their uses have been neglected.

<column-break/>

### WILD ROSEMARY OF RONDELET.

This is a woody shrub two spans high: with a reddish and robust root. It has stiff shoots with the texture of Rosemary; the leaves are equal to the leaves of the Arabian Hyssop, hairy, rough, and hard. Frequently, several leaves emerge from the same point, one of which is much longer than the rest, with a single nerve running along the length of each. It has almost no smell or taste. The flowers cling to the ends of the small branches and are purple; the seed is like that of Viper's Bugloss <note>original: "Echij vel Buglossi"</note>, quite large and ash-colored.

In the *History of Lyon* and by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called the *Bastard Goat-Oregano of Dalechamps*. To the same C. Bauhin, it is also the *Woodier Alkanet* <note>original: "Anchusa lignosior"</note> of Pena. It flowers, however, in the months of March, April, and May at Montpellier on Mount Callepens.

<column-break/>

# FRANKINCENSE-PLANT: OR CORONARY ROSEMARY: German & Belgian *Rosmarin*: French *Rosmarin*. Italian *Rosmarino, Rosmarino coronario*: Spanish *Romero*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Rosemary plant (Rosmarinus officinalis) showing its characteristic woody stem, dense needle-like foliage, and small flowers. The root system is detailed at the base.</image-desc>

The name *Libanotis* <note>from the Greek 'libanos' for frankincense, due to its scent</note>, or Rosemary, was given by Dioscorides to two very different plants. The first is called by him "fruitful and fertile," the leaves of which are similar to fennel leaves: it has a stalk a cubit high, topped with umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note>: and this is the *Ferulaceous Rosemary*, which we shall treat among the umbelliferous plants in Class 27 of this *Sciagraphia* <note>A "sketch" or descriptive outline of the botanical system</note>. The second is another Rosemary, specifically called *Coronary* <note>meaning "used for garlands or crowns"</note>, which differs greatly from the Ferulaceous type.

And this one is again twofold: one is *Ignoble*, which is called *Wild* and *Greater*: and of which we have already proposed various species. The other is truly *Nobler*, which has narrower leaves, and is called *Lesser* and *Fine-leaved Rosemary*.

It is a shrub two cubits or higher: having thin, long stems endowed with an ash color. The leaves arise several together at intervals; they are narrow, crowded, somewhat hard, whitish underneath and green on the upper part. It is crowned here and there with many flowers of a whitish-blue, in the likeness of Sage flowers.

This shrub is of a most pleasant odor, smelling of Frankincense: whence the name *Libanotis* was bestowed upon it; and because it is sought after for little crowns <note>corollas/garlands</note>, it obtained the name *Coronary*. It is called *Dendrolibanus* <note>Tree-frankincense</note> by some and *Campanema*, by others simply *Thymiama* <note>Incense</note>, and by the Italians *Mountain Crown*. To Anguillara it is the *Cneorum of Theophrastus*, and to Hyginus and Virgil it is *Black Cassia*. But most received and by common consent, it is called *Rosmarinus* or simply *Rosemary, Lesser or Fine-leaved Rosemary, Coronary Rosemary, Garden Rosemary with the narrower leaf, and Coronary Frankincense-plant*.

This Rosemary is indeed a foster-child of gardens: but nevertheless, so great is its abundance growing spontaneously in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, that the inhabitants burn no other wood without thought, and use it in Montpellier and neighboring places as fuel for the fire. It flowers in March, April, Autumn, and almost the whole year.

Furthermore, Coronary Rosemary is hot and dry in the second degree, and at the same time partakes of an astringent faculty. It clears the brain, sharpens the senses, and strengthens the nervous parts; it is beneficial for all evils of the head and brain arising from a cold and moist cause. It stops long-standing fluxes of the womb and suppresses flows of blood. Used as a fumigant <note>burning and inhaling the smoke</note>, it restrains catarrhs and coughs; in a decoction, it heals the "royal disease" <note>Jaundice</note>, and it is handed down that by its scent alone it renders a house safe in times of pestilence. Pliny asserts it is given in wine or vinegar against serpents. The oil is more effective for most of these things; it restores limbs suffering from atrophy, and if the neck and temples are anointed with it, it wards off Apoplexy. Rosemary is not only desired for garlands, says Matthiolus, but also for kitchens and the shops of apothecaries, for it wins favor for any meats and drinks, and has a salutary power for many diseases, etc. Practitioners know the method of using it, and We teach it in our *Great History*.

-> END OF CLASS XIII. <-

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XIV.
### WHICH IS OF ROSES, AND CERTAIN RELATED
### thorny Plants.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical floral scrolls, leaves, and blossoms.</image-desc>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a rose bush with multiple full, rounded blooms and thorny stems.</image-desc>

**THE RED ROSE, WITH VERY FULL,**
**semi-double, and single flowers.**
<note>original: "Rosa rubra, flore valde pleno, semipleno & simplici."</note>

The shrub of this variety is smaller than that of the White or the Pale-Red rose. The twigs are not as thick, and the thorns are also fewer and less sharp; indeed, some branches are even without thorns. The leaves grow from a somewhat long stalk, which has ear-like appendages <note>stipules</note> at the base; they grow in groups of three or five, smooth on both sides, greener on the upper surface, and somewhat round. The flowers, or Roses, are large and of an intense red color; some are very full <note>double-petaled</note>, while others have few petals. However, all are fragrant, and most especially so when dried. The flowers are followed by the Fruits, or somewhat long Heads <note>rose hips</note>, which are red when mature. The root is woody and hard. It is cultivated in various places in gardens, but the variety that is intensely red, very full, and most fragrant grows most praiseworthily in the city of *Provins* in Provence <note>France</note>, and from there it is dispersed far and wide.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a rose with a single large bloom and serrated leaves, labeled with the letter D.</image-desc>

**THE ACANTHOS ROSE, OR THE ROSE WITHOUT THORNS;**
**with a full flower, pale-red and white.**
<note>original: "Rosa acanthos, sive sine spinis."</note>

This rose has the form and appearance of the preceding figure, and differs from it almost only in that it lacks thorns and has supple, greener branches. The leaves are rarely in threes, but commonly in fives or sixes; they are somewhat dark green on top and ash-colored underneath. Its Rose is beautiful with a great crowding of petals, of a sweet scent, and sometimes white in color, but most often pale-red variegated with purple lines.

By Clusius, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and others, it is called the *Uncommon rose without thorns, or lacking thorns, with a larger full flower.* It bloomed for us in June in the garden at Montbéliard.

---

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a rose branch with a large, dense flower head and smaller buds.</image-desc>

**THE DAMASK ROSE, ALSO CALLED THE PERSIAN**
**or Alexandrian rose: with a full, flesh-colored flower.**
<note>original: "Rosa damascena... flore pleno incarnato."</note>

The branches of this variety abound with hooked and sharp thorns. The leaves grow in threes, fives, or sevens; they are not bright green as in the red rose, nor polished as in the white. Many flowers grow together from long, bristly stalks; the cup <note>calyx</note> is also bristly. They are large, full, fragrant, and pale-red or flesh-colored.

As Monardes notes, the use of these Roses is now frequent among the French, Italians, Germans, and various nations. They call them *Damask* because they are believed to have been brought from Damascus, a city of Syria. They are given the next highest praise after the Punic <note>Carthaginian</note> roses. From them are made Syrup, Honey of Roses, etc. Is this perhaps the "Campanian" rose of Pliny? Or his "Trachinian" rose, which is less red?

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a rose with distinctively crinkled or "crisped" leaves and a full flower.</image-desc>

**THE ROSE WITH ROUNDISH, CRINKLED LEAVES, AND**
**a multiple flower, pale-red or flesh-colored.**
<note>original: "Rosa folio crispo subrotundo."</note>

This differs from the preceding one only in its leaf.

Furthermore, there are eight *Parts of the Rose*. First, the *Stalk* <note>pediculus</note> which supports the flowers and ends in a solid *Head*, filled with a certain downy wool, placed beneath the leaves and flowers and supporting the whole Rose; this they call the *Calyx* <note>cup</note>. This is surrounded by the *Casing* <note>cortex</note>, which, when the Rose is open, is divided into five little wings or segments. The third part is that saffron-colored center of the flower which sits upon the filaments, called the *Anther* <note>anthera</note>, as if it were the "flower of the rose." The fourth is the thin *Filament* <note>capillamentum</note> itself, the prop and support of that saffron-colored thread. The fifth is the *Petal* <note>folium</note>, the lowest part of which is white and called the *Claw* <note>unguis</note>, which constitutes the sixth part. The seventh is the *Wool* <note>lana</note> contained in the head. The eighth is the *Seed*. And these parts are common to almost all Roses.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of roses, including the Red Rose of Provins, the Thornless Rose, and the Damask Rose, concluding with a detailed anatomical breakdown of the flower's parts.</summary>
<keywords>Red Rose, Thornless Rose, Damask Rose, botanical anatomy, calyx, anther, Provins, Damascus, Montbéliard, medicinal roses</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of rose varieties, following the previous descriptions of larger garden roses. The author continues to cite classical authorities like Pliny and Theophrastus alongside contemporary botanists like Clusius.</meta>

# PLANTS

### THE RED DOUBLE HUNDRED-LEAVED ROSE, called the Dutch Rose, with a thorny shrub.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rosa Centifolia with a large, dense, multi-petaled bloom and thorny stems with serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Theophrastus, Pliny, and Athenaeus <note>Ancient Greek and Roman naturalists</note> mention the hundred-leaved rose <note>original: "Centifoliæ rosæ"</note>: but since they say it is scentless and small, we remain in doubt, along with Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, whether they mean this variety of ours. It is kept today in various places in more cultivated gardens, just as we also nourished various plants in our own garden at Yverdon <note>original: "Ebroduni"</note>. The same Clusius writes that a medium-sized, or middle-magnitude, *White* variety is found among the Dutch: we have not seen it. Could it be the Praenestine rose of Pliny?

<column-break/>

### THE APPLE-BEARING ROSE, WITH HAIRY LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch featuring a single flower and a prominent round, bristly rose hip (fruit).</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are almost a palm's length, in groups of five, approaching the red double rose but longer and less round, saw-toothed, hairy underneath, and quite ash-colored. The heads, or thorny fruits <note>the rose hips</note>, have the size of a round hazelnut, and short thorny stalks support them: there are fewer thorns along the branches. We obtained this from Mount Calcar. Could it be Thalius’s *Cynorrhodos* <note>Dog-rose</note>, or the Virginian dog-rose, with prickly fruit and leaves, which produces "sponges" <note>likely referring to rose galls or mossy growths</note>?

---

### THE SMALLER ROSE, with a red double flower, armed with rough thorns.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose plant with multiple small, dense flowers and stems heavily covered in fine thorns.</image-desc>

This is a shrub armed with rough, hard thorns, growing quite high with many reddish branches. The roses on this are small, on short stalks, full-petaled, and very fragrant: the root creeps widely.

Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, and others label this the Cinnamon Rose. By Camerarius it is called the second Cinnamon Rose, commonly the *Venetian*, by others the Provincial, the *Spermonia* of Pliny, and the *Syrian* by some. To Tabernaemontanus, it is the *Smaller Provincial Rose*: to others a type of *Damask Rose*, the *Flesh-colored Damask Rose*. It blooms in early spring. Could it be the *Gracula* of Pliny, as the *History of Lyon* <note>a famous botanical text</note> suggests? Or the rose from Panga mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny?

<column-break/>

### THE CINNAMON ROSE, WITH REDDISH FLOWERS, thorny.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose with simple, five-petaled flowers and thorny stems.</image-desc>

The leaves of this one are smaller than those of the White, Red, and Reddish roses: the branches are thin, thorny, and reddish: the flowers are small, reddish, fragrant, and simple <note>single-layered petals</note>.

The *Adversaria* <note>a botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> writes that it grows frequently and spontaneously in the countryside of France, Belgium, and England. Some label it the "Cinnamon Rose" <note>original: "Canellam Rosam"</note>, to others it is the *Simple Cinnamon Rose*. Gesner considers it Pliny’s *Lychnis*, and records that a *Greater* and *Lesser* kind grow on Mount Albio, making the former the *Female* and the latter the *Male*.

---

### THE ROSE WITH A SMALL RED FLOWER, SIMPLE, not thorny.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose plant with simple flowers and smooth stems lacking thorns.</image-desc>

Gentler than the others, this one bristles with no thorns, except for the stalk of the flower which is somewhat rough: the pairings of smooth leaves (besides the odd one at the end) are three or four, saw-toothed, green above, whitish below, and smooth. The roses are small, five-petaled, fragrant, and reddish in color. The fruit is round, a little smaller than a small Medlar, turning red when ripe, and containing seeds wrapped in down.

To Tragus it is the *Field Rose*: to Tabernaemontanus and Gerard the *Smaller Provincial*: to many the *May Rose*, the *Meyan rose* of the *History of Lyon*. The *Greek Rose* of Pliny, called *Lychnis* by the Greeks. We found it growing wild on Mount Thoiry in the Geneva region and elsewhere: and we have observed it being cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

### AN ELEGANT KIND OF TINY ROSE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, delicate rose plant with a single open flower and several buds.</image-desc>

The person who brought this to us had collected it in the "Garden of God" <note>likely a specific mountain or meadow known for its flora</note>. Its leaves are an inch long, five-parted, and smooth: the flower is large in proportion to the plant, five-petaled, and white. It should be considered, however, whether this is merely some variation of a preceding kind: for it seems to us that species should not be multiplied beyond necessity; we only strive to demonstrate the Works of God in botany according to our capacity.

The author emphasizes the diversity of the genus while cautioning against over-classifying species.</summary>
<keywords>Rosa Centifolia, Rosa Pomifera, Cinnamon Rose, May Rose, botanical classification, Clusius, Pliny, Yverdon, medicinal plants, rose hips</keywords>

### WHITE ROSE, DOUBLE AND SEMI-DOUBLE.
### Cultivated white rose, with double and simple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall rose branch with multiple leaves and a large, multi-petaled (double) rose bloom at the top.</image-desc>

The stalk rises up with long, woody, and porous branches, upon which are sharp, hooked, and widely spaced thorns. The bark is otherwise polished and smooth. The leaflets are arranged in fives or sevens, notched at the edges, hairless, and somewhat long. At the ends of the branches, several cups <note>calyxes</note> hang from small stalks with non-threatening prickles; when these open, a rose of beautiful scent appears, of a white color, sometimes with many petals and sometimes with few, with yellow tips <note>anthers</note> in the middle. There follow round fruits <note>rose hips</note> which are red when ripe, containing hard seeds wrapped in a woolly down. It endures the cold better than the Red Rose, and the branches that bore flowers must be pruned every year. It blooms very late. It is more bitter than the Red Rose and has a greater power for purging <note>as a laxative</note>. Our illustration, taken from a purchased source, is not entirely satisfactory.

### GREATER MUSK ROSE: German: White Musk Rose; French: Musk Rose.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with several clusters of flowers and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This is a robust, upright, thorny shrub; the trunk is thicker than the others, with very long branches and fewer prickles. At the tops of the branches, from a small stalk armed with a few rare thorns, the roses grow, usually consisting of five or seven petals; they are large and white with some redness, which is most visible when they are dried. The scent is most sweet, because of which excellence it is called "Musk." They are playful <note>variable</note> and bloom at Montpellier in May and Autumn. Gesner writes that in Italy it sometimes blooms the whole year. We, however, have observed it blooming at Yverdon <note>Latin: Ebrodunum</note> in the garden of the aforementioned Mr. Chasseur from the month of August right into Winter.

### LESSER MUSK ROSE, WITH DOUBLE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller rose variety with dense, multi-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

It would be similar in all respects to the simple variety, were there not a difference in the flower: in this one, the outer petals are larger and the inner ones smaller. It seems to Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> that it has shed its wild nature through the art and "adulteration" <note>term: mangonio - refers to the skillful manipulation or "pimping" of plants by gardeners</note> of gardeners, and has become double in gardens.

It is commonly inscribed as the "Many-petaled" or "Many-leaved Musk Rose," and also the "Second Autumn Rose." There are those who think it is the Damascus Rose, and those who think it is Pliny’s Praenestine Rose, and others who think it is his *Coroneola* <note>a garland-rose</note>. In the *History of Lyon*, it is called the Damascus Rose, or the Second Autumn Rose, delighting with its dense mass of petals and extraordinary sweetness of scent.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW ROSE, SIMPLE AND DOUBLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a single, open flower showing prominent stamens.</image-desc>

This golden rose, which was unknown to the Ancients, differs from other kinds of roses in its leaves, flower, and scent. For its leaves are small, round, of a dark greenness, and deeply notched. The stems are very thorny; the flower is golden or yellow, otherwise similar to the others, and as in the white and red, it is either simple or double, with a heavy and unpleasant scent. When the flower has fallen, fruits follow that are so similar in color, shape, and size to Service-berries <note>Latin: Sorbis</note> that an unskilled or unpracticed person could hardly distinguish them. Writers call this the Indian and Alexandrian Rose, which is not unknown today in the more cultivated gardens of Europe; as at Yverdon, the leading citizens of that city, the Messrs. Chasseur, also have it with simple and double flowers.

### LESSER MUSK ROSE, WITH SIMPLE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with simple, five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

Some have thought this to be the *Coroneola* rose of Pliny; others call it the Alexandrian or Damascus Rose. By others it is called the Late Rose and the Autumn Rose. By the Arabs it is called *Nefrin, Nefrim, Nefrin*, and *Neserin*. By Gesner, the Fragrant Musk Rose; but by almost everyone else, the Lesser Musk Rose with a simple flower. It blooms at the same time as the preceding one.

Furthermore, Musk Roses are commonly preserved and eaten in Italy, and especially in Venice; and according to Lobel, they move the bowels pleasantly and quite powerfully, yet they also bring on fainting fits and piercing pains of the stomach and heart. But whether they can move the bowels pleasantly and yet excite such wicked symptoms, let the readers judge.

### WILD ROSE, DOG-ROSE.
### Reddish wild rose, a small shrub.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rose (Rosa sylvestris) with small leaves and simple flowers.</image-desc>

From the cultivated roses we turn the thread of our History to the wild ones, among which the Dog-rose <note>term: Cynorrhodon - from the Greek for "dog-rose"</note> leads the troop. Although this name is sometimes used for a certain kind of Lily, and also for a very thorny rose with a red flower, it is well known that by this term wild roses are understood generally. The shrub of the one we depict here is small, usually a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high. Otherwise, it is similar to the deep red rose, sometimes with thorns on the skin, but few. The leaves are divided into five parts as in that one, more rarely into seven leaflets, serrated, smooth, and dark green on the upper part; finally, it is of almost the same color and form, but the flowers are fewer and smaller. The flower is not small, reddish, with five petals, and a most pleasant scent; it is followed by a little head <note>the hip</note> with a prickly stalk.

<summary>This page describes various species of white, musk, yellow, and wild roses, detailing their physical characteristics, blooming seasons, and medicinal effects. It highlights the distinction between cultivated garden varieties and wild species like the Dog-rose.</summary>
<keywords>White Rose, Musk Rose, Yellow Rose, Dog-rose, Cynorrhodon, botany, medicinal plants, Yverdon, Pliny, Gesner, Lobel, laxatives</keywords>

--- Page 164 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of rose varieties, specifically focusing on wild and dwarf species and their medicinal properties as described by classical and medieval authorities.</meta>

### DWARF APPLE-BEARING WILD ROSE, without thorns, with a reddish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small rose bush with several round seed pods (hips) and a single open flower at the top.</image-desc>

Among the wild Roses, say the *Adversaria* <note>referring to the botanical work *Stirpium Adversaria Nova* by Pena and Lobel</note>, this one is of no small beauty, very familiar to England, and closely related to the sweetbriar. It grows as a dwarf shrub, no higher than two cubits <note>about three feet</note>, and is unscented. The leaf is smaller and very elegant. It is gifted with fruit not unlike the Aronia Medlar, though much smaller, greener in color, turning reddish or nearly scarlet, and ripening through August. The flower is that of a wild Rose.

### FIELD ROSE OF TABERNÆMONTANUS: German: *Feldt Rost*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with dense foliage and a large, multi-petaled flower.</image-desc>

He <note>Tabernæmontanus</note> says this is so common in all places that it requires no description; nor shall we say anything further of it here, as we intend to set forth the Temperament, powers, and uses of Roses alongside the next few tables of Roses.

The Rose, according to Mesuë <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note>, who wrote more distinctly about it than others, is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. It is composed of different separable substances: a moderate watery part, an astringent earthy part, a sweet and aromatic airy part, and finally a thin fiery part, from which comes its bitterness, its effects, and its form. However, the force of the fiery substance, which impressed the redness and appearance, was stronger than that which caused the bitterness; for this reason, the bitterness is lost by drying alone, while the others still remain. If those were to perish, the Rose would no more be a Rose than a dead man is a man.

### WILD ROSE, WITH SMOOTH LEAVES, and a purely white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with smooth leaves and a simple five-petaled white flower.</image-desc>

The variety just mentioned grows around ditches, trenches, and the margins of fields and meadows, especially in damp places. It flowers at various times: June, July, August, September, October, and November. This one, however, grows everywhere in woods and thickets, and flowers a little later than other wild roses: namely in June and July.

Furthermore, the yellow stamens of the Roses, or the tips and calyxes, powerfully dry and bind. Whence Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note> says: "The flower found in the middle of Roses, when dried and sprinkled on, helps with fluxes of the gums." Indeed, the heads <note>the hips or seed pods</note> taken in drink, according to the same author and Pliny, stop blood and the bowels. However, where Pliny says the Rose is heating, it indicates a corrupted passage in his text.

<column-break/>

### VERY THORNY DWARF ROSE, with Burnet-like smooth leaves and a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very thorny rose stalk with small, pinnate leaves resembling burnet (Pimpinella).</image-desc>

This dwarf Rose, a cubit and a half tall, does not allow itself to be touched with impunity in any part; it bristles everywhere with such a dense army of thorns, as much on the stalks as on the branches, of which it has many disordered ones. Along these are winged, smooth leaves in four pairs, scarcely equaling a quarter of the little finger, notched all around, and somewhat round. The small, simple flowers consist of a leafy texture, white, numerous, and beset in the middle with yellow filaments. From these, like little alabaster jars, a thick root creeps and sends out many shoots.

### WHITE WILD ROSE WITH REDNESS, with smooth leaves and a simple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with several flower buds and one large open flower showing prominent stamens.</image-desc>

Fresh Roses, Mesuë continues, are more bitter than astringent. Because of this bitterness, fresh Roses, especially in their juice, are purgative; but when dried, the heat that excites the bitterness having been released, they obtain a styptic <note>blood-stopping</note> and constipating substance. Indeed, the dry Rose is colder and more styptic: and more so that which was not fully matured, and the white more than the red. Furthermore, the Rose resolves <note>disperses inflammation</note>, extinguishes hot distempers, and strengthens parts of the body by pulling them together and tightening them; this is done most effectively by the seed and the hairs found in the middle. Since Roses are red and white, and both may have many or few leaves, curled or flat: in both kinds, that one is more excellent whose natural color is more perfect, and which has few and flat leaves. The white ones purge little or not at all, but they bind and strengthen more powerfully than the red, etc.

### WHITE WILD ROSE WITH SOME redness, and hairy leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with hairy leaves and a flower. Various parts of the plant are labeled with Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV, VII).</image-desc>

This kind of wild Rose is large and branchy, with thorns that are hooked or robust here and there. The leaves are in fives or sevens, somewhat round, wrinkled, whitish, hairy, and somewhat scented. The flowers have five petals, white with some redness, and their stalks are rough with small thorns. It is frequently seen in various places in hedges and thickets. There are those who affirm that the seeds of the wild Rose alone are effective against the stone <note>kidney stones</note> and difficulties of urine. Indeed, within the inner cavity of the "little sponge" of the Dog-rose <note>original: *Cynorrhodi*</note>, larvae are sometimes enclosed; many use these, reduced to powder, successfully to expel intestinal worms.

# THE ROSE CALLED EGLANTINE: German: *Wilderofen* <note>Wild rose</note>
# THE DOUBLE-FLOWERED EGLANTINE ROSE.
->French: *Eglantier* : Italian: *Rose salvatiche* <note>Wild roses</note><--

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rose branch with thorns, leaves, and a single five-petaled flower.</image-desc>

It is similar to the wild roses previously mentioned, but smaller than the common variety. The **stems** are woody and bristling with sharp thorns. The **leaflets** are somewhat round, usually appearing in groups of seven; they are shining and a beautiful green, possessing a most sweet and pleasant scent. The **flowers** are small, having five petals, very fragrant, white, and sometimes blushing with a purplish hue. The **fruit** <note>the rose hip</note> is somewhat long and of a reddish color. Indeed, there are found around the slender stems certain hairy **sponges** <note>original: "spongiolae"; these are "robin's pincushion" galls caused by wasps</note>, such as those that grow around the thorns of the Dog Rose.

In France, England, and Belgium, it is not easily found growing wild. However, we have observed it frequently at Basel, Montbéliard, and Geneva, even with its "sponges."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a large, multi-petaled (double) flower and several buds.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> calls this the Dog Rose with a multiplied flower; to others, it is a species of fragrant wild rose with a full <note>double</note> flower. It is commonly cultivated in gardens for its sweet scent.

To say something further regarding roses in general: they ought to be gathered at the right time, while they are not yet open and mimic the shape of a cone; for those gathered later are preserved for only a short time. They should be dried in a high place facing south, where the rays of the sun may penetrate but do not actually touch the roses. Other matters which might belong here we leave to be sought from our *Great History* <note>referring to the author's larger botanical work</note>. Practitioners and apothecaries <note>term: Seplasiae - an ancient term for perfume or drug sellers</note> are familiar with their particular uses.

---

# THE BRAMBLE or BRIAR: German: *Bremen* : Belgian: *Braemen* : French: *Ronce* : Italian: *Rovo*.
# THE GREATER BRAMBLE, WITH BLACK FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a blackberry bramble with serrated leaves and clusters of dark berries.</image-desc>

The Bramble is also called *Sentis* <note>Thorn-bush</note> by the Latins, because it is felt <note>original: "sentiatur"</note> immediately by those who touch it; the French call it *Ronce*, from the word for weeding <note>original: "runcatione"</note>, which is proper to thickets. The Bramble is so well known that nothing is better known. According to Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note>, there are three kinds of Bramble: the upright and tall, called *Batos* <note>Greek: "Batos" - bramble</note>, which is the Greater Bramble with black fruit to be described next. The second is the low-growing kind, which they call the *Ground-bramble*; we call it the Lesser Bramble with blue-gray fruit. The third is that which is called *Cynosbatos* <note>Greek: "Dog-bramble" or Sweet Briar</note>. Following in the footsteps of Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note>, we distinguish the Bramble into the *Common* kind, which he simply calls *Batos* and which we divide into Greater and Lesser; and the kind called the *Raspberry* <note>original: "Rubum Idaeum" - Bramble of Mount Ida</note>, the varieties of which we shall also present.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large blackberry branch with prominent thorns and heavy clusters of fruit.</image-desc>

It propagates itself from a knotty root with a troublesome fertility, and wanders far and wide with briary, angular, reddish, and biting shoots. The **stems** are clothed with hooked thorns and stinging prickles. The **leaves** grow in threes, are serrated and rough, with a prickly spine on the back; they are whitish on the lower part and dark green on the upper, and hardly fall off in winter. The **flowers** are white, or rosy-white with tips of the same color. The **berries** are red at first, but black when ripe, somewhat rough with certain hairs; the small grains <note>drupelets</note> have a sweet and not unpleasant taste.

It creeps through thickets and is found in forests among other briars, as well as at hedges and the edges of fields. It flowers in May and June, and ripens its fruit in Autumn.

---

# THE LESSER BRAMBLE, WITH BLUE-GRAY FRUIT.
# THE LOW ALPINE BRAMBLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller bramble variety with trifoliate leaves and berries.</image-desc>

This is more compact than the Greater kind; it has smaller leaves and is less thorny. The **flowers** are white and star-shaped. The **fruit** is green at its first appearance, then red, but when ripe it is blue-gray <note>original: "caesius" - likely the Dewberry</note>, and like the preceding kind it is hairy and of similar taste. It delights in the banks of rivers and in moist, thin, and uncultivated fields. The flowers burst forth in the month of May.

Furthermore, the Bramble, according to Dioscorides, is astringent and drying, and it dyes the hair. A decoction of its topmost branches, when drunk, stops the bowels and restrains the female flow. The leaves, when chewed, strengthen the gums and heal sores of the mouth; when applied as a poultice, they restrain "creeping sores" <note>original: "Herpetas" - skin eruptions</note> and are a remedy for hemorrhoids.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing alpine plant with broad leaves and small berries.</image-desc>

This is a very low plant, usually the height of a palm, soft and without thorns. The **leaves** grow in threes, as in the common Raspberry, and are green, not whitish underneath like those. The **berries** are bright red, several growing from a long stalk at the end of the branches, consisting of one, two, or more small heads, with a pleasant acid flavor; in each small grain there is one hard, somewhat long, and wrinkled seed.

By Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, German botanist</note> it is called *Chamaebatos* <note>Greek: "Ground-bramble"</note>, or the second kind of Raspberry. To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse</note> and most others, it is the *Rock Bramble* or Stone Bramble. It grows on the crags which are around the roots of the highest mountains, not on the mountain peaks themselves; we have observed it in such places in Savoy, and also in Burgundy, near Meche, where they call them *Cheurettes* <note>French dialect: "little goats" or "kid-berries"</note>.

<keywords>Eglantine, Sweet Briar, Blackberry, Dewberry, Rock Bramble, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, botany, Renaissance medicine, rose hips</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of thorny shrubs and medicinal plants, moving from brambles (Rubus) to capers (Capparis). # OF PLANTS

### A THORNY PLANT WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A BRAMBLE
->According to Lobelius.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, thorny, upright plant stem with small clusters of leaves and berries at the top, resembling a bramble or exotic Rubus species.</image-desc>

Thus it is described in the *Adversaria* <note>referring to the botanical work by Pena and Lobel, 1570</note>, which records that it was brought from India. They say it is as thick as a wrist, equaling a long spear in length, and is covered in a dense black bark. It is studded with thick, thorny tubercles <note>small bumps</note> like a mace, and the wood is solid, heavy, and very hard. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax* <note>an index of plants</note>, lists it as the 6th Rubus, or the Exotic Bramble: a thorny tree trunk, etc.

<column-break/>

### RASPBERRY: German: Himbeer; Belgian: Hinnebesyan; French: Framboisier; Italian: Rouo Ideo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Raspberry plant (Rubus idaeus) showing trifoliate and pentafoliate leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

It is smaller and gentler than the common bramble, bristling with short and mostly harmless little thorns, and sometimes lacking them entirely. The *leaves* grow in threes or fives, similar to bramble leaves but tender and soft, dark green above and grayish-white beneath. The *flowers* are white. The *berries* are grayish-white, turning red when ripe <insert>sometimes even white</insert>, gifted with hairs between the segments, and full of a sweet juice that smells of violets and tastes of wine, with a flesh-colored tint. The *root* is long, spreading widely through the earth.

Galen, Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta</note>, and Aetius did not mention the Raspberry, perhaps including it under the general heading of Brambles. Dioscorides describes it as a more tender Bramble, provided with tiny thorns. Pliny says the same. It was called "Idaeus" <note>of Ida</note> not because—as Pliny thinks—it grows only on Mount Ida, but because it grows there most abundantly.

---

### A RELATIVE OF THE SMALLER RASPBERRY
->Cloudberry.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cloudberry plant (Rubus chamaemorus) with broad, lobed leaves and a single berry atop a stem.</image-desc>

Clusius describes this plant at length, stating that it is an inhabitant of the highest mountains; it flowers in June and July, and the fruit ripens in August.

The Raspberry flowers in May, June, and July, and the flowers turn into berries which cannot last long, as little worms are born in them within a few days. It delights in marshy and shaded woods, and places that are least sunny, as well as dewy and sandy rocks. It is either larger or smaller, thorny or without thorns, with white or red fruit; the common variety is said to be the one with red fruit, while the white-fruited one is rarer.

Furthermore, according to Dioscorides, it provides the same benefits as the Bramble. Very elegant syrups are made from it, as well as most pleasant wines and distilled waters, which are very useful for those suffering from stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

<column-break/>

### CAPER: German: Capperen; Belgian: Cappers; French: Capres; Italian: Capparo; Spanish: Alcaparras.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caper plant (Capparis spinosa) showing trailing stems, round leaves, and flower buds.</image-desc>

Theophrastus says that the Caper consists not only of a prickly stem and branches, but also has a rough leaf, and it is made worse by cultivation, so that you might call its nature wild. It is a thorny, low-growing shrub, armed with thorns pointing downwards; its branches, bristling with prickles, spread out in a circle along the ground. The *leaves* grow in an alternating pattern, rounded like a circle, and are very bitter in taste. From their joints emerge long, individual stalks on which sit green heads <note>the buds</note>; when these open, they reveal a white flower, rivaling a small rose, with infinite yellow fibers occupying the center. The *seed* is enclosed in an oblong pod, sometimes many, sometimes few.

---

### BEAN-LIKE OR LEGUMINOUS CAPER
->The Peplios of the Parisians, the Ardifrigi of Avicenna.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with succulent-like leaves and small flowers, identified as Capparis fabaginea.</image-desc>

Writers distinguish the plant pictured here by these names; Camerarius reports that it grows among ruins in Rome.

Otherwise, the common Caper grows spontaneously in many regions, especially warmer ones, with little or no cultivation, and with a more abundant yield in dry places and deserted fields. It is also found mild and without thorns; Bellonius writes that it sometimes even grows into a tree. The fruits of this shrub are brought to us from Alexandria in Egypt, from Spain, or from the Provence region of France, sprinkled with salt, because if stored alone they would rot. By this seasoning, they are made more healthful, both for eating and for medical use, of which more shortly.

<column-break/>

### BARK OF THE APOTHECARY'S CAPER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of dried pieces of Caper root bark (Cortex Capparis).</image-desc>

The barks available in the Apothecary shops have thick, hard, whitish, solid walls, not easily broken, with an acid taste; another wrinkled and cracked layer covers them. Sometimes pieces are found that equal two inches in thickness. If they have been stripped from the root, they are simple and have a faded color.

Furthermore, Simeon Sethi determines the Caper to be hot and dry in the second degree, while Fernelius places it in the third. Galen writes that it consists of diverse and conflicting qualities: it wipes away, cleanses, and cuts <note>breaks up humors</note> by its bitterness; it heats and digests by its sharpness; and it contracts, thickens, and binds by its harshness. Therefore, if anything can help those with a hardened spleen, this medicine is effective. The bark—especially of the root—is the most excellent in all these powers.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal virtues of the Raspberry (Rubus idaeus), the Cloudberry, and the Caper (Capparis). It details their physical forms, preferred climates, and their uses in treating ailments such as kidney stones and spleen disorders.</summary>
<keywords>Raspberry, Caper, Cloudberry, Rubus idaeus, Capparis spinosa, medicinal bark, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, spleen treatment</keywords>

# ON THE IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XV.
### DESCRIBING CLIMBING SHRUBS, SUCH AS VINES AND BINDWEEDS,
->and others similar to these in some respect from foreign lands.<-

---

<columns>2</columns>

**THE WINE-BEARING VINE:** German: *Weinreb, Weinstock*. French: *Vigne*. Italian: *Vite*. Arabic: *Harin* or *Kasm*.

The wine-bearing Vine is too well known to require a description. Theophrastus, Varro, and Pliny <note>Ancient Greek and Roman authorities on natural history and agriculture.</note> call it a "tree," but by what right, since with its twisted trunk and its need for external support, nothing seems more lowly than this plant? Columella more rightly denies it is a tree, determining it to be something in between a tree and a shrub.

Democritus alone thought that the types of Vines could be comprehended by number; all others have declared them to be innumerable and infinite. Hence Columella relates that neither the number nor the names of Vines can be reported with certain reliability. We, however, shall cross this shallow water with a completely dry foot <note>A metaphor meaning to pass over a difficult subject quickly or without getting bogged down.</note>, and will briefly review the principal differences of the Vine alongside the next following Table.

<column-break/>

**THE VINE WITH CELERY-LIKE LEAVES.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grapevine branch with deeply lobed leaves resembling celery (apium) and clusters of grapes.</image-desc>

The form of the leaf alone distinguishes this Vine from the others. Otherwise, the Vine is commonly divided into the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*. And of the cultivated, one is the *Greater*, of which there are many species, and the other is the *Lesser*. Of the Greater, again, the *Grapes* differ in color, shape, and size: for the berries are either green, or whitish, or tawny, or blue, or reddish, or blackish; oblong or somewhat round; large or small; crowded together or sparse, and sometimes even none at all. The Lesser usually has black berries, and very rarely white or tawny ones; the seed is very small and soft. They also differ in flavor: sweet, tart, musky, etc. There is also a great difference in the leaves. For they are either larger or smaller; more or less indented; thinner or thicker; green, reddish, spotted; harder or softer; smooth or somewhat hairy, etc.

---

**THE WILD WINE-VINE, OR LABRUSCA;**
->The monstrous bearded grape.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild grapevine with smaller leaves and clusters, and a separate depiction of a "monstrous" bearded grape cluster.</image-desc>

The wild vine resembles the cultivated one in its trunks, branches, jointed shoots, leaves, tendrils, flowers, and fruit: but it runs riot in the growth of its shoots and tree-like offspring, whence it becomes sterile, and produces smaller and sparser grapes; and even these it does not ripen, but leaves them less flavorful and immature.

The Grape pictured here was found in the Palatinate in a village called Friedelsheim in the year 1599; with its yellowish hair, two cubits long <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; this refers to a long, stringy growth or deformity.</note>, it was judged a monster and an error of nature rather than a legitimate offspring of the same.

Concerning the vine and its fruit, we should treat it more extensively here, but the narrowness of this space does not allow for more. Let the reader consult both our *Great History* and our special *Treatise on the Vine and its Fruit*: and the Appendix to it, as well as—

<column-break/>

**THE CORINTHIAN VINE, OR SEEDLESS VINE.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grapevine with small, seedless grapes (currants).</image-desc>

Its native name <note>Corinth, in Greece.</note> bears witness that this Vine differs little in appearance from the common one: but being impatient of a colder climate, it is separated from it only by the slenderness of the clusters and the smallness of the berries. For the small clusters are composed of berries like Peppercorns, or equaling Elderberry grains, and the berries lack seeds <note>original: "Gigartis"</note>, just as certain Pomegranates are empty of pits.

By Theophrastus it is called the *Idaean Vine*. By Pliny the *Alexandrian Vine*, or, as Dalechamps prefers, the *Grecian Vine*. Dioscorides makes it a second species of Wild Vine. Modern and more recent writers call the fruit *Corinthian Grapes*, *Raisins de Corinthe*: *smaller raisins*, *Passulas* and *Corinthian Passulas*, and even *Grapes lacking seeds*.

### CURRANTS : German: St. John’s Grapes : Belgian: Berries over Sea : French: Red Gooseberry : Italian: Red Grapelet.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ribes (redcurrant) plant showing the root system, stems with leaves, and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

This shrub was unknown to the Ancients, or at least passed over in silence. Some contend, however, that it is what the Moors call *Ribes*. Yet, according to the testimony of Fuchs, Mattioli, the *History of Lyon*, and others, the *Ribes* of the Moors is different from ours; although Amatus and Dodoens assert they are one and the same.

Botanical writers observe only two varieties of this shrub: one is commended for its red fruit and the excellence of its juice, which we depict here; the other has black fruit, which is hardly accepted for medical use but is used for ornamental gardening. Some add a third kind which bears white and pleasant fruit, but it is perhaps a species of the "curled grape" <note>Gooseberry</note>.

### THE TRUE RIBES OF THE ARABS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, broad leaves and a central stem bearing small fruit, identified as the "True Ribes of the Arabs."</image-desc>

It reflects the nature of the Celtic Thorn in its manner of growth; it lives perpetually under liquid snow, endowed with a leaf like the Sharp Dock, were it not larger, rounder, and approaching the texture of Papyrus. It bears red berries from the middle fold of the leaves, as seen in the Alexandrian Laurel, and notable in *Hippoglossum* <note>Horse-tongue</note> and *Ruscus* <note>Butcher's Broom</note>. Usually seven stems emerge from the root, in the midst of which the fruits hang down like clusters of grapes, from which a juice is pressed, etc. Thus Belon describes it. Rauwolf describes it somewhat differently, attributing to it only two leaves, like those of the Butterbur, rising from the root; the stalks are rough, purplish, an inch thick and a cubit long. He calls it Sorrel and Dock, but to most others it is called *Serapio’s Ribes* and the *Legitimate Ribes of the Arabs*.

### SAMBACH or ZAMBACH, JASMINE: German: White-vine : French: Jasmine : Italian: Jasmine.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering Jasmine plant with delicate leaves and star-shaped blossoms.</image-desc>

It is called *Jasminum* as if "Violet-like," from the Violets which the Greeks call *Ias*. You might also say *Iosmen*, as if "scent of a violet," or *Jasmen*, as if "medicinal scent." Following the Greeks, the physicians of the Moorish families also named it *Jasemin*, although in their native tongue it is called *Sambach* or *Zambach*. It is also called "Bee-plant" because bees are delighted by its flowers. Modern authors establish three kinds: White, Blue, and Yellow, to which a fourth, Crimson, and another from Alpinus are added. We depict the White here, which some have thought to be the *Pethon* of Theophrastus.

It grows and flowers in the same places and times as the others of which we shall speak soon.

<column-break/>

### THE SO-CALLED BLACK CURRANT, WITH SCENTED LEAF.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Blackcurrant plant, showing serrated leaves and hanging clusters of dark berries.</image-desc>

This differs from the red primarily because the leaves give off a heavy odor, and the berries are oblong and of a dark color. Both are cultivated everywhere in gardens, thriving in the same beds and plots; they flower in April and May, and ripen their berries in June and July. Gesner writes that the Black Currant grows wild at Zurich on the banks of certain streams, and is easily established when moved into gardens. It is commonly called *Ribes niger* or "black-fruited," and in common speech *Ribi*. Some call the black-fruited shrub *Pipirella* and *Garden Pepper*; Mattioli, in his commentary on Dioscorides, calls it the *Small tree bearing clustered Pepper*. Regarding Gooseberries, see the following sections and the Appendix.

### WHETHER THE RIBES OF RAUWOLF, OR a Plant related to it.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, ribbed leaves and a central flowering spike, marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

We received the plant we depict here in dried form under the name of Rauwolf’s Ribes. Furthermore, the so-called *True Ribes of the Arabs* grows on Mount Lebanon, where it is gathered in great quantities to be sent elsewhere, especially to the Emperor of the Turks. A juice is pressed from the crushed shoots, which is thickened by boiling. This Ribes is cold and dry in the second degree. It is endowed with the same virtues as the common kind, which also cools and dries; it moderately binds and strengthens, extinguishes the heat of fevers, represses bile, tempers fervent blood, slakes thirst, wards off putrefaction, and is beneficial for malignant fevers and flux of the stomach.

### YELLOW AND BLUE JASMINE or GELSEMINUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Jasmine variety with smaller, more numerous leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

The leaves, which are seven in number on the common variety, are usually three on these, though other pairings are sometimes added, with an odd leaf always closing the wing <note>the tip of the compound leaf</note>. The Blue is very rarely seen; to some Arabs it is the *Oriental Privet*, to others the *Blue Clematis*. We have observed the Yellow flowering in Summer at Pforzheim, Strasbourg, Padua, and in some thickets of France. The White is planted everywhere in friendly corners of gardens and for the white trellises of estates, and is raised on supports for the decoration of galleries and arches. It flowers after the Rose, but for a longer time; it grows thick with age from the individual leaf-axils, so much so that you can bend it into wicker-work. The seed, however, which it very rarely produces and does not bear in our climate, is similar to a Lupin.

<summary>This page describes various species of Currants (Ribes) and Jasmine, distinguishing between European garden varieties and the "True Ribes" of the Middle East as described by travelers like Rauwolf. It details their physical characteristics, medicinal cooling properties, and ornamental uses in European gardens.</summary>
<keywords>Redcurrant, Blackcurrant, Ribes, Jasmine, Sambach, medicinal plants, Leonhard Rauwolf, botanical classification, cooling herbs, garden history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of climbing shrubs and medicinal plants, specifically focusing on Jasmine and Honeysuckle varieties. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, citing authorities like Prospero Alpini and Carolus Clusius.</meta>

### JASMINE, OR THE ARABIAN SAMBACH, according to Alpini.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Jasmine plant (Sambach) with broad leaves and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

It is a twiggy shrub, says <note>Prospero Alpini, a famous Venetian physician and botanist</note> Alpini, growing in Cairo in Egypt, which raises itself higher by creeping with its shoots; its leaves are very close to those of the Orange tree. The flowers are white, provided with eight petals, similar to the common varieties in size and other features, but with a sweeter and more powerful scent.

The use of the flowers is more for decoration than for health; nevertheless, from them they prepare an Oil which women use in baths to warm the womb. They also drink it warm for a Cough, Pleurisy, and difficulty of breathing, etc. Our own Oil of Jasmine, applied as an ointment, a drink, or an Enema, is also beneficial for diseases of the womb as well as for colicky pains; applied as an ointment, it warms and softens the nerves, and is useful for contracted limbs.

### PAVATE TREE, WITH ORANGE-LIKE LEAVES, The tree that cures Erysipelas.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pavate tree branch featuring large oval leaves and round fruit.</image-desc>

It is a shrub not particularly branched, eight or nine feet in height; its leaves are sparse, similar to the leaves of the Orange tree <note>original: "Mali aureæ"</note>, except for the appendage <note>the winged petiole common in citrus</note> which they lack, endowed with an elegant greenness on both sides. The flower is small and white, with four petals; from its center emerges a white fiber marked with a green tip, with the scent of the Honeysuckle flower, to which it appears very similar to those looking from a distance. The whole seed is the size of a Lentisk berry, turning from green to blackish, and black when it has ripened. The trunk and branches are ash-colored; the root is white. In Malabar it is called *Pauate*; by the Canarinese *Vafaueli*; but by the Portuguese, the *Tree against Erysipelas* <note>a skin infection</note>.

The illustration is incorrect, and perhaps we shall provide a better one in the Appendix.

### PERFOLIATE HONEYSUCKLE, OR that of warmer regions, called Italian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Italian Honeysuckle with perfoliate leaves (stem passing through the leaf) and tubular flowers.</image-desc>

Having spoken of the names of Honeysuckle <note>original: "Periclymeni"</note>, its species and varieties must now be described, beginning with the Common type. This, as Clusius notes, is commonly distinguished into the German and the Italian. That which grows in Northern regions produces many flowers at the ends of the branches, which are very fragrant, and red fruit gathered into a single head. The other, which grows in warmer regions, has broader leaves and flowers that bloom earlier and are less fragrant than the former. Both grow spontaneously in woods and thickets, and are frequently cultivated in gardens to cover arbors. It flowers in April, May, or June. We depict the *Italian* and *perfoliate* <note>where the leaf base surrounds the stem</note> here; the preceding illustration showed the *German* and non-perfoliate type. Regarding its medicinal powers, see what follows.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH JASMINE, WITH A larger flower, reddish on the outside.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spanish Jasmine with pinnate leaves and larger flowers.</image-desc>

It has a growth similar to the common type, but is more elegant in every way; it has five or seven pairs of leaves, always ending with an odd leaf <note>original: "imparé semper alam claudente"</note>, and these are less sharp than in the common variety. The flowers are much larger, sweeter, and more fragrant, with blunt petals (whereas the common ones are sharp), milky white inside and reddish-purple on the outside.

It is most zealously cultivated by the Greeks and Turks, by whom it was brought into our regions and is nourished in various pots. In the *History of Lyon* <note>by Dalechamps</note> it is called *Dalechamps' Reddish Jasmine*, *Red Jasmine*, and *Broad Jasmine*. By Caspar Bauhin in his commentary on Mattioli, it is called *Great-flowered Spanish Jasmine*.

### CLYMENUM, PERICLYMENUM, HONEYSUCKLE; German: Waldgilgen, Geissblatt; French: Chevrefeuille; Italian: Caprifoglio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Honeysuckle (Caprifolium) showing climbing habit and clusters of tubular flowers.</image-desc>

Dioscorides clearly distinguishes *Periclymenum* from *Clymenum*, and treats them in different chapters; nevertheless, he writes that *Periclymenum* is also called *Clymenum* among the "bastard" <note>unofficial or local</note> names. Thus [according to the testimony of Hermolao and Mattioli], *Clymenum* is spoken of by Pliny regarding the *Periclymenum* of Dioscorides, and what he records about *Clymenum* pertains to *Periclymenum*. In this he followed Theophrastus, who himself ascribed to *Clymenum* what Dioscorides brought forth regarding *Periclymenum*. Marcellus also followed Theophrastus, by a great error, since there is a great difference between those plants, according to the learned. Otherwise, almost all writers call it *Periclymenum*, some *Wood-mother* <note>Matrisylva</note>, others *Goat-leaf* <note>Caprifolium</note>, others *Lily of the Valley*, and others *Lily among Thorns*.

### UPRIGHT HONEYSUCKLE, WITH red fruit and non-serrated leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Upright Honeysuckle with paired berries and simple leaves.</image-desc>

It rises on its own trunk, needing no support; the leaves are like those of the common Female Dogwood, softer and less veined, hairy on both sides, and arranged in opposite pairs. In the same number, the flowers—sitting on one and the same stalk—burst forth from the leaf axils; they are pale yellow, in the shape of common Honeysuckle but smaller, with the upper petal bent backwards and fringed, and the lower one hanging down and narrower. The scent of the flowers is sweet, but the berries—which grow beneath them as they fall, like twin testicles hanging from a single stalk, and turning red upon maturity—have a nauseating taste.

It is found in various places among thorns, in hedges, thickets, and shrubberies. It flowers in May.

<summary>This page describes various species of Jasmine and Honeysuckle, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins (Egypt, India, Spain), and medicinal uses for conditions like respiratory issues and "womb ailments." It also addresses the historical confusion in botanical nomenclature between ancient authorities like Dioscorides, Pliny, and Theophrastus.</summary>

<keywords>Jasmine, Sambach, Pavate tree, Honeysuckle, Periclymenum, medicinal oils, botanical nomenclature, Prospero Alpini, Carolus Clusius, Erysipelas, aromatic plants</keywords>

### SMALLER WILD ROSEMARY OF CAMERARIUS. WILD ROSEMARY OF RONDELETIUS.
### Lesser Silesian Ledum of Schwenckfeld.

<image-desc>Two botanical woodcut illustrations of rosemary varieties. The left image shows a smaller, more delicate plant with thin leaves and a fibrous root system. The right image shows a more robust, woody shrub with denser foliage and a thicker main root.</image-desc>

<columns>2</columns>

This is perhaps the same as the previously mentioned scentless wild Rosemary of Clusius: and we believe that the plant depicted was cultivated by Clusius, so similar is this to that one in all respects: only everything is smaller and thinner: or if they are different plants, you might rightly call this the smaller species of wild Rosemary. They also enjoy the same birthplaces, namely the marshy soil of shady forests. Both this one and that one have been observed in Silesia and Prussia, and it flowers in May and June: but when left alone <note>original: "neglecti," implying uncultivated or wild growth</note> it smells more sweet.

<column-break/>

It is a woody shrub two palms high: with a reddish and robust root: stiff shoots with the texture of Rosemary: leaves like the leaves of Arabian Hyssop <note>likely *Origanum syriacum*</note>, hairy, rough, hard, frequently many from the same point, one of which is much longer than the rest, with a single vein running along the length of each: it has no smell or taste: the flowers cling to the ends of the twigs and are purple: with seeds like Viper's Bugloss or Common Bugloss, quite large and ash-colored.

In the *History of Lyon* and by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called *Dalechamp's false Goat-Oregano* <note>original: "Tragoriganum nothum Dalechampii"</note>. To the same C. Bauhin it is also the *woodier Alkanet* <note>original: "Anchusa lignosior"</note> of Pena. It flowers, however, in the months of March, April, and May at Montpellier on Mount Callepens.

<column-break/>

### LIBANOTIS: OR CROWN ROSEMARY: Germ. & Belg. Rosmarin: Gall. Rosmarin. Ital. Rosmarino, Rosmarino coronario: Hisp. Romero.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut of a Libanotis or Rosmarinus Coronarius plant, showing a woody stem with needle-like leaves and small flowers clustered at the branch tips.</image-desc>

The name *Libanotis*, or Rosemary, was given by Dioscorides to two very different plants. The first is called by him "fertile and fruit-bearing": its leaves are similar to fennel leaves: the stalk is a cubit high, topped with umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note>: and it is the Ferula-like Rosemary, which we shall treat among the umbelliferous plants in Class 17 of this *Sciagraphia*. *The second is another Rosemary, namely that called "Coronary" [Crown Rosemary]*, differing greatly from the Ferula-like kind.

And this one is again twofold: one *Less Noble*, which is called *Wild* and *Greater*: and whose various species we have already presented. *The other truly Nobler*, which has narrower leaves, and is called the smaller and thin-leaved Rosemary.

It is a shrub two cubits or higher: having thin, long stalks endowed with an ash color: clothed with leaves arising several together at intervals, narrow, crowded, somewhat hard, whitish underneath and green on the upper part: and crowned here and there with many flowers whitening out of blue, in the likeness of Sage flowers.

This shrub is of a most pleasant odor, smelling of Frankincense <note>original: "Thus"</note>: whence the name *Libanotis* <note>from the Greek 'libanos' for frankincense</note> was given to it: and because it is sought after for Garlands <note>original: "Corollis"</note>, it obtained the name *Coronary*. It is called *Dendrolibanus* <note>Tree-frankincense</note> by some and *Campsanema*, by others *Solu Thymiamia*, and by the Italians *Mountain Crown*. By Anguillara it is called the *Cneorum* of Theophrastus, and by Hyginus and Virgil the *Black Cassia*. But most received and by common consent, it is called *Rosemary* or *Rosmarinum* simply, *Smaller or thin-leaved Rosemary*, *Crown Rosemary*, *Garden Rosemary with a narrower leaf*, and *Crown Libanotis*.

This Rosemary is indeed a foster-child of gardens: but nevertheless, so great is its natural growth in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, that the inhabitants burn no other wood, and use it in Montpellier and neighboring places as fuel for the fire. It flowers in March, April, Autumn, and almost the whole year.

Furthermore, Crown Rosemary is hot and dry in the second degree, and at the same time partakes of an astringent faculty. It dries the brain; sharpens the senses, and strengthens the nervous parts, and is beneficial for all evils of the head and brain arising from a cold and moist cause. It stops long-lasting fluxes of the womb and suppresses flows of blood. By its smoke <note>as incense</note> it restrains catarrhs and coughs, in decoction it heals the "royal disease" <note>Jaundice</note>, and it is said that by its scent alone it renders a house safe during a pestilence. Pliny claims it is given in wine or vinegar against serpents. The oil is more effective for most of these things; it restores limbs suffering from atrophy, and if the neck and temples are anointed with it, it prevents Apoplexy. Rosemary is not only desired for garlands, says Matthiolus, but also for kitchens and for the shops of apothecaries, for it brings grace to any meats and drinks, and has a salutary power for many diseases, etc. Practitioners know the method of using it, and We teach it in our great *History*.
