# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XIV.
### WHICH IS OF ROSES, AND THOSE RELATED TO THEM
->and of some thorny Plants.<-

---

RED ROSE, WITH A VERY FULL FLOWER,
semi-double and single.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose bush with two large, multi-petaled blooms and several buds, showing thorny stems and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

The shrub of this variety is smaller than that of the White or the Pale-Red rose: the branches are not as thick, and the thorns are also fewer and less sharp; some branches are even without thorns. The leaves grow from a somewhat long stalk, which has ear-like appendages at the base <note>stipules</note> in groups of three or five; they are smooth on both sides, greener on the upper surface, and somewhat round. The flowers, or Roses, are large, of an intense red color, some being very full of petals and others with only a few; however, all are fragrant, especially when dried. The flowers are followed by the *Fruits*, or somewhat long heads <note>rose hips</note>, which are red when ripe. The root is woody and hard. It is cultivated in various places in gardens. The variety that is intensely red, very full, and most fragrant grows most praiseworthily in the city of *Provins* in Provence, France, and from there it is dispersed far and wide.

DAMASK ROSE, ALSO CALLED PERSIC, OR
Alexandrian: with a full, flesh-colored flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a single large bloom and a bud, characterized by many small thorns on the stem.</image-desc>

The branches of this variety abound with hooked and sharp thorns: the *leaves* are in groups of three, five, or seven, and they are not green like the red rose, nor polished like the white: the *flowers* grow many together from long, bristly stalks, with a calyx <note>the green outer part of the flower</note> that is also bristly; they are large, full, fragrant, and reddish or flesh-colored.

As Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, a Spanish physician and botanist</note> notes, the use of these Roses is now frequent among the French, Italians, Germans, and various nations. They call them *Damask* because they are believed to have been brought from Damascus, a city in Syria. They are held in the next highest esteem after the Punic <note>Carthaginian</note> roses; from them are made *Syrup, Rose Honey*, etc. Could this be the Campanian rose of Pliny? Or his Trachinian rose, which is less swollen?

<column-break/>

ACANTHOS ROSE, OR THE ROSE WITHOUT THORNS:
with a full flower, reddish and white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a full bloom and a bud; the stem is notably smooth without thorns.</image-desc>

This rose has the shape and appearance of the preceding one, and differs from it almost only in that it lacks thorns and has flexible, greener branches: the leaves are rarely in threes, but commonly in fives or sixes, and they are somewhat dark green on top and grayish underneath: the *Rose* itself is beautiful with a great crowding of petals, of a sweet scent, and sometimes white in color, but most often reddish, variegated with purple lines.

By Clusius, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and others, it is called the uncommon Rose without thorns, or lacking thorns, with a larger full flower. It bloomed for us in June in the garden at Montbéliard <note>The author's botanical garden in France</note>.

ROSE WITH ROUNDED, CRINKLED LEAVES, WITH A
multiple flower, reddish or flesh-colored.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a dense, multi-petaled flower and rounded, crinkled leaves.</image-desc>

This differs from the preceding one only in its leaf.

Furthermore, the *Parts of the Rose* are eight. For the *Stalk* <note>pedicel</note> which supports the flowers ends in a solid *Head*, filled with a certain down, placed beneath the leaves and flowers and supporting the whole Rose, which they call the *Calyx*. This is surrounded, when the Rose is open, by the *Casing* <note>sepals</note>, divided into five little wings or fringes. The third part is that saffron-colored center of the flower which sits upon the filaments, called the *Anther*, as if it were the "flower of the rose." The fourth is the thin *Filament* itself, the prop and support of that saffron-colored part [like a thread]. The fifth is the *Petal*, whose lowest white part, called the *Claw* <note>unguis</note>, constitutes the sixth. The seventh is the *Down* <note>the woolly interior</note> contained in the head. The eighth is the *Seed*. And these things are common to almost all Roses.

# OF PLANTS

### THE HUNDRED-LEAVED REDDISH DOUBLE ROSE, called the Dutch Rose, with a thorny shrub.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a dense, multi-petaled rose (Rosa centifolia) on a thorny stem with several leaves.</image-desc>

Theophrastus, Pliny, and Athenaeus <note>Ancient Greek and Roman naturalists</note> made mention of the Hundred-leaved rose: but because they say it is scentless and small, we hesitate, along with Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, whether they understood it to be this variety of ours. It is kept today in various places in the more cultivated gardens, just as We also have nourished various plants in our own garden at Yverdon <note>original: "Ebroduni"</note>. The same Clusius writes that a *Medium* (or middle-sized) and a *White* variety are found among the Dutch: We have not seen them. Could it be the Praenestine rose of Pliny?

<column-break/>

### THE APPLE-BEARING ROSE, WITH HAIRY LEAVES.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rose branch featuring a prominent round rose hip (fruit) and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves of this one are almost a palm's length, in groups of five, approaching the reddish double rose in appearance, but longer and less round, saw-edged, hairy underneath, and almost ash-colored. The heads, or thorny fruits <note>rose hips</note>, have the size of a round hazelnut, and short thorny stalks support them: there are fewer thorns along the branches. We obtained this from Mount Caleas. Is it perhaps the *Cynorrhodos* <note>Dog-rose</note> of Thalius, or the Dog-rose with prickly stalks, fruit, and leaves, which produces "sponges" <note>likely referring to rose galls or "bedeguars"</note>?

---

### THE SMALLER ROSE, with a MULTIPLIED REDDISH flower, armed with rough thorns.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rose plant with small, multi-layered flowers and stems heavily covered in fine prickles/spines.</image-desc>

This is a shrub armed with rough, hard thorns, growing quite high with many deep red stalks. The *Roses* on this are small, on short stalks, double, and very fragrant: the root creeps far and wide.

Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, and others label this the Cinnamon Rose. By Camerarius it is called the second Cinnamon Rose, commonly the *Venetian*, by others the *Provincial*, the *Spermonia* of Pliny, and the *Sycian* by some. By Tabernaemontanus, it is the *Smaller Provincial Rose*: by others a type of *Damask Rose*, the *Flesh-colored Rose of Damascus*. It blooms in early spring. Is it perhaps the *Gracula* of Pliny, as the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Lugdunensis</note> suggests? Or the *Rose from Pangaeus* mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny?

<column-break/>

### THE CINNAMON ROSE, WITH reddish FLOWERS, thorny.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rose with simpler, fewer-petaled flowers and thorny stems.</image-desc>

The leaves of this one are smaller than those of the White, Red, and Reddish roses: the branches are thin, thorny, and reddish: the flowers are small, reddish, fragrant, and single <note>original: "simplices," meaning a single row of petals</note>.

The *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> writes that it grows wild frequently in the countryside of France, Belgium, and England. Some label it the *Canella* Rose, to others it is the *Single Cinnamon Rose*. Gesner takes it for the *Lychnis* of Pliny, and records that a *Greater* and *Smaller* kind grow on Mount Albis, making the former the *Female* and the latter the *Male*.

---

### THE ROSE WITH A SMALL REDDISH FLOWER, SINGLE, not thorny.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rose with a single layer of petals and a smooth stem without prominent thorns.</image-desc>

Gentler than the others, this one bristles with no thorns, except for the stalk of the flower which is somewhat rough: the pairings of the smooth leaves, besides the odd one at the end, are three or four; they are saw-edged, green above, whitish below, and smooth. The Roses are small, five-petaled, fragrant, and of a reddish color. The fruit is round, a little smaller than a small Medlar, turning red when ripe, and containing seeds wrapped in downy fuzz.

To Tragus it is the *Field Rose*: to Tabernaemontanus and Gerard the *Smaller Provincial*: to most the *May Rose*, the *Meyan rosen* of the *History of Lyon*. It is the *Greek Rose* of Pliny, called *Lychnis* by the Greeks. We found it growing wild on Mount Thuiri in the Geneva region and elsewhere: and we have observed it to be cultivated in gardens as well.

<column-break/>

### AN ELEGANT KIND OF TINY ROSE.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a very small, delicate rose plant with a single flower and small leaves.</image-desc>

The person who brought this to Us had collected it in the "Garden of God" <note>likely a specific mountain or meadow known for its flora</note>. Its leaves are an inch long, five-parted, and smooth: the flower is large in proportion to the plant, five-petaled, and white. However, it must be considered whether it is merely some variation of one of the preceding kinds: for it seems to Us that species should not be multiplied without necessity; we only strive to demonstrate the Works of God in botany according to our capacity.

# THE WHITE ROSE, FULL AND SEMI-FULL.
->Cultivated white rose, with full and simple flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with multiple full-petaled blooms and buds, showing serrated leaves and thorny stems.</image-desc>

The stalk rises up long, woody, and pithy <note>original: "fungosis," referring to the soft, sponge-like center of the stem</note>, upon which are sharp, hooked, and sparse thorns. The bark is otherwise polished and smooth. The leaflets are in groups of five or seven, notched, hairless, and somewhat long. At the ends of the branches, several calyxes <note>the green outer part of a flower bud</note> cling to little stalks with small, non-threatening thorns. When these open, a beautiful, fragrant white rose appears, sometimes with many petals and sometimes with few, with yellow tips <note>stamens</note> in the middle. There follow round fruits <note>rose hips</note> which are red when mature, containing hard seeds wrapped in a woolly fuzz. It tolerates the cold better than the Red Rose, and its branches which bore flowers must be pruned every year. It blooms very late. It is more beloved than the Red Rose and has a greater power for purging <note>as a laxative</note>. Our illustration, taken from purchased stock, is not pleasing.

# THE GREATER MUSK ROSE: German: White
->Musk Rose: French: Rose musquée.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall rose stalk with clusters of smaller flowers and prominent thorns.</image-desc>

This is a robust, upright, thorny shrub; the trunk is thicker than the others, with very long branches and sparser prickles. At the tops of the branches, from a stalk pricked with a few rare thorns, the roses grow. They usually consist of five or seven petals, large and white with some redness that is most revealed when they are dried. The scent is most sweet, because of which excellence it is called the *Muscatula* <note>Little Musk</note>. In Lyon and Montpellier, it blooms in May and Autumn. Gesner writes that in Italy it sometimes blooms the whole year round. We, however, have observed it blooming in Yverdon <note>Latin: Ebrodunum</note> in the garden of the aforementioned Mr. Chasseur from the month of August right into Winter.

# THE LESSER MUSK ROSE, WITH FULL FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose bush with dense, multi-layered (double) flowers.</image-desc>

It would be similar in all respects to the simple variety, were there not a discrepancy in the flower: in this one, the outer petals are larger and the inner ones smaller. It seems to Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> to have shed its wild nature through the art and "adulteration" <note>original: "mangonio," implying clever cultivation or grafting</note> of gardeners, and thus became "double" in gardens.

It is commonly labeled the many-folded or many-leaved Musk Rose, and also the *Second Autumn Rose*. There are those who judge it to be the *Damask Rose*, others Pliny’s *Praenestine Rose*, and others his *Coroneola*. In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is called the Damask Rose, or the Second Autumnal; they delight with their dense mass of petals and extraordinary sweetness of scent.

<column-break/>

# THE YELLOW ROSE, SIMPLE AND FULL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with simple, five-petaled flowers and distinct foliage.</image-desc>

This golden rose, which was not mentioned by the Ancients, differs from other kinds of roses in its leaves, flower, and scent. For its leaves are small, round, of a dark greenness, and deeply notched. The stems are very thorny; the flower is golden or yellow, otherwise similar to the others, and as with the white and red, it is either simple or full. The scent is heavy and unpleasant. When the flower has fallen, fruits follow that are so similar in color, shape, and size to Service-berries <note>Latin: Sorbis</note> that an unskilled or untrained person could scarcely distinguish them. Writers call this the Indian or Alexandrian Rose, which is not unknown today in the more cultivated gardens of Europe; for example, in Yverdon, the Messrs. *Chasseur*, leading citizens of that city, have them with both simple and full flowers.

# THE LESSER MUSK ROSE, WITH SIMPLE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with simple flowers, showing the structure of the stamens and leaves.</image-desc>

Some believe this to be the *Coroneola* rose of Pliny; others call it the Alexandrian or Damask Rose. By others it is called the *Wild Rose* and the *Autumn Rose*. Among the Arabs it is called *Nefrin, Nefrim, Nefrin, and Neferin*. To Gesner, it is the Fragrant Musk Rose; but to almost everyone else, it is the Lesser Musk Rose with a simple flower. It blooms at the same time as the preceding one.

Furthermore, Musk Roses are commonly preserved and eaten in Italy, and especially in Venice. According to Lobelius, they move the bowels pleasantly and quite powerfully, yet they also bring on fainting fits and piercing pains of the stomach and heart. But whether they can move the bowels pleasantly and yet excite such bad symptoms, let the readers judge.

# THE WILD ROSE, OR DOG-ROSE.
->Reddish wild rose, a small shrub.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rose (dog rose) with simple flowers and prominent rose hips (fructus).</image-desc>

From the cultivated roses, we turn the thread of our History to the wild ones, among which the *Cynorrhodon* <note>Greek for "Dog-rose"</note> shall lead the troop. Although this name is sometimes used for a certain kind of Lily, and also for a very thorny rose with a red flower, it is well known that by this term wild roses are understood generally. The shrub of the one we depict here is small, usually about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high. Otherwise, it is similar to the deep red Rose, sometimes with curved but sparse thorns. The leaves, as in that one, are divided into five, or more rarely seven leaflets, serrated, smooth, and a darker green on the upper part; finally, they are of almost the same color and form, but sparser and smaller. The flower is not small, reddish, with five petals and a most pleasant scent, which is followed by a little head <note>the hip</note> with a prickly stalk.

### DWARF APPLE-BEARING WILD ROSE, without thorns, with a reddish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small rose bush with several large, round seed pods (hips) and a single open flower at the top.</image-desc>

Among the wild Roses, say the *Adversaria* <note>referring to the botanical work *Stirpium Adversaria Nova* by Pena and Lobel</note>, this one is of no small beauty, very familiar in England, and closely related to the Eglantine <note>Sweet Briar</note>. It grows as a dwarf shrub, no higher than two cubits <note>about three feet</note>, and is scentless. It has smaller and very elegant leaves. It is gifted with fruit not unlike the Aronia Medlar, though much smaller and of a greener color, turning reddish or a pale scarlet when mature through August. The flower is that of a wild Rose.

### THE FIELD ROSE OF TABERNÆMONTANUS: German: *Feldt Rose*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose plant with a thick, gnarled root system and several stems bearing leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

He <note>Tabernæmontanus</note> says this is so common in all places that it does not require a description; nor shall we say anything further of it here. Instead, here and alongside the following few tables, we shall set forth the Temperament, powers, and uses of Roses.

The Rose, according to the author Mesuë <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note>, who wrote more distinctly about it than others, is cold in the first degree and dry in the second. It is composed of various separable substances: a moderate watery part, an astringent earthy part, a sweet and aromatic airy part, and finally a subtle fiery part, from which comes its bitterness, strength, perfection, and form. However, the force of the fiery substance, which impressed the redness and appearance, was more powerful than that which caused the bitterness; for this reason, the bitterness is lost by drying alone, while the others remain. If those were to perish, the Rose would no more be a Rose than a dead man is a man.

### WILD ROSE, WITH SMOOTH LEAVES, and a completely white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rose branch with multiple leaves and a single large, five-petaled flower.</image-desc>

The variety just mentioned grows around ditches, trenches, and the margins of fields and meadows, especially in damp places. It flowers at various times: June, July, August, September, October, and November. This one, however, grows everywhere in woods and thickets, and flowers a little later than the other wild ones: namely in June and July.

Furthermore, the yellow stamens of the Roses, or the tips and calyxes <note>the leaf-like base of the flower</note>, powerfully dry and bind. Hence Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note> says: "The flower found in the middle of Roses, when dried and sprinkled, helps the flow of humors from the gums." The heads <note>hips</note>, when drunk, according to the same author and Pliny, stop blood and the bowels. However, where Pliny says the Rose is warming, it proves his text is corrupted <note>suggesting a scribal error in the ancient manuscripts</note>.

<column-break/>

### VERY THORNY DWARF ROSE, with Burnet-like smooth leaves and a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very thorny, low-growing rose bush with small, rounded leaves similar to burnet (Pimpinella).</image-desc>

This dwarf rose, a cubit and a half high, does not allow itself to be touched with impunity in any part; it bristles everywhere with such a dense army of threatening thorns, as much on the main stem as on the branches, of which it has many disordered ones. It has winged, smooth leaves in four pairs, scarcely equaling a quarter of the little finger, notched all around, and somewhat round. The small flowers consist of a simple texture of petals, white and numerous, with yellow heads <note>stamens</note> occupying the center, and a few small buds. The root creeps and sends out many shoots.

### WHITE WILD ROSE WITH REDNESS, with smooth leaves and a simple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with several leaves and two open, simple flowers.</image-desc>

Fresh Roses, Mesuë continues, are more bitter than astringent. Because of that bitterness, fresh Roses—especially their juice—purge <note>act as a laxative</note>. But when dried, the heat having been released and the bitterness driven out, they possess a styptic <note>blood-stopping</note> and constipating substance. Indeed, the dry Rose is colder and more styptic; and more so that which was not fully ripe, and the white more than the red. Furthermore, the Rose resolves <note>breaks down tumors or swellings</note>, extinguishes hot imbalances, and strengthens parts of the body by pulling them together and binding them; this is done most effectively by the seeds and the hairs found in the center. Since Roses are red and white, and both may have many or few petals, curled or flat: in either kind, that one is superior whose natural color is more perfect, and which has few and flat petals. White roses purge not at all or very little; rather, they bind and strengthen more than the red ones, etc.

### WHITE WILD ROSE WITH SOME redness, and hairy leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with several flowers and buds. Various parts of the flower and fruit are labeled with Roman numerals (I, II, III, IV, VII).</image-desc>

This large, branchy genus of wild Rose has hooked, sturdy thorns here and there. It has five or seven leaflets, somewhat round, wrinkled, whitish, hairy, and somewhat scented. The flowers have five petals, white with some redness, and their stalks are rough with small thorns. It is frequently seen in various places in hedges and thickets. There are those who affirm that the "sponges" <note>bedeguars or rose galls caused by wasps</note> of the wild Rose are effective against the stone <note>kidney stones</note> and difficulties of urine. Inside the cavity of the *Cynorrhodus* <note>Dog-rose gall</note> "sponge," maggots are sometimes enclosed; many people use these, when powdered, successfully to expel intestinal worms.

### THE ROSE CALLED EGLANTINE: German: *Wilderosen*;
### French: *Eglantier*: Italian: *Rose saluatiche*. <note>Wild roses</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rose branch (Rosa eglentina) with small leaves, thorns, and a single five-petaled flower.</image-desc>

It is similar to the wild roses mentioned before, but smaller than the common variety: the *stalk* is woody and bristling with sharp thorns: the *leaflets* are somewhat round, usually seven in number, shining and a beautiful green, with a most sweet and pleasing scent: the *flowers* are small, five-petaled, very fragrant, white, and sometimes whitening out of a purple hue: the *fruit* is oblong and reddish in color. Indeed, small hairy sponges <note>These are "rose galls" or "robin's pincushions," caused by gall wasps.</note> are found around the slender stalks, such as those that grow around the thorns of the Dog Rose.

In France, England, and Belgium it is not easily found growing wild. However, we have observed it frequently at Basel, Montbéliard, and Geneva, even with the sponges.

<column-break/>

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED EGLANTINE ROSE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rose branch with a large, multi-petaled (double) flower and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a famous German physician and botanist.</note> calls this the Dog Rose with a multiplied flower: to others, it is a fragrant species of wild rose with a double flower. It is commonly cultivated in gardens for its sweet scent.

However, to say something further regarding Roses in general: they ought to be gathered at the right time, and while they are not yet open and mimic the shape of a cone: for those gathered later are preserved for only a short time. They should be dried in a high place facing south, where the rays of the Sun may penetrate, but do not actually touch the Roses. Other matters which could belong to this place we leave to be sought from our *Great History* <note>A reference to the author's larger botanical work, likely the *Historia Plantarum Universalis*.</note>. Physicians and apothecaries <term>Seplasiarii: dealers in perfumes and medicines</term> know their particular use.

---

<column-break/>

### THE BRAMBLE or THORN-BUSH: German: *Bremen*: Belgian: *Braemen*: French: *Ronce*: Italian: *Rouo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a blackberry bramble (Rubus) with compound leaves, thorns, and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

The Bramble is also called *Sentis* <note>Thorn-bush</note> by the Latins, because it is "felt" <note>A wordplay on *sentis* (thorn) and *sentire* (to feel/perceive).</note> immediately by those touching it; and *Ronce* by the French, from the word for weeding <note>original: "runcatione"</note>, which is proper to thickets. Indeed, the Bramble is so well known that nothing is better known. According to Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany."</note> there are three kinds of Bramble: the upright and tall, called *Batos* <note>Greek: βάτος</note>. This is surely the Greater Bramble with black fruit, to be described next. The second is Lowly: they call it the *Ground-bramble*: but we call it the Lesser Bramble with blue-gray fruit: and the third, which is called *Cynosbatos* <note>Greek: κυνόσβατος, "Dog-bramble" or Sweetbriar</note>. We, following in the footsteps of Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist.</note>, distinguish the Bramble into the *Common* kind, which he calls simply *Batos*, and which we separate into the Greater and Lesser: and that called the *Raspberry* <note>original: "Rubum Idaeum," literally "Bramble of Mount Ida"</note>, the varieties of which we shall also set forth.

<column-break/>

### GREATER BRAMBLE, WITH BLACK FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large blackberry branch with heavy clusters of dark fruit.</image-desc>

It propagates itself from a knotty root with a relentless fertility, and wanders far and wide with thorny, angular, reddish, and biting shoots. The *stalks* are clothed with hooked thorns and stinging prickles: the *leaves* are in threes, saw-toothed, rough, with a prickly spine, whitish on the lower part and blackish on the upper, and hardly falling off in winter: the *flowers* are white, or rosy-white with tips of the same color: the *berries* <note>original: "mora"</note> are a shining red, but black when ripe, somewhat sprinkled with certain bristles: with small grains, and a sweet and not unpleasant taste.

It creeps through thickets, and is found in forests among other thorns, as well as at hedges and the margins of fields: it flowers in May and June, and ripens its fruit in Autumn.

---

<column-break/>

### LESSER BRAMBLE, WITH BLUE-GRAY FRUIT. <note>Likely the Dewberry (Rubus caesius).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller bramble species with trifoliate leaves and berries.</image-desc>

This is more compact than the Greater: it has smaller leaves and is less thorny: the *flowers* are white and star-shaped: the *fruit* is green at its first rising, afterwards red, but truly blue-gray <note>original: "caesius"</note> when ripe, and hairy like the preceding, and of similar taste. It delights in the banks of rivers, and moist, lean, and uncultivated fields. The flowers burst forth in the month of May.

Furthermore, the Bramble, according to Dioscorides, is astringent and drying, and dyes the hair. A decoction of its topmost branches, when drunk, stops the bowels and restrains the female flow. The leaves, when chewed, strengthen the gums and heal ulcers of the mouth; but when applied as a poultice, they restrain "creeping sores" <note>original: "Herpetas," likely shingles or cold sores</note> and are a remedy for hemorrhoids.

<column-break/>

### LOWLY ALPINE BRAMBLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing alpine bramble with distinct leaf shapes and a single berry at the terminal.</image-desc>

The plant is quite lowly, usually the height of a palm, soft and without thorns: the *leaves* are in threes, as in the common Raspberry, green, not white underneath like those: the berries are crimson on a long stalk at the end of the branches, consisting of one, two, or more heads, with a pleasing acid flavor: and in each individual grain is one hard, somewhat long, and wrinkled seed.

By Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), German botanist.</note> it is called *Chamaebatos* <note>Greek: "Ground-bramble"</note>, or another Raspberry. To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), influential Flemish botanist.</note> and most others it is the *Rock Bramble* or *Stone Bramble*. It grows on the crags which are around the roots of the highest mountains, not on the mountain ridges themselves: as we have observed in such places in Savoy, and also in Burgundy, near Mecho, where they call it "Chanrostes"—

# PLANTS OF THE BRAMBLE KIND

### A THORNY PLANT WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A BRAMBLE
->According to Lobelius.<- <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall, upright, thorny stalk with dense, scale-like or prickly foliage, resembling a club or a very spiny branch.</image-desc>

Thus the *Adversaria* <note>referring to the "Stirpium Adversaria Nova" by Lobel and Pena</note> titles this plant, which they record as being brought from India. They say it is the thickness of a wrist, equaling a long spear in length, and covered in a dense black bark with thick, lens-shaped, very frequent swellings, prickly in the manner of a club, with solid, heavy, and very hard wood. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register by Bauhin (1560–1624)</note> it is the 6th Bramble, or the Exotic Bramble: a thorny tree trunk, etc.

### A RELATIVE OF THE SMALLER MOUNTAIN BRAMBLE
->Cloudberry.<- <note>Latin: Chamæmorus, literally "ground-mulberry."</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a low-growing plant with broad, lobed leaves and a single flower/fruit at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note> describes this at length, and says it is an inhabitant of the highest mountains, flowering in June and July, but ripening its fruit in August.

The Raspberry <note>Latin: Rubus Idæus</note> flowers in May, June, and July, and the flowers turn into berries <note>original: "Mora"</note> which cannot last long, as little worms are born in them within a few days. It delights in marshy and shady forests, and places with very little sun, as well as dewy and sandy rocks. It is indeed either Greater or Lesser. Thorny or not thorny, with white or red fruit: and the one whose fruit is reddish is called "common," while the one with white fruit is rarer.

Furthermore, according to the author Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist of the 1st century AD</note>, it provides the same benefits as the Bramble. From it are made very elegant syrups, most pleasant wines, and distilled waters very useful for those suffering from stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

### BEAN-CAPER, OR LEGUMINOUS CAPER:
->The Peplios of the Parisians, the Ardifrigi of Avicenna.<- <note>Avicenna was a Persian polymath; "Ardifrigi" is a Latinized version of an Arabic plant name.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with rounded, succulent-looking leaves arranged in pairs along the stems, and small flowers.</image-desc>

Writers distinguish the plant pictured here by these names, which Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598)</note> claims grows among the ruins in Rome.

Otherwise, the common Caper grows wild in many regions, especially the warmer ones, with no or little cultivation, and with a more abundant yield in dry places and deserted fields. It is also found mild and without thorns: and Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), French explorer and naturalist</note> writes that it sometimes even grows into a tree. The fruits of this shrub are brought to us from Alexandria in Egypt, Spain, or the Provence region of France, sprinkled with salt, because if stored alone they rot; and by that seasoning they are rendered more healthful, both for eating and for medical use, of which more shortly.

<column-break/>

### RASPBERRY: German: Himbeer; Belgian: Hinnebesian; French: Framboisier; Italian: Rouo Ideo.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a raspberry bush (Rubus idaeus) with compound leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

It is smaller and milder than the common bramble, bristling with short and almost harmless little thorns, and sometimes it lacks them entirely: the leaves are in threes or fives, similar to Bramble leaves, but tender and soft, dark green above and grayish-white beneath: the flowers are white: the berries are frosted, turning red upon maturity (sometimes also white), provided with hairs between the grains, full of a sweet juice that smells of violets and is a vinous, flesh-colored hue: the root is long, spreading widely through the earth.

Galen, Paulus, and Aetius <note>Ancient Greek medical authorities</note> did not mention the Raspberry, perhaps including it under the Bramble. Dioscorides makes it a more tender Bramble, provided with tiny thorns. Pliny says the same. It was called *Idæus* <note>of Mount Ida</note> not because (as the same Pliny thinks) it grew only on Mount Ida, but because it occurred there most abundantly.

### CAPER: German: Capperen; Belgian: Cappers; French: Capres; Italian: Capparo; Spanish: Alcaparras.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a caper plant (Capparis spinosa) with rounded leaves and large, distinct flowers with long stamens.</image-desc>

Not only, says Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," 4th century BC</note>, does the Caper consist of a prickly stem and branches, but also a rough leaf, and it is made worse by cultivation, so that you might call its nature wild. It is a brambly shrub, low-growing, armed with thorns pointing downwards: its small branches, bristling with prickles, are spread in a circle along the ground: the leaves grow in an alternate arrangement, of a circular roundness, and of a very bitter taste: from their crook come single long stalks, on which sit green heads, which when opened display a white flower, a rival to a small Rose, with infinite fringes of fibers occupying the middle: the seed is enclosed in an oblong pod, sometimes many, sometimes few.

### CAPER OF THE APOTHECARIES, THE BARK.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut showing dried, curled pieces of bark, likely the root bark of the caper plant.</image-desc>

The barks which are available in the Apothecary shops have thick, hard, whitish, solid walls, not easy to break, with an acid taste: another wrinkled and cracked layer covers them. Sometimes some are found that equal two inches in thickness. But if they have been stripped from the root, they are simple and have a faded color.

Furthermore, Simeon Seth <note>11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician</note> established the Caper as hot and dry in the second degree, and Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), French physician</note> in the third. But Galen writes that it consists of diverse and conflicting qualities: and that it wipes away, cleanses, and cuts by its bitterness; heats and digests by its sharpness; and contracts, thickens, and binds by its sourness. Whence, if anything else can, this medicine is able to help mildly hardened parts: and the Bark (especially of the root) is of a more excellent faculty in all these things.

# ILLUSTRATIONS AND DESCRIPTIONS
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XV.
### DESCRIBING CLIMBING SHRUBS, SUCH AS VINES AND BINDWEEDS; and others similar to these from foreign lands.

**THE WINE-BEARING VINE:** German: *Weinreb, Weinstock*. French: *Vigne*. Italian: *Vite*. Arabic: *Harin* or *Kasm*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grapevine (Vitis Vinifera) climbing a wooden trellis, showing leaves and clusters of grapes.</image-desc>

The wine-bearing Vine is too well known to require a description. Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "father of botany."</note>, Varro, and Pliny call it a tree, but by what marriage <note>original: "quo marito"; a metaphor for how the vine "marries" or clings to a support.</note> can this be, when nothing seems more lowly than this plant, with its twisted trunk and its need for external help? Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture.</note> more rightly denies it is a tree, establishing it as something between a tree and a shrub.

Democritus alone thought the kinds of Vines could be counted by number; all others have claimed they are innumerable and infinite. Hence Columella reports that neither the number nor the names of the Vines can be recorded with certain reliability. We, however, shall cross this ford with a dry foot <note>A metaphor meaning to pass over a difficult subject quickly.</note>, and will briefly review the principal differences of the Vine on the side of the next following Table.

**WILD WINE-BEARING VINE (LABRUSCA);**
->The monstrous bearded grape.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild grapevine (Labrusca) with a distinct "bearded" or hairy appearance on the grape clusters.</image-desc>

The wild vine resembles the cultivated one in its trunks, branches, jointed shoots, leaves, tendrils, flowers, and fruit; but it runs riot into a shrubby and tree-like growth, whereby it becomes sterile, producing smaller and sparser grapes, and even those it does not ripen, but leaves them less flavorful and immature.

The Grape pictured here was found in the Palatinate <note>A region in southwestern Germany.</note> in a village called *Friedelsheim* in the year 1599; with its yellowish hair, two cubits long, it was judged to be a monster and an error of nature rather than a legitimate offspring of the same.

Regarding the vine and its fruit, we should treat it more extensively here, but the narrowness of this space does not allow for more. Let the reader consult both our *Great History* and our special *Treatise on the Vine and its Fruit*: an Appendix to this, as well as on *omphacium* <term>juice of unripe grapes</term>, *Must* <term>freshly pressed grape juice</term>, *Sapa* <term>boiled-down grape juice</term>, *Various kinds of Wine*, *Wine Dregs*, and *Water of Life* <term>Aqua Vitae; distilled spirits or brandy</term>, is to be published shortly.

<column-break/>

**VINE WITH CELERY-LIKE LEAVES.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grapevine variety with deeply lobed, laciniated leaves resembling celery (Apium) foliage.</image-desc>

The form of the leaf alone distinguishes this Vine from others. Otherwise, the Vine is commonly divided into the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*. And of the cultivated, one is the *Greater*, of which there are many species, and the other is the *Lesser*. Furthermore, the *Grapes* of the Greater differ in color, shape, and size: for the berries are either green, or whitish, or tawny, or blue, or reddish, or blackish; oblong or somewhat round; large or small; crowded or sparse, and sometimes even none at all. The Lesser usually has black berries, and very rarely white or tawny ones, with a very small and soft seed. They also differ in flavor: sweet, tart, musky, etc. There is also a great difference in the leaves. For they are either larger or smaller; more or less deeply cut; thinner or thicker; green, reddish, spotted; harder or softer; smooth or somewhat hairy, etc.

**THE CORINTHIAN VINE, OR SEEDLESS VINE.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Corinthian grape (currant vine) showing smaller, denser clusters of seedless grapes.</image-desc>

Bearing witness to its native name <note>Corinth, Greece.</note>, this Vine differs little in appearance from the common one; but being impatient of a colder climate, it is separated from it only by the slenderness of the clusters and the smallness of the berries. For the small clusters consist of berries equal to grains of Pepper or Elderberry, and the berries lack seeds <note>original: "Gigartis"; grape stones.</note>, like certain Pomegranates that are empty of pips.

It is called the *Idaean Vine* by Theophrastus. By Pliny, the *Alexandrian Vine*, or, as Dalechamps prefers, the *Grecian Vine*. Dioscorides makes it a second species of *Wild Vine*. Modern and more recent authors call the fruit *Corinthian Grapes*, *Raisins of Corinth*: *smaller raisins*, *Passulae* and *Corinthian Passulae*, and even *Grapes lacking seeds*.

<summary>This page describes various species of grapevines (Vitis), including the common wine-bearing vine, a "monstrous" bearded wild variety found in Germany, and the seedless Corinthian grape. It highlights the botanical debate over whether the vine is a tree or a shrub and notes the vast diversity in grape color, shape, and foliage.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### JASMINE, OR THE ARABIAN SAMBACH, of Alpinus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Jasmine plant (Sambach Arabum) with small, star-shaped flowers and oval leaves arranged on thin stems.</image-desc>

It is a twiggy shrub, says <note>Prospero Alpini, a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian plants.</note> Alpinus, growing in Cairo in Egypt, which raises itself higher by creeping with its shoots; its leaves are very close to those of the Orange tree. The flowers are white, provided with eight petals, similar to the common jasmine in size and other characteristics, but with a sweeter and much stronger scent.

The use of the flowers is more for decoration than for health; nevertheless, from them they prepare an Oil which women use in baths to warm the womb. They also drink it warm for a Cough, Pleurisy, and difficulty of breathing, etc. Our own Jasmine Oil, whether applied as an ointment, drunk, or used as an Enema, is also beneficial for diseases of the womb as well as for colicky pains; applied as an ointment, it warms and softens the nerves and is useful for contracted limbs.

### PAVATE TREE, WITH GOLDEN APPLE LEAVES, The tree that cures Erysipelas.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pavate tree, showing branches with broad, veined leaves and clusters of small berries or flower buds.</image-desc>

It is a shrub not particularly branched, eight or nine feet in height; its leaves are sparse, similar to the leaves of the Golden Apple <note>The "Golden Apple" usually refers to the Orange or Citron in Renaissance botany.</note>, except they lack the appendage <note>Referring to the winged petiole common in citrus leaves.</note> which these lack, endowed with an elegant greenness on both sides. The flower is tiny and white, having four petals; from its center emerges a white fiber marked with a green tip, with the scent of the Woodbine flower, to which it seems very similar to those looking from a distance. The whole seed is the size of a Lentisk berry, turning from green to blackish, and black when it has ripened. The trunk and branches are ash-colored; the root is white. In Malabar it is called *Pavate*; by the Canarines *Vassaueli*; and by the Portuguese *The Tree against Erysipelas* <note>Erysipelas is a bacterial skin infection, historically called "St. Anthony's Fire."</note>.

The figure is incorrect, and perhaps we shall give a better one in the appendix.

### PERFOLIATE HONEYSUCKLE, OR of the warmer regions, called Italian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Periclymenum Perfoliatum (Honeysuckle), showing the characteristic fused leaves surrounding the stem and clusters of tubular flowers.</image-desc>

Having spoken of the names of Honeysuckle <term>Periclymenum: from the Greek 'periklymenon', meaning 'twining round'</term>, its species and varieties must now be described, beginning with the Common sort. This, as <note>Carolus Clusius, one of the most influential botanists of the 16th century.</note> Clusius notes, is commonly distinguished into the German and the Italian. That which grows in Northern regions produces many flowers at the ends of the branches, which are very fragrant, and red fruit gathered into a single head. The other, which grows in warmer regions, has broader leaves and bears flowers earlier and less fragrant than the former. Both grow spontaneously in woods and thickets, and are frequently cultivated in gardens to cover arbors. It flowers in April, May, or June. We depict the Italian and perfoliate <note>Perfoliate leaves are those where the stem appears to pass through the leaf blade.</note> type here; the preceding icon shows the German and non-perfoliate type. Concerning its powers, see what follows.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH JASMINE, WITH THE larger flower, reddish on the outside.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spanish Jasmine, featuring larger flowers and more elongated leaves compared to the first specimen.</image-desc>

It has a growth similar to the common jasmine, but is more elegant in every way; it has five or seven pairs of leaves, with an odd leaf always closing the wing <note>A pinnate leaf structure.</note>, and these are less sharp than in the common variety. The flowers are far larger, sweeter, and more fragrant; the petals are blunt [whereas in the common they are sharp], milk-white inside and reddish-purple on the outside.

It is most zealously cultivated by the Greeks and Turks, from whom it was brought into our regions and is nourished in various places in pots. In the *History of Lyon* it is called the *Purple Jasmine* of Dalechamp, *Red Jasmine*, and *Broad Jasmine*. By C. Bauhin in his commentary on Mattioli, it is called *Great-flowered Spanish Jasmine*.

### CLYMENUM, PERICLYMENUM, CAPRIFOLIUM; Germ. Vvaldgilen, Geissblat: Gall. Cheurefeuille: Ital. Caprifoglio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Clymenum/Caprifolium, showing twining stems and pairs of leaves with flower buds emerging from the axils.</image-desc>

Dioscorides clearly distinguishes *Periclymenum* from *Clymenum* and treats them in different chapters; nevertheless, he writes that *Periclymenum* is also called *Clymenum* among the "bastard" <note>Pseudonyms or local names.</note> names. Thus [according to the testimony of Hermolaus and Mattioli] *Clymenum* is spoken of by Pliny regarding the *Periclymenum* of Dioscorides, and what he relates concerning *Clymenum* pertains to *Periclymenum*. In this he followed Theophrastus, who himself ascribed to *Clymenum* what Dioscorides set forth regarding *Periclymenum*. Marcellus also followed Theophrastus in a great error, since there is a great difference between those plants, according to the learned. Otherwise, almost all writers call it *Periclymenum*, some *Wood-mother* <note>Latin: Matrisylva.</note>, others *Goat-leaf* <note>Latin: Caprifolium; French: Cheurefeuille.</note>, others *Lily of the Valley*, and others *Lily among Thorns*.

### UPRIGHT HONEYSUCKLE, WITH red fruit and non-serrated leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Upright Honeysuckle (Periclymenum Rectum), showing a more shrub-like growth habit with distinct pairs of berries.</image-desc>

It rises on its own trunk, needing no support. The leaves are like those of the commonly called Female Dogwood, but softer and less veined, hairy on both sides, and arranged in opposite pairs. In the same number, the flowers—sitting on one and the same stalk—burst forth from the leaf axils; they are a pale yellowish color, in the shape of the common Honeysuckle but smaller, with the upper petal bent backwards and fringed, and the lower one hanging down and narrower. The scent of the flowers is sweet, but the berries—which follow as twins hanging from a single stalk when the flowers fall, turning red as they mature—have a nauseating taste.

It is found in various places among thorns, in hedges, thickets, and shrubberies. It flowers in May.

<summary>This page describes various species of Jasmine and Honeysuckle, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for women's health and respiratory issues, and resolving taxonomic confusion between classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Jasmine, Sambach, Pavate Tree, Honeysuckle, Periclymenum, Caprifolium, medicinal oils, botanical taxonomy, Prospero Alpini, Carolus Clusius, Dioscorides</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of woody shrubs and climbing plants, specifically focusing on upright varieties of Honeysuckle (Periclymenum) and Bittersweet Nightshade (Glycypicros).</meta>

### UPRIGHT HONEYSUCKLE, with serrated leaves: with fruit not red, but black.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Periclymenum plant with serrated leaves and dark berries, showing the root system and branching stems.</image-desc>

This is much lower than the common variety: it has *leaves* that are more tender than the former, longer, and serrated <note>saw-toothed</note> around the edges. It also differs from it in that it has black *berries*, not red ones. The root of both is hard and woody. Furthermore, this is a rare find, an inhabitant of the Alps, and it flowers and ripens its seed along with the others.

To add something regarding the Powers of Honeysuckle <note>original: "Periclymeni"</note>, it strongly heats and dries, as is perceived from the very taste itself. It dries out moist and foul internal organs, heals <term>impetigo</term> <note>a contagious skin infection</note> and other foulness of the skin, consumes the spleen <note>reduces swelling of the spleen</note>, assists with difficulty breathing, brings about speed in childbirth, expels stones, cleanses the face, etc.

<column-break/>

### A CERTAIN ALPINE GROUND-HONEYSUCKLE: Bone-wood: Gesner’s Ground-cherry.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small woody shrub with opposite leaves and paired berries.</image-desc>

In its entire appearance it approaches the <term>Xylosteum</term> <note>literally "Bone-wood," likely Fly Honeysuckle</note>, four cubits high: with opposite branches, fragile, covered in a cinder-colored bark. The *leaves* are like the said Xylosteum, but much larger, pointed and hairy, especially underneath, and nowhere serrated, situated in opposite pairs. We shall soon depict and describe the *flowers*, as well as the *fruit*.

Gesner indeed concedes that the plant is related to Honeysuckle, but nevertheless thinks it should be called Mountain Ground-cherry, and certainly by a slight argument: namely, because it appears so to the inhabitants of the mountain rocks. It is called Xylosteum by some. However, in the *Adversaria* and by others, it is called the low Alpine *Ground-cherry*. The ancients made no mention of it.

---

### Flowers of the HONEYSUCKLE JUST MENTIONED, AND THE FOLLOWING.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration focusing on the flowering stems of the Periclymenum, showing tubular flowers and developing fruit.</image-desc>

The flowers of the Honeysuckle just mentioned are somewhat long, approaching the flowers of the Upright Honeysuckle, or Xylosteum, gaping with a wide mouth, reddish, sitting upon stalks placed opposite one another, long, arising from the armpits <note>axils</note> of the leaves. The *fruit* moreover is red, sometimes twin <note>paired</note>, marked as if with little eyes, on a long stalk, similar to a Cherry, full of unpleasant and bitter juice: and it contains within itself six, seven, or more white, broad grains <note>seeds</note>. We give here the flowers of the following plant, depicted in the second place.

<column-break/>

### UPRIGHT HONEYSUCKLE, WITH BLUE FRUIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Periclymenum variety with distinct berries and broad leaves.</image-desc>

It is of the same height as the Honeysuckle with the serrated leaf, but it has a somewhat thick stalk, rough and blackish, though purplish on the tender little branches. The *leaves* are arranged in opposite positions to one another, not serrated. The *flowers* are such as are depicted in the second place in the preceding table. The *fruit* consists of individual berries, hanging down on both sides between the leaves on a short stalk, equal to Gesner’s <term>Chamæmespilus</term> <note>Ground-medlar</note>, but a little longer, of a blue color, and full of a wine-like and somewhat acidic juice, containing many full seeds. The woody root spreads widely and is provided with many fibers. Some people diligently collect the fruit and store it for use in dyeing.

---

### SMALL PRUSSIAN HONEYSUCKLE, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing plant with terminal clusters of berries.</image-desc>

This elegant plant is also to be referred to the genera of Honeysuckle: it has little stems nine inches long, to which four, six, seven, and sometimes eight leaves adhere, situated opposite at intervals, ending in a sharp point, and provided with five ribs. From the hollows of the uppermost leaves, little branches come out, provided with two leaves arranged in the same way as on the stem, which bear four other leaves at the summit. From the middle of those little branches, a naked stalk without leaves comes out, on the top of which red berries grow, clinging together in a cluster, sought after by the Prussian peasants among whom it grows abundantly in maritime regions. The *flowers* have not yet been observed. The common sort of writers call it *Ground-honeysuckle* <note>original: "Chamæpericlymenum"</note>.

<column-break/>

### BITTERSWEET, OR SWEET-BITTER: German: *Je lenger se lieber*; French: *Doulce-amére*; Italian: *Dulcamera*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant (Bittersweet Nightshade) with lobed leaves and clusters of berries.</image-desc>

It puts forth woody shoots, two or three feet long, and almost trailing unless they are supported, greenish and somewhat purplish: they are angular, from which grow alternately the leaves of Garden Nightshade, dark green, on an inch-long stalk. The *flowers* are foul-smelling but quite pretty, purplish, or purplish-blue; these are succeeded by berries, of a scarlet color when ripe, of a somewhat long shape, soft, sticky, and of an unpleasant taste, full of small grains. The root is fibrous.

It loves watery and flooded places, and is found around ditches and trenches, leaning on hedges or other shrubs. The flowers come out in July: the berries become ripe in August. It heats and dries in the third degree; it cleanses and dissolves <note>digests/disperses humors</note>.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, moving from previous climbing plants to the various species of Ivy and the medicinal Smilax (Sarsaparilla) group.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

<margin>
**IVY**: To Serapion *Kuffus*: German *Epheuv*:
French *Lierre*: Italian *Hedera*: Spanish *Edera*.
</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common ivy plant (Hedera helix) with its characteristic lobed leaves and climbing stems.</image-desc>

Ivy is believed to be named *Hedera* by the Latins either because it "adheres" <note>Latin: *haereat*</note>, or because it seeks "high places" <note>Latin: *edita*</note>, or even from "eating" <note>Latin: *edendo*</note>: for as an intrusive lover of trees and walls, it finally demolishes, kills, and eats them away. The constraints of this space do not allow for the origins of the Greek name, nor is our discussion here concerning "Ground Ivy" <note>Glechoma hederacea</note>; but of that elsewhere.

According to Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note>, Ivy is manifold. He says some creeps along the ground, while others rise high: and of the tall kinds, many types are evident, but especially three: the White, the Black, and the third, the *Helix*: and each of those has several species. Dioscorides and Pliny establish these same primary genera, and Pliny even adds a distinction of sex. *More in the following.*

<column-break/>

### COMMON SMALLER IVY, FEMALE
->According to Pliny: Ground-ivy: Helix.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of ivy, showing clusters of berries and more rounded leaves.</image-desc>

With thinner and more compliant shoots, it creeps fixed to the ground and produces neither flower nor any fruit. There are several kinds of it, but three are most notable: one is herbaceous and green; another has white leaves; another is variegated.

Of the larger kind than we gave pictured before, which Pliny calls *Maya*, a triple variety is noted: for one is called white, which bears white fruit; another black, which bears black; and a third *Helix*, which bears none.

The White displays white clusters, or fruits, and sometimes even has white leaves: and between the middle of the leaves it sends out as if arms or tendrils, with which it tightly embraces trees so that it can hardly be separated: it has as many beginnings of roots as it has arms, by which, creeping up walls, it remains alive even if cut in several places. *Concerning the Black, shortly.*

---

### GREATER BLACK IVY, DIONYSIAS
->Also called Gold-fruited, and also Bacchic.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large ivy plant with prominent dark berries (Hedera nigra).</image-desc>

This is called Black and *Chrysocarpos* <note>Greek: "Gold-fruited"</note> because it bears fruit that is black or rivaling saffron. It is called *Dionysias* and *Bacchic* because it was believed to be under the protection of Father Bacchus <note>The god of wine, often depicted wearing an ivy crown</note>, and was first brought by him from India into Greece. The illustration is from Dalechamps, who says it is the most beautiful in appearance among its kin.

Black Ivy is common enough, and it creeps everywhere through walls and stone fences: and in forests, fields, and gardens it embraces even tall trees with its roots as if with fingers. It puts forth angular leaves, mostly triangular at first, then more round, hard, and shining with perpetual greenness: the flowers are small, and the berries are green at first, then black, clinging to long stalks like clusters of grapes. *More in the Outline Appendix of this.*

<column-break/>

### ROUGH BINDWEED: Germ. *Prickly* or *sharp Bindweed*: Fr. *Thorny Bindweed*: Ital. *Deer's Bramble*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Smilax aspera (rough bindweed) showing its heart-shaped leaves and prickly stems.</image-desc>

It is called simply *Smilax* by Theophrastus and Anguillara: but by almost all others [on account of the stings/prickles it has] it is called *Smilax aspera* <note>Rough Smilax</note>. However, the word *Smilax* is very ambiguous: for it is used for the Greater and Lesser Bindweed, for the bean-bearing Smilax, for the Smilax tree, for Sarsaparilla, Yew, Ash, and others. As also for the garden bean-bearing Smilax. Here our discussion is properly concerning the Rough Smilax, which is either more thorny and produces red or glowing-red fruits when ripe: or is not so bristling with thorns and has black fruit. It grows in the mountains of warmer regions, in rough and marshy places: and it flowers almost constantly. The leaves and fruit, on the authority of Dioscorides, have the power of an effective antidote.

---

### SARSA PARILLA, SALSA PARILLA, ZARZA
->parilla, Sparta parilla, Peruvian Smilax.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sarsaparilla plant, showing its long, fibrous root system and climbing habit.</image-desc>

Because of the similarity it has with Rough Smilax, the exotic plant which we depict was given these names by the Spanish and Portuguese. For to them *Sarza* or *Zarza* is a bramble, *Paria* is a vine, and *Parilla* a little vine, so that *Sarsa parilla* signifies a "small thorny vine."

We adopt the illustration of Lobelius, because the one of the dried plant which we keep is very poor. He says in his *Observations* that it has a leaf like Rough Smilax, but thorny, with twiggy intertwined shoots, bristling with hooked thorns, and a root intertwined in many places. He says a leaf of the "Robur" <note>Oak-like</note> type is found in Benzo. It grows in Peru and other regions of India <note>The Americas were often called the West Indies</note>, just as Rough Smilax grows in Europe.

<column-break/>

### ROUGH SMILAX OF THE ISLAND OF ZAKYNTHOS
->According to Alpinus. Sarsaparilla: Differences & Virtues.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a specific variety of Smilax from the island of Zakynthos.</image-desc>

Alpinus writes that Egyptian physicians commonly use this to cure the "Venereal plague" <note>Syphilis</note>. How much it differs from European Rough Smilax is shown by the knotless roots and the variety of the leaves.

Furthermore, Sarsaparilla, in its primary qualities, heats moderately: in its secondary, it opens [the pores/vessels] and draws out sweat: in its tertiary, it extinguishes the Venereal poison: it dispels wind <note>gas</note>, etc. It is established that one kind is thicker and another more slender: one darker and another whiter. It differs from Rough Smilax because it has knotless roots, not at all jointed, fibrous, pithy, very long, and splittable like a wicker branch, which are much different in Rough Smilax.

<keywords>Ivy, Hedera helix, Smilax aspera, Sarsaparilla, Bacchus, medicinal botany, syphilis treatments, Theophrastus, Pliny the Elder</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original: STIRPIVM</note>

<margin>
CHINA, CINA, CINNA, CHINNA, CHINEA, SCHIna, & China root: German: Chyna; French: Chine; Italian: China.
</margin>

It takes its name from China, a province of the East Indies bordering Scythia, where it grows in abundance; the Chinese themselves call it *Lampatam, Lampatan*, or *Lampaton*. It first began to become known after the year 1535 and gained authority under Emperor Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1519–1556), who famously used China root to treat his gout</note>, who was nearly the first of all to use this root with the greatest success, as the Asian Scythians of China attest.

Some distinguish two types: one *Western*, which is brought from the West Indies, namely New Spain <note>Mexico</note> and Peru, resembling the root of the larger Reed and considered by many to be a species of Reed. The other is *Eastern*, brought from the China region of the East Indies, as mentioned, which is referred to the Iris genera; more on this follows.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several knobby, tuberous roots of the China plant, showing a textured, bark-like surface.</image-desc>

### FALSE CHINA ROOT OF CLUSIUS: TSINAW.
<note>Clusius (Charles de l'Écluse) was a foundational 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, irregular, branched tuberous root with many nodes and small rootlets.</image-desc>

We are persuaded that this root is the same as the preceding one, which Clusius depicts and describes, having been sent to him from London because it had been brought from *Pvingandecaw*, or Virginia. Moreover, it is very similar to that which they call *Tsinaw*, from which they make bread when it is cut and ground.

Furthermore, in its active qualities, the root of the true China is very temperate; however, in dryness, it reaches the 2nd degree. It is of thin substance yet with some power to bind <note>astringent properties</note>, and a certain moisture of substance, such that men grow fat by its use. It dries out waste humors, but restores or at least preserves the nutritional ones. More follows beside the table.

### CLEMATIS, THE ATHRAGENE OF THEOPHRASTUS TO SOME:
German: *Lynen, Woldräben*; French: *Liferon*; Italian: *Vitalba*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Clematis plant with climbing stems, pinnate leaves, and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

Athragene, says Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note>, is a tree similar to the Wild Vine and Oenanthe, and like those trees, it is climbing. Dioscorides proposed Clematis under two headings: one he calls *Clematis*, the other *Clematitis*. We shall deal with Clematis later, but now with Clematitis.

It is so called because it puts forth *clemata*, that is, shoots or whips similar to vine branches, and like them, it climbs trees. Since various differences are recounted, we will first describe the broad-leaved Clematis, which is commonly referred to the Athragene of Theophrastus. It varies in the division of its leaves: for it is either entire, which we depict here, or jagged, of which more follows.

<column-break/>

### PEAR-SHAPED SPURIOUS CHINA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of three pear-shaped or oblong tuberous roots with horizontal ridges.</image-desc>

This illustration of ours is from a root we possess, very similar to the China root of the Apothecaries, so that it is not easy to discern in what way it differs. Since, however, there is a great agreement with the Spurious China of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist</note>, we have joined them both.

The illustration of the true China placed before was from the root itself, to which we also added a part from Lobelius: as well as a leaf with a thorny stalk from the Appendix of the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the Historia Generalis Plantarum</note>, the figure of which, as he says, was drawn from very fresh China.

The best China root, which alone should be used, is heavy, solid, full, not at all decayed, and tasteless in flavor; the white-reddish is better, and the black is better than both.

### SPURIOUS CHINA WITH THE APPEARANCE OF ACORUS, by Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a long, segmented, rhizome-like root resembling Acorus (sweet flag).</image-desc>

These roots brought from Guinea, not unlike China and like it lacking all taste, were sold in its place. They first became known in Toulouse and were said to be dug up from neighboring places. Lobelius in his *Adversaria* calls it *Aquitanian Acorus* and *Toulouse Acorus*, but in his *Icons* <note>illustrations</note> he calls it *Spurious China with the appearance of Acorus*; Caspar Bauhin also mentions it in his *Phytopinax*.

To add something regarding the use of the genuine China root: It thins, dries, induces sweating, resists rot, strengthens the liver, assists with dropsy <note>edema/swelling</note>, heals malignant internal organs, and is held in high regard for difficult and chronic diseases; but it contributes most of all to the Venereal Disease <note>Syphilis</note>, performing miraculous effects therein. The Arabs, Turks, and Persians call it *Chob-chini* <note>original: "Cophochie"</note>.

### BROAD-LEAVED TOOTHED CLEMATITIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Clematis variety with broader, serrated (dentate) leaves and flowering clusters.</image-desc>

The broad-leaved Clematis abounds with branches somewhat like vines, thick, angular, hairy, and reddish, and flexible with a compliant bend: the leaves are in fives, rivaling Bittersweet, sometimes entire, sometimes toothed and fringed [as we depict here], attached by a twisting middle stalk by which it climbs, entangled in neighboring shrubs in place of tendrils: the flowers sit in clusters on hoary stalks, sweet-smelling, white: consisting of four or five leaves, the center of which is occupied by a mossy tuft of pale stamens: the flowers are followed by several berries bearded with a downy, winged fuzz: the root is somewhat thick, brown, and provided with fibers.

It grows wild everywhere along the edges of fields among briars and thorns, and flowers in July.

<keywords>China root, Smilax china, Clematis, medicinal botany, syphilis treatments, Charles V, Clusius, Lobelius, Virginia, Guinea</keywords>

# IMAGES AND SHADOW-DRAWINGS

P 3

### SPANISH CLEMATIS, ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.
<note>original: "CLEMATIS BÆTICA" — Bætica was the Roman name for the region of Andalusia in southern Spain.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with small, bell-shaped flowers and tendrils, showing detailed leaf structure and root system.</image-desc>

This plant is very similar to the Clematis in form and temperament; for this reason, Clusius—who found it in various places in Andalusia and nowhere else—rightly numbered it among the Clematis species.

However, Gesner, Lonicer, Tabernaemontanus, and Gerard have written about the Clematis in a confused manner. To Dodoens, it is *another species of Cyclamen*; to Lonicer, Turner, and others, it is *Black Bryony* <note>original: "Binia nigra"</note> and *Black Vine*, but incorrectly so. To Ruellius, it is the *Viburnum Herb* and the *Viorna* of the Gauls, specifically because it binds together bundles of branches as if with a cord. According to his opinion, Pliny believed this to be the *Taminian Grape*. It is used for binding bundles, just like willow twigs and other ties. Its taste, however, is burning and sharp, which proves its hot potency.

### UPRIGHT CLEMATIS OR VIRGIN'S BOWER
#### white: known to some as the Flame of Jupiter.
<note>original: "Flammula Iouis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright plant with clusters of small four-petaled flowers at the top and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

The shoots of this plant require no support; by their own strength, they rise to a height of two or three cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>. The leaves, flowers, and its stinging potency are the same as in the preceding plant. It is found to be of two kinds: one has reddish shoots, as well as reddish leaf veins and stalks; the other has green shoots and leaf stalks and produces its flowers later.

It is very rare, except in the felled forests of Austria and Pannonia <note>Pannonia was a Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, along the banks of the rivers flowing into the Danube. It heats and dries in the third degree, or, as some prefer, even the fourth: this is sufficiently clear from the various effects of the waters, oils, and other substances extracted from it.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED PURPLE CLEMATIS
#### climbing.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with large, multi-petaled (double) flowers and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

This belongs to the genus of climbing blue-purple Clematis, but of a different form, specifically with a multiple texture <note>Referring to the "double" or multi-layered petals.</note>. The flower is blue, purple, and a diluted flesh-color; it blooms in June and July. On the outside, the flowers are covered with a greyish down. It is commonly labeled *Double Flesh-colored Foreign Clematis* and *Double-flowered Blue Clematis*.

<column-break/>

### CLIMBING CLEMATIS OR VIRGIN'S BOWER,
#### white and thin-leaved.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine with delicate, narrow leaves and small star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This plant is weak and only strives upward when supported by nearby objects; yet it does not do this with the help of any tendrils, but rather embraces hedges with its leaf stalks. It has ribbed, green, and jointed shoots; the leaves are similar to the leaves of the Upright Virgin's Bower, but shorter and narrower than those previously mentioned. The flowers are white and fragrant, which, with their stinging potency, inflame the lips if they touch them; the seed becomes remarkable for its feathery crest.

It is called the *Other True Clematis* or *Ambuxum*. To some, it is *Epigetis* and *Silicastrum*; but to most, it is *Virgin's Bower* <note>original: "Flammula"</note>, *Virgin's Bower needing support*, and *Creeping Virgin's Bower*. It is called *Flammula* (Little Flame) because when crushed, it raises blisters like a flame; for it is exceedingly hot and sharp. It blooms and ripens its fruit later than the others.

### CLIMBING CLEMATIS OR VIRGIN'S BOWER
#### with purple and blue flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with large, single, four-petaled flowers and broad leaves.</image-desc>

This is more elegant than the common Virgin's Bower, with leaves approaching closer to the *Athragene* <note>A Greek name for a climbing plant, likely another Clematis species.</note>, but varying playfully, sometimes divided, sometimes whole, etc. Its chief grace lies in the purple or blue flowers, which are also recommended for their sweet scent.

It delights in places exposed to the sun, but not entirely arid; it thrives better in rich and not unwatered soil. In Spain and Italy, it grows spontaneously near hedges and the edges of fields. It blooms in July and August, and perfects its seed in September.

### BLUE CLEMATIS WITH SERRATED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with serrated, compound leaves and a single large flower at the top of a long stalk.</image-desc>

This plant is about a span and a half high <note>A "palmus" or palm/span is about 3-4 inches; "sesquipalmaris" suggests about 5-6 inches.</note>, with several long stalks, upon which leaves with frequent divisions are seated in a triple-joined arrangement, as in the Crane’s-bill-leaved Anemone. The flower sits on a very long stalk, composed of only four petals, of a dark purplish color. Caspar Bauhin, who described it from a dried specimen, did not see the seed or the root. It grows on the higher cliffs of Mount Baldo <note>A mountain in the Italian Alps famous for its botanical diversity.</note>.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Clematis and "Flammula" (Virgin's Bower), detailing their climbing habits, medicinal "burning" properties, and geographical locations ranging from Spain to the Alps.</summary>
<keywords>Clematis, Virgin's Bower, Flammula, Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal plants, botany, Mount Baldo, climbing plants, Spanish flora</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### UPRIGHT HUNGARIAN CLEMATIS, with a blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Clematis pannonica surrecta, showing a plant with upright stems, opposite ovate leaves, and bell-shaped flowers at the terminal ends.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational Flemish botanist.</note> depicts this plant, which grows wild in various places along the banks of the Danube, describing it at length: It blooms in May and June, and the seed is ripe in August. It grew for us at Montbéliard in the S.P. garden <note>Likely the garden of the Duke of Württemberg at Montbéliard.</note> from seed, and flowered the following year in June and July. Its temperament is the same as the other Clematis species, and its uses are the same.

### GREATER LAUREL-LIKE CLEMATIS OR PERIWINKLE, with blue and white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Clematis daphnoides (Pervinca major), showing trailing stems with large, broad, opposite leaves and five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

This Periwinkle is larger in all its parts than the common variety: it is pleasant because of the doubling and variety of its flowers. Furthermore, it is well known that Periwinkle delights in woody, shaded tracts and thickets, as well as the margins of fields; it is evergreen, and blooms most especially in March and April. It is also cultivated in gardens.

Apollinaris <note>An ancient medical authority</note> claims it is hot and dry in the third degree: but Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), famous physician and botanist</note> says more accurately that it cools and dries, and moreover strengthens and restrains. Whence the leaves, held in the mouth, or tied to the temples, or wrapped around the neck, check the flow of blood erupting from the nostrils: the green leaves tied to the thighs restrain the abundance of the menses and assist in conception.

### SECAMONE RELATED TO DOGBANE, with a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Apocyno affinis secamone, showing a climbing plant with slender stems, narrow lanceolate leaves, and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

It is a creeping plant, leaping higher and entwining itself around other trees: *with long, hard leaves: it bears white flowers, and long, thick pods, full of white down and small seeds. From the herb, a yellow and burning juice flows, which, when dried (according to Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini (1553–1617), who studied Egyptian plants</note>), the Egyptians say powerfully purges thin humors.*

Guillandinus suspects it to be the *Apocynum* of Dioscorides <note>original: "Apocynum Dioscoridis"</note>: to Clusius (in his Spanish flora) it is another species of the second or narrow-leafed *Apocynum*. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax*, it is *Apocynum 3. with a narrow Willow leaf.* It does not grow wild in our regions, but is kept only in the more cultivated gardens.

<column-break/>

### LAUREL-LIKE CLEMATIS, PERIWINKLE: German: Ingrein, Wintergrein: French: Pervauche, Italian: Pervinca.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Clematis daphnoides (Vinca pervinca), showing a smaller variety of periwinkle with trailing stems and smaller elliptical leaves.</image-desc>

Thus far we have dealt with the climbing Clematis; now we shall speak of the creeping kind. It is called *Clematis* because it has vine-like shoots, as noted above: but because it has Laurel-like leaves, they name it *Daphnoides* <note>from the Greek 'daphne' for laurel</note>: and finally *Vinca* and *Pervinca* <note>Periwinkle</note>, because creeping on the ground, in the manner of a bond <note>original: "vinculi modo"</note>, it overcomes <note>original: "vincit"</note> neighboring things and is tied to them. It varies with blue, purple, violet, or white flowers: and those are either single or double. It is commonly established as two types, *Greater and Lesser.* We depict the *Lesser and Common* variety here; concerning its Location, Time, and Virtues, see the side of the following table.

### DOGBANE, DOG-CABBAGE: German: Hundskraut, Hundsköl: French: Apoynon: Italian: Apoyno.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Apocynum (Cynocrambe), showing a plant with broad, veined leaves and clusters of small flowers, appearing somewhat shrub-like.</image-desc>

*Apocynon* <note>from the Greek 'apo' (away) and 'kyon' (dog), meaning poisonous to dogs</note>, according to Dioscorides, is a shrub consisting of long twigs, flexible and almost impossible to break: the leaves are like Ivy, etc.: the fruit is like Beans: the pod extends to the length of a finger, with small, hard seeds inside.

However, many plants are given the name of *Apocynum*, the series of which we shall review here in order: and first indeed *Apocynum or Periploca, with long leaves and purplish flowers.* It is of two kinds, *Creeping and Climbing*, which we depict here: it is also called *Periploca* [as if "embracing around"], because entwining itself around neighboring stakes, it embraces them. We have seen it at Padua and Montbéliard. It grew for us from seed.

### DOGBANE WITH ROUNDER LEAF, with a flower fading from white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Apocynum folio rotundiore, showing a plant with more rounded leaves and clusters of pale flowers on long stalks.</image-desc>

This plant is a short shrub, not winding itself around its neighbors: but relying on its own strength it stands upright, divided into many branches, with ash-colored bark: *the leaves are born in pairs opposite each other at every node, similar to Ivy leaves, not angular, moderately pointed, thick and soft, clinging to stalks of one to six inches: and from their axils flowers spring forth in abundance resting on long stalks, somewhat mimicking an umbel, white, woven from five oblong petals.*

We have cultivated it in the S.P. garden at Montbéliard.
