<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES</header>

# BROAD-LEAVED CLASPING DOGBANE. The Alexandrian Beidelfar of Alpinus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with broad, heart-shaped leaves and clusters of small flowers, showing its twining habit around a central stalk.</image-desc>

With long, thin, numerous green and jointed shoots, it climbs whatever is nearest, embracing those things with manifold twists and a tight bond. The leaves are like Ivy, soft, of a somewhat ashen color, and swollen with a milky juice (as are the shoots). Many flowers come forth from the crook of the leaves, arranged in umbels <note>umbrella-like clusters</note>, white, small, and consisting of five petals. The pod is full of much down and fluff, in which is hidden the flat, grayish-brown seed. The roots are twiggy and fibrous, and most troublesome in their creeping habit. Is it perhaps a kind of Scammony, as some please to think? We had it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, where it survived one winter but perished thereafter.

<column-break/>

# MONTPELIER OR VALENTINE SCAMMONY: The 4th Broad-leaved Dogbane of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering vine with pointed, opposite leaves and small star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Upon long, thin, tough, two-cubit-long creeping shoots that embrace everything nearby, the leaves grow opposite one another; they are broad, thick, smooth, whitish, and at the stalk (which is an inch long) they are sickle-shaped, ending in a sharp point, and pregnant with milky juice. The flowers are clustered, star-shaped, small, and white; the seed is angular; the root is long and fibrous.

It is the *Volubilis marina* <note>Sea Bindweed</note> of the Pharmacists. To Clusius, it is a kind of Bindweed called Scammony. It is very frequent in the maritime regions of the Kingdom of Valencia and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and it flowers in August. Indeed, they are accustomed to adulterate legitimate scammony so exactly with the juice of this herb and Colophony <note>pine resin</note> that it can scarcely be distinguished.

---

# SYRIAN AND EGYPTIAN DOGBANE, The Alexandrian Beidelfar of Alpinus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, broad leaves and a thick central stem, showing a cluster of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Beidelfar, according to Alpinus, grows in places near Alexandria that are perpetually damp. Christopher Weigel <note>original: "Christophorus Vvelsius"</note> reports that it also grows around Jericho, by the river Jordan. Truly, because it possesses characteristics in its seed, flowers, and other parts not unlike the Dogbane, we have deemed it should be numbered among the Dogbanes. We have seen it, moreover, in pots at Stuttgart and Strasbourg. What Alpinus proclaims concerning his Beidelfar we leave to be sought from his own writings, intending here to treat only of the powers of our own variety. Dioscorides records no use for it for the human body; indeed, he writes that it is fatal to quadrupeds. Pliny also records it as a poison to quadrupeds, but beneficial to humans; and on the contrary, Galen says it is a poison to humans: *let the matter be considered dangerous*.

<column-break/>

# ASCLEPIAS, SWALLOW-WORT, TAME-POISON: Germ. Schvvalbenvvurtz: Gall. Dompte venin: It. Vincetossico.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Asclepias plant, showing its upright growth, opposite lanceolate leaves, and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

What the *Asclepias* of the ancients was, and whether it be known to the Moderns or not, we shall weigh and demonstrate in the Appendix. The learned shall judge; however, we shall in the meantime label the *Vincetoxicum* <note>Tame-poison</note> of the Herbalists as *Asclepias*. It took the name of Asclepias from Aesculapius (called Asclepius by the Greeks), the credited inventor of Medicine, according to that saying:
> Medicine is my invention, etc.

They named it *Hirundinaria* <note>Swallow-wort</note> because its open pods, with their white flying down, are almost similar to a flying swallow. It is called *Vincetoxicum* <note>Tame-poison</note> because there is in it a remarkable power against poisons. Various differences of it are observed: for in some, such as the one we depict here, the flowers are whitish; in others, however, they are black. And there is a certain Indian variety, another from Crete, etc.

---

# ASCLEPIAS, SWALLOW-WORT, TAME-POISON, with the black flower of certain authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Asclepias with darker flowers and similar leaf structure to the previous entry.</image-desc>

By these names Mattioli, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Clusius, Gerard, Lobel, C. Bauhin, and almost all others record this plant. To Dodonaeus, it is another species of *Vincetoxicum*; to Lobel, it is also the *Lesser Periploca*. However, Columna rebukes us who determine it to be an *Asclepias*, and he numbers it among the Dogbanes.

We had it in the garden at Montbéliard from seed; it flowered in July, and in August it bore pods. Elsewhere, both types of Swallow-wort grow on high and sandy mountains and forests, and also on some cliffs and in uncultivated and deserted places nearby: it is frequent enough at Basel on the mountain near Lörrach.

<column-break/>

# INDIAN OR VIRGINIAN ASCLEPIAS. The Cretan Asclepias of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-leaved Asclepias variety, showing a prominent seed pod (follicle) split open to reveal the seeds and silky down.</image-desc>

The plant we depict here was first expressed in an image and described as *Virginian Asclepias* by Gerard. Clusius describes the *Cretan Asclepias*, to which he attributes leaves and seeds similar to the leaves and seeds of the common variety; but he says some are shorter, thicker, and endowed with a cleft point, etc.

As for what pertains to the powers and use of Asclepias: Mattioli makes it moderately warm and dry. It drives away all poison, especially that of a mad dog or poisonous animals, before it reaches the heart. The root, used in a drink or in decoctions, provokes the menses; and in general, it performs all that the Long Birthwort does. Indeed, we have shown in our *Great History* that it is effective against the Plague and Dropsy by certain experiment.

<summary>This page describes various species of Dogbane (Apocynum) and Swallow-wort (Asclepias/Vincetoxicum), detailing their physical characteristics, climbing habits, and medicinal uses as antidotes to poison. It highlights the disagreements between classical authorities like Galen and Pliny regarding their toxicity to humans.</summary>

# OF PLANTS

### OLEANDER OR ROSE BAY: German: Oleanderbaum, Laurel-rose; French: Oleandre; Italian: Oleandro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Nerium (Oleander) plant showing its long, lance-shaped leaves and root structure.</image-desc>

Pliny and Dioscorides bestow the names *Nerium* and *Rhododaphne* <note>original: "Rhododaphnes"; literally "Rose-Laurel"</note> upon this plant, which Dioscorides says is of common knowledge here. More recent authors have also retained these names; and although Pliny writes that it had no Latin name, they devised two, calling it *Oleander* and *Rose Laurel*. However, the illustrations provided by many are unsuitable, especially those of Mattioli, Lonicer, and Tragus. The name *Nerium* was perhaps given to it by the Nereid Nymphs; but it is called *Rhododendron* as if it were a "Tree Rose," and *Rhododaphne* from its rose-like flowers and laurel-like leaves.

It is of two kinds, namely with a red flower and with a white flower. Dioscorides is the authority that it grows in orchards, maritime places, and near rivers. More on this follows.

### THE FRUIT OF THE OLEANDER IN THE SHAPE OF A POD, AN EXOTIC FRUIT CALLED KAYE BAKAS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a long, curved seed pod (siliqua) of the Nerium plant.</image-desc>

Abdala, a native of Gujarat, said that this exotic fruit brought from the Indies was called *Kaye baka*, as reported by Clusius, who described it at length.

To add something regarding the powers of the Oleander: Dioscorides and Pliny say the leaves of the Oleander are poison to four-footed animals, but for man they are a protection against serpents if drunk in wine with added Rue. Galen, on the contrary, writes that Oleander taken into the body is destructive to both cattle and men, but used outwardly it has the power of dispersing <term>digesting; in early medicine, this refers to the breaking down or "ripening" of tumors or swellings</term>. Recent authors busy themselves trying to settle this dispute; we have advised that the use of a doubtful medicine should be omitted.

### BLACK VINE, OR BLACK BRYONY TO SOME: The Thamnus of Pliny, with the leaf of a Cyclamen.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and tendrils, identified as Black Vine or Black Bryony.</image-desc>

Black Bryony is similar in all respects to the White, except that the berries turn black when ripe, and the root is blackish on the outside; also, the White is smaller and does not spread its little vines as widely.

Both climb fences, thickets, and shrubs: yet not by wrapping themselves around like other climbing plants, but by grasping nearby things with their little tendrils <note>original: "clauiculis"; literally "little keys," a common term for vine tendrils</note>, and entwining and implicating themselves in various ways.

The *White* is found in France, Italy, Swabia, the Rhine region, Switzerland, and Belgium, everywhere along roads and at the edges of fields. Hesse, Saxony, Westphalia, Pomerania, and Meissen produce the *Black*, in which places, according to Cordus, the White does not grow. Spring provides the flowers of both, but Autumn provides the grapes. <margin>The narrowness of this space does not contain their powers.</margin>

<column-break/>

### A TREE WITH THE APPEARANCE OF OLEANDER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small tree or shrub with flowers and a bulbous root, described as having the appearance of Nerium.</image-desc>

Lobelius in his *Adversaria* and *Icones*, and Tabernaemontanus, also list a "tree with the appearance of Oleander" and a "tree similar to Oleander": C. Bauhin, however, says it is the third *Nerion* in the *History of Lyon*, in which <unclear>the text is</unclear> transposed.

The Oleander, which is found frequently enough and spontaneously in various places in Italy and France, grows most abundantly in the <unclear>coastal</unclear> tract of Liguria, between Nice and Genoa. We have also observed it cultivated in gardens in Padua, Venice, and Montpellier; and there it flowers in May and June, but brings forth its pods in August.

### WHITE VINE, BRYONY: German: Hundskurbi; French: Coleuvre, Colubrine; Italian: Vua bianca, Bryonia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the White Bryony showing its lobed leaves, flowers, and climbing habit.</image-desc>

Bryony—which all writers except Brunfels and Simon of Genoa admit as the *White Vine* of Dioscorides, besides the one called "wild"—is of two kinds, namely the White Bryony and the Black Bryony: and the White is either spotted or not spotted.

It climbs and overcomes fences, thickets, and shrubs, not like other climbing plants by wrapping itself around, but by grasping all nearby things with its little tendrils, and entwining and implicating itself in various ways.

The Black is similar in all respects to the White: it is only smaller, nor does it spread its little vines so widely, and it has a blackish root and berries that turn black upon maturity. They flower in May.

### MECHOACAN: WHITE RHUBARB: White Mechoacan Bryony: Blackish Mechoacan Bryony, or Jalap.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Mechoacan plant (likely Ipomoea jalapa) showing its large root and climbing vine.</image-desc>

Mechoacan became known to our people in the last century of our ancestors. It takes its name from the province <note>original: "insula"; though the text says island, Mechoacán is a region in Mexico</note> which the Spaniards call Mechoacán. By the natives, however, it is named *Chicohic*. There are those who call it *White Rhubarb*, others *American Scammony*, others *Bryony*, since it seems very similar: but they do so by a great error, as the shape, color, and taste of both the leaves and the cross-sectioned root clearly refute them. Monardes identifies three types from their place of birth: one from the said Mechoacán; another from Nicaragua and Quito, which he says is the best; and finally a third, a wild type which grows on the promontory of St. Helena. Practitioners and scholars <note>original: "Sophiastę"</note> know its powers.

<summary>This page describes the Oleander (Nerium), noting its toxicity and various names, alongside descriptions of White and Black Bryony and the medicinal Mechoacan root from the Americas.</summary>
<keywords>Oleander, Rhododendron, Bryony, Mechoacan, medicinal plants, toxicity, New World botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Monardes</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### HOPS: German: Hopfen; Belgian: Hoppe; French: du Houblon; Italian: Lupolo, Bruscandolo.

#### MALE HOPS

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hop plant (Humulus lupulus) showing its climbing vine structure and leaves.</image-desc>

The climbing Hops <note>original: "Anadendras Lupulus"</note>, being weak by itself, easily follows the roots or nearest supports it has seized. It rises upward not by the help of colors—of which it has none—but by its twisting, rough, angular, purplish, and hollow shoots, clinging to its stakes with a tenacious embrace; otherwise, it is scarcely able to lift itself from the ground.

Some distinguish it into the Cultivated and the Wild; the latter grows of its own accord and differs from the other only in size, having smaller, thinner, and fewer cones. Others distinguish it into Male and Female: they call "Male" that which has sterile flowers, and "Female" that which has pod-like fruit. It is a marvel, however, that the one which flowers does not bear fruit, and the one which bears seed or fruit does not flower.

### HOLY CHARLES: CARLO SANCTO: The root against poisons called Carlo Sancto.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, tuberous root with small stems emerging from the top.</image-desc>

It is similar to Hops and wraps itself around poles in that manner; if these are lacking, it spreads and scatters upon the ground. The leaves are also similar to Hops, green in color but darker, with a heavy scent. It bears neither flower nor fruit. The root has a thick head from which other roots arise the thickness of a finger, whitish in color. The bark, which is easily separated and is the part used, has a bitter taste and an aromatic smell. It grows in the most temperate places of the province of Michoacán <note>A region in Mexico</note>; it is hot and dry in the second degree, and is useful for various things, but especially against poisons. <margin>According to Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax*, this is the third Michoacán Hop; in his *Phytopinax*, it is the Hop-like plant of Michoacán.</margin>

### SMALL BINDWEED: The IASIONE OF THE ANCIENTS, Helxine Cissampelos: German & Belgian: Klein Winde; French: Petit Liseron; Italian: Vilucchio minore.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Bindweed plant with heart-shaped leaves and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

The *Iasione* of Theophrastus and Pliny appears to Gotopio, Gesner, Lobel, and several other learned men to be nothing other than the Small Bindweed, which in the judgment of the learned is the *Helxine* of Dioscorides [not the one called Pellitory, but the Ivy-like one]. It is a plant having leaves similar to Ivy but smaller, with long branches with which it embraces whatever support it happens upon. However, Hieronymus Bock <note>original: "Tragus"</note> denies this, stating that the plant called *Orthauchen* by Theophrastus is "Quinsy" and the "Plague of Herbs." By some, it is also named *Cymbalaria*, like the Great Bindweed, and by others, "Small Scammony."

It varies in the color of the flower: either entirely snow-white, or completely purple, or a middle ground between the two and variegated with stripes. It flowers at the same time as the larger variety and likewise grows in the same places, but sometimes also in neglected fields, where it is troublesome to crops in rainy weather.

<column-break/>

#### FEMALE HOPS

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a female Hop plant with prominent cone-like strobiles (hops).</image-desc>

There are those who believe this was unknown to the Ancients; however, we consider it to be the *Smilax aspera* of Dioscorides, and the *Lupus* or *Lupulus Salictarius* <note>Willow-wolf</note> of Pliny, and that Mesue included it under the genus of twining plants. Leonhart Fuchs writes that it is called *Bryon* by the more recent Greeks, from its similarity to Bryony; it is called *Lupus salictarius* because it climbs willows, and in the Italian countryside *Bruscandula*, as if it were "climbing Bryon," and by some *Humulus*, by others *Lupus septuntium*. Manardus writes that the "philosophers of the East" <note>original: "Tosophis"</note> also call it *Habiola* and *Habilla*.

The wild variety abounds everywhere in hedges and flourishes in thickets and the margins of damp meadows. The cultivated variety is the strength of the Northerners, who diligently cultivate vast tracts planted with Hops for their beers. Furthermore, it cools moderately, restrains the heat of the blood, opens the spleen, promotes urine, cures jaundice, etc. Indeed, the fresh young shoots of spring are not only pleasant in food, but when eaten they purge the blood, loosen the belly, promote urine, and free the liver and spleen from obstructions.

### SMOOTH SMILAX, GREAT BINDWEED: German: glat Winde; Belgian: Winde; French: Liseron, Liset, Campanettes; Italian: Vilucchio maggiore.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis or Calystegia sepium) with large arrow-shaped leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Having dealt sufficiently with Rough Smilax, we must now treat the Smooth variety. What this plant actually is is sharply disputed among writers. We have weighed the opinions and foundations of everyone in our *Great History*; here, however, until something certain is decided on this matter, we shall label it Great Bindweed. This plant is known by the common name "Bindweed" <note>original: "Convolvulus"</note> because it climbs trees and entwines itself around them; it is called "Smooth Smilax" because it lacks rough thorns. Mesue calls it the Great Twining plant, *Lassaria*, and "Rope of the Trees"; among others, it has obtained the name White Bellflower because of the shape of its flowers.

It grows everywhere through thickets and hedges and loves cultivated places. It flowers in Summer and produces seed in Autumn. It is moderately hot, but dry in the 2nd degree. It dissolves, matures, cleanses, opens, etc.

### HELXINE WITH TRIANGULAR POINTED SEED, black: German: Schuvarts Winde; French: Liseron noir.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Black Bindweed (Fallopia convolvulus) showing its twining habit and small flowers.</image-desc>

This plant also seizes whatever is nearest and climbs with a twisting revolution, using no tendrils but its own little vines, many of which it sends out from a thick, many-forked root; these are a palm's breadth, a cubit, or a cubit and a half long, and somewhat reddish. At their joints, on long stalks, grow individual triangular leaves like those of Orach, somewhat reddish. The small, whitish flowers cling together in clusters arising from the hollows of the leaf stalks; the seed that follows is triangular, pointed, and black.

It grows in the fields of cultivated places, among vines and hedges. It flowers in May, but swells with seed in June. Is it the *Centunculus* of Pliny? Or the *Cussus* of Serapion? More on this at the side of the following table.

It also introduces "Carlo Sancto," a medicinal root from the New World used as an antidote to poison.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of climbing plants, specifically focusing on various species of Bindweed (Convolvulus) and their international origins.</meta>

### BEAUTIFUL FOREIGN BINDWEED,
### with Betony leaves and purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with heart-shaped, serrated leaves (resembling Betony) and trumpet-shaped flowers, twining around a vertical stake.</image-desc>

The botanist Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational figure in modern botany</note> named this plant *Convolvulus* because of the little vines with which it entangles itself in neighboring shrubs or herbs. He confesses he does not know which plant described by the Ancients this refers to, unless it is the *lasione* mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny. In the works of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, it is called the *Bindweed with the appearance of Scammony*; in Tabernaemontanus, it is the *Lesser Scammony*.

Clusius writes that it grows in many places in Spain, especially near the Tagus River in rich soil, and that it flowers in March and April. We ourselves have seen it in Montpellier and Basel.

Furthermore, Gesner says that the recently described *Helxine* <note>Parietaria or a similar climber</note> is a plant similar to Bindweed, except for the flower. To him, as well as to Ruellius and Tragus, it seems to be that pest of the crops which writers call *Leontobotan* <note>Lion's herb</note>, and the French call *Tania* or *Tigne* <note>Moth or blight</note>; let the experts judge.

### BLUE BINDWEED: INDIAN GRAIN:
### The "Nil" of some Arabs: The Pest of Asia: French: Blue Bindweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Convolvulus (Morning Glory) with large cordate leaves and a prominent funnel-shaped flower, climbing a support.</image-desc>

With twisting, woolly vines, it seizes everything nearby and strives upward, making it very suitable for topiary frameworks. Regarding this plant, Serapio <note>An Arabic medical scholar</note> says: *It has*, that is, *Nil*, which is *Indian Grain*, etc. There are also other species of Bindweed which are referred to the *Nil* of Avicenna: one is rough with small spines, and the other is without them. There is also the Mechoacan Nil and the American Scammony. However, by most authors, this plant is called *Blue Bindweed* and the *Arabian Nil*; by some, the *Blue Pothos* of Theophrastus; by others, the *Volubilis* or the "downy plant" of Mesue. Because it flowers most powerfully at night and closes at the rising of the Sun, it is commonly called *Fior di notte* <note>Flower of the night</note>.

### INDIAN BELLFLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering vine with ivy-like lobed leaves and large bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This plant is very similar to the Blue Bindweed called the Arabian Nil. It climbs high with twisting, hairy, reddish shoots that wind around poles. The leaves are like Ivy or Cyclamen, pointed—as they first appear in the Arabian Nil—and they are sickle-shaped, hairy above and below, clinging to a reddish, hairy stalk that is longer than the leaf itself. The bell-shaped flowers sit in a cup <term>calyx: the green outer part of a flower</term> divided into five hairy, blackish segments; several flowers are usually joined together on a stalk emerging from the leaves. It is called the *Indian Bindweed with violet flowers* in the Eystettensis <note>The Hortus Eystettensis, a famous 1613 florilegium</note> and the *Purple-violet Indian Bellflower* by the Bry brothers.

<column-break/>

### GROUND BINDWEED:
### The smallest Bindweed of some: Pliny’s Cantabrica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, spreading plant with small, narrow leaves and multiple small flowers.</image-desc>

Various plants are given the name of Pliny’s *Cantabrica*, among which we believe the one we depict here is the *Ground Bindweed*. In the works of Lobel, it is the *Smallest Bindweed with Lavender or Toadflax leaves*. It has many small stalks; the root is thick, woody, and blackish. The stems are reed-like, a span or sometimes a cubit long, hairy, upright, and quite strong. The leaves are narrow, oblong, and hairy. The flowers at the ends of the branches are commonly purplish, and more rarely white, shaped like a small basket. It loves a warm climate and soil; it flowers in May, June, and July, and is frequent in Provence, Spain, and Portugal along the dry edges of sown fields. Perhaps it is the *Lesser Stamminium* of Pliny.

### THE BINDWEED CALLED "GOOD NIGHT,"
### with a large, white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vine with large, broad leaves and a very large, open white flower. Two small round seeds or fruits are shown separately below.</image-desc>

At its first sprouting, it produces two leaves similar to the emerging Indian Bellflower (mentioned above), but slightly larger and thicker. Furthermore, many stems emerge from a single root of this plant, which surround fixed stakes or neighboring plants with many spirals. It is like the *Smilax aspera* <note>Rough Bindweed or Sarsaparilla</note>, having similar leaves but larger and softer; the stems also contain some hooked prickles, like the *Smilax*, but fewer and less harsh. It opens large, white flowers with a moderate central disc; these open in the morning and immediately wither at night, from which it seems to have received the name *Buenas noches* <note>Good night</note>, the phrase with which the Spanish are accustomed to greet one another in the evening. It is usually brought from the West Indies and the Canary Islands.

### EGYPTIAN FIVE-LEAVED BINDWEED,
### of Caspar Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with deeply lobed, palmate leaves (five lobes) and a funnel-shaped flower.</image-desc>

It has thin, jointed, smooth vines. From each joint, a leaf emerges on a long, very thin stalk; the leaf is divided into five narrow, somewhat long segments, and sometimes one or the other of the lower segments is split in two, with a thin, soft prickle sitting on each segment. Above the leaf's origin, an equally thin stalk, two or three inches long and bare, rises up to support a large purple-blue flower, shaped like other Bindweeds. The seed has not been seen. In Caspar Bauhin’s *Prodromus*, it is also called the *Bindweed with jagged or five-lobed leaves*.

<summary>This page describes various species of climbing plants in the Convolvulus family, detailing their physical characteristics, naming conventions across different cultures (Arabic, Spanish, French), and their geographical origins ranging from Europe to the West Indies and Egypt.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SCAMMONY AND SCAMMONIUM; Likewise called *Scammonia* and *Scammonium* by the Germans, Belgians, French, and Italians: Syrian Scammony, with the flower of a Bindweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scammony plant (Convolvulus scammonia) showing its climbing vines, arrow-shaped leaves, and funnel-shaped flowers, with a detailed root system.</image-desc>

Scammony, as Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), a German botanist famous for his dispensatory</note> rightly notes, is the plant from which the liquid *Scammonium* <note>The medicinal resin or juice</note> is derived. Those who call it a tree are in error; for it is not a tree, nor a shrub, but an herb. It has a long, thick root pregnant with a milky juice: from which many climbing vines a cubit long <note>About 18 inches</note> are produced, wrapping themselves around nearby stakes. The leaves are broad and pointed, like the smaller Birthwort, smooth and thin. The flowers are basket-shaped, fading from white to purple. It loves rich soil and grows abundantly in Syria. Among us, it is kept in the more cultivated gardens; it flowers in May, June, and July. The narrowness of this space does not allow for more details.

<column-break/>

### SOLDANELLA, SEA CABBAGE; German: *Meer Winde*: Belgian: *Zee Winde*: French: *Choux de mer*: Italian: *Cauolo marino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Soldanella (Sea Bindweed), showing rounded leaves and bell-shaped flowers with a creeping root system.</image-desc>

The plant called Soldanella today [by some *Soldana*] resembles the Sea Cabbage of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the 1st-century Greek physician and author of De Materia Medica</note> in every way, whence we conclude entirely, along with almost everyone else, that it is the very same. Only Matteo Silvatico writes that Soldanella is the *Cachile of the Arabs*, but with great error: since he attributes to it the leaves of Watercress, whereas they are those of Birthwort, etc.

However, this plant differs from other Cabbages in its entire genus: for it spreads its little vines along the ground, from which grow somewhat round leaves, wider than they are long, similar to the leaves of Lesser Celandine, flowing with a milky juice and resting on long stalks. The flower is large, purple, nearly three inches wide, bell-shaped, and undivided. The seed is angular, black, and sometimes white, contained in round pods. More is found in the broad table following.

---

### A RELATIVE OF SOLDANELLA, the Marine Bindweed: Perhaps the *Iecoraria* <note>Liver-wort</note> or *Ficatelle* of Hermolaus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Sea Bindweed with more heart-shaped leaves and similar climbing habit.</image-desc>

Zwinger <note>Theodor Zwinger (1533–1588), a Swiss scholar</note> used to grow this in his garden at Basel. Furthermore, Soldanella planted in common gardens grows most successfully. But it grows wild everywhere by the sea, especially around Venice and Genoa, and on the Belgian coast. At Montpellier it flowers in Summer and perfects its seed in Autumn. Some establish two species of it: one approaching the Cabbages, the other which is of the Bindweed family, and it is of this latter that we speak here. Besides the purging power assigned to it by Dioscorides, Pliny, Avicenna, and Serapio, it is usefully employed to expel the waters of those with dropsy <note>Edema or swelling</note>. Daily experience teaches that it can be safely given to children and the weak, and that what the Ancients handed down—that no one should use it—is false.

<column-break/>

### SNAKEWOOD: Called *PAO DA COBRA* by the Portuguese, and *Palo della Culebra*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, woody section of Snakewood (Lignum Colubrinum) showing the bark texture and internal grain.</image-desc>

Several plants are gifted with the name Snakewood, because they are useful in a wonderful way against the poisonous strikes and bites of snakes. Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta (1501–1568), a Portuguese physician in India</note> writes that three kinds of this wood are found on the island of Ceylon, describing them and handing down these facts about them in general. He says this wood, or rather the root, is not only effective against the bites of animals that eject venom, but its powder is also believed to kill intestinal worms and remove pimples, rashes, and skin eruptions, etc. We depict here the Snakewood of Garcia, which is called "climbing" by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note>.

---

### IVY-LIKE SNAKEWOOD, with leaves of Bryony, which is Acosta's First Type.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing woody plant with lobed leaves resembling Bryony.</image-desc>

It grows in Malabar <note>A region of southwestern India</note> in the manner of Ivy, with the color of the Greater Dragon-plant or Serpentary. Its leaves are similar to Bryony: yet they are whole at the beginning, provided with a nerve running through the length and five or six veins sloping to the sides. With the passage of time, small holes appear, which gradually grow with the leaves until they finally split the leaves entirely and make them similar to the leaves of a vine. Thus, on one and the same plant, some leaves are whole, others provided with small holes, and some with larger ones—all so different from one another that they hardly seem to be leaves of the same plant. Indeed, this wood has such a similarity to a snake that it easily deceives, and one might think it to be a living snake.

<column-break/>

### SNAKEWOOD, called *DUDA SALI* by the people of Canara; which is Acosta's Second Type.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller woody plant with simple, elongated leaves and a twisting root.</image-desc>

The plant is quite short and thin, and has only three leaves, which are soft, smooth, and a deep green. Neither flower nor fruit has been seen, nor does anyone assert they have seen them. The root is oblong and thin, creeping on the surface of the earth.

In the *History of Lyon* <note>The Historia Generalis Plantarum (1586)</note> it is called the Snakewood of Acosta, Type 1. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical index of 1623</note> it is the Indian Clematis S. Snakes flee from it, nor can they bear the sight of those carrying it.

It focuses on their physical characteristics, their classification by famous botanists, and their effectiveness as purgatives or antidotes to snake venom.</summary>

# OF PLANTS

### SNAKE-WOOD OF CLUSIUS, called PAO DA CO-
### BRA. The Angel Tree. A root resistant to arrows
### smeared with poison.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a thick, gnarled root or piece of wood with a rough, textured surface, showing several cut branch ends.</image-desc>

This fragment of wood, distinguished by the name *Pao de Cobra* <note>Portuguese: "Snake Wood"</note>, was found in that great flagship captured from the Portuguese by English sailors in the year 1581, on which the Viceroy of India was traveling. It is thought by some to be the third type of Snake-wood described by Acosta. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era</note>, identifies it as the sixth type of Indian Clematis.

Indeed, Garcia de Orta writes that a certain root is found in Malacca which provides an immediate remedy against wounds made by arrows smeared with poison <term>Toxico</term> <note>Specifically referring to arrow poisons like curare or similar substances</note>. Bauhin identifies this as the seventh Indian Clematis.

Acosta mentions, under the title of Snake-wood, the *Angel Tree* (*Arbor Angelina*), but since he does not describe what it is, its identity is not yet sufficiently clear.

### THE CACUBALUM OF PLINY TO SOME: Berry-
### bearing Chickweed: Chickweed with black fruit.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a climbing plant with heart-shaped leaves and small dark berries hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

Lobelius doubts whether this plant of ours is the *Cacubalum* of Pliny; Gesner denies it is, while the *History of Lyon* asserts it; let the learned judge.

The *root and seeds* of this plant are like the *Greater Horsetail* <note>original: "Hippiq; majoris"</note>; it has very long, hard, and creeping shoots. The *flowers* are a whitish-green consisting of six petals, which are succeeded by black berries the size of black pepper grains, enclosed in a small husk; they are green at first, but black when ripe, filled with small, flat seeds.

Among the Germans, Belgians, French, and Italians, it is found along the edges of fields among briars and brambles, and it is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms all summer; it cools and constricts.

### INDIAN CRESS WITH ANGULAR LEAVES,
### with the so-called Peruvian Pod.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a climbing plant with lobed, angular leaves and long, curved seed pods (siliqua).</image-desc>

This foreign Cress has broad, angular, and beautifully green leaves. The flower is yellow, hanging backward with a little horn, like the "Royal Flower" which they call *Delphinium* <note>Larkspur</note>. Thus Dodoens describes it, though he did not see the plant itself, but only an illustration. Is it a species of Bindweed? To Lobelius and the *History of Lyon*, it is the *Indian Cress of Dodoens*.

The pod <term>Siliqua</term> depicted with this Cress by Dodoens, Lobelius, and Clusius is labeled the *Peruvian Pod of the Indian Cress*.

<column-break/>

### FOREIGN BLADDER-CHERRY, OR INDIAN
### HEART: Germ. Monk's Head: Fr. Wild Bladder-senna: Ital. Foreign Bindweed:

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a climbing vine with compound leaves and inflated, lantern-like seed pods.</image-desc>

It does not rise from the ground except by the help of tendrils, by which it wraps itself around neighboring objects. It has ribbed, smooth stems; leaves shining with a joyful brightness, divided in the manner of smallage <note>wild celery</note>, and hairy with minute hairs. From the leaf-axils come stalks bearing white flowers, which are followed by swollen bladders containing grains similar to a small pea, partly blackish and partly whitish, upon which the likeness of a Heart is beautifully drawn. The root is the thickness of a finger, fibrous, woody, and somewhat hard.

It is commonly labeled Foreign Bladder-cherry, and *Indian Heart* or *Heart-Pea*. Those who guess it to be *Dorycnium* are very much mistaken. It is cultivated in gardens and blooms in July, August, and September. It is believed that the seed, because of the mark with which it is distinguished, is effective against all ailments of the heart <note>A reference to the "Doctrine of Signatures," where a plant's appearance suggests its medicinal use</note>.

### CLIMBING INDIAN CRESS WITH SHIELD-SHAPED
### LEAVES.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a climbing plant (Tropaeolum/Nasturtium) with round, peltate leaves and spurred flowers.</image-desc>

This Cress has nothing in common with the Cress of our world except for its taste and smell. Whence Gillenius elegantly says: "Did he act rightly who gave this plant the name of Cress because it tastes of its sharpness? Or those who, from the cinnabar-red veins with which the flowers are sprinkled, called it the *Blood-stained Flower*? Why may it not be referred to the Violets, whose most pleasant scent the flowers breathe out? Why not to the Royal Flowers, whose appearance these flowers excellently express? Why not to *Asarum* <note>Wild Ginger</note>, whose leaf it possesses? Why not to the *Bindweeds*, since, like them, it clasps the stem? Let it be 'Cress' because of the taste it truly expresses, and 'Indian' indeed from its birthplace." It is grown in gardens and blooms all summer.

### THE SECOND CYCLAMEN OF THE ANCIENTS.
### Perhaps the second Cyclamen of Lobelius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with large, broad leaves and small clusters of flowers or berries.</image-desc>

With the permission of the learned, we might say with Ruellius that physicians are ignorant of the "Second Cyclamen" of the Ancients. For various plants are presented in its place: *Bittersweet*, Solomon's Seal <note>original: "Sigillum Mariae"</note>, *Black Bryony*, Honeysuckle, and *Creeping Chickweed*. Thus, while many sketch its likeness, none fulfill the description. Whether this plant depicted here with ivy-like leaves, found in the hills of Italy as Lobelius and others suspect, is truly it—let the learned judge.

<margin>
**PEPPER:** German: *Pfeffer*; Belgian and Bohemian: *Piper*; French: *Poivre*; Italian: *Pepe*; Arabic: *Fulful* or *Fufil*.
</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pepper plant branch with clusters of small round berries (peppercorns) and a separate detail of a single berry cluster.</image-desc>

### BLACK AND WHITE PEPPER ACCORDING TO ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing pepper plant with broad, heart-shaped leaves and elongated flower/fruit spikes.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note> makes no mention of a tree bearing Pepper; he says only that it is a fruit, and of it he identifies two kinds: one *Round*, the other *Oblong*. From the records of Dioscorides and Galen <note>Famous ancient Greek medical authorities.</note> we learn that the Pepper trees are small and grow in India. At the beginning of their growth, they produce a very long fruit like a pod, which is *Long Pepper* <note>original: "Piper longum"</note>, and within it are contained grains. These grains, when bitter and immature, make *White Pepper*; when mature, dried, and parched, they make *Black Pepper*. That which is deprived of nourishment, being light and weak, is called *Brafma*. Philostratus compares the Pepper tree to a Vine, and Pliny to a Juniper. Thus the Ancients wrote of Pepper; yet they made a great error in claiming that White and Black pepper come from the same fruit of the same tree.

Acosta <note>Cristóbal Acosta, a 16th-century Portuguese doctor and pioneer in the study of plants from the East Indies.</note> relates that one kind of Pepper is *Domesticated*, which is in common use, and the other is *Wild*, which is neglected due to its bitterness. The domesticated plant, he says, is twiggy and climbs in the manner of Ivy, winding itself around nearby objects. It is equipped with nodes at intervals, from which the leaves grow; these are similar to *Betel* leaves, deep green on the inner side and paler on the outer (they consider the former female and the latter male). At each joint where the leaves hang, from the very base of the leaves, grow clusters containing 30, 40, or 50 grains. The root is small and spreads its fibers in the top of the soil.

He adds that there is a very great similarity between the plants that produce Black Pepper and White; however, the leaves of the White seem thinner and softer, and the fruit is more aromatic and of a better flavor than the Black.

### GRAINS AND CLUSTERS OF TAILED PEPPER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing various botanical details of "tailed pepper" (cubeb), including individual berries with stalks, a cluster of berries, and leaf shapes.</image-desc>

When we previously arranged for the illustration of Tailed Pepper to be prepared, we had not yet seen the clustered variety of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century Flemish botanist.</note> which we depict here. This kind of pepper is so similar to Cubebs that Scaliger doubted whether it might actually be Cubeb.

Anguillara, by whom it is called *Amomum*, writes that in Syria it is called Wild Pepper, and he describes the leaves of the plant as being like those of a Vine. By Lobelius it is called *Tailed Pepper* <note>original: "piper caudatum"</note> and believed to be Amomum. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax*, calls it the Clustered Tailed Pepper from Guinea, and the Amomum of Anguillara.

<column-break/>

### BLACK PEPPER OF CLUSIUS: HAERMIA, or the Little Pepper of Serapion.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pepper plant branch with leaves and small clusters of fruit, showing a more shrub-like habit.</image-desc>

We present various figures here; the one we have just placed was once depicted by Clusius as *White Pepper*. To the sides, under the mark †, is added a tailed grain, which is *Tailed Pepper*; under the mark of a star * is *Haermia*. The one we place here is from the *Exotics* of Clusius, who says the Black Pepper plant is twiggy and so weak and falling that unless it is supported by stakes or planted next to some tree around which it can wind itself, it lies prostrate and spreads on the ground.

*Haermia*, or the *Little Pepper of Serapion* <note>Serapion the Younger, an influential 12th-century Arabic medical author.</note> mentioned above, is a grain that is not very fragrant, shaped like a smaller Pepper, but smaller and lemon-colored, and its scent is like the scent of Aloe-wood.

### TAILED PEPPER: Portuguese: *Pimento del rabo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several elongated, textured seed pods or fruit spikes of the "tailed pepper" variety.</image-desc>

The grains of Tailed Pepper are mostly smaller than the grains of both White and Black pepper, though sometimes equal; they are somewhat longish from a round base, and shaped like a top toward the stalk. As the common name suggests, they are "tailed," of a blackish or dusky color, intermediate between White and Black pepper. The skin is somewhat thick, sometimes smooth and sometimes a bit wrinkled or curled; the marrow and flavor are like that of common Pepper. It is commonly brought from Guinea.

### LONG PEPPER, ACCORDING TO MONARDES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of long pepper spikes (Piper longum), showing the characteristic cylindrical, scaled surface, with one spike shown in cross-section (marked II) and another showing internal structure (marked III and IV).</image-desc>

Long Pepper <note>original: "Piper longum"</note> rivals the catkins of the Birch tree; it is an inch or an inch and a half long, cylindrical, sometimes flat, of a dusky or ashen color, with a net-like pattern and rough on the surface. It contains grains equal to Mustard seeds, blackish on the outside and whitish inside, enclosed separately in their own thin skins. The taste is not inferior to Black or White pepper, although it does not appear immediately. The catkins hang from a slender stalk an inch long. It grows in *Java*, and is preferred by the wealthier inhabitants over other kinds of Pepper because they consider it more healthful than round pepper.

<summary>This page details the botanical characteristics and varieties of pepper, including Black, White, Long, and Tailed (Cubeb) varieties, citing both ancient authorities and Renaissance botanists. It describes their growth habits as climbing vines and distinguishes between their physical appearances and geographic origins like India, Guinea, and Java.</summary>
<keywords>Black Pepper, White Pepper, Long Pepper, Tailed Pepper, Cubeb, Acosta, Clusius, Monardes, India, Java, Guinea, botany, spices</keywords>

# PLANTS: PEPPER FROM FLORIDA.

### LONG PEPPER OF CLUSIUS. <note>Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius) was a foundational 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Piper Longum plant branch with broad, ribbed leaves and a single elongated, textured fruit spike (catkin) shown both on the stem and separately below.</image-desc>

Dioscorides and Galen <note>Ancient Greek medical authorities.</note> believed that the same plant produced both long and round pepper. However, those who have surveyed the regions where they grow testify that the tree producing long pepper is entirely different from the one producing black or white pepper. Hence Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine.</note> says: "The plant," he says, "which produces long pepper has no more resemblance to the one producing white or black pepper than a *Bean* has to *Eggs*."

### ETHIOPIAN POD-PEPPER: The "Anefcen" Grain of Avicenna; Habzeli and Pepper of the Blacks, according to Serapion.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with clusters of pod-like fruits emerging from a central stem, with several pods shown in an upright, radiating arrangement.</image-desc>

This is brought from the region of the Blacks; it is not without use for toothaches.

Johannes Stadius <note>Hans Staden, a German explorer.</note> writes that two kinds of pepper are born in America: one *yellowish*, the other truly *reddish*.

Furthermore, pepper grows commonly in various provinces of the Indies: Malabar, Honnavar, Calicut, etc. It ripens in September and October; it is gathered in November, December, and January. Linschoten writes that in some places it is gathered in May and June. *Long pepper* grows most especially in Bengal, which region is a distance of 50 leagues from Malabar, where *White* and *Black* pepper are held in greater abundance. However, the white pepper plants are rarer, and are not found except in certain places in Malabar and Malacca.

### CROPIOT, A MOST BITING FRUIT, WITH SEEDS similar to Ethiopian Pepper.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two distinct seed pods: one thick and segmented, the other a long, twisted, spiral-shaped pod.</image-desc>

Walichius Syuertz bought these fruits, which were strung on a cord, from sailors returning from America; Clusius, to whom this illustration belongs, obtained them from him. It is endowed with great sharpness, and the Indians mix it with Tobacco leaves when they wish to inhale its smoke to soothe a headache.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of three long, slender, slightly curved botanical specimens, likely the "Piper ex Florida" mentioned in the header.</image-desc>

The fruit of the same plant is tall, oblong, about the thickness of a cord and half a foot in length, consisting more correctly of many small grains joined around an oblong <unclear>stalk</unclear> and arranged in a continuous <unclear>order</unclear>, in the manner of a kidney-bean seed; when these are removed, the bare stem is seen. When fresh it is green; it ripens and turns black in the sun. It is hot in the third degree. <note>Galenic medicine categorized plants by "degrees" of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>

### LONG PEPPER; FELFEL, ACCORDING TO ALPINO. <note>Prospero Alpini, a Venetian physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, succulent-like leaves or stems growing upwards from a base, resembling a type of aloe or sedum.</image-desc>

It has the leaves of a rush, but thicker; when these are cut, a certain yellow juice flows out, which is very sharp and burning, and the whole plant is hot in the 4th degree. It is kept in some pleasure gardens. *So says Alpino.*

To say something of the powers and faculties of Pepper: it heats powerfully. All pepper does this, and the white is more powerful and more fragrant than the black. But, as the plant is very rare, so is the fruit very rare; it is accustomed to be brought only to the tables of Nobles, and it is believed to resist poisons.

Indian Physicians and some practitioners of experience <term>Empirici: medical practitioners who relied on observation rather than traditional theory</term> make Pepper to be "cold," an opinion which We leave to the learned to examine.

The Indians use the leaves of black pepper against colicky pains and other "cold" ailments. Moreover, the clusters are preserved in vinegar or salt while still green and immature, and kept for use.

### QUAMOCLIT, A NEW INDIAN PLANT. The American feathered Jasmine, or Gelsemium, with blood-red flowers, according to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine with finely divided, feathery leaves and small trumpet-shaped flowers, showing the root system and twining habit.</image-desc>

The plant is a climber <note>original: "anadendras"</note>, coming forth with oblong and somewhat broad leaves, initially two joined together; the remaining leaves are similar to the second *Myriophyllum* in Mattioli's work, and are so thin that it might not inaptly be called a "most slender Bindweed." The small stems turn black from red; the flowers please with a most elegant redness, similar to the flowers of the Petum <note>Tobacco</note>. The seed in the oblong capsules is oblong and dark, burning the throat like Pepper.

In the lower part of the illustration, you see two broken-open pods added; in the upper part, two flower calyxes, three separate small petals, and three seeds taken out. Caesalpinus, Camerarius, and Clusius record this as American Jasmine.

<summary>This page describes various species of pepper from the East and West Indies, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for pain and poison, and their classification by early modern botanists. It also introduces the Quamoclit, an American climbing vine noted for its fiery seeds and delicate red flowers.</summary>

<keywords>Long Pepper, Ethiopian Pepper, Cropiot, Quamoclit, Clusius, Alpino, America, India, Malabar, Tobacco, Jasmine, medicinal plants, botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### BODAGLAM EXOTIC FRUIT, OF PALUDANUS.
### Foreign little plant of Clusius. Fragre of the Arabs.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations of various exotic seeds and a slender, segmented plant stalk. The seeds are shown in two rows: the top row contains three larger, textured seeds; the second row contains five smaller, round seeds. Below them is a long, thin, jointed botanical specimen.</image-desc>

An exotic fruit from the collection of Paludanus <note>Bernardus Paludanus (1550–1633) was a famous Dutch physician and collector of "curiosities."</note>, the size and color of gray pepper, which we depict in the upper part of this plate. Below it, however, is the "Foreign little plant" described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a foundational botanist of the 16th century.</note>: perhaps it is the *Feffel* of Alpinus, as it seems to Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era.</note>.

*Fragre*, or the *Fragre* of the Arabs, is compared to the Chickpea by Isaac Eben Amuram <note>An 11th-century Jewish physician from Tunisia.</note>; it has a small, black, round grain inside, but is red on the outside. It is hot and dry in the second degree <note>A reference to Galenic medicine, which categorized plants by their "humoral" qualities.</note>.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN APHYLLON: Leafless in German.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a leafless plant consisting of two clusters of textured, brain-like or floral-like heads atop short, thick stems.</image-desc>

The Dutch found this plant in abundance on the island of St. Lawrence <note>The historical name for Madagascar.</note>; and because it had no true leaves, they named it *Blatterlos*, that is, "leafless" <note>original: "aphyllon"</note>. The more tender branches are said to be useful for the cure of Scurvy. The De Bry brothers <note>Famous engravers and chroniclers of early voyages.</note> mention it, but no others besides Caspar Bauhin, who in his *Pinax* says it is similar to the dried Rose of Jericho.

---

### NEGUNDO EXOTIC TREE: Called SAMBALI in Balaguate: in Malabar, Nochi. MALE NEGUNDO.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a botanical specimen (Negundo Mas) featuring a central stem with serrated, lanceolate leaves arranged in clusters, and small flowers or berries at the nodes.</image-desc>

In Balaguate and Malabar <note>Regions of India.</note> there grows a certain small tree the size of a Peach tree, with frequent branches which, when cut back, grow back more numerous and lush. It has leaves like the Elderberry, serrated around the edges in a similar way and somewhat bristly. The flower is a bright grayish-white; the fruit is black, the size of pepper or a little larger. The inhabitants sprinkle it into their food called *Caril* <note>An early European reference to "Curry."</note>. Thus says Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a pioneer of tropical medicine in India.</note>.

Acosta <note>Cristóbal Acosta, a 16th-century physician who studied Indian plants.</note> describes it slightly differently. Two trees, he says, are found in many places in India, especially in the provinces of Malabar, which are distinguished by sex. The Male is considered to be the size of an Almond tree, with leaves that are green on top and downy and hairy underneath, like Sage leaves, serrated at the edges, which to those looking from a distance seem very similar to Elderberry leaves. Of the Female, more follows.

<column-break/>

### FEMALE NEGUNDO.

<image-desc>Woodcut of the female Negundo plant, showing similar serrated leaves but with a slightly different growth habit and clusters of small fruit or flowers.</image-desc>

The Female, the same Acosta continues, rises to the same height as the Male; but it has larger, rounder leaves, not serrated at the edges, very much like the leaves of the White Poplar. The leaves of both, however, taste and smell of Sage. On many of them, on the reverse side, a certain white foam is seen clinging early in the morning, which emanates from them at night. The flower is gray in color, very closely approaching the Rosemary flower. The fruit is similar to black pepper, sharp in taste, and used very little like pepper, but almost equal to Ginger. The use of this tree for healing is so frequent in those regions that unless God made the pruned branches grow back with manifold offspring, the trees would have been consumed long ago.

---

### AMOMUM ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL
### Amomum of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a woody branch with small, scale-like leaves and clusters of round berries or seed pods at the base.</image-desc>

Amomum, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the father of pharmacognosy.</note>, is a shrub that twists itself from the wood into the shape of a cluster; with a flower like a small white Violet, and leaves similar to Bryony. The Armenian variety is most highly praised, with a color verging toward gold, reddish wood, and being abundantly fragrant. It has the power of heating, binding, and drying. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist.</note> says it is most praised when it is similar to Pomegranate leaves, with a reddish color; the second best is pale; the grass-colored is worse, and the white is the worst.

Among those things which both Dioscorides and other ancients recorded obscurely, Amomum is rightly counted; for none of them gave either a clear image or an accurate description of it. Whence Clusius rightly writes that it is difficult to determine what the true Amomum is; he provides this image in his *Exotics*, and another elsewhere.

<column-break/>

### NEW AMOMUM, with the appearance of common Cardamom, or the Indian cluster.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a cluster of textured, oval-shaped seed pods or fruits, resembling cardamom.</image-desc>

Because in this Indian cluster all the legitimate marks of Amomum recited by Dioscorides and Pliny appear, we might easily believe with Caspar Bauhin that this cluster is the true and legitimate Amomum of Dioscorides and Pliny. The Greeks call it *Amomon*; it is called *Hamama* and *Hamamus* by the Arabs; and *Hamama* by those of Constantinople.

Whether the ancients used the twigs or the cluster of Amomum in Antidotes or other medicines is disputed, and each side has its reasons. However, the opinion of Andromachus <note>Physician to Emperor Nero and inventor of Theriac.</note> is pleasing, who received not the twigs, nor the clusters, but the "clustered Amomum" into his Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" medical ointment or potion.</note>.

<summary>This page catalogs several exotic botanical specimens, including the Negundo tree from India and the mysterious Amomum, attempting to reconcile contemporary findings with ancient Greek and Roman descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>botany, India, Madagascar, Negundo, Amomum, Cardamom, medicinal plants, Clusius, Dioscorides, Theriac</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of aromatic spices and medicinal plants from the previous section, focusing on the identification of Amomum, Cardamom, and the Rose of Jericho. The author frequently cites contemporary botanists like Matthiolus and Lobelius to reconcile ancient descriptions with modern specimens.</meta>

### TRUE AMOMUM OF SOME, AND Amomis or False Amomum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cluster of Amomum plants with small, scale-like leaves and a distinct root structure described in the text as resembling a bird's foot.</image-desc>

The plant sent to us under the name of Amomum represents the spikes of Arabian Stoechas <note>French Lavender</note>, which we depict here because of its aroma. However, since Amomum is called *Hamama* by the Arabs—which signifies a "pigeon's foot"—we have two such spikes joined together here, expressing to a hair <note>original: "ad unguem," meaning perfectly or precisely</note> a hairy pigeon's foot... They consist of many small leaves, compacted in an overlapping arrangement of scales, whitish-yellow in color, fragrant, and possessing a bitter and sharp taste.

Pliny mentions Amomis, and says it is harder and less fragrant than Amomum; he claims it is either a different thing from Amomum, or it is Amomum that was collected when it was least ripe. We received the small plants depicted in the lower part of the table under the name of Amomis.

### Various species of LESSER CARDAMOM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustrations of various cardamom pods, showing different sizes and shapes, including elongated and more rounded varieties, along with individual seeds.</image-desc>

It was not only Castor <note>Castore Durante, an Italian physician and botanist</note> who identified three types of Cardamom, as we just mentioned; for Cornarius also identifies three: the *Greater* with a dusky seed, the *Lesser* with a red seed, and a *Third* with a yellow one. Indeed, Lobelius, Platinus, and Tabernaemontanus establish four types: *Greater*, *Lesser*, *Smallest*, and *Medium*. In this table, we present two species of the podded Lesser Cardamom, having shown the smallest of all on the preceding page.

Both types of Cardamom grow in various provinces of India: but nowhere more abundantly than from the trading center of Calicut all the way to Cannanore. Furthermore, both are warming in the second degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of humors where "degrees" measured the intensity of a plant's effect</note>; they refresh the vital organs, strengthen the innate heat, disperse gas, and aid digestion. The *Lesser* is more fragrant, superior, and more sought after; the *Greater* is less so.

<column-break/>

### CARDAMOM: GRAIN OF PARADISE, Melegueta: Arab. *Cardumeni*: Germ. *Little Cardamom*: French *Cardamom*: Ital. *Cardamomo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a large, textured cardamom pod (Granum Paradysi) and several smaller seeds below it.</image-desc>

Matthiolus writes that Cardamom is not known in this age, while on the contrary, other learned men say it is commonly known. Castor makes three types: the *Greater* resembling a Fig, the *Medium* which is long, and the *Lesser* with a triangular little head. Yet for almost everyone else, there are only two types: namely the *Greater*, which they also call the "cultivated" kind, and the *Lesser*, which is the "wild" kind.

We depict the Greater here, which Matthiolus describes; he says it reflects the appearance of a Fig or a Pear. Lobelius writes in his *Adversaria* that it is called Melegueta or Millegretta from the numerous seeds enclosed in the pods. That seed is commonly called *Grain of Paradise*. Among the Cardamoms known today, none comes closer to the Cardamom of Dioscorides <note>The famous 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> than that which they call the *Lesser*.

### ROSE OF JERICHO, ROSE OF ST. MARY: Germ. *Roses of Jericho*: French *Rose of Jericho*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of the "Rose of Jericho" in its dried, skeletal form, appearing as a woody, branched structure.</image-desc>

In his commentary on Dioscorides, Cordus identifies two species of the *Jericho Rose*: one tasteless and not at all fragrant, which would be Amomis, and another aromatic in taste and very fragrant, which is truly called Amomum. But where he saw this fragrant Rose, we have seen it nowhere, even when we have held it living and fresh.

Andemacus, Frischlinus, Lonicerus Rheginus, Scaliger, and others have also determined it to be Amomum. But Sylvius, Fuchs, Brassavola, Agricola, Ryff, Lacuna, Lobelius, and various others rightly feel that it cannot possibly be Amomum. And we agree with these men, since this Rose has neither a scent, nor the leaves of Bryony, nor the shape of a cluster, which are the characteristics belonging to Amomum. More on this in the margin of the following figure.

---

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE ROSE OF JERICHO.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut of the Rose of Jericho plant in a more leafy, upright state with roots and small flowers/buds visible.</image-desc>

Caspar Bauhin enumerates two species of this Rose: one entirely woody, tasteless, and odorless; the other aromatic and very fragrant. But where did he observe this? Truly, Cordus is more ridiculous than the rest, for he says this Rose is Amomum; and yet, in his *Exposition on Theriac*, he says we lack the true Amomum. Nor is it even Aspalathus, as Gesner wished; it hardly even deserves the name of a Rose.

Giraudet writes, and almost everyone believes, that this Rose expands and opens on Christmas Day at the very hour our Lord was born, and also that it is useful for those in labor. They report that when a woman is in labor, if this Rose is lowered into holy water, it suddenly opens, and the woman gives birth without danger; and at the same time the Rose opens wide, the child is born. But both opinions are full of superstition, for it is certain that this Rose opens at any other time when lowered into warm water; and as for what it contributes to those in labor, the practitioners and midwives know best.

Furthermore, it grows and flowers easily in gardens, as it grew for us in Montbéliard in the garden of the Serene Prince from seed sent from Paris, flowering in June. Whatever the name suggests, it does not grow in the gardens or fields of Jericho in Palestine: but beyond the Jordan, and in the region of Arabia near Jericho.

-> ### END OF THE FIFTEENTH CLASS. <-

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XVI.
### IN WHICH ARE DESCRIBED CLIMBING FRUIT-BEARERS,
->and their relatives.<-

**GOURD: German *Kürbiß* : Belgian *Cauvvorden***
**French *Courge* : Italian *Zucca*.**

**LONG GOURD, WITH SOFT LEAF AND WHITE FLOWER**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a long, slender gourd hanging from a vine with large lobed leaves and tendrils.</image-desc>

The Gourd <note>Latin: *Cucurbita*</note> earned its name among the Latins from its "crookedness" <note>Latin: *incuruata*</note>: because it is easily bent if anything stands in the way of its outward growth. The Greeks called it *Colocynthis* because the offspring it brings forth are stunted and short, even though in the mass of its body it surpasses all fruits of herbs and trees. However, they called this the "edible and cultivated" *Colocynthis*, to distinguish it from the wild variety, which is bitter and purgative, and which we shall discuss in its proper place. Today, however, common usage has prevailed so that the latter is specifically called *Colocynthis*, while the former is called *Cucurbita*. Thus, of the Gourd, one type is cultivated and flowers, another is wild: and of the cultivated type, various differences are reviewed, which we shall soon discuss in order.

**BOTTLE GOURD : German *Fleschenkürbiß*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bottle-shaped gourd (lagenaria) with a bulbous base and narrow neck, growing on a vine.</image-desc>

Its seeds are smaller and darker than those already mentioned: the fruit, however, represents a bottle <note>Latin: *lagena*</note> with a narrow neck and a thick belly: the leaves, flowers, and other parts are not dissimilar. It takes its name from its exterior shape, which sometimes varies: those traveling abroad commonly use it, especially the French, Italians, and Spaniards: for wine is carried more conveniently in it than in a glass, earthenware, or potter's vessel, which are both a burden and more easily broken.

Furthermore, the seeds that are closest to the neck produce tall Gourds; those in the middle produce round ones; and those on the sides produce thick and shorter ones. They grow into whatever shape they are forced, and if granted the freedom of hanging, they are sometimes seen at a length of eight or nine feet. *Columella and Pliny.* <note>References to ancient Roman agricultural and natural history writers.</note>

<column-break/>

**WIDER GOURD, WITH SOFT LEAF, and white flower.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wide, ribbed gourd or squash growing on a vine with large leaves.</image-desc>

This variety varies not only in size but also in the color of its rind. For there are green, yellow, white, and some spotted ones: and the rind of some is marked with furrows, while others are tuberous <note>bumpy or lumpy</note>.

Furthermore, since Pliny distinguished Gourds into the "Chamber" <note>Latin: *Camerariam*</note> and "Plebeian" <note>Latin: *Plebeiam*</note> types: he said the latter is found on the ground, while the former is raised up by the support of neighboring objects, and with its creeping runners, it climbs and covers trellises and vaulted chambers: this variety and the one just mentioned are numbered among the Chamber gourds. But why should you not also call them Plebeian: since they have no strength to stand without support, and, however much they are greedy for height, they are forced to creep on the ground if art and "husbandry" <note>Latin: *mangonio*, referring to the gardener's manipulation</note> remain silent.

**WARTY GOURD.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a warty or bumpy gourd growing on a vine with broad leaves.</image-desc>

In its root, leaf, flower, and tendrils it is similar to other Gourds: but it differs in its fruit, which in others is covered with a flat and smooth rind: in this one, it is tuberous with many knots, in the manner of warts or "skin-growths" <note>Greek/Latin: *achrocordonum*</note>, a pleasing spectacle of nature playing and acting wantonly.

Perhaps this is the *Sicyopepon* or "Scrofulous Cucumber" of Lobelius, of which he says in his *Adversaria*: It is very elegant and rare, with leaves otherwise very close to those of a fig tree, the fruit equaling a large Melon, but resembling Lemons, with a tuberous rind variegated with nipple-like bumps, and likewise a beautiful three-colored bubbling of "swellings" <note>Latin: *strumatum*, referring to the warty texture</note>, etc.

It discusses their naming conventions, physical characteristics, and practical uses as travel vessels, citing classical authorities like Pliny and Columella.</summary>
<keywords>Gourds, Cucurbita, Bottle Gourd, Botany, Pliny the Elder, Columella, Lobelius, Horticulture, Medicinal Plants</keywords>

### GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, ZUCHA: German: Sea Cucumber; French: Sea Cucumber; Italian: Sea Gourd.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a squash or gourd plant with large, lobed, rough-textured leaves and several elongated, striped fruits hanging from a vine.</image-desc>

The crowd of rough-leaved gourds is truly large and almost innumerable; we present six illustrations of them here, though all are from our own sketches and painted with less skill than they might be. Among writers, there is general agreement regarding the naming of these fruits. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist who used the Latinized name Tragus.</note> labels them Indian Apples and Ethiopian Apples; others count them among the Cucumbers; others call them Melons; and most call them all *Zucha* <note>A term derived from the Italian 'zucca', used here as a general category for squashes and gourds.</note>. For our part, we have chosen to keep them in the class of Gourds. By everyone’s account, however, these are foreign fruits, brought not so long ago into our regions from India, Syria, and other places across the sea, which is why they are commonly called Turkish, Indian, or Sea gourds.

### GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, OR ZUCHA, also called Summer Apples, Illustration III.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a gourd plant with broad leaves and two distinct fruits: one round and one elongated, both showing textured or striped skin.</image-desc>

Of all these (adds the same Tragus), the leaves are nearly the same, the stem is the same, and the flowers are the same, although these parts appear larger in some and more meager in others. Indeed, they bear two kinds of yellow flowers representing the shape of a cymbal <note>Likely referring to the flared, bell-like shape of squash blossoms.</note>, the first of which fall away leaving no fruit behind. Those that remain, however, are similar to little bells and possess a sweet scent; when they begin to wrinkle, the fruit immediately follows. The fruit is sometimes oblong, sometimes round, sometimes smooth and hairless, and sometimes striped with many thick, prominent ribs; some are white, some pale yellow, and others blackish—though when these ripen in the Autumn, they take on a flesh-colored hue.

### GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, OR ZUCHA, Illustration V.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a gourd plant with a single, large, round fruit featuring prominent vertical ribs or lobes.</image-desc>

Finally, that which shines with a golden or waxen color in these types of "apples" is frequently changed, for it takes on a green color again, which it keeps for a whole month, then receives the golden color back; thus in alternating months, it is governed by one color and then another, which we have observed more than once with great admiration. There are those who would count these first among the Cucumbers and assert they are called Turkish Cucumbers. But since Cucumbers are extremely prone to rotting and can last a very short time, I cannot approve of their opinion; rather, with Tragus, I will instead grant this fruit the name of Indian Apple or Ethiopian Apple, etc.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, OR ZUCHA: Summer Apples, Indian Apples.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a gourd plant with large leaves and a single, large, round, smooth-skinned fruit.</image-desc>

Of all those who have written about the said Gourds, Cucumbers, Melons, or Apples—however one wishes to name these fruits—Tragus seems to have investigated their nature more <unclear>freely</unclear> than the rest. Among other things, he says, which have been brought into Germany from distant regions within a few years: we do not think the name "Summer Apples" is inappropriate for those which grow to their full substance, flower, and ripen all in one summer. Some of them are large, others small; some are round in shape, others oblong; again, some are sweet, others bitter; some turn out waxen or golden, others yellowish but pale, and some white. More follows.

### GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, OR ZUCHA, Illustration IV.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a gourd plant with a large, round, heavily textured or "warty" fruit.</image-desc>

Furthermore, Tragus continues, the "apples" of all these kinds have a woody outer rind or skin, but inside they are mostly saffron-colored. That which is in the middle between the seeds and the rind in all kinds is considered the most excellent part. Those apples which are white on the outside, and those which are pale yellow, have white flesh. They are rarely similar in form and flavor. Indeed, all their kinds can last for a year and do not become subject to rot in that time, provided they are gathered properly and preserved with the necessary care. More follows on the side of the table.

### GOURD WITH ROUGH LEAVES, OR ZUCHA, Illustration VI.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a gourd plant with a large, round fruit that appears to have a smooth but slightly mottled surface.</image-desc>

Gourds—to continue in their history—are sown and cultivated in gardens, and finally reach maturity around the time of Autumn; however, in warm regions they ripen sooner, especially the early-ripening ones. We teach how they may be made early-ripening in our "Great History."
Furthermore, as Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a Roman writer on agriculture.</note> instructs, when the gourds begin to grow they must be helped with supports. Those which are kept for seeds ought to hang on their vine until Winter; then, having been removed, they should be placed in the Sun or in smoke until the seeds are ready. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of Natural History.</note> writes of a discovered method by which they may be preserved until the next generation of plants: this is done with brine, and by covering them in a shaded place with a layer of sand.
