# IMAGES AND OUTLINE:
<sig>R 2</sig>

### ROUGH GOURD WITH UNLOBED LEAF, very large, white, and flat-bottomed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, round, ribbed gourd growing on a vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and tendrils.</image-desc>

The fruit of this is large, almost equaling the size of a head, but it is compressed, angular, and white. The leaves are rough and somewhat round, and not at all lobed: the flowers are yellow. Dodoens, Cesalpino, and Caspar Bauhin (in his *Phytopinax* and *Pinax*) classify it as a Pumpkin <note>original: "Peponem"</note>. To Lobelius, in his *Observations* and *Icons*, it is the "Greatest compressed Indian Pumpkin with rounder leaves," sometimes weighing 80 pounds.

Is it perhaps the "Calabash" of the Indians, or a type of Gourd growing in India and increasing to a miraculous size, from which various vessels are fashioned once dried?

<column-break/>

### ROUGH PEAR-SHAPED GOURD, small and white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pear-shaped gourd hanging from a vine with jagged leaves and a small cross-section of the fruit showing seeds.</image-desc>

It has rough, jagged leaves; the stems are long with tendrils spread across the ground in the manner of Cucumbers: the flowers are yellow and of two kinds, sterile and fruit-bearing, as in other rough-leaved Gourds. The fruit is beautiful, abundant, white, and smooth, five or six inches long, with a narrow neck above and a bulging belly below. The *rind* <note>original: "Cortex"</note> is hard when it has ripened; the *flesh* is pulpy, hard, and of the same flavor as the others. The seeds are also like theirs: small, broad, and compressed, containing a sweet, white marrow.

---

### SMALLEST SPHERICAL ROUGH GOURD, saffron-colored and variegated.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vine with several small, round, striped gourds.</image-desc>

The flesh of this is sweet, like the others; the seeds are oblong-round, white, and of medium size.

Is this perhaps the "Smaller round Indian Pumpkin" of Gerard and Tabernaemontanus in their *Icons* and *History*? Or the "Round Pumpkin with the appearance of a Melon" of Tragus? Or the "Wild Pumpkin" of Dodoens?

<column-break/>

### SHIELD-SHAPED GOURD, OR SICILIAN: called the Broad Apple-Pumpkin by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flattened, scalloped gourd (pattypan squash) on a vine.</image-desc>

Lobelius, in his *Observations* and *Icons*, calls it the "Broader shield-shaped Apple-Pumpkin," and in his *Adversaria* he says: Gardens nourish "Cucumber-Pumpkins" <note>original: "Sicyopepones"</note>, Cucumbers, and broader shield-shaped Pumpkins, appearing like a round cap or a navelled shield, with a cracked perimeter and a rind wrinkled with folds and fringes, delicate, etc. It is called the "Flat-bottomed Gourd" by Gesner; the "Jagged Gourd" by Dalechamps in the *History of Lyon*; and the "Shielded Apple-Pumpkin" by Tabernaemontanus.

These broader shield-shaped "Cucumber-Pumpkins," sliced into rounds, sprinkled with flour, and fried in a pan, are eaten with pleasure in France, Belgium, and elsewhere, as Lobelius reports.

---

### HEADED GOURD, OR THE SHIELD-SHAPED Gourd of Tabernaemontanus, in German: *Köpffel kürbs* <note>Head-squash</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, rounded gourd with a distinct "cap" or protrusion at the top.</image-desc>

Here we shall hand down something regarding the use and powers of Gourds. Most all writers, following Galen, categorize them as cold and dry in the second degree. Others say they are of an entirely watery nature, and Pliny says that Gourds are nothing other than frozen water. According to the opinion of Simeon Sethi, the Gourd is easy to digest, of good juice, and very nourishing: it quenches thirst, promotes urine, and moves the bowels. It is beneficial for hot and dry temperaments, and soothes inflammations of the stomach and liver. It is conducive to the chest, lungs, and bladder; it diminishes the genital seed and extinguishes the appetite for Venus <note>sexual desire</note>. Applied whole as a poultice, it soothes inflammations. However, the Gourd as food harms those full of phlegm, and if it encounters bad humors, it is corrupted by them.

<column-break/>

### SHIELD-SHAPED GOURD, with a soft and branched rind, and rounded, unequal seed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a scalloped gourd similar to the one above but with more pronounced ridges.</image-desc>

We have previously delivered the powers and uses of Gourds in general from Simeon Sethi, and he shall stand in place of many. Nevertheless, it is pleasing to add something here regarding their particular use.

Some prepare purgatives from the Gourd in this way: they hollow out a fresh Gourd, fill it with wine, and leave it for the space of a night; in the morning, on an empty stomach, they drink that wine. Water distilled from immature little Gourds is drunk most usefully above all others in burning fevers to extinguish the heat, and is applied as a wash to the heart and liver. The same is applied most effectively with great success via linen cloths for heat in the head, especially of infants (which they call *Syriasin* <note>an old term for inflammation of the membranes of the brain</note>); it is likewise useful for the ears, eyes, all limbs, and even for gout. *The reader will find yet more in the following pages.*

<summary>This page describes various species of gourds and squashes, including the pattypan variety, citing major 16th-century botanists. It also details the medicinal properties of gourds, noting their cooling effects and use in treating fevers and inflammations.</summary>

### A SMALL KIND OF SICILIAN GOURD
->by some called the round Apple-pumpkin.<- <note>original: "Melo-pepo". A hybrid term used by early botanists for gourds that resembled melons in shape.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, round Sicilian gourd, shown whole and in cross-section to reveal the seeds and interior structure.</image-desc>

It scarcely exceeds the size of a fist, is almost flat on both ends, white, and marked with inch-wide ribs separated by small spaces: the rind is moderately hard: the seeds are small.

Furthermore, the fresh leaves of Gourds, according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist.</note> [following Cardano], drive away flies when smeared and rubbed upon beasts of burden: the same leaves, when applied to the breasts, dry up the milk of women who have recently given birth. If a Gourd of the same length as the child, or even a Cucumber, is placed in the bed next to a feverish infant while they sleep; the child will soon be free from the fever, according to Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>. The seed of the Gourd tempers the sharpness of urine and provokes its flow in no small measure.

### THE SMALLER ANGULAR INDIAN MELON
->of Tabernaemontanus.<- <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590), a German herbalist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine with broad leaves and small, angular, striped melons or gourds hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

Concerning this Indian Melon, we have nothing certain or worthy of note. However, we present its image and name here, and we suspect it to be some kind of Gourd with a rough leaf, which is why we produce it in this class: which may also be said of the following entry.

### RELATED TO THE SHIELD-SHAPED GOURD
->tapering from the stalk into a cone.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy vine with small, pear-shaped or conical gourds growing among the foliage.</image-desc>

It is also found shaped like a spinning top on both ends: and there are many other variations of this kind: for it varies in size, length, the thickness of the middle, and in its furrows, stripes, and color. Tabernaemontanus labeled this the fourth smaller Indian Melon.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER SMALL KIND OF SICILIAN GOURD
->another flattened Apple-pumpkin of L'Obel.<- <note>Matthias de L'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flattened, ribbed Sicilian gourd, shown from a top-down perspective with its stem.</image-desc>

This kind of flat-bottomed Gourd, which <unclear>Dodoens</unclear> also depicts, is no larger than an orange. It grew for us in our garden at Yverdon <note>original: "Ebruduni". The Latin name for Yverdon-les-Bains in Switzerland.</note>, with a white rind and many ribs arranged in a beautiful order, winged.

The ash of dried Gourds heals burns and ulcers of the private parts. An oil is also prepared from Gourd flowers steeped for a long time in the sun in oil, which extinguishes the heat of the kidneys and soothes headaches in fevers. Gesner <note>Conrad Gesner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist.</note> prepares ointments for <term>achores</term> <note>A medical term for a type of scalp eruption or scabby ulcer.</note> from Gourds. The narrowness of this space does not allow for the other medical uses of Gourds. Simple women know the culinary uses, and so we stop here.

### THE SMALLER INDIAN GOURD OF TABER-
->naemontanus.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vertical climbing plant with large lobed leaves and small round fruits, showing the root system at the base.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus depicts this in his Illustrations: but in his *History*, the image is transposed and poorly placed under the title of the "Long Gourd." Could it be the "Cucumber with an upright stalk and fruit of a small Melon or Pumpkin" mentioned in Cordus's *Forest of Observations*?

### THE SMALL INDIAN GOURD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, round, speckled Indian gourd, accompanied by two individual seeds shown above it.</image-desc>

This kind of Gourd is almost spherical, about the size of a fist, and somewhat pear-shaped toward the stalk: with a very thick rind, yellowish, and marked with dark spots. It was brought among other rare fruits by the Prince of Montbéliard <note>original: "S. Montbelgardensi Principe". Likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg-Montbéliard.</note>.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BITTER GOURD OR BITTER COLOCYNTH, pear-shaped and variegated.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vine with lobed leaves, tendrils, and a small pear-shaped, striped gourd.</image-desc>

Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist</note> calls this the "second Colocynth," or the "German" variety, and demonstrates it to be of a completely different kind from the true Colocynth, not only by the fruit and leaves but by its entire form. Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> in his Latin edition labels it the "Wild Gourd" and says of it: With its small vines, stalks, tendrils, and soft, almost downy leaves, it mimics the cultivated variety; yet in each and every part it is much smaller. It climbs up garden frames, hillocks, and garden sheds; the fruit is similar in shape to the bellied gourds that resemble small flasks, but it is far smaller in size: namely, very tiny, no larger than a common pear, such that it can be enclosed and grasped within the hand, etc.

---

### COLOCYNTH: German: *Coloquint*: French: *Coloquinte*: To the Italians, Spanish, English, and Bohemians: *Coloquintida*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colocynthis plant with deeply incised, palmate leaves and a round, patterned fruit on the ground.</image-desc>

Writers also call it the Little Gourd, the Bitter Gourd, the Wild Gourd, the Goat Gourd, and the Desert Gourd; some call it the Wild Anguria. By Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and author of De Materia Medica</note> it is called the Wild Gourd. By Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> it is called the "second Wild Gourd." To Mesue <note>An Arabic medical authority</note>, because it surpasses all other plants in bitterness, it is called "Gall of the Earth" <note>original: "Fel terrae"</note>. It seems that the same Mesue distinguishes between Male and Female types when he says: The Female is most excellent, especially if it is large, etc. Its "apples" (fruits) are better known to the Apothecary shops than the herb itself: for it is brought to us from Eastern regions, and is not found randomly in our lands, nor does it ever grow wild; even when sown in gardens, it very rarely reaches perfection.

---

### INDIAN GOURD-FRUIT, called CAMOLANGA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, oblong, ribbed fruit (Camolanga) with several oval seeds shown separately to the left.</image-desc>

It equals the size of an Ostrich egg or a large lemon: the external appearance is as it is depicted here: the rind is thick, covered with a yellowish outer skin: the flesh is spongy and whitening: the seeds are small, oblong, and compressed.

But to return to the Citrul or Anguria <note>Watermelon</note>, it grows sweeter in hot regions: and therefore those around Rome, in Campania, Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily are considered superior, being soft and more flavorful. In Germany and Northern regions, however, it is said to be rare, and it rarely ripens. The fruit of the Anguria is cold and moist in the second degree <note>A reference to Galenic humoral theory</note>, and most fit for keeping away thirst: whence it happens, says Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577)</note>, that the Italians refresh themselves with its pulp during the burning Dog Days of summer. The properties of the seed are the same as those of Cucumbers.

<column-break/>

### ROUGH BITTER GOURD, with small, globose fruit of various colors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and a small, round, speckled gourd.</image-desc>

In our garden at Montbéliard there grew a Colocynth with a rough leaf, small, round, a little larger than a palm-sized ball, bitter, with a hard rind that is multicolored on the outside. We have observed that many people provoked vomiting in themselves by eating it. Our illustration is from the Guarinian collection which we bought already engraved. Could it be the "sown second Colocynth with the fruit of an Orange" mentioned by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616)</note>?

---

### CITRUL, ANGURIA, TETRANGURIA: German: *Citrullen*: French: *Citrouille*: Italian: *Citrullo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Citrullus (watermelon) plant with deeply lobed leaves and a large, round fruit.</image-desc>

This has the leaves of a Colocynth, fragile and hairy shoots, yellow flowers, and a large, round fruit: the rind is somewhat hard, smooth, dark green, drenched with spots; the flesh is white and firm, tasteless in some but somewhat acidic in others: the seed is oblong, broad, black, wrinkled, and compressed, etc.

Tragus, Fuchs, and others make it a genus of Cucumber. Not a few establish it as the *Pepon* of Dioscorides, Galen, and Pliny: but Caspar Bauhin <note>Swiss botanist (1560–1624)</note> establishes that the word *Anguria* was first used by Actius. He says it varies in the color of the rind, sometimes green, sometimes spotted: also in the flesh, sometimes reddish, sometimes white: and finally in the seed, being black, red, or tawny.

---

### CUCUMBER, SICYOS, MELON, AND MELO-PEPO: German: *Melonen*: French: *Melons & Pepons*: Italian: *Mellone*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a melon plant with broad leaves and a large, ribbed fruit.</image-desc>

Both the Ancients and the Moderns have written quite obscurely and confusedly about the garden fruits just described. And such is the natural kinship between Cucumbers, Pepons, Melo-pepons, and Gourds, that the Latin and Greek writers frequently confused both their properties and their names. We have weighed this matter according to its importance in our great History: here we shall say only what the narrowness of the space allows.

However, having considered those things which Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> writes about the *Sicyos*, there is nothing that cannot agree with our Melons: and those things which Pliny relates about Cucumbers seem for the most part to refer to our Melons, as do the things Galen has regarding Melo-pepons. Whence also Lobelius, in his *Adversaria*, calls the common Melon the "Cucumber of the Ancients" and the "Melo-pepon of Dioscorides."

# OF PLANTS

### NETTED MELON, A FOOT LONG, AND very thick, with a bright reddish rind.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, oblong melon with a reticulated (netted) skin, still attached to a vine with broad leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

We have often seen this in the garden of His Most Serene Highness <note>Latin: S. P. (Serenissimi Principis)</note> at Montbéliard.

Furthermore, according to the report of Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist</note>, Melons, Pumpkins, and Cucumbers possess leaves, stalks, and flowers of almost the same form; they spread across the ground rather than raising themselves upward, and they possess tendrils—with which they embrace nearby shrubs—that are smaller than those of the Gourd. The leaves of Melons and Pumpkins are round, rough, and smaller than the leaves of the Gourd. The branches or little vines, like those others, burst forth with a double flower from the mud; one of these falls off, while the other (the later one) produces the fruit, which is nothing other than a kind of Apple <note>The author uses "Pomum" in the general sense of a fleshy fruit</note>, but of diverse form, size, and color. The roots of all are straight, fibrous with many white filaments, etc.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH MELON OF TABERNAEMONTANUS & Gerard: LONG MELON.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a long, slightly curved melon with a textured, bumpy skin, marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus and Gerard <note>John Gerard (1545–1612), author of the famous English 'Herball'</note> depict the Spanish Melon. Truly, among our people, <unclear>guilla</unclear> melons <unclear>are offered</unclear> to us which are very long, <unclear>in the body</unclear> <unclear>pines</unclear> <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>they bear</unclear> <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>surpass</unclear> a curved <unclear>body</unclear>.

As for their general nature, as the <unclear>history</unclear> of these <unclear>page</unclear> <unclear>places</unclear> shows, Melons love cultivated soil exposed to the sun, and a moderate earth that is rich and manured. All of Italy, Provence, Narbonnese Gaul, and Gascony hold Melons as a delicacy. In other regions to the North, such as France, Belgium, England, and Germany, they grow with difficulty or are more tasteless; they rarely reach full ripeness, namely on account of the abundance of rains and the lack of heat.

---

<column-break/>

### MUSK MELON, ROUND, SMALL, and pear-shaped: called the SUGAR MELON.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a smaller, rounder melon variety growing on a vine with lobed leaves and tendrils.</image-desc>

Regarding the melon called the Sugar Melon <insert>Dalechampius is the authority that they are called *Succrades* by the French: he distinguishes between Red *Succrades* and White *Succrades*.</insert>

Now it is a timely moment to add something concerning the qualities and powers of Melons. Their flesh is cold and moist: and according to the testimony of Aetius, if it remains too long in the stomach it becomes corrupted and provides an occasion for malignant fevers: however, we would least of all concede to Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> that they are more difficult to digest than the flesh of other Cucumbers. How it may be corrected with salt, or sugar and pepper, is commonly known. A cream of the seed, prepared from a barley decoction <term>ptisana: a medicinal drink made from hulled barley</term>, is most usefully given to those with a cough, those wasting away, and those with fevers: for it cools and extinguishes thirst.

<column-break/>

### ABDELLAVI MELONS OF EGYPT: Peruvian Melons: Very large Indian Melons.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, thick-skinned melon with prominent longitudinal ridges.</image-desc>

The Egyptians have two kinds of Melons, namely the sweeter ones called *Chaiar*, and the more tasteless ones, which they call *Abdellavi*. Moreover, the plant of these which we depict here does not differ much from our own, but it bears fruit that is oblong and sharp.

In the Peruvian valley, Melons grow with such success that the root reaches the thickness of a tree trunk, and remains vigorous in the soil for several years, producing Melons every year. —Acosta <note>José de Acosta (1540–1600), a Jesuit missionary who wrote on the natural history of the Indies</note>.

Indeed, on the island of Madagascar, according to the author Thevet, Melons are found of such great size that one can scarcely embrace them with both arms: they are either reddish, or white, or yellow, and are most healthful.

---

<column-break/>

### COMMON CUCUMBER: German: *Cucumern*: French: *Concombre* & *Cocombre*: Italian: *Cocomero*: Spanish: *Cogombro*.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a common cucumber plant with large leaves and a long, prickly fruit.</image-desc>

The cucumber-bearing plants were discussed before in general: here we treat the Cucumber taken in its stricter sense. It is either Wild [called the Squirting Cucumber, of which more soon] or Cultivated. Whether the cultivated Cucumber is the *Sicyos* of Theophrastus, and whether Dioscorides understands our Cucumbers by the term *Pepones*, must be considered: We have weighed this matter at length in our great History.

Many differences of the cultivated Cucumber are observed: in shape, in color, in size: and thus some are long, others short, some wide, others compressed, some straight, others curved and twisted, some large, others small: and finally some are yellow, others white, some green, others reddish, and some smooth and others rough. Concerning the location, time, and powers, see what follows.

<column-break/>

### CUCUMBER, SMALLER PEAR-SHAPED: German: *klein biren Cucummern*.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a small, pear-shaped cucumber with a dark, textured skin.</image-desc>

Thus Tabernaemontanus and Gerard depict and label it: but wrongly, in our judgment, they say it is similar to other Cucumbers, except that it is like a Pear. Perhaps others more correctly reckon it among the wild Cucumbers.

The common Cucumber is sown in gardens, and loves rich and sunny places. In July and August the fruits are eaten with the seeds themselves: but in September they finally reach perfect maturity.

Furthermore, the larger common Cucumber is peeled and cut crosswise into very thin little disks, sprinkled with salt, and placed between two plates, shaking it until the watery humor is for the most part drawn out: and thus the disks of the shaken Cucumber are eaten with Pepper, Oil, and Vinegar.

### VERY LONG CUCUMBERS, called "of Blood," twisted and furrowed.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a long, coiled, and ribbed cucumber-like plant with large lobed leaves and tendrils.</image-desc>

In their shoots, leaves, and tendrils, these are very similar to the common varieties. However, the fruits are long and twist themselves like a serpent; they are mostly white, channeled, and ribbed. The taste and smell are like those of the common cucumber. There are those who believe they are made winding by artifice <note>i.e., by being grown inside shaped tubes or coils</note>, while others maintain they are naturally so and differ in species from others; let the learned decide.

Cucumbers are indeed cold and humid <note>referring to the Galenic theory of humors, where cucumbers were used to balance "hot" temperaments</note>, but the seed is much less so than the fruit. They possess a power for cleansing and wiping away, they promote urine, and they soothe inflammations of the liver and chest. According to Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note>, those who have a hot temperament may eat cucumbers without harm, but green ones should be chosen, for the mature ones are not fit to be eaten. Small ones are preserved with vinegar, oil, pepper, and fennel, and they wonderfully excite the appetite.

<column-break/>

### EGYPTIAN CUCUMBER, or CHATE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a cucumber plant with broad leaves and a smaller, more rounded fruit compared to the previous entry.</image-desc>

It has smaller, whiter, softer, and rounder leaves than our local ones. The fruits are longer and greener, and they are covered in a full, soft, and even skin. They are considered useful for various things, but especially for the heat of fevers. The physicians of the Egyptians do not fear to allow raw ones to be eaten by those with fever; they are especially believed by the common people to be highly beneficial for those afflicted by the plague. In gouty pains, if the cause is "hot," they apply the juice with milk and rose oil. Indeed, they administer the distilled water to patients for many days to extinguish the "fires" of the liver, inflamed kidneys, and kidney stones.

---

### WILD CUCUMBER: OR, SQUIRTNG CUCUMBER:
German: **Wild Cucumber: Donkey Cucumber**: Belgian: **Wild Cucumber**: French: **Wild Cucumber**: Italian: **Wild Cucumber.**

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a wild cucumber plant with thick, hairy stems, lobed leaves, and small bristly fruits.</image-desc>

<margin>The Wild Cucumber, says Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist</note>, differs from the cultivated one in leaf and fruit, having it much smaller and similar to oblong acorns; the leaves and shoots are similar to the cultivated one; the root is white and large, and the shrub is bitter throughout.</margin>

Theophrastus calls it the *Sicyon sylvestrem* <note>original: "Wild Sicyon"</note>, entirely incomparable to the cultivated one, bearing a resemblance only in appearance. Thus Theophrastus differs greatly from Dioscorides, and not without merit in our judgment: for whoever compares both cucumbers will find a great difference in the shoots, leaves, and root.

Writers commonly call it the wild, rustic, wandering, or "donkey" cucumber. By some Germans it is called *Spritzkürbs* <note>Squirt-gourd</note> and *Pfofien*, because it shoots out its seed and moisture sharply, just as certain pump-machines throw water. Regarding its medical use and the *Elaterium* <note>a potent purgative drug</note> which is usually made from this cucumber, we read in the Appendix; it is perhaps the same thing which some have called "Sun-reagent."

It flowers in the month of August and subsequently produces mature fruit in Autumn. It is an inhabitant of rubbish heaps, sandy areas, and other sterile places in warm regions; it is very frequent in Italy, the Narbonne province, and the regions of France, around walls, courtyards, and stable manure piles. This plant, according to Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, when mature, violently ejaculates its poisonous juice along with its slippery seeds at even the lightest touch. It is very well known to the boys in those places, who, for sport, squeeze the swollen fruit—barely touched by the fingers—into each other's faces, drenching their mouths and eyes with the very bitter and poisonous juice.

<column-break/>

### MOMORDICA, CUCUMBER-LIKE BALSAM,
Wonderful Apple and Jerusalem Apple: German: **Balsam-Apple**: French: **Apple of Wonders**: Italian: **Garanza.**

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Momordica (Balsam Apple) plant, showing its climbing habit, deeply lobed leaves, and distinctive warty fruit with exposed seeds.</image-desc>

This plant has been assigned various names among writers; it is believed to be called *Balsamina* because it can take the place of Balsam in healing wounds.

The root is small and fibrous; the vines are a cubit long, thin, and furrowed. The leaves are like Bryony or grape but smaller, more elegantly divided, smooth, and shining with a cheerful green. The stalk is about an inch long. The flowers are whitish-yellow, consisting of five petals with small yellow stamens. The fruits are red when mature, with scarlet flesh; the seed is like that of a Watermelon <note>original: "Citrulli"</note>, plentiful and rough. Camerarius, Gerard, and Byst recognize a Male and Female variety.

Is it perhaps Pliny’s *Symphos*, a type of Gourd?

It only grows if sown; it prospers better and more successfully in Italy and warm regions than in Germany, where it flowers in August and never, or very rarely, ripens its fruit.

The fruit and leaves dry with a moderate coldness. Applied to fresh wounds, they are believed to glue them together; taken with wine, they are said to soothe pains of the colon and intestines, and are usefully administered for ruptures and convulsions. The oil in which the fruit (with seeds removed) has been steeped in the sun or boiled, wards off inflammations of wounds, and quickly and easily unites and "glues" them. It is usefully applied to punctures and wounds, helps with pains and ulcers of the breasts, and finally, if we believe Fuchsius and the author of the *Pandects*, it possesses powers in healing wounds by no means inferior to *Telephium* <note>Orpine or Stonecrop, known for wound healing</note>.

# OF IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XVII.
### CLIMBING POD-BEARING LEGUMES,
### and other similar non-climbing types.

**PHASELUS, PHASEOLUS, DOLICHOS, GARDEN SMILAX:** German: *Faseln, Vvitscheboxen;* Belgian: *Romseebonen;* French: *Fascioles;* Italian: *Fagiuolo Turchesco.* <note>These are various historical names for the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and its relatives.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing bean plant with broad leaves, flowers, and long seed pods, supported by a thin stake.</image-desc>

Most all learned men establish that those called *Dolichos* by the Greeks—which are named *Phasioli* by Galen and Aegineta—are the *Siliqua* <note>Latin: "pod"</note> of Theophrastus and the *Garden Smilax* of Dioscorides. However, why the name *Phaseolus* is given to the Pod or the Garden Smilax, or what the difference is between *Phaseolus* and *Phafeolus*, we have weighed in the Appendix; the Reader may consult it there.

We intentionally omit the description of this commonly known Legume: intending only to speak of its Varieties, location, sowing, timing, and use. Truly, why Gorraeus and Brunfels call this Garden Smilax of ours a "shrub," we do not see: for what similarity does this Smilax have with a shrub?

<column-break/>

**GUINEA BEANS OF PALUDANUS,**
**Chestnut-colored, very small.**

<image-desc>A collection of nine individual bean seeds shown in various orientations (front, side, and cross-section), illustrating different shapes and markings.</image-desc>

The *Phaseolus* is commonly distinguished into the common (or Native) and the Foreign. And of the Common, again, one is smaller with a narrower pod; another is larger with a longer fruit, better reflecting the shape of a kidney, which is usually white. In thickness and thinness there is also great diversity: but the chief difference is in the color of the flower and the seed. Indeed, the flowers are mostly white, pale, yellowish, or purplish (amethyst-colored). And as Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a famous 16th-century botanist.</note> notes, the fruits follow the color of the flowers, both in the native and the foreign Bean, differing among themselves with a wonderful variety of colors, as will soon be said. We have depicted the common one before; here are the exotic ones.

---

**DWARF FOREIGN BEAN,**
**Black and white.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shorter, bushier bean plant with trifoliate leaves and several hanging seed pods.</image-desc>

It lacks long runners and consists of a firm, short stem, rarely exceeding a foot in length, and therefore needs no stakes. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist.</note> calls them *Alubias de India* <note>Spanish: "Beans of the Indies"</note>; they grew for him in a garden at Vienna. In Caspar Bauhin’s *Pinax*, this is the "Foreign Bean 1," with a smaller white fruit marked with a black spot around the hilum <note>The "eye" of the bean where it attaches to the pod.</note>.

To return to the varieties of this Legume in the color of the fruit: they are snow-white, yellow, faded yellow, purple, red, almost brick-colored, amethyst, violet, dark violet, black, chestnut, distinguished by veins and streaks on one side or both, sprinkled with black spots, variegated with white circles, etc. No less in the American and African types than in the European is the variety of these seeds to be admired.

<column-break/>

**GARDEN SMILAX, OR BEAN**
**Similar in appearance to Anagyris, of a reddish color: *according to Clusius.***

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing bean plant with dense foliage and long, slender pods, twining around a central support.</image-desc>

This Bean has oblong runners coming out from a single stem immediately following the root itself, divided into many branches, supple, twisting themselves obliquely and trailing on the ground unless supported by poles or stakes, around which they wrap themselves in the manner of other Beans. They turn purple near the "wings" <note>The leaf axils</note>, where three leaves grow together, attached by a long stalk. The flowers on the long stalks are usually in pairs, large, pale white on the outside, but bluish-purple on the inner part. These are followed by just as many very long, smooth, and almost cylindrical Pods, in which the fruit is smaller than other Beans, almost similar to the fruit of the true *Anagyris* <note>The "Bean-trefoil" shrub</note>, of a reddish color.

<summary>This page categorizes various species of beans (Phaseolus), distinguishing between common European varieties and "exotic" types from Africa and the Americas. It highlights the immense diversity in seed color and growth habits, such as climbing versus dwarf varieties.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BROAD-PODDED BEAN, WITH SMALL BLACK FRUIT and a white navel.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a climbing bean plant with broad pods, showing leaves, flowers, and a detailed view of a single bean pod and a seed.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> observed this genus of Bean not far from Lisbon; it is so similar to the Common Bean that it was thought to be the Common variety. It covered the trellises of a certain Monastery with ornamental greenery <term>topiary work: the art of clipping or training plants into decorative shapes</term>. Its flower is purple, but the pods are rough, shorter, and broader than those of our Common bean. The fruit is indeed small, the size of a common pea, entirely black except for the part where it adheres to the pod, which is white. He heard that it is frequent in Brazil, and is called by them *Faba brava*, that is, the Wild Bean.

By Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> in his *Observations* and *Icons*, and also by Tabernaemontanus, it is called the *Second Brazilian Bean*; by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called the *American or Second Brazilian Bean, with black fruit the size of a pea*.

### VARIOUS SMALL BEANS.

<image-desc>A collection of eight individual bean seeds of various shapes and markings, arranged in two vertical rows.</image-desc>

The variety of these fruits is quite great. We have small white beans with a very small reddish ring and a small white hilum <term>hilum: the scar on a seed marking the point of attachment to its seed vessel</term>; we have very small white ones with a large likewise reddish ring and a white hilum also in the middle; we have small black ones brought from Italy, in the hollow part of which is a small white hilum, and on the upper and rounded part, a long and wide spot; we have blackish ones with a prominent hilum, not at all unlike the common ones but smaller and denser, and Clusius mentions similar ones in the works of Monardes. Lobelius mentions pale white ones brought from America in his *Icons*, and in the same place he depicts various kinds of small beans with a shape similar to ours.

### BROAD BEAN OF THE NEW WORLD, ENTIRELY WHITE, related to the Garden Bindweed.

<image-desc>Illustrations of four large, flat bean seeds, showing different views of their broad surfaces and veining.</image-desc>

They are called by Lobelius in the second part of his Dutch edition *White Beans from America*. In his *Icons*, *Large, broad, white Beans*; but in his *Treasury*, *The entirely white Bean of the Americans, very compressed, broader and longer than our local ones*. There are also others of this genus: large, broad, entirely white except for certain streaks; there are large, broad, completely black ones; and there are also some the color of roof tiles with black stripes through the middle.

<column-break/>

### SMALL WHITISH AFRICAN BEANS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a bean plant with trifoliate leaves and long, slender pods, including a detail of a single pod and seed.</image-desc>

These were sent to us with this inscription: *Beans from the Island of Saint Thomas, located under the Equator*. The plant climbs in the manner of beans; the leaves are in threes, much smaller and narrower than in the common varieties, a little more than two inches long, not even half an inch wide, veined, smooth, and thick. The flowers fade from a certain dull smoky color into a deathly paleness, scarcely opening. The pods are a span and a half long <note>about 9 to 12 inches</note>, narrower than the common ones, scarcely the width of a stalk, and they contain whitish grains, half the size of our local beans, dark around the germ.

The seed, sown at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden, flowered in August and ripened its seed in September.

### SMALL INDIAN BEANS: SPOTTED, PALE, variegated, shining, etc.

<image-desc>A group of seven bean seeds of different sizes and patterns, some speckled and some solid, labeled with Roman numerals I through VII.</image-desc>

We keep many kinds of these in our treasury of natural things. Some are a dull yellowish or honey-color, sprinkled with a lighter yellow; some are pale and almost whitish, marked with dark spots; some are swollen on both sides, shiny, of a dark color, and marked with spots especially around the navel; some have a black hilum, with the rest of the part being a dull red. Furthermore, the hardness of some is such that from their clashing together—as if they were hazelnuts—a sound is produced. And finally, we have a bean which we received under the name *Egyptian*, scarcely equaling a peppercorn in size, angular, somewhat long, blackish and shining, with a rather long white navel.

### SMALLER SWOLLEN SNOW-WHITE BEANS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a bean plant with heart-shaped leaves and clusters of pods, showing a small insect or beetle at the base.</image-desc>

In size they are generally smaller than the common beans, nor are they curved around the navel like those. However, they are more cushioned and more swollen in every part for their size. In color they are snow-white and shining, but with age they become dull, turning to ivory and finally even to a pale yellow.

Could this be Clusius's *Small snow-white bean of Guatemala* (Spanish: *Frizolas blancas di Guatimala*)? Or Tabernaemontanus's *White African Bean*? Sown in our garden at Montbéliard, it indeed grew, but did not reach maturity.

# OF PLANTS

### THE BRAZILIAN BEAN POD of Clusius.

<image-desc>A large, curved, and textured seed pod (lobe) showing a bumpy surface, likely a Brazilian bean variety.</image-desc>

This pod (he says in *Exotic Flora* <note>original: "Exot." referring to Carolus Clusius's *Exoticorum libri decem*</note>) was very long: for it had a length of ten inches, and a width of one inch, or a little more. Furthermore, it was straight with a cartilaginous skin, and marked with four nerves on the back running lengthwise from the footstalk to the end of the pod; it was of a dark brown color on the outside, and a whitish-gray on the inside, provided with a certain thin membrane distinguishing the individual seats of the beans.

### THE REDDISH-BROWN BRAZILIAN BEAN, Large, with a large black hilum surrounding most of it.

<image-desc>Illustration of a bean plant with broad leaves and a large, round seed showing a prominent dark hilum (eye).</image-desc>

It is the size of a chestnut, <unclear>pointed</unclear>, an inch wide, more or less, cushioned, covered with a wrinkled, reddish-brown husk—sometimes lighter, sometimes darker—but around the <term>hilum</term> <note>The "eye" of the bean where it was attached to the pod</note> it is lighter and almost whitening. Moreover, a dark hilum surrounds almost its entire orbit, a full stem wide, carved with a middle groove along its length, and having an impressed dot at the beginning.

Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Icons*, Tabernaemontanus, and the *History of Lyon* record the Brazilian Bean, called <term>Macauna</term> <note>An indigenous Brazilian name for certain large seeds</note> by those people.

### THE SMALLER AND FLATTER COMMON BEAN, of a reddish color, with narrow leaves.

<image-desc>Illustration of a climbing bean plant with slender leaves and smaller pods.</image-desc>

Columna observed an elegant kind with narrow leaves; Clusius observed the fruit, which is smaller and flatter than the common Bean, of a reddish color, received from the Spaniards under the name <term>Frixoles Guateli</term> <note>Likely a phonetic rendering of "Frijoles de Guatemala"</note>. This is the 6th Foreign Bean in the *History* of Dodoens; a foreign Bean winding itself around poles and neighboring supports, from whose single footstalk three leaves hang, just as in other Beans, but each one is much narrower, and likewise darker. The pods are shorter, flatter, and more compressed, containing also fewer fruits.

<column-break/>

### PODS OF THE BRAZILIAN BEAN.

<image-desc>Six individual beans of varying shapes (round to oval) and markings, some with distinct dark borders or spots.</image-desc>

The beans which were contained in the <unclear>above</unclear> described pod were long, an inch <unclear>wide</unclear>, reddish-brown, becoming <unclear>reddish</unclear> around the <unclear>hilum</unclear>, according to <unclear>Clusius</unclear>.

Indeed, we have and preserve among many natural <unclear>notes</unclear>, Beans of the New <unclear>World</unclear> that are not only reddish-brown, truly scattered with black, but also red, striped, and flat: blood-red, compressed, white; and even others of a reddish color, smaller and flatter than the common kind.

### THE BEAN OF THE BLACKS OF A DARK COLOR.

<image-desc>Illustration of two long, tapered seed pods hanging from a stem, with a single bean shown above them.</image-desc>

This foreign bean was brought from Guinea, according to Clusius in *Exotic Flora*, in the month of February in the year 1598. Its pod was six, sometimes seven, and occasionally even eight inches long (as was reported to him), nearly two inches wide, flat, with wavy edges, provided with a husk that was not very thick, wrinkled, and black on the outer part. In it, however, were three or more fruits, separated by certain little cells, as is observed in other pods of this kind; they were almost circular in their flat shape, an inch in size, of a dark color, with a certain white circle surrounding almost the whole bean.

### A FOREIGN CARTILAGINOUS POD, WITH A blackish-crimson BEAN encircled by a ring: of Clusius.

<image-desc>Illustration of a single large, thick seed pod and one round bean with a dark ring around its middle.</image-desc>

Clusius describes this in *Exotic Flora* thus: It is, he says, four and a half inches long, two inches or a little more wide, consisting of a husk that is cartilaginous rather than hard and woody, marked on the back with a double, as it were, cartilaginous and wavy crest, stretched out even to the end of the pod. It is wrinkled, and of a color more truly black than brown. Although it was of that length, it contained only three Beans, of a circular shape, swelling somewhat in the middle part, about an inch wide, encircled almost everywhere around the perimeter as if by a ring, very hard, and of a blackish-crimson color.

<summary>This page describes various exotic bean species from Brazil and Guinea, detailing their physical characteristics, pod structures, and the colors of their seeds as documented by early botanists like Clusius.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of exotic seeds and legumes, specifically focusing on large beans and pods from the Indies and the Americas. It maintains the descriptive style of early modern botanical catalogs.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE INDIAN BEAN OR KIDNEY BEAN, large, red, and shining.

<image-desc>Three illustrations of a large bean: two views of the seed (one showing the hilum) and one side view of the bean. Labeled with Roman numerals I and II.</image-desc>

It equals an ounce and a half in size <note>The author is likely referring to weight or a specific volumetric measure common in the 16th century</note>; however, it is not of a perfectly circular roundness, but one part is rounder and the other wider. Furthermore, it is quite compressed, and scarcely thicker than an average vetch <note>A common European legume used here as a size reference</note>. The <term>hilum</term> <note>The scar on a seed marking the point of attachment to its seed vessel</note> is remarkable and black, encompassing two parts of the circumference, while the remaining part is devoid of a hilum. The skin is yellow, remarkably smooth, shining, and somewhat hard. Regarding the rest of the clusters, we cannot describe them as we were not permitted to open them.

We have had others of this kind as well, varying only in color from the one painted and described here: ranging from a saffron-purple color, and similar hues.

### PODS OF THE LARGE BRAZILIAN KIDNEY BEANS.

<image-desc>Illustration of a large, curved, segmented seed pod.</image-desc>

Is this perhaps the *Third Kidney Bean of the Black People brought from Guinea*, which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> mentions in his *Exoticorum* Book 2, chapter 11, in these words: "It is," he says, "eight and a half inches long, of a grayish-brown color, containing kidney beans of a chestnut color"? Or is it the third kind of Bean sent by Adolphus Occon, mentioned in the letters of Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, the Swiss naturalist</note>?

By Tabernaemontanus in his *Images and History*, and also by Lobelius in his *Observations and Images*, it is called the *pod of the Brazilian kidney bean*.

### THE TREE-LIKE BEAN, OR KIDNEY BEAN almost similar to a pigeon's egg, of a whitish color.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of an oval seed, one showing the side and one showing the hilum. Labeled with Roman numeral II and a star symbol.</image-desc>

Clusius describes this in his *Exotics* as follows: "The kidney bean," he says, "seemed to have been enclosed in a pod. Its shape, however, was different, for it almost expressed the form of a pigeon's egg, longer than an inch, encompassing almost an inch and a half in circumference, of a whitish color, to which something of yellow was mixed around the end part that had been attached to the pod. It was further marked with a smoky spot; otherwise smooth and shining, heavy and weighty."

<column-break/>

### LARGE FOREIGN KIDNEY BEAN, Chestnut-colored, with a large hilum, smooth.

<image-desc>Two illustrations of a large, rounded bean showing the surface texture and the prominent hilum.</image-desc>

This Kidney Bean is orbicular, half an inch in width, covered with a hard, smooth, and chestnut-colored skin, with a deep, channeled hilum of the same color as the rest of the skin. When the skin is removed, the pulp comes into view; the surface is indeed thin and of a rare color, but white inside, hard, and with the taste of a Vetch. We shall present the pod of these shortly.

### INDIAN KIDNEY BEAN with a short, swollen, and black pod.

<image-desc>Two illustrations: one of a short, thick, dark seed pod and one of the seed itself.</image-desc>

This Indian pod, which was among the natural rarities held by the Most High Prince of Montbéliard, was wider than an inch, double that in length, swollen like a pillow, black or dark brown, in the manner of the bark of the <term>Cassia fistula</term> <note>The "Golden Shower Tree," known for its medicinal pods</note>, wrinkled with moderate streaks, and shining. From one of its ends, the trace of a stalk protruded, and on the opposite side, a curved angle. Inside, in the corner of the pod, the fruits lay hidden, clinging by their own stalks, paired, black, smooth, and compressed to nearly the width of a fingernail. The picture was made from the pod itself, but a little smaller, due to the size of the woodblock.

### THE KIDNEY BEAN, MACOUNA, OR similar to the Brazilian Kidney Bean.

<image-desc>Three illustrations of seeds: one large oval seed and two smaller seeds below it.</image-desc>

It is of a chestnut and blackish color; of a flat and somewhat long shape, with a hilum that is not very large. Clusius labels it the *second foreign kidney bean*, and makes it similar to the *Macouna*: he adds that it was sent from Spain to the Divine Emperor Maximilian II. It goes by the name *Haba de ludia muy larga* <note>Spanish: "Very long bean of the Indies"</note>, that is, the very long Indian Bean. When plunged into water, it seeks the bottom. In the *Images* of Tabernaemontanus, it is the "Foreign Fruit II."

It categorizes the specimens by their physical characteristics such as color, size, and the appearance of the hilum.</summary>
<keywords>botany, kidney beans, Phaseolus, Brazil, West Indies, Clusius, Tabernaemontanus, seed pods, natural history, Maximilian II</keywords>

--- Page 205 ---
### OVAL CHESTNUT-COLORED INDIAN BEAN, with a shorter whitish navel.

<image-desc>Three detailed woodcut illustrations of bean seeds: two showing the side profile (ovoid shape) and one showing the hilum (umbilicus) area.</image-desc>

The color of this bean is chestnut <note>original: "spadiceus"</note>, interspersed with certain spots of a paler hue. But its greatest beauty is in the navel <term>hilum; the scar on a seed marking the point of attachment to the seed stalk</term>, which turns from reddish to white and does not fill more than half the length of the side. It was seen at the home of the late, most Illustrious Princess of Württemberg, and it was not granted to observe it further. We have also seen others of this kind: the *Oval Black Indian Bean*; the *Shining Reddish-Chestnut Indian Bean*, and similar ones, but this one is shorter and narrower than both of those.

### Several species of BROAD INDIAN BEANS.

<image-desc>Six woodcut illustrations of various kidney-shaped and patterned beans, showing different striations and markings.</image-desc>

These are common in Brazil, a province of the New World, and are said to grow from a plant similar to our European one; but they far surpass ours in flavor and length. For they are an inch and a half long, and an inch wide: covered with a shining yellow-reddish skin, variously speckled, but not smooth everywhere. The hilum, however, is white, somewhat long, and surrounded by a dark red area. We present several varieties here, partly from Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist</note>. Furthermore, they vary mostly in the arrangement of their stripes <note>original: "radiorum," literally rays or spokes</note>.

### FLAT MEMBRANOUS POD, BLACK.

<image-desc>A large, flat, oval-shaped seed or pod section with a dark border and a central light area, marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

Regarding this, Clusius <note>The text says "Iusius," likely a typo for Clusius</note> records in his *Exotics* that he obtained it from sailors returning from Guinea in the year 1598. This pod, he says, was entirely flat, two inches long and one inch wide. The end was a little broader; the color was a dark chestnut. However, whether it was ripe or immature, I can pronounce nothing for certain; but since it was clearly a pod and made no rattling sound when shaken, the opinion leans more toward it having been gathered before maturity.

<column-break/>

### BROAD STRIPED OR RADIATED BEAN: and another spotted one, with a dark green husk.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a bean plant showing the climbing vine, leaves, flowers, and a seed pod, with two individual seeds shown below.</image-desc>

The pods of these are large, broad, and compressed; the seeds are also about as long <unclear>v</unclear> and a little less wide, sitting in their own shapes, black, and streaked with frequent white stripes. We also have other seeds, the image of which is in the lowest part of our plate, which can be called white, speckled with black dots and variegated with reddish spots.

Could this be the Brazilian Bean in the images and history of Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a 16th-century herbalist</note>? Or the *Okendigier* in Thomas Harriot’s history of the Virginian Island?

### ALPINUS’S LABLAB BEAN, BLACK AND chestnut, with a long white hilum.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Phaseolus Lablab plant with trifoliate leaves, flowers, and pods, showing its climbing habit.</image-desc>

It is a twiggy tree, says Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini (1553–1617), a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian plants</note>, which grows to the size of a vine, and like a vine, it is extended by its shoots and spreads out with leaves: in shape, it is entirely similar to the common bean. It blooms twice every year, in Spring and Autumn, with flowers very closely approaching the flowers of beans. The pods are long and broad, containing black seeds somewhat similar to beans, of which some are black, others reddish. It lives for a hundred years and more and is perpetually green; it is a frequent food among the Egyptians, and no less pleasant to our people, etc. But that this little tree lives for a hundred years is difficult to believe for those who know the nature of beans and legumes.

### BEAN-LIKE VETCH, BLACK WILD BEAN: German: *Black or Wild Beans, Moorish Peas.*

<image-desc>A woodcut of a flowering plant with pinnate leaves and small pods, marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

This is a legume more than a cubit high, whose stems are thick enough, angular, hollow, and somewhat hairy. The leaves are in fours or sixes, similar to the leaves of the common bean, arranged in two or three pairs; at the bottom, there is no pair closing the wing, which instead turns into tendrils <note>original: "capreolos"</note> with which it catches hold of nearby things. The flowers are like those of the Vetch or Yellow Vetchling, which, when they fall away, are succeeded by moderately long, large, hairy pods. The seeds are almost the size of a pea, of a very heavy and unpleasant taste and smell, turning black upon maturity.

It grows spontaneously in Italy, Aquitaine, and Narbonnese Gaul, and blooms in April; but in other places, it only grows if sown. Some believe this Vetch <note>original: "Aracum"</note> is endowed with the same properties as the common bean; but others more rightly determine it to be of no use, or very little indeed. More in the Appendix.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of legumes, moving from common European beans to exotic and "purgative" varieties brought from the New World and Africa. # IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### COMMON BEAN, THE LEGUMINOUS BEAN:
#### German: Bônen: French: Febues: Italian: Fava.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad bean plant (Faba vulgaris) showing the stalk, leaves, and bean pods.</image-desc>

The common bean is either Wild or *Cultivated*, and the latter is again divided into the *Greater* or the *Lesser* varieties. Beans also differ in the color of their flowers and seeds. For many are white, some are black, and some are a purplish-black color; the flowers are either white with conspicuous black streaks, or a dark purple.

The Greater bean is sown in gardens, the Lesser in fields, especially among the Zealanders <note>People of Zeeland, a province in the Netherlands</note>. The bean flowers in April and May, but the fruit matures in June and July; however, this occurs earlier or later depending on the variety of locations and climates. Indeed, at Montpellier and Florence, we have seen them flowering in February.

Furthermore, beans occupy a middle temperament in heating and cooling; as a food, they are flatulent and difficult to digest, and they both bind and inflate the belly. The reader may seek more information from the Appendix.

### ANOTHER OF THE PURGATIVE BEANS OF THE NEW WORLD
#### Image: The very broad purgative bean.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of three large, flat, rounded seeds or beans, showing their textured surfaces.</image-desc>

The thickness, color, smoothness, and shine are like the others; but these beans are two fingers wide and two inches long, and thus they deviate not a little from the broad, circular shape of the [bean] wings.

Furthermore, this medicine is famous among the Indians <note>Refers to indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>, and it purges bile, phlegm, and thick humors without distress, much more gently and easily than the cathartic pine-kernels. But that thin skin which intersects these beans through the middle, and emulates the outer layer of an onion, must be cast away; otherwise, they purge with such violence from above and below <note>i.e., causing both vomiting and diarrhea</note> that they put the patient's life at risk. They must then be roasted so that their sharpness is broken, then ground into a powder, which is given in a single spoonful mixed with sugar. They are hot <margin>in the second degree, and dry in the first.</margin> <note>Refers to the Galenic system of humoral medicine</note>

### EXOTIC BEANS, SEA KIDNEYS,
#### BEANS OF THE NEW WORLD, OR THE very broad PURGATIVE BEAN, in the shape of a Heart: St. Thomas’s Heart.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, heart-shaped seed with a dark, textured outer rim and a lighter center.</image-desc>

They bring purgative beans of the New World of various sizes: some two inches in width, others almost circular in height but a little wider, especially toward the small cleft where they were attached to the pods. The thickness is that of a finger, and they are moderately compressed, covered in a nut-brown, hard, striated, and shining husk. What is contained inside is white and firm, and by nature divisible into two parts, as are all bean-like plants; the taste is sharp and bites the tongue.

The fertile soil for these beans is Carthage, and especially the island called St. Thomas <note>São Tomé</note>, whence, because of the heart-like shape they possess, they are called by some *St. Thomas’s Heart*. More on this in the margin of the following figure.

<column-break/>

### THE TREE-LIKE BEAN, WITH A FLAT
#### long black bean.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single, large, oval-shaped bean with a prominent dark hilum or border.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> once received this bean from Paludanus <note>Bernardus Paludanus, a Dutch physician and collector</note>. It was sent under the name of the *Tree-like Bean* brought from Guinea, and it was believed to have been taken from a pod similar to that of the very long tree-like bean. It was, however, very flat, two inches long or more, an inch and a half wide, blackish and shining. The same Clusius writes that in the year 1597 he obtained another larger, thicker, and nut-brown one, born on the island of Madagascar, from those who had returned that year to Amsterdam from *Java*.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE INDIAN KIDNEYS
#### and of the stones called "of good fortune."

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with large, heart-shaped leaves and long, dangling bean pods.</image-desc>

Are these the beans of which Lobelius and Pena speak in their *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work from 1570</note>, saying: "We have very rare beans, which they say are found in great abundance on the shores of Cornwall; and, what is no small wonder, no one remembers any ship being wrecked there in that place, and yet new ones are found every year, partly floating, and partly dug out from the shore-sands, as if—as the inhabitants of the Cornish sea believe—they were driven from the New World by favorable South or West winds." <note>These are "sea beans" or drift seeds carried by the Gulf Stream</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bean pod and a single bean, likely the "Sea Kidneys" mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

They say these beans grow among the seaweed on the island of Faro, and are dug out from there; that from their shape they are called *Sea Kidneys*; and by some *Stones of Good Fortune*, because they are believed to ward off or drive away calamity from the cattle, the home, and all the goods of the owner. — Clusius.

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, herbalist</note> displays these in his *Images and History* under the title of the Purgative American Bean. *Purgative Beans from America.* The *History of Lyon* also depicts and describes the same, calling them the Purgative Beans of Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, Spanish physician</note>. Are these similar to the common beans mentioned by Fernão Lopes de Castanheda in the *History of the Indies*, Book 7, chapter 78, which induce vomiting and powerfully purge the bowels?

It highlights their medicinal uses, physical characteristics, and the folklore surrounding "sea kidneys" found on European shores.</summary>

### THE INDIAN TREE-BEAN FROM GUINEA, very broad and nearly square.

<image-desc>A large, flat, rectangular seed or bean with a dark, textured surface and a prominent hilum on one side.</image-desc>

Master Paludanus <note>Bernardus Paludanus (1550–1633), a famous Dutch physician and collector of curiosities</note> sent this fruit under the title of "Climbing Bean" or "Tree-Bean from Guinea." It is flatter than the purgative beans of the New World, measuring three inches in width. It is sharper near the hilum <note>the scar on a seed marking the point of attachment to its pod</note>, broad on the opposite side, and almost square, with a length of an inch and a half. The husk equals the thickness of a chestnut shell; it is blackish-brown in color, obliquely striped, and encloses a somewhat bitter substance. Further inside, it turns blacker and gives off an unpleasant odor.

<column-break/>

### THE VERY LONG POD OF THE TREE-BEAN.

<image-desc>A long, curved seed pod (legume) with a rough, woody texture, marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

<margin>Regarding this, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note> writes thus in his *Exoticorum*: "A very large pod," he says, "was seen at Leiden in the possession of the merchant Henry Tismann, which a Portuguese man is said to have brought from Guinea. For it was endowed with a length of twenty inches and a hard, thick, wrinkled husk; the color on the outside was blackish and sooty, but on the inside nearly chestnut-colored, containing seven large climbing beans, each two and a half inches long and an inch and a half wide, very flat for their size and not at all dense, of a shining blackish-brown color, etc."</margin>

<column-break/>

### LUPIN: German: *Feigbonen*; Belgian: *Vijchboonen* & *Lupinen*; French: *Lupins*; Italian: *Lupino*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Lupin plant with palmate leaves and a vertical flower spike.</image-desc>

The Lupin is not far removed from the Bean family; it is called *Tharmes* by the Greeks <note>original: "Tharmes Græcis dictus"</note> because it is warmer than other legumes. It obtained the name "Lupin" because, just as a wolf (*Lupus*) craves the earth and feeds upon it in hunger, so too—according to Pliny—the Lupin loves the soil so much that even if cast into brambly ground, it reaches the earth with its root through the leaves and briars; or perhaps because it seems exposed and abandoned to the wolves.

According to Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen, there are two kinds of Lupins: the Cultivated and the Wild. We depict the Cultivated and common variety here, intending to treat the wild one shortly. The cultivated Lupin is known to all authors and apothecaries everywhere by the simple name of "Lupin," about which more will be said in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### THE VERY HAIRY EXOTIC LUPIN.

<image-desc>A small, rounded seed or pod with a hairy or textured surface.</image-desc>

We preserve this in our dry herbarium. Could it be the blue-purple Lupin of Clusius, whose leaves are covered in long downy hair?

Pliny, handing down the history of the Lupin, says this one thing: it is sown in unplowed soil and costs nothing to produce. It does not wish to be cultivated, and thus is cast into the soil as is. It is the first of all to be sown, but the last to be harvested; both occur in the month of September because, if it does not precede the winter, it is vulnerable to the cold. It requires sandy, dry, and poor soil, and indeed refuses to grow in well-tended ground. Pliny asserts that it blooms three times—and Dodonaeus follows him in this—first at the end of May, then in June, and finally a third time in July and August. The *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon</note> notes that its leaves, as if sensing the setting of the sun toward evening, become limp and turn downward.

<column-break/>

### LUPIN WITH A YELLOW FLOWER AND VARIEGATED SEED, the "Spanish Lupin" of some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a yellow-flowered Lupin with seeds shown separately below.</image-desc>

Camerarius writes that before the flowers open, they are somewhat bluish, but white inside; however, no one denies that the open flowers of the common Lupin are white. This variety differs from the common one primarily in its flower and seed: for the flower is yellow, and if one were deceived, it might be mistaken for Broom <note>term: Genista (Broom), a shrub with similar yellow pea-like flowers</note>, and it has a sweet scent. The seed, which is white in the common variety, is variegated in this one, spotted with white and brown. Furthermore, there is some variation in the leaves, for they are hairy on both sides.

Moreover, on the authority of Matthiolus, the Lupin is strangled by no other plants; rather, it "strangles" all harmful weeds that grow near it. And, as Pliny writes, it turns daily with the sun, showing the hours to the farmers even when the sky is cloudy.

<column-break/>

### WILD LUPIN WITH A PURPLE FLOWER and a round, variegated seed.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a wild purple Lupin plant with its root system visible.</image-desc>

The title contains the marks by which this differs most from the cultivated kind. It grows spontaneously in sandy places, as we have observed in such locations in Montpellier and Florence, blooming in April.

The cultivated kind seeks fabulous <note>likely a typo in the Latin "fabulosa" for "fabulosa" (sandy/stony) or "fabacea" (bean-like)</note> and dry places, and it blooms and ripens its fruit at the times previously ascribed by Pliny and Dodonaeus. For us at Montbéliard, it bloomed in June and July, and ripened its fruit in August and September.

Dioscorides and Galen differ regarding its medicinal powers: for the former writes that the Wild Lupin performs the same functions as the Cultivated; however, Galen says it is more bitter and more potent in all things than the cultivated. A judgment concerning the knowledge of its powers, which the narrowness of this space cannot contain, we shall provide in the Appendix.

<keywords>Lupin, Guinea Bean, Paludanus, Clusius, Pliny the Elder, Dioscorides, Galen, botany, legumes, medicinal plants, Montbéliard, heliotropism</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>S 4</sig>

### THICK BROWN BEAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Phaseolus plant with broad leaves, climbing stems, and several bean pods hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

Is this perhaps the one sent under the name of the Ethiopian Bean in Clusius’s *History* <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a Flemish botanist</note>, likely named for its blackness, or perhaps because its first origin was from Ethiopia? Caspar Bauhin also mentions the Ethiopian or black Bean in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era</note>. Clusius also possesses an entirely black variety, which he reports is known in Leiden, the seed having been sent from Italy, and that it flowers alongside the common varieties.

### THE ANCIENT CICERA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cicera plant featuring pinnate leaves and small pods along the stem.</image-desc>

The <term>Cicera</term> <note>Lathyrus cicera, or flat-podded vetch</note> differs entirely from the Chickpea (*Cicer*). It is numbered by Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture</note> not so much among the legumes as among the types of fodder. It is distinguished from the <term>Cicercula</term> <note>The grass pea or Lathyrus sativus</note>, which is a *Lathyrus*, only by its color.

According to Columella, it is sown in the first or second furrow in the month of March, as the richness of the soil requires. In Baetic Spain, it is given crushed to oxen in place of bitter vetch. For when it is almost split by the millstone, it is soaked a little until it softens; and thus, mixed with threshed chaff, it is offered to the cattle. We have found nothing else in the writings of authors concerning this Cicera that occurs to be said, other than that Cornarius makes it entirely distinct from the Chickpea. We include the figure depicted here under that name among our purchased specimens.

### MULTI-LEAVED WILD CHICKPEA WITH A thick root, and short, swollen, hairy pods.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Cicer variety with dense, multi-foliate leaves and small hairy pods.</image-desc>

Almost all botanical writers have mentioned the wild Chickpea. Thalius distinguishes it into the "Greater" and "Lesser," and writes that the greater variety grows especially in meadow-like places. Mattioli, in his commentary on Dioscorides, says the wild Chickpea is known to everyone, yet he neither illustrates nor describes it. We present here a figure of the <term>Multi-leaved</term> variety; but we suspect our depicted image—made while we were absent—was based on an illustration in Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616)</note> which does not please us, and was made worse from a poor original.

Furthermore, Chickpeas grow vigorously everywhere, and in Italy, France, and Spain they are sown in the fields. They are sown in spring and flower in June and July. They are by no means harvested unless the pods are dried out; for if they are pulled up too early, the seed becomes wrinkled. Concerning their powers and properties, see the side of the following figure.

<column-break/>

### LABURNUM-LIKE OR EGYPTIAN BEAN, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Phaseolus Laburni plant with trifoliate leaves and long, slender bean pods.</image-desc>

It has thin shoots arising from a single stem immediately near the root; these are very branched, turning purple from green, and they wind themselves around neighboring poles and supports. The leaves grow from the same stalk, as in other types of Beans, always in threes, yet much smaller, dark green, and turning purple around the stalk. The flowers are clustered in the manner of a spike, large, nearly the shape and size of a common Pea, of a yellow color, growing on an oblong, somewhat thick stalk that emerges at the base of the leaves. These are followed by short and narrow pods, in which are three or four seeds, dark or rather greenish-black in color, no larger than the seeds of the Laburnum, but usually with a blunter point at both ends.

In Clusius’s *History*, it is called a <term>type of foreign Bean</term>.

### CHICKPEA, RAM CHICKPEA: German: Zisern, Ziser Erbs; French: Pois Ciche; Italian: Cici.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Cicer Arietinum (chickpea) showing its characteristic serrated leaves and inflated pods.</image-desc>

The Chickpea spreads by its own strength with hairy, somewhat hard, branched stems. The leaves are pinnate, hairy, lacking tendrils, and serrated; from their axils spring single flowers, purple or white in color. The pods are rounded, stuffed with a seed equal to a Pea, white, black, or reddish, with a sort of little horn attached, from which it gets the name <term>Arietinum</term> <note>Latin for "ram-like," referring to the seed's resemblance to a ram's head</note>. In taste, it approaches the Pea.

Theophrastus and Pliny establish many differences among chickpeas based on size, taste, smell, shape, juice, and color. However, Dioscorides and Galen make only two main divisions: the <term>Cultivated</term> and the <term>Wild</term>. And the Cultivated, again according to the opinion of the Ancients and Moderns, is distinguished into the <term>Ram-like</term> (which is depicted here) and the <term>Dove-like</term>. Writers on herbal matters recognize three species of the Ram-like: namely white, red, and black.

### THREE-LEAVED WILD CHICKPEA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a trifoliate wild Cicer variety with small leaves and pods.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus calls this Chickpea "from the borders of the Savoyards." We have seen it at Geneva on Mount Salève.

Furthermore, let us say something of the use and properties of Chickpeas. Chickpeas are hot and moist, and possess a moderate bitterness. As a food, the Chickpea is no less flatulent than the Bean, but it nourishes more strongly than the latter. As a medicine, it has the power of attracting, digesting, cutting through <note>original: "incidendi," referring to breaking up thick humors</note>, and cleansing. It purges the spleen, kidneys, and liver and frees them from obstruction; it stimulates lust, provokes urine, is beneficial for jaundice and dropsy, and breaks down and expels stones of the kidneys and bladder—and if Dioscorides and Galen are to be believed, it shatters them.

<summary>This page describes various species of beans and chickpeas, detailing their physical characteristics, botanical classifications by historical authorities, and their medicinal uses for internal obstructions and stones.</summary>
<keywords>Chickpea, Cicer Arietinum, Phaseolus, Cicera, botany, medicinal herbs, Columella, Clusius, Dioscorides, Galen, legumes, kidney stones</keywords>
