### PEA: German: *Erbs*: French: *Pois*: Italian: *Piso*.
### Common small field pea.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pea plant with several pods hanging from a central vine, showing leaves and tendrils.</image-desc>

Peas <note>original: *Pisa*</note> received their name from the place Pisa, where they once grew in great abundance. Some authors make only two distinctions of them: the *Greater* and the *Lesser*. Others distinguish them more precisely, establishing some as *garden* peas, others as *field* peas, others as *wild* peas, and to these they further add *exotic* varieties. Garden peas, which are generally larger and for the most part white, are further divided into those eaten without the pods (called *leptoloba* <note>Greek: "fine-podded"</note>) and those eaten with the pods themselves. Field peas, however, which are sown in the fields and creep along the ground, include some larger and some smaller varieties; some are white, some green, some reddish or ash-colored, some red, some variegated, and some blue, which are rarer. Finally, there is a certain "proliferous" <note>producing many offspring or clusters</note> garden variety where several pods are joined together. More on this in the following sections.

### LARGE WHITE PEAS: German: *Gross Erbs*: French: *Pois ramiers*: Italian: *Piselli maiori*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall pea plant climbing upwards with large leaves and multiple pods.</image-desc>

The largest white peas are similar to common peas: the flower is sometimes purple, sometimes white. The seeds are white, but not as angular or compressed—rather, they are larger than the edible peas discussed shortly, and not as round. There is also a certain *branching white pea* that grows to a great height, whose pods are large and white and, lacking a tough inner skin, are eaten whole; for this reason, the French call them *Pois mange tout* <note>literally "eat-all peas" or snow peas</note>.

Furthermore, all peas delight in sunny and moist places, requiring a warm climate and soil. They flower in the months of June and July, and subsequently produce seeds in small valves <note>pods</note>. Regarding their use and medicinal powers, see the text beside the following figure.

### TUFTED PROLIFEROUS PEA: German: *Busch-Erbsen*. French: *Pois à bouquets*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "bush" pea variety with a dense cluster of flowers and pods at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

This variety is more upright than the common pea, with a firmer and thicker stalk, especially at the upper part, and it rises by its own strength. It bears no flowers or fruit except at the very top of the stalk, which is densely packed with numerous white flowers arranged in a circle. There, finally, the pods succeed them, crowning the plant in the same radiating row (to use the common Latin term), hanging in pairs or twos from the same little stalk. These peas resemble common peas but are smaller, orbicular, etc.

Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> says that the pea has no active medicinal quality and occupies a middle ground between those things that produce good or bad juices, nourish much or little, are easily or difficultly digested, descend through the bowels slowly or quickly, or are flatulent or free of wind.

<column-break/>

This kind of pea greatly exceeds the height of a man. It bears a flower that is purple in the middle and rose-colored on the wider part. The pods are large and succulent. The peas are very large, not round but angular, or rather compressed, of a beautiful color, and variegated with red and white. They are highly esteemed as food, especially by the Germans. Could this be the *square pea* of Pliny? To Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous botanist</note> it is the *large Italian red pea*. We have seen it in gardens in Basel, Geneva, and Lyon.

### SMALL GREEN OR VARIEGATED PEAS, a beautiful species of pea with angular leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pea plant with smaller, more angular leaves and slender pods.</image-desc>

The smaller peas variegated with red or purple, as well as the smaller green ones, are of nearly the same size and not much larger than Vetches <note>a type of wild legume</note>; they can hardly be distinguished from them by their seeds, although they differ greatly from common Vetches in their foliage, stalk, and pods. These three kinds of peas grew for us at Montbéliard <note>original: *Montelgardi*</note> in the garden of His Serene Highness. The one we depict here with angular leaves is kept in more cultivated gardens, and we likewise had it in the garden of His Serene Highness at Montbéliard.

### INDIAN PEAS WITH SOMEWHAT LONG LEAVES. And concerning various other Indian peas.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an "Indian" pea variety with elongated, pointed leaves and a single large pod.</image-desc>

Indian peas with somewhat long leaves do not grow in the manner of other peas or even kidney beans; instead, they produce many tender leaves, somewhat long, both large and small, attached to long stalks. The tiny flowers are near the base of the leaves; they have no manifest flavor. These peas, sown by us, appeared in the month of June as we express them in the illustration.

We keep various other Indian peas among our natural specimens. Some are orbicular, almost dusky, darkly spotted, and marked with a whitish area at the top. Others are twice as large as the greater pea, orbicular, black, and compressed at the part where the hilum <note>the "eye" or attachment point of the seed</note> is located. Others are larger and more orbicular than the Chickpea, of a faded dusky color, distinguished by white spots. And finally, others are round, variegated with white and red.

It includes early botanical observations on "mange-tout" (snow peas) and tufted varieties, citing authorities like Galen and Pliny.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### VETCHLING, CHICKLING PEA, GREEK PEA
German: *Kichern*; French: *des Gesses*; Italian: *Cicerchia*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lathyrus plant with tendrils, leaves, and seed pods.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> writes that the leaves of the **Vetchling** (*Cicercula*) are oblong; Galen says its substance is similar to the *Ochrus* and the *Phacelis*; Columella compares it to the Pea. Pliny, however, incorrectly makes it a third species of Chickpea <note>original: "Cicer"</note>, but this is an error, for *Cicercula* is a diminutive of *Cicerra*, not of *Cicer*—otherwise it would be called *Cicerrulum*.

Various differences of the Vetchling or Chickling Pea are reviewed in this section, taken from their size, and the shape and colors of the flower and seed, as will be clear from what follows. Here is depicted the *larger species of Vetchling with reddish and smaller white flowers of the thickets*, as it is called in German. It grows in lean and rich soil alike, near hedges, thickets, and thorn-bushes, and climbing by its own tendrils <note>original: "capreolo"</note>, it takes hold and rises above them. It is also cultivated in gardens.

### LARGE NARBONNE VETCHLING
narrow-leafed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Lathyrus plant with narrow leaves and prominent flowers.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are fringed into four at the base of the footstalk; two larger and two smaller, with a split tendril. The **flowers** are large, on a long footstalk, similar to the flowers of the broad-leafed variety, and of a purple color.

Camerarius calls it the *Narrow-leafed Vetchling*, differing from the broad-leafed one only by this mark, and easily enduring the severity of Winter.

We observed this species of Vetchling at Montpellier <note>A major center for botanical study in France</note>, and we also received a dried specimen from there.

### VETCHLING WITH HAIRY PODS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lathyrus variety featuring hairy or textured seed pods.</image-desc>

It has a single, thin, annual root. The stems are angular and longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>. The leaves are in pairs, long and narrow. The flowers on long footstalks are purplish, which are succeeded by long, hairy, and rough **pods** <note>original: "siliquae"</note>, containing small, blackish or reddish seeds, round with a wrinkled surface.

We have found it in various places around the borders of fields, flowering in July and with mature seed in August. When moved into our garden, it grew to a great height for us.

Is it the *Aracus* and *Aracu* of Anguillara? Or the *Aracus* and *Cicera* of the *Adversaria*? Or the *Cicera* of the *History of Lyon*? Or the *Aracus* of Dodoens, which is similar to the Vetchling—a rare legume, and one that is sown by no one except those devoted to botanical matters?

<column-break/>

### LARGE BROAD-LEAFED VETCHLING, WITH
a larger purple flower, more beautiful, of Narbonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Lathyrus with large flowers and pods.</image-desc>

This Vetchling is more beautiful in all its parts than the preceding one, with membranous and veined wings attached along the trailing stems. The **leaves** are in pairs, veiny, somewhat rigid, ending in a blunt point. The **flowers** are many joined together, large, purple, and of a pleasing color. The **pods** are three inches long, or even larger, barely half an inch wide, and somewhat compressed.

By Lobel in his *Observations* and *Adversaria*, it is called the *Broad-leafed Narbonne Vetchling*, the *Clymenum* of Mattioli. It is the *Cultivated Bitter Vetch* of Cordus, and the *Greek Pea* of Bock <note>original: "Tragi"</note>.

We observed it in the springtime in Narbonne, France, on the journey from Montpellier toward Péronne, in the hedges. Birds seek out the seeds of this one, as well as the preceding, and pierce the pods to devour them.

### WILD YELLOW VETCHLING
of the thickets.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild yellow Lathyrus with dense foliage and flowers.</image-desc>

It grows everywhere around hedges and even in meadows, as we have observed at Montbéliard and Belfort, at Basel outside the Stone Gate, and also at Lyon, *in the woods of the Good German woman* <note>original: "au bois de la bonne Allemande"</note>. It commonly flowers in April and March. We have also had it in the garden, both growing spontaneously and planted.

Some maintain it is a *kind of Bitter Vetch* <note>original: "Ervum"</note>; to Tabernaemontanus it is a *species of Vetch*; to Gesner it is *Aphaca*, or *Vetch*, or rather a *kind of Orbus* with yellow flowers; but to all the common people it is the *Wild Chickling*.

### A CERTAIN SPECIES OF VETCHLING, WHICH IS
the Wild Ervilia of Dodoens.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant identified as wild Ervilia, showing branching stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

The stems of this, like other Vetchlings, are angular and one or two cubits long, to which the leaves—oblong, sometimes simple, sometimes ending in tendrils—cling by clasping the stem without any intervening footstalk. The flowers are white; the pod is round; the seed is round, similar to Peas but smaller, bitter, green, hard, and dry. **Botanists** <note>original: "Herbarii"</note> sow it in gardens.

In Mattioli’s commentary on Dioscorides, with a large figure, it is called *Lathyris* and in Italian *Aracus niger* (Black Aracus); but this is a great error in the judgment of Dodoens, since this legume has more similarity to the legitimate **Bitter Vetch** <note>original: "Ervum"</note>. To Lobel and Pena in the *Adversaria*, it is the *Wild Ochrus* or *Wild Ervilia by nature*, etc.

### ANGULAR-SEEDED LATHYRUS <note>Lathyrus angulatus, a type of wild pea or vetchling</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lathyrus plant with climbing tendrils, lanceolate leaves, and seed pods. The roots are fibrous and thin.</image-desc>

The stems of this plant are quite long and divided into many branches; the leaves grow in pairs, are somewhat broad, oblong, pointed, smooth, and streaked, with two appendages at the base that clasp the stem. Emerging from between the leaves, the remainder of the stalk turns into twisting tendrils with which it grips nearby objects. The flowers are white; the pods are broad, and within them are white seeds that are broad, flattened, and angular. The root is fibrous and slender.

Cæsalpinus calls it *Cicercula* <note>Little chickpea</note>, Fuchs calls it *White Ervum* and *Cultivated Ervum*. Lonicer and others call it *Orobus* <note>Bitter vetch</note>; the *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel, 1570</note> calls it another *Narbonne Lathyrus*; but as to why they call it *Lathyris* <note>usually referring to spurge</note>, it would have been better to say *Lathyrus*. Is it perhaps the kind of pea that the Venetians call *Mauerette*, the Romans *Cicerchia*, and the French *des Sars*?

---

### CATANANCE IN GENERAL: The leguminous CATANANCE of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Catanance plant, showing a central stalk with narrow leaves and several flower heads or seed clusters at the top.</image-desc>

The Greeks named this plant *Catanance* <note>from 'katananke', meaning compulsion</note> because it was believed to drive one to love by a fatal and unshakable necessity, and was considered an inevitable lure for love. Pliny thought it superfluous to describe it, as its only use was for love potions; likewise, Dioscorides remained silent on its powers, and Galen and the later Greeks are entirely silent regarding it.

Dioscorides makes two types, but it is admitted by everyone today that the one he established as the First is completely unknown; nor is the Second sufficiently known, in which even the size of the fruit <note>original: "Mali", literally apple</note> is suspected to be an error.

The leguminous Catanance which we depict here bears pods in the gardens of herbalists in July and August, and is also seen in the fields of the northern coasts. *Could it be the Wild Ervum of the herbalists?*

---

### APHACA, VETCH: German: Vvicken; Belgian: Vwitfen; French: Vesse; Italian: Aphaca; English: Fiche <note>Vetch</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aphaca (Yellow Vetchling), showing distinctive large stipules that look like leaves and climbing tendrils.</image-desc>

Following the example of Galen and Mattioli, we join Aphaca here with the Vetch; we shall treat Aphaca more specifically in the Appendix.

Furthermore, of the Vetch, one is cultivated and another is wild; one is larger and another smaller; one has a single flower and another many flowers; one has white flowers and another yellow. Vetches also differ in the color, thickness, roundness, and bitterness of their seeds; that which is thinner and rounder is bitter, and its pod is shorter and rough.

We depict here the common and cultivated variety, a crop very well known to everyone and accustomed to being sown in various places. The seeds ripen in July and August, providing a most welcome food for pigeons; indeed, even humans eat them, but if ducks eat them, they die, nor do chickens easily eat them.

<column-break/>

### THIN-LEAVED LATHYRUS, with red flowers. And concerning the EGYPTIAN LATHYRUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lathyrus variety with thinner leaves and more delicate climbing structures.</image-desc>

It is taller than a cubit <note>about 18-22 inches</note>, with broad pods containing three or four seeds the size of Bitter Vetch, round, rough, covered with dark spots, and with the hilum <note>the seed scar</note> marked with dark lines.

We found it on the journey from Montpellier to Frontignan, in dry and woody places, flowering in April. Is it the *Lathyrus with narrower grass-like leaves* in Lobel's *Icons*? Or a species of *Aracus* called *Arouce* by the French?

The so-called *Egyptian Cicercula* does not differ greatly from the common cultivated variety; the difference is only in the flower, which in this variety is an elegant blue on the inside, and a purplish-ash color on the outside. *Clusius.*

---

### WILD PEA: In GERMAN, Wild Erbsen.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild pea plant (Pisum sylvestre) with broad leaves, tendrils, and developing seed pods.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus and others among the more recent authors have mentioned the Wild Pea. Thus, Camerarius in his *Hortus* has the *Pannonian Wild Pea*, and the *Adversaria* writes that the *Wild Pea* in Switzerland and Upper Germany—not unlike the wild kidney bean—presents itself to those traveling abroad. It is found noted among writers that in Suffolk, England, between Orford and Aldeburgh, on the rocky shores covered by no earth, such a crop of peas sprang up in the autumn of the year 1555 that it sufficed for a thousand men. Clusius likewise observed that peas grow abundantly among rocks on the ridges of the Graben fortress and other places in Hungary <note>Pannonia</note> and Austria. They flower in June; the seed is ripe in August.

---

### COMMON WILD VETCH OF THE CROPS: with small black seeds. CRACCA to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common wild vetch (Vicia), showing small leaflets and clusters of pods.</image-desc>

Gesner calls it the *Lesser Vetch* and *Vogel vvick* <note>Bird vetch</note>; by some Germans it is called *St. Christopher's Herb*. It seems to differ from the cultivated vetch chiefly in the seed, which is very small and round, and numerous in the pods, which are narrower, longer, and more cylindrical than those of the Hedge Vetch, less hairy and almost smooth, turning black when dried.

It very often grows spontaneously in the fields, and is so similar to the Vetch that it retains its name in the fields even today, being called *Wild Vetch*. We have observed it flowering with its purple blossoms everywhere among the crops in Montpellier during the months of April and May.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES:

### WILD VETCH WITH YELLOW FLOWERS.
<note>original: "Vicia sylvestris flore luteo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Vicia sylvestris plant with pinnate leaves, tendrils, and small flowers.</image-desc>

From a single root emerge numerous little stems, which are both winding and angular, divided alternately into "wings" <note>leaf-like appendages or branches</note>: to these cling leaves similar to the cultivated Vetch, ten or twelve in number, more or less, whose midrib ends in a twisting tendril. The flowers are beautiful, yellow, or a pale yellow, and sometimes whitish; these are followed by pods that are shorter, fuller, thicker, and wider than the pods of the common Vetch, ripening with a white hairy down, in which are four or five seeds, dark, spotted, flattened, and angular, with the taste of a legume.

We observed it blooming in Montpellier in March and April, while it matures its seed in June. Every year it sprouts again from the fallen seed and endures throughout the entire Winter.

### YELLOW WILD VETCH, WITH A DARK HOOD.
<note>original: "Vicia sylvestris lutea, cum galea fusca"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vetch plant with larger, broader leaves and distinct floral structures.</image-desc>

We received this from Bologna under the name of Wild Vetch: how much it differs from the preceding ones is clear enough from a comparison of the Illustrations. It was sent to us dried, for which reason it was not possible to depict it exactly: the person who sent it attributed to it a yellow flower with a dark hood <note>the "galea" or upper petal of the flower</note>.

This was sent to us dried from Bologna; whether it is that kind of Wild Lupin of the Italian peasants which grows near rivers and in coastal areas, and with which beasts of burden are fattened and cured of diseases, we leave to the judgment of the more learned.

### SMALL VETCH, OR LESSER CRACCA, with many hairy pods.
<note>original: "Vicia parva, sive Cracca minor"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a delicate vetch with many small, hairy seed pods.</image-desc>

From a slender and weak root, thin and feeble square stems emerge, luxuriating in an troublesome abundance of "wings." The leaves are paired with lush leaves, smooth, pinnate, 15 or 17 attached to the nerve, which, turning into twisting tendrils, seizes and strangles the crops in an unfortunate embrace. From the wings of the leaves, on little stalks born here and there, sit tiny flowers in clusters of 4 or 5, all facing the same way, of a whitish-purple color: these are followed by pods half an inch long, hairy, each containing two grains of Hedge Vetch, smaller, rounder, and more spotted.

Some refer this to *Orobanche* <note>Broomrape, though here likely a misidentification of the vetch</note>. To the German Hieronymus Bock <note>Tragus</note> it is the Smallest Vetch of all; to Tabernaemontanus it is the Lesser Cracca; to Lobel and Pena it is *Aracus* or the Smallest Cracca.

It abounds in the fields, propagating itself every year by fallen seed: and it also grew for us when sown in the garden.

<column-break/>

### PERENNIAL HEDGE VETCH: MOUTH OF THE WORLD: German: St. Christopher’s Herb; Belgian: *Crock*; French: *Vesseron*, Wild Vetch.
<note>original: "Vicia sepium perennis: Os Mundi"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vetch with prominent tendrils and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

The stems of this are two or three cubits <note>about 3 to 4.5 feet</note> long: the leaves are wider where they connect to the rib than in the cultivated or more common wild vetch, and there are more pairs of them than in those; otherwise they do not differ much from them. The flowers are not two-colored, as in the cultivated and common wild vetch, but of a single color, tinted with a deeper purple, and five or six hanging from a single stalk. There is, however, a notable difference in the pods regarding length and smoothness: furthermore, when mature, they are all so black that they almost shine because of their blackness. The seeds are white, smaller and longer than in the cultivated variety, and of various shapes. The root is perennial and self-renewing. It grows abundantly in various places in hedges, and usually flowers in the month of April.

### MANY-LEAVED VETCH WITH BROAD PODS.
<note>original: "Vicia multifolia cum latis siliquis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vetch with dense foliage and broad pods.</image-desc>

In this beautiful kind of Vetch there are very many pairs of leaves—twelve, twenty, or more. They are narrow, however, ending in a point, and upon them are large hairs. The flowers are small, solitary, yellow, hanging from very short stalks. The pods are also solitary, at first very hairy, later less so, but rough to the touch, one and a half inches long, and almost half an inch wide, in which there are usually five grains.

### A SPECIES OF THE SMALLEST VETCH OR CRACCA, with smooth pods.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small vetch with smooth seed pods.</image-desc>

This is more delicate than the preceding: the leaves in this one are also more sparse. The flower, which in that one is usually clustered, is in this one most often solitary, although sometimes two or three are observed. The pod is equal to the pod of the preceding, but smooth and knotted, containing two, three, or even four grains.

It is frequently found on the borders of fields; it flowers in July and matures its seed in August. We believe that Lobel and Pena confused this with the preceding one.

# 148
### THE GREAT WOOD VETCH, similar to the Wild Pea.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing vetch plant with large, pinnate leaves, tendrils, and clusters of flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

Of all the Vetches <note>Latin: Vicia</note> that have been seen thus far, this is the largest, reaching a height of many cubits. The leaves approach the form of the Hedge Vetch. The flowers are numerous and purplish; the pods approach the size of Pea pods and are smooth. The root is thick, interrupted by nodes, creeping, very fertile in producing a lineage of stems, and perennial.

We have observed it growing abundantly around the wonderful spring at Boll <note>A reference to Bad Boll in Germany, known for its mineral springs</note>, as well as elsewhere. Is this perhaps the "Smaller Wild Pea" in the Illustrations and History of Tabernaemontanus? <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a famous 16th-century herbalist</note>

---

### A SMALL KIND OF VETCH WITH A LONG LEAF.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender vetch plant with narrow, elongated leaflets and small flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has an angular stem that turns into tendrils <note>Latin: capreolos</note> at the rib; the leaves are an inch and a half to two inches long, grass-like, scarcely a straw's breadth wide, ending in a point; the small flowers cling to a peculiar long little fork, being many and oblong: the pods are like those of the Smaller Tufted Vetch, but somewhat longer. Caspar Bauhin <note>A preeminent Swiss botanist</note> gave us a branch brought from Montpellier, which he labeled "A small kind of Vetch with a long leaf."

---

### THE VETCH WHICH ANGUILLARA CALLS PITINE, with a broad pod and yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a vetch plant with broad seed pods and tendrils.</image-desc>

This legume is the plant called *Pitine* by Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, an Italian botanist</note>, which almost everyone refers to the Vetches. Dodonaeus and Caesalpinus call it *Aphaca*, and they establish that it was called *Aphace* by Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen.

We have observed it at Montpellier, Bologna, and various other places in Italy and France, growing spontaneously and abundantly among the cornfields; it propagates itself every year by fallen seed. Some also sow it in gardens.

<column-break/>

### WILD VETCH WITH THE POD OF A LENTIL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild vetch with small leaflets and distinct seed pods.</image-desc>

It has a stem about nine inches long, slender, angular, smooth, and branched. The individual leaflets are no larger than those of the Smallest Tufted Vetch, blunt and heart-shaped at the tip—which the illustrator has depicted poorly. The end of the leaf-rib turns into twisting tendrils. From the junction of the leaf and stem <note>the axil</note> grows an inch-long stalk bearing a single flower, similar to a Lentil flower, which is followed by a pod longer than a vetch, half an inch wide, smooth and flattened, enclosing two or three seeds, which are round like those of the Larger Lentil.

We collected this in Gallia Narbonensis <note>Southern France</note> around Nîmes. Our illustrator, however, has poorly drawn the leaves as sharp-pointed, whereas they are somewhat heart-shaped.

---

### A BEAUTIFUL KIND OF MANY-LEAVED VETCH, or a species of Goat's Rue to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lush, leafy vetch or goat's rue species with dense foliage and flower spikes.</image-desc>

To the long rib ending in a tendril are attached sometimes twenty leaves, ending in a point; the arrangement of the flowers is the same, on a long stalk, and they approach the flowers of the Hedge Vetch and are purple. This Vetch is branched.

We obtained this at Strasbourg from the dried plants of Master Agerius, who called it a certain *Galega* <note>Goat's Rue</note> from the Apennine mountains.

---

### BITTER VETCH: <term>Ervum</term> <note>The Latin name for Bitter Vetch, Vicia ervilia</note>: German: *Erven*: Gillyflower-style: *Ers*: Italian: *Ervo*: Spanish: *Iervos*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Orobus (bitter vetch) plant showing its upright habit and seed pods.</image-desc>

What the Greeks called *Orobus*, the Arabs *Erbum* and *Kersene*, the Latins called *Ervum*, from which the "Vetch-like Chickpea" of Theophrastus differs only in its blackness. Moreover, *Ervum* is either Cultivated or Wild, and of both there are again various differences. The Cultivated kind is especially distinguished by either a larger or more slender pod and seed: and that seed is either white, pale, or reddish. However, *Ervum* is by no means the same as *Ervilia* <note>Pellitory or similar</note>, nor is it the *Cicericula* <note>Grass pea</note>, as some have thought.

Furthermore, Bitter Vetch dries to an intense degree in the second stage and heats in the first <note>Refers to the Galenic system of humors/qualities</note>: and because it partakes of bitterness, it cuts through, cleanses, and clears obstructions. It fattens oxen; but humans, as Galen already noted long ago, abstain from it entirely [unless there is a great shortage of crops], because it is most unpleasant and has a bad juice: <margin>because, as we have from the records of Dioscorides, a more frequent use of it in food or drink draws blood through the bowels and bladder along with griping pains.</margin>

<meta>Catchword: vbetior (more frequent/abundant)</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### LENTIL: German: Linsen: Belgian: Lensin: French: Lentille: Italian: Lentichia: Spanish: Lenteyas.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a lentil plant (Lens) showing slender stems, pinnate leaves, small flowers, and seed pods.</image-desc>

They claim the Lentil <note>Latin: *Lens*</note> is named as if it were "gentle" <note>Latin: *lenis*</note>, and that it carries a meaning of mildness because it produces even-temperedness in those who eat it.
This legume spreads out upon the ground on firm stalks unless it has something nearby to climb by clinging with its tendrils. The leaves are pinnate like those of the Vetch, but smaller and hairy; the flowers turn purple or white. The pods are short and flattened, and within them are two or three circular, flattened seeds—white, tawny, or blackish—which are small and very tough <note>Latin: *lentia*, playing on the word *Lens*</note>. When the husk is removed, they split into two parts.
Pliny describes one seed as rounder and blacker, and another of its own specific shape. Commonly, however, two kinds of Lentil are established: the Greater and the Lesser. Some say the latter is more ash-colored, while the former is more so. We depict the Lesser Lentil here.

### THE AMPHICARPOUS ARACHIDNA PLANT: Perhaps the *Aracoides* of Theophrastus?

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Arachidna, showing a plant with rounded leaves and roots that appear to bear fruit or tubers underground.</image-desc>

Theophrastus mentions the *Arachidna* and says it is similar to the *Aracus* <note>Wild Vetch</note>, and he enters it as *Aracoides* <note>Vetch-like</note>. But why does he make it similar to the Vetch when he denies it has leaves, which the Vetch is by no means lacking? Thus we believe his text is corrupted, although Pliny followed him.
Whatever the case, Theophrastus rightly classifies it among the "amphicarpous" <term>amphicarpous: plants that produce fruit both above and below the ground</term> plants, since it bears fruit on both sides—namely, above the earth and beneath it. Some consider it a species of *Dentaria* <note>Toothwort</note>. What we depict here is the Cretan *Arachidna* of Honorius Bellus; we took care to prepare its image from a dried plant, since it did not grow when sown in the garden.

### LEGUMINOUS EARTH-NUT: German: Erdnuss: French: Raue sauuage: Italian: Noce della terra.

Based on the evidence of the root, writers since Ruellius have named this *Chamæbalanus*, as if you were to say a "ground-acorn" or "lowly acorn" <note>From Greek: *chamai* (on the ground) and *balanos* (acorn)</note>. By Fuchs and others it is called *Apios*, by others *Ornithogalum*, and by some *Astragalus*.
It is sown by both seed and root, but it reaches maturity faster from the root. It grows spontaneously in various places in fields and vineyards, and along the edges of plowed lands. We have observed it growing in abundance at Geneva in the vineyards outside the Cornavin Gate, and at Basel in the fields outside the Stone Gate. It flowers in June and July. The Burgundians call them *des Magussans*.
During times of crop failure, the poor in the countryside eat this root. It is moderately warm, but a little more dry; it provokes nausea, but otherwise is harmless. From the flowers, according to Camerarius, a water is distilled which mimics rose water.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATER LENTIL.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a larger variety of lentil (Lens Maior) with similar features to the first but larger leaves and pods.</image-desc>

This is more beautiful and larger in all its parts than the common Lentil.
Furthermore, the Lentil loves a dry climate and a thin soil rather than a rich one, and fields are commonly improved by it. That which cooks easily and which gives off nothing black while being soaked is superior. But if it is eaten constantly, it dims the sight, is difficult to digest, is inconvenient for the stomach, and also inflates the intestines. However, it stops the bowels if eaten with the husk. Boiled with pearled barley and applied as a poultice, it soothes gout. With honey, it glues together cavities, breaks up crusts, and cleanses ulcers; but boiled with vinegar, it dissipates hard tumors and scrofula. So say Dioscorides and Pliny. The reader may seek more from our Appendix and our *Great History*.

### CLUSIUS’S IMAGE OF THE ARACHIDNA.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of another Arachidna variety, showing a sprawling habit with small leaves and pods.</image-desc>

Clusius proposes this in *Exotics*, Book 4, Chapter 16, and describes it at length. We also express it here, taken from that source, with flowers added from Pona’s illustration. The seed is similar in appearance to Vetch, hard to the touch of the teeth, with white marrow and the flavor of peas. Such was the seed we received from Honorius Bellus from Cydonia in Crete, but when sown, as already mentioned, it did not grow. They call this plant *Agriophacon* <note>original: "agrestem Lentem" - wild lentil</note>, which is found among crops and legumes and is neglected.

### THE OROBUS OF CERTAIN AUTHORS WITH A BULBOUS ROOT.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Orobus, showing upright stems with narrow leaves and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

It puts forth slender, upright, firm, and angular stalks about a foot high. The leaves are attached to a single rib at intervals, usually four situated opposite each other, upright and narrow. The flowers grow on long shoots, crowded like a spike, in the shape of Pea or Vetch flowers, six or eight together, of a white color. The pods are oblong and blackish, full of black and sometimes spotted seed. It relies on five or six roots, the length of a little finger, somewhat thick, with oblong bulbs, black on the outside and white within.
It is the Pannonian *Orobus* of Clusius with an Asphodel root. It flowers in April and May, and perfects its seed in June.

It combines classical botanical lore from Pliny and Dioscorides with contemporary observations from botanists like Clusius and Fuchs.</summary>
<keywords>Lentils, Arachidna, Earth-nut, Orobus, medicinal uses of legumes, subterranean fruiting, botanical history, Geneva, Basel, Honorius Bellus, Charles de l'Écluse</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### THE ARACUS OF THE ANCIENTS IN GENERAL.
### CERTAIN SPECIES OF LEGUMINOUS ARACUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a vetch-like plant (Aracus) with pinnate leaves, tendrils, and pea-like flowers, showing the root system and stems.</image-desc>

The Aracus <note>A type of wild vetch</note> is a rough and hard thing in the Law <note>referring to botanical classification rules</note>, says Theophrastus, who makes the *arachidna* <note>wild chickling pea</note> similar to it, as was said before. The seed, according to Galen, is similar to the *Lathyrus* <note>grass pea</note> in use and function, except that the seeds of the Aracus are harder and are not as easily softened by boiling.

However, the plant which we depict here is labeled by some as the *Leguminous Aracus*. The stem is a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> long, or more, thin and smooth. The **leaves** are arranged in fours at intervals, resting on a single stalk, two or three inches in length, as wide as a stalk of grain, ending in a sharp point, streaked, and greenish. The **flowers** cling to the end of a small fork, clustered in groups of five or six, large and purple, like those of the Spring Galega <note>Goat's Rue</note>, sitting upon a long stalk. The root approaches the form of the Spring Galega root. We obtained this from Champagnole in Burgundy.

### SCYTHIAN ROOT, GLYCYRRHIZA, LIQUORICE:
### German: *Susholtz*: French: *Reglisse*: Italian: *Regolitia*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Liquorice plant (Glycyrrhiza) showing its characteristic pinnate leaves and a thick, spreading root system.</image-desc>

The nature of the Scythian root mentioned by Theophrastus and Pliny is not well known today; unless, as Cordus, Tragus, Dodonaeus, and others believe, it is the plant called *Glycyrrhiza* <note>Greek: "sweet root"</note> by the Writers, which the Apothecary shops call by the corrupted name *Liquiritia* <note>Liquorice</note>.

Commonly, two types of *Glycyrrhiza* are established: namely, the prickly-fruited Liquorice of Dioscorides which does not creep, which we depict here: and the Common or German Liquorice with a creeping root, of which we shall speak presently.

The prickly-fruited kind, which some consider the true Liquorice to this day, is said by Dioscorides and Pliny to grow most excellently in Cappadocia, Pontus, and Cilicia. But in our regions, it is cultivated only in some gardens for the sake of pleasure: inasmuch as it is far surpassed in sweetness and grace by the Common variety.

### THE WILD LIQUORICE OF SOME:
### Wild Fenugreek to others.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Wild Liquorice (Glycyrrhiza sylvestris) showing its leaves, flowers, and long, creeping roots.</image-desc>

Tragus names this Wild Fenugreek and the Wild Lotus described by Dioscorides, and Lonicer does not disagree. To Cordus it is *Polygalon* <note>Milkwort</note>, to Clusius and others the Wild *Glaux*. However, the opinion of Gesner, who labels it *Wild Liquorice*, pleases us.

We saw it at Basel, outside the Stone Gate among the thorns and Broom on the hill of La Bestie, flowering in June.

Regarding the Common **Liquorice**, what must be added to the previous remarks is that it is also planted in gardens: and if it once takes hold, it clings with such stubborn fertility that it can hardly ever be eradicated by the roots, for it regrows with such persistent fecundity.

Matthioli mentions a sterile Liquorice, thus making a third species: but to Us, as well as to Lobel and Pena, as many...

<column-break/>

### THE ASTRAGALUS OF SOME, SIMILAR TO THE ARACUS
### of Charles Toffanus.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Astragalus, showing upright stems with small pinnate leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

This plant was sent to Us from Bologna, collected in the meadows surrounding that city. The **flowers** consist of various colors: white, yellow, and lightly reddening. The **root** is bulbous, like that of a peony. The **stems** are a cubit high and angular. The **leaves** have two, three, or four pairs of leaflets, and are longer than the leaves of the Aracus, otherwise very similar: but they do not end in tendrils in the same way. The stalks of the **flowers** are smaller than a palm's breadth, angular, at the ends of which are several flowers, such as those of the yellow Wild Lathyrus: near the base of the leaves and stalks are sharp appendages.

### COMMON LIQUORICE, WITH A CREEPING ROOT,
### called German Liquorice.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the common German Liquorice plant, emphasizing the extensive, horizontal root system (rhizome).</image-desc>

The twig-like **roots** creep far and wide in a tangled, wandering fashion, the color of boxwood inside, but black on the outside, with a flavor like honey. The **stalk** is somewhat hairy, less sweet, and purplish. The **leaves** are arranged in a wing-like shape, in the manner of an Ash tree, dark green and moderately sticky. The **flowers** are in clusters, purplish or dilute blue. The **pods** are smooth, and in them are small seeds.

It is kept in gardens in many places in Italy, and in not a few places in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> it grows spontaneously in great abundance. In the Spains it is indeed most frequent, from whence it is sent to London, Antwerp, and Lyon, and is distributed everywhere at a cheap price. Nor can Germany boast less of this sweet root, and especially the fields of Bamberg, which alone can supply enough Liquorice for all of Germany. More in the following.

### A PLANT APPROACHING IN SOME RESPECTS
### THE WILD FENUGREEK OF TRAGUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant resembling wild fenugreek, with rounded leaflets and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

In many respects this plant also approaches the leguminous star-plant of which we will speak later. We found it around Montpellier, near the Castle of the Bishop of Montpellier, in a dry place.

Furthermore, Liquorice is temperately warm and moist: but the Bark, which has a certain bitterness, partakes of a warmer quality, but it ought to be scraped off. The fresh root full of juice moistens more than the dried one. It is useful for hoarseness, coughs, difficulty breathing, pneumonia, pleurisy, consumption: and it soothes all diseases of the chest that have become roughened, calms inflammations, and mitigates the sharpness and saltiness of the humors. A decoction benefits ulcerated kidneys and bladders, and heals the dripping of urine <note>strangury</note>.

<summary>This page describes various species of Aracus (vetch) and Glycyrrhiza (liquorice), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins in Europe, and medicinal uses for respiratory and urinary ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Aracus, Liquorice, Glycyrrhiza, medicinal roots, botany, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Bamberg, respiratory health, herbal medicine</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE MIMOSA HERB, OR DELICATE HERB.
#### Illustration from Acosta.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mimosa plant with delicate, fern-like leaves and small thorns along the stem.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> says that there is found in certain gardens of Asia a plant five palms in length, leaning upon neighboring shrubs or walls, with a slender stalk endowed with an elegant greenness, not entirely round, and with small, sharp thorns scattered at intervals. The *leaves are like the Female Fern*, but smaller. It delights in damp and stony places; when touched by the hand, it withers and droops, but when the hand is removed, it gradually recovers its former greenness. It has the proper name of *Living Herb* and *Mimosa Herb* <note>original: "Herba viva" and "Herba mimosa"</note>. Acosta also wrote of it as the Soft Herb and the Delicate Herb in his *Book of Aromatics* published in Italian.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER MIMOSA OR DELICATE HERB.
#### Illustration from Clusius, depicted from a dried plant.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a different variety of Mimosa, showing the root system and more detailed leaf structures.</image-desc>

The same Clusius adds that it has a nature very different from the "sad tree" <note>likely referring to the Nyctanthes arbor-tristis, which blooms only at night</note>: for every night at sunset it withers and dries up in a way, so that it appears to have wasted away; but at sunrise it receives its vigor anew, and the more the sun glows, the more it flourishes, turning its leaves toward the sun all day long. In smell and taste it is like Liquorice, and the leaves are commonly chewed by the natives for a cough, to cleanse the body, and to make the voice clearer; it is also said to be useful for pains of the kidneys, and to knit together fresh wounds.

---

### THE ASTRAGALUS OF THE ANCIENTS, AND IN GENERAL
#### The Roman Astragalus, or Shield-bearing Hedysarum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Astragalus plant, featuring pinnate leaves and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

Astragalus, according to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note>, is a small shrub growing from the earth, similar to the Chickpea in its leaves and branches; the *flowers* are purple and small; the *root* is round, like a large Radish, having solid shoots, black and hard like horns, entangled among themselves, and astringent to the taste. But the leaves are not at all like the Chickpea, and what Dioscorides says of the leaves is rather to be understood of the habit of the whole plant.

Indeed, because both its root and its seed resemble the *astragalus* <note>original: "talum," meaning a knucklebone or anklebone</note> in shape and solidity, it was given the name Astragalus. Furthermore, from the various kinds of Astragalus, we depict here the one called Roman, or the shield-bearing Astragalus with a rough pod.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE ROMAN ASTRAGALUS,
#### or Shield-bearing Hedysarum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Roman Astragalus variety, showing the seed pods (siliquae) and root structure.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various gardens of France, Italy, and Belgium. Two illustrations have been made: the first shows the leaves and flowers, the second the seed. The former was made somewhat more rarely from a dried plant brought to us from Italy; the latter from the illustration by Plantin. There are some who contend that this Astragalus is the *Egyptian Helenium*, but in the judgment of Dodonaeus, it cannot be *Helenium*, since it is not fragrant. Camerarius, in his *Hortus*, names it the Shield-bearing Hatchet-vetch, described by Lobelius and Dodonaeus, and the second *Onobrychis* of Dodonaeus.

Otherwise, various other plants are given the name of Astragalus, as will be clear from what follows.

---

### THE GREATER ASTRAGALUS OF FUCHS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Astragalus plant with long, thick roots and upright stems.</image-desc>

The root is quite long, thick, and sweet; the stalks are straight, a cubit high, grooved, and angular. The leaflets are arranged in the manner of Vetches, nine or eleven attached to one rib, oblong from a round base, and somewhat bluish. The flowers grow from long stalks, are quite large and purple, several from the same stalk, in the shape of vetches; these are followed by long, smooth pods.

We have observed it in various places: at Geneva on the hill of *la Bastie*; at Strasbourg and Basel; flowering in May and bearing pods in July. Clusius writes that he saw it in Belgian gardens and reckons it among the Bitter Vetches. However, it is impatient of winter and cold.

Is this perhaps the other *Astragaloides* of the herbalists mentioned by Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants*?

<column-break/>

### ASTRAGALOIDES, OR THE WILD
#### Astragalus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Astragalus Sylvaticus, showing the characteristic leaf arrangement and root.</image-desc>

This plant is related to the Greater Astragalus of Fuchs and the leguminous Ground-nut; in what ways it agrees with them, or differs from them, is clear from a comparison of the illustrations.

By Thalius in his *Harcinia* it is called *Wild Astragalus*, and by some *Christian-wort* <note>original: "Christian Vvurtz"</note>; by Ruellius it is called *Mountain or Rustic Chickpea*, and perhaps it is the Astragalus described by Dioscorides.

We have observed it among the briars in the Duchy of Württemberg near the "Wonderful Spring"; also on Mount Rossberg near Masevaux in the woods and thickets.

It flowers in April and ripens its pods in July.

<summary>This page describes the Mimosa plant, noted for its sensitivity to touch and light, and several varieties of Astragalus (milk-vetch), detailing their medicinal uses for coughs and wounds, as well as their botanical classifications by Renaissance scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Mimosa, Astragalus, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Dioscorides, botany, sensitive plant, Roman Astragalus, Fuchs, wild plants</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of leguminous plants, specifically focusing on various species of the genus Astragalus (Milk-vetch), following the previous descriptions of related pulse-bearing herbs.</meta>

# OF PLANTS.

### UPRIGHT-STEMMED HAIRY MILK-VETCH.
<note>original: "Astragalus recticaulis hirsutus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, upright Astragalus plant with pinnate leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

This plant has an upright stem, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, firm, rigid, and entirely covered with white and woolly hairs, and endowed with a thick covering of leaves. Commonly fifteen of these leaves cling together, in the same order and position as in Goat's Rue <note>Galega</note>, though smaller, narrower, entirely hairy, ending in a point, and having a bitter taste. The flowers sit upon a long stalk, like Meadow Trefoil <note>clover</note>, gaping, pale, gathered into a tuft, protruding from hairy little heads. We do not recall from where we obtained this; however, its elegance, rarity, and variety deserved both a description and an illustration.

<column-break/>

### MONTPELLIER MILK-VETCH.
<note>original: "Astragalus Monspessulanus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing Astragalus with a thick woody root and several stems bearing pinnate leaves and flower spikes.</image-desc>

At Montpellier they call this plant *Astragalus*, being related to the lesser Hatchet-vetch <note>Securidaca</note>, but nevertheless different from it, as we depict here. In our illustration, however, the greatest part of the root is shown stripped of its bark, which remained in the ground while being pulled up. It grows along the road on the journey toward Narbonne near Gigan, one mile from Montpellier, in which place we observed it with purple flowers, and also white ones, in April.

Is this perhaps the *Astragalus* with small leaves of Saint-Foin <note>Hedysarum</note> from the *History of Lyon*? Or the *Astragalus* of Anguillara, which Dioscorides says grows in Arcadia and Memphis? But Memphis is in Egypt, and certainly not in Arcadia.

---

### A CERTAIN MOUNTAIN MILK-VETCH
### Called by some Saint-Foin.
<note>original: "Astragalus quidam montanus, Onobrychis quibusdam"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sprawling mountain Astragalus with numerous small leaflets and clusters of seed pods.</image-desc>

It puts forth many leaves from one and the same root, very much resembling the leaves of Lentils or Tragacanth <note>Goat's Thorn</note>. Small stems arise between the forks of the leaves, nine inches long, lying flat, slender, covered with a certain down, and loaded with the small flowers of the Wild Vetch, turning from blue to purple: these are followed by tiny pods consisting of twin cells full of seed. The root is long and somewhat thick, and puts out many fibers and slanted offshoots: it sends out small branches nine inches long to the sides, spread upon the ground.

It grows on the highest ridge of the Schneeberg, and on the highest rocks of the Rescher, in which two places Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> dug it up in August while it was flowering and already forming pods.

<column-break/>

### WHITER MONTPELLIER MILK-VETCH,
### and the Saint-Foin of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy Astragalus with dense, hairy flower heads.</image-desc>

This *Astragalus* has many things in common with the Montpellier variety, but it differs from it nonetheless. For the leaves are whiter, larger, and longer: and the hairs are also longer. The stems, however, are not much larger, upon which sit many purple flowers, many more than in the Montpellier *Astragalus*, clustered together and hairy with a thick down of hairs. We collected it at Geneva on Mount Salève, flowering in June.

Is this perhaps the purple *Astragalus* from the *History of Lyon* that grows on the rocky hills of Jura, with a large root and leaves like Wild Chickpea, hairy, with a binding <note>astringent</note> taste, and a flower turning from white to purple?

---

### SYRIAN MILK-VETCH,
### The foreign Saint-Foin of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Syrian Astragalus with thick, hairy stems and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

This leguminous plant is very elegant and quite rare, and certainly to be considered of the same kind as the *Astragalus*, since it resembles the *Astragali* in the similarity of its leaves and small stems, and in the entanglement of its creeping roots. It is adorned, however, with the beauty, shape, elegance, and most pleasant red color of its densely clustered flowers.

Brought from Aleppo in Syria, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> cultivated it in hanging gardens, where it flowered in July.

Clusius records it as "Foreign Saint-Foin," which flowered for him in July and the beginning of August. But Lobelius in his *Illustrations* and *History*, Tabernaemontanus, and the *History of Lyon* propose it under the name of Syrian *Astragalus*.

<column-break/>

### WOOLLY SPANISH MILK-VETCH.
<note>original: "Astragalus lanuginosus Boeticus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woolly Astragalus with long, hairy stems and small leaflets.</image-desc>

Clusius observed this on the hills above Lisbon which the Tagus river washes, and he writes that it is called there *Garavancillos*, that is, "small chickpea."

Furthermore, to say something of the powers of *Astragalus* in general: The root, according to Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note>, when drunk in wine stops a loose belly <note>diarrhea</note> and provokes urine; it also works for old dry ulcers when sprinkled on them, and also restrains blood. But because of its hardness, it is pounded with difficulty. Galen also writes that the roots have an astringent quality, and are among those things which dry quite effectively. Whence Pliny also asserts that the same roots in red wine heal dysentery.

<meta>catchword: ASTRA</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### THE ASTRAGALUS OF DIOSCORIDES ACCORDING TO SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Astragalus plant showing a thick, gnarled root system and several stems with pinnate leaves and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

The *Astragalus* of Dioscorides according to Christian <unclear>vourtisii</unclear>, and the true *Astragalus* according to Rauwolf. The illustrator did not give the depicted root its proper proportion: for although the plant is small, it is smaller in the Image than it is in real life.

But since we have again happened upon the mention of the *Astragalus* of Dioscorides, he says that it grows in wind-exposed, shady, and snowy places: specifically in the summer time in Memphis of Arcadia. But since there is no Memphis in Arcadia, we should more truly read—along with Pliny, Galen, and Paul <note>referring to Paul of Aegina</note>—in Pheneus of Arcadia.

### SMALLER ROCK MILKWORT.
<note>original: "POLYGALON MINVS SAXATILE"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polygalon minus saxatile, showing a low-growing plant with numerous small leaves and delicate flower spikes emerging from a central root.</image-desc>

The whole of this plant, as large as it is, scarcely exceeds a span <note>about 9 inches</note> in height; the little root is white and somewhat long. The small leaves are like those of the Cock’s Head <note>Onobrychis</note> but more blunt, covered with white hairs, and some emerging immediately from the base. The little stalks are slender, clothed with similar leaves, and divided at the top: and upon their ends sit little flowers, yellowish or pale, gaping, tiny and few, arranged like those of the *Astragalus*, which are followed by tiny round heads, gifted with several little points at the top.

It grows in low-lying, rough, and rocky places around the citadel of the Bishop of Montpellier; it flowers in June.

### CORTUSUS’S MILKWORT.
<note>original: "POLYGALON CORTVSI"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polygalon Cortusi, featuring a more robust plant with larger, broader leaves and elongated flower racemes.</image-desc>

We saw this at Padua in the garden of Cortusus, who gave it the name *Polygalon*, and we also found it again on Mount Nombre in Rhaetia. Afterwards, having been brought from certain mountains of the Bishopric of Basel to Montbéliard, we cultivated it in the garden of S.P. <note>likely Simon Paulli or a similar contemporary</note>, where it remained green all winter and flowered in May. Could it be the nine-leaved *Lotus* of Dalechamps in the *History of Lyon*?

It has roots longer than nine inches, sometimes simple and sometimes divided into many parts, ending in fibers. These send out several woody little twigs for a stem, nine inches or shorter, spread on the ground, to which the leaves cling in pairs—usually nine in number—short, round, solid, notched and whitish, provided with one nerve along their length. The yellow flowers sit at the end of the branches, which are followed by long pods marked by frequent joints, in which the seeds are contained.

<column-break/>

### MILKWORT ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL,
### Gesner’s Milkwort: Sainfoin to some.
<note>original: "Polygalon Gesneri: Onobrychis quibusdam"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polygalon, showing upright stems with narrow leaves and dense flower spikes at the tips.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides and Pliny, *Polygalon* <term>Milkwort; from the Greek 'poly' (much) and 'gala' (milk)</term> is a small shrub, a span in height, having leaves with the appearance of Lentil leaves, which are believed to produce Milk when drunk, whence it gets its name. However, as Mattioli rightly notes, so few characteristics of this plant are handed down by Dioscorides and Pliny that it is quite difficult to judge which plant presenting itself to us today can rightly be called by the name *Polygala*. Some wish it to be a species of Pimpernel. Others contend it is Gesner’s Milkwort, which we depict here: some say the Smaller Rock Milkwort, and some the Cock’s Head related to Milkwort, about which more presently: let the experts judge.

As for Gesner’s Milkwort, we have observed it in various places in meadows and fields with purple flowers, in the months of April and May.

### COCK’S HEAD RELATED TO
### Gesner’s Milkwort.
<note>original: "CAPVT gallinaceum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Caput gallinaceum, showing a sprawling plant with pinnate leaves and distinct, rounded seed pods or flower heads.</image-desc>

The root is long, somewhat thick, woody, fibrous, and white inside and blackish on the outside. The stems are a span long, thin, slightly hairy, and bear a spike of several inches, crowded with purple flowers like those of Gesner’s Milkwort. In what ways it agrees with that plant, or differs from it, is clear from a comparison of the Images with one another. We found it again in sandy places and plains adjacent to Mount Loup near Montpellier.

### SAINFOIN ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL.
### The purple-flowered Sainfoin of some.
<note>original: "ONOBRYCHIS VETER. ET IN GENERE"</term>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Onobrychis, showing a plant with long pinnate leaves and a tall, slender flower spike.</image-desc>

To *Onobrychis* <term>Sainfoin; from the Greek 'onos' (donkey) and 'brycho' (to bray)</term> Dioscorides attributes leaves similar to the Lentil, but a little longer, a stem a span in height, a crimson flower, and a small, slender root.

But it is not sufficiently clear which herb this is. For some number it among the species of Wild Rue. Others attribute the name of *Onobrychis* to other plants: to Gesner’s Milkwort, to Montpellier Astragalus, to the Shield-bearing Hedysarum, and to the third Melilot of Tragus. Furthermore, Cornarius thinks that *Onobrychis* and *Onopordon* are one and the same herb, one name derived from the sound of breaking wind and the other from the braying of a donkey, because, evidently, from the eating of that herb, the donkey both farts and brays. Finally, there are various species of *Onobrychis* to be described presently.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Milkwort (Polygalon) and Sainfoin (Onobrychis), debating their classical identities based on the writings of Dioscorides and Pliny. The author provides detailed physical descriptions of roots, leaves, and flowers, often citing specific locations like Montpellier and Padua where they were observed.</summary>
<keywords>Astragalus, Milkwort, Polygalon, Sainfoin, Onobrychis, Dioscorides, Pliny, Gesner, botany, medicinal plants, Arcadia, Montpellier, botanical illustration</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### SAINFOIN <note>original: "ONOBRYCHIS"</note> WITH SUB-BLUE flowers, according to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Onobrychis plant, showing a central stem with pinnate leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the branches, with a detailed root system at the base.</image-desc>

From a hard, twisted, woody root that spreads obliquely, it puts forth many small stalks, a foot long, willow-like, then spread out and marked by frequent nodes: and on these are winged leaves, 13, 15, and 17 clinging to a single rib, with the end leaf always making an odd number. Then, from the "wings" <note>the leaf axils</note> come thin stalks or little rods bearing tiny flowers gathered into a spike, in the form of Pea or Vetch flowers, but much smaller, of a dilute blue color, or purplish from blue: which are succeeded by thin, as if doubled, Pods, containing a tiny seed, shaped like a kidney, black.

That variety which we previously described grows in various places along the banks of the Danube, and is also cultivated in gardens, as Meietus had at Strasbourg, and Grieninger at Pforzheim. But the one we depict here is rarer, which bloomed for Us in the garden in July.

<column-break/>

### SAINFOIN WITH A PALE FLOWER, according to some, or Milkwort <note>original: "Polygalon"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Onobrychis flore pallido, featuring upright stems with narrow pinnate leaves and elongated flower spikes.</image-desc>

It rises with branches a cubit and a half high <note>about 27 inches</note>, straight, hard, and green: on which are leaves like Lentils or wild Vetch. Small branches coming from the fold of the axils at the end of the stalk are hand-shaped and furrowed, ending in nine-inch Spikes of little flowers emulating Clover flowers, somewhat oblong and pale, upon which are impressed certain blackish rays: these are then succeeded by pointed Pods, consisting of two valves, in which is a seed almost like Fenugreek, but smaller and black. The root is thick, hard, woody, long, fibrous, whitening, and perennial.

This is very rare, and was seen in only two places by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, to whom, as also to Tabernaemontanus, it is the 1st *Onobrychis*. Gesner calls it *Polygalon* <note>Greek: "much milk"</note>, because it increases the milk in livestock. We have added the pods to Clusius's figure from a dried plant which we had from Gesner.

---

<column-break/>

### SEA MILKWORT <note>original: "GLAVX"</note>, SPANISH MILKWORT: German: *Schielkraut*: French: *Herbe à laict*: Italian: *Glaux*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Glaux plant, showing several stems rising from a common root, topped with dense, rounded flower heads.</image-desc>

*Glaux*, (Γλαύξ) says Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note>, has leaves similar to the Cytisus or Lentil, of which the lower parts are whiter and the upper parts green. It produces five or six small branches along the ground, thin, a palm's height from the root: flowers similar to the Stock-gilliflower, but smaller and purple. So says he, from whom Pliny does not much differ. However, Cornarius writes that he confuses *Glaucium* with *Glaux*, and says that the herb *Glaux* is unknown to the Apothecaries and Herbalists today.

Among the plants which are handed down under the name of *Glaux* by more recent authors, Clusius found none responding more exactly to the description of Dioscorides than this one, which he labels "Spanish," because he observed it nowhere but in Spain, and indeed on the banks of the River Tormes, which flows past Salamanca.

### GOAT’S RUE <note>original: "GALEGA, RVTA CAPRARIA"</note>: German: *Geys Rauten*: French: *Galega*: Italian: *Lananese* & *Lauamani*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Galega plant, showing tall stems with pinnate leaves and long, slender seed pods (siliquae) hanging from the upper branches.</image-desc>

Here and there it spreads thin white roots through the earth: but it raises stalks two cubits <note>approx. 3 feet</note> and higher, furrowed, hollow, branched with many arms. The leaves are like Vetch: the flowers white, or violet-white: the pods are rounded, thin, and long, in which is the seed.

By Fracastoro it is called the "French Herb," by some "Wild Fenugreek," by others *Onobrychis*, by others *Glaux*, by others *Polemonium*, by others *Polygalon*, and by others it is numbered among the species of "Wild Rue."

It grows everywhere in marshy places, on the banks of ditches, in mountains and fruitful fields, and is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms in June and July; the seed matures in Autumn. Concerning its powers, see what follows.

---

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN GOAT’S RUE OF DALECHAMP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Galega montana, showing a thick, twisted root system and stems with broad, rounded leaflets and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

It grows on very high mountains: not indeed in their hidden places or precipices, but on the summits, where a moist plain meets them.

Furthermore, on account of its various uses, *Galega* in general is of great value. A few spoonfuls of the juice are given to children both against worms and against Epilepsy. It is effective, according to Matthiolus, not only against the plague and lethal medicines <note>poisons</note>: but even against the bites and stings of all wild beasts that emit venom with teeth or sting: for which use they exhibit both the herb and its juice in a drink, or apply it, in the manner of a plaster, to the wounded parts.

### SPRING WOODLAND GOAT’S RUE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Galega nemorensis, showing a plant with a fibrous root, stems with paired leaflets, and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

A gift of Spring, the Wild *Galega* has stalks a foot high, rising in great numbers from multiple, fibrous, black, perennial roots: on which are seen leaves very much approaching the leaves of Pellitory-of-the-wall in size and form. The flowers are on a long stalk like a spike, seven or eight, such as are on legumes, of a purple color; which are followed by pods, one or two inches long, black: in which are tiny seeds, round or somewhat oblong. The root sprouts again every year.

It is called "Woodland Bitter-vetch" <note>original: "Orobus syluaticus"</note> by Schwenckfeld, Camerarius, and Thalius. The "First Purple Pannonian Bitter-vetch" by Clusius: the "Woodland Bean" of the *History of Lyon*.

It grows among shrubs under trees and flowers in April and May.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SIMILAR TO WOODLAND GOAT’S RUE; if not the same, with a white flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a flowering plant with pinnate leaves and small clusters of flowers, showing the root system, stem, and foliage.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential Flemish botanist</note> thinks this can be conveniently referred to some genus of *Bitter Vetch* <note>original: "Orobi"</note>, *Wild Kidney-bean*, or *Vetch*. Some indeed, says Dodonaeus, call it *Venus’s Bitter-vetch*.

In the mountains, says Columna, in valleys, in shady places, and everywhere in sunny, rocky areas it arises: it flowers in May, and is completed in the month of June. Clusius found it on the grassy hills of Austria and Bohemia, and asserts it is also cultivated in gardens.

It seems to differ from the preceding one only in this: that the former has purple or shield-shaped flowers, while this one has white. However, we by no means approve of the fact that Columna does not hesitate to establish the plant pictured here (which he describes at length) as the *Astragalus* of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen.

<column-break/>

### MANY-FLOWERED WOODLAND GOAT’S RUE, with purple and white flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant similar to the first, but with more abundant flower clusters (multiflora) and a detailed root structure.</image-desc>

According to Clusius, this is the *First Venetian Bitter-vetch* with a purple flower, and the other, or second type, which differs only in the color of the leaves and branches (which turn pale from green) and in the flowers, which are entirely white. It is the *First and Second Venetian Bitter-vetch* of Clusius, or the purple and white, according to Pona in his description of Mount Baldo. The distinguished botanist and physician of Strasbourg, Master Agerius, offered us the plant pictured here, collected in the garden of Bologna, under the name of *Broad-leaved Bitter-vetch of a whitish color*. Indeed, the same grew for us in the garden at Montbéliard from seed sent from Venice; and it flowered in May.

---

### HATCHET-VETCH, SWEET-BROOM, AX-WORT: German: Linsen unkraut <note>Lentil-weed</note>: French: Securidaca, Hedysaron.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with long, curved seed pods (resembling a sickle or hatchet) and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

*Sweet-broom* <note>original: "Hedysarum"</note>, says Dioscorides (who also calls it *Ax-wort* <note>original: "Pelecinum"</note>), is a shrub with tiny leaves similar to *Chickpeas*, with pods resembling little horns, in which is a reddish-yellow seed, bitter to the taste; the name was given to the plant from its shape, which mimics a double-headed axe <note>term: Securidaca (from the Latin 'securis' for axe)</note>.

Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen mentioned only one *Sweet-broom*, *Ax-wort*, or *Hatchet-vetch*: but the moderns make two kinds of it, the *Greater* and the *Lesser*.

The *Greater* which we depict here is sown in gardens, and grows here and there in various places among the cornfields. Clusius writes that it is very common throughout all of Pannonia, Austria, Styria, Moravia, and Bohemia, both in meadows and in fields, and along the roads. It flowers, moreover, in June, and sometimes through the whole summer, and the seed ripens in July and August.

<column-break/>

### THE OTHER OR LESSER HATCHET-VETCH.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller variety of Securidaca, showing the characteristic curved seed pods and delicate foliage.</image-desc>

Dodonaeus claims it also grows spontaneously, which we have not observed. However, we have had it in the gardens of Geneva and Montbéliard, flowering in May, producing pods, and enduring the winter.

Both types of Hatchet-vetch vary in the color of the flower, which is either yellow, or bright white, or off-white, or intensely purplish.

Furthermore, *Sweet-broom* is useful for the stomach when taken in a drink, according to Dioscorides, and it is also added to antidotes. However, placed as a suppository with honey before intercourse, it is believed to take away the hope of offspring <note>i.e., used as a contraceptive</note>. We have it from the records of Galen that the seed and the little branches of the whole shrub clear out obstructions of the internal organs.

---

### HORSESHOE VETCH, LESSER MOONWORT: German: Mon-raut & Monkraut <note>Moon-rue or Moon-herb</note>: French: Fer de cheval: Italian: Sferra cauallo.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a low-growing plant with crescent-shaped seed pods, resembling horseshoes.</image-desc>

The Alchemists label it *Moonwort* <note>original: "Lunaria"</note>: others call it *Mountain Hatchet-vetch*, others *Lesser Hatchet-vetch*, others *Sweet-broom*, to which its nature is very similar. However, it obtained the name *Horseshoe* <note>original: "Solea equina"</note> rather from the shape of a horseshoe than from the wandering rumor that, when trodden upon, it is believed to pull the iron shoes off of horses.

It arises in the mountains and flowers in May; it was brought to us several times from the summit of the mountains overlooking the city of Yverdon, called *Suchet*.

It is of a hot and dry nature, of little use in medicine, although some use it in wound-healing drinks. As for the wonders the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> tell about it, it is not our purpose to review them.

<column-break/>

### A plant related to HORSESHOE VETCH and BIRD’S FOOT.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with clusters of seed pods that resemble a bird's foot (ornithopodio) or small horseshoes.</image-desc>

In what ways this agrees with *Bird’s Foot* <note>original: "Ornithopodio"</note> and *Horseshoe*, and in what ways it differs from them, is clear from the illustration.

Could this be what Gesner says in his collection of plants: *A low species of Melilot, with two leaflets opposite each other, whose yellow flowers give off a certain sweet milky scent, producing curved pods in the appearance of claws?*

It grows at Montpellier near the gallows, flowering in April and May. At Basel around the *Waterfall*, flowering in June: at Geneva on Mount *Salève*, flowering in May. Moreover, the *Horseshoe Vetch*, which was discussed just before, has also become an inhabitant of gardens: as we have had it in ours, from seed sent from Florence.
