# PLANTS: RADIATE MOONWORT. LEGUMINOUS SCORPION-GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lunaria Radiata, showing a plant with pinnate leaves and distinctive curved, radiating seed pods.</image-desc>

### RADIATE MOONWORT.
<note>original: "Lunaria Radiata"</note>

The seed pods of this plant are quite numerous and most beautiful in their form and elegance. They scarcely exceed an inch in length and are of a reddish-ash color, toothed on both sides, and marked by a nerve running through the middle. Within them, small, compressed seeds are contained in a double row; they possess the color and roundness of a lentil, but are many times smaller and slightly curved, with a legume-like flavor.

Is this the *Foreign Hatchet-Vetch* of Clusius? Or the *Leguminous Scorpion-grass* of Cortusus, or the *Foreign Saint-foin* <note>original: "Hedysarum peregrinum"</note>, which name seems to suit it more aptly?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ornithopodium (Avis Pes), showing a low-growing plant with small leaves and seed pods resembling a bird's foot.</image-desc>

### BIRD’S FOOT: French: Pied d'oiseau: Brabant: Vogeloet.
<note>original: "Ornithopodium, Avis Pes"</note>

The plant called *Ornithopodium* by Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a famous Flemish physician and botanist.</note> puts forth several small stems from a tiny root; these are nine inches long, thin, and divided into branches. The leaves are like those of a small lentil, but smaller. The flowers are pea-like <note>original: "Leguminacei"</note>, yellowish, with several joined together at the tip of a single shoot on very short stalks. The seed pods are abundant, expressing the shape of a bird's clawed foot; they are rounded and marked by five or seven joints, containing six or seven seeds like those of a turnip or rape.

It grows, says Dodoens, in fields, especially after the corn has been harvested; it is also found in uncultivated places, such as on hills, dry and sunny meadows, and along roadsides.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Stella Leguminosa Cortusi, showing a plant with star-shaped clusters of curved seed pods.</image-desc>

### THE LEGUMINOUS STAR OF CORTUSUS.
<note>original: "Stella Leguminosa Cortusi"</note>

We owe this very rare plant to Cortusus <note>Giacomo Antonio Cortuso (1513–1603), director of the Padua botanical garden.</note>; it emerges with leaves like the *Leguminous Scorpion-grass*, but with flowers like *Nipplewort* <note>original: "Lampsana"</note>. The seed is small and dark, contained in tiny pods that are slightly sickle-shaped, attached to a single stalk and clustered in a radiating pattern that represents a star; it has a leguminous and sticky taste.

The *History of Lyon* <note>A reference to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" (1586) by Jacques Daléchamps.</note> calls this the *Leguminous Star of Lobelius*. Whether it is truly the same as that most celebrated "Star" herb honored by the Irish, which is fixed low to the ground, Lobelius says in his *Adversaria* that the credit must remain with those who have seen and reported it.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Scorpioides Leguminosa, showing a plant with long, twisted seed pods resembling a scorpion's tail.</image-desc>

### LEGUMINOUS SCORPION-GRASS.
<note>original: "Scorpioides Leguminosa"</note>

It has a long, thin, simple root; the stems are four to six inches long and hairy. The leaves are equal to those of the *Bird's Foot*, small, hairy, pointed, and somewhat grayish-white, arranged in ten or more pairs of leaflets. The flowers cling in clusters to the ends of the branches, not unlike the flowers of *Bird's Foot*; these are succeeded by twisted seed pods, gradually tapering and moderately compressed.

It grows in the Neapolitan countryside in various places near the roads among the Squills. Lobelius and Pena also record it as *Leguminous Scorpion-grass* in their *Adversaria* and *Images of Plants*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ornithopodium Tuberosum, showing a plant with a complex root system featuring small tubers.</image-desc>

### TUBEROUS BIRD’S FOOT of Daléchamps, with white-reddish flowers.
<note>original: "Ornithopodium Tuberosum Dalechampii"</note>

It is gifted with a manifold root, spread here and there, hairy with thin fibers, and knotty with frequent small tubers that are hard and round. Many small stems are scattered mostly on the ground. The leaves are like those of Vetch, but smaller. The flowers at the tops of the branches are a reddish-white. The seed pods are thin, curved, usually in threes, and distinguished as if by certain joints; within them is a minute seed.

It grows in dry and sandy places.

Some call it *Rupture-wort* <note>original: "Herniaria"</note>, because it is believed to be wonderfully helpful for hernias, whether taken internally or applied externally. It is also effective against kidney stones, breaking them and casting them out.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tribulus Terrestris, showing a prostrate plant with small leaves and spiny fruit.</image-desc>

### LAND CALTROP: German: Feldt kletten: French: Tribule terrestre: Italian: Tribulo terrestre.
<note>original: "Tribulus Terrestris"</note>

The Caltrop we treat here is called "of the land" to distinguish it from the other kind that grows in water, which will be discussed in its proper place. According to the opinion of Theophrastus, Pliny, and most modern authors, the Land Caltrop is again of two types. For one has the leaf of a Chickpea, while the other is thorny and prickly. Theophrastus mentions the latter and attributes to it the leaves of Purslane, but he omitted the other.

It is found in the dusty and sandy shores of the Adriatic, Tyrrhenian, and French Mediterranean seas, where it plagues travelers and renders paths almost impassable <note>The "caltrop" seed pods have sharp spines that can pierce feet or tires.</note>. We have also seen it in the ditches around Montpellier, and we have even cultivated it in the princely garden at Montbéliard. It is counted among the diseases of the crops. More will be said in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several leguminous plants characterized by their unique seed pods, including those resembling bird's feet, scorpion tails, and stars, as well as the spiny Land Caltrop. It includes botanical observations on their habitats, medicinal uses for hernias and stones, and references to classical authorities like Pliny and Theophrastus.</summary>
<keywords>Radiate Moonwort, Bird's Foot (Ornithopodium), Scorpion-grass, Tuberous Bird's Foot, Land Caltrop (Tribulus Terrestris), medicinal herbs, kidney stones, hernia treatments, botanical history</keywords>

# **Images and Outlines.**

### **Lotus**, CULTIVATED LOTUS: German, Belgian, & French.
### *Lotus*: To the Italians, *Loto domestico*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus plant with small leaves and flowers, accompanied by small botanical details of seeds or pods below.</image-desc>

There is the *Lotus* tree, which was discussed previously in Class II, and the *Lotus* herb, which we are dealing with now. Various species of the latter are recorded, differing from one another in their *leaves, stems, flowers, and fruits*. Primarily, it is distinguished into the cultivated and the wild varieties; but since Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, and other ancient authors wrote only very briefly about the Lotus, and since quite different plants are given the name of Lotus by different people, it is by no means easy to say which is the cultivated Lotus of the Ancients, or which is the wild. Thus, we are forced to treat both almost indiscriminately alongside the Melilot <note>Sweet clover</note> and the Trefoil herbs. We depict here the smaller hairy horn-shaped Lotus; the others will be discussed in the following sections.

### GREATER HORNED LOTUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller Lotus plant with larger leaves and distinct seed pods (siliquae) extending from the flower heads.</image-desc>

This is much taller than the smaller variety. Indeed, it rises with stems a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or a cubit and a half high. The *leaves* grow three to a branch from a single stalk, about an inch long, with two others likewise lacking stalks clasping the stem. The *flowers* are clustered in a circle on special forks and at the top of the stem; they are larger, yellow, with certain leaves placed beneath like a crown. There follow numerous *pods* <term>siliquae<note>long, slender seed pods characteristic of the pea family</note></term>, an inch or an inch and a half long. Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous Swiss botanist</note> calls it the *Greater horned trefoil*.

It usually grows in hedges and thickets; it is frequently found between Montbéliard and the village of Souchaut. Could it be the fourth species of Tragus's Melilot, which might be the Melilot of Serapion?

### DARK-FLOWERED PODDED LOTUS,
### Tetragonolobus <note>Four-angled pod</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus variety with broader leaves and large, dark, winged seed pods.</image-desc>

Beyond controversy, this Lotus is by far the most beautiful; it grew for us in the garden at Montbéliard from seed received from Florence under the name of *Sandalida Candia*. It blooms in June, the seeds are ripe in August, and it is an annual plant, seen by us nowhere else, nor described by anyone else.

It is endowed with a simple small root and few fibers: from its head many stems arise, longer than a cubit, rounded, hairy, divided into several "wings," and mostly trailing on the ground. The *leaves* are in threes at certain intervals. The *flowers* emerge from the leaf axils in the shape of a Pea, but smaller, evoking the texture commonly called velvet. The *pods* are an inch and a half long, angular, quite thick, and endowed with four membranes—like the feathers on the shaft of an arrow; in these are contained large, round, yellowish seeds which are hard to the teeth.

<column-break/>

### LOTUS, CULTIVATED LOTUS IN GENERAL.
### Smaller smooth Horned Lotus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender Lotus plant with small leaves and thin, curved seed pods.</image-desc>

There are those who think the cultivated Lotus is that plant which common herbalists and apothecaries falsely call *Melilotus*, and the Sienese Commentator <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli</note> does not disapprove of their opinion. Others want it to be that *Trefoil* which grows everywhere in meadows and elsewhere. Amatus <note>Amato Lusitano</note> judges it to be *Alloluya* <note>Wood sorrel</note>. To us, it is the smaller horned Lotus, both the hairy (male) already described, and the smooth (female) which we depict here.

To Caspar Bauhin, it is the *Smaller horned trefoil*. To Dodoens, the *Horned trefoil*. Might it be the *Crowned melilot* in the *Adversaria* of Lobel and Pena?

Both species grow in meadows and dry hills: we have observed them blooming in May and June at Geneva, Basel, and Montbéliard.

### HORNED LOTUS, WITH PODS
### appearing singly, in pairs, or in threes.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus plant with very thin, elongated seed pods appearing singly or in small clusters.</image-desc>

It clings to the earth with a deep and many-forked root: sending out straight, numerous, foot-long stems, branched, reddish, and covered with long whitish hairs. At their nodes are three *leaves* like those of the noble Melilot, but more oblong and sharper, and two others, no smaller, growing into the stem at the base of the stalk. From the fold of the leaves a single, thin stalk emerges, an inch or more long: at its tip is a yellow flower, gaping open, from a hairy calyx. The pod is usually single (very rarely in pairs), an inch long, rounded, thin, filled with very numerous reddish, round seeds like those of Purslane, and having a legume-like taste.

### PODDED LOTUS, WITH RECURVED PODS
### resembling the toes of crows' feet.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus plant characterized by seed pods that are strongly curved, resembling a crow's foot.</image-desc>

From thin and vine-like little stems hang recurved pods that resemble the toes of crows' feet. Dodoens labels it *Coronopus* <note>Crow-foot</note> from the *Codex Caesareus*; he testifies that it was found by Bernardus Paludanus not far from Tripoli and at the roots of Mount Lebanon. Caspar Bauhin makes it his *57th Trefoil*, and calls it the *Coronopus from the Codex Caesareus* of Dodoens. Why some call it the "Star Herb," we do not see, for what is the great similarity?

<summary>This page describes various species of the Lotus herb (distinct from the Lotus tree), detailing their physical characteristics, seed pod shapes, and the differing nomenclature used by contemporary botanists like Bauhin and Dodoens.</summary>
<keywords>Lotus, Lotus sativa, Horned Lotus, Tetragonolobus, Trefoil, Melilot, Caspar Bauhin, Rembert Dodoens, Montbéliard, botanical classification, seed pods, siliquae</keywords>

# ON PLANTS.

### LOTUS WITH BIRD’S-FOOT PODS, with a yellow flower, streaked with black lines.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus plant with trifoliate leaves and curved, segmented seed pods resembling a bird's foot (ornithopodium).</image-desc>

Since this plant is sufficiently well known from the illustration and the title, we shall only add that the seed is contained most abundantly in the pods, as sometimes even up to 14 seeds are contained in a single pod.

*A peculiar Lotus with Bird’s-foot pods, according to Camerarius. Trefoil 56, or with Bird’s-foot pods, according to Caspar Bauhin in his "Phytopinax."*

### WILD LOTUS FROM THE IMPERIAL CODEX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Lotus plant with an upright stem, trifoliate leaves, and small clusters of flowers/pods.</image-desc>

It is depicted with a straight stem: leaves like Trefoil <note>Trifolium</note>, and from the crook of these, the stalks first bring forth flowers, then pods, which are thin and smaller than Fenugreek, as the image shows.

However, a wild Lotus of this kind has remained unknown and hidden until now, and is found only in the ancient Codex of the Imperial Library <note>referring to the Vienna Dioscorides, a famous 6th-century manuscript</note>, according to the author Dodoens.

*To C. Bauhin it is Trefoil 48, and the Wild Lotus from the Imperial Codex.*

### COMMON MELILOT, Scented Trefoil: German: *Steinklee*; French: *Melilot*; Italian: *Meliloto*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Melilotus (Sweet Clover) showing long racemes of small flowers and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

There are various ambiguities regarding Melilot, as there are with Lotus: the Ancients used to call it *Serta* <note>Garland</note> and *Sertula Campana* <note>Little Garland of Campania</note>, as well as *Gerana regia* <note>Royal Crane-plant</note>. It was called *Sertula* because its flower was dedicated to garlands and wreaths; *Sertula Campana* because it is most highly praised in the Campania region of Italy. Indeed, it was called *Corona regia* <note>Royal Crown</note> because it is crowned at the top with yellow flowers. Today, various plants are gifted with the name of Melilot, but from all of them, in the judgment of Cordus and Mattioli, and our own, the "True" and legitimate one is the so-called Common Melilot, pictured here, which is labeled by most as *Scented Trefoil*.

It grows everywhere (especially on the banks of rivers) and blooms all summer with yellow and white flowers.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW PODDED LOTUS OF MONTPELLIER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lotus species with woody stems and elongated seed pods.</image-desc>

The root of this is thick, long, woody, and provided with many fibers: the leaves are like those of the Horned Lotus, but larger: there is a single flower at the tip of each small stalk, large, yellow, provided with four streaks at the sides, breaking out from a long calyx: the pods are an inch and a half long, in which is a tiny seed, astringent in taste.

According to Clusius, it is frequent in all the meadows of Austria and Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions</note>. We ourselves have seen it blooming in the meadows at Geneva in May: and C. Bauhin collected it not far from Brugg, on the way to the Swiss Thermal Baths. To him, it is *Trefoil 61, or the yellow podded kind.*

Is Caesalpinus’s *Polygala* that grows in maritime regions similar to the common Melilot?

### CRETAN LOTUS OF HIERAZUNI, described by Bellus, or an edible kind of Trefoil.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cretan Lotus with rounded, curved pods and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

This kind of Lotus is edible, if we believe Honorius Bellus: for its pods are found for sale in the marketplace before they begin to harden, and are most gladly eaten by children and women, as they are succulent and sweet, with the taste of fresh peas.

It produces many stems from the root, leaves in threes, somewhat thick and pointed, and yellow pea-like flowers: the pods are round, sickle-shaped, and large in proportion to the plant; the seed is not unlike the seed of the Montpellier Milk-vetch <note>Astragalus monspeliensis</note>.

It is found among the crops and at the edges of fields.

### RELATIVE OF THE COMMON MELILOT, with a smaller and narrower leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant related to Melilot, featuring smaller, narrower leaves and flower spikes.</image-desc>

This plant, says Dodoens, is used by the apothecaries of all Germany in all medicines and compositions in place of the true Melilot of the Ancients. For it is fragrant, almost temperate in heat and cold, and possesses some sharpness; at the same time, it has the power of digesting <note>promoting healing/maturation of humors</note> with some astringency. And for that reason, it is usefully mixed into digesting and resolving plasters and poultices, as well as into <term>ranthroquentibus</term> <note>likely a corruption of 'arthritic' or 'joint-relieving' remedies</note>, and also into <term>acopis</term> <note>medicines to relieve weariness or pain</note>. In truth, on the authority of the Monks, women distill this *Trefoil* to make fumigations and various other playful perfumes.

<summary>This page describes several species of Lotus and Melilot (Sweet Clover), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations, and medicinal uses in early modern Europe. It highlights the "edible Lotus" of Crete and the use of Melilot in German pharmacies and perfumery.</summary>
<keywords>Lotus, Melilot, Trefoil, Bird's-foot, Dodoens, Bauhin, Clusius, medicinal herbs, Cretan botany, perfumes, pharmacy</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### MELILOT WITH LARGE SEEDS, ROUND AND wrinkled: with honey-colored florets like common Melilot.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Melilotus plant with trifoliate leaves, elongated flower spikes, and detailed depictions of the round, rugose seeds and individual florets at the base.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist.</note> depicts this among the Melilots and calls it the *Italian* variety. In his garden, however, he adds to its inscription that it is called the *True Melilot*; in Metz the inhabitants call it *Malatro*, and in the Roman countryside—imitating the Ancients—it is called *Coronella* <note>Latin: "Little Crown."</note>. Could it be the *Uricum* of Anguillara? <note>Luigi Anguillara, an early Italian botanist.</note> To Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist famous for his early classification system.</note> it is *Trifolium 34, or Italian*.

Sown in the garden of the Most Serene Prince of Montbéliard, it flowered in June, but produced mature seeds in August and September: in which month young plants also appeared from the fallen seed. Charles Toussaint had sent the seed to us as *Spanish Melilot*.

### Another Image of the ITALIAN OR SYRIAN MELILOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Melilotus, showing a more robust stem and denser clusters of flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

The previously presented figure by Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), author of a famous herbal.</note> does not please us much, and therefore we provide a better one here. Tragus and Fuchs call this *Italian Melilot* the *Greater Melilot*; Gesner calls it *Joyful Wild Melilot*, and in some places *True Melilot*. Some call it *Syrian Melilot*, first brought from Aleppo in Syria, among them Pena and Lobel <note>Matthias de Lobel, a Flemish botanist.</note>, who consider it the best and most elegant of this family. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Trifolium 44, or scented, with reflected horns*.

We have seen it in the more cultivated gardens of Montpellier, Basel, and Venice; however, we have observed that when sown, it tends to degenerate <note>Lose its specific cultivated characteristics over generations.</note>.

### TRIFOLIUM: German: *Klee, Wisenklee*; French: *Treffle, Triolet*; Italian: *Trifoglio*:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common Trifolium (clover) plant with characteristic three-parted leaves and a globular flower head.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>The primary ancient Greek authority on medicinal plants.</note> mentions only three Clovers in their own chapter, and Pliny has no more. But, as Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous commentator on Dioscorides.</note> rightly notes, Dioscorides' discussion in that chapter is only about *Asphaltite* <note>Bitumen-scented clover.</note>; that the other kinds of Clover were by no means unknown to him is clear from the chapter on *Wild Lotus*.

Clover encompasses many genera, and almost everyone has recognized many species and differences. Caspar Bauhin records seventy known to him; Tragus says innumerable species are found. We also have counted and known many, differing among themselves in root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, taste, location, time, temperament, powers, and use, which we shall now discuss, beginning with the common purple Clover, which we depict here.

<column-break/>

### ITALIAN MELILOT WITH CURVED HORNS, called Italian Clover by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Melilotus Italica featuring curved, horn-like seed pods (cornicula) and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

This is a very tall Clover, three or four cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; this plant is described as 4.5 to 6 feet tall.</note>, and sometimes higher, branched with many arms, and these are thick and firm. The leaves are in threes on short stalks, not much different from the leaves of German Melilot, oblong, saw-toothed, and smooth. From their crook come stalks the length of a palm, the tops of which are adorned with the flowers of *Syrian Melilot*, of a fragrant light and a comb-like scent. These are followed by sickle-shaped pods, an inch long, compressed, furrowed, and hanging winged in a double row.

Lobel calls it *Italian and Paduan Melilot* in his *Observations and Images of Plants*; to some it is *Horned Clover*. Dodonaeus calls it *Italian Melilot*, as does Fuchs, whose image we show, with Tragus and Dodonaeus also having the same.

### ABSUS WITH LEAVES OF ALPINE CLOVER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Absus plant, showing upright stems with trifoliate leaves and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

This is a herb the size of a palm, or somewhat larger, with leaves like Clover or rounder, four attached to each wing <note>Likely referring to the leaf structure or branching.</note>. It bears small white flowers and seeds very close to the seeds of a Pea. According to Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, who wrote on Egyptian plants.</note> in his work on the plants of Egypt, the inhabitants call it *Absus* in their native tongue.

### SILVERY CLOVER WITH YELLOW flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Trifolium Argentatum, showing a low-growing habit with trifoliate leaves and small flower heads.</image-desc>

The base of this unique plant is woody and slender, sending out stems a palm long or more, thin and hairy. The leaves are in threes, shining with a silvery luster on one side, hairy, but green on the other. Large, yellow, hairy flowers cling to the tops of the stems, emerging from a fringed, shaggy calyx <note>The outer protective part of the flower.</note>.

It flowers in the month of August on the road from Montpellier toward Frontignan, and on Mount Seth.

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax* it is *Trifolium 34*. In Lobel’s *Observations and Images of Plants* it is *Lobel’s rougher shrubby Lotus*.

<summary>This page details various species of Melilot and Clover, citing major 16th-century botanists and providing physical descriptions of their seeds, flowers, and growth habits across Europe and the Levant.</summary>
<keywords>Melilot, Clover, Trifolium, Italian Melilot, Syrian Melilot, Absus, Caspar Bauhin, Lobel, Dioscorides, botanical classification, medicinal herbs</keywords>

--- Page 225 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of various clover-like plants (Trifolium), following the previous botanical descriptions. The author continues to cite classical authorities like Dioscorides and Galen alongside contemporary botanists like Bauhin and Caesalpinus.</meta>

### WHITE CLOVER, Snapped, and very hairy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium album plant with trifoliate leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are covered in a gray downy fuzz; the flowers spring forth from the ends of the branches, many joined together, and are pure white. The seed pods are a reddish-brown <note>original: "spadicæ"</note>, and the seed is yellowish. The stems and the cups of the flowers <term>calyces|the leaf-like structure that encloses the flower bud</term> are very hairy. We have observed this plant growing in abundance at Montpellier near the Gramont forest.

Is this perhaps the *Oxytriphyllon* <note>Greek: "sharp-leaved three-leaf"</note> of Scribonius Largus, as some believe? Or the *Glaux* of Caesalpinus which grows in rough places? In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is listed as Mattioli’s Wild Lotus.

### BITUMINOUS OR ASPHALT CLOVER, also called Oxytriphyllon and Menianthes.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Trifolium asphaltites showing trifoliate leaves and dense flower heads.</image-desc>

Dioscorides writes that this Clover is called by these names among the Greeks, although some wish to distinguish *Oxytriphyllon* from the Bituminous Clover. This Clover takes its name, however, from the scent of asphalt <note>bitumen or pitch</note>.

It is called "Stinking Clover" by some, simply "Clover" by others, and an Egyptian species of Lotus by yet others. We have from the records of Galen that it is hot and dry in the third degree, that it provokes urine and menstruation, and helps with pains in the sides.

Nothing is more common than this in Crete; it grows in maritime regions in thin soil, according to Caesalpinus. In Germany and Belgium, however, it never grows of its own accord, but is only sown in gardens. We saw it at Montpellier near Castelnau, flowering in April, May, and June.

### INDIAN CLOVER TREE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody plant with trifoliate leaves and small seed pods at the base.</image-desc>

Caring nothing for supports <note>such as trellises</note>, it rises straight up by itself with a stem, or if you prefer, a square trunk, hairy with very short bristles. It is adorned with leaves that are also hairy on the underside, growing in threes, narrow like Bituminous Clover, on a long stalk. It grew for us when sown at Montbéliard in the Excellence's garden <note>likely referring to the garden of the Duke of Württemberg</note>, but we were not able to observe more than this.

<column-break/>

### BLADDER CLOVER, or Vesicary Clover.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Trifolium halicacabum featuring inflated, bladder-like seed pods.</image-desc>

It puts out stems longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> and covered in a shaggy down. The leaves grow in threes, fours, sixes, or sevens, and are hairy, with the end leaf surpassing the others in size. From the joints of the leaves <term>axils|the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</term> emerge stalks, on the tips of which sit small yellow flowers. These are succeeded by remarkably large, swollen, brown, and downy bladders <note>seed pods</note> enclosing two seeds similar to those of a peanut <note>original: "Arachis"</note>.

It grew for us in the garden at Montbéliard; to Caspar Bauhin, it is Clover number 55.

### AMERICAN CLOVER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Trifolium americanum with broad trifoliate leaves and flowering spikes.</image-desc>

Botanists give this name to this Clover once brought from America to Belgium, where it used to flower in July and August. It seems to be a species of Bituminous Clover, as shown by its heavy scent, which is not unlike that odor. Caesalpinus calls it a certain kind of broad-leaved Clover brought from America with an unpleasant smell; to Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, this American plant is Clover number 11.

Furthermore, we have in our garden a plant entirely related to the so-called Bituminous Clover, whose leaves are completely devoid of any scent, but whose flowers smell sweet—which is a clear distinction.

### THREE-LEAVED AX-WORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Securidaca species with trifoliate leaves and curved, sickle-shaped seed pods.</image-desc>

It has slender but sturdy stems a foot long, furnished with leaves in threes, joined together, wider at the ends and notched. To these stems, as if at the joints and separated by moderate intervals, sickle-shaped pods are attached in a whorl <note>a circular arrangement</note>, similar to the pods of Italian Melilot. There are ten or twelve crowning the stem, more than half an inch long, slender, and flattened. It is the "Wild Fenugreek" of the herbalists.

It grows very frequently in the countryside of Montpellier, near Gramont, and in many uncultivated places in Spain; it is also cultivated in some gardens.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of clover and related legumes, including white, bituminous, and "American" types, noting their physical characteristics, medicinal uses, and geographic origins.</summary>
<keywords>White Clover, Bituminous Clover, Bladder Clover, American Clover, Ax-wort, Montpellier, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Galen, Caspar Bauhin</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### GREATER PURPLE CLOVER, with longer leaf & spike.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a clover plant with long, trifoliate leaves and a tall, elongated flower spike.</image-desc>

It grows to a height of one and a half cubits <note>about 27 inches</note>, with thick, woody, strong stems that branch out in various directions. The leaves occasionally vary in form; sometimes they barely exceed half an inch, while at other times they are two inches long and half an inch wide, oblong, pointed, neatly notched around the edges, very veiny, and crinkled. They sit in groups of three upon a stalk that ends in a very loose sheath, which wraps around the stem for a length of three inches or more. The reddish flowers are arranged in a spike the length of a palm or larger, emerging from calyxes <note>the protective outer layer of a flower</note> divided into long, fibrous segments.

### RHETIAN ALPINE CLOVER, resembling Milk-vetch.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine clover with narrow, pointed leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

The leaf is oblong, pointed, and smooth; the flowers are large, spaced out, and purple. In other respects, it does not differ much from the rest. It is rarely found anywhere except on the highest ridges of the mountains. It is a very rare and perennial plant, with a very beautiful purple flower color.

To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* <note>A famous botanical register from 1596</note> it is *Trifolium 42, or the smallest alpine clover with a yellow flower.* To Pona in his description of Mount Baldo, it is *Narrow-leafed alpine clover, with a root of a somewhat bitter taste.*

### NARROW-LEAFED spiked clover.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leafed clover with long, slender flower spikes.</image-desc>

This has a single root and several firm stems a palm high; the leaves are in threes, grass-like and hairy. The spike is about two inches long, composed of purple flowers held in downy calyxes that extend into five segments.

It grows abundantly near Montpellier <note>France</note> and blooms in June.

To Caspar Bauhin it is *Trifolium 19, or narrow-leafed spiked clover;* to Lobelius and Pena, as well as in the *History of Lyon*, it is *The other narrow-leafed Hare's-foot.*

<column-break/>

### GREATER PURPLE CLOVER, with shorter leaf & spike.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a clover plant with broader leaves and a shorter, more rounded flower head compared to the first entry.</image-desc>

This, along with the preceding one, blooms in the months of May and June. According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note>, it grows with great frequency in the mountains and alpine meadows and woods of Pannonia, Austria, and Styria. We observed it at Geneva near Champel, blooming in June, and at Basel in the garden of Master Felix Platter <note>A famous Swiss physician and botanist</note>.

Tragus and Lonicer call it *Cytisus*, but by a great error. To Lobelius in his *Observations* it is *The second Hare's-foot;* to Dodonaeus *The other greater Hare's-foot;* to Caspar Bauhin *Spiked clover with a feathered leaf.* Could it be the *Purple mountain clover* of the Paris Garden?

### PURPLE STARRY CLOVER of Montpellier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a clover plant with star-shaped calyxes visible in the flower heads.</image-desc>

From a slender, woody root, it sends out stems two palms long, not entirely upright and some even trailing on the ground, all covered in thick down. The leaves are in threes, supported by long stalks, heart-shaped, slightly notched along the upper edges, and entirely hairy. The flower clusters are divided, purple, with a very shaggy calyx whose spread-out segments represent a radiating star.

To Caspar Bauhin it is *Trifolium 35, or the starry clover;* it blooms near the gallows at Montpellier in April.

### WHITE-FLESH-COLORED SPIKED CLOVER, or the Greatest Hare's-foot.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large clover with very thick, hairy flower spikes and rounded leaves.</image-desc>

To Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria*, *Icones Plantarum*, and *Observations*, it is *The greatest Hare's-foot, with the leaf and appearance of Meadow Clover.* To Caspar Bauhin, *Trifolium 36.* To Dodonaeus, *Greater Hare's-foot with a clover leaf.* To the *History of Lyon*, *The greatest Hare's-foot.* It is an annual plant propagating itself from fallen seed, and an inhabitant of meadows located near rivers.

We observed it at Geneva in the meadows near the Arve river, blooming in May.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of purple and alpine clovers, providing detailed physical descriptions and cross-referencing them with the works of major 16th-century botanists. It includes specific geographical sightings in Geneva, Basel, and Montpellier.</summary>
<keywords>Trifolium, Hare's-foot clover, alpine flora, Caspar Bauhin, Clusius, Felix Platter, botanical taxonomy, Geneva, Montpellier</keywords>

--- Page 227 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of Trifolium (clover) species, following the previous descriptions of trefoils and medic plants. The catchword "TRI-" indicates the continuation of the Trifolium genus.</meta>

### SPANISH NARROW-LEAFED TREFOIL,
### or Narrow-leafed Hare’s-foot.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium plant with long, narrow leaves and elongated flower spikes, showing the root system and branching stems.</image-desc>

This plant has a firm stem, marked by certain nodes <note>joints or swellings on the stem</note> and divided into several branches. From each node, leaf-stalks emerge that wrap around the stem and branches quite loosely. At the ends of these stalks sit three leaves, as in the Crimson Clover <note>original: "Trifolio albo incarnato"</note>, yet they are not rounded, but rather somewhat long and narrow, keeled and grayish-white, like the leaves of the common Hare’s-foot <note>original: "Lagopi"</note>. At the tips of the branches is a spike of pale red flowers.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> observed this in the fields of Salamanca <note>Spain</note>, at the edges of vineyards.

### SMALL UPRIGHT TREFOIL, WITH
### clustered flowers and little claws.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, upright Trifolium with trifoliate leaves and small, clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

Rooted with long and thin fibers, it sends out many hop-like stems at once, about a span or a span and a half high <note>roughly 9 to 13 inches</note>. These are cylindrical, smooth, and whitish near the ground, but otherwise dark red or green. The leaves are tiny, in groups of three, smooth, veined, lightly saw-toothed, and some are even heart-shaped; they hang on long stalks, especially on the lower part of the branches. The flowers cluster together in small bunches both at the very top of the stems and from their sides; they resemble a small bird's claw <note>original: "vnguiculum auiculæ"</note> and emerge from relatively large, smooth, striped calyxes <note>the protective outer part of the flower</note> that are toothed at the edges and hard.

It is found in rough and rocky places, but it occurs rather rarely.

### TREFOIL WHOSE STEMS PRODUCE
### oblong clusters from the joints.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium variety with distinct nodes (geniculi) on the stems from which oblong flower clusters emerge.</image-desc>

There are ways in which this Trefoil agrees with the Small Upright Trefoil with clustered flowers, and there are also ways in which it clearly differs, as is plain enough from the illustrations of both. Its little heads are oblong, packed with a dense troop of tiny purple flowers, and they sit upon the joints <note>original: "genicula"</note>; however, there is only one cluster for each joint.

We collected this in the uncultivated rocky areas of Nîmes <note>France; original: "Nemausi"</note>.

<column-break/>

### TREFOIL WITH MASKED CLUSTERS,
### and small purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium with dense, rounded flower clusters and broader leaves.</image-desc>

It sends out several hairy stems from a creeping root that lean toward the ground, a span long, clothed with flowers in groups of three. These are joined together, wider at the end, hairy, small, and purple. The three leaves are large, overlapping like scales, broad, whitish, turning purple along the edges, and streaked with similar stripes; they have a certain resemblance to the petals of the Water Avens <note>original: "Garyophyllatæ aquaticæ"</note>. We observed this at Montpellier <note>France</note> in neglected and dry places around the Bishop’s Castle, and nowhere else.

### TREFOIL WITH A RIGID CLUSTERED
### HEAD and a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium with rigid, globular flower heads and small leaves.</image-desc>

It has a thin, single root provided with few fibers, from which rise several stems about nine inches high, somewhat hairy, dark red, and branching out in various directions. The three leaves are longer than those of the Greater Starry Trefoil, slightly hairy, oblong, and rounded at the end, similar to the leaves of Fuchs’s Hare’s-foot. The tops of the stems are adorned with single, clustered heads, more compact than the "Greater" variety, similar to Bachelor's Buttons <note>original: "Botonariæ"</note>, but prickly with the roughness of Burdock burs <note>original: "Bardanæ echinorum"</note>.

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax*, this is *Trifolium 40. without a globular flower. 4.* It is found blooming in May at Montpellier near the New Castle.

### TREFOIL WITH WOOLLY CLUSTERS
### along the length of the stems.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium with woolly (tomentose) flower clusters distributed along the length of the stems.</image-desc>

The stems of this plant are angular and smooth. The three leaves are joined, ranging from oblong to round, smooth, notched at the edges, and provided with a stalk nearly an inch long. At the base of this stalk is attached a pair of rather large "wings" <note>stipules</note>, broad but ending in a point, which clasp the stem in their embrace. The flowers are tiny, pale, and clustered; they are followed by clusters of woolly, white seed-pods, in which is contained a single reddish, shining seed, provided with a broad outgrowth.

It grows in the neglected places of Provence <note>France; original: "Gallo-Prouinciæ"</note>.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>X 2</sig>

### FOLLICLE-BEARING CLOVER, OR Small Bladder Clover with purple flowers.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a clover-like plant with inflated, bladder-like seed pods (follicles) and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

From a thin and simple root, it produces stems spread along the ground, about nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantales"</note>: adorned with leaves in threes, small, blunt at the tips, notched all around the edges, and hanging from a long stalk. From the junction of these leaves emerges a stalk longer than an inch, supporting small, reddish flowers gathered in a circle; these are followed by parchment-like *little bladders* <note>original: "utriculi"</note>, which are quite loose and open at a two-horned peak.

To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist</note> it is *Meadow Clover of Salamanca*, called *Trebol de prados* by the Spaniards: to Tabernaemontanus it is *Spanish Clover*. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it *Clover 6, or follicle-bearing meadow clover*.

It grew for us in the garden from seed sent from Belgium, and it flowers in April.

### A CERTAIN SMALL CLOVER, OR Dalechamps’ purple meadow Lotus.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a slender, branching plant with small trifoliate leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

The purple meadow Lotus, says the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" by Jacques Daléchamps</note>, produces a slender, whitish root with few fibers; many small stems nearly a foot long, which are twiggy: the leaves are like those of the Lotus, sometimes in threes, sometimes in fours, and very small: the flowers at the tips of the branches are numerous and purple.

It grows in meadows and damp places.

### GREATER WHITE-FLOWERED CLOVER, hoary, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a robust clover plant with large, rounded flower heads and broad trifoliate leaves showing distinct veining.</image-desc>

It rises with three or sometimes four small stalks, a foot high, firm, straight, and rounded: around these grow sparse leaves that are oblong, narrow, hard, veined, and keeled with a raised back; they always come forth in threes from a single point, are hoary <note>covered in grayish-white hairs</note>, and appear toothed along the edges; they are more frequent and larger near the root. The flowers are attached to the ends of the branches into which the stalks divide; they are sparse yet crowded together, forming a sort of spike, white in color, and endowed with some scent. The root is long-lived and equals the thickness of a pinky finger, covered in a dark, thick bark: it is long and provided with several fibers.

Clusius writes that it grows in the drier meadows near Vienna, the capital of Austria, and also in Moravia and Bohemia: and that it flowers in May and June.

<column-break/>

### NAKED-STALKED CLOVER, WITH SMOOTH HEADS: and another small, woody one with heads.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a clover plant with long, leafless flower stalks (scapes) ending in globular flower heads.</image-desc>

From a somewhat thick root come simple, naked, smooth stems, a foot long: they reach a peak in a cluster of purple flowers; they appear rough due to the small leaves beneath them, woven like little nets, and whitish: from the openings of these, the remains of the little flowers still project. The leaves are in sets of three, smooth, nearly an inch long and somewhat round. We have added to this same plate another small, woody variety with clusters. Both grow in the rough places of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. They flower at the beginning of June.

### FOUR-LEAVED PLANT RELATED TO CLOVERS, the dusky plant of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a plant with four-lobed leaves (quadrifoliate) and globular flower heads.</image-desc>

To Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> in his *Observations* and *Icons* it is the *Dusky brown four-leaved garden plant*. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is the *White four-leaved garden plant*. To Tabernaemontanus it is the *Four-leaved Lotus*. But why they all make this plant "four-leaved" is a mystery, since in Lobelius’s own illustration it even appears with five leaves.

### MEADOW CLOVER, WITH WHITE FLOWER, the smaller and female, smooth.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a low-growing clover with creeping stems and small, rounded flower heads.</image-desc>

It has a more compact habit than the Male variety, with shorter, weak stems spread across the ground: along which grow leaves in threes, small, round, smooth, and notched at the tip. The flowers are clustered, smaller, hanging from longer stalks, and white in color.

We have observed it growing here and there spontaneously in various places. In Montpellier, however, we saw the *Small white hairy clover* flowering in April, with a few white flowers, two or more joined together. That plant was quite stunted.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the "Trifolium" (clover) genus and related three-leaved plants, transitioning from common meadow varieties to rare Cretan species and the "Hepatica" (liverleaf).</meta>

### MALE YELLOW MEADOW CLOVER, with smaller flowers and many seeds.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium plant with small leaves and multiple flower heads, showing the root system and branching stems.</image-desc>

This Clover grows to a height of one or one and a half feet: however, the stems are not entirely upright. It produces many hairy stems from a deep root that is as thick as a pinky finger, tastes like a legume <note>original: "saporis Leguminosi"</note>, and is difficult to pull out. The leaves are hairy like those of the purple and white Clover. The flowers are small and yellow, composed of many tiny florets gathered into a small globe, shaped (if one may compare small things to great) like those of a Broom <term>Genista: a genus of flowering shrubs in the pea family</term> or a Bladder Senna. These are followed by many seeds somewhat similar to the Common Melilot <note>Sweet clover</note>.

Tragus calls it "Small Melilot"; Dodonaeus calls it "Medick"; Tabernaemontanus calls it "Field Clover"; Gesner calls it "Yellow Clover"; and Fuchs calls it "Yellow Saxifrage." We have found it growing wild in Geneva, Lyon, and almost everywhere.

<column-break/>

### FEMALE YELLOW MEADOW CLOVER, with more beautiful flowers, or Hop-Clover.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trifolium plant with larger, more distinct flower heads resembling hops (Lupulus), including detailed views of individual seed pods.</image-desc>

This plant has much in common with the preceding one: a thin, hard root; slender, hairy stalks; and three-parted, veined leaves. It differs in the yellow flower, specifically in the size and shape of the individual florets. The clusters on this plant are two or three times larger, imitating the heads of Hops <note>original: "Lupulorum capitula"</note>, though smaller and with the scales arranged in an opposite direction. Each of these scales is crested and forms the uppermost leaf of the florets, hiding the other three within its fold.

Furthermore, there are commonly held to be two species of this most beautiful Clover: a smaller one occurring everywhere, and another large and robust one rising to a foot in height with beautiful large flowers. Some follow the author Brunfels in calling it "Hare's-foot Yellow Hop-Clover." We found this larger variety on the margin <margin>of fields near Masevaux <note>original: "Masmunster," a town in Alsace</note>, flowering in October.</margin>

---

### CRETAN SHIELD-BEARING CLOVER, with pale yellowish florets.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cretan Trifolium with distinctive peltate (shield-shaped) seed pods and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

It has a thin, somewhat long root provided with fibers, which produces two or three stalks from itself, a few inches high and smooth. The leaves are small, attached to somewhat long stalks. About five florets rest upon the top of the stalk, clustered together and pale yellowish in color. These are followed by pods that are compressed and somewhat broad, containing a small, broad, and flattened seed. According to Honorius Bellus <note>An Italian physician and botanist famous for his Cretan studies</note>, while these are tender and fresh, they are very sweet and fit for eating; but when they have hardened, they are very bitter. The name indicates its place of birth <note>Crete</note>.

<column-break/>

### PRICKLY CRETAN CLOVER, with a lovely, large, purple-violet flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a prickly Cretan Trifolium with sharp-pointed seed heads and broad leaves.</image-desc>

This rare Clover is a gift from Crete, like the preceding one. However, it grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince from seed sent from Italy, and it flowered at the beginning of July. Casabona, the Overseer for the Serene Duke of Florence, sent seed from his Pisan Garden with this inscription: "Orbitochorto. Prickly Clover, with a Cistus-like flower, a very rare plant of Candia <note>Crete</note>." We also saw it at Mainz in the garden of his Most Reverend Highness, from seed indeed sent from Italy, but received from Crete.

---

### LIVER CLOVER, HEPATICA: Germ. Leberkraut: French. Hepatique: Ital. Hepatica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Hepatica (Anemone hepatica) showing the characteristic three-lobed leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

This plant varies chiefly in its flower, which may be either simple or double, and blue, white, or red. The leaves are attached to long stalks and are three-cornered; on the underside, they are purplish like a Cyclamen, but on the upper side, they are sprinkled with certain white spots. The stem rising from the root is thin, supporting a star-shaped flower at the top—blue, white, or red—and, as mentioned, either double or simple. The seed does not differ in color and is oblong. The many roots are somewhat reddish.

It seeks marshy and shaded places and is frequent in thickets.

<column-break/>

### LIVER CLOVER, HEPATICA, or Herb Trinity, with white and red flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another Hepatica variety, showing the plant in bloom with detailed views of the flowers and roots.</image-desc>

The "Herb Trinity" (or Blue Hepatica), such as we have observed it, was given pictured in the preceding table. Here, however, we present the white and red varieties growing wild in Silesia, Pannonia <note>The Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary/Austria</note>, and the Viennese territory, according to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note>, who writes that they are also cultivated in Belgian gardens. He notes that the Viennese woods nourish all Hepaticas except for the one with the double flower. We ourselves have seen the white and red (or flesh-colored) varieties growing wild near Jena in Thuringia and in the mountain forests of Savoy.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Images and Outlines," focusing on various species of trefoils and clovers, specifically the Hepatica and the Medica (Alfalfa) groups.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THREE-LEAVED LIVERWORT, HEPATICA, or Herb of the Trinity, with double flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hepatica plant showing its distinctive three-lobed leaves and a dense fibrous root system. The flower is shown in a "pleno" or double-petaled state.</image-desc>

This plant of rare and foreign elegance is found crowded with multiple purple-blue flowers; Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> writes that it grows spontaneously in several places in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>. Otherwise, it is not unlike the preceding plants in its root and leaves.

It is called *Hepatica Trifolia polyanthos* <note>Many-flowered three-leaved liverwort</note> by Lobelius in his *Observations and Icons of Plants*; by Clusius in *Pannonia* it is called *Trifolium nobile* with a <unclear>bluish</unclear> flower; by Tabernaemontanus, *Hepatica aurea multiflora* <note>Many-flowered golden liverwort</note>. By Camerarius in his notes on Mattioli, it is called *Trinitatis* with a double flower.

### MEDICA: German: Cattle-clover, healing fodder; French: Healthy Hay; Spanish: Alfalfa, Ervaye.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Medica (likely Medicago sativa or Alfalfa) showing upright stems, trifoliate leaves, and spiked flower clusters.</image-desc>

Medica <note>Alfalfa</note> is of the genus of Trefoils, and its name indicates its origin and the place from which it came. It was once called <term>Mēdikē</term> <note>Greek: "Median herb"</note> by the Greeks, for as Pliny says, it was brought from the Medes during the Persian wars which Darius waged. From this, it obtained its national name. Pliny makes it similar to the Trefoil in general; Dioscorides says it is so only when sprouting, but as it grows, the leaves contract, etc.

The name Medica is attributed to various trefoils: the creeping, the sharp, the yellow, and the purple. It is also wrongly attributed to Yellow Saxifrage, Horse-iron, and Laburnum. However, the truer Medica, accepted by Hermolaus, Marcellus, Gesner, Mattioli, Bacchanellus, Dodoens, Clusius, and Caesalpinus—and also by us—is the *Medica maior*, which is more upright with purple flowers, which we depict here.

### MARINE MEDICA, OR Snail-shell Sea Trefoil.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing coastal Medica plant with small trifoliate leaves and distinctive coiled, snail-like seed pods (cochleatum).</image-desc>

As great as it is, it is entirely covered in a shaggy and hoary down. The stems are a foot or even a cubit long, branching with frequent limbs; through these, the leaves grow in threes from short stalks—small, blunt, and numerous, with no manifest taste. The flowers are many, crowded together, and yellow; the pods are circular and twisted into themselves. The root is thick and longer than a cubit.

It flowers for the Venetians at the seashore in the months of May and September; it grows here and there in Spain and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, in the obscure maritime places of the South.

<column-break/>

### THE EPIMEDIUM OF CERTAIN AUTHORS, with purple flowers and yellow tips.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Epimedium plant with heart-shaped leaves and delicate flowers on thin stalks.</image-desc>

Anguillara names this *Epimedium*, and says that Dioscorides was mistaken in thinking that it lacks flower and seed. The authors of the *Adversaria* suspect it to be *Epipetrum*. In the *History of Lyon*, and by Tabernaemontanus and Camerarius, it is called *Epimedium*. Dodoens, however, doubts whether it is *Epimedium*, because Dioscorides and Pliny deny flower and seed to the Epimedium. Let the learned judge. Caesalpinus says it is a plant growing in the mountains of Liguria. We ourselves have seen it at Stuttgart in the Ducal garden, flowering in May; and we have observed it being cultivated in the more refined gardens of Italy. In our large *History*, through the carelessness of the printer, the image of this was wrongly placed for *Anonis* <note>Restharrow</note> and vice versa.

### WILD MEDICA, WITH A YELLOW FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Medica variety with smaller leaves and curved seed pods.</image-desc>

We observed this in May, hiding in hedges and cornfields near Montpellier and Lunel. In this variety, everything is smaller, more contracted, and narrower than in the preceding one; it never grows luxuriously, though it supports the cultivator with a compliant return; the stems are as numerous as they are long. The leaves are in threes, oblong, and notched along the outer edge, which is blunt. The flowers are copious, arranged as if in a spike, turning purple. The pods are twisted like a goat's horn, in which is a tiny and white seed. The root is long, thin, and woody. It was introduced from Spain by our ancient ancestors into the Neapolitan territory; today, however, it is sown in many other places, and in some it even grows spontaneously.

### SHIELD-SHAPED MEDICA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Medica variety featuring large, shield-like or plate-like (scutellata) coiled seed pods.</image-desc>

It has robust and hairy stems a cubit long, and these are upright; the leaves are in threes, somewhat large, rather broad, pointed, hairy underneath, and notched all around. The flowers are few and yellow, followed by wrinkled, top-shaped pods, composed as if of four or five little shields (*scutellis*), so that the lower, larger one receives the convex part of the one above it. The root is woody and simple.

It grows here and there at Montpellier, especially in cornfields, flowering in Spring. Tabernaemontanus calls it English Medica, but he has a false illustration and a description tailored to it.

<keywords>Hepatica, Medica, Alfalfa, Epimedium, Clusius, Dioscorides, Pliny, Tabernaemontanus, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, 16th-century botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the genus Medica (Medick or Burclover), following the previous discussions of leguminous plants. The catchword "MEDI" indicates the continuation of the genus name.</meta>

### ROUNDED MEDICK.
<note>original: "Medica Orbiculata"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Medica plant with rounded, coiled seed pods and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

This plant has a small, woody root, sending out infinite stems, a palm or a foot in length, spread across the ground. The leaves are in threes <note>trifoliate, like a clover</note>, small, smooth, almost triangular, broad at the tip, and somewhat notched, speckled with black spots. The flowers are tiny, yellow, and provided with long stalks. The pods <note>siliqua</note> are as they are depicted here, the size of a fingernail: the seeds are flat, reddish, and curved.

It is gathered in the Euganean Hills <note>near Padua, Italy</note>, as well as at Montpellier. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is the "Scutellate Trefoil with a blunter, more wavy leaf."

<column-break/>

### GREAT TOP-SHAPED MEDICK.
<note>original: "Medica Magna Turbinata"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger Medica plant with more prominent, turbinate (top-shaped) seed pods.</image-desc>

This plant puts forth stems a cubit or a cubit and a half long <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>, which are hairy and split into many branches. The leaves are in threes and hairy: the flowers are small and yellow. The fruit consists of six or more tightly joined coils, which are hard; each spiral is raised with a double row of small teeth, with a continuous little belt or band cutting through the middle. The seed is compressed and curved like a kidney, similar to the seed of Fenugreek.

It is an annual plant and flowers in June. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is the "10th Trefoil, or snail-like with a compressed, oblong fruit."

---

### GREAT HAIRY PRICKLY MEDICK.
<note>original: "Medica Echinata Magna Hirsuta"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hairy Medica plant with spiny, burr-like seed pods.</image-desc>

The first leaves of this plant are somewhat round, later becoming somewhat pointed and saw-toothed, with three resting on a single stalk. The stems are spread across the ground for two or three cubits: many flowers are clustered together on a long stalk, yellow in color: several pods cling together, forged of two, three, or even five spirals, made rough with very short, blunt spines. It grew for us in the garden at Geneva and Montbéliard, and flowered in July. However, the "sea-urchin" <note>the prickly seed pod, termed an "echinus"</note> which is shown separately in this small table belongs to the following Medick.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY MEDICK with stiffer prickles.
<note>original: "Medica Hirsuta Echinis rigidioribus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Medica plant with more rigid, prickly seed pods and a visible root system.</image-desc>

It expands itself across the ground with stems a cubit or more in length: the leaves are small, hairy, and broad at the outer edge: the flowers are yellow: the snail-like prickles <note>seed pods</note> are few and usually solitary; they bristle with long, somewhat rigid spines pointing up and down, which are not very dense: there are three or four coils.

In our figure, it puts forth spines that are too short and crowded; therefore, we have expressed it better in the preceding table, where the prickle was depicted separately.

It is found by the sea at Montpellier in the month of September. Is it perhaps the "Annual Medick with a tiny, hairy seed" from Camerarius's garden?

---

### HAIRY PRICKLY MEDICK.
<note>original: "Medica Echinata Hirsuta"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hairy, spiny Medica plant with upright growth and small flowers.</image-desc>

The root is white, somewhat thick and long. The stems are many, thin, a span or a cubit long, spread across the ground, striped and hairy: the leaves are in threes, somewhat round, hairy, and whitish. The flowers are small, yellow, and several are crowded together: the heads are no larger than a pea, consisting of twisted spirals, globe-shaped, four or five or even more, prickly with soft little spines.

It grows everywhere among the cornfields at Montpellier, and especially near the gallows <note>a common landmark in early botanical texts</note>: we also found it near Pérols on the seashore, and we had it in the garden at Geneva. Is it perhaps the "Other Italian Lotus" in Lobel's *Observations*?

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST PRICKLY MEDICK.
<note>original: "Medica Echinata Minima"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small, delicate Medica plant with tiny spiny pods.</image-desc>

This plant has stems about a foot long or smaller, which are adorned with leaves in threes, similar to the leaves of the Prickly Medick, small and hairy: the little flowers are puny, yellow, and many are crowded together. The little prickly burrs are joined in groups of three, four, or five, and are no larger than a grain of bitter vetch <note>original: "Otobi," likely referring to Orobus</note>. The roots are thin.

It grows in sandy places and also in meadows. It is frequent in the meadows near the Hospital <note>original: "Nosodochium"</note> in Geneva. To Camerarius in his garden, it is the "Puny Medick with prickly capsules." Is it perhaps the "Wild Trefoil of Dalechamps" in Pona's *Mount Baldo*?

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and classifications for several varieties of Medick (Medica), focusing on their growth habits, leaf shapes, and the distinct morphology of their coiled, often prickly seed pods. The author cross-references these plants with the works of contemporary botanists like Bauhin, Camerarius, and Lobel, noting specific locations where they were observed, such as Montpellier and Geneva.</summary>

<keywords>Medick, Burclover, Trifolium, botanical illustration, seed pods, Montpellier, Geneva, Caspar Bauhin, Joachim Camerarius, medicinal plants, Renaissance botany</keywords>

--- Page 232 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of trefoils and legumes, focusing on the "Medica" (Medick/Alfalfa) varieties and their medicinal or agricultural properties.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALLEST CROWNED MEDICK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flowering plant with trifoliate leaves and tiny, crown-like seed pods.</image-desc>

This little plant is to be considered among the rare ones; it grows in dry and barren places between Nîmes and Viertu <note>Nemausum is the Latin name for Nîmes, France</note>, and its seed pod <note>original: "echinus," literally a sea-urchin or prickly husk</note> sits at the very top with a sort of crown of small teeth.

Now is an opportune time to say something regarding the powers and excellence of the Medick. It manures the field, and is so sweet and nutritious that it is necessary to keep cattle away lest they be consumed by it <note>likely meaning they might overeat or bloat</note>. Thus (as Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> notes) in Spain, where its use is daily, they report that the draft animals and all cattle rejoice in no food more—whether green or dry—and are fattened and made sleek by it. However, it should be given to few at a time, since it causes bloating and creates too much blood. The dried seed, for the sake of its pleasant scent, is mixed into seasoned salt. Indeed, the whole herb heals the ailments of animals.

<column-break/>

### MOON-SHAPED OR SICKLE MEDICK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with trifoliate leaves and distinct crescent-shaped or sickle-shaped seed pods.</image-desc>

The pod is broad, compressed, and larger than a thumbnail; it approaches the "Mouse-ear" of Camerarius, but is more beautiful, larger, and striated: and there are even somewhat long small spines around the edge, which makes it represent a rooster's comb <note>original: "Cristam galli"</note> quite well.

But let us add something further regarding the powers and excellence of the Medick. There is not good agreement among the agricultural writers <note>term: Geoponicos — authors who wrote on husbandry and farming</note> as to whether it increases or extinguishes milk in animals: for Aristotle denies it, but on the contrary, Varro, Columella, and Palladius assert it: *We leave the dispute before the judge* <note>A Latin legal proverb meaning the matter is undecided</note>. The reader will find its virtues listed beside the following figure.

---

### CAMERARIUS’S MOUSE-EAR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with small rounded leaves and curved seed pods.</image-desc>

Camerarius does not know where it grows spontaneously, unless perhaps in Crete, from where the seed is brought mixed with Dodder <note>original: "Epithyrao"</note>. To us, however, it grew in the garden of Montbéliard from seed sent from Stuttgart. To C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Trefoil 29. Similar to the sickle-podded Trefoil*. By Camerarius in his garden book, it is called *Mouse-ear from the seed*, and *Hare's-ear from the shape of the leaves*.

Regarding the <term>MOON-SHAPED</term> or sickle Medick, of which we were treating a little before: on the authority of Theophrastus and Pliny, its virtue is so great that from one sowing it lasts more than thirty years: and very often, when cut back and shorn, it emerges better and more flavorful. Manuring does not benefit it; rather, it perishes because of manure and urine.

<column-break/>

### RUSTIC WOUNDWORT, Great Anthyllis, Leguminous Anthyllis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with pinnate leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

This plant has been gifted these names by various people; by some it is also inscribed as *Broad-leaved Lotus, Glaux, and Lepidium*. It grows in dry, lean, and sandy places, and on the margins of fields, and in some places it is even a garden plant.

The root is long, straight, and woody. The stems are nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantales"</note>, rounded, thin, hairy, and somewhat reddish. The leaves are pinnate, somewhat fatter than Goat’s Rue <note>original: "Galega"</note>, hairy underneath, and a yellowish-green above, with a taste somewhat sweet and somewhat sharp. But those leaves which are placed under the flowers at the ends of the branches are broad, finger-like, and have long membranes. The flowers are clustered at the top of the small branches, yellowish: which are sometimes also red or white, endowed with no remarkable scent.

---

### FENUGREEK: German: Bockshorn, Kühorn; French: Fenugréc & Senegré; Italian: Fengreco.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Fenugreek plant showing its characteristic long, pointed seed pods and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

By Hippocrates it is called *Epiceras*, by Theophrastus *Buceras*: by Dioscorides *Telis*, and by Pliny *Silicia*: and it obtained its name among the Greeks from the similarity which the seed has with a horn <note>The Greek roots "keras" and "buceras" refer to horns or ox-horns</note>. The whole plant is a cubit high and branched: and it was admitted into the class of Trefoils on account of the leaves, which are in threes, rather large, oblong, and notched. The flowers are equal to the flowers of lupines, whitish: the pods are sickle-shaped and pointed: the seed is yellowish, scented, and almost square: the root is woody and angular.

It grows spontaneously and is sown in gardens: but, if Pliny is to be believed, the worse it is treated, the better it grows. It is certainly a wonderful thing to say, that there is something which benefits from negligence? More in the Appendix.

That which we depict here is the *Wild Fenugreek of Dalechamps*.

<column-break/>

### HARE’S-FOOT TREFOIL OF SOME: German: Hasenfuß, Katzklee; French: Pied de Lievre; Italian: Pie de Lepre.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Hare's-foot" clover, showing the soft, fuzzy flower heads.</image-desc>

The name is taken from the evidence of its appearance, which—with its soft, ash-colored, and purplish down—imitates the feet of hares: with small, white flowers like the Scorpion-tail plant. The seed is small and tawny: the stalks <note>original: "caliculi"</note> are a palm high and budding with hoary down: the leaves are in threes and hairy: the root is small, woody, and twisted.

It grows spontaneously in plowed fields, and is also sown in gardens: it flowers and flourishes in June and July.

It possesses no small amount of astringency: and so much dryness that the seed mixed [with liquid] provides a defense for those suffering from a flux <note>likely diarrhea or hemorrhage</note>. It stops the bowels if drunk with wine: and, according to Dioscorides, it is tied on as an amulet for inflammations of the groin.

### WOOD SORREL, OR SOUR TREFOIL: Cuckoo’s Bread: Germ. *Guekgauchklee*: French *Pain de Cocu*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Wood Sorrel showing its trifoliate heart-shaped leaves and delicate flowers with visible roots.</image-desc>

This plant is numbered among the trefoils <note>Plants with three leaves, from the Latin *trifolium*</note> because of the heart-shaped form of its three leaves. It is called "Cuckoo’s Bread" either because the cuckoo bird feeds upon it, or because the cuckoo begins to sing its song when this plant first breaks through the ground. It also obtained the name "Sour Trefoil" from its acidic flavor.

Furthermore, the Wood Sorrel with white and purplish flowers, which we depict here after the work of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany</note>, grows both wild and sown in gardens. It grows wild in shady places near hedges and paths, and flowers in April and May; however, in the mountains, it flowers later.

According to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an influential Italian physician and botanist</note>, the entire plant is cooling in the manner of Sorrel: and when eaten, it extinguishes thirst and the burning of the stomach, and strengthens the liver and the heart.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW WOOD SORREL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Yellow Wood Sorrel showing a more upright growth habit with seed pods and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

By creeping along the ground, it spreads slender little stalks a palm or a palm-and-a-half long. Three leaves hang together supported by very thin stems; they are smaller than those of the common Wood Sorrel and more deeply cleft at the end, more clearly representing the shape of a little heart (as it is commonly painted) and more hairy, with an acidic taste. The star-like shape of the flower is the same, but the color is yellow. These are followed by "little horns" or pods nearly an inch long, looking upwards, somewhat thick, leafy, and composed of five cells. When these reach maturity, at the slightest touch, the small, reddish, rough seeds leap out from the sides, the openings closing up so quickly that the fissure from which they burst forth cannot even be seen. The root is somewhat long, slender, and fibrous.

It grows wild in shady places and can be planted in any soil; it produces flowers almost all summer long.

---

### RESTHARROW: Germ. *Heckelkraut*: French *Arreste bœuf*: Ital. *Bonaga*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Restharrow showing a woody stem with small leaves and pea-like flowers, including a detailed root system.</image-desc>

It is called *Anonis* by Dioscorides, but Theophrastus, Pliny, and Galen called it *Ononis*; both the Latins and Greeks use these same names. It is called *Anonis* from "not helping" <note>Greek *a-* (not) and *oninemi* (to help/profit)</note> because it is especially hostile to plowmen <note>The tough roots "arrest" or stop the plow</note>, which is also why the name *Resta bovis* <note>Latin: "Stay the ox"</note> was given to it. It is called *Ononis*, however, because the *Onos* (Donkey) very gladly rubs itself against it.

We depict here the common variety, which has flowers that are either white, or purple and flesh-colored; there are other differing types of *Anonis* which follow. This common variety of ours is found abundantly everywhere in grain fields and cultivated lands, and it flowers in Summer. There are also those who transplant it into gardens. Regarding its medicinal powers, see below.

### NON-SPINY RESTHARROW with purple spiked flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a non-spiny variety of Restharrow with a dense spiked inflorescence.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a Flemish botanist</note> writes that this is cultivated in the meadows of Silesia and Slavonia.

Otherwise, the Restharrow has a root that is heating in the third degree. Its bark is of the greatest use, having a certain power of cleansing and cutting. Thus, it not only provokes urine but also grinds down stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones</note>; by the same faculty, it clears away the crusts of ulcers. It is most highly recommended for the obstructions of all the internal organs. A decoction of the root in vinegar-water <note>original: "posca"</note> soothes toothaches if the mouth is rinsed with the decoction; the decoction, when drunk, heals hemorrhoids. The Ancients used to pickle the whole herb in brine before it became spiny, because when taken in food, it was believed to correct foul breath.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW NON-SPINY RESTHARROW, the *Natrix* of Pliny according to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a yellow-flowered, non-spiny Restharrow with trifoliate leaves and glandular hairs.</image-desc>

This has shrubby stalks a cubit high, split into frequent branches and free of spines. The leaves are in threes, oblong, hairy, notched at the edges, sticky, and fragrant. The flowers rest on long stems, yellow and well-formed. The pods are an inch long, rounded, and hairy. The seed is a dark, dusky color. The whole herb is hairy and greasy, and also fragrant, but smelling somewhat like a goat.

It usually grows in dry, gravelly, and sandy places, and flowers in June and July. It is quite common in Spain and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. We observed it in abundance near Geneva by the Arve river. However, as Pona notes in his work on Mount Baldo, many err greatly by using this in place of true Melilot.

### A SMALL, SMOOTH, SHRUBBY RESTHARROW related to the Trefoils, with white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, smooth, shrubby Restharrow with white flowers and trifoliate leaves.</image-desc>

We observed this around Montpellier in rocky and neglected places, flowering in May. In the same places, a hairy variety of the same genus with whitish flowers is also found. Furthermore, in our illustration, the leaves are of almost the same size as the natural leaves.
