# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### STRAWBERRY, STRAWBERRIES: German: *Erdtbeerkraut, Erdtbeer*: French: *Fraisier, Fraises*: Italian: *Fragaria, Fraga & Fragole*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a strawberry plant (Fragaria) showing trifoliate leaves, small flowers, and berries on thin stems.</image-desc>

It is common knowledge that the Strawberry approaches the Trefoils <note>plants with three leaves, like clover</note> in the number of its leaves, although Brassavola writes that in the region of Verona, five leaves are commonly found on a single stalk.

Tabernaemontanus calls it the "Berry-bearing Trefoil," and some call it *Fragula*; however, it is not yet clear what this plant was called by the Greeks, although Apuleius writes that it was called *Comaron* <note>original: "Comaron"</note>.

Furthermore, one type of Strawberry is not edible, or does not bear fruit (about which more follows), while the other is edible and fruit-bearing. This latter kind produces strawberries that are either red or white, or of an intermediate yellowish color; these ripen later and can be called late-season. There are also differences in size and shape, and some are said to bear fruit twice a year. *More on this beside the following figure.*

### PENTAPHYLLON OR CINQUEFOIL: German: *Funfblat*: French: *Quintefeuille*: Italian: *Cinquefoglio*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping cinquefoil plant (Pentaphyllon) with five-lobed leaves and a long taproot.</image-desc>

According to the description by Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist from the 1st century AD</note>, it bears thin, twig-like branches a palm's height, upon which is the fruit. It has leaves similar to Mint, five on each stalk—rarely more—split around the edges like a saw. The flower is a reddish-pale color, and the root is reddish and long, etc.

Theophrastus and Pliny add that it begins with the Vine and ends with it, and takes its name from the number of its leaves. The former commonly calls it *Pentapetes* <note>five-leaved</note>, *Pentaphyllon*, or *Pentatomon* <note>five-cut</note>, and even *Pseudofelinum* <note>false flax</note>, *Calipetalon* <note>beautiful leaf</note>, and *Xylopetalon* <note>woody leaf</note>; the reasoning for these names is shown in the Greek Nomenclature. We depict here the common and creeping variety, which grows everywhere in various places, both wild and cultivated in gardens.

### SHINING ALPINE CINQUEFOIL with a golden flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine cinquefoil with serrated leaves and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This beautiful species of Cinquefoil grows on the highest grassy ridges of the Austrian Alps and flowers toward the end of June; however, when moved into gardens, it flowers in May.

It is called by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note> in his *Pannonian History* the "Pentaphyllon or Cinquefoil with a golden flower"; by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*: "Cinquefoil 6, or the smaller, creeping, yellow Alpine variety." By Schwenckfeld: "Shining Alpine Cinquefoil."

<column-break/>

### NON-FRUIT-BEARING STRAWBERRY, OR NON-edible: Sterile Strawberry.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sterile strawberry plant, similar in leaf structure to the fruiting variety but without berries.</image-desc>

Botanists commonly label this the "Sterile Strawberry" and the "Strawberry without edible fruits."

Strawberries are produced mostly in the mountains, and not infrequently also in valleys and other somewhat shaded places; they also grow successfully in gardens. The herb is green all year round; it flowers in Spring, and in June—sooner or later—the fruits become ripe.

Serapio (according to Fuchs) claims the Strawberry is "hot and dry" in the second degree; but this is a great error, as it is "cold and moist" in the first degree <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors used in ancient medicine</note>. The fruits are suitable for those with bitter bile <note>pichrocolis</note>, but if eaten too copiously, they affect the head. However, water distilled from Strawberries is a most excellent remedy for all internal inflammations of the liver, lungs, and the rest of the body, and is useful for quenching thirst; it is also good for mouth ulcers and for redness and spots on the face.

### UPRIGHT CINQUEFOIL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright cinquefoil (Pentaphyllon rectum) with distinct five-parted leaves and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

This elegant kind of Cinquefoil rises to a height of a span and a half or nearly a foot, and has saffron-colored flowers.

Furthermore, Cinquefoil in general dries without biting <note>astringent without being irritating</note> and has very little heat; it penetrates and binds. It is a remedy for flows of the bowels, dysentery, prolapse of the intestines, St. Anthony's Fire <note>igni sacro; a skin infection now known as erysipelas</note>, and wounds. It is drunk against the cycles of fevers. The juice of the leaves, drunk for many consecutive days, heals the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>. However, what they say is superstitious: *“that if anyone carries Cinquefoil with them, it gives help and aid; and if anyone wishes to ask something of a king or a prince, it renders the princes well-disposed.”*

### SMALLER CINQUEFOIL, downy with soft fuzz, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, pubescent cinquefoil plant with a thick rootstock.</image-desc>

So Clusius labels it in his *Pannonian History*. By Camerarius in his *Hortus* it is called "Bavarian Cinquefoil, frequent in rough places around Munich"; by C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*: "Cinquefoil 4, or the first smaller creeping yellow variety."

Furthermore, nothing is more common than this along the roads in the dry and bare places of Pannonia, Lower Austria, Moravia, and Bohemia. It begins to flower at the start of Spring.

It contrasts edible varieties with sterile ones and notes the folklore surrounding the cinquefoil's ability to influence royalty.</summary>
<keywords>Strawberry, Fragaria, Cinquefoil, Pentaphyllon, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Clusius, botanical classification, herbal remedies, folklore</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Cinquefoil family, focusing on smaller and upright varieties found in Central Europe and the Alps.</meta>

### SMALL HAIRY CINQUEFOIL.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum parvum hirsutum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Pentaphyllum plant with hairy stems, several five-lobed leaves, and small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This is provided with a thick, long, black **root**: the *leaves* are small and hairy, on stalks of two inches: many *stems* are spread upon the ground, four or five inches long: the *flowers* are yellow.

It grows everywhere in various places: as we have frequently observed at **Montbéliard** <note>A city in eastern France, then a center of botanical study</note> toward **la Crotte**, at **Belfort** toward the **Castle**, and at **Geneva** *in the open Palace* <note>original: "en plein Palais," likely referring to the Place du Bourg-de-Four or a similar public square</note>. It flowers in Spring and Autumn, and sometimes even in November.

### LARGE UPRIGHT CINQUEFOIL.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum rectum maius"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller, upright Pentaphyllum plant with larger serrated leaves and more prominent flowers.</image-desc>

By Lobelius and Pena in the *Adversaria* <note>A famous 1571 botanical work</note> it is called *white and purple Cinquefoil*, being taller and more beautiful than the others. In the *Observations*, however, it is called *greater Cinquefoil with a pale yellow flower*, and sometimes white and red.

Thus it varies in the color of the flowers—white, yellow, and red; and a certain kind is found more shaggy than the rest, and a certain species which has a bulbous root.

It is found growing wild in various places, and is also cultivated in gardens.

### CREEPING CINQUEFOIL-LIKE PLANT.
<note>original: "Pentaphylloides supinum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, creeping Pentaphylloides plant with long-petioled leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The leaves are numerous, on long stalks, from a somewhat thick, long root with many heads; they are joined in pairs, each serrated, approaching the leaves of the creeping Geranium. The stems are a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note> and hollow: they bear numerous small, yellow flowers on short stalks. Small heads succeed them, similar to unripe strawberries.

By Lobelius in the *Observations* and *Images of Plants* it is called *creeping Cinquefoil with the appearance of Tormentil*: by Tabernaemontanus, Dodonaeus, and Schwenckfeld, *creeping strawberry-bearing Cinquefoil*. Clusius writes that it is frequent in the Viennese territory, at the outer edges of meadows along the woods: and Schwenckfeld finds it in the grassy places of the mountains of Silesia.

<column-break/>

### A LARGER species OF THE SMALLER CINQUEFOIL, with leaves whitish underneath.
<note>original: "Pentaphylli minoris maior species"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pentaphyllum variety with leaves that appear lighter on the underside, showing a thick root and upright stems.</image-desc>

It rests upon a long **root** with thick fibers: the *stems* are a palm's breadth high, at the top of which are yellow flowers sitting on short stalks. The *leaves* are long, serrated, coming forth in fives and sometimes sevens from long stalks.

Is this the *medium Cinquefoil* of Thalius, being intermediate in its leaves between the larger and smaller? Or the *tiny Cinquefoil* of Tragus?

### UPRIGHT CINQUEFOIL WITH DEEPLY cut leaves, silvery underneath, with a yellow flower.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum rectum foliis profunde sectis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright Pentaphyllum with deeply incised leaves and a robust root system.</image-desc>

It is labeled *greater rock Cinquefoil* by Tabernaemontanus and Lobelius. By Thalius it is called *hoary Cinquefoil*.

It grows everywhere in various places on embankments and by the water, in lean and sandy soil. At Montbéliard it is frequently found on the walls of certain gardens around la Crotte, flowering in Summer: at Basel it abounds between the stone bridge and the ash-bridge <note>original: "pontem lapideam & cinereiceam"</note>, flowering in July: at Geneva it is green in April and flowers in June.

### ERECT CINQUEFOIL-LIKE PLANT?
<note>original: "Pentaphylloides erectum?"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an erect Pentaphylloides plant with dense foliage and small flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

Is this the *5th or strawberry-bearing Cinquefoil* of Clusius in his *History of Pannonia*, perhaps unknown to Pliny? By Caspar Bauhin in the *Phytopinax* it is called *14th or strawberry-bearing Cinquefoil*: but to me, it is known by the name of *wild strawberry* <note>original: "Fragariae sylvestris"</note>. It grows, according to Clusius, in Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Austria region</note>, not only in coppiced woods but also in grassy fields. It flowers in May, and the fruit matures a little later, shedding its seeds just as in the rest of the Cinquefoils.

Writers claim that the herb, root, and seed of both this and the preceding plant possess the power of drying and binding <note><term>astringent</term>: a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, used to stop bleeding or secretions</note>.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of Cinquefoil (Potentilla) and related plants, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe, and medicinal astringent properties.</summary>
<keywords>Cinquefoil, Pentaphyllum, botany, medicinal herbs, Montbéliard, Geneva, Clusius, Lobelius, astringent, wild strawberry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Images and Outlines," focusing on the Cinquefoil family (Pentaphyllum) and its relatives, including Tormentil.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### WHITE CINQUEFOIL.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum Album"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pentaphyllum album plant, showing its root system, stems, and five-lobed leaves.</image-desc>

We have observed this in several gardens in Stuttgart and Montbéliard. Schwenckfeld writes that it is found most abundantly in the shady and damp forests of Silesia; Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a famous German physician and botanist</note> notes it grows among massive rocks and stony places.

It is astringent, drying, strengthening, and repelling: and it can provide all those benefits, if we believe Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an influential Italian physician</note>, which the common creeping Cinquefoil does. But that this White Cinquefoil was not at all known to that Commentator from Siena <note>Referring again to Mattioli</note> is demonstrated by the variation that exists in his descriptions in various places; and Camerarius rightly notes in his *German History* that Mattioli's descriptions do not match his own figures.

### CINQUEFOIL, OR RATHER SEVEN-
### leaved Silverweed, with mossy flowers.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum, sive potius Heptaphyllum argenteum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a silver-leaved heptaphyllum with serrated leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

In the *Adversaria* and *Images of Plants* by Lobelius and Pena, it is called *the smallest alpine rock Cinquefoil, very similar to Tormentil*. In Gesner’s garden works, it is *Rock Silverweed*. By some it is called *White Tormentil*, by others *Silvery Stitchwort*.

It occurs on the higher ridges of mountains and on cold cliffs, such as those in the Aosta Valley of Savoy, on Mount Calcaris in Narbonne, and similar places. We observed it flowering in May on the mountains near Geneva.

### THE PLANT WITH THE APPEARANCE OF CINQUE-
### foil, called Leucas by some, according to Valerandus. Is it Leucas?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, serrated leaves and a thick, scaly root system.</image-desc>

The root is thick, black, and scaly: the whole plant, however, which is an inch or an inch and a half tall, is covered in a grayish down; the leaves are usually in threes, in the manner of a Strawberry, but smaller, more hairy, whiter, and serrated.

It is quite rare to find, and is only discovered on the slopes of mountains.

According to the testimony of Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria*, those who look upon this hoary plant with the appearance of a Cinquefoil and judge it to be *Leucas* <note>A Greek name for various white-leaved plants</note> are not entirely without reason. In the *Images* of Tabernaemontanus, it is called *Montpellier Silverweed*, or in German *Welsch Silberkraut* <note>Foreign Silver-herb</note>.

<column-break/>

### CINQUEFOIL, OR RATHER
### Seven-leaved, with red flowers.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum, vel potius Heptaphyllum, flore rubro"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a red-flowered heptaphyllum with seven-lobed leaves and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It is commonly titled *Purple Cinquefoil, Red Cinquefoil*, and *Marsh Cinquefoil*: as well as *Marsh Five-leaf with purple or reddish flowers*.

It delights in the marshy and decayed places of mountains, growing as a shrub near fishponds and swamps; it flowers in June.

As Camerarius notes, the whole herb is astringent, and especially the fruit: for which reason it is believed to be beneficial for flows of blood.

### THE INDIAN CINQUEFOIL OF CLUSIUS.
<note>original: "Pentaphyllum Indicum Clusii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Indian Pentaphyllum showing a long, curved root and distinct leaf structure.</image-desc>

In the small baskets of Master Nicolaas Kool, a physician, Clusius says in his *Exotics* that in the year 1601, a plant of *Indian Cinquefoil* was brought from the East Indies to Amsterdam, along with two others of the same genus, entirely similar in form, but differing somewhat in size. Whether it bore a stalk and flowers remains unknown to me. The leaves were tender, supported by a somewhat long stalk, of the form shown in the figure. The root was tuberous and solid, like the root of Tormentil, etc.

### TORMENTIL, SEVEN-LEAFED: German: Tormentil.
### French, English, &amp; Belgian: Tormentille: Italian &amp; Spanish: Tormentilla.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tormentilla plant with small flowers and characteristic seven-parted leaves.</image-desc>

Since this plant almost always has seven leaves, and rarely fewer, Tragus, Gesner, Valerius Cordus, and others err greatly in thinking it is the *Pentaphyllum* <note>Five-leaf</note> of Theophrastus: for, besides the number of leaves, there are other distinguishing marks.

It enjoys shady and dry woods, and lean, mountainous places: it flowers late, and only in Summer.

It possesses very little heat, but dries in the third degree, and partakes of an astringent quality. Administered in various forms, it is very useful for checking dysentery, chronic diarrhea, and any other flows of the bowels: it is added to wound-drinks, plasters, and ointments; as well as to medicines administered against plague and poisons.

<keywords>Cinquefoil, Tormentil, Silverweed, medicinal herbs, astringents, botany, Mattioli, Clusius, Camerarius, dysentery treatments</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### POTENTILLA, SILVERWEED, GOOSEGRASS: Germ. Gänserich: Gall. Argentine: Ital. Argentina.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Potentilla (Silverweed) plant, showing its characteristic pinnate leaves with serrated edges and a creeping runner system.</image-desc>

By what name the Greeks and Latins called this plant is not at all known. More recent authors have called it *Potentilla* <note>from the Latin 'potens', meaning powerful</note> because of the strength of its medicinal powers; but *Argentina* because of the silvery color of its leaves; and *Anserina* <note>from 'anser', meaning goose</note> because geese do not at all despise it. Some call it Wild Agrimony because of the similarity of its form. It also approaches the Milfoil <note>Yarrow</note>, and there are those who refer it to the *Heptaphyllon* <note>Seven-leaf or Tormentil</note>, while others believe it to be the *Stephanomelis* of Pliny: let the learned judge.

It loves marshy and watery places, and grows everywhere around paths and near rivers: in May, June, and July it displays yellow flowers. Furthermore, it does not differ much from the *Pentaphyllon* <note>Cinquefoil</note> in its characteristics. More details in the appendix.

<column-break/>

### LION’S FOOT, OR ALCHEMILLA: Germ. Sinauw Sanickel: Gall. Pied de Lion: Ital. Pie de Leone.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alchemilla (Lady's Mantle) plant, featuring its distinctive palmately lobed, fan-shaped leaves and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

It is named *Pes Leonis* <note>Lion's Foot</note> because its leaves resemble the broad and round feet of lions; but *Alchimilla* because it has been celebrated by the proclamations of the Alchemists. However, Fuchs, Mattioli, and Dodoens rightly contend against Brunfels, Roesslin, and Cornarius that this is by no means the *Leontopodium* or *Leontopetalon* of Dioscorides. It is better called *Sanicula Major* <note>Greater Sanicle</note> by others, because it is very similar to that plant in both appearance and powers.

It is a lover of meadows, hills, and mountains, growing successfully in various places: and it is also transplanted into gardens. In May and June, it flowers with grassy-green clusters with yellow tips. Concerning its powers, see the Appendix.

---

### AGRIMONY OR EUPATORIUM: Germ. Odermennig: Gall. Eupatoire, Agrimoine: Ital. Agrimonia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Agrimonia (Agrimony) plant, showing an upright stem with pinnate leaves and a long spike of small flowers/buds.</image-desc>

Dioscorides and Pliny say its leaves are similar to Hemp leaves: it is clear from their descriptions that our Agrimony is their *Eupatorium*. However, Cesalpino calls this into doubt, whose error is opposed by Bock, Fuchs, Cordus, Dodoens, and Ferrante Imperato. No less do those err who wish it to be *Argemone* or Wild Sage.

Those skilled in herbal matters distinguish *Hepatica*, *Hepatorium*, and *Eupatorium* thus: *Hepatica* is Liverwort <note>Lichen</note>, *Hepatorium* is common *Eupatorium* <note>likely Hemp-agrimony</note>, but our *Eupatorium* is Agrimony. Because these three are suitable for strengthening and healing the liver <note>Greek: 'hepar'</note>, they are all commonly called *Eupatoria* for convenience, a name they claim is derived from its discoverer, King Eupator. Regarding the location, season, and powers, let the reader consult the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### CARYOPHYLLATA, HEALTHY AND CLEAN: Germ. Benediktenwurz: Gall. Refte, Galliot: Ital. Garyophyllata.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Caryophyllata (Wood Avens/Herb Bennet), showing the basal rosette of leaves and the flowering stalks with seed heads.</image-desc>

The name *Caryophyllata* <note>Avens</note> claims this plant for itself because of the very fragrant scent of Cloves <note>Latin: 'caryophyllus'</note> which the root breathes out: but the common folk, on account of its divine efficacy, have called it *Sana munda* <note>Healthy and Clean</note>.

There are those who call it *Lagopus* <note>Hare's foot</note>, some *Leporis oculus* <note>Hare's eye</note>, some *Avantia*, some *Baccharis*, some *Our Lady’s Glove*, some *Herba benedicta* <note>Blessed Herb</note>, and some the *Daughter of Glory*: to Bock it is Wild Nard, to Scaliger it is *Getia*, and to some it is the *Geum* of Pliny: and this opinion seems free from danger, because the same property is present in the roots of both.

It is commonly distinguished into the Aquatic, the Mountain, and the Common variety, which we depict here. It delights in a wonderful way in shady hedges and thickets, from whence, because of its great utility, it is transplanted into gardens. It flowers in May and June. Concerning its powers, in the following sections.

---

### MOUNTAIN AVENS, with a large yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Mountain Avens, showing larger, more prominent flowers compared to the common variety.</image-desc>

This plant possesses the same powers as the other, but more excellent ones. That a heating and drying temperament is in them is shown by the manifest evidence of their roots, which are found to be fragrant and astringent to the taste: they provoke the menses and blood clots, open obstructions, and act against poisons. Taken in food, drink, or medicine in any way, they succor the brain, refresh the vital spirits, and when chewed, they correct and strengthen foul breath and preserve against contagion. If they are placed in wine, they commend it with the best and most pleasant smell and taste, and render it most effective for various purposes.

<column-break/>

### WATER AVENS, or Marsh Avens, with a red striped flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Water Avens, showing nodding flowers and characteristic leaf structure.</image-desc>

This plant delights in watery places, and flowers in May and June, and, according to de l'Obel, it grows in great numbers in the woods of England and Brabant: it is also transplanted into gardens, as we have had in ours at Geneva.

Furthermore, the roots of the Mountain Avens especially, when washed of mud and filth, are dried, and when sprinkled with a rain of vinegar, they commend chests and clothes with a pleasant scent. By smelling them, they refresh the spirits and strengthen a cold brain. In summary, the argument that *Caryophyllata* is not ineffective in its powers is, as the Sienese commentator states, that its roots breathe out the commanded scent of Cloves.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XVIII.
### CEREALS, GRASSES, REEDS, Rushes, and similar plants.

**GRAIN, WHEAT:** German: *Korn* <note>Grain</note>; French: *Froment*; Italian: *Fourmento & Grano*; Arabic: *Hantha, Heniba, & Hencha.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single stalk of wheat (Triticum) with a detailed ear and roots.</image-desc>

Under the category of "Fruits of the Earth," as the first and highest kind, are contained among others the Cereals: namely, those which consist of a jointed stalk and reed-like leaves, and produce from their spikes or tufts a seed suitable for bread-making or porridges. Of all these, Wheat is the most common and noble in very many lands. Moreover, "Wheat" <note>original: "Triticum"</note> signifies every kind of grain which is threshed from the spikes and cleaned by winnowing; it is the same as what the Greeks call *Pyros*.

We depict here the common variety with a "mute" spike <note>meaning awnless or beardless wheat</note>, which grows in almost all inhabited and cultivated regions of the world. It requires a rich and fertile soil, and one that is sunny and dry rather than waterlogged. It is sown in Autumn, flowers in June, and is harvested in July. More information is found in the following pages and in the Appendix.

**ASH-COLORED WHEAT** provided with **VERY LARGE BEARDS**, which sheds its husks during threshing.

Modern authors commonly distinguish Wheat into *Robus* <note>Hard red wheat</note> and *Siligo* <note>Winter wheat or fine white flour</note>, and also into *Six-month* or *Winter* wheat, which is sown before winter, and *Three-month* or *Summer* wheat, which is sown at the beginning of Spring. Rembert Dodoens <note>A famous Flemish physician and botanist</note> distinguishes Wheat into the *Robus* of Columella, the *Siligo* of Pliny, and *Setanium* <note>A three-month wheat</note>. Jacques Daléchamps <note>French botanist</note> divides it into *Red Wheat*, which he identifies as the *Robus* of the Ancients, and *White Wheat*, which is their *Siligo*: and of this latter they make two species, one whose spike has beards <note>bristles</note>, and another whose spike lacks beards, called *Mutica* <note>Mute/Beardless</note> by Varro, and *Blé mutet* by the French.

Furthermore, according to Galen <note>The influential Roman-era physician</note>, Wheat is of the first order of heating substances, and is neutral in dryness and humidity. The narrowness of this space does not allow for more; let the reader consult the Appendix and our great *History*.

<column-break/>

**BRANCHED WHEAT, OR WHEAT WITH A MULTIPLE SPIKE:** French: *Blé qui truche* (as called by the people of Lyon); Italian: *Gran del grappo.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a stalk of branched wheat (Triticum racemosum) showing multiple smaller spikes branching from the main head.</image-desc>

As Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" from Ancient Greece</note> notes, various differences of Wheat are recounted, taken from the location, the time, and the variation in size, color, and form of the stalk, leaves, and parts of the spike. Whence, he says, some is early-ripening, some late; some is large and high-yielding, some meager and bearing little; some produces a grand spike, some a small one; some consists of a thin stalk, some a thick one; some is clothed in many tunics <note>husks</note>, some in few; some has a single stalk, some many stalks, etc. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> holds almost the same views as Theophrastus. Columella <note>Roman writer on agriculture</note> lists three: *Robus, Siligo,* and *Three-month Wheat*; Dioscorides <note>Greek physician</note> lists two: *fresh, well-ripened and yellow-colored*, and the *Three-month* which is *Setanium*. We shall review the differences handed down by more recent authors alongside the following figure.

**RYE:** German: *Rocken, & Rockenkorn*; French: *Seigle & Segle*; Italian: *Segala.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a stalk of rye (Secale) with a long, bearded ear and slender leaves.</image-desc>

It is commonly distinguished into *greater* and *lesser*, and into *Spring* and *Autumnal*. Some divide it into *Winter* and *Summer* rye; the former is established as the greater, the latter as the lesser; thus the difference is drawn from the size and the time of sowing. Caspar Bauhin <note>Swiss botanist</note> mentions a *Broad-leafed* and luxuriant Rye in his *Pinax*. There are indeed some who refer Rye to the *Olyra* of the Ancients, and others who refer it to their *Siligo*; let the judgment belong to the learned.

Furthermore, Rye grows in many regions, especially those subject to the North: and it grows in any soil whatsoever, no matter how stiff with frost or dry it may be, yet it fares better in more fertile and rich ground. It is sown in Autumn and Spring: but the Summer variety is more slender than the other, with fewer stalks, a shorter and thinner spike, and a lighter grain. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page categorizes and describes various types of wheat and rye, citing classical authorities like Theophrastus and Pliny alongside contemporary botanists to explain their physical characteristics and cultivation cycles.</summary>
<keywords>wheat, rye, Triticum, Secale, cereal grains, agriculture, botany, Theophrastus, Pliny the Elder, Columella, Dioscorides, plant classification</keywords>

# OF GRAINS

<columns>2</columns>

### SPELT OR HULLED WHEAT AND SEED: Germ. Speltz, Dinckel, Einkorn: French. Espeaute: Ital. Spelta.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spelt plant (Zea sive Spelta) showing the roots, stalk, and a single drooping ear of grain.</image-desc>

The stalk and leaves correspond to those of Wheat; the ear is a palm or a palm and a half long, sometimes without awns <note>bristles</note>, sometimes surrounded by awns, with shorter clusters and a double row of grains. Or the grains are so arranged that the middle of one corresponds to the beginning of the next alternately. The husks cling tenaciously and do not release the seed even under the blow of the threshing sledge; by this name it is distinguished from common Wheat, though otherwise, once stripped of the husks and tunics, the grains can hardly be told apart.

The *Zea* of Theophrastus and Pliny is the same as the <term>Zea</term> <note>A Greek name for a specific husked grain</note> of Dioscorides: of which there are two kinds, one simple, the other bearing two grains joined in each husk, and for that reason called <term>dicoccos</term> <note>two-grained</note>, which we depict here.

### SPRING SPELT: Germ. Immer: OLYRA, TYPHA, EMMER, Chondrus, Alica, Athera, Gluten, Tragus, Starch.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Zea Verna (Spring Spelt/Olyra) showing a cluster of stalks with multiple ears of grain and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

The kind of *Zea* we depict here is called <term>Immer</term> <note>Emmer wheat</note> by the people of Württemberg, and by various writers <term>Far</term>, <term>Halycastrum</term>, <term>Zeopyrum</term>, <term>Starch-wheat</term>, <term>Second Wheat</term>, and <term>Olyra</term>.

Furthermore, <term>Olyra</term>, which Pliny calls <term>Arinca</term>, is ascribed by Dioscorides to the *Zea* family, and various authors make it one and the same with *Typha*: others, following Galen’s example, distinguish this from that. Whatever the case, *Olyra* and *Typha* are a small kind of Wheat, used for the nourishment of peasants, and bread made from *Olyra* is considered superior to that of *Typha*. *Far* is otherwise a natural grain, called *Zea*, of which we spoke before; at other times it is a processed thing, even if not a work of nature. In this way also are made the processed items <term>Athera</term> <note>a type of gruel</note>, <term>Tragus</term> <note>groats</note>, <term>Gluten</term> <note>paste</note>, <term>Halica</term> <note>spelt grits</note>, and <term>Amylum</term> <note>starch</note>: the use and method of preparing these is not our purpose to teach here.

### TURKISH OR INDIAN WHEAT: Germ. Turkish or Heathen corn: French. Blé Sarrafin: Ital. Grano Indiano.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Maize (Triticum Turcicum) showing the broad leaves and a large ear of corn partially enclosed in husks.</image-desc>

Gesner <unclear>calls</unclear> this foreign and Indian Millet or Saracen Millet: but Fuchs calls it <term>Turkish Wheat</term>. However, Dodoens and Mattioli contend against him that it should rather be called "Indian," because it was first brought from the West Indies and not from Turkey, as Fuchs maintained. But since Pliny skillfully sketches the description, height, and fruitfulness of this plant—at a time when the West Indies were known or accessible to no Europeans—it might rather be that it was brought then by sailors from Greater Turkey, bordering the Indians: and so in this part we stand with Fuchs and Lobelius.

In our regions, it is sown more for delight than for bread-making: nor is there any use for it among the Turks except in times of grain scarcity.

<column-break/>

### SIMPLE ZEA AND ONE-GRAINED SPELT, BRIZA: Germ. Einkorn, Birken: French. Blé locar.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Einkorn (Zea Simplex) showing a slender stalk with a single upright ear of grain.</image-desc>

Some also call this "Second Spelt" and "Husked Grain." Furthermore, it grows in many rough and mountainous places in Germany. It is sown in Autumn with the rest of the crops, but later, and then matures only in the month of September. Moreover, the bread made from this *Zea* is dark and unpleasant to men.

However, the <term>Dicoccos</term> <note>Two-grained</note> *Zea*, of which we spoke before, grows in many places in France, Italy, and Germany. It grows in any soil whatsoever: yet it thrives better in rich and fertile ground. It is sown like Wheat in the months of September and October; it flowers in June, and in July it reaches maturity and is harvested. Furthermore, in its overall quality, *Zea* is in a way midway between Wheat and Barley: and breads made from *Zea* are more nourishing than those of Barley, but less than those of Wheat.

### RICE: Germ. Reiß: Belg. Ryß: French. Ris: Ital. Ris: In Greek, Oryzon or Oryza.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rice plant (Oryza) showing the branching panicle of grain and dense root system.</image-desc>

Marcellus and Mattioli deemed it useless to describe Rice, as it is very well known and familiar to everyone in food. There is no doubt that our common Rice is the *Oryza* of Theophrastus, Pliny, and Dioscorides. Ruellius makes two kinds of it: one with a white grain, which is in common use, the other with a reddish grain, which Pliny writes reaches a cubit in height. Others distinguish between cultivated Rice and Rice growing spontaneously, which to us is <term>Dens caninus</term> <note>Dog's tooth grass, often confused with wild rice</note>, of which more soon. Pliny also mentions a Rice with a round root, which Lobelius writes differs from our kind. In the East Indies, Rice is distinguished into the best and the cheaper sorts. More in the Appendix.

### PERUVIAN WHEAT, Indian Grain, Indian Millet, called Maize: French. Turkish Wheat.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Peruvian Wheat/Maize plant showing the large stalk, broad leaves, and the developing ear (cob) with visible kernels. Small detail drawings of individual kernels are labeled I, II, III, IV.</image-desc>

This kind of Wheat, which has long since become a resident in our world, varies greatly in the color of its flower and seed: for the color of the flower is either purple, or reddish, or yellow, usually according to the nature of the future fruit. And the color of the fruit is also manifold: first, either solid or mixed. The solid colors are white, yellow, violet, or black: the mixed is variegated in various ways, whence Gerard describes 11 kinds of ears, and Tabernaemontanus 16.

It seeks manured earth, is sown in March, and matures toward the end of Summer. It is not yet certain what power it may have in Medicine: but in nourishment it is considered inferior to all Wheats, and the bread prepared from it, although it is white, is hard and dry like biscuit; it nourishes little, descends slowly, and is binding <note>causes constipation</note>.

<summary>This page describes various husked grains like Spelt and Einkorn, the cultivation of Rice, and the introduction of Maize (referred to as Turkish or Peruvian Wheat) to Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Spelt, Einkorn, Emmer, Rice, Maize, Corn, Botany, Cereal Grains, Herbalism, Agriculture</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal survey of cereal crops, specifically focusing on diseases of grain and the various species of barley. It maintains the encyclopedic style of the previous sections, citing classical authorities like Theophrastus, Pliny, and Dioscorides.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMUT, RUST, AND BLIGHT.
#### German: *Brandt*; French: *Brusleure, Nielle*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a cereal plant (likely wheat or barley) affected by smut or rust, showing blackened, diseased grains on the ear and withered leaves.</image-desc>

A common defect of crops or grains, especially those with spikes—and most frequently seen in oats, rye, and wheat—is <term>smut</term> <note>original: *ustilago*; a fungal disease where grain turns to black powder</note>, which Theophrastus called *Erysibe* and Gaza called <term>Rust</term> <note>original: *Rubigo*</note>. This occurs when the stalk develops into a spike with the appearance of grain, but if it is soaked by rain and then feels the harsh rays of an uncertain sun, the stalk does not fail to grow, but the grains are transformed into a dark, sooty dust. This dust, either on its own or mixed with a salty liquid or other substance, stains everything with that same color.

According to Theophrastus, grain-bearing plants are more susceptible to rusts than legumes; among the grains, barley is more affected than wheat; and among barleys, some varieties are more susceptible than others, especially the variety called *Achilleis*.

### BARLEY: German: *Gersten*; Belgian: *Gerste*; French: *Orge*; Italian: *Orzo*; Spanish: *Cenada*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a barley plant with a single long-awned ear and characteristic leaves.</image-desc>

Barley <note>Latin: *Hordeum*</note> is named either from "bristling" <note>Latin: *horror*; referring to the prickly awns</note>, since its beard is sharper than that of wheat, or from its speed of "arising" <note>Latin: *oriendi*</note>, or from the word *hordus*, which means "heavy with seed."

It differs from wheat because it has a broader leaf, a shorter stalk, and a rougher husk than wheat; also because its grains are arranged in rows on the spike, which is not observed in wheat.

In the genus of barley, some have two rows, some three, some four, and most have six. Those with more rows are always denser and stand more upright. The spikes are larger in some varieties, smaller and more frequent in others, further from the leaves in some, and closer in others. More on this follows.

### NAKED BARLEY, OR GYMNOCRITHON:
#### A species of Spelt and the "Wheat-Barley" of some authors.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of naked barley, showing the roots, leaves, and a dense ear without the typical long husks.</image-desc>

You might call <term>Gymnocrithon</term> <note>Greek: "naked barley"</note> a hybrid, as its spike mimics that of barley. The **grains** are reddish and wrapped in a simple husk; they pop out with a light rub of the fingers and have no orderly rows. The leaf is broad and clasps the stalks closely; it is used in the same way as common barley.

Barley cools and dries in the first degree; it cleanses, promotes urine, and when cooked, it aids digestion and ripening <note>referring to the "ripening" of bodily humors or abscesses</note>. However, it causes gas and is hard on the stomach. Barley bread passes very quickly through the bowels and provides little nourishment to the body. So say Dioscorides and Galen; however, Pliny claims that barley is the most ancient of human foods. For things made from barley, the reader should consult our *Great History*.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF
#### SMUT OR RUST.

<image-desc>A second botanical illustration of a diseased cereal ear, showing the fungal growth (smut) more prominently on the spikelets.</image-desc>

Smut arises in the months of April and May, when the weather is frequently inconsistent—sometimes rainy and sometimes clear and hot. For then, while the tips are wet with moisture, they are corrupted by the heat of the sun and are, in a manner of speaking, "scorched" <note>original: *aduruntur*</note>.

We must remember, says Pliny, that there are two kinds of injury from the heavens. One we call "Storms" <note>original: *Tempestates*</note>, which include hail, tempests, and the like; when these happen, it is called "Greater Force" <note>Act of God</note>, and these come from the harsh constellations. Others occur when the sky is silent and the nights are clear, with no one noticing until the damage is done. Many call this Rust, <term>Blight</term> <note>original: *Vredo*</note>, or <term>Coal-blight</term> <note>original: *Carbunculus*</note>; all result in infertility.

### A KIND OF BARLEY, GERMAN RICE.
#### A species of Spelt? Or Olyra? Or Clusian Grain?

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a variety of barley with a very long, straight awned ear.</image-desc>

In its stalk, leaves, and joints, it agrees with the common barley already depicted, but there is a clear difference in the spike. It is praised as a food because of its whiteness.

Of barleys, says Theophrastus, one is rounder and smaller, another is oblong, larger, and more spread out on the spike; one is white, another inclining toward purple. Thus he says; but in the writings followed by Pliny, he adds that a wild version is found among the Indians. Barley is described and distinguished by Dioscorides as an "imperfect" grain.

More recent authors, along with Columella and Palladius, divide barley into <term>Six-rowed</term> <note>original: *Hexastichum*</note> (formerly called "Pack-horse barley"), which is larger and sown in Autumn, and <term>Two-rowed</term> <note>original: *Distichum*</note> (called "Galatian"), which is smaller and sown in Spring.

### STINGING BARLEY OF NEW SPAIN,
#### Mouse barley, Wild barley.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of wild barley (Hordeum murinum), showing a smaller, bristly ear and slender leaves.</image-desc>

Castor and Monardes mention a "stinging barley" of New Spain <note>Mexico</note> called *Orzada* and *Ceuadilla* <note>Sabadilla</note>; they say it possesses different properties than our native barley. They attribute to it a burning and caustic power, acting in place of fire wherever a cautery is needed.

There is also a certain defect of barley common in our regions, which Lobelius called <unclear>s</unclear> barley, others call *Aristida*, others *Phoenix grass*, but most call it <term>Mouse Barley</term> <note>original: *Hordeum murinum*</note> or "Spurious Wild Barley." It has the roots and leaves of barley and raises stalks a cubit high, but they are thinner and the spikes are lighter, armed with soft bristles and a thin husk that covers no grain. It grows everywhere.

<summary>This page describes various cereal diseases like smut and rust, alongside a detailed classification of barley species, including their medicinal properties and regional varieties.</summary>
<keywords>Barley, Smut, Rust, Ustilago, Hordeum, Ancient Medicine, Botany, Theophrastus, Pliny, Agriculture</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of cereal grains and grasses, specifically focusing on varieties of Millet, Sorghum, and Oats. It maintains the encyclopedic style of the previous entries, citing classical authorities like Pliny and Dioscorides.</meta>

# MILLET: German: *Hirs* & *Hirss*: Belgian: *Hirs* & *Milie*: French: *Mil.* & *Millet*: Italian: *Miglio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Millet plant (Milium) showing long, slender leaves and a dense, drooping seed head at the top of a tall stalk.</image-desc>

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> claims that the name *Milium* is derived from the Greek word *Melines*, but this is incorrect, since Dioscorides and Galen understand *Melines* to mean Italian Millet <note>original: "Panicum"</note>. Festus more rightly suggests it is taken from the word for "a thousand" <note>original: "miliari summa"</note>, as if it bears a thousand grains; from this, the "millet-birds" <note>original: "Miliariæ aves"</note> are named, which flock together to this crop to feed upon it.

Differences in the plant are chiefly observed in the color of the seed, which is most often tawny or golden, very rarely black or reddish-brown, and sometimes found to be striped.

It requires a smooth and thin soil: it is sown toward the end of March, and the seeds ripen in the Summer.

It cools in the first degree, but dries in the third <note>Refers to the Galenic system of "degrees" of medicinal properties</note>. *More in the Appendix.*

---

**SORGHUM: OR WHITE INDIAN MILLET: Called *Dora* by some: More noble Indian Millet.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of White Indian Millet (Sorghum), featuring broad, corn-like leaves and a large, upright, branched seed cluster (panicle).</image-desc>

This Indian Millet is similar to the Sorghum already mentioned, and is believed to be the *Hareoman* of the Arabs. It consists of reed-like leaves, very tall and jointed stalks, and a spreading mane <note>the seed head</note>: but its seed is much larger, rounder, and white, contained in hairy husks, which constitutes a clear difference.

Belon <note>Pierre Belon, a French naturalist</note> writes that it is sown in Cilicia and Epirus. Furthermore, the seed of Sorghum or Indian Millet is similar in flavor and temperament to Italian Millet. It is gathered by peasants, ground into flour, and made into loaves, but these are crumbly and provide little nourishment. It is sown in Tuscany, but rather for the fattening of pigeons and poultry than for human food.

---

**NAKED OATS:**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Naked Oats (Avena nuda), showing a slender stalk with drooping spikelets that lack the typical husks or awns.</image-desc>

Theophrastus writes that Nature has most especially covered the Oat: but on the contrary, Pliny declares the seed of the Oat to be most *naked*: but he said this long ago because, when the membranes gape open at maturity, the naked seed appears.

The Oat pictured here is titled *Naked Oat* and *Third Oat* by authors. It clings less stubbornly to the husks of the grain, which is a yellowish-white, and has the appearance of the grain of the other Oat.

Furthermore, the Oat is food for beasts of burden, not for men, unless perhaps in extreme hunger they are forced to make bread from it. As a medicine, it dries and disperses, and, as Galen says, it possesses a power similar to Barley. Simple women <note>original: "mulierculæ," often referring to folk healers or housewives</note> are familiar with its culinary use.

<column-break/>

**SORGHUM, INDIAN MILLET: German: *Sorgsamen*: French: *Blé Barbu*, Italian: *Sorghi, Melego*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sorghum (Milium Indicum), showing a robust stalk with alternating leaves and a very dense, heavy seed head.</image-desc>

This plant has stalks taller than a man, reed-like leaves, and a mane <note>seed head</note> a palm or a foot long, in which are very numerous grains, equal in size to lentils, compressed, and somewhat oblong: sometimes white, sometimes dusky, and occasionally black: and thus it varies chiefly in the color of the seed.

It is called *Sagina* <note>meaning "fattening"</note> by some from the act of fattening; to others it is the *Calamogrostis* of Dioscorides, but to most it is the *Indian Millet* of Pliny.

It loves a rich and moist soil, and is commonly found in Italy, Spain, and other warmer regions, and is among the Summer sowings. *We shall provide its use shortly.*

---

**WHITE AND BLACK OATS: Greek: *Bromos*: German: *Habern*: French: *Auoine*: Italian & Spanish: *Auena*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Common Oats (Avena sativa), displaying the characteristic loose, hanging panicle with pointed glumes.</image-desc>

The Oat, says Dioscorides, has certain joints: in leaf and stalk it imitates Wheat: and at the tops it bears hanging structures like two-footed locusts <note>a classical description of the oat spikelet</note>, in which the seed is contained.

Commonly, however, the Oat is distinguished into the cultivated <note>original: "farinam"</note> and the *wild*: the former is simply called Oat, White Oat, Milder Oat, Edible Oat, First Oat, and Common Oat by authors: and by Cordus in his commentary on Dioscorides it is called *Grain Oat*. The *Wild* kind they call *Black and Bearded Aegylops* and *the vice of grain*. It was called *Calamina*, which is a type of pipe <note>flute</note> mentioned by Virgil in Eclogue 1.

Furthermore, the Oat loves watered places: it is sown in Spring, and matures toward the end of Summer. *More in the following pages.*

---

**HAIRY OATS: The *Aegilops* with recurved bristles of some.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pilose or Wild Oats (Avena pilosa), showing long, twisted awns (aristae) protruding from the spikelets.</image-desc>

Although this agrees with the others in its leaves and stalks, it has a very beautiful ear a foot long: and the grains are surrounded by yellowish hairs which shine beautifully like fine linen <note>original: "byssi instar"</note>; these are generally longer than the grains of the common Oat, usually appearing in pairs, and sometimes singly. From the husks emerge twin bristles <note>original: "aristæ"</note>, long, two or three inches, nodding and curved, like the legs of wild locusts.

It is found in the fields of Germany and Belgium: however, its properties are unknown and not yet explored. Furthermore, all Oats exhaust the soil, whence Virgil says in the first book of the Georgics:

> For a crop of flax burns the field, and so does the Oat. <note>original: "Vrit enim Lini campum seges, vrit Auena."</note>

It highlights the distinction between food for humans and fodder for animals, while citing classical authorities like Virgil and Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Millet, Sorghum, Oats, Avena nuda, Indian Millet, Agriculture, Botany, Classical Medicine, Virgil, Pliny, Dioscorides</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### AEGILOPS: German: *Taubhaber* <note>literally "deaf oats" or "empty oats"</note>; French: *Auoine-sauuage*, *Aueneron*, *Auoine sterile* <note>Wild oats or sterile oats</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild oat-like grass (Aegilops) with long awns and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

One and the same name has been maintained among the Greeks and Latins; it is a small herb that grows of its own accord, specifically when barley degenerates into it, and it is commonly called "most abundant bearded oats," "black oats," "silly oats," or "wandering oats." It obtained its name from the fact that it heals *Aegylopas* <note>original: "oculorum Aegylopas"; a type of ulcer or fistula in the inner corner of the eye</note> of the eyes.

However, various plants are gifted with the name of *Aegilops*, such as the Turkey Oak, the Hedge Beech, Columbine, Royal Larkspur, Wall Barley, and others, concerning which we treat elsewhere. Thus, there is no agreement among authors as to which plant is the true *Aegilops* today. We present this figure from Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note>.

In summer it is found along roadsides, in meadows, at the margins of fields, and among the standing corn. It is that "Fescue-grass" which is handed down as *Aegilops*.

### BULBOUS GRASS FROM ALEPPO.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with distinct bulbous swellings at the base of the stems.</image-desc>

From many olive-shaped bulbs, covered in torn layers <note>original: "tunicis"; referring to the papery skins of the bulb</note>, there emerge stalks a foot or a foot and a half high, distinguished by narrow leaves the length of a palm. The spike is similar to Wall Barley, a palm's length: with dense, long husks pressed against the reed, looking upwards, and each ending in a short bristle <term>awn<gloss>the hair-like beard of a grass spike</gloss></term>.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called "Bulbous grass from Aleppo," and "Knotty grass," from the shape of the root.

### OAT-LIKE GRASS with red spikelets.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall grass with drooping, oat-like spikelets (locustae).</image-desc>

It varies; the stalk is smooth in mountainous areas, but somewhat rough in thickets. We observed it flowering at the beginning of May on rocks around Saint-Hippolyte and Saint-Ursanne. Indeed, Caspar Bauhin writes in his *Phytopinax* that it is found in July and August in mountainous and shady places around the castle of Badenweiler in the Margraviate, and Richenstein near Basel. In his *Phytopinax* it is called "Grass 41," or "non-downy oat-like grass," having some similarity to the "Spiked grass" of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary figure in 16th-century botany</note> from Pannonia.

<column-break/>

### AEGILOPS, perhaps the "GREAT GRASS" of Montbéliard: German: *Dort* and *Lulch* <note>Common names for darnel or tares</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with multiple bristly seed heads branching from the top of the stalks.</image-desc>

Is it the first *Lolium* of Tragus? Or the "Sterile Brome" of Lobelius in his *Observations*? Or the "Wall Grass" of Dalechamps? Or the "Gramineous Fescue with hairy husks" of Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax*?

It varies in its spikes, which are sometimes gathered as if into a bundle, and sometimes dispersed; and furthermore, sometimes they are smooth, and sometimes hairy.

It grows up like others of this kind, specifically through frequent rains, when the constitution of the year and winter is mild and warm. It is properly a defect of rye, and is only very rarely found with other grains.

### GRASS WITH SMALL WHITE HAIRY SPIKELETS, and oat-like seed: German: *Haber grass* <note>Oat grass</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tufted grass with small, hairy, pale spikelets.</image-desc>

To Clusius in his *Pannonia* and *History*, it is "Mountain grass similar to oats." To Tabernaemontanus, it is "Oat-like grass."

It grows, according to the same author Clusius, in the mountainous and shady places of Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, Austria, and Bohemia; it matures its seed in the month of July.

By Tabernaemontanus in his *Icons* and *History* it is called "Oat-like grass," or *Haber grass*. By Gerard, "Two-rowed barley"? By Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* and *Phytopinax*, "Downy mountain oat-like grass."

### OAT-LIKE GRASS WITH RARER GRAIN, of the groves, Danish.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender grass with sparse, drooping grains.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is scattered at the top of the turf, spread out, but with longer tufts attached: the stalk is a foot and a half or two feet high, shining, bright, and trembling: the leaves are those of the "Oat-like wood grass": the <term>spikelets<gloss>locustae; the small flowering units of the grass</gloss></term> are rarer and shorter than in the others.

Lobelius collected it in mountainous beech forests, not far from Kronborg, in damp soil.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called "Oat-like grass, or grass with rarer spikelets."

It includes descriptions of their physical characteristics, such as bulbous roots or hairy spikelets, and their typical habitats in Europe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of cereal-like grasses and grains, specifically focusing on darnel (Lolium) and various species of millet (Panicum).</meta>

# DARNEL, PHOENIX, DARNEL-GRASS:
->German: *Dort*. French: *Turaye*. Italian: *Loglio*.<-

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Lolium (darnel), showing a tall stalk with alternating spikelets and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Darnel <note>original: *Lolium*</note> is called "drunken wheat" <note>original: *Triticum temulentum*</note> and "foolish grain" <note>original: *Frumentum fatuum*</note> by some. The Greeks called it *Airan* <note>original: *αἶραν*</note> because its harmful vapors are carried upward to the brain. It varies in form, and is sometimes observed without awns <note>bristle-like appendages on the grain</note>, but commonly it possesses them.

It grows in fields with Wheat and Barley when their seeds have been corrupted or, as Galen says, transformed into a worse state. It grows especially in marshy soil during wet weather, particularly in the winter months.

The grain is contained in a hard husk. The stalk, root, and the rest are like those of Wheat or Rye; and therefore, as was long ago handed down by Theophrastus, this pest—this defect of the crops—is believed to return again into Wheat or Rye. More on this is found beside the following figure.

### MILLET <note>original: *Panicum*</note>: German: *Fench*, *Fuchs schwants*. French: *Paniz*. Italian: *Panico*. Spanish: *Panizo*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Panicum (millet), showing two stalks with dense, bristly seed heads and broad leaves.</image-desc>

Millet <note>specifically Foxtail Millet</note> is thought to be named from its "panicles" <note>the branched cluster of flowers</note>. To some, it is a wild or small version of Common Millet <note>original: *Milium*</note>. Ruellius calls it *Melica* <insert>but incorrectly, as Matthioli notes</insert>. To the Greeks, it is *Elymos*.

Dioscorides touches upon its history in a few words: Millet, he says, is numbered among the cereal grains, similar to Common Millet, and is kneaded into bread in the same way; it also has the same uses, though it provides less nourishment and is more astringent.

It varies in the size, shape, and color of the panicles: for they may be large or small, compressed or spread out, yellow, reddish, or white. We depict the common variety here.

### MILLET WITH A SPREAD-OUT SPIKE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Panicum variety with a more open, branched seed head (divulsa) and scattered seeds shown at the bottom right.</image-desc>

Pliny says that Millet should be sown first in cold and watery ground, and later in warm fields. They forbid it to be sown among vines or fruit-bearing trees, believing the earth is exhausted by this crop. Furthermore, the same author adds that a certain herb, whose name is unknown, if buried in the four corners of the cornfield, drives away the plague of Starlings and Sparrows from the Millet—so that, wonderful to say, no bird will enter! But what that herb is, which through so many centuries has not yet become known to the curious inquirer, remains a mystery.

<column-break/>

### THE CYNOPS OF THEOPHRASTUS ACCORDING TO SOME.
->Perhaps the Wall-Grass of Dalechamps?<-

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Cynops, showing a slender grass with a single, elongated, bristly spike.</image-desc>

To proceed with the history of the previously discussed Darnel and *Phoenix*: *Phoenix* <note>likely a species of Ryegrass</note> grows in fields, along roadsides, and on the roofs of buildings; it is found almost everywhere in Italy and France. There is such a great similarity between it and Darnel that he who knows the latter will also know the former.

Darnel heats in the beginning of the third degree and dries at the end of the second <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors</note>. When it is in bread, it very quickly causes vertigo, numbness, and "drunkenness" <note>Darnel is often infected with a fungus that causes intoxicating or toxic effects</note>, and brings a fog to the eyes. It does no harm to hens and fattened poultry. Applied or laid on in various ways, it is effective against scrofula, spreading sores, rotting ulcers, and gangrene. Indeed, applied to the forehead with lard, it drives away its own harmful effects. Thus, as Pliny says, even the pests of the crops are of some use.

### MILLET WITH A COMPRESSED SPIKE AND PURPLE-
->tinted awns.<-

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Panicum variety with a very dense, cylindrical, compressed spike.</image-desc>

The illustration previously proposed from our purchased collection was less pleasing, therefore we present another one here.

Furthermore, although one may read in the *History of Lyon* <note>the *Historia Generalis Plantarum*</note> that there is no use for Millet today, neither in the apothecaries nor in bread-making—because the seed is very dry and meager, providing very little nourishment, and is therefore left to the small birds—Clusius nevertheless asserts that Millet is of great use throughout all Germany, Hungary, and Bohemia. For it serves as food, and porridges are made from its husked seed, which are of a not unpleasant flavor.

### BLUE OR INDIAN MILLET.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Indian or Blue Panicum, featuring very broad, corn-like leaves and a thick, dense seed head.</image-desc>

This elegant kind of Millet was brought into Europe from the province of Peru. It has stalks far thicker, firmer, and taller than common Millet; the leaves are reed-like, long, wide, and hard. The spike is about the length of a finger, densely packed, and of almost equal thickness everywhere. The seeds are smooth and of a bluish color, and the roots are fibrous, larger, and stronger than those in common Millet.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics and medicinal uses of Darnel (Lolium) and various species of Millet (Panicum), including a variety recently introduced from the Americas.</summary>
<keywords>Darnel, Millet, Lolium, Panicum, botanical history, medicinal plants, agriculture, Peru, Dioscorides, Pliny</keywords>

--- Page 244 ---
### THE FOOT-AND-A-HALF LONG SPIKE OF AMERICAN MILLET.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut of a large, thick corn-like ear (Panicum Americanum) showing individual kernels and a textured surface.</image-desc>

Regarding the spike of this Millet <note>original: *Panici*</note>, which is thick, very firm, and well-compacted, though not uniform throughout—tapering gradually and perceptibly at the furthest end—and over a foot and a half long (though not entirely whole), Charles l'Écluse <note>Clusius, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> says: "James Garret sent this to me from London in the year 1591, having purchased it from an English sea captain returning from his voyage." It contained innumerable seeds, enclosed in a rough husk <note>glume</note> on a short stalk. He calls it *Ethiopian Millet* from *Guinea*; Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* calls it *Indian Millet with a very long spike*. It represents not poorly a spike of Plantain or Long Pepper.

### A KIND OF WILD MILLET, OR Dog’s Tooth I. In French: *Panicette*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a wild grass (Panicum Sylvestre) with long, slender leaves and two upright stalks ending in spiked seed heads.</image-desc>

This is a plant hated by gardeners, encountered everywhere, and ripening its seed in August. It varies, sometimes with an oblong spike, sometimes short and round.

Is it Pliny’s *White Herb*? Or his *Miliaria*, which kills Millet? Or Cesalpino’s *Foxtail*? Or Ruellius’s *Hospium*? Or Gorraeus’s *Tailed Grain*? Or the *Phalaris* of Dioscorides, as it seemed to Lonicer and Tragus? Fuchs, whose illustration we provide here, thinks it is the *Phalaris* of Pliny; others think it is *Wild Millet*, and by some it is called *Panicastrella*.

### A KIND OF GRASS, DOG’S TOOTH III. Manna Grass, in German: *Himmelthau* <note>Heaven's Dew</note> & *Mannagrass*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tufted grass (Gramen Mannae) with multiple flowering stalks and a dense root system.</image-desc>

It is an annual plant, also very hateful in gardens, which first begins to appear in July.

Boys insert the tips into their nostrils and pull them out to draw blood, and from this effect they call it *Sanguinella* <note>Little Blood-plant</note>. Matthiolus writes that in some parts of Germany it is sown with great care, no less than other types of Grain and Legumes, because they eat its seed; its power is such that when boiled in a rich meat broth, it is no less pleasing than Rice. But it must be pounded in a mortar to free it from its husk. Gesner writes that it is eaten in vinegared dishes.

<column-break/>

### Phalaris, as called by the Greeks, Latins, Germans & French.
->In German it is also called *Canarien saet*: In French *Froment de Canarie* <note>Canary Wheat</note>.<-

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Phalaris (Canary grass) showing the distinct oval-shaped seed heads and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It rests on a rather stout root, from which come stalks a cubit and a half high <note>about 27 inches</note>, barley-like and knotted, upon each of which sit single, cone-shaped spikes. The leaves are like barley, the flowers pale, and the seed like Millet, a favorite of birds.

Some distinguish it into *Cultivated* and *Wild*; others into *Greater* and *Lesser*. Is the *Phalaris* of the Ancients unknown today?

It was formerly brought from Spain and the Canary Islands <note>Fortunate Islands</note>, but today it is kept in the more cultivated gardens. Furthermore, the leaves and seed are believed to be beneficial for torments of the bladder; and specifically, according to Lobelius, breads made from the seed are most useful against kidney stones. However, the chief gift of the seed is for feeding Canary nightingales, which is why a great abundance of it is commonly found among shopkeepers.

### A KIND OF GRASS called DOG’S TOOTH II.
->or Wild Millet with a divided panicle.<-

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass with divided panicles (seed heads) and broad, blade-like leaves.</image-desc>

From a root consisting of several somewhat thick fibers, it sends out stalks <note>reeds</note> two or three cubits high; the leaves are reed-like, ending in a sharp point. The crest <note>juba</note> is a span or a span and a half long, reddish or blackish-red, composed of crowded spikes with a dense troop of Millet-like grains in pointed husks, sometimes blunt and sometimes bearded <note>awned</note>. It is frequent near the embankments of fields and elsewhere, a plant met everywhere and troublesome to gardens.

<margin>Is it the species of Rice called *Schnader-Et* by the Germans in Cordus's commentary on Dioscorides? Or a kind of Darnel? Or Pliny’s *Miliaria*? Or Matthiolus’s *Marsh Millet*?</margin>

### HAIRY FINGER-GRASS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of "hairy finger-grass" (Gramen Digitatum Hirsutum) showing the finger-like arrangement of the seed spikes.</image-desc>

It rests on a perennial and firm root, from which it sends out stalks one or two cubits high, thin, knotted with reddish joints, more frequently tongue-shaped, otherwise branched. The leaves are three or four inches long, narrow, and hairy with scattered long hairs; they arise partly from the root and partly from the stalks. The reddish panicle is crested with four or five spikes, similar to Manna Grass, except they are more brownish-purple and shaggy with soft down, with a soft beard protruding from the tip of the husks; the little tongues of the flowers speak with a deeper purple.

It grows in dry and neglected places; it is frequent at the Alban orchard in Basel.

It focuses on botanical identification, naming conventions across languages, and medicinal or practical uses like birdseed and kidney stone remedies.</summary>
<keywords>American Millet, Phalaris, Canary seed, Manna grass, Sanguinella, botany, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Matthiolus, Basel, 16th-century plants</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

**JOB’S TEARS or MARY’S TEARS: *German: Mary’s Tears; French: Our Lady’s Tears; Spanish: Tears of Moses.***

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Job's Tears plant (Lachryma Iobi) showing its roots, long grass-like leaves, and distinctive bead-like seeds hanging from the stems.</image-desc>

It is provided with stalks one or two cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note> high, which are jointed. The leaves are like those of Turkish corn <note>Maize/Corn</note>. From the axils of the branches spring forth stalks, through each of which the grains are pierced—usually one at a time, more rarely in pairs. They are of a highly polished smoothness, shining, yellowish before they are ripe, but turning from white to reddish when mature. They have a stony hardness and are equal in size to a chickpea; the upper part is cone-shaped, from which emerges a blunt spike of empty husks.

Is it perhaps a species of Stone-seed <note>original: "Lithospermi"; likely referring to Gromwell</note>?

<column-break/>

**ANOTHER IMAGE OF JOB’S TEARS.**

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Job's Tears plant, showing a more upright specimen with detailed seed clusters.</image-desc>

In more cultivated gardens and among all plants, this is considered an exotic. It is especially grown in the green spaces of monasteries because of its stony seed; for when the seeds are ripe and soaked in boiling water, they prepare prayer beads <note>Rosaries</note> from them, as they are called.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> writes that it is effective against the Stone of the kidneys and gravel of the bladder when used as a powder or decoction. As for our two images, which we bought already engraved, we would have preferred a single one that was better depicted.

---

**GRASS IN GENERAL, CALLED AGROSTIS BY THE GREEKS: *German: Grass; French: Grass or Herb; Italian: Couch-grass.***

<image-desc>Woodcut of a common grass plant with fibrous roots and several flowering spikes.</image-desc>

The Greeks called grass *Agrostis*, from the word *agros*, meaning a field or land. The Latins call it *Gramen*, from *gradiendo* <note>walking/stepping</note>, because it creeps by crawling and, as it were, "steps" forward. The Arabs call it *Nagen, Negé, Negieu,* and *Negil.*

There are, moreover, many and various kinds of grass. Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> identified four: the Common, the Reed-like, that which grows on Parnassus, and that which grows in Cilicia, which the natives call *Cinna*. Pliny also lists the first three, and three others of a prickly kind. By some, forty-five differences are numbered; by others fewer, and by some more, to be distinguished by the root, the spike, the tuft, the leaf, and the flower. We shall subjoin those known to us to the ones mentioned before. The grass we depict here is that called *canaria* or *caninum* <note>Dog-grass or Couch-grass</note>, not much different from the common sort; it is either the Greater or the Lesser, and is found in gravelly, uncultivated fields.

<column-break/>

**KNOTTY, BULBOUS, OR TUBEROUS GRASS: *German: Knot grass.***

<image-desc>Woodcut of bulbous oat-grass showing the characteristic chain of small bulbs or tubers at the base of the stems.</image-desc>

It has stalks two or three cubits high, which are slender. At their nodes, leaves arise that wrap around the stalk almost to the next node; from there they spread out, being nearly an inch and a half wide, a palm <note>about 3-4 inches</note> long, and smooth. The panicle <note>flower cluster</note> is two palms long and consists of oat-like husks provided with a small, soft crest, from which the trembling filaments of deep purple flowers hang. The *roots* are tuberous with chained bulbs, hairy with very frequent long fibers, and have a somewhat acidic taste. It grows among crops, along the edges of fields, and on hills among other grasses.

---

**CROSS GRASS OR THE NEHEMELSALIB OF THE EGYPTIANS, according to Alpinus.**

<image-desc>Woodcut of "Cross Grass" (Dactyloctenium aegyptium) showing the flower spikes arranged in a cross-like shape at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

It creeps with white, jointed, sweet roots—possessing some sharpness—very close to common grass. The jointed stalk rises to the height of a finger. Its leaves are similar to those of common grass, but smaller. At the ends of the small branches, there are four spikes, like those of *Ischaemon* <note>a type of finger-grass</note>, forming a perfect cross, in which they are all shaped in the same way. For this reason, the Egyptians call it *Nemelen*, as if they were saying "Grass of the Cross," in which very tiny seeds are produced, similar to the seeds of common grass.

The seeds are of great use among all people, specifically for those who suffer from stones of both the kidneys and the bladder, and for breaking up stones formed in the bladder—a type of disease that is very common there, and almost endemic.

<column-break/>

**BROOM GRASS WITH PANICLES OF ISCHAEMON, French, according to Lobelius.**

<image-desc>Woodcut of a brush-like grass (possibly a species of Digitaria or similar) with multiple spikes radiating from the top of the stem.</image-desc>

The form is like grass, similar to the common *Ischaemon*. The stalk is slender, stiff, jointed, and a cubit high. It bears four, five, six, or more very elegant, shining, spiked little tails at the top, similar to *Ischaemon* grass; the leaves are likewise not dissimilar. It grows abundantly in the sandy places of France.

From its very long, very slender, and stiff roots—a cubit or more in length—are fashioned those very common little brushes <note>hairbrushes</note> used for arranging shining hair, which are most suitable and commonly used for rubbing the head, as Lobelius notes in his *Adversaria*.

<summary>This page describes various grasses and seed-bearing plants, notably Job's Tears used for rosaries and "Cross Grass" used in Egyptian medicine to treat kidney stones. It also details the physical characteristics and practical uses of common and bulbous grasses, including their use in making hairbrushes.</summary>

<keywords>Job's Tears, medicinal plants, kidney stones, rosary beads, botany, grasses, Dioscorides, Pliny, Lobelius, Egypt, hairbrushes, Agrostis</keywords>
