# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### CREEPING APOTHECARY GRASS: German: *Gras*; French: *Dent de chien*; Italian: *Gramigna*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping grass plant (Gramen repens) showing long, jointed rhizomes and upright flowering stalks.</image-desc>

Some record this as "Medicinal Dog-grass" <note>original: *Gramen caninum medicatum*; likely Couch Grass, *Elymus repens*</note>. It grows everywhere of its own accord, especially in plowed and sown fields, and is no small nuisance to the crops. For this reason, the farmers advise that those about to sow should weed it out with rakes in September, and even by hand in early Spring. It is rarely found in meadows.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a famous Flemish botanist</note> considers the whole plant edible and grain-like. It is very widely accepted for medical uses, specifically for clearing obstructions of the kidneys and other internal organs, and for killing intestinal worms. However, the root is more effective for these purposes than the rest of the plant's parts.

The image is of the Creeping Grass described by Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), German physician and botanist</note>.

### COMMON MEADOW GRASS, with a reed-like spike: HAY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of common meadow grass (Gramen pratense) with a fibrous root system and a branched panicle.</image-desc>

It occupies the entire sod with hair-like fibers, sending up smooth, green, and tender stalks. The tops of these are marked by wide-spreading, soft, and hairy tufts <note>original: *panniculæ*; panicles</note>, which lack bristles or awns, yet in some way resemble a reed. There is a notable variety in this grass depending on the location and the size of the spikes. This meadow grass is as well-known as anything can be, and when it has dried, it is called **Hay**.

Many physicians use its seed, shaken out from the spikes in barns and collected, to dispel gas <note>original: *flatus*</note> and for other ailments. The French call it "Flower of Hay" <note>original: *Fleur de foin*</note>.

C. Bauhin <note>Gaspard Bauhin (1560–1624), Swiss botanist who developed an early system of plant classification</note> mentions a larger variety with a narrower leaf.

### HAIR-LIKE GRASS: CORN-FIELD GRASS: German: *Acker Strauss grass*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tufted grass (Gramen capillatum) with very fine, hair-like panicles.</image-desc>

The tufts of this plant are beautiful, sometimes greenish, sometimes yellowish, and sometimes reddish; hence it is commonly recorded as "Corn-field Grass with a beautiful tuft."

It grows in fields among Barley and Grain, as we have frequently observed among the crops at Geneva and Montbéliard.

In C. Bauhin's *Phytopinax*, this is Grass 18, or "tufted corn-field grass"; in his *Pinax*, it is "tufted field grass 1," or "the tallest corn-field grass with a scattered tuft." Could it be the "jointed-stem grass" of Thalius <note>Johannes Thal (1542–1583), author of the first regional flora</note>?

<column-break/>

### PRICKLY LOW-LYING GRASS: Italian: *Gramigna spinosa*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, prickly grass (Gramen supinum aculeatum) with sharp, pointed leaf sheaths and small flower heads.</image-desc>

It takes root with short fibers, but presses many branches to the ground in a circle. These are a palm's breadth <note>about 3 inches</note>, or a palm and a half, and some even a foot long, while others are occasionally only an inch, and somewhat stiff. At their joints, like a small brush, a striped leaf encloses numerous clustered husks, held within a grouping of leafy scales. It then extends straight out to the side into a stiff, sharp point, an inch or less in length. At the end of the stem of this species, several leaves and small pouches full of husks display a somewhat prickly <note>original: *echinati*; like a hedgehog</note> appearance.

It grows among rubble and on walls collapsed with age; likewise, rougher and drier paths sometimes have it. It possesses the same medicinal powers as the "Medicinal Dog-grass" mentioned just above.

### LOBELIUS’S FIELD GRASS: Wind-spike of the fields.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of "wind grass" (Gramen agrorum) showing a large, dense, nodding panicle.</image-desc>

It is called "Wind-spike of the fields" because it has a broad, hairy, expanded spike that is commonly driven to one side by the winds. In its leaves, root, and size, it is otherwise almost equal to the Corn-field Grass. Its crest <note>original: *juba*</note> is also not unlike the crest of Millet Grass. These are the observations of Lobelius, to which Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590), an early German herbalist</note> adds: It has a small, shaggy root; long, narrow leaves that are not pointed; and a stalk thinner than other reed-like plants.

It is found among the crops in the fields.

### THIN, HARDISH GRASS, almost like a rush.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thin, stiff grass (Gramen tenue duriusculum) with small, rounded flower heads and a dense fibrous root.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes that it is found in sandy places and the desolate, drier fields of France, England, Germany, and Belgium. We have observed it at Montbéliard, in the joints of rocks and on walls and rubble-strewn areas, with very small white flowers or tips. It clings so firmly to rocks and walls with its thin, hair-like, blackish fibers that it can hardly be pulled out.

In Lobelius’s *Images* and the *History of Lyon*, it is called "slender grass"; in Tabernaemontanus’s *Images* and *History*, it is "smaller hardish grass."

It cites major 16th-century botanists like Lobelius, Bauhin, and Tabernaemontanus to provide a scholarly consensus on identification.</summary>

### SMALLER HARD NORWEGIAN GRASS
### or Danish, related to Broom Grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, tufted grass with thin, upright stems and a dense root system. A small asterisk is placed near the roots.</image-desc>

Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that this grass thrives in the crevices of rocks in the thin, sterile soil of rocky Norway, and likewise on the withered, cracked trunks of trees in the forests of Denmark. It is observed to be packed in a very dense and scattered troop of stiff, rush-like leaves, an inch and a half high and very thin. The remaining stalks are a span long <note>about 9 inches</note>, numerous, curled, jointed, and thread-like; their uppermost leaves are somewhat broad, like a small sheath, which enclose or embrace the spiked, inch-long panicles <note>the flowering part of the grass</note>. The root is nine inches long, maned like hair, and the color of pale Boxwood.

<column-break/>

### GRASS WITH A SOFT REDDISH
### PANICLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with multiple flowering panicles and a fibrous root base.</image-desc>

The <term>radicles</term> <note>small, fine roots</note> of this plant are matted together under the sod: from which many leaves immediately grow forth, three to four inches long, very narrow, soft, and smooth; those observed on the stalks are smaller, and there is one at each joint. The <term>culm</term> <note>the hollow stem of a grass</note> is a foot long, sometimes smaller and sometimes larger. It bears a <term>panicle</term> <note>a loose, branching cluster of flowers</note> one to one and a half inches long, spread out, turning from green to purple, ending in crowded, thin husks that terminate in short, and sometimes twisted, awns <note>bristle-like appendages</note> that are soft and almost silky.

We have observed this grass in various places: in the meadows of Montpellier, at Geneva above the walls, at Basel on this side of the custom house, and on the dry walls at Montbéliard.

---

### SMALLER WHITE PANICLED GRASS:
### German: Small white street grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with spreading, branched panicles and a dense root cluster marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

The root of this is thin and hairy, tangled as if from many fibers: the leaves are quite narrow, small, sharp, and smooth: the stalks are small and uniform, not exceeding half a span in height: the panicles are extended, white, and somewhat shining.

There is also a red variety of this kind, similar in all respects to the white one already mentioned, except that its stalks and panicle turn reddish, and the panicle is more compact.

The white variety grows everywhere in gardens and vineyards: the red, however, is seen quite rarely; nor does it grow in every land. We saw it not far from Byzantium <note>likely referring to a location near Venice, or perhaps a specific estate, rather than Constantinople</note> in the Venetian territories.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY NARROW-LEAFED GRASS
### of Caspar Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with hairy leaves and a single, dense flowering head.</image-desc>

From a small, fibrous, reddish <term>root</term>, a single <term>culm</term> <note>stem</note> rises, higher than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, and for the most part smooth: at its summit is a white <term>panicle</term>, soft and lightly scattered, composed of many small scales, each of which contains minute, blackish, and somewhat round seeds. It has few leaves, which are narrow, a span long, and hairy, with some surrounding the stalk. It grows in the marshy meadows of Michelfeld.

---

### SMALLEST GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small, delicate grass with fine roots and thin stems.</image-desc>

Thin <term>radicles</term> like hairs grip the sod firmly: the stalks are numerous, an inch long, without joints, soft, and very thin, ending in a <term>spike</term> beset with the alternating husks of meadow grass: tiny, very small, tender leaves accompany the base of the stalks for some distance.

We observed this near that great spring at the Temple of Diana in Nîmes, and nowhere else.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPS' SMALLEST GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, bulbous-based grass. Below the main plant are three detailed views of the seeds/glumes, one marked with an asterisk.</image-desc>

It is like a rather large, round clod of earth: with many short, white <term>radicles</term>: leaves no longer than a finger, rounded, with a very slender, small spike: red flowers emerging immediately at the first mildness of the air. It grows in plowed fields.

In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Jacques Daléchamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> it is called "Dalechamps' smallest grass": by Caspar Bauhin in the *Phytopinax* it is called "Smallest grass like a thickish clod."

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### YELLOW-FLOWERED SPIKED GRASS.
<note>original: "Gramen Anthoxanthōn Spicatum." Likely Sweet Vernal Grass.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tufted grass with thin, upright stems ending in dense, spike-like flower heads.</image-desc>

In its leaves and hair-like roots, it most closely resembles Meadow Grass: but the leaves are smooth: the stalks are about nine inches long <note>term: "dodrantales" — a Roman measurement of about 9 inches or 3/4 of a foot</note>, sometimes taller than a cubit <note>term: "cubit" — about 18 inches</note>, thin, somewhat frequent, and jointed. Each stalk bears a single spike, one or two inches long, yellowish-green in color, shaped like a cone.

We saw this flowering in May near St. Hippolyte in Burgundy.

### DALECHAMPS’ WOOLLY GRASS.
<note>Named after Jacques Daléchamps, a 16th-century French physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass plant with broad, soft-looking leaves and several branched, feathery panicles.</image-desc>

The whole plant is quite soft; not only are the somewhat long leaves covered in downy hair <note>term: "tomentóque" — botanical down or fuzz</note>, but also the stalks and the joints themselves. The moderately spread-out panicles <note>term: "panicula" — a branched flowering cluster</note> mimic a spike, appearing purplish, ash-gray, or a mixture of these colors.

It loves high and rugged mountains, as well as well-watered meadows. The *History of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugdunensis," a famous botanical work by Daléchamps</note> writes that it is called *Woolly Grass* because it feels soft to those who touch it. Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous Swiss botanist</note> calls it *Meadow Paniculate Grass 1* and *Soft Paniculate Grass* in his *Pinax* and *Phytopinax*.

### SMALL PRICKLY GRASS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small, low-growing grass with short, stiff leaves and prickly, burr-like seed heads.</image-desc>

It is rooted by long, whitish fibers, provided with several stalks about a palm’s length <note>about 3-4 inches</note> or a little longer; these are hard, reddish, and marked by frequent intervals of nodes. The leaves almost entirely wrap around these stalks, extending scarcely an inch from them; they are gifted with bristly hairs along the edges but are otherwise smooth. The inch-long spike is woven from a dense crowding of husks <note>term: "glumarum" — the leafy scales of grass flowers</note> that are prickly with beautiful little teeth: these contain the seed in a prickly core, which is tiny, oblong, and reddish-brown.

<column-break/>

### VARIEGATED GRASS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass with creeping rhizomes and upright stems bearing small, clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

This should also be counted among the creeping grasses, as it spreads its hard, jointed roots far and wide, with thick fibers sent deep down, which makes it so that it can hardly be pulled out from the cracks of rocks. The stalks are clothed with frequent leaves and are nine inches long; each bears a spike like that of the Yellow-Flowered Grass, only a little shorter and purple, which is pleasing because its color changes depending on how the light hits it.

### ROUGH GRASS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tall grass with prominent nodes on the stem and elongated, bristly flower spikes.</image-desc>

The stalk is two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> or taller, jointed, and rough, especially at the nodes and at the top. The leaves are also rough, as is the panicle, which is stiff and thick, whitish or reddish: often it is less spread out, other times more so, with small clusters on long, rough stems. The flowers are either yellow or reddish.

Daléchamps, the *History of Lyon*, and Caspar Bauhin classify this as a spiked grass; they add that its leaf is never jointed. It is found in the meadows of cold mountains.

### TINY GRASS, with a round thorny head.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a very small, delicate grass with tiny, round, spiny flower heads at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

It is rooted by a few small fibers clinging to the very top of the turf: the leaves are an inch long, somewhat stiff, and slightly broad. The stalk is one or two inches high, hard, stiff, and striped; on its summit sits a clustered Head, whitish and prickly with star-like teeth that are quite rigid and stinging.

We collected this at Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausi"</note> near the mills in the hollows of stones and rocky places, and never found it larger anywhere else: the Figure represents the actual size of the little plant.

<summary>This page catalogs six varieties of grasses, detailing their physical characteristics, preferred habitats (such as Burgundy and Nîmes), and botanical nomenclature according to authorities like Bauhin and Daléchamps.</summary>

### GRASS WITH A BRIGHT GLOBULAR HEAD
->According to Tabernaemontanus.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with fibrous roots, long thin leaves, and several stalks ending in globular, white flower heads.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is thin and fibrous; the leaves are like those of common grass. The stalk is smooth, quite delicate, and a span <note>about 9 inches</note> long. At the top are translucent, globe-shaped spikes, densely packed with small white flowers; when these open, they release a very tiny seed.

It grows in uncultivated places and on rough, dry hills. Tabernaemontanus and Caesalpinus call it "Bright Grass"; Anguillara calls it the "Luziola Herb." Could it be the *Combretum* mentioned by Pliny? <note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist; early botanists often tried to match their finds to his ancient descriptions.</note>

### KNOTTED GRASS OF TABERNAEMONTANUS
->German: *Knoden Grass* (Knotted Grass).<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with thick, knotted (geniculate) stems, broad leaves, and elongated, fuzzy flower spikes.</image-desc>

The root, composed of many fibers, pushes out many knotted or jointed stalks, which are then divided into others. The leaves are long, narrow, and pointed, with a raised vein running through the middle. The spike is long, thin, and hairy, consisting of white husks containing the seed.

It grows in fields, meadows, and grassy places. It varies in size: in Montpellier <note>France</note> it is smaller than a palm's breadth, but in Basel <note>Switzerland</note> and elsewhere, it is sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> tall.

### BEAUTIFUL SMALL GRASS, with a wide, flattened panicle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small grass plant with thin roots and a wide, flattened, umbrella-like panicle at the top of the stalk.</image-desc>

The roots of this lovely little grass are hair-like, reddish in color, and a span long. The leaves are few, one, two, or three inches long, and thin. The stalks are three-sided, solid, numerous, and between one and one-and-a-half spans high. At their ends sit flower clusters <term>panicles: a loose, branching cluster of flowers</term> without stalks, somewhat mimicking an umbrella; they are beautiful, flattened, and reddish-green in color, containing minute black seeds.

It abounds in damp places, flourishing in June, July, and August. It is frequent near the Biese river in Basel in marshy areas, and in Michelfelden.

<column-break/>

### CRESTED GRASS, OF CASPAR BAUHIN

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall grass with narrow leaves and a dense, one-sided, comb-like (crested) flower spike.</image-desc>

It rises with stalks a cubit and a half tall, which are very thin and jointed. It is not without leaves, which embrace the stalk like a sheath for a considerable distance and then pull away, being a span long and narrow. The spike is four inches long, with two rows turning toward one side; it displays trembling, hair-like fibers of pale, crested, or fringed flowers that are tawny or yellow, while the back of the spike is bare of husks. The roots are thin and curled.

Because the spikes mimic a rooster's comb, this grass is cleverly named "Crested" by Caspar Bauhin, as Lobelius says. Nothing is more frequent than this in the various meadows of the London countryside, where the country folk use it—as well as several other grasses—to decorate floral displays, arbors, and other ornamental garden works.

### QUAKING GRASS, OR GRASS OF LOVE
->German: *Liebgrass* (Love-grass) & *Zydern* (Shivering); French: *Amourettes*, *Amourettes tremblantes* (Little Lovers/Trembling Lovers).<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of "Quaking Grass" with delicate, drooping, heart-shaped spikelets hanging from thin branches.</image-desc>

We present here three kinds of Quaking Grass: the Small, the Large, and the Largest. It obtained the name "Quaking" because whether one holds a single stalk or many in the hand, all its flower clusters are perpetually trembling. This most elegant genus of grass was called "Grass of Love" because of the beauty of the clusters, which are either white or dark purple.

It grows spontaneously in various places and is also cultivated in gardens for its beauty.

### ANOTHER BEAUTIFUL SMALL GRASS,
->with a flattened, blackish panicle.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small grass similar to the previous "pulchrum" variety but with darker, more compact flower heads.</image-desc>

This differs from the other small one just illustrated because it is larger and sturdier, and has wider and longer leaves. Furthermore, it has a flattened and blackish flower cluster, whereas the other's is wide and reddish-green.

It grows, however, in the same places as the preceding one.

By Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax* and *Pinax*, it is called the "Smallest Sedge-like Grass with a blackish panicle," and by Lobelius in the second part of his *Adversaria*.

-># IMAGES AND OUTLINES.<-
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### SMALLER MOUSE-TAIL GRASS.
<note>original: "GRAMEN CVM CAVDA MVRIS MINVS"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small grass plant with a fibrous root system and several thin stalks ending in elongated, fuzzy seed heads resembling mouse tails.</image-desc>

This plant has a long, slanted, somewhat thick root, from which thin fibers are divided upward into several heads. From these grow many leaves, 4 or 5 inches long, similar to the leaves of Meadow Grass. It has several stalks a span <note>about 9 inches</note> or a foot high. The spike is four inches long, like that of the Greater Mouse-tail Grass, but thinner.

It grows in dry places and grassy fields, and is called by some Cat-tail Grass or Cat-tail-like Grass. <note>original: "Gramen Typhinum vel Typhoides"</note>

### GREATER MOUSE-TAIL GRASS
### larger and long: Greater Cat-tail Grass.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a larger grass variety with more robust foliage and longer, thicker cylindrical seed heads.</image-desc>

This has thin roots. The stalks begin with something like a small oblong bulb; they are a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high and sometimes taller. The leaves are rough, with a longer sheath clasping the spike. The very top supports a spike a span long, and often even longer, which is rounded and resembles the tail of a large mouse. It is soft if you stroke it upward with your hand, but rough if stroked the opposite way. It is ash-colored and consists of countless small scales ending in two short bristles <term>awns<gloss>stiff bristles growing from the ear of a grass</gloss></term>.

### PURPLISH MOUSE-TAIL GRASS.
### Called Foxtail Grass by some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass plant with dense foliage at the base and several upright stalks with fuzzy, slightly tapered seed heads.</image-desc>

From a dense cluster of smooth grass leaves, several stalks emerge; some are a foot high, others a cubit or a cubit and a half. They are sometimes purple, clothed with deeper-colored, broader leaves, and marked by a few small joints. At the top they bear a purplish spike, a span or shorter in length, shaped like a mouse's tail but packed with a confused order of sterile husks, from which short and tender bristles <term>awns</term> leap forth. Its little flowers are pale yellowish tips <note>anthers</note>, hanging from very thin filaments. The root consists of nothing but fibers.

It flowers in June in dry places around Montbéliard. <note>A city in eastern France where the author likely observed these specimens.</note>

<column-break/>

### SMALL CREEPING MOUSE-TAIL GRASS
### with a knotted root.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass plant with a creeping, knotted root system and multiple stalks with short, fuzzy seed heads.</image-desc>

From a fibrous root that is knotted with little bulbs, several small stalks emerge, a cubit or a cubit and a half high. They are thin, smooth, and bent back at the joints. From the very bottom, they are accompanied by several smooth, short, narrow leaves. Furthermore, a single small leaf protrudes from each joint. Upon the summit rests a small spike, bristly, in the shape of Lobel’s Cat-tail Grass, two inches long and very densely packed with small scales.

Two kinds of this are found: one has a knotted root, the other is not knotted at all. We have observed both near Belfort, not far from the village of Danjoutin <note>original: "Danuuin"</note> in the thickets and along the river banks.

### LOBEL’S CAT-TAIL GRASS,
### Cat-tail Grass II of Tabernaemontanus.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a dense tuft of grass with numerous upright stalks, each topped with a distinct, cylindrical, fuzzy seed head.</image-desc>

It delights in sandy places and coastal births <note>habitats</note>. The root is tiny and hair-like; the stalk is nine inches to a foot high. Thus Lobel describes it. But the description is too brief, and nothing certain can be gathered from it. If you consider the figure, the Cat-tail Grass II of Tabernaemontanus pictured here represents it well, for he depicts the bulbous beginnings of the stalks. Size alone creates doubt.

It grows in damp and sandy places.

### ROUGH HARE’S-TAIL GRASS,
### or Mouse-spike.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a grass plant with thin, slightly drooping stalks and elongated, bristly seed heads.</image-desc>

It sends up several stalks, slender, somewhat stiff, a foot or a foot and a half high. At their summit are short spikes, not unlike a fox's tail in size and shape, but with rough crests, prickly on both sides, with somewhat long and lightly curved bristles <term>awns</term> which nod at the top of the stalk from a short bend. In their hollows are small, useless husks. The leaves are of moderate length, somewhat stiff and smooth. The dense root sends down a numerous offspring of hairy fibers.

It is very common in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Mouse-tail" and "Cat-tail" grasses (likely Phleum and Alopecurus species), detailing their physical structures, roots, and habitats across Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Mouse-tail grass, Cat-tail grass, Foxtail, botanical taxonomy, Montbéliard, Belfort, Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, awns, spikes</keywords>

-># IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### LOBELIUS’S REED BENT-GRASS.
### Reed-like grass: Babylonian grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, reed-like grass with long, slender leaves and a feathery seed head (panicle) at the top.</image-desc>

It varies according to its location: for that which grows in sandy places has a thicker spike, while that in mountainous areas and damp thickets has a thinner one. Its nature is intermediate between a Reed and a Grass.

It is hardly suitable for fodder, unless the draft animals are very hungry and suffer greatly from a lack of better feed; nor do flocks eat it, for it causes them to become thin, wasted, and thirsty. It also wounds the tongue and the esophagus; hence the lips and throats of beasts of burden are observed to be dripping with blood if they have eaten it during haymaking. Thus, its nature is intermediate between a Reed and a Grass.

This genus of grass is familiar in wet meadows that are otherwise thin, meager, and sandy.

<column-break/>

### GREATER REED-LIKE GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust grass with broad leaves and dense, spiked flower clusters.</image-desc>

It has a hair-like root creeping along the ground; the leaves on either side are sharp or cut quite severely. The stalks are jointed reeds similar to the Reed, along with the spike, except they are smaller.

It seeks out shores, marshes, and well-watered meadows; it is a flat plant of very common knowledge.

---

### LESSER REED-LIKE GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of reed-grass with multiple spiked seed heads emerging from the stem joints.</image-desc>

The root and the knotted reed correspond to the previous plant; however, the leaves are both wider and longer; the spikes are also more numerous and more spreading.

It grows, like the preceding one, in damp and marshy places.

It is called *Lesser reed-like grass* by Tabernæmontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernæmontanus (1522–1590), a famous German botanist</note>; and *Spiked reed-like grass* by C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a Swiss botanist who revolutionized plant naming</note>.

<column-break/>

### LOBELIUS’S GREAT WATER GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an aquatic grass with broad, ribbed leaves and a large, branching panicle.</image-desc>

Among the grasses of common knowledge is this one, and it is found in abundance almost everywhere near waters and streams; in Holland <note>original: "Batavia"</note> it is even cut as fodder for cows. It has leaves a thumb-width wide, and a cubit and a half or two cubits long <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>. The stalks are four or five feet in height, with a millet-like tuft. The root is fibrous.

We have described the greater and lesser reed-like grass in our *Great History*.

---

### WATER GRASS WITH A VERY LONG TUFT.
### Very long grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very tall aquatic grass with an elongated, drooping seed head.</image-desc>

Duck grass, *Duck-grass* <note>original: "Entengrass"</note> according to Tragus; *River grass, Float-grass* <note>original: "Flutgrass"</note> according to Tabernæmontanus; *Grass floating in water* according to Lobelius; *Spiked aquatic or floating grass with multiple spikes* according to Gerard <note>John Gerard (1545–1612), author of a famous English Herbal</note>.

There is also a certain genus of grass said to be very long, sometimes exceeding a height of two or three cubits, which peasants use to make collars for the horses that pull plows, and for pastoral cloaks with which shepherds cover themselves against the rains.

<column-break/>

### TABERNÆMONTANUS’S KNOTTED WATER GRASS.
### Finger-like, dark purple grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with distinct nodes (geniculate) and finger-like (digitate) seed spikes.</image-desc>

It has a fibrous root, from which grow several rounded, knotted stalks about a foot and a half long; they are clothed at the joints with grass-like leaves that are short, wide, and pointed. At the tops of the stalks grow long, thin spikes, similar to the spikes of the "finger-grass" <term>Ischæmum: a genus of grasses often called "blood-grass" or "finger-grass"</term>, but shorter and of a dark purple color, according to Tabernæmontanus.

It grows here and there in lake-side and marshy areas.

<keywords>botany, reed-grass, aquatic plants, fodder, Tabernæmontanus, Lobelius, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal herbs, agricultural history</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### A THINNER BLACK SPECIES OF DOG'S TOOTH GRASS WITH DIVIDED SPIKES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with fibrous roots and several spiked seed heads branching from the top of the stems.</image-desc>

Compared to the first and second *Dog's Tooth* grass <note>original: "Dentis canis"; likely a species of Cynodon or Digitaria</note>, this one has more subtle and thinner leaves and jointed stalks: its flower-heads are not unlike *Ischaemon* <note>a type of "blood-stanching" grass</note>, black in color. The seed is black on the outside, but once the husk is removed, it is white inside.

It is called Panic-grass by most. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it *Wild Panic-grass with a black spike*.

<column-break/>

### SPIKED MOUNTAIN GRASS, with a grassy, soft stalk, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass plant with a thick, knotted rhizome root system and a single, long, dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

He says it is found in certain mountain meadows, two miles above the baths of Baden: as well as in the coastal areas of Flanders, and that it opens in <unclear>July</unclear>. In Tabernaemontanus's *Icons*, it is the 1st Wild Grass, or *Waldgrass*.

The root is the thickness of a finger, split into two or three parts, and fibrous. The leaves are five, six, or more in number, oblong and somewhat keel-shaped, embracing one another at the very base. From their ribbed fold, a stalk or stem emerges, sometimes a foot long, smooth, bare, and without joints: which, at its highest peak, produces many small flowers crowded into a dense spike, endowed with a grassy color.

---

<column-break/>

### WOODLAND DEW-SHINING GRASS, or Wood-rush.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tufted grass with broad, hairy leaves and a branched inflorescence of small flowers.</image-desc>

The Shining Grass rests upon a large, fibrous, jointed, reddish root. When it flowers, the stalk is nine inches long, provided with one or two embracing leaves. The spikes are in twos, threes, fours, or fives, and are short; one of these sits directly on the stem, while the others hang from stalks of half an inch or an inch. The individual flowers consist of six radiating, chestnut-colored petals, with as many yellow stamens, and a green center producing a black filament; these are succeeded by three-cornered heads containing three small white seeds.

Since there are commonly held to be three types of Wood-rush—the largest, the middle, and the smallest—we depict the *middle* one here, which is found in various places in meadows.

<column-break/>

### THE LARGEST WOOD-RUSH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, robust grass with wide, lanceolate leaves and a large, spreading panicle of flowers.</image-desc>

This is less common than the preceding one, which they call the *middle* or *common* kind. Its root, stalk, leaves, flowers, capsules, and seeds were discussed under the previous heading; now we shall proceed with the description.

The leaves of the Common Shining Grass are four inches or a palm's breadth long, somewhat stiff, sharp, upright, streaked on the outside, and smooth: but on the sides, they are covered with a long, grey, and tender down <note>fine hairs</note>, which even runs onto the leaf itself. Therefore, when this down or the hairs (which fall off easily) are touched, they collect dew which shines at night under the radiating stars or the Moon, so that it is a source of wonder to those who see it—hence the name of the Herb <note>Luzula is derived from the Italian 'lucciola', a firefly, or 'lux', light</note>. However, when the dew falls away, those searching for it cannot find it.

---

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLEST WOOD-RUSH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, delicate grass with thin leaves and a small cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

This Wood-rush is more frequent than the other two; in it, everything is thinner and smaller. It seems to come very close to the *Small Hairy Galingale-grass* of Lobelius. We have observed this one, as well as the Middle or Common kind, flowering at the beginning of May in the valley of the acidic springs called *Griesbach*. The Largest kind, however, grows on the mountain and in the nearby dark forest.

It grows from a root with a beard of thin fibers. The leaves are thin, raised upwards, narrow, pointed, and somewhat shaggy with hairs and bristly down. The reed <note>stalk</note> is very slender, endowed with two joints, from which a few leaves emerge both in the middle of the reed and at its summit. At the top, it is divided into three or four parts [like little heads], similar to the parts of the Long Galingale.

<column-break/>

### SMALL HAIRY GALINGALE-GRASS, of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender, hairy grass with small, dark, rounded flower heads.</image-desc>

It was noted before that this agrees in many ways with the Smallest Wood-rush: yet it is clear from a comparison of both that it differs in certain respects. Tabernaemontanus and others call it *Hairy Cyperus-grass*.

Lobelius found it in sandy places. Tabernaemontanus, however, says it grows in damp, sandy, and grassy places along roadsides. Furthermore, it varies, having sometimes wider and sometimes narrower leaves.

It cites prominent botanists like Clusius, Lobelius, and Tabernaemontanus to distinguish between similar species.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

<margin>Aa 3</margin>

### BLACK GRASS, OR BLACKISH-YELLOW.
### Perhaps the "Rabbinic Grass" of some?
<note>original: "Gramen Rabinum" — A historical name for a specific grass, possibly referring to its use or a specific regional name.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall grass with slender leaves and dark, spiked flower heads at the top of the stalks.</image-desc>

We have given it this name because of its spikes, which are entirely black at first; later, when the flower has opened, they are for the most part yellow.

There is a larger and a smaller variety; the former is found in damp meadows, the latter in dry ones. They bloom in March and April.

By Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1525–1590), a famous German herbalist.</note> in his *Images and History* it is called Pink-flowered Grass, or *Nail-grass* <note>original: "Naglen graß"</note>. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called Spiked Grass with Betony-like leaves.

### THE MORE COMMON WATER SEDGE-GRASS.
<term>Cyperoides: Sedge-like. From "Cyperus" (a genus of sedges) and the Greek suffix "-oides" (resembling).</term>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dense tuft of aquatic grass with long, tapering leaves and several dark, cylindrical flower spikes.</image-desc>

It puts forth three or four, and sometimes more, roots that are long, black, and an inch thick, similar to the Long Cyperus. The leaves are also similar, growing not only from the root but also from the nodes of the stalk. The stalk <note>original: "Calamum"</note> is triangular and a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> long. Finally, it bears spiked flowers, which are followed by spikes—sometimes five at once—of a bright rusty color. It is found everywhere in watery, marshy, and stagnant places. It varies, however, with a tuft <note>original: "panicula"</note> that is either more compact and shorter, or more spread out and wider.

### WOODLAND CYPERUS-GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with fibrous roots and multiple thin stalks bearing small, dark flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rests upon a fibrous, hair-like root. The leaves are narrow, nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantalia"</note>, and pointed, like the leaves of common grass. Near these, three or four stalks emerge, which are round, narrow, and a foot long. Each of these produces two or three spikes, of a yellowish-purple color and three inches long.

It is found here and there in woods, in marshy, grassy, and sandy places.

<column-break/>

### SEDGE-GRASS WITH BLACK TUFTS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Cyperoides grass with a thick, knotted root system and dark, drooping panicles.</image-desc>

This Sedge-grass varies in size, and in the shape and length of its chestnut-green spikes, as well as in its leaves, which are either narrow or broad. The one we depict here we observed at Zurich, blooming near the river in May; it also grows abundantly at Montbéliard.

The roots proceed joint by joint, exactly like the roots of the Long Cyperus, from which hang somewhat thick fibers. The leaves are a cubit or a cubit and a half long, and keeled <note>V-shaped in cross-section</note>, like those of the Cyperus. The stalk is three-sided, without nodes, bare, and two cubits high. At its summit are several leaves, from whose crook the tufts or spikes burst forth, turning blackish-purple, in which is a hard black seed.

### TABERNAEMONTANUS’S THIRD CAT-TAIL GRASS, with multiple black spikes, approaching the Sedge-grasses.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with a bulbous, knotted root and a single stalk topped with multiple dark, bristly spikes.</image-desc>

It is secured by a slanted, knotty root, an inch or more thick, adorned with many thin fibers like hairs. From these come long leaves that clasp the jointed stalks <note>original: "ulmos" - likely a typo for "culmos" (stalks)</note>, which are provided with smaller leaflets. At the base of these, above the middle of the stalk's length, the spikes rise up, long, rough, and black. The taste is sour and astringent.

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Pinax* it is the *Cat-tail Grass with multiple spikes*; in Gerard’s <note>John Gerard (1545–1612), English herbalist.</note> it is the *Cat-tail Cyperus*. It is a lover of wet meadows.

### A KIND OF SEDGE-GRASS: The "False-Cyperus" of Lobelius, with tufts hanging from long stalks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass with long, arching leaves and distinct, heavy flower spikes hanging from long, thin stalks.</image-desc>

It bears tufts similar to the aquatic Sedge-grass with black spikes, but they differ in this: they hang from long stalks in the manner of *Quaking Grass* <note>original: "Gramine tremuli"</note>, rather than standing upright; and they have longer hairs. There are both larger and smaller varieties. Gesner, Lobelius, Dodonaeus, Caspar Bauhin, and others label it *False-Cyperus* or *Wild Cyperus*; Thalius calls it Water Grass.

It grows in damp places around the Baths of Abano <note>original: "Thermas Apponenses"</note> in the territory of Padua.

<summary>This page describes various species of sedges and grasses characterized by dark or black flowering spikes, detailing their physical structures, habitats, and the differing names given to them by prominent Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>botany, sedge-grass, Cyperoides, black grass, aquatic plants, Tabernaemontanus, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal herbs, Zurich, Padua</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### III. TYPHA-LIKE GRASS OF TABERNÆMONTANUS with multiple black spikes, approaching the Sedge-like Grasses.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass-like plant with multiple dark, cylindrical flower spikes (typhinum) emerging from a basal tuft of long, narrow leaves.</image-desc>

It is anchored by an oblique, knotty root, an inch or more thick, adorned with many slender fibers like hairs. From these emerge long leaves that clasp the jointed stalks; these stalks are provided with smaller leaflets, at the base of which—above the middle of the length of the stem—rise long, rough, and black spikes. The taste is sour and astringent.

To Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era</note> it is *Typhoid grass with multiple spikes*; to Gerard <note>The English herbalist</note> it is *Typha-like Sedge*. It is a lover of damp meadows.

### A KIND OF SEDGE-LIKE GRASS: The False-Sedge of Lobel, with panicles hanging from long stalks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sedge-like plant with drooping, elongated panicles hanging from long stalks (pedicels).</image-desc>

It bears panicles <note>loose, branching flower clusters</note> similar to the Aquatic Sedge-like Grass with black spikes; but they differ in this: that they hang from long stalks <note>original: "pediculis"</note> in the manner of Quaking Grass, rather than standing upright, and they possess longer hairs. Both a Greater and Lesser variety are found. Gesner, Lobel, Dodoens, Caspar Bauhin, and others record it as *False-Sedge* or *Wild Sedge*; Thalius calls it *Aquatic Grass*.

It grows in damp places, around the Abano Springs <note>original: "Thermas Apponenses"</note> of the Paduans.

### SEDGE-LIKE GRASS WITH A DIVIDED SPIKE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sedge with a divided or branched inflorescence consisting of several distinct, bristly spikes.</image-desc>

The leaves are nine inches <note>original: "dodrantalia"</note> or shorter, narrow in the manner of meadow grass. The stem is triangular, gifted with no sheath <note>original: "vtriculo"</note>, a cubit or a cubit and a half in height; it carries a divided panicle at the very top, like a less showy Sedge, with a wrinkled leaf placed beneath it. The fibers of the roots are slender and twisted.

By Lobel it is called *Small aquatic sedge-like grass*; by Tabernæmontanus, *Lesser marsh sedge-grass*.

We observed it with its spikes in the month of August on the mountain near Gesardmagni.

<column-break/>

### WOODLAND SEDGE-LIKE GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woodland sedge with a single, elongated, interrupted spike of small flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rests upon a fibrous, hair-like root. The leaves are narrow, nine inches long, and pointed, like the leaves of common grass. Next to these, three or four stalks emerge, round, narrow, and a foot long, each of which produces two or three spikes, of a yellowish-purple color, <unclear>two</unclear> inches long.

It is found here and there in the woods, in marshy, grassy, and sandy places.

### TRIANGULAR MARSH SEDGE-LIKE GRASS, with an integrated spike.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh sedge with a sharply triangular stem and a dense, integrated terminal spike.</image-desc>

It raises a triangular <note>original: "triquetrum"</note> Sedge-like stem, a cubit or a cubit and a half high. The top is adorned with a *spike* somewhat similar to the spike of Millet <note>original: "Panici"</note>, but of a looser texture, an inch and a half to two inches long; it contains seeds in triangular blackish or greenish-red chambers, the seeds being almost equal to Millet and flattened. The roots are fibrous and tangled, tufted with the fibers of fallen leaves. The leaves are moderately wide and almost equal the stem in length.

There is another of this kind with smaller and less compact spikes. Both grow in watery places.

### PRICKLY MARSH GRASS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh grass with "echinate" or prickly-looking flower heads arranged along the upper stem.</image-desc>

It is related to the Marsh Sedge-like Grass, but yields to it in size. At the top of the stem, a few small spikes grow, half an inch long, greenish, with smaller triangular chambers also containing a three-sided seed, and prickly <note>original: "muricatæ"</note>. Overlooking these and occupying the very summit is an incomplete reddish spike, almost twice as long but scarcely a sixth part as thick, soft, and woven from awnless scales. The roots are entirely blackish.

It grows in marshes. It varies, however, with longer or rounder spikes, <unclear>often</unclear> even on a single plant. By Caspar Bauhin it is called *Italian prickly marsh grass*, or *Adonis grass*.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

### GRASS WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A SMALL HYACINTH
### Arrowgrass, with yellow flowers. <note>original: "Triglochin, floribus luteis."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Triglochin plant showing a fibrous root system, long thin leaves, and a tall central stalk with small flowers/seeds.</image-desc>

It has an oblong and tufted *bulb*, in the manner of Alpine Garlic, sometimes simple and other times multiple: it takes root from fibers sent down from its base. The *leaves* are very thin, smooth, a span long <note>A "span" (palmaris) is roughly 8-9 inches, the width of an outstretched hand.</note>, three or five in number, rising directly from the root. A somewhat hard *stalk*, rounded, slender, bare, and without joints, rises between the leaves, a span or a span and a half high, bearing a long *spike* of tiny yellow flowers, from the middle of which a somewhat long style <note>The pollen-receiving part of the flower.</note> extends.

We dug this up in June in certain desolate maritime locations of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and near that wonderful triple-arched Bridge of the Gard river.

<column-break/>

### MARITIME RUSH-GRASS DENSELY
### packed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime rush-like grass with dense, upright stems and a thick root mass.</image-desc>

In its *root* and *leaves* it is like the spiked maritime Grass of Zeeland <note>A province in the Netherlands</note>, hard and black. The *stalks* bear spikes like those of the aquatic *Rush*. Otherwise, it is neither better nor more useful than maritime grass. Lobelius <note>Matthias de L'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that it is found on the shore at Middelburg: however, we describe many more varieties of rush-grass in our great History.

By Lobelius, in his History of Belgium, it is called *Densely spiked maritime rush-grass*. By Tabernæmontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, an early German botanist</note> in his Illustrations, it is called *Lesser aquatic rush-grass*.

---

<column-break/>

### SMALL FOREST GRASS
### thin-leaved and somewhat rigid: German: Waldgraff.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small forest grass with thin leaves and a delicate flowering head.</image-desc>

The *root* protrudes from a single multiple fibrous source: the *leaves* are narrow, similar to common Grass, but more solid, and packed in a dense order. Several *stalks* proceed from these, thin, round, and only a span high. The *spikes* at the top of these are soft, hair-like, and somewhat reddish. It grows in damp, marshy, and sandy soil. *Tabernæmontanus.*

By Gerard <note>John Gerard, English herbalist</note> it is called *Forest grass*: by C. Bauhin <note>Gaspard Bauhin, Swiss botanist</note> in his Pinax <note>A famous botanical register</note>, *Smooth woodland grass 13, or woodland grass with a soft reddish spike*.

<column-break/>

### FOREST OR WOODLAND GRASS
### small, thin-leaved with a prickly spike.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woodland grass with a more pronounced, prickly-looking seed head (spica aculeata).</image-desc>

The *root* is multiple from a single origin, small, and filled with filaments: the *leaves* are narrow, ending in a point, about a span long. From these arise eight or nine *stalks*, thin, leafless, equal in height, and a span long. The tops of these are occupied by spreading, prickly *spikes*.

This varies with a wider leaf in thickets, and a narrower one in meadows. In Tabernæmontanus it is *Forest grass III, or woodland grass*.

---

<column-break/>

### TOAD GRASS: German: Kroottengrass. French: Her-
### be aux Crapaux, Crapaudine. The rush-like Holosteum of Mattioli.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Toad Grass (Gramen Bufonium) showing a branching structure and small seed pods.</image-desc>

This plant is a span or a span and a half high, with frequent, thin, somewhat reddish little stalks divided into many branches: the *leaves* are sharp, two or three inches long, and narrow: the *flowers* are numerous both along the branches and at the tips, which are succeeded by *small vessels* <note>seed pods</note> enclosing a tiny, reddish, transparent seed: the *roots* are hair-like.

It grows everywhere in mossy meadows and other decayed and damp places. Could it be Mattioli’s <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, famous Italian physician and botanist</note> *rush-like Holosteum*?

<column-break/>

### THE ESPARTO OF PLINY AND THE LATINS,
### or the Grass for fig baskets.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Esparto grass with long, tough, linear leaves forming a dense tuft.</image-desc>

This *Esparto* <note>original: "spartum"</note> of the Latins and of Pliny differs greatly from the *spartum* of the Greeks, which is a Broom <note>Genista</note>, and which was treated in Class XI of this Outline: for that is a shrub, while this is an Herb.

It is called *Pliny's Esparto* by Clusius, Tabernæmontanus, and Gerard: by some *Esparto grass*: by Dalechampius *Iberian and Spanish Rush*: and it is believed by some to be the *Linospartium* of the Ancients.

It grows in the Baetica region <note>Southern Spain/Andalusia</note> in a part of Spain, and especially in the kingdom of Murcia, and near the city called Murgia: so that not without cause was that entire tract called the *Esparto Plain* <note>original: "spariarius Campus"</note> by the Ancients. It also grows in the kingdom of Valencia, and there indeed more abundantly and lushly. Concerning its use, see what follows.

<keywords>Arrowgrass, Triglochin, maritime rush, forest grass, Toad Grass, Esparto grass, Spain, botanical taxonomy, Pliny, Mattioli, Lobelius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical classification of grasses, specifically focusing on the "Spartum" (esparto) varieties and their practical uses in early modern Europe, drawing heavily on the works of Carolus Clusius and Pliny the Elder.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SPARTUM GRASS II. ACCORDING TO CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a clump of Spartum grass with long, thin blades and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It grows in the same locations as the preceding variety, but in damper spots. It is more tender than the former, and its use is quite rare because it is not at all suitable for making mats and similar handiwork.

Furthermore, this herb is *thornless, fruitless, and leafless*, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note>, growing spontaneously and unable to be sown. It is properly a rush of dry soil, a defect given to a single land: for it is an ailment of the Earth, and nothing else can be sown or born there. From this, the country folk make their bedding; from this, fires and torches; from this, footwear and the clothing of shepherds. It is harmful to animals, except for the tenderness of its tips. For other uses, it is pulled up with great labor, with the legs and hands protected by linen wraps, etc.

### FEATHERED GRASS, OR AUSTRIAN SPARTUM, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall grass with feathery, plume-like seed heads and a dense root system.</image-desc>

It grows on very dry hillocks and in sunny, stony places; it is found in abundance on certain mountains situated along the Danube, and in other open and grassy places in Austria and Hungary.

Moreover, according to the reports of Clusius and Amatus <note>Amatus Lusitanus, a 16th-century physician</note>, Spartum is currently in the same use among the Spaniards as it was in the time of Pliny. For from the raw and dried grass, they fashion tapestries or wall-hangings, mats, baskets, cables, and other ropes. Even those baskets in which figs and raisins are transported are made from Spartum. But from that which has been soaked in water, softened like flax, then dried and beaten, a type of footwear is made which they call *Alpergates* <note>original: "Alpergates"; modern Spanish: alpargatas or espadrilles</note>; and it is used for these and other fine works. It is a marvel, as Pliny says, how much it is in use in all lands, for the rigging of ships, the machinery of buildings, and other necessities of life.

### OUR SMALL SPARTUM, Rush-leaved Spartum grass, of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, tufted grass with thin, needle-like leaves.</image-desc>

Thus he depicts it. Truly, besides those described, there are still several varieties and differences of the Spartum herb. *Variegated Spartum grass* of C. Bauhin. *Broad-leaved maritime Spartum. Basel Spartum grass, with hair-like leaves. Smaller or Dutch Spartum grass*, of C. Bauhin. *Montpellier Spartum grass, with hair-like leaves* by the same author. *Spartum grass resembling horse-hair*, also by the same. And others of this kind, concerning which our Great History <note>referring to a larger botanical compendium</note> may be consulted.

<column-break/>

### SPIKED SPARTUM GRASS, OR Pungent Oceanic Spartum, of Clusius: in Belgian, *Halm*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coastal grass with upright, spiked inflorescences.</image-desc>

It is found in several places in France and Flanders and on the sandy embankments facing the Ocean. It is not very different from the former Spanish type, but much larger and stiffer; it is <unclear>very troublesome</unclear> to the legs of those who walk along those embankments; for its leaves prick and penetrate the skin. It grows in the same manner as the ones above, but it creeps more widely, in the fashion of common grass. It bears a spike almost like that of Rye.

Its use is that, with its broad and very thick tufts and its roots spreading out sideways, it makes the sand firmer and binds it together on the embankments, so that it is not so easily washed away by the sea winds and waves; and so that they may more easily withstand the storms which are frequent on the Ocean.

### AEGYLOPS BROMOIDES GRASS OF TABERNAE-montanus, with very long awns: in German, *Haberwacht*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild grass with long, drooping awns (bristles) on the seed heads.</image-desc>

By G. Bauhin in the *Phytopinax* and *Pinax* it is called *Festuca with very long awns* <term>awns: the hair-like bristles found on the ears of grass or grain</term>. It delights in sandy places and drier meadows. Tabernaemontanus testifies that it is encountered most especially on the roads between Worms and Frankenthal, a city of the Palatinate.

The root is manifold and fibrous: from which emerges a numerous troop of small, narrow, rush-like leaves. Among these rise three or four stalks, a cubit or a cubit and a half high: which bear spikes at the top similar to the husks of oats, but empty of seeds, with winged and long awns.

### PROSTRATE DARNEL-GRASS OF LOBELIUS, of C. Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, spreading grass with small, alternating seed spikes along the stem.</image-desc>

This is a tiny grass, humble and spread upon the ground, with innumerable stalks of two or three inches, spread out with divided joints and provided with thin tips. The leaves are an inch in length and somewhat broad, with stalks that are quite thick for the size of the plant. The root is dark and hairy. The whole herb turns white during the hay-making season, and it abounds near Kronborg in Danish Zealand.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### REED; CANE, STALK: German: *Rohr*:
### French: *Canne, Roseau*: Italian: *Canna*: Spanish: *Canas*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall reed plant with long, tapering leaves and a feathery flowering head (panicle).</image-desc>

Theophrastus established many differences among Reeds: based on whether the body of the Reed is solid or hollow; on shortness, height, thickness, or slenderness; on the abundance or scarcity of leaves; on whether they grow in dry or aquatic places; and finally on their use. However, he makes two primary types: the *Flute-reed* <note>original: "Tibialem," used for making musical instruments</note> and the *Common-reed*.

Pliny described twenty-nine species: yet Theophrastus and Pliny agree in this, that both make the Reed *Male* and *Female*, the former being solid and the latter hollow.

According to Dioscorides, however, there are five kinds of Reeds: the *Solid* <note>original: "Nastos"</note>, the *Female*, the *Pipe-reed* <note>original: "Syringias"</note>, the *Thick and Hollow*, and the *Hedge-reed* <note>original: "Phragmites"</note>. We depict here the Common Marsh Reed, about which more follows.

### THE BROADEST REED LEAF
### serrated, called Papyrus by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad, serrated leaf with prominent parallel venation, shown in detail.</image-desc>

We have received the leaf which we depict here under this name: and we have added it among our *Natural Wonders*.

Furthermore, Galen reports that the root and the <insert>young shoots</insert> of the Reed have a cleansing property; but the neck <note>the part near the root</note> is effective for thinning out dense humors and has a dispersing faculty, and it dries and heats in the third degree. The leaves are remarkably cold and dry, which is why in summer they are strewn in the chambers where the sick lie who suffer from burning fevers, so that the air may be corrected and rendered cooler, and the patients refreshed; when fresh, indeed, they are beneficial for Erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note> if bruised and applied. The root boiled in vinegar or wine and drunk stimulates menstruation and urine.

### THE SOLID REED, OR STUFFED, SMALLER,
### called Poisonous by Theophrastus, figured, Indian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two segments of a thick, jointed reed (bamboo-like), showing the solid interior and the exterior texture.</image-desc>

The juice of the Reed (to continue further in describing the use of Reeds), if mixed with honey, heals the bruising of the lips and cracks in the tongue: but others rub the bruised pith on the feet and <unclear>ankles</unclear> to provoke sweating. The one called *Phragmites* <note>Hedge-reed</note> is useful for making fences because of its thickness and firmness.

Furthermore, the Reed called *Nastos* by Dioscorides is called the *Poisonous Stalk* by Theophrastus, and by some *Papyrus*, but erroneously, since it is round, whereas Papyrus has triangular sides.

Is this the Indian Cane which Princes, Nobles, Leaders of military forces, and those whose strength has been broken by old age or disease use for walking sticks? More on this at the side of the following Figure.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATEST AND GARDEN REED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very tall, robust reed with large leaves and a thick stalk.</image-desc>

The *Common Reed* refuses no soil: yet it grows more prosperously in loose soil than dense, in moist than dry, in valleys than on slopes, and on river banks and in thickets rather than in the middle of fields. It is, moreover, long-lived, and rises better after being burned: its stalk is thick and numerous, for which reason it is stubborn in dying, and when wounded it easily knits back together. It is a marvel, indeed, what is reported: that the length of some upright ones is 30 paces; while those creeping on the ground are 50 paces, with a thickness of three cubits.

The one called *Garden Reed* is diligently cultivated in gardens for various uses, and equals the longest spear in length, with stalks thicker than a thumb, strong, hollow, frequently jointed, and yellowish: with large broad leaves: a tufted mane <note>the flowering head</note>, and a root creeping far and wide.

### THE SOLID REED, OR STUFFED, THICK
### and larger: The poisonous stalk of Theophrastus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two large, thick sections of a solid reed, showing the internal density and external nodes.</image-desc>

In Ethiopia, to continue with the uses of Reeds, the people live on the roots ground into flour. Some are remarkably large and robust, so that they serve in place of spears: some are so thick that individual sections between the joints serve in place of boats. With their coverings, the Northern peoples roof their houses, and the roofs are hard as bone. The peoples of the Orient finish their wars with reeds: they add arrowheads to the stalks, harmful with an unremovable hook. With these arms they overshadow the Sun itself, and because of this they especially hope for serene days, and hate winds and rains, which force peace among them. Thus says Pliny. From burnt Reeds the Umbrians make a salt, which they use in place of the natural kind.

### THE SOLID REED, OR STUFFED, OR
### Poisonous, slender and flexible, Indian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several slender, flexible reed stalks, some showing a slight curve or bend.</image-desc>

Lobelius mentions this and the preceding one in these words: for a walking stick, he says, they use a certain most beautiful *Assidine* <note>a type of cane</note>, distinguished by beautiful joints, remarkably stuffed, woody, hard, covered, smooth, shining, reddish or chestnut-colored, variegated along its length, with curly lines running here and there, shaping little teeth like a saw in a most beautiful appearance. For the sake of beauty, rarity, lightness, and convenience, they are accustomed to carry them, and they encircle them with silver.

There are many other varieties of Indian Reed. On the Island of Bali there are *Reeds flowing with gold*. There is a kind of Reed having 15 paces in length, and three palms in thickness, from which columns, planks, and roof-tiles are made—

<keywords>Arundo, Reed, Cane, Bamboo, Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, Galen, medicinal plants, Indian Cane, walking sticks, botany, ancient technology</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### SUGAR CANE AND SUGAR:
German: *Zuckerrohr*; French: *Canne à sucre*; Italian: *Canna di Saccharo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall sugarcane plant with segmented stalks and long, blade-like leaves, showing the root system at the base.</image-desc>

The *Sugar Reed* <note>original: *Saccharinus Calamus*</note> appears to be an intermediate between the millet-like and reed-like plants. It puts forth stalks seven or eight feet high, thicker than a thumb, provided with dense joints, and stuffed with a spongy, very sweet, succulent, and whitish pith. The leaves are two cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note> long, but they are narrow, rough, numerous, and striped along their length. The flower is tufted, somewhat like Sorghum. The root approaches the root of the Common Reed, but is sweeter, more succulent, and less woody.

They commonly call the sugar reed *saccharina*, *saccharata*, and *saccharifera* <note>meaning sugar-bearing</note>; and also *Sugar Cane*, *Honey Cane*, and *Cane of Sugar*. Indeed, Theophrastus, Aristotle, and Strabo call Sugar the *Honey of Indian Reeds*. More on this in the Appendix.

### LONG OR GREATER CYPERUS, WITH A
thicker, less spreading panicle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyperus plant (galingale) with a triangular stem, long leaves, and a clustered inflorescence at the top, showing a creeping rhizome root system.</image-desc>

It raises a triangular stalk to the height of a cubit or a cubit and a half: which is surrounded by grass-like leaves, striped, keeled, and hunched with a sharp back. At the top of the stalk, two or three shorter, narrower leaves arise: from whose crook dark panicles <note>branched flower clusters</note> unfold, with pale little flowers. The root consists of several olive-shaped bulbs, dark on the outside, white within, of a hard and sweet substance.

It flowers in June and July, and is troublesome in gardens due to its creeping habit.

Now, Cyperus—which is called <term>kypeiros</term> or <term>kyperos</term> by the Greeks—is believed by them to have taken its name from the shape of the root, which imitates a small box or a tiny vessel.

### ROUND OR LESSER CYPERUS,
the scented variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Cyperus variety with thinner leaves and a distinct cluster of small, round tubers along the root system.</image-desc>

This kind of Cyperus has numerous small roots in the shape of an olive, connected by a middle fiber like a thread, and is very fragrant. It is commonly called *Cyperus resembling an Olive* in the marshes of Rome; likewise *More Fragrant Cyperus from Syria and Alexandria*; and by Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax*: *Round Oriental Scented Cyperus*.

It is clear that our Cyperus—namely the long greater kind and the minor round kind (discussed here)—differs in some part from that of Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>; although it is not inferior in its medicinal powers. Theophrastus calls that "Cyperus" which Theodorus translates as "Gladiolus."

It grows in marshy, swampy, and cultivated places.

<column-break/>

### CYPERUS: German: *Wild Galgant*; Belgian: *Wild Galgaen*; French: *Souchet*; Italian: *Cypero*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyperus plant with a dense, spreading panicle of flowers and a thick, horizontal rhizome.</image-desc>

One Cyperus is bitter, another sweet: and the bitter is either scented or odorless; the sweet is either broad-leaved or narrow-leaved: and both are reddish, either round or long. Other differences are also taken from the shape of the flower clusters and their places of birth.

We depict here the *Long Cyperus with a spreading panicle*: its roots flourish with an intrusive creeping habit, being long and soon swelling into olive-shaped portions, of a pleasant scent and dark color. The stalks are three-sided, two cubits high, and striped, accompanied from the roots by many long leaves. At the top of the stalks are several leaves, pale flowers, and a dark, spreading panicle.

It grows in cultivated, marshy places.

### SYRIAN AND CRETAN CYPERUS,
or the round variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing several detached, rounded tubers of the Cyperus plant, some showing the fibrous exterior and others the smooth interior.</image-desc>

These roots were once given to us as Syrian Cyperus; they are knotty, solid, full, reddish on the outside, and encircled by transverse ridges or small zones. On the inside, they turn from reddish to white, being top-shaped or globular: with a vigorous, sharp, and somewhat bitter taste, similar to Zedoary <note>A root similar to ginger</note>.

As for the Cretan variety, we were given a Cyperus with a root like a small olive, wrinkled, black or dark on the outside, scented, aromatic, and bitter. We refer both of these to the Cyperuses of Theophrastus.

Furthermore, it is brought into Italy and exported at great price, not only from the moist mountains of Syria, but also from similar birthplaces in Illyria and Apulia, where it grows spontaneously.

### NORTHERN WATER CYPERUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an aquatic Cyperus with long, arching leaves and a distinct flowering head, showing the root structure adapted for water.</image-desc>

Lobelius says that in ditches and streams, by the most pleasant flows of the Scheldt river behind "New Antwerp," it grows with the same leaves and a maned panicle: putting forth some roots, but few, which are smooth, olive-shaped, bulbous, astringent, and odorless.

Regarding the **Powers** of Cyperus in general, it should be known that among all parts of the Cyperuses, only the root is of use. It warms and dries without biting, it cuts and thins [humors], and opens the mouths of the veins. It moves the urine, stirs up delayed menstruation, and is most usefully drunk for stones and dropsy <note>original: *aqua inter cutem*, "water under the skin"</note>. Also, on account of a certain drying power, it is very suitable for ulcers of the mouth and private parts. And, as Alpinus reports, there is great use of it, especially among the Egyptians.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### ROUND SHORE CYPERUS, odorless, English.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyperus plant showing long, slender leaves and a complex root system with small tubers.</image-desc>

In the coastal areas of Northern England and the Netherlands, along the banks of slow-flowing rivers and sea-marshes, there arises this quite elegant kind of Cyperus. It spreads its offspring far and wide by the roots, which are entangled with many filaments two cubits long <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; "two cubits" implies a length of about 3 feet.</note>, similar to the Round Cyperus. The leaves are angular; the stalk is a cubit or a cubit and a half high, shining and three-sided, upon which a cluster of branched tufts is gathered. It is slightly astringent to the taste, but the root is devoid of scent.

*For in Tuscany they call the plant "Noccum" a False-Cyperus: according to Caesalpinus.*

### GRASSY CYPERUS: FALSE-CYPERUS: Millet-like Cyperus Grass.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass-like Cyperus with a dense, drooping seed head (panicle).</image-desc>

It raises a three-sided stalk a cubit in height; the *leaves* accompany it, embracing the bottom of the stalk almost to the middle. Where they recede from the stalk, they surpass its top; they are keeled and twice as wide as common Grass, but otherwise not dissimilar. At the very summit of the stalk, millet-like *panicles* <note>A loose, branching cluster of flowers.</note> spread out widely, heavy with seeds like those of a Rush; beneath their point of origin, leaves are placed which would be similar to the lower ones if they were not smaller. The *root* is fibrous.

It grows abundantly in Geneva, Basel, and Montbéliard, and flowers in May.

### NILOTIC PAPYRUS OF ALPINUS, called BERD by the Egyptians: The Syrian Bible-plant of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Papyrus plant with a tall stalk topped by a large, feathery umbel.</image-desc>

Pliny confuses this with the Babylonian variety; but as the name and the thing itself indicate, the *Papyrus* of Theophrastus is no different from the *Papyrus* of Dioscorides. It is a very beautiful plant of great size, similar to the Cyperus in its girding and its origins, as well as its Egyptian nomenclature. It grows in the region along the streams in the marshes of the Nile; it does not emerge from the deep, but only flourishes in the shallows, not far from the banks.

We have seen this Papyrus—just as Theophrastus and Pliny describe it—brought from the Egyptian shores and made an inhabitant of the Pisan garden (the most pleasant of the whole Tyrrhenian coast and most rich in rare plants), where we saw it flowering.

Water distilled from the fresh stalks is beneficial for cataracts <note>original: "suffusiones"</note>, dimness, and obscurities of the eyes.

<column-break/>

### LONG ODORLESS WILD CYPERUS, according to Lobelius: Spurious Cyperus according to Gesner.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Cyperus with long leaves and a terminal cluster of spikelets.</image-desc>

Another smaller, odorless species of our local Cyperus, generally neglected, which the followers of Theophrastus in Switzerland used to mix into their "quintessences" <note>Highly concentrated herbal extracts or "fifth elements" in alchemy/early pharmacy.</note>.

Perhaps this is C. Bauhin’s *Long odorless Cyperus, wild or mountain*. Others commonly label it the Long Odorless Cyperus. It is called *Spurious Cyperus* by Gesner, growing in the watery places of Geneva around the Arve river, and flowering in the month of May.

### TRASI, THE MALINATHALLE OF THEOPHRASTUS: The Anthallium of Pliny: The Habalzelin of the Arabs: In Italian, Dolcichini.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with small tubers attached to the roots, resembling Cyperus esculentus.</image-desc>

Is *Trasi* thus the *Malinathalle* of Theophrastus and the *Anthallium* of Pliny? We hold this to be so, along with Caesalpinus, Clusius, and Dalechamps; and also that it is the Grass *Aizelin* of the Arabs, as Belon wishes. Whether it is also the *Mahebi* of Lery, we leave for the readers to examine.

Amatus, Lobelius, and others determine it to resemble Cyperus, whence Dodonaeus says: "Our age calls the plant itself *Dolcichinum*, and the roots *Trasos, Tragos*, or *Traseos*." It is a species of Cyperus, but sweet, and was not unknown to Theophrastus. Gesner and Pona (in his work on Monte Baldo) deny this plant a stalk, flower, and seed; but Matthiolus, Dodonaeus, Lobelius, and Columna—whose illustration we have adopted—attribute these to it. More on this in the Appendix.

### TRAGUS'S COTTON-WEED, OR COTTON RUSH: In German, Meadow-flax, Meadow-wool.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of cotton-grass (Eriophorum) with fluffy white seed heads.</image-desc>

It is rooted with tangled *fibers*, raising rushes that are straight, without nodes, and leafy. At their summit, from a two-holed sheath, the downy *panicles* hang by long and smooth stalks; they are white and surpass the work and softness of silkworms. Those who identify this as the *Gnaphalium* of Dioscorides are in error; it is more correctly called *Downy Grass* by others. Could it be Pliny’s Egyptian type of flax called *Orchomenium*?

It grows in damp and boggy places, just as we observed in the Griesbach valley where there are acidic springs, and in those boggy meadows on the way to *Cologny* near Geneva, and elsewhere. It is powerful in its astringent and thickening properties.
