### CAMEL GRASS OR SWEET RUSH:
->German: *Camelstro* <note>Camel-straw</note> : French: *Schoenanth* : Italian: *Squinantho*.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Schoenanthos (Camel grass), showing long, slender stalks emerging from a fibrous root system, with small flower clusters at the tips.</image-desc>

This is a rush-like and grass-like plant: which brings forth from a small, dry, somewhat hard and knotty root many very hard stalks, which are thick, round, flat (not hollow), and shining; they grow a foot high and are slender at the top. The leaves are stiff, about a span and a half long <note>approximately 12 inches</note>, pointed, and pale; they embrace the grassy shoots and, often being rolled together, they form what looks like a stem. Their tips are adorned with a series of small, pale reddish and downy flowers.

Cæsalpinus calls it *Round Rush*: Matthiolus, Amatus, and Cornarius call it *Sweet Round Rush*: Acosta calls it *Aromatic Flowering Rush*: by some it is called *Squinanthum*, and by others *Schoenanthum*, as if it were *Schoeni anthos* <note>Greek: σχοίνου ἄνθος</note>, that is, the flower of the rush. The Arabs call it *Adher* and *Adhir*.

->*Concerning the varieties, location, season, and medicinal powers in the following sections.*<-

### SHARP RUSH WITH A COMPACT PANICLE:
->The Rush of Matthiolus.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sharp rush (Iuncus acutus) with a dense, non-spreading seed head at the top of a tall, leafless stalk.</image-desc>

Here we shall treat the native location of Rushes. Every kind of unscented Rush is of common knowledge; and almost all its species are found near stagnant waters.

Dioscorides writes in Book 1, Chapter 16, that the most highly praised Sweet Rush is obtained from Nabataea <note>An ancient kingdom in the Middle East</note>: the next best is the Arabian kind, which some call Babylonian: while the worst is brought from Africa. Finally, one should choose that which, when rubbed in the hands, gives off the scent of a Rose. Brassavolus reports, on the authority of Pliny, that it grows in Apulia and Campania; but Pliny does not assert this as a certainty: nor are the flowers or the chaff brought from there, wherefore Matthiolus rightly doubts it, and determines that the Rush used by the perfumers <term>seplasiæ</term> <note>referring to the Seplasia, a famous street of ointment-sellers in ancient Capua</note> is brought from Alexandria.

### LEAFY RUSH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy rush (Iuncus foliaceus) with several stalks and prominent leaves rising from the base.</image-desc>

It creeps by means of a slanted root that sends down white fibers: the stalks are two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> or higher, provided with a thin pith: two or three leaves wrap around these, later turning into smooth, rush-like stems: from the slits in the sides, more scattered panicles <note>flower clusters</note> emerge.

<column-break/>

### RUSH WITH A REED-LIKE PANICLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rush with a reed-like panicle (Iuncus panicula arundinacea), showing a feathery, spreading seed head.</image-desc>

Caspar Bauhin distinguishes the Rush according to the opinions of Theophrastus, Pliny, and Dioscorides: "The Rush," he says, "is either scented or unscented: one grows in dry places, the other in watery ones: and this latter grows either in fresh water or by the sea. Again, in both kinds, some end in a sharp point, others in a blunt tip: and thus some are smooth, others rough: some with a sharper tip, others blunter. And the smooth Rush that is sharp at the tip is either the *Oxy-schœnos* <note>Sharp-rush</note> or the *Holoschœnos* <note>Entire-rush</note>: and of the *Oxy-schœnos*, one is male, fertile with no seed, the other female, bearing black seed."

It is called *Iuncus* by the Latins from *iungendo* <note>joining</note>, just as it is called *Schœnos* by the Greeks because of thongs and ropes <note>referring to its use in weaving cordage</note>.

### PUNGENT RUSH OR SHARP RUSH
->with Sorghum-like heads.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pungent or sharp rush (Iuncus pungens) with distinct, rounded seed clusters resembling sorghum heads.</image-desc>

Here we shall treat the medicinal powers of Rushes. Dioscorides writes that the seed of the common Rush, toasted and drunk with wine, stops the flow of the bowels and the red discharge of women <note>menstruation or uterine bleeding</note>: and the leaves nearest the root are suitably applied as a salve against the bites of venomous spiders <term>Phalangiorum</term>. He adds that the seed of the Ethiopian Rush induces sleep.

Regarding the Sweet Rush, there is use for the flower, the stalks, and the root. It has the power to provoke urine, drives out the menses, and disperses flatulence: the flower in a drink is useful for those spitting blood: but the root is more astringent than all the other parts of the plant. These are the words of Dioscorides. Galen writes that it heats moderately.

### LEAFY RUSH WITH TRIANGULAR
->capsules.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy rush with triangular capsules, showing dense clusters of star-like seed pods.</image-desc>

It varies not a little in size, sometimes with stalks a span long, sometimes a cubit long, somewhat compressed, spongy, and branched. The leaves, both from the root and at the joints, embrace the stalks for some distance and are grassy and sharp. On the shoots sent out from the divided stalk sit five, six, or more or fewer capsules, joined together, three-sided, oblong, pointed, reddish-black, and shining. It grows abundantly in damp places.

<summary>This page describes various species of rushes (Iuncus), distinguishing between aromatic varieties like Camel Grass and common unscented rushes, while detailing their physical characteristics and medicinal uses according to classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Schoenanthos, Camel Grass, Rush, Dioscorides, Pliny, Matthiolus, Galen, botany, medicinal herbs, astringent, Nabataea</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of rushes (Juncus species), providing descriptions of their physical forms, habitats, and flowering times. It maintains the systematic approach of the previous sections, likely following the classifications of Caspar Bauhin.</meta>

-># IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-

### THREE-FORKED RUSH.
<note>original: "Juncus trifidus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Juncus trifidus plant, showing a dense cluster of fibrous roots and thin, upright stems topped with small, delicate floral structures.</image-desc>

This is listed as *Rush 5, or the three-forked rush with a bent point*; it is described by Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous Swiss botanist (1560–1624) known for his early classification system.</note> in his *Prodromos* as follows: From a black, jointed, and fibrous root, several thin rushes rise up, exceeding a palm <note>A unit of measure based on the width of the hand, roughly 3-4 inches.</note> in height. At the top, these are divided into three, or more rarely four, very thin stalks of three or four inches; at the tips of these, after the rush divides, small panicles <note>A loose, branching cluster of flowers.</note> are located.

It grows on the "Broken Mountain" <note>Mount Pilatus</note> of Lucerne, in the Pyrenees, and in the mountains of Moravia.

<column-break/>

### GREAT ROUND-HEADED RUSH.
<note>original: "Juncus maximus holoschoenos"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Juncus maximus holoschoenos, featuring tall, thick, leafless stems emerging from a robust root system, with spherical flower heads near the tips.</image-desc>

It puts forth bare and knotless stalks, the tallest and thickest of all, with a pith that is porous and dry. Around their summits, scattered panicles break out, woven from large, cone-shaped heads, packed together in a scaly and overlapping <term>imbricated<note>Arranged like roof tiles or fish scales.</note></term> fashion, and hairy. The stalks are sometimes longer, sometimes shorter, and almost non-existent; the three-cornered seed lies hidden within the scales.

It delights in ditches, lakes, and places that always or frequently hold water.

<column-break/>

### SMALL RUSH WITH ROUND SEED-VESSELS.
<note>original: "Juncus parvus cum pericarpis rotundis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Juncus plant with numerous thin leaves at the base and stems ending in small, round seed pods (pericarps).</image-desc>

It produces rush-like stalks often a palm's length, and sometimes no less than a cubit <note>An ancient measure, roughly 18 inches.</note>. It is gifted with many grass-like leaves around the bottom, rising immediately from an oblique, fibrous root. Their stalk unfolds into a disordered <term>umbel<note>A flower cluster where stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs.</note></term>, in the manner of Dropwort <note>Filipendula</note>, whose individual heads are polished, round, and carry the enveloped seed in blackish husks, which finally gape open into three keels.

It is observed in meadows and watered areas.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST LEAFY RUSH.
<note>original: "Juncus foliatus minimus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small, leafy Juncus plant with a fibrous root and small clusters of flowers/seeds among the leaves.</image-desc>

It sends out stalks of one or one-and-a-half inches, many rising from a tuft, without knots, bearing a tiny, bunched panicle that hides a triangular seed within reddish husks. It has two opposite leaf-like "horns," one standing upright and the other turning downward along the stalks. The leaves are narrow, rising from fibrous, hair-like roots, reaching about an inch in length.

We collected this near Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausium," the Latin name for the city in France.</note>.

<column-break/>

### SMALL MOUNTAIN RUSH WITH SMALL YELLOW HEADS.
<note>original: "Juncus parvus montanus cum parvis capitulis luteis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Juncus variety with dense basal foliage and stems bearing small, distinct flower heads.</image-desc>

This is a perennial plant growing in damp places, which we have observed in various locations flowering in May.

It is rooted with frequent fibers, from which it sends out stalks a palm or nine-inches <note>original: "dodrantales"</note> long, thin, and beset with many leaf-wrappers near the ground. These stalks, otherwise smooth and knotless, carry a head at the very summit, two or three times shorter than the Clubbed Rush, with tiny yellow flowers shining out from between the longer scales.

Caspar Bauhin mentions a small mountain rush that lacks a sharp point.

<column-break/>

### RUSH WITH LONG HEADS, OR CLUBBED RUSH.
<note>original: "Juncus capitulis longis, sive clavatus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Juncus plant with long, club-shaped (clavate) flower heads and a creeping rhizome root system.</image-desc>

It rests upon a creeping root, headed with many fibers. The stalks are streaked, not rough, rounded, knotless, and without leaves; they are nearly a cubit long, spongy, and reddish around the bottom. Their summit does not end in a sharp point, but in a club-shaped spike overlapping with reddish scales. It varies in its appearance, sometimes with wider spikes, other times three times narrower.

We observed it at Geneva in watery places around the Arve, and elsewhere in muddy and stagnant waters; it flowers in the months of May and June.

<summary>This page catalogs six varieties of rushes, detailing their physical characteristics, root structures, and specific habitats ranging from the Alps to the French city of Nîmes. It cites the work of the prominent botanist Caspar Bauhin to provide scientific authority for the descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Juncus, rushes, Caspar Bauhin, Nîmes, Geneva, aquatic plants, mountain flora, herbals</keywords>

# PLANTS

### FLOWERING MARSH RUSH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering rush (Butomus umbellatus) showing the root system, long linear leaves, and an umbel of flowers atop a tall stalk.</image-desc>

Distinguished by its flowers, this Rush raises naked, straight stalks, two or three cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches, the length of a forearm.</note> high and nearly the thickness of one's smallest finger. Their tips support a large umbel emerging from a papery sheath, arranged unequally, consisting of white flowers, purplish flowers, or white-purplish flowers, with yellow stamens occupying the center. These are succeeded by small heads containing tiny seeds. The root is somewhat thick, rush-like, and fibrous; from it sprout several keeled leaves, like those of the Galingale <note>Cyperus</note>, and no smaller than the stalk.

It is observed everywhere in coastal areas and lakes, especially among other Rushes. In Italy, it is particularly frequent in the lakes and coastal areas of nearly the whole country, as well as in wet meadows and rush-beds.

It is found in both a larger and smaller variety, and both flower from May all the way until August.

### TIPHA, TYPHA, MARSH TYPHA: Greater Typha.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large cattail (Typha latifolia) with its characteristic thick, cylindrical brown flower spike and long, sword-like leaves.</image-desc>

Galen, Paulus, and Aetius passed over the Marsh Typha in their lists of simple medicines, perhaps because they had many other things that provided the same use which Dioscorides attributes to the Marsh Typha. We believe Pliny likewise did not treat it, although Tragus and Bauhinus suspect mention was made of it among the aquatic reeds.

This Typha is commonly distinguished into the *Greater* and the *Lesser*: Clusius adds a third species, namely the *Middle* one.

It grows most frequently in marshes, ponds, and lakes, both the larger and smaller kinds; indeed, stagnant waters are very rarely found that do not teem with Typha. The panicles <note>The fuzzy flower spikes</note> flourish in July and August.

### SPARGANIUM: Germ. Riedigrass: French. Sparganion: Ital. Sparganio: Arab. Saphareramon.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bur-reed (Sparganium) showing its branched inflorescence with spherical, spiky flower heads and long leaves.</image-desc>

It takes its name from a Greek word designating "swaddling bands," because nurses use its broad leaves—which are flexible like wicker—in place of bandages.

Some call it *Xiphidion* and *Gladiolus* <note>meaning "little sword"</note>; by others it is called *Carex*: by Dodonaeus and Thalius it is called *Platanaria*, on account of the similarity of its fruits to the little balls of the Plane tree. By Theophrastus it is called *Butomos*, and it is of two kinds, *Male* and *Female*. Truly, those who think it is the *Calamogrostis* of Dioscorides are much mistaken, as are those for whom it is the *female Phleos*. And finally, Ruellius and Lonicerus are mistaken, who call it *stinking spatula* <note>Iris foetidissima</note>.

It has leaves like the Gladiolus, says Dioscorides, but narrower and more drooping toward the ground: at the top of the stalk, little balls project, as it were, in which the seed is contained.

<column-break/>

### TIPHA OR TYPHA: Germ. Kolben; Messkolben; French. Masses de ionc: Ital. Mazza Sorda.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cattail plant showing the root structure and the developing flower spikes.</image-desc>

This Typha is called "Marsh" to differentiate it from the "Grain-like" Typha mentioned previously: and perhaps for the same distinction, *Tiepha* is written with an "i": from the Greek word <term>Tiphos</term> <note>original: "Tiphos"</note> designating its place of birth <note>meaning a pond or marsh</note>.

By some it is called *Fool's Mace*, by some *Ulva*, by others *Rough Rush*, and by others—though incorrectly—*Stinking Spatula*: but by almost everyone it is called *Typha*, *Typha*, and *Marsh Typha*. Is it the *Scirpus* of Ovid in the 6th book of the Fasti? Or a species of *Papyrus*, the *Reed for making mats* of the French Dodonaeus?

In the French countryside they called them *Maces*, says Ruellius, because the polished stalk, topped with a woolly density of flowers, rivals the scepters of kings given by this name.

### LESSER MARSH TYPHA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller species of cattail (Typha angustifolia) with narrower leaves and more slender flower spikes.</image-desc>

This differs from the greater and middle variety chiefly in that all its parts are shorter and thinner, and that it has two cylindrical maces separated by a small gap between them.

We present the <unclear>former</unclear> image; however, the other two made while we were absent do not please us at all; we could wish they were better.

Furthermore, Marsh Typha is believed to have obtained a certain moderate Temperament <note>In Galenic medicine, a balance of hot/cold/moist/dry</note>. The downy fluff of the maces is sought after by the lowest class of people for making pallets <note>straw beds</note> in place of feathers. The use of the leaves is for preparing mats, making women's chairs, and covering glass vessels: even for joining the seams of barrels faithfully and tightly. More in the *Appendix*.

### SECOND SPARGANIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Sparganium, showing distinct spherical, bur-like fruit clusters along the stem.</image-desc>

Thus it is labeled by Caesalpinus, the History of Lyon, and Tabernaemontanus. To Caspar Bauhin it is the *unbranched Sparganium* and the *broad-leaved Sparganium* of Gerard. He also mentions in his *Prodromus* the smallest Sparganium, which he labels the Third.

Otherwise, Sparganium comes out in marshy places and those having perennial waters, and also along the margins of certain brooks and rivers. It produces its little balls in the month of August.

Dioscorides shows that the root is given with wine against the bites of serpents.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of grasses and reeds, following the systematic classification of species. It focuses on alpine rushes, creeping grasses, and the highly debated identity of the "Aromatic Reed" (Calamus aromaticus).</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### ALPINE RUSH WITH A RABBIT’S TAIL. CREEPING GRASS WITH A PANICLE of Manna-grass: Finger-grass to many.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations side-by-side. On the left, a tufted alpine rush with a soft, fuzzy seed head resembling a rabbit's tail. On the right, a creeping grass with multiple finger-like spikes (panicles) extending from the stem.</image-desc>

It raises numerous stalks from small roots, about nine inches <note>original: "dodrantales"</note> or sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high; these are channeled and crowded with leaves near the ground, which also wrap around the stalks to some extent. Otherwise, the rush-like leaves end in a sharp point, turning reddish a little above the root, and often breaking down into hairy fibers. Furthermore, each stalk tapers into a cone-shaped "tail" composed of grayish, downy scales, which invites the touch with its silken softness. It is rooted by many fragile fibers.

Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax*, *Prodromus*, and *Phyto-Pinax*, calls it *Rush with a woolly head* <note>Latin: "Iuncus capitulo lanuginoso"</note>; and because the head is not unlike a rabbit's tail, it is also called *Rush with a reed-hare tail* <note>Latin: "Iuncus schoenolaguros"</note>.

We collected this on that very high mountain through which the path leads from the Grieffach Valley into the city of *Dornstetten* in the Duchy of Württemberg.

<column-break/>

Some believe this to be the *Ischaemon* of Pliny <note>a plant used in antiquity to stop bleeding</note>, which does not please Clusius at all. He calls it a "legitimate grass," adding an illustration of it that had been provided by no one else. He describes it thus: It rises, he says, with stalks a foot high, round, purplish, and jointed; from these it puts forth narrow leaves, tapering to a point, and hard. The stalks themselves, or reeds, end in four or five panicles <note>flower clusters</note>, of a mixed dark and purple color. It is secured by long, knotty roots, divided by joints, whitish, and of a somewhat sweet taste with a certain astringency. These roots creep far and wide, sprouting in many places and producing new stalks and leaves.

He adds that nothing is more common than this grass throughout all of Spain and even France, in fields, vineyards, and coastal areas, where it grows more lushly and abundantly.

---

### HAIRLESS GRASS SIMILAR TO FOXTAIL, with somewhat long hairs on the spike: Onocordon to many.

### AROMATIC REED: German & Belgian *Kalmus*: French *Calamus aromatique*: Italian *Calamo aromatico*.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations. On the left, a grass with a dense, cylindrical spike (foxtail-like) and a separate detail of the root system. On the right, three detailed depictions of aromatic reeds (Calamus), showing the segmented stems and the flowering spadix.</image-desc>

Its root is fibrous. The stalk is a cubit or higher, divided by long segments <note>internodes</note>, and gifted with two long, narrow leaves. At the top of the stalk sits a spike equal to *Phalaris* <note>Canary grass</note>, but of a different texture: it is composed of short, delicate husks and soft, somewhat long, ash-colored bristles <note>awns</note>.

It is found repeatedly in flat fields and near paths.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Grass 43, or Phalaris-like*; in his *Pinax* it is *Phalaris-like Grass I, either the greater or the Italian*.

<column-break/>

We shall cast out from the entryway those remote and metaphorical meanings of "Calamus" where it is used for various types of reeds, for a writing stylus, for a hollow pipe suitable for a flute, for small stalks of grain, for sugar cane, or for anything rolled up like a tube. Here we shall speak only of the "Scented Reed" understood in its proper sense.

Whether this *Aromatic* or *Scented Reed* commonly so-called—and named *myrepsicus* or "perfumer's reed" by Hippocrates—is the true and genuine aromatic reed of the Ancients, or whether it is instead *Acorus* <note>Sweet Flag</note>, is a matter writers contend over with fierce words and ferocious expressions. We propose, weigh, and refute their arguments at length in our *History*. However, if we believe Dodonaeus, Tragus, Clusius, and especially Mattioli, the "Scented Reed" of the Ancients is not a root, but a most precious reed that has not been brought to us until now. The legitimate and genuine one is *Acorus*, which the apothecaries display and sell as *Calamus aromaticus*. Then there are the followers of Briantius Calopodius who believe it is *Schoenanthum* <note>Camel grass</note>, and others who think it is *Cubeb*, and those who confuse it with *Galangal*. Whether this should be called "aromatic reed" and not "scented reed" (an epithet Garcia ab Horto disapproves of), we leave for the learned to investigate.

Rather, what Mattioli depicts as Aromatic Reed—and after him Lacuna, Lonicer, Acosta, Castore Durante, the *History of Lyon*, Tabernaemontanus, and Gerard—is nothing other than a fiction, differing not at all from a common garden or "stinking" reed.

Dioscorides says it grows in India; Theophrastus, Pliny, and Plutarch say also in Arabia, an error for which Guilandini rightly accuses them.

Following Vegetius, he makes two kinds of Aromatic Reed: *one Syrian*, growing on the banks of Lake Gennesaret (which others call the Sea of Galilee, after the city of Tiberias), not much different from the common sort; the *other Indian*, described and designated by Dioscorides of old, which is very different from the Syrian. Pliny, according to the same Guilandini, ignorantly mixed and confused these types of Reed, which differ greatly from one another.

The superior kind, however, invites one immediately from a distance with its *scent*; it is reddish or whitish, soft to the touch, less brittle, and breaks into splinters rather than snapping like a radish. When chewed, it is sticky and binds the tongue with a sharp taste; its hollows are full of "cobwebs" <note>a pithy substance resembling spider webs</note>.

It heats and dries in the second degree; it is mildly astringent, and by the thinness of certain parts, it opens the passages, promotes menstruation, provokes urine, restores the breath, and aids the natural heat of the body.

In our plate, we depict one Reed with its root from Clusius’s edition of Garcia, and two others with branches from a dried plant which we keep among our natural specimens.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES OF PLANTS
## CLASS XIX.
### PRESENTING BULBOUS HERBS AND THEIR RELATIVES.

| | |
|---|---|
| **ONION**: Arabic *Baffil & Bassal*: German *Zvvibel & Zibel, Bollen & Zipellen*: Belgian *Ajuin*: French *Oignon, Ciboule*: Italian *Cipolla*. | **ASCALONIAN OR FISSURE ONION** <note>The Shallot</note>; German *Aslaticis Leuchel & Esleychen*: French *Challettes, Branlettes, Appetis*. |

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an onion plant (Cepa) showing the bulb, roots, long tubular leaves, and a spherical flowering head (umbel) on a tall stalk.</image-desc>

Of all the bulbs found anywhere in the domain of nature, the most well-known is the Onion <note>original: *Cepa* or *Cæpe*</note>, named in the neuter gender. Among the Latins, it earned its name from the size of its "head" <note>Latin *caput*, referring to the bulb</note>. Turner writes that it was once called "Union" <note>original: *Vnionem*</note> because a single plant grows from a single root; and from this, perhaps, it is called *Oignon* by the French.

Dioscorides mentions only long and round, yellow and white onions. However, Theophrastus and Pliny describe a great variety of onions distinguished by their location, size, pungency, tenderness, and so on. Among more recent authors, many other differences of onions are reviewed. For in terms of size, some are called larger, others smaller. In form, some are long, others round, others flat-bottomed. In color, some are reddish, others white, others green, others blushing, others pale red. In flavor, some are very sharp, others moderately sharp, and others having no sharpness at all. Regarding their membranes or skins, some are clothed in a double membrane, others in a triple one. In planting, some are grown from seed, others are set down as bulbs.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Ascalonian or "fissile" onion (shallot), showing a cluster of smaller bulbs joined at the base with multiple leaf stalks.</image-desc>

It has several bulbs joined together at once, nearly equal to medium-sized leeks, oblong and fibrous; it has the flavor of the common onion. The leaves come forth tube-like, rounded, and smooth, endowed with the same flavor.

Theophrastus called it the "fissile" <note>splitting</note> and sterile onion, and "Ascalonian" after Ascalon, a town in Judea; it is given the same names by Gesner and others, and is even inscribed as the "Palestinian" onion. Could this be the *Setanian Bulb* of Theophrastus and Pliny?

Many onions of this kind are joined together, small and long: and it is their nature that if one is planted separately, many soon propagate from the same root, clinging together like a cluster of grapes.

There is also a certain onion called *Gethium*, without a head, whose entire growth is in the foliage. He relates that German women call this the "Onion" because it grows more into a herb than into a bulb, which is why it is sown from seed, but rarely set as a bulb. Dalechamp noted that there are also onions which bear bulbs in place of seeds <note>likely referring to top-setting or "walking" onions</note>.

---

| | |
|---|---|
| **LEEK**: German *Lauch*: French *Pourreau*: Italian *Porro, Praso*. **BULBOUS LEEK**. | **CUT LEEK, CHIVES** <note>original: *Schoenoprasum*</note> to some: German *Schnittlauch*: French *des Porrettes, oignonettes*. |

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leek (Porrum capitatum) with a distinct bulbous base, broad flat leaves, and a large globular flower head.</image-desc>

The Leek, a herb of common knowledge, had its name among the Latins because it "goes forward" <note>original: *porrò eat*</note> and spreads far and wide.

Dioscorides mentions two kinds of Leek with two different heads, but Pliny mentions three: and three are also found in Theophrastus: the Headed <note>Bulbous</note>, the Cut <note>Chives</note>, and the Vine or Wild Leek.

The Headed Leek is depicted here, though not perfectly: the reason for its name is taken from the fact that it grows into a head. However, the headed leeks do not differ in kind from the cut leeks; indeed, gardeners know that the former can be made from the latter.

Furthermore, they flower in June and endure almost every kind of weather. Thus they are found in abundance in various places; truly large ones are found in Padua, Lyon, and Geneva. Athenaeus mentions some that equal the size of a Turnip, though we have seen them nowhere. More on this in the following pages.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of chives (Schoenoprasum), showing a dense tuft of thin, grass-like tubular leaves and small fibrous roots.</image-desc>

In kind, as said before, it does not differ from the preceding, since they are produced from the same seed, but it differs only in cultivation.

It is commonly called *Schoenoprasum* <note>Rush-leek</note> and "Reed-leafed Leek," "Shaven Leek," and "Tarentine Leek," and by some "Ascalonian Head" or "Palestine," but erroneously. It makes up in number what it lacks in size: for its single plant sometimes consists of two hundred little leeks: yet in such a way that they can be pulled apart from each other and split to be planted, or many can be planted joined together. This kind of leek is met with almost everywhere.

It provides the same benefits as the headed leek (whose powers we will discuss shortly), but with slightly less effect. The greatest use of this "cut" leek is in the springtime, in foods, salads, broths, various sauces, and the German *Pfannenkuchen* <note>pancakes/omelets</note>.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Allium family (leeks and garlic), following the previous discussions on garden leeks. # IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
Cc

### WILD LEEK, VINE-LEEK: Germ. Wildlauch: Gall. Pourreau sauvage: Ital. Porro Sylvatico.
<note>Latin: Porrum Sylvestre, Ampeloprason. The Greek name Ampeloprason literally means "leek of the vineyard."</note>

### GARLIC: Greek Scorodon: Germ. Knoblauch: Gall. Ail & Aulx: Ital. Aglio & Ayo.
<note>Latin: Allium.</note>

*Illustration of a wild leek showing long, slender leaves, a flowering stalk with a small umbel, and a bulbous root with fibers.*

Galen calls this the "Rustic Leek," and recorded that it differs from the common leek only as much as a wild plant differs from a cultivated one within the same family. To some it is *Dog’s Onion*, to others *Dog’s Garlic*.

It shoots up with a stalk two cubits high <note>about 3 feet</note>, with leek-like leaves but narrower, a white flower, and a bulbous root. It grows in vineyards, which is why it is named *Ampeloprason* <note>Vine-leek</note> by the Greeks from its place of birth. However, it is also found at the edges of fields.

It is eaten by peasants and farmers in salads in place of fresh garlic. According to the School of Galen, every leek is hot and dry in the third degree; it thins thick humors and cuts through slimy fluids. However, by its sharpness, it "bites" the nerves, and by sending vapors up to the head, it induces dimness of sight.

<column-break/>

*Illustration of a garlic plant with broad leaves and a flowering head containing small bulbils.*

Many derive the name for Garlic <note>Allium</note> from its heavy, breath-fouling odor <note>halante</note> and write it as *Alium*; others seek Greek origins for the Latin word, which we shall not review here.

The primary differences in Garlic are taken chiefly from location and time. Thus, one kind is of the garden, another is Wild; one is early-ripening and another is Late. Garlic also varies in size, thickness, sweetness, and odor; but these differences are mostly assigned to the nature of the soil and cultivation. Hence Pliny denies that Garlic without cloves <note>nuclei</note> exists; on the contrary, Dioscorides claims such a thing grows in Egypt. Mattioli <note>a famous 16th-century Italian botanist</note> reports that in Tuscany and various places in Italy, there is a Garlic consisting of a single, solid head, which is called the *Male*.

---

#### ANOTHER IMAGE OF GARLIC.

*Illustration of three garlic bulbs, showing the outer skin and the fibrous roots at the base.*

Garlic is found among almost all nations, but the largest are in Lyon. There is no need to linger longer on a matter commonly known to everyone. We shall only add something regarding its virtues and harms.

Galen writes that Garlic dries and heats in the fourth degree: and that the Wild is stronger than the cultivated, just as all wild things are. It possesses a sharp power, says Dioscorides; it heats, bites, expels wind <note>gas</note>, disturbs the bowels, creates thirst, blisters the surface of the skin, and dims the eyesight when eaten. It is most effective against the poisons of serpents, rabid dogs, and the plague. Therefore, the powers of Garlic are very great—so many and so significant that the narrow limits of this space cannot contain them.

<column-break/>

#### A THIRD IMAGE OF CULTIVATED GARLIC.

*Illustration of a large garlic bulb with multiple cloves visible through the skin and a thick root system.*

We have touched upon its powers and uses before: we will add only what is said in the well-worn proverb, *Onions, Leeks, and Garlic are the dishes of the poor*. But as nothing is ever blessed in every part, besides the harms previously recounted, one must detest the foul and very strong odor in Garlic which affects the brain. Thomas More <note>the English statesman and author</note> prescribes it to be corrected thus:

> If you wish to drive away the foul stench of an Onion,
> Chewing Garlic will easily do this for you.
> But if after the Garlic a heavy breath still remains:
> Either nothing, or only Rue <note>The text jokingly suggests "Dung" (Merda) but corrects it to "Rue" (Ruta)</note> can repel it.

---

### LEEK-GARLIC: Germ. Aberlauch, Ackerknoblauch: Gall. Ail pourreau: Ital. Aglioporro.
<note>Latin: Scorodoprasum.</note>

*Illustration of Scorodoprasum (Leek-garlic) with twisting leaves and a distinct bulb.*

Just as the name *Scorodoprasum* reflects both Garlic <note>Scorodon</note> and Leek <note>Prason</note>, so too, according to the opinion of Dioscorides, Paulus, and Galen, it possesses the qualities and powers of both: it does whatever Garlic and Leek do, but a little more mildly. As a vegetable, on the authority of Dioscorides, it is used for food, and is cooked and sweetened just like a Leek.

Clusius learned from Busbecq <note>an ambassador to the Ottoman Empire</note> that this is a delicacy among the Turks.

It flowers in June and July, and grows in gardens in the manner of a Leek.

<column-break/>

### A KIND OF GARLIC, SNAKE-GARLIC: Germ. Welsch knoblauch: Schlangen knoblauch.
<note>Latin: Ophioscorodon.</note>

*Illustration of Ophioscorodon (Snake garlic) showing the characteristic coiled or "snake-like" flowering stem and bulbils.*

Because the head of this plant, along with the top part of the stalk, twists itself like a serpent, this kind of Garlic obtained the name *Ophioscorodon* <note>Snake-garlic</note>.

It is called *Amphicarpum*, *Ampeloprasum*, and *Scorodoprasum* by some: others (Lobelius) call it *Serpentine Moly*. Is it what was called *Moly serpentinum* by Lobelius in his *Observations and Images*? Or what was called *Amphicarpon*, another kind of cultivated Garlic, by Cordus in his *History of Plants*?

At the beginning of June it twists its head, but in July it straightens up, and in the same month brings its bulbs to maturity: just as was observed by Us in the garden of the Prince <note>S.P. likely refers to Serenissimi Principis</note> at Montbéliard, where we cultivated it.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Allium genus, including wild leeks, garlic, and snake garlic, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal properties, and culinary uses according to classical and contemporary authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Garlic, Wild Leek, Scorodoprasum, Snake Garlic, Galen, Dioscorides, medicinal herbs, botany, Montbéliard garden, Thomas More</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### WILD GARLIC: German: *Wilder Knoblauch*:
### French: *Ail sauvage* : Italian: *Aglio salvatico*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild garlic plant with a bulbous root, long slender leaves, and a spherical flower head at the top of a tall stalk.</image-desc>

Many kinds of Wild Garlic are found in the mountains, forests, and fields, differing among themselves in their leaves, flowers, or heads. Here, however, is depicted the broad-leaved Mountain Moly <note>Moly is a mythical or ancient name for a magical herb, often associated with wild garlic species</note> of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, who says that it grows commonly in the mountains of Hungary, Styria, Austria, and Moravia, flowering in June and producing bulbs in July. He attributes to it a flower of a dilute purple color, and to the whole plant a heavy smell of Garlic.

### TWO-HORNED PURPLE WILD GARLIC, prolific.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic variety with two distinct horn-like appendages emerging from the flower head and small bulbils forming among the flowers.</image-desc>

It grows frequently on the island of Lio <note>Lido di Venezia</note> in the Venetian territory, and is also found among the thickets at Basel. From the bulbs which we received from Venice, it grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of S.P. <note>likely referring to the Prince's garden or a specific patron's collection</note>, bearing flowers in July and August.

Is this the second Mountain Moly of Clusius, which he discusses at length in his *History of Pannonian Plants*? Or the Prolific Vine-Leek <term>Ampeloprassum: a wild leek or garlic often found in vineyards</term> in the illustrations of Plantin?

### PURPLE SPHERE-HEADED Wild Garlic.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic plant with a dense, perfectly spherical flower head and long, narrow leaves sheathing the stem.</image-desc>

The bulb is woven from many white cloves <note>original: "nucleis"</note>, wrapped in a white tunic, fibrous, and endowed with a heavy smell of Garlic. There are three or four leaves, a palm's breadth long, sometimes smaller depending on the nature of their birthplace; they embrace the stalk with a tube-like sheath. The stalk is a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or a cubit and a half high, rush-like in color and form, rounded, solid, and firm. At the very top, it bears a sphere equal to a pigeon's egg, or larger, consisting of crowded small purple flowers made of six petals with stamens of the same color, on short stalks.

This is most beautiful when it blooms, and is found in various places, in vineyards and grain fields, and is even transferred into gardens. Is it the *Ampeloprason* of Cordus?

<column-break/>

### TWO-HORNED WILD GARLIC with a green flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic plant with two long, leaf-like bracts extending from the flower head, which contains several small bulbils and flowers.</image-desc>

We have observed several specimens of this kind at Montbéliard, at the rock of Bavans, near the Doubs river. The flowers were composed of six petals, green on the outside, but whitening on the inside, and streaked with a purplish line.

Is this the Mountain Moly of Clusius with the "faded flower," of which he says: "The head spreads out widely between loose membranes and tunics that have a long point, full of flowers of a very faded color; the root produces cloves on the sides," etc.? Or the Garlic with reddish cloves in Plantin's illustrations?

### WILD GARLIC, with a pale YELLOW FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic plant with a loose umbel of drooping, bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

An umbel sits upon a rounded, cubit-high stalk, unfolding from a gaping membranous husk. It consists of yellow flowers sitting on stalks about an inch long, with six petals, round stamens, and a somewhat long, thin style. The seed is three-cornered and black. The leaves are narrow, a foot long. The root is bulbous and fibrous, also producing cloves by which it is propagated. It has the smell of Garlic.

To Clusius, in his *Pannonian History*, this is the fourth species of Garlic. To Caspar Bauhin, however, in his *Phytopinax*, it is Garlic number 11, or "Mountain garlic with a pale, scented flower."

### TWO-LEAVED SPHERE-HEADED GARLIC, with purple flowers crowded into a globe.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic plant with two prominent leaves and a dense, round cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

It grows spontaneously in the fields, displaying purple flowers at the top of a tall stalk, conspicuous in color and form. We found it flowering in July near the Castle of Belfort, as well as around Montbéliard in the plain of Berchamp toward Audincourt in the grain fields; from there we transferred it into the garden of S.P. In Clusius's *Pannonian History*, it is the Purple Mountain Moly with a most elegant flower.

Is it the *Scorodoprason* <note>Garlic-Leek</note> of the Adversaria <note>referring to the botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note>, or the "Garlic-Onion," the description of which is maimed and imperfect?

The illustrations for this and the preceding one are from purchased stock, and do not please us much.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### WILD ROCK UMBEL-BEARING GARLIC, with numerous purple flowers.
<note>original: "ALLIVM SYLVESTRE PETRÆVM VMBELLIFERVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild rock garlic plant with a long stalk, a bulbous root with fibers, and a spherical flower head at the top.</image-desc>

Conrad Gesner <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss naturalist</note> used to call this Rock Garlic, or Rock Leek growing among stones. We found it blooming in June at Burmium; we saw it at Basel in the garden of Master Felix Plater, and we ourselves cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince. Could it be the Rock Garlic, Vomiting Bulb, or Moly with Narcissus leaves mentioned in Camerarius's garden catalog?

Our illustration, which we have engraved, shows slender plants uprooted from a drier location.

### VERY SMALL WILD RUSH-LEAVED GARLIC with white flowers.
<note>original: "ALLIVM SYLVESTRE PERPUSILLVM iuncifolium"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small wild garlic plant with thin, rush-like leaves and a small cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

The stalk is a palm's breadth high, straight, and somewhat stiff; from its summit, about six shoots break out, from which small white flowers emerge, arranged as if in an umbel <note>a parasol-shaped flower cluster</note>, consisting of five or six petals. These are followed by small round heads, three or four in number, three-sided, containing oblong black seeds. Small, white, somewhat oblong bulbs lie beneath, with the unpleasant odor of garlic. The leaves are tiny, rush-like, very thin, four or five in number, and scarcely an inch long.

It is found on the hills near Montpellier, with flowers breathing the very sweet scent of Musk.

### ALPINE GARLIC: The MALE VICTORIALIS of some: German: *Laulauch*, *Sigwurz*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alpine garlic (Victorialis) showing broad leaves and a distinct fibrous net-like covering over the bulb.</image-desc>

It loves the mountains, yet we have observed it cultivated in gardens at Geneva and Montbéliard, and we have seen it in various other places and gardens, such as Basel, Strasbourg, and elsewhere. The flowers are similar to those of onions.

It obtained the names <term>Victorialis</term> <note>Victory Root</note> and <term>Sigwurz</term> <note>German: Victory Root</note> because those who work in the excavation of metals <note>miners</note> proclaim that it possesses great and certain powers against the attacks of impure spirits, by whom they are very frequently beset. There are those who report that when hung up, it protects against the contraction of limbs; and others write that it soothes the kind of convulsion called <term>Krampff</term> <note>German: Cramp</note>.

<column-break/>

### TWO-LEAVED ROUND-HEADED ITALIAN GARLIC.
<note>original: "ALLIVM SPHÆROCEPHALVM BIFOLIVM Italicum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a round-headed garlic with two leaves and a dense, spherical inflorescence.</image-desc>

It scarcely reaches a height of a palm and a half. The small root rests on an olive-shaped bulb, fibrous and white, provided with no trace of outer tunics <note>skins</note>. The stalk is stiff and, in proportion to the plant, quite thick and round; it rises dark green, clothed with two thick, channeled leaves. At the top it bears flowers gathered into a ball, conspicuous for their elegant purple color, from which certain small, mucous, flame-like tongues flow out. The taste is not unlike the taste of Garlic.

It bloomed for us throughout May at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince which we tended; the figure expresses the size and proportion of the plant almost exactly.

### TWO-LEAVED SPRING WILD GARLIC: German: *Beerhundslauch*: French: *Ail d'Ours*: Italian: *Aglio de li Orsi*.
<note>Commonly known today as Ramsons or Bear's Garlic</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ramsons (Wild Garlic) with broad, elliptical leaves and a loose umbel of flowers.</image-desc>

Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> records it thus: "There is," he says, "also a certain wild garlic which they call Bear's Garlic, with a mild odor, a very thin head, and large leaves." There are those who judge it to be the <term>Scorodoprason</term> <note>Leek-garlic</note> of Dioscorides, or his <term>Ampeloprassum</term> <note>Vine-leek</note>, or <term>Ophioscordon</term> <note>Snake-garlic</note>, but they are mistaken.

We have observed it in various places: in gardens at Bologna, Padua, and Ferrara; at Geneva on the hill of La Bastie; and at Montbéliard near the <unclear>Vauigouret</unclear> bridge. It produces numerous white flowers radiated in the manner of a star. It is said that when put into milk, it curdles it.

### PERHAPS A KIND OF GARLIC, the second *Scorodoprason* of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a garlic variety with a tall stalk and a dense flower head, possibly a type of leek-garlic.</image-desc>

The bulb is an inch and a half or longer, fibrous, top-shaped, and composed of many reddish skins. There are two or three thin leaves, a palm long, wrapping around the stalk; the stalk is a foot high, firm, round, and without joints, upon which sits a small umbel of pale flowers, smaller than those of the Rock Garlic.

We do not remember where we obtained this plant. However, it has the odor and taste of Garlic; likewise the bulb, flowers, and leaves, but all parts are more slender. Is it perhaps the fourth Garlic, or Spherical Garlic, in Caspar Bauhin's <term>Phytopinax</term> <note>An early botanical index</note>?

# OF PLANTS
## THE MOLY OF THE ANCIENTS AND THE GENUS OF MOLY IN GENERAL
### The small Moly of Dioscorides according to some, with a white flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Moly plant with a bulbous root, two broad leaves, and a single stalk topped with a cluster of small white flowers.</image-desc>

Moly is believed to take its name from the Greek verb <term>mōlyein</term> <note>original: "μωλύειν"</note>, meaning "to drive away diseases." Pliny called it the most famous of herbs, discovered by Mercury, and noted its supreme use against sorcery—observations which, like most of his work, he borrowed from Theophrastus. Both authors record that it grows around Pheneus and near Cyllene in Arcadia; Homer says the same. However, Theophrastus does not write that it is difficult to dig up, as we find in the accounts of Homer and Pliny.

The plant pictured here, which almost everyone accepts as the Moly of Dioscorides, was observed by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> at Cadiz, in that part of the ancient city which extends into the sea. We ourselves have seen it flowering in April in the public garden at Padua, as well as at Bologna.

### THE GREAT MOLY OF THEOPHRASTUS, WITH
### white star-shaped flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a larger Moly species with a large bulb, several long leaves, and a tall stalk ending in a dense, star-shaped floral umbel.</image-desc>

Two types of Moly are proposed by Pliny: one with a round root and one with a long root. Yet Theophrastus and Dioscorides mention only one, and some think the Moly of Dioscorides is different from that of Theophrastus. In Galen’s writings, it is called *Myle* rather than *Moly*, perhaps through the fault of the transcribers. The Moly pictured here is cultivated in gardens by those devoted to botany, and it flowers in the month of May.

Furthermore, it puts forth two or three leaves from a bulbous root (blackish on the outside, white within); these are long, broad, somewhat thick, and embrace one another. The stalk is bare, larger than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, thick, hollow, whitening, and round. The flowers at the summit are arranged in an umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster</note>, star-shaped, and white, growing from somewhat long little stems; these are followed by three-cornered heads containing black seed.

### INDIAN MOLY, OR THE CAUCASON
### of Lobelius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Indian Moly, showing a bulbous root and a stalk topped with a dense, globular cluster of bulbils or flowers.</image-desc>

He says <note>referring to Matthias de l'Obel</note> it is similar to the Moly of Theophrastus in its leaves and general form. However, it never produced flowers for me, nor for many others; instead of flowers, it bears a foot-long stalk, nearly flat, and so weak that it cannot be raised up unless supported by some prop. At the very top, it bears a clustered head consisting of many parts like cloves of Garlic, the size of a common Medlar; these are green at first, then turning pale. Even when not placed in the earth, these germinate; yet when committed to the soil, they grow into larger bulbs and produce leaves and stalks, though not every year. The root is onion-like, round, white, and covered with many tunics <note>layers</note>, the outermost of which is dusky, separating itself with age and spreading into other bulbs. Such is the plant whose image and description we present; however, Clusius and Imperato depict and describe it differently, as will be clear from what follows.

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLER MOLY WITH THE SMALL
### round flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller Moly variety with a round bulb and a spherical flower head.</image-desc>

The description of Moly in Dioscorides is, in the judgment of Cornarius, that of the famous Homeric *Moly* which Mercury gave to Ulysses against the sorceries of Circe. However, Matthiolus and Clusius freely admit that this plant is entirely unknown to them and others, and has not been seen anywhere.

The one we depict here is the "Smaller Moly" in Clusius’s *History*; of it he says: It is very similar to the Moly of Dioscorides. The stalk is a span high <note>about 9 inches</note>, green, supporting ten or more flowers consisting of six snow-white roundish petals, with six little threads in the middle. There are two leek-like leaves; the root is round, whitening, and the size of a hazelnut <note>original: "Nucis Ponticę"</note>.

### THE YELLOW MOLY OF THE BOTANISTS, BROAD-LEAVED,
### with the scent of Garlic.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a yellow-flowered Moly with broad leaves and a large, rounded floral cluster.</image-desc>

It has yellow flowers, gifted with six petals and several stamens of the same color, very similar to the flowers of the Yellow Star-of-Bethlehem. It has two rather broad leaves, similar to the leaves of the Bologna (or Apennine) Tulip, though usually one is broader than the other. The root is also similar, but shorter. It is found in the Pyrenees mountains.

The whole plant, say the *Adversaria* <note>a botanical reference book by Pena and Lobel</note>, gives off the scent of Garlic, and for that reason, it is closer to Moly than to the Yellow Star-of-Bethlehem; the name "Yellow Star-of-Bethlehem" is wrongly given to it by the root-cutters <note>herbalists/druggists</note> because it is more easily sold under that name.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF INDIAN MOLY, by Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of another variety of Indian Moly, featuring twisted, wavy leaves and a central stalk with a cluster of bulbils.</image-desc>

Clusius says in his *History of Spanish Plants*: "Those devoted to botany in our country say there is also another kind of Moly which they call Indian (others use the foreign name *Caucason*), because they say it was first brought from India to Spain, and from there passed to the Italians, from whom the Belgians received it." The leaves, bulb, and the rest are similar to the Lily-flowered Moly, or that of Theophrastus, etc. The same Clusius also reports that it grew in Constantinople and was brought from there to Vienna. The plant shown to Ferrante Imperato under the name of Indian Moly and Caucason is a species of bulb which has small bulbils instead of flowers and seeds, each having its own little husk.

<summary>This page describes various species of Moly (wild garlic), blending classical mythology—specifically the herb given to Odysseus by Hermes—with 16th-century botanical observations from across Europe and the Indies.</summary>
<keywords>Moly, Allium, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Pliny, Clusius, Caucason, Garlic, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
->Cc 3<-

**HYACINTH: German & Belgian: Hyacinthen : French: Hyacinthe : Italian: Hyacintho.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hyacinth plant with a bulbous root, long slender leaves, and a flowering stalk with bell-shaped blossoms.</image-desc>

The Hyacinth, says Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist from the 1st century AD</note>, has leaves similar to a Bulb; a stem a palm's breadth in height, smooth and thinner than the little finger, and green; upon which rests a drooping crest full of purple flowers; and a root that is also itself like a Bulb.

Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle</note> recognized both the Wild and the Cultivated varieties. But as will be clear from what follows, many other variations of the Hyacinth are observed. Whether the Hyacinth of Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, Ovid, Virgil, and Galen is actually the "Purple Lily" of more recent authors, as Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius, a 16th-century German humanist physician</note> maintains, we leave to the judgment of experts.

However, the one we depict here is the Spring Hyacinth, grape-like, smaller, blue, with narrower leaves, and fragrant. It blooms in March in gardens, and in some places it grows wild in fields and mountains.

<column-break/>

**SPRING GRAPE HYACINTH, smaller, broad-leaved, blue, unscented.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hyacinth plant similar to the first, but with broader leaves and a denser cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

This variety plays with its leaves <note>meaning the leaf shape varies</note>, which are more or less broad depending on how rich or cultivated the soil is. It blooms earlier than the preceding one and grows in the same locations.

Furthermore, Pliny records this regarding the origin of the Hyacinth. In Book 21, chapter 11, he says: "A double myth accompanies the Hyacinth: displaying the grief for the one whom Apollo had loved <note>referring to the youth Hyacinthus</note>, or as having sprung from the blood of Ajax; with its veins running in such a way that the shape of the Greek letters 'AI' <note>an exclamation of grief</note> may be read inscribed upon it." That this myth was also known to Virgil is clear from his verses:
> *Tell me in what lands flowers are born*
> *inscribed with the names of Kings, etc.* <note>original: "Dic quibus in terris inscripti nomine Regum Nascantur Flores"</note>

---

**WHITE UNSCENTED GRAPE HYACINTH: Perhaps the "Dipcadi" of the Italians?**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hyacinth plant with a tall flowering spike and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> distinguishes two species: One, which has an entirely milky flower and a whitish stem; the other, in which the snowy color of the flower is seen suffused with a very dilute purple. It is an inhabitant of gardens and groves; it blooms in April, and even in May if the spring season begins later due to the harshness of the preceding winter. Is it perhaps the twin variety of Lobelius's "Dipcadi with white flowers" mentioned in his *Observations*?

<column-break/>

**GREATEST GRAPE HYACINTH with a blue crest.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Hyacinth variety with a thick bulb and a prominent, feathered flowering head.</image-desc>

By some it is called the "Edible Bulb," by others *Pancratium* and the "Greater Squill." Clusius reports that it grows wild in many provinces of the Christian World, and he identifies two types: one early-blooming, with a broader leaf and larger bulb, the other late-blooming. We have seen it growing wild in the fields, meadows, and roadsides of Basel, Montpellier, Ferrara, and Geneva. Camerarius, Gerard, and other botanists label it the "Greater Tufted Hyacinth"; C. Bauhin calls it the "Greater Racemose Hyacinth."

---

**AUTUMN HYACINTH, Greater and Smallest.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Hyacinth plants of different sizes, showing the autumn-flowering variety with smaller blooms.</image-desc>

We observed this one and the following in the gravelly and rugged places near Montpellier at the beginning of Autumn. They are also cultivated in hanging gardens, with blue flowers shining out from the middle to the top of the stalk.

Some have thought this to be the *Bulbine* of Pliny; but the description of *Bulbine* in his own work clearly contradicts this, since he attributes leek-like leaves and a reddish bulb to it. With no less an error, others have thought it to be the <term>Tiphyon</term> <note>An unidentified plant mentioned by ancient Greeks</note> of Theophrastus, since the characteristics of *Tiphyon* do not fit this Hyacinth in the least.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER AUTUMN HYACINTH.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small autumn Hyacinth with a delicate flowering stalk and thin leaves.</image-desc>

We have observed this frequently in various places: at Paris, at Narbonne near the Marian waters, and at the "New Cell" in Montpellier, in gravelly and rugged areas.

Regarding Hyacinths in general, Pliny, Dioscorides, and Galen attribute these powers to them. The root, they say, dries in the first degree and cools in the second; applied as a liniment with wine, it keeps boys from reaching puberty <note>a common ancient belief regarding the inhibition of secondary sex characteristics</note>; taken as a drink, it stops the bowels, drives out urine, and helps those bitten by serpents. The seed gently cleanses and binds, and drunk in wine, it heals the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>; it dries in the third degree, standing in the middle between heat and cold.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Hyacinths, including spring and autumn varieties, while debating their classical nomenclature and medicinal uses. It cites major botanical authorities like Pliny, Dioscorides, and Clusius to distinguish between species based on bloom time, leaf shape, and color.</summary>
<keywords>Hyacinth, Grape Hyacinth, Botany, Medicinal Herbs, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, Clusius, Montpellier, Jaundice, Ancient Medicine</keywords>

### THE ORIENTAL OR CONSTANTINOPOLITAN HYACINTH, with the larger flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hyacinthus orientalis with a large bulb, long leaves, and a tall stalk bearing several bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

There are various species of the Oriental Hyacinth, called "of Constantinople," which the Turks hold in high esteem and call *Zembulcu der* <note>original: "Zembulcu der"; likely a Latinization of the Turkish "Sümbül," meaning hyacinth</note>. These are kept in various cultivated gardens across Germany, France, Italy, and the Low Countries. They vary in the size, number, and color of their flowers. The kind we depict here bears larger flowers, and those are for the most part purple. However, the Oriental Hyacinth that has smaller flowers usually bears more of them and in greater numbers, though sometimes it has only two or three. We have seen the larger one pictured here in gardens in Ferrara, Bologna, and Padua; and we ourselves have kept purple, blue, and white varieties in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>S.P. likely refers to "Serenissimi Principis," the Most Serene Prince</note> at Montbéliard.

### ANOTHER MANY-FLOWERED ORIENTAL HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a polyanthes hyacinth with a thick cluster of flowers on a single stalk and broad leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> has observed the distinctions of the Oriental Hyacinths more diligently than others. He says they vary greatly in the intensity or lightness of their color: they are either entirely blue, or ash-colored, or a lighter and more cheerful purple, or a deep purple approaching the color of a dark violet.

Furthermore, all Oriental Hyacinths were sent under the name *Zambul*, with the word "Indian" added when they are from India, or some other word when they wish to indicate the place from which they were received. Moreover, they all bloom in April.

### THE ORIENTAL HYACINTH, reddish-purple.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hyacinth with a dense floral spike and a prominent bulb with roots.</image-desc>

The illustrations of Plantin <note>The famous printing house in Antwerp</note> also depict this one. By Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, an Italian botanist</note> it is called the *Hyacinth of Theophrastus and Dioscorides*, and by the Turks *Zembiecuder*. Clusius writes of it thus: "I have," he says, "one plant endowed with a very broad leaf of a deeper green; its stalk is thick and succulent, but more sparing in bearing flowers, as it gives no more than ten, and these do not face or turn toward one side, but spread out in different directions, being of a deeper purple. The heads are also seen to be a deeper green, as if sprinkled with a purple color."

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLER MANY-FLOWERED ORIENTAL HYACINTH: German: *Gefulter fremder Hyacinth* <note>Filled/Double foreign Hyacinth</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller polyanthes hyacinth with multiple flower heads emerging from the stalk.</image-desc>

A plant was born from the seed of this variety in the year 1585 for Clusius; its stalk was a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, thick and firm, and it bore seventeen flowers. They were not the same color as the parent plant, but a more florid purple; and beneath them were small branches, each of which was loaded with five flowers. Otherwise, this plant is more sparing in bearing flowers, sometimes giving no more than ten. They by no means always face or turn to one side, but are sometimes scattered equally on every side. Our illustration is from the Plantin Illustrations, page 195.

### THE WHITE ORIENTAL HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a white oriental hyacinth with a slender stalk and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a major Flemish physician and botanist</note> relates this concerning these Hyacinths: "The Hyacinth," he says, "which Italy and the Low Countries call 'Oriental,' has richer and broader leaves, and thicker, more powerful, and larger stalks, which emerge earlier. One of these produces many flowers, while another produces fewer." Indeed, L. Bellius and Pena in the *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by L'Obel and Pena</note> say that the variety of the Greek Oriental Hyacinth, which the Indians call *Zumbel*, has a stalk knotted in the manner of a Dragon-plant, and twisted leaves.

Our illustration is from the Plantin collection.

### THE WHITE WINTER HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a winter white hyacinth with a distinct bulb and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

Although this plant agrees with most others in the form of its leaves and flowers, it claims this unique trait for itself: that it breaks through the earth immediately after the Winter Solstice <note>original: "Solis Hybernum tropon"</note>, sometimes even pushing its stalk through the middle of the snow. Around the beginning of January, it displays a most beautiful, loose, white flower, which is nevertheless somewhat bluish at the start and around the top edges. As this color fades gradually in the month of February, it becomes entirely milk-white, most fragrant in scent, persisting in that appearance for more than a full month. The root is bulbous, white inside and reddish on the outside. It does not enjoy damp places at all, but is ruined by moisture sooner than by cold; for that reason, it is even kept in earthenware pots.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE HIGHLY FRAGRANT HYACINTH, called Dipcadi and Muscari.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus odoratissimus (Muscari) showing a bulb with roots, long linear leaves, and a tall stalk ending in a raceme of small bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This most elegant plant was brought from Constantinople, which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> describes thus: The bulb, he says, is quite large, whitish, interwoven with many tunics <note>layers or skins</note>, to which are attached thick and long fibers, though few in number, which are perennial. There are five or six leaves, about nine inches long or more, nearly an inch in width, with six somewhat thick ridges running lengthwise; they are keeled, quite thick, and succulent. The stalk is fairly thick, angular, rounded, bare, and remarkably weak for its thickness: from about the middle to the top, it is surrounded by clusters of *flowers* clinging together in a raceme, which are whitish, pale blue, yellowish, or blackish, yielding a most pleasant scent of musk or spices. The flowers are followed by very large, three-cornered, and winged seed-pods, in which is contained round black seed.

### THE STARRED SPRING HYACINTH OF THE THICKETS, two-leaved: with blue and white flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus stellatus showing a bulb, two broad lanceolate leaves, and a flower stalk with several star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Because of its flowers, which spread out like rays in the shape of a star, it earned the name *starred* among students of botany. Since it is found with both blue and white flowers: the blue variety varies, with flowers that are more saturated and tending toward violet, or approaching a flesh-colored hue. Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist</note> distinguishes them into *Male* and *Female*. Since this plant comes forth in the spring, specifically in the months of February and March, it has come to pass that botanists call it the *March flower*.

### THE SMALL STARRED SPRING HYACINTH with blue-gray flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller variety of Hyacinthus stellaris with a bulb, narrow leaves, and small star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This is a plant scarcely a palm's breadth high, with narrow leaves, four or five in number, from the middle of which a *small stalk* emerges. The root is small, white, oblong, and has few fibers: the *flowers* grow in threes or fours, star-shaped, of a blue-gray color, composed of six small petals and as many blue stamens and tips: with a pistil in the middle with a gray-blue knob or point.

George *Le Seigneur* enriched the collection of *Bryania* <note>likely a reference to a specific garden or estate</note> with this plant, as well as many other new ones brought from France. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), Flemish physician and botanist</note> in the second part of his *Adversaria*.

<column-break/>

### THE HIGHLY FRAGRANT HYACINTH, called Dipcadi and Muscari, yellow.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration similar to the first, representing the yellow variety of the Muscari, with a prominent bulb and raceme of flowers.</image-desc>

It is also inscribed as the *Yellow Musk-Hyacinth of Chalcedon* or *of Constantinople*. By Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590)</note> in his *Icons* it is called the *Yellow Chalcedonian Grape-Hyacinth*: Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it *Hyacinth 18, or the Yellow Musky Racemose Hyacinth*. Furthermore, a variety of it is found whose flowers are pale blue in March and become golden in April.

We have seen this and the preceding one at Padua in the Medical Garden <note>The Orto Botanico di Padova, the world's oldest academic botanical garden</note>, and we ourselves have cultivated them at Montbéliard in the garden of His Serene Highness.

By Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577)</note> in his Italian and Latin *Commentaries* with large figures, it is called the *Vomiting Bulb*: but as Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585)</note> notes, he describes it with no distinguishing marks in the meantime, and supports his opinion with no reasons or testimonies. Yet almost the same thing happened to Dodonaeus himself that he criticized in Matthiolus, so meager is his description.

### THE THREE-LEAVED SPRING HYACINTH OF THE THICKETS: with blue and white flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a three-leaved Hyacinthus vernus with a bulb and a cluster of star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

It grows, like the preceding one, in the woods: and it is for this reason that the French—among whom, by the testimony of Pliny, it grows excellently—call it the *woodland* or *wild onion*, as Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), French physician and botanist</note> is the authority. They are frequently found in the small forests and fields of Switzerland and Germany. *We* observed them flowering in March at Genoa on the hill of *la Bastie*, as well as across the river *Arve*, in the region of *Champel* in the wooded areas: also at Montbéliard on the hill going toward *Vauvaucourt*, and even in the groves around *Arbouans*. Truly, however, nowhere is there a greater abundance of them than in the woods not far from the village of *Lustnau*, near Tübingen.

### THE WHITISH LATE-BLOOMING STARRED HYACINTH.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a late-blooming white Hyacinthus stellaris showing the bulb and star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

It flowers later and has more slender leaves: the flower, however, is pleasant to look at and is whitish. It was brought into Belgium from the mountains of Biscay: *Lobelius*. We present its image here, in which the flower is depicted with five petals; however, we do not know how accurately, since the flowers of starred hyacinths are commonly observed to consist of six petals.

Could it be the *White Narcissus* of Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), whose name translates to 'Tragus' in Latin</note>, as Caspar Bauhin thought?

# OF PLANTS

### RARE BLUE HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rare Blue Hyacinth, showing a bulbous root with fibers, long slender leaves, and a stalk topped with several six-petaled star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is bulbous, large, and provided with white fibers: it has three or four leaves, like those of the Starry Hyacinth: the stalk is slender, purple, shining, angled, and about a span <note>a "palmaris" or span is roughly 9 inches</note> or a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height; it is usually single, but sometimes there are two, three, or more. The flowers at its very top are four, five, or six in number, composed of six leaves <note>petals</note>, which are somewhat long, pointed, blue or rather violet, with a whitish "claw" <note>the base of the petal</note>, and a darker violet line running down their length; they are so spaced from one another down to the little stem that they mimic a radiating star. The center is occupied by a round, channeled head, the size of a small pea, white, which is the rudimentary seed-vessel: this is surrounded in order by six stiffish violet filaments, which are whitish near the bottom: from the middle of the head, a violet style <note>the female part of the flower</note> stands out.

It bloomed for us in April at Montbéliard in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>original: "S. P." likely referring to the Prince of Württemberg's garden</note>.

### ANOTHER BYZANTINE STARRY HYACINTH, most elegant and late-blooming.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Byzantine Starry Hyacinth, featuring a large bulb, broad leaves, and a cluster of star-shaped flowers on a central stalk.</image-desc>

This one is far more elegant than the early-blooming variety, coming forth with beautiful, shining, starry, blue flowers along little stalks that are a span and a half long, bright, flat, and reddish: it has the leaves of the German Starry Hyacinth: the seed in the pods is round, white, and shining. The root is equal to the bulbous Stock <note>Leucojum</note>, white inside and reddish on the outside, and it is propagated by attached offsets <note>small "bulblets" or "nucleis"</note>.

Brought from Constantinople to London, it was observed there in some of the richest gardens of exotic plants by Lobelius, as recorded in the second part of his *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Matthias de l'Obel</note>.

### SUMMER STARRY HYACINTH, with flowers turning from blue to purple.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Summer Starry Hyacinth, showing a bulb, upright leaves, and a tall flower spike with numerous small blossoms.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note> first saw this kind of Hyacinth, laden with its flowers, in the month of May in the year 1606, in the highly cultivated garden of a certain citizen of Leiden named Perturbanus, who asserted it had been brought to him from Portugal: when Clusius noticed that neither a description nor an illustration of it had been provided by anyone before that time, he described it at length in his *Exotics*.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S SPRING BYZANTINE STARRY HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spring Byzantine Starry Hyacinth, showing a bulb with roots, spreading leaves, and a stalk with several star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

It has four or five leaves spread upon the ground, long, keeled <note>ridged like the bottom of a boat</note>, of a pale green color, like a Hyacinth: the stalk is a finger's length, slender and weak, supporting three, four, or five flowers consisting of six petals, of a pale blue color, scentless, which, when illuminated by the rays of the Sun, unfold themselves like the common Hyacinth, and display six small white filaments, the tips of which turn purple, with a style shining in their midst. These are followed by triangular heads <note>seed pods</note>, as in the common variety, but they are mostly empty. The root is bulbous, not large, covered with a black skin, and provided with fibers underneath.

It bloomed for Clusius in April.

### MANY-FLOWERED STARRY HYACINTH of an ash-gray color.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Many-flowered Starry Hyacinth, featuring a large bulb and a dense, conical cluster of many small flowers atop a thick stalk.</image-desc>

This plant has many leaves lying on the ground: among which comes forth a little stalk a span high, bearing twenty, thirty, or sometimes more flowers, of a color between blue and ash-gray, crowded together like a spike or a cluster of grapes: a central boss <note>umbone</note> occupies the middle with six filaments. The flowers are followed by triangular heads containing seed. The root is bulbous and bright white. It blooms at the same time as the common ones, that is, toward the end of March, though a little later than the common variety. It is found today in British gardens and is propagated by the bulb. According to Lobelius.

### THEOPHRASTUS’S TWO-LEAVED HYACINTH of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Two-leaved Hyacinth, showing a bulb with two distinct leaves and a small cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

<margin>By Lobelius in the *History of Belgium* it is called "Blue May-flower" <note>original: "Blauwer Meybloemken"</note>: and in the *Images of Plants* it is called "Theophrastus's two-leaved Hyacinth." By Caspar Bauhin in the *Phytopinax* it is called "Hyacinth 4, or Theophrastus's two-leaved Hyacinth of Lobelius."</margin>
