### BYZANTINE TASSEL HYACINTH
<note>original: "Hyacinthus comosus Byzantinus"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus comosus Byzantinus, showing a bulb with roots, a tall stalk with small flowers at the top, and long, slender leaves.</image-desc>

Around the year 1578, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note>—who paints and describes it at length—it was first brought from Constantinople with other bulbs of various kinds. Since that time, few have been sent, perhaps because it is not much sought after, as it is endowed with no great elegance of flower. By what name it is distinguished by the Turks, he adds, is unknown to me, for it was always mixed in with *Muscari* <note>Grape Hyacinth</note> bulbs. However, I have named it the *Byzantine Tassel Hyacinth* because of a certain similarity of its tuft and flowers to the Greater Tassel Hyacinth.

<column-break/>

### WHITE TASSEL HYACINTH WITH
->blue stamens.<-
<note>original: "Hyacinthus comosus albus cum cæruleis staminibus"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus comosus albus, featuring a bulb, roots, and a flowering stalk with distinct florets.</image-desc>

Regarding this Hyacinth, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes thus in his Appendix: Of this kind (namely the Tassel Hyacinth), he says, another is found in certain gardens of the Belgians, with flowers indeed similar, but with a white flower decorated inside with blue stamens, etc. And in the *illustration*: Clusius cultivated one not very different from the Byzantine Tassel Hyacinth, both in Belgium and in Vienna, endowed with no tuft or a very tiny one, whose flowers of a faded whitish color closely approach the flowers of the Byzantine one. However, the little stalks supporting the flowers do not grow long; the seed and root agree well enough.

---

### A PLANT RELATED TO HYACINTHS, PERHAPS THE
->Peruvian Wool-bearing bulb.<-
<note>original: "Bulbus Eriophorus Peruvianus"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant related to Hyacinthus, showing a large bulb with fibrous outer layers and a stalk with clustered flowers.</image-desc>

A somewhat thick stem, the stalk of which produces a great number of little four-inch flower-stalks, green around their origin and purple higher up. Each one of them bears a rather large purple flower, similar to the rare flowers of our Hyacinth, consisting of five somewhat long petals, with the tips occupying the middle. Finally, round, somewhat thick *seed* pods succeed them, ending in a point. Furthermore, at the origin of each little stalk, small tongues <note>bracts</note> grow, as in the Star of Bethlehem, long, whitish, and translucent.

<column-break/>

### ELEGANT PERUVIAN HYACINTH.
<note>original: "Hyacinthus Peruvianus elegans"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus Peruvianus elegans, showing a large, scaly bulb and a dense, conical cluster of flowers on a thick stalk.</note>

In Montbéliard, in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, at the beginning of June, the beautiful Peruvian Hyacinth which we paint here bloomed. The leaves are spread almost upon the ground, about a finger's width, nearly sea-green, four inches or a palm long, with a sticky taste. The stem is not much larger than a palm, round, thick, and firm. Countless flowers come forth from the middle of the stem, surrounding it alternately, arising from stalks of nearly three inches, blue or purplish, with six blue tips and a blue style in the middle, beneath which lies the beginning of the seeds.

---

### ANOTHER PERUVIAN HYACINTH.
<note>original: "Hyacinthus Peruvianus alius"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of another variety of Hyacinthus Peruvianus, showing a bulb and a flowering stalk with star-shaped blossoms.</image-desc>

We received this most beautiful dried plant at Lyon from a certain German Baron returning from Spain; he called it the Peruvian Hyacinth. However, one must consider how much this plant differs from Clusius's Peruvian Wool-bearing Bulb pictured before, in whose illustration "tongues" (which Clusius himself calls "appendages") appear on the stalks. Certainly, it has a great agreement with the preceding Hyacinth, if they are not one and the same.

<column-break/>

### ENGLISH OR BELGIAN HYACINTH,
->with a whitish flower.<-
<note>original: "Hyacinthus Anglicus, sive Belgicus"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Hyacinthus Anglicus (Bluebell variety), showing a bulb and a nodding raceme of bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> describes it thus: The leaves, he says, are narrow, oblong, smooth and shining, narrower and smaller than the leaves of a Leek. The stem is devoid of leaves, smooth, and round; its tuft of flowers, weighed down by their weight and mass when they first begin to open, is curved downwards. The flowers are oblong, round, hollow, opening wide, reflected at the edges, mostly blue in color, but sometimes whitish, bright white or snowy, and occasionally representing the diluted purple of a black Violet. The seed in the triangular pods is small and round; the root is bulbous, white, perennial, full of a slow-flowing juice, as is the whole herb.

In Belgium, it grows frequently in the fields and along the edges of the fields; and in England in the grassy glades. —Lobelius.

# OF PLANTS

### SPANISH HYACINTH WITH A DULL-COLORED
### flower, similar to the English variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hyacinthus Hispanicus showing a tall flowering stalk with bell-shaped flowers, long basal leaves, and a bulbous root system with fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It grows naturally, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note>, in certain places in Spain, from where it was first brought into Belgium and bloomed for several friends; from them, through the sharing of seeds, several plants were born to me. It germinates late and keeps its leaves into Autumn: however, it flowers in June along with the Lilies. Indeed, the flowers—even when the seeds are taken from the same head—are seen to be some more dull-colored than others, and some even greenish: such is the varying nature of these plants.

By Camerarius in his *Hortus* it is called *Spanish Hyacinth with a dull flower*: by Lobelius in his *Adversaria*, the *Duller Spanish Hyacinth, with the compressed seed of the Montpellier Pancratium*. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it *Hyacinth 10, or from a pale purple and greenish flower*.

### INDIAN HYACINTH, WITH A TUBEROUS
### root and white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tuberose (Hyacinthus Indicus) featuring a thick, tuberous root, upright stem with small leaves, and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Lobelius in his *Adversaria* calls this a foreign, rare, and distinguished Hyacinth; Clusius calls it an exceedingly rare plant. Because of the very thin filaments—like spider webs—which appear when the leaves clinging to the stalk are broken into small pieces, he thought it was a type of *Eriophoros* <note>literally "wool-bearer" or Cotton-grass</note>, although both the stalk adorned with leaves and the shape of the flowers argue against this. Furthermore, the plant had been sent to him with this inscription: *Indian Bulb producing a white flower, rivaling the flower of the Oriental Hyacinth*.

### STARRY LILY-LEAVED HYACINTH,
### blue.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Starry Hyacinth with broad, lily-like leaves spreading from the base and a central stalk bearing star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This Hyacinth is quite rare, says Lobelius, and elegant; one might aptly call it "Lily-like." For its root and bulb are like a lily's, but smaller and more oblong, yellowish, like that of the Cross-lily or Martagon. The leaves are very similar to the White Lily, six or seven in number, between which springs up a central, bare, leafless stalk a span high, at the top of which are the blue-purple flowers of the Starry Hyacinth.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Hyacinth 5, or with the root and leaves of a Lily*.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER SPANISH HYACINTH,
### narrow-leaved, blue and white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Spanish Hyacinth variety with narrower leaves and two flowering stalks emerging from bulbs.</image-desc>

The same Clusius depicts and describes these in his *Exotica, part 1*, writing that he received from Bordeaux very small bulbs of this Hyacinth, which, when committed to the earth, produced plants with blue flowers and white flowers. They bloomed in the month of June and ripened their seed in July, which was exactly similar in both kinds: namely, round, black, and shining. The same Clusius also had another Hyacinth of the same kind, which was a dilute and pleasant red, with certain deeper-colored rays running along the length of the tips of the petals.

### DALECHAMP’S BROAD-LEAVED HYACINTH,
### with elegant purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Dalechamp's Hyacinth, characterized by broad, ribbed leaves and a dense spike of flowers.</image-desc>

It grows spontaneously in the *Golden* mountain of Auvergne <note>Mont d'Or in France</note>: with a fibrous root similar to a Lily: with six or eight leaves, blackish, thick, broad, almost like a Lily's: with elegant purple flowers, opening bit by bit: with seed in round, herbaceous heads: *History of Lyon*. However, in Dalechamp’s figure, the root does not seem to correspond to the description. We have seen this plant only once, namely at Padua, in the public garden, and the flowers were white.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Hyacinth 18, or the broad-leaved of Dalechamp*.

### TRIPOLI HYACINTH.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tripoli Hyacinth with very slender, grass-like leaves and a few flowers atop a thin stem.</image-desc>

It has long, very thin leaves, similar to our *Phalangium* <note>Spiderwort</note>. The stalk, however, is quite large, at the top of which are four flowers, beautiful in color and size, similar to the three upright petals in a small blue Iris. The roots are similar to Tulips in shape and color. These things says Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a physician and botanist who traveled the Levant</note>, who saw it blooming in Tripoli in April, and writes that it is called *Agur* by the people of Tripoli.

By Camerarius in his *Epitome of Mattioli*, as well as by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called the *Tripoli Hyacinth*.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Hyacinths and related bulbous plants, citing the observations of famous Renaissance botanists like Clusius, Lobelius, and Rauwolf. It details their physical characteristics, origins ranging from Spain to India and Tripoli, and their various Latin botanical synonyms.</summary>
<keywords>Spanish Hyacinth, Tuberose, Starry Hyacinth, Clusius, Lobelius, Dalechamp, Rauwolf, botanical classification, bulbs, medicinal gardens</keywords>

<sig>Dd 2</sig>

### BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE: German: White February-flower; French: White Bells.
<note>original: "Leucoium Bulbosum". This plant is likely the Spring Snowflake (Leucojum vernum).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Leucojum bulbosum (Snowflake) plant showing the bulb, roots, long slender leaves, and a single nodding bell-shaped flower on a stalk.</image-desc>

The Snowflake of which we treat here is not that which is found in the works of Theophrastus, Pliny, and Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek and Roman authorities on natural history</note>; that name denotes not only the *White Violet*, as the meaning of the name suggests, but also other kinds of Violets, which were discussed previously. Rather, this is a bulbous plant, the various species of which we shall describe here.

Among the spring flowers, says Theophrastus, it shows itself first, as soon as the weather has become a little milder, and even before Winter has fully passed.

It grows wild in shady woods and other places, and is also planted in gardens. Near Tübingen, above and below the Monastery of *Bebenhausen*, Leonhart Fuchs <note>A famous 16th-century German botanist</note> writes that it grows most abundantly. We ourselves have seen it at Montbéliard between Audincourt and Mandeure, on the road leading to *Dampierre*, and elsewhere; it flowers in March.

### SMALLER THREE-LEAVED BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Leucojum with three leaves, showing the bulb, roots, and a single flower. To the right, a detail of the flower head and seeds.</image-desc>

The whole plant is smaller than the preceding Snowflake, and it comes forth quite early with it—scarcely, in fact, when the snows have melted, and sometimes even penetrating through them. We have observed it in various places flowering toward the end of February, and we have even had it elegantly unfolding its flowers in December in our garden at Montbéliard.

Charles de l'Écluse <note>original: "Clusius", a highly influential Flemish botanist</note> notes that the flower closes itself at night and opens again with the Sun, even when removed from the earth and kept in heated rooms <note>original: "hypocaustis"</note>.

### MANY-FLOWERED BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE, late-blooming, with smaller flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Leucojum variety with multiple flowers on a single branching stem, showing the bulb and roots.</image-desc>

It is accustomed to sprout later than the Snowflakes mentioned above, and finally produces flowers in the month of May. It is cultivated in the more refined gardens of Germany, the Low Countries, and other places, and sometimes it is even found growing wild in meadows. We had it at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden where it flowered in April and May, and we also saw it at Florence, in the garden of Niccolò of Ferrara.

<column-break/>

### Another illustration of the SIX-LEAVED BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Leucojum with six leaves, showing the bulb, roots, and a single nodding flower.</image-desc>

The bulb of this Snowflake consists of many white layers (though the outermost is dark), and it is hairy with white fibers, having a sticky taste. The leaves are like those of a leek <note>term: "porracea" (leek-like)</note>, numbering three, four, five, or six. The stalk is nine inches long <note>term: "dodrantalis" (a span or nine inches)</note>, angular, streaked, hollow, and bare; it is wrapped together with the leaves, even up to the middle, by a white sheath. The flower has a scent that is not pleasant; it is usually solitary, sometimes in pairs, rarely in threes, nodding, a white rival to a small bell <note>original: "cymbali æmulus"</note>, hanging from a long little stem, with six yellow tips. The flower is followed by a small membrane-like head containing the seeds, which are somewhat dark, rather oblong, and hard.

We present two illustrations, one of which shows the plant beginning to flower, and the other when it produces its seed.

### EARLY BYZANTINE BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Byzantine variety of Leucojum with two broad leaves and a single flower.</image-desc>

This one is two-leaved, but otherwise not unlike the smaller three-leaved Snowflake. According to the report of Clusius, it first began to be brought from Byzantium <note>Istanbul</note> to Vienna in the year 1592; in that same year, it was also sent to him from Naples, having been dug up from Mount Virgineo.

In Caspar Bauhin's *Phytopinax*, it is the *8th Snowflake, or another species of the smaller bulbous kind*; in Lobelius's *Adversaria* part 2, it is the *White-Narcissus-Lily* <note>original: "Leuco-Narcisso-Lyrion"</note>.

### SMALLER AUTUMN BULBOUS SNOWFLAKE, thin-leaved, the Andalusian of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an autumn-flowering Leucojum with very thin leaves and multiple small flowers on a stem.</image-desc>

Clusius once dug up this bulbous Snowflake in the furthest part of Andalusia <note>original: "Baetica"</note>, where it borders Portugal, at the beginning of November. The flower was of a completely milky color.

The *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Lobelius and Pena</note> mentions a blue three-leaved bulbous Snowflake found in Albania.

Fuchs attributes a dispersing and lightly astringent power to the roots of the bulbous Snowflake; but the opinion of those who determine that the bulbous Snowflake is generally of no medicinal use is more approved by us.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of the bulbous Snowflake (Leucojum), detailing their physical characteristics, flowering times, and geographical locations across Europe and the Near East. The author cites prominent contemporary botanists like Fuchs, Clusius, and Bauhin while noting personal observations from gardens in Montbéliard and Florence.</summary>
<keywords>Snowflake, Leucojum bulbosum, botany, 16th-century gardens, Montbéliard, Leonhart Fuchs, Charles de l'Écluse, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal plants, Byzantine flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of bulbous plants, specifically focusing on the Bulbocodium and Pseudo-Narcissus (wild daffodils), following the previous discussions on spring-flowering bulbs.</meta>

### BULBOCODIUM : German: Morning-flowers <note>original: "Mornungs-blumen"</note> : French: Yellow bells, Coquelourdes : Italian: Little bell.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bulbicodium plant showing a single bulb, long slender leaves, and a bell-shaped flower atop a stem.</image-desc>

Codion, as Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), a French physician and botanist</note> says, is the flower of a bulb, bursting forth at the beginning of Spring, and again toward the end of Summer, fleeing both the cold and the winter. From these descriptions, it is easily established what the Bulbocodia are. Various kinds of them are recorded, of which we depict the most common here. It is called the Yellow False-Narcissus by some, and the Common False-Narcissus by others; others call it Campanilla, and Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, the Swiss naturalist</note> calls it Codiaminum.

It is accustomed to grow in meadows, fallow lands, and the borders of fields, in woods and places planted with trees, in moist soil, appearing toward the end of February. Indeed, it abounds nowhere more than in the meadows near London, and on Mount Bar in Montbéliard, and the meadows neighboring that city. That it is also cultivated in gardens is well enough known.

### BULBOCODIUM WITH A FULL OR multiple flower, according to Lobel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bulbicodium with a double or multi-petaled flower (flore pleno).</image-desc>

The Bulbocodium varies most greatly in its flower, says Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist to King James I</note>: for while a single flower usually sits upon each stem, sometimes two are found. The flower is either simple or full <note>meaning "double-flowered," having extra layers of petals</note>: and it is almost always yellow, although sometimes white ones are also found. Furthermore, the same Lobel observed other varieties: that this kind of Bulbocodium sometimes has a larger flower, which is paler and narrower at the tips of the flower petals; and finally, with leaves broader than the rest and slightly curved back.

### A BEAUTIFUL KIND OF BULBOCODIUM WITH A FULL FLOWER : From the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a highly ornate, double-flowered variety of Bulbicodium with broad leaves.</image-desc>

It produces four green leaves from a bulbous root, between which comes forth a smooth, knotless, green stem, a foot high, supporting a thin, skin-like husk at the very top: from which emerges a flower provided with pale petals arranged in a double row, with a cup or oblong tube protruding from its center, having edges somewhat turned back, and these are curled and notched, of a purely golden color: etc. — Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note>.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH BULBOCODIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spanish Bulbicodium variety with a distinct bulb and flower structure.</image-desc>

According to the testimony of Lobel in his *Observations*, it is not unlike the Mountain Narcissus of Theophrastus in appearance, but with broader and larger leaves that are entirely yellow.

It is endowed with a hot and dry temperament <note>referring to the Galenic theory of humors used in medicine</note>, and nearly the same as the Narcissus. Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician</note> says it is proven by certain experience that two drachms of the fresh root, boiled in wine or water with a little <term>zz.</term> <note>An old apothecary abbreviation for ginger (Zingiber)</note> and seeds of Anise or Fennel, purges slow and viscous phlegm through the lower parts. The *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Lobel and Pena</note> asserts that a decoction of the root purges in the manner of the Iris <note>original: "Xyridis"</note>, and that the country folk provoke vomiting with it.

### BULBOCODIUM OR MULTIPLE PSEUDO-NARCISSUS, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a multi-flowered Pseudo-Narcissus with multiple blooms on a single stem structure.</image-desc>

This Bulbocodium, he says, is nourished in gardens, and is similar to the other multiple Bulbocodiums in both leaves and bulb: but the flower lacks a cup <note>the central trumpet</note>, and in its place has innumerable petals similar to the six outer ones, of a pale color.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called Narcissus 22, or the multiple kind lacking a cup: by Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History*, it is called the Yellow False-Narcissus <unclear>gestult</unclear> Joseph's <unclear>stablein</unclear> <note>Likely "Stäblein," meaning "Little Staff of Joseph"</note>.

### CYPRIAN MANY-FLOWERED BULBOCODIUM: or the Yellow Cyprian Narcissus with a full flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyprian variety with multiple flowers emerging from a single bulb.</image-desc>

This very elegant kind of exotic Narcissus is owed, says Clusius, to that excellent London gentleman, Master <term>Leette</term> <note>Nicholas Leate, a prominent London merchant and plant collector</note>, a merchant in Constantinople, who shared its bulbs (brought from the Island of Cyprus with many others) with his friends. In the month of December, it produced leaves a foot long, an inch wide at the base and narrower at the top, and several multiple yellow flowers from a single stem, from a bulb thicker than the bulbs of the Narcissus and covered in a chestnut-colored wrapping.

<summary>This page describes various species of Bulbocodium and Pseudo-Narcissus (wild daffodils), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins ranging from London to Cyprus, and their medicinal uses as purgatives.</summary>
<keywords>Bulbocodium, Pseudo-Narcissus, daffodils, botany, medicinal herbs, London meadows, Cyprus, Nicholas Leate, Clusius, Lobel, purgatives</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of bulbous plants, specifically focusing on small varieties of wild daffodils and related species as categorized by 16th-century botanists.</meta>

-># IMAGES AND OUTLINES.<-
-># THE SMALLER BULBOCODIUM OF CLUSIUS. THE SMALLEST CROWNED BULBOCODIUM.<-
<note>The term "Bulbocodium" was used historically for various small bulbous plants; here it refers to types of wild daffodils or hoop-petticoat narcissus.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with long, narrow leaves and a single nodding flower, showing the bulb and roots.</image-desc>

It is suspected to be one and the same as the *Small Broad-leaved Spanish False-Narcissus*, which in early Spring puts forth three or more leaves, similar in shape and color to the larger variety, but much smaller and narrower: a tiny flower, yet very similar in both shape and color to the larger Spanish type: sitting upon a thin, green stalk the length of a finger, emerging from between the leaves. The flower is followed by a three-sided, yet blunt-angled and almost round *Seed-head*, in which the seed is uneven, black, and quite large in proportion to the plant. The *Root* is bulbous, small, and blackish on the outside.

### THE THIN-LEAVED BULBOCODIUM WITH A YEL-
### low flower, of Clusius.
<note>Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius) was one of the most influential 16th-century botanists.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with thin, grass-like leaves and a bell-shaped flower.</image-desc>

Clusius says that a type of False-Narcissus grows on certain hills of Portugal, which has leaves that are not broad like the previous ones, but very narrow, or rather rush-like. The *Stem* is thin, bare, and a palm's breadth high, at the end of which sits a flower emerging from a sheath; it consists of pale-greenish spreading petals, the center of which is a yellow cup <note>original: "calyx"</note>, provided with edges that are not wavy and fringed like the ones above, but smooth. The *Root* is similar to a small Narcissus, white inside and blackish outside. It was blooming in January when we set out from Lisbon for Spain: and it was called *Campanilla* <note>Spanish for "little bell"</note> by the locals.

### THE BULBOCODIUM, OR FALSE-NARCISSUS
### with a white flower, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with broad leaves and a large, drooping white flower.</image-desc>

From a bulbous root, somewhat oblong and blackish on the outside, it puts forth three leaves, about nine inches long, very similar to the leaves of a Narcissus, and keeled <note>ridged like the bottom of a boat</note> on the upper part: between which comes forth a bare *stem*, slender, nine inches high, bearing a papery *little pouch* <note>original: "folliculum"</note> at the very top, from which hangs a completely white flower, similar in shape to the more common False-Narcissus, but a little smaller: which is followed in a triangular head or casing by round, black, and shining seed.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small bulbous plant with two flowers on long stems.</image-desc>

Is this the *very small kind of False-Narcissus from Pannonia, sent from Spain by the Royal Herbalist of Spain* mentioned by Clusius? Or the *Narcissus 16, or the small yellow one, a very small kind of False-Narcissus of Clusius* in Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax*? Or the *Smallest Crowned Mountain Narcissus* of Lobelius, called *Klein gecroonde Berg Narcisse* <note>Dutch for "Small crowned mountain Narcissus"</note> by the Belgians?

### ANOTHER THIN-LEAVED BULBOCODIUM,
### with a fringed yellow flower, of Lobelius.
<note>Matthias de l'Obel (Lobelius) was a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with thin leaves and a fringed yellow flower.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes that this was brought from the mountains of Biscay <note>a province in northern Spain</note> into Belgium, and was accustomed to be kept and cultivated there in earthenware pots in its season. Clusius, in his later *History*, has an illustration like that of Lobelius under this title: *Thin-leaved False-Narcissus 2, with a yellow flower*, and adds: *The other False-Narcissus with rush-like leaves had slightly thinner leaves, though they were upright: a yellow flower, that is, a cup lightly and thinly fringed along the edges, and those six little petals surrounding the cup were a pale greenish color. After the flower, a somewhat round black seed follows in the Seed-head. The root is tiny, blackish on the outside, bulbous, and secured by thin fibers coming from the base.*

### THE SMALLEST THIN-LEAVED WHITE
### Bulbocodium, of the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small bulbous plant with thin leaves and a white flower.</image-desc>

Clusius writes in his later *History* that he learned from the Spaniards that a certain kind of Narcissus is found in Spain which has entirely rush-like leaves and produces a white flower, and for that reason it is called *Iunquillos blancos* <note>Spanish for "white jonquils"</note>.
It is called *Narcissus 15, or the rush-leaved one with a white flower* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*: and Lobelius also mentions the *Rush-leaved Narcissus with entirely white flowers* in the second part of his *Adversaria*.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of small, bulbous "False-Narcissus" (wild daffodils) found in Spain and Portugal, citing the works of famous botanists Clusius, Lobelius, and Bauhin. It details their physical characteristics, such as leaf shape, flower color, and root structure, while noting local Spanish names like "Campanilla."</summary>
<keywords>Bulbocodium, False-Narcissus, Clusius, Lobelius, Bauhin, Spain, Portugal, botany, bulbs, wildflowers, Iunquillos blancos, Campanilla</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of plants, moving into the genus Narcissus. The catchword from the previous page was "NAR-".</meta>

### NARCISSUS, LIRION : German: Narcissen Roslin : French: Narcisse : Italian & Spanish: Narcisso.

### NARCISSUS WITH PURPLE CENTER, single-flowered.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single-flowered Narcissus with a bulbous root, long slender leaves, and a single bloom showing a distinct central cup.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> describes the Narcissus thus: It brings forth leaves, he says, similar to a Leek, thin, much smaller and narrower. The stalk is hollow and without leaves, rising above nine inches. The flower is white, saffron-colored within, and in some varieties purple. The root is white inside, round and bulbous. The seed is as if in a tunic, black and long.

In the description of the Narcissus, Theophrastus and Dioscorides agree in almost every part. Nor is there any difference in the leaf, although Theophrastus compares it to the Asphodel, while Dioscorides compares it to the Leek: for Dioscorides also attributes the leaf of a Leek to the Asphodel. It was also called <term>Lirion</term> <note>Greek for Lily</note> by both, just like a Lily: although Homer encompasses every kind of flower with the name <term>Lirion</term>.

<column-break/>

The differences of the Narcissi are drawn chiefly from the flowers, which are either single or double, and again either saffron-colored, or purple, or entirely white. That which is called purple, however, is not so all over, but only the center or circle of the flower in it is purple. Pliny adds a "grassy-green" variety, which we have observed nowhere, nor have we read of it being observed by others. The remaining differences which are sought from place, time, leaves, etc., we shall set forth in the following sections.

---

### NARCISSUS WITH PURPLE CENTER, purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus with a darker central cup (corona) and pointed petals.</image-desc>

Regarding the etymology of the Narcissus: the people of Thespiae prattle that the Narcissus was born from a youth seized by love for himself and turned into a flower, pointing out the place where the most foolish boy used to gaze at himself; who, not knowing how to distinguish his own shadow, perished suffocated in those waters, and by the mercy of the Gods was finally turned into a flower, of which Ovid says:
> They find no body, but a saffron flower
> In its place, etc. <note>original: "Nusquam corpus erat, croceum pro corpore florem / Inveniunt, &c." from Metamorphoses</note>

But, as Euellius notes, the very ancient poet Pamphilus refutes this fable, who sang of Proserpina being captured by Pluto many years before Narcissus existed, while she was gathering Narcissi. Therefore, Pliny and Plutarch judge it better said to be from <term>narce</term> <note>Greek: narkē</note>, that is, numbness or torpor, since it weighs down the head.

---

### NARCISSUS WITH SINGLE WHITE FLOWER, double.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered Narcissus (pleno) with multiple layers of petals and a bulbous root.</image-desc>

The best Narcissus grows (according to Dioscorides) in mountainous places, and that one is fragrant: the rest resembles a Leek and gives off a grassy scent. But on the contrary, Theocritus reports in Idyll 19 that the fragrant kind also grows in meadows, where he sings that Europa, having entered the meadows with her girls, plucked the sweet-smelling Narcissus.

According to Dodonaeus, those which are purple-centered come out in most of France, and among the Hedui and Sequani <note>Ancient tribes of Gaul/modern Burgundy and Franche-Comté</note> in the meadows. We have often observed them growing spontaneously in the meadows around Montpellier. Indeed, most Narcissi are today inhabitants of the gardens of Germany, Belgium, England, and France.

---

### NARCISSUS WITH SAFFRON CENTER, thin-leaved, of Lobel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus with very thin, grass-like leaves and a small flower.</image-desc>

All Narcissi are late-blooming, as Theophrastus already noted long ago. Furthermore, the root of the Narcissus, according to Dioscorides, whether it is eaten or drunk, induces vomiting: it is beneficial for burns from fire when ground with honey: it also binds together severed tendons when applied: likewise for sprained ankles and long-standing pains of the joints when ground with honey: it draws out embedded thorns with darnel flour and honey: etc. Pliny attributes the same powers and faculties to it. Indeed, from the flowers of the Narcissus is made <term>Narcissinum Oleum</term> <note>Narcissus Oil; called an ointment by Dioscorides</note> for softening hardness and warming those parts which they claim.

<column-break/>

### NARCISSUS BEARING MANY FLOWERS, yellow-centered, of Narbonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a multi-flowered Narcissus (polyanthos) with several blooms emerging from a single stalk.</image-desc>

Clusius says it grows in most places in Spain which face the Mediterranean Sea, and in almost all the meadows around Montpellier. And he mentions that not far from Villeneuve, a small town near Maguelone, he dug up a bulb whose top stalk sustained sixteen flowers, so that it could deservedly be called <term>polyanthes</term> <note>Greek: many-flowered</note>. It flowers there in February, but among the Belgians not until March and April.

Theophrastus indeed attributes a "quince-yellow" (that is, yellow) flower to the Narcissus: but that is to be understood as being of the center of the flower, which Pliny calls the cup, and which is seen surrounded by white petals, as is clear from Ovid's verse:
> They find a saffron flower in place of a body,
> With white petals surrounding the center. <note>original: "Croceum pro corpore florem / Inveniunt, folijs medium cingentibus albis."</note>

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical and mythological description of various Narcissus species, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides, Pliny, and Ovid. It covers their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for pains and burns, and their geographical distribution across Europe.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### WHITE NARCISSUS, YELLOW IN THE MIDDLE with several flowers.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long leaves, and two flowers blooming from a single stalk.</image-desc>

The leaves are very similar to the white Narcissus, but with a larger stalk; it usually bears two or three whitish flowers, with a <term>corolla</term> <note>the inner circle of petals or the "cup"</note> yellow like ochre.

According to Dodonaeus in his *Latin History*, this is the Narcissus of Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> with a yellow center, which has longer leaves than the purple-centered variety, as well as wider and slightly less green leaves. The stalks are taller and bear two or more flowers on each, similar to the others, but with a yellow middle <term>calyx</term> <note>the cup-shaped part of the flower</note>. The seed and root are as in the other types.

### PISAN YELLOW-CENTERED NARCISSUS, bearing many flowers.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, several long leaves, and a cluster of four flowers at the top of the stalk.</image-desc>

It has broad leaves and very beautiful flowers, with a yellow corolla in the middle. It was sent to Pisa, and some say it was brought from Constantinople. According to Lobelius.

Dodonaeus, in his book on flowers, seems to provide a description of this under the name of the yellow-centered Narcissus—if indeed it is correctly read there as having "smaller flowers." To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is Narcissus 8, or the 4th yellow-centered variety.

### NARCISSUS WITH A LARGE FLOWER, and a full golden crown, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long leaves, and a single large, multi-petaled (double) flower.</image-desc>

Clusius records this as the second Narcissus with a full flower in his *History*, describing it thus: He says the leaves, bulb, and stalk are so similar to the previous [double] one that neither can be distinguished from the other. Only the flowers make the difference; these also emerge from a small sheath sitting atop the stalk, three or four at a time, equal in size to the previous kind and consisting of six white petals. These surround a large, golden-colored cup, which is so wonderfully and intricately folded that they somewhat mimic the many-petaled flower of a yellow <term>Leucoium</term> <note>likely referring to a Wallflower or similar stock</note>. The scent is just as sweet as in the previous one.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER NARCISSUS WITH A SAFFRON-COLORED CENTER and several flowers.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long leaves, and two flowers on a single stalk.</image-desc>

In May, it produces two, three, or four beautiful, large flowers from a single small stem, consisting of six, seven, eight, and sometimes nine petals, so that they appear "full" or double.

For us at Montbéliard, in the <term>S. P. garden</term> <note>likely the Princely Garden of the Duke of Württemberg</note>, an elegant specimen grew in which the flowers were joined with their own stems, creating a very multi-layered flower. Clusius writes that he was told it grows wild in England.

### NARCISSUS WITH MANY FULL FLOWERS and a yellow corolla.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long leaves, and a dense cluster of small, double flowers.</image-desc>

Every year, this was sent from Constantinople to Vienna for Clusius under the name *Zirim cada catamer*. For the Turks are accustomed to calling Narcissi *Serin cade*, that is, the "Royal Cup," because that yellow cup in the middle of the flower represents a chalice in some way.

By Camerarius, it is called the "Exotic Narcissus of Constantinople with full flowers, most fragrant."

### NARCISSUS WITH A SMALLER FLOWER and an entirely yellow crown, also from Clusius.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long leaves, and a cluster of small flowers with distinct centers.</image-desc>

The leaves and all other parts are almost similar to the one above (the two full ones), but a little smaller. The flowers in this variety are also smaller, consisting of white petals; they have a full and yellow middle cup, with somewhat long and narrow small petals springing from the center, arranged like a cross or a star. These are white in color, but mixed with green on the outside and a pale hue on the inside. The scent is almost like the previous one, but breathing something more aromatic—a middle ground between the scent of a Narcissus and a <term>Muscari</term> <note>Grape Hyacinth</note>.

<keywords>Narcissus, botanical history, Carolus Clusius, Rembert Dodoens, Constantinople, double flowers, floral morphology, Montbéliard</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Narcissus varieties, following the descriptions of Narbonne and Mediterranean types. The catchword "NAR-" indicates the continuation of the Narcissus genus.</meta>

### ALL-WHITE NARCISSUS WITH MANY FLOWERS; Described by the same Clusius. <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus plant with multiple white flowers, showing the bulb, roots, long leaves, and a central stalk with several blooms.</image-desc>

It has three or four leaves, very closely resembling the Narbonne Narcissus with the yellow center <note>original: "Narcissi mediolatei Narbonensis"</note>, but greener, longer, and narrower. From the middle of these springs a somewhat broad, angled, and hollow stalk, upon which sit six, seven, and sometimes ten flowers, similar to the previous ones but a little more oblong and entirely snow-white; specifically, that middle cup (which was yellow in the previous kind) is also white. The scent is similar to the previous one, as is the root.

### FLAT RUSH-LEAVED NARCISSUS; with a LARGE cup.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus juncifolius with a large cup-shaped flower, showing the bulb, thin leaves, and a single stalk with two flowers.</image-desc>

This Narcissus was observed by Clusius in the month of April, 1595, laden with its flowers, at the home of Theodorus Clutius <note>Dirck Outgaertsz Cluyt, the first curator of the Leiden botanical garden</note>, the director of the Academy garden in Leiden <note>original: "Lugduni Batavorum"</note>.

Could this be the *Yellow polyanthos Narcissus* mentioned in Camerarius’s *Hortus* <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, author of "Hortus Medicus et Philosophicus"</note>—that is, bearing many flowers on one stalk—which is most impatient of the winter's cruelty and therefore must be kept in an earthenware pot?

### SMALLEST WHITE THIN-LEAVED BULBOCODIUM: Described by Clusius. <note>Bulbocodium refers here to a hoop-petticoat daffodil or similar small bulbous plant.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Bulbocodium plant with very thin leaves and a single bell-shaped flower, showing the bulb and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It has four or five very thin and hair-like leaves, green, trailing on the ground and scattered. Between these emerges a weak little stalk, a palm's breadth high, thin and bare, supporting a single delicate flower at the top coming out of a papery sheath. It is entirely white, very small, and with the edges of the cup fringed. The seed is as in other *Bulbocodiums*, and the root, as in those also, is bulbous and fibrous.

By Lobelius in his *Appendix* and C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called the *Smallest white mountain Narcissus of all*.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW-FLOWERED RUSH-LEAVED NARCISSUS;

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a yellow-flowered Narcissus juncifolius, showing the bulb, thin rush-like leaves, and a stalk with several small flowers.</image-desc>

This has a stalk a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, bare of leaves, at the top of which two or more flowers burst forth from a papery sheath on six-inch stems. They are similar to the flowers of the common Narcissus but smaller, composed of six radiating petals, all yellow. Not only is the oblong tube endowed with this color, but also the crown encircling the middle. A few narrow leaves accompany the stalk, joined in thinness and greenness. The root is bulbous and fibrous.

Clusius observed it in the mountain meadows not far from Toledo; we, however, have possessed and cultivated it in the Botanical Garden <note>original: "S. P." likely referring to "Schola Publica" or a specific academic garden</note> at Montpellier.

### EARLIER SPRING NARCISSUS WITH A YELLOW FLOWER, and the Blue-flowered Narcissus: Described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spring Narcissus, showing the bulb, broad leaves, and a stalk with two drooping flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius depicts the *Earlier Spring Narcissus with a yellow flower* in this way in his *Exotics*. He also mentions in his *Pannonian History* a *Blue Narcissus* sent to him from Spain by the King’s Gardener.

Likewise, men of no small credit asserted to Lobelius and Pena that Narcissi with entirely purple flowers are found near the river Lez <note>original: "Lanum fluuium"</note>, not far from Montpellier; but the same authors record in their *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> that they hunted for them there long and often in vain.

### YELLOW-FLOWERED RUSH-LEAVED NARCISSUS; Also by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of yellow Narcissus juncifolius, showing the bulb, rush-like leaves, and a stalk with multiple flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

We have presented a Narcissus of this kind before; but Clusius describes this one as follows: It has, he says, two or three angled, fleshy, oblong, and almost round leaves, somewhat similar in suppleness and color to the greener and pithy Rushes <note>term: "Iuncis" - Rushes, referring to the Juncus genus</note>, and no less flexible. Between these springs a middle stalk, round, hollow, and adorned with no leaves. At its summit, from a certain thin papery wrapping, three, four, or five flowers come forth, oblong [sometimes in pairs], entirely yellow, and similar in shape to other Narcissi. These are followed by triangular heads <note>seed pods</note> full of black and angled seed. The root is white and covered with blackish membranes, etc.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Narcissus and Bulbocodium, detailing their physical characteristics, flowering habits, and the geographical locations where they were discovered or cultivated by 16th-century botanists like Clusius and Lobelius.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
->Ee<-

### YELLOW OR PALE NARCISSUS, with narrow leaves, from Thrace.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus plant with a bulb, long narrow leaves, and a single six-petaled flower with a central corona.</image-desc>

The leaves are similar to the all-white Narcissus and narrow; the flower is entirely yellow or pale and very fragrant. The <term>seed</term> <note>original: "semine"</note> is like that of other Narcissi, and the root is not very large, covered with reddish-brown tunics. It obtained the name "Thracian" because it is believed to have been first brought from Thrace.

<column-break/>

### WHITE RUSH-LEAVED NARCISSUS, with twisted petals: with a long nodding cup.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender Narcissus with a small bulb, thin rush-like leaves, and a nodding flower with a long cylindrical cup (calyx).</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> depicts this rush-leaved Narcissus in his *Adversaria*, featuring twisted petals and a large, long, nodding <term>cup</term> <note>original: "calyce"</note>, with a slightly protruding, thin pistil.

Is this the same as the "smallest white mountain Narcissus of all" in his Appendix? Or the "smallest white mountain Narcissus with a pipe-like stalk" (Narcissus 10) in Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax*?

<column-break/>

### PERSIAN NARCISSUS WITH A QUINCE-COLORED CROCUS FLOWER, related to the Meadow Saffrons, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Narcissus plants emerging from bulbs, featuring broad leaves and flowers resembling crocuses.</image-desc>

This Narcissus is entirely without a stem, provided only with a flower stalk, just like the Crocus and the Meadow Saffron <note>original: "Colchicum"</note>. The oblong flower emerges from a papery sheath, as if from a small vessel or case, emulating the flower of a Crocus or Meadow Saffron. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneer of modern botany</note> reports it was brought from Constantinople, and he depicts and describes it at length.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER AUTUMNAL NARCISSUS, with a white flower and yellow cup: also from Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Narcissus plants with bulbs; one shows a developing seed pod, the other a six-petaled flower with a small cup.</image-desc>

The illustration we provide skillfully expresses the form and size of the small plant described by Clusius. He labels it the "smallest late-blooming" variety and adds that it is called <term>Tonada</term> by the Spaniards, among whom it is frequently found. Caspar Bauhin, from whom we received it, said it grows on Mount <term>Spiegel</term>.

<column-break/>

### AFRICAN OR EXOTIC NARCISSUS, two-leaved, described by Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus with a large, scaly bulb and two broad, thick leaves emerging from the top.</image-desc>

From a thick and tough root, compressed on both sides, scaly, and appearing as if compacted from kernels, it produces only two leaves, two inches wide or wider, and five inches long, green and smooth. However, according to Lobelius, this foreign bulb—which equals a small fist in size—is provided with the rudiments of two other leaves beneath the earth.

<column-break/>

### AFRICAN NARCISSUS with rounder leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Narcissus with a large bulb and two very broad, rounded leaves spreading horizontally.</image-desc>

In the second part of his *Adversaria*, Lobelius calls this the "African Narcissus with rounder folded leaves." The distinguished gentleman Mr. Jacob de Keiser provided an abundance of these along with the preceding variety. He writes that their bulbs were dug up in places near the Port, or the <term>Cape of Good Hope</term>, and were first brought by him into Belgium.

# PLANTS

### SQUILL, PANCRATIUM: German: *Meer Zvvibel* <note>Sea Onion</note>; French: *Scirpoule, Squille, Oignon marin*; Italian: *Squilla, Scilla*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Scilla (Sea Onion) plant, showing a large bulb with thick roots and long, broad, wavy leaves emerging from the top.</image-desc>

The Squill <note>original: *Scilla*</note> seemed so well known to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> that he felt it did not need to be illustrated. By Theophrastus, however, it is placed among those plants which have multiple and leathery layers in their roots. Pliny divides the Squill into the edible and the medicinal types.

Ruellius identifies two kinds of Squill: the Male with white leaves, and the Female with black <note>darker</note> leaves; he adds a third kind that is pleasant for food and tender in use. Matthiolus and Amatus, on the contrary, think it more agreeable to reason to attribute the black to the male and the white to the female. To Dodonaeus there are two species of Squill: one with narrow leaves, which is the true Squill, and another with broad leaves, which is commonly used for Squill. Pena and Lobel also take two differences from the color: the outermost layers, they say, are reddish in one and white in the other. More on this in the Appendix.

### THE LILY-NARCISSUS, having the appearance of the Montpellier Pancratium or the Valentian Day-lily.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Pancratium plant, featuring a round bulb with roots and a tall stalk topped with several lily-like flowers.</image-desc>

Proceeding here with the history of the Pancratium <note>A genus of bulbous plants in the Amaryllis family</note> in general, we shall add something from Matthiolus. The Pancratium, he says, is called by some the "tiny Squill," because today it is not accepted for use in medicines; therefore it is neglected by Physicians and Apothecaries <note>original: *Seplasiariis*</note>. Hence there are perhaps few who either know it or notice it, even though it grows in various places in Italy, and especially in Apulia, where there is a great abundance of Squills. But even if it is not kept in the Shops, I think no loss is made to medicine, because the larger Squill—which is even more potent—performs its function.

### ANOTHER SPRING INDIAN PANCRATIUM.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of another Pancratium variety, showing a bulb, roots, and a flowering stalk with distinct petals and stamens.</image-desc>

To be associated with the Narcissi, says Lobel in his *Adversaria*, is this Indian bulbous plant with the appearance of the Montpellier Pancratium, endowed with lily-like flowers, for the most part white, but sometimes brownish. It has a great similarity and openness in its leaves and bulbs to the Montpellier Pancratium. The Distinguished Gentleman <note>original: *C. V.* - Clarissimus Vir</note> Johannes Huffenius, Councilor and Prefect of the Maritime Society of Zeeland, etc., gifted me with the bulb.

<column-break/>

### PANCRATIUM, THE MONTPELLIER PANCRATIUM: called by many the small white Squill.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of the Montpellier Pancratium, showing a bulb with long roots and upright, narrow leaves.</image-desc>

The Pancratium obtained its name among the Greeks from "conquering and putting to flight" <note>from Greek *pan* (all) and *kratos* (strength/victory)</note> diseases. Pliny, Dioscorides, and Galen record that it is held to be a type of Squill. Thus also Paulus compared it to the Squill in both appearance and virtues. Among the more recent authors, Cordus makes it a species of Squill, although inferior in power to the larger one. Likewise, Matthiolus writes that the Pancratium is called the "tiny Squill."

However, some call the Pancratium we depict here the "Epimenidian Squill" of Theophrastus and Pliny, but incorrectly; nor are others any better who wish it to be the *Hemerocallis* <note>Day-lily</note> of Dioscorides.

It abounds along that whole shore from the Waters of Maria <note>near modern Maguelone</note> all the way to the maritime parts of the city of Narbonne. It is eaten by the inhabitants of the coast, fishermen, and hungry pirates, but it excites nausea.

### INDIAN PANCRATIUM, OR CLUSIUS’S GREAT AUTUMNAL INDIAN NARCISSUS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Indian Pancratium or Narcissus, showing a large, complex bulb with thick, tangled roots and a flowering head.</image-desc>

The root of this is a span long and as thick as an arm, scaly with many dingy onion-like layers, the outermost skins being reddish-brown or of a dilute chestnut color. The larger seated part is equal to a medium-sized fist, supported by numerous, fleshy, and quite thick fibers, like a Pancratium or Squill, gathered as if into a trunk or node. The flowers are eight or ten in number, star-shaped, equal to the flowers of the English white Meadow Saffron <note>original: *Colchici albi Anglici*</note>, but longer, somewhat lute-like, of a murky white, and endowed with six longer white stamens.

### THE WOOL-BEARING OR LANIFEROUS BULB of Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a wool-bearing bulb plant, showing a tall inflorescence and a bulb with fibrous, wool-like coverings.</image-desc>

Could this be the Wool-bearing Bulb of Theophrastus? He indeed writes of his Wool-bearing Bulb in Book 4, Chapter 13 of his *History of Plants*: "There is a certain kind of bulb growing on shores, which between the outermost bark and the part that is the stalk, has wool, from which small rugs and certain garments are made."

The one we depict here was brought to Clusius from Constantinople under the name of the "Greater Muscari"; he gave it the name "laniferous" <note>wool-bearing</note> because of the abundance of downy hair <note>original: *tomentum*</note>, which can be drawn out into threads in the manner of wool.

Is it the Narcissus of Matthiolus? We saw it at Basel in the garden of Dr. Smielecius; and we ourselves have planted and cultivated it at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden.

It also features the "Wool-bearing Bulb," noted for its fibrous texture used in textiles.</summary>
<keywords>Squill, Sea Onion, Pancratium, Lily-Narcissus, Wool-bearing Bulb, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Pliny, Clusius, botanical classification, medicinal herbs, maritime plants</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### STAR OF BETHLEHEM: German: Little Earth-nut; Belgian: Field Onion; French: Charles; Italian: Hen's Milk.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Ornithogalum plant showing a bulbous root, long slender leaves, and a cluster of star-shaped flowers at the top of a central stalk.</image-desc>

Theophrastus and Galen <note>Ancient Greek authorities on botany and medicine</note> did not know the Star of Bethlehem, nor did their rivals Aelius and Paulus. Pliny calls it *Ornithogalum* <note>original: "Ornithogalum"</note>; but Dioscorides describes it thus: The Star of Bethlehem, he says, is a tender stalk, whitish, thin, a foot and a half tall, with three or four soft shoots joined at the top, from which come forth grass-like flowers, which when they open wide are seen to be milky-white: among which, when <term>cut open</term> <note>original: "dissectu"</note> in the manner of a Safflower, little heads spring out. We depict here the common variety and the one called <term>of the spring</term> <note>original: "veris"</note>, which is either <term>larger</term> or <term>smaller</term>: and it abounds quite copiously in various places in meadows and among cornfields, so that if it is sought in the month of May (these are the words of Mattioli), and the characteristics attributed to it by Dioscorides are weighed, it may be easily found by everyone.

### YELLOW STAR OF BETHLEHEM, or Fuchs’s Wild Bulb: BULBOCODIUM with a full flower.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a yellow Ornithogalum variety, featuring a single bulb, narrow leaves, and a more complex, multi-petaled flower head.</image-desc>

The Yellow Star of Bethlehem is a gift of the spring, quite frequent in various places in Germany around hedges and at the edges of fields: and it is very fond of a warmer sky: nevertheless, We have seen it in the orchards of the city of Lyon.

It has been called <term>Partridge-herb</term> <note>original: "Perdicium"</note>, because Partridges roll themselves in it and dig up the earth; by others <term>Bulbine</term>, by others <term>May Bulb</term>, and by some <term>Edible Bulb</term> <note>original: "Bulbus esculentus"</note>, though how rightly this is done we leave to the learned to examine. There are those who call it <term>Vomiting Bulb</term> <note>original: "Bulbus vomitorium"</note>, because it has been found by use that a decoction of the root stirs up vomiting and powerfully leads the bowels.

However, the image provided here is not of the aforementioned Yellow Star of Bethlehem, but an exceptional variety of the <term>Full-flowered Bulbocodium</term>.

### PALE-FLOWERED STAR OF BETHLEHEM.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a pale-flowered Ornithogalum, showing a bulb with roots and a stem bearing several star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This is not very unlike Fuchs’s Wild Bulb, according to Clusius in his *History of Plants*, Book 7: yet it consists of a larger leaf and a thicker stalk, though a weak one: the two or three flowers which it supports are larger, less yellow, but somewhat pale from a grassy green. It blooms in May. Clusius observed it in the meadows of the Styrian and Austrian Alps, where the forests usually end.

<column-break/>

### PALE BLUE STAR OF BETHLEHEM, and the Lesser Spanish Star of Bethlehem.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a blue/pale Ornithogalum, showing a round bulb and a tall stalk with several flowers.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes in his *Observations* that the plant we depict here is indeed similar to the Autumn Hyacinth: yet in almost every part it is very closely related and akin to the Star of Bethlehem. <term>Could it be Clusius’s Lesser Spanish Star of Bethlehem?</term> He says it blooms in April, and was sent to him from Spain under the label of a Starry Hyacinth with a <term>late-blooming white flower</term>.

Furthermore, the Star of Bethlehem <note>original: "Ornithogalum," from the Greek 'ornis' (bird) and 'gala' (milk)</note> takes its name from the fact that a milky color shines in its flower, similar to that observed in the wings of birds or the eggs of hens.

### SINGLE-LEAFED BULB WITH A WHITE FLOWER: AND concerning the Edible Bulb and the Vomiting Bulb.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a single-leafed bulbous plant with a white flower.</image-desc>

This plant is very rare, according to Clusius, who bought it from a French root-cutter who brought it from Portugal, suspecting it to be <term>THEOPHRASTUS’S BULBINE</term>. Others have given the name of Theophrastus’s Bulbine to the one we gave pictured in the preceding table; and some present the same plant as both the <term>Vomiting</term> and the <term>Edible</term> Bulb of the Ancients. Thus, the opinions of Modern authors concerning these Bulbs of the Ancients are so diverse that it is quite difficult to establish anything certain about them.

Whatever the case: it should be observed generally that all oily roots which have a resemblance to Bulbs—<term>Turnips</term>, <term>Rapes</term>, <term>Onions</term>, <term>Garlic</term>, etc.—were called "Bulbs" by the Ancients: but two specifically: namely the <term>Edible</term> and the <term>Vomiting</term>. More on this in the Appendix and in our great History.

### LESSER YELLOW STAR OF BETHLEHEM.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a smaller yellow Ornithogalum, showing a bulb with fine roots and a stem with small flowers.</image-desc>

It comes forth with a single small leaf, narrow and of a whitish color: the little stalk supports one or two small leaves: from the middle of which two small flowers spring out, star-shaped, yellow inside, and purplish-green on the outside: which are succeeded by tiny triangular heads, full of small and uneven reddish seed. The root is white, round, and covered with an ash-colored husk.

It seems to delight more in a sunny spot, and grows more abundantly in sunny places facing the South.

<summary>This page describes various species of Ornithogalum (Star of Bethlehem), debating their identification against classical texts by Dioscorides and Theophrastus while noting their medicinal properties as emetics.</summary>

### SPIKED STAR OF BETHLEHEM WITH GREENISH FLOWERS: Dodoens’ Bulbous Asphodel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering bulbous plant (Ornithogalum spicatum) with long, narrow leaves and a tall central spike of small flowers.</image-desc>

<margin>
Perhaps the *Hyacinth-like Asphodel* of Galen <note>Galen was a prominent Greek physician whose botanical observations remained influential in the Renaissance</note>: According to Camerarius in the German edition of Mattioli, it is *Galen’s Bulbous Asphodel*.
</margin>

Lobel, in his *Observations*, gives it this name. He says it blooms in the months of May and June, and sometimes even later; among the Belgians, it is found only in gardens. However, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a foundational figure in modern botany</note> writes that it is found frequently among the grain crops in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>.

### SPIKED STAR OF BETHLEHEM WITH WHITE FLOWERS, from Montpellier or Narbonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with a dense, upright spike of white flowers and long, slender leaves.</image-desc>

<margin>
Called by Clusius in his Pannonian history the *Greater Star of Bethlehem of Montpellier*: by Mattioli in his commentary on Dioscorides (with a large figure) the *Other Oriental Hyacinth*. Could it be the *Epimenidium* of Theophrastus?
</margin>

It is abundant in Italy and throughout the Spains, and it also grows in the countryside of Montpellier among the grain fields; it blooms in April and May. Clusius notes it also grew in Vienna from seed sent from Paris; it grew for us as well at Montbéliard in the Prince’s garden, but it must be stored away during the winter.

### CRETAN AND PANNONIAN STAR OF BETHLEHEM, with white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller bulbous plant with a cluster of flowers at the top of the stem and curved leaves at the base.</image-desc>

The bulb is larger than a hazelnut, provided with thin fibers like those in onions. From this, a stem one foot high emerges, bearing flowers at the summit like those of the Greater Star of Bethlehem, but fewer in number, arranged in the manner of a spike. They consist of six petals, green on the outside and white on the inside; in their center is a sort of little ball surrounded by stamens. The seed is small, black, wrinkled, and elegantly marked as if with tiny spider-like punctures; it is round, except for being slightly pointed on one side, hard inside, white, and with a somewhat sweet taste.

It is abundant in the open and grassy places of the mountains in Pannonia.

<column-break/>

### Another Image of the SPIKED STAR OF BETHLEHEM WITH GREENISH FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the first, showing the bulb, roots, leaves, and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

This image, which is among those we purchased, pleases us more than the preceding one in certain respects, especially regarding the spiked flower. Since it depicts the bulb and leaves more accurately, we have decided that both should be retained for that reason. We have often observed this kind of Star of Bethlehem at Geneva, on the hill called *la Bastie*, where it blooms in May.

### THE BYZANTINE STAR OF BETHLEHEM OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with a thick flowering spike and broad, lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

It received the name "Byzantine" because it was brought from Byzantium <note>Constantinople/Istanbul</note> with other bulbs, without any name attached. In the judgment of Clusius, it seems to come very close to the Spiked Star of Bethlehem called "of Montpellier," but it is shorter, and the flowers are less snowy-white. Our illustration, however, does not please us, as it was less skillfully made.

### THE GREAT SYRIAN STAR OF BETHLEHEM: OR THE Lily of Alexandria.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust bulbous plant with a large, dense cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

At the top of the stem, it bears a large flower, equal to a Narcissus with a saffron-colored center, consisting of five <note>original: "quinque," though these plants typically have six</note> radiating petals ending in a blunt point, which are entirely white. The center is occupied by a large *Head* <note>original: "Capitulum"</note>, the beginning of the seed vessel, surrounded by several pointed small tongues <note>referring to the filaments or appendages of the stamens</note>.

Clusius writes that it was brought from Constantinople with other rare plants, adding that it is very sensitive to the cold and cannot endure winters in the garden at all, but must be kept in earthenware pots.

### IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
Ee 3
<meta>catchword: gardens.</meta>

### NEAPOLITAN STAR OF BETHLEHEM, OF CLUSIUS. ASPHODEL, ROYAL STAFF, ALBUCUS: German: Goldwurz <note>Gold-root</note>: French: Asphodel, Royal Axe: Italian: Asphodello

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Ornithogalum neapolitanum, showing a bulbous root system, long linear leaves, and a tall stalk topped with a cluster of bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> received this elegant species of Star of Bethlehem from Naples; he illustrates it in his *Exotic Flora* and describes it at length. He attributes to it three or four leaves, which are long, keeled, green, and narrow: not unlike those of a Hyacinth. From among them emerges a firm stalk, about nine inches <term>dodrantalem | a span or nine inches</term> wide, smooth and green. It supports five or more flowers that hang forward, colored a white-ashy green. These are followed by three-sided seed pods, somewhat thick, ending in a blunt point; their weight causes the stalk to droop. They contain wrinkled black seeds. The root is bulbous and whitening.

### GREATER ASPHODEL, WITH WHITE FLOWERS, Branched: of Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Asphodelus maior, featuring a thick cluster of tuberous roots, long pointed leaves, and a branched flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The Asphodel is a plant wonderful and pleasant to behold when dug up whole, because of the vast number of bulbs that hang from it on all sides. According to Pliny, no other plant is more prolific, having eighty bulbs gathered together at once, resembling moderate-sized turnips. The stalk has two peculiar features: 1. although smooth and narrow, it eventually splits into small branches at the top; 2. it creates worms which, as Theophrastus says, transform into small winged creatures resembling little flowers; finally, when the stalk has matured and withered, they fly out from the eroded seed-vessel.

This Asphodel and the one already mentioned grow wild in the higher rocky places of Portugal, Spain, and France, blooming in March and April; in Germany and Belgium, however, they are kept only in gardens.

### SMALLEST WHITE ASPHODEL, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Asphodelus minimus albus, showing a smaller variety with a single flowering spike and slender leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius calls this a new and late-blooming kind of Asphodel, as it begins to produce flowers at the start of July, when the other kinds have already shed theirs.

Furthermore, regarding Dioscorides' claim that the Asphodel is a plant known to most people, Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius, a Saxon physician and translator of Greek medical texts</note> judges this to be true in Italy; but in Germany, it is not so at all, as few or none there know the Asphodel, and there is no use for it in German waters.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tall Asphodelus plant with a dense, upright spike of flowers and long, sword-like leaves rising from the base.</image-desc>

According to the author Dioscorides, the Asphodel is a plant known to many: it has leaves similar to a large Leek, and a smooth stalk which bears a flower at the top called the <term>Anthericum | the flowering stalk of the asphodel</term>. Beneath are oblong, round roots, similar to acorns, sharp in taste and warming in their properties.

Theophrastus, like almost all the Greeks, called its stalk—which is a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> and often two cubits long—the *Anthericum*; the root, however (that is, the bulbs), they called the *Asphodel*. Our people call the roots *Albucum* and the stalk the *Royal Staff* <note>Latin: Hastula regia</note>. More on this in the following sections.

Since various species of Asphodel are soon to be discussed, the Greater Asphodel with white flowers, non-branched, is depicted here. This illustration is from our own purchased collection.

### LESSER ASPHODEL, WITH WHITE FLOWERS, and hollow leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Asphodelus minor, showing a cluster of thin, tube-like leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Some have distinguished the Asphodel by sex, finding in it Male and Female; others distinguish them by color, size, and the variety of leaves and stalks. Pliny records two kinds: the white, whose stalk is larger than a cubit, pure and smooth; and another, which has a berry-like stalk. However, Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta</note>, being content with one kind, did not distribute it into various species. Marantha recognized four: "Dioscorides," he says, "describes one kind of Asphodel; but we have found three others," etc.

This plant must also be referred to the Class of Asphodels; Clusius writes that it grows wild in many places in the Kingdom of Granada, and also along the paths between Arles and Marseille.

### YELLOW ASPHODEL.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Asphodelus luteus (Yellow Asphodel), showing a thick flowering spike and dense foliage at the base.</image-desc>

Many roots spring from a single head on this plant, but they are much smaller than those of the Greater White Asphodel; they are yellow in color and propagate themselves by fibers stretched out crosswise. The stalk is a cubit and a half tall, single, and adorned from the leaves to the top with Asphodel flowers, but yellow ones. These are followed by seed-vessels containing the seed. The leaves are leek-like and sea-green <note>Latin: glauca</note>, similar to Asphodel leaves, were they not smaller and narrower.

The Ancients made no mention of it, but today it is kept in various cultivated gardens in Germany, Belgium, France, and Italy.

It details their physical characteristics, geographical distribution, and the nomenclature used by different cultures.</summary>

### ENGLISH MARSH YELLOW ASPHODEL,
### with Iris-like leaves, according to Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh asphodel with long, narrow leaves and a spiked flower head, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This plant is handed down by various authors under the name of *Yellow Marsh Asphodel*; girls make their hair blonde by soaking it in a lye made from its flowers. Indeed, land snails pursue the stalk of every *Asphodel* in a wonderful manner, and dry it out by sucking upon it.

Furthermore, as Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "Father of Botany."</note> says, the *Asphodel* has many parts useful for nourishment: for the *Anthericus* <note>The flowering stalk of the asphodel.</note> comes into use as food when lightly toasted by the fire, as does the roasted seed, but most of all the Root. Whence Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet.</note> not undeservedly pronounced those men fools who do not know how much good is in Mallow and Asphodel. The Root, according to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note>, possesses a cleansing and dispersing faculty: it is a great remedy for those suffering from jaundice, etc. The Ancients believed it to be an Amulet against the doom of sorcery when placed before the gates.

### ANOTHER MORE BEAUTIFUL SPIDERWORT,
### conspicuous with the spotless whiteness of a Lily.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spiderwort (Phalangium) with lily-like flowers and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

We call this "more beautiful" in respect to the preceding one, but not in respect to the one following. It grows spontaneously on hills near streams, and is also kept in more cultivated gardens.

By Lobelius, Dodonaeus, and Tabernaemontanus <note>Famous 16th-century botanists.</note> it is called the *unbranched Spiderwort*; by Camerarius, the *Spiderwort with the larger flower*; and by some *Liliago* <note>St. Bernard's Lily</note>, but incorrectly.

It has leaves almost similar to the leaves of the preceding; and almost the same stalk: the flowers are a little larger, white, numerous, representing a spike, which are succeeded by somewhat long little heads <note>seed pods</note>, in which are round seeds. Could this be the *Many-rooted Lily* of Micon?

### CROCUS OR SAFFRON: Germ. Saffran: Belg.
### Saffraen: Fr. Saffron: It. Zaffarano: Arab. Sahafaran.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus plant showing the bulbous root, thin leaves, and flowers.</image-desc>

Antiquity fables that because of the love of the youth *Crocus*, the maiden Smilax was changed into a shrub, and the boy *Crocus* was turned into the flower of his own name. But we pass over these things by design, intending to search out another origin for the Name.

Since, therefore, among the Greeks *Kroke* <note>original: "Crocen"</note> signifies a thread or a tuft of wool—of which sort are the stamens of the Crocus, or those tufts called *Croeides* <note>thread-like</note>, which are seen in the middle of the flower in groups of three or more—and because these alone come into use, the name of *Crocus* is given by excellence to this whole plant. We derive the Latin name from this, though Theophrastus and Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist.</note> establish its nature as being entirely like a pot-herb.

<column-break/>

### THE SPIDERWORT OF THE ANCIENTS, AND IN GENERAL:
### The less-branched Spiderwort with a small white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Phalangium plant with small white flowers and a thick root mass.</image-desc>

Which herb deserves to be called the *Spiderwort* <note>term: Phalangium (from the Greek 'phalangion' for spider), used for plants believed to cure spider bites</note> of the Ancients is not very easy to assert today, whence Matthiolus says: "Even if there is no lack of Herbalists today who substitute certain herbs, whatever they may be, for Spiderwort (as they do for many other unknown plants), and often show them to those little-skilled in herbal matters; I myself, to confess frankly, have not yet seen the True *Spiderwort* in Italy, nor do I know of it being found by others, although I would not deny that it grows there."

However, the one we depict here is both sown in gardens and grows spontaneously on hills situated on slopes near running waters, at Geneva, Lyon, Montbéliard, and elsewhere; it flowers in June and July.

### SPIDERWORT WITH THE LILY FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Phalangium with lily-like flowers and prominent roots.</image-desc>

It is rooted with many long, white, rather thick fibers: the leaves are those of the *Spiderwort*: the stalk is a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, or even smaller, round, smooth, and unbranched: at its summit, large flowers are seen to come forth from short stalks, two, three, or four, similar to small Lilies, and pleasing with the same scent, white, almost two inches long: the seed heads are somewhat long.

We have seen it in the meadows near Burnium, and at Geneva on the wine-growing mountain *Thuri*: and having been brought from there, we have cultivated it in the garden. It flowers in July, and two species of it are held, the *Greater* and the *Lesser*.

Furthermore, *Spiderwort* is praised against every poison.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE CROCUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a different variety of Crocus, showing the flower and bulb.</image-desc>

We bought these images already carved, and neither pleases us in all respects: for which reason we place two, so that what is lacking in one, the other may supply.

Furthermore, the *Crocus* consists of a sweet bulb, the size of a hazelnut, hairy with many fibers: five or eight leaves, a palm or nine inches long, very narrow and striped: among these rises a short stalk, sustaining a single flower, similar to the flower of Meadow Saffron, consisting of blue petals, in the middle of which are several stamens of a flaming redness and very fragrant.

Moreover, the Crocus is either domestic or wild: and both are either *Greater* or *Lesser*: *Vernal* (Spring) or *Autumnal*: thus again they vary in leaves and the color of the flowers.
