# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### BROAD-LEAVED SPRING CROCUS WITH A WHITE FLOWER, variegated with purple veins.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Crocus plants with bulbs, roots, and flowers. The left plant shows a closed bud and an open flower; the right plant shows two open flowers. A small numeral 'I' is placed between them.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> depicts this and describes it at length in his *Later History*; he wonders greatly that he found no genus of Crocus flowering in the spring time in the mountains of Austria, Syria, or Hungary, even though he surveyed them diligently: since, however, the Swiss Alps—even colder than those—nourish several genera of it spontaneously.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER SPRING CROCUS, WITH A NARROWER LEAF, and a smaller purple flower.

In the highest mountains of the Swiss, and in the place called *Jura*, various species of wild Crocus are found, varying chiefly in the color of the flower.

The Turks call the Crocus *Zafran* <note>Saffron</note>, and they add the words *ak, mor, sari*, when they wish to express the colors white, violet, or yellow.

---

### WHITE SPRING CROCUS WITH BLUE EDGES on the side of the leaf, according to Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Crocus plants. The left plant has a single flower and a distinct bulb; the right plant (labeled 'II') shows a flower with striped petals and a bulb with roots.</image-desc>

The leaves sufficiently resemble the leaves of the cultivated and "legitimate" Crocus <note>The Saffron Crocus, *Crocus sativus*</note>, except they are shorter: among them, however, two or three *flowers* come forth, consisting of six pointed petals, which are pale or white, with streaks of dark purple, with the stamens of a mountain Crocus, and a pale *style*. The seed in the triangular heads is round, turning from reddish to white. The root is brown on the outside, white within.

The image marked II represents the broad-leaved white variegated Spring Crocus of Clusius, of which more follows.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED VARIEGATED SPRING CROCUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single Crocus plant with a large, striped flower and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

Clusius proposes two types; namely, with a single flower and with a multiple flower: the former we depict in the preceding table under Number II. The latter, however, Clusius depicts under the title, *Broad-leaved Spring Crocus with a double flower*.

Is this the *Double white wild Crocus, Greater and Lesser* in the *Observations* of Lobelius? Or the *Spring Crocus with a variegated flower* in the garden of Camerarius?

---

### SPRING CROCUS WITH A WHITE FLOWER, variegated with purple streaks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus plant with two flowers showing prominent veins/stripes, and a separate detail of a six-petaled flower head at the bottom left.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> reviews various differences of the domestic Crocus taken from their locations: *Corycian, Lycian, Aegean, Cyrenaic, Thessalian*, etc. Today, however, the Crocus is cultivated everywhere in gardens. Not only the regions to the South—Cyrene, Sicily, France and others—but also those situated to the North—England, Germany, and Austria—possess and cultivate the Crocus, and use it both in foods and in medicines. Ruellius writes that according to the opinion of the Ancients, the best is that which is fresh, with a fragrant odor and golden color, etc. *Concerning the cultivated variety, see what follows.*

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED PURPLE SPRING CROCUS with a variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus plant with a single dark-shaded flower and a bulb with long roots.</image-desc>

It is sown from the bulb of the root, and it puts forth the flower before the leaf, or as Theophrastus and Pliny <note>Classical natural historians</note> have it, it "drives out" the flower with the leaf. It is harmed most of all by mice and moles, which gnaw its bulbs underground. But it loves to be trodden upon and worn down, and it comes forth better by being trampled: therefore it is most lush next to paths and fountains. It ought to be harvested when the middle stamens of the flowers shine with a pleasing color, the "hairs" <note>the stigmas</note> having been pulled from the middle of the flower and dried for three or four days: it must be dried in the shade.

It highlights the plant's transition from a wild mountain flower to a common garden specimen used in both cuisine and medicine.</summary>

### BROAD-LEAVED SPRING CROCUS, with yellow, golden, and pale flowers, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus vernus latifolius plant, showing the bulb, roots, long narrow leaves, and a single upright flower.</image-desc>

Saffron <note>original: "Crocus"</note> warms in the second degree and dries in the first. Its moderate use benefits the brain, makes the senses more vigorous, rouses one from sleep, and creates joy by refreshing the heart. It brings the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine believed governed health.</note> to a state of digestion and blesses the prudent user with many benefits.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED SPRING CROCUS, with a single variegated yellow flower, according to the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus vernus latifolius with a variegated flower, showing the bulb and two flowering stems.</image-desc>

This Crocus varies, as does the following double-flowered variety, in the color of the flower, being more or less intensely yellow or reddish-gold.

Furthermore, to proceed in recounting the uses of Saffron: the Irish people <note>original: "Gens Hybernica"</note> use Saffron in their undergarments to drive away troublesome guests and enemies of rest and sleep—namely, lice—and it cleanses clothes stained with filth; for this reason, it is of no small use in military service.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED SPRING CROCUS, with a double variegated yellow flower, by the same author.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus vernus latifolius with a double variegated flower, showing a large bulb and broad petals.</image-desc>

Saffron has its uses and its harms; for if anyone uses it beyond measure, they will contract paleness and a headache, and it will cause sleeplessness and a loss of appetite for food. Therefore, let its use be meager, not excessive, and let the best be chosen, since nothing feels the frauds of the perfumers <note>original: "Seplasiarum"; referring to the Seplasia, a famous street of ointment-sellers in ancient Capua known for adulterating goods.</note> quite as much. The test of the genuine article is that it should crackle when pressed by the hand, as if brittle, and not give way like something diluted or damp. Then, when the hand is brought to the mouth, it should gently "bite" the face and eyes <note>referring to the pungent, stinging aroma of high-quality saffron</note>.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED SPRING CROCUS, with a blue flower, according to the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus vernus angustifolius, featuring narrower leaves and a curved stem emerging from the bulb.</image-desc>

Clusius proposes three species of this, the smallest of which we depict here. By Lobelius, in his *Images of Plants*, it is called the *Spanish Wild Crocus*, commonly known as the *Greater Notilicha*.

Clusius observed this only at Cadiz, along with two others of this kind, in rugged and open places, flowering in January and February.

<column-break/>

### AUTUMNAL MOUNTAIN CROCUS, with a smaller and paler purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Crocus montanus autumnalis plants, showing slender stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

The flower is like that of the cultivated Saffron, but paler and smaller, with three saffron-colored *stamens* inside, and a yellow style divided at the top into several *small filaments*. It has four leaves similar to those of the Saffron, but shorter. The root is smaller than in the cultivated variety, white, full, and as if distinguished by segments <note>original: "internodiis"</note>, with a somewhat sweet taste.

Among the Belgians, according to Lobelius, it has become a garden plant and a resident, brought from the maritime hills of Portugal, where Clusius observed it, as well as in Vienna, Austria, and Frankfurt am Main.

<column-break/>

### BLUE BYZANTINE MOUNTAIN CROCUS, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus montanus byzantinus, showing a bulb with roots and a flower with distinct petals.</image-desc>

The root of this is the thickness of a finger or even a thumb, nearly orbicular, white, and solid. The flower is odorless, or of a very thin and vanishing scent; the rest is as it is in other kinds of mountain Crocus.

This Crocus was sent to Clusius from Byzantium <note>Modern-day Istanbul</note> by the name *Zaffran maby*, which is to say, "Blue Saffron."

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

<meta>catchword: FE</meta>

### WILD BYZANTINE CROCUS,
Late-blooming white, slightly bluish.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Crocus plant showing the bulb, roots, and two flowers with long stems and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

The entire plant reaches five or six inches in height: it has a delicate little stalk about a palm's breadth high, provided with a small sheath. The flowers are white, variegated with a dilute blue shade, smaller than the flowers of the *Colchicum* <note>Meadow Saffron</note>, composed of six petals with yellow stamens. The root equals a nutmeg in size, or even exceeds it; it is white inside and covered with a brownish bark on the outside. We have observed it blooming in several of the more cultivated gardens of Belgium throughout the entire month of November. There are also other varieties of Crocus: but who could describe them all? Who could unlock all the treasures of wealthy Nature?

### WHITE COLCHICUM WITH PURPLISH
lines.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with a large bulb, fibrous roots, and a single prominent flower with striped petals.</image-desc>

Some distinguish *Colchicum* into *Oriental* and *Occidental*. Others divide it into the *Poisonous* and *inferior* kind which has long roots—this is the *Ephemerum* <note>A name used by ancient authors for short-lived or poisonous plants</note> of Dioscorides, Galen, Paul, and Aetius—and into the *Non-Poisonous* kind, which Mesue says is better and more perfect, and which is properly called *Hermodactylus* <note>literally "Hermes' fingers," a root used in gout medicine</note> in the Apothecary shops. Others have also observed a difference in the flower, which, while commonly purple or flesh-colored, is also occasionally found white. A variety has also been observed in the leaf: broader in the mountains, narrower in the plains. Finally, Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a famous 16th-century herbalist</note> busied himself with discerning the sex, making one *Masculine* and the other *Feminine*: but he neither demonstrates in what way they differ, nor are the Figures very dissimilar.

### ORIENTAL AND SYRIAN COLCHICUM
according to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with a large bulb and a single flower on a long stem.</image-desc>

This comes forth with smaller leaves, narrower and more pointed, with a round stalk, a larger flower, and a bulbous root, evidently split and pregnant with a milky juice: the Italians call it *Zaffarano Orientale* <note>Oriental Saffron</note>. Is it perhaps a *Tulip of the Apennine kind*, as it seems to Clusius?

The *Adversaria* <note>A reference to the botanical work "Stirpium Adversaria Nova" by Pena and L'Obel</note> reports that a certain Venetian Surgeon mixed this *Colchicum* into decoctions of Guaiacum <note>A medicinal wood from the Americas</note> to treat the Venereal Pox <note>Syphilis</note> and other diseases by inducing sweat, to the great benefit and shortcut of the sick: *This is a matter of experiment.*

<column-break/>

### COLCHICUM, EPHEMERUM: German: Autumn-flowers, Meadow-saffron; French: Dog's death, Kill-dog; Italian: Colchico.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with two flowers emerging from a single bulbous root system.</image-desc>

Theophrastus seems to have understood the plant *Ephemerum* only as a deadly one. Dioscorides assigns no lethal power to *Ephemerum*. Pliny considers it not only not destructive, but even healthful. The Mauritanians <note>Arab physicians</note> and the Doctors of the previous age who followed them confused *Ephemerum* (the poisonous *Colchicum*) with *Hermodactylus*.

However, so that all ambiguity may be removed, we, along with the learned, shall make a Threefold *Ephemerum*. Namely, one kind that is lethal and causes strangulation, such as *Colchicum*, which we discuss here. Another that is not strangulating, like our local variety, which we will treat in Class 1 of this Outline. And a Third that is purgative, and safe, such as the Syrian kind, which has the name *Hermodactylus* in the Apothecary shops.

### TWO-FLOWERED COLCHICUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum biflorum showing two flowers emerging from a bulb with dark outer skin.</image-desc>

In Autumn, the *Colchicum* produces a flower like the Crocus, warning us of the approaching Winter, with no leaves at all. Although it usually appears only at the end of Autumn, it nevertheless not infrequently decorates the mown meadows around the Feast of St. James <note>July 25th</note>, and from that time until the end of September it is seen in them. The leaves, however, are produced after the flowers. It grows everywhere in all the meadows of Germany and various other regions, so that few damp meadows are found that do not abound with it.

### SMALL MOUNTAIN COLCHICUM
yellow, called Narcissus by others.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small mountain Colchicum with a flower and emerging leaves from a dark bulb.</image-desc>

It brings forth a naked flower from a thin, skin-like sheath, composed of six oblong and narrow petals, unequal in size, but all of them merely yellowish on the outside, while entirely yellow on the inside, with yellow stamens also in the middle. This flower is fragrant, and resting on a lone stalk, it does not rise high above the ground. When the flower has withered, three or four leaves begin to emerge, narrow, shining, and contrary to the habit of others, twisting themselves. The seed in the small pods is round and black: the root is tiny, covered with a black tunic, and secured at the bottom by thin fibers. Is it a kind of Narcissus?

The author attempts to clarify the confusing historical terminology surrounding "Ephemerum" and "Hermodactylus" used by ancient and medieval physicians.</summary>

# OF PLANTS.

### SPRING COLCHICUM OF CLUSIUS.
<note>Charles de l'Écluse, known as Clusius, was a pioneering 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Colchicum vernum plants showing bulbs, stems, and emerging flowers.</image-desc>

Colchicum is hot and dry in the second degree <note>referring to the Galenic system of humoral medicine</note>. The Arab physicians wrote that its root is useful for those suffering from joint disease <term>gout or arthritis</term>: this is a matter of proven experience, especially if it is applied externally. However, when taken as food, as Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> reports, it kills by strangulation, much like poisonous mushrooms. Those who have eaten it are helped by the same remedies as those who have consumed mushrooms, particularly donkey's milk or cow's milk.

### MANY-FLOWERED WHITE COLCHICUM, variegated with elegant redness.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum polyanthes with a large, multi-petaled flower head and a bulbous root.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> testifies in his *Adversaria* <note>original: "Adversaria," a botanical notebook</note> that this plant is held among the delights of gardens because of the loveliness of its flowers. They are endowed with several rather broad leaves, some entirely white, others truly tinted with a diluted redness, others with a cheerful mix of white and red, divided in half along the length of the leaf, and finally others streaked with white lines in the middle.

### ENGLISH WHITE-FLOWERED COLCHICUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with slender leaves and a single open flower.</image-desc>

Because this plant is mentioned nowhere else by herbalists, and because England produces it most abundantly of its own accord <note>growing wild</note>, and it is not easily found elsewhere, we call it "English," as Lobelius does in his *Adversaria*. It is a very beautiful plant, he adds, with milk-white flowers, larger than those of the Star-of-Bethlehem <note>original: "Ornithogalum"</note> or the Asphodel, and equal to the wild mountain Crocus. The stem is a span and a half high <note>about 12 inches</note>. The root and leaves are otherwise like the common meadow variety.

<column-break/>

### SPRING COLCHICUM OF CAMERARIUS, of a faded purple color.
<note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger was a famous German physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Colchicum vernum specimens, one showing the flower bud and the other the full bloom with bulb.</image-desc>

To drive away and exterminate all kinds of lice, especially the broad ones of the private parts <term>crab lice</term>, the roots of Colchicum are boiled in water, and the affected parts are washed with it.

Indeed, it is a custom among the Turks, when they wish to become intoxicated, to soak Colchicum flowers in wine, which they afterwards drink; from this they are rendered so senseless that they fall as if into an ecstasy.

### MANY-FLOWERED WHITE COLCHICUM, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum polyanthes with multiple long leaves and a cluster of flowers emerging from the bulb.</image-desc>

It brings forth seven, ten, twelve, or even more flowers of a milky whiteness, an elegant sight. The leaves are equal to the leaves of the common Colchicum, but of a paler green. The seed is abundant in loose, triangular heads, and is somewhat reddish. The root is larger than the common bulb. In Autumn, the meadows near Vienna, the capital of Austria, are seen adorned with this kind of Colchicum. —Clusius.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED COLCHICUM, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered Colchicum with a dense, ruffled bloom.</image-desc>

The flower is very similar in color to the common variety, but consisting of many more petals <note>original: "foliis," literally leaves, but referring here to petals</note>, namely twenty or more, very crowded together, of which the six outer ones are larger than the rest, yet narrower than the petals of the common variety: among which are the stamens, as in the common sort, endowed with yellow tips <term>anthers</term>.

It is an elegant and excellent ornament of meadows and gardens.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BYZANTINE BROAD-LEAVED COLCHICUM <note>Meadow Saffron</note> Many-flowered.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with a large bulb, thick roots, and a cluster of several flowers emerging from a single stem.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are very large, differing neither in shape nor size from the leaves of the White Hellebore <note>original: "Hellebori albi"</note>. The flowers are numerous and large, otherwise similar in form and color to the flowers of the common variety. The root is very thick, equaling a fist in size, or even larger. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational figure in modern botany</note> received the bulbs from Constantinople.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER BYZANTINE COLCHICUM with variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with a bulb and a single, multi-petaled flower on a long stem.</image-desc>

It is a late-blooming variety, and later [namely, not until October] than the preceding one, it produces its flowers in twos, threes, or fours; they are small and rest upon a very short stalk, so that they are scarcely raised above the earth.

Clusius received this as a gift from an Illustrious Lady who cultivated it in her highly refined suburban garden near the city of Vienna; he illustrates it and describes it at length.

---

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN COLCHICUM with purple flower: Clusius’s.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with long, narrow leaves and two flowers emerging from the base.</image-desc>

Clusius first unearthed this on the hills near Salamanca <note>in Spain</note> in very stony soil; afterwards, he had it in his garden at Frankfurt am Main, as well as at Leiden, and also at Vienna.

He calls it the Spanish Mountain Colchicum, or the fifth <unclear>under the title</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἐπιγραφῇ</unclear>, meaning "under the heading"</note>; it is called *Merenderas* by the people of Salamanca.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER MOUNTAIN COLCHICUM with variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with three distinct flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This variety does not differ much in its leaves and bulb from the Larger Variegated Mountain Colchicum called "Spanish"; however, it differs in its flowers. The petals of all these flowers are long and narrow, but the inner ones are entirely white, while the outer ones are green in the middle part and somewhat flesh-colored on the other. —Clusius.

---

<column-break/>

### DWARF THIN-LEAVED COLCHICUM: Lobelius’s Galician variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Colchicum plant with very thin, grass-like leaves and a single flower.</image-desc>

He says: We cultivate this new kind of dwarf Colchicum in our garden, brought from Galicia <note>a region in Northwest Spain</note>. It has leaves smaller than the Mountain Crocus, spread upon the ground in groups of two, three, four, or five, being two inches or an inch and a half long. The root is like that of a Colchicum, equaling the kernel of a small hazelnut. The flower emerges together with the leaves, consisting of six narrow purplish petals, and is provided with as many stamens and yellow tips <note>anthers</note>, rising slightly from the earth on a short stalk.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED BYZANTINE COLCHICUM of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant with broad, ribbed leaves spreading at the base and a central flower bud.</image-desc>

It has a thick bulb and very large leaves that lean toward the ground. The flowers are of a color distinguished by white and purple, coming quite close to the color of a Fritillary <note>a bell-shaped flower often with a checkered pattern</note>. However, our illustration shows only the leaves and the bulb.

Is this the same as Clusius’s Portuguese Colchicum, with a color mixed of purple and white? Or is it perhaps the same as his Boissot’s Broad-leaved Colchicum?

<keywords>Colchicum, Meadow Saffron, Carolus Clusius, Matthias de l'Obel, Byzantine flora, Spanish botany, bulbs, botanical illustration, Merenderas</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of bulbous plants, transitioning from Colchicum (meadow saffron) and Hermodactylus to the various species of Tulips. The catchword from the previous page was "Tulipa," indicating the start of this major section.</meta>

### THE YELLOW-FLOWERED COLCHICUM OF SOME. ILLYRIAN OR GREEK COLCHICUM, non-poisonous, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum plant showing the bulb, roots, long leaves, and a single lily-like flower emerging from the center.</image-desc>

This type of Colchicum <note>Meadow Saffron</note> is late-blooming, which some call the Greater Autumn Narcissus, and about which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> writes the following: "Some," he says, "call this plant the Autumn Narcissus, others the yellow-flowered Colchicum, even though it has nothing in common with Colchicum except for the flower, while the rest of its parts belong to the Narcissus. Indeed, if this is to be called a Colchicum, then it would be permissible to call all types of Crocus 'Colchicum' as well." It was brought from Thrace <note>Modern-day Bulgaria/Greece/Turkey region</note> under the name *Cedenfari*.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colchicum Illyricum, similar to the first but with slightly broader leaves and a more robust bulb structure.</image-desc>

Anguillara labels it thus; Lobelius in his *Observations and Icons of Plants* calls it the *Non-poisonous Hermodactyl of the Apothecaries*. To Tabernaemontanus and Gerard, it is the *Illyrian Colchicum*. In the *History of Lyon*, it is the *Illyrian or Greek Colchicum, non-poisonous*, of Anguillara. To Clusius, it is unknown.

---

### HERMODACTYLUS: German: Hermodatteln; French: Hermodattes; Italian: Hermodattilo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Hermodactylus roots, showing two distinct tuberous shapes, one whole and one sliced to show the interior.</image-desc>

It was said before that the Hermodactyl <note>literally "Hermes' Finger"</note> is of the genus *Ephemerum* <note>plants that last only a day</note>, and that one *Ephemerum* is poisonous, another is non-poisonous, and a third is called the Syrian purgative; and finally, the name *Hermodactylus* was bestowed upon this one in the apothecary shops.

The meaning of the name signifies "the finger of Hermes," as witnesses testify; the roots in some way resemble fingers, whence some conclude that the Hermodactyl is the "Theriac" <note>a universal cure or panacea</note> for joint diseases <note>such as gout or arthritis</note>.

However, Mesue <note>an influential Arabic medical scholar</note> identifies two kinds of Hermodactyl: one with a long root which is nothing other than *Behen* <note>Sea Lavender or similar</note>; and another with a round root, which is again twofold: for it either has a root that is black or reddish on the outside, which is the Autumn Colchicum; or it is white, thick, and moderately hard, which is the Hermodactyl of the Apothecaries. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### TULIP OR LILY-NARCISSUS; German: Tulipan; French: Tulipe; Italian: Tulipa.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tulip plant with a large, bell-shaped flower, broad wavy leaves, and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

This foreign plant is rightly numbered among the bulbous plants, most pleasing to everyone on account of the remarkable variety of colors in its flower, about which Posthius wrote:

> It surpasses every kind of flower with its manifold color.
> Hither, the Tulip has been sent from the Gothic ridges.

Many doubt by what name it was called by the Ancients. There are, however, some among the more skilled who think it should be referred to the *Satyrium* of Dioscorides, specifically the one named *Triphyllum* <note>three-leaved</note>, to whose description it certainly conforms in many ways. Others refer it to the Narcissi, others to the Lilies, and others establish it as a certain mixture of Lily and Narcissus, calling it the *Lily-Narcissus*. The common people call it the *Tulip*. *More in the following pages.*

---

### EARLY YELLOW TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Precocious Yellow Tulip" with a slender stem, pointed leaves, and a single upright flower.</image-desc>

Some suspect the Tulip to be the *Potion* of Theophrastus; others wish it to be understood that Homer meant this under the name of *Lotus* when he sings in the *Iliad* of Jove having relations with Juno, with the earth bringing forth Lotus, Crocus, and Hyacinth beneath them.

There are various differences among Tulips, and these are taken either from the *leaves*, which are usually in threes, fours, or more, pointed or narrow, nodding and hanging down or upright, keeled, thick, etc. Or from the *stem*, being more or less long, thick, firm, round, spongy, simple, or multiple. Or from the bulbous *roots*, more or less thick, long, or round. Or from the *flower*, and these are almost innumerable, so much does it vary in color. The principal differences, however, are taken from the *time* of blooming: whence some Tulips are called *Early* <note>original: "Præcoces"</note>, others <unclear>Late-blooming</unclear> <note>original: "Serotinæ"</note>, and others "Doubtful."

<column-break/>

### EARLY RED TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Precocious Red Tulip" showing the flower in full bloom with distinct petal markings.</image-desc>

The color of the Red Tulip is sometimes more golden, sometimes paler and of a most pleasing appearance; occasionally it is even inelegant and faded. The "claws" <note>the base of the petals</note> of the leaves are either entirely yellow, or as if sprinkled with a light soot upon the yellow. In some, a black spot stains only the middle of the yellow claw; in others, it occupies almost the whole part, so that nothing is seen except a certain yellow line surrounding the black claw. Sometimes those claws are so large that they occupy half the petal. The scent of the whole flower is otherwise pleasant, like a golden apple <note>likely an orange or citrus</note>, but for the most part, it is very faint, or smelling of the wild poppy. And those variations observed in this Tulip are also found in others, or similar ones.

<summary>This page describes various species of Colchicum and Hermodactylus before introducing the Tulip, discussing its botanical classification, its possible mentions in ancient Greek literature (Homer and Theophrastus), and its physical variations.</summary>
<keywords>Colchicum, Hermodactylus, Tulip, Lily-Narcissus, Autumn Narcissus, Clusius, Dioscorides, botany, medicinal roots, flower varieties</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### EARLY WHITE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a single flower, a bulb with roots, and long, slightly curved leaves. The flower is shown in full bloom.</image-desc>

The earlier Tulip bears a single stem, mostly a foot long, sometimes larger, round, green, and sprinkled with a certain short and grayish down; it is not hollow, but filled with a firm pith. The flower, moreover, is entirely white: only the three outer petals seem to have something of a grayish or sometimes even a bluish color mixed on the back. The claws <note>The "claw" or *unguis* is the narrow base of a petal where it attaches to the stem.</note> are yellow, and sometimes as if sprinkled with soot. The tips and stamens are pale.

<column-break/>

### EARLY PURPLE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip similar to the first, but with slightly more pointed petals and a distinct bulb structure.</image-desc>

Three leaves usually embrace the stem of the early Tulip: sometimes four or five. The lower ones are quite broad and Lily-like, yet longer and thicker, keeled <note>original: *carinata*; shaped like the hull of a ship</note>, spreading themselves out above the ground and twisting. The upper leaves, however, are smaller and narrower, and these are either hanging and nodding, or upright. All of them are of a color between blue-green or copper-rust, and as if sprinkled with flour <note>A description of the "glaucous" or waxy, powdery coating found on tulip leaves.</note>.

---

### EARLY VARIEGATED YELLOW TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a more open flower head and seeds or small petals falling from the bloom.</image-desc>

A single large flower sits at the top of the stem of the Early Tulips (sometimes twins are also found, either growing joined at the top of the stem, or attached to a cleft stem), looking upward, consisting for the most part of six petals, and sometimes seven or eight. At the beginning, it is the same color as the stem, and sometimes it bends itself toward the ground and rests upon it, so that it mimics the head of a viper or a snake lying on the ground: then, it gradually raises itself and changes color, and finally unfolding itself, it opens at the bottom like a basket or a drinking cup.

<column-break/>

### EARLY VARIEGATED RED TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a tall stem and a flower that appears to have variegated or striped petals.</image-desc>

As many petals as the flower of this kind of Tulip consists of, just as many stamens come forth from its base—sometimes pale yellow, sometimes blackish. The filaments <note>original: *pediculi*; the stalks supporting the anthers</note> which support the stamens also vary in a wonderful manner. Furthermore, the outer petals of the flower are commonly pointed for the most part, while the inner ones are rounded: and usually both are provided with large edges, shining with the brightness of gold. We cannot describe the rest of the variety of colors here.

---

### EARLY VARIEGATED WHITE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a drooping leaf and a prominent bulb.</image-desc>

After the flower has been shaken off, there follows a large, somewhat oblong or shorter seed-vessel <note>original: *Capsulatis*</note>, triangular and membranous, with a more prominent belly. When this gapes open into three parts from the top, six rows of seeds are seen, full, cartilaginous, almost like those of a Lily, and sometimes of a nearly perfect circular roundness. On the other side, however, which reaches the center and interior of the head, they are mostly somewhat oblong, pale, tawny or reddish, and if the rains have been more frequent, even dark brown.

<column-break/>

### EARLY VARIEGATED PURPLE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a sturdy stem and a flower head showing detailed petal layering.</image-desc>

The root of these Tulips is bulbous, sometimes shorter, sometimes more oblong: with the inner seat somewhat protruding, almost like the root of a Meadow Saffron <note>original: *Colchici*</note>. It is gifted with several thin fibers [roots], and covered on the outside by a brownish or blackish membrane. Sometimes it is full of a very thick woolly down, so that the Bulb rests very softly. The bulb is solid, firm, and white like the white of a boiled egg, and to the taster it is sweet, or at least not unpleasant.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions of various early-blooming tulip varieties, categorized by color (white, purple, yellow, red). It documents their physical characteristics from the bulb and leaves to the seed-vessel and petals.</summary>
<keywords>Tulipa Præcox, early tulips, botanical illustration, bulb anatomy, seed pods, floral morphology, 16th-century botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical classification of tulips, moving from the early-blooming varieties discussed on the previous page to the late-blooming and "doubtful" intermediate varieties.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### VARIEGATED AMETHYST EARLY TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an early-blooming tulip with a single flower, showing the bulb, roots, and leaves.</image-desc>

Finally, there is the greatest variety of color in the early tulip, so much so that a greater variety is hardly observed in any other flower. For it is either entirely yellow, or red, or white, or purple: and sometimes even two or more of these colors are seen mixed together in the same flower. Nor are there lacking those who claim to have seen some of an entirely blue color <note>Blue tulips were a legendary "holy grail" for early botanists, though true blue tulips do not exist in nature.</note>.

Thus far concerning the nature and varieties of Early Tulips: now concerning the Late-blooming ones.

### SMALLER MULTI-BRANCHED LATE TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a late-blooming tulip with multiple flower heads on a single stalk (polyclonos), including bulb and roots.</image-desc>

At the top of the stalk of the late-blooming Tulips sits a single large and oblong flower, concave in the manner of a cup <note>original: "cyathimodo"</note>, consisting of six petals <note>original: "foliis," literally leaves, but referring here to petals</note>, with the very tip being entirely pointed or rounded: or with only the three outer ones pointed and the inner ones rounded, as in the Early variety, and vice versa. The flower is followed by a triangular seed-head, parchment-like, usually thicker and with a somewhat protruding belly; when this opens from the top, six rows of flat, gristly seeds are seen, tawny or reddish, larger than in the Early variety.

### CONCERNING THE SO-CALLED "MIDDLE" TULIPS, THE FIRST GREAT DOUBTFUL TULIP OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "doubtful" tulip variety, showing the flower, stem, and bulb.</image-desc>

The tulips that bloom in the time between the Early and the Late-blooming: those which unfold their blossoms as the flowers of the Early ones are withering, and which are already growing old when the late ones begin to bloom—indeed, sometimes they even bloom alongside them—can in a certain way be called "Doubtful" <note>term: "Tulipa Dubia" (Doubtful Tulip). These were intermediate varieties that Carolus Clusius, the famous botanist, found difficult to categorize strictly as early or late.</note>, since they reflect the nature of both kinds. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### THE LATE TULIP IN GENERAL, THE LATE TULIP WHICH HAS 4 LEAVES ON THE STALK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a late-blooming tulip with four leaves on the stem, showing the bulb and roots.</image-desc>

The Late Tulip is of greater size, for it has a stalk a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or three feet high, firmer, thicker, round, full of spongy material, and even sprinkled with a short and grayish down, or a certain bloom. This stalk is clasped alternately by usually four leaves, sometimes five or six, which are keeled <note>v-shaped like the hull of a ship</note>, firmer than in the Early variety, and for the most part upright, not nodding or bent toward the ground: and with the edges sometimes so turned back that they appear wavy, though sometimes they are all uniform.

### THE GREATER MULTI-BRANCHED LATE TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger late-blooming tulip with multiple flower heads (polyclonos <note>from Greek: "many-branched"</note>).</image-desc>

The root of the Late-blooming tulips is similar to the root of the Early ones, but it consists of a longer and larger bulb, generally agreeing with them in other respects.

Just as the Early tulip usually consists of a single stalk, the late one sometimes has a multi-branched and ramified one: and of this kind, one is the *Greater* which we depict here, and the other is the *Smaller*, presented in the preceding table.

### THE SECOND GREAT DOUBTFUL TULIP OF THE SAME AUTHOR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another "doubtful" tulip variety, showing the flower and bulb.</image-desc>

There are among those called "Middle" tulips some whose flowers and the plant itself equal the size of the Late-blooming ones: but others which do not exceed the Early ones, nor are they different from them in form. And these are indeed either endowed with very large flowers, or ones no larger than the Early variety: and there are even some lower than the early ones. We neither wish nor are we able to express the infinite variety of colors here; let the reader consult the *History, number 106* <note>A reference to Carolus Clusius's "Rariorum plantarum historia" (1601).</note>.

<summary>This page categorizes various tulip species by their blooming periods—Early, Late, and "Doubtful" (mid-season)—detailing their physical characteristics such as stalk height, leaf structure, and seed pods.</summary>
<keywords>Early Tulip, Late Tulip, Doubtful Tulip, Carolus Clusius, botany, bulbous plants, multi-branched tulips, floral morphology</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE SECOND MEDIUM TULIP, the first medium of Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a single large flower, a long stem, and one prominent leaf, showing the bulb and roots at the base.</image-desc>

It has a flower of an elegant yellow color, of which all the petals are pointed, with black "claws" <note>The 'unguis' or claw is the base of the petal where it attaches to the stem</note>, black tips, and stems stained as if with soot.

This illustration by Clusius is also found in the *Book of Plant Images* with this inscription: *White Lily-Narcissus, with sweetly reddening edges.*

<column-break/>

### THE THIRD DUBIOUS TULIP, THE SECOND MEDIUM OF THE SAME, with a flower equal to the early-blooming ones.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a closed flower head, two leaves on the stem, and a bulb with roots.</image-desc>

Of the *Dubious Medium* tulips, whose flowers are equal to the Early-blooming ones: their stems are also of the same size as those stems, and sometimes equal the height of the Greater Dubious tulips. There are many kinds; it is more difficult to distinguish their differences than those of the Early ones, so varied is the confused mixture of colors throughout the flowers.

---

<column-break/>

### THE SECOND DUBIOUS MEDIUM TULIP, VARIEGATED.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with an open, star-shaped flower, two broad leaves, and a bulb with roots.</image-desc>

We have reviewed the various mixtures of this type in our great *History* <note>Likely referring to the author's larger botanical compendium</note> based on Clusius; he writes that every year some new kind of tulip, never seen before, is born. *Thus God shows His admirable power even in these flowers.*

<column-break/>

### THE BULB-BEARING TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip plant featuring small bulblets (bulbils) growing in the leaf axils along the stem, with a bulb at the base.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a famous German herbalist</note> also has this one, labeling it the *Bulb-bearing Tulip*, and in German *Narcissus-Lily*. Schwenkfeld also calls it the *Bulb-bearing Tulip*, and the *Bulb-carrying Lily-Narcissus*. We present the illustration of Clusius, who relates that a certain merchant of Antwerp received a large number of these bulbs from a friend in Constantinople along with some linen cloths. Since he was ignorant of their use and excellence, and thinking they were onions, he ordered them to be prepared for him under the coals, and ate them with oil and vinegar in the manner of common onions.

---

<column-break/>

### YELLOW TULIP WITH BLUNT PETALS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a cup-shaped flower, two leaves, and a bulb with roots.</image-desc>

The illustration placed by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist</note> in his *Observations*, page 65, corresponds best to this under the title: *All-yellow Chalcedonian Narcissus, equal to blood-red.* Is this the kind of tulip from the *History of Lyon* <note>The 'Historia Plantarum Lugdunensis' (1586)</note> which the Greek commoners call *Oulandia*? Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a major Flemish physician and botanist</note> in his *Book of Flowers* uses its image for the tulip in general. Indeed, it often grows for us at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden.

<column-break/>

### PHOENICIAN YELLOW-EDGED TULIP, with a spreading flower.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tulip with a wide, open flower, two leaves, and a bulb with roots.</image-desc>

Lobelius records this under the title *Phoenician Narcissus with yellow edges, spreading flower*: but the *History of Lyon* records it under the title *Yellow Tulip*.

As for what pertains to the *powers and properties* <note>The medicinal or pharmacological uses</note> of Tulips, as Dodonaeus writes, nothing certain has been discovered so far. However, Clusius reports that some have preserved tulip bulbs like the roots of Orchids, and found them quite pleasant and agreeable to the palate. Whether they truly provide what is attributed to the *Satyrium* <note>A plant believed in antiquity to be a powerful aphrodisiac</note>, he does not know.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of "Medium" and "Dubious" tulips, citing major 16th-century botanists and including a humorous anecdote about an Antwerp merchant eating tulip bulbs like onions. It also notes the lack of known medicinal properties, though mentions their potential use as an aphrodisiac.</summary>
<keywords>Tulip, Carolus Clusius, Matthias de l'Obel, Rembert Dodoens, bulbifera, botany, Constantinople, horticulture, medicinal plants, aphrodisiacs</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### THE SCARLET OR CRIMSON GLOWING TULIP.
### For Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a famous Flemish botanist whose Latinized name was Lobelius.</note> it is the Scarlet or Crimson glowing Lily-Narcissus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tulip with a long stem, pointed petals, and a bulb with roots. A small asterisk is placed near the base of the stem.</image-desc>

Furthermore (to fill this empty space), not all flowers endure equally long in the elegance and beauty of their color; indeed, the more fragile parts of some wither quickly, while those of others are firmer and retain the grace of their color longer, especially the late-blooming and "doubtful" <note>The author uses "dubiae" (doubtful/uncertain) to categorize tulips that bloom between the early and late seasons.</note> varieties. Certainly, all of them contract themselves when the sky is cloudy and are easily ruined by rain, and vice versa.

<column-break/>

### THE SCARLET TULIP WITH WHITE EDGES, LILY-
### Narcissus with white edges, according to Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tulip similar to the first, but with slightly broader petals and a distinct bulb. A small asterisk is placed near the base of the stem.</image-desc>

Nor indeed, to proceed with what was just said, do all the multicolored ones—both the early and the late-blooming—perpetually retain the same grace of color every year, but we have observed them to vary in alternating years.

In the Book of Illustrations by Plantin <note>Christophe Plantin, the famous printer of Antwerp.</note> on page 230, the illustration presented here is found with this inscription: Scarlet Lily-Narcissus with white edges.

---

### THE ENTIRELY SNOW-WHITE TULIP: OR THE
### Entirely snow-white Lily-Narcissus, of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tulip with two flowers on one stem, showing a closed bud and an open bloom.</image-desc>

None among the early tulips is more fertile than the red and the white; however, the most fertile is the late-blooming red, which is so prolific that even when grown from seed and scarcely two years old, it generates other offspring two or three years before it begins to flower—which some of the *Doubtful* ones also do.

Moreover, all tulips, while not yet mature and before they begin to produce a flower, usually tend to descend deeper every year in a straight line, as if by a plumb line, to a depth of nine inches or a span. We except, however, the Apennine tulips and some others, which do not descend deeply but rather to the side and at an angle.

<column-break/>

### THE TULIP WITH MINGLED WHITE AND RED;
### Lily-Narcissus with mingled white and red: of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tulip with a single large flower and broad leaves.</image-desc>

All tulips, of whatever kind they may be, as long as they do not bear a flower, produce no stalk, and are accustomed to produce a single leaf each year; but if, when it has emerged and begins to unfold itself, a second leaf appears enclosed within it, there is hope that the plant will produce a flower that very year.

---

### THE DWARF DOUBTFUL TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller tulip variety with a single flower and a prominent bulb.</image-desc>

It does not exceed a foot in height; indeed, for the most part, it stays below that, closely approaching the Early tulip in its leaves and flower.

Furthermore, the spring sowing of all tulips is almost useless because, as has been said, many tulips sink deep into the ground and are thus lost. I have known of some who place stone slabs beneath the bulbs <note>A horticultural trick to prevent the "dropper" bulbs from burrowing too deep into the soil to be recovered.</note>.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER DWARF TULIP.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another small tulip variety with a slightly different petal shape and bulb structure.</image-desc>

The propagation of tulips from seeds is plainly uncertain in the *early* and *doubtful* kinds; the *late-blooming* ones, however, seem for the most part to preserve their type, and can be propagated from seeds.

Moreover, no region is more fertile for tulips than Thrace <note>A historical region in the Balkans, then part of the Ottoman Empire.</note>, in which they bloom even in the middle of winter; just as Ogier de Busbecq <note>The Flemish diplomat who famously introduced tulips from the Ottoman court to Europe.</note> reports that he observed a vast abundance of tulips there in the month of January during his journey to Constantinople.

<summary>This page describes various tulip species, including scarlet, white, and dwarf varieties, while offering horticultural observations on their growth habits and propagation. It highlights the role of botanists like Lobelius and the diplomat Busbecq in the study and dispersal of these flowers.</summary>
<keywords>Tulip, Lily-Narcissus, Lobelius, Plantin, Thrace, Busbecq, botany, bulbs, horticulture, scarlet tulip, dwarf tulip</keywords>

--- Page 297 ---
### SMALL YELLOW TULIP OF NARBONNE.
->Yellow Lily-Narcissus of the mountains, according to Lobelius.<- <note>Lobelius refers to Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a small tulip with a single flower, long slender leaves, and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

The smaller Tulips have narrower leaves, almost like those of a leek <note>original: "potraceis"</note>, with thinner and shorter stems, and smaller flowers that do not spread out in width at all. The bulbs are also smaller. Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a famous Flemish herbalist.</note> writes that it grows wild in Italy and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW TULIP OF BOLOGNA.
->Yellow Lily-Narcissus of Bologna, from the History of Lyon.<- <note>Refers to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a tulip with a larger flower, broader leaves, and a detailed bulb showing offsets and roots. To the left of the main plant are two smaller sketches of the bulb and seed pod.</image-desc>

The stem usually breaks out from the middle of the bulb: but when the stem and leaves are already withered and dried, if you dig up the bulb, you will see a new bulb born at its sides (which also happens in the bulbous Iris <note>original: "Inde bulbosa"</note>, Meadow Saffron <note>Colchicum</note>, and related plants) gradually growing up and receiving the sap of the whole plant for itself, at which time it can be dug up most conveniently.

The excavated bulb can be kept out of the ground for a long time and can be transferred to other places, even far distant ones, without harm.

---

### DWARF NARROW-LEAVED WHITE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a dwarf tulip with a star-shaped flower and two broad leaves emerging from a bulb. A separate sketch of the bulb is shown to the right.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes in his *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work published in 1570.</note> that this is held in the highest esteem and is diligently cultivated. The flower has six petals <note>original: "foliorum"</note> and is white: the three inner ones are a brilliant white and broader, while the three outer ones are narrower; likewise white on the inside, but reddish-brown on the outside. The leaves are narrow, five or six in number, lying flat on the ground: the stem is higher than a palm's breadth: the root equals the bulb of the Bologna Tulip in size and is brownish on the outside.

<column-break/>

### DWARF WHITE PORTUGUESE TULIP.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a dwarf tulip with a single upright flower and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This flower is dry and white, provided with six small petals and as many stamens. The bulb is very small, in the likeness of other Tulips, covered with a hard, scaly husk. It grows wild on the mountain near St. *Ove* <note>Likely a reference to a local Portuguese landmark or chapel.</note> by the sea shores.

Concerning the powers and medicinal properties <note>original: "viribus & facultatibus"</note> of Tulips, nothing has been discovered by anyone up to this point. —Dodoens.

---

### THE "SATYRIUM ERYTHRONIUM" OF SOME:
->The "Dog's Tooth" species to others.<- <note>Now known as Erythronium dens-canis, the Dog's-tooth violet.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with mottled leaves and a nodding flower. Below the plant are detailed sketches of the seed pods and roots.</image-desc>

The root of this is white, somewhat thick, and two inches long: the leaves are usually in pairs, rarely in threes (sometimes there is only one), somewhat round, ending in a point, and variegated with purplish spots. There is a single small stem, smooth, rounded, and a palm's breadth high. The flower is single, nodding downward, purple or white, or a pale mixture of purple and white. It is followed by a triangular head <note>seed capsule</note> of a greenish-brown color, containing somewhat oblong seeds of a yellowish hue.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE THREE-LEAVED SATYRIUM ERYTHRONIUM.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a similar Satyrium species with a nodding flower and distinct root structure.</image-desc>

This kind of Satyrium is called *Hermodactylus* <note>Finger of Hermes</note> by some, and *Pseudo-Hermodactylus* by others: Dodoens calls it *Dens caninus* <note>Dog's tooth</note>: Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a central figure in 16th-century botany.</note> in his Pannonian history calls it *Dentalis 1, or the purple-flowered*, and *Dentalis 2, or the milk-white flowered*.

The purple-flowered variety grows abundantly at the base of certain mountains in grassy soil. We have observed the white-flowered variety in various places—Lyon, Bologna, Geneva, and elsewhere—both in gardens and on grassy hills.

<summary>This page describes various species of small and dwarf tulips from Italy, France, and Portugal, as well as the Erythronium (Dog's-tooth violet). It notes their physical characteristics, growth habits, and the lack of known medicinal uses for tulips at the time.</summary>
<keywords>Tulips, Erythronium, Dog's-tooth violet, botany, bulb cultivation, Dodoens, Lobelius, Clusius, Narbonne, Bologna, Portugal</keywords>

### ILLUSTRATION OF THE TWO-LEAVED RED SATYRIUM.
<note>original: "Satyrii Erithronii Bifolii". Likely Erythronium dens-canis, known today as the Dog's-tooth violet.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Satyrium Erithronium plant, showing two broad leaves at the base, a slender stem, and a single lily-like flower at the top with a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

We present three illustrations of this Satyrium, of which the last two, which we purchased already engraved, do not entirely please us. Nor do the illustrations by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> or those in the *History of Lyon* satisfy us; but the one by Mattioli is truly the worst. However, Camerarius, in his commentary on Mattioli, provides a beautiful one under the titles of *Pseudo-Hermodactyl* and *Horse-tooth*.

Furthermore, the powder of this so-called Red Satyrium, when sprinkled into porridges, kills and expels intestinal worms in children. Drunk in wine, it mitigates the pains of colic, nourishes, and restores the body's strength; taken in water, it helps children suffering from epilepsy. Lobelius writes that this Satyrium is extremely effective for arousing sexual desire <note>original: "ad excitandam Venerem"</note>.

We treat the Satyriums in general elsewhere.

### THE MELEAGRIS OR FRITILLARY, paler and less showy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Fritillaria plant with a checkered, bell-shaped flower hanging downwards, narrow leaves, and a bulb.</image-desc>

Following the example of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary figure in 16th-century botany</note>, we provide a double illustration of the common Fritillary: the more deeply colored one mentioned before, and the paler one described here, which we depict as being less showy and blooming later. For this flower is either very early-blooming, early, or late-blooming.

It is sown in gardens and grows spontaneously in the meadows of Saintonge, Poitou, and other parts of France, and is also found in the Northern provinces.

### THE AQUITANIAN MELEAGRIS OR FRITILLARY, with reflexed edges, late-blooming, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Aquitanian Fritillaria with a nodding flower, the petals of which are slightly reflexed at the edges.</image-desc>

The flower of this plant consists of six petals; on the outside, all are marked from the base of the petal to the outer edges with streaks of dull purple, beneath which is a bit of yellow. On the inside, however, they possess a color of pale green, like a green silk cloth with a yellow weft.

Plants of this genus were called *Fritillaria* because of their resemblance to a *fritillus* <note>a dice-box, referring to the checkered pattern on the petals</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE MELEAGRIS or FRITILLARY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Meleagris (Fritillaria) plant with a large, checkered, bell-shaped flower and long, thin leaves.</image-desc>

This plant obtained the name *Meleagris* because its petals are painted with various colors, like the feathers of the Meleagris bird, which the common people usually call the Guinea hen or the Barbary partridge. Others call it *Fritillaria* because its multicolored checkered squares somewhat rival a dice-board <note>original: "Fritillum"</note>.

Those who extend the name of Narcissus broadly refer to it not only the Tulip, but also the Meleagris, which is more similar to Tulips than to Narcissi. It is called by Lobelius the *Fritillaria*, or the *Lily-Narcissus*, variegated by a skillful mixture, checkered, black, or either a deep or pale purple.

### THE PYRENEAN MELEAGRIS OR FRITILLARY, with a smaller flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pyrenean Fritillaria with a smaller nodding flower and a separate detail of the seed pod/bulb.</image-desc>

This plant has a slender green stalk about a foot high, surrounded by six or seven leaves of a grayish-green, much like those in other Fritillaries. At its summit grows a flower smaller than that of other Fritillaries, consisting of six petals, of a dull color on the outside, but on the inside yellowish-green and shining, with many deep purple spots arranged in a checkered pattern. From the center <note>original: "umbilico"</note> emerge six short stamens provided with long pale tips, with a three-pronged style proceeding from the middle of them. The scent is heavy.

### THE YELLOW MELEAGRIS OR FRITILLARY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a yellow Fritillaria with a nodding flower and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This produces a flower consisting of six petals, nodding like the other kinds; but some of these are of a yellow color marked with red spots, while others are of a greenish color with a slightly prominent central vein. It bloomed for us in April at Montbéliard in the Prince's garden <note>original: "in S.P. horto", likely referring to the garden of the Duke of Württemberg</note>.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE
<margin>Signature: Gg 2</margin>

### MELEAGRIS OR WHITE FRITILLARY marked on the inside with purplish veins. According to Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Fritillaria (Snake's Head Lily) showing the bulb, roots, long slender leaves, and a single bell-shaped nodding flower with a checkered pattern.</image-desc>

Lobel mentions in his *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Matthias de l'Obel, 1571</note> a White Fritillary checkered with dark purple, and also Fritillaries with white flowers sprinkled with random marks, which may be found among the Pictones <note>The Poitou region of France</note>.

However, the Fritillary has no medicinal use; it is cultivated in gardens solely for the elegance and beauty of its flowers.

### LILY: German: *Lilien* or *Gilgen*: Belgian: *Lelia*: French: *Lis*: Italian: *Giglio*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a common white lily (Lilium candidum) featuring a bulbous root, a tall straight stem with multiple lanceolate leaves, and several trumpet-shaped flowers at the top.</image-desc>

The Lily, a delight among flowers, rises from a bulbous root consisting of many scales. It sends up a straight stem, a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>About 18 to 27 inches</note>, or sometimes even taller; it is single and round. The leaves are attached to it from bottom to top without any stalks. Several flowers appear on the stalk in a certain sequence; they do not open at the same time. They possess an extraordinary sweetness of scent and a milky color, imitating a basket with six thick, curving petals. In their center stands a somewhat long, whitish-green three-parted style, surrounded by stamens equal in number to the petals, upon which sit saffron-colored tips <note>Anthers</note>.

Theophrastus calls the Lily "Narcissus"; Dioscorides treats it with very few words as it is known to everyone; Pliny says it is next in nobility to the Rose and depicts it skillfully.

### SYRIAN WHITE LILY OF RAUWOLF.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Syrian white lily, showing a thick stem with dense, broad leaves and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Theophrastus writes that Lilies differ from one another chiefly in color. Thus Dioscorides mentions two kinds: the White and the Red. Likewise, for Pliny, the Lily is threefold: White, Red, and Purple.

More recent authors identify more kinds: namely, one blood-red, another yellow, a certain orange-red, and a certain white and common one, which is simply called the Lily. There is also a certain small one called the Lily of the Valley. There is also the Great Persian Lily, commonly named the Imperial Crown. To these are also joined various species of Day-lilies and Martagons. Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a 16th-century physician and botanist</note> writes that the one we depict here grows in marshes, ponds, and wet places.

<column-break/>

### TIGER: thought to be a SPECIES OF DRACUNCULUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with a bulbous root, long pointed leaves, and a flower with spotted petals, resembling a Tiger Lily or a species of Dracunculus.</image-desc>

We have seen this depicted with green, oblong, narrow, and pointed leaves, springing from a dark bulbous root; the flower is yellow, varied with many small, random reddish spots, from the middle of which rises a lovely red style.

However, to all students of botany—a complaint shared by Dodonaeus, Lobel, and C. Bauhin—this plant remains unknown to this day.

*Is it a species of Dracunculus?* <note>Dragon Arum</note>

### COMMON WHITE LILY.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a common white lily, similar to the previous lily but shown with a more mature flowering head and distinct leaf arrangement.</image-desc>

Greek fables claim the Lily was born from the milk of Juno <note>Hera</note>, and for that reason, it obtained the name "Juno’s Rose." Nicander sang that it was called and nicknamed the "Charm of Venus," as if it were a delight. But setting aside the trifles of the Ancients, the nobility of this flower is more than sufficiently illustrated by its extraordinary whiteness, its sweetest scent, and the elegance of its form. Indeed, it has Truth itself as the herald of its praise: "Consider how the lilies grow; they toil not, nor do they spin. But I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these." Matthew 6.

### CONSTANTINOPLE WHITE LILY called SULTAN ZAMBACH by Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Sultan Zambach lily, featuring a thick, leafy stem and a dense cluster of lily flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Clusius says the roots of this were sent from Constantinople as the "Martagon of Constantinople," and it is commonly called *Sultan Zambach* <note>Turkish for "Sultan's Lily"</note> among the Turks. It seems to have obtained this name either because of the pleasantness and beauty of the flower or because it was dedicated to the Great Sultan.

Lobel records it thus in his *Observations*: He says the root is like that of the blood-red Lily, but varied with small purplish marks and spots, recently sent from Constantinople. The leaf is like our white Lily; the flower is white and of a beauty worth seeing, if ever there was one.

But what Theophrastus writes is true: the Lily for the most part consists of a single stem, and rarely a double one; and then from each head, one or more Lilies emerge.

# OF PLANTS.

### THE GREATER RED OR SAFFRON LILY.
### DAY-LILY. MARTAGON.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily plant with a bulbous root, long slender leaves, and several downward-facing flowers on a single stalk.</image-desc>

Various writers have bestowed the name of Day-lily <note>original: "Hemerocallis"</note> and Martagon upon the red or saffron-colored Lily.

The Day-lily, however, as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> describes it, has leaves and a stem similar to the Lily, green like a Leek: the flowers are on the stem itself, three or four on each shoot, similar in shape to a Lily, and when they begin to open, they are of a very pale color. The root is large and bulbous.

Pliny also mentions the Day-lily and points out the same plant as Dioscorides: but the Day-lily mentioned by Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a successor to Aristotle.</note> among the "garland shrubs" <note>Plants used for weaving wreaths and crowns.</note> is different from that one. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLER RED OR SAFFRON LILY.
->Germ. *Red Lily, Yellow Lily:* French *Red Lily, Orange Lily.*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller lily variety, showing a bulb, lanceolate leaves arranged along the stem, and a cluster of upright-facing flowers at the top.</image-desc>

To those things which we said just before regarding the Day-lily, we shall here add something from Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician and botanist.</note>. Of Day-lilies, he says, one is a shrub, the other a flower. The Day-lily shrub is of the kind used for garlands and is woody: about which Theophrastus writes in book 6 and Pliny in book 21, chapter 11. But the other Day-lily is a flower, which Dioscorides describes.

More recent authors establish many kinds: taking the differences from the color of the flower, the location, the size, etc., which we will soon treat in order. And they count among them both the great *Persian Lily*, which is commonly called the *Imperial Crown*, as well as various species of Day-lilies and Martagons. The one which is pictured here grows in marshes and damp places.

<column-break/>

### THE DILUTED PURPLE LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with numerous small leaves along the stem and several flowers blooming along the upper half of the stalk.</image-desc>

Various authors record it under this name: but to Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish botanist.</note> in his *Icons* it is called *the second Martagon of the Alchemists*, and elsewhere the *diluted purple lily*: to Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is the *5th Lily, or the purple one*.

<column-break/>

### THE BROAD-LEAVED BLOOD-RED LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with broad, overlapping leaves and a single large flower bud at the top, emerging from a scaly bulb.</image-desc>

It rests upon a bulb exactly like that of the *White Lily*: but it is gifted with a stem that is not thick like other Lilies, which produces a single blood-red flower consisting of six broad petals. At the top of the stem the leaves are few and very broad, similar to Plantain.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATER BULB-BEARING LILY, with a large red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbiferous lily showing small bulbs (bulbils) in the leaf axils and large, open flowers at the summit.</image-desc>

It sometimes rises with a stem two cubits high <note>About 3 feet or 90 cm.</note>, firm and thick: with leaves like a Lily, somewhat sharp, carrying thick bulbs in the upper joints <note>The "axils" where the leaf meets the stem.</note> and large red flowers. It blooms in June and perfects its seed in August.

This plant, however, as well as the other two bulb-bearing kinds of which we shall speak soon, are usually greatly infested by ants as soon as they first show their flower buds, not unlike the flowers of the Peony before they unfold.

<column-break/>

### THE HOARY BULB-BEARING LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with many narrow leaves and flowers at the top, characterized by a downy or "hoary" appearance on the upper stem.</image-desc>

It scarcely exceeds a cubit in height, with a firm, ribbed stem: provided with leaves that are blackish-green, which nevertheless grow hairy with a hoary down toward the top of the stem. The flowers do not glow with a fiery redness as in the one above, but are more pale. The stems of the more mature plants carry small bulbs in the upper joints. The root is stained with a yellow ochre color. It grows wild in the mountain meadows of Austria and Styria. *Clusius.* <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary figure in 16th-century botany.</note>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

### CREEPING BULB-BEARING LILY with flowers dyed with much Saffron.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall lily plant with multiple flowers and small bulbs (bulbils) visible along the stem and at the base.</image-desc>

It propagates itself extensively by creeping bulbs, and it bears small bulbs <note>original: "bulbulos"; these are aerial bulbs that grow in the leaf axils</note> before it produces a flower: otherwise it grows to a great height and bears many Lilies. We have seen it in abundance at Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France, then a center of botanical study</note> in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, multiplying itself from the falling small bulbs.

<column-break/>

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED SAFFRON LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with a large, dense, multi-petaled (double) flower head.</image-desc>

Is this Gesner’s <note>Conrad Gesner, a famous Swiss naturalist</note> red seed-bearing Lily? Or Clusius’s <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note> Pannonian <note>From the region of modern-day Hungary/Austria</note> purple Lily, or the smaller red bulb-bearing one? The smaller bulb-bearing Martagon, and the early bulb-bearing Martagon? Or Lobelius’s <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> Lily with the glowing Martagon flower?

---

### NARROW-LEAVED BLOOD-RED BULB-BEARING LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with narrow leaves and several flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Icons* it is called the narrow-leaved blood-red Martagon, with a small stem divided into wings, and not bearing bulbs composed upon them.

By Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who categorized thousands of plants</note> in his *Phytopinax* it is called the eighth Lily, or the narrow-leaved bulb-bearer, and by some the narrow-leaved blood-red Martagon.

<column-break/>

### LILY WITH A NODDING FLOWER, PURPLISH MARTAGON, spotted with blood-red.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Martagon lily with downward-facing (nodding) flowers, showing details of the bulb and seed pod.</image-desc>

Called by some the Wild Day-lily <note>original: "Hemerocallis syluestris"</note>, and by others the Apothecaries' Asphodel. Commonly called the Martagon and the Alchemists' Lily, the Wild Lily, the Mountain Lily, and in manuscripts the Saracen Lily. Thus it is inscribed by Authors. However, there is a Greater and a Lesser of this kind, and both are found in various places in mountains and woods, and wooded mountains, especially indeed in Styria and Austria, and not far from Frankfurt. We have also frequently observed it transferred into gardens at Ferrara, Padua, Genoa, etc.

---

### GREATEST LILY WITH A NODDING FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very tall lily with numerous narrow leaves and nodding flowers at the top.</image-desc>

This has a very large bulb, hiding deep in the earth: stems of several cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; this implies a very tall plant</note>: a huge number of flowers, and those less spotted: many narrow leaves, and some of them arranged in whorls <note>original: "verticillatim"; leaves growing in a circle around the stem</note>.

We observed this in the city of Thann in Alsace, in a certain highly cultivated garden: and from there we transferred it to Montbéliard, and cultivated it there for many years.

<column-break/>

### NODDING VERMILION-FLOWERED MARTAGON, or the Chalcedonian Day-lily to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with recurved, nodding petals and a prominent bulb with roots.</image-desc>

This glory of the gardens is accustomed to emerge in the new Spring: and it flowers in June, or a little later; and on account of the beauty of the flower it is called in most Italian places *Riccio de la Signora* <note>Italian: "The Lady's Curl," referring to the recurved petals</note>.

By Lobelius in his *Icons* and *History* it is called the many-flowered blood-purple Chalcedonian Day-lily: or the second Byzantine Day-lily.

# OF PLANTS

### EARLY MARTAGON WITH VERMILION FLOWERS, or the Early Lily with nodding red flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Martagon lily with a bulbous root, a tall leafy stem, and several nodding flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Two primary differences are observed in the Martagon with nodding vermilion flowers: the *Early* variety, which produces a stem of two or three finger-widths from a lush root and bears five, six, or even ten flowers upon it (which we depict here); and the *Late-blooming* variety, of which more follows.

<column-break/>

### LATE-BLOOMING MARTAGON WITH VERMILION FLOWERS, or the Late-blooming Lily with nodding red flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Martagon lily, similar to the previous one but with slightly different flower positioning and leaf density.</image-desc>

Besides the differences taken from their timing, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist</note> observed another distinction in this Lily. For he says the flowers are either paler or more saturated in color: those plants which bear paler flowers have greener stems and leaves than those with saturated flowers. Furthermore, those with purplish roots produce paler flowers, while others, by contrast, produce more saturated ones.

---

<column-break/>

### EARLY YELLOW MARTAGON, OR the Early Lily with nodding yellow flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lily with a scaly bulb and a tall stem bearing multiple nodding flowers.</image-desc>

It is cultivated in gardens and is found growing wild in the mountains; the open flower is sometimes observed to be marked with spots.

This kind of Lily grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>original: "S. P." likely referring to the Prince of Württemberg's garden</note>, with eight yellowish flowers reclining downward. It was blooming at the beginning of June.

<column-break/>

### PERSIAN OR SUSIAN LILY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Persian lily with a large bulb and a dense spike of small, bell-shaped nodding flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has a large and tuberous root, a tall stem densely packed with narrow leaves, and at its summit is a cluster <term>thyrsus: a dense, tufted flower stalk</term> of numerous flowers hanging from stalks about an inch and a half long. These face the ground and are dyed a deep purple, consisting of six petals and resembling small bells, etc.

It blooms in April, and its seed is mature at the same time as the Tulip <note>original: "Tufæ," likely a typo for Tulips</note> or shortly after. It is probable that it was first brought from the city of Susa in Persia to Constantinople, and from there into these regions.

<insert>Alphonso Pancio described it thus: *The Persian Panachia is a most beautiful plant, a species of Lily or Martagon, distinct from the Crown Imperial.*</insert>

---

<column-break/>

### YELLOW LILY WITH AN ASPHODEL ROOT, OR the Yellow Lily-Asphodel of certain authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Daylily (Hemerocallis) with fibrous, tuberous roots and lily-like flowers.</image-desc>

Called *Lily-flowered Asphodel* and *Lily-Asphodel* by Lobelius and Pena, and *Liliaceous Asphodel* by others, with an elegant and fragrant yellow flower. To Camerarius, it is the *Non-bulbous or reed-like Lily*, with a very fragrant yellow flower. It may be the shrub which Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> recounts among the garland-flowers called *Elion*.

It blooms with the larger purple Lily, or a little before, preceding the white Lilies. In our regions it is a stranger, but it is frequent in Hungary, from whence it was translated into our gardens, where it is commonly cultivated.

<column-break/>

### SCARLET LILY WITH AN ASPHODEL ROOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a red Daylily, showing the characteristic tuberous root system and trumpet-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Called *Reddish Liliaceous Asphodel* by Tabernaemontanus; *Scarlet Lily-Asphodel* by Lobelius; *The Turks' Red Reed-like Lily* by Belon; and *Non-bulbous or reed-like Lily* with a red-saffron flower by Camerarius.

It grows luxuriantly in many German gardens, though it is quite troublesome because of its creeping root.

We shall deliver the QUALITIES, POWERS, AND USES OF LILIES in the Appendix.
