# CROWN IMPERIAL, TUSAİ: German: *Kaysers kron*; French: *Couronne Imperiale*; Italian: *Corona di Re*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Crown Imperial (Fritillaria imperialis) showing a tall stalk topped with a cluster of bell-shaped flowers and a tuft of leaves.</image-desc>

This royal plant varies in many ways: in the number and length of its stalks, and in their "tuft" <note>The cluster of leaves at the very top of the flower spike</note>, which is not always single, as others sometimes tower above the first. It varies in the number of flowers, since one and the same plant is found laden with five, six, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, and even seventy of them. It varies in the color of the flowers, which is sometimes yellow or pale, and other times red. It varies in its season and leaves; for one is the "Early" kind, which blooms immediately in March, and has a broad leaf of a diluted green and a paler flower; another is the "Middle" kind, whose leaf is narrower and paler, and the flower more diluted; and finally another is the "Late-blooming" kind, with dark green broad leaves and deep crimson flowers.

<column-break/>

# MONSTROUS CROWN IMPERIAL.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a "monstrous" or fasciated Crown Imperial, showing a much thicker, flattened stem and a denser, more chaotic cluster of flowers and foliage at the top.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist</note> writes that the bulbs of the Crown Imperial were brought from Persia to Constantinople, and from there to Vienna; and thus this plant reached us. By the Turks it is called *Tusai*, *Tousai*, *Tusihai*, and *Thushiai*, which words signify a "royal scepter." Indeed, on account of its resemblance, it obtained the name of the Imperial or Royal Crown, and the common sort of herbalists have retained this name until now.

It blooms in April and even in March, and the seed is ripe in June. However, none of our people have seen it growing wild. It is dedicated more to the delight of the eyes and the ornament of gardens than to the nose, or to culinary or medicinal uses.

---

# GLADIOLUS OR SWORD-LILY: German: *Schovertel*; French: *Glais*, *Glayeul*; Italian: *Gladiolo*, *Monacucie*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Gladiolus plant, showing the long, sword-shaped leaves, the flowering spike, and the bulbous root system.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that a variety is found in the flowers: and that the Narbonne Gladiolus has one row of flowers, while the Italian has two.

It is common in woody and brushy places, and also in meadows and fields where it grows among the crops, for which reason it is called "Corn-flag" <note>original: *Segetalis*</note>. It is also cultivated in gardens. In meadows it has a paler flower and sometimes a white one; but in fields and woody or brushy places, it is a pleasant red or a deeper purple.

Its root, and especially the second one which is higher up, has the power of attracting, dispersing, and drying: according to *Galen* <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>. Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> writes that the upper root, drunk with wine, stimulates sexual desire <note>original: *Venerem stimulare*</note>, but the lower one makes people sterile, etc.

<column-break/>

# IRIS: German: *Blauw Gilgen*, *Blauw Schovertel*; French: *Flambe*, *Glayeul*; Italian: *Iride*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of an Iris plant, showing the characteristic broad leaves, a single large flower, and the rhizome root.</image-desc>

The Latin speakers have retained the Greek name *Iris*. However, the distinction that the common folk make between the words *Iris* and *Ireos* according to the popular verse:

> Iris bears the purple flower: Ireos the white;

is utterly vain. Whence Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), French physician and botanist</note> says: "There are those who, by a shameful error, assign one herb to the nominative case and another to the genitive case <note>A joke about Latin grammar; *Ireos* is simply the Greek genitive form of *Iris*</note>, so that *Iris* is thought by herbalists to be distinguished from *Ireos* as if it were a purple color; but this opinion is to be numbered among old wives' tales, and is not even worthy of being hissed at, let alone exploded by the unlearned and the rude." It received its name from the fact that it represents and expresses the appearance and colors of the heavenly Rainbow <note>original: *Arcus cœlestis*</note> in its flowers. Furthermore, here is depicted the *broad-leaved bulbous Iris, with a blue and white flower*.

---

# BULBOUS IRIS, ENTIRELY VIOLET or blue.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a bulbous Iris with dark, violet-colored flowers.</image-desc>

Various differences are observed in the Iris: From its place of birth, whence one is called cultivated, another wild, another "ours," German, Venetian, Florentine, Thracian, Macedonian, African, Carthaginian, or Illyrian. From the shape of the roots, it is either called *rhizotomos* <note>root-cutting</note> by Pliny, or *Raphanitis*—having acquired the name from its resemblance to a radish—and called *Astragalitis* by Galen, Paulus, and Aetius, because its root has a resemblance to the root of the *Astragalus* <note>Milk-vetch</note>. From the diverse color of the flowers, which varies not only in the individual but also in the species, so that one may see white, pale, yellow, purple, blue, or ash-colored ones. And finally from their form, size, powers, and scent, as will be said more at length as we proceed.

<column-break/>

# MULTI-BRANCHED VARIEGATED BULBOUS IRIS of Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a multi-branched bulbous Iris with variegated flowers.</image-desc>

Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophistae*, Book 15, is witness that Pliny writes that the flowers of the Iris are called *Lupi* <note>Wolves</note>, because they are similar to the gaping mouth and lips of a wolf. Moreover, the Iris is called in general by some—Virgil, Palladius, and Columella—the *Hyacinth*, by others *Lialis*, by others the *Celestial Lily*; and among the Germans, Belgians, Italians, and Spaniards it has obtained the name of *Lily*, but *Gladiolus* among the French. By the Greeks it is called "heavenly" and "admirable"; and among them, by Theophrastus, the "preserver"; but by Dioscorides *Illyrica*, not *Myrica*, as some have badly read, by a slippery error in writing the letter Delta ($\Delta$) which, when doubled, makes an M.

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical and etymological description of the Crown Imperial, Gladiolus, and various species of Iris, noting their origins, physical variations, and medicinal properties according to classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Crown Imperial, Gladiolus, Iris, botany, medicinal plants, Clusius, Dioscorides, Galen, plant taxonomy, flower varieties</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### BULBOUS IRIS OF VARIED BLUE AND WHITE, with narrow leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a bulbous iris with narrow leaves and a prominent flower showing detailed petals and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

Regarding the birthplace of the Iris: it delights in births that are not excessively hot, such as Africa, nor excessively cold, such as the North; but rather in temperate and well-watered mountainous places, as in such locations it is highly fragrant and most praised. For the Spaniards possess the Common and most well-known variety almost everywhere, according to the testimony of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note>; the people of Provence have it in gardens, or growing upon walls and roofs. We observed it blooming at Montpellier in March and April; at Verona, Florence, and Lyon, growing abundantly and spontaneously near hedges; and at Geneva and Basel blooming in gardens in September. Thus it grows in almost all regions of Europe; and although this variety is of lesser reputation, it is still to be considered good, and all the more so the more fragrant it is.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW BULBOUS IRIS, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a bulbous iris, similar to the first but with slightly different petal structure and a smaller bulb.</image-desc>

According to the judgment of Theophrastus, Pliny, and Dioscorides, the most praised Iris grows in Illyria <note>The western Balkan Peninsula</note>: and there indeed not in the maritime districts, but in the inland parts situated more toward the North, and in the wild woods of the Drilon and Narona rivers. The next best is in Macedonia, which is very long, whitish, and slender. The third place is held by the African variety, the largest among them all, and most bitter in taste.

Among the Illyrian and Macedonian types, the best, in the judgment of Dioscorides, is that which has a thick <term>root</term> <note>original: radix; here referring to the rhizome</note> and is somewhat blunt to the sight, difficult to break, and of a yellowish color: and which is highly fragrant, bitterer in taste, pure in scent, not smelling of mold, and which moves one to sneezing when it is rubbed.

---

### COMMON VIOLET OR PURPLE IRIS, of the garden or the wild.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a common iris with broad, sword-shaped leaves and a thick rhizome root.</image-desc>

The common cultivated Iris is very well known in gardens, and the wild variety corresponds to it in flavor, scent, and other qualities. But it has smaller leaves which do not appear in winter, whereas the leaves of the cultivated variety stubbornly resist the severity of winter. It is also shorter in the stalk: and for that reason the flowers burst forth almost twenty days before the flowers of the cultivated kind, and are of a deeper purple color. The <term>root</term> <note>The underground stem or rhizome</note> also does not form such a tuft as the cultivated one produces. Moreover, it grows in elevated and sloping places among thickets. By these marks alone is this one distinguished from that. *We would have hoped for a better illustration; this one is from the empirical practitioners.*

<column-break/>

### GREATER DALMATIAN IRIS, with a flower less violet than the common.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large Dalmatian iris with broad leaves and a robust rhizome.</image-desc>

This Iris is of remarkable beauty and size, which is very similar to the blue Asiatic Iris—the largest of all Irises—if it is not indeed the same.

However, to proceed with what was just said, the Illyrian Iris is held first among all Irises: not indeed because it differs in genus or species from the others, but because by the suitability of that climate and soil, it possesses more excellent powers; just as <term>Wormwood</term> <note>original: Absinthium</note> which grows in Pontus, <term>Sweet Flag</term> <note>original: Acorum</note> in Colchis and Galatia, <term>Cattail</term> <note>original: Typha</note> in Syria and the Cyclades islands, and <term>Costus</term> in Arabia, and many others are preferred because of their locations, since they come forth with the most excellent natural gifts.

---

### LESSER DALMATIAN IRIS, with a pale purple flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller Dalmatian iris with slender leaves and a rhizome.</image-desc>

The common Florentine Iris of the shops is not badly used as a substitute for the Illyrian, and is valued more by Merchants than the Venetian, because it is whiter and more fragrant. Nevertheless, from Illyria (today called Slavonia), Iris is usually carried to Venice, wherefore the "Venetian" is considered by everyone to be the legitimate Illyrian Iris.

The German Iris, however, although it has much affinity with the Illyrian or Florentine if you consider its form and temperament, and although it burns the tongue when tasted no less than those do: it is nevertheless not as hard and solid, nor even so fragrant. Thus, as we also have from the records of Theophrastus and Galen, *the diversity of regions produces great diversity in plants.*

<column-break/>

### GREATER BROAD-LEAVED IRIS, PALE BLUE, with a white sheath.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a broad-leaved iris with a large flower head and detailed rhizome structure.</image-desc>

Various diversities of the greater broad-leaved Iris are proposed by Clusius and others: one excellent in its flower with purple veins, others with smaller flowers, others with purple edges, others with edges approaching yellow; one with a multicolored flower, fading from white with purple veins, with seed pods marked with purple veins, one with a purple flower and a naked stalk: and not a few others distinguished from one another by certain marks. All of these things, says Clusius, are most difficult to express in words, and concerning which that line of the Poet <note>Ovid, Metamorphoses 2.13-14</note> may truly be said:
> They do not all have one face, 
> Nor yet are they different; just as it should be for sisters.

It cites classical authorities like Dioscorides and contemporary botanists like Clusius to categorize the plants by color, scent, and root structure.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE VIOLET PORTUGUESE SPRING IRIS of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris plant with a large bloom, long slender leaves, and a bulbous root system.</image-desc>

This is the same as the ninth large broad-leaved Iris of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational Flemish botanist</note> with purple veins.

We have found through experience that the roots of the Iris become more fragrant with age, and Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> teaches this as well; which is surprising, since other roots tend to rot when they are old. But this occurs through drying, as Cronemburgius correctly determined.

<column-break/>

### IRIS WITH A WHITE FLOWER: German: *Weiss Schwertel*: Belgian: *Wittisch*: French: *Flambe blanche*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris plant with a white flower, broad leaves, and a thick rhizome.</image-desc>

Anyone who correctly knows the common purple Iris will understand this white one with no trouble, as it has no difference worthy of note in its roots or in the shapes of its leaves and flowers; it differs only by the distinction of its color, which is white approaching a sea-green gray. Why some have called this the "Florentine Iris," however, we do not see.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATER BROAD-LEAVED YELLOW IRIS, with spreading variegated flower petals.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Iris with variegated petals and broad, ribbed leaves.</image-desc>

Clusius recounts several varieties of this. We have seen it in the gardens at Basel, and we have kept it in our own garden at Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France where the author maintained a botanical collection</note>, blooming in May.

Furthermore, as we have from the records of Dioscorides, Pliny, Paulus, and Mesue, the Iris is hot and dry in the third degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine referring to the intensity of a plant's "humoral" effect</note>, sharp and composed of thin parts. It cleanses, ripens, dissolves, softens, and opens obstructions; it soothes pains and purges thick phlegm and the bile mixed with it; and besides these, it gently purges watery humors, etc.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATER BROAD-LEAVED IRIS, OF SUSA OR Chalcedon, with a variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Susiana Iris with a large, heavily patterned flower head.</image-desc>

Clusius attributes to this plant the largest flower of all the Irises he has seen, variegated with white and black. He labels it "of Susa" because it was brought to Constantinople from Susa, the capital of the province of Susiana <note>Modern-day Shush, Iran</note>.

Among the particular uses of the Iris—all of which it is not our purpose to list here—Gesner, Hollerius, and others recommend the water distilled from the purple flowers with the <term>Diatrionfantalon</term> <note>A medicinal powder made of three types of sandalwood</note> and cinnamon as being most effective for those suffering from dropsy <note>Edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE TWO-FLOWERED PORTUGUESE IRIS, with a violet flower, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris with two flower heads on a single stalk.</image-desc>

It grows in many places in Portugal in the fields and rich soil; when moved into gardens, it blooms in Spring and Autumn, which is why the name *Biflora* <note>Two-flowered</note> was given to it. Clusius writes that a purple-flowered variety of this kind is also found.

In his *Observations*, Lobelius says: In Spring and Autumn, it produces a fragrant violet flower on individual stalks a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>About 18 to 27 inches</note>, one or two to a stalk, fringed with a shaggy whiteness; in its root, appearance, and leaves, it is similar to the Dalmatian Iris, etc.

<column-break/>

### IRIS WITH A VIOLET FLOWER AND GREEN LEAF, perhaps the 25th of Clusius, with a stem bare of leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris with a single bloom and leaves emerging from the base of the stem.</image-desc>

This plant has a unique characteristic among the other Irises: it retains no leaves through the winter. Instead, they all wither and dry up, and the plant is seen bare; then, at the beginning of Spring, it puts forth new shoots.

Having brought it from Belgium, we cultivated it for several years at Montbéliard in the <note>original: "S. P. horto"</note> Prince's Garden; it used to bloom in April.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called "Iris 12, or the Iris that loses its leaves in Winter."

<summary>This page describes several Iris varieties, including the Portuguese, Florentine, and Susiana types, detailing their physical characteristics, seasonal growth patterns, and medicinal applications for treating humors and dropsy.</summary>
<keywords>Iris, botany, Clusius, Lobelius, medicinal plants, Susa, Montbéliard, pharmacology, horticulture</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
<margin>Page 242</margin>
<margin>Signature: R r 2</margin>

### LOW BROAD-LEAVED DWARF IRIS, violet-colored, found among rocks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing Iris plant with broad leaves and a single large flower, showing the rhizome and root structure.</image-desc>

The root is thick, white, wrinkled, and sharp to the taste; from which several leaves emerge similar to those of the common Iris <note>Iris germanica</note>, half an inch wide and two or three inches long. The **stalks** are very short, about nine inches high; the flower is violet and purple, as in the common Iris, but smaller in all its parts and without scent.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> calls this the smallest and rarest of all Irises: with the flower, seed, and pod of the Stinking Gladwin <note>original: "Xyridis foetidae"</note>.

### LARGER STEMLESS LOW BROAD-LEAVED IRIS, of a deep violet color, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a stemless Iris with broad leaves and a prominent flower, showing detailed rhizome and roots.</image-desc>

The flowers are supported by no stalk, but are succulent and rest only upon weak little stems, like those of the Saffron <note>Crocus</note>, Meadow Saffron <note>Colchicum</note>, and similar plants. Of this kind of Iris, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note>, two varieties are held: for one has larger and broader leaves, scarcely yielding in width to the leaves of the Great Iris; the other has slightly smaller and narrower leaves, yet they are broader than the leaves of the Narrow-leaved Iris. We depict the Larger one here.

### MOST ELEGANT SMALL LOW BROAD-LEAVED IRIS, variously colored.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, broad-leaved Iris with a variegated flower pattern, including roots.</image-desc>

It differs from the others neither in root, nor leaves, nor the shape of the flower: only the color of the flowers is different, which is so variously painted that, according to Clusius, it is difficult to express it exactly in words. It displays its beauty along with the other Dwarf Irises in April: nor is there any pleasant scent in it: the flower is followed by a three-sided seed head.

<column-break/>

### SNOW-WHITE OR PURE WHITE DWARF IRIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dwarf Iris (Chamæiris) with upright leaves and a single flower, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This grows in great abundance, according to Lobelius, in the region of Narbonne <note>Southern France</note>, in dry and rocky places, near that cave which is very frequently visited at Montpellier, where the road goes toward Frontignan, common in the crevices of the rocks. It is also cultivated in gardens. In his *Later History*, Clusius notes it is a lower kind of Iris, growing in the rocky and sea-breeze-swept places of Portugal above Lisbon.

### SMALL STEMLESS LOW BROAD-LEAVED IRIS, of a deep violet color.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, stemless, broad-leaved Iris with a dark flower and visible roots.</image-desc>

This plant has slightly shorter and narrower leaves: the flowers are also a little smaller: the three-sided and pointed seed heads are likewise smaller, and the seed even smaller still. However, there is the greatest variety in the flowers: although almost all have blue fringed hairs <note>the "beard" of the iris</note> above the stamens, but yellow ones below. Clusius describes many of these varieties, which we leave to be sought from his writings.

### SMALL NARROW-LEAVED IRIS, the fourth of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leaved Iris with multiple flower buds emerging from the foliage, showing the root structure.</image-desc>

The root is slanted and knotted, under which are thick white fibers: the leaves are narrow, grass-like, ending in a point: the stalk is shorter than the leaves themselves, on the uppermost part of which are large heads or pods, such as emerge from a thin sheath in the Gladwin or common Stinking Iris.

The image was depicted from a dried plant: for which reason we cannot add the color of the flowers. Is it the *Medium* of Dioscorides? Or the *Maritime Iris of Narbonne* from the *Adversaria*? Or the *Maritime Gladwin* of the *History of Lyon*?

<summary>This page details several varieties of dwarf and stemless Irises (Chamaeiris), noting their physical characteristics, flowering times, and specific geographic origins in France and Portugal. The text relies heavily on the observations of renowned botanists Clusius and Lobelius to distinguish between these similar-looking species.</summary>

<keywords>Dwarf Iris, Chamaeiris, Clusius, Lobelius, Narbonne, Montpellier, botanical illustration, rhizome, maritime plants, 16th-century botany</keywords>

### IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

### GRASS-LEAVED IRIS WHOSE LEAVES PERISH ANNUALLY, with a variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris graminea plant, showing its long, grass-like leaves, fibrous roots, and a single flower stalk with a bloom.</image-desc>

In such a great variety of Irises, this small one also offers a beautiful sight to the eyes; we call it *Grass-leaved* because of its thin, very narrow leaves, which are not rigid, but green and long. The scent of the flowers is pleasant—to us it smells of Plums, to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> it smells of Apricot. It grows in meadows situated at the foot of mountains and is also cultivated in gardens, as we have kept it in our own at Geneva and Montbéliard, and have observed it in others. It blooms in May.

### ANOTHER LARGER NARROW-LEAVED IRIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris angustifolia, featuring slender leaves and a prominent flower with distinct petals and sepals.</image-desc>

According to Clusius, it also grows wild in damp meadows in places near the city of Vienna; he writes that he had never seen it before he traveled to Austria. However, we have kept it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince; and Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist</note> also observed it in the gardens of the Low Countries, reporting on it thus: "Varieties of the wild narrow-leaved Iris," he says, "are seen cultivated in our gardens through the diligence of the Belgians," etc.

### THE THIN-LEAVED IRIS OF MICHELFELDEN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris tenuifolia, showing a cluster of narrow leaves and a flower stalk with a large bloom, including a detailed view of the root system.</image-desc>

This Iris grows wild and frequently in the marshy areas of Michelfelden near Basel: the stem exceeds two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> in height; the flower is quite large, blue or purplish; the seed pod is large and long; and the leaves are a cubit long, narrow, and even narrower than those described by Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, renowned Italian physician and naturalist</note>.

It blooms in May, and sometimes even in June if a harsher winter has preceded it. Could this be the thin-leaved Iris of Valerius Cordus that grows in sunny, level meadows, thickets, and moist fields?

<column-break/>

### LARGER THIN-LEAVED IRIS, WITH A BLUE and striped flower: according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger Iris tenuifolia variety, showing the plant with its characteristic long leaves and a detailed flower showing striations on the petals.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is composed of many white fibers: the leaves are a cubit or a cubit and a half long, half an inch wide, pointed, and when rubbed they smell somewhat like garden herbs. The stem is longer than the leaves, cylindrical, and divided into three or four small forks: upon each of these sit flowers the size of the *Dwarf Iris*, but of a more pleasant elegance. For the three curved-back petals are violet at the edges, variegated with white and violet further down, and painted with very beautiful long, diagonal, violet, whitish, and rust-colored stripes; above these are placed three other cleft petals of a purple-violet color, which hide purple tongues: the remaining three violet parts stand upright.

It grows wild in meadows near marshes in Vienna, Austria.

### NARROW-LEAVED IRIS WITH A WHITE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a white-flowered Iris angustifolia, showing the plant's structure from the fibrous roots to the pointed leaves and flower.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is gifted with many fibers; the stem is a foot and a half or two feet high: the leaves are a foot long and a small finger's width; the flowers are white and most sweet in appearance. For the three broader curved-back petals are pleasantly marked with sweet reddish nerves or veins, and also elegantly striped at the edges with shorter lines of the same color: there are three other petals resting upon them, and just as many narrower upright petals that are entirely white.

Lobel writes in his *Adversaria* <note>his botanical notebook</note> that it grows in the hanging gardens of Adonis.

### THE TUBEROUS IRIS OF THE BELGIANS, WITH A dark reddish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iris tuberosa, highlighting the distinct tuberous root system and the unique shape of the flower and foliage.</image-desc>

It appears to be a kind of wild Iris: and therefore, from the shape of its roots, it can be called the *Tuberous Iris*. It is an exotic plant which is said to have been brought from Eastern parts and the regions near Constantinople into both Italy and the Low Countries. Mattioli suspected it to be the *Hermodactyl* <note>a medicinal root often confused with Iris or Colchicum</note>, but erroneously: nor do others fare better who wish it to be the "first Lonchitis," thinking that no plant more closely resembles the Lonchitis.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Iris, including the grass-leaved, narrow-leaved, and tuberous types, noting their physical characteristics, scents, and geographic origins across Europe and the Near East.</summary>
<keywords>Iris graminea, Iris angustifolia, Iris tenuifolia, Iris tuberosa, botany, Clusius, Lobel, Mattioli, Vienna, Basel, garden cultivation, medicinal plants</keywords>

### YELLOW MARSH IRIS, FALSE ACORUS: German: Yellow water-sword; French: Bastard Iris.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Yellow Iris (Iris pseudacorus) showing the tall flowering stalks, sword-shaped leaves, and thick rhizome root system.</image-desc>

The apothecary shops incorrectly call this <term>Acorus</term> <note>original: "Acorum"; likely referring to Sweet Flag</note>, and with even greater error they use its roots in place of the legitimate <term>Acorus</term>: therefore, most people more appropriately name it <term>Pseudo-Acorus</term> <note>False Acorus</note>.

It grows everywhere in marshes or in nearby and adjacent places, such as well-watered meadows and the banks of rivers. It flowers in April and May; around Yverdon in Switzerland, and especially on the road leading to Grandson, they are so common in the marshes that people transplant them into gardens and cultivate them there.

Furthermore, its taste abundantly demonstrates that the root possesses an immense astringent quality: thus its powers are entirely different from the root of the true Acorus.

<column-break/>

### LARGE SISYRINCHIUM RELATED TO THE BULBOUS IRIS, of a blue color.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Sisyrinchium (Barbary Nut) showing the flower, stem, and a distinct bulbous root with a smaller offset bulb shown to the side.</image-desc>

And this plant, according to Theophrastus, although it differs entirely in color and does not consist of scales, nevertheless seeks to be reduced in some way to the genus of Bulbs, because it has a rounded root.

Clusius observed two kinds of this plant during his travels in Spain. The Larger, which we depict here, and the Smaller. The Portuguese, he says, call them <term>Nozelhas</term>, as if "little nuts," because the boys there eat its bulb just like hazelnuts and consider them a delicacy.

---

<column-break/>

### SMALLER SISYRINCHIUM RELATED TO THE BULBOUS IRIS: with a blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Sisyrinchium species with a single flower and a small bulbous root.</image-desc>

Clusius observed this in the Spanish kingdom of Valencia; he reports that it is called <term>Lirio</term> by the inhabitants, and <term>Maçucas</term> by some. Could this be the <term>Sisyrinchion</term> <note>original Greek: Σισυρίγχιον</note> or <term>Sithyrinchion</term> of Theophrastus?

Moreover, there is a marvel in this Sisyrinchium: the lowest roots grow in Winter; but in Spring, when the violet has appeared, they diminish and contract, and only then does the bulb grow plump.

According to Clusius, it is useful for stomach cramps: but once the root is swallowed, the body must immediately be exercised by dancing.

<column-break/>

### STINKING SPATULA, CALLED XYRIS BY MOST: German: Foreign sword-lily, bedbug herb; French: Stinking Iris.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spatula Foetida (Iris foetidissima) showing the seed pods and fibrous root system.</image-desc>

According to Cordus, Cornarius, Mattioli, and other most esteemed writers, this is the <term>Xyris</term> of Dioscorides, which obtained its name among the Greeks from the edge of a razor <note>original Greek: ξυρόν (xyron) meaning razor</note>. It is a species of Gladiolus which the shops call <term>Spatula foetida</term> <note>Stinking Spatula</note>, both because of the shape of the leaf (for <term>spathe</term> <note>original Greek: σπάθη</note> signifies a sword) and because it exhales a heavy odor. The similarity of most parts—leaves, flowers, stalks, and roots—demonstrates that it is a relative of the Irises; therefore, they are numbered among the wild Irises. Nothing seems to distinguish it from the common sort except for the deeper purple of the flowers.

---

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE XYRIS, CALLED STINKING SPATULA.

<image-desc>Alternative woodcut illustration of the Xyris plant, focusing on the foliage and root structure.</image-desc>

In Italy, Provence, Narbonnese Gaul, and England, it grows spontaneously near damp meadows and coastal embankments. In Belgium, however, Germany, and other Northern places, it is kept only in gardens. In Montpellier, it grows everywhere among the thickets along the roads; it produces a flower in May, June, July, and August, ripening its seed in Autumn.

Furthermore, although this plant smells of bedbugs, Dioscorides writes that its root is effective against head wounds and fractures; and by the same witness, it draws out all weapons and thorns without pain. Peasants attempt purgings with a decoction or infusion of this root. The figures which are from purchased sources do not please us, nor do the images of Fuchs and Mattioli.

<column-break/>

### ACORUS OR ACORUM, SWEET FLAG: German: Calamus; French: Bastard Iris; Italian: Acoro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Acorus calamus (Sweet Flag) showing the characteristic spadix inflorescence and creeping rhizome.</image-desc>

As well-known as the root and its ancient name were to the perfumers <note>original: "Seplasijs," referring to the Seplasia, a famous street of perfume-sellers in ancient Capua</note>, the appearance of the whole plant remained unknown for many centuries. The Ambassadors of the Roman Emperors brought it from Constantinople; by their gift, it became an inhabitant of the city of Vienna, and was thereafter shared in various places, so that it is now very common. Clusius saw it at Vienna, Cesalpino at Florence; we ourselves have seen it at Pforzheim and Paris, and we successfully nourish it in our own garden at Yverdon. It delights in water and produces [yellowish] flowers in June, July, and August. The root which we use is sharp and moderately bitter, and not unpleasant in taste: whence, in the judgment of Galen, it is established that its faculty is hot and of a thin consistency. More in the Appendix.

It highlights the botanical confusion between the Yellow Iris and true Acorus, and notes the introduction of Sweet Flag to Europe via Constantinople.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

# GALANGA: German: Galgan, Galgan-root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Galanga root, showing a thick, knotted rhizome with smaller offshoots.</image-desc>

The root which is called *Galanga* by the pharmacies and more recent physicians does not differ greatly from the Sweet Flag <note>original: "Acoro"</note>. However, nothing at all was handed down about it by Dioscorides and the ancient Greeks; it is also clear that it was not sufficiently understood by the Arabs, from the fact that Avicenna and Serapio wrote two different chapters about it. They called it *Calungen* or *Galangen*, from which the Greek and Latin names are thought to have been derived.

In the appendix of this Outline, we uncover the error of Lonicer, Brassavola, and Fuchs, who established that Galanga is the true and legitimate Sweet Flag of Dioscorides. Furthermore, we reject the opinion of the Monks—who write that Galanga is the root of the *Juniper-scented* plant—as being foreign to reason, agreeing with Matthiolus, Garcia, and the History of Lyon.

# ROOT OF ST. HELENA, PATER NOSTER, A species of Galanga.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Radix S. Helenæ, showing a gnarled, vertical root structure with fibrous details.</image-desc>

It grows commonly in damp places in Florida; it is called *Pater noster* <note>Latin for "Our Father," likely referring to the bead-like shape of the root segments used for rosaries</note> of *St. Helena* by Monardes, because it grows in a certain port so named. In the History of Lyon it is called *Pater noster*, or *Root of St. Helena* according to Monardes. To Clusius, it is the *Root of St. Helena*. Could it be a type of *Cyperus* <note>Sedge</note>? The Indians, when about to bathe, rub their whole body with its powder.

Furthermore, it is hot and dry in the third degree, like the Galanga mentioned before; it greatly benefits those troubled by stomach moisture, gas, and indigestion, and it is considered the supreme remedy for whitlows <note>term: Paronychia; an infection of the fingertip</note>. Moreover, it is so common among the people of Malabar that they use it not only for curing diseases but also make bread from it, called *Atas*, which they consider a delicacy.

# CONTRAYERVA ROOT, RELATED TO THE DRACKENA ROOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Contrayerva root, depicting two oblong, textured root pieces.</image-desc>

Clusius purchased this from shipmasters returning from the East Indies, having heard it was of great value among the Indians.

Truly, from the Charcas province of Peru, certain roots are brought that resist poisons; they are similar to Iris roots but smaller, and have the scent of a fig leaf. The Spaniards living in the Indies gave them the name *Contrayerva*, which means *antidote* <note>original: "alexipharmacum"</note>. This is not without reason, since its powder taken in white wine is considered a most immediate remedy against almost every poison, of whatever kind it may be. It is also reported that Contrayerva expels intestinal worms <note>original: "ventris animalia"</note>, etc.

<column-break/>

# IMAGE OF GALANGA; ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Galanga plant with broad, pointed leaves emerging from a central stalk, and a detailed view of the root system below.</image-desc>

Galanga is commonly distinguished into *Greater* and *Lesser*, as we depict both roots in the preceding table from Clusius. The *Greater* rises to a height of two cubits, with leaves like an Orchid, pointed, and clasping the stem; the flower is white, and the seed is tiny and ignored. The *Lesser* is only two spans high, with leaves like Myrtle, a knotted root, and it grows spontaneously.

It is an exotic plant known more by its root than its seed, although it may also grow when sown from seed. The Greater variety grows more abundantly in Java in the Indies, where they call it *Lauvaz*; the Lesser grows in the region of China, from which it is carried into India, called *Lavendea* by the Chinese. *Regarding its use, see what follows.*

# DRACKENA ROOT OF CLUSIUS: BEZOARDIC ROOT of Tabernaemontanus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Drackena or Bezoardica root, showing several twisted, tuberous segments.</image-desc>

The Knight Sir Francis Drake <note>original: "Fr. Dracke"</note> brought this root back with him from that voyage in which he circumnavigated the whole world, and gave it to his friends; for that reason, Clusius, who illustrates and describes it, also labels it with the name of the donor. By Tabernaemontanus, it is called the *Bezoardic* root <note>note: "Bezoardic" refers to its use as an antidote to poison, similar to a bezoar stone</note>.

# CURCUMA: OR THE PHARMACY'S "TERRA MERITA": Called Curcum by the Arabs: Saroth by the Turks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Curcuma (Turmeric) plant, showing long, ribbed leaves and a thick, segmented rhizome.</image-desc>

We, along with Sylvius, Ruellius, Amatus, Cordus, Dodonaeus, Clusius, Matthiolus, and most other recent authors, establish that the *Curcuma* or *Terra Merita* <note>term: Turmeric; "Terra Merita" literally means "meritorious earth"</note> of the pharmacies is the Indian Cyperus of Dioscorides. No characteristic contradicts this, as Matthiolus skillfully demonstrates. By Acosta and some others, it is called *Indian Saffron*, and there are those who think the Curcuma is the root of Celandine, but they are mistaken.

Cordus, in his commentary on Dioscorides, recognizes two differences: the *long* and the *round*.

It grows in Cannanore, in Calicut, and Goa; a great quantity of it is carried to the Arabs, Persians, and Turks, all of whom acknowledge it is imported from India.

It is in frequent use among painters and chemists, and among physicians, it is used as a hair-dye <note>original: "philothri"</note>.

<summary>This page describes various medicinal roots from the East and West Indies, including Galanga, Turmeric (Curcuma), and the "Drackena" root brought to Europe by Sir Francis Drake. It focuses on their botanical identification, geographical origins, and their uses as antidotes and digestive aids.</summary>
<keywords>Galanga, Turmeric, Curcuma, Contrayerva, Sir Francis Drake, Clusius, medicinal roots, Indian Saffron, antidotes, Florida, Java, Peru</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

**GINGER: German: Imber; French: Gingembre, Zingembre; A SPECIES OF GINGER CALLED MECHINUM.**
**Italian: Zenziero; to the Arabs, Persians, and Turks: Gengibil. Secacul: Zerumbet: Zedoary.** <note>These are various aromatic roots of the ginger family (Zingiberaceae) used in medieval and early modern medicine.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a ginger plant (Zingiber) showing its long, lanceolate leaves and the characteristic rhizome root structure below. To the right, a separate detailed illustration of a dried ginger root segment.</image-desc>

Pliny correctly established that Ginger is not the root of the Pepper-bearing tree, as it seemed to some. For, according to Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, Ginger is a plant of its own kind, growing for the most part in Troglodytic Arabia: its roots are small like those of the Cyperus <note>Galingale or sedge</note>, whitish and fragrant, and they imitate the taste of Pepper.

Those who have seen the plant in India say it is similar to the Water Iris, but with darker leaves; they say the root creeps along with jointed segments, and its leaves turn green again two or three times a year.

It grows in many regions of India, sown from seed or root; the best is that which is brought from Malabar, where it is most common; it is grown there with great care, otherwise it is of very poor quality.

<column-break/>

Another root is available in the Apothecary shops today called Mechinum, and formerly called Secacul, which is related and very similar to Ginger; yet it differs from it—not indeed in maturity or "wickedness" <note>original: "improbitate," referring here to a lack of potency or poor quality</note> as some have truly written—but in its appearance, its density, its transparency, its moisture, its solidity, its sharper taste, and a heat that is devoid of moisture. Thus, this root does not suffer from decay, to which Ginger is liable on account of its inherent moisture.

But to return to the history of Ginger: when the Ginger is dug up, a joint of the root is usually left in a dug-out pit for the sake of the plant's permanence; for covered with earth, it sprouts the following year and produces other roots and new leaves. More on Ginger in the Appendix, where also on Zedoary and Zerumbet.

---

**COSTUS, AND ITS VARIOUS SPECIES: INDIAN COSTUS OF CLUSIUS.**
**Arabian Costus similar to Ginger.** <note>Costus is a medicinal root, often Saussurea lappa, used as incense and medicine.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several segments of Costus root, showing a rough, woody texture and irregular shapes. To the right, two larger vertical specimens of Costus Indicus are depicted.</image-desc>

Antiquity used to offer Costus to its Gods just like Frankincense; for which reason, both for the sake of this superstition and for the sake of perfumes and luxuries, it was held in high value.

It is a foreign plant, celebrated indeed by the Ancients, but not accurately enough marked or described by its features; hence its true identification has not yet been perfectly clear to more recent writers. All indeed declare with one voice that it is a root, and that its shrub is of no value except for the root; but from what stock it comes, and whether from only one or several, no one has yet asserted without doubt.

If, however, faith is not denied to the Ancients, we shall recognize three kinds of Costus: the Arabian which we depict here, the Indian, and the Syrian.

<column-break/>

Antiquity, as was said, made a threefold kind of Costus; and Serapio and Dioscorides distinguished it into Arabian, Indian, and Syrian—who, acting as if dealing with a well-known thing, only outline the types and the selection. Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> has the Arabian and Indian indeed, but for the Syrian he says there is a third bitter kind of heavy odor, which is not named *Garyophyllata* <note>Clove-scented</note>. Thus he seems to establish a certain "sweet" kind, of which neither Dioscorides nor Pliny made mention, and which serious writers contend does not exist in nature. But the Monks and others wish it to be had; and the Apothecary shops, following Avicenna and Mesue, make two kinds of Costus, the bitter and the sweet; and perhaps that one is called sweet which merely has less bitterness: let the judgment be for the most expert.

---

**SWEET COSTUS OF THE APOTHECARIES. COSTUS WITH THE APPEARANCE OF ELECAMPANE.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of thick, tuberous roots labeled as Costus Dulcis and Costus Helenii, showing a more rounded and bulbous form compared to the previous specimens.</image-desc>

It is so labeled by Tabernaemontanus and Camerarius, whose figures we express here in one plate.

As for what pertains to the powers of Costus: since Costus is somewhat bitter, it is moderately astringent; and because it is sharp, it heats significantly, and by the grace of its excellent sweet odor, it affects and cheers the heart and spirits.

Finally, there are various ambiguities regarding Costus. For there are those who establish that common Zedoary is Costus. Others sell the roots of Giant Fennel for Costus; others, by a heavier error, the roots of Thapsia. Costus is also called Petasites <note>Butterbur</note> by some. Concerning the Elecampane of Comagene, believed to be Costus, it was discussed before, and it is a species of our local Elecampane.

<column-break/>

The roots of Elecampane coming from Comagene, a region of the East, such as we depict here, are sold by some for Costus; and in the *Images of Plants* they are labeled "Adulterated Comagene Costus of the Apothecaries." C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it "Bitter Costus of the Apothecaries, or the Elecampane of Comagene of Dioscorides": the root of the Elecampane of Comagene.

True Costus grows in many tracts of India, such as in Gujarat, and around Ahmedabad, a very famous city of that region.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics, origins, and medicinal varieties of Ginger and Costus, noting the confusion among ancient and contemporary authorities regarding their classification.</summary>
<keywords>Ginger, Costus, India, pharmacology, Dioscorides, Pliny, Avicenna, botanical illustration, trade, Gujarat</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### INDIAN CANE, OR REED, by some called the Crab Flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Canna Indica plant with broad leaves and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

This plant, having become a resident in our world <note>original: "Inquilina Orbi noftro facta"; referring to its introduction to Europe from the Americas</note>, is unknown by what name it was gifted by the ancients. Some in this age have called it the *Crab Flower*, because its flower, when not yet opened, reflects the shape and color of the claws of the common crab. Others have preferred to call it *Indian Cane*, because it was first brought from America, and its shoots are knotty in the manner of canes or reeds. The Spaniards and Portuguese call them *Cuentas* <note>Spanish for "beads"</note>, from their number, because prayer beads <note>rosaries</note> suitable for counting prayers are usually made from its seeds.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> observed it very frequently in certain monasteries in Portugal, planted against walls under the eaves. We, however, have seen it in various gardens in Lyon, Bologna, Genoa, and Basel.

### YELLOW ORCHIS OR THREE-TESTICLE ORCHID with rather long leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a tall flower spike and elongated leaves.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called the *Third yellow Triorchis* of C. Gemma, *with rather long olive-shaped bulbs of the root*. By C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*: *Yellow Triorchis with a long fibrous root*.

The same Lobelius in his *Observations* also has another orchid of this kind, which, like the *History of Lyon*, he titles the *Second*, and says the leaf is greener than that of the *Third* pictured here; and that it has much affinity with the Oriental Sad Orchid, of which more will be said shortly.

### GREATER MILITARY ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large military orchid (Orchis strateumatica) showing the root system and flower spike.</image-desc>

The orchids called *Strateumatica* <note>Military</note> or *Anthropina* <note>Human-shaped</note> surpass the others in beauty in the judgment of many. For the hooded flowers have the appearance of little men with truncated hands and feet; they are white inside, dappled with purple spots, and more deeply red on the outside. The stem is prominent, and the leaf is very large in length and breadth.

It blooms on the wooded slopes of mountains from the beginning of May until the end.

Most call it the *Strateumatic* or *Military Orchid*, and some, including Gemma, call it the *Basilea* <note>Royal orchid</note>.

<column-break/>

### ORCHIS, DOG-ORCHIS, SATYRION: Germ. Knabenkraut: French Couillon de chien: Ital. Testiculo di cane.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cynosorchis with twin testiculate bulbs and a dense flower head.</image-desc>

In the same tribe of genus as the bulbous plants, those plants must also be placed which are called *Testiculi* <note>Little eggs/testicles</note> from the likeness of their roots; but from their effect, because in the manner of Satyrs they make one prone to Love <note>original: "Venerem"; referring to sexual desire</note>, they are called *Satyria*. Among these, the *Satyria* have one bulb, the *Orchis* a twin pair, and there are those with three, called *Triorchides* for that reason. Yet all are related in their powers and are friends to Venus; for which reason they are almost always confused in the apothecaries' shops. However, Matthiolus, Dodonaeus, and the *History of Lyon* note that this should not be done indiscriminately.

Various *Differences* of Orchids are reviewed, from which we depict here the *Stinking Bearded Orchid*, which grows on mossy hills in rich soil and blooms in May and June.

### ORCHID WITH HOOD AND WINGS ALMOST cinereous.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with hooded flowers (galea) and broad leaves.</image-desc>

This genus is divided into two species as far as the flower is concerned: one of which puts forth a purple head of flowers, the other a white one.

Could it be the *Male Satyrion* of Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock</note>, which some say is the first and most common, blooming in the month of May?

Furthermore, Galen says that *Orchis* and *Cynosorchis* are names for the same herb, and the power of its root, which is bulbous, is doubly moist and hot. Indeed, the larger root seems to have much superfluous and flatulent moisture. Wherefore, when drunk, it excites Venus; but the other, more refined root, since it is of a drier temperament, not only does not excite Venus, but even inhibits and represses it entirely. More in the following pages.

### LESSER MILITARY ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller military orchid with its root system.</image-desc>

In this plant all parts are smaller: the flower is indeed very charming, but, as in the preceding one, scentless.

C. Bauhin titles it the *Lesser Military* in his *Phytopinax*; Tabernaemontanus in his *Icons* and *History* calls it the *Lesser Strateumatic Testicle*.

It grows in the same places as the Greater.

To those things said before from Galen regarding the powers and faculties of the Orchid, we shall add some things from the monuments of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny. Regarding this, they say it is told that if the larger root is eaten by men, they beget males; but if the smaller root is eaten by women, they beget a female. And it is further told, they add, that women in Thessaly give the tender root to be drunk with goat's milk to excite Venus, but the dry root to inhibit it; from which it happens that if drunk from the other, <unclear>the powers are extinguished</unclear>.

<summary>This page describes the Canna Indica and several species of Orchids (Orchis), focusing on their physical characteristics, nomenclature by various Renaissance botanists, and their traditional use as aphrodisiacs or fertility aids based on the Doctrine of Signatures.</summary>
<keywords>Canna Indica, Indian Cane, Orchids, Satyrion, Military Orchid, botany, medicinal plants, aphrodisiacs, Galen, Clusius, Bauhin, Renaissance herbal</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of orchids (Orchis species), maintaining the botanical classification system used in the previous sections. The catchword from the previous page was "ORCHIS".</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### DODONÆUS’S FIRST DOG-ORCHIS
<note>original: "Cynosorchis prior Dodonæi"</note>
->with abundant, dilute purple flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid plant (Cynosorchis) showing broad basal leaves, a tall flowering spike, and two distinct testiculate tubers at the root.</image-desc>

It has broad, fleshy leaves, almost similar to the leaves of a Lily: a stem a foot or more in height, angled, and upon it many flowers arranged in a spike, of a pale reddish-purple color, resembling an open hood or helmet. For roots, besides the fibers attached above, there are twin bulbs, like testicles <note>The name "Orchis" is derived from the Greek word for testicles, referring to the shape of these tubers</note>, somewhat oblong in shape, of which one is fuller and more vigorous, while the other is more shriveled.

*The "Adversaria" <note>A famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> calls this the most well-known Dog-orchis of all, very common in meadows and by streams. In the "Observations" of Lobel and the "History of Lyon," it is called the Serapias of Dioscorides by Cornelius Gemma.*

### GREAT ORCHIS WITH BROAD LEAVES AND A HELMET
->of dark or blackish color.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large orchid (Orchis magna) with broad, pointed leaves and a dense, dark flowering spike.</image-desc>

It has four or five leaves, large, like a Lily, a hand-span or a hand-and-a-half long, about three inches wide, streaked, shiny, and besides these, the beginnings of two leaves at the ground. The stem is streaked, a cubit and a half tall <note>about 27 inches</note>, becoming purplish toward the top: upon which is a head of flowers that are dark purple on the outside, but variegated with reddish-white on the inside: the scent is light and not unpleasant: the taste is sticky and disagreeable.

We observed this in the Duchy of Württemberg, flowering in May, not far from the city of *Dornstetten*.

### DELPHINIAN ORCHIS WITH SPOTTED LEAVES,
->with a purple-violet flower, according to Lobel.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid (Orchis delphinia) with spotted leaves and a slender flowering spike.</image-desc>

It has stalkless leaves that are spotted and somewhat blunt: the flower is purple-violet: the stem is a cubit and a half tall, rather large, with a twin bulb that is broadly olive-shaped. Lobel labels this the *Delphinian Dog-orchis* in his "Images of Plants." By Caspar Bauhin in his "Phytopinax," it is called the *Eighth Testiculate plant, with stalkless spotted Fool's leaves*.

Whether our illustration, which was purchased, matches this plant must be considered.

<column-break/>

### BIRD-BEARING ORCHIS WITH SPOTTED LEAF
->of Lobel and Cornelius Gemma.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid (Orchis ornitophora) with spotted leaves and flowers resembling small birds.</image-desc>

The flowers of this plant, resembling a bird in flight, gave the plant its name <note>from the Greek "ornithos" (bird) and "phora" (bearing)</note>. There are many accidental variations of it: in the flowers, which are either purple, purplish, or white; and in the leaves, which are very large or small, oval in shape, tapering from broad to a point, or from a point to a wide and rounded base. It blooms in April and May.

As for the roots of the Orchis—to proceed in describing the powers of these plants—when boiled with wine and honey, they heal ulcers of the mouth and any of its defects; the roots of the scented variety are especially effective for this.

### TRAGUS’S FOURTH ORCHIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid (Orchis quartus) with a thick flowering spike and paired tubers.</image-desc>

It is of two kinds, if you consider the flower, which one produces as entirely purple, while the other produces a rosy-white marked with small purple spots. The plant is quite large in all its parts, whose green and soft leaves almost resemble a Lily. Its roots, which are succulent and sweet, can be compared to two oblong eggs of small birds, or the testicles of an old rooster. *Tragus* <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note>.

We believe this illustration, which we bought as a woodcut, corresponds well enough to this *Fourth* Testiculate plant of Tragus.

### SECOND SMALL DOG-ORCHIS
->with spotted leaves on the stem and purple flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller orchid (Cynosorchis minimis) with spotted leaves clasping the stem.</image-desc>

Lobel labels it thus in his "Images of Plants." In Caspar Bauhin’s "Phytopinax," it is the *Seventh small Testiculate plant with spotted leaves*.

We have observed it flowering in April in various places: around Montbéliard and Belfort in meadows and among thickets; near Pont-de-Roide in Burgundy; near the Abbey of Masevaux in the Sundgau, and elsewhere.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### ALL-PURPLE FEMALE ORCHID, with unspotted leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with two large round tubers, long lanceolate leaves, and a dense spike of flowers.</image-desc>

It is provided with twin large bulbs <note>The "testiculate" tubers characteristic of many orchids</note>, one of which is somewhat oblong. It has four or six leaves, long, broad, smooth, and shining. The stem is between nine inches and a foot and a half tall <note>original: "dodrantali & cubitali"</note>, thick, and becoming purple at the summit. The flowers are many and crowded together, purple, and sometimes whitening, with almost no scent. The lip <term>labellum: the prominent lower petal of an orchid</term> is divided into three parts; the middle segment is more extended and marked with sparse purple dots on a greenish-white background. The wings <note>the lateral sepals or petals</note> are purple both outside and inside, with a sufficiently long purplish spur. It is found in the same locations as the preceding variety.

<column-break/>

### BIRD-BEARING ORCHID WITH GRASS-GREEN FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with two tubers, broad leaves at the base, and a flowering spike where individual flowers resemble small birds.</image-desc>

It is furnished with four, five, or six leaves, long and two inches wide. The stem is more than a foot long, with flowers of a greenish-herbaceous color. The part that hangs down like a fringe <note>the lip</note> is oblong and almost quadrangular.

Could this be the "Fox's Testicle with larch-like leaves pressed to the whole stem, with flowers simulating flying butterflies or birds balancing themselves with spread wings" mentioned by Lobelius in his *Adversaria*? <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616) was a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

---

### WHITE BIRD-BEARING ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid similar to the one above but with distinct floral structures, showing the "bird-like" shape of the blossoms.</image-desc>

In this genus, a double variety of flowers is found: for in one, the lip is whitish, having scarcely a tiny bit of purple; in the other, the whole flower with the spur is white, inclining somewhat toward yellow. Furthermore, this Orchid varies greatly in size.

We observed it flowering in April in the damp meadows around Montbéliard <note>original: "Mörtbelgardum," a city in eastern France where the author likely botanized</note>; but at Geneva in May.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER PURPLE ORCHID, AND OF OTHER colors, with others being green.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller orchid with two round tubers and a slender flowering spike.</image-desc>

The root is divided into two round "testicles," one superior and the other inferior, with several fibers attached. It has eight or eleven leaves, some large, two inches or a little more in length, and narrow. The stem is four to six inches high, and sometimes taller. The flowers grow spontaneously, are striated <note>streaked or veined</note>, opening all at once, reddish, with a wider lip than in the preceding variety, fringed, and with a shorter spur, distinguished by deeper crimson dots on a white or flesh-colored background. The wings are green on one part, though more so on the inside than the outside, and reddish on the rest. Next to the stalks of each individual flower is a purplish leaf <note>a bract</note>. It is found in the same locations as the preceding.

---

### GREATER ALL-PURPLE ORCHID, with spotted leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust orchid with spotted leaves and a thick flower spike.</image-desc>

The Greater All-Purple Orchid with spotted leaves, which we depict here, should be considered shortly as to how it differs—aside from the black spots on the leaves—from the one we previously called the "Greater All-Purple Unspotted Orchid."

In the *Icons and History* of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany</note>, this is the "Narrow-leaved Male Orchid" (*Schmall Knabenkraut Menle*). Or is it the "Male Dog-Orchid" or "Two-kind Testicle" of Tragus? <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), who wrote under the name Tragus.</note>

<column-break/>

### A SMALL KIND OF ORCHID, WITH AN ENTIRELY purple flower, of a most sweet scent.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, slender orchid with two tubers and a thin flowering spike.</image-desc>

This is the fifth kind of "Testicle" according to Tragus, who makes it two-parted in Article 5, both with leaves similar to Lily leaves. The flowers are entirely purple and approach the most sweet scent of the Clove-pink <note>original: "Garyophyllæam," referring to Dianthus caryophyllus</note>. This Orchid usually grows on rough mountains, under Junipers, rejoicing in strong, white soil.

Is it perhaps the "Most Elegant or Third Kind of Orchid" in the *History* of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), an influential botanist</note>, provided with two thick bulbs, one full of juice and the other more yellow (as is common in Orchids), with narrow, long leaves, etc.?

# OF PLANTS

### ORCHID WITH SMALL RED OR SCARLET FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a slender stem, several leaves at the base and along the stalk, and a dense, elongated flower spike at the top.</image-desc>

It is scarcely larger than a palm's breadth: with several small leaves that closely clasp the stem. The flowers are an inch and a half long and nearly an inch wide—small, red, and almost of a single uniform color. Could this be the *Third Fool's Orchis* <note>original: "Testiculus morio tertius"</note> of Dodoens? Or the *Orchid with most elegant red flowers* described by Clusius in his Pannonian history? Caspar Bauhin labels it "Orchid 19 with most elegant red flowers" in his *Phytopinax*. We ourselves have seen it blooming in June in the meadows near *Souchaux* in Montbéliard.

### DUTCH ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid featuring a bulbous root system with two tubers, a central stem with leaves, and a rounded, dense cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

It rises with a stem about nine inches high: which is surrounded by three or four narrow leaves. The top of the stem supports a short spike of flowers of an elegant, intense red color, with a three-lobed lip hanging down.

It is rare to find and grows only on coastal embankments, unless it is transferred into gardens, where it unfolds its head of flowers more broadly.

### ORCHID WITH MANY SMALL SPOTTED FLOWERS: Perhaps Clusius’s 4th Pannonian Orchid?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with two distinct tubers at the root, several broad leaves at the base, and a tall stem ending in a long, tapered spike of small flowers.</image-desc>

The bulbs of this one, as in the others, are two: one shaped like an olive, the other rounder, from which fibers <note>rootlets</note> grow. The stem is a span and a half high, surrounded by five to seven leaves, a palm long and an inch and a half wide; some of these are turned back, while others wrap around the stem. The flowers are crowded into a fairly short spike; they are tiny, with a very short greenish spur and a rust-colored hood <note>the "galea" or helmet-shaped part of the orchid flower</note>. Others are entirely greenish or half-purplish, marked with red dots. The lip is somewhat similar to a small four-legged animal, divided into three or four parts, winged, entirely whitish on the outside, but marked on the inside with very frequent deep purple spots: the tips in the "mouth" of the flower are yellow. It blooms in May in the meadows.

Could this be the *Lesser orchid with blood-spotted flowers* in Camerarius’s garden catalog?

<column-break/>

### LESSER GOAT-ORCHID WITH SOOTY FLOWERS; in German: *klein Bocks Hödle* <note>literally "little buck's testicles," a common folk name for orchids due to the shape of their tubers</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a pair of tubers, a stem with several leaves, and a flower spike that appears darker or "sooty" in texture.</image-desc>

<margin>Lobelius, in his *Observations and Icons of Plants*, calls this the "Lesser and truer Goat-Orchid of Cornelius Gemma," or the "Bedbug-scented Orchid" <note>original: "Coriosmites vel Coriophoca"</note>, because the flower is the color of soot, and its shape, color, and smell are like those of a bedbug. The leaf is not unlike the smaller *Delphinium Satyricum*: it delights in well-watered places and blooms at the same time as the Delphiniums.</margin>

In the *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" by Dalechamps</note> it is also called the *Lesser truer Goat-Orchid of Gemma*.

### LESSER NARROW-LEAVED ORCHID with broad leaves at the top.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with two tubers, long narrow leaves along the stem, and a dense flower head.</image-desc>

<margin>Tabernaemontanus calls this *Testiculus 16* or "Little Boy's-Wort" <note>German: "Klein knaben-wurtz"</note>: however, in his usual fashion, he provides no description of it. But if the illustration matches the plant, it is a notable kind of Orchid, differing from the others in that the upper leaves near the flowers are long, whereas in others they are short.</margin>

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax* it is Orchid 29; in Tabernaemontanus it is the 16th, the lesser.

### DALECHAMPS’ ROUND ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with two round tubers and a single stem topped with a perfectly spherical flower head.</image-desc>

<margin>He says the root consists of a pair, like testicles, fleshy and fibrous at the top; a single stem, a cubit high and round: with at most three or four leaves, bright, veined, and pale, unfolding from their embrace of the stem like a Reed. The flower is scarlet, in globose and somewhat flattened heads: not unfolding into a long stalk like other kinds.</margin>

It delights in the sloping meadows of cold mountains.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### PURPLE ORCHID WITH THE LARGEST FLOWER.
<note>Likely *Orchis purpurea*, the Lady Orchid.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with broad leaves and a tall flower spike, showing the root system with two tubers.</image-desc>

In the works of Mattioli, it appears without a description in his *Commentaries* with large Latin and Italian figures under the title *Image of the third Testicle* <note>The term "Testiculus" was commonly used for orchids due to the shape of their twin tubers.</note> featuring a very large flower: and in the same small plate there is an image of another plant which has long spurs, which perhaps should be referred to the *White orchid with a long spur*.

This genus of Orchid, moreover, was brought to us from Italy.

<column-break/>

### DRONE-FLOWERED ORCHID, WITH purplish helmet and wings.
<note>Likely *Ophrys holoserica*, the Late Spider-orchid.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with narrower leaves and distinct flowers resembling insects.</image-desc>

Of the leaves of this plant, which correspond to the leaves of the narrow-leaved Plantain, some are spread upon the ground, others are raised up surrounding the stem. On a stem a span or nine inches high <note>term: "palmari & dodrantali" - measurements based on hand width and the span of the thumb to little finger.</note> are sparse flowers, lacking a spur, with purplish helmet and wings <note>The "helmet" (galea) and "wings" (alae) refer to the upper sepals and petals of the orchid.</note>, and a greenish line running from top to bottom: that which is in the place of the lip is a full and rich leaf, beautifully expressing a drone <note>term: "fucum" - a drone bee.</note>, of a sooty color, varied with an elegant yellowish pattern of running lines: with a concave green mouth, above which yellow tips lie hidden in the little beak: with a curved, pot-bellied stalk.

Perhaps it is the second kind of Fuchs’s *Triple-orchid* <note>original: "Triorchidis"</note>, possessing flowers distinguished by diverse colors, namely purple, white, green, and blackish: and in its lower part clearly displaying the likeness of a drone.

---

### TABERNÆMONTANUS’S BEE ORCHID.
<note>Likely *Ophrys apifera*, the Bee Orchid.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with a slender stem and small, insect-like flowers.</image-desc>

It is so titled by Tabernæmontanus: by the *History of Lyon* it is called *Gemma’s Bee Orchid*: and by Lobel in his *Observations and Images of Plants* it is called *The Bee Orchid, or the one expressing the little corpse of a Bee*. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Orchid 24. The smaller drone-mimicking orchid with greenish lily-like leaves*. *The orchid resembling a bee, the second Satyrium of Dioscorides according to some*.

<column-break/>

### WASP ORCHID OR TESTICLE, with a hairy flower.
<note>Likely *Ophrys sphegodes*, the Early Spider-orchid.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with flowers that have a large, rounded, hairy labellum.</image-desc>

It expands green helmet and wings, and with a darker and more faded sooty color it resembles a hornet <note>original: "aurescam" - likely a hornet or large wasp.</note> rather than a bee: the lowest leaf, which serves as the lip, is hairy, in which there is no pattern of yellow lines as in the drone-flowered Orchid, but only two clear lines, smoother and lower than the rest of the leaf, joined by a small transverse line, forming the capital letter H of the Romans: and elsewhere meeting in two places they circumscribe an island of oval shape, woody and hairy.

To Dodonaeus it is the *Lesser second Serapias orchid*: to Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, the *Third drone-bearing orchid*.

---

### FLY ORCHID WITH GRASS-GREEN HELMET AND WINGS.
<note>Likely *Ophrys insectifera*, the Fly Orchid.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with small flowers resembling flies.</image-desc>

Three, four, or five leaves, an inch wide and sometimes narrower, about a span in length: the stem is thin, a span or two spans high or more: and upon these are upright, pot-bellied stalks, on which sit sparse flowers, without a spur, indeed representing the little body of a Fly in shape: and in a rusty and faded color, and with an unlovely purplish darkness, expressing a Drone.

It blooms in May, quite common in the meadows of Montbéliard <note>original: "Monthelgardi"</note>.

<column-break/>

### FLY ORCHID WITH A RATHER LARGE FLOWER.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an orchid with a robust stem and larger fly-like flowers.</image-desc>

In Lobel’s *Observations and Images of Plants* it is the *Other fly orchid of Cornelius Gemma, with broader leaves and a rather large flower*: Perhaps it is the same as the *Fox-testicle with wrinkled Plantain leaves, if it exists*, etc., in Lobel and Pena’s *Adversaria*. In the *History of Lyon* it is *Gemma’s second Fly Orchid*. In Tabernæmontanus’s *Images and History* it is the *4th Fly-testicle*. In Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax* it is *Orchid 28. The larger fly-mimicking orchid*.

<keywords>Orchidology, Ophrys, Bee Orchid, Fly Orchid, Mattioli, Lobel, Bauhin, botanical illustration, insect mimicry, Montbéliard</keywords>
