<meta>This page continues the catalog of orchid species, focusing on yellow, creeping, and spiral varieties. The catchword from the previous page was "ORCHIS".</meta>

### SMALL YELLOW FLY ORCHID.
<note>original: "ORCHIS HVMILIS MYODES LVTEA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small orchid with broad basal leaves and flowers resembling insects (bees or flies), showing the root system with two rounded bulbs.</image-desc>

Among all those kinds of Orchids whose flowers in some way resemble a Butterfly, a Fly, or a Drone, that one is deservedly considered rarer and more excellent whose flower is entirely yellow. <term>Pena and Lobel</term><note>Pierre Pena and Matthias de l'Obel, famous 16th-century botanists</note> discovered this in the sweltering and arid, barren slopes of <term>Narbonne</term><note>A region in Southern France</note>, among the male Rock-rose and the berry-bearing Holm-oak; as well as in the grassy areas near the forest of Grammont.

### LOBEL’S HAIRY FRISIAN COASTAL ORCHID.
<note>original: "ORCHIS FRISIA HIRSVTA LITTORALIS Lobelij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a tall, slender flowering spike and two prominent ribbed leaves near the base. The root system shows two small round bulbs.</image-desc>

It has two leaves, says Lobel, similar to <term>Twayblade</term><note>Listera ovata</note>, a little smaller than the narrow-leaved Plantain, hairy and rough to the touch. The stalk is a span high. The little flowers are many, of a yellowish-green, as in the larger Hyacinth. The roots are two, small and round.

In his *Observations* and *Icons of Plants*, Lobel calls this the Coastal Orchid of Gemma <margin>Gemma</margin><note>Likely referring to the physician Cornelius Gemma</note>. <term>Tabernaemontanus</term><note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a German botanist</note> in his *Icons* and *History* calls it the Yellow Testicle-plant or Yellow Orchid.

### CAMERARIUS’S CREEPING-ROOT ORCHID.
<note>original: "ORCHIS RADICE REPENTE, CAMERARII"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two orchid specimens; the left one shows a creeping rhizome-like root system (radix repens) and a flowering spike, the right one shows a similar plant with a more developed spike.</image-desc>

This plant has a creeping and jointed root: the *leaves* are thick and dark: and the *little flowers* are white. It grows naturally in shady woods and in the decaying debris of trees that have wasted away with age. When moved to gardens it survives, but it requires a paler color <note>perhaps meaning it loses its deep green/black hue</note>, and the leaves do not remain so thick.

Furthermore, it is recorded that if the root of an Orchid, especially the fragrant kind, is boiled in wine with a little honey added, it heals putrid ulcers of the mouth.

<column-break/>

### SMALL AUTUMN YELLOW ORCHID.
<note>original: "ORCHIS PARVA AVTVMNALIS LVTEA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender orchid with a long, thin flowering spike and narrow leaves. The root system consists of a single elongated bulb with small fibers.</image-desc>

It is provided with two or three *leaves* similar to the five-ribbed Plantain, veined, smooth, and clasping the bottom of the stalk: the stalk itself is indeed <unclear>verò</unclear> rush-like, a foot long, and sometimes half that size; it bears a long spike of tiny flowers, turning from a whitish color to yellow, fragrant with almost the sweet scent of Musk, protruding from the stalk like a pressed-down husk. A single small *bulb* clings to the bottom of the stalk, from which fibers spread out, to which one or two hanging bulbs are attached.

Could this be the "Small, pale, fragrant Orchid" mentioned by <term>Clusius</term><note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> in his *Pannonia*?

### FRAGRANT WHITE SPIRAL ORCHID.
<note>original: "ORCHIS SPIRALIS ALBA ODORATA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid characterized by a spirally twisted flowering spike (inflorescence). The base shows two oblong, hairy bulbs.</image-desc>

It rests upon a double bulbous root, oblong, hairy, and provided with several fibers. The stalk is nine inches or a foot long, rounded, clothed in pointed, green, succulent little leaves like a sheath. The spike of fragrant, whitish flowers, which cling like little keys, nods in such a way that it turns around toward the top like a spiral: these are yellowish-green on the inside, while at the side two small white leaves cling like wings. Little pods follow, as in almost all other Orchids, filled with small, dust-like seed.

It delights in high, uncultivated, and arid places: and puts forth flowers in August and September: it is quite common near Basel at the castle of Birseck; and also at Montbéliard in the wildlife park.

### LESSER LILY-FLOWERED ORCHID OF THE ZEALAND SANDS.
<note>original: "ORCHIS LILIFLORA MINOR SABVLETORVM Zelandiæ"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small orchid with a dense flowering spike and several small bulbs at the base of the stem.</image-desc>

In its origin and compact appearance, which has a series of scales, it is very similar to the bulbous Cotton-grass, with its fibers fixed in the ground and greenish bulbs protruding. The little stalk is a span high: as for the flowers, they were not noted by William N., a Dutch merchant, who gave this description in <term>German</term><note>original: "Teutonicè"</note>, and says it grows near the maritime sandy embankments closest to Haarlem in the "Earthy Wood," commonly called *Erden bosch*, etc. — Lobel.

<summary>This page describes several orchid species, including the Yellow Fly Orchid and the Spiral Orchid (Ladies-tresses), noting their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe, and medicinal uses for mouth ulcers.</summary>
<keywords>Orchid, Lobel, Clusius, creeping root, Spiral Orchid, Zealand, botanical taxonomy, medicinal uses, mouth ulcers, Haarlem</keywords>

### WHITE ORCHID WITH A LONG SPUR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a long, slender flowering spike, two broad basal leaves, and a tuberous root system with several finger-like projections.</image-desc>

This genus of Orchid has two leaves, and sometimes three, and is very fragrant. It is found in the drier meadows of hills and mountains; as we have frequently observed in such places on the road from Montbéliard to Héricourt; as well as in the mountains overlooking the Griesbach valley, where it was blooming in June with a most pleasant scent.

There are those who recognize a threefold difference in it: the broad-leaved, the narrow-leaved, and a third variety in which all parts are snow-white.

<column-break/>

### HERMAPHRODITIC TWO-LEAVED ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid featuring two large basal leaves and a dense spike of flowers. The root consists of two distinct rounded tubers.</image-desc>

It delights only in marshy soil. It bursts forth toward July, entirely white and delicate. It is called "hermaphroditic" <note>In early botany, this term often referred to plants sharing characteristics of two different groups</note> because it holds a middle place between the orchids called *Cynosorchis* <note>literally "Dog-orchis"</note> and *Serapias*, especially regarding the shape of the root.

By Lobelius in his *Observations* and in the *History of Lyon*, it is called *Gemma's Hermaphroditic Orchid, or the two-leaved butterfly-like Orchid.*

---

### A GENUS OF ORCHID CALLED THE CASTRATED OR EUNUCH SATYRIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with wavy-edged leaves along the stem and a thick flowering spike. The root system shows two large, elongated tubers.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called *The castrated or Eunuch Satyrium of the Cynosorchis genus of Cornelius Gemma;* in the *History of Lyon* it is *Gemma's castrated Satyrium;* by Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History* it is *Testicle-plant 6, castrated;* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Satyrium 15, whose root is not at all bulbous and round, but divided into two oblong parts.*

<column-break/>

### ORCHIDS CALLED THREE-LEAVED GNATS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with three leaves on the stem and a sparse flowering spike. The root has several small, rounded tubers.</image-desc>

In the *Images of Plants*, an illustration is placed with this inscription: *Three-leaved Gnats.* <note>original: "Culices triphyllæ"</note> Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it the smaller three-leaved Orchid, and *Smaller three-leaved Gnats.*

We possess a three-leaved genus of Orchid which has small, spiked purple flowers on a stem the length of a palm or a foot; and four thick roots, an inch or an inch and a half long. Truly, we do not remember from where we obtained it.

---

### FROG-LIKE ORCHIDS, OF CORNELIUS GEMMA AND LOBELIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust orchid with broad leaves and a very dense, dark flowering spike. The root system is complex with multiple thick tubers.</image-desc>

They are considered to be of that genus which is of ambiguous sex: so that you might not wrongly call it a "Hermaphroditic Testicle-plant": for they are intermediate between the *Serapias* and the *Cynosorchis*, especially in the form of the roots.

In the *History of Lyon* it is *Gemma's Frog-like Orchid;* by Tabernaemontanus *Frog-like Orchid;* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Orchid 37, or the Hermaphroditic Orchid.*

<column-break/>

### TINY ORCHID WITH A PURPLE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very slender, small orchid with narrow leaves and a thin flowering spike. The root consists of two small, round bulbs.</image-desc>

That there is a remarkable variety of Orchids is more than evident from the preceding pages: this variety is also observed in size, whereby it is possible to find large, medium, and very small ones in various places. Furthermore, the one we depict here was sent to us from Strasbourg some time ago by Master Aggerius, a most diligent seeker of plants; we have also observed many of them near the village of Souchaux, close to Montbéliard.

# OF PLANTS

### ROYAL SATYRIUM, THE PALMATED ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with palmately lobed tubers, a leafy stem, and a dense spike of flowers.</image-desc>

Orchids and Satyriums <note>Satyrium was a name used in antiquity for orchids believed to have aphrodisiac properties, named after the lustful Satyrs of Greek myth.</note> are often confused in apothecary shops because they possess nearly the same medicinal powers; however, even according to the judgment of Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and pharmacologist.</note>, they differ greatly from one another in their characteristics and appearance.

Up to this point, we have presented the history and illustrations of the Orchids; now we must treat the Satyriums properly so-called. Dioscorides proposes two types, the second of which Galen and later Greek writers omitted. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of Natural History.</note> has two, but they are not the same as those of Dioscorides. Even today, the Satyriums of Dioscorides are scarcely well known. Nor is it entirely clear what he means by the "Royal Satyrium" <note>original: "Satyrium Basilicum"</note>. However, of all the species available today, the *Palmated* orchid—called the "greater unspotted male"—which has purplish flowers, is depicted here.

### ANOTHER FEMALE SPOTTED PALMATED ORCHID:
#### The Female Serapias Palm of Christ, according to Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid similar to the first, but with spotted leaves and a slightly different flower spike structure.</image-desc>

This does not grow to the same height as the species already mentioned; however, it agrees with them in its roots. The flowers are endowed with a purple color and marked with deep-colored dots; they raise up crests that lack "wings" <note>referring to the lateral sepals or petals of the orchid flower.</note>. Next to each flower is a pointed leaf of a deep purple color.

By Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist.</note> in his *Illustrations of Plants*, it is called the *Female Marsh Serapias Palm of Christ*; by Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish botanist.</note> in his work on flowers, it is called the *Second Royal Satyrium*.

### PALMATED ORCHID, OR MARSH SERAPIAS
#### Broad-leaved, with a white-to-purplish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh orchid with broad leaves and a thick flower spike.</image-desc>

In the *History of Lyon* <note>A famous botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps.</note> it is called the *Female Broad-leaved Marsh Dog-Orchis*; by Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a German herbalist.</note> in his *Illustrations and History* it is called the *Marsh Palm of Christ*, or in German <term>Water Hand-Root<note>original: "vvaffer Hendekens vvurts"</note></term>; by Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called the *Broad-leaved Marsh Serapias, the Broad-leaved Marsh Dog-Orchis with smooth leaves and a white-purplish flower*.

<column-break/>

### FEMALE PALMATED ORCHID WITH RED OR
#### Pale Purple Flowers and Spotted Leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spotted orchid with palmately lobed roots and a tall flowering stem.</image-desc>

The synonyms are *Royal Satyrium*, or *Royal Orchid*, *Palm of Christ*, or *Palmated Orchid*, and *Serapias Orchid*. Some, including Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, an influential Italian physician.</note>, refer the <term>Zuzides<note>A term from Arabic pharmacology.</note></term> of the Arabs and the yellow <term>Aureana's Fingers</term> to this plant; but the Monks <note>likely referring to the "Commentary of the Monks of Cassino" or similar medieval botanical authorities.</note> and the *History of Lyon* resist this. We, however, waver with an uncertain mind between their contrary opinions.

The names *Palm of Christ* and *Palmated* were given to the plant because of the resemblance it has to a human hand or fingers <note>referring to the finger-like lobes of the root tubers.</note>.

Furthermore, their differences are many: taken chiefly from their sex <note>In early botany, "male" and "female" often referred to size or robustness rather than biological sex.</note>, size, leaves, and especially the flowers.

### WHITE SPOTTED PALMATED ORCHID,
#### or Palm of Christ.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with pale, spotted leaves and a slender flower spike.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus labels this the *Spotted Mountain Palm of Christ* in his *Illustrations and History*; Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who began the transition to modern plant classification.</note> calls it the *Spotted Royal Mountain Orchid* in his *Phytopinax*.

It grows in mountainous places. The preceding types, however, are observed everywhere along roadsides and in thickets; and when moved into gardens, they bloom most joyfully.

### PALMATED ORCHID, OR PALM of CHRIST;
#### With white or whitish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with unspotted leaves and a dense spike of white flowers.</image-desc>

This has leaves like a Lily, of a pale green, and marked with no sprinkling of spots. The stem is a span high, at the very top of which the flowers are arranged in a spike; they are white, or of a pale whitish color, distinguished by no dots. At the front, they resemble gaping hoods <note>original: "cucullis"</note>, eared on both sides, with a somewhat broad, pale lip hanging down. On the back part, they have a little horn <note>the nectar spur</note>, like the *Royal Larkspur* <note>original: "Consolida regalis"</note>, and are heavily scented. The roots are twin, distributed like a palm into two or more fingers.

There is also a variety of this kind with purple flowers. Both are quite common around Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France where the author likely observed these specimens.</note>.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Palmated" orchids (Satyrium), so named for their hand-shaped roots, and attempts to reconcile the naming conventions of ancient authorities like Dioscorides with contemporary 16th-century botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Satyrium, Palm of Christ, Orchid, Serapias, Dioscorides, Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, botanical nomenclature, Montbéliard, medicinal plants</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

### MARSH HAND-ORCHID, NARROW-
### leaved violet, spotted and unspotted.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with spotted leaves and a dense flower spike, showing the root system with palmated tubers.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called the second Marsh Dog-Orchid <note>original: "Cynosorchis"</note> of Cornelis Gemma, flowering later, with a violet tuft, leaves sometimes smooth and not spotted, but at other times spotted: In the *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published by Rouillé in Lyon</note> it is the second narrow-leaved Marsh Serapias of Gemma: By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is the 3rd Satyrium, the greater royal, second broad-leaved variety.

<column-break/>

### MARSH HAND-ORCHID, NARROW-LEAVED, MOST COMMON
### of the marshes.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender orchid with narrow leaves and a smaller flower spike, showing palmated tubers.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants* it is called the Marsh Dog-Orchid with smooth and narrow leaves, thin-leaved, the most common of all, according to Cornelis Gemma: In the *History of Lyon*, the thin-leaved Dog-Orchid of Gemma: By Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History*, the Marsh Palm of Christ <note>A common name for orchids with hand-shaped tubers</note>: By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, the 16th Satyrium, marsh-dwelling with smooth leaves.

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN HAND-ORCHID SERAPIAS, WITH
### smooth leaves, of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust orchid with broad leaves and a large, dense conical flower spike.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants* it is called the Mountain Serapias with smooth leaves, and the Mountain Dog-Orchid with smooth leaves, of Cornelis Gemma: In the *History of Lyon*, the Mountain Serapias with smooth leaves of Gemma: By Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History*, the Mountain Serapias, or "Mountain Boy's-Herb" <note>original: "Berg Knabenkraut," a German common name for orchids</note>: By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, the 11th Satyrium, the mountain royal, two cubits tall.

<column-break/>

### HAND-ORCHID WITH DEEP RED FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with a tall flower spike and several leaves along the stem.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants* it is called the Dragon-Orchid <note>original: "Dracontias"</note> with deep red leaves and flowers, of Cornelis Gemma: In the *History of Lyon*, the Dragon Dog-Orchid of Gemma. It flowers around the end of April or the beginning of the month of May. It grows in damp and swampy places, especially where the earth is darker.

<column-break/>

### CLOUDY MARSH HAND-ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an orchid with spotted leaves and a loose flower spike.</image-desc>

Its flower is almost the same as the other spotted varieties: for which reason we have also depicted the common form of the Satyrium as it fades, together with the little horns <note>seed pods/spurs</note> in which the tiny, atom-like seed is entirely enclosed.

Lobelius, in his *Observations* and *Images*, titles this the Crested or Cloudy <note>original: "Nephelodem," likely referring to the clouded or mottled appearance</note> Marsh Dog-Orchid of Gemma. Tabernaemontanus in his *Images* and *History* calls it the Marsh Palm of Christ.

<column-break/>

### LONG-STEMMED HAND-ORCHID OR DOG-
### orchid, gesturing, of Cornelis Gemma.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall orchid with a long flower spike and distinct palmated tubers.</image-desc>

By Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called the long-stemmed Dog-Orchid, or the Gnat-Orchid <note>original: "conopsea," referring to the Fragrant Orchid</note>, or the gesturing orchid of Cornelis Gemma: In the *History of Lyon*, the Gnat Dog-Orchid: By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, the 12th Satyrium, the mountain variety two cubits tall.

It flowers around the middle and end of the month of May, and nearly until the middle of June.

### CLOVE-SCENTED PALMATE ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Palmata Caryophyllata plant, showing a tall flowering spike, long leaves, and a palmate (hand-shaped) root system.</image-desc>

The female Clove-scented Serapias Orchid, pregnant with seed. <note>original: "Orchis Scrapias Caryophyllata femine, prægnans"</note> The flower of the Clove-scented Serapias Orchid, according to Lobelius in the *History of Belgium* and *Images of Plants*: and according to Caspar Bauhin in the *Phytopinax*, the first Great Royal Satyr-orchid. <note>The "Satyr-orchid" or Satyrium was a general term for orchids believed to have aphrodisiac qualities.</note>

Regarding the use of the Palmate Orchid, there are those who believe its roots can drive away quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every four days.</note>; Nicolaus Florentinus reports that he cured a certain bookseller of this fever using only these roots.

### REDDISH PALMATE WITH LONG SPURS,
### Palm of Christ, and the Greater Palm of Christ, according to Mattioli.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Palmata Rubella plant with a dense flower spike and characteristic palmate roots.</image-desc>

The Palmate orchid rests upon a double root, which exerts itself in a beautiful cycle of annual alternation: for that root which supplies nourishment to the stem appears entirely flaccid and exhausted; whereas the one that is to produce the stem in the following year is full and succulent. Otherwise, they are endowed with many "fingers," sometimes up to 14 inches long. The stem is a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>About 18 to 27 inches.</note>, surrounded by narrow leaves, which are longer at the bottom and shorter toward the top. Furthermore, the summit is occupied by a very pleasant head of reddish florets, endowed with a very long and curved spur; these are succeeded in striated pods by a dusty, rust-colored seed.

It grows in various places, and is frequent around Montbéliard. The illustration is from the purchased collection.

### SMALLEST REDDISH PALMATE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of the Palmata Rubella plant.</image-desc>

We saw this in the meadows between Belfort and the village of Danjoutin: but the preceding variety we saw on Mount Braulio in Raetia, and on Mount Salève in Geneva.

Furthermore, the powder of the plant called the Lesser Palm of Christ by Mattioli, drunk in water in which glowing steel has been quenched, is believed to be extremely beneficial for those suffering from dysentery. According to Avicenna—who classifies them as a type of "henna-fingers" <note>original: "digitorum cyprinorum"</note>—the roots heat and dry in the second degree. A drachm's weight of the seed powder drunk in wine aids those with the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>, and the whole plant and its individual parts are recommended for various other things, for which practitioners should be consulted.

<column-break/>

### SPOTTED NARROW-LEAVED PALMATE
### purple.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Palmata Angustifolia plant with spotted leaves and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

It has narrow leaves, sometimes spotted and sometimes not, appearing five or six in number alternately along the stem: the lower ones are somewhat broad, yet much narrower than an inch, reflexed, and four or five inches long; the upper ones are shorter and very narrow. The stem is a cubit high, sometimes larger, and occasionally even smaller. The flowers are many, forming a shorter spike, and are purple. The roots consist of several fingers. The illustration is from the purchased collection.

### SMALLEST HIGHLY SCENTED PALMATE:
### Lesser Palm of Christ to many: Avicenna’s Yellow Fingers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, fragrant variety of Palma Christi.</image-desc>

It has leaves like Saffron: a stem nine inches long, reed-like and smooth: and at its summit a purple flower, rivaling the Amaranth, which when fresh gives off a most sweet scent.

To Dodoens, it is the Lesser Royal Satyr-orchid, and to Mattioli the Lesser Palm of Christ; Mattioli argues sharply against the hesitant Monks that these are Avicenna’s "Yellow Fingers": but he does so with little modesty, as the *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel.</note> rightly notes, since he brings forth his affirmative opinion without even a shadow of reason.

Benedictus Aretius labels it the Lesser Palm of Christ, and a scented and most excellent species of Satyr-orchid. The *History of Lyon* and others call it the Lesser Palm of Christ: Tabernaemontanus calls it the Female Palm of Christ.

### MATTIOLI’S ERYTHRONIUM SATYR-ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Satyrium Erythronium, showing a cross-section of a bulbous root and a separate view of the whole root structure.</image-desc>

Various plants are handed down under the name of *Satyrium erythronium*: the Dutch Phallus, discussed in Class XI of this *Sciagraphia*; the marrow of the *Nux Cynephora*, in Class III; some species of Tulip, and the Wood Hyacinth, discussed previously in this same Class; and finally the *Satyrium erythronium* of Dioscorides, the true nature of which is not yet agreed upon among writers. Here, however, the roots of the said Satyr-orchid are depicted according to Mattioli; they consist of a thin, reddish bark, but the pulp inside is white, not unpleasant to the mouth, and sweet in taste.

Regarding these, the *Adversaria* relates the following: they say that Giacomo Cortuso used to show them to us, and—shaking us with laughter almost against our will—he claimed that merely by touching them with his hands, his whole body was truly aroused to lust.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of palmate-rooted orchids (Palmata), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats near Geneva and Montbéliard, and medicinal uses for fever, dysentery, and epilepsy. It also notes the historical debate over the identity of "Avicenna's fingers" and the alleged aphrodisiac properties of the Satyrium.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of parasitic and orchid-like plants, focusing on the Broomrape (Orobanche) and the Bird's Nest Orchid. ### BROOMRAPE: Germ. Spyn or Wind-herb: French Tigne: Ital. Orobanche.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Orobanche plant with a thick, scaly stem and hooded flowers, showing the fibrous root system.</image-desc>

This plant is called *Orobanche* by the Greeks, as if it were the "strangler of vetch" <note>original: "Ervi angina"</note>, because it strangles the *Orobus* or Bitter Vetch. Some also call it *Negam*, as if it were "the killer" <note>original: "Necam"</note>, because by seizing the nutrients of the legumes among which it grows, it kills them; it is also seen to be called the "Wolf" by some.

As Theophrastus rightly advises: "Certain things are clearly common to many; but because they have greater power in certain cases, they are considered to belong to those, such as the Broomrape of the Vetch, or the Cleavers of the Lentil; the *Limodorum* or rather *Haemodorum* <note>A parasitic plant, likely a species of Orobanche or an orchid</note> of Cumin and Fenugreek."

Furthermore, from the various species of Broomrape, we depict here the one which has a larger, hairy, purple flower.

---

### SMALLER PURPLE-FLOWERED BROOMRAPE, branched.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, branched Orobanche plant with multiple flowering spikes.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various places among crops, and even in fields sown with Hemp.

The common Broomrape, however, grows in fields sown with Oats, Peas, Beans, Lentils, and similar legumes, of which it is a blight. It is also found in woods and on sandy sea shores; it flowers in May and June.

Regarding the powers and properties of Broomrape: Clusius writes that a powder made from the dried plant, drunk in warm wine, is praised among the Belgians as a most present remedy for the pains of Colic. Some, says Matthiolus, call it "Cow-herb" and "Bull-herb," because cows, having devoured it, immediately seek out the Bull.

---

### BIRD'S NEST, RELATED TO BROOMRAPE: Germ. & Belg. Vogels Nest: French Nid d'oiseau.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bird's Nest Orchid (Neottia nidus-avis) showing the characteristic tangled, nest-like root mass.</image-desc>

Clusius considers that this plant—which is called "Abortive Broomrape" and "Abortive Satyrion" <note>An old name for orchids</note> by Lobelius and Dodonaeus, and "Morning Tears" <note>original: "Morgentréhen"</note> by some Germans—should undoubtedly be numbered among the *Leimodoris* [*Haemodoris*]; some also believe it to be the *Coagulum* of Pliny.

It grows in damp and shady woods and flowers in the month of May. We have seen it frequently near Basel towards Augst, around Zurich, and on Mount <unclear>Kar</unclear>, which is half a mile distant from Montbéliard. The color of the flowers is tawny or pale.

<column-break/>

### BROOMRAPE WITH SMALLER FLOWER, HAIRY and purplish:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender Orobanche specimen with smaller flowers and a hairy stem.</image-desc>

Two types of Broomrape were established by the Ancients: one of which is only a reddish little stalk, which Dioscorides describes; the other is truly a legume, or rather the blight and pest of legumes—especially of the Vetch—which we are dealing with here.

Various species of it are reviewed by more recent authors: some are wider, others low-growing; some white, some whitish, some yellowish, some brown, and others of a bluish color. Some grow upon the roots of other plants, while many subsist by themselves and grow alone among other plants and buds. Most of them, however, are endowed with a single and simple stem, though occasionally they have one that is branched and many-cleft.

---

### GREAT PURPLE BROOMRAPE, of Montpellier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust Orobanche species with a thick stem and dense floral spike.</image-desc>

This flowers near Montpellier in April in the Gramont Woods. Its stem is the thickness of a finger and two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> in height; the stalk is purplish, upon which quite short, stem-clasping leaves are pressed in a certain series facing upwards. Purple flowers occupy the stalk, similar to the flowers of an Orchid, with two-horned spurs, each separated by a small leaf. The root is not endowed with any bulbous fibers.

There are those who call the Broomrape "evil flower," and "Evil Henry," and "evil herb"; and if it grows upon Thyme, Maranta wishes it to be called *Epithymum*; nor are there lacking those who refer the "Broom-rape" <note>original: "Rapum Genistae"</note> to the *Orobanche* genus.

---

### PURPLE AUSTRIAN FALSE-LEIMODORON, related to Broomrape and Bird's Nest, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Limodorum species with a tall, scaly stalk and distinct orchid-like flowers.</image-desc>

The entire plant is endowed with a deep purple and plainly violet color, and it flowers in June.

By Lobelius it is called "Bird's Nest" from the species of Abortive Satyrion, "Abortive Orchid," and "Abortive Satyrion."

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of various plants, focusing on leafless and tuberous species like Dentaria and Arum. It maintains the encyclopedic style of 16th-century herbals, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary botanists.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SMALL LEAFLESS TOOTHWORT OF TABER-
->naemontanus: German: Small bald-herb.<- <note>original: "Klein kaal kraut." Tabernaemontanus was a famous 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dentaria Aphyllos plant, showing a leafless stalk with small flowers and a scaly, horizontal rhizome root.</image-desc>

This is a delicate little plant, about a span high <note>a "span" is roughly 9 inches</note>, succulent, white, and without leaves. The small stalk appears to be marked by certain traces of joints: and several delicate little flowers occupy its summit, approaching very closely to the flowers of the Orchid. The root is white and tooth-like <note>hence the name "Dentaria" or Toothwort</note>. It grows in the mountains in August.

### ARUM: German: Arum, Arum-herb: French: Calf's foot, Dog's penis: Italian: Arum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Arum plant (Cuckoopint) featuring large, arrow-shaped leaves and a central spadix enclosed in a spathe, with a tuberous root system.</image-desc>

The leaf of the Arum, says Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note>, is quite large and broad, hollow and like a Cucumber: it has no stalk and likewise no flower, etc.

Marcellus and Cordus <note>Renaissance commentators</note> criticize Pliny: the former because he confuses Arum with Dragon-plant <note>Dracunculus</note>; the latter because he writes that it has a large root.

According to Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note>, the Arum puts forth leaves like the Dragon-plant, but longer and marked with fewer spots: a stalk nine inches long, somewhat purplish, in the appearance of a pestle <note>the "spadix" or central spike</note>, from which comes a saffron-colored seed: and a root like the Dragon-plant, but white.

Moreover, the Arum is given various other names: for it is also called *Aras*, *Iarus* of the Apothecaries, *Colubrina* <note>Snake-like</note>, *Serpentaria* <note>Serpent-herb</note>, *Calf's foot*, *Beard of Aaron*, *Priest's penis* or *little pillar*, etc. *More in the following pages.*

### ARISARUM: German: Monk's testicles. <note>original: "Münch hoden." A common folk name for the plant's twin tubers.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Arisarum plant, showing the characteristic "friar's cowl" shaped flower and rounded tuberous root.</image-desc>

In the opinion of Dioscorides, Arisarum <note>Friar's Cowl</note> is a small herb whose root fills the size of an Olive. Galen and Paulus make Arisarum smaller than Arum, and attribute the same root to it, nor do they have more to say about Asarum. Pliny mentions it under the name *Aris*, of which some wish *Arisarum* to be the diminutive: but what the *Aris* of the Ancients properly is, or what Hippocrates (who first wrote of it) understood by it, is not yet sufficiently clear.

However, although the Ancients left to posterity the history of only one Arisarum: the Moderns recognize two kinds of it, namely the Broad-leaved which we depict here, and whose flower, resembling a Monk's hood, is of a dark color at the tip and white in the rest, and the Narrow-leaved, of which more follows.

<column-break/>

### CORDUS’S AMBLATUM, OR LEAFLESS PLANT
->approaching the Broomrape.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Amblatum (Lathraea) plant, showing a dense cluster of scaly, succulent stems with drooping flowers and a thick, branching root system.</image-desc>

This plant has a manifold root, packed with a wonderful mass of tooth-like scales, white, soft, and juicy. The stalk is nine inches long, the thickness of the little finger, round, succulent, and brittle: near which, at long intervals on both sides, certain membrane-like parts come forth mimicking leaves. Several gaping flowers occupy the highest part of the little stalk, nodding and facing forward, all reddish or purplish. These are followed by little vessels the size of a Hazelnut, very densely stuffed with small, round, black seed.

It is found in shady mountains, where it blooms in May. It is astringent, cooling, and cleansing. *More in the Appendix.*

### BYZANTINE ARUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Byzantine Arum, showing spotted leaves and the flowering spathe.</image-desc>

Several differences of Arum are observed, by reason of location, by reason of the leaf, and by reason of the pestle <note>spadix</note>. Thus Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note> calls this one the Constantinopolitan or Byzantine, because the roots were brought from Constantinople. A difference is also observed in the leaves: for they are larger or smaller, sharper or rounder, sprinkled with white, purple, or black spots. Thus the pestle also varies, in color either purple, or from white to yellow.

In Italy they have three species of Arum, one with black spots, another with yellow, and a third without spots. Indeed, the one with blackish spots puts forth leaves in the fields, in vineyards, in paths near hedges, and almost everywhere on the roads, as soon as Winter has passed. *More in the Appendix.*

### NARROW-LEAVED ARISARUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the narrow-leaved Arisarum, showing slender leaves and the hooded flower.</image-desc>

Clusius writes that the Broad-leaved Arisarum is common in the hedges of Portugal, on salt-flats and hills, and near roads. But the Narrow-leaved is found growing wild in the heaths and fern-beds of Liguria <note>Northern Italy</note>: and according to the testimony of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, it is accustomed to be cultivated in Belgian, French, and English gardens.

Its leaves are long and narrow, green, shining, five or six in number: after which comes forth the Hood, longer and more hooked, turning white at the back of the tip: from which an oblong mouth comes out like a tongue, a span in length, bent, of a purplish color, or greenish-purple, and pointed. The fruit here is crowded like a cluster of grapes and white.

Furthermore, according to Dioscorides, Arisarum is of far greater sharpness than Arum, and is powerful for curing spreading sores <note>original: "nomas," referring to gangrenous or eating ulcers</note>.

<keywords>Dentaria, Arum, Arisarum, Toothwort, Cuckoopint, Byzantine Arum, botany, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Clusius, Renaissance science</keywords>

IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
Kk 2

<margin>
SNAKEWORT, DRAGON-PLANT <note>original: *Serpentaria, Dracunculus*</note>: German *Schlangen-kraut*: French *Serpentaire*: Italian *Serpentina*.
</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Serpentaria plant with a spotted, snake-like stalk and palmate leaves.</image-desc>

The smooth stalk, sprinkled with purple spots, represents a snake's body with its variegated appearance, and its reddish tail represents a twisted dragon: from which it happened that in all languages a name was given to it based on its serpentine shape.

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note>, contrary to his usual habit, neglected the description and deals only with its powers. Pliny confuses it with Arum. Dioscorides, however, distinguishes between the *Greater* and *Lesser* varieties and describes both. Yet, they are one and the same thing under different names: which is why Galen, Paulus, Aetius, Serapio, Oribasius, Marcellus, Connarius, Amatus, Mattioli, and almost all other writers recognize only one Dragon-plant in Dioscorides, and consider the chapter on the second one to be a forgery.

### COLOCASIA, EGYPTIAN BEAN, CULCAS:
->*Mantle of our Lady.*<- <note>original: *Manta di nostra Senora*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Colocasia plant with large, broad, heart-shaped leaves.</image-desc>

Dioscorides, in describing the Egyptian Bean, followed Theophrastus almost exactly, and Pliny certainly interprets him. However, the root is by no means thorny, as Theophrastus claims. We have depicted neither flowers nor fruits: because, as Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, a physician and botanist who traveled to Egypt</note> warns, no one has ever seen the Colocasia called *Culcas* endowed with flowers or fruits, although Dioscorides attributes both to it, and Mattioli wrongly adds them to his illustration. Why the Ancients called it the "Egyptian Bean" when it bears no beans is not sufficiently clear.

It produces much seed and excites lust: concerning its origins and culinary use, see later under the entry *Faalim*.

### THEVET’S FAALIM, Similar to ELECAMPANE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Faalim plant, showing large ribbed leaves and a thick root structure.</image-desc>

This herb is similar to Elecampane <note>original: *Helenium*</note> especially in its leaves; it is very fertile on the island of Mombasa, and is called *Faalim* in the native language. *Thevet* <note>André Thevet, a 16th-century French explorer and writer</note>.

It works against the poisons of all serpents, with which that region abounds, and is a most ready and excellent remedy for them.

Furthermore, Alpinus writes that among the Egyptians, fields are seen full of Colocasia (which we discussed just above) much like our Turnips: and they eat them both raw and prepared in various ways. Belon found it in abundance in Crete near streams, Clusius found it in Portugal, and it is also cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

### WATER DRAGON-PLANT, OR MARSH DRAGON.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a water dragon plant (Calla palustris) with heart-shaped leaves and a spadix.</image-desc>

It is accustomed to grow here in damp, marshy places, and in the swamps themselves, and in the sluggish streams of the fields. It blooms for the most part in May. The preceding Dragon-plant, however, is produced in shady spots around hedges and stone walls. Mattioli saw both—the Greater and the Lesser, forsooth—at Trent and Venice. We certainly have known only one, and of the kind which, except for the leaves, Dioscorides describes in both chapters.

As for its powers: the Dragon-plant, according to Galen, possesses something very similar to Arum in both leaves and root: but it is both sharper and more bitter than that: and therefore more heating and composed of subtle parts. From its "signature" <note>The Doctrine of Signatures: the belief that a plant's appearance indicates its medicinal use (e.g., snake-like spots cure snakebites)</note>, more recent authors attribute to it power against serpents. The aquatic variety, however, is less potent in all respects.

### THEVET’S HETICH: PLINY’S OETUM: American TURNIP. The Plant that Collects Water.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Hetich plant, showing its foliage and large tuberous roots.</image-desc>

Thevet writes that two kinds of Hetich are found: one which turns yellow when cooked, like a Quince: the other which turns white when cooked. Both have Mallow-like leaves. This plant bears no seed, but is propagated by roots divided into slices and committed again to the earth.

Moreover, these roots are persistent in American soil, and almost nothing else serves them for food. Dalechamps thinks it is the *Oetum* of Pliny, of which he says: They also chew the *Oeum*, which has few and very small leaves (*large* ones, says Theophrastus), but a large root.

Among the Siberos, an American nation, there is also found a plant having very large leaves, in which (as well as in the root) a very great amount of water is contained and preserved, as *Bergi* writes.

### BATATAS, A FOREIGN INDIAN PLANT, also called *Camotes, Amotes & Ajies* by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sweet potato plant (Batatas) with trailing vines and tubers.</image-desc>

Clusius is uncertain whether it was known to the Ancients, and for that reason he adds no Greek or Latin name.

It grows spontaneously in the New World and in all provinces of the Indies, from where it was first brought into Spain. Now, however, it is sown in many places in Baetica <note>Southern Spain/Andalusia</note>, either whole or cut into slices: the smaller roots are planted whole, the larger ones cut into pieces.

Monardes says it is temperate in nature, of a substance midway between meat and fruit, and of much nourishment, but flatulent. The root is very useful, taking the place of corn, and is eaten by the inhabitants either raw or cooked: and even now it is a delicacy among the Spaniards because of its pleasant flavor.

It compares classical descriptions from Dioscorides and Pliny with contemporary reports from explorers like Thevet and Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>Snakewort, Colocasia, Sweet Potato, Batatas, Thevet, Clusius, Dioscorides, Botany, New World plants, medicinal herbs, Doctrine of Signatures</keywords>

### IGNAME OR INHAME <note>The Yam</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large, tuberous root system with thick, gnarled tubers and some leafy stems emerging from the top.</image-desc>

Roots of various shapes and sizes, related to the Sweet Potato <note>original: "Batatis"</note>, grow spontaneously on the Island of St. Thomas and others situated not far from the New World. The individual bulbs are rounded and oblong, equaling a turnip that is blunt at both ends; their color is dusky on the outside and white within. The flavor is very pleasant, much like a delicate millet or crushed beans.

They reach a length of a foot or more and the thickness of an arm, and are endowed with many small fibers and a rough, uneven skin.

<column-break/>

### Another Illustration of the IGNAME OR INHAME ROOTS.

<image-desc>A second botanical illustration of the Inhame root, showing two distinct, elongated tubers connected by a thin stem.</image-desc>

The islanders use them roasted and boiled, both as food and as an aphrodisiac <note>original: "Veneris illicio," an enticement to Venus</note>; they also eat them with salt, oil, and vinegar.

The substance of the roots is white, tough, and succulent, and somewhat lumpy, yet tender and not of an unpleasant flavor; some say it recalls the taste of Cassava, though it is more tender.

These roots are called *Postades* in the vernacular by both the <unclear>twins</unclear> <note>likely a reference to specific local groups or a misprint for a nationality</note> and the Spaniards.

---

<column-break/>

### AGES, GUARAGUAX, TUNNA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration showing two small palm-like plants or shrubs with radiating leaves at the top of slender stems.</image-desc>

The species of *Ages* <note>A Caribbean term for types of sweet potatoes or yams</note> are innumerable, as we learn from the *History* of Peter Martyr <note>Pietro Martire d'Anghiera, a 16th-century historian of the Age of Discovery</note>. Their differences are distinguished by their leaves and flowers.

One species is called *Guaraguax*, which is whitish inside and out; another is *Guaraguei*, having a violet color on the outside but white within; another is *Zazagueio*, which is reddish on the outside and white within; another is *Squinetes*, which is whitish inside and out; another is *Tunna*, which is violet throughout; another is *Hobos*, yellowish in skin and flesh; another is *Aribumae*, with violet skin and white flesh; another is *Aniguamar*, violet outside and white inside; another is *Guacanacca*, with whitening skin and violet flesh.

They cultivate these on the island of Cuba and use them in place of fruits, just as our people use Turnips, Navews, Radishes, Tubers, etc.

The figures pictured here are placed in the *Universal History* under the following title, and perhaps suit that better.

<column-break/>

### MANIHOT, YUCCA AND CASSAVA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Manihot (Cassava) plant, showing a large, tapered root and a stem with palmate, finger-like leaves.</image-desc>

The West Indians have a type of bread which they commonly call *Cassava*. It is made from *Yucca* or *Manihot*. Now, the Yucca or Manihot is a root the thickness of a turnip, which produces no seed of its own, but only certain knotty and solid canes with green leaves, like Hemp. Some call it Yucca, others *Manihot*.

There is not just one kind of Yucca: one is sweeter and more precious than the other, from which food is prepared for the petty kings <note>original: "Regulis," referring to local chieftains or caciques</note>. There is also a kind which the nobles eat, and another which the common people eat. For almost countless ages the Indians have sustained their lives with such bread, and even today the Spaniards who live in those regions subsist on it.

---

# OF IMAGES AND THE SKETCH
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS 20.
### CONCERNING RAMPIONS, BELLFLOWERS, AND THEIR RELATIVES.

**RAMPION, THE COMMON RAMPION:**
German: <term>klein Rapüntzel</term> <note>Small Rampion</note>: French: <term>Raiponce</term>: Italian: <term>Raponzoli</term>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rapunculus vulgaris showing a long, tapered taproot, basal leaves, and a tall flowering stalk with small bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Whether the Ancients made mention of Rampions is a matter of controversy among more recent authors. Ruellius, Cornarius, Fuchs, Gesner, and Dodoens <note>Prominent 16th-century botanists</note> considered it to be the "Wild Turnip" <note>original: "Rapum Sylvestre"</note> of the Ancients. Ruellius and Cornarius affirmed this all the more undoubtingly because the descriptions of the Wild Turnip by Dioscorides and Pliny seem to agree in every part with the Rampion. However, it appeared otherwise to Mattioli, Laguna, and others; they argue that whatever Ruellius and Cornarius may say, the Rampion does not correspond to the descriptions of Dioscorides and Pliny. Could it be the <term>Iasione</term> of Pliny? Or the <term>Siser</term> and <term>Sisarum</term> <note>Skirret or parsnip-like plants</note> of Columella? Or the <term>Locust's Foot</term> <note>original: "Pes Locustae"</note> of Avicenna, as some maintain? Let the learned and the experienced judge. More on this in the following sections.

---

**MOUNTAIN RAMPION, OR MOUNTAIN THROATWORT, with a flower whitening from blue.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rapunculus montanus featuring a thick root system and a dense cluster of flowers at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

The common Rampion grows on hills, in meadows, in wooded areas, among crops in sown fields, and in unsown fields—almost everywhere, in warm regions as well as cold. It is also sown in gardens so that it may produce larger roots for use in salads <note>original: "acetariorum"</note>.

In summer it is pregnant with seed, but in winter it remains green throughout. We have observed it flowering at Montpellier in April; at Padua and Basel, on the way to the Mountain, in October.

<column-break/>

**A KIND OF RAMPION WITH ROUNDER SERRATED LEAVES.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rapunculus variety with rounded, serrated leaves and larger bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

There are various species and differences of Rampion. The common variety has a root roughly the thickness of the little finger, resembling a small Navew <note>a type of rapeseed or small turnip</note>, white and sweet. The leaves are oblong but rounded at the ends, spread across the ground, somewhat notched, and hairy. The stalk is a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>, hairy, yielding a milky sap, and clothed with sharper leaves that lack stalks.

The flowers resemble little bells <note>original: "nolas"</note>, fringed at the edges, and blue, which are supported by oblong little vessels.

Our first illustration, which is from the marketplace <note>original: "empiticiis," likely referring to a common or commercial woodblock</note>, does not please us, but this one shows a beautiful variety.

We shall soon treat its location, season, use, and medicinal powers.

---

**THE SMALLEST RAMPION, WITH THIN GRASSY LEAVES.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rapunculus minimus showing very thin, grass-like leaves and a slender flowering spike.</image-desc>

This plant has a somewhat thick root; the slender little stalk, two inches high, bears a tufted blue flower like that of the Spiked Rampion. The leaves accompany the stem, being almost longer than the stem itself, as thin as thread, and numerous.

Furthermore, to return to the use and properties of the common Rampion: the root, in terms of heat and cold, is not far from temperate, nor indeed in its other qualities. It is eaten in salads, either raw or cooked, and is very pleasing to the taste and stimulates the appetite. In Geneva, Montbéliard, and other places, in Spring and Winter (if it is not too harsh), not only are the roots taken for salads, but the leaves as well.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Rapunculus genus (Rampion), following the previous discussions of bell-flowers and related herbs.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SPIKED OR TUFTED RAMPION,
### white & blue: With spotted and unspotted leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two Rapunculus plants with spiked flower heads and basal leaves; one shows spotted leaves (maculato) and the other plain leaves.</image-desc>

Its places of birth, says *Schwenckfeld* <note>Caspar Schwenckfeld (1563–1609), a Silesian physician and botanist</note>, are mountainous and chalky meadows, and woody valleys. The spike flourishes in June.

Some label it the Greater Rampion <note>original: "Rapuntium maius"</note>: in German *Gross Rapüntzel*: in Belgian *Grote Raponcele*: in French *Grande Raiponce*. To some it is the Wood or Wild Rampion: to others the Foxtail Rampion <note>original: "Rapunculus alopecuroides"</note>.

There is a Male of this kind, which has spotted leaves, and a Female, which has unspotted leaves. It varies, moreover, by a longer or shorter spike: and by the color of the flowers, being white, ash-gray, and purple: and also in the shape and size of the leaves.

### SMALL ALPINE TUFTED
### Rampion.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small alpine Rapunculus with a dense, tufted flower head and a thick, scaly rootstock.</image-desc>

It is provided with a root that is, as it were, composed of scales from the remains of old leaves—as can almost be seen in Celtic Spikenard <note>term: Nardus Celtica; a highly aromatic alpine plant used in ancient pharmacy</note>—somewhat thick, and gradually tapering: it puts forth numerous leaves, one or two inches long and a stalk's breadth wide, approaching the Celtic Spikenard, resting on long petioles: among which rises a small stalk of two inches, not without leaves, though these are narrower: upon the summit of which sit the blue flowers of the Tufted Rampion.

Master *Agerius* sent this from Strasbourg, having collected it in the mountains of Styria. However, because it has some things in common with the Rampion of Mount Baldo, we have taken care to have some of its parts depicted separately here.

### RAMPION WITH A GLOBULAR PURPLE
### flower, and a long root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rapunculus with a globular flower head and a long, slender taproot.</image-desc>

It rises to a cubit's height <note>about 18 inches</note>, with a sufficiently slender stalk, the lower part being somewhat purplish, but the upper part green. The leaves are four inches long, serrated around the edges, resting on a nine-inch petiole, and those attached to the lowest part of the stalk are twice as wide as the rest. The very top of the stalk ends in a spike of purplish-blue flowers.

We collected this at Geneva, but we could not dig up the root because it grew among rocks and in broken, rugged places.

Is this perhaps Clusius's Foxtail Rampion with a nearly circular spike?

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE
### Spiked or Tufted Rampion.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of spiked Rapunculus with broad, serrated leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

At Geneva, the white variety with a long spike grows in various places, as it does at Montbéliard between the City and Charmontay, and also in the Forest of Le Chesnay.

The root, however, both of this and the preceding one—before it pushes out the stalk—being boiled and steeped with salt, vinegar, and oil, creates an appetite for food, benefits the stomach, and draws out urine <note>i.e., acts as a diuretic</note>.

### LARGE ALPINE TUFTED RAMPION,
### from Mount Baldo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large alpine Rapunculus from Mount Baldo, featuring a prominent tufted flower head and broad basal leaves.</image-desc>

The stalk is a span high <note>about 9 inches</note>, scaly at the bottom, with the lowest leaves similar to the Blue Daisy called *Bottonaria*, the upper ones like the Great Daisy, deeply serrated, and wider than the lower ones; such leaves are also placed in a dense radial pattern at the top of the stalk, which is tufted, beneath the flower. The individual flowers are also quite large, resembling an inflated skin-bottle, wider at the bottom and whitish, gradually thinning into a violet neck, from which a thin blackish stamen, ending in what look like twisted tendrils, shines out, overtopping the flower by a long way.

Our illustration was made from a dried plant which we still possess: we believe it to be *Ponz’s Lesser Rock Throatwort of Mount Baldo*.

### CRETAN RAMPION CALLED
### Pietra-Marola, with a purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cretan Rapunculus with multiple flowering stems and small, jagged leaves.</image-desc>

This is a Cretan plant, and it does not grow naturally anywhere else: it is found on the margins of fields along the roads, in rich soil, and among walls. It flowers at the beginning of Summer.

It is called *Petremarola*, as if to say "Rock Lettuce," although according to Honorius Bellus <note>an Italian physician and botanist who lived on Crete</note>, it has nothing in common with Lettuces. By others, because it is believed to stimulate lust, it is called by the obscene name *Petrocauli*.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Rampion (Rapunculus), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins ranging from the Alps to Crete, and their medicinal uses as appetizers and diuretics.</summary>
<keywords>Rampion, Rapunculus, Alpine flora, Mount Baldo, medicinal roots, botanical classification, Styria, Geneva, Crete</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BELLFLOWER, THROATWORT: German: *Halskraut* <note>literally "throat-herb"</note>: French: *Gands nostre Dame* <note>Our Lady's Gloves</note>, *Gantelée*: Italian: *Campanula*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Campanula plant showing the root system, broad serrated leaves, and bell-shaped flowers on a central stalk.</image-desc>

The Bellflowers are joined by a close affinity to the Rampions; they possess a flower that gradually loosens itself from a narrow base into a broad width, in the shape of a small basket or a bell, which has given them the common name of "Bellflowers" <note>original: "Campanularum"</note>. There are, moreover, various species of them, the series of which we set forth here.

That which we depict in this small plate is called the Greater and Rougher Bellflower, with a nettle-like leaf: some call it a type of Wild Rampion, others the Greater Throatwort <note>original: "Trachelium maius"</note>, *Cervicaria* <note>from "cervix," meaning neck</note>, and *Uvularia* <note>referring to the uvula in the throat</note>.

It varies with a snow-white flower, a pale purple, or inclining toward blue. A leaner <note>more shriveled</note> variety is also found. It grows spontaneously in various places everywhere, and is also kept in gardens.

### ALPINE SMOOTH BELLFLOWER, with a very pale blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alpine Campanula with a tall flowering spike and lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

Doctor Agerius <note>Nicholas Ager (1568–1634), a French botanist and physician</note> once collected this on the peaks of the Tyrolean mountains, from whom we received it.

### CREEPING BELLFLOWER WITH A SMALLER blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping Campanula with small flowers and rounded, serrated leaves along a slender stem.</image-desc>

It possesses a cooling faculty, like the others, and is somewhat astringent; it is even eaten in salads. By Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, the famous Swiss naturalist</note> it is called the Lesser Rampion with creeping roots: by Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, the Flemish herbalist</note> the fourth kind of Rampion. It grows abundantly in various places, and because of its creeping habit and the fact that it can hardly be eradicated, it is greatly detested <note>by gardeners</note>.

<column-break/>

### GREATER BELLFLOWER OR THROATWORT, smoother, with a large white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Cervicaria plant with a thick root and broad leaves.</image-desc>

This differs greatly from the preceding one. For its leaves are smooth and have scarcely any visible hairs: the serrations are also smaller and not so unequal. The flower is otherwise large and white.

Furthermore, the Bellflower is powerful in its faculty for cooling, binding, and drying: therefore, a decoction of it is useful for ulcerations of the mouth, and it contributes to the beginning inflammations of the tonsils and other ailments of the throat which require astringency: and it is also undoubtedly useful for any other ulcers, on account of the remarkable drying faculty which it possesses.

The white, tender root is eaten in salads, especially during the Spring fast <note>Lent</note>.

### BOLOGNESE BELLFLOWER or THROATWORT, with a small blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bolognese Campanula with a very tall, dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

It is inscribed as "Bolognese" because this very elegant plant grows abundantly at Bologna <note>original: "Bononiæ"</note>; it is not so small, as its summit, clothed in flowers, is a foot long and abounds with many seed capsules.

### BEAUTIFUL BURGUNDIAN BELLFLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Burgundian Campanula with star-shaped flowers and pointed leaves.</image-desc>

This has flowers of a whitish-blue, partly nodding and partly turning upwards, sitting upon or hanging from a short, purplish stalk. Having been brought to us from Burgundy, we cultivated it for many years in the Princely Garden of Montbéliard <note>original: "S. P. horto Montbelgardi"</note>, where it bloomed in the months of June and July.

<summary>This page describes several species of Bellflowers (Campanula), detailing their physical characteristics, Alpine and regional origins, and their medicinal use as an astringent for throat ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Bellflower, Throatwort, Campanula, Cervicaria, medicinal herbs, mouth ulcers, tonsillitis, Alpine flora, Bologna, Burgundy, Montbéliard, Nicholas Ager</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### SMALL BELLFLOWER, WITH ROUND LEAVES
called the Cantabrian of Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara (c. 1512–1570) was an Italian botanist; "Cantabrian" refers to the Cantabria region of Spain.</note>, with a deep purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small bellflower with rounded basal leaves and thin stems bearing narrow leaves and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

We have found this growing wild in various places: Lyon, Basel, and Geneva. However, it grows nowhere more extensively than at Montbéliard, on the walls of the citadel and upon the gates.

### CAMPION-LIKE BELLFLOWER WITH NARROW,
hairy leaves; with a flower of purplish-white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bellflower with hairy, narrow leaves and larger, upright bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Myconus <note>Francisco Micó (1528–1592), a Spanish physician and botanist.</note> called this a species of Campion <note>original: "Lychnis"</note> because of the shape of the leaves and a certain similarity in the flowers, although it is not as "hot" <note>A reference to the Galenic humoral system where plants were classified by their perceived temperature and moisture.</note> as the other Campions described by Dioscorides and Galen.

It grows in mountains and very dry places, and it blooms in May.

### NARROW-LEAVED BELLFLOWER, BLUE
and white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall bellflower with long, narrow leaves and multiple flowers on a single stalk.</image-desc>

It is tall, reaching two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note>, with an angular, rigid stem that shines with a dark green color. The leaves are scarcely wider than a stalk of grain but longer than a palm's breadth; they are rigid, slightly toothed, and grow alternately close to the stem. From their axils <note>the "wings" or crotch where leaf meets stem</note> emerge little stalks supporting one, two, or more flowers. These are bell-shaped but more spreading, usually blue in color, more rarely white, with tips of the same color. There follow little seed-heads pierced by three holes, with five small leaves rising above the center. The root is smaller than a Rampion <note>a common edible bellflower</note>, but more fibrous and twisted.

<column-break/>

### IVY-LEAVED BELLFLOWER, A SPECIES
of Anguillara’s Cantabrian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a delicate plant with ivy-like (lobed) leaves and small bell flowers.</image-desc>

This is a very delicate little plant with thin stems, a palm or a palm-and-a-half high; along these are tender leaves of a cheerful green, like those of Ivy or Toadflax <note>original: "Cymbalaria"</note>, but sharpened into four lobes. A single small flower sits upon a stalk as thin as a thread and somewhat long; it is slender, oblong, fringed at the very edges, and blue, though otherwise pale.

### THYME-LEAVED BELLFLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, creeping plant with small, thyme-like leaves and bell flowers.</image-desc>

It has shrubby little vines like Wild Thyme <note>original: "Serpyllum"</note>, long and numerous, divided into various thinner branches. On these, the leaves are placed in opposite pairs, mimicking Thyme; they are of unequal size, notched, somewhat hairy, and attached by very short stalks. From the ends of the branches rise flower-stalks, nearly a palm long and bare of leaves, on which grow two or three nodding flowers. They are shaped like bellflowers, smaller than a pinky fingernail, and blue in color.

### NARROW-LEAVED BELLFLOWER, BLUE
and white, another Illustration.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of narrow-leaved bellflower, showing the root system and upright habit.</image-desc>

Both varieties are cultivated in gardens solely for the sake of pleasure, just as we cultivated them for a long time in the Illustrious Prince's <note>likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg</note> garden at Montbéliard, and as we have kept them in our own. We have also observed them growing wild in various places: in Alsace, between the cities of Soultz and Cernay, at Geneva around Mount Salève, as well as on the hill of La Bastie, and elsewhere.

<summary>This page describes several small and narrow-leaved varieties of bellflowers (Campanula), noting their physical characteristics, medicinal comparisons to ancient authorities like Galen, and specific locations where they were found or cultivated in Europe.</summary>
<keywords>botany, Campanula, bellflowers, Montbéliard, Alsace, Geneva, Anguillara, Myconus, medicinal plants, garden history</keywords>

### IMAGES AND OUTLINES:

### THROATWORT: German: *Halskraut*; French: *Gantelée*, *Gands nostre Dame* <note>Our Lady’s Gloves</note>, *Herbe de la nuque* <note>Nape-of-the-neck herb</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Throatwort plant with bell-shaped flowers and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This plant is called *Trachelium* and *Cervicaria* <note>Latin terms derived from 'trachelos' (Greek) and 'cervix' (Latin), both meaning neck</note> because of the remarkable qualities by which it is beneficial to the throat (the neck or gullet); it is designated by the same name among the Germans, Belgians, French, and Italians.

There are, moreover, two types of Throatwort, namely the greater and the lesser, which two kinds are subdivided into various species of which we shall speak presently.

The one we depict here is *Pona’s greater rock Throatwort* <note>referring to the botanist Giovanni Pona</note>, with a white flower: which he found only among the crevices of the roughest stones of Mount Baldo, where it sprouts around the shrine of the Crown, and nowhere else.

### VERY TALL HAIRY THROATWORT, rougher, with narrow leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, hairy Throatwort with narrow leaves and clustered flowers at the top.</image-desc>

It rests upon a thick and somewhat sweet root: it raises a stem two or three cubits high <note>about 3 to 4.5 feet</note>, somewhat thick, hairy, and adorned with narrow, long leaves approaching the leaves of Viper's Bugloss, and rough: the flowers are crowded together in a cluster, as in the lesser Throatwort, bell-shaped, but smaller, even though the plant itself is larger.

We found it flowering in June between the Alsatian cities of *Sultz* and *Senn*.

### BRANCHING THROATWORT, with mostly solitary flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branching Throatwort with large, single bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

The root of this one is somewhat thick, four inches long, and slightly fibrous: there are many leaves at the root on short stalks, one or two inches long and half an inch wide: the stem is hairy, divided into branches a foot long, which end in short, wide leaves, from the middle of which arise large, purple bells, usually appearing singly.

<column-break/>

### SIMILAR TO PONA’S GREATER THROATWORT, if not the same.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the first, with broad serrated leaves and bell flowers.</image-desc>

We received this plant from Verona; the image of which we provide here: since it bears little bells, we do not see why Caspar Bauhin <note>a famous Swiss botanist</note> called it by the name *Crista galli* <note>Cockscomb</note>. We certainly maintain that it is the same as Pona’s greater rock Throatwort, in whose illustration long hairs were poorly depicted instead of the notches on the leaves.

### LESSER WHITE THROATWORT?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Throatwort variety with rounded, notched leaves.</image-desc>

This kind of Throatwort grows spontaneously in various places, especially sunny ones, in meadows and gardens, and is also cultivated in gardens. It keeps its flowers in June, July, September, and October: indeed, in early spring the leaves are eaten in salads, having the flavor of Rampion.

The one we express here in this image, we saw in Strasbourg in the highly cultivated garden of Meier; and perhaps cultivation made all its parts larger.

### THROATWORT WITH GOAT'S-BEARD LEAF, with a purple flower, by Fabio Colonna.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Throatwort with long, narrow leaves resembling Goat's-beard (Tragopogon) and upright flowers.</image-desc>

This differs from the rest of the Throatworts in the form of its flowers and leaves, and in its abundance of milky sap. However, like the others, the root is suitable for eating.

### THROATWORT OR MARSH GENTIAN
#### Of Gerard the Englishman.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trachelium plant with serrated leaves and bell-shaped flowers arranged along a central stalk, showing the root system.</image-desc>

We have not seen this plant ourselves, nor does anyone possess it except for Gerard <note>John Gerard (1545–1612), the famous English herbalist</note>, from whom we have borrowed this description.

### ERINOS, ERINEOS, ECHINOS:
#### Greater Erinos, of Fabio Colonna.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Erinos maior plant, featuring a branching stem with small leaves and delicate flowers, including a detailed root structure.</image-desc>

Erinos, according to the author Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, grows near springs and rivers: it has leaves like Basil, but smaller and divided at the upper part: *with five or six shoots about nine inches long, a white flower, and a black, bitter seed.* The leaves and stems swell with a milky juice.

Pliny calls it *Erineos*, while Galen calls it *Echinos*: this is not due to a slip of the scribes, as some believe, but is a reading approved by the judgment of Ruellius, Mattioli, Massaria, and Agricola <note>A list of prominent Renaissance botanists and commentators</note>.

In assigning medicinal properties, Pliny and Galen agree with Dioscorides; nor does Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century medical writer</note> depart from them, though by proposing the same plant twice—first from Dioscorides and second from Galen—he demonstrates that it was not known to him personally.

### PYRAMIDAL OR COLUMNAR BELLFLOWER:
#### Pyramidal Campanula.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, pyramidal flowering plant (Campanula) with large basal leaves and a spike of flowers.</image-desc>

According to Dodoens, there are those who assert that the larger or largest Bellflower is the "Columnar" plant of Pliny, even though the name "columnar herb" is not actually found in Pliny's writings. It is commonly held to be of two types: *smooth* and *hairy*. We depict the hairy variety here, which has sometimes grown to such a height for us that the stem easily equaled a spear's length. This stem is hairy, stuffed with white pith, and clothed with leaves that are hairy and pointed at both the top and bottom. The serrated flowers imitate Bellflowers in a long series; they are no larger than the flowers of the common rampion, blue in color, fringed along the edges, with several growing from a single stalk.

<column-break/>

### WHITE ENGLISH THROATWORT
#### The Greater.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Trachelium Candidum Anglicum, showing a sturdy stalk with broad, serrated leaves and clusters of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

<margin>
The **Leaves** of this are like Foxglove: the **Flowers** are like Throatwort, but larger and longer, of the purest white: the stem is two feet or a few cubits high, <unclear>cylindrical</unclear>: the **Root** is fibrous, <unclear>thick</unclear>, milky, <unclear>long-lived</unclear>, and <unclear>spreading</unclear>: the **Seed** is like Throatwort, but larger.
</margin>

### LESSER ERINOS OF FABIO COLONNA

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Erinos minor, a smaller, more delicate version of the Erinos plant with fine stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

Various plants are held by writers under the name of Erinos, Erineos, or Echinos: *Sweet Spurge, Tufted Rampion, Barrenwort, Great-rooted Figwort*, etc. We have from Dioscorides that it is called by some *Hydreron*, that is, a "water herb." According to others, Erinos is the *Lactoris* of Pliny. There are even those who ask whether the *Touch-me-not* <note>Impatiens noli-tangere</note> is Erinos or not.

However, more recent authors distinguish Erinos into the Greater and Lesser types; they assert that the one we have just described responds to the ancient descriptions of Erinos in the shape of its leaves, its abundance of milk, and its flavor. It also matches in its place of birth, as it is very frequent in watery places, on riverbanks, and at the feet of mountains.

### THE "MEDIUM" OF DIOSCORIDES, ACCORDING TO RAUWOLF.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Medium Dioscoridis plant, showing a central stalk with lanceolate leaves and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Among thickets and hedges, he says, it rises up high, and the plant is very similar to the *Canterbury Bell* of Dodoens. Only in the leaves is there something worthy of note: they are more divided, like Chicory. The flowers also open wider, consisting of eight small petals arranged in a circle.

By Rauwolf and the *History of Lyon*, it is called the *True Medium of Dioscorides*; and the *Mindium of Rhazes* <note>Referring to the Persian physician Al-Razi</note>. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it the *Foreign Canterbury Bell with jagged leaves*.

Rauwolf found it in a deep, dark, and rugged valley of Lebanon.

Regarding *Medium* and *Epimedium*, let the reader consult the Appendix.
