### MARIAN VIOLET OF DODONÆUS, by some called
### The "Medium" of Dioscorides
<note>Likely the Canterbury Bell (Campanula medium).</note>

*Woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with bell-shaped flowers and long, narrow leaves along the stem.*

The Marian Violet is also so named by Tabernæmontanus, C. Bauhin, Gerard, Clusius, and others. Gesner calls it the largest kind of Wild Turnip <note>original: "Rapi Sylu. genus maximum"</note>; by some it is called the Wild Turnip of Dioscorides; by others his Wild Radish. Cæsalpinus considers it a larger kind of Rampion <note>term: Rapunculus (Rampion), a common edible bellflower</note>; and finally, many call it the *Medium* of Dioscorides, but erroneously, for the description does not match, as is evident from a comparison of that plant with the Marian Violet.

The Marian Violets usually bear flowers of a violet or purple color; however, they also bear white, sometimes off-white, occasionally ash-colored flowers, and even mixtures of white and violet, either in stripes or spots. *More details are provided beside the following figure.*

### SYLVIUS’S BIRD-PLANT ACCORDING TO SOME
### with purple-violet flowers.
<note>original: "AVICULARIA SYLVII"</note>

*Woodcut illustration of a plant with pinnate leaves and clusters of small flowers at the top of the stems.*

Dodonæus once suspected this to be *Onobrychis* <note>Sainfoin or Holy-hay</note>; but later he changed his opinion. Thus, Lobelius and the *History of Lyon* incorrectly displayed it under Dodonæus's name for *Onobrychis*. Gesner more accurately titled it the Wild Bird-plant, and a certain "Anonymous Vetch."

It grows abundantly among grain crops, and we have often observed it among them in Montpellier, Basel, and Geneva, flowering in June and July. We kept it in our garden at Montbéliard, where it bloomed for us at the same time.

### FOXGLOVE: German: Fingerhutt, Vualdschell. French:
### Digitale, Doigtier, Gantelée: Italian: Gantelli.

*Woodcut illustration of a Foxglove plant with large, drooping bell-shaped flowers on a tall spike.*

Some refer this plant to the second kind of *Alisma* mentioned by Pliny. Others join it to the Mulleins <note>original: "Verbascis"</note>, specifically the species called *Lychnitis*, as it bears a great resemblance in its stalks and leaves. However, if you look at the flower or its properties, it seems to Tragus that it should be referred to *Galiopsis*, which Dioscorides discusses in Book 4, Chapter 10. We call it the Bell-flower or Wild Little Bell; and also, with Fuchs and others, *Digitalis* <note>from the Latin 'digitus' for finger</note>, from the likeness of the flowers, which resemble a thimble.

It is divided into various species or differences, of which the one called "purple" is pictured here, which grows spontaneously in various places and is cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

### THE MARIAN VIOLET OF DODONÆUS
### Another Image.

*Woodcut illustration of a similar bell-flowered plant, showing the root system and upright flowering stalk.*

We provide two images here so that what is missing in one, the other may supply.

This Violet grows spontaneously in forests, mountains, and many shady places; as Matthiolus notes, in the regions of Germany and Italy. We have observed it cultivated in gardens in Basel, Padua, and Bologna, and we ourselves have kept it in the garden at Geneva and Montbéliard. It does not bloom all at once, but bit by bit, in the months of June and August.

Dodonæus writes that it possesses a cooling and somewhat astringent power, and that, like other wild turnips, the root is suitable to be added to salads.

### ALPINE FOXTAIL, ACCORDING TO SOME
### The Mountain Bugloss of Dalechamp.
<note>original: "Echium montanum"</note>

*Woodcut illustration of a plant with a dense, fuzzy flower spike and broad, ribbed leaves at the base.*

This plant bears a flower-head <note>original: "Thyrsum"</note> of three inches, or a palm’s breadth if the plant is large; the flowers emerge from between the leaves, turning from blue to pale, being oblong and fringed along the edges, with small filaments breaking out from the center.

Others label it the "Thyrse-like Throatwort" or the "Greater Thin-leaved Neckwort," and some the Mountain Bugloss of Dalechamp.

It grows in the highest mountains of Savoy.

### YELLOW FOXGLOVE, WITH A LARGER FLOWER,
### and a broader leaf.

*Woodcut illustration of a yellow Foxglove variety with broad leaves and a dense spike of flowers.*

This varies from the purple kind not only in the color of the flower, but also in the leaves; in the purple they are similar to Mullein and narrower, but in this one they are broader, blackish-green, and woolly. The flowers of this yellow kind are hairy inside and out, and are colored a pale yellow on the outside, but inside they are variegated with a deeper saffron and a faint yellow.

We found it growing wild between Montbéliard and Marvelize; and we cultivated it in the public garden of Montbéliard.

# PLANTS

### RUSTY FOXGLOVE, with narrower
### leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Digitalis ferruginea plant, showing a tall central stalk with numerous small bell-shaped flowers and long, narrow basal leaves.</image-desc>

Foxglove with a pale yellow flower, otherwise called rusty, with a narrower cup and dark green leaves, according to Lobelius in his *Observations*. Narrow-leaved Foxglove with a rusty flower, according to Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*. <note>These are references to famous 16th-century botanists Matthias de l'Obel and Caspar Bauhin.</note>

It bloomed beautifully in the Illustrious Prince's garden at Montbéliard in June and July, and it is a most elegant plant.

<column-break/>

### FOXGLOVE WITH SMALLER PALE YELLOW FLOWERS,
### and narrower leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Digitalis plant with smaller flowers and narrower leaves than the previous specimen.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various places near Spelunca, blooming in June. Also at Basel on Mount Mureto, and on the road leading there from the city; in the mountains near Geneva; and at Montbéliard, on the road that goes to Étupes. <note>original: "Dun" likely refers to the lordship of Étupes/Dun near Montbéliard.</note>

Furthermore, the Foxglove herb is bitter, and consequently hot and dry; it stimulates menstruation, heals wounds, acts as a <term>purgative</term> <note>original: "cathartica"</note> and an <term>emetic</term> <note>induces vomiting</note>, and can do almost everything that Gentian can.

<column-break/>

### MEXICAN JASMINE, the Mexican
### Flower; Marvel of Peru.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Mirabilis jalapa (Four o'clock flower), showing broad leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers, and a detailed view of the seed/root structure at the bottom left.</image-desc>

This elegant and very beautiful exotic plant is found bestowed with these names, which some also record as the *Flaccum* or *Flacquetin* of the Indians. In the *History of Lyon* it is called *Dalechamps' Red Jasmine, the Scarlet Flower*. Cesalpino writes that it is called Mandrake by Theophrastus: but the powers do not match, nor do other features. Camerarius feels more correctly about this plant in his *Hortus*: he says it is called Indian Jasmine, since it was shared with others from the Indies under that name and has always retained it afterward, although it is a plant of its own kind and has few things in common with the Jasmines. It would be more properly called the Mexican Flower from its place of birth. Some have called it *Thaumantin* from the Spanish word *Maravillas* <note>meaning "Marvels" or "Wonders"</note>.

Sown in the Illustrious Prince's garden at Montbéliard, it came forth successfully and produced several plants. It is believed to be endowed with a powerful ability to disperse fluids, and the root, taken internally in a dose of two <term>drachms</term> <note>an ancient unit of weight, roughly 1/8 of an ounce</note>, is excellent for drawing off water <note>acting as a diuretic</note>.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW FLAX-LEAVED BELLFLOWER.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Campanula linifolia, featuring slender stems with narrow leaves and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This plant must also be assigned to this Class, and it is not without reason that it is numbered among the Bellflowers. The leaves along the stems—which are almost a span and a half high—are arranged alternately, oblong and narrow, mimicking the leaves of Flax, and smooth. The stems branch out at the top, bearing flowers of remarkable size, longer than an inch, shining with a saffron color, with the <term>calyx</term> <note>the outer green part of the flower</note> split into five long bristles, like Flax, but more cone-shaped. The root is long, thick, and woody.

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXI.
### POD-BEARING HERBS, MOSTLY SHARP-TASTING, AMONG WHICH ARE MANY CULINARY VARIETIES.

**CABBAGE: German: *Keel* <note>Modern German: Kohl</note>; French: *Choux*; Italian: *Cauolo*.**

**MOST TENDER ITALIAN CABBAGE, BUNCHED, with a white flower.**

---

### WHITE HEADED CABBAGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, tightly headed cabbage (Brassica capitata alba) with broad, outer leaves.</image-desc>

We shall now discuss the Cabbage, a plant familiar to gardens and kitchens, and by which the Ionians <note>An ancient Greek people</note> once used to swear their oaths.

It was called *Crambe* by the Greeks, as if it were *Coramble* <note>original: "Coramble", a Greek wordplay</note>, because it is said to dim the pupils of the eyes; or as if it were *Corambe*, inasmuch as it is believed to oppose the effects of a hangover more effectively than anything else. Varro <note>A Roman scholar</note> claims it was called *Brassica* by the Latins, as if it were *praeseca* <note>meaning "cut off before"</note>, because its stalk is cut off into small pieces. There are those who wish it to be so named as if it were *passa* <note>spread out/dried</note>, because it is cut from the stem into small bits to be prepared like raisins; or from the Greek *apo tou bibrōskein* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ βιβρώσκειν"</note>, that is, "from devouring," since it is eaten entirely by the common people, sometimes raw, sometimes cooked, and sometimes preserved in brine.

We depict here the White Headed variety, the most frequent in use, which is cultivated in various places both in gardens and in fields.

<column-break/>

<margin>This is thought by some to be the *Lacuturris* cabbage of Pliny: by many it is called Curled Cabbage, and by some Savoy Cabbage: German: *Krauss Kölkraut*; French: *Chou d'Italie*, *Chou de Savoye*. It is an inhabitant of gardens and is impatient of the cold.</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Savoy cabbage (Brassica sabaudica) with characteristic crinkled, textured leaves.</image-desc>

Furthermore, to settle upon the general history of the Cabbage: because Cato <note>Cato the Elder, Roman statesman and author</note> preferred it above all other vegetables, it is understood—according to Varro—by the very name "Vegetable" <note>original: "Oleris", implying it is the vegetable par excellence</note>. And since it swells with a stalk larger and stronger than others, it has claimed the name of the whole genus for itself. Indeed, we have it from the records of the Ancients that they even called the Radish a "Cabbage."

---

### WRINKLED SAVOY CABBAGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy cabbage variety with deeply veined and ruffled foliage.</image-desc>

Various distinctions of Cabbages are established by both the Ancients and the Moderns. Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany"</note> divides them into three parts: the *Curled*, the *Smooth*, and the *Wild*. Cato also has three species: the *Curled*, the *Smooth*, and the one called *Crambe*. Pliny has the same, but adds others: the *Cumaean*, *Arician*, *Pompeian*, *Brutian*, *Lacuturris*, and *Tritian*. But best of all, Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note> makes three main kinds: the *Cultivated*, the *Wild*, and the *Sea* cabbage. Thus the Ancients; we shall soon hand down the species proposed by the Moderns.

However, the one we depict here is commonly labeled the "slightly curled Cabbage" and the "Summer Savoy": which is believed by some to be the *Lacuturris* of Pliny, but by others his *Sabellica*.

---

### MANY-FLOWERED CABBAGE <note>Cauliflower</note>: German: *Blūm-köl*; French: *Choux fleuris*; Italian: *Caulifiori*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cauliflower plant showing the developing curd surrounded by large protective leaves.</image-desc>

Among the Moderns, Gesner <note>Conrad Gesner, Swiss naturalist</note> mentions the *white*, *black*, *curled*, *shaggy*, and *red* Cabbage. Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius, German botanist</note> mentions the *Cyprian* or *Pompeian* (which is this many-flowered one of ours), the *Turnip-stemmed* <note>Kohlrabi</note>, the *Curled Bee-cabbage*, and the *White Genoese* (which is our finely-cut Cabbage). Lonicer <note>Adam Lonicer, German herbalist</note> lists the *white*, *broad*, *curled*, *headed*, and *low-growing*. Ryff <note>Walther Hermann Ryff</note> lists the *smooth*, *curled*, the *Crambe* properly so-called, and the *headed* types. Cornerarius makes two most noble kinds: one *low-growing* and *headed*, the other with *extended leaves*. Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, author of famous herbals</note> has four species: the *Smooth*, the *Curled*, the one called *Crambe*, and the *low-growing with a spreading head*. More [will be found] at the side of the following Figure.

<summary>This page provides a botanical and historical overview of the cabbage family (Brassica), citing classical authorities like Pliny and Cato alongside Renaissance botanists to classify different varieties such as headed cabbage, Savoy cabbage, and cauliflower.</summary>
<keywords>cabbage, Brassica, cauliflower, Savoy cabbage, botany, horticulture, Pliny the Elder, Cato the Elder, Dioscorides, Renaissance herbals, etymology</keywords>

--- Page 334 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Brassica (cabbage) genus, following the previous descriptions of leafy greens. The catchword "BRASSICA" confirms the ongoing subject.</meta>

### COMMON WHITE CABBAGE: In German, *Ginnvveiß koel*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common white cabbage plant with broad, textured leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

This plant produces a very tall stalk and provides enough leaves for a single dish. By Lobelius and Pena <note>Matthias de l'Obel and Pierre Pena, famous 16th-century botanists</note> it is called *the most common cabbage, whitening from a dark base*; by Mattioli, *smooth white cabbage*; in the *History of Lyon*, *common white cabbage, smooth, cultivated, of Theophrastus, Cato, and Pliny, with leaves turning white from a bluish-green, and with flowers sometimes yellow, sometimes white.*

Among more recent authors, the *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Lobelius</note> further distinguish Cabbage into *White and Red Headed, Savoy, Fringed (white, red, and black), Sea Cabbage, Kohlrabi, and Clustered or Many-flowered Cabbage.*

Mattioli writes that the varieties held in highest esteem among the Italians are *Curly Cabbage, Headed Cabbage, and Turnip-Cabbage.*

### KOHLRABI OR STEM-TURNIP
Germ. *Küben Koel* : French *Chou raue*. To the Italians, *Torzuti*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a kohlrabi plant, showing the characteristic swollen, globe-like stem above the ground with leaves sprouting from it.</image-desc>

It is believed to have been unknown to the ancients, unless perhaps it is Cato’s *Rapitius Caulis* <note>Turnip-stemmed cabbage</note> and Pliny’s *Lacuturris*. The stalk swells out in the manner of a Turnip, and the marrow <note>the fleshy interior</note> is eaten cooked in a rich broth.

Dodoens, Tabernaemontanus, Dalechamps, and others also recount various species of Cabbage. But because it would be a long task to describe every detail from every author, they should be sought from the original sources themselves.

### ENGLISH SINGLE-SEEDED CABBAGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sea cabbage or similar wild brassica variety with wavy-edged leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves are almost the same as those of the black cabbage, but thicker and of a more pleasing appearance, adorned with wavy fringes and very intricate folds. There is an elegant, dense, and umbrella-like cluster of pale white flowers. The pods are short and somewhat thick, in each of which resides a single seed. The *Adversaria* write that it is found in the coastal regions of England.

Thus, from the seed, the location, the clustering of leaves, the notches, the flatness, the smoothness, the roughness, and the various colors—and also from the head (whether curly, clustered, fringed, or low-growing) and the various shapes and lengths of the stalks, as well as the color of the flowers—the various distinctions of Cabbages are derived; regarding which there is more to follow.

<column-break/>

### TUFTED CABBAGE ACCORDING TO TABERNAEMONTANUS:
Germ. *Büchel Koel*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, leafy cabbage variety with elongated, ruffled leaves.</image-desc>

Regarding the Location, Time, and Cultivation of Cabbages in general: Cabbage is indeed sown for food, planted, and cultivated everywhere among all nations and places. However, all its varieties do not flourish equally in all regions. Some require one type of cultivation, others another; hence one is called *Savoy*, because it delights more in the region of Savoy. In general, the best placement for Cabbages is in cold and rainy areas. We have it from the records of Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> that Cabbages are helped by salt water, and that they become better when watered with it. Furthermore, frosts contribute a great deal of sweetness to every kind.

### RED HEADED CABBAGE: Germ. *Rote Cappes Kraut* : French *Chou cabu rouge*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dense, round-headed red cabbage.</image-desc>

The leaves are somewhat similar to the white variety, but they play with a great variety of color. For some are dark purple, some dark green, or even a paler green; some are also bluish-gray with a glaucous dusting like a mist. But all are interwoven with red ribs and veins. The flowers are yellow. It also gathers into a head and easily endures the winter. There is a great yield of it in the Netherlands.

The *Cymae* or *Cymata* <note>Cabbage sprouts or "tops"</note>, on the authority of Pliny and Celsus, are the more tender and delicate little stalks sprouting as Spring approaches, which from the first cutting are called *Protocomi* <note>Greek: "first-hairs"</note>, and from their tenderness *Haphosides*.

### COMMON RED CABBAGE: Germ. *Roter koel* : French *Chou rouge*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common red cabbage plant with open, spreading leaves.</image-desc>

This variety is taller than the others, and sometimes acquires a tree-like height and firmness; it is very rarely harmed by the cold of winter. It is sown abundantly everywhere in gardens.

Pliny says it would take a long time to go through the praises and virtues of the Cabbage, since the physician Chrysippus dedicated a private volume to it, and Pythagoras and Cato celebrated it no less sparingly. It is worth following Cato's opinion quite diligently, so that it may be known what medicine the Roman people used for 600 years <note>Cato famously claimed Romans stayed healthy for centuries using only cabbage as medicine</note>.

If we believe Cato, Cabbage stands above all other vegetables. According to Galen, the juice has a purgative quality; however, the body of the plant itself, by its common drying nature, binds the bowels more than it incites them to be emptied, etc.

<summary>This page catalogs various cabbage varieties, including white, red, and kohlrabi, citing classical authorities like Pliny and Cato on their cultivation and medicinal properties. It highlights the plant's diversity in form and its historical significance as a primary Roman remedy.</summary>
<keywords>Cabbage, Kohlrabi, Red Cabbage, Botany, Horticulture, Roman Medicine, Pliny the Elder, Cato the Elder, Galen, Herbalism</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
## Page 271

### CURLY FRINGED CABBAGE
#### German: *Krauser Koel*; French: *Chou crespe*.
<note>This is likely a variety of Kale (*Brassica oleracea var. sabellica*).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a kale plant with highly ruffled, curly leaves and a thick central stalk with visible roots.</image-desc>

This is the most elegant of all; it puts forth leaves from long, eared stalks. The leaves are oblong, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or more in height, elegantly decorated with white veins and interwoven by their many branchings. Along its edges, it is greatly curled with many winding, coiled spirals. One wonders if this is the "Curly Cabbage" of Theophrastus, which he records in the first place among the cabbages.

Cabbage stands out with great nobility, as Carpanus writes: for it is both Food and Medicine. Indeed, the Romans knew no other remedy for so long a time, for both external and internal diseases.

---

### VERY THINLY FRINGED CABBAGE,
#### Called "Parsley-like": French: *Chou a feuille deschiquetée*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall brassica plant with deeply lobed, feathery leaves and a flowering stalk at the top.</image-desc>

To those things which were previously handed down concerning the powers and qualities of Cabbage, the opinion of Fiera <note>Baptista Fiera, a physician-poet</note> must be added, which encompasses much in a few words. For he sings thus:

> Unless dry Cabbage prepared the Socratic bile,
> It would rightly be enough for all diseases.
<note>original: "Arida Socratica pararet ni Brassica bilem, / Iure erat in morbis omnibus illa satis." This suggests that while cabbage is a "cure-all," it was thought to provoke melancholy or "Socratic" temperament.</note>

Thus, Cabbage is not without its harms. According to the authors Galen, Simeon Sethi, and Dodonaeus, it generates a juice that is not at all good—thick and melancholic—providing little nourishment, dulling the sight, and disturbing sleep.

---

### WILD CABBAGE: and the Thorny variety
#### German: *Vuilde Zee Koel*; French: *Chou sauuage*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild cabbage variety with broad, slightly lobed leaves and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

Dioscorides touches upon the history of the Wild Cabbage in a few words. He says it grows for the most part in maritime and rugged places. It is similar to the cultivated kind, but whiter, hairier, and bitter.

Pliny, as Dalechamps notes, confuses the history of the Sea Cabbage and the Wild Cabbage. This variety is described by Matthiolus as having leaves similar to the Domestic kind, but hairy in the manner of Henbane (*Hyoscyamus*).

Thalius lists various species of it: the *Greater broad-leafed* kind growing in sunny mountains and clearings; the *Middle Wild*, the *Lesser Wild*, the *Wild with Beet-like leaves*, and the *Wild with membrane-like leaves*.

We provide here an image of Caspar Bauhin’s *Thorny Cabbage*, since no other is available.

<column-break/>

### WHITE FRINGED CABBAGE

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a brassica plant with broad, jaggedly toothed (laciniate) leaves.</image-desc>

Matthiolus writes that cabbage seed, crushed coarsely and boiled in meat broth, then drunk along with the broth itself, aids those suffering from the pain of colic as an immediate remedy.

Indeed, many take Cabbage to protect themselves from drunkenness, either before drinking or after. Thus the Sybarites, as Timaeus says, fortified themselves by eating Cabbages before they drank. Thus, according to Athenaeus, it was a rule among the Egyptians to eat Cabbage before all other food, and so prepare themselves for drinking parties. For Amphis says, *no remedy is more ready for the drunken.*

---

### SMALLER THYRIOID CABBAGE / RED CABBAGE

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cabbage plant with a dense, upright growth habit and elongated leaves.</image-desc>

This belongs to the genus of Red Cabbage; in its flower, pod, and seed, it approaches the more common Red Cabbage. However, its leaves are spreading, reddish from a dark green, and occasionally fringed. Through these leaves, here and there on the back side, a new offspring of curly little leaves rises up—beautiful ribbons, a remarkable game of nature—springing up on this side and that. Sometimes they hang from a short, thin filament; sometimes they cling to a somewhat broad stalk, and even then they spring forth in another sequence of pipes and bands.

The RED CABBAGE we depict here is the SMALLER variety; what it has in common with the other is clear from comparing the image with the description.

---

### WOAD-LEAVED CHICORY-LIKE PLANT, TOWER-MUSTARD.
<term>Turritis: A genus of flowering plants in the cabbage family, often called Tower Mustard.</term>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, narrow, lanceolate leaves resembling woad (Isatis tinctoria) or chicory.</image-desc>

What we call the Woad-leaved Chicory-like plant is labeled by Clusius as the second *Turritis*.

Is it the *Branched Wild Cabbage* of Cordus? Or the *Broad-leafed Wild Cabbage* of Thalius? Or the *Cabbage 10* in Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax*, otherwise known as the *Wild cabbage with leaves inserted in the manner of Chicory around the root*? Or the *White Mustard* of the History of Lyon? Or the *Cowherb* of Tabernaemontanus?

It grows of its own accord <note>original: "Spontè prouenit"</note> on stony and rugged hills; it flowers in May. We found it in the sandy areas near the Rhine around Basel, on the road to Krentzach.

<summary>This page describes various specialized cabbage varieties, including kale, wild cabbage, and red cabbage, detailing their physical appearances, medicinal uses for colic, and their historical use as a remedy for drunkenness. It also attempts to cross-reference these plants with the works of famous botanists like Bauhin, Clusius, and Matthiolus.</summary>

<keywords>kale, red cabbage, wild cabbage, medicinal botany, Roman medicine, drunkenness remedies, colic, botanical taxonomy, Basel, Rhine flora</keywords>

### THE INDIAN ACHANACA CABBAGE
### With leaves like the Water Lily: Cabbage-like *Caion-a*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, bifurcated leaves and a thick central stalk, labeled as Achanaca.</image-desc>

The leaves of the Achanaca are forked and pointed, very similar to the leaves of the larger Cabbage, but not as thick, and with a thinner midrib. In the middle of these, a fruit grows about the size of a grape <note>original: "ubi" likely a typo for "uvae"</note> and of a yellow color, which is highly prized among those people. The stalk is about the thickness of a man's arm. The Indians use a decoction of this herb to treat the venereal disease <note>Syphilis, which was often associated with the Americas in early modern botany</note> to which they are very prone.

Regarding the *Caion-a*, Jean de Léry <note>A French explorer and author of "History of a Voyage to the Land of Brazil"</note> writes thus: "I have seen," he says, "a kind of cabbage which the wild men (of America) call *Caion-a*, which they sometimes use in broths: its leaves are broad, and almost like those of the Water Lily," etc.

### THE TURNIP OR RAPA, THE CULTIVATED TURNIP:
### German: Rüben; French: Raue; Italian: Rapa.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, bulbous turnip root with leafy greens emerging from the top.</image-desc>

According to the judgment of Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note>, the miracle of nature in the Turnip is by no means to be overlooked. Namely, that from such a tiny seed, in almost three months, a root of sometimes a hundred pounds can be produced.

Both the Ancient and Modern writers establish two main kinds of Turnips: the cultivated and the wild. And the cultivated kind, which we depict here, is further distinguished into the long and the round; they say the latter is the male and the former the female. Both are found in larger or smaller sizes. They also differ in color, being found as green, white, or reddish-purple; there are even some that are yellowish both inside and out.

Both kinds are sown in gardens and fields in the months of June and July, for the food of both humans and livestock.

### THE NAPUS <note>A variety of rapeseed or swede-like root</note>: In Greek: *Bounias*; German: Steckrüben; French:
### Naueau & Nauet; Italian: Nauoni & Napo:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a long, tapered root vegetable (napus) with serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Theophrastus did not name the *Bunias* unless he understood it to be the male Turnip. Nor did Dioscorides describe the Napus; nor did Pliny, who, thinking that the "raphanides" of Theophrastus were Napus plants, now forgot himself and confused everything into only two types.

In their leaves and roots, the Napus plants resemble Radishes; but in their stalk, flowers, and seed, they emulate the Turnip; hence Valerius Cordus writes that they are of the same genus as Turnips. And perhaps this is why Galen and Paulus Aegineta established no distinction between the turnip and the napus.

Furthermore, the Napus is distinguished into the cultivated, which we are discussing, and the wild, which follows. Most people divide the cultivated kind again into white, yellow, and black.

<column-break/>

### PODDED PERFOLIATA, A SPECIES OF WILD
### Cabbage. Podded Napus-leaved plant.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender plant with perfoliate leaves (stem passing through the leaf) and seed pods (siliques).</image-desc>

It is a cubit and a half <note>About 27 inches</note> or taller, with a smooth, thin stalk divided into branches emerging from the hollow of the leaves. The leaves are undivided, oblong, somewhat round, with the sea-green color of the Napus, somewhat stiff and fragile in shape; the stalk seems to pass right through them <note>This is the "perfoliate" characteristic</note>, and they have a vegetable-like taste. The flowers are whitish, with pods like those of the Cabbage which are very long and narrow, containing the seed. The root is thin and white, with the taste of Cabbage.

By some it is called the napus-leaved perfoliata; but by most, it is called a species of wild Cabbage. As far as I know from Dodoens, it is not used for food or medicine.

Is it perhaps the Succory-like Woad-leaf, as Cordus wishes? However, it is wrongly called the second *Cotyledon* of Dioscorides by Hieronymus Bock <note>referred to here by his Latin name, Tragus</note>.

### WILD TURNIP: German: Vuild rüben;
### French: Raue sauuage; Italian: Napo Sylvestre.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild turnip plant with a smaller root and more spreading foliage than the cultivated variety.</image-desc>

This wild Turnip is very common among the Flemings and Germans, who sow it so that the leaves may serve as fodder for oxen. It grows so luxuriously in the number of its leaves that the root is not tuberous or swollen like a turnip, but slender. Otherwise, it is not unlike the cultivated round, top-shaped Turnip; only its leaves are more curled and wrinkled.

Our illustration is from Mattioli; Tabernaemontanus also has it, as do Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria*.

Cæsalpinus, Turner, and Anguillara openly profess that they have never seen a plant that completely fulfills the description of the wild Turnip proposed by Dioscorides; and Pliny’s description is also entirely corrupt.

### WILD NAPUS: German: Vvilde Naueuen; French:
### Naueau sauuage, Nauette.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild napus plant with thin roots and flowering tops.</image-desc>

It is called Wild Napus by Fuchs, Dodoens, Lobelius, and almost all others. It is called Wild Turnip by Bock and Schwenkfeld. It is called *Nauera* by Ruellius, and by some, the Wild *Bunias*.

It is sown in the fields in Autumn and flowers in April and March, as you may see in great abundance in the fields of Montbéliard and neighboring areas, as well as among the Mediomatrici <note>People of the region around Metz, France</note>, and in other places where nuts are not available for making oil. The root is not usually taken for food, but the leaves are sometimes used while they are tender. Oil is made from the seed; and with the same seed, bird-catchers feed small birds kept in cages, such as goldfinches, buntings, finches, and similar kinds. Let the reader consult the appendix.

<keywords>Achanaca, Turnip, Napus, Wild Cabbage, medicinal herbs, botany, Jean de Léry, Mattioli, rapeseed oil, fodder</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>The title "Icones et Sciagraphia" refers to the visual illustrations and the descriptive sketches or profiles of the plants.</note>

### WILD MUSTARD OR HORSE-RADISH: German: Hederich; French: Velar, Tortelle, White Mustard; Italian: Remoracia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rapistrum plant with broad, lobed leaves and clusters of small flowers at the top of branched stems.</image-desc>

From the report of wild plants, some would judge this to be *Wild Mustard* <note>original: "Rapistrum"</note>, which some label as *Hedge Mustard* <note>original: "Erysimum"</note>, others as *Nipplewort* <note>original: "Lampsanam"</note>, many as *Horse-radish* <note>original: "Armoraciam"</note> or *Wild Radish*, and others as *Wild Mustard* <note>original: "Sinapi Sylvestre"</note>: thus the opinions of authors vary regarding this plant.

It varies in its leaves, sometimes being wavy-edged <note>sinuated</note>, at other times not cut; in its flowers, which are white or yellow, and occasionally even purple; and in its seed, which is sometimes solitary in the pods.

It flourishes greatly among crops (especially barley or turnip fields) even against the will of farmers, and sometimes covers the fields entirely during June and July, flowering in those same months. We depict here the *Wild Mustard* with a yellow flower.

### SINGLE-SEEDED WILD MUSTARD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rapistrum Monospermon, showing a central root system, deeply lobed basal leaves, and tall stems with small flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

The root of this is somewhat long, whitish, and slightly fibrous; the stalks are a foot long, round, branched, and lightly hairy; the leaves are scattered on the ground, thick, similar to turnip leaves, lightly wavy and somewhat hairy; the flowers are yellow or golden, arranged as if in a spike; the seed pods are round; and in them is a slightly oblong, round seed, from which it takes its name <note>Monospermon means "single-seeded"</note>.

We have seen it growing spontaneously at Montpellier, and also at Basel in the fields on the way to Augst <note>Augustam Rauracorum</note> near the Red House.

### RADISH: German: Rettig; French: Raifort; Italian: Raphano & Radice.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Raphanus (Radish) plant, featuring a large, thick taproot and large, pinnatifid leaves.</image-desc>

The affinity that exists between the Turnip, Wild Mustard, and Radish requires that this be joined to them.

The kinds of radishes are distinguished by Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> by their leaves, roots, colors, flavors, and other such traits. Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note> makes two kinds, *Cultivated* and *Wild*, to which Amatus adds a third called *Smallage-like* <note>Apium</note>, but erroneously: for Dioscorides treats those in various Chapters and Books; nor does he call Mountain Smallage or Wild Radish by that name, but records only that it is so called by others.

Pliny, and Gesner following him, recognized three kinds: *Smooth*, *Curly*, and *Field*: thus perpetually attributing to the Radish what Theophrastus and the ancient Greeks set forth concerning Cabbage <note>Brassica</note>, who also designated Cabbage by the word *Raphanos*. More on this in what follows.

<column-break/>

### WILD MUSTARD WITH WHITE STRIATED FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rapistrum variety with more delicate, serrated leaves and distinct floral clusters.</image-desc>

It has leaves similar in their division to Mustard or Rocket, hairy, with a vegetable-like flavor; the stalks are branched and hairy; the flowers are whitish, like those of the Great Rocket, variegated with thin streaks, with yellow tips; the pods are beautiful, almost a finger's length, and when mature are marked with joints like a scorpion's tail, and are striated; in these, the seeds match the number of joints; the root is quite thin, white, sometimes simple, sometimes divided into many parts.

It grows in the same places as the preceding one and flowers at the same time.

It possesses a drying, cleansing, and somewhat digestive faculty. The leaves and stalks are sometimes taken as food. The seed is hot and pungent; it provokes urine and serves the use of Mustard among country folk.

### DALECHAMPS' KNOTTY CHICKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine Nodosa, showing a cluster of thin, upright stems with small, narrow leaves and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

It grows in great abundance in the territory of Montpellier; with a simple, long root, slightly hairy, of a yellowish-white color; many longish, narrow leaves near the ground, not much different from the leaves of Chickweed; many stalks a foot high; a white flower composed of five petals; the seed is in many knotty and striated globules, following one another in order, and pierced as if by a little stalk <note>verucula</note> in a completely peculiar shape.

In the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Lugdunensis</note> it is called *Knotty Chickweed*. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Chickweed with globular seeds*. Is it perhaps a kind of *Wild Mustard*?

### THE "LITTLE FROG" RADISH OF THE CRETANS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Raphanus Ranula, showing a thick, dark root and a dense rosette of lobed leaves with flowering stalks.</image-desc>

According to the opinion of more recent authors, one Radish is *Cultivated*, of the garden and home, tender and more delicate, which we commonly eat; the other is *Wild*. And the former is reddish, either early or late-ripening; small or large; with white or purple flowers; round or long; white, black, or red; and there is also found a yellow one, and a red one which has reddish fibers running through its substance.

Indeed, the round kind of Radish seems to some to be what Theophrastus called *Corinthian* and Pliny called *Syrian*. But the very long Radish of Theophrastus is the *Cleonaean* root, called *Algidensian* by Pliny.

However, that which is called the *Ranula Radish by the Cretans*, depicted here, seems altogether to be referred to our garden or cultivated variety.

<keywords>Wild Mustard, Radish, Rapistrum, Raphanus, Botany, Medicinal Herbs, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, Montpellier, Basel</keywords>

### WILD RADISH, HORSE-RADISH: German: *Meerrettich*: French: *Raifort sauvage*: Italian: *Ramoracia*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild radish plant (Raphanus sylvestris) showing large, broad leaves with serrated edges and a thick, tapering taproot with smaller lateral roots.</image-desc>

The leaves of the Wild Radish, which the Romans call *Armoracia* <note>Modern horseradish, Armoracia rusticana</note>, says Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician, c. 40–90 AD</note>, are similar to the cultivated kind, but they more closely resemble the *Lampsana* <note>Hedge mustard or nipplewort</note>: the root is slender, tender, and somewhat sharp. We also have Pliny as a witness that it is called *Armoracia* by the Romans: others, by a transposition of the first letter, have called it *Amoracia*. To Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, 16th-century botanist</note> it is the *Greater Thlaspi*, the *Other Thlaspi*, and *White Nasturtium*. To others it is *Crateuas's Thlaspi*, *Greater Radish*, *Great Radish*, *Greatest Radish*, *Nasturtium*, *Persian Mustard*, and *Hydropiper* <note>Water-pepper</note>. It is the *Molybdæna* of Pliny, *Radish*, *Rustic Radish*, *Wild Radish*, *Medicinal Radish*, and the *Radish of the Caterers*. Regarding its location and powers, see the side of the following figure.

### MUSTARD: German: *Senff*: French: *Moustarde*: Italian: *Senape*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mustard plant (Sinapi) featuring deeply lobed, pinnatifid leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of the branching stems.</image-desc>

Mustard is neither described nor divided into types by Theophrastus or Dioscorides. Pliny, however, says there are three kinds: one slender; the second with leaves like a Turnip; the third like Rocket <note>Eruca</note>: Matthiolus and the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Generalis Plantarum by Dalechamps</note> also hold this division.

Ruellius, and following him Charles Estienne, and finally Gesner in his *Horti*, list three kinds: the Wild, which grows everywhere of its own accord and is thinner; and the Cultivated, which has many flowers and higher branching arms, with leaves like a Turnip but smaller and rougher, and which varies in its seed, being either reddish or entirely white.

More in the following sections. We depict here the common Garden variety.

### MUSTARD SIMILAR TO TRAGUS’S HEDGE-MUSTARD, with a yellow flower and tiny dark seed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mustard variety resembling Erysimon, showing a tall, branched plant with narrow, deeply incised leaves and long, slender seed pods (siliques) along the upper stems.</image-desc>

It grows in dry places along borders and among rubble near cities: it is recorded as *Wild Mustard* by Matthiolus, Pena and Lobelius, Dodonaeus, the *History of Lyon*, and almost all others.

Renodaeus <note>Jean de Renou, French physician</note> seems to distinguish the Mustards best of all. He first establishes two types: the Cultivated, of which more soon, and the Wild, of which he says: The Wild grows everywhere of its own accord in dry places, and sometimes even in damp ones, along borders and rubble. It is smaller than the others and bears smaller, jagged leaves approaching the leaves of Shepherd's Purse, but sharper: it puts forth small yellow four-petaled flowers: and afterwards gives seed in pods, which varies in color, being either white or reddish.

<column-break/>

### TABERNAEMONTANUS’S WATER RADISH, with a yellow flower: German: *Wasser Rettich*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a water radish (Raphanus aquaticus) showing a plant with basal leaves that are deeply lobed and upper leaves that are more entire, with a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Because of the flavor of Radish, this plant is assigned to that genus, although, as is apparent from the illustration, it differs greatly in all other physical characteristics from the common Radish. However, the Wild Radish called *Armoracia*, mentioned before, grows spontaneously in several places: and because of the great use it provides in the kitchen during the winter time, it is also kept abundantly in gardens in shady and damp places. We have observed it growing wild near *Wittenberg*: and on the road from Montbéliard to Héricourt, next to the hemp fields. We have seen it cultivated in gardens at Padua, Verona, Basel, Geneva, and Lyon: but it is troublesome because of its creeping nature.

Regarding its powers, see the appendix.

### WHITE GARDEN MUSTARD: German: *Weisser Senff*: French: *Seneve blanc*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of white garden mustard (Sinapi hortense album) showing a robust plant with large, lobed leaves and prominent, bristly seed pods (siliques) containing visible seeds.</image-desc>

The one pictured previously has a somewhat broad, smooth pod, red seed, yellow flower, and the inner leaf is broad, hairy, and dissected: This one, however, has a hairy pod, yellow flower, leaves endowed with hairs and small spines above and below: and the seed is yellow or white, but most often white, and not as sharp as common Mustard.

As we proceed here in presenting the various species of Mustard, different distinctions are taken by different authors: from the location, the leaves, the stalks, the flowers, and the seeds: according to how they vary in color, hairiness or roughness, sharpness or sweetness, position, cultivation, and other factors: since it is not possible to report all of these from every source here, we leave them to be sought from the original sources themselves, or from our *Great History*.

### WILD MONTPELLIER MUSTARD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Montpellier wild mustard (Sinapi sylvestre monspessulanum) showing a slender, highly branched plant with very fine, linear leaves and long, thin siliques.</image-desc>

This has a broad leaf, a very small yellow flower, a very long pod, and very sharp seed.

Renodaeus, as said before, distinguishes Mustard into the Wild kind already described, and the Cultivated. This latter he makes two-fold: one, namely, bearing leaves similar in shape to a Turnip, but a little smaller and much rougher: with a smooth, bristly, rough stalk, two cubits high and branched with many small arms: around which small yellow flowers break out, arranged in an excellent series: which are succeeded by pods that are oblong, thin, and rough, enclosing small, round seed, yellowish-white in color, and sharp in taste. The other kind differs from the first only in the leaf, which greatly approaches Rocket, and in the seed, which is reddish-black.

### IMAGES AND OUTLINE
<sig>Mm 2</sig>

### WILD GENEVAN MUSTARD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sinapi Genevense plant, showing a tall stem with serrated leaves and small flowers at the top, with a detailed root system.</image-desc>

We call this the Genevan variety because we saw it among the ruins at Geneva and nowhere else; however, it seems to have a great deal in common with the Montpellier variety with the very long pods already mentioned.

Both types of domestic Mustard are sown in fields, and wherever it springs up, it usually sprouts with no cultivation; nevertheless, it loves plowed and especially well-heaped soil. For sowing and for use, however, old seed is useless, which when broken by the teeth is found to be dried out and tawny or white. But, even in the judgment of Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note>, one should choose that which, when broken, appears succulent and green or bluish-gray, as it is fresh and established in its vigor.

---

### PRICKLY MUSTARD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sinapi Echinatum, featuring a central stalk with broad, lobed leaves and clusters of flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

This blooms in the grain fields around Montpellier in the months of March and April, and puts forth yellow flowers, similar to the flowers of Rocket <note>original: "Eruca"</note>.

To proceed in describing the use of Mustard: it hardly serves as a food; sometimes it is a medicine, and often a condiment. For when mixed with viscous foods, it cuts through and thins them. Especially in the winter time, it is most conveniently mixed with those dishes for which the stomach grows sluggish and feels a loathing for unpalatable food. But because it is very sharp and strikes the taste unpleasantly, it is not only ground with vinegar to mitigate its heat, but also mixed with must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> for greater sweetness and pleasantness; and thus it becomes a most grateful condiment, free from much of its burning; it is commonly named **Mustard** <note>original: "Mostarda," derived from "mustum ardens" or burning must.</note>.

---

### WATER MUSTARD OF PADUA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sinapi Aquaticum Patavinum, showing a plant with deeply lobed, almost feathery leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

Because this plant is found in and near the water, and resembles Mustard, we have labeled it "Water Mustard." The leaves are indeed finely divided, with the division of the Skeleton-weed <note>original: "Chondrilla"</note> shown by Mattioli; those near the root, however, are broader and less divided, and serrated along the edges of the segments. The roots are about the thickness of a small finger, a hand-and-a-half long, tender, white, and provided with few fibers; the taste is sharp and bitter, which the leaves also possess.

We observed it at Padua near the Livia Gate in and near the water. Could it be the "Wild Little Root" of Dodoens?

<column-break/>

### SMALL MONTPELLIER MUSTARD, with rough hairy pods and the leaf of the smaller Rocket.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sinapi Monspessulanum Parvum, showing a slender plant with small leaves and elongated seed pods.</image-desc>

We found this in the month of Autumn between Montpellier and Mount Espérou. We observed a large variety in the damp ditches between Montpellier and the Balaruc Baths.

Furthermore, Mustard is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of "humors" where the 4th degree is the most intense level of a quality.</note>: it cuts, thins, and draws out. Held in the mouth, it draws out phlegm; ground and applied to the nostrils, it provokes sneezing. It is useful for many other things and gave its name to a noble medicament which they call a *Sinapism* <note>A mustard plaster or poultice.</note>, which is highly celebrated for many ailments. But it hurts the vision and a "hot head" because, as Pliny also noted, its force is carried upward in a dense vapor. Therefore, let those with weak and dim eyes especially avoid it.

---

### WILD MUSTARD WITH A PURPLE FLOWER by Fabio Colonna.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sinapi Agreste, showing a plant with broad, rounded leaves and clusters of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

In the valley above the shrine of the Blessed Mary of Life, among Brambles, Mercury, Dandelions, and Buttercups, this new and elegant plant arises; Fabio Colonna <note>A famous Italian botanist (1567–1640) known for his detailed copperplate illustrations.</note> records that it does not know how to grow elsewhere, nor does he remember seeing it in other Herbals.

It flowers in March and is finished by the month of April.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called "Rocket 10" or "Mustard with a purple umbrella-shaped flower."

---

### DWARF ALPINE MUSTARD OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sinapi Pumilum Alpinum, showing a small, low-growing plant with distinct seed pods and small leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are like those of a Daisy; the little stalk is tender, slender, and a palm's breadth high. The flowers are white, umbrella-shaped, consisting of four small petals. The pods or "little horns" are like those of Bittercress; the seed is tiny, flat, and reddish; the root creeps along the surface of the earth.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the "Stirpium" (Plants), focusing on the various species of Rocket (Eruca). It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, citing classical authorities like Plinius and Dioscorides alongside contemporary botanists.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

<margin>ROCKET: German: *Rauchen*; Belgian: *Recken*, *Raket*, etc.; French: *Roquette*; Italian: *Ruchetta* and *Rucula*.</margin>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with small flowers and long seed pods, identified as Eruca sativa (Garden Rocket).</image-desc>

Theophrastus mentions Rocket among the pot-herbs, and attributes to them a woody root. Dioscorides also mentions Rocket <note>original Greek: Εὔζωμον - *Euzomon*</note>, but does not describe it. Pliny writes that it was called *Euzomon* <note>meaning "well-flavored"</note> because of the great pleasantness it possesses for seasoning foods.

It is commonly distinguished into the Garden and Wild varieties, of which we have observed various differences soon to be set forth.

**The greater annual garden Rocket**, with a white striped flower which we depict here, is cultivated in gardens in Montpellier, Lyon, Geneva, Basel, Montbéliard, and various other places, and remains green in them throughout the whole winter. However, Mattioli, Lonicer, and Laguna wretchedly confuse this and other species of Rocket with various kinds of Mustard.

### PERENNIAL THIN-LEAVED ROCKET, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply lobed leaves and clusters of flowers at the top, identified as Eruca tenuifolia.</image-desc>

This has a thick, white, and quite long root: from which come forth stems with frequent hollow wings, striped, and slightly hairy: the *leaves* are divided by frequent incisions: the *flowers* are yellow and fragrant, arranged in the same sequence as the garden variety: the *seed pods* are long and narrow.

This is both a garden and wild plant, for it is cultivated successfully in gardens: as we have had in ours at Montbéliard, and also in the garden of the S. P., where it took over a wall, multiplying itself by falling seed: and it also grows spontaneously everywhere around walls, and in walls and rubble. Both the garden and the wild variety easily endure the winter: and both flower in July and August.

### SMALLEST MONTPELLIER ROCKET, with a yellow flower and a seed pod an inch long.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, branching plant with narrow leaves and upright seed pods.</image-desc>

We record this as the Montpellier variety because we have seen it only in Montpellier, flowering on walls in July.

To those things which were said before regarding the powers and properties of Rocket, it should be added: the crushed leaves applied to the eyelids are believed to sharpen the sight: the root, moreover, boiled in water, is said to extract fragments of bone: and it is of a different nature from Lettuce, and for that reason it is almost always joined to it in meals, because, as Pliny says, when an equal heat is mixed with excessive cold, it balances the temperament.

<column-break/>

### ROMAN OR NOBLE ROCKET, with a broad leaf, a white or yellow flower, and a narrow seed pod.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with broad, serrated leaves and long, thin seed pods.</image-desc>

<margin>Is this the Greater Spanish or Noble Rocket of Lobel and Pena in the *Adversaria*? Or the English Rocket of Camerarius with broad leaves, tiny yellow flowers, and leaving behind small seeds in very tight pods?</margin>

It is called *Euzomon* by the Greeks because of the peculiar grace it has in sauces and broths: but by the Latins it is called *Eruca*, because when tasted it eats away at and stings the tongue <note>Latin: *erodit*, to gnaw or erode</note>: or as if it were *Vruca*, because it has almost the power of burning <note>Latin: *urere*, to burn</note>. Some have called it White Mustard, because it may serve in place of Mustard. In another sense, *Eruca* is a small beast which is called *Campa* <note>caterpillar</note> by the Greeks.

### WILD NARROW-LEAVED ROCKET with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild variety of Eruca with narrow, jagged leaves and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

<margin>*Wild narrow-leaved Rocket*, in the Observations and Icons of Lobel, the History of Plants of Lyon, and C. Bauhin in *Phytopinax*.</margin>

Furthermore, Rocket heats and dries in the third degree: it thins the spleen, removes the heavy stench of the armpits, heals the bites of the shrew-mouse, and provokes urine; it removes freckles, moles, and spots on the face. Moreover, it aids digestion and is suitable for the bowels: and both its seed and the raw herb excite <term>Venus</term> <note>meaning it acts as an aphrodisiac</note> if eaten rather abundantly. Whence the Poet says:
> Let him who wishes to be lustful seek out Rockets.

### SCENTLESS ROCKET: HERB OF ST. ALBERT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with small flowers, identified as Herba S. Alberti.</image-desc>

It rests upon a long, simple, and slender root: the stem is branched, a cubit high: the *leaves* are almost nine inches long, with the division of the cultivated yellow Rocket: the *flowers* are a pale yellow, consisting of four small petals: the *seed pods* are slender, two inches long. Truly, there is no scent to the plant.

Is this the Herb of St. Albert of Cesalpino?

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>Mm 3</sig>

### PURPLE ROCKET, CALLED BLUE BY OTHERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with serrated leaves and small four-petaled flowers, showing the root system and upright stems.</image-desc>

The flowers of this plant are purple or blue, or dark purple, and sometimes white. It is found in both a Larger and Smaller variety, depending on whether it grows in a lush or a barren place; it also frequently varies in size when growing on walls.

We have seen it blooming in March in various places: around the church and the Castle of Belfort; on the walls of Byzantium <note>modern-day Istanbul</note>; it abounds in the vineyards of *Pisa*, and on the walls of the town of St. Hippolyte. One wonders if this is Galen's *Vella* <note>original: "Vella"</note>, a herb unknown today, of which he says: "Vella is a herb with leaves smaller than Rocket, with a violet flower, heating to the taste, and slightly biting," etc.

<column-break/>

### CREEPING WILD ROCKET, WITH SMALL purple and yellow flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping plant with deeply lobed leaves and small flowers clustered at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

This grows abundantly at Geneva, in the *Plainpalais*; at Lyon in the *Bellecour*; at Basel on the road leading to *Neuhaus*, and at Montbéliard, both at the bridge and at the banks of the *Allan* <note>original: "Alominis"</note>. It also grows in the garden of S. P., where its creeping habit makes it hateful to his gardener. We do not doubt that others have found it in different locations. It blooms in July.

---

### GREATER MARSH ROCKET.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust marsh plant with large, deeply pinnatifid (lobed) leaves and dense flower clusters at the top.</image-desc>

It is supported by a thick, woody, and rough root; it is gifted with several stems that are large, round, and of moderate height. Upon these sit many tiny white flowers consisting of four small petals; as these fall away, they are succeeded by oblong, thin seed pods <term>siliquae: long, slender seed capsules characteristic of the mustard family</term> enclosing seeds of a sharp flavor. The leaves are large, pointed, and serrated.

<column-break/>

### PODDED MOUSE-EAR, OR PODDED Shepherd's Purse.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with a basal rosette of leaves and upright stems bearing small flowers and elongated seed pods (siliques).</image-desc>

Of this genus, there are found the larger, smaller, and smallest varieties, and it varies greatly in its leaves, stem, and roots. The small flowers are white, arranged in no particular order. Like the common Shepherd's Purse, the pods are long, rounded, and thin, hanging from fairly long stalks. Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, 16th-century Swiss naturalist</note> was of the opinion that it should be classified among the *Myagrum* <note>Gold-of-pleasure or false flax</note> genus.

We saw it blooming in the fields of *Vete* at Montpellier; at Geneva in March and April; and on the walls of the Palace in Bologna. At Belfort, however, we saw the smallest of all growing upon the wall in the citadel.

---

### THE CAKILE OF SERAPION TO SOME, SEA Rocket or Sea Radish to others.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sea rocket plant with fleshy, lobed leaves and clusters of flowers and distinctively shaped seed pods.</image-desc>

Although thin, the root of this plant is quite long; it produces numerous stems over a span <note>approx. 9 inches</note> in height. The leaves are like those of *Reseda* <note>Mignonette</note>, but smaller and fleshier, with a sharp, somewhat salty taste. The flowers sit on peculiar side-shoots, having the position and form of Rocket or Cabbage, and are purple in color. The pods are somewhat thick and short, each enclosing two seeds.

By Anguillara and Lobelius <note>Luigi Anguillara and Matthias de l'Obel, renowned botanists</note> it is called the *Cakile* of Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger, an influential Arabic herbalist</note>, commonly known as Sea Rocket. In the *History of Lyon* it is called Great Nasturtium, Sea Rocket, and Serapion's Cakile. That work actually provides three figures for one and the same plant.

<column-break/>

### CAKILE, OR BROAD-LEAFED SEA ROCKET.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed variety of the sea rocket, showing thick, succulent leaves and developing seed pods.</image-desc>

The leaves of this variety are jagged, but not divided into small parts as in the common sort; for they are broad and usually only wavy at the edges.

When we were at Montpellier, we came across both types of *Cakile* by the sea, bearing pods in August. In our garden at Geneva and Montbéliard, it bloomed for us in March.

Myconus <note>Francisco Micó, Spanish physician and botanist</note> recommends a warm distilled water made from *Cakile*, drunk in a weight of four ounces, for the torments of colic and kidney stones <term>nephritic: relating to the kidneys</term>.

<summary>This page describes various species of Rocket (Eruca) and Sea Rocket (Cakile), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and medicinal applications for digestive and renal pain.</summary>
<keywords>Rocket, Sea Rocket, Cakile, botany, medicinal herbs, Montpellier, Geneva, Belfort, Conrad Gessner, Matthias de l'Obel, kidney stones, colic</keywords>

--- Page 342 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of cruciferous plants (mustard family), focusing on hedge mustard, winter cress, and various wallflowers. The translator has maintained the distinction between the different species as categorized by Renaissance botanists.</meta>

### HEDGE MUSTARD OR ERYSIMUM: German: Hedrich, Eisenkraut; French: Velar, de la Tortelle; Italian: Irione.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Irio or Erysimum plant, showing its long, thin seed pods (siliques), small flowers, and deeply lobed leaves.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> says that *Erysimum* has leaves like wild rocket: with small stalks that are pliable and flexible like a leather thong: yellow flowers: and seed pods at the top shaped like little horns and slender, like Fenugreek, in which small seeds are enclosed similar to Garden Cress, and with a burning taste.

Besides this *Erysimum*, there is also another which Theophrastus and Galen <note>Ancient Greek authorities on plants and medicine</note> reckon among the legumes: and Pliny shamefully confuses this one with the one already described.

As for the Etymology of *Erysimum* and *Irio*, it is held among the Greeks to come either from the multiple divisions of the leaves: or from the excellence of the pot-herb, as if it were precious: or from the drawing faculty <note>The ability to draw out humors or splinters</note> with which it is endowed. *Irio* truly comes from "rushing in" <note>Latin: irruendo</note>, because it rushes onto the palate with a fiery force.

### WINTER CRESS, CARPENTER'S HERB, DRABA: German: St. Barbara's Herb; French: Carpenter's Herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Barbarea plant, featuring clusters of small flowers at the top and broad, lobed basal leaves.</image-desc>

Its root is white and oblong, moderately thick: the stalks are nine inches long and striated: the leaves are like Radish, but smaller, shining with a dark green color: the flowers are small and yellow: the seed pods are many, thin and rounded, and in them is a tiny reddish seed.

The French common folk call this *Carpentaria* and the Carpenter's herb, according to Ruellius. To some of the Ancients, it is the "Royal Broom": but to Fuchs, Tragus, Dodonaeus, Gesner, and many others, it is *Barbarea* and St. Barbara's herb. Some wish it to be the *Sideritis* of Pliny. Furthermore, Tabernaemontanus divides *Barbarea* into Male and Female varieties.

It grows spontaneously in fields, uncultivated places, and in marshy and damp areas. It flowers in the months of May and June. It is quite frequent in Padua, Bologna, and Genoa.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED YELLOW WALLFLOWER, Multiple yellow Violet, or many-flowered.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered yellow wallflower (Leucoium luteum), showing dense clusters of petals and a separate detail of a seed pod on the left.</image-desc>

The flower of this plant is very densely packed and crowded with small petals, of a most sweet scent, with no seed pods and no seed, as that juice which ought to have gone to the pods and seeds passes away into the fullness of the flower; by these marks, and by its longer duration, and because it becomes more woody, it differs from the single-flowered variety pictured previously.

The single variety grows spontaneously in various places on walls: and commonly flowers in the months of April, May, June, July, and August, and sometimes, as we observed at Montpellier, throughout the whole Winter.

However, it is cultivated to become many-flowered: and the double-flowered version is kept in many gardens: where it flowers in April and May, and is propagated by branches fixed into the earth.

<column-break/>

### MATTHIOLI'S SECOND ERYSIMUM, with small pods, called by some Toothwort.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second type of Erysimum, characterized by more upright growth and smaller seed pods along the stem.</image-desc>

We depict here Matthioli's second *Erysimum*, which he says is endowed with all the marks of *Irio*; Camerarius truly says it abounds near the sea of the Venetians. Could it be the *Irio* of the Ancients?

The preceding illustration is the *Erysimum* of Tragus with yellow flowers: which Lobelius, Gerard, and many others among the Moderns believe to be the *Erysimum* or *Irio* of the Ancients.

Moreover, *Erysimum* grows, according to Dioscorides, around cities, the courtyards of houses, and gardens. We have often observed it in those places, and also at crossroads, in graveyards, and among ruins, in flower in the month of May, at Genoa, Lyon, Basel, Montbéliard around the Chancery in the Castle, and at Yverdon near the walls "behind the lake" <note>original: "derriere le lac"</note>.

Galen says that in its faculty it is fiery and heating.

### WALLFLOWER: Arabic: Cheiri & Alcheri; German: Veyelen; French: Violier; Italian: Viola.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a standard Leucoium (Wallflower), showing the root system, lanceolate leaves, and cruciform flowers.</image-desc>

The *Leucoium* <note>Literally "White Violet" in Greek, though here referring to the Wallflower</note> is very well known, and because it is known, Dioscorides does not describe it, but only notes the differences. *It is white*, he says, *or blue, or purple.* But, since Pliny, in enumerating the kinds of *Leucoium*, mentions only purple, yellow, or white: Hermolaus, Marcellus, Fuchs, and other learned men contend that the word "blue" in Dioscorides is suspicious and foreign. We, however, since it is found in all the Greek manuscripts of Dioscorides, judge that it should by no means be erased: even by the example of Tragus, who reckons five kinds of *Leucoium*, differing only in color: namely *yellow, white, purple, rose, and red.* Here, however, is pictured the yellow *Leucoium* with a single flower.

### WILD YELLOW WALLFLOWER, with a double yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild yellow wallflower with multiple blooms on branched stems.</image-desc>

Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Clusius have this as the Wild *Leucoium*: to Lobelius in his *Observations* it is the Sea *Leucoium* with a yellow flower.

Furthermore, although the name *Leucoium* signifies "White Violet" if you look at the Greek composition of the word: nevertheless, among almost all writers, all kinds of Violets, of whatever color they may be, are designated by this single name of *Leucoium*. Yet there is no reason why you should understand by "purple" here that plant which is properly called <term>ion</term> <note>Greek: ἴον - the true violet</note> by the Greeks and <term>Viola</term> by the Latins: for it belongs to another family from those we are dealing with here, and they are contrary to it in quality, faculty, and form.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### WINTER STOCK, LONG-LASTING, purple and rose-colored, and also white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with long, narrow leaves and clusters of four-petaled flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

In this purple Stock <note>original: "Leucoio"</note> there are various differences, due to the color being either lighter or deeper. Likewise, it is sometimes multicolored; and while some plants last only a single summer, others last for several years. In Montpellier they have Stocks mixed of white and purple, which bloom throughout the entire Winter. In Lyon we have seen variegated ones, and some with jagged leaves.

By means of cultivation <note>term: mangonio — the art of improving plants through grafting or specialized care</note> and more frequent transplantation of the purple winter Stock, its flowers attain a magnificent size; being pregnant with a multiple birth of petals, they rival the Musk Rose, though in other respects they do not differ from the purple Stock with a simple flower.

### WINTER STOCK, LONG-LASTING, with a white flower, and smooth, lead-colored green leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the first, with dense foliage and several flower heads.</image-desc>

Besides the differences taken from the flowers, the duration, and the season, there are also several others drawn from the leaves and the native habitat. We present one of these here, which bloomed for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>original: "S. P. horto," likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg</note> in August; it lasts for several years, but must be kept in a cellar during the Winter.

### BROAD-LEAVED MARITIME STOCK, with a purplish-blue flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader leaves and smaller flower clusters.</image-desc>

Having described those things which contribute to the knowledge of the Stock in its genus and species, it is now timely to hand down its powers and uses.

The yellow Stock (which is the *Keiri* of the Arabs, or *Alkeiri* with the article prefixed) is of primary use in Medicine, according to Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>. Its dried flowers (though fresh are better) boiled for use in a sitz-bath, are effective for inflammations of the womb and for inducing menstruation. When taken in a wax salve <note>term: Cerato — a medicinal ointment made of wax and oil</note>, they heal cracks in the seat, and with honey, they heal foul ulcers of the mouth. The roots applied with vinegar suppress the Spleen and benefit those suffering from gout. The seed, in the weight of two drachms drunk with wine or applied with honey, draws out the menses, the afterbirth, and the fetus. More on this in the following pages.

<column-break/>

### SUMMER STOCK, WITH PURPLE, rose, and white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with slender leaves and distinct four-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

It is sown in many gardens, just as we also had it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince.

Regarding the Stock in general, Dioscorides has this to say:

This kind of Violet, he says, some call Royal or *Basilicon*, the Romans call it the White Violet, others the Imperial <note>original: "Augustam"</note>, and some call it the Matronly Violet, or the Sparrow-Violet, or *Polyphuram*.

Hermolaus Barbarus writes, relying on the testimony of Columella, that it was called the Ligustrian Violet by the Romans.

### LARGE BROAD-LEAVED MARITIME STOCK, with a purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust maritime plant with thick leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Called the Greater Sea Stock by Clusius and Camerarius; by the *History of Lyon*, by Pena and Lobelius, and by most others.

We observed it by the Mediterranean Sea near Montpellier, and others have seen it elsewhere. We also saw it at Stuttgart in the Duke's garden, still flowering in October.

### SMALLER NARROW-LEAVED MARITIME STOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller maritime plant with narrow leaves and a single flower at the top.</image-desc>

Most authors label it thus: to some it is *Tripolium*, to others the *Hesperis* of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher known as the "Father of Botany"</note>.

It grows spontaneously in many coastal areas of Zeeland, as well as in Narbonne, France, and in several maritime locations throughout Spain; it flowers in July and August. When moved into gardens, it dies in the same year it was sown.

Its scent, according to the testimony of Pliny and Dodonaeus, becomes stronger toward nightfall as the sun sets, whereas otherwise during the day it is faint.

<summary>This page details various species of Stock (Leucoium), including winter, summer, and maritime varieties, noting their physical characteristics and medicinal uses as described by classical authorities like Dioscorides.</summary>
<keywords>Stock, Wallflower, Leucoium, medicinal plants, Dioscorides, Montbéliard, maritime flora, botany, gynecology, herbal remedies</keywords>

--- Page 344 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Leucoium (Stock) and Hesperis (Dame's Rocket) families, following the previous descriptions of maritime and garden varieties.</meta>

### SMALL MARINE STOCK, with thick green leaves and purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small marine stock plant with slender stems, small leaves, and four-petaled flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

We shall add here something regarding the powers and faculties of the Stock <note>original: "Leucoium"</note> in general. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist</note> attributes a warm temperament to it, and the same strengths are assigned to the juice as were previously recorded for the seed. The water, drunk twice a day in a measure of 4 or 5 spoonfuls, is especially conducive to treating defects of the liver and kidneys, and it stimulates Venus <note>An early modern euphemism for increasing libido or fertility</note>.

From the flowers of the yellow Stock, an oil is prepared by infusion, much like oil of Chamomile, suitable for dissolving humors <note>In Galenic medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids that needed to be balanced</note>, soothing cold pains, and strengthening the nerves.

### HESPERIS: Hesperis with purple, white, and variegated flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hesperis (Dame's Rocket) plant with broad, serrated leaves and clusters of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

To the Hesperis <note>Dame's Rocket</note>, according to the author Theophrastus, the name was given because it smells more fragrant at night than during the day <note>The name derives from the Greek 'hesperos', meaning evening</note>. Because this also happens with the Matronal Violet, some have gifted it with the name Hesperis as well.

However, Hesperis is by no means to be confused with the *Leucoium* of Dioscorides, as Fuchs does; nor with the Persian Violet of Hermolaus, as Tragus does; nor with the Rampion <note>Rapunculo</note>, as the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Lugdunensis, a famous 16th-century botanical work</note> does.

It grows spontaneously in various places, under hedges along the Rhine, in England, and elsewhere in meadows. Therefore, those who call it Damascene, Parthian, or exotic act with little counsel. It is also cultivated in gardens.

### MATRONAL HESPERIS WITH VIOLET LEAVES, with a green or unattractive white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Hesperis with elongated leaves and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

This grew for us in the Princely Garden of Montbéliard <note>S. P. horto Montbelgardi</note>, from seed sent from Stuttgart, and it bloomed in August and September.

It is to be referred to the common variety, which varies greatly in the color of the flower: sometimes white, sometimes dilute purple, sometimes red, sometimes green, sometimes an unattractive white, etc.

It is worthy of note, however, that the purple Hesperis, as it grows old, sometimes changes color and acquires a very beautiful variegated pattern, striped with white and purple.

<column-break/>

### CAMERARIUS’S MARITIME STOCK, the Sea-Starwort related to Stocks, according to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime stock with thick, succulent-like leaves and flowers, showing a curved taproot.</image-desc>

This grows between Scylla and Charybdis <note>The Strait of Messina between Sicily and Italy</note> around St. George. The leaves are similar to Plantain, but narrower and thicker; from the middle emerges a stem a palm high, divided into three branches. The flowers are similar to the flowers of the March Violet; the root is white, sharp, the color of a Radish, thick, and not fragrant, as some wish to claim based on Dioscorides. The leaves are also wrongly said to be similar to Plantain leaves: for what is the similarity?

### ODORLESS PANNONIAN HESPERIS, with a whitish or purplish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pannonian Hesperis with deeply lobed or pinnatifid leaves and terminal flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist</note> says this is so similar to the common Matronal Violet that the seed pods <note>Cornicula</note>, root, and flowers agree with it entirely, nor can any difference be seen from a comparison of the two. They differ only in the scent of the flower, in the judgment of the same Clusius, which in this variety has no charm.

It grows at the base of mountains and at the edges of vineyards situated on hills; it blooms at the same time as the preceding one, namely in the months of May, June, and July, and sometimes even into September.

### SYRIAN HESPERIS, OR SYRIAN STOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Syrian Hesperis with wavy-edged leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

It grows in the maritime regions of Syria, from whence the seed was brought, says Clusius. We have indeed seen it in various gardens: at Pforzheim in the Margraviate, at the house of Grüninger, a distinguished pharmacist; at Basel at the house of Doctor Felix Platter, and elsewhere. It was blooming in July.

<summary>This page describes various species of Hesperis (Dame's Rocket) and maritime Stocks, detailing their medicinal uses for the liver and kidneys, their fragrance patterns, and their geographic distribution from the Rhine to Syria.</summary>
<keywords>Stock, Hesperis, Dame's Rocket, medicinal oils, botanical classification, Montbéliard, Clusius, Felix Platter, maritime plants</keywords>
