# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
->creeping, with whitish flowers: WHITLOW GRASS.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flowering plant with serrated leaves and clusters of four-petaled flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

This is the second *Draba* according to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note>: the white podded *Draba* of Caspar Bauhin: and the <term>Wall Rue</term> <note>original: "Ruta muralis"</note> of the herbalists of the *History of Lyon*.

It grows in ruins and the cracks of walls among stones: thus we have seen it growing on the walls of St. Urbain, Clairvaux, and elsewhere. Indeed, at Lyon and Geneva it grew for us in the garden, flowering in April and May, and sometimes even in November and January.

### SIMILAR TO THE ALPINE OR WALL ROCKET
->Tall and large WHITLOW GRASS, with white flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller plant with elongated, serrated leaves and a dense cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Phytopinax* it is the 4th *Draba* with flowers and pods like Hedge Mustard. Is it perhaps the medium Mustard or Penny-cress of Lobel and Pena in their *Adversaria* and *Plant Images*, and also of the *History of Lyon*?

It grows in the mountains of Burgundy between St. Hippolyte and Maîche.

### MOUNTAIN SNOWBELL TO SOME:
->Small Moonwort: Alpine Violet with Asarum-like leaves.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded, kidney-shaped leaves and nodding, bell-shaped flowers with fringed edges.</image-desc>

This plant is recorded by various names, having either larger or smaller leaves; the leaves are sometimes a deep green and sometimes a paler green, both above and below: the flower is also sometimes deep purple, sometimes pale, and occasionally even snow-white.

The *Adversaria* <note>A botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> records that it is gathered in the steep mountains and high Alps that surround Innsbruck and Salzburg. Clusius notes it also grows in the Alps of Austria and Styria. For us, however, it grows successfully at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince.

Some assert that when the leaves are applied, they close wounds wonderfully with both flesh and scar; and that when the top skin is peeled off and applied to the abdomen, they draw out fluids <note>likely referring to treating dropsy or edema</note>: we have not seen this ourselves.

<column-break/>

### RELATED TO THE ALPINE OR WALL ROCKET,
->the succulent WHITLOW GRASS, with white flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with thick, succulent-looking leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

It is called <term>Arabis</term> or the second *Draba* by Pena and Lobel.

Clusius writes that it grows spontaneously in several mountains of Austria. In gardens, however, once sown, it flourishes, according to the testimony of Lobel.

### GARLIC MUSTARD: German: Leuch, Garlic-
->herb: French: Garlic-herb: Italian: Alliaria.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, heart-shaped, toothed leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The name is undoubtedly derived from the fact that the leaves, when crushed with the fingers, smell of Garlic.

Some call it <term>Sea Frog</term> <note>original: "Ranam marinam"</note>, or <term>Alliallum</term>, while Lonicer calls it common <term>Thlaspi</term>. It is by no means *Scordotis* <note>Water Germander</note>, as some think: for the leaves argue against it—in this plant they are like Oak <note>likely a comparison of texture or margin</note>, in that like Nettle: the stem in this one is quadrangular and reddish, in that one round and yellowish: and there is also the smell of Garlic, which fills the nostrils more in Garlic Mustard.

It grows spontaneously in various places, both in gardens and elsewhere: it is green in February, flowers in March, and bears pods in May.

It heats and dries in the intense second degree, and by a singular power and property it resists rot, wipes away, and cleanses.

### GREATER MOONWORT: German: Moon-Violet,
->Silver-flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, heart-shaped leaves and clusters of flowers, likely Lunaria annua.</image-desc>

The Greater Moonwort varies with either a longer or rounder pod: and with flowers that are purple, beautifully red, bluish, or white: and these are either fragrant or scentless.

It is an inhabitant of mountains and mountain forests: it abounds on Mount Salève near Geneva. We have observed it cultivated in gardens at Lyon, Geneva, Bologna, and Montbéliard, flowering in May and June.

By what name the Ancients designated this plant, according to Gesner, is not yet clear. Some herbalists call it <term>Bulbonac</term>, others <term>Bulbonach</term>: but in what dialect or with what meaning is still unknown, as is why it was nicknamed <term>Royal Greek</term>. Is it a type of <term>Thlaspi</term> <note>Cress/Penny-cress</note>, as some learned men wish?

# OF PLANTS

### WATERCRESS OR WATER NASTURTIUM: German: *Brunkreß, Vafferkreß;* French: *Cresson;* Italian: *Crescione.*

<note>The Latin title "Sisymbrium Cardamine" refers to what we now know as *Nasturtium officinale*.</note>

There is a second kind of Sisymbrium according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>: which, by his own testimony, some call *Cardamine*, and others call *Sion*. It is, he says, an aquatic herb that grows in the same places as the *Sion* <note>Water-parsnip</note>. It is called *Cardamine* [or *Nasturtiaria* by some, because in taste it represents *Cardamum*, that is, *Nasturtium* <note>original: "quod gustu Cardamum, id est, Nasturtium, repraesentet"</note>]. The leaves first come forth round: but as they grow, they are divided in the manner of Rocket <note>A leafy green in the mustard family</note>.

According to Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note>, who confuses this with the former Sisymbrium of Dioscorides, Sisymbrium is said to grow in well-watered places and is similar to Nasturtium.

To Avicenna <note>Persian polymath and physician</note> it is *Water Rocket*, *Water Parsley*, and *Pupil of the Eye*. It is, however, wrongly called *Lauer* by some, *Senecio* by others, and *Vella* by others; it is similar to the former Sisymbrium (of Dioscorides) in name alone. More on this in the following sections.

### A CERTAIN TASTELESS SPECIES OF WATERCRESS.

This was collected at Padua on Mount Castello by C. Bauhin <note>Caspar Bauhin, a famous Swiss botanist</note>, and sent as the *Vella* of Galen. We, however, saw it at Strasbourg in the garden of Meyer: and we ourselves had it in the Princely garden at Montbéliard.

Could it be the *Second Accipitrina* of Caesalpinus?

This Watercress grows most luxuriantly on the walls of wells, and around fishponds and pools. In warmer springs it floats upon the water, and in the months of May, June, and July it is observed to produce very small white flowers; it remains green all winter and is used in salads. Just as the people of Geneva have it "in the open palace" <note>original: "en plain palais"</note>, those of Yverdon have it by the public road called "the Causeway" <note>original: "la Chaussée"</note>, and others elsewhere.

### GERMAN SERIPHIUM, SIUM OR LAUER: German: *Waſſermerck;* French: *Berle.*

The plant we depict here, called German Seriphium, is to Caesalpinus the "common Accipitrina," to some "Wild Nasturtium," and to most of Thal's followers *Arum* and *Sophia*. Lonicer, however, errs greatly, confusing it with Wormseed <note>original: "Semine Sanctonico"</note>.

It comes forth in old masonry, in rubbish heaps, stony and sandy places, and other uncultivated spots: and it flowers from June until Autumn, but bit by bit. It possesses, moreover, a drying, somewhat cooling, and astringent quality.

Furthermore, regarding *SIUM* or *LAVER*, the legitimate *Sium* of Dioscorides grows mostly in the streams of bubbling springs, whose waters are warm in Winter but grow cold in Summer. More in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### WATERCRESS, OR WATER NASTURTIUM with a larger flower, taller.

Because of its great similarity to Sisymbrium, Thalius, Camerarius, Gesner, and others call this plant Sisymbrium and Water Nasturtium, or "another Sisymbrium." To C. Bauhin it is "Water Nasturtium with a larger flower"; to Matthiolus, *Sinapigara*, called *Sio* by the Italians.

This Watercress varies much, for it grows in both wetter and drier places, although it does not differ in its properties: for it is found in dry places with smaller leaves and thinner stalks. All these varieties of Sisymbrium flower in white, with yellow tips. Concerning the location and properties, see the notes beside the following figures.

### HAIRY WATERCRESS.

The other Sisymbrium Cardamine of Dioscorides proposed by Matthiolus agrees with this one in almost all respects, if it is not the same. Could it be the "third species of Water Nasturtium" of Thalius? Or the "Broad-leaved Cardamine" of Gerard?

This plant is a dweller of springs, clear rivulets, and shady places near water: and it flowers in Spring.

Furthermore, aquatic Sisymbrium is heating, according to Dioscorides, and it provokes urine: and it is, if we believe Galen, of the third order of heating and drying things, but when moist and green, of the second order. It is recommended for obstructions of the liver and spleen, for dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, and for scurvy, and it is commonly eaten raw in salads.

### FUCHS'S IBERIS, WILD NASTURTIUM: German: *Gauch blum, Wilder kreſſ;* French: *Passerage sauvage.*

By Galen and Paulus it is called *Lepidium*: by many "Field, Wild, and Meadow Nasturtium": by some *Cardamine*, by others *Sisymbrium* and *Sium*, and by certain people *Cuckoo Flower* <note>original: "Flos Cuculi"</note>.

It varies chiefly in the flower, which is sometimes simple, as we depict here, and sometimes full or multiple: sometimes from white it turns slightly purple, sometimes it is entirely white, and sometimes it is marked with purple spots.

<summary>This page describes various species of Watercress (Sisymbrium) and related aquatic plants, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses for liver ailments and scurvy. It reconciles different names used by classical authorities like Dioscorides and Galen with contemporary 16th-century botanical findings.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
<sig>Nn i</sig>

### FUCHS’S CRESS, OR CRESS
->of the meadows, with a full flower.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with small, dense clusters of flowers and serrated leaves, showing the root system.</image-desc>

The plant called *Iberis* <note>Cress or Bittercress</note> by Fuchs grows in many places, but in uncultivated ones: and especially by public roads and around meadows. At Basel, outside St. Alban’s gate, we have seen it by the Birs river, and at Geneva between the bridge of the *Arve* and *Lancy*, in the hedges. If indeed it is cultivated in gardens, as we had it at Montbéliard in the Prince's garden <note>original: "S. P. horto" referring to the Serenissimi Principis garden</note>, it displays a multiple flower, although it is also found growing wild with a full flower.

It appears in the springtime, and most especially in the month of April, and pours forth its milky flower around the beginning of Summer.

### MYAGRUM: German: Gold-of-Pleasure, Flax-weed:
->French: Cameline: Italian: Sevenzina, Durella.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myagrum plant with slender stems, small flowers, and elongated seed pods, including a detailed view of the seeds and pods to the right.</image-desc>

Myagros, says Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist</note>, which some call *Melampyron* <note>Black wheat</note>, is a twiggy herb, two cubits high: with leaves similar to *Rubia* <note>Madder</note>, but pale: it bears a seed similar to Fenugreek, which is oily. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist</note> holds almost the same views.

The flowers, which Dioscorides does not mention, are small, yellowish, and four-petaled: each of which is followed by a seed vessel <term>pericarpia: the part of a fruit that encloses the seeds</term>, somewhat swollen, oblong, and angular: containing many oblong, triangular seeds. The root is woody and fibrous: the stems are thin, rounded, straight, slightly hairy, branched, and stuffed with a spongy pith.

Commonly, however, *Myagrum* is distinguished into the *Cultivated* and the *Wild* varieties. More on this in the following.

### A PLANT RELATED TO MYAGRUM, WITH LONG
->pods, and small yellow flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with long, narrow seed pods (siliques) and small flowers.</image-desc>

Near *Chastenoy* in the district of Montbéliard, it flowers in July and August, on the bank of the water near the Mill. We have also seen it in the Burgundian village of *Courchaton*, and we cultivated it in the Prince's garden at Montbéliard.

Moreover, *Myagrum* grows in abundance among the cornfields everywhere: but most especially in Alsace and along the Rhine tract, where it abounds in the fields; and also, as we have from Ruel, in various places in France. Around Montbéliard they have fields planted with *Myagrum* for its oil, and near *Granges*, a town of Burgundy, it renews itself every year from fallen seed. We have seen it cultivated in gardens at Padua and Geneva, flowering in March and April.

<column-break/>

### A THREE-LEAVED RELATIVE OF FUCHS’S CRESS
->Clusius’s Cuckoo-flower.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cardamine plant with trifoliate leaves and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note> found this in wooded mountains and in bare rather than grassy soil, at the roots of Firs and very tall trees.

By him it is indeed inscribed as *Alpine Cardamine 1. three-leaved*: by Lobelius, the History of Lyon, and Gerard as *Three-leaved Cardamine*: by Tabernaemontanus and C. Bauhin as *Three-leaved Alpine Cress*.

Furthermore, Fuchs, rendering the reason for the German, Belgian, and French names of this plant, says it is so called because it "infatuates" <note>makes foolish</note> most people. And he adds, it could also conveniently be called *Wild Cress*. But when he concludes it is a type of *Iberis* solely from its milky flower, he seems to do so on very slight conjecture. And anyone who compares this with the *Iberis* of the Ancients will easily notice that he is mistaken.

### TURKISH MYAGRUM: German:
->Turkish Gold-of-Pleasure.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myagrum Turcicum with distinct lanceolate leaves and seed pods.</image-desc>

They call this "Turkish" because it is rarer: otherwise it is also called Wild Myagrum. It has more tender twigs and smaller seed than the preceding. Thus says Camerarius.

Otherwise, it has retained its name *Myagrum* both with the same Camerarius, and with Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria*, as well as with Gerard and most others; Tabernaemontanus also calls it *Myagron* and *Chamaelinum*; some call it *False-Flax*, and the Apothecaries call it *Sesame*.

But in Dioscorides the name *Melampyrum* is thought doubtful: and it perhaps happened to it, as with many other names, that one name is used for many things; Cornarius wishes it to be read as *Melampycnon*.

### SINGLE-SEEDED MYAGRON, WITH A YELLOW
->flower, and a jagged lower leaf.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myagron Monospermon showing deeply lobed (laciniate) lower leaves and flowering tops.</image-desc>

The seed in this plant is contained singly in individual little pouches <term>burſulis: small seed pods</term> that face upward, with the stems and branches pressed close.

We observed this plant growing spontaneously between *Dampierre* and *Colombier Fontaine*, by the Doubs river.

Furthermore, *Myagrum* approaches very nearly to the powers of Sesame; it warms and moistens moderately. Its seed is most pleasing to small birds: and an oil is made from it, most useful not only for the light of lamps, but also for the seasoning of food: and which Tragus writes is more grateful and pleasant than Olive oil. But let him keep that for himself; to us, Olive oil seems preferable for many reasons.

# OF PLANTS

### ANOTHER PLANT RELATED TO MYAGRUM.
<note>original: "Myagro affinis planta alia." Myagrum is likely Gold-of-Pleasure or a similar crucifer.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender plant with small flowers along the upper stems and narrow leaves at the base.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is woody: the *stalks* are one to two cubits <note>about 18 to 36 inches</note> high, hairy, brittle, and divided into many branches: the *leaves* are like those of Myagrum, but smaller, rough, and hairy: the *flowers* are very thin and pale: the *seed-heads* are tiny and round: it contains a single yellow *seed*, which is oily, etc.

It bloomed for us in June in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>S. P. likely refers to Serenissimi Principis</note> at Montbéliard.

---

### SESAME or SISAMUM: German: *Leindotter, Flachsdotter*: French: *Iugoline*: Italian: *Sesamo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with lanceolate leaves and clusters of small seed pods or flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

The plant pictured here is called *Sesamum* by Dodoens, Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, and Alpinus—who also calls it *Sempfen* and *Sempfeni*. In the *History of Plants of Lyon*, by Camerarius and others, it is called *True Sesame*. But if anyone carefully weighs the passages concerning Sesame in Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny, he will easily gather that none of these plants commonly accepted as Sesame by these authors is the true Sesame <note>The author is correctly noting the confusion between European "False Flax" (Camelina) and the tropical Sesame (Sesamum indicum) known to the ancients.</note>.

Thus, Mattioli is greatly "blind" <note>original: "caecutit," meaning he is groping in the dark or mistaken</note> in his explanation of Sesame and Myagrum, thrusting the latter forward in place of the former. Nor did Cornarius sufficiently indicate what he meant by his *Schvvaden*, which he presents as true Sesame. The *Sesame* of Valerius Cordus and Hieronymus Bock <note>Tragus</note> is, to us, the *Camelina Myagrum*. However, we have seen the plant we depict here in gardens at Venice and Basel.

---

### SCORPIOIDES: German: *Scorpion kraut*: French: *Scorpioides, Aureille de Lieure* <note>Hare's Ear</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with broad leaves and distinctive curled, caterpillar-like seed pods resembling a scorpion's tail.</image-desc>

*Scorpioides* <note>Scorpion-grass or Caterpillar-plant</note>, says Dioscorides, is a small herb with few leaves and a seed in the likeness of a Scorpion's tail, which, when smeared on, provides immediate aid for Scorpion stings: Pliny holds the same. Galen says it is heating in the third degree, but drying in the second.

However, that brief description by the Ancients has caused herbalists to present one plant after another as *Scorpioides*: such as *Great Heliotrope, Marigold*, and the *Scorpioid Telephium* mentioned a little earlier. The *Scorpioid Telephium with a rough pod-casing*, which we depict here, is to be treated shortly.

Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, and others label it *Scorpioides with a Bupleurum leaf*: to some, however, it is the *Clymenum of Dioscorides* and the *Second Clymenum of Pliny*, and to others *Catanance*.

<column-break/>

### A PLANT SIMILAR TO MYAGRUM, WITH A WHITE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a basal rosette of lobed leaves and a flowering stalk with small four-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

It sends out numerous *leaves* immediately from the root, which are smooth and somewhat jagged. Among these rise *stalks* filled with pith, the bases of which are surrounded by winged leaves that are jagged as if with small teeth. The *tiny flowers* at the tips are white and small: these are followed by *little vessels* <note>seed pods</note> that are somewhat round, pointed, and cling to a long stalk, approaching the Myagrum with round seeds. The *root* is long, white, and has few fibers.

We saw it flowering between Bologna and Florence.

---

### SCORPIOID TELEPHIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with succulent-like leaves and highly curled, textured seed pods.</image-desc>

Various plants have obtained the name of *Telephium*: *Scorpioid Bladder-senna: Live-forever or Orpine: and the so-called Scorpioid Telephium* which we depict here, and which (even in the judgment of Guillandinus) agrees in all respects with the description of Dioscorides and Pliny; the others being irrelevant.

It obtained the name *Scorpioides* from the shape of its pods; Cesalpino writes that it is nicknamed the *Herb of Love* by the Italians.

We have observed it cultivated in the gardens of Lyon, Geneva, and Basel: but it grows wild in the cultivated fields of Montpellier: it flowers in April, May, and June.

Galen writes that it is heating in the first degree and intensely drying in the second.

---

### MOUNTAIN SCORPIOIDES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small mountain plant with a basal tuft of narrow leaves and a single stalk bearing a few flowers.</image-desc>

The *root* is somewhat thick, black, and fibrous: the *leaves* are many, long, narrow, and woolly: the *stalk* is a palm high <note>about 3-4 inches</note> and puts forth few leaves: the *tiny flowers* are three or four in number, blue, and bunched together into a small, round *head*. It is a rare plant and familiar only to the inaccessible solitudes of the mountains.

However, the *Scorpioides with a rough, curved pod* <note>original: "siliqua Campoidis hispida"</note>, which we described a little earlier, is found growing wild in several places, such as near the gallows at Montpellier, where it is seen adorned with yellowish flowers in April. It is also gathered in gardens, as we have quite often observed at Basel and Padua, and we ourselves have kept it in the garden of the Most Serene Prince at Montbéliard.

<summary>This page describes various plants related to Myagrum and Sesame, alongside several "Scorpioides" species named for their curled, scorpion-tail-like seed pods. The author critiques previous botanists for misidentifying the "True Sesame" of the ancient Greeks.</summary>
<keywords>Myagrum, Sesame, Scorpioides, Telephium, botanical identification, Dioscorides, Galen, Renaissance gardens, Montbéliard, Montpellier, medicinal herbs</keywords>

### HYPECOUM: Germ. *Reemisch Felvyss*: French *Hypecoon*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hypecoum plant, showing slender stems, finely divided leaves, and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

Hypecoum, according to the author Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, is called *Hypopheon* by some. It grows among grain and in plowed fields; it has a leaf similar to Rue and small branches. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist</note> records the same things. However, Galen and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina</note> write that it has a cooling effect in the third degree, and that it is not far removed from the Poppy <note>original: "papaverisque à Papavere abesse"</note>.

The Hypecoum of the Ancients is not sufficiently known today, as different people thrust forward various plants in its place. The one we depict here is categorized by some as a species of *Iberis* <note>Candytuft</note>. It has the flowers and seeds of Cress.

We saw it at Montpellier, not far from the bathhouse known as Balaruc; and at Basel in the garden of Plater. We ourselves have also kept it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>S.P. likely refers to Serenissimi Principis</note>.

---

### VARIOUS CORALLOIDES, Seven-leaved Coralloides; Seven-leaved Toothwort.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Coralloides plant with seven distinct leaflets on a single stem and a cluster of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

The number of leaves emerging from the same stalk gave this plant its name; those who label it "five-leaved" do so by a great error.

It varies in the color of the flower, sometimes white, other times purplish.

We saw it growing wild at Basel on Mount Mutetz, at Geneva on Mount Salève, and at Montbéliard on Mount Bar. In gardens, it blooms in April and May.

Several plants are nicknamed *Coralloides* <note>Coral-like</note> and *Alabastrites* because they have roots that rival coral. There are those who refer them to the *Solidagines* <note>Goldenrods</note> and *Symphyta* <note>Comfreys</note>; others among the *Saxifragas*; others among the *Saniculas*; others, though recklessly, reckon them among the *Aconites* <note>Wolfsbane</note>. In this controversy, let it be permitted for us to place it here until someone else seeks out a more suitable location.

---

### FEMALE BALSAM: Germ. *Balsamkraut vveible*: Ital. *Balsamina maggiore*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Balsamina Foemina plant with serrated leaves and flowers emerging from the leaf axils.</image-desc>

We saw it in gardens at Esslingen and Padua, blooming in June; we also had it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince. Some call it *Balsaminum* in the neuter gender. By certain Italians, it is called "Saint Catherine’s Herb." The illustration is not pleasing <note>The author expresses dissatisfaction with the quality of the woodcut</note>.

<column-break/>

### TOOTHWORT, SCALEY-WORT: Germ. *Schupenvvurtzel*: French *Dentaria*: Ital. *Dentaria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dentaria plant showing a scaly root system and upright stems with small flowers.</image-desc>

It obtained the name *Dentaria* or *Squamaria* because its root is composed of many scales or "teeth."

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> calls it "White Violet" because of the similarity of the flowers to Stock-gillyflowers; others call it "Five-leaved Sanicle"; Jesius calls it *Pantaphyllæon* from the number of five leaves clinging to the stalk; but almost everyone calls it *Dentaria* for the reasons stated.

It loves shady places and emerges immediately at the start of Spring.

From the various species of *Dentaria*, we depict the five-leaved one here, with a flower of purplish-white.

---

### CORALLOIDES, OR THREE-LEAVED TOOTHWORT; Small Toothwort to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dentaria Triphyllos plant, characterized by three leaflets per leaf and a cluster of drooping flowers.</image-desc>

The number of leaves gave the name to this one as well; the flowers are a pale herbaceous color; it blooms in April, and in May it is found pregnant with seed.

It comes forth in the shady forests of Styria, Austria, Carinthia, and Pannonia <note>Modern-day western Hungary and surrounding regions</note>; not only at the foot of mountains, but also around their middle region where there are forests of very tall trees. —Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note>.

---

### WOLF-KILLING ACONITE OF DODOENS (Pod-bearing), perhaps to be referred to the Coralloides.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Aconitum plant with broad, lobed leaves and long seed pods (siliques).</image-desc>

An image of it is found in a very ancient manuscript, a Greek Codex, which is preserved at Vienna in Austria in the Library established by the Lord Maximilian, Most Sacred and August Emperor. Its leaves are not entirely like those of the Plane tree, but broad; the stem is thin and smooth; the pods are thin and oblong; the roots, however, seem to resemble not just tendrils, but the Sea Squills themselves.

To us, the image seems fabricated, and the description appears to have been tailored to fit a counterfeit illustration.

It includes a critical note on a potentially forged botanical illustration in the Imperial Library.</summary>
<keywords>Hypecoum, Toothwort, Coralloides, Balsam, Aconite, Dioscorides, Clusius, botanical gardens, Renaissance botany, medicinal plants</keywords>

### LOOSESTRIFE, OR WILLOW-HERB: German: *Yellow Loosestrife*: French: *Corneille, Water Marigold*: Italian: *Lysimachia*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lysimachia plant with long, serrated leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Pliny says that King Lysimachus discovered the herb Loosestrife, which takes its name from him, and it was also celebrated by the physician Erasistratus. <note>Lysimachus was a general of Alexander the Great and later King of Thrace; ancient botanists often attributed plant discoveries to royalty.</note>

According to Dioscorides, it sends out stalks a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note>, or even taller, which are slender and shrub-like. From the joints of these stalks come leaves similar to those of a Willow, with an astringent taste. The flower is yellow or golden. [Pliny attributes a purple flower to it.]

Thus, from the records of the Ancients, two kinds of Loosestrife are held to exist: namely the yellow and the purple, which are likewise recognized by more recent authors. There are also other differences, which we shall discuss presently.

We depict the yellow variety here, which is found in both a Greater and Lesser form.

### LOBEL’S OTHER YELLOW LOOSESTRIFE with globular yellow flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lysimachia plant with whorled leaves and globular flower clusters at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

We learn from Dioscorides that Loosestrife was also once called *Lytron* <note>original: "Lytron," likely referring to "lythron," meaning gore or blood, relating to its color or styptic properties</note>. Besides the etymology derived from King Lysimachus its discoverer, there are those who derive the Greek origin of the name <term>from the releasing of strife</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ λύειν τὴν μάχην"</note>, because it possesses the power to calm the fierce tempers of beasts and their mutual hostile encounters. Concerning its other powers and properties, we shall speak later.

### PURPLE SPIKED LOOSESTRIFE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with a dense, spiked inflorescence at the top.</image-desc>

It grows abundantly at Montpellier and Geneva, as well as at Basel near the Birs river, and it flowers in June and July. It is also frequent at Montbéliard near *Audincourt*, and on the road leading to *Sochaux*; likewise in various places at Yverdon.

However, our illustration, taken from purchased plates, does not please us; we would have wished for a better one. *Could it be a species of Goldenrod?*

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER YELLOW SPIKED LOOSESTRIFE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a long, tapering flower spike.</image-desc>

We have observed the yellow Loosestrife, both the Greater and the Lesser, as well as this one and the preceding, growing wild in various places, flowering in July. At Geneva in the *Plainpalais*, near the Arve river; at Basel outside St. Alban’s gate; at Montbéliard in the moats near the citadel, and elsewhere. But nowhere is it more beautiful than at Yverdon above the Mill.

### PURPLE PANNONIAN LOOSESTRIFE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with slender leaves and a terminal flower spike, showing the root system.</image-desc>

By Clusius in his *History of the Plants of Pannonia* <note>Pannonia was a Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note> it is called *Lysimachia 2* and *Lesser Loosestrife with a red flower*. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Lysimachia 4, or red non-podded Loosestrife*.

Furthermore, as we have from the records of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen, Loosestrife has a predominant astringent quality, because of which it both knits wounds together and stops outbreaks of blood from the nostrils if the nose is plugged with it; it restrains all other eruptions of blood as well. Indeed, whether drunk or infused as a clyster <note>an enema</note>, it heals dysentery, the spitting of blood, and the female flux. When burned as incense, it gives off a very sharp smell, so much so that it drives away serpents and kills flies. And its power is so great that, if placed upon the yoke of quarreling beasts of burden, it restrains their wildness.

### HAIRY PODDED LOOSESTRIFE, with a larger purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hairy plant with seed pods (siliques) and flowers.</image-desc>

It is found along the edges of ditches, moats, rivers, and streams, and in other damp places, and sometimes even in drier spots. We ourselves found it growing wild in such places, both damp and dry, at Ferrara and Montpellier, at Basel near *Muttenz*, and at Montbéliard between *Dasle* and *Audincourt*. It flowers throughout the whole summer in July.

<summary>This page describes various species of Loosestrife (Lysimachia), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and their medicinal uses as astringents and animal calmatives.</summary>
<keywords>Loosestrife, Lysimachia, Willow-herb, medicinal plants, astringents, King Lysimachus, Dioscorides, Pliny, botany, European flora</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### HAIRY PODDED WILLOWHERB, with a smaller purple flower.
<note>original: "LYSIMACHIA SILIQVOSA HIRSVTA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Lysimachia plant with hairy stems, serrated leaves, and long seed pods (siliques) extending from the upper axils.</image-desc>

It is nearly two cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> tall, though at other times it barely exceeds one cubit; the stem is reddish and round, branching out into many opposite limbs almost immediately from the root. The leaves are hairy, oblong, notched, and end in a moderate point. Small flowers, pale reddish or whitish in color, sit upon long pods. The root is hairy with many fibers.

### SMOOTH PODDED WILLOWHERB, with pale purple flowers.
<note>original: "LYSIMACHIA LÆVIS SILIQVOSA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a smooth-stemmed Lysimachia with lanceolate leaves and upright seed pods.</image-desc>

It has earned the name "smooth," not because it is entirely devoid of any hairs, but because it is endowed with such thin ones, both on the stems and the leaves, that they almost escape the sharpness of the eyes.

### TOUCH-ME-NOT: German: *Springkraut*: French: *Noli me tangere*.
<note>original: "NOLI ME TANGERE"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of the Impatiens noli-tangere plant, showing its characteristic irregular flowers and seed capsules.</image-desc>

This plant has a fibrous root and a stem one cubit high, very pale green and translucent. The leaves are like those of Dog’s Mercury <note>original: "Cynocrambe"</note>, but broader, blunter, saw-toothed around the edges, and quite soft. The flowers are reddish-yellow and spotted with darker red dots; in their center are whitish stamens. These are followed by pods like those of the Greater Celandine, which are angular; when the seed is ripe, they burst open at the slightest touch, scattering the seed and striking fear into many <note>The sudden "explosion" of the seed pod can startle the unaware.</note>, curling up like little worms. From this, the name "Touch-me-not" was given.

We found it growing wild and flowering in June in a damp place between Basel and Waldenburg; however, it is also cultivated in gardens. More on this in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### SHOWY WILLOWHERB, called by some *Onagra*.
<note>original: "LYSIMACHIA SPECIOSA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with narrow leaves and large four-petaled flowers, identified as Onagra.</image-desc>

It is a shrub, says Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note>, appearing like a tree and quite large; having leaves similar to the Almond, but broader and more closely resembling the leaves of a Lily. The flowers are like Roses and large; the root is white and long, which when dried gives off the scent of wine.

Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author of Natural History.</note> holds the same view, and he, like Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note>, attributes the same scent to the dried root; he adds that it has the potency of wine, which is why the name *Onagra* <note>Literally "wild ass-catcher," as the scent was thought to soothe wild animals.</note> was given to the plant.

Whether this Willowherb of ours is the one called *Onagra* by the Ancients must be weighed carefully. Some call it St. Anthony’s Herb. We have seen it growing wild at Basel and Montbéliard near Audincourt, and also on Mount Ballon. It flowers in June, and the flowers vary in color: purple, white, and blue.

### SHOWY NARROW-LEAFED PODDED WILLOWHERB, with a purplish flower.
<note>original: "LYSIMACHIA SILIQVOSA SPECIOSA ANgustifolia"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a narrow-leafed Lysimachia with long, slender siliques.</image-desc>

It is similar in appearance to the ones above, and the difference is only in the leaves, which in this variety are equal in length and width to Toadflax <note>original: "Linaria"</note>.

We observed it at Geneva near the Arve river.

Is it Gesner’s "St. Anthony’s Herb," or "The son before the father" <note>A common name for plants where flowers or pods appear to precede the leaves or main growth.</note>? Or Lobelius’s *Chamaenerion*?

Is it the *Epilobium* of others?

### WILD OR MARSH RADISH: German: *Wilder Raettig*: French: *Raifort d'eau*.
<note>original: "RADICVLA SYLV. SIVE PALVSTRIS"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a water-radish or similar marsh plant with pinnatifid leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The plant pictured here also claims a place for itself in this Class, although it was recorded later. It varies greatly in its leaves according to the diversity of its location; for some are broad and merely serrated, with a single stem, sometimes reddish, rising to two or three cubits and divided into branches. The flowers are yellow, very small, and many times smaller than those of the Wild Rocket. The pods are likewise shorter, thicker, and rounded. The root is usually a single fiber.

Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Caspar Bauhin call it Water Charlock; some call it Marsh Radish.

We observed it flowering in Geneva in May; but in Montbéliard in July, in the village of Courcelles.

It includes observations on their physical characteristics, habitats near Basel and Geneva, and various regional names.</summary>
<keywords>Willowherb, Lysimachia, Touch-me-not, Onagra, Epilobium, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Basel, Geneva, medicinal plants, seed pods</keywords>

# WOAD or GLASTUM: German: *Weid*, *Endich*; French: *Guesde*, *Pastel*; Italian: *Guado*.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Isatis plant (Woad), showing its tall stalk, lanceolate leaves, and clusters of small flowers and seed pods at the top.</image-desc>

Two kinds of Woad are handed down by Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>: *Domestic Woad* and *Wild Woad*. Regarding the Domestic, he says: *Cultivated Woad, which the dyers of wool use, has a leaf similar to Plantain, but fatter and blacker: a stem exceeding two cubits in height. The Wild is similar to the one just mentioned, but it has larger leaves, approaching very closely to the leaves of Lettuce; the stems, however, are thinner, many-branched, somewhat reddish, from the tops of which many small pods hang down, resembling the shape of tongues, in which is the seed: the flower is honey-colored and delicate.*

Almost all writers have mentioned Cultivated and Wild Woad in this way: and there are those who call it *Vitrum* <note>Latin for glass</note> from the German word *Glaß*, which others mistakenly turn into *Nitrum* <note>Nitre or saltpeter</note>. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> depicts only the cultivated Woad, and says the wild differs from it in nothing except that it is not planted in every location. On the other hand, Tabernaemontanus in his *Images and History* displays only the Wild. However, both are depicted, named, and described by Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria*, *Observations*, and *Images of Plants*. Ruellius writes that Woad was formerly called *Glastum* by the Greeks, but is now called *Guadum*, or rather *Gualdum*, and by some *St. Philip’s Herb*, by others *Indigo*, and by others *Pastel*. That word *Pastelli* or *Pistelli* appears in Pliny Valerianus, Book 2, chapter 3. In Avicenna <note>Persian polymath</note>, chapter 512, it is called *Nil*; moreover, the dyers call the floating foam, which the Woad solution belches out during boiling, *Indigo*. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

# ANOTHER IMAGE OF WOAD OR GLASTUM.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of a different variety of Isatis, featuring broader, more serrated leaves and a similar branching flowering structure.</image-desc>

Some, along with Cornarius, contend that the descriptions of Woad handed down by Dioscorides are erroneous: and that the qualities he attributed to the Wild variety actually belong to the Cultivated: and thus what is called Wild among us today is the Domestic of Dioscorides: and vice versa.

According to the opinion of Constantinus, Dioscorides embraces two plants under the name of Woad, with only the distinction of "Wild" or "Cultivated" added. Pliny distinguished each more effectively by its own name: calling the cultivated *Glastum*, and the wild *Isatis*. And, in the judgment of the same Constantinus, the translators ought to have imitated Pliny rather than confusing the names and calling both plants *Glastum* without any authority. In the midst of such a discrepancy of opinions, we leave the matter undecided.

Furthermore, Woad is sown in fertile and rich fields, and is most abundant especially in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> and in Italy, as well as in the Erfurt region of Germany; a great profit is perceived from it because the dyers of wool use it. We have also observed it being cultivated in gardens: in the public garden at Padua, and in that of Dr. Felix Platter at Basel, and we ourselves have had it in the garden of the Prince of Montbéliard.

Wild Woad grows in uncultivated and rich places: and we have seen it in such spots at Tübingen, Basel, and in Alsace. It flowers along with the cultivated variety in the months of May and June.

Besides the use of Woad known to dyers, the smeared leaves—according to Dioscorides—disperse all tumors, glue together bloody wounds, heal creeping ulcers, and stop the flow of blood.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXII.
### CONTAINING HERBS THAT BEAR CAPSULES OR SMALL VESSELS.

<margin>CRESS: German: *Kres*, *Garten kres*; French: *Cresson*, *Cresson alenois*; Italian: *Nasturtio*, *Agretto*.</margin>

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a Nasturtium plant with tall stems, small flowers, and a detailed root system.</image-desc>

Authors do not describe this plant, as it is considered well-known. However, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany" (c. 371 – c. 287 BC).</note> suggests it is a cultivated variety when he says: *In the month of June, Cress is usually sown, emerging from the seed on the fifth day,* etc. <note>original: "Mense Iunio Nasturtiu ferere assolens, exit à satu die quinto"</note>. And he grants it very few varieties, adding: *they maintain that a diversity of kind is entirely lacking in it.* Likewise, Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist, author of "De Materia Medica."</note> mentions only one. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of "Natural History."</note> records two, making one white and the other black, also mentioning a wild variety to which he attributes a greater effect in all matters. We depict here the Common and Ordinary variety, intending to discuss the remaining differences in the following sections. It generally remains green in gardens throughout the winter, and in March and April it puts forth flowers, which are either white or purplish.

### BROAD-LEAFED CRESS.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a broad-leafed Nasturtium variety.</image-desc>

The flower, pod, seed, taste, and smell in this variety are the same as in the Common one: but it has a white and woody root, sending out many stiff fibers from the sides; a stem the thickness of a finger, a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> high, and divided into frequent branches immediately from the root, bushing out densely. Finally, the lowest leaves are spread along the ground, five inches long, about an inch and a half wide, notched, and sometimes somewhat wavy and ear-shaped around the stalk, though this is rarer; the upper leaves are narrower.

We have cultivated this in the garden at Geneva and Montbéliard, and it remained green for us throughout the winter.

Is this the Spanish Cress of Gesner and Tabernaemontanus? <note>Conrad Gessner and Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, influential 16th-century botanists.</note> We know of no one who has described it.

<column-break/>

### CURLY CRESS.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a curly-leafed Nasturtium variety.</image-desc>

More recent authors commonly distinguish Cress into Wild and Garden varieties: and for them, the Garden variety is further divided into one with simple leaves—which is either smooth and whiter, or slightly hairy and less white—and another with deeply divided leaves; and this again is either larger or smaller, or curly or not curly.

The Curly variety which we depict here agrees in the appearance of its stems, flowers, and seeds with the Common and Ordinary variety; but the leaves differ greatly, being slashed in many ways and fringed with curly edges, though with the taste and smell of the more common Cress.

This grew for us at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden, from seed brought from Belgium.

### WILD CRESS ACCORDING TO US:
### Narrow-leafed Penny-cress according to Fuchs.

<image-desc>Botanical illustration of a wild Nasturtium variety with narrow leaves and elongated seed pods.</image-desc>

This is larger than the cultivated variety by nine inches <note>original: "dodrante," a Roman unit of measure equal to three-quarters of a foot.</note>; otherwise similar to it in appearance, except that the leaves, flowers, pods, and everything else are smaller.

Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist.</note> in his *Illustrations* and *History* provides only an image without a description, under the title of Narrow-leafed Penny-cress <term>Thlaspi: a genus of herbs in the cabbage family, often called Penny-cress</term>. To Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), who used the name Tragus.</note> when illustrating it, it is a kind of Penny-cress, but when describing it, it is a kind of Cress. To almost all others, it is a kind of Penny-cress.

Is it the Smallest Madwort of Clusius, as Schwenckfeld believes? Or a species of Iris according to Brassavola?

We have observed it in abundance at Basel near the paper mills; at Geneva near the hospital, as well as near Belfort, flowering in June.

<summary>This page describes various species of Cress (Nasturtium), detailing their physical characteristics, seasonal growth, and the differing classifications provided by historical botanical authorities like Theophrastus, Pliny, and Fuchs.</summary>
<keywords>Cress, Nasturtium, Penny-cress, Thlaspi, botany, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, Leonhart Fuchs, Montbéliard, Geneva, Basel, medicinal herbs</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### SMALL ALPINE CRESS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flowering plant with thin stems, small leaves, and clusters of tiny flowers at the tips, showing the root system.</image-desc>

We found this Small Cress on Mount Nombre in Rhaetia <note>The Rhaetian Alps, likely in modern-day Switzerland/Italy</note>, where it was blooming in July. It was scarcely three inches wide, with a woody root provided with few fibers. There are two or three small stalks, at the tops of which are the seed pods of the common Cress, arranged in a similar order. The leaves are small, simple, narrow, and thinner than an inch; the little flowers are small and white.

Cress was called *Kardamon* <note>original Greek: Κάρδαμον</note> by the Greeks, as if to say "subduing the head" <note>original Greek: κάρα δάμον; a reference to its pungent smell affecting the head</note>. Among the Latins, however, according to Pliny, it takes its name from "torment of the nose" <note>Latin: *nasus* (nose) and *tormentum* (torment), referring to the sharp, sneezing sensation caused by its spice</note>. The French called it *Creisō*, because it grows with perennial offspring, even in the greatest heat or the rigors of winter, which it disregards. And by some, perhaps from its nourishing quality, it is called *Cresson d'aleno*.

### SMALL ALPINE CRESS, VERY FINELY
->dissected: with many white flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with more complex, finely divided (dissected) foliage and numerous small flower clusters.</image-desc>

We have from Gesner <note>Conrad Gesner, 16th-century Swiss naturalist</note> that it grows in the Swiss Alps; and from Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, influential Flemish botanist</note>, who found it blooming in August in the Austrian Alps.

Cress was once a very common side dish. Indeed, Xenophon, Strabo, and Cicero deny that anyone used anything except Cress for seasoning when they first embraced frugality, before the Empire grew and they fell into every kind of luxury. And so, says Pliny, they cleared themselves by frequent spitting and clearing the mucus from the nostrils—evils to which they were greatly subject—and even by the shedding of tears. Thus today it is still commonly used for seasoning foods and sauces; and it also comes to the table during Summer with Lettuce and other herbs, with oil, vinegar, and salt.

<column-break/>

### WILD CRESS OF VALENCIA
->of Clusius: Peruvian Cress with Lentil-like leaves.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Nasturtium variety with elongated leaves and small flowers, including the root structure.</image-desc>

We depict here a plant found in the Kingdom of Valencia, which has pale flowers and many things in common with the common Cress. Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, Spanish physician who wrote on New World plants</note> mentions a Peruvian Cress with leaves like those of a Lentil.

Furthermore, the seed of Cress is of a burning and caustic faculty, according to Galen. It thins, cleanses, opens, and cuts <note>referring to the "cutting" of thick humors or phlegm</note>. It disturbs the bowels, diminishes the spleen, expels stillborn fetuses, provokes the menses, stimulates lust, is contrary to the stomach, drives out intestinal worms, wipes away leprosy and skin eruptions, moves sweat, is effective against Scurvy <note>Latin: *Scorbutum*</note>, dissolves clotted blood, and prevents it from gathering or clotting anywhere; it is helpful for those who have fallen from a height or been cast down. The herb has the same effect, but to a lesser degree.

### WARTY CRESS; SWINE'S CRESS
->of Ruellius: German: *Wartzen kraut*: French: *Pied de Corneille*.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with deeply lobed leaves spreading from a central root, typical of Coronopus.</image-desc>

<margin>Ambrosia, and the first Ambrosia according to Matthiolus and Camerarius. Creeping Coronopus according to Ruellius, Field Coronopus according to Tabernaemontanus, Hartshorn to some, a species of Buckshorn according to the French Dodonaeus.</margin>

It grows spontaneously in Geneva and Basel, and around the city of Montbéliard, as also in the S. P. garden, where it renews itself every year from fallen seed; it blooms in June and July.

### PENNYCRESS: German: *Bisem kraut*: Belgian: *Boeren kerse*:
->French: *Seneue sauuage*: Italian: *Thlaspi*.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Thlaspi (Pennycress) showing the characteristic flat, heart-shaped seed pods (silicles) along the stem.</image-desc>

From a root that is quite thick, fibrous, woody, white, and somewhat sharp, there rise hairy, round, rigid, and branched stalks. The leaves adhere to these without a stalk; they are long, becoming gradually narrower, and are saw-toothed or notched. They embrace the stem with a double little wing, having a sharp, biting taste. The little flowers are minute, white, and many, arranged as in Shepherd's Purse, consisting of four small petals, with as many greenish tips supporting them. The seed pods occupy the flower with a premature birth; they are leafy, somewhat round, flattened, and notched at the top, in which is a sharp seed like Mustard or Cress.

Hippocrates called it *Thlaspios*; Galen called it *Thlaspen* and *Thlaspion*. Some perhaps called it *Thlaspidion* as a diminutive; others called it Country Mustard, Roof Cress, and Wandering Cress.

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE
->more common Pennycress.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Thlaspi with similar seed pods but slightly different leaf structure.</image-desc>

From the work of Dioscorides and Pliny, a double Thlaspi is drawn out: namely, the narrow-leaved and the broad-leaved, which they call Persian Mustard. Cornarius writes that it is gathered from Galen that the first kind of Thlaspi is twofold, and there is a third which Dioscorides and Pliny made their third. Among more recent authors, three kinds of Thlaspi are noted: the Greater, the Lesser, and the Middle; to which others given this name are referred, which we have already reviewed.

Furthermore, Thlaspi grows most abundantly in cultivated and uncultivated places of almost all regions: especially in ditches, paths, and hedges. In the months of May and June, it is adorned with flowers and pregnant with seed. We have also observed it in gardens at Basel, Geneva, and Petaut.

<summary>This page describes various species of Cress and Pennycress (Thlaspi), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations in the Alps and Europe, and their historical uses as both a frugal food and a potent medicine for conditions like scurvy and blood clots.</summary>
<keywords>Alpine Cress, Pennycress, Thlaspi, medical botany, Scurvy, Galen, Pliny, Clusius, Gesner, Valencia, Switzerland, botanical taxonomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Thlaspi genus (Penny-cress), maintaining the systematic descriptions of varieties and their medicinal properties as established in previous sections.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### PENNY-CRESS WITH HAIRY CAPSULES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender Thlaspi plant with small flowers and hairy seed capsules along the stem. Two detailed views of the hairy seed pods are shown to the left of the main stem.</image-desc>

Hairy Penny-cress, Shaggy Penny-cress, and Bristly Penny-cress to some; the Cretan Penny-cress of Galen according to Anguillara. <note>Luigi Anguillara was a 16th-century Italian botanist.</note>

We have kept this at Montbéliard in the Sacred Botanical Garden, where it propagates itself from fallen seed.

<column-break/>

### PENNY-CRESS WITH BROAD PODS: AND WHITE FLOWERS like Shepherd's Purse.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thlaspi plant with broad, flat seed pods and small white flowers. Two detailed views of the broad pods are shown to the right of the stem.</image-desc>

In the French edition of Dodoens, it is called *Thlaspi*, *Thlaspidion*, Wild Mustard, *Capsella*, and *Scandulaceum*; by some *Myitis*, *Bytron*, *Dasmophon*, and *Myopteron*. He says the name *Thlaspi* <note>original: "Thlaspi"</note> was derived among the Greeks from the fruit, which resembles a small, flattened shield. <note>The Greek 'thlao' means to crush or flatten, referring to the shape of the seed pod.</note>

Lobelius, in his *Observations and Icons of Plants*, calls it *Draba* and *Chamaelina*-leaved Penny-cress. Schwenkfeld calls it the Greater Broad Penny-cress. Cordus calls it Cress-like Penny-cress; Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it Penny-cress with broad leaves and pods.

It grows spontaneously in fields and is also sown in gardens.

---

<column-break/>

### CRETAN PENNY-CRESS TO SOME, WITH REDDISH-WHITE FLOWERS: to others the DRYOPHONON of Pliny.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering Thlaspi plant with clusters of flowers at the top and elongated leaves. A detailed view of a flower cluster is shown to the right.</image-desc>

Cretan Penny-cress, Cappadocian Penny-cress, and Candy <note>An old name for Crete</note> Penny-cress, according to Lobelius, Schwenkfeld, and others. To Caspar Bauhin, it is the Cretan Umbel-type Penny-cress with Iberis-leaves, the *Dryophonon* <note>literally "oak-slayer"</note> of Pliny to some, and the *Draba* of Dioscorides to others. To Camerarius, it is the Cretan Penny-cress with purple and whitish flowers and a very bitter leaf. In the French Dodoens, it is the Moderns' Candy Penny-cress, the *Dryophonon* of Pliny to some, and *Draba* or *Arabis* (by an easy slip from *Arabina*).

We have seen it in gardens in Basel, Geneva, and Stuttgart, flowering and producing seed in July and August.

There is also found a Cretan Penny-cress with undivided or Flax-like leaves.

<column-break/>

### UMBEL-FLOWERED FIELD PENNY-CRESS WITH WHITE, or purplish-white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thlaspi plant with umbel-like flower clusters and broad, notched seed pods. Detailed views of the pods are shown to the right.</image-desc>

We depict two here in the same plate, of which the *Greater* we saw in the fields among the crops at Geneva, flowering in June; as also in various fields at Montbéliard, traveling from *Arbouans* to *Audincourt*, around *la Chaux*, and elsewhere. The *Lesser* variety we found between Montpellier and Pérols at the edges of fields, flowering in May. To Tabernaemontanus and other writers, it is the *Narbonne Penny-cress*.

---

<column-break/>

### SMALL UMBEL-FLOWERED PENNY-CRESS, with snow-white fragrant flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing Thlaspi with dense flower clusters and small leaves. A detailed flower cluster is shown to the left.</image-desc>

Here we shall treat the powers and faculties of Penny-cress. The seed, as we learn from Dioscorides, is sharp and heating; it purges bile both upwards and downwards when a measure of one small cup <note>original: "acetabuli"</note> is drunk, and administered as an unsalted enema, it cures sciatica. Taken as a drink, it also draws blood and ruptures internal abscesses. It provokes the menses and causes miscarriage. Pliny, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina</note> repeat these same points. Among the more recent authors, Fuchs and Schwenkfeld declare the matter more briefly. The seed, they say, heats and dries in the fourth degree; it is sharp, it cuts through, thins, provokes, and burns, just like Watercress.

<column-break/>

### PENNY-CRESS WITH GLOBULARIA LEAVES, AND MILK-COLORED FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thlaspi plant with rounded leaves resembling Globularia and clusters of pale flowers.</image-desc>

In the month of May, we saw this with flowers and nearly ripe pods in stony places near Saint-Vincent.

Could this be the Round-leaved Penny-cress of Camerarius and Caspar Bauhin?

As for the choice of Penny-cress: Galen prefers the Cappadocian variety over the others, especially for *Theriac* <note>A famous ancient "universal" medicinal paste or antidote</note>; and not just any brought from Cappadocia, but specifically that which grows on Mount Saurus, which is unlike the Cretan variety or that which grows everywhere.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of Thlaspi (Penny-cress), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations (including the author's personal observations in Montbéliard and Geneva), and their potent medicinal uses as described by ancient and Renaissance authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Penny-cress, Thlaspi, botany, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Galen, Pliny, Caspar Bauhin, pharmacology, Theriac, Montbéliard, Crete</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### PENNY-CRESS WITH HEART-SHAPED CAPSULES, and a tiny purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thlaspi plant with a single upright stem, small heart-shaped seed pods (capsules), and a small root system.</image-desc>

It grew for us in the Illustrious Prince's <note>original: "S.P." referring to Serenissimi Principis</note> garden at Montbéliard, from seed brought from Zurich, and it was blooming in July and August.

### SMALLER PENNY-CRESS TO SOME, with a yellow flower: Small Alyssum to many.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Thlaspi variety with multiple stems branching from the base and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> says it grows everywhere in the Viennese countryside, at the edges of fields and vineyards where they are separated from the public road, and even in the dry and grassy fields of other places. We have observed it in the same types of places at Geneva, Lyon, and Montbéliard, flowering in April and May.

### HOARY PENNY-CRESS WITH ELONGATED CAPSULES, and a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thlaspi plant with elongated seed pods and hairy or hoary (incanum) leaves.</image-desc>

It grows in many places in Austria and Moravia, along roadsides, at the edges of fields, and in uncultivated grassy places; it flowers in July. It grew for us in the Illustrious Prince's garden at Montbéliard.

Is this the *Third Penny-cress* in Mattioli's <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, renowned Italian physician and botanist</note> later Latin and Italian Commentaries? Or perhaps the *6th Hoary Shrubby Penny-cress of Franconia* in Camerarius's Garden? Or the *Low-growing White Penny-cress* of Lobel and Schwenckfeld?

<column-break/>

### MARITIME PENNY-CRESS TO SOME, to others Maritime Watercress.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime Thlaspi with thick, succulent-looking leaves and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

It grows into a shrubby plant a span and a half <note>about 13 inches</note> or almost a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high: with woody, quite brittle, hairy, reddish branches spread across the ground. Along these are narrow leaves <note>original: "folia vocialia" likely referring to the shape or arrangement</note>, very slender, covered in hoary hairiness, with the taste of Watercress <term>Nasturtium: a peppery-tasting herb</term>. The tiny flowers are clustered at the ends of the branches, white with some blue parts, fragrant, and similar to Watercress. These are followed by a few *Capsules*, which are oblong and pointed at both ends, containing a tiny, reddish seed. The *root* is somewhat large, thick, and white.

We observed it flowering in April, August, and October in the sandy salt marshes near Montpellier. Tabernaemontanus and the *History of Lyon*—as well as Pena and Lobel—present it under the names of Narbonne Penny-cress, Narrow-leaved Centunculus, and Italian Alyssum.

### YELLOW MOUNTAIN PENNY-CRESS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Thlaspi with broad, deeply lobed or incised leaves and spreading stems.</image-desc>

It flowers in the months of June and July. It varies in its leaves, which are sometimes found without lobes, but more often are cut into deep, very narrow segments right down to the midrib.

### EVERGREEN WHITE PENNY-CRESS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an evergreen Thlaspi with small, narrow leaves and clusters of white flowers.</image-desc>

This plant is branched, with many small, oblong leaves that are hoary or white. The *flowers* are white in umbrella-like clusters; the *pods* are small and somewhat round.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the Illustrious Prince's garden from seed sent from Stuttgart.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Thlaspi (Penny-cress), detailing their physical characteristics, flowering seasons, and specific geographic locations where they were observed or cultivated, such as Montbéliard and Montpellier.</summary>
<keywords>Penny-cress, Thlaspi, Alyssum, botany, Montbéliard, Clusius, Mattioli, medicinal plants, herbals</keywords>

# IMAGES AND SKETCHES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### ANOTHER SHRUBBY PENNY-CRESS of Lobel's.
<note>Thlaspi fruticosum alterum Lobelii. Matthias de Lobel (1538–1616) was a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

Lobel describes this quite meagerly, nor does he note the place where he found it. We have depicted here a branch of the dried plant sent to us under that name.

<column-break/>

### SHRUBBY PENNY-CRESS WITH LEAVES OF THE SMALLER SEA-STOCK. Tree-like Penny-cress.
<note>Thlaspi fruticosum folio Leucoii marini minoris. Thlaspi arborescens.</note>

This plant has numerous twigs, crowded with many leaves like those of the smaller Stock; the *flowers* are white and plentiful, and the seed is compressed like that of the small Penny-cress. The root is fibrous and woody.

It is found in the gardens of Belgium; however, in Speyer <note>original: "Spirae"</note>, where the Imperial Chamber is located, we observed in the highly cultivated garden of a certain Assessor a *Penny-cress* that was not only shrubby, but clearly tree-like, with leaves like Toadflax <note>original: "Linariae"</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### THORNY PENNY-CRESS, called Thorny Stock by some.
<note>Thlaspi spinosum, Leucoium spinosum quibusdam.</note>

Because some of its branches turn into somewhat long, rigid, sharp, and straight thorns, it has therefore been given the name "thorny."

We collected it among the steep rocks and crags of Mount Lupus <note>likely the Wolfsberg or a similar "Wolf Mountain" landmark</note>.

<column-break/>

### PENNY-CRESS WITH GARLIC-MUSTARD LEAVES, and a white, four-petaled flower like Watercress.
<note>Thlaspi folio Alliariae, flore Nasturtii aquatici.</note>

This grew for us in the garden of the Prince of Montbéliard <note>original: "S. P. horto," likely referring to the Princely garden</note>, from seed brought from Stuttgart: it endured the winter, bloomed all summer, and propagated itself by dropped seed.

It is called *Pannonian Penny-cress* by Lobel in his "Images of Plants" and by Camerarius in his "Garden"; Clusius calls it *Mountain Penny-cress*; and Caspar Bauhin in his "Phytopinax" calls it *Penny-cress 4, or Woad-leaved*.

---

<column-break/>

### ALEXANDRIAN PENNY-CRESS OF CORTUSUS.
<note>Thlaspi Alexandrinum Cortusi. Giacomo Antonio Cortuso (1513–1593) was the director of the Padua Botanical Garden.</note>

We formerly received this plant from Cortusus under this title: *A beautiful plant of Alexandrian Penny-cress*.

<column-break/>

### IVY-LEAVED PENNY-CRESS.
<note>Thlaspi hederaceum.</note>

This little herb creeps among various maritime rocks in England; it has slender, grooved, reddish stems about nine inches or a span long: the *leaves* are lobed, ivy-like, and fleshy. The *flowers* are white, and the seed is small, in which the taste and character of Penny-cress is expressed.

# OF PLANTS

### GARLIC-CRESS OF ULISSE ALDROVANDI.
<note>original: "Scorodothlaspi Ulyssis Aldroandi." A name combining the Greek words for garlic (skorodon) and cress (thlaspi).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scorodothlaspi plant with broad, serrated leaves and small clusters of flowers at the top of several stems.</image-desc>

The seed, brought from Bologna and sown in the garden of His Serene Highness at Montbéliard, grew for us into that plant whose image we give here: in July it produced small white flowers, like those of the common Shepherd's Purse. It is a new plant, and as far as we are aware, has not been described by anyone until now.

### SMALLEST SHIELD-SHAPED MOONWORT, WITH YELLOWISH FLOWERS: by some called the smaller buckler-cress.
<note>original: "Lunaria peltata minima... Thlaspi clypeatum minus."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Lunaria peltata plant with rounded, peltate leaves and thin stems ending in small flower clusters.</image-desc>

This little plant is shorter than a palm's breadth, which Lobelius and Caspar Bauhin call the smaller buckler-cress.

It grows in the territory of Narbonne and Montpellier, in desolate and sandy places, near the tiny Buglosses <note>original: "Anchusas"</note>.

### THE ALYSSUM OF ANGUILLARA: OR PERHAPS THE GREEK CRESS of Lobelius and Pena?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alyssum plant with small, narrow leaves and clusters of tiny flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

The Ancients did not write with one mind concerning Alyssum. To Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> it is a small, somewhat rough shrub: having round leaves, around which is the fruit in the shape of a double shield, in which the seed is found, being somewhat broad. He adds that it grows in rough and mountainous places.

Pliny seems to make the Greater Madder into Alyssum; Aetius calls the *Sideritis Heraclea* <note>Ironwort</note> Alyssum; and Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta</note> defends his opinion: but Cotuarios rightly contends that it is not called Alyssum except improperly.

Others refer it to the Madder, others to the Crosswort, others to the Spider-king <note>original: "Liliaginem"</note>, others to Horehound: but it is shown in our *Great History* that they all do so with a great error.

It moderately dries and disperses, and cleanses somewhat: according to Galen.

<column-break/>

### DOUBLE-SHIELDED MOONWORT, WITH A SMALL YELLOWISH FLOWER: by some called buckler-cress.
<note>original: "Lunaria biscutata... Thlaspi clypeatum."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lunaria biscutata plant featuring distinctive double-shield shaped seed pods (silicles) along the stems.</image-desc>

This is that plant which Lobelius and Pena, in their *Adversaria*, call the small Hawkweed-leaved Cress, or the Yellow Moonwort of Montpellier, and the Yellow Sea-Stock, and the second smaller Moonwort. By the judgment of all, no place is more suited for this than among the Cresses <note>original: "Thlaspi"</note>.

It is found in the meadows of Montpellier and other places near Montpellier: and in Italian gardens it was first called Sea-Stock, though not with great similarity. At Montbéliard, in the garden of His Serene Highness, it bloomed for us in May.

### ALYSSUM OR ALYSSOS: YELLOW OR GREEK MOONWORT, the Greater Moonwort of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger Alyssum or Lunaria plant with elongated leaves and dense clusters of flowers and developing pods.</image-desc>

The plant we depict here is called Alyssum by the moderns and by Dioscorides. To Dodoens, Gesner, Cesalpino, and almost everyone else, it is known as such; and Pena and Lobelius thought no plant better matched the Alyssum of Dioscorides. Others record it under the name of *Greater Moonwort, Yellow Moonwort, and Moonwort with broad rough pods*.

We have seen it in gardens at Padua, Ferrara, and Bologna, and we ourselves have had it in our own at Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard; it flowers in April and May.

It is called *alysson* <note>original: "ἄλυσσον"</note> by the Greeks, and similarly *Alyssum* by the Latins, because it wonderfully helps those bitten by a mad dog, on the authority of Galen, Aetius, Paul, Pliny, and Pausanias. More on this in the margin of the following figure.

### THE LEADWORT OF RONDELET.
<note>original: "Dentillaria Rondeletii." Now known as Plumbago europaea.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dentillaria plant with long, lanceolate leaves and spikes of flowers.</image-desc>

It puts forth many shoots a cubit and a half long, striped, blackish, frequently divided into alternating branches. The leaves embrace the stem with wings; they are smooth, dark green, of a burning taste, equal to the leaves of Fleabane <note>original: "Conyzae"</note>, but much smaller through the ends of the branches. The flowers cling to the tips, crowded together in heaps, oblong, purple, with a hairy calyx. The seeds are large, black, and sharp.

It is the *Plumbago* of Pliny, commonly called the Herb of St. Anthony, and by some the *Lepidium* of Aegineta: but to most it is the *Dentillaria* of Montpellier and the *Molybdena* of Narbonne.

We saw it flowering in September at Montpellier and near Avignon: but we have had it in the garden at Lyon and Montbéliard.

It is a sharp herb, the root of which is recommended for toothache <note>The name "Dentillaria" refers to its use in treating dental pain.</note>.

<keywords>botany, Alyssum, Moonwort, Leadwort, medicinal plants, Montbéliard garden, Dioscorides, Pliny, Renaissance science</keywords>
