# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shepherd's purse plant (Bursa Pastoria) showing its distinctive heart-shaped seed pods, basal rosette of leaves, and fibrous root system.</image-desc>

### SHEPHERD'S PURSE: German: *Seckel-kraut*, *Teschelkraut*; French: *Bourse de Pasteur*; Italian: *Bursa Pastori*.

Many have considered Shepherd's Purse <note>original: "Bursa pastoris"</note> and Pennycress <note>original: "Thlaspi"</note> to be one and the same plant, as noted by Cesalpino and Mattioli <note>Andrea Cesalpino and Pietro Andrea Mattioli, influential 16th-century botanists</note>. But since they differ greatly in their medicinal powers, and the leaves of Shepherd's Purse are jagged around the edges and do not at all match what Dioscorides and Pliny recorded about Pennycress, their opinion seems clearly to be rejected.

Guido <note>likely referring to Guy de Chauliac</note> is no less foully mistaken in thinking it is Knotgrass <note>original: "Polygonum"</note>; as is Cornarius, who believes it to be Medick <note>original: "Herba Medica" or Lucerne</note>; for those skilled in plants know how much they differ.

Thus, various types of Shepherd's Purse have been observed both by us and by others: of which we depict the **Greater** variety here. More will follow.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Bursa Pastoria with more elongated, narrow leaves and smaller seed pods.</image-desc>

### SMALLEST SHEPHERD'S PURSE, with oblong pods, blooming in spring: with white or purple flowers.

Dodoens depicts and describes this under the title of common Whitlow-grass <note>original: "Paronychia vulgaris"</note>. To Tabernaemontanus it is the Smallest Chickweed. To Camerarius it is the Smallest Siliquose Mouse-ear.

It varies in its flowers, leaves, and size: for the flowers, which are commonly white in the ordinary kind and others, are sometimes seen as purple in this one. The leaves are sometimes whole, but at other times jagged. The whole plant is sometimes larger and sometimes smaller.

It grows spontaneously in various places in sandy fields and everywhere along roadsides and in hedges: it blooms in March and April: it is frequent at Geneva in the *Plainpalais* <note>A famous open square/district in Geneva</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader, clasping leaves and clusters of small flowers/pods at the top.</image-desc>

### A plant related to SHEPHERD'S PURSE with a somewhat long seed-vessel.

It grows in the fields of Montpellier and Basel: it blooms in April and May.

When crushed, the herb Shepherd's Purse cools the inflammation of gatherings <note>abscesses or swellings</note>, restrains the humors flowing thereto, and is applied to "sacred fires" <note>erysipelas or skin rashes</note> and a burning stomach; the juice is effective for the same.

For hemorrhages, from whichever part the blood may flow, the water, juice, and decoction are applied in various ways, internally and externally, and they perform wonders. Many are of the opinion that blood flowing from the nostrils or other parts and wounds is restrained if the herb, having been carried, grows warm against the person from whom the blood flows. Cesalpino rubs the herb with vinegar and applies it to the wrist <note>original: "carpo"</note> to stop the flow of blood and to check the shivering of a Tertian ague <note>a fever occurring every third day, often malaria</note>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with small, smooth leaves and clusters of tiny flowers.</image-desc>

### SMALL SHEPHERD'S PURSE, with a smooth, thick leaf.

Caspar Bauhin distinguishes Shepherd's Purse into the first greater kind with a notched leaf; a second with a whole and un-notched leaf; and into a middle Shepherd's Purse and a smaller Shepherd's Purse.

This one which we depict here has a single root, but subdivided into thinner parts: the first leaf is simple, round, and small; but others thereafter are somewhat jagged in the manner of the Greater Shepherd's Purse, thick, smooth, and scarcely two inches long <note>original: "sextantalia"</note>: the stalks are single or several, nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantales"</note> or even smaller: many little flowers together, white: the pods are rounder than in the common kind.

By Tabernaemontanus it is called Rock Cress <note>original: "Nasturtium petraeum"</note>. It grows on walls and at the edges of plowed fields.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with perfoliate leaves (stem passing through the leaf) and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

### SHEPHERD'S PURSE with perfoliate leaves.

Camerarius depicts it under the title of Mouse-ear: but Clusius, Tabernaemontanus, the *History of Lyon*, and Caspar Bauhin classify it among the types of Pennycress <note>original: "Thlaspi"</note>: to Schwenckfeld it is the Lesser Shepherd's Purse.

We have observed it growing spontaneously in various places. It blooms in April and May.

Regarding the powers of Shepherd's Purse: It is of the class of cooling, drying, and astringent medicines, but as to what degree of coldness it possesses, writers do not agree: we have their opinions and weigh them in our *Great History*. Its decoction is highly commended for "hot gout" <note>inflammatory gout</note> and tumors of the throat and private parts. More is found at the side of the following figure.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Draba or Arabis plant with serrated leaves and dense clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

### DRABA OR ARABIS: German: *Tureckisch Kress*; French: *Draue*; Italian: *Draba*.

Some call it Babylonian Cress. However, Cornarius believes the *Draba* in Dioscorides to be a later insertion, both because mention is made of it twice in the same book, and because no other writer mentions either *Drabes* or *Arabis*.

Others (such as Cordus), because the final words of Dioscorides regarding *Draba* are handed down by Pliny regarding *Dryophonon*, think that the *Draba* of Dioscorides and the *Dryophonon* of Pliny are one and the same, but this is based on slight conjecture.

Serapio numbers it among the kinds of Cress and calls it Oriental Cress. Others judge that *Arabis* and *Draba* are names for one and the same plant, with only the 'D' changed to an 'A', as has been demonstrated before.

We have two images, in which since some significant variety is observed, we present both.

<summary>This page details the botanical classification and medicinal uses of Shepherd's Purse (Bursa Pastoria) and its relatives, correcting historical misidentifications by earlier scholars. It highlights the plant's primary use as a cooling astringent to stop bleeding and treat inflammations.</summary>
<keywords>Shepherd's Purse, Bursa Pastoria, Draba, Arabis, botanical classification, astringent, hemorrhage, herbal medicine, Dioscorides, Caspar Bauhin</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
## SCURVY-GRASS
<meta>Catchword: SCURVY-GRASS</meta>

### ANOTHER FIGURE OF DRABA OR ARABIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Draba (whitlow-grass) plant, showing a central stalk with alternating leaves and clusters of small flowers/seed pods at the top.</image-desc>

The Draba <note>likely *Lepidium draba*, commonly known as Hoary Cress</note> scarcely exceeds a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height, with a round, striated stem rising from a woody, multiple root. The leaves clasp the stem alternately at their base; they are oblong, an inch and a half wide, and wavy-edged. The tops of the stems branch out into very numerous shoots, which are themselves leafy. Upon these sit small white flowers in an umbel-like cluster; when these fall away, small pods emerge shaped like a little heart, putting forth a tiny style from the tip. These contain two small reddish seeds in their two compartments.

Around Vienna, and throughout almost all of Lower Austria, the edges of fields are covered with this plant, and it occasionally creeps into the cultivated fields themselves. It is also found at Montpellier at the edges of some fields; we have truly seen it in the public garden at Padua, flowering in March.

### NON-CREEPING LEPIDIUM, approaching the Lepidium of Paul, of which more follows.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lepidium (pepperweed) plant, featuring a tall, slender stalk with small, serrated leaves and a long raceme of flowers/seeds.</image-desc>

Under this name, among our Guarinian Figures <note>referring to illustrations from the collection of the printer Guarinus</note>, we found this and the following one, which seem to moderately represent the non-creeping Lepidium.

Furthermore, to proceed with what was said shortly before: Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Caesalpino, a famous Italian botanist</note> follows our opinion when he says: Galen thinks that *Iberis* is the same as *Lepidium*; but in Dioscorides, a distinct mention of them is found. *Iberis* has its strength in the roots, while *Lepidium* has it in the leaves; moreover, the latter is used in food, while *Iberis* is not at all.

We prefer, therefore, to think that the *Lepidium* of Paul <note>Paul of Aegina</note>, Pliny, Dioscorides, and Galen are one and the same. However, the *Iberis* in Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, and others is the same plant that is also called *Lepidium*, but it is different from the one just mentioned.

### THE LEPIDIUM OF PAUL AND PLINY, PEPPERWORT: German: Senffkraut; French: Poivrée; Italian: Piperella.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lepidium Pauli (Dittander), showing a robust plant with large, broad, lanceolate leaves and a branching floral structure at the apex.</image-desc>

From a root the thickness of a finger, a single straight, slender, smooth stem rises, creeping along the ground, filled with a spongy pith, two cubits high or more. The leaves are like those of a Citron tree, often larger, notched around the edges, stiff, turning from green to yellow, with the taste of Mustard; the flowers are numerous, tiny, and whitish, with greenish tips.

It grows wild in several places, such as at Montpellier by the river. In gardens, however, this plant also grows abundantly, though its creeping habit makes it hateful to gardeners.

It is of a very hot nature, and is extremely useful for provocations <note>stimulating the skin</note>, mustard-plasters, and other such purposes.

<column-break/>

### IBERIS: by some called LEPIDIUM: German: Gauchblum, Uvilder Kress; French: Passerage; Italian: Iberide.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Iberis (candytuft) plant, showing a woody base with multiple stems and dense clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

*Iberis* or *Cardamantica* <note>original: "Cardamantica"</note> is described by Dioscorides in Book 1, Chapter 147. It has leaves like Watercress, greener in the spring, and a stem a cubit or less in height. It grows in uncultivated places. Regarding the *Lepidium* treated by the same Dioscorides in Book 2, Chapter 170, Galen, Paul, Aetius, Oribasius, and Matthiolus believe it to be the same as *Iberis*. We, however, embrace this opinion as true: nor would we concede to Gano, Cornarius, and Matthiolus that *Lepidium* is the same as *Iberis*. For from Pliny, and perhaps from the context of Dioscorides, a great difference appears: *Iberis* is wild, while *Lepidium* is cultivated. *Iberis* has the leaf of Watercress, while *Lepidium* has Laurel-like leaves, etc. More on this in the following sections.

### ANOTHER FIGURE OF THE NON-CREEPING LEPIDIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Lepidium, showing a tall, upright stem with narrow leaves and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

Since we cannot always write everything pertaining to a plant next to its image, we are forced to borrow space from neighboring plants and those somewhat related to them. And so, here is more concerning *Iberis*.

Along roadsides, on walls and near walls, and at the edges of fields, it grows wild in Italy and France; in Northern regions, however, it is kept only in gardens. Its flowers are white, which it puts forth in August.

The power of *Iberis* is sharp and heating, wherefore the crushed root is a most present help for those with sciatica <note>original: "Ischiadicis"</note>; it likewise benefits those with spleen complaints. It is also believed that the root, when hung from the neck, frees one from the pain of teeth <note>toothache</note>.

### ANOTHER FIGURE OF THE LEPIDIUM OF PAUL AND PLINY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another Lepidium variety, showing broad basal leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

We easily persuade ourselves that the plant we present here, and represent with these two Guarinian figures—namely *Piperitis* <note>Pepperwort or Dittander</note>—is the *Lepidium* of Pliny, Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul. Yet it is a different plant from the *Iberis* of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Democrates, as we also warned a little earlier. Ruellius referred it to the radish or *Raphanus* family. By Cordus it is called *Lepidium* or the Greater *Iberis*, likewise *Piperina* and *Zingiberina* <note>Ginger-like</note>, but why he writes it thus is unclear. More on *Iberis* and *Lepidium* in the Appendix.

<summary>This page discusses the botanical identification and medicinal uses of various cresses and pepperworts, attempting to reconcile conflicting descriptions from classical authors like Dioscorides and Pliny. It highlights the plants' "hot" nature and their use in treating sciatica and toothaches.</summary>
<keywords>Draba, Lepidium, Iberis, Pepperwort, Dittander, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, medicinal plants, sciatica, botany, Renaissance herbal</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes Class 22 of the botanical compendium, focusing on medicinal herbs and exotic spices. It maintains the encyclopedic style of the previous sections, blending classical citations with contemporary observations from the author's garden in Montbéliard.</meta>

# SCURVY-GRASS: German: Leffel-kraut; French: Herbe aux cuilleres; Italian: Cochlearia.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Cochlearia (Scurvy-grass) plant, showing its broad, spoon-shaped leaves and clusters of small flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

Scurvy-grass, or *Spoon-wort Thlaspi*, is a plant related to the *Cresses* with white flowers, which we depict here. It is called *Telephium* by Lacuna <note>Andrés Laguna, a 16th-century Spanish physician</note>, and Hadrianus Junius calls it *Pliny's Britannica*; but incorrectly, for it does not at all correspond to the descriptions of either *Telephium* or *Pliny's Britannica*, as Lobelius and Gesner have rightly noted. It obtained the name *Cochlearia* <note>from the Latin 'cochlear' meaning spoon</note> because the ends of its long leaves are rounded into the shape of a spoon.

It grew for us and bloomed in March in the garden at Montbéliard. It grows abundantly and spontaneously by the Dutch sea, from which it is also called *Batavian*.

It is hot and dry, and very similar to the virtue, taste, and quality of Watercress: and it effectively cures Scurvy, a disease familiar to that region.

<column-break/>

# CAPSICUM PEPPER, German: Calecutischer Pfeffer; French: Poivre d'Espagne; Italian: Pepe d'India.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Capsicum (Chili pepper) plant with long, pointed seed pods hanging from the branches.</image-desc>

Of the various and greatly differing plants presented under the name of Pepper, there remains that which is handed down under the names *Capsicum, Calicut, Siliquastrum, Indian, Brazilian*, and *American*, and which is also called *Piperitis*, and *Pliny's Siliquastrum*.

*Siliquastrum*, in the opinion of Fuchs, was named most appropriately by Pliny, from the large, long, or round and wide pods <note>Latin: 'siliquis'</note> which it produces.

The same plant is also named *Piperitis* by the same author, because its seed, when tasted, displays the flavor and sharpness of Pepper. However, it is different from the plant commonly called *Piperitis* <note>Dittander</note>. Some have thought it to be the *Dog's Ginger* of Avicenna. It was perhaps called *Capsicum* because the seed bites when eaten, from the word <note>original Greek: κάπτω</note> "to bite" or "to gulp down."

---

### CAPSICUM PEPPER WITH WIDER & rounder pods.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a variety of Capsicum with broader, more rounded fruit pods compared to the previous image.</image-desc>

There are various differences of the Pepper called Capsicum, Indian, Calicut, etc. For it is either *larger* or *smaller*: and there is a distinction in the pods, stem, leaves, flowers, and seed. For the *pods* are either long, or wide and somewhat round; the stem is either smooth or hairy, and endowed with white hairs. The *leaves* are either wide or narrow; the *fruit* is either rounder or ending in a long pointed appendage: and its color, which is commonly green or black at the start, is saffron-yellow or ruddy-red at maturity: and finally the flower, which is commonly white, is either larger or smaller; either whitish or tinged with a deep redness.

It is cultivated most diligently throughout all of Castile, both by gardeners and by women in the hanging gardens of their houses. We also had it in the garden of His Serene Highness at Montbéliard.

<column-break/>

### A VARIETY OF CAPSICUM PEPPER, WITH SMALL pods, and leaves and flowers of Garden Nightshade.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller variety of pepper plant with small, upright fruits and leaves resembling those of nightshade.</image-desc>

This grows abundantly in Brazil and is in manifold use, for which reason it is called *Brazilian*.

Furthermore, Capsicum Pepper powerfully heats and dries: it partakes of heat and dryness in the third degree, according to Dodoens, or in the fourth, according to Monardes. It has the same faculties as common Pepper: differing from it only in this, according to the testimony of the same Monardes, that the former is bought for many gold pieces, while this is acquired solely by sowing. But it tints the foods with which it is mixed a saffron color, and its too frequent use is harmful, because it is secretly endowed with a certain malignant power which kills dogs if they eat it: just as Avicenna once attributed the same power to his *Z. Z.* <note>Zingiber</note> *caninum*, which some among the more recent authors believe to be the same as this Pepper.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXIII.
### IN WHICH ARE CONTAINED THE SOFTENING AND MOSTLY POT-HERB PLANTS.

**MALLOW: German: *Papelen* <note>Modern German: Pappel</note>: French: *Mauve*: Italian: *Malua*: Spanish: *Malvas*. Common Mallow.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Malva plant showing its root system, broad lobed leaves, and several flowers on upright stems.</image-desc>

Many plants are held under the title of "Mallow" among Botanists. There are various species of *Althea* <note>Marsh-mallow</note> and *Alcea* <note>Hollyhock or Rose-mallow</note>: *Petasites* <note>Butterbur</note>, which some call *Horse Mallow*: *Mallow-leaved Geranium*: and *Anagyris* <note>Bean-trefoil</note>, called by some *Ground Mallow*. But of these we do not speak here; they are treated in their own place. However, the *Mallow* whose history we hand down here is that of which Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> writes. It consists of an annual stalk, only the rib of which is eaten, and it constantly turns around with the Sun. And hence the line of Lucius Columella <note>Roman writer on agriculture</note>:
> The Mallow, which follows the Sun with its head first.

For it is well enough known that the leaves of Mallows—which is to be understood especially of the smaller ones—by a prodigious miracle of Nature, follow the path of the Sun, and are bent with it toward the West.

<column-break/>

**ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COMMON MALLOW.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Malva vulgaris, showing a more slender stem and detailed leaf structure.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> makes one Mallow *Cultivated* and another *Wild*, but, because they are so well known, he describes neither. Thus Galen <note>Prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> also mentions the *Cultivated* and *Wild*. Pliny recognizes two kinds of *Cultivated*, and just as many of the *Wild*: he says the former is called *Malope* by the Greeks, and the latter *Malache*.

More recent authors reckon many differences. For they make one Mallow *Garden* or *Cultivated*, and another *Wild*, which grows not in the woods, but in uncultivated places and paths, and which is the *Common* variety, which is dealt with here. Again, various species of this *Wild Mallow* are observed, differing from one another in size, leaves, and flowers. For some produce red "roses" <note>The author uses "roses" metaphorically for the blossoms</note>, others white, others whitening into purple: and these again are either larger or smaller, consisting of a single or multiple texture of petals. Furthermore, some leaves of the Mallow are lobed, others round, and some curled. And finally, among the Mallows, some rise up higher, and some are dwarf-like and lie upon the ground.

---

### STARRED MALLOW.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Malva Stellata, characterized by deeply lobed, star-like leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The stalks of this beautiful species of Mallow are thin, a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, and branched: the first leaves on the tender plant are small, round, and saw-toothed on long stalks, but when it has grown enough, they are quite large and divided into three parts. The flower is large, purple, and striped, consisting of five heart-shaped petals: in the middle of which is a white pistil composed of many tips, and in it are three points expressing a star in a certain way. The rest is as in the Common variety.

Master Friedrich Meier had this in his garden at Strasbourg.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER BEAUTIFUL WILD MALLOW
#### species, with a crescent-shaped flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Mallow species with rounded leaves and flowers showing distinct petal markings.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> depicts this Mallow thus, painting those crescent-shaped flowers with purple "claws" <note>the base of the petal</note>. Here, however, we shall treat the origins of the common Mallow.

It comes out in uncultivated and neglected places, yet in fertile soil, not sterile, near roads, garden fences, the edges of fields, and in somewhat damp places. It is delighted by a rich and moist place, and enjoys the borders of gardens.

It brings forth flowers from the month of June well into Summer.

Concerning its powers, see the following sections. We will only add here that it is peculiar to the Mallow that, when applied to the stings of Wasps and Bees, it eases the pains: and it makes the soil in <unclear>which</unclear> it is planted richer.

<summary>This page describes the Common Mallow and its varieties, noting its heliotropic behavior (turning toward the sun) and its preference for fertile, damp soil. It cites classical authorities like Theophrastus and Pliny while providing specific botanical descriptions of the "Starred Mallow" and wild varieties.</summary>
<keywords>Mallow, Malva, botany, heliotropism, medicinal herbs, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, Pliny, Clusius, Strasbourg gardens</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Mallow family, following previous entries on common mallows. It focuses on ornamental and exotic varieties like the Hollyhock and Tree Mallow.</meta>

# ROSE MALLOW, OR GARDEN MALLOW: German: *Garten Papein*; French: *Maulue de iardin*; Italian: *Malua maggiore*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a tall Malva Rosea (Hollyhock) with large, lobed leaves and several large, open flowers blooming along a central stalk.</image-desc>

If this plant provided as sweet a scent to the nostrils as the Rose does, there is no doubt it could compete with Roses themselves in excellence and beauty. Furthermore, it reaches the height of an elm tree <note>The author likely refers to the height of a young elm or a very tall shrub, as Hollyhocks can reach 8-10 feet</note>, with a thick, solid, hairy, and straight stalk, only rarely branching into a few arms. The leaves arise individually from the stem on long, downy stalks in an alternating pattern; they are broad, lightly indented into nearly five divisions, notched around the edges, dark green above, whiter underneath, and hairy on both sides. From the armpits of the leaves <note>The leaf axils</note>, several flowers burst forth in succession, possessing the size and color of a Rose—that is, red, or scarlet, or deep blood-red, or flesh-colored, or white. These are sometimes simple, and sometimes luxuriant with a multiple "offspring" of petals <note>double-flowered varieties</note>, with a cone possessing yellow tips occupying the center.

# CURLED OR FRINGED MALLOW, with pale purple flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Malva Crispa, featuring distinctive curled or "crisped" edges on the leaves and smaller flowers clustered at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

This plant obtained the name "Curled" because the leaves are not only fringed but also curled along the edges with frequent bends and folds.

It is cultivated in gardens, as we had at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>S. P. likely refers to Serenissimi Principis</note>, flowering in June and July.

Furthermore, every Mallow is moderately warm, and because of both its moisture and its stickiness, it easily softens the bowels. For this reason, the Ancients were even accustomed to eat Mallow in the manner of other pot-herbs for the sake of loosening the belly, whence Martial says:

> The farm-wife brought me Mallows 
> to unburden my stomach, etc. And:
> Eat lettuces and use soft mallows:
> For you have the face of a constipated Phoebus. <note>original: "faciam durum Phoebe cacantis habes" - a crude Roman joke about the strained expression of someone who is constipated</note>

# ALCEA, BISMALVA: German: *Sigmars-kraut*; French: *Guimauue*; Italian: *Bismalua*, *Malua Syluatica*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Alcha (Bismalva) showing a branched stem with smaller, more deeply lobed leaves and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

The COMMON ALCEA <note>Hollyhock Mallow or Musk Mallow</note>, which some call "pinguinus," has stalks up to a cubit high, hairy, rough, and stuffed with a spongy pith. The leaves are like those of the common Mallow but more upright and larger, usually divided all the way to the stalk into three, five, or six segments, dark green and hairy. From their armpits, beautiful red flowers—of a purplish flesh color—hang from four-angled hairy stalks; these are composed of five striped petals, the center of which is occupied by a small cluster of white tips. The gathered seeds mimic the shape of a compressed little cheese <note>A common historical description of mallow seed pods, often called "cheeses"</note>, just like the common Mallow. The root is as long as a finger.

Some call it Wild Mallow, Hungarian Mallow, Hungarian Herb, and the Herb of Simeon; Anguillara calls it Wild Hemp-Mallow; but almost everyone calls it Alcea.

<column-break/>

# ROSE MALLOW, OR GARDEN MALLOW, another Illustration.

<image-desc>A second botanical woodcut of a Malva Rosea, showing a single tall stalk with large flowers and a thick root system.</note>

To proceed with the description of this Mallow: the flowers sit upon a double calyx <note>the green outer casing of the bud</note> which is covered in white downy hair and leaves the seed behind it. The root is long, white, and yields a sticky slime. A species of this is also found with a broad leaf like a *Fig*, deeply fringed.

By Cordus it is called the Little Garden Mallow—rare to the sight and almost unknown—and the Roman Mallow. By some, it is called the Noble Rose, the Foreign Mallow, the Tree Mallow, the Venetian Mallow, the Mallow of Theophrastus and Dioscorides; the Overseas Rose, the Autumn Rose, the Vintage Rose, and the Winter Rose.

We have seen it in gardens at Padua, Bologna, and Lyon, and we ourselves have had it at Geneva and Montbéliard, both the simple and the double-flowered varieties. It flowered, moreover, in June and July, and even into Autumn.

# TREE MALLOW: DENDROMALACHE, a type of Indian Mallow.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Malva Arborea, showing a thick woody stem and large, rounded, lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It grows with a thick, woody stalk, four or five cubits high, and is perennial. The leaves are very large, curved in the manner of the Creeping Mallow, but with the downy softness of the Marshmallow. The flowers along the stalk are mallow-like and small.

Rauwolff writes that he saw a Tree Mallow of such great height in Aleppo that the inhabitants would quite often walk under its pleasant shade. We have seen beautiful ones in gardens at Montpellier and Basel, and especially at Esslingen.

Clusius suspects that the type of Mallow we depict here is "Indian" (*Exotica*, Book 2, chapter 15). We shall add one thing further concerning the Mallow: namely, that it is useful for so many things that it was not undeservedly called "All-Disease-Healer" <note>original: "Omnimorbia"</note> by the Ancients.

# SMOOTH TREE ALCEA, called HERMIA or Ketmia, with large white flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Alcea Arborescens, featuring a woody stem and large, pale flowers with prominent stamens.</image-desc>

Among the species and differences of Alcea which we shall now review is this exotic plant which some of the more refined gardens possess, and which Robin, the Royal Gardener, once showed to us in Paris.

To Clusius, it is a *rare and elegant shrubby type of Marshmallow*; to Camerarius, it is the *Tree Alcea* and *Syrian Alcea*. To Imperato, it is a *Shrubby species of Marshmallow, called Ketmia, which is cultivated in Syria for the delight of the eyes*. However, the common Alcea, which was discussed a little earlier, grows in various places in uncultivated fields, the edges of lands and ditches, and next to roads, hedges, and paths; we have observed it in abundance at Montpellier, Geneva, and also Montbéliard.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Mallow family, including the Hollyhock and Tree Mallow, noting their physical characteristics, medicinal uses as laxatives, and their presence in famous European botanical gardens.</summary>
<keywords>Hollyhock, Mallow, medicinal herbs, laxatives, botanical gardens, Leonhard Rauwolff, Carolus Clusius, botany, Renaissance medicine</keywords>

### HEMP-LEAVED MALLOW : WILD CANNABIS
<note>original: "ALCEA CANNABINA : CANNABIS SYLVESTRIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alcea cannabina, showing a tall plant with serrated, palmately divided leaves resembling hemp, and several flowers along the stems.</image-desc>

It reaches the height of a man, with rough, round stalks divided into many branches. The leaves are quite similar to Hemp <note>Cannabis</note>, but less rough. The flowers appear singly or in pairs, similar to the common Mallow. The seeds are like those of the Curled Mallow. The root is perennial, white both outside and inside.

Camerarius and Caspar Bauhin <note>famous 16th-century botanists</note> record this as the "Wild Cannabis" of Dioscorides; others call it the "Five-leaved Hemp Mallow." It was grown for us in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard; it bloomed in July and the seed ripened in August.

### HAIRY MALLOW, WITH PURPLISH FLOWERS.
<note>original: "ALCEA VILLOSA, FLORE PVRPVRASCENTE."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alcea villosa, depicting a plant with hairy stems and deeply lobed, serrated leaves, with multiple flowers blooming at the top.</image-desc>

The name "Hairy Mallow" was given to this plant because of the dense, somewhat stiff and rough hairiness with which the entire plant bristles. Many branches, a palm or nine inches long, smooth and hairy, arise immediately from a simple, slender root of a palm's length. The leaves are small, mostly cut into deep serrated segments, and downy. The purplish flowers are composed of five petals, followed by a circular "cake" of blackish seeds.

It is common in vineyards around Montpellier, especially in drier spots and on desolate hills.

### FOREIGN SUN-FOLLOWING MALLOW, called by some the Venetian Mallow.
<note>original: "ALCEA PEREGRINA SOLISEQVA, ALCEA Veneta"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alcea peregrina solisequa, showing a plant with trilobed leaves and flowers that appear to follow the sun.</image-desc>

In its root, stalks, leaves, and almost all other parts, it resembles the common Mallow; but the leaves are more hairy, and the flowers are a greenish-yellow, and more pleasing than the common Mallow due to their foreign elegance.

Some call it the "Bologna Mallow," many the "Venetian," others the "Italian." However, the *Adversaria* <note>a botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> rightly wonders at this, since it is found nowhere in Italy, let alone Venice, except in gardens. They preferred to name it the "Foreign Sun-following Mallow." Dodonaeus and C. Bauhin call it the "Bladder Mallow"; Matthiolus calls it *Hypecoum*, but erroneously. There are those who call it in French *La gloire du monde* <note>The glory of the world</note>, and in German *Latternblum* <note>Lantern flower</note>.

It grows for us every year in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard; however, our illustration from <unclear>purchased sources</unclear> is not satisfactory.

<column-break/>

### FINE-LEAVED CURLED MALLOW.
<note>original: "ALCEA TENVIFOLIA CRISPA."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alcea tenuifolia crispa, featuring a plant with highly divided, curly (crisped) foliage and small flowers.</image-desc>

It differs from the common Mallow only in this: that it has a leaf very finely divided into numerous thin, curled segments; in other respects, it does not differ much from it. It is perhaps merely a freak of nature.

Lonicer calls it "Oak Mallow" and "Lion's Tooth"; Rysso in his commentary on Dioscorides calls it "The other Mallow, fringed with deeper segments." Camerarius in his garden catalog calls it "Fine-leaved Mallow, with a curled leaf."

It is frequent in the Black Forest <note>Hercynia sylua</note> and near the Rhine. We have also seen it near Saint-Cosme in the Sundgau.

### BROAD-LEAVED MALLOW, DEEPLY fringed, smooth; with a purplish flower.
<note>original: "ALCEA AMPLISSIMO FOLIO PROFVNDÈ laciniato..."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved Alcea, showing large, deeply lobed, smooth leaves and a prominent flower with a dark center.</image-desc>

Since it could not be done before, we will here review the medicinal powers of the Mallow. Galen omitted it in his list of simple medicines; but Paul <note>of Aegina</note> and Dioscorides write that, drunk with wine, it heals dysentery and internal erosions, and the root even more so when taken with honey-water. Pliny also offers it in wine or water for ruptures, convulsions, dysentery, and diarrhea; and Tragus confirms this as well. It is celebrated by empirical practitioners for dimness of sight; and there are those who believe that the root of the Mallow, hung from the neck, sharpens the eyesight beyond measure and protects it. It is drying and moderately warm, and as is easy to gather from the sticky sliminess of the leaves and root, it is rightly placed among the <term>emplastic</term> <note>medicines that are sticky or adhesive, used in plasters</note> medicines.

### PERHAPS A KIND OF INDIAN MALLOW according to Clusius.
<note>original: "ALCEÆ MALVÆVE INDICÆ FORTE genus Clusij."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an "Indian" Alcea or Mallow, showing a sturdy plant with large, palmate leaves and a prominent, bristly seed pod or flower head.</image-desc>

Clusius writes in his *Exotics*, book 2, chapter 15, that this fruit was brought by the Dutch from a voyage to Java; he illustrates and describes it, presenting it perhaps as some kind of Mallow or Alcea. The experts shall judge.

<keywords>Alcea, Mallow, Cannabis sylvestris, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Clusius, Montbéliard, botany, dysentery, eye health</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### MARSHMALLOW OR BISMALVA: German: Ibisch,
### Healing-root: French: Guimauve: Italian: Malvavisco.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Althaea plant (marshmallow), showing its upright stem, lobed leaves, and flowers, including a detailed view of the root system.</image-desc>

By Galen it is called *Didrema lache* and *Anadendromalache* <note>original: "ἀναδενδρομαλάχη"</note>, the tree-like or arborescent Mallow. By Palladius it is called *Ibiscum*, *Ebiscum*, and *Eviscum*, and by some *Malvaviscum*, a name composed from Mallow and Hibiscus. By more recent authors, however, it is called *Althæa*, *Bismalva*, Spanish Mallow, and Wild Mallow.

The leaf of the Hibiscus is like that of the Mallow, says Theophrastus, but larger and more hairy: with soft stalks having the taste of Mallow: a honey-colored flower: the fruit of a Mallow: and a white, fibrous root. Dioscorides writes that the leaves of the Althæa are like those of the Cyclamen, round and turning white with downy hair, with a rose-colored flower, a stalk two cubits high <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; thus about 3 feet tall.</note>, and a tough root that is white inside. Pliny writes thus: Of the wild Mallows, he says, that which has a large leaf and white roots is called *Althæa*. We depict the Common variety here.

### MARSHMALLOW WITH THE LARGE FLOWER OF THE HOLLYHOCK: Perhaps
### that of Camerarius of Thuringia? Or Clusius's 2nd Pannonian?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-flowered Althaea, showing broad leaves and large blossoms, with a separate detail of the thick, woody root section.</image-desc>

Regarding the powers and temperament of the Marshmallow: among all the mallow-like genera, the Hibiscus possesses remarkable faculties for curing diseases, and whatever is said of the Mallow should be understood as being twice as potent in the Marshmallow: for which reason they even wish it to be called *Bismalva* <note>Literally "Twice-Mallow".</note>. Its temperament is hot and dry.

The root, decocted in wine or honey-water and drunk, heals any internal faults of the chest and lungs, erosions of the intestines, etc.; and, to say much in few words, it is beneficial to the entire body.

The same root, boiled in milk or water until it turns into a pulp and applied as a plaster, softens and matures <note>Refers to "ripening" an abscess or swelling to a head.</note>: boiled in vinegar and held in the mouth, it helps with toothache. The leaves, when smeared on, thoroughly heal the stings of wasps.

### A SPECIES OF MARSHMALLOW, BY SOME CALLED TREE-LIKE
### or another with a Bryony leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a species of Althaea with leaves resembling Bryony, showing a climbing or sprawling habit with distinct leaf shapes.</image-desc>

This grew for us in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard, and it grew to the height of a man, with a stalk shining with greenness: the branches appearing as if sprinkled: and some of the upper leaves being whiter underneath, some somewhat long, without lobes.

Is this the *Tree-like Marshmallow* of Camerarius's garden, or rather a shrubby perennial plant, different from the Spanish one of Clusius, etc.? By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Althæa 6, or shrubby, with Bryony leaves, perennial*.

<column-break/>

### MARSHMALLOW WITH DEEPLY SERRATED, OR
### TOOTHED, LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Althaea with deeply serrated or toothed leaves, showing the characteristic jagged edges of the foliage.</image-desc>

The leaf is soft, hairy, imitating the Common variety, yet beautifully divided, deeply and finely serrated: with a rather large, reddish flower, the central stalk <note>The stamen column characteristic of mallows.</note> adorned with purple or blackish tips.

The Common Marshmallow grows naturally in marshy and rich places, in damp and swampy meadows, as well as in ditches: and it flowers in the months of July and August. We have seen it growing wild at Montpellier near the sea; but at Basel, Geneva, and Montbéliard, we have cultivated it ourselves in gardens.

Furthermore, it is called *Bismalva*, or *Vismalva*, as if it were a "viscous mallow": and *Althæa* from the word <term>althainein</term> <note>original: "ἀλθαίνειν"</note>, which means to heal, because it is powerful with many strengths and remedies for healing, which is why that name was given to it by Physicians.

### TREE-LIKE MARSHMALLOW.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tree-like Althaea (Hibiscus syriacus type), showing a woody stem and distinct trilobed leaves.</image-desc>

It grows to the height of a small tree, with woody, firm trunks covered in a downy bark: the leaves are the size of the smaller Mallows, sometimes gently lobed, other times, in the manner of the Marshmallow, cut into oblong segments, whitish, woolly, mixed with a sufficiently long, shaggy stem: the purplish flowers are equal to the flowers of the common Mallow: and the seeds are also similar.

Lobelius writes that in certain places with a more fertile climate (such as in the maritime parts of Provence near Hyères), it grows with such rare abundance that it suffices for constructing hedges. It is usually cultivated in gardens, as we have seen in various places; Paris, Basel, Pforzheim, etc.

### MARSHMALLOW CALLED SIDA BY SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sida variety of Althaea, showing a smaller plant with more delicate leaves and a prominent root marked with an 'X'.</image-desc>

It has the root of a garden Mallow: a stalk of two cubits: flowers like the Rose Mallow, of a deep purple: leaves like the Abutilon, which we will discuss soon.

By Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria* and *Observations*, it is labeled *Marsh Althæa with a Cytinus flower*: and a plant closer to the *Sida* of Theophrastus: but Dodoens wishes the *Sida* of Theophrastus to be referred to the Water-lilies: let the learned judge. However, both Lobelius and Tabernaemontanus depict the one they call Marsh Althæa poorly in their Illustrations and Histories.

It grew for us in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard.

The author notes personal cultivation of these plants in various European botanical gardens, including Montbéliard.</summary>

### THEOPHRASTUS’S MALLOW WITH YELLOW FLOWERS,
->called by some Abutilon.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with heart-shaped, serrated leaves and small flowers, identified as Althaea Theophrasti.</image-desc>

This is a foreign plant, not seen anywhere except in gardens. We have kept it in our own gardens at Geneva and Montbéliard. It blooms toward the end of Summer.

By the consensus of many learned men, it is concluded to be the *Althaea* of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek successor to Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany."</note> and the *Abutilon* of Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980 – 1037) was a Persian polymath whose medical texts were standard in Europe for centuries.</note>. Only the *History of Plants of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugd." referring to the Historia Generalis Plantarum (1586).</note> considers it to be neither Theophrastus’s mallow nor Avicenna’s abutilon, though it refutes the opinion of others with no reasoning.

Lobelius, in his *Images of Plants*, labels it "mallow with yellow flowers." But in his *Observations*, he asks whether the mallow with yellow flowers might be the *Ibiscus* of Theophrastus and the *Abutilon* of Avicenna. Matthiolus freely confesses that he has never seen the mallow with the yellow flower, and yet he provides a drawing of it.

---

### BAMIA, THE BELMUSCUS OF HONORIUS BELLI: Bamia of Great Cairo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Bamia (Okra) plant, showing large lobed leaves and long, pointed seed pods (fruit).</image-desc>

It has leaves very closely resembling the leaves of the Hollyhock <note>original: "Maluae roseae"</note>: from the "armpits" <note>axils</note> of which yellow flowers burst forth. These are followed by a seed pod, standing upright along the stem, nearly three inches in length, tapering to a point like a top, covered with bristly hairs, and five-sided. Inside, between the dividing walls, grow as many rows of seeds, which are similar to Bitter Vetch <note>original: "Orobo"</note>.

This elegant exotic plant is cultivated in gardens and in hanging jars. Its seeds are used for food among the Egyptians, just as Peas, Kidney Beans, and other Legumes are used among us. The leaves, applied as a warm compress or a plaster, resolve inflammations, soothe pains, soften tumors, and bring them to suppuration <note>the process of forming pus to heal an infection</note>.

The *Belmuseus* of these same Egyptians, which tastes of Musk, very much rivals the Bamia.

---

### BEET: German: Mangolt: French: Bete, Reparée: Italian: Bietola.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Beta (Beet) plant with large, broad leaves and a thick taproot.</image-desc>

The vegetable which the Greeks call *teutlon* or *seutlon*, and the Arabs *Becka* and *Celb*, is the *Beta* to the Latins. It took this name for itself because it seems to represent the shape of the Greek letter $\beta$ (Beta) when it is swollen with seed, as it has a top that is bent back at the summit. This is elegantly expressed in the poem of Lucius Columella:

> Then by a Greek name, as the letter next to the first,
> It is planted, etc. <note>original: "Nomine tum Graio, ceu litera proxima primæ..." referring to the letter Beta being second after Alpha.</note>

Various differences of Beets are handed down, taken from various locations. Thus, in Pliny, one is called *Spring* and another *Autumnal* based on the time of sowing; based on its birthplace, one is cultivated, another wild, another Sicilian, another Cretan, etc. Based on color, one is white, another red, and another yellowish. We illustrate the white Beet here.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN ABUTILON.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Abutilon Indicum plant, featuring broad, cordate leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

Camerarius writes that the Indian Abutilon could be referred to the Mallows. The flower is pale or somewhat yellowish, resting on a slightly hairy stalk, as are the young leaves and the stem, which turns reddish near the joints. The flower is followed by a blackish little pod arranged in a star shape, also containing black seed. The outer casing, however, turns from green to yellow. The root is pale and fibrous. Dr. Doldius described it as it once appeared to us.

---

### SABDARIFFA, RELATED TO THE BAMIA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sabdariffa plant, showing deeply lobed, palmate leaves.</image-desc>

This exotic plant is also referred to the Mallow family. Rauwolf, who describes it and records that it is called *Lubee Endigi* (that is, Indian Kidney Bean) by the Arabs, thinks it is the *Trionum* of Theophrastus. He labels it with that same name among his illustrations, as does the *History of Lyon* in its Appendix. But, in our judgment, this plant was unknown to the Ancients.

Lobelius, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, the same *History of Lyon*, and others have called it *Sabdariffa*. C. Bauhin calls it *Indian Alcea* in his *Phytopinax*.

We have seen it in the more cultivated gardens of Basel and Strasbourg; and we ourselves had it in the princely garden at Montbéliard, blooming in September and October.

---

### RED BEET, CALLED THE BLACK BEET: German: Rott Mangolt: French: Bete ou Reparée rouge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dark-leaved beet variety (Beta Rubra) with a prominent root system.</image-desc>

To the differences of the Beet already related, Pliny adds one more based on its effect: "A marvelous difference," he says, "the white ones loosen the bowels, the Black ones stop them."

The Beet which they call "White," based on the evidence of the root and leaves, has a woody root the thickness of a little finger, moderately long, and white. The leaves are a paler green, like Dock <note>original: "Lapathi"</note>, thick and succulent, with a salty taste. The stem is two or three cubits high, slender, striped, and hollow at many "wings" <note>axils</note>. The flowers are silent <note>inconspicuous</note>, small, star-shaped, consisting of five leaves. The seed is round, brown, and rough with a curled surface.

The "Black" one, which we illustrate here, is very similar to it, yet the leaves are shorter and reddish or dark green.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### RED, YELLOW, AND RUSSET BEET: BEET-TURNIP: Red Turnip: Thick-rooted Beet.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a beet plant with large, broad leaves and a thick, tapering root system.</image-desc>

There is, furthermore, a certain Beet called "Red," which likewise has shorter and dark-green leaves: but which, besides the distinction of the leaves, is also recognized by another feature in the root: it is bellied <note>swollen or bulbous</note>, like a Navew <note>a type of rapeseed or French turnip</note>, and is stained inside and out with a deep blood-red color. Consequently, it has a twin nature of both a Pot-herb and a Bulb. Brunfels, Tragus, Lobelius, Camerarius, and others title it *Red Beet*, *The Commoner Red Beet*, and *Thick-rooted Red Beet*: Schwenkfeld calls it *Red Turnip*: Cornarius in his commentary on Dioscorides calls it *Cultivated Red Turnip*. However, the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586</note> rightly concludes that it is not a Turnip. We truly believe it to be the one that Mattioli calls *Russet*.

There is also found a *Yellow* variety, differing from the aforementioned only by its boxwood-colored root. This is called *Lutea* <note>Yellow</note> by Camerarius and *Flava* <note>Golden</note> by Gesner.

### GOOD HENRY, ALL-GOOD: German: Guter Heinrich: French: Toute Bonne: To the Italians: Herba infarinata <note>Floured herb</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Good King Henry plant (Blitum bonus-henricus), showing upright stems, triangular leaves, and spiked flower clusters.</image-desc>

This plant is called *Tota bona* <note>All-good</note> on account of its remarkable virtues: and for the same reason it is called *Bonus Henricus* <note>Good Henry</note>, just as, conversely, they call a certain destructive plant *Malus Henricus* <note>Bad Henry</note>.

It rests upon a thick root like that of Sharp-dock <note>Oxylapathum</note>: the stalks are many, thin, striated, and partly erect, partly trailing: the leaves are triangular, like those of Orach, dark green, and sprinkled with a fine meal <note>referring to the powdery texture on the leaves</note>: the little flowers are mossy and herbaceous in a cluster: the seed is round, somewhat similar to Radish seed.

It grows spontaneously in courtyards, dung-heaps, and at the edges of fields; it flowers in September and October. Truly, we have observed it nowhere more abundant or more beautiful than in the courtyard and near the house of those noblemen, the Lords Chabraeus, Chief Consuls of Geneva, at Tempe, which is situated in the Village of Genthod by the Lake <note>Lake Geneva</note>. *Regarding its powers, see the Appendix.*

### SPINACH, OR SPINACIA: German: Spinet, or Binetsch: French: Espinars: Italian: Spinacei.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spinach plant with pointed, lobed leaves and a fibrous root.</image-desc>

Spinach takes its name from the notable mark of the spikes on its seeds <note>Latin: "spina" meaning thorn/spine</note>, or from the Moorish word *Hispanach*, which denotes a Spanish vegetable, because it was first brought from Spain. Certainly, and strangely, the Ancients handed down nothing concerning it: nor is it very easy to examine the causes of their silence in this matter.

However, in the judgment of Constantinus and Mattioli, Amatus, Caesalpinus, and others are greatly hallucinating <note>mistaken</note> when they contend that it is a domestic Dock. Those who think it is Pliny's *Boulepathum* are also deceived, as are those who believe that Orach and Spinach are of the same genus. Some have named it *Seutlomalachen*, that is, "Mallow-Beet": but they would have done better to call it *Seutlo-Lapathum* <note>Beet-Dock</note>: since it seems to be of a nature midway between a Beet and a Dock.

<column-break/>

### CRETAN BEET WITH PRICKLY SEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cretan beet variety with elongated leaves and visible seed pods along the stem.</image-desc>

This seems to be referred to the Docks or to Spinach: although it is handed down by almost everyone under the name of Beet. We have observed it in several gardens.

Otherwise, Beets of every kind are sown everywhere in gardens today: and nothing is more frequent in kitchens than the common Beet.

It consists, however, of contrary properties: for the juice, which is hot and nitrous, cleanses, provokes the belly to flow <note>acts as a laxative</note>, twinges the stomach, opens obstructions of the liver and spleen, and, when applied to the nostrils, excites sneezing. But the body of the plant consists of thick parts; it is flatulent, difficult to digest, provides little nourishment and is cold, and it binds the belly <note>causes constipation</note>: and therefore it is served only at the tables of rustics and the poor. *More in the Appendix.*

### PLINY’S SYMPHONIA: German: Widerschein, Papageyfedern <note>Reflection, Parrot-feathers</note>: French: Jalousie: To the Italians: Herba de la maraviglia <note>Wonder-herb</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Amaranthus (Joseph's Coat), showing its characteristic long, pointed leaves and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

It has a short, white, forked root: a single stem, a foot long, reddish: leaves like those of Blite, painted alternately with green, rose, and yellow colors, so that in individual mature and perfect leaves, it resembles the feathers of Parrots—a most pleasant sight. It bears seed in a small shaggy spike adhering to the stem without a stalk, marked with hairs like those of Buttercups: and this takes the place of a flower, just as if nature had first bestowed so much beauty and grace upon the leaves that afterwards, as if forgetting the painting of the flowers, she left them scarcely begun.

Is it Gesner’s *Spotted Blite*? Or Lobelius’s *Three-colored Amaranth*? Ruellius calls it *Gelosia*; some call it *Gomphrena* or *Cremphena*.

It is cultivated in gardens for use in salads and for the delight of the eyes. It is, moreover, a nourishing plant.

### SPINACH WITH NON-PRICKLY SEED: with a larger and rounder leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smooth-seeded spinach variety with broader, more rounded leaves.</image-desc>

The distinction observed in the seeds and leaves of Spinach is manifest both from this Image and from its title. But we find in several writers that Spinach is further distinguished by sex and location. Thus Scaliger calls that one *Male* whose seed is prickly, and *Female* that whose seed is without prickles. And so also in Camerarius and the *History of Lyon*, two kinds of Spinach are established, *Cultivated* and *Wild*: and of the cultivated again two, *Male* and *Female*—the Male which bears seed, and the Female which, being unfruitful of seed, remains sterile <note>Note: This reflects early botanical misunderstandings of plant reproduction</note>.

It is sown everywhere in gardens in March and September, and it comes up seven days after sowing, rejecting no soil.

It belongs to the first class of cooling and moistening things, and nothing is more frequent than it in broths. When eaten, it softens the bowels, increases milk, etc.

->IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-
<sig>Qq</sig>

<margin>ORACHE: German: *Melten*, *Milten*; French: *Arrouches*, *Bonnes Dames*; Italian: *Atriplice*.</margin>
### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF GARDEN ORACHE, WHITE AND RED.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a garden orache (Atriplex hortensis) showing the root system, broad leaves, and flowering stalks.</image-desc>

Orache is commonly distinguished into the Cultivated and the Wild varieties. The Cultivated kind, which we depict here, is either white or red. It not infrequently reaches the height of a man. The white garden Orache has a stem that is rounded at the bottom and angular at the top. The leaves are like those of a Beet, but smaller, almost winged at the footstalk, somewhat wavy around the edges, and sprinkled with a thick mealiness <note>referring to the "dusty" or "mealy" texture characteristic of the genus Atriplex</note>; the color fades from green into yellow. The flowers are numerous, consisting of small yellow or grass-colored tips; these are followed by broad, leaf-like pods containing seed like that of Amaranth—black, small, shining, slippery, round, and compressed. The root is straight, about a palm's length, and fibrous.

The appearance of the red cultivated Orache is no different, except that it is entirely colored with a blood-red hue. More on this follows.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A second botanical woodcut of Atriplex hortensis, showing a slightly different growth habit with more pronounced seed clusters.</image-desc>

*We provide two figures because they were engraved from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany</note>. Otherwise, one well-painted image might suffice, since both Fuchs and others provide only a single description for garden Orache, whether white or black. Likewise, the "History of Lyon" <note>referring to the Historia Generalis Plantarum by Jacques Daléchamps</note>, which also includes the white and red varieties and no others, contains only a single illustration.*

Tragus mentions a reddish variety, one turning pale from yellow, and one turning black from yellow. Mattioli and Lonicer mention green, red, white, or pale yellow types. However, we conclude with Gesner, Dodoens, Pena and Lobel, Gerard, Caspar Bauhin, and almost all other learned men, that there are only two primary kinds of cultivated Orache: namely, the White and the Red.

---

<margin>WILD ORACHE: German: *Scheiss Melten*; French: *Arrouches sauvages*; Italian: *Reppice aluatico*.</margin>
### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF WILD ORACHE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of wild orache (Atriplex sylvestris) with narrower, more jagged leaves and elongated flower spikes.</image-desc>

Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen <note>The three primary authorities of ancient medicine and natural history</note> establish two main divisions of Orache in general: namely, the *Garden* and the *Wild*, or the *Cultivated* and the *Spontaneous*. We believe it cannot be better divided; for the third type (*Maritime* or Sea Orache) which Marantha adds, can be reduced to the Wild and Spontaneous category.

Regarding the garden Orache, which only grows when sown, we have dealt with it above; now we must speak of the Wild or spontaneous kind. Except for the fact that its leaves appear whiter, it corresponds so closely to the Garden variety in all characteristics that anyone who knows the latter will recognize the former with little effort.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A second woodcut of wild orache, showing the plant in a more mature state with dense seed racemes.</image-desc>

As with the garden variety, we have two figures of this Wild Orache from Fuchs, and following his example, we include both.

Spontaneous or Wild Orache occupies almost everywhere: roads, paths, ditches, the edges of fields, city walls, and dung heaps; it also grows in gardens. It flowers at the same time as the cultivated kind, namely in the months of July and August. The seed ripens in September.

There are those who derive the name *Atriplex* from its dark color <note>original: "ab atro colore"</note>. However, the Greeks wish it to be called *atraphaxis*, because it "breaks through" <note>original: "atrax nyxei"</note>, for it leaps forth from the sowing on the eighth day, and is immediately seen to advance in growth. Dioscorides called it *Chrysolachanon*, that is, *Golden Herb*, because it represents the color of gold.

---

### SMALLER NARROW-LEAVED LACINIATE WILD ORACHE.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a smaller, narrow-leaved variety of wild orache.</image-desc>

We now pass to the various differences of Wild Orache. Regarding the *Powers of Orache*, Dioscorides records the following: "Cooked," he says, "it is eaten as a vegetable and softens the belly; it disperses swellings <note>original: "Panos"</note> whether applied raw or cooked. The seed drunk with honeyed water cures the royal disease <note>Jaundice</note>." Galen also authorizes its use as a vegetable, and almost everyone asserts it was born for the kitchen rather than for medicine. Yet it has its praises in medicine: for, as Galen himself testifies, it is cold in the first degree and moist in the second; it is rightly numbered among the emollient herbs, and most easily and effectively moves the bowels. It is devoid of any strong quality, being dull and tasteless, smelling of a watery and marshy nature. However, the garden variety is colder and moister than the wild.

<column-break/>

### WILD ORACHE WITH ENTIRE LEAVES, CLUSTERED.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a wild orache variety with entire (non-jagged) leaves and clustered flowers.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various places in the Sundgau <note>A region in Alsace</note>, around dung heaps.

To the virtues of Orache, we shall add something regarding *its harms*: Pliny writes that it was accused by Pythagoras of causing dropsy, jaundice, and paleness, and of being very difficult to digest. He even reports that nothing grows near it in gardens except what is sickly. Likewise, Dionysius and Diocles wrote that many diseases are birthed from it, that it is inconvenient for the stomach, and should not be cooked unless the water is changed frequently.

<summary>This page describes the botanical characteristics, nomenclature, and medicinal properties of Garden and Wild Orache (Atriplex), citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Galen alongside Renaissance botanists like Fuchs.</summary>
<keywords>Orache, Atriplex hortensis, Atriplex sylvestris, botanical illustration, Leonhart Fuchs, Dioscorides, Galen, medicinal herbs, jaundice, emollient, Sundgau</keywords>

### COMMON NARROW-LEAFED ORACHE, with seed pods.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender plant with narrow leaves and clusters of seed pods along the upper stems.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are quite dark green, almost appearing black, and closely resemble the leaves of Knotgrass <note>original: "Polygoni"</note>, though they are broader, pointed, and sometimes very slightly lobed. It grows to a height of one and a half to two feet <note>original: "cubitalem & sesquicubitalem," referring to the cubit, an ancient unit of length</note>. The flower and root are like those of the lobed Wild Orache. It bears pod-like seed vessels, often diamond-shaped and crowded together; when these open, they reveal the seeds, one in each pod, which are round and flattened.

<column-break/>

### Another Illustration of COMMON NARROW-LEAFED ORACHE with seed pods.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a similar narrow-leafed plant, showing a more branched structure and dense seed clusters.</image-desc>

While this Orache typically has oblong, narrow leaves that are not lobed, it is also sometimes found with leaves that have two "wings" at the base and are narrower, as depicted here.

It grows in vineyards and along the edges of fields.

---

<column-break/>

### MARITIME ORACHE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, spreading plant with thick, fleshy leaves and prominent roots.</image-desc>

It spreads numerous stems along the ground, about a foot and a half long, arising from a fairly thick root; these stems are entirely whitish. From them grow pale, lobed leaves, similar to the leaves of the Goose-foot plant. The small flowers are clustered in bunches, mostly at the ends of the branches, and resemble the flowers of Sea Purslane.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that it is found everywhere along the Mediterranean and Adriatic coasts, spread across the ground. Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Italian physician and botanist</note> notes it is frequent at Trieste near the salt works on the seashore.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER SPECIES OF MARITIME ORACHE by Valerand Dourez.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright maritime plant with broader, lobed leaves and spiked flower clusters.</image-desc>

Maritime Orache possesses the same medicinal power as the other Oraches; however, because of the saltiness with which it is filled, it moves the bowels more effectively and cleanses more thoroughly if given as a decoction in meat broth, according to *Matthiolus*. If indeed one trusts Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist</note>, it aids digestion, cuts through phlegm, thins the humors, dissolves blockages, protects against rot, opens the system, dries a moist bowel, assists those with dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, thins those who are overweight, and purges by scraping away waste.

---

<column-break/>

### ORACHE CALLED GOOSE-FOOT: German: *Ganss fuss, Sonn fuss*; French: *Pied d'Oye*; Italian: *Pede di Ocha*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust plant with broad, deeply lobed leaves resembling a goose's foot.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves like the Maritime Orache—large, jagged, and dark green—and possesses a scent that weighs heavy on the head. The small flowers are branchy and moss-like. The seed is tiny and round; the root is fibrous and becoming woody; the stem is somewhat thick, straight, and about a foot and a half tall.

It grows near old walls, roads, paths, and in other uncultivated, deserted, and somewhat damp places. It thrives and flowers along with the rest of the Oraches, as has been frequently observed by us in Lyon, Geneva, Montbéliard, and elsewhere.

However, it is considered clearly lethal and poisonous, especially if devoured by cattle, on the authority of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566)</note> and Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), known as Tragus</note>.

<column-break/>

### Another Illustration of the ORACHE called GOOSE-FOOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of the "Goose-foot" plant, showing more elongated leaf lobes.</image-desc>

In the *Illustrations* and *History* of Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590)</note>, it is called <term>Chenopodium</term> <note>from the Greek for "Goose-foot"</note> and the second type of Goose-foot. To Tragus, it is the fifth kind of Blite and Orache, just as the preceding one was his fourth. It differs very little from the aforementioned plant, except that it is more branched and has darker leaves.

It is found in old courtyards and ditches in villages.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Atriplex Foetida, showing a central stalk with broad, serrated leaves and small clusters of flowers/seeds at the leaf axils and apex.</image-desc>

### STINKING ORACH OR VULVARIA: Germ. *Schamkraut, Hunds Melten*: Gall. *Herbe de bouc* <note>French: "Goat herb"</note>.

Tragus writes that this is a faulty species of Orach rather than anything else; however, he and Lonicerus wrongly label it "Good Henry" <note>original: *Bonum Henricum*</note>. Caesalpinus called this little herb a relative of Dog’s Mercury. Tragus and others call it "Dog’s Orach" because they believe it grows from the urine of dogs. Some call it *Garosmon* <note>Greek: "Garum-smell"</note> because it smells like *Garum*, or fish sauce. Some call it "Stinking Blite." It is called *Canina* <note>Dog-like</note> and *Vulvaria* because it smells like the female parts: so say Caesalpinus, Lobelius, and the *History of Lyon*. Almost everyone calls it "Stinking, Foul, or Goat-like Orach" due to its foul odor.

It grows next to walls and in sandy places, especially those frequently sprinkled with the urine of dogs; it flowers in mid-summer. *We shall provide its powers and uses in the Appendix.*

---

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Ocimastrum Verrucarium, featuring a slender stem with opposite, pointed leaves and small, delicate flower clusters.</image-desc>

### WARTY BASTARD-BASIL, CIRCÆA to some: Parietaria III I. Rival Helxine.

From a thin, fibrous, dark root rises a single stem, round, slightly hairy, jointed, reddish-green, and shining. The leaves are opposite at the joints, like those of common Nightshade but sharper, dark green, and lightly wavy around the edges. The flowers in the clusters are quite pretty, four-petaled, flesh-colored, and enclosed in a two-holed sheath before they open. Small stamens of the same color occupy the center, set upon hairy little globes which later turn into small burrs; in each of these, sometimes one and sometimes two oblong seeds are enclosed.

It comes up frequently in the darker, marshy places of forests, as well as sometimes by streams and rotten tree trunks; it is found almost everywhere in the forest of Le Chesnoy at Montbéliard.

---

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Mercurialis Mas, showing a plant with upright stems, serrated lanceolate leaves, and small spiked inflorescences.</image-desc>

### MERCURY: Germ. *Bingel kraut*: Gall. *de la Mercuriale*: Ital. *Mercorella*. MALE MERCURY.

Because Mercury is believed to have discovered this, it obtained the name *Hermobotana* <note>Mercury's Herb</note> and *Hermopoa* among the Greeks, and *Mercurialis* among the Latins. The Greeks also called it *Linosostin*, and some *Parthenium*.

It is either Cultivated or Wild, and both are either Male or Female. We shall follow the commonly accepted or cultivated kind here; the Wild or Creeping kind, which is called *Cynocrambe* <note>Dog-cabbage</note>, we shall describe later.

Mercury is found in vegetable gardens, vineyards, and other damp and shaded places, along the fences of gardens and trees.

Furthermore, both types of Mercury, as Dioscorides dictates, move the bowels when eaten like a vegetable; but when boiled in water and the broth drunk, it draws out bile and water, purges phlegm, and its medicated juice is very useful for many things.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Parietaria, showing a tall plant with many lanceolate leaves and small flower clusters at the nodes.</image-desc>

### PELLITORY-OF-THE-WALL, HELXINE, PERDICARIA: Germ. *Maurkraut*: Gall. *Parietaire*: Ital. *Parietaria*.

Dioscorides describes it under the name *Helxine* thus: He says it bears thin and reddish stalks; leaves slightly hairy like Mercury; around the stems are small, rough seeds that stick to clothing. The flowers are grass-like, pale, and mossy.

Pliny confuses this *Helxine* of Dioscorides with his *Parthenium*. It is called *Helxine* by the Greeks because it sticks to passing clothes. They also call it *Perdicaria* or *Perdicium* because partridges <note>Latin: *Perdices*</note> are accustomed to eat it. To the Latins, it is *Parietaria* and *Muralis* <note>Wall-herb</note> from its place of birth. There are those who call it *Vitriaria* <note>Glass-herb</note> and *Urceolaria* <note>Pitcher-herb</note> because it is very suitable for scouring jars and glass vessels.

It is either Greater or Lesser, and both grow next to walls, partitions, in hedges and ruins, and on the walls themselves.

---

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Corchorus Theophrasti, showing a plant with serrated leaves and distinct elongated seed pods.</image-desc>

### CORCHORUS OF THEOPHRASTUS AND PLINY: and the Melochia of Serapion.

The stem of this is smooth and a cubit high; the leaves are almost like Dog’s Mercury or common Mercury, but larger, serrated around the edges, and have at the lowest part a small beard or outgrowth, like a little tongue. The pods hang on short stalks, single, 4 or 5 inches long, striated, gradually tapering to a point; they enclose many seeds, ash-colored, angular, small, and slimy to the taste. The flowers, according to Alpinus, are small, saffron-colored, and smaller than a Stock-gilliflower.

It grew for us in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard from seed sent from Basel, and it flowered at the beginning of September.

In its properties, it is clearly similar to Marshmallow; nothing is more familiar to the Egyptians in their food: for they cook it in water or meat broth, etc. *Alpinus. More in the Appendix.*

---

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Mercurialis Foemina, similar to the male variety but with distinct fruiting bodies at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

### FEMALE MERCURY.

Neither the root, nor the leaves, nor the flowers distinguish Male and Female Mercury. For both have a tender and fibrous root; an angular, smooth stem about a span high and jointed; and leaves approaching the leaves of Pellitory, but smooth, shining with a dark green color, and serrated on the edges. In the FEMALE, however, straight little tongues spring from the leaf axils, which clustered, mossy flowers surround in a whorl, as if in a spike; these, unfolding into four grass-like leaflets, display the fringes of yellowish or greenish tips, perishing with no following seed. In the MALE, however, short stalks rise from the same axils, on each of which sits a small testiculated purse, somewhat compressed and hairy, enclosing twin seeds approaching the seeds of Cleavers.

It highlights the distinction between male and female plant varieties as understood in early modern botany.</summary>
<keywords>Stinking Orach, Pellitory-of-the-Wall, Mercury (plant), Corchorus, botanical classification, medicinal herbs, Montbéliard, Dioscorides, Pliny</keywords>
