<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of various herbs, focusing on the "Dog's Mercury" (Cynocrambe), the "Leaf" plant (Phyllon), and varieties of "Dock" (Lapathum). It maintains the classical distinction between "male" and "female" forms of plants, which in early modern botany often referred to different growth habits or flowering structures rather than modern biological sex.</meta>

### DOG’S MERCURY, OR CREEPING MERCURY:
German: *Wildt Bingelkraut*: French: *Mercuriale sauvage*:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dog's Mercury (Mercurialis repens) plant, showing its roots, serrated leaves, and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

With many fibrous, perennial, and tough little roots, the Dog’s Mercury—both the MALE and the FEMALE—creeps along the ground. They possess several stems that are rounded, hollow, jointed with long spaces between the nodes, about a foot high, and becoming purplish near the ground. The *leaves* are paired opposite one another at the joints, very smooth, slightly downy, similar to the leaves of common Mercury, tender, pointed, and saw-toothed around the edges, with short stalks. From the axils <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> of the leaves, stalks emerge; in the Male, which we depict here, they are shorter, about 4 or 5 inches long. Upon these sit small flowers of a grassy color, consisting of three small petals, with two horn-like tips reflected outward. These are followed by two small seeds, appearing in groups of three on each stalk, enclosed in compressed, hairy pods.

### PHYLLON, OR THE LEAF: German: *Welsch Bingelkraut*. Phyllon Arrhenogonon <note>Greek: "Male-begetting"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Phyllon Arrhenogonon plant with upright stems and paired, pointed leaves.</image-desc>

Theophrastus mentions *Phyllon* among those plants believed to have the power to influence the procreation of a male or female child. Dioscorides, following Crateuas, assigns it these same powers, with Pliny in agreement.

Galen, Paulus, and the later Greeks never mentioned it, perhaps because they saw no medical use for it and had little faith in what the earlier writers handed down about it; or perhaps because the legitimate *Phyllon* was unknown to them, just as it is to us.

Matthioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> also argues that the text of Dioscorides has been corrupted in this section, because in many details it departs from Theophrastus. He demonstrates that those who wish to claim *Phyllon* is no different from Mercury are "entirely in error" <note>original: "toto caelo errare," literally "err by the whole sky"</note> based on a consideration of the characteristics and properties of both.

### DOCK, SORREL, OR SHARP DOCK:
German: *Ampffer*, French: *Lapais, Parelle*: Italian: *Lapazio, Rombre*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lapathum Acutum (dock) plant with large, wavy-edged leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

We treat Dock, Sharp-Dock <term>Oxylapathum: from the Greek 'oxys' (sharp) and 'lapathon' (dock)</term>, and Great Water-Dock in the Appendix in a general way. However, Dioscorides identifies five kinds of Dock; Pliny and Theophrastus identify only two, and the latter confuses Wood Sorrel with Sharp-Dock.

The one we depict here is *Sharp-Dock* or *Oxylapathum*. It grows to a height of a cubit and a half <note>about 27 inches</note>. The stem has many branches, is hollow, channeled, and somewhat reddish. The *leaves* are like those of a Beet, but longer, more wrinkled, somewhat curled at the edges, and sometimes pointed or rounded, with a slightly acidic taste. The *flowers* are mossy, abundant, and composed of fibers; these are followed by a three-sided seed enclosed in three membrane-like leaves that turn from green to reddish. The *root* is nine inches long, a finger's breadth thick, saffron-colored, and bitter in taste.

<column-break/>

### DOG’S MERCURY, OR MERCURY
creeping, or Cynia, Female.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the female Cynocrambe plant, showing longer flower spikes emerging from the leaf axils.</image-desc>

In the Female Dog’s Mercury, three stalks rise from the leaf axils, 4 or 5 inches long, thin and channeled, upon which the flowers are arranged in a mossy spike. They are composed of outer grassy petals containing several grassy stamens; these wither away without producing any seed. The whole herb (as in the Male) has a loathsome taste and a poisonous smell.

We have observed the Male and Female Dog’s Mercury in various places: breaking through at Geneva in March and April; growing green at Basel near the mountains as late as October; and flowering at Montbéliard on Mount Bar in May. They share the same habitats as common Mercury and possess the same medicinal powers. More is found in the Appendix.

### PHYLLON THELIGONON <note>Greek: "Female-begetting"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Phyllon Theligonon plant, similar in structure to the previous Phyllon but with distinct flowering characteristics.</image-desc>

Various plants are handed down under the name of *Phyllon*. What is to us *Woolly Chickweed* is called Phyllon by Agerius. What is to us *Adder's Tongue* is so called by Amatus. What we call *Twayblade* is called so by Gesner. What we call *Our Lady's Thistle* is so called by some. And finally, there is the *Phyllon of Montpellier* with hoary leaves, the *Theligonon* which is pictured here, and the *Arrhegonon* (incorrectly called *Arrenogonon* by Pliny) which was shown just before. The "Libyan and Ethiopian Phyllon" of Hippocrates is actually *Silphium* <note>an extinct medicinal plant of antiquity</note>.

In this Montpellier *Phyllon* of ours, both sexes are recognized by Dodoens, L'Obel, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Caspar Bauhin, and other writers. The chief difference is that in the Female, the flowers are spiked and clustered, just as in the Female Mercury.

### SMALLEST SHARP DOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Lapathum (dock), showing a more compact growth habit and smaller leaves.</image-desc>

As we intend to set forth the species of Dock observed by more recent authors, we encounter, after the common Sharp-Dock which we have already pictured and described, this *Smallest Dock*.

It is very similar to the common one in all its parts; however, it seems to have this peculiar trait: almost immediately from the root, the stem begins to divide into branches, in which the flowers grow at certain intervals in whorls. They are mossy and yellowish, with a small leaf like a little tongue attached to almost every whorl, though the outermost whorls lack them.

It grows wild everywhere in the same places as the common variety—namely, in the mountains, in meadows, ditches, and gardens—and both flower as June approaches.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### DOCK, OR SHARP DOCK, with obtuse leaves.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM, SIVE OXYLAPATHVM, folio obtufo."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dock plant (Lapathum) showing its long, slender leaves, flowering stalk with small clusters, and a detailed root system.</image-desc>

The leaves are blunt at the top, and shorter and rounder than in the common Sharp Dock <note>Lapathum acuto</note>: yet it is scarcely to be distinguished from that one by its seed, stalk, flower, root, or properties. It grows around rubble and open courtyards, in the same places as the most common variety.

A decoction of Sharp Dock made with wine and drunk for several days drives away jaundice <note>original: "auriginem"</note>, and restores the skin to its former brightness. Water distilled from the roots is very effective for erasing pimples, white leprosy <note>original: "alphos"</note>, skin discolorations <note>original: "vitiligines"</note>, ringworm <note>original: "lichenas"</note>, and finally all spots of the skin, especially of the face. Some superstitious folk believe that those who carry the root of the Dock with them, dug up while the Moon is waning, will never suffer from bleary eyes.

### GREAT DOCK, OR MONK'S RHUBARB:
#### German: Monk's Rhubarb: French: Monk's Rhubarb.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM MAIVS, VEL RHABARBARVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Monk's Rhubarb, featuring large, broad, wavy-edged leaves and a tall, branched inflorescence.</image-desc>

It sometimes reaches the height of a man: rising with a **stalk** that is channeled, reddish, and divided toward the upper parts into numerous small twigs. The **flowers** are in a long series along almost all the branches, appearing mossy. The **seed** that follows is angular, surrounded by membrane-like husks. The **leaves** are a foot or a foot and a half long, broad, pointed, hard, stiff, and reddish, hanging from long reddish stalks. The **root** is long and thick, provided with many attached fibers, and intensely saffron-colored.

It is kept in several gardens in Germany, France, and Italy; nor is Switzerland <note>original: "Heluetia"</note> without it, as it is cultivated and grows successfully in the garden of the Nuns in the city of *Estavayer* <note>original: "Estavai"</note> in the territory of Fribourg. The leaves burst forth in March, the flowers in June. More on this in the Appendix.

### SMALLER WATER DOCK.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM AQVATICVM MINVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller water dock, showing lanceolate leaves and a flowering stem emerging from a thick rhizome.</image-desc>

The birthplace of this plant is also in the water, as the *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> says, but only in clear and spring waters. Through these waters it thrusts up from the bottom rather tender, drooping, slender little stalks, not without filaments crowding and hanging here and there, as with other aquatic plants. The **leaves** are thin and somewhat soft, yet not floating in the manner of Pondweed <note>original: "Potamogetonis"</note>, but upright, dark green, lance-shaped, and much narrower than those of Pondweed.

Pharmacists say that the leaves of this plant, above all others, are required for that most confused jumble of names and ingredients known as *Soldier's Ointment* <note>original: "Vnguenti Martiati"</note>.

<column-break/>

### COMMON LARGE WILD DOCK.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM SYLVESTRE MAGNVM vulgare"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of common wild dock, showing a robust plant with large leaves and a dense, branched seed head.</image-desc>

This herb is of common knowledge, frequently growing in damp places in the courtyards of villages near stables; and also in the mountains, especially in those places where cattle are accustomed to be stabled for a long time, and where the soil is made rich by their dung.

It is called *Wild Horse-dock* <note>original: "Hippolapathum sylvestre"</note> by Tabernaemontanus; *Most Common Dock*, and *Apothecary's Dock*, by Schwenkfeld. By certain Germans, among other names, it is called *Butter-sorrel* <note>original: "Butter ampffer"</note>, because the peasants bring butter to the cities for sale wrapped in its leaves.

Indeed, it has the same powers as Sharp Dock.

### GREATEST WATER DOCK:
#### German: Water Sorrel: French: Great Marsh Dock.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM MAXIMVM AQVATICVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Great Water Dock, showing very large, elongated leaves and a tall, sturdy flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The **flower** and seed are like those of the Sharp Dock: and it also has similar **leaves**, but they are smoother and less wrinkled, almost a cubit and a half long <note>approx. 27 inches</note>, with somewhat curled edges. The **stalks** rise to two cubits. The **root** is black on the outside, boxwood-colored within, and divided into many fibers.

It grows in watery, marshy, and stagnant places, and in damp ditches.

The root softens the bowels and dispels Jaundice <note>original: "Icteritiam"</note>; the leaves, however, are beneficial for hot gout <note>original: "podagris"</note>.

### ROUND-LEAVED ALPINE DOCK, with very abundant mossy flowers.
<note>original: "LAPATHVM FOLIO ROTVNDO, ALPINVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alpine Dock (Monk's Rhubarb type), characterized by large, rounded, heart-shaped leaves and a dense floral spike.</image-desc>

It is commonly called Round-leaved Dock and Round Horse-dock by almost all writers, and by some of the more recent ones, *False Rhubarb*.

It grows in the mountains, in damper places, and especially in those where herds, having their station there in the summer months, are most frequently accustomed to gather for the sake of watering.

Some say it purges the bowels if the root is administered at double the dose of true Rhubarb.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of the Dock family (Lapathum), detailing their physical descriptions, preferred habitats in marshes or mountains, and their medicinal uses for skin conditions, jaundice, and gout.</summary>
<keywords>Dock, Rhubarb, medicinal herbs, botany, jaundice, skin treatments, Switzerland, aquatic plants, Alpine flora</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### YELLOW-FLOWERED DOCK.
<note>original: "Lapathum Anthoxanthum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Yellow-flowered Dock plant, showing upright stems with small flowers at the tips and long, narrow leaves at the base.</image-desc>

It has a thin, twiggy, fibrous root that is hard and woody. There are two or three stalks, angled, about a palm's breadth in height. The leaves are like those of Sharp Dock <note>Oxylapathum: Rumex acutus</note>, oblong and narrow; the flower at the tops of the branches is golden, from which it takes its name.

It grows in ditches and marshy places; it is especially frequent around Nuremberg.

### BEAUTIFUL SINUATE DOCK OF BOLOGNA.
<note>original: "Lapathum Pulchrum Bononiense sinuatum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lapathum Pulchrum Bononiense, featuring a basal rosette of broad, wavy-edged (sinuate) leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

From a thick root it puts forth many leaves, most of them two inches long, on thin stalks of nearly the same length; they are an inch wide, deeply wavy-edged <term>sinuate: having a wavy or indented margin</term> on both sides, and somewhat round. The stalk is a palm high, and upon it are prickly husks arranged at the joints. *We received this from Bologna.*

### BLOOD DOCK, OR DRAGON'S BLOOD herb: German *Drackenbluet.*
<note>original: "Lapathum Sanguineum, sive Sangvis Draconis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lapathum Sanguineum, showing a plant with prominent veining on the leaves and a tall, branched inflorescence.</image-desc>

The distinction of this plant from the rest of the Docks is easy, due to the blood-red juice with which it teems, and the veins running frequently through the leaves (which are pointed like the Smaller Dock), which by their various weaving together impart a dark blood-red color to the green leaves. With this juice it stains both hands and leather, first with a purple color, which soon fades into blue. The stalks of the leaves are also soaked in this same juice. In other features of its shape, it is not much different from the Sharp Dock.

It grows spontaneously in Northern gardens, but more rarely in warm regions. We had it in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard, flowering in June and propagating itself by dropped seed.

In taste it is more salty/nitrous than Sharp Dock; its other properties are shared with it. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### SINUATE SEA DOCK.
<note>original: "Lapathum Marinum Sinuatum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lapathum Marinum Sinuatum, showing a plant with decumbent (lying on the ground) stems and small, lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It puts forth small stalks trailing on the ground, and sometimes standing obliquely upright, nine inches long, divided into small branches that are angled and streaked. The leaves cling to these on stalks nearly an inch long, placed alternately; they are oblong, with two notable jagged lobes dividing the bottom part. At the top of the small branches, the little flowers are gathered as if into a spike, of a faded color, and turning somewhat white from a yellowish-green. The root is reddish, provided with few fibers. It is found frequently near *Aigues-Mortes* <note>A coastal town in southern France</note>.

### FLOATING DOCK, WITH LONG SERRATED LEAVES.
<note>original: "Lapathum Fluitans, Longo Serrato folio"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lapathum Fluitans, an aquatic plant with long, narrow, serrated leaves trailing as if in water.</image-desc>

Its root is jointed, and from each joint it puts forth fibers by which it clings to the shallow bottom, being reddish at the first segments. It produces many stalks, round, five or six cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> long, floating in the water. The leaves are a palm's breadth long, or even more, narrow, notched around the edge, growing alternately along the stalks. At the top of the stalks a flowering head stands out, exactly of the appearance seen in Pondweed <note>Potamogeton</note>.

It grows in the shallows of all sluggish rivers, such as the Saône <note>Latin: Araris</note>.

### RHAPONTIC: German *Rhapontick*: French *Rhapontique*: Italian *Repontico*: To the Arabs *Raued* and *Rauend*.
<note>original: "Rhaponticum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thick, woody Rhaponticum root, shown in two sections to display the internal texture and exterior bark.</image-desc>

The Rhapontic root which the druggists <term>Seplasiæ: sellers of perfumes and medicines</term> display is about the thickness of an average radish, heavier and more compact than Rhubarb. It is covered with a wrinkled and dark bark; when cut crosswise it shows spirals of various colors, and is less red than Rhubarb. Its taste is somewhat bitter and astringent, but it has almost no smell.

It takes its name from its native soil; for it grows on the banks of the river *Rha* <note>The Volga River</note> above the Black Sea and the Cimmerian Bosphorus. Hence we read in Pliny and Dioscorides that it is brought from the regions above the Bosphorus.

Moreover, we have from the records of the ancient Greeks that there are two kinds of *Rha* or *Rheum*: *Rha Barbarum* (Foreign Rhubarb), which will be discussed shortly, and the *Rha* or *Rheum Ponticum* (Rhapontic) which we describe here. *More on this in the Appendix.*

<summary>This page describes various species of Dock (Lapathum), including maritime and aquatic varieties, and introduces Rhapontic (a type of Rhubarb), detailing its physical characteristics, geographical origins near the Volga River, and its distinction from "Foreign" Rhubarb.</summary>

<keywords>Dock, Sorrel, Blood Dock, Rhapontic, Rhubarb, medicinal roots, Nuremberg, Bologna, Montbéliard, Volga River, botany, aquatic plants</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
Xx

RHUBARB: Germ. *Rhabarbarum*: French *Rhubarbe*: Ital. *Rhabarbaro*. <note>original: "Rhabarbarum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Rhubarb plant (Rhabarbarum) showing large, broad, textured leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

Rhubarb, as it is depicted by some, has a stem the size of a palm, and leaves twice as long; they are narrower at the part where they cluster together without a stalk, but broader elsewhere and bent downwards. They say that another thinner stem grows from within the leaves where it lies hidden, at the top of which are flowers resembling the March Violet in shape and color, but with a powerful and unpleasant scent. The root, which is the only part that reaches us <note>referring to the dried medicinal root imported to Europe from Asia</note>, is very thick, round, and reddish-black on the outside, but yellowish-red on the inside, wavy with a pattern of reddish lines. It is spongy yet heavy, with a bitter taste and a slight astringency that is not unpleasant; it tints the liquid in which it is infused with a saffron color. More details are in the Appendix.

### CURLED SORREL: Germ. *Krauser Ampffer*. <note>original: "Oxalis Crispa"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Oxalis Crispa, featuring upright stems with crinkled or ruffled (crisped) leaves and clusters of small flowers/seeds at the top.</image-desc>

In its native habitat, season, and manner of growth, this plant differs not at all from the preceding or Common variety, except that nature plays wonderfully with the curled leaves in this species.

The common Sorrel with the long leaf, depicted in the previous plate, produces stems higher than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, which are striped, hollow, and divided into branches. The leaves are like those of Bistort, but smaller and pointed; where they attach to the stalk they are sickle-shaped or winged, succulent, dark green, and sour in taste. The flowers and seeds are like those of the Sharp Dock. The root is fibrous, yellow, and has a strongly drying and astringent taste.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> writes that it flourishes everywhere in meadows and gardens at any time of year, as we have also observed.

### CREEPING SORREL WITH ROUNDER LEAVES: French *Ozeille franche, Ozeille ronde, & Ozeille Romaine*. <note>original: "Oxalis folio rotundiore repens"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping Oxalis with rounded leaves (Oxalis folio rotundiore repens), showing a low-growing habit and smaller, heart-shaped or rounded foliage.</image-desc>

This plant occasionally plays with the shape of its leaves: sometimes they are round, very close to Scurvy-grass or Lesser Celandine; sometimes they are gifted with winged appendages; at other times they are pointed like an arrow and winged, like the end of Spinach leaves, bluish-gray in color, somewhat fatty, and endowed with a delicate sourness. The stems are hollow and longer than a cubit. The small flowers are composed of yellowish-red fibers, as in the others, to which the seed corresponds. The thin root creeps, as do the stems, and is less sour in taste than the leaves.

It is found in almost all gardens and even grows on walls. Concerning its use and powers, see the following sections.

<column-break/>

SORREL OR DOCK: Germ. *Saurampffer*: French *Ozeille, Salsette*: Ital. *Azedera*. <note>original: "Oxalis sive Acetosa"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Oxalis or Acetosa (Common Sorrel), showing a tall, slender flowering stalk and lanceolate leaves with basal lobes.</image-desc>

Up to this point, we have described the Sharp Docks, which, because they have a sharp leaf, were allotted the name <term>Oxylapathon</term> <note>original Greek: ὀξυλάπαθον, from oxys (sharp/acid) and lapathon (dock)</note>. But there are also other plants of the same name which, on account of their acid taste, have also been given the name Oxylapathi from the Greek word <term>Oxys</term> <note>original Greek: ὀξὺς, meaning sharp or sour</note>, which must now be discussed.

Here, therefore, we speak of the *Oxalis*, which the Greeks also called *Anaxyris*, and which is the *Acetosa* of the Latins. The Romans used to call it *Rumex* because, on account of its acid juice, it is usually sucked by the thirsty just like a breast, which the Ancients called *Ruma*.

Two main divisions or kinds are established: namely, the Cultivated and the Wild. Each is distinguished into various species, of which we shall speak in order.

### TUBEROUS-ROOTED SORREL. <note>original: "Oxalis tuberosa radice"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Oxalis tuberosa radice, showing a plant with distinct tuberous swellings along the root system and upright stems with small leaves.</image-desc>

Above the ground, it resembles the meadow Sorrel; the leaves are of the same size and shape, some embracing the stem with their "wings" (lobes), others resting on a longer stalk. The flower is thread-like, yellowish, and grows in clusters. The root is tuberous, like Dropwort or Water Dropwort.

We saw it flowering in June at Heidelberg, in the garden of Sprenger. Indeed, Clusius and Caspar Bauhin <note>renowned Renaissance botanists</note> mention a Sorrel with a very large leaf and tuberous, knotty joints.

### SMALL PRICKLY SORREL OF CRETE. <note>original: "Oxalis minor aculeata Candiae"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Oxalis minor aculeata, showing a smaller, more delicate plant with multiple branching stems and small, pointed leaves.</image-desc>

It produces several branches, a cubit or nine inches long, spread on the ground, wavy and winding, slender and striped; the color is reddish near the earth, otherwise green. The leaves are few, like Sorrel, but appearing mutilated at the wings. The flowers, appearing at intervals along almost the entire length of the branches, are mossy and yellowish; these are followed by a three-cornered, purplish seed. The root is purple, slender, and clings to the surface of the soil.

It is cultivated at Montbéliard in the garden of His Most Serene Highness <note>likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg's botanical gardens</note>, and it flowers in June.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and illustrations of Rhubarb and several varieties of Sorrel (Oxalis), including their physical characteristics, medicinal roots, and regional names.</summary>
<keywords>Rhubarb, Sorrel, Oxalis, botany, medicinal roots, Lobelius, Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, Heidelberg, Montbéliard</keywords>

### SMALL EARED CREEPING SORREL:
->German: *Sheep's Sorrel, small Sorrel.*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping plant with small, heart-shaped or eared leaves and a slender flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It has long, woody, and very fibrous *roots*, reddish in color, creeping here and there, and often divided into several heads: these send out oblong leaves, an inch or half-inch long, eared at the base, with a sour taste like the rest of its kind. The small flowers form long clusters, followed by a triangular seed.

It is commonly called by writers *Smaller Oxalis, Smallest Oxalis, Little Sorrel, Wether Sorrel, Small Dock, and Small Lance-shaped Sorrel.* <note>The author lists various Latin synonyms: Oxalis minor, Acetosilla, Acetosa veruecina, etc.</note>

It grows in many places in sandy and uncultivated fields; it is troublesome due to its creeping habit, and it flowers in June.

It is more pleasing to the palate than the Common Sorrel, and it performs all the same functions beautifully. More information is in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### MOST ELEGANT AFRICAN SORREL,
->with small flowers of a yellowish-green color.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with trifoliate leaves (resembling clover or oxalis) and a cluster of flowers at the top of a leafless stalk.</image-desc>

This grew for us at Montbéliard in the Prince's garden <note>original: "S.P. horto," likely referring to the garden of the Serenissimi Principis</note> from seed sent from Paris <note>original: "Lutetia"</note>, and with a small yellow flower.

We have designated this place for explaining the *powers and properties* of Sorrel in general. Therefore, these are cold and dry in the second degree: they digest, open, and cut through sluggish humors <note>In Galenic medicine, "cutting" humors meant breaking down thick fluids in the body</note>: they temper the heat of the stomach and liver, stimulate the appetite for food, and resist bilious and pestilential fevers. The root unlocks obstructions of the liver and the mesenteric veins: the seed is used in cordial medicines. The leaves and their juice are a useful seasoning for many foods in the summer months; they stimulate the appetite and drive out putrefaction.

---

### BUCKWHEAT: German: *Heathen corn, Beech-wheat:*
### French: *Horse-drench, Saracen wheat:* Italian: *Big Wheat.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buckwheat plant (Fagopyrum), showing broad, heart-shaped leaves, branched stems, and clusters of small flowers and triangular seeds.</image-desc>

Because of the similarity it has with Sorrel in its leaves and seeds, it claims this place for itself. It rises with a reddish stem to two feet or higher, channeled, smooth, and divided into several branches. The leaves, on long reddish stalks, are like Ivy, dark green, with a dull taste: from their axils <note>the angle between leaf and stem</note> emerge individual stalks, four or five inches long, thin, which support the small flowers in clusters; these are first flesh-colored, then white, each consisting of five small petals with reddish tips. The seed is three-cornered, covered in a black husk, containing a very white, tasteless flour. The root is woody, white, long, and provided with many fibers.

It grows in any soil whatsoever, nor does it reject any, however arid or lean. More in the appendix.

<column-break/>

### MOONWORT OF THE ARABIAN MAGI.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded, slightly lobed leaves and a single stem bearing small flowers and seed pods.</image-desc>

Lobelius writes in his *Observations* that this rare plant is called Moonwort <note>Latin: Lunaria</note> because of the similarity its leaves have to the waxing Moon; but it was called Moonwort of the Arabian Magi so that it might be distinguished from other Moonworts. Caspar Bauhin calls it Round-leaved Sorrel Moonwort in his *Phytopinax*.

The tender leaves emerge in March from a woody, winding, ash-colored root, similar to the first emerging leaves of round-leaved Sorrel, and almost equal to Ivy-leaved Scurvy-grass. We have not seen the flowers or seeds. However, as mentioned, we found and collected the plant as it was emerging in a valley of the Allobroges <note>The Savoy region of the Alps</note> between the very high mountain commonly called Mount Cenis and St. Jean de Maurienne.

---

# ON THE IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXIV.

### THE LETTUCES, ENDIVES, AND OTHERS OF THAT KIND,
->whose flower passes into down <note>original: "pappum"; referring to the fluffy seed heads like those of a dandelion.</note><-

**LETTUCE, COMMON CULTIVATED LETTUCE: ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COMMON CULTIVATED LETTUCE.**
German: *Laich*: French: *Laictuë*: Italian: *Lactuca*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a lettuce plant with broad, rounded leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Lettuce <note>original: "Lactuca"</note> obtained its name from the abundance of milky juice <note>original: "lactei succi"</note> which it pours out when it is broken.

Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> distinguishes between the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*: Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany," a student of Aristotle.</note> seems to establish the same two main divisions, when he says that one has a small leaf, a whiter stalk, and is copious in milk, which he makes the *wild* variety: but the other is white, sweeter and more tender, of which he makes three species: the *Broad-stalked*, the *Round-stalked*, and the *Laconian*.

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History.</note> also mentions the *Broad-stalked*, *Round-stalked*, and *Laconian* Lettuce, but he adds many other differences taken from the location and the time of sowing: Thus he records the *Cappadocian*, *Grecian*, *Goat-lettuce*, *Mecenis*, *Abylida*, and—with a reproach for its bitterness—

<margin>one called Picris <note>meaning "bitter."</note>. Likewise, more recent authors have observed many differences, as will be clear from what follows.</margin>

Recent authors have distinguished the species of Lettuce in various ways. By location and cultivation, establishing one as *cultivated* and another as *wild*. By the leaves, which are longer, broader, flat, curled, or wavy at the edges, or closed into the shape of a head, from which comes the name *Headed* <note>original: "Capitata"; i.e., Cabbage lettuce.</note>. By color, from the diversity of which one is called *white* (which is more common), another *red*, and another *black*. And finally by the seed, which in these last two is black, but in all the others is white. To these is added yet another Kind, commonly called *Roman* <note>known today as Romaine lettuce.</note>.

We depict here in a double plate from Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German botanist.</note> the *common cultivated Lettuce*, the *Headed*, and the *Non-Headed* as they split from the stalk: we shall treat the *Wild* variety later in its own place.

<column-break/>

**LONG SWEET ROMAN LETTUCE.**

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Roman lettuce variety with elongated, upright leaves.</image-desc>

The leaf is sweet, oblong, moderately jagged, and armed on the lower part along the rib with small prickles; the flowers are yellow and small like common lettuce, and the stalk is also like common lettuce. It swells into a *head* if it is tied at the top; and it turns out more tender and whiter if earth is drawn around it up to the tip.

It is called *Black Lettuce* by Caesalpinus: by some *Dusky Lettuce*: by Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Schwenckfeld, *Endive-like Lettuce*.

It is cultivated abundantly in gardens, as are the Common Headed and Non-Headed varieties: and this Roman variety is sometimes found whiter, other times darker: and it is given the highest praise in foods. We saw a Headed variety with many heads at Porcutruum, in the garden of Mr. Rittner.

**LETTUCE WITH A LONG AND VERY NARROW leaf.**

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a lettuce variety with very narrow, pointed, and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

In this lettuce, many leaves rise immediately from the root, a span or a span and a half long <note>about 9 to 13 inches.</note>, one or two inches wide: the upper ones, however, are as narrow as they are short, provided with certain small prickles along the margins, and both are pointed: the stalk is a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>about 18 to 27 inches.</note>, and branched: the flowers and seed are the same as in common Lettuces, but the color of the seed is dusky.

We have observed this in several gardens, especially between Bedford and the silver mines in Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines <note>original: "Girarmegne".</note>. Some (Castore Durante and others) label it *French Lettuce*.

<summary>This page describes various species of lettuce (Lactuca), detailing their physical characteristics, naming conventions based on their milky sap, and classifications by ancient and contemporary botanists. It specifically highlights the common cultivated, Roman, and narrow-leafed varieties, noting their cultivation methods and culinary value.</summary>
<keywords>lettuce, Lactuca, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Roman lettuce, plant classification, medicinal herbs, gardening, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of various lettuce species, following the previous discussions on garden herbs. The focus here is on both cultivated and wild varieties, their medicinal properties, and their geographical locations.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### CURLED LACY LETTUCE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Lactuca crispa laciniata plant, showing a thick central stalk with highly ruffled, curled, and deeply lobed leaves spreading outwards.</image-desc>

Crescentius <note>Pietro de' Crescenzi, a 14th-century Italian writer on agriculture</note> writes that Lettuce can be sown and transplanted almost the whole year round: and both he and others hand down many other details regarding its sowing, cultivation, and "sophistication" <note>original: "mangonio" - referring to techniques used to improve the plant's appearance or flavor</note>. But since these things are commonly known to both kitchen-gardeners and ordinary women, we shall refrain from enumerating them.

*As for its powers*, this vegetable is moist and cold, according to the testimony of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>; yet not extremely so, for if it were, as he says, it would not be fit for eating, but rather possesses a coldness similar to spring water. And while every other vegetable generates very little blood, and that of a faulty nature: Lettuce produces more abundant blood, and with less fault. Therefore, Galen writes that he used it very much; in his youth indeed to moderate the heat of the mouth of the stomach, but in declining age to bring on sleep.

### WILD LETTUCE, BROAD-LEAFED, with poisonous juice.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a wild lettuce plant (Lactuca sylvestris) with a tall, branching flowering stalk, small flower heads, and broad, serrated basal leaves.</image-desc>

We now proceed to describe the Wild Lettuces. That which we depict here has a *root* the thickness of the little finger, white, and hairy with a few fibers: a *stalk* three cubits high <note>about 4.5 feet</note>, round, smooth, hollow, and branched: the lowest *leaves* are broad, very close to the cultivated Endive, blackish, and as if saw-toothed with soft little spines around the edge: the upper leaves indeed are wavy and, where they face the ground, bristly with little spines along the length of the rib: the *flowers* are crowded together, yellow like Lettuce, with a scaly, reddish calyx. The *seed* is black, hanging from a downy tuft. *The engraver has corrupted our figure.* <note>A common complaint by early botanists when the woodcut artist made anatomical errors</note>

It grows on stony cliffs and rocky places, and sometimes out of the very cracks of the rocks. It is called Endive by some, and by almost everyone *Wild Lettuce*.

### WILD WALL LETTUCE, with deeply jagged leaves, and small yellow lettuce-like flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a wall lettuce plant, featuring a slender, branched stem with small flowers and deeply lobed, pinnatifid leaves.</image-desc>

It grows at Montbéliard on the walls of the Castle, and in shady woods, flowering in July: we have also observed it at Basel outside the stone gate, and at Geneva on roofs and walls.

To many, it is a kind of Sow-thistle: to others, a species of *Wild Scariola*: to others, *Woodland Lettuce* with yellow flowers.

### LETTUCE FROM PERU.

Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, a Spanish physician who wrote on plants from the New World</note> mentions a certain *Lettuce-leafed* herb brought from Peru: and he commends it greatly for diseases of the kidneys: as also for toothaches, if its leaves are placed upon the affected tooth or if their juice is dripped in, or if a decoction is held in the mouth for a long time on the side where the teeth ache. They call it the *kidney* herb. Is it perhaps the *Dwarf Wild Lettuce* of the History of Lyon?

<column-break/>

### FINELY CUT CURLED LETTUCE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a finely dissected curled lettuce, showing a dense head of very narrow, frilly, and intricately divided leaves.</image-desc>

Cultivated Lettuces, as can be gathered from the records of Dioscorides and Pliny, are cooling, pleasing to the stomach, induce sleep, soften the bowels, and increase milk: when boiled, they are more conducive to sexual desire. The seed, when drunk, resists sexual desire, restrains flowing dreams and sexual imaginings in sleep. However, the herb itself, if eaten too frequently, harms the clarity of the eyes. The juice, according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century herbalist</note>, when smeared with <term>verrucolaceo</term> <note>likely a preparation involving wart-wort or similar resin</note> on the forehead and temples, not only brings sleep to those with fever, but also soothes headache: used as a gargle with the juice of a Punic Apple <note>Pomegranate</note>, it helps inflammations of the uvula.

### WILD LETTUCE, OR ENDIVE, as called by many, with jagged leaves and a prickly back.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a wild lettuce or endive-like plant with a prickly midrib on the underside of its deeply lobed leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It has irregular *leaves* along the stalk, jagged and saw-toothed like the Sow-thistle, provided with spines along the rib on the back side, and full of bitter milk: the *stalk* indeed is two cubits or more, prickly at the base: which at the top goes off into many small branches, which are adorned with small, yellow, lettuce-like *flowers*, turning into downy tufts.

It is the domestic <term>Seris</term> <note>a Greek name for chicory/endive types</note> to some, the *Lactucina* of Dioscorides to others, the wild *Badiuia* and *Budinia* to others, and to Ruellius, Mattioli, Dodoens, Lobel, and others, the *Common Endive of the Apothecaries*.

It grows by roadsides and the edges of fields and meadows, as well as near ditches: it is also found in vineyards and gardens among the vegetables: and very easily, if once sown, it returns every year.

### PURPLE WOOD-LETTUCE, OR purple-blue.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a purple wood-lettuce, showing a tall stem with alternate, clasping leaves and a terminal panicle of small flowers.</image-desc>

It has a *stalk* two cubits or higher, smooth, round, and full of white pith: which the *leaves* clothe alternately at intervals; they are wavy, smooth, tender, pale green beneath, green above, and otherwise as the small picture outlines. The *stalk* is divided into several branches, and spread out again into other smaller ones, which support small Lettuce flowers, composed of five petals, but of a cheerful purplish color, which turn into down: the seed is oblong and black: the *root* is the thickness of a thumb and fibrous.

It is the *Wild Sow-thistle* and the sterile *Libanotis* of Theophrastus according to Tabernaemontanus: and the *Blue-flowered Sow-thistle* according to Camerarius.

We have seen it at Montbéliard on Mount *Estobens*: at Geneva on Mount *Thuyri*, and at Basel, on Mount *Wasserfall*. It flowers in August and September.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### WILD AND CULTIVATED CHICORY:
#### German: Wild Chicory; French: Chicory; Italian: Chicory, Sunflower. <note>original: "Wegvvart" (Wegwart), "Tornafole". The Italian "Tornafole" likely refers to the plant's tendency to follow the sun.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Cichorium sylvestre plant, showing its long, jagged leaves and multiple flowering stems with small blossoms.</image-desc>

The root is the thickness of a thumb and full of milky sap; it puts forth winding stalks, swollen with the same juice, and spreading out into various branches. The leaves are like those of the Dandelion <note>original: "Dentis Leonis"</note>, sometimes whole, other times very finely divided, curled, and hairy. The flowers emerge successively from the sides of the stalks and the axils of the uppermost leaves; they are like those of the Dandelion, but blue in color, and occasionally white. The entire plant is found to be remarkably bitter—root, stalks, leaves, and flowers. Through cultivation, it becomes larger and milder.

We present only one illustration, taken from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a famous German botanist</note>, and it seems sufficient for both Wild and Cultivated Chicory; for it is not so changed by cultivation that it does not retain a great resemblance to the wild variety. More will be found in the Appendix.

### THORNY CHICORY OR
#### Thorny Gum-Succory. <note>original: "Chondrilla spinosa"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cichorium spinosum, characterized by its low-growing, tangled, and thorny branches with small leaves at the base.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are like Chicory, but narrower, green, and lobed, with many growing from the same point. The stalk is smooth and divided into somewhat stiff, disordered branches that spread out in many directions, ending in hard thorns. The flowers are placed at the branchings of the stems and at the very tips of the forks; they are blue and consist of notched petals. They are two or three times smaller than those of common Chicory, and the seed is similar.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the Saint-Pancrace garden from seed sent from Naples; it flowered in July and August.

### ENDIVE OR CHICORY: German: Endive,
#### Escarole; French: Endive, Escarole; Italian: Endive.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Intybus (Endive), showing broad, wavy-edged leaves growing from a central root and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The plant pictured here is called *Seris*, *Scariola*, and *Endivia*, as well as *Intybum*.

It has fibrous roots full of milky sap. Before the stalk grows, the leaves are spread across the ground—long, broad, and sometimes narrow, similar to Lettuce leaves, occasionally notched around the edges and somewhat bitter. Through the "trickery" of gardeners <note>original: "mangonio" - referring to cultivation techniques like blanching</note>, they are sometimes seen to be curled and white. The stalk is a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>, smooth, grooved, hollow, branched with many arms, winding, and pouring out milk when wounded.

The blue flowers emerge from the axils of the leaves (which on the stalk are shaped like Ivy), resembling Wild Chicory, and the seed is also very similar.

<column-break/>

### WART CHICORY; WART-WORT
#### Italian: Knight’s Mace. <note>original: "Mazza di Caualiero"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cichorium verrucosum, showing upright stems with small, scale-like leaves and flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

It raises its stalks only a little from the ground; they are slender, brittle, and branched. Along their sides grow small, stalkless flowers, and others at the ends of the branchlets, which are yellow. When these vanish into downy tufts, they are succeeded by very beautiful seed-vessels arranged in radiating circles, the size of a Lupin seed, containing many seeds like those of Lettuce, though not as compressed. The leaves are oblong, like Dandelion, jagged, with many spread on the ground and few on the branches. The root is long and fibrous.

The power of this plant to remove warts is marvelous. Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist</note> writes that the weight of three seeds taken in a drink, or the leaves eaten just once in a salad, will certainly accomplish this. We ourselves have observed quite often that the leaves, when applied as a poultice, completely destroy them.

### BULBOUS OR SCROPHULOUS CHICORY:
#### Small, maritime, bulbous, yellow Gum-Succory.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Cichorium bulbosum, featuring distinct bulbous swellings along the roots and thin, dandelion-like leaves.</image-desc>

As rare as it is beautiful, this kind of Chicory creeps far and wide with innumerable thin fibers, to which are attached solid bulbs the size of a hazelnut, with the whiteness of alabaster marble. The leaves are an inch and a half or two inches long, half an inch wide, lightly lobed, smooth, ending in a blunt point, somewhat thick, and reddish. Among them rise small stalks a palm's breadth high and hairy, on the tips of which sit yellow flowers like Hawkweed <note>original: "Hieracij"</note>, which vanish into downy tufts.

It creeps through the sand and flowers in April, near Mount Seth by the sea. Its roots are very helpful for scrofula <note>original: "strumas" - a swelling of the lymph nodes, often treated with "signature" plants like this bulbous root</note>.

### CULTIVATED NARROW-LEAFED ENDIVE.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Intybum sativum angustifolium, showing narrower, more deeply lobed leaves compared to the previous endive variety.</image-desc>

From *Intybus*, as Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius, a 16th-century Saxon physician</note> notes in his commentary on Dioscorides, the word *Endivia* is corruptly derived. From *Seris*—a word which, according to Pliny, the Ancients used specifically for cultivated endives—is derived *Seriola*, and later *Scariola*. To Amato <note>Amato Lusitano</note> and others, this is the cultivated narrow-leafed endive, just as to Cornarius and others, *Endivia* is properly the cultivated broad-leafed endive. However, *Serriola* is actually a type of Wild Lettuce.

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a pioneer of German botany</note> holds four differences, or rather varieties, of cultivated endive: distinguishing them into Large, Curled, Small, and Small with a white flower. Almost all other authors make three types: Broad-leafed, Narrow-leafed, and Curled.

<summary>This page describes various species of Chicory and Endive, detailing their physical characteristics, cultivation, and medicinal uses, such as treating warts and scrofula. It references major botanical authorities like Fuchs, Mattioli, and Pliny to classify the different varieties.</summary>
<keywords>Chicory, Endive, Escarole, Cichorium sylvestre, Cichorium spinosum, Cichorium verrucosum, medicinal plants, wart treatment, scrofula, botany, Mattioli, Fuchs</keywords>

--- Page 379 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of salad herbs and thistles, specifically focusing on cultivated endive and various species of sow-thistles (Sonchus).</meta>

### CULTIVATED CURLY ENDIVE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy chicory or endive plant with curly, ruffled leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

Cultivated Endive <note>original: "Intybum Sativum"</note> is made *larger* or *smaller* depending on the soil and cultivation: the *curly* variety is produced through transplantation and the clever manipulation <term>mangonio: the artful "doctoring" or improvement of plants by gardeners</term> of gardeners; otherwise, it does not differ from the others.

It is sown in gardens; that which is sown in the Spring grows quickly, flowering in the Summer itself, produces seeds, and then dies away. However, that which is sown in July remains into the Winter; when covered with earth in September or October—the leaves having first been tied together—it is rendered as white as snow <note>This refers to the process of "blanching" to make the leaves less bitter</note>, and is then brought to the table during the Winter months in place of other salad greens.

### SMOOTH LOBED SOW-THISTLE, OR the non-prickly variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sow-thistle with deeply lobed (laciniate) leaves and several flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

It relies on a small, fibrous, and white root: with a stalk a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, hollow inside, and turning purple. The leaves are long, smooth, almost blue-grey <note>glaucous</note>, divided like a Dandelion <note>original: "Dentis Leonis"</note>, and pregnant with milk <note>referring to the milky sap or latex</note>; they come out alternately, sometimes with a long stalk, other times with none, but embracing the stem with a wider base, appearing toothed around the edges, and armed with either no spines or very soft ones. The flowers are leafy and yellow, but the outermost part of the petals turns purple on the reverse side. The seed is small, oblong, and a reddish-brown.

Cordus calls this the "Smooth or Mild Sow-thistle": but to Fuchs, it is another type of Sow-thistle, more tender and edible and less dark, and the "Hare's Lettuce" of Apuleius. In the *History of Lyon*, it is the "Lesser Andryala" of Dalechamps.

### CREEPING SOW-THISTLE TO MANY, TO SOME the Greater Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a perennial sow-thistle with creeping roots and dandelion-like flowers.</image-desc>

The flowers of this one are a little larger than the other Sow-thistles, yellow, and held together by a hairy structure of dark green leaves, which eventually turn into downy tufts <note>pappos: the fluffy seeds dispersed by wind</note>.

It is found in marshy willow-thickets and reed-beds, near ponds and stagnant waters; it is common everywhere in the fields of Montbéliard and Geneva, and in some gardens it is considered hateful because of its creeping habit. It flowers in July.

In our illustration, which is taken from Fuchs's works, the creeping root is missing.

<column-break/>

### SOW-THISTLE, CICERBITA: German *Sawdistel*, French *Laicteron*, *Palais de Lieure*: Italian *Lattucella*, *Soncho*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common sow-thistle with prickly-edged leaves and small flower buds.</image-desc>

It is called *sonchos* by the Greeks <foreign language="Greek">ἀπὸ τοῦ σῶον ἔχειν</foreign> <note>original Greek: "apo tou sōon echein"</note>, that is, because it pours out a "wholesome" juice. The Romans called it *Cicerbita*, and that name is still retained today in Tuscany.

Theophrastus mentions the Sow-thistle among the prickly-leaved plants; likewise, Galen says the *Sonchus* is among the prickly plants, but only after it has fully matured. Pliny creates two kinds, the white and the black, both similar to Lettuce, were they not prickly. Indeed, Dioscorides seems to have mentioned three: namely, the wild and more prickly one, another softer and edible one, and a third tree-like one with broad leaves.

We depict here the less-lobed, pricklier, or rougher Sow-thistle with a yellow flower, belonging to the Hawkweeds: we shall discuss the remaining differences observed by us in the following sections.

### PRICKLY LOBED SOW-THISTLE, Rough Sow-thistle, Rough Cicerbita.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a prickly sow-thistle with sharp, spiny margins on the leaves.</image-desc>

Almost all writers have mentioned this. Tabernaemontanus, however, makes three types of smooth lobed Sow-thistle: the broad-leaved smooth lobed Sow-thistle, a second smooth one with a yellow flower, and a third smooth one with a yellow flower. We have shown in our *Great History* that the writings of Matthiolus and Schwenckfeld regarding these Sow-thistles were quite foolish.

Both the smooth and the prickly lobed Sow-thistle grow wild in various places: everywhere around Geneva and Montbéliard, and most frequently in gardens: and at Basel, outside the city between the Stein and Eschen gates. Both flower until November.

### BROAD-LEAVED BLUE SOW-THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved blue sow-thistle with large, dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

For this Sow-thistle, which is two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> or higher, the top of the stalk is bristly and bears a wand-like cluster <term>thyrsus</term> of flowers similar to the common Sow-thistle, but shining with a blue color, and quickly crumbling into downy tufts.

We obtained this from Alsace; it grows in the highest mountains in shady places, and flowers in July and August. We suspect it is the same as the Blue Sow-thistle of Clusius.

<summary>This page describes various species of endive and sow-thistles (Sonchus), detailing their cultivation, physical characteristics, and the differing classifications provided by classical and contemporary botanists. It highlights the transition from garden vegetables like blanched endive to wild, prickly, and even blue-flowered thistles found in the mountains.</summary>
<keywords>Endive, Sow-thistle, Sonchus, Cicerbita, botanical classification, gardening techniques, medicinal plants, Montbéliard, Geneva, Basel, blue sow-thistle</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of chicory-like plants, specifically focusing on sow-thistles and gum-succories. It maintains the structure of providing the Latin name, common synonyms, and descriptions of habitat and medicinal use.</meta>

### DALECHAMPIUS’S TREE SOW-THISTLE;
#### Related to Wall Lettuce.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sonchus Dendroides plant, showing a tall central stalk with serrated leaves and multiple flowering heads at the top.</image-desc>

This Sow-thistle <note>original: *Sonchus*</note>, if the *History of Lyon* <note>The *Historia Generalis Plantarum* (1586) by Jacques Daléchamps</note> is to be believed, has many things in common with that kind of Sow-thistle which Dioscorides mentions in the third place; the learned shall judge. Indeed, that it also has much in common with the so-called Wall Lettuce, no one, we believe, will deny.

It grows, says Daléchamps, on the rocky slopes of cold mountains.

Furthermore, both types of sow-thistle are cooling, according to Dioscorides, and moderately astringent. The juice, when applied to a burning stomach and to inflammations, soothes the gnawing pains of the stomach. The milky sap flowing from it aids in collections of bile and disorders of the womb. *Regarding its culinary use, see the side of the following table.*

### EARTH-CRACKER, RELATED TO THE SOW-THISTLES;
#### or Terracrepolum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Terracrepolum plant, featuring deeply lobed basal leaves and several thin stalks ending in small flower buds.</image-desc>

It has a root similar to Endive, small, curved, and white; many stalks, a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, covered in leaves; and leaves similar to Endive, but whiter and less indented, flowing with a milky juice. The flower is yellow, vanishing into downy seeds.

The country folk of Tuscany call this wild vegetable *Terracrepolum* <note>literally "earth-cracker"</note>; it is the *Small Hawkweed* of Dioscorides, and the *Crepis* of Theophrastus and Pliny. Perhaps it is the <term>epiphyllokaulos</term> <note>original: ἐπιφυλλόκαυλος; a plant where the flower appears to grow upon the leaf</note> of the same Theophrastus.

It grows spontaneously on the earthen banks of the Montpellier territory, as well as on the walls of buildings and rocky hills; it is also cultivated in gardens.

This vegetable is eaten raw with oil and vinegar; and because it is sweet and slightly astringent, it is held in high esteem.

### YELLOW GUM-SUCCORY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chondrilla Lutea, showing a branched plant with narrow leaves and small composite flowers.</image-desc>

The whole plant, just as in the blue variety, swells with milky juice. On its smooth and hairless stalk, it has leaves approaching those of the Smooth Sow-thistle, but much smaller, with divisions almost like the Blue Gum-succory; their extremities resemble a Stork with spread wings vibrating in the air. They are also finely toothed around the edges, which is worthy of note, as by this mark the plant can be distinguished from the blue or white varieties even when not in bloom.

From the crook of the leaves, small branches emerge, upon each of which sits a single yellow flower, like a Sow-thistle's, vanishing into downy seeds.

It blooms in March on the walls at Montpellier; and throughout the whole summer, it is found in gravelly vineyards and olive groves.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPIUS’S WOOLLY SOW-THISTLE,
#### with the golden flower of Groundsel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sonchus Lanatus, showing a plant with woolly or fuzzy stems and leaves, and large, drooping flower heads.</image-desc>

The whole plant swells with milky juice, in the manner of Chicory, and is endowed with a bitter taste, but less so than the rest of the Chicories, whose properties it also possesses, though more weakly.

It grows at Montpellier near *Perault*, blooming in the month of June in rocky and sunny places. Some call it *Stellugine*, yet it is different from the *Mollugo* of Pliny.

Furthermore, there is frequent use of the common Sow-thistle in salads during the winter; and the roots especially, since they are tender and sweet, are sought after for the table. Galen said the same of it long ago. It is eaten green and tender, just like other wild vegetables.

### GUM-SUCCORIES or CHONDRILLA: Germ. Klein Sonnenwirbel: French. Laiteron: Ital. Chondrylla, Terracrepolo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla species, showing a long taproot and a slender, branching stem with minimal foliage.</image-desc>

Galen writes that the Gum-succory <note>original: *Chondrilla*</note> is a species of *Seris* <note>a type of wild chicory</note>; Dioscorides, however, says it is called Chicory by some and *Seris* by others. He identifies two kinds, which Pliny confuses with one another, attributing to one what the former gave to two.

Thus, even today, it is not easy to distinguish the plants of the Gum-succory genus among writers with certain names; especially since they have not yet accurately examined the history of the Endive-like and Gum-succory-like plants. They have proposed either names and descriptions without illustrations, or illustrations without descriptions.

However, a huge abundance of Gum-succory plants offers itself almost everywhere, on walls, in vineyards, and in sunny, elevated places. *We illustrate the Blue Gum-succory here.*

### TWIGGY GUM-SUCCORY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chondrilla Viminea, characterized by its stiff, rod-like (vimineous) branches and small leaves.</image-desc>

First, leaves sprout scattered in a circle along the ground, with the jagged edges of a *Hedypnois* <note>a wild salad green</note>; they are smooth and wither as the plant rises into a stalk. The stalk itself is quite bristly with thick small spines near the ground and rises to two or three cubits, becoming shrubby with frequent twig-like branches spreading out in various ways, with either no leaves or very few, and those of a grass-like thinness. Yellow flowers, equal to those of lettuce, cling to the ends of the branches. A seed follows that is round, streaked, oblong, and ash-colored, with a shaggy down attached. The root is a single taproot, an inch thick, long, and pregnant with milky juice.

It grows in fields and at their margins in many regions. It is frequent in various places in Montpellier, at Basel by the Rhine, and elsewhere. It blooms in Summer and Autumn.

<summary>This page describes several species of sow-thistles and gum-succories (Sonchus and Chondrilla), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in France and Switzerland, and their culinary and medicinal uses as cooling herbs.</summary>
<keywords>Sow-thistle, Gum-succory, Chondrilla, Sonchus, Montpellier, botany, medicinal herbs, salads, Dioscorides, Galen, Daléchamps</keywords>

--- Page 381 ---
### A CERTAIN LACINIATED PLANT RELATED TO CHONDRILLA: Perhaps the *Trinciatella* of Camerarius? <note>original: "Chondrillis affinis quaedam laciniata"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla plant with deeply laciniated leaves and several flower heads on long stems.</image-desc>

This plant is related to the Chondrillas <note>Gum-succories</note> or the Hieraciums <note>Hawkweeds</note>: from a thick, long root, several heads emerge, from which many leaves grow two inches long, laciniated <note>deeply jagged or fringed</note>, the ends of which are somewhat round, smooth, and quite thick. The stalks are rush-like, branched, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, and sometimes smaller; and at their extremities are individual flowers, rather large, yellow, ending in downy tufts <note>pappus</note>. Indeed, the whole herb yields milk.

It flowers around Montpellier in April.

### THE CRETAN CHONDRILLA OF SOME: Perhaps the Cretan Hawkweed of Camerarius and Gesner?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla Cretica with prickly stems and dandelion-like flowers.</image-desc>

The root is like Dandelion <note>original: "Dentis leonis"</note>: the stems are bristling with small spines, variously divided into wings with no regular order: the leaves are like Wild Lettuce: the flowers like Sow-thistle: the seed is beautiful and curved, ending in a small rose-shape from a finely-toothed base, turning reddish-brown when mature.

It flowers in June and July, and sometimes even in October, and is a short-lived plant. It grew for us in the garden at Montbéliard from seed sent from Crete.

### CHONDRILLA WITH AN UNDIVIDED LEAF, and a bare stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla with smooth-edged leaves at the base and a bare flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant differs from the preceding one only by its stalk being bare of leaves; we received it from Valerand Dourez under the name *Syrian Chondrilla*.

We recount many other varieties of Chondrilla in our great History: *Chondrilla with a hairy leaf and a single large yellow flower: Chondrilla with a whitish root and small yellow flowers: the Greater and Lesser Chondrilla, with a yellow Goat's-beard flower: Chondrilla with a bristly stalk provided with many nodes: Chondrilla with a rough cubit-high stalk and downy flowers: a smaller Chondrilla with leaves turning red on the back: Chondrilla with leaves armed with small spines around the edge, etc.*

Furthermore, Chondrilla is of the same temperament as lettuce. Decocoted in wine and drunk, it resists the poison of serpents.

The juice, if taken internally, stops flows of the bowels. This juice, as well as the gum that forms around the branches, if inserted into the womb, draws out the menses.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY CHONDRILLA WITH A REDDISH FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hairy Chondrilla with small flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

It has a simple white root, hard, endowed with fibers and pouring out milk: the stems are a foot or a cubit high, solid, branched, thin, striated, and endowed with individual leaves: upon each of these sits a single flower on a single stalk, of a color between white and purple, crowded with dense petals notched along the outer edge. The leaves are spread along the ground either immediately from the root or from the bottom of the stem; they are scarcer on the rest of the stem, with the jagged edges of *Hedypnois* <note>a type of wild endive</note>, hairy on both sides, and with a heavy scent. The seeds are long and thin, with down.

We have observed it in various gardens: and we ourselves had it flowering in July and August in the garden of S.P. at Montbéliard.

### CHONDRILLA WITH AN UNDIVIDED LEAF, and a leafy stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla with non-dissected leaves and a leafy stem.</image-desc>

It is anchored by a long, thick root, swollen with milky juice and divided into several heads: it sends out many leaves, a palm's breadth or longer, about half an inch wide, similar to the leaves of narrow-leaved Plantain, pointed, smooth, thick, like the Blue Chondrilla and of nearly the same color. The stems are numerous, rush-like, nine inches or a foot high, smooth, spongy, usually bare of leaves, and sometimes, as we show in this illustration, leafy; they are mostly divided into two branches: upon each sits one large yellow flower, vanishing into downy tufts, to which the thin, long, dark and reddish seeds adhere.

We found it around Chur in the Grisons <note>original: "Curiam Rhaetorum"</note>, flowering in June.

### LAMPSANA OR LAPSANA, THE NIPPLE-WORT: German: *Hederich*: French: *Lampsana*: Italian: *Lampsana*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lampsana plant with broad, lobed leaves and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

It pours out a bitter milk when wounded, whether in the root (which is white and a finger's thickness), or in the stems (which it raises above a cubit, hairy, reddish, branched, and hollow), or finally in the leaves, which are shaped like the plant called Winter-cress <note>original: "Barbareae"</note>, but are softish and hairy. The flowers are star-shaped, yellow, like Hawkweed but small, which similarly turn into downy tufts.

By Ruellius it is called the *Chrysolachanum* <note>Golden-vegetable</note> of Pliny; by some *Napium* or *Wild Turnip*. To Gesner it is related to the *Sonchus* <note>Sow-thistle</note>, and to Gerard it is the *Wild Sow-thistle*.

It grows everywhere frequently on ruins, rubble, and the edges of walls and gardens.

It dries, cleanses, and digests: and it heals ulcerated nipples when applied to them; and because of this peculiar efficacy, it obtained the name "Nipple-wort" <note>original: "papillaris"</note>. More in the Appendix.

<keywords>Chondrilla, Nipple-wort, Lampsana, botanical classification, medicinal herbs, Montpellier, Montbéliard, Chur, 16th-century botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### HAWKWEED OR HAWKWEEDS: German: Hawk-weed <note>original: "Habichs Kraut"</note>; French: Hawk-herb <note>original: "Herbe à l'Espervier"</note>; Italian: Hawkweed <note>original: "Hieracio"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with jagged, lobed leaves and a single flowering stem at the top.</image-desc>

Regarding Hawkweed according to the opinion of the Ancients, and concerning its names and ambiguous terms <term>Equivocals: terms that might refer to multiple different species</term>, we treat these generally in the Appendix. Here, however, we shall set forth the various differences and varieties observed both by us and by others.

The Hawkweed we depict here is beautiful: the root is not large, with several somewhat thick fibers; the leaves, in their jagged edges, shape, and hairiness, very closely resemble Wild Chicory, and the higher they grow, the smaller they become. There is a single stem, straight, grooved, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, and hairy, clothed with leaves arising alternately which have a broad base with "wings" but no stalk. The flowers at the summit are numerous, each on its own small stalk, yellow, turning into downy tufts <term>pappos: the fluffy seed heads like those of a dandelion</term>. It flowers in May.

### HAIRY YELLOW HAWKWEED: by others called Hairy Yellow Chicory.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed with deeply serrated leaves and multiple flower buds on a branching stem.</image-desc>

In its entire appearance, it is very close to Wild Chicory: it has thick, long, fibrous roots that pour out a bitter milk. From these rise several stems, one or two cubits high, hollow with many branches <note>original: "alis," literally wings or side-branches</note>, channeled, and reddish; at times they are quite hairy, at other times almost smooth and empty. The leaves are similar to those of Chicory; the flowers are each provided with their own stalks, shaped like the flowers of Nipplewort <note>original: "Lamp-sanæ"</note>, yellow, passing from a hairy, channeled head into downy tufts. The seed is tiny, grooved, and dark.

### A SMALL SPECIES OF HAWKWEED: by some called Rough Narrow-leaved Pig-succory <note>original: "Hioseris angustifolia aspera"</term>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Hieracium with thin, narrow leaves and three distinct flower heads.</image-desc>

It is gifted with a tiny but somewhat thick little root, appearing somewhat cut off as if it had been bitten off <note>a reference to "Devil's bit" roots</note>, adorned with many fibers. It has long, narrow, hairy leaves spread out on the ground; two or three smooth stems spring from the root, not much more than a palm's breadth long, usually divided into two branches toward the top. On the ends of these sits a single flower, yellow, full, quite large; the whole plant has a bitter taste. By Tabernaemontanus <note>a famous 16th-century herbalist</note> it is called Narrow-leaved Pig-succory.

It greatly loves [sunny] places, and is also frequently found in sandy soil and along roadsides.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY HAWKWEED WITH ROCKET-LIKE LEAVES <note>original: "Erucæ folio," referring to Eruca or Arugula</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, deeply lobed (eruca-like) leaves and a large, thistle-like flower head.</image-desc>

It rises with a single stem to the height of a foot, entirely hairy, clothed with leaves that are also hairy, one to six inches long, of an ash-gray color, with jagged edges like Chicory or Rocket, and the tip of the leaf is almost triangular. At the top of the stem is a single, rather large, golden flower.

### SMOOTH YELLOW HAWKWEED: by others called Smooth Yellow Chicory.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed with smooth, lobed leaves and several flower heads.</image-desc>

This differs from the preceding one only in its smoothness, or because it is less hairy. Both abound in Geneva, Montpellier, and other places, as well as in Basel on the way to the mountain and near the Birs river. They flower in March, April, and May, and sometimes even in October. This illustration is from Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, and is presented by him as the "Hedypnois" of Pliny; the preceding one, however, is from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs</note>.

### BEAUTIFUL BRANCHING HAWKWEED, hairy, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branching Hieracium with hairy stems and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

The whole plant is hairy, especially on the outer branches where the hairs are longer. We saw it at Heidelberg, in the garden of Sprenger, a distinguished pharmacist and botanist, flowering in June.

Furthermore, according to Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note>, both types of Hawkweed have a cooling and moderately binding <term>astringent</term> power; therefore, it helps the stomach and is conveniently applied to inflammations. But if the juice is swallowed, it soothes gnawing pains of the stomach. Pliny attributes the same properties to it. Concerning its powers according to the opinion of more recent authors, see the following pages.

<sig>R 4</sig>

### BROAD-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED,
### with leaves like the Greater Montpellier Fleabane, and a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with broad, serrated leaves and multiple flower heads on a single stalk, showing the root system.</image-desc>

We observed this in the mountains around Geneva, flowering in June and July, and ripening its seed in August.

Modern writers, following Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the standard botanical text for 1,500 years</note>, attribute a "cold" temperament to the Hawkweeds. Because of this, they say it is especially beneficial for all burning fevers and inflammations, and particularly for abscesses and piercing pains in the chest: provided that either the juice or the water is drunk somewhat frequently, or if it is applied using linen cloths; for this reason, it is called the "Abscess-herb" <note>original: "Apostematicam"</note>.

Eye-washes <term>Collyria: medicinal lotions or drops for the eyes</term> prepared from the same water also disperse dimness of vision and spots on the eyes. It is also common for simple women <note>original: "mulierculæ," often referring to laypeople or folk-healers</note> to wash their faces with this water to rub out blemishes, so that they may obtain a pure and spotless countenance.

### ALPINE HAWKWEED WITH HAIRY LEAVES,
### with a yellow Hawkweed flower: according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine Hieracium with a hairy stem and leaves, featuring a large, solitary composite flower head and a thick rhizome.</image-desc>

To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note> this is the *5th Pannonian Alpine Hawkweed*. It is found on the grassy ridges of the Alps, where it flowers in July and August. In gardens, however, it flowers in May and perfects its seed in June.

To Gaspard Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is the *5th Mountain Hawkweed, hoary with hairiness*. To Camerarius in his garden catalog, the *5th Pannonian Hawkweed*. To Gerard, *Clusius’s 5th Pannonian Hawkweed*. To Tabernaemontanus, the *Broad-leaved Mountain Hawkweed*.

### HAWKWEED WITH HEADS LIKE BLESSED THISTLE,
### the largest kind, called by some Viper's Bugloss-like.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, robust Hieracium species with large, prickly-looking flower heads resembling thistle buds and long, wavy-edged leaves.</image-desc>

It is supported by a many-forked root, a finger's breadth thick, white, and pouring out a bitter milk. The stalk is two cubits high <note>about 3 feet</note>, matching the thickness of the root; it is streaked, reddish, and bristling with very dense, sharp, rigid spines—though these easily break off the stalk—and it likewise pours out a milky juice from any wound. It is branched with many arms; the leaves are wavy like Bugloss, long, and bristling with threatening spines. The flowers are like Hawkweed, turning saffron-colored, ending in downy fluff <term>pappum: the feathery hairs on seeds like a dandelion</term>, emerging from a channeled cup with bristly scales.

It is an annual plant, sowing itself; it flowers in June and July, as we have observed at Montbéliard, Basel, Heidelberg, and elsewhere, in our own gardens and those of others.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED PANNONIAN HAWKWEED
### of Clusius, spotted and non-spotted.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pannonian Hieracium with broad basal leaves (some showing spots) and a tall stem with a few flower heads.</image-desc>

Clusius has three kinds of Pannonian <note>from Pannonia, a Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note> Hawkweed: two broad-leaved and one narrow-leaved. Of these, we depict the first broad-leaved one here, which most closely approaches the Greater Mouse-ear or Yellow Lungwort. It has five or six leaves spread on the ground, somewhat wavy around the edges, sometimes even jagged, soft, hairy, and very often marked with blackish spots, though sometimes not at all. Its flower is similar to the flower of the *Hedypnois* <note>a type of wild chicory</note>, but paler.

It is found, says Clusius, in many of the grassy and sunny mountain locations and artificial meadows of Hungary, Upper Austria, and Moravia. It flowers in May.

### STARRY HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Hieracium stellatum, showing a branched stem with multiple small flower heads and elongated, slightly toothed leaves.</image-desc>

It rises to a height of a cubit, with thin, branched, and hairy little stalks. The leaves of the first sprouting are like *Hedypnois*, somewhat wavy and hairy. The flowers are simple, small, like Nipplewort, and yellow; these are succeeded by the radiated stars of the seeds, which are hairy and afterwards curve inward like a sickle. The whole plant pours out milk.

By Lobelius and others, it is inserted as the *Narbonne Hawkweed with a sickle-shaped pod*. Truly related to this is Cesalpino’s *Rhagadiolus*, called *Ragaggiolo* in Tuscany, which is eaten raw in meals, like Chicory.

It abounds in rich soils around Montpellier and around Bologna.

### ROUGH HAWKWEED, WITH COLTSFOOT FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rough Hieracium with many small flower heads on slender branches, resembling the flowers of coltsfoot.</image-desc>

This has many things in common with the preceding plant. To Thalius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Gaspard Bauhin, it is *Yellow Chicory* and *Wild Chicory with a yellow flower*. To Tragus, the *3rd and 4th Chicory with a yellow flower*.

It grows everywhere at Montbéliard and in various other places, along the edges of fields and vineyards, flowering in the months of July, August, September, and October.
