# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALLER HAWKWEED WITH A BITTEN-OFF ROOT, Or the Smaller Hawkweed of Fuchs. <note>original: "Hieracium minus Fuchsii"; Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566) was a founding father of German botany.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with a distinct "bitten-off" (praemorsa) root system, thin stems, and several composite flower heads.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is fibrous, appearing blackish at the bottom where it is "bitten off" <note>The term "praemorsa" refers to roots that end abruptly, looking as if the tip was bitten off by a devil or animal, a common botanical descriptor of the era.</note>, while the rest is whitish and swollen with milky sap. It bears yellow, leafy *flowers*. It varies significantly in the size and diversity of its jagged leaf edges. To Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590), an influential herbalist.</note> and many others, this is the *Smaller Hawkweed of Dioscorides*. Could it be the *Hare's Lettuce of Apuleius* mentioned by Anguillara?

It grows very frequently around Basel, as well as in the meadows near the Arve river in Geneva. It blooms in June, July, and August.

### A VARIETY OF THE SAVOY HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Hieracium Sabaudum, showing a more robust stem with numerous lanceolate leaves and multiple flower buds at the apex.</image-desc>

The plant called Savoy Hawkweed <note>original: "Hieracium sabaudum"</note> varies greatly, not only in its stems—which are sometimes taller than a cubit <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 cm.</note>—but also in its leaves, where there is great variation or "playfulness" of form, as is apparent from the images displayed here.

### LONG-STEMMED AND LONG-ROOTED HAWKWEED: with the yellow flower of Succory-Gum. <note>original: "Hieracium Macrocáulon et Macrorhizon: flore Hedypnoidis luteo."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium with a long, thick taproot and basal rosette of leaves, with branching stems bearing flowers.</image-desc>

By Tabernaemontanus it is called *Endive-like Hawkweed*. By Caspar Bauhin, *Hawkweed with Dandelion leaves and an oblong root*. By Gerard, *Hypocharis, Swine's Succory, and Long-rooted Hawkweed*. Could it be the *Apargia of Theophrastus*? Why Tabernaemontanus calls it *Stinging Hawkweed* <note>original: "Hieracium vnticante"</note> we do not know, since in his description he makes it branched, and the illustration also indicates this.

We have observed it on the walls at Geneva, and in the meadows at Montpellier, blooming in May.

<column-break/>

### UPRIGHT STIFF HAWKWEED, Known to some as Savoy Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, upright botanical specimen with a stiff stem and serrated leaves, topped with several flower heads.</image-desc>

It rises to two cubits with hairy, stiff, reddish stems, which branch out at the top into several shoots; each of these supports a single yellow flower, like that of the common Hawkweed. The *leaves* are stiffer than all other Hawkweed leaves, curved with stiff little teeth, hairy, dark green, and placed alternately along the stem. The *root* is hard and provided with long fibers.

### ANOTHER VARIETY OF SAVOY HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Hieracium Sabaudum, featuring broader, more deeply toothed leaves and a cluster of flower heads.</image-desc>

Guilandinus [followed by Lacuna, Lonicer, and others] believed the Savoy Hawkweed to be the *Erinus* of Mattioli, and that it was called *Military plant* <note>original: "Militarem"</note> by Galen and *Milk-weed* <note>original: "Lactaridem"</note> by Pliny. But, if Colonna and Lobel are to be believed, the plant Mattioli depicts—a small, flowerless thing—is not *Erinus*, and no one has ever seen it except as he drew it. Rather, they suggest it is a somewhat impudent fabrication of a commentator; the learned shall judge.

### NODDING-FLOWERED HAWKWEED: or Hawkweed with a drooping flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium species characterized by nodding or drooping flower heads (flore nutante) and a basal rosette.</image-desc>

This is the *Hawkweed with the appearance of Succory-Gum* according to Lobel. It is called the *Smallest Hawkweed of Clusius* and the *Smaller Hawkweed with a nodding head* by Caspar Bauhin; Tabernaemontanus and Gerard call it *Male Swine's Succory*.

We have seen it at Montpellier, Basel, and Montbéliard, blooming in March and April.

It highlights the Savoy Hawkweed and species with "bitten-off" or long roots, noting their locations in Basel, Geneva, and Montpellier.</summary>
<keywords>Hawkweed, Hieracium, Savoy Hawkweed, botanical nomenclature, Mattioli, Caspar Bauhin, Tabernaemontanus, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany, Basel, Geneva</keywords>

# OF PLANTS.

### GREATER BROAD-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with broad, serrated leaves and several flower heads on a branched stem.</image-desc>

Almost all authors record it under this name. We do not know why Gerard calls it the *Spanish Gum-succory with a purple flower* <note>original: "Chondrillam Hispanicam flore purpureo"</note>, since he uses the illustration of Tabernæmontanus, who identifies it as a German plant and attributes yellow flowers to it.

It has leaves that are long, broad, curled, grayish-white, and covered in a stiff down, etc. It is an inhabitant of the highest peaks of the Harz Mountains <note>original: "Herciniæ"</note>.

### BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED with a bitten-off root and a single stalk, related to the Greater Mouse-ear.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick, "bitten-off" root, basal leaves, and a single stem branching into multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is fibrous and "bitten-off" <note>A botanical term for a root that ends abruptly, appearing as if the end were severed or bitten</note>. The leaves are about a span long and an inch wide: some are longer, others shorter; some are gifted with very short and barely visible hairs on the margin, while others have obvious hairs. There is a single stalk, leafless, supporting many yellow flowers crowded at the top, which eventually turn into downy tufts; at each division of the stalk, there is a thin, narrow little leaf. It loves the woods.

### ROUND-LEAVED HAWKWEED OF NARBONNE, with a leafless stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded basal leaves and two leafless stalks bearing flower heads.</image-desc>

Immediately from the root, it sends out leaves on winged stalks, eight or ten in number, more or less; these are round, notched around the edge, but gifted with harmless little points like stings; they are smooth and lack any distinct taste. From the center of these leaves, two rush-like little stalks emerge, scarcely longer than a hand's breadth, naked like those of the Dandelion <note>original: "Dente leonis"</note>. The tops of these support a yellow flower, smaller than that of the aforementioned plant, but turning into an elegant, pale, yellowish down <note>term: "pappus" (the feathery bristles on seeds like a dandelion)</note>. The seed is tiny, long, reddish, and streaked.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium with smooth, broad leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

This plant enjoys the same birthplaces as the preceding one and, like it, flowers in May. However, its root is smaller, and the leaves are narrower and a little shorter. The lower leaves are also provided with a longer stalk; the others lack a stalk and embrace the stem. All parts are tender and soft. The stem branches into five, six, or seven stalks, upon each of which sits a single yellow flower, equal to the flowers of the preceding plant but a little smaller. The whole plant is bitter.

### MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED with a jagged, downy leaf, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply lobed (laciniate) basal leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

By Tabernæmontanus it is called *Narrow-leaved mountain Hawkweed with Succory leaves*. By Clusius, in his Pannonian history and later works, it is called *Mountain Hawkweed with a jagged leaf*. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is listed as *Hawkweed 13, with a jagged downy leaf*.

Clusius observed it growing in Leytemberg and flowering in June. We have found it in the high mountains of Lorraine <note>original: "Lotharingiæ"</note>.

### HAWKWEED OF NARBONNE, with a leafless stalk and a jagged, hairy leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with hairy, sinuate leaves and several leafless stalks bearing flower heads.</image-desc>

It relies on a root that is dark on the outside and white within, sending down many fibers. The leaves are a span or longer, half an inch wide, jagged, and hairy. The stalks are a foot, a foot and a half, or a cubit high; they are thin, streaked, unbranched, hairy, and hollow. The flower is like that of a Dandelion, with a hairy cup <note>term: "calyce" (the green outer part of the flower head)</note>.

It grows everywhere in the meadows of Geneva and Montbéliard, flowering in May, June, and July.

--- Page 386 ---
### IMAGES AND OUTLINE SKETCHES.

### SMALL HAIRY HAWKWEED, with a leafless stem, curled when dried.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small hawkweed plant with a single flowering stem, basal leaves, and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

It raises a simple stem a foot high, rough to the touch and solitary: upon its summit is placed a single yellow flower, which vanishes into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos"</note>. There are many leaves from a slender root, spread across the ground, dense, and with a stiff down that somewhat imitates little thorns; they are hairy and grayish-white, an inch and a half or two inches long, sufficiently broad, with the division of the Purple Rocket <term>Eruca</term> <note>A type of mustard or rocket plant</note> as it is called by us, and these appear curled when dried. The root is thick.

We received it dried from Montpellier.

---

### HEDYPNOIS OR LION'S TOOTH: German: *Pfaffenrorlin, Pfaffenblatt*; Belgian: *Pappencruyt*; French: *Dent de Lion*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dandelion-like plant with deeply lobed (runcinate) leaves and a single flower head on a leafless stalk.</image-desc>

Various names are attributed to this plant by authors. Some label it the *Hedypnois* of Pliny, others the *Aphaca* <term>Aphaca</term> of Theophrastus (concerning which, see the Appendix), the smaller Hawkweed <term>Hieracium</term>, a species of *Chondrilla*, some a species of wild Chicory <term>Cichorium</term>, others the *Sonchites* of Dioscorides, others *Urinaria* <note>referring to its diuretic properties, hence the common name "piss-a-bed"</note>; the apothecaries call it *Taraxacon* <term>Taraxacon</term>. Others call it *Heliotropium*; others, from its time of flowering, the March flower; others, from its color, the yolk-colored flower [ *Eierblumen* ]; others, because the tops of the stalks are similar to shaved heads, Monk’s Head [ *Münchkopf* and *pfaffenblatt* ]; others, from the shape of the leaves, Lion's Tooth <term>Dens leonis</term>; and finally others, because it seems to belong to the wild lettuces due to its form and milky juice, call it the Wandering Lettuce <term>Lactuca erraticam</term>.

It grows in gardens, in fields, near hedges, and on the ruined walls of buildings; as well as in vineyards, meadows, and orchards.

---

### MOUSE-EAR, PILOSELLA: German: *Nagel-kraut, Meussöhrlin*; Belgian: *Nagelcruyt, Muys-oor*; French: *Pilosella*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mouse-ear hawkweed with oval, hairy leaves and a single flower stalk.</image-desc>

Mouse-ear <term>Pilosella</term> is hardly hidden from anyone, reclining on the ground and repeatedly propagating new offspring through low-lying fibers and creeping, hairy shoots. The leaves are covered in hairs, similar to the ears of mice, green above and grayish-white beneath; the flowers are like those of the Lion's Tooth, but smaller, yellow or golden, with the outermost edges turning purple, with a hairy dark calyx, and flying away in downy seeds. The roots are numerous and thin, but cling tenaciously to the ground.

It grows in thin and arid soil, on hills and uncultivated places, on the grassy borders of fields, and everywhere along the roads. It flowers chiefly in the months of May and June.

It is strange, however, that the Ancients did not remember this most well-known herb, nor gave it any name. More recent writers call it *Pilosella* from the copious hairs <note>Latin: "pilis"</note> with which both the little stems and the leaves are clothed.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED, with an oblong, undivided leaf: the 6th of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain hawkweed with long, narrow, slightly toothed leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

This varies with leaves that are sometimes not divided, and sometimes with leaves somewhat jagged on the sides; and with a yellow flower that is more or less reddish. But all parts of the plant are full of milky juice and have a somewhat bitter taste.

It loves mountains and flowers in May. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> reports that it grows in all those mountains extending from Kahlenberg overlooking the Danube to the Alps: we, however, have observed it in various mountains of Alsace.

---

### MONTPELLIER HEDYPNOIS, OR Montpellier Lion's Tooth.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Montpellier dandelion with a thick root, basal leaves, and a branched flowering stalk.</image-desc>

From a somewhat thick root rises a stem a palm high, which through cultivation even becomes a cubit or two cubits high; it is somewhat thick, hollow, and divided a little above the root into three, four, or five branches: each of which bears a single large, fragrant flower of the common *Hedypnois*. It is reddish on the outside but otherwise yellow, and finally vanishes into downy seeds. It grows at Montpellier in meadows, walls, and dry places: and it flowers in the months of April and May, as well as in Autumn.

Furthermore, Lion's Tooth is astringent, strengthening, and cleansing; it is of a cold temperature, and it effectively provides all those things which Hawkweed <term>Hieracium</term> does, the powers of which were described previously. Its more tender and white shoots are eaten in salads or put into broths. More in the Appendix.

---

### SMALLER MOUSE-EAR WITH NARROWER, less hairy leaf, creeping.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, creeping variety of mouse-ear hawkweed with narrower leaves.</image-desc>

This also creeps remarkably with leaves scattered along the ground, which are narrower, smaller, and smooth both below and above, if you except certain rare hairs situated on the opposite leaf; the lower leaves are somewhat round, the upper ones longer. The stems are taller, sometimes higher than a cubit, not without leaves, and divided into several stalks near the top: where there are two, three, or four flowers, yellow like the other variety, but smaller.

In Camerarius's <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, German physician and botanist</note> *Hortus* it is called the "Creeping Wild Little Lettuce," wavering between a Hawkweed <term>Hieracium</term> and a wild lettuce, and is bitter. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is "Lettuce 14, the Wild Little Lettuce of Camerarius."

It grows everywhere in the woods; flowering in May and June.

# OF PLANTS.

### GREATER BROAD-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed plant with broad, serrated leaves and multiple flower heads on a branched stem.</image-desc>

Almost all authors record it under this name: nor do we know why Gerard calls it the *Purple-flowered Spanish Succory* <note>original: "Chondrillam Hispanicam flore purpureo"</note>, since he uses the illustration of Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590), a famous German botanist</note>, who identifies it as a German plant and attributes yellow flowers to it.

It has long, broad, curled leaves, grayish-white in color, covered with a stiff down, etc. It is an inhabitant of the Harz Mountains <note>original: "Herciniæ," referring to the ancient Hercynian Forest region of Germany</note>.

### BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED with a bitten-off root, a single stem, related to the Greater Mouse-ear.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed plant showing a thick, "bitten-off" (praemorsa) root system, a basal rosette of leaves, and a single stem branching at the top into several flower heads.</image-desc>

This plant has a fibrous and "bitten-off" root <term>praemorsa: a root that looks as if the end has been bitten off, typical of certain species like Devil's-bit Scabious</term>; the leaves are about a span long <note>roughly 9 inches</note> and an inch wide: but some are longer, others shorter, and some are provided with very short and barely visible hairs on the margin, while others have obvious ones. There is a single stem, leafless, supporting many yellow flowers crowded at the top, which eventually turn into downy tufts; at each division of the stem, there is a thin, narrow little leaf. It loves the woods.

### ROUND-LEAVED HAWKWEED OF NARBONNE, with a leafless stem.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a basal rosette of rounded leaves and several leafless stalks (scapes) ending in flower heads.</image-desc>

Immediately from the root, it sends out leaves on winged stalks, eight or ten in number, more or less; they are round, notched around the edge, but provided with harmless little points like stings; they are smooth and lack any distinct taste. From the center of these, two rush-like stalks emerge, scarcely longer than a palm's breadth, naked like those of the Dandelion <note>original: "Dente leonis"</note>: the tops of which support a yellow flower, smaller than that of the aforementioned plant, but turning into an elegant, pale downy head. The seed is tiny, long, reddish, and streaked.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed with smooth, broad leaves that appear to clasp the stem (amplexicaul), and several flower heads.</image-desc>

It enjoys the same birthplaces as the preceding one, and like it, blooms in May. However, its root is smaller, and the leaves are narrower and a little shorter; the lower ones are also provided with a longer stalk, while the rest lack a stalk and clasp the stem: all parts are indeed tender and soft. The stem branches into five, six, or seven small stalks, upon each of which sits a single yellow flower, equal to the flowers of the preceding plant but a little smaller. The whole plant is bitter.

### MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED with jagged downy leaves, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply lobed (laciniate) basal leaves and a single flower head on a long, slightly hairy stalk.</image-desc>

It is called by Tabernaemontanus the *Narrow-leaved Mountain Hawkweed* with Chicory-like leaves: by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note> in his Pannonian and later histories as the *Mountain Hawkweed with a jagged leaf*: and by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* as the *Hawkweed with a jagged downy leaf*.

Clusius observed it growing in Leithagebirge <note>original: "Leytemberg," a mountain range on the border of Austria and Hungary</note> and blooming in June. We have found it in the high mountains of Lorraine <note>original: "Lotharingiæ"</note>.

### HAWKWEED OF NARBONNE, with a leafless stem and hairy, wavy leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hawkweed with hairy, sinuate (wavy-edged) leaves and multiple leafless stalks bearing flower heads.</image-desc>

It relies on a root that is dark on the outside and white within, sending down many fibers: the leaves are a span long or more, half an inch wide, wavy-edged, and hairy: the stalks are a foot, a foot and a half, or a cubit high, thin, streaked, unbranched, hairy, and hollow: the flower is like that of a Dandelion, with a hairy cup <note>calyx</note>.

It grows everywhere in meadows around Geneva and Montbéliard, blooming in May, June, and July.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALL HAIRY HAWKWEED, with a leafless stem, curled when dried.
<note>original: "Hieracium parvum hirtum, caule aphyllo, crispum ubi siccatum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with a single flowering head, basal rosette of leaves, and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It raises a simple stem a foot high, rough to the touch and solitary: at the top of which is placed a single yellow flower, vanishing into downy seeds <note>pappus</note>: *many leaves from a slender root, scattered along the ground, dense, and with a stiff down somewhat imitating little thorns, hairy and grayish-white, an inch and a half or two inches long, sufficiently broad, with the division of the "Purple Rocket" <note>original: "Erucæ purpureæ"</note> as named by us, and these appear curled when dried.* The root is thick.

We received a dried specimen from Montpellier <note>original: "Monspelio"</note>.

---

### HEDYPNOIS OR DANDELION: German *Pfaffenrohr* <note>Priest's pipe</note>, *Pfaffenblatt* <note>Priest's leaf</note>: Belgian *Pappencruyt*: French *Dent de Lion*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dandelion (Taraxacum/Hedypnois) showing the characteristic jagged leaves, hollow stalks, and flowering heads at various stages.</image-desc>

Various names are attributed to this plant by Authors. Some label it the *Hedypnois* of Pliny, others the *Aphaca* of Theophrastus (about which see the Appendix), some the *Lesser Hawkweed*, a *species of Chondrilla*, and a *species of wild Chicory*; others the *Sonchites* of Dioscorides, others *Urinaria* <note>referring to its diuretic properties</note>; in the apothecary shops *Taraxacon*: others *Heliotropium*: others, from its time of flowering, *March flower*, others from its color, yolk-colored flower [*Egg-flowers*:] others, because the tops of the stalks are similar to shaven heads, *Monk's head* [*Münchkopf* & *pfaffenblatt*:] others from the shape of the leaves, *Lion's tooth*: and finally others, because it seems to belong to the wild lettuces by its shape and milky juice, *Wandering Lettuce*.

It grows in gardens, in fields, near hedges, and on the ruinous walls of buildings: as well as in vineyards, meadows, and pleasure gardens.

### MOUSE-EAR, PILOSELLA: German *Nagelkraut* <note>Nail-herb</note>, *Meussöhrlin* <note>Little mouse-ear</note>: Belgian *Nagelcruyt*, *Muys-oor*: French *Piloselle*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pilosella (Mouse-ear hawkweed) with stolons/runners, hairy leaves, and a single flower head.</image-desc>

Hardly anyone is unaware of the *Pilosella*, lying low on the ground, and repeatedly propagating new offspring by sending down fibers from creeping, hairy shoots: *leaves covered in hairs, similar to mouse ears, green above, grayish-white below; flowers like the Dandelion, smaller, yellow or golden, with purplish tips, the cup <note>calyx</note> hairy and dark, and flying away in downy seeds: the roots are numerous, thin, but clinging tenaciously to the ground.*

We <unclear>found</unclear> it growing in <unclear>sunny</unclear> soil, in <unclear>pastures</unclear> <unclear>limy</unclear> <unclear>mountainous</unclear> <unclear>dry</unclear> <unclear>hard</unclear>.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED, with an oblong, undivided leaf: the 6th of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Hieracium with long, narrow, undivided leaves and a thick rootstock.</image-desc>

This varies with leaves sometimes not divided, and sometimes with leaves somewhat jagged on the sides; and with a yellow flower more or less reddish: But all parts of the plant are full of milky juice, and of a somewhat bitter taste.

It loves mountains, and flowers in May. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> reports it grows in all those mountains running from Galemberg overlooking the Danube to the Alps: We, however, have observed it in various mountains of Alsace.

### MONTPELLIER HEDYPNOIS, OR Montpellier Dandelion.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mediterranean variety of Hedypnois with smaller, more upright flower buds and a distinct basal rosette.</image-desc>

From a somewhat thick root rises a stem a palm high, which through cultivation even becomes a cubit or two cubits high, somewhat thick, hollow, divided a little above the root into three, four, or five branches: each of which bears a single large, fragrant flower of the common Hedypnois, reddish on the outside, otherwise yellow, and finally vanishing into downy seeds. It grows at Montpellier in seaside meadows and dry places: and it flowers in the months of April and May, as well as in Autumn.

Furthermore, the Dandelion is astringent, <unclear>and it binds wounds</unclear>, <unclear>it strengthens and cleanses</unclear>, <unclear>and it is digestive</unclear> <unclear>and provides a peculiar power</unclear> <unclear>with all efficacy</unclear> <unclear>so that</unclear> <unclear>with the juice of the Hawkweed</unclear> <unclear>the power of the root, either raw or cooked, crushed and taken in place of food, is accustomed to be used for sexual desire</unclear> <unclear>and the instinct of Venus</unclear> <note>original: "veneris"</note> <unclear>Paracelsus also praises it</unclear>.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of salad plants and thistles, following the previous discussions on chicory and endive varieties. The catchword "SONCHVS" (Sow-thistle) indicates the transition to the next major genus described.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### CURLY CULTIVATED ENDIVE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a curly-leafed endive plant (Intybum sativum crispum) showing its dense, ruffled foliage and fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Cultivated Endive is made *larger* or *smaller* depending on the soil and cultivation: but the *curly* variety is produced by the transplantation and <term>husbandry</term> <note>original: "mangonio," referring to the skillful manipulation or "doctoring" of plants by gardeners to achieve desired traits</note> of gardeners; nor is this variety different from the others in any other way.

Endive is sown in gardens, and that which is sown in the Spring grows up quickly, and flowering in the Summer itself, produces seeds and then dies away. However, that which is sown in July remains into the Winter; having been buried in the earth in September or October, with the leaves first tied together, it is rendered white as snow <note>This refers to the process of "blanching" to make the leaves less bitter</note>, and then in the Winter months it is brought to the table in place of other salad herbs.

### SMOOTH LOBED SOW-THISTLE, OR THE NON-prickly kind.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smooth sow-thistle (Sonchus laciniatus laevis) with deeply lobed leaves and several flower heads at the top of a tall stalk.</image-desc>

It rests upon a small, fibrous, and white root: with a stalk a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, hollow inside, and turning purple. The leaves are long, smooth, almost blue-gray, with the jagged divisions of a Dandelion, full of milk <note>sap</note>; they come forth alternately, sometimes with a long stalk, sometimes with none, but embracing the stem with a broader base, appearing as if toothed around the edges, armed with either no spines or very soft ones. The flowers are leafy and yellow, but the outermost part of the petals turns purple on the underside. The seed is small, oblong, and reddish-brown.

Cordus calls this the *Smooth* or *Mild Sow-thistle*: but to Fuchs it is the *second kind of Sow-thistle*, more tender and edible and *less dark*, and the *Hare’s Lettuce* of Apuleius. In the *History of Lyon*, it is called *Dalechamp’s smaller Andryala*.

### CREEPING SOW-THISTLE OF MANY; BY SOME called the Greater Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping sow-thistle (Sonchus repens) featuring broad, jagged leaves and multiple flowering stems rising from a thick root.</image-desc>

The flowers of this one are a little larger than the other Sow-thistles, yellow, and held together by a hairy structure of dark green leaves, which finally turn into downy tufts <note>pappus, the fluffy seeds blown by the wind</note>.

It is found in marshy willow-thickets and reed-beds, near fishponds and stagnant waters; it is common everywhere in the fields of Montbéliard and Geneva, and in some gardens it is a hateful nuisance because of its creeping habit. It flowers in July.

In our illustration, which is taken from Fuchs’s works, the creeping root is missing.

<column-break/>

### SOW-THISTLE, CICERBITA: Germ. *Sawdistel*, French *Laicteron, Palais de Lieure*: Ital. *Lattucella, Soncho*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common sow-thistle (Sonchus) with prickly-edged leaves and small flower buds.</image-desc>

By the Greeks it is called <term>sonchos</term> <note>original: σόγχος</note> <term>from the phrase "to pour out health"</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ σῶον χεῖν</note>, that is, because it pours out a wholesome juice. The Romans called it *Cicerbita*, and that name is still retained today in Tuscany.

Theophrastus mentions the Sow-thistle among the prickly-leafed plants, and likewise Galen says the *Sow-thistle* is among the prickly plants: but only after it has reached full maturity. Pliny makes two kinds, the *white* and the *black*, both similar to Lettuce, were they not prickly. Indeed, Dioscorides seems to have mentioned three: namely the wild and more prickly kind, another softer and edible kind, and a third tree-like kind with a broad leaf.

We here depict the Sow-thistle that is less lobed and more prickly or rough with a yellow flower, belonging to the Hawkweeds: we shall discuss the remaining differences observed by us in the following pages.

### PRICKLY LOBED SOW-THISTLE, ROUGH Sow-thistle, Rough Cicerbita.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a prickly sow-thistle (Sonchus laciniatus spinosus) showing sharp, spiny margins on the leaves and clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

Almost all writers have mentioned this one. However, Tabernaemontanus makes *three types of smooth lobed Sow-thistle*: the smooth lobed broad-leafed Sow-thistle; a second smooth Sow-thistle with a yellow flower; and a third smooth Sow-thistle with a yellow flower. We have shown in our *Great History* that the writings of Matthiolus and Schwenckfeld regarding these Sow-thistles were quite foolish.

Both the smooth and the rough lobed Sow-thistle grow spontaneously in various places: everywhere around Geneva and Montbéliard, and most frequently in gardens; also outside the city of Basel, between the Stein and Eschen gates. It flowers and thrives even into November.

### BLUE BROAD-LEAFED SOW-THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a blue-flowered sow-thistle (Sonchus caeruleus latifolius) with broad, deeply lobed leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

For this Sow-thistle, which is two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> or higher, the top of the stalk is hairy and bears a cluster of flowers similar to those of the common Sow-thistle, but shining with a blue color, and quickly fading into downy tufts.

We obtained this from Alsace where it grows in the highest mountains in shady places, and it flowers in July and August. We suspect it is the same as Clusius’s *Blue Sow-thistle*.

It reconciles various names used by classical authorities like Pliny and Dioscorides with contemporary botanical observations in regions like Geneva and Basel.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>Rr 4</sig>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sonchus Dendroides Dalechampii, showing a plant with jagged leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

### DALECHAMPS’ TREE-LIKE SOW-THISTLE;
->Related to the Wall Lettuce.<-

This Sow-thistle <note>original: "Sonchus"</note>, if the *History of Lyon* is to be believed, has many things in common with that kind of Sow-thistle which Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> mentions in the third place; the learned shall judge. However, that it also has much in common with the plant called Wall Lettuce, no one, we believe, will deny.

It grows, says Dalechamps <note>Jacques Dalechamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist.</note>, on the rocky slopes of cold mountains.

Furthermore, both types of Sow-thistle are cooling, according to Dioscorides, and moderately astringent; the juice, when applied to a burning stomach and to inflammations, eases the gnawing pains of the stomach. The milky sap flowing from it helps with gatherings <note>swellings or abscesses</note> of the seat and the womb. *Regarding its culinary use, see the side of the following table.*

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sonchis Affinis Terracrepolæ, showing a tall stalk with thistle-like flowers and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

### A SOW-THISTLE RELATED TO THE EARTH-CRACKER;
->or the Earth-cracker.<-

It has a root similar to Endive, small, curved, and white; many stalks, a cubit high, covered in leaves; and leaves similar to Endive, but whiter and less jagged, flowing with a milky juice. The flower is yellow, vanishing into downy fluff <note>pappus</note>.

This wild vegetable is the *Small Hawkweed* of Dioscorides, but the *Crepis* of Theophrastus and Pliny. The country folk of Tuscany call it "Earth-cracker" <note>original: "Terracrepolum"</note>. Perhaps it is the same as Theophrastus’ <unclear>leaf-stemmed plant</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἐπιφυλλόκαυλος</unclear>.

It grows spontaneously on the earthen banks of the Montpellier territory, as well as on the walls of buildings and rocky hills; it is also cultivated in gardens.

This vegetable is eaten raw with oil and vinegar; and because it is sweet and slightly astringent, it is held in high esteem.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chondrilla Lutea, showing a branching plant with small flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

### YELLOW GUM-SUCCORY.

The whole plant, just like the blue variety, swells with a milky juice; and on its smooth and hairless stalk, it has leaves approaching those of the Smooth Sow-thistle, though much smaller, with a division almost like the Blue Gum-succory, their tips resembling a Stork with spread wings vibrating in the air. They are also toothed around the edges, which is worthy of note, so that this plant can be distinguished from the blue or white variety when not in bloom.

From the crook of the leaves, small branches emerge, on each of which sits a single yellow flower, like a Sow-thistle's, vanishing into downy fluff.

It blooms in Montpellier on walls in March; and throughout the whole Summer, it is found in gravelly vineyards and olive groves.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sonchus Lanatus Dalechampii, showing a plant with broad, fuzzy leaves and a flowering head.</image-desc>

### DALECHAMPS’ WOOLLY SOW-THISTLE,
->with the golden flower of Groundsel.<-

The whole plant swells with milky juice, in the manner of Chicory, and is endowed with a bitter taste, but less so than other Chicories, whose properties it also possesses, though more weakly.

It grows in Montpellier near Peraux, in rocky and sunny places, blooming in the month of June. <margin>Pliny’s Soft-wort.</margin> Some call it Soft-wort <note>original: "Mollugo"</note>, yet it is different from the Soft-wort of Pliny.

Furthermore, the common Sow-thistle is frequently used in salads in Winter; and especially the roots, which, since they are tender and sweet, are sought after for the table. Thus Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> used to say of the same. It is eaten green and tender, just like other wild vegetables.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chondrille, showing a slender plant with a long taproot and small flowers along the stem.</image-desc>

### GUM-SUCCORY or CHONDRILLIA: German: Klein Sonnenwirbel; French: Laicteron; Italian: Chondrilla, Terracrepolo.

Galen writes that Gum-succory <note>original: "Chondrilla"</note> is a species of Wild Endive <note>original: "Seridis"</note>; Dioscorides, however, says it is called Chicory by some and Wild Endive by others. He makes two kinds of it, which Pliny confuses with each other, attributing to one what the former gave to two.

Thus, even today, it is not easy to distinguish plants of the Gum-succory genus among writers with certain names; especially since they have not yet accurately examined the history of the Endive-like and Gum-succory-like plants: and they have proposed either their names and descriptions without images, or images without descriptions.

However, a huge abundance of Gum-succory-like plants offers itself almost everywhere, on walls, in vineyards, and in sunny, elevated places. We depict the Blue Gum-succory here.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chondrilla Viminea, showing a plant with many thin, rod-like branches and small flowers.</image-desc>

### TWIGGY GUM-SUCCORY.

First, leaves sprout scattered in a circle along the ground, with the jagged edges of a Dandelion-relative <note>original: "Hedypnoidis"</note>, smooth, which wither as the plant rises into a stalk. The stalk itself is entirely bristly with thick small spines near the ground, and rises to two or three cubits, becoming shrubby with frequent twig-like branches spreading out in various ways, with either no leaves or very few, and those as thin as grass. Yellow flowers, equal to those of Lettuce, cling to the ends of the branches. A round, streaked, oblong, ash-colored seed follows, with a shaggy down attached. The root is a single thumb's thickness, long and pregnant with milky juice.

It grows in fields and at their edges in many regions. It is frequent in various places in Montpellier, at Basel by the Rhine, and elsewhere. It blooms in Summer and Autumn.

# OF PLANTS

### A CERTAIN LOBED PLANT RELATED TO THE GUM-SUCCORIES: Perhaps the *Trinciatella* of Camerarius? <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598) was a famous German physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla plant with deeply lobed (laciniate) leaves and several flower heads on long stems, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This plant is related to the Gum-succories <note>original: *Chondrillis*</note> or the Hawkweeds <note>original: *Hieraciis*</note>. From a thick, long root, several heads emerge, from which grow many leaves two inches long and deeply lobed <note>original: *laciniata*</note>; the tips of these leaves are somewhat round, smooth, and quite thick. The stalks are rush-like, branched, about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, and sometimes smaller. At their tips are solitary flowers, rather large and yellow, which turn into downy seed-heads <note>original: *pappos*</note>. Indeed, the whole herb yields a milky sap.

It flowers near Montpellier <note>original: *Monspelium*</note> in April.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY GUM-SUCCORY WITH REDDISH FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with hairy stems and leaves, showing small flower heads and a thick root.</image-desc>

It has a simple white root, hard, provided with fibers, and yielding milk. The stalks are one to two feet high, solid, milky, thin, streaked, and furnished with individual leaves. Upon each of these stalks sits a single flower on a single stem, of a color between white and purple, densely packed with petals that are notched <note>original: *crenatis*</note> along the outer edge. The leaves spread across the ground either directly from the root or from the bottom of the stalk; they are more sparse on the rest of the stalk, shaped like the lobes of the *Hedypnois* <note>a type of wild chicory</note>, hairy on both sides, and have a heavy scent. The seeds are long and thin, with down.

We have observed it in various gardens, and we ourselves had it flowering in July and August at Montbéliard <note>original: *Montbelgardi*</note> in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>original: *S. P. horto*, likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg's garden</note>.

---

### THE CRETAN GUM-SUCCORY OF SOME AUTHORS: Perhaps the Cretan Hawkweed of Camerarius and Gesner?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla Cretica with jagged, dandelion-like leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

The root is like that of a Dandelion <note>original: *Dentis leonis*</note>. The stalks are rough with small spines and divided into "wings" in a varied and disorderly fashion. The leaves are like those of the Wild Lettuce; the flowers like those of the Sow-thistle <note>original: *Sonchi*</note>. The seed is beautiful and curved, ending in a little rose-shape from a small-toothed base, turning reddish-brown when mature.

It flowers in June and July, and sometimes even in October; it is a short-lived plant. It grew for us in the garden at Montbéliard from seed sent from Crete.

<column-break/>

### GUM-SUCCORY WITH UNDIVIDED LEAVES and a leafy stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with undivided, lance-shaped leaves and several flower heads.</image-desc>

It is anchored by a long, thick root, swollen with milky juice and divided into several heads. It puts forth many leaves, a palm's breadth or longer, about half an inch wide, similar to the leaves of the Narrow-leaf Plantain; they are pointed, smooth, thick, like those of the Blue Gum-succory and nearly the same color. The stalks are numerous, rush-like, nine inches to a foot tall, smooth, spongy, usually bare of leaves, though sometimes leafy as we show in this illustration. They usually divide into two branches, and upon each sits one large yellow flower that vanishes into down, to which the thin, long, streaked, and reddish seeds adhere.

We found it near Chur in Switzerland <note>original: *Curiam Rhætorum*</note>, flowering in June.

---

### GUM-SUCCORY WITH UNDIVIDED LEAVES and a bare stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chondrilla with a leafless flowering stalk and a basal rosette of undivided leaves.</image-desc>

This plant differs from the preceding one only by having a stalk bare of leaves; we received it from Valerand Dourez under the name *Syrian Gum-succory*.

We have reviewed many other varieties of Gum-succory in our great *History*: *Gum-succory with hairy leaves and a single large yellow flower; Gum-succory with a whitish root and small yellow flowers; the Greater and Lesser Gum-succory with a yellow Goat's-beard flower; Gum-succory with a bristly stalk provided with many nodes; Gum-succory with a rough cubit-high stalk and downy flowers; the Lesser Gum-succory with leaves turning red on the back; Gum-succory with leaves armed with small spines around the edge, etc.*

Furthermore, this Gum-succory is of the same temperament as Lettuce. Boiled in wine and drunk, it resists the poison of serpents.

The juice, if taken internally, stops fluxes of the bowels. This juice, as well as the gum that forms around the branches, provokes the menses if inserted into the womb.

<column-break/>

### LAMPSANA OR LAPSANA, THE NIPPLE-WORT: German: *Hederich*; French: *Lampsana*; Italian: *Lampsana*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lampsana plant with broad, lobed lower leaves and small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

When wounded, it pours out a bitter milk, whether from the root (which is white and the thickness of a finger), or from the stalks (which rise above a cubit and are hairy, reddish, branched, and hollow), or finally from the leaves, which are shaped like those of the plant called *Barbarea* <note>Wintercress</note>, but are softish and hairy. The flowers are star-shaped, yellow, like Hawkweed but small, and they similarly turn into down.

By Ruellius it is called the *Chrysolachanum* of Pliny; by some *Napium* or *Wild Turnip*. Gesner calls it a relative of the *Sow-thistle*, and Gerard calls it *Wild Sow-thistle*.

It grows frequently everywhere on walls, in rubble, and at the edges of fields and gardens.

It dries, cleanses, and dissolves <note>original: *digerit*, referring to "digesting" or dispersing humors</note>. Applied to ulcerated nipples, it heals them; and because of this particular efficacy, it obtained the name *Papillaris* <note>Nipple-wort</note>. More on this in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Chondrilla (gum-succory) and Lampsana (nipple-wort), detailing their physical forms, habitats in places like Montpellier and Montbéliard, and their medicinal uses for snakebite and skin ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Chondrilla, Hawkweed, Nipple-wort, Lampsana, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, Montpellier, Montbéliard, Valerand Dourez, herbal medicine</keywords>

# HAWKWEED OR HAWKWEEDS: German: Habichs Kraut; French: Herbe à l'Esperauer. Italian: Hieracio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with a single tall, striated stem, alternating leaves, and several flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

Regarding Hawkweed <note>original: "Hieracio"</note> according to the opinion of the Ancients, and concerning its names and ambiguous terms, we treat these generally in the Appendix. Here, however, we shall set forth the various differences and varieties observed both by us and by others.

The Hawkweed we depict here is beautiful: it has a *root* that is not large, with several somewhat thick fibers; the *leaves* closely resemble Wild Chicory in their jagged edges, shape, and hairiness, and the higher they grow, the smaller they become. There is a single *stem*, straight, grooved, about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, and hairy, clothed with leaves arising alternately which have a broad base with "wings" but no stalk. The *flowers* at the summit are numerous, each on its own little stalk, yellow in color, and turning into downy seed-heads <note>original: "pappos"</note>. It blooms in May.

### HAIRY YELLOW HAWKWEED: called by others Hairy Yellow Chicory.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium with deeply lobed, hairy leaves and multiple flowering stems emerging from a central base.</image-desc>

In its entire appearance, it is very close to Wild Chicory: it has thick, long, fibrous *roots* which pour out a bitter milk. From these rise several *stems*, one or two cubits high, hollow with many branches, channeled, reddish; sometimes they are quite hairy, at other times almost smooth and empty. The *leaves* are similar to those of Chicory. The *flowers* are each provided with their own stalks, shaped like the flowers of Nipplewort <note>original: "Lampasanæ"</note>, yellow, emerging from a channeled, hairy head and turning into down. The *seed* is tiny, grooved, and dark.

### A SMALL SPECIES OF HAWKWEED: called by some Rough Narrow-leaved Swine's-succory.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller species of Hieracium with a thick rootstock and several thin stems ending in single flower heads.</image-desc>

It is gifted with a tiny but somewhat thick *rootlet*, rather succulent, appearing as if it had been bitten off <note>a common botanical description for "praemorse" roots</note>, and adorned with many fibers. The *leaves* are long, narrow, hairy, and spread out upon the ground. There are two or three *stems*, smooth, coming forth from the root, not much longer than a palm's breadth, usually divided into two branches toward the top. Upon the ends of these sits a single *flower*, yellow, full, quite large; the whole plant has a bitter taste. By Tabernaemontanus <note>a famous 16th-century herbalist</note> it is called Narrow-leaved Swine's-succory <note>original: "Hioseris angustifolia"</note>.

It greatly loves groves, and is also frequently found in sandy soil and along roadsides.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY HAWKWEED WITH ROCKET-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium with jagged, thistle-like leaves and large, bristly flower heads.</image-desc>

It rises with a single *stem* to the height of a foot, entirely hairy, clothed with *leaves* that are also hairy, about four to six inches long and ash-colored, with jagged edges like Chicory or Rocket <note>original: "Erucæ"</note>, and the tip of the leaf is almost triangular. The *flower* at the top of the stem is a single, rather large, golden-colored bloom.

### SMOOTH YELLOW HAWKWEED: called by others Smooth Yellow Chicory.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smooth-leaved Hieracium with multiple branching stems and flower buds.</image-desc>

This differs from the preceding one only in its smoothness, or because it is less hairy. Both types abound in Geneva, Montpellier, and other places, as well as in Basel on the way to Montets and near the Birs river. It blooms in March, April, and May, and sometimes even in October. <gloss>This illustration is from Lobelius, and is presented by him as Pliny's "Hedypnois"; the preceding one, however, is from the works of Fuchs.</gloss>

### BEAUTIFUL BRANCHING HAWKWEED, hairy, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branching, hairy Hieracium with multiple flower heads and a thick root.</image-desc>

The whole plant is hairy, and especially so on the outer branches, where the hairs are longer. We saw it blooming in June at Heidelberg, in the garden of Sprenger, a distinguished pharmacist and botanist.

Furthermore, according to Dioscorides, both types of Hawkweed have a cooling and moderately astringent power; for this reason, they are usefully applied to a <unclear>failing</unclear> stomach and to inflammations. But if the juice is sipped, it soothes griping pains of the stomach. Pliny attributes the same properties to it.

*The opinion of modern authors concerning its powers follows in the next section.*

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Hawkweed (Hieracium), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats near cities like Basel and Heidelberg, and their medicinal uses for stomach ailments according to classical authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Hawkweed, Hieracium, Chicory, botany, medicinal herbs, Heidelberg, Geneva, Basel, Dioscorides, Pliny, Lobelius, Leonhart Fuchs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of Hieracium (Hawkweed) species, focusing on broad-leaved and mountain varieties. The translator has maintained the botanical nomenclature used by 16th and 17th-century authorities like Clusius and Bauhin.</meta>

### BROAD-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED,
### with leaves like the Greater Montpellier Fleabane, and a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with broad, serrated leaves and two flowering heads, showing the root system.</image-desc>

We observed this in the mountains around Geneva, flowering in June and July, and ripening its seed in August.

Modern writers, following Dioscoride <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, attribute a cold temperament to the Hawkweeds. Because of this, they say it is especially beneficial for all burning fevers and inflammations, and particularly for abscesses and piercing pains in the chest: provided that either the juice or the distilled water is drunk frequently, or if it is applied using linen cloths; for this reason, it is called "Apostematica" <note>The Abscess-herb</note>.

Eye-washes prepared from the same water also disperse dimness of vision and spots in the eyes. Common women are also accustomed to washing their faces with this water to wipe away blemishes, so that they may achieve a clear and spotless countenance.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED PANNONIAN HAWKWEED
### of Clusius, both spotted and unspotted.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with spotted leaves and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential Flemish botanist</note> describes three kinds of Pannonian <note>From Pannonia, a Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note> Hawkweed: two broad-leaved and one narrow-leaved. Of these, we depict the first broad-leaved type here, which very closely resembles the Greater Mouse-ear or Yellow Lungwort. It has five or six leaves spread upon the ground, somewhat wavy around the edges, sometimes even jagged, soft, hairy, and very often stained with blackish spots, though sometimes not at all. Its flower is similar to the flower of the *Hedypnois* <note>A type of wild chicory or succulent</note>, but paler.

It is found, says Clusius, in many of the grassy mountains and sunny places of Hungary, Upper Austria, and Moravia, as well as in fertile meadows. It flowers in May.

---

<column-break/>

### ALPINE HAWKWEED WITH HAIRY LEAVES,
### with a yellow Hawkweed flower: according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a hairy-leaved alpine Hieracium with a thick root and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

To Clusius, this is the *5th Alpine Pannonian Hawkweed*. It is found on the grassy ridges of the Alps, where it flowers in July and August. In gardens, however, it flowers in May and perfects its seed in June.

To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is the *5th Mountain Hawkweed, hoary with hairiness*. To Camerarius in his garden catalog, the *5th Pannonian Hawkweed*. To Gerard, *Clusius’s 5th Pannonian Hawkweed*. To Tabernaemontanus, the *Broad-leaved Mountain Hawkweed*.

<column-break/>

### STARRED HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium stellatum with deeply lobed leaves and star-like seed heads.</image-desc>

It rises to the height of a cubit <note>About 18 inches</note>, with thin, branched, and hairy stalks. The leaves of the first emerging plant are like *Hedypnois*, somewhat wavy and hairy. The flowers are simple, small, yellow, and like those of Nipplewort; these are followed by the radiated stars of the seeds, which are hairy and afterwards curve inward like a sickle. The whole plant pours out a milky sap.

By Lobelius and others, it is classified as the *Narbonne Hawkweed with sickle-shaped pods*. Related to this is the *Rhagadiolus* of Cesalpino, called *Ragaggiolo* in Tuscany, which is eaten raw in meals like Chicory.

It abounds in rich soils around Montpellier and around Bologna.

---

<column-break/>

### HAWKWEED WITH HEADS LIKE BLESSED THISTLE,
### the largest kind, called by some Bugloss-like Ox-tongue.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Hieracium with prickly, thistle-like flower heads and long leaves.</image-desc>

It is supported by a large, spreading root, a finger's breadth thick, white, and pouring out a bitter milk. The stalk, two cubits high, equals the thickness of the root; it is streaked, reddish, and bristling with very dense, sharp, stiff spines that nevertheless easily break off the stalk. It likewise pours out a milky juice from any wound. It is branched with many arms. The leaves are like Bugloss, wavy, long, and bristling with threatening spines. The flowers are those of a Hawkweed, saffron-colored, turning into downy fluff, emerging from a cup-like base with bristly, channeled scales.

It is an annual plant, sowing itself. It flowers in June and July, as we have observed at Montbéliard, Basel, Heidelberg, and elsewhere, in our own gardens and those of others.

<column-break/>

### ROUGH HAWKWEED, WITH THE FLOWER OF COLTSFOOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rough Hieracium with leaves resembling Tussilago and a single flower head.</image-desc>

This plant has much in common with the preceding one. To Thalius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Caspar Bauhin, it is *Yellow Chicory* and *Wild Chicory with a yellow flower*. To Tragus, it is the *3rd and 4th Chicory with a yellow flower*.

It grows commonly in Montbéliard and various other places, along the edges of fields and vineyards, flowering in the months of July, August, September, and October.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### SMALLER HAWKWEED WITH A BITTEN-OFF ROOT, or Fuchs’s Smaller Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with several flowering heads and a distinct, short, "bitten-off" root system.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is fibrous, appearing blackish where the lower part is bitten off <note>The "bitten-off" appearance of the root is a common botanical descriptor for certain species, often associated with folklore about the devil biting the root.</note>, while the rest is white and swelling with milky sap: the *flowers* are indeed yellow and leafy. It varies significantly in the size and diversity of its jagged edges. To Tabernaemontanus and many others, it is the *Smaller Hawkweed* of Dioscorides. Could it be the *Hare's Lettuce* of Apuleius mentioned by Anguillara?

It grows very frequently around Basel: as well as in Geneva in the meadows near the Arve river. It blooms in June, July, and August.

### A VARIETY OF THE SAVOY HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Hieracium Sabaudum, showing a taller stalk with alternating leaves and multiple flower buds at the top.</image-desc>

The plant called Savoy Hawkweed varies greatly, not only in its stems, which are sometimes taller than a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>, but also in its leaves, in which there is great difference or "play" of nature, as appears from the images displayed here.

### LONG-STEMMED AND LONG-ROOTED HAWKWEED: with the yellow flower of the Succory-Gum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium with a thick stem and a long, substantial taproot, featuring dandelion-like flowers.</image-desc>

By Tabernaemontanus it is called *Chicory-like Hawkweed*. By Caspar Bauhin, *Hawkweed with Dandelion leaves and an oblong root*. By Gerard, *Hypocharis, Swine's-Succory, and Longer-rooted Hawkweed*. Could it be the *Apargia* of Theophrastus? Why it is called *Single-stemmed Hawkweed* by Tabernaemontanus we do not know, since in his description he makes it branched, and the Illustration also indicates this.

We have observed it on the walls at Geneva, and in the meadows at Montpellier, blooming in May.

<column-break/>

### UPRIGHT STIFF HAWKWEED, known to some as Savoy Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rigid, upright Hieracium with hairy stems and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

It rises to two cubits with hairy, stiff, reddish stems, which at the top divide into several shoots, each of which supports a single yellow flower of the common Hawkweed: the *leaves* are stiffer than all other Hawkweed leaves, curved with stiff little teeth, hairy, dark green, and placed alternately: the *root* is hard, provided with long fibers.

### ANOTHER VARIETY OF SAVOY HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Hieracium Sabaudum, showing denser foliage and more numerous flower heads.</image-desc>

Guilandious thought that Savoy Hawkweed was the *Erinus* of Mattioli [followed by Lacuna, Lonicer, and others], and that it was called *Military* by Galen and *Lactaris* by Pliny. But, if Colonna and Lobel are to be believed, the *Erinus* depicted by Mattioli is not this plant—it is a small, flowerless plant that no one has seen except as he drew it: rather, they consider it the invention of an over-bold Commentator; the learned shall judge.

### HAWKWEED WITH DROOPING FLOWERS: or the Nodding-flowered Hawkweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium characterized by nodding or drooping flower heads.</image-desc>

Called *Hawkweed with the appearance of Succory-Gum* by Lobel. *Clusius’s Smallest Hawkweed*, and *Smaller Hawkweed with a drooping head* by Caspar Bauhin; by Tabernaemontanus and Gerard it is called *Male Swine's-Succory*.

We have seen it at Montpellier, Basel, and Montbéliard, blooming in March and April.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Hawkweed (Hieracium), detailing their physical characteristics, blooming seasons, and the conflicting classifications provided by various Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Hawkweed, Hieracium, Savoy Hawkweed, botanical taxonomy, Basel, Geneva, Montpellier, Mattioli, Caspar Bauhin, Tabernaemontanus</keywords>

# OF PLANTS.

### GREATER BROAD-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant with broad, serrated basal leaves and several flowering heads on a branched stalk.</image-desc>

Almost all authors record it under this name: nor do we know why Gerard calls it the Spanish Purple-flowered Gum-succory <note>original: "Chondrillam Hispanicam flore purpureo"</note>, since he uses the illustration of Tabernæmontanus, who identifies it as a German plant and attributes yellow flowers to it.

It has leaves that are long, broad, curled, grayish-white, and covered with a stiff down, etc. It is an inhabitant of the highest peaks of the Harz Mountains <note>original: "Herciniæ"</note>.

### BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED with a bitten-off root, a single stalk, and related to the Greater Mouse-ear.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick, truncated (premorsa) root, a single stalk, and several dandelion-like flower heads.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is fibrous and "bitten off" <note>term: "præmorsa" - a root that ends abruptly as if the bottom has been bitten off, common in species like Devil's-bit Scabious</note>; the leaves are about a palm's length and an inch wide: but some are longer, others shorter, and some are provided with very short and barely visible hairs on the margin, while others are more obvious. It has a single stalk, leafless, supporting many yellow flowers clustered at the top, which eventually turn into downy tufts; at each division of the stalk, there is a thin, narrow little leaf. It loves the woods.

### ROUND-LEAVED NARBONNE HAWKWEED, with a leafless stalk.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded basal leaves and two long, leafless stalks ending in flower heads.</image-desc>

Immediately from the root, it sends out leaves on winged stalks, eight or ten in number, more or less; they are round, notched around the edge, but provided with harmless little points like stings; they are smooth and lack any distinct taste. From the center of these, two rush-like stalks emerge, scarcely longer than a palm, naked like those of the Dandelion <note>original: "Dente leonis"</note>. The tops of these support a yellow flower, smaller than the aforementioned plant, but fading into an elegant, pale downy seed-head. The seed is tiny, long, reddish, and streaked.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH BROAD-LEAVED HAWKWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with multiple flower heads, showing smooth (glabrous) foliage.</image-desc>

It enjoys the same birthplaces as the preceding one, and like that one, it flowers in May. However, its root is smaller, and the leaves are narrower and a little shorter: the lower ones are also provided with a longer stalk, while the others lack a stalk and clasp the stem: all of them are indeed tender and soft. The stem branches into five, six, or seven stalks, upon each of which sits a single yellow flower, equal to the flowers of the preceding plant but a little smaller. The whole plant is bitter.

### MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED with downy, jagged leaves, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply lobed (laciniate) leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

It is called by Tabernæmontanus the *Narrow-leaved Mountain Hawkweed* with Chicory-like leaves: by Clusius in his Pannonian history and later works, the *Mountain Hawkweed with a jagged leaf*: by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, the *13th Hawkweed with a jagged downy leaf*.

Clusius observed it growing in Leytemberg and flowering in June. We have found it in the high mountains of Lorraine <note>original: "Lotharingiæ"</note>.

### NARBONNE HAWKWEED, with a leafless stalk and a hairy, wavy leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with hairy, sinuate leaves and several leafless stalks bearing flower heads.</image-desc>

It relies on a root that is dark on the outside and white within, sending down many fibers: the leaves are a palm's length or longer, half an inch wide: wavy-edged and hairy: the stalks are a foot, a foot and a half, or a cubit high, thin, streaked, unbranched, hairy, and hollow: the flower is like a Dandelion, with a hairy cup <note>term: "calyce" - the green outer part of the flower head</note>.

It grows everywhere in the meadows of Geneva and Montbéliard, flowering in May, June, and July.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Hawkweed (Hieracium), detailing their physical characteristics, preferred habitats in regions like the Harz Mountains and Lorraine, and reconciling naming discrepancies between early botanists like Gerard and Clusius.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SMALL HAIRY HAWKWEED, with a leafless stem, curled when dried.
<note>original: "Hieracium parvum hirtum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hieracium plant showing a basal rosette of jagged leaves and a single long, leafless stalk topped with a composite flower head and a secondary bud.</image-desc>

It raises a simple stem a foot in height, rough to the touch and solitary: upon its summit is placed a single yellow flower, vanishing into downy seeds <note>pappus: the feathery bristles on seeds like dandelions</note>. There are many *leaves* from a slender root, scattered along the ground, dense, and with a stiff down that somewhat imitates little thorns; they are hairy and grayish-white, an inch and a half or two inches long, and sufficiently broad. They have the division of the purple <term>Rocket</term> <note>Eruca: a genus of flowering plants in the mustard family</note> as it is called by us, and when dried, they appear curled. The root is thick.

We received a dried specimen from Montpellier.

---

### HEDYPNOIS OR LION'S TOOTH: German *Pfaffenrorlin, Pfaffenblatt*: Belgian *Pappencruyt*: French *Dent de Lion*.
<note>This is the common Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a dandelion-like plant (Hedypnois) with deeply lobed (runcinate) leaves and a single flower head on a leafless scape.</image-desc>

Various names are attributed to this plant by authors. Some label it the *Hedypnois* of Pliny; others the *Aphaca* of Theophrastus (of which more in the Appendix); some call it *Lesser Hawkweed*, a *species of Chondrilla*, or a *species of Wild Chicory*. Others call it the *Sonchites* of Dioscorides, others *Urinaria* <note>referring to its diuretic properties, hence the English folk name "piss-a-bed"</note>; the apothecaries call it *Taraxacon*. Some call it the *March Flower* from its time of blooming; others the *Yolk Flower* from its color <insert>Egg-flowers</insert>. Others call it *Monk's Head* <insert>Münchkopf & pfaffenblatt</insert> because the tips of the stalks resemble shaven heads. Others call it *Lion's Tooth* from the shape of the leaves; and finally others call it *Erratic Lettuce*, because in its form and milky juice it seems to belong to the wild lettuces.

It grows in gardens, in fields, near hedges, and on the ruined walls of buildings; as well as in vineyards, meadows, and pleasure gardens.

---

### MOUSE-EAR, PILOSELLA: German *Nagelkraut, Meussöhrlin*: Belgian *Nagelcruyt, Muys-oor*: French *Piloselle*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pilosella showing a creeping habit with stolons, small oval leaves, and upright flowering stems.</image-desc>

Hardly anyone is unaware of the *Pilosella*, lying low on the ground and repeatedly propagating new offspring through drooping fibers from creeping, hairy shoots. The *leaves* are covered in hairs, similar to mouse ears, green above and grayish-white below. The *flowers* are like those of the Lion's Tooth, but smaller, yellow or golden, with the outermost edges turning purple; the cup <note>calyx</note> is hairy and dark, and the seeds fly away in downy tufts. The *roots* are numerous and thin, but cling tenaciously to the ground.

It grows in thin and arid soil, on hills and uncultivated places, on the grassy borders of fields, and everywhere along the roads. It flowers chiefly in the months of May and June.

It is strange, however, that the Ancients did not remember this very well-known herb, nor gave it any name. More recent writers call it *Pilosella* from the abundant hairs <note>Latin: pilus</note> with which both the little stems and leaves are clothed.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED MOUNTAIN HAWKWEED, with an oblong, undivided leaf: 6th of *Clusius*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Hieracium with long, narrow, lanceolate leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

This varies with leaves that are sometimes not divided, and sometimes with leaves somewhat jagged on the sides, and with a yellow flower that is more or less reddish. But all parts of the plant are full of milky juice and have a somewhat bitter taste.

It loves mountains and flowers in May. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> reports that it grows in all those mountains running from the Kahlenberg overlooking the Danube to the Alps; we, however, have observed it in various mountains of Alsace.

---

### MONTPELLIER HEDYPNOIS, OR Montpellier Lion's Tooth.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a French Hedypnois with a thick root, basal leaves, and a branched flowering stalk with several buds and flowers.</image-desc>

From a somewhat thick root rises a stem a palm's breadth high, which through cultivation even becomes a cubit or two cubits high <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>; it is somewhat thick, hollow, and divided a little above the root into three, four, or five branches. Each of these bears a single large, fragrant flower like the common *Hedypnois*, reddish on the outside but otherwise yellow, and finally vanishing into downy seeds. It grows at Montpellier in meadows, on walls, and in dry places; it flowers in the months of April and May, as well as in Autumn.

Furthermore, the Lion's Tooth is astringent, strengthening, and cleansing; it is of a cold temperature and effectively performs all those things which Hawkweed does, the powers of which were described previously. Its more tender and white buds are eaten in salads or put into broths. *More in the Appendix*.

---

### SMALLER PILOSELLA WITH NARROWER LEAF, less hairy, creeping.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Pilosella with narrower leaves and a creeping stem.</image-desc>

This also creeps remarkably, with leaves scattered along the ground that are narrower, smaller, and smooth both below and above—if you except certain rare hairs situated on the opposite leaf—of which the lower ones are somewhat round and the upper ones longer. The stems are taller, sometimes higher than a cubit, not without leaves, and branched into several stalks near the top, where there are two, three, or four flowers, yellow like the other variety, but smaller.

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, German physician and botanist</note> in his *Hortus* calls it: *Creeping wild little lettuce, wavering between Hawkweed and wild lettuce, bitter*. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it: *Lettuce 14. The wild little lettuce of Camerarius*.

It grows everywhere in the woods, flowering in May and June.

# OF PLANTS

### HAIRY AND TALLER MOUSE-EAR, not creeping.
<note>original: "Pilosella hirsutior et elatior non repens"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Pilosella plant with a fibrous root system, a basal rosette of hairy leaves, and a tall, single stem topped with several flower heads.</image-desc>

It has a fibrous root swelling with a milky juice: the stem is very hairy, as are the leaves, some of which are narrower, others broader, and some longer, others shorter. The flowers are seen sitting upon hairy stalks, like those of the yellow Hawkweed <note>original: "Hieracij lutei"</note>, with a striped cup <term>calyx|the green outer part of a flower that holds the petals</term> covered in black downy hair.

To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, this is *Pilosella 3, or the greater, upright*. Is it perhaps the *Other greater Mouse-ear* of the Lusitanian Garden?

It grows on walls around Montbéliard, and in the forests near Basel.

<column-break/>

### SPANISH MOUSE-EAR OR RAT'S EAR: by some called Hungarian Hawkweed.
<note>original: "Pilosella sive Auricula muris Hispanica: quibusdam Hieracium Pannonicum"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Pilosella plant featuring a thick root, a rosette of broad leaves, and a branched stem with multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

We observed this beautiful plant, which seems to be of the kind of the French Lungwort <note>original: "Pulmonariæ Gallorum"</note>, at Stuttgart in the Princely Garden, and in the garden of the wonderful spring at Boll <note>referring to Bad Boll, known for its medicinal springs</note>, and nowhere else.

The root is fibrous, purplish, and bitter, with a milky juice flowing out: according to Clusius, it puts forth shoots from itself like the Mouse-ear of Fuchs. The leaves are also very close to the leaves of Mouse-ear. The stems are a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or a cubit and a half high, bristling with black hairs: at the ends of these are deep saffron-colored flowers.

---

### THE GREATER MOUSE-EAR TO SOME, TO OTHERS Yellow-flowered Lungwort.
<note>original: "Pilosella maior quibusdam, aliis Pulmonaria flore luteo"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a tall Pilosella plant with deeply lobed (pinnatifid) basal leaves and a branched inflorescence with numerous small flower heads.</image-desc>

This plant has a jointed red root with fibers, flowing with milk that is bitter in taste: from which rises a stem similarly full of milk, as are the leaves; it is a cubit high, thin, and hairy. In the "wings" <note>axils</note> arising toward the top, sit yellow flowers like Hawkweed, which turn into downy seeds <term>pappos|the feathery bristles on seeds like a dandelion's</term> as they wither. The leaves spring forth immediately from the root, wavy-edged, green and hairy on the upper side, and turning white with thicker down underneath, sometimes marked with beautiful spots; they have a bitter and salty <note>nitrous</note> taste, with reddish, shaggy stalks, some long and others shorter.

It grows in shady groves, and sometimes on old walls situated in perpetual shadow, and it blooms in June. More on the following side. Figure.

<column-break/>

### A MORE JAGGED SPECIES OF GREATER MOUSE-EAR, OR LUNGWORT.
<note>original: "Pilosellæ maioris, sive Pulmonariæ species magis laciniata"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Pilosella species with highly dissected, laciniate leaves and a branched flowering stalk.</image-desc>

By Tabernaemontanus in his *History and Icons*, it is called *Female French Lungwort*: but the preceding one is called *Golden or French Lungwort*, and *Male French Lungwort*. But he does not mention spotted leaves in his description, nor does Tragus, who titles it *Saracen's Woundwort* and *Greater Mouse-ear*.

By Robert Constantinus and Amatus it is called *Lungwort*: by Lobelius, *French Lungwort with a Hawkweed flower*. By Gesner in his book on gardens, *French Lungwort related to the Lettuce kind, the Royal Broom of Pliny*, and in his Catalog, *Pliny's Hyoseris*. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, *Lungwort 1, or French Lungwort with very hairy leaves and a Hawkweed flower: the Corchorus of some, after Theophrastus and Pliny*.

---

### A SMALLER SPECIES OF THE GREATER YELLOW JAGGED MOUSE-EAR, OR LUNGWORT.
<note>original: "Pilosellæ maioris, sive Pulmonariæ, luteæ laciniatæ species minor"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a smaller Pilosella species with deeply cut leaves and several flower heads on a single stem.</image-desc>

The root of this is so thick and provided with many somewhat thick fibers that it can only be pulled out by being torn. The stems are reddish in the lower part, round, hollow, and divided into many branches: at the ends of which sit solitary flowers, quite large, yellow, and downy. The leaves are seven inches long, the rest as they are depicted here.

We observed it on the wall of the bridge of the city of Clairvaux, and nowhere else.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED YELLOW GREATER MOUSE-EAR, OR LUNGWORT.
<note>original: "Pilosellæ maioris, sive Pulmonariæ, luteæ angustifolia"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Pilosella plant with narrow, elongated leaves and a branched flowering stem.</image-desc>

It relies on a shorter root than the preceding ones, provided with longer fibers: the leaf is indeed long, like the former, but narrower, hairy, downy, widely divided but not deeply jagged; it does not only spring from the root but also clasps the stem all the way to the top, being whole and not jagged at the summit where the "wings" <note>axils</note> emerge. The stem and flower correspond to the previous ones.

<keywords>Pilosella, Mouse-ear, Lungwort, Pulmonaria, Hawkweed, botanical taxonomy, Caspar Bauhin, Tabernaemontanus, medicinal plants, 17th-century botany</keywords>
