<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Images and Outlines," focusing on various species of Hawkweed, Groundsel, and Starwort. The text relies heavily on classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny to establish the medicinal properties and physical descriptions of these plants.</meta>

### MOUSE-EAR, OR YELLOW LUNGWORT, with narrower leaves, very hairy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pilosella plant with a single stalk, hairy leaves at the base, and several composite flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

It is pleasing here to record the strengths and capabilities of the Mouse-ear <note>original: *Pilosella*</note> in general. The entire plant is powerfully astringent, binding, restraining, cooling, and drying. It heals dysentery, flows of the bowels, abdominal afflictions, intestinal hernias <note>original: *enterocelas*</note>, ruptures, relaxation of the womb, and other such conditions where binding and drying are needed, whether administered as a drink, a fomentation, a gargle, or applied in any other manner. It is added to wound-healing potions, ointments, and plasters. The juice of the leaves not only binds fresh wounds but also heals stubborn ulcers, especially of the mouth and private parts. The juice or a decoction of it even hardens the edge of iron or steel when frequently dipped into it. However, sheep that graze upon this are affected by such a great binding of the bowels that they die.

### GROUNDSEL WITH UNLOBED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Senecio plant with smooth, non-laciniated leaves and small flower heads.</image-desc>

This herb is a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height, with thin, white, woody, and sweet roots. The stalk is somewhat hairy, round, hollow, and stuffed with a downy pith. On this, the leaves are small, hairy, saw-toothed around the edges, thick, somewhat green, and reddish underneath—which sometimes stain the hands with a wine-like color. At the top of the stalk are yellow flowers, which immediately turn into downy seeds <note>original: *pappos*</note>.

It grows in the same places as the common variety previously illustrated: namely, in stone walls, on walls, and around towns, and sometimes even in gardens; it blooms in Spring and Autumn.

### ATTIC STARWORT, GROIN-WORT: Germ. *Schartenkraut*, *Sternkraut*: Belg. *Sterncruyt*: Gall. *Petite Espargoutte*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aster Atticus with lanceolate leaves and a large radiate flower head.</image-desc>

Regarding the Attic Starwort <note>original: *Aster Atticus*</note>, Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> records it thus: It is a woody shrub, he says, having a purple or yellow flower at the summit, divided around the edge in the manner of a Chamomile head; the leaves that surround the stalk are oblong and hairy.

According to Linio, the stalk is raised with two or three oblong leaves, at the summit of which are heads radiated in the manner of a star.

Various differences of this plant are observed, taken from the color of the flowers, the shape of the leaves, the place of birth, and other factors. We depict here the common variety with purple and white flowers, intending to treat the others in the following sections.

It grows on rough and uncultivated hills and in various valleys, and it blooms in August.

<column-break/>

### GROUNDSEL OR ERIGERON: Germ. *Creutswurtz*: *Grindkraut*: Belg. *Cruyskruyt*: Gall. *Senezon*, *Senesson*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Senecio (Erigeron) plant with deeply lobed (laciniated) leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> reckons *Erigeron* among the chicory-like plants. Pliny says it is an herb with the appearance and softness of *Trixago* <note>likely Germander</note>, with small round stalks. It is described most diligently by Dioscorides in these words: Groundsel <note>original: *Senecio*</note>, he says, has a stalk a cubit high, reddish; the leaves are crowded and divided at the ends like a caterpillar <note>original: *Brucae*</note>, but much smaller; the flowers tend toward yellow, which indeed open quickly and, as they fade, turn into downy seeds. The root is useless. Furthermore, it grows in stone walls and around towns.

The name *Erigeron* was obtained among the Greeks for this plant because in the spring the flowers grow white like hair; and because of this same whiteness, it was also called *Senecio* <note>from *senex*, meaning "old man"</note> by the Latins. The figure from the marketplace <note>original: *empitijs*</note> is not pleasing.

### BLUE GROUNDSEL, BLUE FLEABANE, Dyer’s Flower of Tragus, and the "Tooth-wort" of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a blue Senecio or Conyza with serrated leaves and clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

Authors record this plant by various names; it usually grows in marshy heaths and on hills among junipers, blooming in July.

Furthermore, Galen <note>Influential Roman physician</note> attributes a cooling and moderately dispersive power to Groundsel. According to Dioscorides, it cools; and the downy seeds and leaves, if applied by themselves or with wine, heal inflammations of the testes and the seat <note>the anus</note>. Fontanus records that this plant accelerates suppurations <note>the formation of pus</note>; Caesalpinus notes that the leaves are included in salads. But what Pliny writes about it regarding toothache is clearly superstitious.
*Regarding synonyms, see the Appendix.*

### MONTPELLIER ATTIC STARWORT, purple, with narrower leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Montpellier Aster with narrow leaves and a dense, radiate flower.</image-desc>

This is a relative of the common Attic Starwort, with straight, cubit-high, round, and hairy stalks, along which are crowded, smooth, and veined leaves. They correspond in size and shape to the leaves of Toadflax <note>original: *Linaria*</note>. The flowers, on numerous stems—some a palm's breadth, others an inch long—imitate an umbel; they are similar to the Starwort of Euchius <unclear>previously</unclear> depicted, yet a little smaller, with violet petals around the edge and a yellow disk, which dissolve into downy seeds. It is found at Montpellier near the sea.

<summary>This page describes several species of Pilosella, Senecio, and Aster, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses as recorded by classical authorities. It emphasizes the astringent properties of Mouse-ear and the distinctive "old man" downy seeds of Groundsel.</summary>
<keywords>Pilosella, Groundsel, Aster Atticus, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Pliny, astringent, wound healing, botanical illustration, Montpellier</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Stirpium" (Plants), specifically focusing on the various species of the Aster genus and their medicinal properties as understood in the 16th and 17th centuries.</meta>

### YELLOW ATTIC ASTER, PROSTRATE and thorny.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a low-growing Aster with thin, branching stems and small, spiky flower heads. A small 'x' mark is placed near the central stem.</image-desc>

It is endowed with many small stalks coming forth from a single root, for the most part spread out upon the ground, furrowed and hairy: the *leaves* are numerous, almost similar to the previous variety but greener: indeed, each of the branches supports a hard and leafy little stalk, upon which sits a yellow flower of a circular roundness, rivaling the Ox-eye <note>original: "Buphtalmi"</note> or the Corn Marigold <note>original: "Chrysanthemi"</note>: as this fades away, the cups <note>the calyx or base of the flower</note> turn into *heads* so hard and woody that they can scarcely be broken with a fingernail to remove the seed which is contained within them and firmly attached.

It is found in the rough and uncultivated places of Germany, Italy, France, and Bohemia, in woods, on hills, and also even in meadows: flowering in June, July, and August.

### MOUNTAIN ASTER, WITH A LARGE YELLOW FLOWER, called by some CHRIST’S EYE.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a taller Aster with a single large, composite flower head and lanceolate leaves. An asterisk '*' is placed at the base of the plant.</image-desc>

Thus the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" published in Lyon, 1586</note> titles it. By others, however, it is called the *hairy yellow mountain Aster*. We have observed it on fabulous mounds and arid places on the road from Lyon to Vienna.

Furthermore, plants are gifted with the name of *Aster*, or *Stellaris* <note>Star-like</note>, in various ways: *Woodruff, Bubonion, Buck’s-horn, Lady’s Mantle, our native Star Thistle, Sea Fleabane, Middle Fleabane, Camomile, Samphire, Sea Starwort, Sea Holly, Wolf’s Grape, White Horehound, Hemp, Cow Parsnip, Masterwort, and Pellitory-of-the-wall*. Indeed, Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, a Venetian scholar</note> bears witness that the *Heads of Poppies* are called "Little Stars" <note>original: "Asteriscos"</note> by the Greeks.

Our illustration was made from a dried plant, which is why its flowers are less spread open.

### Similar to the HAIRY MOUNTAIN ASTER, with a LARGE flower, or Christ’s Eye, if not the same.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a flowering plant with multiple stems, hairy leaves, and three distinct flower heads in various stages of bloom.</image-desc>

To Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> this is the third Fleabane <note>original: "Conyza 3"</note>. It flowers in June, and grows in dry and arid places, which are nevertheless herb-bearing.

Otherwise, as we read in Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician</note>, Attic Aster helps as a liniment for a burning stomach, inflammations of the eyes and groins, and for a prolapsed anus. And that part of the flower which turns purple, drunk with water, is believed to help those suffering from quinsy <note>severe throat inflammation</note> and many with the Falling Sickness <note>epilepsy</note>. If the flower is applied fresh to an inflammation of the groin, it is beneficial: but if it is gathered dry with the left hand of the sufferer and bound to the groin, it frees them from pain. But this is superstitious, and like other things, we pass over it by choice. Pliny adds that it is drunk for snake bites, and he differs from Dioscorides in several other points.

<column-break/>

### PURPLE MOUNTAIN ASTER.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a mountain Aster with a thick rootstock, several stems, and large, daisy-like flower heads with distinct ray florets.</image-desc>

The flower of this one is larger than the common purple Aster, but in other respects it is similar to it in all things. It flowers on the ridges of the Austrian Alps in July.

Furthermore, the number, position, and form of the leaves in the flower of the *Attic Aster*, by which it radiates in the manner of a star, have made this herb—otherwise common and growing in hedges—named after the stars. Later, through use and the assembly of Physicians, it was recognized as useful for the groins, called *Bubonion* in Greek, and *Inguinalis* in Latin. It is called *Attic* Aster, however, because it was believed to grow there more frequently than elsewhere. Some have also called this plant *Huophthalmum*, as if to say *Pig's Eye*, because its whole flower seems to resemble the eye of that animal.

### YELLOW NARROW-LEAVED ASTER.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a narrow-leaved Aster with several upright stems topped by composite flower heads.</image-desc>

This genus of Aster is beautiful, with a slender, somewhat stiff stem, and densely packed with leaves that are narrow, smooth, pointed, veined, green, and without any stalks: upon its little branches are placed individual flowers, rather large, yellow, like the Marigold <note>original: "Calthæ"</note> or the "Britannica" of the Lyon authors: with a scaly cup, of a grayish-green, and hairy.

It grows in the shady mountain meadows near the city of Vienna, and also on the grassy hills themselves, and flowers in July and August.

### Similar to the PURPLE MOUNTAIN ASTER, approaching the Globularia.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with a single, globular flower head and small leaves arranged along the stem. An asterisk '*' is at the base.</image-desc>

It has a black root, thick in proportion to such a tiny herb: the little stalk is four inches long, clothed with alternate leaves, somewhat broad, ending in a blunt tip: a single flower sits at the top of the stem, clustered with many small filaments, similar to the Globularia which is called "leafless-flower" <note>original: "aphyllanthes"</note>. The leaves approach the leaves of the purple mountain Aster, but are narrower and more delicate, and not so hairy. We received this from Strasbourg, from the dried plants of Master Agerius.

<keywords>Aster Atticus, Christ's Eye, Bubonion, Inguinalis, Dioscorides, Pliny, Clusius, Vienna, botanical taxonomy, herbal medicine, 16th-century botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE THIRD PANNONIAN STARWORT OF CLUSIUS:
### called by some the British Fleabane-like plant.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with lanceolate leaves and composite flower heads, showing the root system and stem structure.</image-desc>

It has hairy, rounded stems, more than nine inches <note>original: "dodrante," a Roman measurement of about 9 inches</note> high; along which grow alternating leaves supported by no stalks, shaped like willow leaves, veined, covered in hairs, about half an inch wide and two or three inches long, ending in a gentle point. The flower sits at the top of the stem, similar to a Marsh Marigold <note>original: "Calthae"</note>, yellow in color: the root is quite fibrous. It grows in glades and flowers in August.

### A KIND OF GREATER FLEABANE,
### called Baccharis by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with broad, serrated leaves and clusters of small flower heads at the apex.</image-desc>

The roots of this are woody, brittle, not deeply fixed, fragrant, and bitter: the stems are three or four cubits <note>about 4.5 to 6 feet</note> high, dark purple, and shaggy with gray down. The *leaves* are like those of the Black Mullein, but smaller, lightly notched, fragrant, with a sharp and somewhat bitter taste. The *flowers* are crowded together: heavy-smelling, yellow, and downy, emerging from rough, soft husks <note>term: "calyculis," the protective outer part of a flower</note> variegated with green and red.

It grows spontaneously in many high mountain forests, on walls, and along roadsides; it flowers in Autumn.

Lonicer, Fuchs, Dodonaeus, and most others label this the *Greater Fleabane* or the male variety: whereas Lacuna, Camerarius, Lobel, the *History of Lyon*, and others call it *Baccharis*. More on this in the Appendix.

### THE MANY-FLOWERED RELATIVE
### of the Middle Montpellier Fleabane.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with numerous small flower heads arranged in a flat-topped cluster at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are smooth, stiff, quite crowded along the stem and wide at the ends: the *flowers* are yellow, very numerous, representing a sort of umbrella-shape <note>term: "umbellam," a flat-topped flower cluster</note>, and are smaller: We counted up to twelve on the plant we depict here, which was sent to us dried.

<column-break/>

### FLEABANE, PULICARIA: German: *Geelmüntz*, *Duruwurtz*;
### French: *Herbe aux Puces*; Italian: *Conyza*, *Pulicaria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with narrow leaves and small flower heads, including the root.</image-desc>

*Fleabane* <note>original: "Conyza"</note>, according to the author Theophrastus, has one variety that is *Male* and another that is *Female*. Indeed, the female is more slender, with a narrower leaf, and smaller overall. The male, however, has a larger and thicker leaf, a more brilliant flower, and a heavy scent, which is sharper in the female. Furthermore, both are fruit-bearing. Pliny says the same, having borrowed his facts from Theophrastus. However, Dioscorides and Galen establish three types of Fleabane: the *Greater*, the *Lesser*, and the *Middle*.

There are various other *Differences in Fleabanes* observed by more recent authors, as will be clear from what follows. We have long depicted the Greater Montpellier variety here. But the image from Fuchs's works does not please us, for it is not complete; the flowers and the serrations on the leaves are missing.

### THE MIDDLE MONTPELLIER FLEABANE:
### considered by some a kind of Attic Starwort.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with lanceolate, slightly serrated leaves and a single prominent composite flower head.</image-desc>

The stem is a foot or more than a cubit high, grooved, smooth, hard, and clothed with leaves placed alternately: these are hard, stiff, veined, smooth, distinct from the stalk, half an inch wide, and more or less three inches long, ending in a point. The flowers are like Gold-flowers <note>original: "Chrysanthemi"</note>, of conspicuous size, yellow, emerging from a rough head, each sitting at the ends of individual shoots: these are followed by a downy fluff. The root is long and fibrous.

We saw it flowering in July between Vantancourt and Dampierre, in dry places near hedges, as well as near the vineyards of Mount Su Chan, in the County of Montbéliard.

### MATTHIOLI’S MIDDLE FLEABANE, WITH A
### yellow flower, growing in damp places.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with several flower heads and a thick root system.</image-desc>

By Tragus it is called the *Greater Fleabane*, or the Male. To Lobel and Pena in their *Adversaria*, it fits the descriptions of Dioscorides' *Middle Fleabane* perfectly: others label it differently. It grows in moist and grassy places, such as the banks of rivers, dried-up ditches, marshes, and drier meadows, and sometimes even near hedges.

<summary>This page describes various species of Fleabane (Conyza) and Starwort (Aster), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and the differing classifications used by classical and Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Fleabane, Conyza, Aster, Pannonian Starwort, Baccharis, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, botany, medicinal plants, Montbéliard</keywords>

--- Page 401 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Conyza (Fleabane) genus, following the larger varieties discussed previously. It focuses on medium and minor species, providing geographical locations and synonyms from other Renaissance botanists.</meta>

### A SMALLER SPECIES OF THE MIDDLE FLEABANE, with a flower scarcely radiated.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Conyza plant showing the root system, a slender stem with small leaves, and several flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

It grows almost everywhere in marshy places and damp fields: it is most frequent at Basel and Montbéliard, and especially at Yverdon-les-Bains, between the lake and the city walls, and next to the branch of the river called *the old Thiele* <note>original: "la vieille Tesle"</note>.

Is this Tragus’s *Female Fleabane of Theophrastus*? By Lobelius and Pena in their *Adversaria* it is called *Smallest Fleabane*. At Montpellier they call it *Saint Roch’s Herb* <note>Saint Roch was the patron saint of plague victims; herbs named after him were often used for skin ailments or protection.</note>.

### A WOUND-HEALING HERB RELATED TO THE FLEABANES, called the third Saracen’s Consound by Tragus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, serrated leaves and a cluster of flower heads at the apex.</image-desc>

In a dried plant which we received from Speyer, we observed a smooth, hairy stem embracing the *leaves* with round wings; the leaves are supported by no stalks, are pointed, an inch or a palm long, about half an inch wide, and somewhat shaggy. The very top of the stem goes off into several small stalks, each of which bears a golden flower that turns into downy seeds <note>term: pappos (pappus) — the feathery bristles on seeds, like those of a dandelion, that allow them to be carried by the wind.</note>.

### HAIRY HELENITIS FLEABANE, of the same Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with hairy stems and leaves, featuring multiple small flower heads along the upper branches.</image-desc>

In its leaves, root, and flowers, it comes very close to the preceding plant. However, it differs from that one in that it has stems and leaves that are quite rough and hairy.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Fleabane 10, or the very hairy Alpine species*. For it is so hairy that by some it is called *Alpine Hairy-plant*.

<column-break/>

### A SPECIES OF MIDDLE FLEABANE, WITH LEAVES OF GOLDENROD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with larger, lanceolate leaves and several prominent flower heads.</image-desc>

We observed and collected this at Speyer in the garden of the distinguished and famous jurist Tengnagel, Assessor of the Imperial Chamber, while it was flowering in June. It appears to be a certain species of the Middle Fleabane.

### HOARY HONEYED HELENITIS FLEABANE of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick stem, elongated leaves, and a dense cluster of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

It sends up a stem a foot and a half high, woolly and hoary, from a fibrous root not unlike the root of the common *Baccharis* <note>term: Baccharis — likely referring here to the Ploughman's Spikenard.</note>: the *leaves* are oblong, related to Foxglove leaves, whitish or ash-colored on the underside, and purple-green on the upper side, like the leaves of Rhapontic Rhubarb: the *flowers* are yellow, similar to the flowers of other Fleabanes, with the scent of virgin honey and a somewhat sharp taste.

It grows in certain woods of Artois, from where, on account of its rarity, it was moved into gardens.

### THE TRUE MINOR FLEABANE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, bushy plant with numerous small flower heads and a thick root.</image-desc>

This so resembles the *greater* variety that whoever knows that one will also recognize this one when it is presented: it has a similar scent, but more vigorous. It is only smaller, and about a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high; for the most part it is branched, which you do not see by chance in the other. The *leaves* are much thinner, narrower, shorter, somewhat hairy, and sticky: the *flowers* are the same, and in the same spiked order, but smaller and more numerous.

By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Theophrastus’s Female Fleabane and Dioscorides’s Minor*. By Lobelius and the *History of Lyon* it is called *True Minor Fleabane*. By Dodoens in Latin: *A Fleabane besides the Greater, Middle, and Smallest, another minor one, more fragrant than those*.

It grows spontaneously at Montpellier and Basel: and it flowers in September.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### SYRIAN FLEABANE OF SOME AUTHORS.
<note>original: "CONYZA SYRIÆ QVIBVSDAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Conyza plant with thick, segmented stems, serrated leaves, and small flower heads at the tips.</image-desc>

It produces several small stalks from the same *root*, a foot or more high: some of these are upright, but the greatest part lie flat on the ground, and by putting out new fibers, they subsequently produce other stalks a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> long. It has somewhat long *leaves*, fleshy, slightly hairy, and of a fairly heavy scent, though a certain sweetness is mixed in: otherwise, in its *flowers* and other characteristics, it is not very different from the Greater Fleabane.

Leonhard Rauwolf, the author of the description, observed it around Tripoli in Syria.

### NODDING-HEADED FLEABANE.
<note>original: "CONYZA CAPITE NYTANTE"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Conyza plant with nodding flower heads (capite nutante) and broad, lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

The *roots* of this one are fibrous, like those of Black Hellebore: the *stalks* are several, a cubit high, and hairy, which split into various small branches: the *leaves* are long, fairly wide, like Fleabane, and more rarely serrated: the *flowers* are yellow and nodding <note>drooping or hanging downward</note>. It is found on sunny mountains near Basel and elsewhere.

Is this perhaps the second *Hydropiper* <note>Water-pepper</note> of Dalechamps' *History of Lyon*?

Furthermore, we have shown in our Great History that various other plants are given the name of Fleabane (*Alpine Water-plantain, Ragweed, the Terrible Herb, Stinking Goosefoot, Wild Marjoram, Winter Savory, Smartweed, Fleawort, Wild Rue, and Hemlock*).

### ANOTHER OF RAUWOLF’S GUM-SUCCORIES, RELATED TO SEA FLEABANE.
<note>original: "CONYZA MARINÆ AFFINIS CHONDRILLA alia Rauvvolffij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a bulbous root, long thin stems, and dandelion-like flower heads.</image-desc>

It is clearly similar to Sea Fleabane in its root and flowers: however, the leaves are wider and hairier, and more ash-colored, just like the *Holosteum* <note>Jagged Chickweed</note> of Montpellier. Rauwolf considers it to be another kind of Dioscorides' *Chondrilla* <note>Gum-succory</note>, and reports that it grows in stony fields around Aleppo.

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN FLEABANE OF MICÓN, WITH HAIRY COMMON HYSSOP LEAVES.
<note>original: "CONYZA MONTANA MYCONI, FOLIO Hyssopi vulgaris villoso"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Conyza with upright stems and narrow, hairy leaves resembling hyssop.</image-desc>

Micón, a skilled Physician and a student of botany, judged the plant pictured here to be a species of Fleabane based on the shape, scent, and taste of the leaves and flowers, and named it *mountain* after its place of birth.

For it grows in rocky, steep, and mountainous places, and especially among the cracks of rocks, flowering most greatly in August.

### SEA FLEABANE.
<note>original: "CONYZA MARINA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sea Conyza with a thick, woody root system and clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

It drives long *roots* underground, not without fibers, finally ending in a sort of tuberous bulb. Several *stalks* emerge at once, about nine inches long, hairy, and clothed with frequent *leaves*, two or three inches in length and scarcely a stalk's width, rigid, and endowed with a single vein running lengthwise. The stalk, divided *at the top*, bears yellow *flowers* like the Greater Fleabane, which vanish into downy seeds <note>pappus</note>.

It grows abundantly in the coastal regions of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

### ALPINE FLEABANE WITH CHRYSANTHEMUM FLOWERS:
#### Also called the Broad-leaved Ragwort by some.
<note>original: "CONYZA ALPINA FLORE CHRYSANTHEMI: Iacobæa latifolia altera quorundam"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine Conyza with broad, deeply lobed leaves and large daisy-like flowers.</image-desc>

Here we shall assign the temperament, powers, and faculties of Fleabane.

It possesses a hot and dry temperament: when decocted and drunk warm, it effectively draws out suppressed menses, dead fetuses, and the afterbirth; it dispels the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note> and opens obstructions of the liver. Decocted in vinegar and drunk, it rouses those who have collapsed from the "comitial disease" <note>epilepsy</note>. Indeed, as a fumigant or a bed-covering, it puts snakes to flight, drives away gnats, and kills fleas, from which it also obtained the name **FLEABANE** <note>original: "PVLICARIÆ"</note>: chopped and applied, it draws out the venom of serpents.

<summary>This page describes several regional varieties of Conyza (Fleabane) from Syria, the Alps, and the French coast, detailing their physical characteristics and habitats. It concludes with a summary of the plant's medicinal uses, particularly for women's health, jaundice, and repelling insects and snakes.</summary>

<keywords>Fleabane, Conyza, Leonhard Rauwolf, Francisco Micón, medicinal herbs, Syria, Basel, Montpellier, jaundice, epilepsy, insect repellent, botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of flowering herbs, specifically focusing on the Jacobaea (Ragwort) family and its varieties across Europe.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

**ST. JAMES’S WORT, OR ST. JAMES’S FLOWER: German: St. James’s Flower <note>original: "S. Iacobsblumen"</note> :**
**French: Herb or flower of St. James : Italian: Greater Carduncello.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Jacobaea plant with tall stems, serrated leaves, and multiple daisy-like flower heads.</image-desc>

When it finds a rich soil, it reaches a height of three cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note>, with a straight, reddish, and grooved stem. The *leaves* are placed alternately and are like those of Groundsel <note>original: "Senecionis"</note>, but larger and smooth to the touch. The *flowers* are numerous and joined together, like Groundsel but larger and yellow, with a center of the same color, eventually turning into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos"; the fluffy seeds typical of the daisy family.</note>. The *root* is white and fibrous.

It abounds everywhere in various places. We saw it blooming in Montpellier in April and May; in Basel, on the way to *Moutier* and by the river *Birs* in October; and in various places in Geneva and Montbéliard.

### BROAD-LEAFED ST. JAMES’S WORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Jacobaea (Jacobaea latifolia) with large, deeply lobed basal leaves and a cluster of flowers at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

It has a *stem* three cubits high, round, reddish, and filled with white pith, divided into branches like the other variety. At the ends of these are large, yellow, star-shaped *flowers*, like the common sort, which finally vanish into a downy fluff. But the *leaves*, as is evident from the illustration, differ greatly. The *root* is slanted and hairy with many fibers.

We observed it blooming in August in the Sundgau <note>A region in Alsace, France.</note>, on the bank of a small stream.

### PANNONIAN ST. JAMES’S WORT WITH UNSERRATED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pannonian Jacobaea with lanceolate, non-laciniated leaves and several flower heads.</image-desc>

It grows in many mountainous and cleared forests of Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note> and Lower Austria. It blooms at the beginning of June, and by the end of the same month, the seed is ripe. — *Clusius* <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a famous Flemish botanist.</note>.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF ST. JAMES’S WORT, OR THE FLOWER OF ST. JAMES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Jacobaea, showing a single tall stalk with dissected leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

We present two figures from Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist.</note>, not because they are different species, but only as variations.

The Flower of St. James, however, possesses not only the same form but also the same powers and medicinal properties as Groundsel, so that it may rightly be used in its place. It is primarily used to heal wounds, inflammations, and fistulas <note>A term for an abnormal passage or ulcer in the body.</note>.

### BROAD-LEAFED PANNONIAN ST. JAMES’S WORT, with Ox-eye flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Pannonian Jacobaea with large, prominent flower heads resembling "ox-eye" (Buphthalmi).</image-desc>

Thus Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who developed an early system of plant classification.</note> names it in his *Phytopinax*. To Clusius, however, in his *History of Pannonian Plants*, it is the third Broad-leafed Pannonian Jacobaea.

It grows in the Austrian and Styrian Alps. It blooms in June and July, and when moved into gardens, in May.

### SEA ST. JAMES’S WORT, OR CINERARIA, with honey-yellow flowers turning to down.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Jacobaea marina (Cineraria), featuring highly dissected, silvery-looking foliage and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

It is called Sea Chrysanthemum and Sea Mugwort by Lobelius and Foesius; by Tabernaemontanus and many others, it is called *Sea Jacobaea and Cineraria*. It is commonly called *Cineraria* <note>From the Latin "cinis," meaning ashes.</note> because of the whitish, ash-like color it displays. Alpinus calls it White Mugwort and writes that it is called *Achaean* by the Egyptians, and that it is of great use among them for stones of the kidneys and bladder, and for obstructions of the internal organs.

Its leaves are similar to those of the Oak; in other respects, its appearance is very similar to the St. James’s Wort, which gave it its name, while its maritime birthplace added the distinction.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Jacobaea (St. James's Wort), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical locations across Europe, and medicinal uses for treating wounds and internal obstructions.</summary>
<keywords>St. James's Wort, Jacobaea, Cineraria, medicinal herbs, Pannonia, Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, botanical illustration, kidney stones, wound healing</keywords>

--- Page 404 ---
### IMAGES AND OUTLINE:
<sig>Tt 2</sig>

### ALPINE GOLDEN-FLOWER OF JUDENBURG Related to Ragwort, according to Clusius. <note>original: *Chrysanthemum Alpinum Iudebergense Iacobææ affine, Clusij*. Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius) was a foundational 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with deeply lobed leaves and daisy-like flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

It has many rather long leaves near the root, similar to the so-called umbelliferous Wormwood, thick, about a thumb's length, divided into several segments, green, and bitter in taste. It has several stalks a span high, adorned with sparser and finely dissected leaves, upon which sit clusters like umbels of ten or twelve flowers, not unlike the flowers of the common Ragwort and of the same scent. The root is somewhat thick and hairy with many-branched fibers.

It grows in Judenburg <note>A town in Styria, Austria.</note> and certain other ridges of Styria. According to Clusius.

### GOAT'S BEARD: German: *Bocksbart, Gauchsbroot*; French: *Barbe de bouc*; Italian: *Barba de becco*. <note>original: *Tragopogon*. From the Greek *tragos* (goat) and *pogon* (beard).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tragopogon plant with long, narrow leaves and a large flower head, including the long taproot.</image-desc>

Goat's Beard is commonly found in meadows; it has a root swelling with milk, sweet, the thickness of a pinky finger, and long. The stalk is a cubit high, clothed from bottom to top with leaves that are almost like leeks, keeled <note>V-shaped in cross-section like the hull of a ship.</note>, and clasping the stalk. From the crotch of these leaves branches grow out, on the tips of which sit large flowers, crowded with a dense troop of radiating petals, yellow, which turn into downy seed-heads <note>original: *pappos*. The fluffy "clock" of seeds like a dandelion.</note>. The attached seed is two inches long, slender, streaked, rough, and turning black when mature.

It grows almost everywhere in meadows, as we have observed in Padua, Lyon, Montpellier, Geneva, Basel, and elsewhere, flowering in March, April, May, and sometimes August.

### GOAT'S BEARD WITH JAGGED LEAVES, with a yellow or pale flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Tragopogon with more jagged, laciniate leaves and several flower stalks.</image-desc>

We have seen this species of Goat's Beard in Padua, Bologna, and Basel, flowering in June and July. By Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, an Italian botanist.</note> it is called the *Acorus* of Theophrastus, and the Herb of Venus.

Indeed, the herb which the Paduans call *Herba lissa*, and the rural folk of Tuscany call *Saffifica* or *Saffeffrica* <note>Likely Salsify.</note>, we think should by no means be distinguished from Goat's Beard. Some have called it the Rock Herb, because in stony places it seems to break out as if from the middle of the rocks. Athenaeus is the authority for the claim that the name *Tragopogon* is also given to a part of the *Tragus* fish <note>A species of sea-fish.</note> which is blackish under its throat.

Furthermore, it should be noted, especially in Goat's Beard, that the flowers of all species always turn toward the East.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE AND SCHERIAN GOLDEN-FLOWER Related to Ragwort, by the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with finely divided, feathery leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

Numerous leaves grow close to the root, corresponding to the leaves of the Greater Southernwood, but shining with a paler greenness, and with a scent that is not unpleasant if they are rubbed, though the taste is bitter and not at all pleasant. From these come stalks a foot high, loaded with smaller leaves, sometimes divided into several small branches; these sustain single or twin flowers, larger than the flowers of common Chamomile, odorless, and entirely yellow. The root is fibrous and blackish.

It is found, says Clusius, on the high ridges of the Alps of Styria, and it flowers in August.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF GOAT'S BEARD OR OLD MAN'S BEARD. <note>original: *Tragopogonis sive Gerontopogonis*. *Gerontopogon* literally means "old man's beard" in Greek.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tragopogon plant showing the closed flower bud, the open flower, and the seed head (pappus).</image-desc>

Various differences are observed in Goat's Beard, taken chiefly from size, location, the color of the flowers, and the shape of the leaves, as will be clear from what follows. The main difference, however, is in the color of the flowers, which is either yellow, or whitish, or purple, or crimson.

Indeed, *Gerontopogon*—that is, the beard of an old man or a priest—is almost entirely similar to Goat's Beard, except that it flows with milk and has a bitter root, not a sweet one. Nevertheless, the number of illustrations should not be multiplied because of this, as the *Histories of Lyon* <note>A reference to the *Historia Generalis Plantarum* published in Lyon.</note> and others do.

Nor would we have cared to have this one painted, if the illustration by Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, author of a famous 1542 herbal.</note>, which we showed in the first place, had been satisfactory.

### GRASS-LEAVED GOAT'S BEARD with a white and yellow flower with a tiny bit of purple.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass-leaved Tragopogon with a distinct flower and root.</image-desc>

It grows in damp, uncultivated places, and flowers in June and July.

The apothecaries <note>original: *Officinæ*. The shops where medicines were prepared.</note>, however, show a false Goat's Beard instead of the true one. For the true one pleases with the smooth hairlessness of its stalk and leaf, while that false one irritates the one who touches it with a biting down; the true leaf grows slender like a Saffron leaf, while in that false one it extends to a quite ample width; again, in the true one a "beard" hangs down sent out from the calyx <note>The green outer part of the flower.</note>, while that one has a beardless top.

Furthermore, Goat's Beard is a help to the liver, stomach, kidneys, and chest. Water distilled from the herb and root is a most excellent remedy against abscesses <note>original: *Apostemata*.</note> and pains in the sides. The herb is mixed into salads, as is the root, which, eaten raw or cooked, is said to expel stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note> and to cure the dripping of urine.

<summary>This page describes various species of Alpine Golden-flower (Chrysanthemum) and Goat's Beard (Tragopogon), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in Styria and Italy, and medicinal uses for the liver and kidneys.</summary>
<keywords>Alpine Golden-flower, Goat's Beard, Tragopogon, Clusius, Styria, medicinal herbs, botany, Salsify, kidney stones, botanical illustration</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Tragopogon genus, specifically focusing on the Scorzonera varieties and introducing Goldenrod (Virga aurea).</meta>

### SPANISH GOAT'S BEARD, OR Escorzonera, or Scorzonera.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tragopogon hispanicus plant, showing long, slender leaves, a thick root system, and several flower heads in various stages of bloom, including one with pappus (seed head).</image-desc>

The root is a foot in length and an inch thick, full of a very sweet milk—though not without some astringency. The stalk is a cubit and a half high <note>about 27 inches</note>, hollow with many "wings" or ridges, and covered in a soft, scrapable down. This same down appears on the lower leaves, which embrace the stalk with a wider base; they are long, like those of the Goat's Beard <note>Tragopogon</note>, an inch and a half wide or narrower, ending in a very long, narrow point. Single flowers sit at the ends of the branches, like those of the Goat's Beard, yellow in color, emerging from scaly, smooth, tightly-packed cups <note>calyxes</note>. The seed is tufted <term>papposum: having feathery hairs for wind dispersal</term>, like the Goat's Beard.

This herb is of the same family as the Goat's Beard; the Spaniards call it *Scorzonera* or *Escorzonera* because it serves as an immediate remedy for those bitten by the viper, which they call *Scorzo*. More on this follows.

### A SPECIES OF GOAT'S BEARD, Low-growing narrow-leafed SCORZONERA, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Scorzonera with narrower leaves and a single prominent flower head.</image-desc>

This differs from the preceding primarily in the narrowness of its leaves; the flower, however, is yellow or gold like the others. It blooms in April and May, and the seed ripens at the beginning of June.

We have the testimony of Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous German physician and botanist</note> that Scorzonera with both simple and full flowers is found in many parts of Germany, and that it differs from the Spanish variety only by reason of the soil and climate. Likewise, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> writes that it grows wild in several woody, marshy mountains of Pannonia <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and Serbia</note>. We ourselves have observed it in various cultivated gardens in Padua, Lyon, Speyer, and elsewhere. However, it is unlikely that these local varieties are endowed with the same powers as that celebrated Spanish one.

### SPIKED THIN-LEAFED GOAT'S BEARD, from the History of Lyon.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tragopogon with very thin, grass-like leaves and a spiked inflorescence.</image-desc>

In its root, leaves, and jointed stalk, it is similar to the other types of Goat's Beard; only the stalk is more slender, the root thinner, and the leaf narrower. But it differs from the others most notably in its flower, which is yellow and gathered together in a spike.

How great the efficacy of Scorzonera is against the bites of the *Scorzo* (the viper) and other venomous animals, we pass down from Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a renowned Italian doctor and botanist</note> in our great History, as well as the method of use. The distilled water is also given for pestilential and malignant fevers, for it provokes sweat wonderfully when nature attempts this movement; it is also mixed into compresses beneficial to the heart.

Regarding the Goat's Beard from the records of the Ancients, see the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### A SPECIES OF GOAT'S BEARD, Low-growing broad-leafed SCORZONERA, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Scorzonera species with two flower heads.</image-desc>

Clusius observed this in Austria, on the mountain overlooking the baths of Baden and other neighboring places.

Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist</note> classifies Scorzonera as a foreign Goat's Beard; he says it was first made known in Tarraconensian Spain through the industry of a certain Moor, and it is thought to be the same plant with which Cardanus <note>Gerolamo Cardano</note> records that Ptolemy was once cured.

It was first called "Spanish," as Thalius writes, until the name *Scorzonera* was added to it. It possesses evident differences according to the nature of the leaves and flowers: one has a somewhat sweet root, the other a bitter one, which is more endowed with antidotal power.

### A SPECIES OF GOAT'S BEARD, Larger narrow-leafed SCORZONERA, with a bluish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger, narrow-leafed Scorzonera with multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

This is nearly equal to the preceding, only it has longer and narrower leaves, and slightly smaller flowers of a purplish-blue color. Clusius includes it among his Pannonian plants.

The entire Scorzonera plant is of great use in dispelling various diseases. As an immediate remedy against the bites and stings of vipers and other venomous animals, as well as any pestilential diseases, the juice is taken from both the leaves and the root and offered as a drink. It is also used when preserved as a confection <term>Conservæ: a medicinal preserve made with sugar or honey</term> for headaches, dizziness, "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, and heart ailments. *More is written at the side of the following figure.*

### GOLDENROD: German: *Güldin Rute*, *Güldin Wundkraut*; French: *Verge d'Or*; Italian: *Virga aurea*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Goldenrod (Virga aurea) plant with a tall, leafy stem and a dense cluster of small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

This plant received the name Goldenrod because the branches, heavy with flowers, resemble a rod of gold. There are those who claim it is the *Leucographis* of Pliny; by others, it is referred to the *Solidago* and *Consolida* <note>wound-healing plants</note> groups because of its powers. Some have called it the "Pagan" or "Jewish" herb; Jochius and Gesner called it "Saracen's Woundwort," though Mattioli did not venture to do so—and not without reason, since these two plants differ significantly.

The common broad-leafed variety which we depict grows spontaneously in various places: on embankments, near roads, and in stony places.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Scorzonera (Viper's Grass), detailing their physical characteristics and their celebrated use as an antidote for snake bites and fevers. It also introduces Goldenrod (Virga aurea), noting its various regional names and its reputation as a wound-healing herb.</summary>
<keywords>Scorzonera, Goat's Beard, Goldenrod, Virga aurea, viper bites, antidotes, Clusius, Gesner, Mattioli, medicinal botany, 16th-century medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Images and Outlines," focusing on the Goldenrod family and coastal plants like Sea Starwort. It maintains the systematic descriptions of leaf shape, habitat, and medicinal history found in the preceding sections.</meta>

### BROAD-LEAVED SERRATED GOLDENROD,
->known by some as Saracen’s Woundwort.<- <note>original: "Solidago Sarracenica"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed plant with serrated edges and clusters of small flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

The leaves of this variety are three times wider than the common sort, and also longer, though similar in other respects, as are the stalks and branches; but the *yellow flowers are downy and do not grow in spikes along the branches, but cling to the very tops and ends, forming a shape like an umbrella.* <note>The "umbrella" shape refers to an umbel, a cluster of flowers where stalks spread from a common point.</note>

We have found it in various places: on the *Rossberg* mountain near *Masevaux*, and on the *Münchenstein* mountain near Basel. It blooms at the same time as the common variety, in September and October.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED SERRATED GOLDENROD,
->also called Saracen’s Woundwort by some.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with narrower, serrated leaves and a more upright, branched flowering structure.</image-desc>

By Tragus, Dodonaeus, and Fuchs <note>Renowned 16th-century botanists Hieronymus Bock, Rembert Dodoens, and Leonhart Fuchs.</note> it is called *Strong Herb* <note>original: "Herba fortis"</note>, by some *Cudweed* <note>original: "Filago"</note>, or rather, as Fuchs notes, *The Leaf-Guardian* <note>original: "Cartaphylax"</note>. Others have called Goldenrod in general *Consolida* and *Saracen’s Woundwort* or *Turkish Woundwort*, because the Turks frequently use it to join the edges of wounds together.

For Goldenrod has a dry temperament, and possesses the same powers for healing wounds as Sanicle: and although, as Tragus notes, other plants may be more excellent, this holds the first rank among the "vulnerary" <note>wound-healing</note> herbs.

---

<column-break/>

### RELATED NARROW-LEAVED GOLDENROD
->Dalechamp’s "Bird’s Tongue."<- <note>original: "Lingua avis Dalechampii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with long, narrow leaves and multiple flowering heads at the apex.</image-desc>

The stalk is two or three cubits <note>about 3 to 4.5 feet</note> high, hollow and grooved: along which, at long intervals, grow alternate leaves not much different from the leaves of Saracen’s Woundwort. They are attached without stems, a palm or a palm-and-a-half long, about half an inch wide, serrated around the edges, ending in a sharp point, and covered underneath as if with down. The top of the stalk divides into many small forks, and these again into little stems, upon which sit the yellow flowers of the Saracen’s Woundwort.

In our judgment, Dalechamp wrongly places this among the Rampions; others more correctly refer it to the Fleabanes.

<column-break/>

### WATER PLANTAIN OR DAMASONIUM: DOREA
->and the Goldenrod of Montpellier.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, lanceolate leaves and a tall, branched inflorescence.</image-desc>

A larger and smaller variety of this kind is found at Montpellier on the riverbank near Castelnau, and they bloom in May, June, July, and August. We have also seen them in gardens at Padua, Ferrara, and Zurich; indeed, we cultivated it in the Princely Garden at Montbéliard, where it bloomed in August.

It comes very close to the Goldenrod or *Consolida aurea*, and is commonly called *Dorea* (by the people of Narbonne) from its golden color. Those who call it *Doria* are quite mistaken, as if the praise for its discovery should be attributed to *Doria*, the commander of the galleys. <note>A reference to the famous Genoese admiral Andrea Doria.</note> *Perhaps it is the Panax Chironium of Theophrastus. See the appendix for the opinions of the Ancients on Alisma and Damasonium.*

---

<column-break/>

### SEA STARWORT: Arabic, German, & Belgian: Turbith; French: Blue Daisy; Italian: Tripolio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coastal plant with fleshy leaves and daisy-like flowers.</image-desc>

Today some call this a maritime herb, a cubit or a cubit-and-a-half tall, clinging by a fibrous root. The *leaves* approach the leaves of the Great Sea-Lavender, but are narrower, nearly equal in length, provided with straight veins like Plantain, smooth, and growing in no particular order along the branches. The top of the *stalk* is branched and bears *flowers* clinging to the ends of the forks, blue or purple, which vanish into downy tufts.

Its flower, according to Dioscorides, is said to change color three times a day: so that it appears white in the morning, purple at noon, and crimson in the evening.

Commonly, two types of Sea Starwort are established: the *Greater*, which we depict here, and the *Lesser*, of which more follows.

<column-break/>

### LESSER SEA STARWORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of the Tripolium plant with similar leaf and flower structures.</image-desc>

Sea Starwort grows, as Dioscorides further says, in maritime places which the wave washes over and leaves behind as it recedes. And in such maritime places of Belgium our variety is found, as in the islands of Zeeland: neither truly in the sea, nor on dry land, but in places which the surging sea strikes and then deserts as it ebbs, flows, and moves back again. According to Lobel, the shores of Narbonne, England, and Venice abound with this, as do the banks of rivers which the reflux and tide of the sea inundate, where almost no other herb appears.

The root, which is sharp to the taste, is "hot in the third degree" <note>A classification in Galenic medicine indicating a very potent, heating effect on the body.</note>. *See Pliny in the Appendix.*

<keywords>Goldenrod, Saracen’s Woundwort, Sea Starwort, medicinal herbs, vulnerary, botany, Dioscorides, Montpellier, coastal flora, plant taxonomy</keywords>

# PLANTS

### ADULTERINE EUPATORIUM, EUPATORIUM
of Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard European textbook for centuries.</note>: German *Hirtsklee* <note>Hemp-agrimony</note>: Belgian *Herts claueren*:
French *Eupatoire bastard*: Italian *Terzola*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Eupatorium adulterinum (Hemp-agrimony), showing the plant with its serrated, lanceolate leaves arranged in clusters and terminal flower heads, including the root system.</image-desc>

Writers on botanical matters distinguish between *Hepatica*, *Hepatorium*, and *Eupatorium* in this way: *Hepatica* is Liverwort <note>original: "Lichen"</note>, *Hepatorium* is the common Eupatorium, but the true *Eupatorium* is Agrimony. And these three are often and rightly called "Eupatoria" because they are suitable for strengthening and healing the liver <note>The name derives from "hepar," the Greek word for liver.</note>.

We provide the history of Liverwort, as well as Agrimony, elsewhere; but here our discussion concerns *Hepatorium*, the common Eupatorium, the male Eupatorium; the Eupatorium of Avicenna, *aquatic Eupatorium*, *hemp-like Eupatorium*, *water hemp*, and that called *adulterine Eupatorium* or *False-Eupatorium*. In Tiago <note>likely a regional dialect or specific locale</note> it is called *Herb of St. Kunigunde*. In the apothecaries of Belgium, it is wrongly called *Eupatorium of the Greeks*.

It dwells on the banks of waters, growing to a remarkable height of two, three, or more cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; the plant stands 3 to 4.5 feet tall.</note>: with a straight, round, downy stem, purplish-green in color, full of white pith, breathing out a pleasant and aromatic scent when it is cut, and hollow with many branches. The leaves are arranged at intervals, hemp-like, saw-toothed, hairy, oblong, and pointed, with several coming out from the same joint. The flowers are clustered in tufts, consisting almost entirely of small filaments; they turn from white to purple, finally turning into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos," the feathery bristles on seeds like dandelions.</note>. The root is fibrous and white; its taste, like the leaves, is bitter.

<column-break/>

### FEMALE ADULTERINE EUPATORIUM,
Verbesina, Water Hemp.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Eupatorium adulterinum foemina (likely a species of Bidens or similar aquatic plant), showing opposite leaves and a distinct flowering head, including the root system.</image-desc>

Writers have bestowed various names upon this plant. Thus, some have called it *Eupatorium of Avicenna*, others *water Hepatorium*, others *female False-Eupatorium*, others *water Hemp*, others *prostrate Verbena*, others *Fleabane-like Eupatorium 1 & 2*, others *water Chrysanthemum*, others *water Goldenrod*, others *water Stellaria*, others *water Comfrey*, etc. Indeed, Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel (1474–1537), a French physician and botanist.</note> judged it to be *Hydropiper* <note>Water-pepper</note> by a great error.

A double variety of it is found: for it has either a more beautiful or less beautiful flower, but in both, it is yellow.

It grows in damp and marshy places and in ditches, as well as within the open beds of certain rivers. It is frequent in England, Belgium, and Germany. It flowers and flourishes through the greater part of Summer, and finally perfects its seed.

As far as its temperament and powers are concerned, it is bitter, and therefore hot and dry. It drives away serpents and venomous animals, just like *Conyza* <note>Fleabane</note>. It is beneficial for wounds, especially when taken internally; and it can also be applied to consuming ulcers that creep far and wide.

---

It grows around the edges of trenches, streams, and stagnant waters, on the banks of rivers, and in other boggy places, as well as on old and damp walls. But although it loves watery things and places near water, it by no means requires to be entirely flooded. It flowers and flourishes in July and August: the root is perennial <note>original: "restibilis," meaning it grows back each year</note>, but the leaves and stems perish in winter. It is met with almost everywhere.

It is a herb of remarkable powers, although the Ancients were silent about it. It has a bitterish taste, yet a scent no less sweet than scented Agrimony, to which it is very close in power, and in some conditions, it is even more excellent. Those who repeatedly said it stinks were of "too dull a nose," according to the testimony of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>. It is hot and dry in the second degree; it heats, thins, cleanses, cuts through [phlegm], and opens [obstructions]; it is especially useful in conditions of the liver and viscera. Practitioners and druggists <note>original: "Seplasiæ," referring to sellers of perfumes and medicines.</note> know its particular use.

# END OF CLASS XXIV.

# IMAGES AND DESCRIPTIONS
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXV.
### HEADED PLANTS WITHOUT SPINES, SUCH AS SCABIOUS, KNAPWEED, AND SIMILAR TYPES: AND SPINY ONES, SUCH AS THISTLES: ETC.

---

<columns>2</columns>

**SCABIOSA PSORA <note>original: "Psora" is a Greek term for a skin disease; the plant was named for its supposed ability to cure it.</note>: German: Scabiosen: French: Scabieuse: Italian & Spanish: Scabiosa.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scabiosa plant showing the root system, stem with opposite leaves, and a single flower head at the top.</image-desc>

Whether the Ancient authors made mention of Scabious or not is not yet sufficiently established.

However, the name can be applied to several plants (not unlike the *Psora* of Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>), such as Knapweed, Devil’s-bit, and others related in appearance and properties, which we shall discuss as we proceed. There is also a great variety of Scabious plants, as will be clear from what follows.

The most common variety grows among the grain; it has a long, straight root: stems two cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> high, quite hairy and hollow: leaves growing opposite one another from the joints, covered with a greyish downy fuzz, shaped like the Greater Valerian, sometimes deeply jagged, other times less so, with a somewhat sharp taste: blue flowers gathered from crowded, four-parted joints.

<column-break/>

**GREATER SCABIOUS WITH UN-JAGGED LEAVES.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scabiosa variety with broader, less divided leaves and a flowering head.</image-desc>

Cesalpino <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), an Italian physician and botanist who classified plants by their fruits and seeds.</note> is undoubtedly speaking of these Scabious plants of ours when he says: "Some consist of divided leaves, others of whole leaves: those which bear divided leaves grow mostly in the fields in Summer among the stubble left from the harvest: with a stem a cubit or more in height, with branches spread to the sides: a few somewhat hairy leaves divided on both sides, etc. Upon the tips of the small branches sits a Head, spread out in width, with little flowers verging toward blue: with heaped, somewhat hairy seeds: and a single root." The whole plant is quite bitter and slightly astringent: it is thought to be the *psora* of Aetius, by the use of which "ant-larvae" <note>Likely referring to a type of skin eruption or small parasitic infestation.</note> are killed.

---

**ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE BROAD-LEAFED GREATER SCABIOUS.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Scabiosa with a thick root and multiple flower buds.</image-desc>

We also preserve this variety of Scabious among our dried plants, which has very broad and short leaves: in which, as in several others, a not insignificant diversity occurs.

Furthermore, it is well known that the Greater Scabious, both with the jagged leaf and the least jagged leaf, is found almost everywhere among crops, in open fields, and in meadows. It abounds in the said places around Geneva, Lyon, Basel, and Montbéliard, and it flowers in May, June, July, and August, sooner or later, and then produces its seed.

Moreover, according to some, the name "Scabiosa" was given to this plant from the rough <note>Latin: *scaber*</note> habit of the herb, which is a common explanation: or according to others, because it cures the Itch <note>Latin: *scabies*</note>, which is the explanation accepted by everyone.

<column-break/>

**GREATER SCABIOUS WITH BEAUTIFUL SEEDS: The Starred Greater Scabious of Salamanca, according to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), one of the most influential botanists of the 16th century.</note>.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scabiosa variety featuring a prominent star-shaped seed head and detailed foliage.</image-desc>

It has leaves similar to the common Scabious, namely jagged, deeply cut, soft, and covered in downy fuzz: the stems are knotty, round, and sometimes a cubit high: from the joints of which the leaves emerge opposite one another. Upon the highest branches sit the Heads, composed of many membrane-like and chaff-like husks, containing individual white flowers: when these fall off, in the middle of what might be called the centers of each small stem, a certain small blackish star is seen, consisting of four, five, or sometimes six small rays: gradually, however, these husks grow and expand until the seed, which is hairy and thick, begins to ripen.

<summary>This page describes various species of Scabious (Scabiosa), detailing their physical characteristics, their naming conventions related to skin diseases, and their geographical distribution in Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Scabious, Scabiosa, botany, medicinal herbs, skin diseases, Cesalpino, Clusius, plant morphology, 16th-century science</keywords>

--- Page 409 ---
### THE GREATEST SCABIOUS OF THE THICKETS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Scabiosa plant with large, serrated leaves and multiple flower heads on long stems.</image-desc>

It is accustomed to grow among thickets and in the damp meadows of mountains, just as we observed at Basel on Mount *Monteri* <note>likely Mont Terri in the Jura mountains</note>, and in mossy places around Zurich. It blooms in October, and in its entirety is similar to Devil's-bit <note>original: "Succisæ"</note>; only the flowers are larger and more gaping.

Furthermore, all kinds of Scabious possess a warm and dry temperament: they are very friendly to the heart, liver, and all internal organs, so much so that when three ounces of their juice is drunk with two scruples <note>a small unit of apothecary weight</note> of Mithridatium or Theriac <note>famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "cure-alls" used against poisons and plague</note>, deadly and pestilential fevers are driven away. The same juice, when applied, wipes away all foulness of the skin, and is most useful for every kind of Scabies <note>The plant's name "Scabiosa" derives from its use in treating "scabies" or itchy skin eruptions</note>. *More in the Appendix.*

### SMALL FRAGRANT SCABIOUS, with flower petals stained with spots.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scabiosa variety with deeply lobed leaves and a single prominent flower head.</image-desc>

This Scabious, most beautiful and very pleasing to both the eyes and the nose, has a woody and long root from which various leaves emerge: for at the bottom they are either like wild Rocket or Buck's-horn Plantain <note>original: "Coronopo"</note>, but smaller and hairy; yet on the stalk they are like the jagged leaf of the common Scabious. The flowers, as in other Scabious plants, are purple, or bluish-purple, similar to exotic Basil <note>original: "Ocymo exotico"</note>, with the petals stained with spots and fringed: these same flowers—which is not observed in other Scabious plants—are pleasantly scented.

It loves mountains and blooms in Summer, and even in Winter in warmer places; it is also found with undivided leaves.

### SMALL MARITIME SCABIOUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller maritime Scabiosa with thin, divided leaves and several flower heads.</image-desc>

It puts forth a somewhat long and sufficiently thick root with many heads: from which emerge stalks nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantales"</note>, and if cultivation is added, even a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note>: the leaves are thin and like grass. The *flower heads* are large for the size of the little plant, filled with large purplish florets, with small leaves surrounding the said heads: the *seed* is almost like that in the Greater Scabious with beautiful seed.

It grew for us at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi"</note> in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>likely referring to the gardens of the Dukes of Württemberg</note> from seed sent out of Italy.

<column-break/>

### COMMON SMALLER SCABIOUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the common small Scabiosa, showing its characteristic leaves and flower structure.</image-desc>

It grows in meadows and open fields, in uncultivated lands, and at the edges of fields, along paths, and on earthy hills; it blooms at various times of the year depending on the exposure of the place: in May, June, July, and August.

Many differences or varieties of this plant are observed: for one has very finely dissected leaves, another does not, and a certain one has leaves that are not dissected at all. The flowers also vary: some are blue, others bluish-purple, and others white, which they call the *Female*. It also varies in size.

### SMALLER SCABIOUS WITH BEAUTIFUL SEED: or the Small Starry Scabious.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "starry" Scabiosa, featuring distinct seed heads that appear star-like or bristled.</image-desc>

It is fixed by a simple, woody, and whitish root, hairy with a few—and indeed small—fibers: the stalk is nine inches long, hollow, and hairy: with finely dissected leaves, covered in hairs: and those leaves which are placed beneath the *flower heads* are arranged like rays. The *seed* is downy, crowned with a membrane-like basket, almost the size of a fingernail, translucent and striped: in the middle of which is a small five-parted star: moreover, from the hollow of the seed, certain somewhat rigid filaments project.

It differs only in size from the Greater Scabious with beautiful seed previously described.

We found it in the maritime regions of the Adriatic.

### PROLIFEROUS SCABIOUS, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "proliferous" Scabiosa, where smaller flower heads appear to grow out of the primary head.</image-desc>

It is kept only in the more cultivated gardens, and has flowers of a purplish-blue color crowded into a head, at the side of which, in a circle, are poured out somewhat long stalks from which hang other smaller flowers, similar in color to the larger ones; from these sometimes even a third set grows, but they are imperfect. The first flowers are succeeded by seeds, such as those in the common Scabious. The root is brownish and endowed with many fibers, but it is not long-lived.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### RED FOREIGN SCABIOUS, called by some "Indian."
<note>original: "Scabiosa rubra peregrina, quibus-dam Indica." Scabious (Scabiosa) was historically used to treat skin conditions like scabies.</note>

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a Scabiosa plant with multiple flowering heads, long stems, and deeply lobed basal leaves.</image-desc>

Although this plant is unique and singular, and similar to the common smaller Scabious, it nevertheless produces several species differing in the shape of their leaves, just as that one does. Indeed, the lowest leaves which are near the root are broader than the rest; some are notched, some divided by lobes—though less deeply—and they cling to a long stalk, appearing as if turned back. Those that follow toward the upper parts are cut more deeply and divided by more profound lobes, as if subdivided into many others. Among these are some cut even more deeply and finely; the uppermost consist of either a few incisions or none at all, and are entirely uniform around their edge, narrow, and provided with shorter stalks. The lowest leaves and the stem are moderately hairy.

---

### GREATER MOUNTAIN SCABIOUS of warm regions, according to Lobelius.
<note>Matthias de Lobel (Lobelius) was a Flemish physician and botanist to King James I.</note>

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a mountain Scabiosa with a thick root system and several flower heads on branching stems.</image-desc>

It loves the hills of more temperate regions, such as Piedmont and Narbonne. Its leaves are narrower, whiter, and slightly hairy, and more lightly lobed at the base of the stem. The flowers are few, like Scabious or Knapweed <note>original: "Jaceae"</note>, with heads composed of scales, where the seed—like that of Bitumen Trefoil <note>original: "Trifolij Asphaltitidis"</note>—is dark and abundant, held in membranous coverings fashioned with narrow elegance, containing the narrow folds of the small arched structures.

---

### BROAD-LEAVED SCABIOUS with a red flower.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a broad-leaved Scabiosa with large, serrated leaves and three distinct flower heads.</image-desc>

The stems of this plant are a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, round, knotted, hollow, and not at all hairy. At each joint, two leaves grow opposite one another; they are not many-cleft like other Scabious varieties, but broad, yet notched around the edge, hanging from a short petiole, and endowed with a paler green color and a bitter, sharp taste. From the crook of the "armpits" <note>the leaf axils</note> leafy branches also emerge, which push out stalks from their sides adorned with the flowers of the common Scabious, of a reddish color and no scent. Then come the seeds, crowded together, angular, hairy, and marked with a star-shaped crown. The root is long, blackish, and equals the thickness of the little finger.

It grows in almost all cleared woods near hedges and in shady places throughout all of Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Balkans</note> and Austria below the Enns river <note>original: "Onasum"</note>. It blooms in May and June, at which time the seed usually also ripens, according to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary 16th-century botanist</note>.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH SCABIOUS, with rigid, green leaves.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a smooth Scabiosa with rigid leaves and two prominent flower heads.</image-desc>

It grows to a remarkable size, with rigid and grooved stems, along which the leaves are placed opposite each other, as if from joints. There are many of them, a palm and a half or nine inches long <note>original: "sesquipalmaria, quędam dodrantalia"</note>, clinging to long stalks. They are two or three inches wide, divided in the lower part by a few widely spaced segments; the final segment which forms the tip is three inches long or less. They are rigid, greenish, and smooth on both sides. On special shoots, a palm or nine inches long, the flowers cling from rather large, shaggy, whitish, hairy heads. The seed is long and hairy.

In Tabernaemontanus's *History* <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, early German botanist</note> it is called *Foreign Mountain Scabious* and *Narbonne Scabious*.

---

### CLUSIUS’S FIFTH SCABIOUS, related to the Daisy.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a low-growing Scabiosa with a creeping rootstock and leaves resembling a daisy (Bellis).</image-desc>

It spreads branches creeping along the ground, which occasionally take root by sending down fibers; otherwise, it has a primary root that is woody and somewhat thick. The leaves, similar to Globe Daisy <note>original: "Globulariae"</note>, are deep green, smooth, and whole at the edges, but cleft and heart-shaped at the tip, on a somewhat long stalk, with a bitter taste. The short stalks (sometimes quite long) rising from between the leaves bear a blue, clustered flower like the Globe Daisy, whose seed it also resembles.

It grows, as Clusius reports, in all the rugged mountains of Pannonia and Austria among the rocks; also in some grassy and uncultivated fields around Wiener Neustadt <note>original: "Neapolim Austriae"</note> in Austria; it blooms in May.

---

### SHRUBBY SCABIOUS, with undivided leaf, foreign.

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a shrubby Scabiosa with undivided leaves and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

The leaves grow in order along the stem from opposite, somewhat long stalks that clasp the stem; they are oblong, pointed, broader in the middle, hoary, and like Plantain, were it not for a different path of the veins. The stem is round, tree-like, hairy, and whitish, supporting a purplish, clustered flower. The seed is beautiful, white, somewhat long, and rather thick, ending in a broad membrane, like the Great Scabious with the beautiful seed. It grew for us at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden <note>original: "S. P. horto" - likely the garden of the Duke of Württemberg</note>.

By Lobelius in his *Observations* it is called *Foreign Scabious of rare elegance*, not yet recorded in literature; in his *Images of Plants* it is *Foreign Scabious*; by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is *Scabious 17, or the starry one with undivided leaf*.

<sig>Vu</sig>
