### SILVER GRASSY SCABIOUS.
<note>original: "SCABIOSA GRAMINEA ARGENTEA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut of Silver Grassy Scabious showing a plant with long, narrow, grass-like leaves and several flower heads on tall stems, with a detailed view of a single flower head to the right.</image-desc>

Along a downy stem, which is densely jointed, two leaves arise positioned opposite one another; they are silver in color and covered in a delicate hairiness, similar to the <term>French Toad-flax</term><note>original: "Holostei Monspeliensis"</note>, but longer, narrower, and sharper, resembling the Grasses, and provided with a single vein along their length. The very top of the stem is occupied by a Scabious flower head of moderate size, thick with silvery downy hair, and surrounded by numerous pointed small leaves.

We collected this in the Euganean Hills <note>near Padua, Italy</note>, flowering in June. Zwinger and Paschalis Gallus found it on the mountain of Vicenza called Sumano: indeed, it is frequently found in the iron mines of Styria <note>Austria</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLEST OF ALL MOUNTAIN SCABIOUS.
<note>original: "SCABIOSA MONTANA OMNIVM MINIMA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut of the smallest mountain Scabious showing a smaller plant with basal leaves and two flowering stalks.</image-desc>

It puts forth a few small stalks, a span or a foot in height: the leaves at the bottom are more often provided with narrower shapes, somewhere between <term>Sesamoides</term> <note>a genus of Resedaceae</note> and the Lesser Scabious. When flowering, they are a pale purple with scaly flower heads. It grows in chalky and uncultivated mountains.

*Is it perhaps a species of small Verbena? The "Adversaria" <note>a botanical work by Lobelius and Pena</note>, the "History of Lyon," and almost all others record this as our Mountain Scabious and the Smallest Scabious of all.*

---

<column-break/>

### GLOBE SCABIOUS, which some call "cuinam."
<note>original: "SCABIOSA GLOBVLARIS QVAM cuinam vocant"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut of Globe Scabious showing a plant with a thick rootstock, basal leaves, and multiple globular flower heads on stems.</image-desc>

It has a hard and woody root, whitish and fibrous, sometimes divided into several heads: it produces many stems a span long, sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, branched, sometimes simple, slender, and hairy. And on these are small hairy leaves, half an inch or an inch long, softer and curled (somewhat saw-toothed according to Lobelius), but those which are around the roots are longer than two inches. These have no evident taste. The flowers cling to the ends of the small branches, clustered like the <term>Leafless-flower of Anguillara</term> <note>Aphyllanthes</note>, containing small blue stamens, and are small. It grows on the margins of fields and flowers in June; it grows more vigorously in Northern regions than in hot ones.

<column-break/>

### ANGUILLARA’S LEAFLESS-FLOWER, OR Globe-flower related to the Daisy.
<note>original: "APHYLLANTHES ANGVILLARÆ, SIVE Globularia Bellidi affinis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut of Aphyllanthes showing a dense cluster of basal leaves and several globular flower heads.</image-desc>

Because of the shape of the very beautiful clustered flower, some have called it the Globe-flower <note>Globularia</note>. It consists of very thin stamens densely packed together: sitting upon the summit of a stem a span, a span and a half, and sometimes even a cubit high, which is round, sea-green, and reddish: it is clothed with many leaves, sometimes a single one, sometimes multiple from the same root. Other leaves are spread along the ground, very close to the leaves of the Daisy <note>Bellis</note>, firmer, smooth, veined, and bitter in taste. The root is woody, hard, and provided with red fibers stretching outward.

*The Mountain Daisy growing in thickets, according to Cesalpino. Indeed, Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, C. Bauhin, and almost all others record it under the name of the Blue Daisy. We have observed it in various places, in grassy fields, flowering in Summer.*

---

<column-break/>

### SUCCISA, OR DEVIL’S-BIT: German: *Teuffels abbiss*: French: *Mors du Diable*: Italian: *Morso di Diavolo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of Succisa (Devil's-bit Scabious) showing the characteristic "bitten off" root and flowering stems.</image-desc>

Where the long white fibers grow around the root (which is nearly the thickness of a pinky finger), the root appears cut off or bitten off <note>hence the name "Devil's-bit," from the legend that the devil bit the root out of envy for its medicinal properties</note>, and it has a mixed taste, sharp and bitter. The leaves are oblong, pointed, like those of Scabious: although not dissected, but either whole or just slightly saw-toothed, especially those which occupy the higher position: they are greener above than below, and here indeed provided with hairs, there with none, the outer margins being tinged with a trace of redness; they grow in pairs opposite each other along the stem, with a weaker taste than the root. The stem is higher than a cubit, straight and divided into "wings" <note>branches</note>. The flowers are blue or purple-violet, like Scabious.

It occurs almost everywhere in meadows and public ways and flowers in Summer. More in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### LEOPARD'S-BANE: German: *Wolfsbeer, Dolvurtz*: French: *Herbe de la Tore*: & Spanish: *Contecha*.
<note>original: "DORONICVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut of Doronicum (Leopard's-bane) showing the rhizome and a single large composite flower head.</image-desc>

Whether the *Doronicum* is the plant the Ancients called *Aconitum Pardalianches* <note>Leopard-strangling Aconite</note> mentioned by Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta</note>, or whether one should marvel at the same, is sharply disputed among writers. However, there is <unclear>no</unclear> time here to recite or weigh their opinions. That is done in our great History, which the reader may consult, as well as the Appendix of <unclear>this</unclear> Sketch.

Moreover, various species of *Doronicum* are <unclear>produced</unclear>, differing among themselves in the thickness and length of the roots, the roughness or smoothness of the leaves, and several other things.

The one we depict here is the GREATEST LEOPARD'S-BANE with a roundish, saw-toothed yellow flower. According to Clusius, it grows on the ridges of the Austrian and Styrian Alps among the rocks: it flowers in June.

<keywords>Scabious, Devil's-bit, Leopard's-bane, Globularia, botanical taxonomy, Alpine flora, medicinal roots, Styria, Euganean Hills</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the "Doronicum" genus (Leopard's-bane), providing detailed physical descriptions, habitats, and medicinal uses of various species found in the Alps and European gardens.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BROAD-LEAVED LEOPARD'S-BANE, with a large flower.
<note>original: "Doronicum folio lato, flore magno"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Doronicum plant with a large, daisy-like flower head, broad serrated leaves at the base, and smaller leaves clasping the stem.</image-desc>

The Leopard's-bane has a stem a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, round, channeled, green, and hollow inside. At the top of the stem is a large head, crowded with many small, yellow, hollow florets divided into five parts; this is surrounded by other rather long leaves <note>ray florets</note> that are notched at the tip and shine with the luster of gold, and it is not without scent. The seed is channeled, greenish, and easily vanishes with its downy tuft <note>pappus</note> at a light golden breeze. The leaves around the root are attached to long stalks, nearly circular and saw-toothed; however, those that surround the stem are longer, with a sharp and bitter taste. The root is a bright white within its greenness, as thick as the little finger, jointed and appearing scaly, divided by segments; however, the nodes tend upward rather than downward. From the lower part of the joints, it sends out long, white, fairly thick fibers.

### LEOPARD'S-BANE WITH AN ELONGATED LEAF, almost like Plantain. Called Grassoy Leopard's-bane.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Doronicum variety with elongated, ribbed leaves resembling plantain and two flowering heads.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> illustrates and describes this, calling it the "Lesser Leopard's-bane of the Apothecaries"; he reports it is common in Belgian and English gardens.

Indeed, the industrious pharmacist Johann Heitz showed us in Basel a plant growing in a pot under the name *Grassoy* Leopard's-bane, the green root of which he had received from the Rhaetian Alps <note>the Swiss Alps</note>. There are those who wish it to be eaten against Vertigo; yet its nauseating, though sweet, taste seems more likely to cause Vertigo by upsetting the stomach.

### GERMAN LEOPARD'S-BANE, with hairy leaves always growing in pairs.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with opposite, hairy leaves and three flower heads on long stalks.</image-desc>

According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist</note>, it sends out three or four leaves from the surface of the earth, nearly equal to Broad-leaved Plantain, marked with veins, soft, green, somewhat hairy, whiter and smoother underneath, always growing in pairs opposite one another. It has a stem nearly a cubit high, bare, round, and shaggy; at its summit is a shaggy calyx <note>the cup-like base of the flower</note>, from which emerges a large disk consisting of many yellow florets. That disk is surrounded by fifteen or more leaves <note>petals</note>, similar to the Rock Leopard's-bane, somewhat broad and notched at the end, of an elegant yellow color. The seed follows the flowers, as in other types of Leopard's-bane, and vanishes into down. The root equals the thickness of the little finger, divided by nodes and fibrous.

It is found in meadows situated at the feet of mountains, and is quite frequent in the very pleasant fields and woods situated near Frankfurt by the Main. It blooms in May.

<column-break/>

### GREATEST LEOPARD'S-BANE: with leaves clasping the stem in the manner of Peruvian Henbane.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall Doronicum with large, wavy-edged leaves that clasp the stem and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

To Clusius, who describes it at length, this is the Greatest Austrian Leopard's-bane. It is found near streams flowing down from the mountains in shady mountain areas, and it blooms in June. However, when cultivated in gardens, it gives flowers in May; for we have observed it kept in the more refined gardens of Rome, Florence, Basel, and Lyon.

As for what concerns the *uses and powers* of Leopard's-bane: its roots are recommended for obstructions of the body, and especially of the womb. According to Matthioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician</note>, they kill and expel intestinal worms, open obstructions of the intestines, provoke urine, and act against poisons; they also work against fainting and heart palpitations. And although they are reported to be deadly to dogs <note>hence the name "Leopard's-bane"</note>, we have Gesner and Lobelius as witnesses that they can be eaten by humans without harm.

### LONG-LEAVED HAIRY LEOPARD'S-BANE and Long-leaved Saw-toothed Leopard's-bane.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a slender Doronicum with narrow, hairy leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

The Long-leaved Hairy Leopard's-bane, which we illustrate here from Clusius, he observed on the ridges of Austria and Styria, blooming in July and sometimes even August, and subsequently ripening its seed in the same month. He says it grows in no greater abundance than on the highest ridge of Erigher, among rocks lightly covered with thin, black earth. We, however, found the Long-leaved Saw-toothed Leopard's-bane with flowers in the Rhaetian mountains in the same month. Its leaves indeed agree with the common Leopard's-bane in their soft down and yellowish-green color; however, the shape is different, being long, not very wide, and saw-toothed around the edge.

### A RELATIVE OF LEOPARD'S-BANE, Matthioli's Alisma, or rather Mountain Plantain.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with a basal rosette of leaves and a single, long-stemmed flower head, identified as Alisma or Plantago montana.</image-desc>

Matthioli is mistaken in thinking that this plant represents the *Alisma* of Matthioli to all drinkers; so much so that he does not hesitate to assert it is the legitimate *Alisma*. It would indeed present the same appearance if the flower were not yellow, and if it did not inhabit mountains but rather loved watery regions, as Dioscorides <note>the ancient Greek father of pharmacology</note> reports of his *Alisma*.

By Tabernaemontanus it is called *Damasonium*; by Dodonaeus, "Broad-leaved Gold-flower"; by Gesner and others, "Alpine Flowering Alisma," "Son of Plantain," "Leopard's-bane Pipe," etc. By Clusius, it is the "6th Pannonian Leopard's-bane."

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Doronicum (Leopard's-bane), detailing their physical characteristics, Alpine habitats, and medicinal properties, while correcting botanical misidentifications by contemporary scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Doronicum, Leopard's-bane, Alisma, Mountain Plantain, Clusius, Matthioli, Lobelius, Gesner, Alpine flora, medicinal herbs, botany, 16th-century science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of alpine and field plants, following the previous discussions on mountain herbs. The catchword "CYANVS" indicates the transition to the extensive section on cornflowers.</meta>

### ALPINE COLTSFOOT, LONG-LEAVED, with flowers like Leopard’s Bane or Alpine Marsh Marigold.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tyssilago Alpina, showing a plant with broad, serrated basal leaves and a single long stalk topped with a composite flower head, including a detailed view of the root system.</image-desc>

The root of this Alpine Coltsfoot <note>original: "Tussilaginis huius alpinæ"</note> somewhat imitates the fibers of Hellebore. The leaves are thick, some longer than a palm's breadth, hairy on the underside, and serrated along the edges; they are much shorter and wider in the young plant than in the adult. The stalk is sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, the top of which is adorned with a flower like Leopard's Bane <note>original: "Doronici"</note>, or Marsh Marigold, or Alpine Plantain. This flower is usually solitary, though sometimes two are observed. We saw it blooming in July on Mount Thoiry near Geneva. The flower eventually turns into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos"</note>.

<column-break/>

### GOLDEN WOOD-CONSOLID, with Sea-Lavender leaves: called by some Mountain Water-Plantain.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Consolida Avrea Nemorvm, featuring a plant with a basal rosette of smooth, elongated leaves and a branched flowering stalk with multiple small composite flower heads.</image-desc>

The leaf, as Pena and Lobelius say in their *Adversaria*, is like that of the Black Beet, or rather Sea-Lavender <note>original: "Limonij"</note>, but a darker green, fleshy, somewhat hairy, thick, veined, and similar to the Roe-deer's ear <note>original: "Dorcæ"</note>. It clasps two or three foot-long stalks like those of Leopard's Bane. The flowers are radiate, like Leopard's Bane or Marigold, and of the same color; specifically, they are an elegant sight, with small leaves joined and arranged like the teeth of a comb before they open. The root is spread into a thick tuft with many white filaments, in the manner of a Daisy.

It is found in the densest forests of Orléans, France, and blooms in June and July.

---

### CORNFLOWER: FIELD CORNFLOWER: German: Kornblumen: French: Blaueole, Bluet, Aubifoin: Italian: Fior campese.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Cyanus Segetum (Cornflower), showing the characteristic slender, branched stems, narrow leaves, and distinct fringed flower heads.</image-desc>

Our discussion concerns the Cornflower <note>original: "Cyano"</note>, the plant, not the gemstone. It has a woody root with many hair-like fibers. From this rise stalks a cubit or a cubit and a half high, narrow, hollow, grayish with downy fuzz, and divided into branches. The lowest leaves are notched with sharp segments, in the manner of Scabious or Dandelion; others are long, as wide as a straw, veined lengthwise, and of a bluish-gray or whitish color. The flowers unfold from heads composed of compact scales; they consist of fringed little horns, commonly blue in color—or as the name implies, <term>cyanean</term> <note>a deep greenish-blue</note>—though sometimes white or reddish-purple. The seed grows within the heads that support the flower; it is oblong, shiny, and crested with down. The taste of the whole plant is somewhat nauseating, but it has no scent.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE CORNFLOWER, FIELD CORNFLOWER, GRAIN-FLOWER, or "Scythe-Blunter."

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Cyanus Segetum, showing a more robust plant with multiple flower heads in various stages of bloom.</image-desc>

This plant is called *Cyanus* from the blue color of its flower; most nations have named it "Flower of the Grain" because, with its troublesome abundance, it kills off the crops—especially Rye—almost everywhere, even in the coldest lands. Others label it <term>Battisecula</term>, <term>Blaptisecula</term>, or <term>Baptisecula</term> <note>literally "harm-the-sickle"</note>, because it hinders the reapers and mowers by dulling the sickle when it is encountered. According to some, it is the <term>Struthium</term> of Theophrastus; to many, it is the <term>Lychnis coronaria</term> of Dioscorides, which he calls <term>athanaton</term> <note>immortal</note>. Pliny mentions it in express words when he says: "In the name of the Cyanus also is a flower; it blooms after the Rose and precedes the Amaranth."

There are those who assign it to the Succory <note>Chicory</note> family, but where is the resemblance? Tragus more rightly refers it to the Scabious family. More on this in what follows.

---

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED FIELD CORNFLOWER, or Multiple Cornflower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "double" Cornflower (Cyanus multiplex), showing a dense, multi-petaled flower head.</image-desc>

Many variations of the Cornflower are observed in size, flowers, leaves, root, and seed, as well as according to the nature of the place where it grows. Thus, one is the *garden* variety, another the *field* or *wild* variety; one is large, another small; *one*, as said before, is cyanean or blue, *another* white, *another* purple, etc. And again, one has a simple flower, another a double flower, which we depict here. Lobelius has two illustrations of this, and Tabernaemontanus has three; but to what end, since the difference lies only in the color of the flower, which the engraver is least able to express. We purchased the two preceding illustrations of the simple-flowered Cornflower already engraved: the first, which has wider leaves, is the *Domestic Garden Cornflower*; the second, with narrower leaves, is the *Wild Cornflower growing in the fields*.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE CORNFLOWER WITH A PERENNIAL ROOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Cyanus Alpinus, showing a thick perennial rootstock and large, deeply lobed leaves with a single large flower head.</image-desc>

It is fixed by a root of numerous and moderately thick fibers joining into one, which is hardy and perennial, with an unpleasant taste. The stalks are very shaggy with down and are angular; upon them grow leaves like those of the Rose Campion <note>original: "Lichnidis coronarię"</note>, but longer, wider, downy, and soft, some of which are continuous with the stalk all the way to the next leaf. Scaly heads support flowers like the common Cornflower, but much larger, fringed, and of a purplish-blue, sometimes even white, with "horns" about an inch long turning purple; the stamens are also endowed with this color, though their tips are ash-colored.

Tragus labels it <term>Verbasculum</term> <note>Little Mullein</note>; Tabernaemontanus calls it *Mountain Cornflower*; most writers call it the *Greater Cornflower*.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### CORNFLOWER WITH BEAUTIFUL SEEDS, of the lesser Centaury: with purplish flowers, etc.
<note>original: "CYANVS PVLCHRO SEMINE, CENTAVRII minoris"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyanus plant with a slender stem, small leaves, and a thistle-like flower head at the top.</image-desc>

This plant improves, like the others, through cultivation; when growing wild it is scarcely a palm <note>about 3 inches</note> high, as is well known to individuals, but in gardens it grows to two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> and is branched with many arms. It grew for us at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden <note>likely the garden of Sieur Pantaleon, a known botanical site</note>; however, Lobelius saw it growing wild on the hills of the territory of Narbonne and Tuscany. By him, by Tabernaemontanus, and by others, it is called *Rare Succory, Spanish Succory*, and *Purplish Succory*. The entire plant has a somewhat bitter taste.

### CREEPING FLAX-LEAVED CORNFLOWER.
<note>original: "CYANVS LINIFOLIVS REPENS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping Cyanus with narrow, linear leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

According to Tragus, the distilled water of "Bachelor's Buttons" <note>original: "Aqua Babtiseculæ," a common name for Cornflowers</note> is dropped into reddened eyes, and when applied with linen cloths, it benefits their inflammation. The juice of crushed Cornflower blossoms, dropped in, or the powder of dried ones sprinkled on, is effective against rotting internal organs. The same juice is also beneficial for thrush and putrid ulcers of the mouth when used as a wash. An elegant color is still obtained from the flowers for sugar-work, the use of which is thereafter free from any danger. Likewise, if they are thoroughly pounded with water and then passed through a linen cloth, and if an extract <term>ecchylisma: a medicinal juice or thickened extract</term> of almonds is drawn out with that water, it will please with a beautiful blue color; even more so if it is brought to the table in bright white dishes, sprinkled with currants <note>original: "uuis Corinthiacis"</note>, without salt.

### EVERLASTING.
<note>original: "XERANTHEMVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Xeranthemum plant with stiff stems and star-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

The name *Xeranthemum* <note>from the Greek for "dry flower"</note> was given to this plant because of the dryness and parched nature of the flowers, even when they are fresh.

It has an angular stem, hoary, downy, a palm or more in height, spreading out into branches. Along the stem, the leaves are arranged alternately, covered everywhere with a dense white fuzz, two or three inches long and a stalk's width broad. At the ends of the individual small branches hang single oblong heads, woven from bright, shining, white scales ending in a point, with a reddish streak. The flower is star-shaped and dry, consisting of pointed, reddish petals with numerous stiff, white, hairy stamens, among which lie hidden broad, soft seeds. The root is angular and woody.

<column-break/>

### VERY BITTER CREEPING CORNFLOWER, with Lavender leaves: and a Knapweed flower of a faded purple color.
<note>original: "CYANVS PERAMARVS, REPENS, FOLIO LAVendulæ"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping Cyanus with lavender-like leaves and a flower head resembling a Knapweed.</image-desc>

The *Adversaria* <note>a famous botanical work by Pena and Lobel</note> records that this plant is found hiding beneath the branches of Meadow Saxifrage in various places in the region of Montpellier.

Here, however, as well as alongside the following table, we shall list the Powers and Properties of the Cornflowers.

The Cornflower is of a cold temperament. The flowers cool by binding, drying, and repelling. Mattioli recommends them, boiled with the seeds, for the bites of spiders and scorpions. These same flowers are administered in Plantain water to those who have fallen from a height or those spitting blood. Women use the smoke of them for "suffocation of the womb" <note>a historical term for hysterical or uterine distress</note>; some use the powder for the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>. More in the following sections.

### SAW-WORT of TABERNÆMONTANVS. German: *Schartenkraut, Ferberscharten*; Italian: *Cerretta, Serretta*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Serratula (Saw-wort) with serrated leaves and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

With a straight, stiff, grooved, smooth, and reddish stem, it rises to two cubits, and at its summit, it splits into many branches. The leaves are sometimes whole, like those of Betony, and other times jagged like Scabious; both types are dark green, hairy, and serrated with a sharp row of tiny spines. Numerous oblong, ragged, dark green heads sit upon the ends of the forks, from which burst forth flowers like those of the Black Knapweed, of a purple or flesh color. The root is composed of small fibers. It takes its name from the leaves being finely serrated all around. It occurs everywhere in wooded areas and sloping meadows adjacent to forests. It is hot and dry in the second degree: useful for wounds and ulcers; and it is given to be drunk in wine for ruptures or for those who have fallen from a height.

### ANOTHER EVERLASTING, or the Sneezewort of some.
<note>original: "XERANTHEMVM ALIVD, SIVE Ptarmica quorumdam"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Xeranthemum with broader flower heads.</image-desc>

Clusius describes this under the name of Austrian Sneezewort. He gave it the name *Sneezewort* <note>original: "Ptarmica"</note> not because it provokes sneezing, but because it agrees in its other characteristics with the Sneezewort of Dioscorides. For it has slender twigs and hoary leaves like the Olive, though softer, and a flower almost like Chamomile. He gave it the epithet "Austrian" because he first found it growing wild in Austria, below the river Enns, and especially around Vienna, the capital of Austria.

We have seen it in the mountains of Savoy and cultivated it at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden, where it bloomed in July. By some, it is called the **Cornflower of Jerusalem**.

### CERTAIN SPECIES OF DRY-FLOWER
<note>original: "Xeranthemi". From the Greek 'xeros' (dry) and 'anthos' (flower), referring to the papery, everlasting quality of the blooms.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with thistle-like heads and narrow, alternate leaves.</image-desc>

The little stem of this plant is less divided than in the preceding one, measuring about a span or a span and a half in height <note>roughly 9 to 13 inches</note>. The leaves are larger, like those of an Olive tree, and more hoary or grayish-white, not at all serrated. The flower heads are fuller, with shining silvery scales, and have an insipid taste that is not at all bitter.

Some label this the "Olive-leaved Knapweed." By Lobelius, in his *Observations and Icons of Plants*, it is called the *Small hoary second Jacea with Olive leaves*, a species of Sneezewort. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is *Jacea 25, or Olive-leaved*.

---

### A RELATIVE OF CATANANCE, THE SESAMOID
->the small kind, with a more complete flower, according to Camerarius.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with multiple stems, small leaves, and several flower heads.</image-desc>

Camerarius believes this plant should be referred to the succory-like plants <note>Intybacea</note>, because the root does not swell with much milk, and this opinion is pleasing to many experts in herbal matters. The flowers correspond in shape to Chicory; some consist of a simple texture of petals, while others are more densely packed, of an elegant blue color, having yellow stamens in the middle. From these is left a blackish seed, narrow and tiny, enclosed in scaly heads. Whether it truly possesses the power of purging, he does not dare to assert, nor does he think anyone has learned so by experience. He did, however, determine one thing: that when administered in a small quantity, it achieves nothing.

---

### KNAPWEED WITH SCALES LIKE EYELASHES
->hairy.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant with prickly flower heads and lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It divides into slender, angular, streaked branches, somewhat hairy, clothed with leaves an inch or an inch and a half long, and about half an inch wide, hard and slightly hairy. A deeper purple surrounds the stamen-like flowers, similar to the common Knapweed <note>Jacea</note>, coming from a similar head that is entirely blackish, of which each individual scale possesses short hairs in pairs all around, like eyelashes <note>original: "cilii instar"</note>. It grows in the mountain meadows of Austria and Hungary <note>Pannonia</note>, and flowers in July and August.

To the same Clusius, in his *History of Hungarian Plants*, it is the *Mountain Knapweed with a hairy head*.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPS’ CATANANCE, WITH THE FLOWER
->of a Cornflower, and the leaf of a Buckshorn Plantain.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply lobed basal leaves and several flower heads on long stalks.</image-desc>

Some label this the *Lesser Sesamoid of Mattioli*; by Gessner, in his collection of plants, it is called *A certain Buckshorn with a blue flower*; others, as Caspar Bauhin notes in his *Phytopinax*, count it among the *Chondrilla* <note>Gum-succories</note>, while others refer it to the *Catanance*. We observed it flowering in the months of June, July, and August, in the garden of Master Plater at Basel; but growing wild between Nîmes and Montpellier, as well as near the bridge of Saint-Esprit. The author of the *History of Lyon* states it grows on the desolate and even the grassy hills of the Narbonne region and Lombardy.

However, just as truly as Mattioli wrote in his earlier *Commentaries* that he had no knowledge of the *Lesser Sesamoid*, he just as falsely says in his later work that this plant was found with all the marks agreeing very well with the *Lesser Sesamoid* of Dioscorides.

---

### KNAPWEED, OR BLACK KNAPWEED:
->German: Black Flokenblum. French: Jacea, Black Jacea. Italian: Lombruna.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with lanceolate leaves and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

The Knapweeds <note>Jacea</note> are wild herbs; they have flowers of a violet color, from which the name was perhaps given to them: for *IA* to the Greeks are violets <note>original: "IA enim Graecis violae sunt"</note>. Scaliger in some places writes *Getia* for *Jacea*, as if the name were made from *Geo* <note>Earth</note>, doubtless because the one nicknamed "Black" in this genus has roots as fragrant as <term>Phytanimum</term> <note>A term used here to compare the scent to Avens or "Geum", which has a clove-like smell</note>.

Furthermore, being about to describe various species of Knapweed, we will begin with the one pictured here, which is labeled "Black," to distinguish it from the three-colored violet <note>the Pansy</note>, which is also called *Jacea*.

It frequently arises in meadows and neglected cultivated grassy places, and also next to the hedges of fields and estates. It can be counted among the pests of the sowers; for oxen and beasts of burden abstain from it, nor do they eat the hay in which it is mixed. It flowers in June and July.

---

### MOUNTAIN KNAPWEED WITH FEATHERED SCALES,
->or with a shaggy head.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with deeply divided leaves and a large, scaly flower head.</image-desc>

Clusius makes two kinds of this genus: the *taller* and the *lower*; and he says both grow in the mountain meadows of Austria and Hungary, and flower in July and August.

Could this be Thalius’s *Entire-leaved greatest mountain wild Cornflower, of the Knapweed kind*?

Clusius, in his work on Hungary, mentions the use of the seed of the *Greater scaly mountain Knapweed*, growing in the mountain meadows of Hungary and Austria; and also the *Lesser scaly mountain Knapweed*, with a whitish seed, acknowledging the same birthplace; and he writes that they flower in June and August, but this one earlier.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Jacea" (Knapweed) varieties, focusing on species found in Montpellier, Narbonne, and Salamanca. It maintains the systematic botanical descriptions typical of early modern herbals.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### MONTPELLIER KNAPWEED, with black fringes on the scales.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant with a large, scaly flower head and jagged, lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

In the wild it barely exceeds a span <note>about 9 inches</note> in height, and is sometimes stemless; however, through cultivation it grows to a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, producing many stems from a somewhat thick root, which are grooved, hairy, entirely spongy, and very branched. The small leaves are scattered along the ground, mimicking the leaves of the Cornflower <note>original: "Cyani"</note>, covered in a hoary down, and jagged: some are whole, while the rest grow randomly positioned along the branches. The heads are surrounded by oblong leaves that are not at all divided but pointed; they are of moderate size, somewhat soft, and composed of rather long scales. The flower is white or purple, thread-like, turning into downy seeds <note>term: pappos (the feathery bristles on seeds like a dandelion)</note>; it is frequently found at the edges of sown fields and blooms in Spring.

### DWARF MOUNTAIN KNAPWEED, with a large pine-cone head.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing thistle with a very large, prominent, cone-shaped flower head and deeply lobed leaves.</image-desc>

This was presented to us at Montpellier, brought from Mount Ceti. By Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous botanist</note> it is called *Dwarf or Pygmy Knapweed*: and the *Pine-thistle of Narbonne*. In the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the Historia Generalis Plantarum by Dalechamps</note> it is called *Mountain Knapweed of sunny and gravelly mountain places, blooming in April*. Perhaps it is the *Non-prickly Chameleon* of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was an ancient Greek philosopher known as the father of botany</note>.

Furthermore, to say something of the powers of Knapweed: it is hot and dry; but not as much as Devil's-bit Scabious. Used as a gargle, it heals ulcers of the mouth, throat, and larynx, and corrects any defects; it also benefits those who are wounded, whether used as a powder, a decoction, or consumed in any other manner.

### MOUNTAIN KNAPWEED OF NARBONNE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender thistle with multiple small flower heads and narrow, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This has a slender root, a span long, and not very remarkable: the stems are nine inches to a foot long. The leaves are like those of the *Yellow Knapweed* and the *Smooth Chameleon* of Theophrastus, hoary on one side and slightly hairy. The flowers are like the *Common Knapweed* or the *Plume Thistle*, but smaller. We saw it among the rocks and hills of the Montpellier territory near Castelnau.

By Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants*, and also in the *History of Lyon*, it is called *Mountain Knapweed of Narbonne*. By C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is *Mountain Knapweed 15*.

<column-break/>

### SALAMANCA STOEBE-TYPE KNAPWEED, with soft downy leaves and a low stem.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branching plant with multiple small, round flower heads and deeply pinnatifid leaves.</image-desc>

It has entirely soft and downy leaves, jagged like those of *Rocket* <note>original: "Erucæ"</note>: the stem is very low, even trailing on the ground. The flowers grow at the tips of the branches, with the outer fringes mimicking the Cornflower, purple in color, with certain yellow hairs mixed in occupying the center of the flower: the seed is similar to the seed of the Cornflower: the root is the width of a finger, whitish, and not at all long-lived.

It grows abundantly in the territory of Salamanca, at the edges of fields and vineyards: and it blooms in June.

### KNAPWEED WITH SILVER SCALED HEADS, by some called Silver Scaled Scabious.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle with a single large flower head showing distinct silvery scales and deeply cut foliage.</image-desc>

Supported by a woody root, it sends out stems one or two cubits high, grooved, slightly hairy, and hollow in many parts. The leaves are divided by many-fold cuttings, thin and somewhat blackish. At the ends of the small branches, at the very top, grow cone-shaped spikes, covered in an overlapping pattern of elegant, shining, and whitening scales.

In the territory of Salamanca, at the edges of fields and vineyards, it occurs frequently and blooms in June.

### BROAD-LEAVED KNAPWEED, with beautiful spiny heads and purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust thistle with broad, spiny leaves and a large, prickly flower head.</image-desc>

It is branched with many arms, a cubit long, grooved, angular, slightly hairy, rough to the touch, and sometimes hollow. The lowest leaves are about a foot long and a span wide, divided into deep, wide, wavy segments, hairy and rough: the upper leaves along the branches are much smaller, similar in division and size to the leaves of *Hawkweed* <note>original: "Hieracij"</note>, crowded right up to the head itself. Furthermore, the heads clinging to the ends of the branches are cone-shaped, and equal to the heads of the Common Knapweed. The flowers are purple and thread-like, finally turning into downy seeds. The seeds are somewhat similar to the oblong Safflower <note>original: "Cnico"</note>, but much smaller and variegated: the root is somewhat thick.

We saw it blooming in June at Strasbourg in the garden of Friedrich Meier. Perhaps it is the *Mountain Knapweed with a prickly head* of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary founder of modern botany</note> in his *Pannonia*.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and classifications for several varieties of Knapweed (Jacea) found across Europe, noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses for throat ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Knapweed, Jacea, Montpellier, Salamanca, Narbonne, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, Theophrastus, Lobelius, Clusius, thistle varieties</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### MUSK KNAPWEED.
<note>original: "Iacea Muschata"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with a thick taproot, basal leaves, and several flower heads on slender stems. A small "XX" mark is placed near the root.</image-desc>

The root is woody and flexible; the stem is round and a foot high. The **leaves** are long, soft, and downy <note>tomentosa: covered with densely matted woolly hairs</note>, divided into long segments, and are white or ash-colored. The **flower heads** are similar in shape and color to the second Knapweed (which is called Wall Centaury). The entire plant is endowed with a sufficiently sweet scent, and has a somewhat bitter taste with a certain astringency: thus describes Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590), a famous German botanist</note>.

We recalled the *Spanish Purple Prickly Knapweed* in our great History; as well as the *Fine-leaved Knapweed with Purple Spiny Heads*: let the Reader consult those, as this page does not contain them all. This plant grows on mountains and sandy hills.

### STOEBE AND PHLOEOS: THE FIRST STOEBE OF SALAMANCA (of Clusius), or Succory-leaved Knapweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, branching plant with deeply lobed leaves and multiple thistle-like flower heads.</image-desc>

The **stems** are two feet high <note>cubitales: the length of a forearm</note>, striped, slightly hairy, filled with a spongy pith, and very leafy. Along these stems and branches are seen **leaves** like those of Chicory, jagged and saw-toothed, blackish, hairy, two or three inches long, and scarcely a straw's breadth wide. The **flower heads** cling to the tops of the branches, equal to the heads of Great Centaury but more cone-shaped; they are overlapping with scales that are smooth, shining, polished, whitish, and turning red at the edges, from which the purple threads of the flowers spring forth. When these wither, the downy seed-head <note>pappus</note> appears as the stalk opens.

The *Greater Stoebe* of Tabernaemontanus, who observed it in uncultivated places and along the roads between Worms and Frankenthal. Called *Greater Knapweed with Chicory leaves, or Stoebe* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*.

### GREAT CENTAURY; German: Reupontick; French: Rheponitice; Italian: Centaurea maggiore.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-leaved plant with a thick, scaly root and a single large flower head atop a tall stem.</image-desc>

Various plants are given the name of Great Centaury: *Greatest Alpine Scabious, several species of Knapweed mentioned just before, Feverfew, Spiked Loosestrife, Wood-ruff, Columbine, Henbane*, and *Gentian*. Cornarius, Tragus, and Cordus <note>noted 16th-century botanists</note> indeed concede that it is called the *Rhaponticum* of the Apothecaries; but only improperly, and solely because in the scarcity of true Rhapontic <note>a type of rhubarb</note>, Great Centaury is usually substituted for it. On the contrary, without any evasion and without any controversy, Amatus, Gesner, Tabernaemontanus, Mattioli, C. Bauhin, and many others conclude it to be the *Rhaponticum of the Apothecaries*. Furthermore, it was a great slip by Theodorus <note>Gaza</note> who wrongly called it *Gall of the Earth* <note>original: "Fel terrae"</note>, since this name better suits the Lesser Centaury on account of its remarkable bitterness. *More on this in the following pages.*

<column-break/>

### SPINY KNAPWEED WITH A YELLOW FLOWER, by some called a species of Hill Centaury.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant with spiny flower heads and deeply incised leaves.</image-desc>

It rises with a stiff and straight **stem**, four feet high <note>bicubitali</note>, striped, angular, smooth, and many-branched and hollow. The **leaves** are two inches long, more or less one inch wide, cut into deep segments, stiff, hard, and rough to the touch. The **flower heads** cling to the ends of the small branches, nearly the size of a Walnut, armored with scales that are yellowish-green and sometimes unarmed <note>without spines</note>, but most often ending in a biting spine, somewhat long and blackish. The threads of the **flowers** unfold in a circle: they are yellow in color. The **root** is at least a finger thick and fibrous.

Many label this the *Greater Yellow Knapweed*. We saw it at Montpellier on the path leading to Peraux. It blooms in June and July.

### HEADED STOEBE WITH ROSEMARY LEAVES (of Pona): or Cretan Garden Ground-pine, by Bellis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with narrow, rosemary-like leaves and small flower heads.</image-desc>

In Caspar Bauhin's *Phytopinax* it is called *Shrubby Knapweed with Pine leaves*; we have cultivated this and the preceding one in gardens at Geneva and Montbéliard.

Furthermore, that *Stoebe* was commonly known to everyone in the time of Dioscorides is evidenced by the fact that he described it with no specific characteristics at all, but merely said it was of common knowledge. Theophrastus says some call it *Stoebe*, others *Stiba*, and others *Phleos*; among them is the one which has a leaf next to the thorn: etc.

Pliny followed Theophrastus, but understood him poorly: for he wrongly says it has a *thorny leaf like Broom*; *Stoebe* does not have a thorn on the leaf, but on the stem. *More in the Appendix.*

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE COMMON GREAT CENTAURY, with the Walnut leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with large, pinnate leaves resembling walnut leaves and several flower heads.</image-desc>

The **stem** is straight, reaching the height of a man, divided into branches near the top. The **leaves** are a span long <note>about 9 inches</note>, three or four inches wide, arranged in the shape of a wing <note>pinnate</note>, saw-toothed around the edge, veined, smooth, and deep green: though when they first come forth, they show no serration. The **flower heads** sit on the ends of the stalks, being rough or scurfy: from which spring **flowers** composed of purple threads, vanishing into down: the **seed** is shining and oblong. The **root** is reddish, somewhat thick, long, and straight. Our figures, taken from those available for purchase, in which a notable variety appears, do not please us in all respects.

This Great Centaury with the Walnut leaf is planted in gardens, as seen in various herbaria in Geneva, Lyon, Padua, Chur, etc.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Knapweed (Iacea) and Great Centaury, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal nomenclature, and the historical confusion regarding their identification by ancient authorities like Pliny and Theophrastus.</summary>
<keywords>Knapweed, Great Centaury, Stoebe, Rhaponticum, botanical history, Tabernaemontanus, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany</keywords>

--- Page 418 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of Centaury species, focusing on their physical descriptions, historical nomenclature, and medicinal properties as cited by classical authorities.</meta>

### CENTAUROIDES WITH SMOOTH LEAVES and yellowish flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Centauroides plant with a tall, branched stem, multiple flower heads, and deeply lobed, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This plant is a cubit or a cubit and a half tall <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>, with a smooth, branched, rounded stem. The leaves are a span long <note>about 9 inches</note> or more, smooth and bluish-grey, divided into many segments all the way to the midrib. These segments sometimes correspond in opposite positions and sometimes not at all; they are somewhat thick, with a split vein extending through their length, notched with sparse small teeth around the edges, or sometimes entire, with a flavor like pot-herbs. Furthermore, single heads sit upon each small branch, the size of an olive but conical in shape, shining and overlapping like tiles, woven with such an accurate joining of small scales that they appear smooth and are not troublesome with any roughness. From these spring forth thread-like flowers, imbued with a pale yellow color.

It is frequently found on Mount Baldo; it is also kept in gardens, as we have cultivated it at Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince's garden, flowering in August.

<column-break/>

### GESNER’S HILL CENTAURY.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Centaurium Collinum showing a single upright stem with a large flower head and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

This has a great similarity to the Greater Centaury. By Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, 16th-century Swiss naturalist</note> it is called *a hill species of Greater Centaury, with divided leaves*; by Lobelius and Pena in the *Adversaria* it is called *Greater jagged black Knapweed, substituted for the common one by the ignorant Matthioli*. By some it is called *Greater mountain Scabious*. Is it Tragus’s *third Scabious*? Or Dodonaeus’s *third Aphyllantes with more incised leaves*? In the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Plantarum Lugduni</note> page 1066, it is *Matthioli’s Greater Scabious*; likewise on page 1108, *Dalechamps' Mountain Scabious*. In both places the same plant is described and depicted, which the severe Censor did not observe.

At Basel in <term>Waterfall</term>, <term>Ertzach</term>, and <term>Leirach</term> <note>local place names near Basel</note> we have observed it with purple and white flowers. At Montbéliard it abounds near the vines, and belongs to the fields rather than the meadows; it is also cultivated in gardens.

---

### BROAD-LEAVED GREATER CENTAURY, with a wide or undivided leaf.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Centaurium Maius Latifolium with broad, undivided, serrated leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

In its stem, flowers, seed, and root, this approaches the Greater Centaury with Walnut-like leaves; but the leaf is like Dock <note>Lapathum</note>, long, wide, simple and undivided, yet serrated around the edge. And Dodonaeus believes this to be the one mentioned in the book *On the Virtues of Greater Centaury*, which is ascribed to Galen; where two species of Greater Centaury are recounted, the *Greater* and the *Lesser*: and the *Greater* is said to have leaves like *Dock*.

Above Lisbon, on the stony hills near the Tagus river, Clusius found it; he says it is entirely foreign to Belgium and neighboring places, although the one with divided leaves is seen commonly in almost all gardens.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER GREATER CENTAURY, with a narrow Dock-like leaf.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Centaurium variant with narrower leaves and a prominent flower head.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are much narrower, like those of sharp Dock, turning greyish on the underside. The stem is upright, topped with a head armored with small scales and full of purple threads, the same color as *Artichoke* or *Thistle*. The seed is like *Wild Saffron*, compressed. The root is that of Greater Centaury, but a little more spongy.

It would take a long time to go through the praises of Centaury, says Ruellius; since Galen himself dedicated a private volume to it, organized by the individual members of the human body. Whence also Humelbergius says: It is a wonder that Physicians have blundered for so long, and that it is even yet unknown which plant is the Greater Centaury, and they themselves have used a far different and diverse herb in its place. It is nothing other than Rhapontic <note>False Rhubarb</note>, etc. We shall say more of *Rhapontic* elsewhere.

---

### GREATER CENTAURY WITH ELECAMPANE LEAF, hairy and greyish underneath.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Centaurium Maius Enulae showing broad leaves with visible veining and a sturdy stem.</image-desc>

The root of Great Centaury—to proceed in narrating the powers of this plant—just as it possesses contrary qualities in taste, so also, as Galen attests, it provides contrary effects in use.

The same root is suitable, according to the pronouncement of Dioscorides, for ruptures, convulsions, pleurisy, difficulty breathing, an old cough, and for those spitting blood. Similarly also for griping pains and pains of the womb; it brings on the menses and the fetus, and is fit for wounds, drawing them together and gluing them. Indeed, it even joins meats together while they are cooking, if one cooks the bruised root along with them.

Pliny also attributes the same to it, adding many other things. Moreover, what the root provides, the juice provides even better.

<column-break/>

### THIN-LEAVED SPECIES OF GREATER CENTAURY.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a thin-leaved Centaurium species with multiple small flower heads and finely divided foliage.</image-desc>

We classify this as a species of Greater Centaury by the evidence of the heads. It has a root the thickness of the little finger, a span long, with the nauseating taste of Cornflower. The leaves are like the silvery scaled Scabious, finely divided, whiter, and endowed with a bitter taste. The stems are sometimes one, two, or three cubits high, split into many branches, clothed with even thinner leaves like those of Pontic Wormwood. The flowers are in the shape of Cornflower, thread-like, smaller, turning purple, springing from the somewhat swollen and top-shaped heads of the silvery scaled Scabious. The seeds are small, oblong, reddish, striped with four small ribs, to which hairs adhere.

Around Basel, Montpellier, Montbéliard, and Breisach we have observed it on walls and in rough places, flowering in July and August. Tabernaemontanus, the *History of Lyon*, and others label it *White Jacea*.

# PLANTS

### CIRSIUM: German: *Voelsch Ochsenzunng* <note>Modern German: Ochsenzunge, meaning "Ox-tongue"</note>; French: *Cirsion*; Italian: *Buglossa*.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Cirsium plant (thistle) with large, jagged, spiny leaves and several flower heads at the top of a thick stem.</image-desc>

We treat the subject of *Cirsium* <note>A genus of perennial thistles</note> in general in the Appendix: let the Reader consult it there. However, various plants are bestowed with the name of *Cirsium*: the Meadow Thistle of Tragus, the Bulbous Thistle of Montpellier, the Greater and Lesser Bugloss, Hawkweed, Viper's Bugloss, and others.

But the *Cirsium* shown in this small illustration is woolly, having many white roots hanging from a single head in the manner of a common Peony. The leaves are longer than a cubit <note>About 18 inches</note>, soft, covered above and below with a hoary down, fringed around the edges, and beset with softer spines. The stem is thick, downy, and divided into branches. Individual flowers sit upon individual stalks, scarlet in color, like those of the common *Cirsium*, springing forth from a scaly head; these, turning into downy seeds <note>original: "pappos"</note>, leave behind a small white seed.

<column-break/>

### GREATEST CIRSIUM WITH A BULBOUS ROOT of Clusius.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a tall thistle with a distinct bulbous root structure and large, broad leaves.</image-desc>

The *Root* of this is firm, with many thick fibers almost resembling the <unclear>tubers</unclear> of Asphodel. The *Stem* is a cubit high, furrowed, and <unclear>covered</unclear> with a tomentose <note>densely matted woolly hairs</note> down: the *leaves* are large <and> bristly, full, green, <not> jagged, and beset with soft <spines>. The *Heads* at the top of the stem are large, opening into thread-like flowers shining with a purple color, which at maturity dissolve into down.

It grows in mountain meadows and at the damp margins of fishponds, among Amerian willows and reeds: and it blooms in July.

Clusius also refers this mild kind of Thistle to the *Cirsium* genera, and labels it the Greatest *Cirsium*, with a hoary leaf and bulbous root. Could it be the second *Cirsium* of Caesalpinus?

---

### MONTPELLIER CIRSIUM, WITH A LONG SMOOTH LEAF; of Matthiolus.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a thistle with long, smooth-edged leaves and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

It is called the *Cirsium* of Matthiolus by Gesner, the *History of Lyon*, and Lobelius; also by Camerarius and Caspar Bauhin. For Matthiolus depicts this plant as *Cirsium*, having received it from Pisa from Luca Ghini, who wrote that it grows in marshy places. We observed it at Montpellier near the Mill, in a swampy place. Indeed, Lobelius reports that it is found in great abundance near the olive press and behind the flour mills, in the shallow places of the Lez river at Montpellier, and in the coastal meadows sloping southward from the Grammont grove; he notes it is very well known to students there, although elsewhere in Italy or France it is little known or frequent.

<column-break/>

### ENGLISH CIRSIUM.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a slender thistle with narrow leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

It is so labeled by Lobelius in his *Icons* and by the *History of Lyon*. It seems, however, to resemble a white thorn with a stem a span long <note>about 9 inches</note> and the leaves of a *Cirsium*. The flower is solitary, like the Bulbous Thistle. The root is fibrous in the manner of a Daisy or Black Hellebore. It grows in the meadows in a village called *Avon* in the local tongue, with a sharp, astringent taste, and moderately warm. This description is by Lobelius and is too brief. It must be examined how much the British *Cirsium* of Clusius (of which more soon) differs from this one.

---

### CIRSIUM WITH NON-JAGGED LEAVES; with the greenness of Cabbage, and a long stem.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a thistle with broad, non-laciniated leaves and a thick stem.</image-desc>

Dodoens labels it thus, describing it so: Among the number of Thistles and Thorns, he says, is also the *Cirsium*. Its leaves are oblong, somewhat like lettuce, but pointed, and prickly around the edges. The stems are straight, two cubits high, divided into two wings: on each of which a prickly and bristly Head stands out, which after the vigor of the flower nods downward, and finally dissolves into a downy fluff. The flower is a reddish-purple color. The seed shines smooth like many other Thistles, etc. The root is quite thick, fibrous, and perennial. It blooms in June. Clusius calls it the Mountain *Cirsium*, as he observed it in certain mountain forests of Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>.

<column-break/>

### PANNONIAN MEADOW CIRSIUM of Clusius with a non-jagged leaf.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a thistle with a thick root and leaves that are not deeply lobed.</image-desc>

Immediately from a root provided with many dark and hard fibers, it puts forth leaves about three inches long and one wide, gradually ending in a point, but with a wider base around the stalk, somewhat hairy, and provided with frequent small spines around the circumference. From their midst springs a stem a foot high, thin, firm, beset with a certain down, along which are scattered leaves smaller than those already mentioned. It usually bears a single head at the top, sometimes a second and third, which, like the flower and seed, entirely resembles the common *Cirsiums*.

It grows, says Clusius, among trees on the slopes of certain mountains of Pannonia: but much more abundantly in the mountain meadows that extend along the Danube. It blooms in June, and soon after even produces seed.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### CREEPING BRITISH THISTLE, with a reddish-purple flower, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant with a single flowering head and serrated leaves along the stem.</image-desc>

The plant has a single stem, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or more in height. The leaves are alternate along the stem, long, and have very small, non-stinging spines around the edges; their upper sides are green, while the undersides are whitish and covered with a downy fuzz. At the top of the stem is a head similar to the heads of other thistles, with a large reddish-purple flower. The root is blackish and fibrous.

It grows in the meadows at the foot of Ingleborough mountain—the highest in all of England—in the county of Yorkshire, and it blooms in July and August. Whether the *Cirsium* <note>thistle</note> described by us and Clusius corresponds to the powers described by the Ancients, we confess, along with Clusius, that we do not know; it is difficult to pass judgment on them, for Dioscorides attributed no powers to his *Cirsium* except those he described from hearsay.

<column-break/>

### THISTLE: German: *Distell*; French: *Chardon*; Italian: *Cardo*. MEADOW THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle with a large, rounded flowering head and deeply lobed, spiny leaves.</image-desc>

The family of Thistles makes up the largest number of "headed" plants, which Nature has fortified in a manifold way with peculiar care. Indeed, here the stem, there the leaves bristle with spines; there you may see the flower and seed, and in most cases the down <note>pappus</note> springing forth from the tops of the stems and from the heads, nevertheless protected by threatening thorns.

Among the various differences of Thistles (of which we shall treat frequently alongside the figures in general), the one depicted here is commonly called the "Meadow Thistle" because it grows in many meadows; and because its leaves are eaten in food like other pot-herbs, it is also called "Grassy Cabbage."

To Tragus, it seems to be the <term>akanos</term> <note>original Greek: ἄκανος; a prickly plant</note> of Dioscorides and Pliny. Could it be the <term>Limonia</term> of Theophrastus? Or the <term>Cirsium</term> of Dodoens?

---

### BULBOUS THISTLE OF MONTPELLIER, with the jagged leaves of certain wild Acanthus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle with multiple flowering heads and broad, jagged leaves.</image-desc>

Although Dioscorides mentioned only one Thistle, and that briefly, many more kinds of Thistles are handed down by Theophrastus, Pliny, and other approved writers, both Ancient and Modern. For Thistles are either wild or cultivated, and there are diverse kinds of wild ones, just as there are many types of cultivated ones. We, however, shall first treat those which grow spontaneously under Nature's care.

We gave the Meadow Thistle of Tragus in the preceding illustration. This one, however, is frequent in wet places in the meadows around Montpellier, among Narcissi and Birthworts, blooming in May.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMP’S THIN-LEAVED THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall thistle with several small flowering heads and narrow, spiky leaves.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves placed at intervals, one by one, which are somewhat long, narrow, and rough with a few soft spines. The stem is rounded, a foot high, and at its summit are four or five whitish heads, which are not at all prickly. The flower is purple; the seed is small, oblong, and downy.

This thistle was called <term>Areophyllos</term> <note>from the Greek for "thin-leaved"</note> by Dalechamp because the stem is clothed with sparse leaves. It is a pity, however, that Dalechamp did not add the location where he observed it.

---

### SOFT THISTLE WITH DOCK-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick stem, large broad leaves resembling dock, and a single thistle-like flower head.</image-desc>

It rises with a foot-long stem, somewhat thick, grooved, and slightly downy. The leaves are like those of Dock, or "Good King Henry." The flower is a bluish-purple; the seed is wrapped in down, not very different from the seed of a Cornflower, but a little larger and whitish. The root is black, provided with several thin fibers, hard and long-lived, spreading shoots from its sides.

Clusius writes that it grows among rocks in the Austrian mountains and blooms in the month of July.

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN THISTLE, with leaves of Elecampane, non-spiny, with a red head, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain thistle with large, broad leaves and a single flowering head.</image-desc>

It is frequent in the mountains of the Hermunduri <note>an ancient Germanic tribe in Thuringia</note>, growing around the mining towns; it does not differ much from the broad-leaved soft Thistle of the same Clusius.

Camerarius, in his *Hortus*, lists it under the same title as ours and also calls it the <term>soft thistle</term>. By Clusius, in his *History of Pannonian Plants*, it is called an elegant, very tall kind of softer Thistle with a creeping root; the same Clusius also mentions a low and narrow-leaved soft mountain Thistle in the same place, reporting that it blooms in July and August on the highest ridges of the Schneeberg.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of thistles (Carduus and Cirsium), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats ranging from Yorkshire to the Alps, and their classification by Renaissance botanists like Clusius and Dalechamp.</summary>
<keywords>thistles, botany, Clusius, Dioscorides, Ingleborough, Yorkshire, Montpellier, medicinal herbs, mountain flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of thistle species, following the previous descriptions of prickly plants. The text focuses on the Milk Thistle and its relatives, providing botanical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal properties.</meta>

### MILK THISTLE, OR MILKY THISTLE
#### German: Our Lady’s Thistle, White Way-thistle.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut of Carduus Marianus (Milk Thistle), showing its large, prickly, variegated leaves with white veins and a flowering head at the top of a tall stalk.</image-desc>

The French call it *Chardon de nostre Dame* <note>Our Lady's Thistle</note>: the Italians *Cardo Mariane*. On this plant, one sees broad and long leaves, variegated with a wavy pattern of milky-white and green streaks, indented at the edges, and bristling with fierce, shining prickles. The stalk is the thickness of a finger, grooved, hoary with a downy fuzz, and grows two or three cubits <note>about 3 to 4.5 feet</note> high, dividing into several branches. The flower heads <term>Echini</term> <note>literally "hedgehogs," referring to the prickly involucre</note> are difficult to handle, armed with very stiff and sharp spines, similar in size to a modest Artichoke <note>original: Scolymus</note>; they unfold purple flower filaments from a callous, sweet, and edible cartilaginous base of scales. These are followed by seeds like those of Safflower. The root is long, thick, and edible. More is found beside the following figure.

### SOFT THISTLE, WITH LACY LEAVES,
#### and a scaly head with a purple flower.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Carduus Mollis, featuring deeply lobed (laciniate) leaves at the base and a single thistle flower head atop a slender stem.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> says it is found throughout that entire chain of mountains which extends from Calenberg and the Danube (which it overlooks) all the way to the Alps, and then through Leytenberg, and again through Prellenberg and Hamburgenberg, turning back two miles above Bratislava <note>original: Posonium</note>. It flowers in May and perfects its seed in June and July.

Furthermore, these virtues of the *Milk Thistle* (mentioned before) are recorded: The root warms, cleanses, opens <note>refers to opening "obstructions" in the body</note>, promotes flow, and thins the humors. A decoction of it is usefully given as a drink for obstructions of the liver and spleen <note>original: valorum, likely a typo for viscerum or splenis</note> and for retained urine: it benefits those with dropsy <note>edema</note>, jaundice, and kidney ailments. Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, Flemish physician and botanist</note> testifies that the tender leaves, once the spines are removed, may be added to cooked greens without disadvantage.

### NODDING THISTLE

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Carduus Nutans (Nodding Thistle), showing a branched stem with several drooping or "nodding" flower heads and spiny leaves.</image-desc>

It is a low-growing plant, with a stalk one or two feet high, split into various slightly hairy branches, winged along their length with spiny membranes. The leaves are small, rough, frequently but not deeply jagged, spiny and hairy; at the ends of the branches, they are round and covered in downy spines. Each branch bears one large flower head, similar to the head of the Milk Thistle, but nodding downward and composed of prickly scales. The numerous small flowers are purple, and sometimes white, spreading out widely. The root is reddish or blackish.

It flowers in August and is abundant at Montbéliard, around the walls and ditches of the city, as well as in the fields, such as between Audincourt and Arbonhans.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE MILK THISTLE: Called Chardon de nostre Dame by the French and Cardo Mariano by the Italians.

<image-desc>A second woodcut of Carduus Marianus, focusing on the upper portion of the plant with its distinctively patterned leaves and a large, spiny flower head.</image-desc>

This is common by the roadsides not far from Montpellier: it flowers in Spring.

It grows commonly in various places, and is considered a common Thistle, as mentioned shortly before: just as we have seen the "True Thistle" <note>original: C. veruz</note> frequently at Lyon, Basel, and Montbéliard, both in gardens and in uncultivated places. It flowers in the second year after it has sprouted, and meanwhile reaches maturity in its seed; once the seed is ripe, the plant dies, as do most Thistles, which have no longer a life than until the perfection of the seed.

Tragus, Fuchs, Camerarius, Dodonaeus, and others call it White Thorn, *Acanthium Leucen*, and the *Bedeguar* of the Arabs. But this is a great error, as Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus</note> notes: nor is it better named "White Chameleon" by Amatus, or "Wild Artichoke" by Lonicer.

### MONSTROUS THISTLE

<image-desc>A woodcut of a "monstrous" thistle, showing a highly distorted, flattened, and curved stem (fasciation) ending in a wide, fan-like flowering structure.</image-desc>

Regarding this Thistle of monstrous form, presenting a "horn of plenty" shape, which Ferrante Imperato exhibits in Book 2, Chapter 1 of his *Natural History*, and which he believes was the *Onopyxon* of Theophrastus, we have nothing to say at present. We would wish that Imperato had described it more diligently and compared it with the *Onopyxon* of Theophrastus, and noted the place where he found it, so that posterity might have more easily investigated the truth. <note>This "monstrous" growth is a botanical phenomenon now called fasciation.</note>

### THISTLE WITH A WOOLLY HEAD, AND MULTICOLORED FLOWER,
#### violet and white.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a thistle with woolly (tomentose) flower heads and spiny, deeply cut leaves.</image-desc>

It is called *Carduus Eriosephalus* <note>Woolly-headed Thistle</note> by Clusius and Camerarius: by Lobelius it is called the *Carduus Eriocephalus* of Dodonaeus, the *Woolly Thistle*, and the *Friar's Crown* of Hesychius.

Is it perhaps the *Monstrous Thistle* with a head covered in down mentioned by Mattioli in his commentary on Dioscorides?

Or the other *Acanthium* of Caesalpinus, growing everywhere on the borders of fields, larger and gray?

Or the kind of Thistle lacking a stalk mentioned by the Monks in *Mel.*, which is called *Friar's Crown*?

Or the *Woolly Thistle* found by Rauwolf near Marseille, not unlike the *White Thorn*?

It grows spontaneously in various places, both uncultivated and even in gardens: it flowers in July, August, and September.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of thistles, notably the Milk Thistle (Carduus Marianus), detailing their physical appearance, medicinal uses for liver and kidney health, and various botanical synonyms used by Renaissance scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Milk Thistle, Carduus Marianus, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, liver health, fasciation, Clusius, Dodonaeus, Renaissance botany</keywords>
