<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of thistles (Carduus), focusing on various "lance-shaped" and "smooth-stemmed" varieties, including their physical descriptions, habitats, and classical nomenclature.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### LANCEOLATE THISTLE, OR the wild thistle of Dodoens.
<note>original: "Carduus lanceolatus, sive sylvestris Dodonaei." Rembert Dodoens was a famous 16th-century Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall thistle with lanceolate, prickly leaves and a single flower head at the top, showing the root system.</image-desc>

It possesses a stem two or three cubits high <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>, covered in a white down, angular, reddish, winged along its length with thorny membranes, branchy, and rigid. It is adorned with leaves in an alternating arrangement, one or two palms long, hairy above and below, and divided by deep, frequent incisions. Each segment of these leaves ends in a formidable prickle, imitating the point of a lance. The **flower head** <note>original: "Echinus," literally "hedgehog," used here for the prickly involucre</note> is oblong, approaching the harmlessness of the **Burdock** <note>original: "Lappa"</note>, yet with stiffer prickles on both sides; these are not hooked with a turned-back point, but are straight and interwoven with white down. From the head, it brings forth tufts of **flowers** of a purplish color, which are succeeded by downy seeds <note>pappus</note>, to which long, shining seeds are attached.

It grows in abundance at Montbéliard around the castle garden and the city ditches, both inside and out; flowering in July, August, and September.

### SMALL LANCEOLATE THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller thistle variety with similar lanceolate leaves and a prickly flower head.</image-desc>

This plant very closely resembles the fiercer Lanceolate Thistle; however, it is smaller in all its parts if you examine each of its individual features specifically, and it is also significantly less "fierce" <note>less prickly</note>.

This plant and the two preceding it acquired the name "Lanceolate" from their leaves, the individual segments of which end in a formidable prickle, imitating the points of lances.

### SMOOTH-STEMMED THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle with a smoother stem and deeply lobed, prickly leaves.</image-desc>

To Gesner, Tabernaemontanus, and the Portuguese Garden, this is the *Field Thistle*; to some, the *Corn Thistle* and the *Oat Thistle*. Tragus labels it the *Wild Thistle*. Could it be the second *Onopyxus* <note>Ass-whipping thistle</note> of the *History of Lyon*? Or the *Spina ceanotus* of Theophrastus, Anguillara, and Lobelius?

It grows in many places in Germany and France, flowering in July and August. It is abundant everywhere at Montbéliard, in fields and vineyards, and even in gardens, both within the city and outside.

Furthermore, all the types of thistles already described, which are frequently a hindrance to farmers and reapers, we judge to be "vices of the crops," about which Virgil wrote in this manner:
> *The Thistle and the Christ's-thorn rise with sharp spines.*

<column-break/>

### FIERCER LANCEOLATE THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust thistle with very large, densely prickly flower heads and sharp, winged stems.</image-desc>

This belongs to warm regions, such as Gallia Narbonensis <note>Southern France</note> and similar areas. The leaves have almost the same divisions as the Lanceolate Thistle pictured before, but they are much more rigid and are densely covered with small spines on the underside and around the edges. On the back, where the rigid nerve or rib breaks out into a terminal spine, they are covered with a certain amount of down, though only a little. The stem is also thicker and firmer, like that of the Woolly-headed Thistle.

As for the small heads at the top, there are usually three, and they are larger than the heads of the [standard] Lanceolate Thistle; they bristle so much with a fence of spines that it is not safe to touch them rashly. We obtained ours from Paris <note>original: "Lutetiae"</note>.

### CURLY-STEMMED THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle characterized by "curly" or highly ruffled winged stems and multiple flower heads.</image-desc>

This has a stem a cubit and a half high, a finger thick, somewhat hairy, greenish, and endowed with laciniated, thorny membranes that are wavy with a curly entanglement attached along the length; it is hollow and has many concave wings. The leaves are wavy, nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantalia"</note>, dark green, rough, and stinging with frequent, biting prickles. The flowers, composed of purple filaments, turn into down; beneath them are the heads, the size of a hazelnut, covered with softer spines. The root is half a palm long, endowed with very frequent fibers.

Tabernaemontanus and the *History of Lyon* call it *Polyacanthos* or the *Many-spined plant* of Theophrastus.

It is abundant around the Castle and in the garden of Saint-Privat at Montbéliard.

### THISTLE, SCOLYMUS, ARTICHOKE: German: *Strobildorn*: French: *Artichaut*: Italian: *Cardo, Carcioffo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cultivated thistle or artichoke-like plant with a large, scaly flower head.</image-desc>

The Thistle which the Greeks called *Scolymus* and the Latins *Cinara* is of common knowledge. There are, however, two kinds of *Scolymus* held: the *Cultivated* and the *Wild-growing*, about which we will speak later. And again, in the Cultivated kind, one is *thorny* and prickly, the other *not thorny*.

The thorny one bears leaves like the non-thorny one, but more divided and more jagged, surrounded by thin spines. The stem is also similar to the non-thorny one, striated and somewhat whitish, at the summit of which swells a prickly and thorny head, with a hyacinth-colored flower and a seed smaller than Safflower <note>original: "Cnici"</note>. It rests on a thick, firm root that is not unpleasant [to the taste]. Thus, the *thorny* does not differ from the *non-thorny* except for the spines or prickles which the latter lacks.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of thistles, specifically the Lanceolate and Curly-stemmed types, providing detailed botanical descriptions and their locations near Montbéliard. It also introduces the Scolymus (Artichoke) group, distinguishing between cultivated thorny and smooth varieties.</summary>
<keywords>thistle, Carduus, Artichoke, Scolymus, Montbéliard, botany, medicinal plants, Dodoens, Theophrastus, Virgil, plant morphology</keywords>

--- Page 423 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical classification of thistles and artichokes, following the previous discussions on the Acanthus family.</meta>

### CULTIVATED SCOLYMUS, OR ARTICHOKE, another Illustration.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a cultivated artichoke plant with large, jagged leaves and a central flowering head.</image-desc>

In addition to the two primary types of cultivated Scolymus <note>original: "Scolymi satiui"; likely referring to the Globe Artichoke</note> previously presented, others also grow. For Caspar Bauhin, in the works of Matthiolus, distinguishes them thus: the cultivated Scolymus, he says, is twofold, *spiny and non-spiny*; and again, the shape of the head is sometimes oblong, sometimes round. These are again categorized as largest, medium, and small: and its scales end in a spine that is sometimes short, sometimes weak, sometimes robust, and sometimes almost non-existent. In color, they are sometimes reddish, sometimes green.

We have also observed other differences in the stalk, leaves, scales, and heads, which we pass over as mere whims of Nature.

Thus *Scolymus* differs from Scolymus. Indeed, some wish to distinguish Scolymus from the Artichoke <note>original: "Cinara"</note> in this way: that Scolymus is the wild Thistle, while the Artichoke is the cultivated variety.

### THISTLE, OR WILD SCOLYMUS: The Scolymus of Dioscorides: The "Agriocinara" of the Cretans.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild thistle-like plant with sharp spines on the leaves and flower heads.</image-desc>

It is very similar to the garden Scolymus, with a tall stalk, sometimes reaching the height of a man. The leaves have the very wide notches of the cultivated variety. The heads are smaller than those of the cultivated type. The thread-like flower is similar and purple. The seed is like that of the Safflower <note>original: "Cnici"</note>. However, the spines on this plant are longer and sharper everywhere: and the entire fruit bristles with very sharp spines.

It abounds in many places around Montpellier, in fertile fields and along roadsides.

Pierre Belon calls it "Agriocinara" <note>Greek: "Wild Artichoke"</note> in a letter to Clusius: and he says it is never without spines. Many others go hunting for the wild Artichoke and the wild Scolymus. Is it perhaps "Brancauors": *Acantha leuce* <note>Greek: "White Thorn"</note>, or White Spine, or Bedeguar? More will be found in the Appendix.

### WILD ACANTHUS, OR SPINY Bear's Breech.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Acanthus plant with a tall, spiked inflorescence and deeply lobed, spiny leaves.</image-desc>

Dioscorides made two kinds of Acanthus, *cultivated and wild*. Pliny also has two: *smooth and prickly*: and Ruellius writes that the latter is wild, threatening with its protruding menaces, and rejects the work of the Gardener; while the *urban* <note>cultivated</note> variety is smooth and hairless, and rejoices in cultivation and sowing.

The urban or cultivated Acanthus, according to Dioscorides, grows in gardens and in stony, moist places. We have seen it frequently in Montpellier, Lyon, Padua, Bologna, Basel, Geneva, and Montbéliard, both in gardens and in moist meadows: and flowering in April, May, and June. The wild variety grew for us in the garden from seed sent from Crete. You will find more on the Bear's Breech, Reader, in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### THISTLE, OR GREATEST SCOLYMUS, non-spiny: The Greatest Artichoke of Lobel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, non-spiny artichoke head on a thick stalk.</image-desc>

Palladius Balbus confirms that the Artichoke is brought back to a state without spines through cultivation and "adulteration" <note>term: mangonio; refers to the horticultural art of improving or altering a plant's natural state</note>. Palladius, so that the heads of the Thistles might lack spines, grinds down the tips of the seeds, and thus they are sown <unclear>rarely</unclear> <unclear>lest</unclear> they be those about which Augustus Caesar consulted.

Galen and Aetius write that the Scolymus Thistle <unclear>heats</unclear> in the beginning of the third degree, and the berried type in the second. Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, Oribasius, and Aetius say that the root, boiled in wine and drunk, draws out foul-smelling urine: and it miraculously cures the "goat-smell" <note>body odor</note> of the armpits and the stench of the whole body. Indeed, the Scolymus is so frequent among the delicacies of the glutton <note>original: "ganeæ"</note> that no sumptuous or inaugural banquet is held without this food, unless the season of the year forbids it.

More on Scolymus and the Artichoke in the Appendix.

### ACANTHUS THISTLE, BEAR'S BREECH: German: *Berenklauw*: French: *Branche vrsine*: Italian: *Branca vrsina*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Acanthus mollis (Branca ursina) with broad, soft, lobed leaves and a tall flower spike.</image-desc>

Although there is a great affinity in the names *Acanthus, Acanthium, Acanthon, and Acanthian*, their meanings are very different. For by *Acanthus* or *Acanthian*, the Bear's Breech is commonly understood: *Acanthium* denotes a small spine. But *Acanthos* is another thing, namely the Egyptian or Arabic Thorn: and *Acantha leuce* is another, or White Thorn, about all of which we shall speak in order.

The Bear's Breech, which we depict here, has leaves spread on the ground, deeply fringed, soft, shining with an intense green, and hairy. Among these rises a stalk of two or three feet, straight, which from the middle to the very top bears a wand <note>term: thyrsium; a compact panicle or flower cluster</note> of white flowers: the seed is contained in oblong pods. The root wanders far and wide, black on the outside, white within.

### ACANTHUS-LIKE THISTLE, WITH PALE purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant with multiple small flower heads and very spiny stems.</image-desc>

This plant has smaller leaves than the Milk Thistle <note>original: "Mariæ carduo"</note>, and is more spiny around the edges, sprinkled with many milky spots, but covered with a gray down, especially on the underside, with moderately deep notches. The stalk is two cubits high, winged with four rows of spiny "wings." The heads are small, somewhat long, crowded together at the ends of the branches, not separated by stalks. The flowers are pale purple, which are succeeded by whitening down <note>pappus</note>.

Furthermore, the leaves of the cultivated Acanthus are placed in the middle between hot and cold, and are somewhat moist: they possess a softening and lightly digestive power, like that of the Mallow, which is why they are also usefully boiled down for use in enemas.

<summary>This page details various species of artichokes and thistles, distinguishing between cultivated and wild varieties while citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny for their medicinal and culinary uses.</summary>
<keywords>Artichoke, Scolymus, Acanthus, Bear's Breech, Thistle, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, Montpellier, medicinal plants, botany, horticulture</keywords>

### WHITE THISTLE OR WHITE SPINE: German: Way-thistle; French: White thorn; Italian: White spine.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall, prickly thistle-like plant with large, jagged leaves and several flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

No small contention arises among Authors as to which, in the genus of prickly plants—of which Nature has produced so many—can be called the legitimate "white spine" <note>original: "spina alba"</note>, with all identifying marks agreeing. Thus, some display certain herbs in its place, and each considers his own to be the true one: the *Marian Thistle* <note>Milk Thistle</note>; and various other kinds of Thistles, the *Wild Clove Rose*, the *Sharp-thorn*, the *White-thorn*, etc. Indeed, those who confuse the *White-thorn* <note>original: "Leucacanthan"</note> with the *White Spine* <note>original: "Acantha leuce"</note> are in manifest error; even Galen, who had sometimes written of them as if they were one plant, finally distinguished them as different under the letter L.

The one we depict here is labeled by some as the White Spine with the hedgehog-like head.

<column-break/>

### WILD WHITE SPINE ACCORDING TO FUCHS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a thistle with smaller, more numerous flower heads and deeply lobed, spiny leaves.</image-desc>

It produces a stem three or four cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> high, furrowed and downy, covered with various and very prickly membranes. From these come leaves about a cubit long, wavy-edged, bristling with spines, hairy and white on both sides. The heads, clinging to the ends of the branches, unfold a purple flower that turns into downy fluff. The seed is like that of the *Safflower* <note>original: "Cnici"</note>, but smaller, variegated, and bitterish. The root is tender, white, and somewhat sweet.

Many writers call it *Acanthium*, others *Onopordon*, the Garden of Lous calls it <unclear>common</unclear> *Acanthium*, Johann Agricola calls it the *Thistle of Peru*, and Lobelius calls it the *More common road-thistle* and the *Very prickly common thistle*.

It grows in both parts of Germany <note>Upper and Lower Germany</note> along the roads, and flowers from June until August.

---

### GLOBE THISTLE: German: Foreign thistle: Giant thistle; French: Foreign thistle. Greater Globe Thistle.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Globe Thistle (Echinops) with a large, perfectly spherical flower head and spiny leaves.</image-desc>

Various differences are observed in the Globe Thistle <note>original: "Echinopi"</note>: in the leaves, which are either narrower or broader; in the flowers, which are either white or blue; and in size, whence one is the Greater and another the Lesser.

The Greater, which we depict here, has a stem one or two cubits high and the thickness of a finger, covered with purplish down, furrowed, oily to the touch, and sweet to the taste. The leaves are broader at the base and oblong, entirely sticky, profusely fringed, dark green above, hairy on both sides, though much more so on the underside than the upper; on the ends of the stems and in their "wings" <note>axils</note>, exactly spherical little heads are born, with whitish-blue florets. The *Root* is of middling thickness.

It grows spontaneously in rocky places and on hills overhanging rivers; it is also cultivated in gardens. More in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### LESSER GLOBE THISTLE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a smaller variety of Globe Thistle with multiple spherical flower heads.</image-desc>

The root is smaller than a finger, wrinkled, split into several heads, from each of which one stem sprouts, a span <note>about 9 inches</note> or longer, entirely whitening with dense down; from this come frequent alternate leaves, very finely cut right to the midrib, prickly, pubescent below with soft, white down, and green above. On the very top of the stem sits a spherical little head, smaller than that of the Greater Globe Thistle, clustered with florets of a deep blue color.

We have seen it between Montpellier and Péronne; and we have cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of S.P. It flowers in July, August, and September.

Could it be the *Rutrum* or *Ritrum* of Theophrastus? By Camerarius, it is called the Annual Round-head with a blue flower.

---

### ACANTHIUM, ILLYRIAN ACANTHIUM, called by some Onopordon.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall, branched thistle with winged stems and small flower heads.</image-desc>

Acanthium, says Dioscorides, bears leaves similar to the white spine, prickly at the very tips. Thus he says, and no more. Whence it is not easy to understand which Spine or Little Spine was called *Acanthium* by him.

However, the Thistle depicted here is called *Illyrian Acanthium* by some. It has a great similarity to the White Spine of Fuchs. The leaves are similarly covered with whitening down, more deeply cut, and entirely armed with spines. The stem is winged with prickly membranes, six or seven cubits in height. At the ends of the branches, it bears purplish flowers, like the Thistle already mentioned, also from a similar "hedgehog" <note>the spiny involucre</note>. Could it be the *Onopordon* of Pliny?

We have seen it at Strasbourg and Lyon, and we ourselves have cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of S.P.

<column-break/>

### BLESSED THISTLE: German & Belgian: Blessed Thistle; French: Blessed Thistle; Italian: Blessed Thistle.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Cnicus benedictus (Blessed Thistle) showing its characteristic bristly flower heads and lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It rests upon a root with blood-colored juice: the leaves are fringed, with the division of a Sow-thistle or Dandelion, armed with stinging prickles, and hairy. The stem is a finger's thickness, concave with many wings, partly trailing and partly erect, purplish, furrowed, and villous <note>shaggy</note>. The flowers are small and yellow, walled in by reddish branched spines, between which much down intervenes; beneath them are scaly, matching heads in which the oblong, yellowish seed is contained, attached to tufts of fluff. The whole plant is endowed with a remarkable bitterness.

Belon writes that it grows frequently in the island of Lemnos in the Mediterranean Sea, in flat places without any care being applied. We, however, have nowhere found it growing wild; but in gardens, especially among the Germans and Belgians, it is studiously cultivated, and flowers in July and August. More in the Appendix.

### BLACK CHAMELEON, German: *Schwartz Eberwurtz*; French: *Chardonnerette*; Italian: *Chamæleone nero*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a low-growing thistle-like plant with jagged, spiny leaves and a thick, fibrous root system.</image-desc>

We are by no means dealing here with the Chameleon lizard, which Egypt, Africa, and India see everywhere and daily; but rather with the plant of that name, whose etymology <note>The origin of the word</note> and other details that do not fit within the narrow constraints of this entry, we provide in the *Appendix*.

Furthermore, Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, and more recent authors unanimously recognize two kinds of Chameleon: namely, the Black and the White. However, the word "Chameleon" used on its own denotes both the white and the black.

The Black Chameleon, which we present here, is depicted thus by Marantha; and Marantha, Anguillara, Sarracenus, and others assert that all the characteristics assigned to the Black Chameleon by Dioscorides correspond beautifully to this one.

### TEASEL, OR FULLER'S THISTLE: German: *Kartendissel*; French: *Chardon à carder*; Italian: *Cardo*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a tall Teasel plant (Dipsacus) with a prickly stem, opposite leaves forming a basin at the stem, and an oblong, spiny flower head.</image-desc>

Teasel, or the Fuller's Thistle, is commonly established as being of two types: the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*.

The *Cultivated* <note>original: "Satiuus"</note>, which we depict here, reaches a height of two or three cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>: with a stem the thickness of a thumb, straight, rigid, hollow with many "wings," furrowed, and bristling with certain small spines. The leaves are in pairs, opposite and so continuous with one another that the stem pierces through them, and they form a hollow lip fit for receiving water <note>Teasel leaves often collect rainwater at the stem joint</note>; they are large, long, and no less bristly than the stem. The heads are the size of a fist, oblong, and armed with very rigid hooked barbs pointing downward: and among these, little flowers shine out like small tubes, of a purplish-white color. The root is smooth and white. *More in the following sections*.

### TEASEL, OR FULLER'S THISTLE, with jagged leaves.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a Teasel variety with deeply lobed or laciniate leaves and a spiny flower head.</image-desc>

This differs from those already mentioned by the white color of the flower, the thickness of the root, and because its leaves are very large, long, and wide, and deeply jagged <note>original: "laciniata"</note>. It grows abundantly in Alsace between Horburg and Colmar, and also between Rouffach and Colmar.

The Cultivated variety, however, of which we spoke before, is sown in many places in Italy, and especially in the territory of Bologna, with singular diligence applied by the cultivators. The merchants <note>original: "Magones"</note> of Yverdon also bring a great abundance of them in the suburb called *la plaine*. It flowers in June and July, but the prickly heads are gathered in Autumn. Concerning the use, name, and *Ambiguities* of the Teasel, see the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

### WHITE CHAMELEON, German: *Weiss Eberwurtz*; French: *Chamæleon blanc, Carline*; Italian: *Chamæleone bianco*.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a Carlina thistle with a large, flat, radiating flower head and spiny leaves.</image-desc>

This is the illustration of Bock <note>original: "Tragi"</note>, who labels it *White Chameleon* according to common <unclear>usage</unclear>. Lonicer also names it thus. By Cordus it is called *White Chameleon*; by Clusius, the *Lesser Carlina*. Perhaps it is the monks' <image-desc>small circular symbol</image-desc> kind of "Horned Discharge" <note>original: "Cerata Elatrum"</note>: so called because the large head stands like a Father: while the smaller heads stand like his Sons and Brothers in the manner of a crown, surrounding the Father himself.

It grows on the rough and stony mountains of Pannonia <note>Modern-day western Hungary and surrounding regions</note>, as well as on grassy hills and drier meadows: and also on the edges of fields in England and Gallo-Belgium. We ourselves saw it at Montbéliard near the *Vautaucourt* meadow, flowering in July: but in Burgundy near Vaucluse and Chastillon, they flower in September among the mountain valleys.

### WILD TEASEL, OR WILD FULLER'S THISTLE.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a wild Teasel, similar to the sativus variety but with straighter, non-hooked spines on the flower head.</image-desc>

Just as the Wild Teasel is of the same genus as the Cultivated, so it agrees with it in many characteristics. Namely, with an equal height of the spiny stem and branching of the limbs. The size of the leaves is also not dissimilar, as is the lip-like joining <note>forming a water basin</note>, and they are armed everywhere with threatening spines. The burrs bristle with spines that are actually longer than the cultivated kind: but they are softer and less rigid, and not hooked. From their recesses, purplish flowers shine out. The root and seed are similar to the Cultivated.

It grows almost everywhere, by ditches and in watery places in Lyon, Geneva, Basel, etc. It flowers in Autumn.

### COMMON SHEPHERD'S ROD.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a smaller Teasel-like plant (Small Teasel) with more slender stems and smaller, globular flower heads.</image-desc>

In its whole appearance it resembles the Teasel, four or five cubits high: with a stem the thickness of a finger, smooth, furrowed, hollow, branched into many arms, and armed with biting little spines. The leaves are born in pairs at the joints, opposite, not at all clasping the stem, but hanging from a short stalk, and provided with two "ears" at the lowest part; they are saw-toothed and armed with spines arranged along the veins that look toward the ground. The heads are smaller than the heads of the Teasel. The flowers are small and white, with hairy and somewhat soft spines, unlike in the Teasel.

It comes up of its own accord in various places, flowering in August: at Basel in the paths to the vineyards, at Montpellier in the meadow near the city, and elsewhere. Is it a species of Wild Teasel, as some prefer? Or is it Pliny's *Plumbago*, as the *History of Lyon* suggests?

# CARLINA, CAROLINA: German: Boar-root <note>original: "Ebervvurtz"</note>: Belgian & French: Carlina: Italian: Carlina.
# WILD CARLINA TO SOME, TO OTHERS Atractylis: German & Belgian: Three-Thistle <note>original: "Drey Distel"</note>.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Carlina plant with a thick taproot, spiny leaves radiating from the base, and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

Carlina or Cardopatium, says Gesner <note>Conrad Gesner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist</note>, is a genus of Thistle (Boar-root) to many herbalists. Its varieties are distinguished by size and the color of the flower—white in some, purple in others—and finally by the stem, which some lack and others possess: so he says. Others distinguish between the Garden and Wild varieties.

Apollo writes that the White Thorn <note>original: "Spinam albam"</note> is considered by some to be Carlina, and is distinguished by sex into male and female.

It grows on high mountains, in deserted places, and along roadsides, and it flowers in July and August.

The stem-bearing variety is more frequent among the Germans: indeed, we found it in abundance near Blamont, from where we transferred it into the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>abbreviated "S. P." for Serenissimi Principis</note> at Montbéliard. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a wild Carlina (Atractylis) with a more slender stem and smaller flower heads compared to the first image.</image-desc>

Not inaptly, says Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note>, is it written as Wild Carlina: for it rivals the flower of the Carlina, nor is it very different in its leaves. Tragus and Lonicer called it *Atractylis* and *Cnecumum* or Wild *Cnicus*. Gesner called it the Middle *Atractylis* as well as the Common *Atractylis*: some call it the Country Distaff <note>original: "Colum rusticam"</note> and the Wild Spindle <note>original: "Fusum agrestem"</note>: Clusius, Lobelius, Caesalpinus, Dodoens, and the History of Lyon identify it as the *Acarnan* of Theophrastus.

We saw this plant flowering in August outside the walls of Basel at the Stein gate: and also in abundance at Montbéliard, on the hill next to the garden of the Most Serene Prince and in other places: whether it may be called "Cultivated" by some, we declare in the Appendix.

---

# SMALLER WILD CARLINA THISTLE of Clusius, with a yellow flower.
# ATRACTYLIS OF THE ANCIENTS, THE TRUE ATRACTYLIS with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Carduus Carlina Minor, showing a stem with multiple spiny leaves and a thistle-like flower head.</image-desc>

Clusius found this nowhere except in dry, stony, and deserted places around the city of Salamanca, where it was flowering in August.

It is a variety of Wild Carlina to Lobelius: the Small Carlina of Clusius to Camerarius: the Smaller Wild Carlina to Dodoens, Vara in Baldo, and Tabernaemontanus.

Furthermore, the name *Carlina* was obtained from Charlemagne <note>Charles the Great</note>, the first Roman Emperor of that name, whose army is said to have been preserved and liberated from the plague in former times by the root of this plant, following the warning of an Angel. Others wish it to be called *Carlina* as if it were *Cardina* or *Carduina* <note>derived from "Carduus," the Latin for thistle</note>.

More concerning Carlina in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Atractylis Vera, featuring a central stem with sharp, jagged leaves and a flower head at the apex.</image-desc>

From a small, somewhat slanted root, a single stem is produced, straight, slightly hairy, and filled with white pith; it is clothed with alternate leaves, dark green, veined, and cut into deep and sharp segments, provided with no stalk <note>sessile leaves</note>. The top of the stem breaks into several wings, the ends of which are occupied by heads composed of long, biting, leafy scales. The flowers are thread-like, yellow, and dissolve into downy tufts <note>pappus</note>.

It is frequent and grows spontaneously at Lyon and around Geneva; but to the Germans and Belgians, it is a garden plant. However, it flowers and matures its seed late.

It took the name *Atractylis* from the fact that ancient women used it as a spindle; for <unclear>atractos</unclear> <note>Greek: ἄτρακτος</unclear></note> signifies a spindle. More in the Appendix.

---

# YELLOW THORN, THE SCOLYMUS OF THEOPHRASTUS, the Yellow Eryngium of Montpellier.
# HACUB OR SILYBUM TO SOME.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Spina Lutea (Scolymus), showing a very prickly plant with dense, sharp foliage and a thick root system.</image-desc>

It is handed down by writers under these names, and is also called the *Eryngium* of Vegetius; whence also Anguillara says the *Eryngium* of Vegetius is the same plant as the *Scolymus* of Theophrastus.

It is called yellow or citron-colored because the flowers, which sit tufted among the leaves, shine with a golden color. It grows everywhere around Montpellier, and flowers in the Spring, and sometimes also in Summer and Autumn: at Montbéliard, in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, it grew for us from seed: but in Crete, according to Belon, it grows spontaneously everywhere and is called *Ascolombres*.

We saw it for sale in the markets at Ravenna and Ancona: for they use the root and leaves of the sprouting plant before it develops a stem, both raw and cooked.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Hacub or Silybum, showing a robust plant with broad, spiny leaves and a large, prickly flower head.</image-desc>

In early Spring it pushes forth "asparagus" <note>tender young shoots</note>, which the inhabitants cut, and cook and eat in the manner of our own people. The whole plant is very similar to our native Carlina. However, it is larger than that, and raises a taller stalk; upon the top of which sit prickly heads, from which reddish florets spring forth.

To Rauwolf, the author of the description, it is called the *Hacub* of Serapion and the *Silybum* of Dioscorides.

It grows around Aleppo in dry and rugged places. The root, when infused and drunk, produces nausea and vomiting.

It also discusses the edible uses of the Scolymus and Hacub plants in the Mediterranean and Near East.</summary>
<keywords>Carlina, Atractylis, Charlemagne, medicinal plants, botanical history, edible thistles, Montbéliard, Aleppo, Scolymus, Silybum</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### CNICUS, CNECUS, CARTHAMUS: Ger. *Wild Saffron*: Fr. *Bastard Saffron*: Ital. *Saracen Saffron*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cnicus (wild saffron) plant, showing a central stalk with spiny leaves and a thistle-like flower head at the top, with a detailed root system.</image-desc>

The Carthamus <note>Safflower</note> rises with a single stalk, which is divided into branches at the top. The leaves along the stalk and branches are scattered, veined, smooth, and gifted with short little spines around the edges; they are an inch and a half or two inches long, almost an inch wide, ending in a point, and attached to the branches by a narrow neck. Sitting at the ends of the branches are the *Heads*, scaly and nestled among leaves: from which the *flowers* unfold, dyed with a deep, thread-like saffron-red. The seed is attached to a downy tuft <note>pappus</note>, being oblong and white, with a sweet white marrow.

No differences are noted by Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, except that he says the seed sometimes consists of white, and sometimes of reddish. But Theophrastus, Pliny, and Mesue distinguish it better into the *wild* and *Domestic* types.

<column-break/>

### CNICUS, OR CARTHAMUS, with a BLUE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a blue-flowered Carthamus, similar in structure to the previous plant but with slightly different leaf shapes and flower head density.</image-desc>

Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, and Lobel have made mention of this, both in their Observations and in their Illustrations of Plants. Clusius also has it and describes it at length: however, its flower is not yellow like the preceding one, but consists of many threads of a blue color. Clusius found it among the cornfields around Córdoba: but we have had it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg's gardens</note>, flowering at the same time as the other.

The common or yellow kind is sown in various places in gardens and fields, as we shall declare more fully in the Appendix; there we shall treat more extensively of its location, season, sowing, cultivation, temperament, powers, and its various names.

---

### ERYNGIUM: Ger. *Brackendistel, Manstreuv*: Fr. *Sea Holly, Thistle of a hundred heads*: Ital. *Eringio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Eryngium vulgare (Sea Holly), featuring deeply lobed, spiny leaves and multiple flower heads on branched stems.</image-desc>

The common Eryngium <note>Sea Holly</note> which we depict here, rests upon a very large root, the thickness of the little finger, and white: the stalk is hollow and grooved, whitish, a cubit or a cubit and a half long <note>about 18–27 inches</note>, filled with a white spongy pith, and divided into frequent branches near the top. The leaves are broad, almost sea-green, stiff, and threaten on all sides with smooth spines; they are deeply jagged, and their segments are similarly subdivided. The prickly heads are very numerous, almost equal to a shepherd's rod, and they bring forth whitish flowers among biting spines, gifted with tips of the same color, below which the leaves are arranged in a circle, grooved, somewhat long, with a spiny point and margins. More on this in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### BLUE ERYNGIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Eryngium caeruleum, showing a more upright growth habit with distinct spiny bracts surrounding the flower heads.</image-desc>

Matthioli, Anguillara, Castore, and Gesner (in his book on gardens) distinguish this blue Eryngium from the common one only by the color of the flower.

Is the plant improperly called the *Rose of Jericho* the same as this in the Appendix?

By Lobel in his *Adversaria* it is called the Blue Mountain Eryngium, not to be accepted as the one described by Dioscorides.

To Caesalpinus, it is another Eryngium with blue tops, which they call the "Thorn of St. Francis" on Mount Avernus in the Apennines: to Camerarius in his garden, it is the "All-Blue Eryngium" in the mountains of the Savoyards: in the German History of Matthioli, it is another kind of Eryngium with a blue flower, occurring only in the Avernus of the Apennines.

We ourselves have seen it in various gardens, at Strasbourg, Esslingen, Stuttgart, and elsewhere.

---

### SMALL FLAT ERYNGIUM OF MUTONI.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Eryngium species with flatter, less divided leaves and small flower heads.</image-desc>

Of this, Lobel writes thus: It is rarely seen, he says, in the countryside or in the gardens among the Belgians; its leaves are much smaller and narrower than the Teasel; with stalks nine inches or a foot long, winding and spreading: at the top of which, and along their length, are flowers smaller than the field Eryngium. The root is like that of Wild Asparagus.

Furthermore, it is believed that Eryngium contracted its name from the nature of the thing: namely from the "belch" which the Greeks call <term>eryge</term> <note>original: ἐρυγὴν</note>: because if by chance any she-goat should come upon and swallow a stalk or twig of Eryngium, the whole flock immediately stops, abandoning their desire to graze, standing as if stunned, until the goat has cast out the Eryngium by a belch, or the shepherd has snatched it from its mouth.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAFED FLAT ERYNGIUM, with a small round head: and a whitish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Eryngium with small, round head and a thick root.</image-desc>

This grows frequently in the meadows situated along the Danube above and below Vienna, where it flowers in July. The Silesian mountains also have it growing wild, and it also grows easily when brought into gardens. As we have cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince, flowering in August and September: however, with age, the flowers turn toward blue.

As far as the powers and faculties of Eryngium are concerned; its root heats, but only moderately; it opens the passages, moves the menses and urine, expels sand from the kidneys and bladder, and provokes the languors of Venus <note>acts as an aphrodisiac</note>. What its differences and varieties are is clear both from what has been said before and what is soon to be said.

Concerning the various names, see the Appendix.

### VERY BEAUTIFUL ALPINE ERYNGIUM
<note>Commonly known today as Alpine Sea Holly or Queen of the Alps.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Eryngium alpinum plant, showing its distinctive jagged, thistle-like leaves and a flowering head with a spiny involucre.</image-desc>

The *root* has several heads, is about a thumb's width thick, and is tufted toward the ground. The first *leaves* rest on stalks more than a cubit <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches.</note> long; they are like those of the Marsh Marigold, curved in the same way near the stalk, but with a sharper point and saw-toothed around the edge. Other leaves along the stems are fringed at the branching of the stalks and deeply cut; these are blue, especially the uppermost ones, as is the stem itself along with the branches. The *flower heads* <note>original: "Echini," literally "hedgehogs," referring to the prickly burr-like heads.</note> are large and oblong, hedged in by a very dense rampart of numerous crested blue leaves that rise above the head.

We observed it in abundance on Mount Thoiry near Geneva, where it flowers in July. Sown at Montbéliard in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>original: "S. P. horto," likely referring to the Prince of Württemberg's garden.</note>, it grows successfully.

---

### STAR THISTLE, OR CALCITRAPA
#### German: Wallen-distel; French: Chaussetrappe; Italian: Cacatréppola.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Carduus stellatus (Star Thistle), featuring deeply lobed leaves and flower heads surrounded by long, radiating spines resembling a star.</image-desc>

It is a cubit or a cubit and a half high. The *stem* is angular, somewhat hairy, and hollowed with many "wings" <note>referring to the leafy ridges along the stem</note>. The *leaves* are quite soft, sometimes a foot long, somewhat grayish-white, and deeply dissected into irregular fringes. The *small heads* clinging to the ends of the twigs are smooth, equal in size to the heads of a Cornflower, with each scale ending in stiff and biting spines an inch or an inch and a half long, so that they seem to imitate a radiating star. The stamens of the *flowers* are purple, or more rarely white. The *seed* is slippery, small, and oblong. The *root* is a foot long, a finger thick, soft, juicy, and whitish.

It obtained the name *Calcitrapa* <note>The "caltrop," a multi-pointed weapon used to puncture the feet of horses or soldiers.</note> because it is crushed not by the hands, but by the heels. Concerning its location, season, and medicinal powers, see the Appendix.

---

### ACARNA

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Acarna plant, a thistle-like herb with narrow, spiny leaves and a terminal flower head.</image-desc>

One *Acarna* differs from another *Acarna*: for as Hesychius says, *akarna* <note>original Greek: ἄκαρνα</note> is the Iris or Laurel; but *Acarna* is also a *spinous plant* <note>original Greek: ἀκανθώδης φυτὸν</note>. Indeed, it seems to Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany."</note> that *Acarna* is a certain kind of *Atractylis* <note>Distaff thistle.</note>. He says the spine of the *Acarna* serves as its leaf, similar to the cultivated Safflower, only reddish in color and with a fatty juice.

The *Acarna* of Theophrastus, as Anguillara writes, is found in Illyria and grows copiously on the Island of Lesina <note>Modern Hvar, Croatia.</note>, with yellowish spines, but otherwise entirely white, with many branches, yellowish flowers from small prickly heads, and a seed similar to Safflower of a reddish color; it is an annual plant. We have depicted here the kind we received from Valerius Dourez.

<column-break/>

### SEA ERYNGIUM
<note>Commonly known as Sea Holly.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Eryngium marinum (Sea Holly), showing its thick, leathery, spiny-edged leaves and rounded flower heads.</image-desc>

The *roots* of this plant are very long, wandering deeply in every direction, with an aromatic flavor. The *leaves* are not at all or very little fringed, almost round, yet somehow wider than they are long, thick and therefore dense, whitish or sea-green <note>original: "glauca"</note> like the whole plant, and armed with biting, stiff little spikes. The *stem* is a cubit high and very branched. The *heads* sit at the ends of the twigs among stinging leaves, bringing forth whitish *flowers*. The two *seeds* are broad and inseparable; since they are beset on all sides by spines, they can hardly be removed without injury.

The Venetian shores are seen to be filled with this everywhere. It grows naturally and frequently not only in warmer regions, but also in the maritime areas of Northern and colder regions. It is also kept in gardens.

---

### THE LEUCACANTHA OF THE ANCIENTS, THISTLE, or Solstitial Spine.
<note>Likely the Yellow Star-thistle (Centaurea solstitialis).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Leucacantha (Yellow Star-thistle), showing a slender, branched stem with small spiny flower heads.</image-desc>

Botanists commonly call this plant the Solstitial Spine or Thistle, and some call it *Leucacantha* <note>White-thorn.</note>. It is divided into frequent branches; the *stem* is slender, two cubits high, covered everywhere with a white down, and "winged" with membranes fitted along its length. The *leaves* approach the leaves of the Cornflower, being whitish and hairy. The *small heads* are also equal to Cornflower heads, but are dangerous with long, stiff, yellow spines born from the tip of each scale. The stamens of the *flowers* are yellow, which finally vanish into down <note>original: "pappos," the fluff that carries seeds on the wind.</note>. The *root* is long and woody. It abounds naturally at Montpellier and flowers in Autumn. More in the Appendix.

---

### CHAMELEON SIMILAR TO ACARNA
#### Of Salamanca (from Clusius); German: Spanish Boar-root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Acarnae similis Chamaeleon, showing a robust thistle with broad, very spiny leaves and a large central flower head.</image-desc>

The *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" by Dalechamps.</note> says that this plant is very closely related to the *Acarna* in its origin, leaf, and entire appearance. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist.</note> says it is very frequent in the fields of Salamanca; it produces a flower in July and ripens its seed in August.

By Dodoens it is called in Latin the *Black Chameleon of Salamanca*; by Tabernaemontanus in his Illustrations and History, it is called *Clusius's Spanish Chameleon*.

<keywords>Eryngium alpinum, Sea Holly, Star Thistle, Calcitrapa, Acarna, Leucacantha, Chameleon thistle, botanical illustration, Renaissance botany, medicinal herbs</keywords>

### THE FIERCE LION, RELATED TO THE ACARNA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spiny thistle-like plant with deeply lobed, prickly leaves and a single flower head at the top of a short stem.</image-desc>

Modern writers have called this plant the "Fierce Lion" <note>original: "Leonem ferocem"</note>, easily the phoenix of the entire thistle family <note>original: "Acanacei generis"</note>, because of its little spikes and most troublesome thorns. Indeed, you would see nothing else from its deep, divided leaves and heads but spikes and brambles, an inch or an inch and a half long. The little stalk scarcely equals a palm's breadth; the flower is like that of the Wild Safflower <note>original: "Cuici syluestris"</note>, pale, and surrounded by raging and bristling thorns and prickles. According to Lobelius.

It is called the Lion and the Fierce Thistle by Lobelius; to Tabernaemontanus, it is a rare plant and scarcely known, growing on certain arid hills of Italy, not very far removed from the Apennines.

### THE LITTLE THISTLE OF MOUNT LUPUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with a rosette of jagged, spiny leaves and several flower heads on short stalks.</image-desc>

Immediately from a simple root, several leaves grow, two inches or a palm long, somewhat stiff, divided into spiny segments half an inch long and spaced rather far apart, similar to the leaves of the Star Thistle. For the most part, there is no stem, though sometimes it is a palm and a half high, clothed with a few smaller leaves and slightly hairy with short down; it bears a large head at the summit, solitary and long, beset with stiff, fearsome, and spiny leaves, beneath which lie oblong and harmless scales, confining the downy seed-head <term>pappum: the feathery part of a thistle seed that allows it to fly</term> which the purple flower leaves behind as it withers.

### A KIND OF SMALL THISTLE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender thistle with small, pinnate leaves and multiple small flower heads at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

This is a quite beautiful thistle, resting on a somewhat long but slender root, from which several stems rise, thin, a palm's breadth or higher, divided into branches, along which are little leaves an inch long and a stalk's width, endowed with small spines along the margins and slightly hairy. The little heads, clinging to the ends of the small branches, are enclosed within a lattice-work of feathered leaves, similar to the heads of the Cornflower <note>original: "Cyani"</note>, but smaller.

Moreover, this thistle, as seen by us, is not much larger than the illustration itself. We obtained it among the plants of Valerandus Dourez.

<column-break/>

### THE MANY-SPINED THISTLE, SIMILAR TO THE ACARNA;
->The Male Lion-Thistle of Casabona.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, very spiny thistle with long, narrow leaves covered in sharp prickles and small flower heads along the stem.</image-desc>

This is a beautiful thistle, about a cubit and a half tall <note>roughly 27 inches</note>: its round stem is white and smooth, and its branches and leaves—which shine with a dark green on top but are covered with a whitening down underneath—are armed with biting, yellowish small spines. These are stretched out at intervals in twos, threes, or fours, and more rarely singly, from the veins that end in them. The seed is small, oblong, shining, and blackish. The heads, as well as the stem, branches, and leaves, are beset with stiff spines. It grew for us from seed in the garden of the Prince of Montbéliard.

### LOBELIUS’S HEDGEHOG-MELON-CACTUS;
->The Spiny Melon-Thistle of the History of Lyon.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a globular, ribbed cactus (Melocactus) covered in clusters of spines, with a distinct cephalium at the top.</image-desc>

We saw this Indian <note>meaning from the West Indies/Americas</note> thistle at Basel at the house of Caspar Bauhin. Regarding it, Lobelius and Pena report these things in their *Adversaria*: They say it is a thistle of wondrous rarity and beauty, which the western islands of the New World produce spontaneously, and especially that which is sacred to Saint Margaret <note>the island of Margarita, off the coast of Venezuela</note>, from whence returning English sea captains brought it. It seems to be, as it were, a certain whim of Nature <note>original: "Naturæ cinnus"</note> composed of a Gourd, a Melon, and a Thistle; and for that reason, we have called it the Hedgehog-Melon-Cactus, or the Spiny Melon-Thistle, using a descriptive rather than a traditional name.

### NANA, ANANAS, OR YAYAMA.
->The Illustration of Acosta.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pineapple plant (Ananas comosus) showing the fruit with its tuft of leaves (crown) sitting atop a leafy stalk.</image-desc>

In certain places, as the writers of Indian matters claim, these fruits grow spontaneously; but where cultivation is added, they are far sweeter than those, abundantly repaying the labor of the cultivator. At first, they are green, but upon ripening, they finally acquire a golden color with a certain moderate redness. Inside, however, they are always white and very easy to slice. They have a most fragrant scent and a flavor like that of a well-ripened peach <note>original: "mali Persici"</note>, far surpassing all other fruits in delicate taste. Some are the size of a melon. According to Maffei, it is a low plant, from whose branches the fruits hang down like pine cones, very soft, etc. Concerning its use, see the following table at the side.

<summary>This page describes various prickly plants, ranging from European thistles like the "Fierce Lion" to exotic New World species including the Melocactus and the Pineapple.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### OF THE SAME EXOTIC FRUIT
->Linschoten’s Illustration.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pineapple plant with two harvested fruits at the base, showing the scaly exterior and leafy crown.</image-desc>

It grows on the ground, says Linschoten <note>Jan Huyghen van Linschoten (1563–1611), a Dutch voyager whose travelogues revealed East Indian secrets to Europe.</note>, resting upon a rough and spreading herb, not unlike <term>Aizoi</term> <note>original: "Aizoi"; a Greek-derived term for "ever-living" plants, likely referring here to the Houseleek or Sedum family</note>, or the Spanish Ever-living plant, as far as the leaves are concerned. It is common throughout all of India and held in great esteem among the inhabitants. However, there is very little agreement among writers whether it is hot or cold, and whether it is healthy and pleasant when raw, or not; most claim it <unclear>erodes</unclear> the throat, and that it is hot and moist. They even say that if it is cut through the middle and the parts are joined back together, and a small knife is left in it for the space of a day or night, that entire part of the blade which stuck in the wound is found to be eaten away. It is preserved and kept in sugar.

<column-break/>

### WILD PINEAPPLE WITH ALOE LEAVES,
->with a cypress-like fruit.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild pineapple plant with long, serrated leaves and a central stalk bearing a cone-like fruit.</image-desc>

This one rises up higher and has a trunk the size of a spear, very smooth, quite thick, and bristling with spines. The leaves are also provided with thorny tips and are hedged around the edges with soft spines, approaching the appearance of Aloe leaves. The flower turns yellow, and the fruit rivals the cone of a Cypress tree.

The Arabs—according to Acosta <note>Cristóbal Acosta (1515–1594), a pioneer in the study of Oriental plants.</note> who describes it at length—call it <term>Quara</term>, while the Persians call it <term>Ananasa</term> and <term>Angali</term>.

The more tender leaves of the heads are eaten and taste like Thistles. Indeed, the Arabs recommend the juice for heat in the liver and kidneys, for pus in the urine, and for Diabetes <note>The author uses the Greek term for "passing through," recognizing the condition of excessive urination.</note>.

---

### AN EXOTIC-LOOKING WATER-AIZOI
->plant: Pineapple.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pineapple fruit with a prominent leafy crown, viewed from a slightly elevated angle.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), one of the most influential botanists of the Renaissance.</note> took this same illustration from Lobelius, as did we, and ascribes these notes to it: The sea captains who returned from Java in the year 1599 brought back the <term>Ananas</term> fruit preserved in sugar, along with the green shoots of that plant mixed in, the illustration of which I have taken care to place here. That fruit was sweet, etc. I had previously seen leaves brought from Guinea, not very different from the leaves of the Water-Aizoi, yet less thick and serrated or toothed around the edge.

<column-break/>

### THISTLE FROM MADAGASCAR IN THE INDIES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thistle-like plant head from Madagascar, showing thick, pointed bracts.</image-desc>

This is not a fruit, says Clusius, but the head of a most elegant Thistle, gathered in that great bay of the island of Madagascar in which the Dutch, on their first voyage, obtained both water and other necessities for food, staying there for several days before proceeding to Java. Furthermore, a single head of this Thistle was found in the wooden boxes brought back by the sea captains; no name was attached to it, but only a slip of paper indicating it had been gathered in the aforementioned bay.

---

# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXVI.
### CORYMB-LIKE OR CORYMB-BEARING PLANTS, AND THOSE
->bearing smaller heads, and others somewhat similar.<-

---

**OTHONNA : INDIAN MARIGOLD : AFRICAN**
**Flower :** *German:* Indian Clove-pink <note>original: "Indianisch Nägelin"</note> : *Belgian:* Tunis flower : *French:* Flower of Rome ; *Italian:* Indian Clove-pink.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tagetes (Marigold) plant showing the root system, serrated leaves, and a single flower head.</image-desc>

It produces striated <note>grooved or striped</note> stalks, about nine inches long, spongy inside, and hollow at some of the wing-junctions. The leaves are similar to Tansy, pinnate <note>feather-shaped</note>, consisting of five or eight pairs with an odd one at the end; their odor is poisonous and heavy. The flowers cling to the ends of the branches, appearing singly; they emerge from a swollen, oblong calyx <note>the green outer cup of a flower</note> and are radiated with a single row of petals, with a color ranging from yellow to rusty-red, imitating a velvet fabric. The center is occupied by numerous yellowish stamens, to which are attached thin, oblong, black seeds. The root is short and fibrous.

Since, furthermore, several varieties of Marigold are observed, distinguished by size, flower, and location, we depict here the one with the smaller single flower.

<column-break/>

**OTHONNA, MARIGOLD, AFRICAN FLOWER;**
**Greatest Marigold with a single flower.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger variety of Tagetes with more robust foliage and a single large flower head.</image-desc>

This flower is content with a single row of petals, but it is many times larger, turning pale from yellow, and far less pleasant than the smaller single variety mentioned above. In the leaves and other parts, there is no great difference.

By Tragus it is called the *Greatest Indian Clove-pink*; by Caesalpinus, the *Common Flower of India, the Othonna of Dioscorides and Pliny*. By Tabernaemontanus and Gerard, the *Greater African Flower with a single flower*.

The Marigold grows spontaneously in many places in Africa, and was first brought from there when the Emperor Charles V gained that famous victory at Tunis <note>The Conquest of Tunis in 1535</note>; thus it obtained the surname *African and Tunisian*. Today, however, it is kept in almost all cultivated gardens.

---

**OTHONNA, MARIGOLD, AFRICAN FLOWER,**
->with a very large double flower.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tagetes with a "double" or "multiplex" flower head, showing dense petals.</image-desc>

It sometimes exceeds the height of a man, with a straight and rigid stalk: the flowers are pale yellow, crowded with innumerable petals, of such great breadth that they cover the palm of the hand.

The *Greater many-flowered Othonna* by Lobelius: *Indian Clove-pink with a double flower* by Gesner; *Greater many-flowered African Flower* by Tabernaemontanus. *Greater African Tansy with a full flower* by C. Bauhin.

It is sown in gardens, and is also kept in earthenware pots and small boxes for the sake of the pleasing sight. For us at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi"</note> in the Most Serene Prince's garden, it grew to the height of a man.

Furthermore, the Marigold warms and dries; it cleanses and opens: yet it is not entirely devoid of a poisonous and destructive faculty. More on this in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

**CHRYSANTHEMUM, CALTHA, CALENDULA,**
*German:* Marigold <note>original: "Ringelblumen"</note> : *French:* Marigold <note>original: "Soucy"</note> : *Italian:* Flower of every month.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caltha or Calendula (Marigold) plant with multiple flower heads and broad leaves.</image-desc>

The golden splendor of the *flowers* has made the Caltha <note>Pot Marigold</note> noble; for they are more saturated with a reddish-gold than actual gold, in the form of the Corn Chrysanthemum: yet they do not emerge from a scaly head like that one, but from a many-cleft, hairy calyx. They are fragrant, with a yellow or dark disk, leaving behind a curved, double seed, roughened in a certain way with small grains. The stalks are thin, somewhat angular, hairy, and sticky to the touch. The leaves are shaped like a tongue without stalks, oblong, fleshy, hairy, and grayish-white, with a taste that is at first herbaceous and a little later somewhat warm. The root is woody.

Various differences of this plant are given: of which the one depicted here is the more common variety, with a single flower.

<summary>This page describes various species of Marigolds (Tagetes and Calendula), detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal properties, and historical origins, including their introduction to Europe following Charles V's victory at Tunis.</summary>
<keywords>Marigold, Tagetes, Calendula, African Flower, botany, Charles V, Tunis, Montbéliard, medicinal herbs, horticulture</keywords>

--- Page 432 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of flowering plants, moving from previous entries into the various species and historical classifications of Marigolds and Chrysanthemums.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED CALTHA OR CALENDULA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caltha (Marigold) with a large, dense, multi-petaled (double) flower head and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

It is not yet established, as Turner <note>William Turner (1508–1568), often called the "Father of English Botany."</note> also noted, by what name the *Caltha* was called by the Greeks. Indeed, it is difficult to find any specific mention made of it, although in Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical text for 1,500 years.</note> in the chapter on the Chrysanthemum, some read, *Chrysanthemum, or Caltha*, while others read *Buphthalmos* <note>original: "Buphtalmos," meaning "Ox-eye."</note>, etc. The learned shall judge.

It is called *Calendula* by the Latins, and *Flower of every month* <note>original: "Fior di ogni mese"</note> by the Italians, because it is seen to bloom on the first day (the Calends) of every month. The German name is taken from the seed, which is twisted and driven into a circle. The French name comes from the fact that it nods in a circle toward the sun. Some monks, however, called it "the head" <note>original: "caput"</note> from the shape of the small seed-head that remains after the flower falls.

<column-break/>

### PROLIFEROUS CALTHA, OR CALENDULA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "proliferous" Marigold, showing smaller flower heads emerging from the base of the primary large flower head.</image-desc>

The flower sometimes gives birth to others around its circumference that are smaller than the mother, growing from hairy stalks about a third of a palm long. And this mother flower is sometimes very large and "double," almost filling the palm of the hand, and beneath it are the small beginnings of other flowers.

Furthermore, Mataradus maintained that the Caltha was the *Leontopodium* <note>Lion's foot</note>; Matteo Selvatico called it the *Paralysis herb*; Fabio Columna called it the *Clymenum* of Dioscorides; Dalechamps, in his commentary on Pliny, called it the *Chrysanthemum and Buphthalmos* of the same Dioscorides; and some call it the *Scorpion*. But we have shown in our "Great History" that those of the same name, and even those who call it *Heliotropium* <note>Sun-turner</note>, are in great error. It is more tolerably called by some the *Bride and friend of the Sun*, inasmuch as it wakes with him and lies down to sleep at twilight.

---

### SMALLEST CALTHA, OR CALENDULA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, slender variety of Marigold with thin stems and smaller flower heads.</image-desc>

It puts forth stems an inch long or shorter, and thin; upon each sits a tiny, yellow flower of the *Caltha* type, emerging from a green, leafy calyx. The leaves are like those of *Linaria* <note>Toadflax</note>, narrow, and half an inch long. The root is simple, thin, and equal in length to the stem.

Regarding the origins of the Caltha, it grows everywhere of its own accord in the fields and gardens of Montpellier, blooming all year round, even in Winter. We have observed it to abound in gardens at Parma, Padua, Lyon, Basel, Geneva, and elsewhere, with both *simple and double* flowers, blooming in June, July, August, September, and October. We had the proliferous variety at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince.

*Regarding its medicinal powers, see the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### CHRYSANTHEMUM OF THE ANCIENTS: Greater Chrysanthemum, with deeply jagged leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chrysanthemum with deeply lobed, laciniate leaves and a daisy-like flower head.</image-desc>

The Chrysanthemum, or Caltha—called by some Buphthalmos—says Dioscorides, is a certain slender herb, but with the appearance of a shrub, which produces smooth stems and many-cleft leaves; the flowers are honey-colored and exceedingly bright, like an eye set in a circle, which is why it was so named. It grows around cities. *So says he.*

However, various plants are gifted with the name of Chrysanthemum: *Anthemisia, Sea Ragwort, Scentless Mayweed, Foreign Golden Chamomile, Goldilocks, Everlasting Flower, Sweet Buttercup*, etc. Yet, in the judgment of many learned men, the Chrysanthemum (which the Greeks so named from the golden color of its flowers) is our *Caltha or Calendula*.

---

### CRETAN CHRYSANTHEMUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cretan Chrysanthemum with distinct foliage and a central flower head.</image-desc>

Our previously pictured Chrysanthemum, the image of which is from Fuchs's works <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), author of "De Historia Stirpium."</note> and does not please us much, we have seen in various gardens: with Gesner at Zurich, with Fuchs at Tübingen, and in the public garden at Padua.

By Laguna it is called *Chrysanthemum and Caltha*; by Tabernaemontanus and the "History of Lyon" it is called *Matthioli's Chrysanthemum*; by Anguillara it is called the *Chrysanthemum most well-known in Italy, and especially in Tuscany, and in the Paduan garden*.

This one, however, grown from seed sent from Crete, is depicted by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist.</note> and labeled as "Cretan." Perhaps it is the Chrysanthemum <unclear>maranthi</unclear> of Honorius Bellus, which is eaten by the peasants.

<column-break/>

### CHRYSANTHEMUM WITH BROAD SERRATED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chrysanthemum variety characterized by broad, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

We obtained this one from the Paduan garden. Furthermore, from the words of Dioscorides passed down before, and the fact that Pliny records the same things about the Buphthalmos as the former does about the Chrysanthemum or Caltha: there are those who believe that *Buphthalmos and Chrysanthemum* are <unclear>spurious</unclear> <note>original Greek: "notheia," referring to a confusion or illegitimate naming</note> and are the same plant. But by manifest signs, a great difference is detected between those plants; and this was best noticed by Dioscorides, who deals with them specifically in different books and different chapters. The Chrysanthemum of Matthiolus, which he says agrees with the Chrysanthemum of Dioscorides (with no one objecting), we label as *Corn Marigold* <note>original: "Chrysanthemum segetum"</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the classification and nomenclature of Marigolds (Caltha/Calendula) and Chrysanthemums, citing various Renaissance botanists and ancient authorities like Dioscorides. It highlights the confusion in naming these "golden flowers" and describes several varieties, including double-flowered and Cretan types.</summary>
<keywords>Marigold, Calendula, Chrysanthemum, Dioscorides, Botany, Renaissance Science, Horticulture, Plant Taxonomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Golden-flowered" plants (Chrysanthemums) and large-statured herbs, following the previous descriptions of field daisies and marigolds.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### CHRYSANTHEMUM WITH SMALLER CUT LEAVES, sea-green; related to the Corn Marigold.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with deeply lobed, serrated leaves and a single composite flower head at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

This plant agrees in most respects with the Corn Marigold <note>original: "Chrysanthemo segetum"</note>, as is easily apparent from a comparison of the two. For the *flower* is golden, like the Chrysanthemum, sitting upon a scaly green cup <note>the calyx</note>, with a granulated central disk of the same color. The *root*, *stalk*, and *flavor* are the same. However, the *leaves* are of the sea-green color of Honeywort <note>Cerinthe</note> or Woad <note>Glastum</note>; they are oblong, fleshy, smooth, and not very deeply divided. Our figure, which is taken from the works of Fuchs, is not entirely satisfactory in all details.

The cornfields of the colder regions of France, Germany, England, and the Low Countries abound with this plant, where it adorns the harvest of Ceres <note>the grain harvest</note>; it is rarer in hot regions. Some also keep it in gardens, as Fuchs formerly did at Tübingen.

### SEA SAMPHIRE, THE THIRD OF MATTHIOLUS: The "Coastal Chrysanthemum" of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coastal plant with thick, succulent, segmented leaves and a small flower head.</image-desc>

This is a maritime sub-shrub, sending out many shoots directly from the root itself, more than a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, upright, robust, rounded, and reddish. Along these are very dense leaves, longer than an inch, narrow, thick, rounded, and smooth, endowed with a sharp, salty, and aromatic flavor. The stalks of the shoots split into leafy branches, upon each of which sits a rather large yellow flower that vanishes into downy seeds <note>pappus</note>.

Tabernaemontanus calls it the *Maritime Starwort* <note>Aster Atticus marinus</note>; Camerarius, in his Epitome, calls it *Vitraria*.

We have seen it blooming in August at Montpellier near the salt lakes and the sea; at Bologna in the garden of St. Salva; and at Pforzheim in the garden of Master Grienninger.

### THE GREATEST HERB, OR INDIAN SUN-PLANT, another Illustration.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large sunflower (Helianthus annuus) showing the broad leaves and the large, heavy flower head bowed downwards.</image-desc>

There is a certain smaller species of this genus, but one which compensates for its smallness with a multitude of flowers. Indeed, in Italy there are those who have observed 24 flowers on a single plant, and even more in Spain. We have seen ten in Germany. It varies, moreover, in the size of the leaves and stalk, in height, and even in the color of the flowers (which is sometimes white), as well as in their size and the number of seeds; for a flower has sometimes been observed of such great breadth that it contained 2,362 seeds.

Thus it is sufficiently clear from what has been said how justly the name "Greatest Herb" <note>Herba Maxima</note> was bestowed upon this plant. Concerning its other names, origins, and virtues, see the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### SMALL CHRYSANTHEMUM, OR THE SMALL BROAD-LEAVED YELLOW DAISY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller flowering plant with serrated leaves and a single flower head.</image-desc>

This is very similar to the Greater Daisy, whose leaves it possesses; they are an inch long, serrated, and arranged in the same order along the stalk. The stalk is single, a foot high, and slightly hairy; at the very top it bears a single flower, a little smaller than the aforementioned Daisy, with ray-petals of a deep saffron color encircling a thready central boss of the same color. These are supported on the underside by pale green, slightly hairy leaves <note>bracts</note>. The *root* is short, slender, and many-forked.

This plant was sent to us from Italy; we place it here until a more suitable location for it can be found.

### THE GREATEST HERB, THE INDIAN SUN: Germ. Sonnenblum: Gall. Tournesol: Ital. Pianta massima.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall sunflower plant with a thick stem and a large, radiant flower head.</image-desc>

The stalk is single, the thickness of an arm, reaching a height of 10 or 12 feet in our gardens, but truly twenty-four feet in Spanish soil. The leaves are arranged irregularly along it, shaped like Coltsfoot <note>Cacalia</note> but not of the same size, being a span or a span-and-a-half long <note>9 to 13 inches</note>, not much narrower, pointed, rough, hairy, serrated around the edges, and attached by long stalks. The very top of the stem supports a single nodding flower, circular, with the appearance of a Marigold <note>Helianium</note>, but so large that it easily measures a foot in diameter. It has golden-colored petals shining with yellow surrounding the center; the disk is flat, broad, without leaves, and pregnant with the fertility of innumerable seeds that are broad, dark or white, oblong, and compressed. The root is fibrous, and one would not expect it to produce such a massive sprout.

### ELECAMPANE: Ger. Alant, Alantwurz: Gall. Aulne: Ital. Enola.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Elecampane plant with large, broad basal leaves and composite yellow flowers.</image-desc>

Elecampane <note>Helenium</note> grows remarkably large, to a height of three or four cubits. The stalk is upright, channeled, hairy, reddish, and somewhat hollowed at the joints. The leaves grow directly from the stalk without any intervening stems; they are like those of the broader Mullein <note>Verbascum</note>, hoary, woolly, and notched around the edges. The *flowers* are fragrant, though faintly so, having the form of the Ox-eye <note>Buphthalmum</note> but many times larger, tufted with a golden glow. Beneath them sits a scaly, rather broad head containing slender, oblong seeds. The *root* is of a notable thickness, dark on the outside and white within, with an aromatic flavor mixed with sharpness and some bitterness. Let the reader consult the *Appendix* for more.

<summary>This page describes various yellow-flowered composite plants, including varieties of Chrysanthemums, Sea Samphire, and the first European observations of the giant Sunflower (Herba Maxima) and Elecampane.</summary>
<keywords>Chrysanthemum, Sea Samphire, Sunflower, Helianthus annuus, Elecampane, Inula helenium, botanical gardens, Fuchs, Italy, Spain, medicinal herbs</keywords>
