<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on the Maluccan herb and various species of daisies (Bellis). The catchword from the previous page, "olera" (pot-herbs), connects to the description of the daisy's culinary use at the end of this page.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### THE MALUCCAN HERB OF ACOSTA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Maluccan herb showing a central stalk with small leaves and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

The stalk of this plant is two, three, four, or five cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> long, thin, rounded, and hollow; unless it is supported by trellises, it creeps along the ground, spreading many branches which, by taking root here and there, occupy a large space in a short time. The leaves very closely approach the leaves of the Elder tree in size and shape: the flowers are like those of Chamomile, and like them, they are saffron-colored.

It stays green and flourishes throughout the entire year: it is diligently cultivated in all the provinces of India, and especially in Maluku <note>The Moluccas or Spice Islands in modern Indonesia.</note>, and is held in great value because it is a most present and certain remedy for all ulcers and wounds.

<column-break/>

### DAISY: German: *Maßlieben*, *Zeitlosen*: French: *Marguerite*, *Pasquette*: Italian: *Margarite*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common daisy (Bellis) with a slender stem, small leaves at the base, and a single flower head.</image-desc>

The Daisy is commonly distinguished into the *Garden* and the *Field* or *wild* variety: and both are again divided into the *Greater* and the *Lesser*: and there are, as will be clear from what follows, various other differences of the Daisy.

The Lesser wild daisy, which we present here, grows everywhere in meadows and many marshy places: it flowers in the Spring months, and sometimes even in the Autumnal ones. Moreover, in all its parts, it most closely resembles the Garden variety, of which we speak next. Our illustration, taken from Fuchs's works <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a famous German botanist.</note> and purchased sources, does not please us: for the leaves are poorly drawn, and the roots are poorly drawn; nor should those stalks have been added. We will perhaps offer a better one in the Appendix, where we treat the Daisy in general.

---

### GARDEN DAISY, OR THE DOUBLE-FLOWERED DAISY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered garden daisy with dense, rounded flower heads and broad basal leaves.</image-desc>

It is thick with leaves spread in a circle, like Mouse-ear Hawkweed or Butterwort, somewhat notched, otherwise entire, hairy, with an astringent taste: among these arise stems a palm's breadth high <note>About 3-4 inches.</note>, thin, reddish, and hairy: these support flowers that are white or purplish, with a yellow center, in the manner of Chamomile. In other cases, however, a numerous luxury of petals overshadows the "navel" <note>The central disk of the flower.</note>: the color is either white or red, or red on the edge and white in the middle, or alternating, or green; in short, wherever chance has led it, it is commendable for its randomly multicolored variety of petals.

<column-break/>

### GARDEN DAISY, DOUBLE-FLOWERED, or the Proliferous Daisy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "hen and chickens" daisy, where smaller flower heads emerge from the sides of the main central flower head.</image-desc>

Not content to have propagated itself by the creeping of its fibrous root, the Garden Daisy produces new offspring from the edges of the flower, not unlike the Proliferous Marigold: but these are smaller than the mother, as is fitting.

The white florets, says Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), known as Tragus, a German botanist.</note>, which become double through cultivation, unless they are plucked early, generate others from themselves, so that from one head—or, if I may speak thus, from the "brain" of the first flower—four or five others break out, in which matter the fruitfulness and wonderful power of nature is commended to us.

The Daisy abounds commonly in gardens: and it flowers in the Spring and Autumn months.

---

### LESSER WILD DAISY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild daisy with a thick rootstock and long-petioled leaves.</image-desc>

The root of this is also fibrous, but thicker than in the common Lesser Daisy. The leaves are larger, oblong, rounded at the end, and somewhat serrated around the edge, hairy, sometimes even reddish, provided with a long stalk. Several naked little stalks come out from the root, nine inches or a foot long, and even larger, each supporting a single flower, like the Greater Daisy but a little smaller, with white radiating petals and a yellow disk.

Tabernaemontanus, Lobelius, Clusius, and C. Bauhin <note>A list of prominent 16th-century botanists.</note> record this as the "Middle Daisy."

Furthermore, as for what pertains to the powers and temperament of the Lesser Daisy, Fuchs makes it hot and dry, Dodonaeus cold and moist, and Tragus temperate regarding cold and dryness. More notes are at the side of the following figure.

<column-break/>

### LESSER MOUNTAIN DAISY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain daisy with a single flower head and narrow, serrated leaves along the stem.</image-desc>

It has a stalk a cubit and a half high, and it is simple and undivided: many leaves near the ground are half an inch long, somewhat round at the end, serrated, resting on long stalks: others along the stalk are alternate, grass-like, about two inches in length, and occasionally notched. A single, rather large flower sits at the very top, larger than the Meadow Daisy, white with a yellow disk, with a head composed of blackish scales.

It grows in the mountains, in parched and uncultivated places.

That the Daisy is a <term>vulnerary herb</term> <note>A plant used for healing wounds.</note> is confessed by all: and it is especially useful in wounds of the head. The juice of the herb is also usefully drunk by the wounded, and from this, the name <term>Consolida</term> <note>From the Latin 'consolidare', meaning to make firm or heal together.</note> was bestowed upon it. The leaves are included among the pot-herbs <note>original: "olera"</note>.

<summary>This page describes the Maluccan herb, noted for its wound-healing properties, and details several varieties of daisies (Bellis), including garden, wild, and mountain types. It discusses their physical characteristics, medicinal uses as "vulneraries," and provides conflicting opinions from famous botanists on their elemental temperaments.</summary>

<keywords>Maluccan herb, Daisy, Bellis, Acosta, wound healing, vulnerary, botany, garden plants, medicinal herbs, Consolida</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of flowering herbs, specifically focusing on the larger daisies and various species of chamomile. It maintains the systematic approach of citing classical authorities like Dioscorides alongside contemporary Renaissance botanists.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### THE GREATER DAISY: German: *Genßblum* <note>Modern German: Gänseblümchen, though here referring to the larger Ox-eye daisy.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bellis Maior (Ox-eye daisy) showing a single tall stem with a large flower head, smaller buds, and serrated leaves rising from a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

It creeps with a fibrous root, sending out several stalks, nine inches <term>dodrantales</term> <note>A Roman measurement of about 9 inches or a "span".</note> or higher, square-shaped, and sometimes divided into branches. The *leaves* are oblong, fleshy, and serrated, with a somewhat sharp taste. The *flowers* are like those of the Ox-eye or Pellitory, with a yellow center <term>umbilico</term>, white petals around the edge, and no remarkable scent: the small leaves of the calyx have a blackish fringe.

Dodoens, Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, Caesalpinus, and almost all others record this as the *Bellis maior* or *Bellium maius*.

It abounds in many places in meadows, and flowers especially in June and July, and sometimes remains green throughout the whole Winter.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE GREATER DAISY.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Bellis Maior, showing a slightly different growth habit with more curved stems and detailed leaf structure.</image-desc>

Our images of the Greater Daisy are from purchased blocks <note>original: "empititiis", likely meaning pre-existing woodcuts bought from another printer</note>: and could have been painted sooner. Furthermore, Tabernaemontanus reports that they have a balanced temperament of moisture and dryness. Drunk, or applied as a plaster, it is extremely useful for wounds and ruptures: and, if we believe Lobel, it has the same powers as the smaller daisies when used in the same manner. In the month of February, it is eaten in salads by the Italians.

Lobel, in his *Adversaria*, records the Lesser Daisy as the *Bellis minor*, the *Consolida minor* of the Apothecaries, and the *Primula Veris* of Tragus.

---

<column-break/>

### ANTHEMIS, OR CHAMOMILE: German: *Chamillen, Camomillen*: French: *Camomille*: Italian: *Camomilla*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of Anthemis (Chamomile) featuring highly branched, feathery foliage and multiple small daisy-like flowers.</image-desc>

Theophrastus says there are many kinds of *Anthemis*. Dioscorides also has many: but three are principal for him: *Leucanthemon* <note>Greek: "White flower"</note> which has a white flower; *Eranthemon* <note>Greek: "Spring flower"</note>, that is, flowers of the spring; and *Chamæmelum* <note>Greek: "Earth-apple"</note>, so called because it has the scent of an Apple.

Modern authors also establish many differences. However, we here depict the Common Chamomile, which grows everywhere in cornfields, and which Mattioli accepts as the *Leucanthemon Anthemis* of Dioscorides and Galen. Cordus writes that this *Anthemis* is well known to the common people and the Apothecaries. And we judge it to correspond to the description of Dioscorides, which Pliny followed word for word.

<column-break/>

### ROMAN CHAMOMILE, most fragrant creeping Chamomile, with a single flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut of Roman Chamomile, showing a low-growing, creeping habit with dense, fine foliage and single flowers.</image-desc>

The Common Chamomile pictured before relies on a thin and fibrous root, not deeply fixed. The *stalks* are thin, nine inches high, upright, and clothed with leaves thinner than those of Mayweed <term>Cotula</term>, with a faint but sweet scent. The *flowers* are white on the outside, whose petals surround a central disk <term>umbonem</term> consisting of yellow florets.

But this variety is not the Common one; it does not rise with an upright stalk, but the root sends out many small trailing shoots upon the ground, a little shorter: clothed with thicker leaves, endowed with a more vigorous and lovely scent. The flowers are not much different from the flowers of common Chamomile, with white radiating petals crowning a yellow center.

It abounds around the Tiber not far from Rome: as also in grassy, dry places one mile from the city of London. Elsewhere it is cultivated in gardens.

---

<column-break/>

### ROMAN OR NOBLE CHAMOMILE with a double flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut of Double-flowered Roman Chamomile, showing dense clusters of "double" flowers where the yellow center is largely replaced by white petals.</image-desc>

This has the same fragrance of scent as the Noble Chamomile just mentioned, nor is the form of the leaves or the manner of growth much different. But the flowers which are there simple and white with a yellow center, here luxuriate with a manifold offspring of petals occupying the center.

It is said to grow spontaneously around Aurelia <note>likely Orléans, France</note>: otherwise it is familiar in well-furnished gardens, and is also abundant in the princely garden at Montbéliard under our care.

It is spread along garden beds, mounds, and walkways: and from its flowers and juice a syrup is made that is excellent for dropsy and both types of Jaundice <term>Icterum</term>: and its uses are the same as the preceding one.

<column-break/>

### FOREIGN GOLDEN CHAMOMILE, with a head without petals.

<image-desc>Woodcut of a "naked" or rayless chamomile, showing flowers that consist only of the yellow central cone without white outer petals.</image-desc>

This is the *Chamæmelum Chrysanthemum* for Dodoens, the *Yellow Chrysanthemum* for Tabernaemontanus, and the *Scented Naked Chrysanthemum* for Gerard. For Lobel and Pena, and also the *History of Lyon*, it is the *Anthemis Chrysanthemos*. Regarding this plant, the *Adversaria* writes thus: "The plant called *Chrysanthemos Anthemis*, they say, with its golden turned-back heads, is like Roman Chamomile in the appearance of its leaves, scent, and taste. But it is surpassed in size, and its slightly prominent center is surrounded by no radiating petals: its use is not dissimilar."

It does not grow wild, but is cultivated with great diligence in the gardens of Germany, Belgium, and England.

<summary>This page describes the physical characteristics, nomenclature, and medicinal uses of the Ox-eye daisy and various species of Chamomile, including Roman and "double" varieties. It highlights the plants' geographic distribution from Rome to London and their cultivation in botanical gardens like Montbéliard.</summary>
<keywords>Ox-eye daisy, Chamomile, Roman Chamomile, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany, Dodoens, Lobel, gardening, jaundice, wounds</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### AN OX-EYE ALLIED TO CHAMOMILE, THE ITAL-
->ian Field variety, very tall.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with feathery leaves and daisy-like blooms, showing the root system and upright stems.</image-desc>

It has simple stems through which are scattered leaves like those of certain yellow Chamomiles, or the Ox-eye of Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, though somewhat rougher. There is a single flower at the summit, equal to the flower of the aforementioned Ox-eye, consisting of a single row of white petals radiating in a circle around a yellow center. We saw it at Pforzheim in flower during the months of May and June. In Italy, however, it rises so high that it even overtops the grain crops. It differs truly from Stinking Mayweed, lest anyone be deceived.

<column-break/>

### THE GOLDEN-FLOWERED CHAMOMILE OF SOME:
->called Ox-eye by many.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with multiple stems arising from a thick root, featuring composite flowers and finely divided foliage.</image-desc>

With stems a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or more in height, slender and covered in a hoary down; several are reddish near the ground, arising obliquely from a woody root, and branched. The leaves grow on them likewise covered in down, like Yarrow, with small-toothed pinnate leaflets; they are much smaller and have the scent of Chamomile. At the summit of each branch is a single Golden-flower. It sits in a hoary cup-like base <note>original: "calyce"</note> which is scaly like the Golden-flower.

It grows in the fields among crops of Oats and Wheat, and is considered a weed to them. It also grows spontaneously by roadsides and at the edges of sown fields; it is also cultivated in gardens. It possesses the same powers as the fragrant Chamomile.

---

<column-break/>

### PURPLE CHAMOMILE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy plant with dense, feathery foliage and several flower heads.</image-desc>

In its leaves, branches, and heads, this kind of Chamomile is grander and fuller than the other kinds, and is distinguished by the purple circle of petals surrounding the flower heads. Before the flower opens, it is confined within a leathery and compact wrapper. It grows in rugged places.

This plant is rare and known to very few; it is called *Anthemis Eranthemos* <note>Spring-flowered Chamomile</note> in the *History of Lyon*: *C. Bauhin* <note>Caspar Bauhin, a Swiss botanist</note> names it *Adonis* in his *Phytopinax*.

Furthermore, in the judgment of Gesner, Tabernaemontanus, and other learned men, our common Chamomile—which the <term>Apothecary Shops</term> <note>original: "Officinæ"</note> call *Chamomilla*, *Camomilla*, and *Gamamilla*—is the true Chamomile of the *Ancients*, as its scent and powers demonstrate.

<column-break/>

### SCENTLESS CHAMOMILE, OR THE
->non-stinking Mayweed.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick taproot and spreading stems with composite flowers.</image-desc>

It has a sufficiently thick root, hairy with many fine fibers; in the appearance of its leaves and flowers, it is so similar to Stinking Mayweed that it can be distinguished from it only by the judgment of the nostrils.

It grows in various places among the crops and flowers in May and October, with a weak scent or none at all, whence some call it *Fool's Chamomile*. Fuchs asserted it was an Ox-eye, but by a great error, as Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> rightly notes.

Its powers and properties are the same as common Chamomile, whose roots, leaves, and herb moderately heat, digest, thin the humors, loosen, and disperse gas; they provide remarkable use for various ailments, as the Practitioners and <term>Perfumers</term> <note>original: "Seplasiæ" - sellers of ointments and medicines</note> well know.

---

<column-break/>

### STINKING CHAMOMILE, OR STINKING
->Mayweed.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with deeply lobed leaves and a prominent root.</image-desc>

If the Stinking Mayweed of the shops finds a fertile soil, it lacks little of reaching two cubits in height, with many branches crowded together. On these are leaves like Chamomile, finely cut, with an abominable odor; the flowers are like common Chamomile, white and radiating. The root is fibrous and the thickness of a finger.

It grows abundantly everywhere in various places and flowers in May and June, and even in October. At Basel by the Birs river, as well as on the way to Krentzach, and both inside and outside the city, between the Ash Gate and the Stone Gate.

Leonicenus inscribed it as *Genta*, *Cotta*, and *Cota*. Some call it *Dog-herb* <note>original: "Cynobotanem"</note> or *Dog-flower* <note>original: "Cynanthemon"</note>, and almost everyone calls it *Stinking Mayweed*. Those who believe it to be the *Parthenium* of Pliny are in error.

<column-break/>

### GREATEST STINKING CHAMOMILE, OR
->Greatest Stinking Mayweed.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust flowering plant with large, serrated leaves and composite flowers.</image-desc>

The stems and branches of the Greatest Stinking Mayweed are grooved and reddish, clothed in a white down, as are the leaves, which are whitish and more minutely divided. The flowers are white, with their petals surrounding a yellow center.

Furthermore, the scent and taste demonstrate that Stinking Mayweed is hot and dry. Crushed and applied to wounds like a plaster, it glues them together and cleanses them. In cases of "suffocation of the womb" <note>a historical term for hysteria or uterine distress</note>, it serves as a remedy through smelling it, fumigation, or as a warm wash or sitz bath. However, its scent is harmful to the head. Beekeepers and common women know that it is extremely hostile to bees; for when the hives must be harvested, or the attacks of fierce bees restrained, the beekeepers carry this herb and rub their hands with it.

In our absence, a false figure <note>illustration</note> was placed here.

OX-EYE: German *Rinds aug* <note>Ox-eye</note>: French *Oeil de bœuf*: Italian *Occhio di bue*.

OX-EYE WITH THIN LEAVES SIMILAR TO THE
Golden-flower of Valencia described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Buphthalmon plant with daisy-like flowers and finely divided leaves, showing the root system.</image-desc>

Ox-eye <note>original: Buphthalmon</note>, according to the author Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, puts forth tender stalks, and in some manner thin: *leaves like Fennel*. The flowers are honey-colored, larger than those of Chamomile <note>original: Anthemidis</note>, resembling eyes, from which the herb also drew its name. It grows in open fields and around towns. Thus he says, from whom Pliny and Galen do not much differ.

However, various plants are gifted with the name of Ox-eye. *The Golden-flower, the scentless Chamomile, the stinking Chamomile, the Golden-chamomile, the thin-leaved Hellebore, the Great Daisy, the Marigold* <note>original: Calthe</note>, and the two following next: from which that which is depicted here by Tabernamontanus and Gerard is held to be the true and legitimate Yarrow <note>original: millefolio</note> of the Ancients: but it is commonly inscribed as *Thin-leaved Ox-eye with a Yarrow leaf*.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second variety of Buphthalmon, similar to the first but with slightly different leaf structure.</image-desc>

Found at the margins of plowed fields and near paths in the Kingdom of Valencia, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> dug this up, having observed it nowhere else. It was blooming, moreover, in the month of March.

It differs greatly, however, from the Ox-eye of the Province of Narbonne, concerning which Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist</note> hands down these details. The thin-leaved Ox-eye of Narbonne, he says, comes from the cold regions of Provence and Narbonnese Gaul: *with yellow radiated flowers*, like Ox-eye: and *leaves of common Chamomile*, or non-stinking Mayweed, small, and somewhat grayish-white: the root equals a span in length; the stalks are a foot long, etc.

The flowers of Ox-eye, according to Dioscorides, when ground with wheat, disperse swellings and hard tumors. Otherwise, this plant is of little use.

---

FLOWER OF ADONIS: German *Adonis Röszlein*: French *Fleur d'Adonis*: Italian *Fior di Adone*.

ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE FLOWER OF ADONIS, OR ADONIS-PLANT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Flos Adonis (Adonis flower) showing its upright stem, feathery leaves, and single terminal flower.</image-desc>

**From a root** thinner than the little finger, white, and straight: stalks rise up gifted with many branches <note>original: alis, literally "wings"</note>, channeled, and perforated with a narrow tube. *Leaves like Fennel-flower* <note>original: Nigellæ</note>, yellow-green, smooth, with a somewhat sharp taste. *Flowers* at the ends of the branches like Chamomile. *Seeds* as if gathered into a little cluster, densely packed, and pointed.

Turner <note>William Turner, the "Father of English Botany"</note> makes it a species of *Wild Poppy*: others wish it to be *Eranthemum* <note>Spring-flower</note>: but Turner denies this, and with him Lobel in his *Adversaria*, who along with many learned men asserts it to be an Anemone. By Dodoens in French and by Tabernamontanus it is called *Purple Chamomile*: by Gerard *Stinking Mayweed*: in the Portuguese Garden *Purple Adonis-plant*. More in the following sections.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Another woodcut illustration of the Flos Adonis, showing a slightly more mature plant with seed heads forming.</image-desc>

That this flower of extraordinary beauty, commonly called *Adonis's* or the *Adonium*, is not Eranthemum but a species of Anemone, is shown by the scarlet flowers, saturated with an intense blood-red color, and shining somewhat with a blackish tint. *The Leaves, Stalks, Branches, and Roots* are like those of Mayweed, or the *Montpellier* Anemone, and the seed is in small oblong, somewhat longer pointed heads like Crowfoot <note>original: Ranunculi</note>, or like Asparagus when it first sprouts, as Dioscorides notably advised regarding the Anemone, the whole being somewhat sharp in taste, etc.

We place two images here from purchased stock because they were already engraved, although there is little difference between them. It is better for the sake of the Third one soon to be added.

---

YET ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE FLOWER OF ADONIS.

<image-desc>A third woodcut illustration of the Flos Adonis, showing the plant in full bloom with its characteristic dissected foliage.</image-desc>

It is very frequent of its own accord, says Clusius; it grows among the crops, not only in Narbonnese Gaul: but also throughout all Spain, and even in Austria and Moravia. We ourselves have seen it blooming in the fields in April between Montpellier and Nîmes, and blooming at Basel in May among the crops on the way to Doroacum. In gardens, however, we have cultivated it at Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard.

Tabernamontanus makes the Adonis-plant hot and dry in the second degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of humors</note>: Camerarius recommends it for kidney stones: and Dodoens records that it is of no use in Medicine, and is cultivated in gardens only for the sake of pleasure.

<column-break/>

FEVERFEW, MOTHERWORT: German *Metram, Mutterkraut*: French *Matricaire*: Italian *Matricaria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Parthenium (Feverfew), showing its branched stems, lobed leaves, and numerous small daisy-like flower heads.</image-desc>

There is a certain *Parthenium* called Helen's, which is not at all dealt with here. However, which plant today represents the *Parthenium of the Ancients* is a dispute among authors: for some assert it to be the *Noble Chamomile* of Dioscorides, others *Stinking Mayweed*, others *Athanasia* called Tansy, others *Mercury*, and others the *Artemisia* called Lapparia by Pliny: but most indeed say it is the *Common Feverfew* <note>original: Matricariam vulgarem</note> which we depict here.

It rests upon a very fibrous root: raising stalks one or two cubits high, channeled, filled with a spongy pith, and divided into many branches. *Leaves like Mugwort* <note>original: Artemisiæ</note>, divided into many fringes, yellowish-green, with a heavy odor and a bitter taste. *Flowers* yellow in the middle, with white outer petals <note>original: foliis</note>, in the manner of Chamomile.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED FEVERFEW.
<note>Latin: Matricaria flore pleno</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Matricaria plant with dense, double flowers (flore pleno), showing detailed leaves and root structure.</image-desc>

It is similar in all respects to the common Feverfew <note>Matricaria vulgaris</note>, except for the flower, which in this variety is very crowded with multiple layers of petals.

This is sown in gardens, just as a great abundance is kept under our care in the Illustrious Prince’s garden at Montbéliard. According to Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, the dried flowers, when committed to the earth with the seed already ripe, produce many plants. However, the preceding variety with the simple flower, which they call the *Common* type, is more frequent: for it not only grows in various gardens but also springs up in hedges, along old walls, and delights in rubbish heaps. It blooms in June and throughout the Summer.

### SCENTLESS MAYWEED, OR THE Achaouan of the Egyptians.
<note>Latin: Parthenium inodorum, sive Achaouan Aegyptiorum</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Parthenium inodorum, showing a tall stem with multiple small flower heads and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

This herb is very close to Chamomile, yet it does not rise quite so high, but spreads out a little wider at the top: with leaves like Feverfew, though smaller and denser, and flowers rivaling those of Chamomile. The herb is perceived to be devoid of taste and smell, but the flowers breathe out a heavy and very obscure odor.

Furthermore, the Egyptians, for whom this plant is native, use a decoction of the flowers and leaves for Jaundice <term>Icterus: a yellowing of the skin and eyes</term> and obstructions of the internal organs, according to Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, a physician and botanist who studied Egyptian flora</note>.

### TANSY, IMMORTALITY: German: Rheinfarn, Wurmsot; French: Tanasée; Italian: Tanaceto.
<note>Latin: Tanacetum, Athanasia. The name Athanasia comes from the Greek for "immortality," likely due to the flowers' long-lasting nature.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tansy plant (Tanacetum), showing its characteristic flat-topped clusters of button-like flower heads and deeply feathered leaves.</image-desc>

Since there are several varieties of Tansy, as will be clear from what follows, we depict the *Common* one here. It grows to a fairly great height, two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> and higher: with smooth stems, not at all striated or hairy, filled with a white spongy pith. The leaves are feathered, turning from green to yellow, notched around the edges, and attached to a central rib; they have a powerful smell and a bitter taste. The tops of the stems are occupied by yellow clusters <note>corymbs</note>, smaller than those of the Cypress-herb, composed only of scales or little flames, which finally turn into seed that blackens upon maturity. The root creeps far and wide.

It grows spontaneously in various places, along roads, on embankments, along the edges of fields, and garden fences, and even in the gardens themselves.

<column-break/>

### SCENTED FEVERFEW OF TABERNÆMONTANUS: German: Wolriechend Metram, Spanish: Megablum.
<note>Latin: Matricaria odorata Tabernæmontani</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Matricaria odorata, showing a flowering plant with distinct leaf shapes and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

Tabernæmontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a pioneer of German botany</note> mentions this, though in his work nothing is found besides the illustration and the names. He calls it *Scented fine-leaved Mugwort* and *Spanish Feverfew*, and says it is called *Argentina* <note>Silvery</note> by physicians and herbalists.

It heats in the third degree and dries in the second <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors</note>: it cleanses, purges, opens, and successfully performs whatever bitter things are able to do. It contributes not a little to uterine affections; it rouses delayed menses and brings forth the afterbirth and deceased fetuses, whether a decoction of it is drunk, or it is boiled in a bath, or even applied to the pubic area as a poultice. It also helps with "suffocations of the womb" <note>a historical term for hysterical or uterine distress</note>.

### SMALL-LEAVED FEVERFEW OF MYCONUS.
<note>Latin: Parthenium Smikrophyllon Myconi. "Smikrophyllon" is Greek for "small-leaved."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small-leaved Parthenium, showing a compact plant with numerous flower heads.</image-desc>

This herb is a palm and a half in height <note>about 6-9 inches</note>: with a small, woody, white root with few fibers. From this rise several small, round, reddish stems, on which—especially at the lowest part nearest the ground—the leaves are thin and fennel-like, so similar to the leaves of Southernwood that one egg could not be more like another. At the tops of the stems are umbels, and in them many small, white, compact flowers, such as are seen in common Yarrow. The taste of the plant is bitter and the smell heavy, as in common Feverfew.

### CURLED OR CRESTED TANSY; with a yellow flower, English.
<note>Latin: Tanacetum crispum, sive cristatum</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Curled Tansy, showing the distinctively "crisped" or curled foliage and flower clusters.</image-desc>

To one who knows common Tansy, the recognition of Curled Tansy is more obvious than the herb itself. Indeed, this is rarer, though similar in other respects to the common one already described; but it has most elegant leaves, divided by frequent incisions, curled with many twists and turns of the segments, imitating military crests. It has a heavier smell and a bitter taste.

We have seen it in gardens in Chalon-sur-Saône and Paris: and we ourselves have also kept it, both at Montbéliard in the Illustrious Prince’s garden, and at Yverdon, in the garden adjacent to the large house of Lord d'Orges near the market, which we cultivated there for several years. It blooms in July and August.

<keywords>Feverfew, Tansy, medicinal herbs, Montbéliard garden, uterine health, Tabernæmontanus, botany, 16th-century medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of herbaceous plants, specifically focusing on Tansy, Lavender Cotton, and Yarrow varieties. The catchword from the previous page was "Mille."</meta>

### WHITE MOUNTAIN TANSY, scentless.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tanacetum album montanum plant, showing a thick root system, tall stems with pinnate leaves, and several daisy-like flower heads.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is thick, black, and fibrous, with many small fibers attached to it. The stalks are a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> to a cubit and a half high, hairy, striped, and in some cases hollow. The leaves are like those of Tansy, pinnate <note>feather-shaped</note>, hairy on the underside and smooth on top, dark green, with no scent and an astringent taste. The flowers are like those of the Great Daisy, star-shaped and white, with a yellow central boss.

Botanists commonly record this as the "Scentless Tansy." By Tabernaemontanus and Camerarius <note>noted 16th-century botanists</note> it is called *Tanacetum Leucanthemum* <note>White-flowered Tansy</note>; in the *History of Lyon* it is called *Athanasia Leucanthemos*, which some maintain is the "White Vehna" (others say "Achna") of Avicenna <note>referring to the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>.

It grows in the forests of the Aedui <note>modern-day Burgundy, France</note> and in lower mountains, especially in Hungary and Austria. It blooms in May and June.

### GROUND-CYPRESS, SANTOLINA: German: *Cypreskraut*; French: *Cypres, Garderobe*; Italian: *Santolina*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamæcyparissus (Santolina) plant, featuring a woody base, dense upright stems with small, scale-like leaves, and small rounded flower heads at the tips.</image-desc>

One might not wrongly count this among the undershrubs. From a woody root, it sends out woody, tender twigs over a cubit high, covered in a grayish down. On these are leaves about an inch long, gray, finely toothed, with a medicinal scent that has a certain heavy sweetness, and a taste partly sharp and partly bitter. At the tip of each small branch sits a single yellow flower, like those of Tansy.

More recent authors call this *Cyparissus Santolina* <note>Lavender Cotton</note>, and many writers call it "Female Southernwood." However, some—especially Anguillara—deny that it is Female Southernwood. Others have given it the name *Unguentaria* <note>The Ointment-plant</note>.

### YARROW: German: *Garben, Schafrip*; French: *Millefeuille*; Italian: *Mille foglio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Millefolium (Yarrow) plant, showing its characteristic finely divided, feathery leaves and flat-topped clusters (corymbs) of small flowers.</image-desc>

Because of the plurality of leaves and their manifold divisions, many plants take the name *Millefolium* <note>Thousand-leaf</note>, such as *Achyllea*, *Sideritis*, and others. However, Yarrow holds the name *Stratiotis* or *Militaris* <note>The Soldier's plant</note> because it heals inflicted wounds and is therefore extremely useful to soldiers.

Commonly, the "Thousand-leaf Soldier-plant" is divided into the Aquatic type (which will be discussed in its proper place) and the Terrestrial type, which we depict here.

This plant, as Dioscorides describes it, is a small shrub about a palm's height, having leaves like the feathers of young birds. The leaf-growths are very short and divided by incisions. It bears small shoots at the summit, on which are umbels <note>flat-topped flower clusters</note> in the manner of Dill. The flowers are small and white.

<column-break/>

### Another Illustration of the WHITE MOUNTAIN SCENTLESS TANSY.

<image-desc>A secondary woodcut illustration of the Tanacetum album montanum, showing a slightly different perspective of the foliage and flowering stems.</image-desc>

Since the previous figure taken from Fuchs's works did not please us, we subjoin another here from Clusius; we have determined his "Scentless Tansy" to be the same as ours.

As for the temperament and powers of Tansy: it is hot and dry in the second degree. It expels intestinal worms, settles pains of the belly, draws out sweat, provokes urine, and eases pains of the bladder. Its juice, smeared on the spine with oil of roses before the onset of a fit, is said to remove the rigors of fevers; the same juice cures cracks and fissures of the feet and hands to a miraculous degree. We leave the remaining excellent uses of the root, leaves, and flowers to be sought from our *Great History*.

### Another Illustration of CYPARISSUS OR SANTOLINA.

<image-desc>A secondary woodcut illustration of the Cyparissus (Santolina) plant, emphasizing the root structure and the branching pattern of the flowering stalks.</image-desc>

Dodoens makes two types of *Cyparissus* in his French History, but five types in his Latin History. Lobel lists three, and Clusius two. We also have observed two types: for besides the one already proposed, we have seen another which has smaller leaves but cut with larger teeth. And this one which we depict here is endowed with a less heavy scent.

It grows abundantly in the vineyards and open fields of Nîmes, and other maritime places of Provence, flowering in May and June. We have seen the cultivated variety in Montpellier, Padua, Ferrara, Bologna, Basel, Lyon, and Geneva.

The seed of Santolina, according to Dodoens, is bitter to the taste, and dry and hot in the third degree.

### HOARY ALPINE YARROW, with beautiful flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alpine Millefolium, showing a more compact growth habit with distinct, rounded flower clusters.</image-desc>

This is a small plant about a palm high, with a simple root, reddish and almost black. From this come leaves two or three inches long, sparsely pinnate, woolly, clinging to rather long or nearly inch-long stalks. Similar leaves also cling to the aforementioned woolly stems, but somewhat smaller and gifted with shorter stalks. On their summits sit five or six flowers, scaly and clustered; the scales, marked with dark veins, are conspicuous on them and render the flower more beautiful.

We have gathered this occasionally in the mountains of Valais. The preceding common variety, according to Dioscorides, grows in somewhat rough fields and especially along roadsides. Furthermore, that one has white or purplish flowers and blooms from June until September. As the White variety is more than well-known in meadows and fields, the pale red variety is found here and there among the crops and near the edges of plowed fields, meadows, and gardens.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### YELLOW WOOLLY YARROW <note>original: "Millefolium Tomentosum Luteum"</note> of Montpellier or Narbonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with finely divided, feathery leaves and a thick, creeping root system with numerous fibers.</image-desc>

This herb is about nine inches high <term>dodrantalis; a Roman measurement of about 9 inches</term>, with a thick, hard, creeping root, featuring fibers similar to those of Hellebore. It sends out several stems, which are upright and quite robust; at their tips shine dense clusters of flowers <term>umbellæ; umbrella-like flower clusters</term> like those of the common land Yarrow, glowing with a golden color both in the petals and the center. The *leaves* along the woolly little stems are like those of the Water-Soldier Yarrow, but much smaller, finely cut, and covered with a grayish downy hair.

We observed this between Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausum"</note> and Valence; it flowers in June. Gerard calls it Golden Stechas.

### CRETAN YARROW.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, narrow, pinnate leaves and a cluster of small flowers at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

We saw this at Basel flowering in November, in the garden of Dr. Zwinger, where it had grown from seed sent from Crete by the distinguished botanist Honorius Bellus.

Regarding the powers and properties of Yarrow: According to Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, it is of extraordinary use for stopping blood flowing from anywhere, and for ulcers both old and new, as well as fistulas. Galen and more recent authors report the same. As for the fact that Yarrow can cause a nosebleed, that happens through irritation. Therefore, it is an astringent, drying, and wound-healing herb. They say the root and leaves, when chewed, soothe toothache.

### AGERATUM, JULIA’S HERB, German: Kunigundkraut. French: Ageratum. Italian: Herba Giulia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with small, rounded leaves and a terminal cluster of button-like flowers.</image-desc>

Because this is commonly labeled as the true and genuine Ageratum of Dioscorides, we will provide his description here.

Ageratum, he says, is a shrubby herb, simple, low-growing, rising to the height of a palm's breadth: very similar to Oregano. It bears a cluster in which the flower shines with golden buttons, smaller than Everlasting <note>original: "Helichryso"</note>. The name was given to it because the flower preserves its colorful appearance for a very long time <note>The name "Ageratum" comes from the Greek for "not growing old"</note>.

It grows in the mountains, abundantly around Montpellier; and it is planted by some in gardens for its scent, flowering in July and August. It is proven to be hot and dry by its smell and bitter taste: hence Dioscorides also says the power of its decoction is fervent, etc. More in the following pages.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE YARROW, TO WHICH IS RELATED the Mountain Musk-Iva of the Rhaetians.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain plant with a thick rootstock and clusters of feathery leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

The Alpine Yarrow is smaller than the common or water variety, a little longer than a palm's breadth, with very similar leaves: but with a smaller cluster at the top of the stem. However, its individual flowers are four times larger, with radiating petals at the edge, large and white, with yellow tips in the middle, emerging from a scaly, blackish, fringed head. The plant is somewhat hairy.

In our Rhaetian travels <note>The Rhaetian Alps, covering parts of modern Switzerland, Italy, and Austria</note> we found it on the mountain near Vresen. Could it be the *Ciaij* of the Parisians?

### FRAGRANT ACHILLEA YARROW: German: Edelgarb, Reinfahrn; French & Italian: Achillea.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, leafy plant with a dense corymb of small flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Related to the land Yarrow is *Achillea*, sometimes branching out with stalks three cubits high <note>about 4.5 feet</note>, and sometimes only a palm high, and striated. The leaves are like common Yarrow, but wider, shorter, and many-cleft. It bears clusters of flower-heads like the aforementioned Yarrow, with small white petals surrounding a golden central disk. The root is woody.

It loves only rich and fertile soil in high fields, such as in the Roman and Tuscan territories of Italy. We found it flowering in June between Nîmes and Valence, and we also had it in the garden between Basel, Haguenau, Montbéliard, and Geneva, where it stayed green all year. Its powers are the same as Yarrow. More in the Appendix.

### DALECHAMPS' PURPLE AGERATUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with small leaves and drooping flower heads.</image-desc>

It has a short, hairy, yellowish root; small leaves, numerous and scattered around the root, similar to the leaves of Ageratum; many small stems hanging through the crevices of rocks, adorning and covering them like tapestries; very abundant purple violet-like flowers, smelling most sweetly; and finally, tiny seed in oblong vessels.

We observed it in abundance in the mountains of Salève and Thoiry near Geneva. Some call it Moschatellina.

Most authors label the Ageratum of Dioscorides as the Eupatorium of Mesue. "Julia’s Herb" takes its name from the month of July, in which it begins to flower. More in the Appendix.

# OF PLANTS

### FERULA-LEAVED AGERATUM described by the same Dalechamps.
<note>original: "Ageratum Ferulaceum eiusdem Dalechampij." Ageratum refers to "ever-young" flowers; Ferulaceum implies leaves like the Ferula or Giant Fennel.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with finely divided, fern-like leaves and small clusters of flowers at the top, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This herb grows to a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height, with stems that are quite robust and channeled. These are adorned with leaves finely divided in the manner of Chamomile; the higher they reach toward the top, the smaller and more minutely cut they become, while the lower leaves are longer than a palm's breadth and very close in form to the Ferula. The top of the stem branches into numerous small stalks, and upon these, the disordered flowers mimic an umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster</note>; they are similar to the flowers of Ragwort but smaller, eventually turning into downy seeds. The root is somewhat long, of moderate thickness, and fibrous.

It is not very common, according to the testimony of Lobel, except on the higher ridges of Calcar and the "Garden of God" near Narbonne, where it flowers in July and August.

<column-break/>

### HERB OF THE RUPTURE.
<note>original: "Herba de la Rotta." Likely Achillea erba-rotta, used historically for internal "ruptures" or bruises.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems, small serrated leaves, and flat-topped flower clusters (umbels).</image-desc>

From the root, it sends forth stems less than a span <note>about 9 inches</note> high, which are smooth; along these, the leaves are seen placed alternately. They are similar to the leaves of Ageratum, an inch long, narrow, saw-toothed around the edges, and smooth, with an aromatic and bitter taste, almost like Tansy. The tops of the stems branch into umbels of small flowers, smaller than those of Alpine Yarrow, with white petals surrounding the centers, arising from heads decorated with scales marked by black lines.

In Piedmont and elsewhere it is called *Herba rotta*: and it abounds in the Lanzo valley of Piedmont, and in the valley of Santa Giustina <note>original: "S. Fidei"</note> in Padua.

It dissolves curdled milk and blood <note>referring to internal clots</note>, and is recommended for pleuritic abscesses and many other ailments.

---

### CORYMB-BEARING MINT, GREEK, ROMAN, Saracen Mint, or Garden Costus.
<note>original: "Mentha Corymbifera... Costus hortensis." This is likely Costmary (Tanacetum balsamita).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, serrated leaves and clusters of small round flower heads at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

It puts out slanted roots, equal to the roots of Mint, rounded, from which many fibers hang down. The stems are a cubit or a cubit and a half tall, channeled, hairy, branched, and pale green in color. The leaves are like those of Pepperwort <note>original: "Lepidij"</note>, the same color as the stems, saw-toothed, rarely jagged, with the intense scent of Ageratum and a violently bitter taste. On the highest branches sit golden clusters <note>term: corymbi - flat-topped flower clusters</note> like those of Tansy.

Given the names of Greek, Roman, or Saracen Mint, this Mint is entirely different in kind from the rest of the Mints, and therefore had to be separated from them.

It is a garden plant, cultivated everywhere in gardens, and in warmer places it flowers in January, February, or March.

<column-break/>

### A SPECIES OF SARACEN MINT, with the flower of Chamomile.
<note>original: "flore Anthemidis."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the previous Mentha but with daisy-like flowers (white petals around a central disk).</image-desc>

It grows especially in cold places in the Pyrenees mountains near streams; hardly anywhere else: and it flowers in the months of July and August. They boil it in meat broths for the sake of the flavor.

The Corymb-bearing Mint is considered hot and dry in the second degree: and on the authority of Matthiolus, it heats, dries, opens <note>obstructions</note>, thins <note>humors</note>, strengthens, cleanses, and provokes <note>menstruation or urine</note>. It assists in afflictions of the womb and cures those with dropsy <note>edema</note>: its smoke puts snakes to flight, and its whole substance resists their poisons. The seed, no differently than Lavender Cotton, expels intestinal worms and belly-mites. *More in the Appendix.*

---

### SNEEZEWORT: WILD PELLITORY: Germ. Wilder Bertram: French. Herbe à esternuer: Ital. Ptarmica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with narrow leaves and small, round flower heads.</image-desc>

Sneezewort, says Dioscorides, is a small shrub having many thin, rounded shoots like Southernwood: around which the leaves are oblong, very close to Olive leaves, and numerous; and at the summit is a small, round head like Chamomile, which provokes sneezing with its sharp scent, from which it also received its name.

The leaves, when smeared on with the flowers, are effective for removing bruises <note>original: "sugillata"</note> under the eyes, while the flowers most effectively provoke sneezing. It grows in mountainous and rocky places: so he says. However, it has been observed by more recent authors <note>original: "Neotericis"</note> to grow also around the edges of fields and meadows in shady places, and is even transferred into gardens. It flowers in Summer. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### GARDEN TARRAGON, OR TARCHON: Germ. Dragoncel: French. Targon: Ital. Dragoncello.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with long, narrow, undivided leaves and small clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

This shrubby plant puts forth stalks of two cubits or more, hard, slender, somewhat angular, divided into irregular branches. The leaves are undivided when they first emerge, but when it has matured, it is loaded with leaves equal to those of Flax, dark green, shining, and entirely without divisions, with a sharp yet somewhat sweet and aromatic taste. The clusters are arranged on the highest branches in the same order as in Southernwood: with the tips of the flowers barely visible, which are followed by an acidic seed. The root is long, quite thick, and perennial.

It is cultivated in gardens, especially and most abundantly in Lyon and in Italy, and is more often planted from cuttings than from seed; it flourishes throughout the whole Summer.

It strongly heats and dries, cuts <note>thick humors</note>, digests, stimulates the appetite, and provokes <note>urine</note>. *More in the Appendix.*

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Helichrysum plant with thin, upright stems and small clusters of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

### HELICHRYSUM, HELICHRYSON, AND HELEIO-chrysum, German & French: Helichryson; Italian: Helichryso.
<note>The name derives from the Greek *helios* (sun) and *chrysos* (gold), referring to the bright yellow flowers.</note>

We shall treat the Helichrysum of the Ancients, and the various plants circulated under that name, in the Appendix.

However, for the true Helichrysum of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician whose herbal was the standard botanical authority for 1,500 years</note>, the plant we depict here is currently presented. It has straight, robust stems, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, along which and the branches are seen leaves like Southernwood, very dense where they first break out, very finely divided, short, hairy, and somewhat whitish. The flowers cling to the highest twigs, yellow, in the form of Chamomile flowers, with a powerful scent. The root is hard and woody.

It grows copiously in warmer regions in rough, uncultivated, and deserted places, in lean valleys, and on parched hills; it is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms in August.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with linear leaves and rounded flower heads, identified as Helichrysum Tragi.</image-desc>

### TRAGUS’S HELICHRYSUM, WITH TOADFLAX LEAVES, yellow clusters, and black seed.

Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> makes this plant the third species of Toadflax; Lonicer makes it the fourth, calling it *Linosyris*. Among the moderns, Lobel in his *Observations* calls it *Osyris*; Clusius calls it Austrian *Osyris*; Gerard calls it Purple-blue *Osyris*; and some call it Golden Toadflax.

Tragus writes that it grows in sandy, damp, and uncultivated places, and on the sunny borders of fields. It also comes up in gardens, as we have observed in various places, and we have even cultivated it at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden. It blooms in August and September.

To this plant, as to the preceding one, are ascribed the same strengths and powers as those the Ancients attributed to their Helichrysum, concerning which see the Appendix.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Stoechas Citrina plant with broad leaves and clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

### VARIOUS GOLDEN STOECHAS: German Golden Stoechas, with a broader leaf.

The Golden Stoechas <note>commonly known today as "Everlasting" or "Strawflower"</note> are referred to and belong among the Helichrysums and Amaranths; they differ greatly from the Stoechas properly so-called <note>French Lavender</note>, which we shall present in Book 28 of this *Outline*.

The one we depict here has stalks nine inches or a cubit long, clothed in gray down, sometimes solitary and sometimes many; along these are woolly, gray leaves, an inch wide (especially around the root). At the ends of the twigs, clusters compact with small scales shine with the brightness of gold. The root is long, woody, and fibrous.

In the regions adjacent to the Rhine, it occurs in dry, rough, and sandy places; it blooms in June and July.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Stoechas Citrina plant with detailed flower heads labeled I, II, III, and IV.</image-desc>

### GOLDEN STOECHAS, BEAUTIFUL IN BOTH THE SIZE AND COLOR OF THE FLOWER.

It is entirely covered in down and gray. The leaves, which are also gray, are thick and broader than in the Narbonne variety (of which more shortly), namely one or two inches wide. At the very top of the stems, which are not branched and are a cubit high, sit many clusters, brightly shimmering, yellow, rivaling gold, much larger than those of the German or Narbonne Golden Stoechas, being nearly the size of a Chickpea.

Camerarius labels this as a Stoechas sent from Crete, having larger tufts. By Caspar Bauhin in his *History* and in Mattioli, it is called the 3rd Oriental Helichrysum, with a yellow and shining flower. We saw the plant at Basel, sent from Crete.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Stoechas Citrina with narrow leaves (tenuifolia).</image-desc>

### NARROW-LEAVED GOLDEN STOECHAS OF NARBONNE, with a yellow or pale flower.

By Mattioli, Gesner, Dodoens, Laguna, Castore, and the *History of Lyon*, it is called simply Golden Stoechas. By Fuchs, Laguna, and Lonicer, it is called Yellow Amaranth; by some, *Chrysocome* <note>Goldy-locks</note>; by Lobel in his *Adversaria* and *Observations*, our Golden Stoechas, Yellow Amaranth, Golden Toadflax, and *Tinearia* <note>Moth-herb, as it was used to repel moths</note>. By Amato, Camerarius, and others, it is called Helichrysum. By Sylvius, it is called the Helichrysum of Dioscorides and the Amaranth of Galen. However, Mattioli, Lobel, and Robert Constantinus write that those who think this is the legitimate Helichrysum of Dioscorides are hallucinating.

Germany has less of it; but a beautiful and very fragrant variety grows in the arid and stony places of Spain, and it is very abundant in Narbonne, France. It blooms in May.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Stoechas Citrina identified as the Italian variety.</image-desc>

### ANOTHER NARROW-LEAVED GOLDEN STOECHAS, or the Italian variety.

This is a branched plant, with leaves similar to the Narbonne Golden Stoechas but thinner; at the summit of each stalk is a small, golden, divided cluster-bearing umbrella. The root is thin and fibrous.

It is also called Helichrysum by some; but by Mattioli and the *History of Lyon*, it is called Cretan Helichrysum.

It grows in Crete, as well as between Naples and Pozzuoli.

### A RELATIVE OF GOLDEN STOECHAS, with spreading, sparse, scaly heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with multiple stems, narrow leaves, and scaly flower heads at the tips.</image-desc>

It grows like a shrub in the manner of the Golden Stoechas <note>original: "Stoechadis citrinæ"; likely *Helichrysum stoechas*, also known as Goldilocks or Everlasting</note> of Narbonne: however, the twigs are shorter and white with downy fuzz. The leaves clothe these twigs just like those of the Golden Stoechas, with smooth, even margins, and are covered with a woolly down underneath. The *Heads* are placed at the ends of individual small branches, appearing either singly, in pairs, or even in threes; they are shorter than half an inch and scaly. The *Flowers* are of a dull and faded color, not golden, and the centers of their tips turn into downy fluff <note>term: pappos (pappus); the feathery bristles on seeds like a dandelion, used for wind dispersal</note>. This plant has nearly the same scent as the aforementioned Stoechas.

We observed it at Montpellier on walls at the beginning of Spring. Is it perhaps Lobelius’s second Golden Stoechas? Or the scentless species of Golden Stoechas mentioned by Camerarius in Mattioli? Or the Yellow Amaranth of Tabernaemontanus?

### A RELATIVE OF GOLDEN STOECHAS from Mr. Bernh. Paludanus, called "Ialoux."

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, fuzzy leaves and several rounded flower heads on long stalks.</image-desc>

The tops and flower heads of a certain herb were sent to us under this name, approaching the Golden Stoechas, or rather more correctly the scaly heads of the Cudweed <note>original: "Gnaphalij"; Cudweed or Everlasting</note>. These, however, are not golden but ash-colored, like the said Cudweed, though shorter and covered with white hairs. From these, the very white petals of the florets emerge. Certain small leaves also cling to them, smaller than the leaves of Wild Thyme and somewhat round, the back part covered in hoary down, and the opposite side a dark green. Mr. Bernh. Paludanus <note>Bernardus Paludanus (1550–1633), a famous Dutch physician and collector</note> called it *Ialoux*.

### GERMAN CUDWEED OF FUCHS. Called "Wicked Herb" by some, after Pliny.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, slender plant with small leaves and clusters of tiny flowers along the stem and at the apex.</image-desc>

It hardly exceeds the height of a span and a half <note>about 12 inches</note>. It is endowed with several stems, some upright and some spreading on the ground, branched and covered in hoary down, which also coats the leaves. The leaves are similar to Lavender leaves, with a taste that is drying without being biting. The *Flowers* are sessile <note>term: sessile; attached directly at the base without a stalk</note>, pale yellow, and crowded together, found both at the ends of the small branches and in the angles where the branches divide. The *Root* is woody, white, and fibrous.

We have seen it in fields at Lyon, Geneva, Padua, and Montbéliard; elsewhere it commonly abounds in sandy places and on sunny embankments. Belon calls it "Bastard," as he admits only the *Maritime* variety as legitimate. However, by the consensus of many, it is determined to be the *Wicked Herb* <note>original: "Herbam verò Impiam"; so called because the younger flowers overtop the older ones, like children rising above their parents</note> of Pliny. More in the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

### A RELATIVE OF GOLDEN STOECHAS with longer heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with woody stems and elongated, scaly flower heads.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub with woody twigs, one to sometimes two cubits high <note>approx. 18–36 inches</note>, divided into many branches and covered in white hairs. The *Leaves* are like those of Arabian Stoechas, downy and hoary below, and almost blackish above. At the summit of each branch sits sometimes one, sometimes two, or sometimes three *Heads*, an inch long, cylindrical, beautifully shingled with scales, somewhat reddish, containing a downy fluff longer than the heads themselves.

Lobelius calls this the "other scentless Golden Stoechas"; Tabernaemontanus calls it *Yellow Amaranth*, but his illustration is poor, which Gerard places under a false title with an even more serious error.

### CUDWEED, CENTUNCULUS: German: *Rhurkraut*; French: *Herbe à cotton*, *Herbe à la dissenterie*; Italian: *Gnaphalio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, lanceolate leaves and small flower clusters, showing the root system and a detail of a seed/flower.</image-desc>

It is anchored by a thick, long, woody root, black and provided with very few fibers. This sends out several stems, nine inches long, somewhat thick, hairy, and white. On these, the *Leaves* are packed in a dense order; they are oblong, half an inch long, and somewhat round at the tip. When crushed, they turn entirely into tufts of cottony wool, and are capable of soaking up oil in lamps <note>note: This refers to the plant's use as a makeshift wick</note>. At the summits of the branches, the *Heads* are arranged almost in the form of an umbel; they are somewhat thick, white, and hairy, but yellow in the middle. Within these is a somewhat long, white *Seed*, curved into the shape of a bow.

Clusius, among others, labels this *Gnaphalium* and *The True Gnaphalium of Dioscorides*; almost everyone else calls it *Marine* or *Maritime* Cudweed, because the sea coasts are made white by it.

### LOBELIUS’S SMALLEST CUDWEED, *Allerminste Ruercruyt*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, branched plant with tiny leaves and flower heads.</image-desc>

Lobelius described this Cudweed in his *Observations* with the following words: "The smallest Cudweed," he says, "is the height of a palm, with the small flowers of Southernwood and whitish, downy leaves." I wish, however, he had noted the locations where he collected it. By C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called *Gnaphalium 5* or *The Lesser*. To tell the truth, we are still ignorant of what this plant is, nor have we seen it anywhere; if Lobelius had noted the birthplaces <note>note: i.e., the native habitats</note> where he collected it, more diligent students of botany might have been able to investigate it.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Images and Outlines" (Icones et Sciagraphia) of botanical specimens, specifically focusing on various species of Gnaphalium (Cudweeds) and Leontopodium (Lion's Foot or Edelweiss types).</meta>

### UPRIGHT CUDWEED; The Great Branched Cudweed of Caspar Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, upright Gnaphalium plant with narrow leaves and small flower clusters along the upper stem.</image-desc>

This plant has a straight and rigid stem, nine inches high <note>original: "dodrantem," a span or nine inches</note>, round and covered with a white downy fuzz, yet nonetheless rough to the touch, more so on the back than on the front. The leaves grow thickly on the stem in no particular order, about four inches long and scarcely a straw's breadth wide, mostly shaped like a keel. From the axils of these leaves, along the stem from the middle to the very top, grow small, oblong, scaly heads joined together. These are a shiny blackish-green, which open into tiny yellowish-green filaments. The root beneath is small and black.

We found this in the mountains between Belfort and Masmünster; it also abounds between Montbéliard and Pont-de-Roide <note>original: "Pontem Vancianecurt"</note>, and it flowers in August.

### SINGLE-STALKED CUDWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gnaphalium plant with a single central stalk and clusters of flowers at the nodes.</image-desc>

It rises with a single small stalk, provided with several little branches twisting in different directions, which are surrounded here and there by somewhat broad, soft, and hoary <note>gray-white</note> leaves. At the joints of the branches, among the cluster of leaves, grow five, six, or more small heads crowded together, a grayish-yellow in color and full of much down. The root is of no use, but new plants are reborn every year from the fallen seed.

It occurs in drier fields, especially among harvested crops, according to Clusius.

### ANOTHER BEAUTIFUL KIND OF ALPINE CUDWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing alpine Gnaphalium with broad, fuzzy leaves arranged in a rosette-like fashion.</image-desc>

Lobelius depicts this in his *Images of Plants* under this inscription: *Leontopodium*, or Lion's Foot. The herbalists have labeled this and the preceding Cudweed as *Leontopodium* <note>Lion's Foot</note> because of the shaggy appearance of the leaves and flowers, which somewhat resembles a leg attached to a foot.

As for the etymology of *Gnaphalium*: Galen says it is so named because we can use its soft leaves <term>instead of flocks of wool <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ γναφάλων (anti gnaphalon)</note></term>, that is, for stuffing. Thus the downy leaves of Dittany are also called "Gnaphaloid" <note>wool-like</note> by Dioscorides.

<column-break/>

### CUDWEED Resembling Stoechas.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a branched Gnaphalium plant with small, dense flower heads resembling Stoechas.</image-desc>

The root of this is seen to be small, fibrous, and somewhat woody. The leaves are those of a Cudweed, two or three inches long, one or two straw-breadths wide, downy, hoary, and soft. The stems are shaggy and white; they are straight, sometimes branched, and between nine inches and a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height. Only at the very tips do the flowers cling, with small heads resembling the yellow Stoechas <note>a type of lavender or everlasting flower</note>.

We saw this at Montpellier, and in the mountains around Espérou, flowering in Autumn.

Is it perhaps the "Second Golden-locks" of Clusius? Or the "Wild Golden-locks and Sun-gold" in the *Images* of Lobelius?

### BEAUTIFUL ALPINE CUDWEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine Gnaphalium with distinct, star-like woolly flower heads.</image-desc>

It has stems a palm's breadth, nine inches, or even higher, which are downy. These are clothed in oblong, narrow, shaggy leaves, three or four inches in length and wider than a straw. The very top bears flowers that are quite large, clustered, tufted with down, composed of bright yellow filaments, sitting close to the stem, and interwoven with soft down in the middle of <unclear>whitening</unclear> leaves that imitate a wide, radiating star. There are many leaves near the ground not much different from the upper ones. The root is black, quite thick, and fibrous.

Is this the true *Leontopodium* of Dioscorides, as Mattioli maintains?

It abounds in the mountains around Geneva and flowers in July and August.

### SMALL LION'S FOOT of Lobelius, Related to Alpine Cudweed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Leontopodium (Edelweiss-type) plant with a single stalk and woolly bracts.</image-desc>

He says it has a single small stalk nine inches high. The leaves are those of the Mountain Cudweed, hoary with dense down. The tiny flowers at the top of the stem are also like Mountain Cudweed, a pale yellow. It has a meager and woody root. Lobelius writes this in his *Observations*, page 256, concerning his "Small Lion's Foot," the image of which he provides under the same title in *Images of Plants*, page 484, as does Tabernaemontanus in his *Images and History*, where he calls it in German <term>Small Lion's Foot <note>original: "Kleinen Löwen fuss"</note></term>. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called "Cudweed 11, or the Lesser Alpine."

We shall treat the use and virtues of Cudweed in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several species of Gnaphalium and Leontopodium (Cudweeds and Lion's Foot), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in the Alps and France, and their botanical nomenclature according to contemporary authorities like Lobelius and Bauhin.</summary>
<keywords>Gnaphalium, Leontopodium, Cudweed, Lion's Foot, Edelweiss, botany, Alpine flora, Caspar Bauhin, Lobelius, Clusius, medicinal plants, Belfort, Geneva</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Gnaphalium (Cudweed) and Pilosella (Hawkweed) families, focusing on their physical characteristics and the differing opinions of contemporary Renaissance botanists.</meta>

### SMALLEST UMBEL-BEARING CUDWEED.
<note>original: Gnaphalium Umbellatum Minimum</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a small Gnaphalium plant with multiple stems ending in clustered flower heads and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

This little plant scarcely exceeds an inch in size. Sometimes it is an inch tall and simple, other times divided into several "eyes" <note>likely referring to the flower heads</note> consisting of whitish, hairy leaves. Between these, an "eye" is visible, almost as wide as the nail of the little finger, somewhat rough, and turning from yellow to green. Small leaves also clothe the little stalks, smaller than those mentioned before; they are poorly depicted here, as is the "eye." The root consists of pure fibers of a woody hardness, black, twisted, and longer than the plantlet itself.

We collected it in flower during May in the sandy areas of Mount Cetus <note>The Kahlenberg near Vienna</note> and in maritime sand-dunes.

<column-break/>

### AMERICAN OR EXOTIC CUDWEED.
<note>original: Gnaphalium Americanum, sive Exoticum</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a taller Gnaphalium species with lanceolate leaves and dense clusters of flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

This plant rises to the height of a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, and sometimes grows even taller. We first saw it at Pforzheim in the very well-cultivated garden of Höchstetter, in full flower in November. However, for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>S.P. likely refers to Serenissimi Principis</note>, it flowered in the months of July and August. It obtained the name "American" because it was first brought into our regions from America. By Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called Clusius's *American Cudweed*; in Mattioli, however, it is called *Foreign Broad-leaved Cudweed*, etc.

---

<column-break/>

### HAWKWEED, A KIND OF CUDWEED: SMALLER HAWKWEED.
<note>original: Pilosella Gnaphalii Genus: Pilosella minor</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Pilosella minor showing a basal rosette of leaves and long, thin stems with small flower heads.</image-desc>

It spreads oblong leaves all around on the ground, rounded at the end, and covered with a hoary down on the underside. Between these rise stalks a span or nine inches high, and even a cubit high, woolly and whitish, clothed with long, narrow leaves. At their summit hang many clustered flowers, sometimes larger and more beautiful, sometimes smaller and less lovely, and also now white, now more or less purple; in the middle are many tips, followed by long downy seeds <term>pappus: the feathery bristles on seeds like a dandelion</term>. The fibrous roots creep along.

There is, moreover, one Hawkweed larger and another smaller; one of our country and another exotic; and there is a difference in the length of the leaves and, as said before, in the color of the flowers.

<column-break/>

### GREATER HAWKWEED.
<note>original: Pilosella Maior</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Pilosella maior, featuring broader leaves in a basal rosette and more robust flowering stalks.</image-desc>

Regarding the Hawkweed which we present here, we have nothing from the Ancient writers. Without a doubt, those are hallucinating—in the judgment of Mattioli and Laguna—who believe this herb is the *Holosteum* <note>Stitchwort</note> which the common sort of Herbarists call Hawkweed. Those who put forward *Mouse-ear* <note>Auricula Muris</note> in its place are also in great error, in the judgment of Fuchs; for that has blue flowers, while in this they are white, purple, or flesh-colored. They are also mistaken, in the judgment of Ruel, who think it is *Elatine* <note>Fluellen</note>, as its place of birth openly contradicts this.

Others more correctly refer it to the genus of Cudweed and call it *Mountain Cudweed*; among these are Dodoens, Lobel, Tabernaemontanus, Caspar Bauhin, and the *History of Lyon*.

---

<column-break/>

### EXOTIC MULLEIN-LIKE HAWKWEED.
<note>original: Pilosella Phlomodis Exotica</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Pilosella phlomodis showing broad, textured leaves and a cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

Lobel labels this the *Greatest Syrian Hawkweed*; Tabernaemontanus the *Greater Syrian Hawkweed*; Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it the *Fourth or Syrian Hawkweed not yet seen*.

Our common Hawkweed, both the greater and the smaller, grows on mountainous and grassy hills, as well as in clear-cut and open woods and sandy mounds. We saw it at Geneva on Mount Salève, and in the Griesbach valley—both the Greater and the Smaller, with white and purple flowers—blooming in May.

It has no use in Medicine, although by nature it is strongly drying and astringent.

<column-break/>

### DIOSCORIDES' BACCHARIS ACCORDING TO RAUWOLF.
<note>original: Baccharis Dioscoridis Rauvvolfio</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Baccharis Dioscoridis with serrated leaves and multiple small flower heads on branching stems.</image-desc>

This is also a foreign plant, observed near Lebanon by Rauwolf, reaching a cubit in height and endowed with woolly leaves. It grows with leaves similar to <unclear>...</unclear> and a stem, as in the <unclear>...</unclear> Peruvian Henbane of Dodoens, clasping the stalk. The tops are occupied by whitish-purple flowerlets, densely packed together, as in the Yellow Amaranth or Fuchs's Mouse-ear. The small root is fragrant, similar to the roots of Black Hellebore.

Thus Rauwolf describes it, but he is found to hesitate regarding this plant: for no one pronounces it to be Dioscorides' *Baccharis* with absolute certainty; indeed, he doubts whether it is the *Baccharis* of Dioscorides.

Could it be a <unclear>...</unclear> of Mountain Cudweed, as it seems to Clusius?
