<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of medicinal herbs, focusing on the various species and subspecies of Wormwood (Absinthium). It maintains the encyclopedic style of comparing classical descriptions from Dioscorides with contemporary observations from 16th-century botanists like Lobelius and Clusius.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### WORMWOOD: German: *Elfs, Eltz, Wermuth*; French: *Absynthe, Aluine*; Italian: *Assenzo, Assentio, Medico*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wormwood plant (Absinthium) showing its root system, branched stems, and feathery leaves.</image-desc>

Although Wormwood is a herb well known to the common people, as Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> reports, hardly two authors agree in identifying and describing its species. However, leaving aside the variations of opinion for the sake of brevity—and having relegated them to a specific Treatise—we say there are three differences of Wormwood: Common Wormwood, Pontic Wormwood, and Seriphian Wormwood, about which we shall speak specifically in the following sections.

*The lesser common Wormwood, also called Common Mountain Wormwood, which we depict here, grows in many places in the mountains; it is entirely similar in both root and stems, as well as leaves and flowers, to the very common larger Wormwood (of which more shortly), but it is more slender, less liked, and has a less abominable odor.*

### LOBELIUS’S TREE-LIKE WORMWOOD: German: *Baum Wermuth*; Italian: *Assenzo de Comasco*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody, shrub-like wormwood plant with a thick central stem and dense foliage.</image-desc>

It is not so different from the common variety in leaf and flower, but it takes on the habit of a woody shrub, in the manner of Southernwood <note>original: "Abrotoni"</note>, reaching the height of a man. It has a whiter and slightly smaller leaf which is evergreen, a bitter aromatic taste, and a not unpleasant odor.

By Camerarius in his notes on Matthiolus, it is called "Tree-like Wormwood, odorless and sweet." By Dodonaeus in Latin, it is called "Female tree-like Southernwood."

Lobelius writes that it is found especially in Belgium. However, a tasteless, odorless, and dull variety, unknown to the Ancients, is found in some gardens. Furthermore, the common variety grows almost everywhere; it is both sown and grows by itself in gardens, and especially loves rocky and uncultivated places. *More in the Appendix.*

### FINE-LEAVED SERIPHIAN WORMWOOD, or Sea Wormwood of Narbonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sea wormwood plant with fine, delicate leaves and small flower heads.</image-desc>

It grows with many shrubby shoots a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, becoming woody and hoary-white. Along these, the leaves are crowded, very finely divided, whitish, with a salty taste combined with bitterness; when they first sprout, they are succulent and green. Finally, it becomes heavy with minute seeds.

This comes forth around the shores of the Mediterranean Sea in most provinces of Europe, and especially in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>; however, it is more heavy-scented and less white than the Seriphian Wormwood of Meissen or Belgium.

Furthermore, Sea Wormwood is commonly labeled "Seriphian Wormwood," namely from the island of Seriphos where it grows most abundantly; for which reason it does not please some that it be called simply "Seriphium."

<column-break/>

### COMMON LARGE WORMWOOD: Tasteless Wormwood: Italian: *Assenzo bas lordo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the common large wormwood plant, showing a robust root and tall, flowering stalks.</image-desc>

The most common Wormwood has several stems, woody, hoary, shrubby with many branches, one to three cubits high, and sometimes taller. The leaves are like the leaves of Mugwort <note>original: "Artemisiæ"</note>, more finely divided, somewhat soft, entirely hoary, though more so on the underside than the top, with an aromatic, pungent odor and a bitter taste. Clusters of flowers <note>term: "Corymbi" - flat-topped flower clusters</note> shine forth very abundantly in long rows on the branches everywhere with a tawny color, followed by minute seeds. The root is somewhat thick, woody, and pleasantly aromatic, washing the whole mouth with flavor without any bitterness.

*Cordus calls it "Rustic Wormwood." There is also a certain tasteless Wormwood, similar in all respects to the common one, except that it is destitute of all taste and smell. Regarding its origins, see what follows.*

### SEA WORMWOOD, OR SERIPHIUM: Broad-leaved Maritime Wormwood.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime wormwood variety with broader leaves than the Narbonense type.</image-desc>

It grows with dense branches a cubit or more high, and these are woody, whitish, and crowded with a great multitude of leaves. The leaves are covered all over with a hoary down; sometimes they are entire and mimic the leaves of the Olive, being delicate; sometimes they are divided into two, three, or four segments, with the odor of Mugwort and a not unpleasant taste. The flower clusters are yellow, smaller than those of common Wormwood; the seed is minute; the root is woody. *Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, and others call it "Sea Mugwort."*

We have seen this in various gardens in Padua, Paris, Esslingen, and elsewhere. However, according to Matthiolus, it grows spontaneously on very many shores of both the Tyrrhenian and Adriatic seas, and especially those of Apulia and Trieste.

### FINE-LEAVED AUSTRIAN WORMWOOD

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Austrian wormwood, characterized by slender stems and fine foliage.</image-desc>

The stem of this plant usually equals a foot in height, and sometimes reaches a cubit; it is firm, becoming gray, and provided with many thin leaves which surround it in a confused manner. It branches out into many small stalks in the upper part and is full of drooping clusters of small flowers. The root is fibrous. The whole plant is very bitter, elegant, and rare.

Clusius, the author of the description, says it grows on hills and certain open places near the city of Vienna.

*In the Illustrations and History of Tabernaemontanus, it is called "Nabataean Wormwood of Avicenna." Could it be the "Sea Wormwood" of Anguillara? Or the "Seriphian Wormwood" mentioned in various chapters by Belon in his Observations?*

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of Wormwood (Absinthium), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins, and the differing nomenclature used by prominent 16th-century botanists. It distinguishes between common, tree-like, maritime, and Austrian species, noting their medicinal and aromatic qualities.</summary>
<keywords>Wormwood, Absinthium, Seriphium, botany, medicinal herbs, Dioscorides, Lobelius, Clusius, maritime plants, herbals</keywords>

--- Page 447 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of Wormwood (Absinthium) varieties, following the general descriptions of the genus. The catchword "ABSYN-" from the previous page leads directly into these specific subspecies.</meta>

### LOW-LYING OR CREEPING WORMWOOD: called by some Golden Camomile:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, creeping plant with small, finely divided leaves and several upright flowering stalks with small button-like flower heads.</image-desc>

It has a simple and singular stem, about a cubit <note>approximately 18 inches</note> long, smooth and rounded: along which leaves grow at intervals, similar to the leaves of Noble Camomile <note>Anthemis nobilis</note>, finely divided. A little above the middle of the stem, all the way to the top, flowers sprout alternately, with clusters similar to Southernwood <note>Abrotanum</note>: the lower ones rest on stalks half a cubit long or more, while the upper ones cling to very short stalks and are pressed, as it were, against the main stem. The root is woody, twisted, many-branched, and fibrous.

Leonhart Fuchs used to call it *Golden Camomile*. However, Conrad Gesner, Tabernaemontanus, and Matthias de l'Obel called it *Creeping* and *Low-lying Wormwood*.

It is found in certain cold mountains of the Swiss, where it is unable to grow tall due to the severity of the climate.

<column-break/>

### FINE-LEAVED WHITE VALAIS WORMWOOD, or White Herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender, upright plant with very fine, feathery foliage and small clusters of flowers along the upper stem.</image-desc>

Rembert Dodoens writes of this as follows: Among the "spurious" <note>false or hybrid</note> Wormwoods, he says, the one called *White Herb* by the Swiss is the first to be encountered. This entire plant is soft, as if covered in down, and whitish: similar to *Seriphium* or Sea Wormwood, but whiter, reflecting it also in scent and taste, yet somewhat sweeter, approaching the scent of Camphor. Gesner writes that it grows in Valais <note>a region in Switzerland</note> on the hills near Sion, etc.

In the judgment of the same Gesner, the white color and the strength—which is somewhat less than the maritime varieties—along with a similar scent and taste, seem to indicate that it could be called the female *Seriphium Wormwood*.

---

<column-break/>

### COMMON PONTIC WORMWOOD: German: Pontischer Wermuth: Italian: Assenzo Pontico.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy plant with deeply lobed, feathery leaves and numerous small flower heads on branched stems.</image-desc>

It spreads numerous small roots, interwoven with frequent fibers, woody, and endowed with an aromatic taste. It raises several stems from the same root, a cubit or a cubit and a half high, rounded, smooth, greenish, or turning reddish or grayish from the green, branched from the bottom all the way to the top. With leaves no less finely cut than Southernwood, but with shorter and neater segments, they are covered in a short down, especially on the lower part, which is even grayer than the upper; it has a sweet scent and a somewhat bitter taste. The flower clusters are smaller than in Common Wormwood, honey-colored, and breathe a stronger scent than the leaves.

Charles de l'Écluse <note>Clusius</note> identifies two kinds of this: *One* entirely gray-white: and *Another* which has reddish little stems.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER Illustration of COMMON PONTIC WORMWOOD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a similar variety of Wormwood, showing a robust root system and dense, feathery foliage with flowering spikes.</image-desc>

Those who think "Common" Wormwood is something different from "Roman" and "Pontic" are mistaken: for it was once called "Common Roman" because it was sacred to the Roman Commoners, and because it is found everywhere among the ancient ruins in the Roman countryside. It is called "Pontic" after Pontus <note>a region on the Black Sea</note>, where it is said to grow in great abundance. But why is it named after the Roman or Pontic locations, when it is also found in various other places? Pietro Andrea Mattioli and Clusius write that it grows in Hungary, Bohemia, and various places in Austria, in rocky, rugged, and grassy fields. We have also seen it growing wild at Tübingen, not far from the Neckar river: as well as around Speyer and Worms. In England, Belgium, and France it is a garden plant: at Lyon and Geneva you call it *du prin fort* <note>likely a local French dialect name for a strong herb</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### EGYPTIAN WORMWOOD: Italian: Assenzo d'Egitto.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader, lobed leaves and clusters of small flowers, showing the root and branching habit.</image-desc>

The whole herb is hairy and gray-white, in the manner of Ground-Cypress, with a bitter taste and a <term>worm-seed</term> <note>original: "semine contra vermes" - seeds used to expel intestinal parasites</note> almost like that of the Apothecaries, with a nearly aromatic scent. We depict it here from a dried plant. Mattioli describes it thus: It is a stunted plant, he says, growing in Egypt, with tiny leaves, almost like female Southernwood: with many shoots, slender, short, and leafy: with a tiny seed and a bitter taste, though not vehemently so: and it is endowed with all the other qualities which the Italian variety has. So he says: but Rauwolf and others reject this Wormwood from the Class of Wormwoods.

We have placed two illustrations of the so-called Pontic Wormwood above, not because they are different plants, but because we found them already engraved among our purchased plates.

<column-break/>

### UMBEL-BEARING WORMWOOD: called Mutellina by some: French: Mutelline blanche, Herb of the Abscess.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with basal leaves and an upright stem ending in an umbel-like cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

Under the name *Mutellina*, we found a type of Wormwood among our dried plants, supported by a thick root: sending out several stems, a palm's breadth <note>about 3-4 inches</note> or a little larger, through which (as well as at their tips) rather sparse flower clusters are seen, quite large, and if we are not mistaken, yellow. The leaves are thin with the divisions of *Seriphium* Wormwood, very white, hairy: with a bitter, unpleasant taste.

In his *Observations*, L'Obel calls it *Another Italian Umbel-bearing Wormwood, not yet recorded in Literature*: in Camerarius's garden it is called *Small and Gray Wormwood*. It was called "lowly" by Gesner and "stunted" by Clusius. Clusius, in his history of the plants of Pannonia, calls it a *Stunted kind of Wormwood, scarcely exceeding a palm in height, etc.*

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and synonyms for several varieties of Wormwood, including creeping, Swiss, Pontic, Egyptian, and alpine (Mutellina) types. It highlights the disagreements among Renaissance botanists regarding the classification and naming of these medicinal herbs.</summary>
<keywords>Wormwood, Absinthium, Pontic Wormwood, Mutellina, Egyptian Wormwood, Mattioli, Clusius, Gesner, botanical classification, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Artemisia family, specifically focusing on varieties of wormwood and mugwort. It follows previous descriptions of common wormwood.</meta>

->IMAGES AND OUTLINES:<-

### WORMWOOD WITH WHITE FLOWERS and shaggy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering wormwood plant with deeply lobed leaves and small, rounded flower heads at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that this rare kind of wormwood was mentioned by no writer in his time. However, Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist</note> states that it holds a nature midway between Wormwood and Feverfew; to him, as to several others, it is called *white wormwood, or white-flowered wormwood*.

It is a small plant, about six to nine inches high: with a hoary, white stem, along which are observed leaves an inch long, somewhat broad, covered in a hoary down, divided into segments in the manner of common wormwood—deeply jagged—yet much smaller. At the top, the flowers are arranged in the form of an umbel <note>a cluster of flowers where stalks spring from a common center like umbrella ribs</note>, beautiful, seven or eight in number, clinging to moderate stalks, consisting of radiating white petals, with many tips, supported by shaggy heads. The root is thick, perennial, and fibrous.

### WORM-SEED, SANTONIC SEED: Germ. Wurmkraut: Gal. Barbotine: Ital. Semenzana.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Santonicum plant (Wormseed) showing upright stems with small, scale-like leaves and clusters of tiny flower heads.</image-desc>

Various plants are thrust forward by various authors as the plant bearing the so-called "Worm-seed." By some, it is called *Seriphian or Marine Wormwood*; by others *Santonic Wormwood*, or rather *Xantonic*, which took its name from the region of Saintes in France <note>original: "Xantonum in Gallia Tractus"</note>, where it grows in great abundance. By others, it is called *Wormwood itself*, as by Lacuna. Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician</note> also has his own peculiar variety, which we depict here. Thus to Pena <note>Pierre Pena, a French botanist</note>, whose opinion we do not reject, the "Worm-seed" of the Apothecaries <note>original: "Offic." for Officinarum</note> seems to be none of the three wormwoods.

The whole plant is similar to common wormwood, but smaller and less white, with seeds that are not quite so tiny, and small flowers.

### MUGWORT: Germ. Beyfust: Gall. Armoise, Herbe de S. Iean: Ital. Artemesia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mugwort plant (Artemisia) with large, deeply pinnatifid leaves and a tall, branched flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This perennial and shrub-like herb has a root the thickness of a finger, creeping, hairy with many fibers, woody, with a somewhat sweet and aromatic taste. The stems are two or three cubits high <note>about 3 to 4.5 feet</note>, stubborn to break, channeled, slightly hairy, mostly reddish in color, but more rarely hoary or green, with many hollow "wings." Its leaves are sweet-smelling, with a taste somewhat sweet and slightly sharp; they attach alternately to the stems and branches, hoary underneath and greenish above, divided into sharper segments than those of common wormwood. The flower clusters <note>term: "Corymbi" - flat-topped flower clusters</note> are fragrant, hoary, and shaggy, displaying little yellow fibers.

There is one Mugwort that is white and another that is red: and another fine-leaved variety, of which more shortly: another is the common and broad-leaved variety, which we depict here, and which is familiar throughout all of Europe.

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN WORMWOOD WITH Chamomile flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain wormwood with a single, large, daisy-like flower head atop a slender stem with finely divided leaves.</image-desc>

From a woody, small, black, winding, and prostrate root, it sends out thin, woolly leaves divided by deep incisions—midway between Sea Wormwood and male Southernwood—arranged in a circle. In spring, it puts forth several trailing stems, with a few leaves clinging to the bottom. In summer, however, it bears single flowers clinging to the top of each stem, in the manner of female Southernwood, but in the shape of Chamomile flowers. In taste and smell, it resembles *Common Pontic Wormwood*, which is why it obtained the name of Wormwood rather than Southernwood, to which it is more similar.

This rare plant grows on the high mountain called "Of the Blessed Virgin Mary" <note>likely referring to a specific peak in the Alps</note>; it grows in the crevices of rocks and nowhere else.

### WORM-SEED, OR THE SANTONIC Wormwood of Rauwolf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Wormseed, showing two branched stalks with very fine, needle-like foliage and small seed heads.</image-desc>

Santonic Wormwood, he says <note>referring to Leonhard Rauwolf (1535–1596), a German physician and traveler</note>, grows around Bethlehem and abounds in the Holy Land, with small, ash-colored leaves moderately approaching our local Wormwood: with many thin branches, and an abundance of small, yellowish seed, of a heavy odor and a very bitter taste, and sharp with a smoky quality. Such is the description by him whose illustration Camerarius prefers over all others handed down by others.

This Seed is given various other names: for it is called "Seed" simply, "Zedoary Seed," "Seed against worms," "Zina Seed," "Sementina," and "Holy Seed" <note>original: "Semen Sanctum"</note>, though the latter is a corrupted word, since it should have been called "Santonicum."

### FINE-LEAVED MUGWORT, OR LEPTOPHYLLOS: by some called Wild Southernwood.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a fine-leaved Mugwort (Artemisia tenuifolia) with highly dissected, feathery leaves and a dense, upright flowering habit.</image-desc>

This has a many-forked, woody, perennial root. The stems are slender, streaked, rigid, and in other respects approach the stems of common Mugwort. The leaves are whitish, hairy, with the division of Seriphian Wormwood, and an odor approaching Southernwood. The flower clusters are reddish, crowded in spikes on the branches, in the form and color of Southernwood. It is also accustomed to bear a mossy, scaly growth at the forks of the branches.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), an influential botanist</note> reckons three variations of fine-leaved Mugwort, but most refer the one we depict here to the "second Ambrosia" of Matthiolus.

We have observed it in various places: at Basel by the Rhine, on the way to Krentzach; at Montpellier everywhere in the hedges and the margins of fields, and elsewhere. It blooms in Autumn. *More concerning the Mugworts in the Appendix.*

<summary>This page describes several varieties of the Artemisia genus, including rare white-flowered wormwood, medicinal worm-seed used for parasites, and common mugwort. It cites prominent 16th-century botanists like Lobelius, Camerarius, and Rauwolf to distinguish between these similar-looking species.</summary>
<keywords>wormwood, mugwort, worm-seed, Artemisia, Santonicum, medicinal herbs, botany, 16th-century science, Rauwolf, Clusius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of medicinal herbs, focusing on Southernwood (Abrotanum) and its varieties, followed by Ambrosia and Moschatellina. The text maintains the encyclopedic style of 16th and 17th-century herbals, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary botanists.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

**Southernwood**: German: *Stabwurtz*; French: *Auron, Auronne*; Italian: *Abrotono & Abretano*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Abrotanum (Southernwood) plant, showing its woody base, branched stems, and fine, feathery foliage.</image-desc>

It grows from a woody root into a shrub with many shoots, three or four cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> high, hard, brittle, full of white pith, reddish, furrowed, and branched. There are many leaves along the stalks, finely divided, a little broader than fennel, grayish-white, with a powerful scent and a bitter, sharp taste. Indeed, the lower leaves are many-cleft, in the manner of Chamomile, while the upper ones are divided into only one or two segments, and very often are nothing more than a single thin filament. The flowers, crowded along the small branches, mimic the clusters <note>original: "Corymbos"</note> of Wormwood, possessing a yellowish color. This plant varies according to the season of the year and its cultivation. *More in the following.*

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER FIGURE OF COMMON SOUTHERNWOOD.

<image-desc>A second woodcut of Abrotanum, depicting a more mature or differently shaped specimen with denser foliage and visible flower clusters at the tips.</image-desc>

Southernwood, as the interpreter of Nicander <note>Nicander of Colophon, a Greek poet and physician</note> testifies, took its name from the fact that it appears tender, soft, and delicate to the sight: <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁβροῦ καὶ ἀπαλοῦ φαίνεσθαι" - meaning "from appearing delicate and soft"</note>; for which reason the Grammarians wish it to be called *Habrotanum*.

Its differences are taken especially from its *location*, its *flavor*, and its *size*: hence one is established as *Urban* (Garden) and another as *Wild*; one as *Male*, which is smaller, more slender, and called "twiggy" by Dioscorides, and another as *Female*, which is larger and, on the authority of the same Dioscorides, is said to grow like a shrub in the form of a tree. Pliny makes one *Field-grown* and another *Mountain-grown*: and he says that by the latter he understands the *Male*, and by the former the *Female*.

---

### YET ANOTHER FIGURE OF SOUTHERNWOOD.

<image-desc>A third woodcut of Abrotanum, showing a tall, slender variety with distinct branching patterns.</image-desc>

Southernwood grows everywhere in gardens and in open fields; it flowers in August and produces seed in September. We have seen it in various gardens: at Padua, Zurich, Geneva, and Montbéliard. The Field variety is very common in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, but is infrequent in Germany.

Furthermore, Southernwood is hot and dry in the third degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine regarding the intensity of a plant's "humoral" properties</note>, and is powerful in its ability to digest and thin out fluids. The tops, boiled in wine or water, are recommended for ailments of the chest, kidneys, bladder, and womb, and they soothe all manner of internal pains. Distilled water of the same plant contributes to these effects and cleanses the female parts if they are washed with it.

<column-break/>

### SOUTHERNWOOD WITH BEAUTIFUL CLUSTERS.

<image-desc>A fourth woodcut of Abrotanum, specifically highlighting the "beautiful corymbs" (flower clusters) at the ends of the branches.</image-desc>

This variety is lower than those previously mentioned, and has leaves divided with a great resemblance to Southernwood, but less white and more fragrant, in which they resemble Lavender Cotton <note>Santolina</note>. The clusters <note>corymbs</note> are abundant from the branches and shine with a yellow color even at the very top; the seed is quite fertile; the root is like the others.

Lobelius writes that it is a garden variety among the Belgians, which he depicts under the name *Fragrant Southernwood*. By C. Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Southernwood 10, or the smaller narrow-leaved Male*. Dodonaeus pronounces it without doubt to be the *Sicilian Southernwood* of Dioscorides, and names it as the third kind.

Furthermore, Southernwood extracts arrows, thorns, iron, and other things fixed in the body, if it is applied in the manner of a poultice <note>original: "Cataplasmatis"</note>. *More in the Appendix.*

---

**Ambrosia**: German: *Ambrosien*; Belgian: *Ambrosie*; French: *Ambroisie*; Italian: *Ambrosia*.

<image-desc>Woodcut of an Ambrosia plant, showing broad, lobed leaves and an upright flowering spike.</image-desc>

The plant which we depict here we first saw in Gesner’s garden, and we ourselves cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of S.P., where it flowered in Autumn. Lobelius and others call it *Sown* or *Garden Ambrosia*. Some call it *Ambrosia* and *Ambrosiana*; but Caesalpinus believes it to be the legitimate *Ambrosia* of Dioscorides, of which he relates thus: *Ambrosia*, he says, *is a tiny shrub, branched, three palms in height: with leaves like Rue, small around the base of the stalk. The little stems are heavy with seeds just like small clusters of grapes, which never produce a flower, with a wine-like, sweet scent: the root is thin and a foot and a half long.* Its power is to restrain, repel, and bind <note>astringent properties</note>. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### CORDI’S MOSCHATELLINA, WITH LEAVES OF BULBOUS FUMITORY: and flowers of a grassy color.

<image-desc>Woodcut of Moschatellina (Adoxa moschatellina), showing its characteristic basal leaves and small, globular flower head on a slender stalk.</image-desc>

Because this plant breathes out the scent of Musk in its flowers and leaves, it obtained the name *Moschatellina*: and in German it is called *Bisemkraut*, from Musk <note>Bisam</note>: and not *Besemkraut*, from brooms <note>Besen</note>, as some have wished.

Some label it *Denticulata* <note>Toothed</note>, from the shape of the root; others *Alabastriten*, because of the splendor of the root's translucent and shining skin, which is similar to Alabaster. To some it is the *Smallest Bulbous Fumitory*; to Lobelius in his *Adversaria* it is the *Smallest Northern Ranunculus with a mossy flower*.

Dalechampius writes that it grows near the bubbling sources of springs, by streams watering the meadows, and in shady hedges. It flowers in March and perishes quickly. It is very frequent on the hill of La Bastie in Geneva.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Southernwood (Abrotanum), detailing their physical characteristics, classical nomenclature, and medicinal uses as a digestive and poultice. It also introduces Ambrosia and Moschatellina, noting their botanical classifications and preferred habitats.</summary>
<keywords>Southernwood, Abrotanum, Ambrosia, Moschatellina, Adoxa, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny, Lobelius, Bauhin, Gesner, Caesalpinus, herbal medicine</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<meta>Original Latin: ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA</meta>

### RUE: German: Rauten; Belgian: Ruyten; French: Rue; Italian: Ruta; Spanish: Ruda, Aruda.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ruta (Rue) plant with detailed leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

Rue is commonly divided into *Sown* <note>cultivated</note> or domestic and *Wild*, and both are divided into *Greater* and *Lesser*; the plant called *Harmala* is also referred to the Wild varieties.

Rightly indeed do they place Rue among the shrubs; its woody branches bush out thickly, reaching two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> high or more, divided by frequent "wings" <note>leafy axils</note>. The *leaves* have a poisonous <note>heavy/stinking</note> smell and an equally unpleasant taste; they are bluish-green, often in threes or more, like a shrubby Trefoil. The *flowers* at the ends of the small branches are star-shaped and yellow, similar to the Wallflower but smaller; after they fall, a *seed-head* emerges, usually four-angled, divided into as many partitions and compartments as there are angles, in which is a small black *seed*, slightly oblong within its roundness.

### LESSER WILD RUE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of wild rue with more delicate, segmented foliage.</image-desc>

It sends up a stalk higher than a cubit, the stem of which is divided into frequent short forks, burdened with crowded herbaceous *flowers*. After these fall, they are followed by four-grained seed-heads, but much smaller than the preceding. The *leaves* are quite thick and very finely divided. It has the *heat* and *potency* of the Greater Wild Rue.

Wild Rue grows in many places in Montpellier, but especially near *Castelnau* among the rocks, and it blooms in Summer. We ourselves have had it in the gardens of Lyon and Geneva, still beautifully green in November and January.

The Sown variety is an inhabitant of gardens and is cultivated everywhere in them, blooming in Summer and Autumn. *Concerning its Potencies, see the Appendix.*

### FUMITORY, CAPNOS, SMOKE OF THE EARTH: German: Erdrauch; French: Fumeterre; Italian: Fumaria.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Fumaria (Fumitory) plant showing its characteristic spindly stems and fine leaves.</image-desc>

Fumitory, says Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, is a shrubby little herb, very tender, similar to Coriander: with many very bright leaves everywhere of an ash-gray color: with a purple *flower*. Thus he spoke, passing down nothing regarding the seed, which is tiny and round, following the flowers in a long and spreading spike.

However, although he depicts Fumitory only with a purple flower, it is also found with a white one, and that is judged by some to be better and more excellent. Nor was Dioscorides ignorant of this, if Marantha <note>Bartolomeo Maranta, a 16th-century botanist</note> is to be believed: but perhaps because he thought it was the same as the purple, he did not wish to distinguish them. *Concerning its origins, differences, and potencies, see the following pages.*

<column-break/>

### WILD RUE: Greater Wild Rue.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the larger wild rue variety with prominent seed pods.</image-desc>

Very few distinctions are established for the Sown Rue: however, Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a notable German botanist</note> distinguishes between the *broadest* and the *narrow-leafed*; he records that the latter corresponds to the others in all respects, except that it consists of much smaller parts in every way.

But of the *Wild* kind, two species are commonly recognized, the *Greater* and the *Lesser*. The Greater, which we depict here, has much smaller and thinner leaves than the garden variety, yet larger than the other wild kind; it also has larger seed-heads following the flowers, which are not four-angled like the garden variety. Both have a poisonous and very sharp odor, and neither can be applied to the sensitive parts of the body without harm.

### THE RUE WHICH IS USUALLY CALLED HARMALA: To the Arabs, Harmel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Harmala plant (Peganum harmala) with its distinct root system and upright stems.</image-desc>

Concerning this, Dioscorides records these things: They still call it, he says, Wild Rue, which in Cappadocia and Asiatic Galatia is called *Moly*, because it maintains a certain similarity with Moly <note>A mythical herb from Homer's Odyssey, often associated with Allium species</note>; for it has a black root, but a white flower. Its leaves are longer and thinner than the other Rue. There are those who call this Rue *Harmala*, and the Syrians call it *Besasa*; it grows on hills and in joyful, fertile soil, etc.

It is commonly called *Harmala* by writers, and is the third kind of Rue in Dioscorides. Bellonius <note>Pierre Belon, a French explorer and naturalist</note> records that it grows in sandy places around Alexandria in Egypt; Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note> says it grows most abundantly in New Castile around Madrid, and blooms there in July and August. It is also cultivated in gardens.

### LESSER OR THIN-LEAFED UPRIGHT FUMITORY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, upright variety of Fumitory.</image-desc>

From thin, upright roots it produces stems a palm or a span <note>about 3 to 9 inches</note> high, or smaller. The *leaves* are smaller and more finely divided than in other Fumitories. The *flowers* are packed into a short and dense spike, and are very beautiful to see because of their variety.

Herbalists commonly label this Thin-leafed Fumitory and *Thin-leafed Capnos*; Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> calls it *Spanish Fumitory*, with a flower most elegantly variegated with red, white, green, and yellow colors.

Clusius writes that it is found in many regions of Spain, at the edges of plowed fields, and next to roads and paths. We have observed it in various places in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>.

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical description and classification of various species of Rue (Ruta) and Fumitory (Fumaria), citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and contemporary botanists like Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>Rue, Ruta, Harmala, Fumitory, Fumaria, Dioscorides, Clusius, botany, medicinal plants, herbals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Fumaria genus (Fumitory) and introduces Melanthium (Nigella). It maintains the systematic classification used in early modern herbals, citing authorities like Dioscorides and Galen.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### FUMITORY WHICH IS CALLED SPLIT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Fumaria plant with delicate, divided leaves and small clusters of flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

It produces numerous tender and delicate stems about nine inches long: through which are seen leaves like those of Maidenhair fern <note>original: "Adianthi"</note>, but much smaller, quite soft, and sea-green <note>original: "glauca"</note>, especially on the lower part, with a remarkably sharp taste. The flowers, yellow or white, leave behind little pods like those of Bulbous Fumitory, but smaller, full of black, shining seed. The root is somewhat thick and blackish.

This species of Fumitory, unknown to Dioscorides and the Arabs, grows almost nowhere except in the mountains: hence it is also commonly labeled Mountain Fumitory. In Illyria <note>The Balkan Peninsula</note> it grows on hills in cultivated fields, from which it obtained the Illyrian name *Split*. It is also cultivated in gardens, as we have kept it in the Serene Prince’s garden at Montbéliard.

Whether this is the *Fumaria corydalis* of Galen <note>Galen was a prominent Greek physician whose botanical observations remained influential for centuries</note>.

<column-break/>

### FUMITORY WITH TENDRILS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing Fumaria plant with tendrils (capreolis) and small flowers.</image-desc>

It has a thin but sufficiently long root. The tender branches are raised up, wound around neighboring plants by the help of little tendrils <note>original: "clauicularum"</note>: clothed with <unclear>spiky</unclear>, tender, entire leaves, clinging to very thin stalks. The flowers are whitish.

It varies with broader or narrower leaves, and with flowers either white or faintly reddish. Some maintain this is the *Capnon* of Pliny.

It grows around hedges, lentil fields, the edges of fields, and old walls: and it blooms at the same time as the others.

The Common Fumitory, however, described previously in the first place, grows spontaneously in many locations: in vineyards, fields, gardens, and along roadsides: and it blooms in Spring and Autumn.

---

### BULBOUS FUMITORY, WITH A HOLLOW ROOT, LARGER with a green flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with a hollow root (radice cava), broad leaves, and a spike of flowers.</image-desc>

Bulbous Fumitory is also labeled *Hollow Root* <note>original: "Radix caua"</note> because its root is hollow, broad, and flat: yet it is gifted with several fibers; the color inside and out is like boxwood, the taste bitter: and sometimes it equals the size of a nut, while at other times it is larger than a very large fist. And besides that difference which is observed in the size of the root, there is also some in the leaves, which in this variety are broader. It is likewise in the color of the flowers, which in this one is green. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> depicts it in his illustrations under the title "Hollow root with a green flower."

<column-break/>

### BULBOUS FUMITORY, OR SMALLER HOLLOW ROOT, with purplish and white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller bulbous plant with a hollow root and flowering stem.</image-desc>

This grows abundantly around Montbéliard and in the Serene Prince’s garden, and it blooms in the months of February, March, and April.

It is better known than it ought to be reported or refuted that the apothecary shops <note>original: "Officinas"</note> have wrongly used this in place of Round Birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochia rotunda"</note>. Among writers, Brunfels, Apollinaris, Cornarius, and Georgius Pictor believed it to be Round Birthwort. But it is rightly denied by Cordus (in his commentary on Dioscorides), Tragus, Fuchs, Mattioli, Turner, Lonicer, Lobelius, Guilandini, Tabernaemontanus, and Bauhin. <note>This list represents the "who's who" of 16th-century European botany</note>

---

### BULBOUS FUMITORY, WITH A SOLID ROOT; with a spur and crested leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous plant with a solid root (radice solida) and a crested leaf structure.</image-desc>

This has a solid root, not hollow, the size of a hazelnut, sometimes larger, not fixed as deeply as the one with the hollow root; it is boxwood-colored on the outside, whitish inside, bitter, and has capillary fibers growing onto it. The plant is a palm's breadth high and sometimes a foot: the flowers are purple.

The *History of Lyon* calls it "Hedge Celandine" <note>original: "Chelidoniam phragmitem"</note> and says that Aetius calls it *Capnium*: while Pliny names it *Capnos phragmites*, as well as *Cock's Feet* <note>original: "Pedes Gallinaceos"</note>, on account of the seed pod being similar to the spurs of roosters.

It is a solid species of common Birthwort according to Gesner and Tragus. A full, firm, and solid species of Hollow Root according to the French Dodonaeus. The origins and powers of Fumitory in general will be handed down in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### MELANTHIUM, GITH, NIGELLA: German: Black Coriander; French: Nielle, Barbue; Italian: Melanthio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Nigella plant (Melanthium) with fine, feathery leaves and a distinct seed pod at the top.</image-desc>

Melanthium, or Gith, called *Nigella* in the apothecary shops, is a plant rising with thin shoots to a height of eighteen inches <note>original: "binum dodrantum"</note>, or even more, with leaves like Groundsel but much thinner: with a small head at the top, like a Poppy, oblong, provided inside with certain partitions, within which lies the seed—black, sharp, and fragrant. Thus Dioscorides describes it.

However, various differences of Melanthium are given, by place of origin, head or calyx, flowers and seeds, as will be clear from the following descriptions.

We depict here the Melanthium with the larger head and flower, which we have observed growing spontaneously in gardens at Geneva, Montbéliard, and Basel, blooming in May.

<summary>This page details several varieties of Fumitory (Fumaria), distinguishing between hollow-rooted and solid-rooted bulbous types, and begins the description of Melanthium (Nigella or Love-in-a-Mist).</summary>
<keywords>Fumitory, Nigella, botanical classification, medicinal plants, Montbéliard, hollow root, solid root, Renaissance botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>Bbb 2</sig>

### MELANTHIUM WITH SMALLER CALYX AND FLOWER; With black and yellow seed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Melanthium plant with thin stems, feathery leaves, and small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

The leaves are finely divided, with a vein running through the middle, and they cling to striated stems about a foot long. The flowers at the ends of the branches are irregular, pale white, smaller than the others, and composed of five petals. Many tips <note>stamens</note> occupy the center, surrounding a small head. This head is smaller than that of the preceding plant, which he calls Damascus Melanthium <note>original: "Damascenum Melanthium"</note>, and is equipped with five or six small horns. It is filled with smooth, angular seeds, or black fragrant ones.

This grows very easily in gardens and blooms in August and September.

It is called *Common Cultivated Melanthium* <note>original: "Melanthium vulgare Satiuum"</note> and *Cultivated or Garden Nigella* by almost everyone.

---

### WILD OR FIELD MELANTHIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Melanthium with more robust, branching stems and distinct seed pods.</image-desc>

This plant is a span or nine inches high and very closely resembles the Damascus Melanthium. The stems are sometimes simple, sometimes branched and striated right from the root, which is woody. The leaves are like Dill, or rather like the Damascus Nigella. The flowers are star-shaped, consisting of five petals, of a blue or pale color, and are not gifted with any thin "beards" <note>fine bracts</note> like the Damascus variety. These are followed by seed heads like those of Columbine <note>original: "Aquilegiæ"</note>, with five little horns. The seed is black and has little scent.

It grows in fields and blooms in September.

Furthermore, Melanthium powerfully warms and dries; it kills intestinal worms, dissipates gas, and promotes menstruation. The crushed seed, when smelled, helps those suffering from a rheum <note>a cold or sinus drip</note>. More can be found in the *Appendix*.

---

### UPRIGHT ROYAL CONSOLIDA, with a larger PURPLE or violet flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Consolida Regalis (Larkspur) with upright growth and spurred flowers.</image-desc>

The Royal Consolida <term>Consolida regalis: commonly known today as Larkspur</term>, or the Greater Royal Flower with a purple blossom, as Camerarius and C. Bauhin testify, has this peculiarity: if the petal attached to the "horn" <note>the spur</note> is opened, it shows the letters A. I. A. I. A. inscribed upon it. For this reason, it is held by Caesalpinus to be the *Poet’s Hyacinth* <note>original: "Hyacinthus Poëtarum"</note>; of which Ovid writes in the Metamorphoses:

> He inscribes his own groans upon the leaves, and AI AI <note>The Greek cry of woe, "ai ai," linked to the myth of Hyacinthus</note>

The flower has the inscription, and the mournful letter is drawn there. And Theocritus says:

*Now, Hyacinth, let your letter sound out, namely AI AI.*

<column-break/>

### MELANTHIUM WITH A SMALLER HEAD, and a manifold or double flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Melanthium with a dense, "double" flower head and feathery foliage.</image-desc>

From a small, simple root, a single stem rises, a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>approx. 18–27 inches</note>, rounded, striated, hairy, hollow, and divided into "wings" <note>branches</note>. The leaves arise alternately, attached to long, keeled stalks; their color verges from green to yellow, and the divisions are much wider than in the common Melanthium, and hairy. The flowers are a herbaceous white color, full with a manifold crowding of petals, with many central tips.

It is called *Very Yellow Melanthium by Tabernaemontanus*; and *Yellow Nigella with a double flower* by most others. It is cultivated in gardens and blooms in July and August.

---

### ROYAL CONSOLIDA: Germ. Ritter sporen; French. Pied d'alouette: Ital. Sperone di Cavaliero.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Consolida Regalis showing the characteristic long spur on the flower.</image-desc>

We depict here the *Royal Consolida* with the smaller flower. Since it is wild and does not exult in any richer cultivation <note>original: "mangonio," referring to "faking" or enhancing growth through fertilizers</note>, it turns out entirely more scrawny; it rarely exceeds nine inches in height as long as it is left to its own devices. Nor does it luxuriate in the number or width of its leaves. The flower, even more dull and smaller, testifies to this neglect, and is blue in color. In other respects, it is hardly different from the one with the larger flower, which is discussed next.

It grows wild everywhere among the grain crops. The flower is called simply "Flower" by some; by others *Royal Flower*; by Cordus *Calcatrippa*; and by some *Knight's Spur* <note>original: "Calcar equitis"</note>, or *Ritter Sporn* <note>German for Knight's Spur</note>, because it seems to resemble the shape of a spur.

---

### UPRIGHT ROYAL CONSOLIDA, with a double purple or violet flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered Consolida Regalis with dense floral spikes.</image-desc>

It grows with stems a cubit and a half high, upright, and slightly hairy. The description of the leaves is a little larger than the previous two, with frequent, short, narrow segments. The flowers are arranged in a row a span and a half long; they cling to half-inch stalks that are hairy and shaped like a small trumpet <note>original: "buccinum"</note> before they open. When unfolded, they are seen to be full with a manifold layering of petals, of a more cheerful purple-violet color, with tips occupying the center and a long spur. There follows a hairy *little horn* <note>seed pod</note>, which is usually without seed.

<summary>This page describes various species of Melanthium (Nigella) and Consolida Regalis (Larkspur), detailing their physical forms, medicinal uses for parasites and respiratory issues, and their mythological associations with the "Poet's Hyacinth."</summary>
<keywords>Melanthium, Nigella, Consolida Regalis, Larkspur, Hyacinthus, Ovid, medicinal herbs, botany, Ritter sporen, Calcatrippa</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Consolida regalis (Larkspur) family, concluding Class 26 of the herbal. It transitions from specific varieties to a discussion on the historical identity of the Delphinium.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### THE GREATEST HAIRY ROYAL CONSOLIDATE,
### with a large white flower.
<note>original: "Consolida regalis maxima villosa". This is the Great Larkspur.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a tall, leafy plant with multiple stems and small flowers, labeled with an asterisk at the base.</image-desc>

The stem is long, thick, twisted, and quite hairy: the *leaves* are a palm's length, hairy, and deeply divided. The *stalks* along almost the entire stem and branches are bent upwards, a palm's length or smaller—the higher ones being always shorter—hairy, and not without certain oblong little tongues, as if they were small leaves. A single *flower* sits upon each stalk, large and white: its spur and outermost petals are woolly on the outside and endowed with a certain greenness. The little pods <note>seed pods</note> which follow are likewise covered in very thick hair. We do not recall from where we obtained this variety.

<column-break/>

### THE FOREIGN ROYAL CONSOLIDATE, WITH THE FLOWER
### of the thin field variety, blue.
<note>original: "Regalis peregrina".</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a slender plant with fine, feathery leaves and a single flower spike, labeled with an asterisk at the base.</image-desc>

This is not found except in gardens, nor are the four preceding varieties.

Furthermore, Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> writes that water distilled from the Royal Consolidate is beneficial for all inflammations, whether drunk or applied topically. The flowers, by constant gazing upon them, strengthen the eyesight; for which reason some are accustomed to hang bunches of the aforementioned flowers in their rooms for that purpose. The juice of the whole plant drives away the little worms of putrid ulcers. The same is used in wound-drinks, according to Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician</note>, because it consolidates and glues <note>heals and closes wounds</note>: from which it also earned the name *Consolidate*. It is commonly counted among the Garland-flowers <note>term: Coronarias; flowers used for weaving wreaths or crowns</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLER ROYAL CONSOLIDATE, WITH A DOUBLE
### flower, white and blue.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with deeply lobed leaves and dense, double-petaled flowers, labeled with an asterisk at the base.</image-desc>

Besides the listed species of Royal Consolidate, we have had others at Montbéliard in the garden of His Serene Highness: such as the *Smaller Royal Consolidate, with a simple flower of two colors, blue and white*; the *Smaller Royal Consolidate, with a double flower, blue and white*, which we depict here; the *Royal Consolidate with a larger flower, of a pale purple, with a streaked lip*; the *Branching Royal Consolidate with a larger blue and white flower*; and finally the *More upright Royal Consolidate, with a double flesh-colored flower*.

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus, a German herbalist</note> writes that preserves are prepared from the flowers of the Royal Consolidate, and that a dose the size of a hazelnut is recommended for the griping pains <note>colic</note> of infants.

<column-break/>

### THE DELPHINIUM OF THE ANCIENTS, THE HERB OR FLOWER
### of Saint Ottilia to some.

Delphinium (as Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note> is said to have recorded) puts forth branches from a single root two spans in length: around which the *leaves* are thin, white <note>likely meaning pale green</note>, very long, and divided by notches. They are in the shape of dolphins, from which it also found its name. It bears a *flower* similar to the white violet [some add: "to the white violet"], of a purple color. It has *seed* in pods equal to Millet. It grows in rough places. There is also a second Delphinium, which some call *Hyacinth*, but the Romans call *Buccinum* <note>Trumpet-flower</note>, similar to the one just mentioned, but with more slender leaves and twigs.

However, since the Delphinium is not described anywhere by Galen, nor by Oribasius, nor by Paul <note>of Aegina</note>, nor by Pliny, nor by other Greeks or Latins, many—especially Cordus and Matthiolus—consider its chapter, which is found in Dioscorides, to be spurious and added later. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, however, feels otherwise: it must be investigated whether those Classical authors wrote about it under perhaps another name or not. His opinion pleases us not a little: since in such great obscurity of facts and diversity of opinions, one can hardly establish anything for certain.

Marcellus refers the Delphinium to the *Senna* of the Moors; others to the plant which is called *The Son before the Father* <note>term: Filius ante patrem; a name given to plants where the flower appears before the leaves</note> by herbalists. To some it is *Antora* <note>Yellow Monkshood</note>; others compare it with *Lychnis*, others with *Linaria* <note>Toadflax</note>: to Cratopus, it is that plant which some call *Touch-me-not*. Is it perhaps the *Royal Consolidate*, as some suppose?

---

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXVII.
### CONTAINING UMBELLIFEROUS PLANTS. <note>Plants that bear flowers in umbrella-like clusters (umbels), such as carrots, parsley, and fennel.</note>

**MARATHRUM OR FENNEL: German: Fenchel: French: Fenouil: Italian: Finocchio.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Fennel plant (Marathrum/Foeniculum) showing the tall stalk, feathery leaves, and umbel flowers.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany."</note> classifies Fennel among the many ferulaceous <note>Giant fennel-like or reed-like plants.</note> sub-shrubs; he attributes to it a fibrous stem and a naked, sweet-smelling seed. Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and author of De Materia Medica.</note>, however, does not describe it, as it is very well known. Pliny, imitating Theophrastus, relates that it is of the ferulaceous kind and makes it very similar to Thapsia <note>A genus of plants in the carrot family, often called "deadly carrots."</note>.

Furthermore, there is one Fennel of the garden and home, and another of the wild; one larger, another smaller. Moreover, as will be clear from what follows, other differences are observed in taste and flavor, the color of the flowers, and both the shape and color of the seeds.

We depict here the common smaller variety, with a sharper and darker seed, which grows everywhere in rocky, southern locations.

<column-break/>

**SWEET FENNEL, WITH LARGER AND WHITE SEEDS.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sweet Fennel (Foeniculum Dulce) with detailed views of the seeds and flower clusters.</image-desc>

The common Fennel has a root the size of a finger, and even larger: straight, white, with a flavor of a certain aromatic sweetness. The stem is three or four cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; this suggests a height of 4.5 to 6 feet.</note> high, straight, furrowed, jointed, dark green, stuffed with a spongy white pith, and hollow at the many branch-junctions. The leaf-stalks embrace the stem and branches like a sheath, upon which sit the leaves, divided into long, very thin filaments, dark green, with a sweet taste and pleasant odor. The flower umbels are loose, yellow, and fragrant; the seed is oblong like Anise, blackish, more slender, with a sharp taste.

But the variety we depict here differs little from the common one in its roots, leaves, stems, and flower. However, its seeds are larger, furrowed, whitish, sweet, and less sharp. The illustration shows the seeds of both.

---

**ROUND FENNEL WITH WHITE FLOWERS.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Round Fennel with white flowers, showing the root system and dense foliage.</image-desc>

It rests on a fibrous, slender root; with a smaller and shorter stem; the leaves are broader and also shorter than those of common Fennel. The umbel is white and round, bearing flowers and seed in the first year; the seed is smaller than the common oblong and round Fennel. It endures the winter easily, and if the seed is committed to the earth in Autumn, it will turn out taller and more effective.

It does not differ from the common variety in taste and smell, but it is lower to the ground, with a white umbel and smaller seeds than the common kind.

It is a garden variety, as is the preceding one; it is commonly labeled Italian Fennel, and Florentine Fennel, and even Roman Fennel, on account of the sweetness which it is accustomed to acquire in those places from diligent cultivation.

<column-break/>

**GREAT FENNEL, HIPPOMARATHRUM, And Chaa, the Herb of Japan.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Great Fennel or Hippomarathrum, showing a robust stalk and thick root.</image-desc>

Hippomarathrum <note>Literally "Horse-fennel," a larger wild variety.</note> (as Bellus writes in a letter to Clusius) produces thin leaves, somewhat similar to Fennel; a smooth stem, two or three cubits long; the thickness of the little finger, and jointed. The flower is yellow; the seeds are large, similar to *Cachrys* <note>A genus of plants with corky seeds.</note>; the root, however, is firm, large, and fragrant.

The seed of this plant is commonly boiled by women in lye for dyeing the hair a golden color.

Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the 17th century.</note>, reduces to the Fennel family the herb *Chaa* <note>Tea (Camellia sinensis).</note> in Japan, from the powder of which (according to Linschoten <note>Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, a Dutch traveler.</note>) they prepare a precious decoction and offer it to more distinguished guests.

More concerning Fennel in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various species of Fennel (Foeniculum), distinguishing between common, sweet, and "round" varieties, while also identifying "Chaa" (tea) from Japan as a related plant. It details their physical characteristics, medicinal or cosmetic uses—such as hair dyeing—and their cultivation in Italy.</summary>
<keywords>Fennel, Foeniculum, Hippomarathrum, Botany, Herbal Medicine, Tea, Japan, Hair Dye, Theophrastus, Caspar Bauhin</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of umbelliferous plants (those with umbrella-like flower clusters), following the previous discussions on fennel varieties. The catchword "MEVM" from the previous page likely refers to Meum athamanticum (Spignel), which often precedes these entries in Renaissance herbals.</meta>

### TWISTED FENNEL of Montpellier,
### called Marseille Spignel by many.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Foeniculum tortuosum plant, showing its thick, twisted stems, feathery leaves, and umbel flowers, including a detailed view of the root system.</image-desc>

In Montpellier, they call this a cubit-high herb <note>about 18 inches</note>, and sometimes larger: with a ribbed stalk filled with white pith, which soon divides from the root into various twisted, bent branches; it is somewhat thick and interrupted by short spaces between the joints. The leaves are fennel-like, though not as thin, shorter, more sparse, and harder, with a color much like Dill. The small flower umbels consist of five white petals (which Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note> describes as turning purple). The seeds are white and ribbed (like Celery, according to Clusius). The root is long, white, somewhat thick, and aromatic, as is the entire plant.

Many label this as Marseille Spignel <note>original: "Seseli Massiliense"</note>: Clusius calls it the Foreign Spignel. It grows abundantly and widely around Montpellier.

### DILL: German: Dyllen or Tillen; Belgian: Dillet;
### French: Aneth; Italian: Aneto.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Anethum (Dill) plant, featuring fine, thread-like leaves and broad umbels of flowers and seeds.</image-desc>

Dill is very similar to Fennel, with a hollow, ribbed stalk: the leaves are very finely cut into hair-like filaments and are fragrant, though less pleasantly so than Fennel. The flowers in the umbel are yellow, followed by fennel-like seeds that are broader, with a sharp taste, and also less pleasant than those of Fennel.

In Greek it is called <term>Anethon</term> <note>Ἄνηθον</note>, <term>from "running upwards"</term> <note>παρὰ τὸ ἄνω θέειν</note>, because it grows quickly: or because it is <term>blameless</term> <note>ἀναίτιον</note>, because it excites the appetite for food.

It is commonly sown in gardens, and once planted, it propagates itself every year from fallen seed with a persistent fertility; it endures every state of the weather but thrives in warmer conditions. More on this in the Appendix.

### ASCLEPIUS’S ALL-HEAL: German: Heylwurtz;
### French: Panaces; Italian: Panace Asclepio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Panaces Asclepium, showing a tall stalk with large umbels and detailed foliage resembling fennel but broader.</image-desc>

Asclepius’s All-Heal <note>Panaces Asclepium</note>, as Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> recorded, sends up a thin stalk from the earth a cubit high, marked by joints: around which are leaves similar to Fennel, but larger, hairier, and fragrant: and at the top is an umbel in which the flowers and tips are gold-colored and fragrant. The root is small and thin. The flowers and seeds have power against ulcers, swellings, and spreading sores <note>phagedænas</note> if ground and applied with honey: they are drunk with wine against serpents and smeared on with oil.

Theophrastus and Pliny make the leaves similar to Thapsia <note>Deadly Carrot</note>: yet Dioscorides does not differ in this, since according to Marcellus, Thapsia has a fennel-like leaf. We depict here Guilandini’s "Asclepius’s All-Heal," which he says has a white flower and a leaf like a Carrot.

<column-break/>

### WATER YARROW resembling Fennel,
### bearing umbels.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an aquatic Millefolium plant with submerged-style feathery leaves and an upright flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The leaves are scattered, a wide green, very similar to Fennel-leaves and not unlike them in their cut; they have a pleasant smell but no notable taste. It bears flowers in umbels on a stalk. The roots somewhat approach the roots of White Hellebore; they are fibrous, white, hanging in clusters from a single head, longer than a palm’s breadth, and hollow.

Is it the "Soldier's Yarrow" <note>Millefolium Stratiotes</note>, as Schyrenkfeld determined? Or the legitimate "Myriophyllum" of Dioscorides, as it seemed to Mattioli?

It is a marsh plant in Silesia and various other places, familiar in non-flowing waters. We saw it around the ditches of Padua in the month of April.

### A PLANT SIMILAR TO DILL,
### the true Gingidium of Dioscorides.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Gingidium, showing a dense, bushy plant with complex umbels and a thick root.</image-desc>

Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, physician and botanist</note> labels this plant the true Gingidium of Dioscorides: and writes that it grows in the steep places of Mount Lebanon in Syria. It is a plant, he says, very similar to our local Gingidium, with a small whitish root: with fennel-like leaves, thinner than in the Wild Parsnip, and more bitter in taste. The umbel, which has a blue "little head" <note>capitulum</note> in the middle, has thin leaves beneath it, like Black Cumin <note>Melanthio</note>. The seeds are round, crowded together into a single head. So he says: for us, from seed sent by Rauwolf, the plant we depict here grew in the princely garden at Montbéliard.

### THE SECOND ASCLEPIUS’S ALL-HEAL
### of Dalechamp.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second variety of Panaces Asclepium, showing a robust stalk and distinct leaf structure.</image-desc>

In place of Dioscorides' Asclepius’s All-Heal, Anguillara and Mattioli present a plant with leaves like Giant Fennel <note>Ferula</note> and a yellow flower, which they say is called "Seseli" in Crete, but "Peucedanum" <note>Hog's Fennel</note> in Sicily.

However, the "History of Lyon" <note>Historia Lugdunensis</note> writes that Dalechamp’s second variety of Asclepius’s All-Heal grows in rough places and hills near Montpellier, with a root like Celery—white, thin, sharp, and fragrant: yet with a leaf like Celery or Coriander rather than Fennel, and hairy: with a yellow flower in perfectly circular umbels.

Concerning Chiron’s All-Heal and Hercules’s All-Heal, see the Appendix.

It highlights the differences in regional naming conventions and cites prominent Renaissance botanists like Clusius, Rauwolf, and Mattioli.</summary>

# SPIGNEL: German: *Beerwurtz*, *Hertzwurtz*; French: *Meum*. ANOTHER ITALIAN SPIGNEL ACCORDING TO SOME.
# Spignel: Italian: *Meo* & *Finocchiello*. Another false Italian Spignel.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Meum plant, showing its long, thick root system and feathery, dill-like foliage extending upwards into multiple umbels of small flowers.</image-desc>

Spignel, which they call *Athamanticum* <note>original: "Athamanticū"</note>, says Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note>, grows most abundantly in Macedonia and Spain: it is similar to Dill in its stalk and leaves, yet thicker than Dill, rising to two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note>, with scattered roots that are thin, slanting and straight, long, fragrant, and warming to the tongue.

Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> identifies two kinds: the more noble, which they call *Athamanticum*, either from its discoverer Athamas, or because it is most highly praised in Athamas; and another, which is less upright.

Whether the *Common Spignel* depicted here is the legitimate Spignel of Dioscorides, and whether his Spignel grows in our regions, is debated: Mattioli doubts it, but the Portuguese [Amatus Lusitanus], Anguillara, Lobelius, and others assert it, and we subscribe to their opinions. The learned indicate this to be so.

<column-break/>

Regarding *Common Spignel* and the true kind, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> records thus in his *Adversaria*: "I have seen," he says, "many plants of the true Spignel growing most joyfully in the alpine regions of Germany, Italy, France, and Spain. The root has a sweet scent, like Nard or Angelica; the stalk and leaves are like Dill, the flower cluster is white, blooming in June and July; the seed is like Horse-fennel, fragrant, etc."

Regarding the *False* kind which we depict here, he writes thus in his *Observations*: "The *other false Italian Spignel* is not unlike common Spignel: but the leaves, stalks, and flower clusters are all thicker and more robust. The root is likewise larger, dark on the outside, with the appearance and consistency of Hog's Fennel <note>term: Peucedanum (Hog's Fennel), a plant often used for its resinous root</note>, and of a foul and unpleasant scent and taste." These details from Lobelius shall suffice.

---

# SPIGNEL WITH THE APPEARANCE OF CANDY CARROT,
# THE SMALL MOUNTAIN PARSLEY OF CLUSIUS, with leaves of Fennel or Hog's Fennel, a white flower, and the seed of Parsley.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations side-by-side. On the left, a plant with a thick, dark, branched root and dense, fine foliage. On the right, a smaller plant with a similar root structure and more compact umbels of flowers.</image-desc>

The Spignel depicted here, which grows in the coldest and highest mountains of the Savoyards and the Sequani <note>Regions in the western Alps and eastern France</note>: there are those who hold it to be the genuine kind. Its *root* is half a foot longer, black on the outside like the Candy Carrot <note>term: Daucus Creticus (Candy Carrot), a medicinal plant from Crete</note>, white inside, branched, and fragrant. The *stalks* are many, and fibrous like Fennel, three or at most four fingers high. The *leaves* are short and hair-like, similar to Fennel. The *flower* is white, in dense clusters. The *seed* is very small, bitter, and sweet-smelling. *History of Plants of Lyon.*

From what was said before, the native habitat of Common Spignel is established: indeed, Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a major Flemish herbalist</note>, imitating Lobelius, reports that it grows in many places in Italy, Spain, France, and Germany, which has also been observed by us. More will be found in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

To the notes added to the title, something must be added regarding the root. In its uppermost part, it swells into a thick head, shaggy with many fibers (which are the fibers of the previous year's leaves); it is short and as if coiled in a circle; spongy and white inside, dark and wrinkled on the outside, usually split in two at the bottom, and ending in sparse fibers.

This meager and dwarfed kind of *Selinum* <note>term: Selinum (Mountain Parsley)</note> described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> is found by some in dry and deserted—yet still green—margins of fields, and on the bare grassy mountains of Lower Austria and Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note>; it blooms at the beginning of May, and is believed to be a biennial, as are most umbrella-bearing plants.

---

# THE SAXIFRAGE OF MATTIOLI AND THE ITALIANS.
# SAXIFRAGE WITH MULTI-CLEFT LEAVES, the Pannonian kind of Clusius.

<image-desc>Two botanical illustrations. On the left, a plant with thin, wiry stems and small, sparse leaves. On the right, a plant with a thick root crown and more robust, divided foliage.</image-desc>

Mattioli records that the Greeks call this *Saxifragan* and *Seselingion*, and the Italians *Sassifraga* <note>note: The name literally means "stone-breaker," referring to its use in treating kidney stones</note>. It is well known in Italy, and especially Tuscany, and breaks out from the hardest rocks: with hair-like leaves, not unlike Dodder-of-Thyme. And finally, it is sought after for stones of the kidneys and bladder, as well as for delayed urination.

We suspect that the *Ferula-like Saxifrage of the Italians* described by Lobelius is the same as that one, about which he writes: "Some," he says, "cultivated in Italian gardens a Saxifrage two cubits high, with leaves like Giant Fennel or Fennel, less or not at all jointed, thinner, and dark green: with umbrella-like flowers, whitish, appearing to be a species of Spignel; the roots are whitish, with the taste of a Parsnip."

<column-break/>

Much smaller than Hog's Fennel, he says, is the *Pannonian Saxifrage*, and endowed with shorter leaves, almost rivaling the head of the leaves: among these, however, come out small stalks a foot high, slender, jointed, adorned with a few tiny leaves, supporting an umbrella of white little flowers at the very top. The *root* is not much different from the root of Hog's Fennel but shorter, sharper, and stimulating saliva, producing many shaggy heads at the top, from which the leaves and stalks emerge.

This was discovered by Clusius, the author of the description, in many places in Hungary and Lower Austria, namely on the slopes of mountains, in stony and rugged soil. It blooms in July. By Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who developed an early classification system</note> it is called *Mountain Carrot with short, multi-cleft leaves*.

<keywords>Spignel, Meum, Saxifrage, Mattioli, Clusius, Lobelius, medicinal herbs, kidney stones, botany, Alpine flora, umbellifers</keywords>

# PLANTS

### A RELATIVE OF THE FINE-LEAVED SAXIFRAGE, known to some as Caucalis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with feathery, carrot-like leaves and multiple umbels of small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, a 16th-century Italian botanist</note> calls this *Caucalis*, and reports that it grows in the Peloponnese and many other places among rocks. It has leaves like Fennel, a stalk a cubit long, a white flower cluster, and seeds like Bishop’s Weed <note>original: "Ammi"</note>. It is eaten, has the scent of Parsley, and is called by the inhabitants *agrioselinon*, that is, Wild Celery.

Lobelius also names it *Caucalis*; Pena calls it *Caucalis* in the *History of Lyon*; Tabernaemontanus calls it *English Caucalis*; C. Bauhin in his *Pinax* and *Phytopinax* calls it *Caucalis with 12 fennel-like leaves*. Could it be the *Fistra findula* of the people of Apulia?

### PELLITORY-OF-SPAIN: German: Pertram; French: Pyrestre; Italian: Pyretro; Arabic: Macharcaraba.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pyrethrum plant with deeply lobed leaves and a single large umbel of flowers.</image-desc>

The name was given to the whole plant by the Greeks because of the fiery quality <note>original: "Pyrethrum" from the Greek "pyr" meaning fire</note> left in the mouth <note>literally: "the carrying organ"</note> when the root is chewed. The Latins call it the "Saliva Herb" because of the abundance of spit it draws out when held in the mouth.

According to Dioscorides, it is a herb that produces a stalk and leaves like the Wild Carrot and Fennel, but a flower cluster shaped like the wheel of Dill. The root is as thick as a large finger, extremely hot to the taste, and draws out phlegm, etc.

Furthermore, in our great *History*, we have reviewed other plants given the name of Pyrethrum: Pellitory, Saxifrage, Tansy, Wild Valerian, Tarragon <note>original: "Dracunculum hortensem"</note>, and those pictured here.

### CUMIN or CYMINUM. German: Kymmel, Kymmich; French: Cumin; Italian: Comino.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cumin plant with thin, linear leaves and small umbels of seeds/flowers.</image-desc>

*Cuminum* or *Cyminum* is the name of both the seed and a certain plant similar to Fennel. Two kinds are commonly recognized: the Garden or Cultivated kind, which we depict here, and the Wild kind, of which we speak next.

The *Cultivated* kind is a small herb, a foot high, with thin leaves cut into many narrow segments. It has white flowers and the seed in the cluster is oblong, pointed at both ends, angular, gristly, yellowish, somewhat sharp, somewhat bitter, and pleasantly scented with a certain heaviness. The root is oblong and thin.

There are again two types of it: one somewhat black and of a more vehement sharpness, the other whitish and somewhat sweet. *More in the following pages and in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### CELERY, WHICH IS THOUGHT TO BE DALECHAMP’S ROCK-PARSLEY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild celery or parsley variety with broad, serrated leaflets and thick roots.</image-desc>

This has a somewhat long and thick root, blackish on the outside, white on the inside, with a tufted head and a bitter taste. From this grow several stalks, angular, furrowed, a foot long (and sometimes only a palm's breadth), clothed in leaves similar to the blue-green leaved Carrot. The stem of the stalks is mostly divided into three parts and bears clusters of small whitish flowers. The seed is like that of common Parsley.

The *History of Lyon* <note>A famous botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps</note> testifies that it grows in rocky mounds near Grenoble.

### GESNER’S PELLITORY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Gesner's Pyrethrum, showing a thick, vertical taproot and finely divided foliage.</image-desc>

He says it relies on a long, simple root with moderate fibers, pale, a finger thick, and of a burning and scorching taste. Leaves come forth similar to Dill; the stalk is like Fennel; the flower is in a cluster of rounded circularity. Whether this is the true *Pyrethrum* of Dioscorides is rightly doubted.

Common Pellitory is indeed recorded among the plants native to European regions; however, it grows more abundantly and happily in warmer and Eastern lands, being especially familiar to Italy and Spain.

The root of Pellitory is extremely hot, ascending to the fourth degree of heat <note>A reference to the Galenic system of medicinal "degrees"</note>. Held in the mouth, it casts out phlegm copiously; therefore, it is useful for toothache arising from a "cold" cause, as well as for all afflictions that proceed from phlegm congested in the head.

### WILD CUMIN: The first Wild Cumin of Dioscorides.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Wild Cumin with more spreading, delicate foliage and distinct seed heads.</image-desc>

Galen, Aetius, and Paulus passed over Wild Cumin in their accounts of simple medicines. Pliny says it is very slender, with four or five leaves that are as if saw-toothed, and more effective for all uses than the cultivated kind.

Dioscorides mentions two kinds: one he makes similar to the cultivated kind, saying it bears seed like Black Cumin <note>original: "Nigellae"</note>; the other has five or six round, soft heads at the top, in which is a chaffy seed, sharper to the taste than the cultivated kind; it grows in elevated places.

This latter kind, by the judgment of almost everyone, is depicted here; it is usually labeled by herbalists as Wild Cumin, or *The first Wild Cumin of Dioscorides*. *Regarding its use and powers, see the Appendix.* Dalechamp calls them "Strong Cumin" and "Sweet Cumin."

<summary>This page describes various umbelliferous plants including Caucalis, Pellitory-of-Spain, and Cumin, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal "heat," and their classification by ancient and Renaissance botanists.</summary>
