# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### AMMI, AMMI, AMIVM, AND AMMIVM: Ger. Ammy, Ammey: Gal. Ammi: Ital. Ammi, Ammio. <note>Commonly known today as Bishop's Weed or Laceflower.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ammi plant (Bishop's weed) showing its tall, slender stalk, finely divided pinnate leaves, and large compound umbels of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Ammi, says Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, is called Ethiopian Cumin by some, and Royal Cumin by others: others have claimed that Ethiopian Cumin is of one nature, and Ammi of another. It is commonly known as a small seed, much smaller than Cumin, with the flavor of Oregano, etc.

Thus Fuchsius <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German botanist</note> says: It is very similar to Cumin, which the Greeks call Ammi, and which some consider to be Ethiopian Cumin, etc.

As far as the differences are concerned: these are taken from the location, the size, the scent, etc. Whence one is called Cultivated, another Wild: one is the Greater and common variety, whose leaves, stalks, umbels, seeds, and in general all parts, are larger; which we depict here. Another is the Lesser and thin-leaved variety, which is not so frequent: one has the scent of Oregano, another is most fragrant, etc.

<column-break/>

### AMMI WITH THE SCENT OF OREGANO: CRETAN AMMI or Ammi of Candia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Cretan Ammi plant, featuring a more robust stem, denser umbels, and slightly broader leaf segments compared to the previous specimen.</image-desc>

Regarding the Stalk: this one has branched, striated, and jointed stalks: the lowest leaves are indeed somewhat broad and many-cleft, but the upper ones are much more finely dissected, with a very aromatic scent if rubbed, like Oregano, and a similar taste. There are frequent umbels of very tiny, whitish flowers. The seed has the appearance of Anise, but smaller, and is remarkably aromatic. The root is somewhat thick.

Cæsalpinus describes it under the name of Cultivated Cumin, but Turner <note>William Turner, the "Father of English Botany"</note> understands it as the second kind of Ammi recently discovered in Italy. To most writers, however, it is Cretan or Candian Ammi, Aromatic Cretan Ammi, or the Aromatic of Syria or Crete. It is the Ammi of Laguna, Castore, and Camerarius.

In our regions, when sown, it deceives us <note>original: "nos deludit" — likely meaning it fails to thrive or changes its character in northern climates</note>, according to the testimony of Lobelius.

---

### AMMI WITH VERY THIN AND MOST FRAGRANT SEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very fine-seeded Ammi variety, characterized by extremely delicate, thread-like foliage and small, airy umbels.</image-desc>

This herb is a foot tall, and sometimes two feet: with a thin, brittle, fennel-like stalk, full of white pith. The leaves are at first long, deeply cut everywhere: and the upper ones are indeed similar to fennel or dill, yet a little thinner: at the ends of the branches hang small, unequal umbels, woven with white flowers: the seed is very small, most fragrant, with a hot and sharp taste: the root is small, slender, and woody.

This is much smaller than the Cretan variety, and the scent is also a little weaker: the leaves also differ. We have had this in abundance in gardens at Lyon, Geneva, Basel, and Montbéliard. It blooms in August, and sometimes in November, and propagates itself by fallen seed: Concerning its medicinal powers, see the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### BUNION AND PSEUDO-BUNION: The BUNIUM of Dalechamps. <note>Likely Earthnut or Pignut.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Bunium plant (Earthnut), showing its characteristic tuberous root (bulb-like), upright stem, and umbelliferous flower heads.</image-desc>

Bunion, says Dioscorides, produces a four-angled stalk, long, and a finger's breadth in thickness: the leaves are indeed similar to Celery, but much thinner, approaching the leaves of Coriander: the flower of Dill: the seed is fragrant, smaller than the seed of Henbane. It stirs the urine, warms, and draws out fluids. Others say Pseudo-Bunion is a small shrub a palm's height in Crete, having leaves and branches similar to Bunium.

Furthermore, almost all nations use the name of Bunium. The Greeks, Latins, Germans, English, and others. Some (such as Cornarius) think that both Buniums, the true and the false, are unknown today: however, the *History of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" by Dalechamps</note> maintains that the Bunium we depict here is the true Bunium of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen. The learned shall judge.

---

### BULBOCASTANUM: Germ. Small Earth-nut. Belg. Small Earth-nuts: In Savoy, Fauerottes. <note>Great Earthnut (Bunium bulbocastanum).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Bulbocastanum (Great Earthnut), emphasizing the distinct round tuber at the base of the root system and the delicate, branching stems.</image-desc>

Gesner, Dodonaeus, and Tabernaemontanus called it Bulbocastanum <note>literally "Bulb-chestnut"</note>, as did Castore and Gerard: Turner called it Celery and Ground-acorn: Dodonaeus in French, Laguna, and Gesner called it Bunium: some call it Earth Chestnut and Pig's Chestnut: Lobelius calls it the Earth Nut of the Northerners: Cortuso, Castore, and Mattioli call it a species of Oenanthe: some call it Bulbium: others Thrasi: and by a great error, Guypylus, Andernacus, and Mattioli call it Balanocastanon.

There is one Greater Bulbocastanum, and another Lesser. Dalechamps distinguishes them by sex: and calls one the Male, which others label as the Bunium of Dioscorides, and the other the Female, which we name the Water Oenanthe. More in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### SESELI: MARSEILLES SESELI: Germ. Common Sesel, Horse Cumin: Gall. Sermentain, Large Cumin. <note>French Hartwort.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Seseli Massiliense (French Hartwort), showing thick, ribbed stems and dense, flat-topped umbels of flowers.</image-desc>

The stalk is like Giant Fennel, a cubit long, jointed, and hard. The leaves are like Fennel, but larger, broader, and thicker. The flowers in the umbels are whitish: the seeds are oblong, woodier and broader than those of fennel, and very sharp. Thus some describe it, others differently: from Dioscorides we add that the root is long and fragrant.

It is commonly labeled as Marseilles Seseli or *Massiliense*, and by some as Mountain Siler.

One reads in Mattioli that it is gathered in almost all the mountains of Trent: but Pena and Lobelius rightly deny this: more truly, he says it abounds around Marseilles: it also abounds around Montpellier in rough places, and is cultivated in various gardens. More in the Appendix.

# THE PLANTS: VISNAGA. ANOTHER IMAGE OF VISNAGA OR BISNAGA. PEUCEDANUM: German: *Haarstrang*, *Seuvfenchel*; French: *Peucedane*; Italian: *Peucedano*. GREATER ITALIAN PEUCEDANUM. LIBANOTIS. LIBANOTIS WITH YELLOW FLOWERS ACCORDING TO SOME, with the seed of Giant Fennel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Visnaga plant, showing a tall stalk with fine, feathery leaves and multiple large, dense umbels of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

This plant is about a cubit and a half tall <note>approx. 27 inches</note>, with a root that has few attached fibers. The stalk is like that of Dill, striated, smooth, and jointed. The leaf is like that of the Wild Parsnip, and smooth. The flower umbels are bright white, and the seed is small, like the Apothecary’s Celery <note>Smallage</note>, and pungent.

We have had this plant in abundance in gardens in Lyon and Geneva, and especially in Montbéliard, where it bloomed in July and August and was swollen with seed in Autumn.

Dodonaeus and Anguillara thought this was the legitimate *Gingidium* <note>a type of wild chervil</note>, or another kind of *Gingidium*. However, their opinion does not please Castore and Matthiolus, nor does it please us; we cannot agree with Matthiolus and Castore themselves when they determine it to be a larger Wild Parsnip. Those who wish for Matthiolus’s *Scandix* to be *Gingidium* are also greatly in error.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Visnaga (Bisnaga), similar to the first but with slightly different leaf structure and umbel density.</image-desc>

Our images are from early sprouts and do not satisfy in all respects. The last one is placed in Fuchs’s work as the *Seseli* of Marseilles; likewise, Dodonaeus (in French) and Lonicer also place *Visnaga* as the true *Seseli* of Montpellier—but the learned know by what merit they do so. It is commonly called *Visnaga* and *Bisnaga*, and Camerarius is the authority that it is also called *Basniaguem*. We have the testimony of Dioscorides and Dodonaeus that it is called *Lepidium* in Syria, but *Bisacatum* by some.

Matthiolus contends that it matches the Parsnip in its medicinal powers; others attribute the qualities of *Gingidium* to it. However, those qualities suit it as truly as it is truly called *Gingidium* <note>The author is being skeptical of these identifications</note>. The stalks of the umbels, which are longer at first, become hard and somewhat rigid; because of their sweet scent, they come into use for many people as toothpicks, especially in Spain.

---

### PEUCEDANUM: German: *Haarstrang*, *Seuvfenchel*; French: *Peucedane*; Italian: *Peucedano*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Peucedanum plant, featuring deeply lobed, fan-like leaves and broad umbels.</image-desc>

*Peucedanum* <note>Hog's Fennel</note>, as Dioscorides describes it, produces a thin, slender stalk similar to Fennel. It has a copious and dense tuft of foliage around the root, a yellow flower, and a black root that has a heavy odor, is thick, and is full of juice. It grows in shaded mountains, etc.

Theophrastus writes that *Peucedanum* grows in Arcadia; Pliny says it is held in the highest esteem there. Otherwise, in describing *Peucedanum* and assigning its powers, Pliny agrees with Dioscorides.

The Pine tree, which is called <term>Peuke</term> <note>original: Πεύκη</note> by the Greeks, gave its name to *Peucedanum*. This was not because the plants are of the same genus or even similar, but because the beautiful and lofty tree "adopted," as it were, a shrub lower than itself that shared a similar leaf.

<column-break/>

### GREATER ITALIAN PEUCEDANUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Peucedanum Maius Italicum, showing a more robust stem and larger umbels than the previous variety.</image-desc>

*Peucedanum* is commonly distinguished into the *Lesser* or *German* variety, and the *Greater* or *Italian* variety. That which is depicted in the preceding table is the *Peucedanum* of Tragus, Fuchs, Cornarius, and Tabernaemontanus, who also calls it "Hog's Tail." Lobelius also names it *Peucedanum* and "First Fennel." To Caspar Bauhin, however, in his *Pinax* and in his commentaries on Matthiolus, it is called *German Peucedanum*.

What this table shows is the latter *Peucedanum*, inscribed by various authors as *Greater Peucedanum*, *Italian Peucedanum*, and *Greater Italian Peucedanum*; and by some as *Black Libanotis*.

Furthermore, it grows in shady and dark places, both in gardens and elsewhere, and blooms in July and August. More on this in the Appendix.

---

### LIBANOTIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Libanotis plant, showing a thick root system and delicate, compound leaves with small umbels.</image-desc>

Theophrastus made two kinds of *Libanotis* <note>often identified as Moonwort or Rosemary in antiquity, but here referring to umbellifers</note>: one that bears a shoot and another that bears fruit. Pliny treats *Libanotis* confusedly and with such uncertain understanding that it is by no means easy to distinguish them from *Conyza* and Rosemary in his work. For Dioscorides, there are four types of *Libanotis*: 1. with a Fennel leaf and white seed and root; 2. with a similar leaf but black seed and root; 3. with a similar leaf but without a stalk, flower, or seed; and 4. finally, one with a leaf like Lettuce. For Galen, there are three *Libanotides*: one sterile and two bearing fruit. From the various plants of very different genera that are gifted with the name *Libanotis*, we depict here the one called *Cachryophoron* with yellow flowers, observed by us in various gardens in Basel, Padua, and elsewhere.

<column-break/>

### LIBANOTIS WITH YELLOW FLOWERS ACCORDING TO SOME, with the seed of Giant Fennel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Libanotis variety with yellow flowers, showing detailed seed structures (semine Ferulae) and fine foliage.</image-desc>

Dodonaeus thinks this is the *Panaces Asclepium* of Dioscorides; but to Lobelius, Anguillara, and others, it is the *Panaces Asclepium* with the appearance of Giant Fennel. It is found frequently in Crete and Sicily, and it has often grown successfully for us in the garden of the Most Serene Prince at Montbéliard from seed sent from there.

Since 27 or more plants are referred to the category of *Libanotis*, it must be investigated which of them can be accepted as the *Libanotis* of the ancients. We have weighed this matter more primarily in our *History*.

Furthermore, all *Libanotides*, by the testimony and judgment of Galen, possess the same medicinal faculty: namely, cleansing, digesting, and cutting <note>referring to the thinning of bodily humors</note>. More in the following and in the Appendix.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

Ccc 3

# THE LIBANOTIS OF THEOPHRASTUS ACCORDING TO SOME, Ethiopian Seseli according to Mattioli, Black Cervaria.
<note>Theophrastus was an ancient Greek botanist; Mattioli was a 16th-century Italian physician. "Cervaria" refers to Hart-wort.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Libanotis plant with a thick, gnarled root, a tall stalk with several umbels of flowers, and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

It has the root of the Black Cervaria, thick, very firmly fixed, and hairy at the top, but white in color: the stalk is knotted, two or three cubits high <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>: the leaves are singular, five or ten times larger than those of the Black Cervaria, somewhat round, serrated, smooth, almost sea-green <term>glaucous<gloss>a pale greyish-green or blue-green color</gloss></term> underneath, and green on top. The umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note> are broad, the flowers white: the seed is paired, endowed with eight angles, and possesses a certain bitterness.

Dodoens, in his French edition, identified this as the Libanotis of Theophrastus: but in his Latin edition, he gives it the title of Ethiopian Seseli. Fuchs, Bock <note>Tragus</note>, and sometimes Mattioli depicted it as the legitimate Ethiopian Seseli: Lonicer depicted it as the *Elaphoboscum* of Dioscorides. We found this plant flowering in June among rocks; in gardens, it also flowers in June.

<column-break/>

# THE BITTER COSTUS WITH CURLED SEEDS, very similar to the Libanotis of Theophrastus according to some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant similar to the first, but with more delicate, finely divided leaves and smaller umbels.</image-desc>

We received this plant from Italy, collected on Mount Sumano, under the inscription of Bitter Costus: it was very similar to the Libanotis of Theophrastus just described: only the leaves were larger and less serrated, the umbel more ample, and the seeds oblong, curled, and somewhat bitter with a sharp pungency.

Furthermore, to say something regarding the etymology of *Libanotis*, it is admitted by almost all Greeks and Latins that it is so named because it smells of Frankincense <note>original: "Thus"</note>, whence Pliny says in Book 19, Chapter 8: "Libanotis yields the odor of Frankincense, and hence its name": for <margin>libanōtis <note>original: λιβανωτὶς</note></margin> is the Greek word for Frankincense. Apuleius seeks another etymology: namely, that before Frankincense was known to our world, the nations used the smoke of this herb as a substitute for Frankincense; but that is hardly likely.

---

# THE LIBANOTIS OF THEOPHRASTUS ACCORDING TO SOME, with less rounded leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Libanotis variety with more elongated, serrated leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

We observed this variety of the so-called Libanotis of Theophrastus at Heidelberg in Sprenger’s garden: with a very large stalk, a cubit high, divided into three parts, and with branches again divided into three, mostly ending in three small leaflets, somewhat long, serrated, and of which the last is sometimes three-cleft: on the underside, they are more whitish.

The Garland Libanotis of Dioscorides we label as Rosemary, and we refer to it elsewhere: and we wonder greatly, along with Marcello, why it was gifted with the name of Libanotis, since it has almost nothing similar or in common with Libanotis, as is easy to understand from the history of both, which are entirely and in every way different.

<column-break/>

# ANOTHER LIBANOTIS ACCORDING TO SOME, TO OTHERS Black Cervaria: German: Black Heart, Heart-root.
<note>original: "Schwartz Hertz, Hertzwurtzel"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with very fine, feathery leaves and multiple small umbels of flowers.</image-desc>

The roots of this are the thickness of a finger, with a head hairy like a mane, fixed deep in the ground, blackish on the outside, white within, flowing with a slow mucus when wounded, with an aromatic, resinous, and pleasant taste. The leaves arise both from the root and from the stalk, attached to long petioles, somewhat in the form and division of Macedonian Parsley, but stiffer, smooth, of an almost sea-green color, notched, with a milder taste than the root. The stalks are like Giant Fennel <term>Ferulaceous<gloss>resembling the Ferula or giant fennel genus</gloss></term>, striated, two or three cubits high, and divided into wings: they support very large umbels of whitish florets, which consist of five small petals, and turn purplish before they open. The seed is broad, approaching the seed of the broad-leaved parsnip. More <unclear>regarding</unclear> <unclear>its</unclear> following figures.

---

# THE LESSER LIBANOTIS OF THEOPHRASTUS, ACCORDING TO LOBEL: a species of Panax to some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller Libanotis plant with dense, fine foliage and a single main flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It has much more slender leaves, very close to those of Venetian Saxifrage: the stalk is two cubits high and taller: the seed is like Dill, white: the flowers in the umbels are white: the root is aromatic, of a grateful and pleasant odor.

By Tabernaemontanus it is called *Libanotis Panacea*, by Thalius the *Lesser White Libanotis*; by Lobel the *Lesser Libanotis of Theophrastus*. Is it the same as the Black Cervaria, or the "Other Libanotis of some" described just above? For we have observed it in various places: at Basel, on Mount Mutetis, and on the mountain near Krentzach, flowering in Autumn: at Geneva, on Mount Salève: at Montbéliard at La Chaux, near the vineyards, and also between Raupach and St. Germain.

<column-break/>

# A SPECIES SENT UNDER THE NAME OF "VALDE BONA," the second Libanotis of some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a plant with broad, opposite leaves and small clusters of flowers at the leaf axils and stem tip.</image-desc>

This entire plant approaches the Black Cervaria: but the color of the leaves is more green, and not so sea-green. There are also fewer pairings in the leaves, but they are much larger, bitter, and somewhat sharp. The flower is yellow, from smaller umbels than in the Libanotis already named, and when chewed it yields an odor somewhat vinous and aromatic. We once received it dried from Strasbourg, under the name of the *Welgutta* of the Bolognese and *Valdebona nigra*. The seed sown by us finally produced a stalk in the third year: and it ripened its seeds in June and July.

It is found at the foothills of the Apennine mountains, from whence we obtained it: and it flowers in June.

### GIANT FENNEL, FERULAGO, NARTHETICUM: Germ. Ferulkraut: French Ferule: Ital. Ferola.

### GIANT FENNEL WITH FENNEL-LIKE LEAVES, AND BROADER, ROUNDER SEEDS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ferula plant with a tall, segmented stalk, fine feathery leaves at the base, and multiple umbels of flowers at the top. A small detail of the seed is shown to the left of the main stem.</image-desc>

The Giant Fennel genus, as Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> noted long ago, is divided into many species: but here we speak of the Giant Fennel properly so-called. Some derive its name from *feriendo* <note>Latin: striking/beating</note>, others from *ferendo* <note>Latin: bearing/carrying</note>, and most—because its stalks serve as props for shrubs and as walking sticks for the elderly—derive it from "bearing": just as <term>Narthex</term> <note>Greek: Νάρθηξ</term> among the Greeks signifies a twig, a small staff, or a wand.

From the various species of the Giant Fennel genus, we present here the one called *Narthecium* by Theophrastus and *Ferulago* by Gaza: and which the *History of Lyon* says has the stalk and leaf of Fennel, a yellow flower, oblong seed, and a white, fibrous, somewhat sharp root, nine inches long, and small in proportion to the size of the plant.

<column-break/>

Two plants of this name are commonly established, which seem to differ only in cultivation, stature, elegance, and abundance of juice: depending, of course, on whether they have obtained a choice, dry, well-baked, fertile, and warmer soil.

Others distinguish between the *Male Giant Fennel* and the *Female Giant Fennel*: to these, the Female is inscribed as the *Giant Fennel with sea-green leaves* (of which more shortly), and by some, the one we proposed under the preceding title. The Male, however, is the one we depict here. It grows to five or six cubits <note>roughly 7.5 to 9 feet</note>, with a thick stalk full of spongy pith, and branched; the leaves are very large, like Fennel, or similar to the sea-green Giant Fennel. The umbels <note>umbrella-like flower clusters</note> are broad with yellow flowers, which, when fallen, are followed by a large, leaf-like seed. The root, when wounded, pours out a milky tear.

---

### THAPSIA WITH THE APPEARANCE OF GIANT FENNEL, OR THE TURBITH OF THE FRENCH, and the Ash-colored Turbith of the Apothecaries.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with feathery foliage and a large, thick, branched root system. A single seed is illustrated to the right of the stem.</image-desc>

The bark of the root is dark on the outside but pale within, and it abounds with a milky and gummy juice. The stalk is like Sulfur-wort, and more slender than Giant Fennel. The leaves are broader and shorter than Fennel. In the umbels is the seed of the Lesser Giant Fennel, oblong, narrower, and like Mountain Parsley. Thus it is described by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist</note>, who calls it *Thapsia of Aquitaine*, and *Spring Thapsia* in the Aquitaine of the Basques. He adds that it is called *Thapsia* not only, as Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> pleased, from the island of *Thapsos* (one of the Sporades): but also because of the flaming color it induces when applied to the body. Otherwise, it is very similar to *Thapsia* in its whole habit and powers; although it is more excellent in its purging power: and most all Northern Apothecaries use its root, etc.

---

### GALBANUM-BEARING GIANT FENNEL AND GALBANUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ferula variety with dense, feathery leaves and a thick root. To the left, a separate detail of the flowering umbel is shown.</image-desc>

Lobelius describes the Galbanum-bearing Giant Fennel thus: This very beautiful plant, he says, arises in our gardens with abundant, broad, leaf-like, aromatic seed. In its whole appearance it resembles Giant Fennel: the leaves are slender, likewise with flowers in more cheerful umbels: the root is thick and pregnant with juice. However, we have not yet clearly perceived which plant this of Lobelius might be.

Furthermore, *Galbanum* is, according to Dioscorides, the juice of a Giant Fennel growing in Syria, etc. Whence also Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> says: Syria also gives Galbanum on Mount Amanus from the Giant Fennel. Thus, those even moderately practiced in medical matters know that it is the liquid of a Giant Fennel plant, which is known and in use today in the Apothecaries under the same name. The narrowness of this space does not allow for more on this subject.

<column-break/>

### GIANT FENNEL WITH SEA-GREEN LEAVES, AND BROAD, ROUND, AND LONG SEEDS: By some called Ferulaceous Thapsia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ferula plant with broad, flat seeds shown in detail to the left of the main flowering stalk. The leaves are finely divided.</image-desc>

It is a wonder how large the root of this is: the stalk far exceeds the height of a man. The leaves are large, Fennel-like, of a sea-green color, especially underneath. They drip a milky juice with a heavy odor and sharp taste. The flower of the umbel is yellowish: the seed is large, compressed, striped, and black.

Is it the *Female Giant Fennel* of Caesalpinus? Or the *Fertile Ferulaceous Rosemary* of Dioscorides according to Lobelius? Or the *Greater Thapsia* of Cordus in his History?

We have seen this ripening seed in various gardens in July, at Padua, Lyon, and elsewhere. Moreover, Felix Plater <note>Swiss physician and professor</note> writes that the root grew to such a mass that it weighed 70 pounds, where we saw it. More on the Giant Fennels in the Appendix.

---

### THAPSIA, OR GARGANIC TURBITH, with very broad seeds.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thapsia plant featuring very large, broad, winged seeds and feathery foliage.</image-desc>

The origin of the name Thapsia was noted before. In its whole nature it is similar to Giant Fennel, yet with a more slender stalk: the leaves are similar to Fennel: the umbels on each branch are similar to Dill, in which the flower is honey-colored. The seed is like that of Giant Fennel, somewhat broad, but a little smaller. The root is black on the outside, white within, long, sharp, and covered with a thicker bark.

We have recorded the census of plants circulated under the name of Thapsia in our Great History, but here there is no time to review them. We show at least this one, which has the broadest seed: and it is commonly called *Garganic Turbith*, both from its powers similar to Turbith, and from its place of birth, Mount Gargano in Apulia. More in the Appendix.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE.
## CONTINUATION OF THE HISTORY OF CRETAN DAUCUS: Caraway-leaved.
Ccç 3

**DAUCUS, CRETAN DAUCUS: German: *Mohren-kummel* <note>literally "Moorish cumin"</note>: French: *Panet sauuage* <note>Wild parsnip</note>: Italian & Spanish: *Dauco*.**

Daucus, as Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> reports, is called *Dircæum* by some. But the Cretan variety has leaves similar to Fennel, though smaller and thinner: the stalk is nine inches long, the flower-head <note>original: "umbella"</note> like Coriander, with white flowers: and among these is the seed, which is sharp, white, hairy, and has a sweet scent when chewed. The root is the thickness of a finger and nine inches in length. There is truly another kind similar to wild Celery, smelling of spice, sharp, fragrant, and of a pleasant taste. The Cretan is the most highly prized. There is furthermore a third kind with flowers like Coriander, white, with the head and seed of Dill, etc. Thus he distinguishes them. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist and author</note>, however, holds only two types of Daucus: the Cretan, which is also his most highly prized, and another growing in any dry places.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Daucus Creticus plant, showing a central stalk with feathery leaves and a large umbel of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Because our previous figure from Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century botanist</note> was less than good, it was our intention to substitute a better one here for another: but since we lacked the industry of a woodcutter, we have depicted another of this family here, which we observed flowering in Autumn in various thickets in the County of Montbéliard, and we have labeled it CARAWAY-LEAVED <note>original: "CARVIFOLIA"</note>. Those little flowers are white on the upper part, but reddish on the back.

Furthermore, the rugged rocks of the highest mountains nourish the so-called Cretan Daucus: such as Salève and Thuiri among the Genevans: Wasserfall among those of Basel, and similar places. Whence some also call it *Mountain Daucus*. In gardens it is green in March, flowers in May, and swells with seed in June.

---

**DAUCUS III. WITH CORIANDER LEAF, and yellow flower.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Daucus plant with Coriander-like leaves and multiple flowering umbels.</image-desc>

This has the leaves of Coriander, but smaller and somewhat thick: the stalk is about two feet long, the flowers in the head are yellow, and the seed is like Cumin.

In truth, the roots and leaves are eaten, which are of an aromatic taste.

Otherwise, various plants have claimed the name of Daucus for themselves among writers: *Mutellina*; *Common Meum* <note>Spignel</note>, *Carrot*, *Visnaga*, *Seseli*, *Lappula*, *Caucalis*, *Anthriscus*, *Hippuris*, Cordus's *Celery-like Daucus*, his *Clove-scented Daucus*, and also his *Blue-footed Daucus* and *Cone-leaved Daucus*: and others which vary in leaf, stalk, seed, or flower: moreover, we have Galen <note>Prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> as a witness in his 2nd book *On Foodstuffs* that the *Wild Parsnip* was once called *Daucus*.

<column-break/>

**DALECHAMPS' MEADOW DAUCUS, WITH Meadow Yarrow leaf.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a meadow Daucus with finely divided, yarrow-like leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It grows with many white, round roots, scattered in different directions from the bottom part of the stalk, short, sweet, and fragrant. With leaves similar to Meadow Yarrow, soft, and bright green: the stalk is like Fennel, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, divided into two or three branches: and the flower-head is somewhat reddish at the beginning, afterwards white, bitter, and smelling somewhat dry. It grows in mossy meadows and flowers in May.

As far as the powers of Daucus are concerned: The seed of all of them has the power of heating: taken as a drink it stimulates menstruation, labor, and urine, frees one from griping pains, and soothes an old cough. It also helps those bitten by the Phalangium spider when drunk in wine, and applied as a poultice it disperses swellings. —Dioscorides.

---

**GLAUCOUS-LEAVED DAUCUS, SIMILAR TO Twisted Fennel: The Rock Fennel of Tabernaemontanus.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Daucus with glaucous (blue-green), fennel-like foliage and thick roots.</image-desc>

Some refer this plant to the *Peucedana* <note>Hog's Fennel</note>, others to the *Libanotides*. It grows in rocky places, on high mountains and cliffs. It is found abundantly in the grassy places around the gallows at Montbéliard: it flowers in June, July, and August, and the seed matures in September.

This Daucus is endowed with the same powers as Fennel: it is hot in the second degree and dry in the first: it expels stones and moves the urine.

Concerning the use and powers of Daucus, these things among others are found in Galen. The wild kind, he says, is less fit for eating than the cultivated, but is more potent in all things. The cultivated can indeed be eaten, but it is weaker.

---

**MYTELLINA OR MUTRINA: The Alpine Meum of some.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Mutellina plant, showing a thick root system and delicate, finely cut leaves.</image-desc>

It has the leaves of the Wild Carrot <note>original: "Staphylini syluestris"</note>, yet smaller, and very minutely cut, about three fingers in length, and smooth in a circle. The stalk is short, and only a few inches high, bearing a purplish flower-head. The root is hairy near the ground, long and thick enough, blackish on the outside, with the scent and taste of common Meum.

It is commonly called *Mutellina* in the Rhaetian Alps, where we collected it in flower in June. Its powers and properties are the same as those of Cretan Daucus. The dairy farmers of Glarus and Valais season their colostrum <note>first milk</note> and their whey-cheese with it. From its grazing, cows gather the most and best milk, just as they do from the grazing of Meum in Apulia <note>a region in Southern Italy</note>.

<summary>This page details several varieties of Daucus (wild carrots and parsnips), describing their physical characteristics, habitats ranging from Montbéliard to the Alps, and their medicinal uses for digestion and respiratory issues.</summary>
<keywords>Daucus Creticus, Caraway-leaved, Coriander, Mutellina, Alpine Meum, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, Montbéliard, medicinal plants, botany, diuretics, digestive health</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Stirpium" (Plants), specifically focusing on the various species of parsnips and carrots, following the previous discussions on root vegetables.</meta>

### THE PARSNIP OF THE ANCIENTS, THE STAPHYLINOS: German: *Pasteney*; French: *Pastenades*; Italian: *Pastinaca*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a parsnip plant (Pastinaca sativa) showing the root, stalk, leaves, and umbel flowers.</image-desc>

The name *Pastinaca* <note>original: "Pastinaca"</note> seems to have been derived from the fact that it resembles and possesses the form of a *pastinum* <note>A "pastinum" was a two-pronged gardening tool used by Romans for digging and planting; the author suggests the root looks like this tool.</note>. The Greeks called it *Staphylinos*. There are two types of Parsnip: the cultivated and the wild; the wild variety is further divided into many kinds. However, the term "Parsnip," when used without any additional description, is commonly understood to mean the cultivated kind. According to the opinion of Cesalpino <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), an Italian physician and influential botanist.</note>, Theophrastus called this *Daucus*; but Dioscorides, Galen, and others determine that the name *Daucus* better suits the wild Parsnip, and they establish that the wild Parsnip and *Daucus* are of one and the same genus. We leave this dispute to the judge <note>A Latin idiom meaning the matter is still undecided among experts.</note>.

### A BETTER REPRESENTATION OF THE CULTIVATED PARSNIP, OR CARROT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a carrot plant (Carota) with a thick taproot and feathery foliage.</image-desc>

If the Parsnip called the Carrot <note>original: "Carota"</note> is permitted to grow a stalk, it raises a stem of two or three cubits <note>roughly 3 to 4.5 feet</note>, which is hairy, ribbed, hollow, and branched. At its junctions are leaves nine inches long, divided as if into wings, each cut with a certain notch like Smallage <note>Wild celery</note>, hairy, and with a pleasant enough smell and taste. The flowers are in somewhat broad umbels <note>umbrella-shaped clusters</note>, tiny and reddish. Care is chiefly given to the root, which is a foot long, thick, brittle, yellow or red, succulent, and of a sweet and aromatic taste.

Some call the cultivated Parsnip the "domestic *Daucus*," and many call it the "Carrot." It varies only in the color of the root, which is either white, pale yellow, bright yellow, or dark red.

### THE SYRIAN PARSNIP OF RAUWOLF; The *Secacul* of the Arabs and certain Moors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Syrian Parsnip (Secacul) showing a tuberous root system and flowering umbels.</image-desc>

It relies on a root that is ash-colored on the outside and bright white within, smooth, tender, a finger thick, and a finger-and-a-half long. In place of fibers, small nodes or "warts" protrude from it. It has a sweet taste similar to Carrots, which this Parsnip resembles in its stalk, leaves, and umbel (except for the tiny flowers, which are entirely yellow).

Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf (1535–1596), a German physician and botanist famous for his travels in the Levant.</note>, the author of the description, reports that it is a species of Rampion <note>a type of bellflower with edible roots</note>, called *Gerelen* by the Germans; it grows among cornfields and near the hedges and gardens of the city of Aleppo, especially in sunny places. He adds that it is edible and of a pleasing taste.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE CULTIVATED PARSNIP by Fuchs.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of cultivated parsnip from Fuchs's herbal.</image-desc>

Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), one of the three "German fathers of botany."</note> has two figures for the cultivated Parsnip, which we also present here. Furthermore, various plants are gifted with the name of "cultivated Parsnip": by Lobelius it is called <unclear>Giser</unclear>, by Tragus *Siserum* <note>Skirret</note>, by others *Silaum*, Caraway, *Pisnaga*, *Althea*, etc., but less properly so. Commonly, however, the white, yellow, red, and black Carrots are called "cultivated Parsnips" and "cultivated *Staphylinos*." The *Secacul* of the Arabs, which is a type of Rampion, is grouped by some with the Syrian Parsnip. Olivier de Serres <note>A famous French soil scientist</note> is greatly mistaken in concluding that the *Beram rapaccum* is a species of Parsnip.

### WILD PARSNIP, OR THE *STAPHYLINOS* of the Greeks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of wild parsnip (Pastinaca sylvestris) with slender roots and smaller umbels.</image-desc>

It is easy to recognize the appearance of the wild Parsnip from the cultivated one. The root is smaller and more pungent; the stalks are equal in height (about two feet), ribbed, hairy, and divided into wings. The leaves are similarly cut into smaller segments, dark green, and hairy. The flowers in the umbel are also similar. When the flowers have fallen, they are succeeded by short, ribbed, hairy seeds; and then the umbel curls inward, forming a cavity in the middle like a small bird's nest.

Some distinguish between a Male and Female variety; they say the former has a reddish tiny flower in the center of the umbel, while the latter does not.

It grows in stony and thin soil in the fields, and also grows spontaneously in gardens. More on both this and the cultivated variety in the Appendix.

### SEA PARSNIP: Called by some *Secacul*, and Prickly Samphire.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sea Parsnip (Pastinaca marina) with spiny leaves and thick roots.</image-desc>

This has a thick, tender, white root, very pleasing to the taste, sweet and wrinkled like the German and broad-leafed cultivated Parsnip. The leaves are thick, nearly two spans <note>about 18 inches</note> long, prickly, cut with frequent divisions, and have an aromatic taste with a certain saltiness. The stalk is a cubit high, divided into many branches, upon which sit prickly umbels provided with small white flowers.

The people of Montpellier call this plant "Sea Parsnip"; some call it the *Hippophaes* of Dioscorides, others "Sea Caltrop," Anguillara calls it *Secacul*, and Apollo calls it the "True *Secacul*." Tabernaemontanus and others call it "Prickly Samphire."

We saw it blooming in August by the sea at Montpellier, and at the seashore in Venice; we have also kept it in our garden. Its medicinal powers are the same as those of common Samphire.

It also introduces exotic and coastal varieties like the Syrian Secacul and the Sea Parsnip.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BROAD-LEAVED CULTIVATED PARSNIP, GERMAN, with a yellow flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pastinaca sativa plant showing its broad leaves, thick root, and umbel-shaped flower head.</image-desc>

The roots of this Parsnip are very well known in German kitchens; they are unique, long, less thick, white, and endowed with a hard nerve in the middle. Their flavor is more pleasant than that of the Skirret <note>original: "Sifarum"; a root vegetable popular in the Renaissance</note>. From these roots rises a stalk two cubits high or taller, furrowed, hollow, and concave with many "wings" <note>referring to the leaf attachments</note>. The leaves approach the leaves of the Greater Burnet <note>original: "Pimpinellæ maioris"</note>, but are many times larger, hairy, and have a pleasant, aromatic taste. The flowers in the large umbrella-cluster are yellow. The seed is broad, leaf-like, double, flattened, and similar to the seed of the plant commonly called Angelica.

It loves meadow-like places and is also sown in gardens, as we have kept them in our own at Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard. It blooms in July or August. *More regarding this is on the side of the following figure.*

---

### WILD GERMAN PARSNIP, called by some, Elaphoboscum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild parsnip (Pastinaca germanica sylvestris) with jagged leaves and a long taproot.</image-desc>

This differs from the cultivated variety in no other way than by its growth: the form of all parts is the same, but more compact, and the flavor is more vigorous.

Matthiolus, and Lacuna who followed him, propose this image alone for the legitimate *Elaphoboscum* <note>Greek: "deer-feed," a plant mentioned by Dioscorides</note>: thus Dodoens (in French) and Castore Durante also call it *Elaphoboscum*; Tabernaemontanus calls it *erraticum* [wandering]; Tragus, Anguillara, Cordus, Gesner, Thalius, and Camerarius call it *Syluestrem* [wild]; and Gerard calls it *Spondylium*.

It grows everywhere among wild plants, on the hills of fields and vineyards, in grassy places and dry meadows. It blooms in July and August.

---

### THE ANTRISCUS OF PLINY, ACCORDING TO SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Antriscus plant with slender stems and small umbel flowers.</image-desc>

The *History of Lyon* <note>referring to Dalechamps' Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> depicts the Antriscus and describes it thus: certain Herbarists contend that the plant pictured here is the *Antriscus*, a view I neither oppose nor support. It is produced at the edges of meadows and near the beds of flowing streams. It has a root like Fennel, white inside, fragrant, and sharp; leaves like Celery <note>original: "Apij"</note>, obliquely cut along the edges, almost always five to each stalk; a stalk a cubit high and sometimes taller, angular; a white flower in an umbrella-cluster; and a double, oblong seed, tipped with two thin points, sharp and fragrant.

<column-break/>

### Another Image of the BROAD-LEAVED CULTIVATED PARSNIP, German.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the German broad-leaved parsnip, showing the plant in a more mature state with seeds.</image-desc>

Many wish this Parsnip to be the *Siser* of the Ancients, just as Fuchs exhibited it in the first place under the title of Cultivated Siser. Tabernaemontanus, however, labeled it *Cultivated Elaphoboscum*. Lacuna and Lonicer, on the other hand, confuse it with *Carrots*.

Furthermore, the root of this is more bitter and more fragrant than the root of the common Parsnip, having something more aromatic and being more pleasing to the taste. For this reason, it is still sown by many and most greedily sought after in foods; whence we have it from the author Pliny that the Emperor Tiberius wished it to be brought to him every single year. But those who gather its roots in Winter should beware of *Hemlock* <note>original: "Cicuta"</note> or *Water-Hemlock*.

---

### CAROS, CARUS, CARUM AND CAREUM: German: Field Caraway; French: Carui, Cumin, Sifot; Italian: Caro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Caraway plant (Carum carvi) showing its feathery leaves and distinct root system.</image-desc>

Pliny writes that the *Careum* [Caraway] was named after its nation, namely from the region of Caria, where it grows most praiseworthily.

The plant is not unlike the wild Parsnip, says Matthiolus: with several stalks from one root, four-angled, a cubit high; the umbrella-cluster filled with white flowers; the seed longer than Anise, angular and blackish underneath; and a long root. In the Apothecaries' shops, it is commonly called *Carui*, etc. It grows on hills, mountains, grassy plains, and lush meadows, and from the month of May until August it produces flowers and seed; it is especially frequent among the Germans, Bohemians, and Hungarians, and is a principal ingredient in their kitchens, to use Pliny's words. Concerning its powers, see the Appendix.

---

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF ANTRISCUS.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Antriscus plant, showing a slightly different growth habit.</image-desc>

We present two images of Antriscus from our acquisitions, so that what seems to be missing from one may be had from the other.

The plant which we depict here as *Antriscus* grows everywhere near hedges and blooms in May, July, and August; it is frequent in Lyon, Geneva, Basel, and Montbéliard. Some label it *Caucalis*; Tabernaemontanus calls it *Wild Chervil* and *Onobelinon*; Gesner calls it *Hedge Parsnip*; Gerard calls it *Wild Celery*; Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* calls it *Wild Chervil 2*, but in his *Phytopinax* he calls it *Caucalis*.

<summary>This page provides botanical descriptions and synonyms for the cultivated parsnip, wild parsnip, caraway, and the mysterious "Antriscus." It highlights the culinary preferences of Emperor Tiberius and warns of the dangers of confusing edible roots with poisonous hemlock.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of umbelliferous plants (herbs with umbrella-like flower clusters), specifically focusing on the Scandix genus and its relatives, commonly known as Shepherd’s Needles.</meta>

# THE SCANDIX OF THE ANCIENTS, THE SCANDIX OF CERTAIN AUTHORS with white flowers, etc. VENUS’S COMB: German: *Venus Strell* <note>Modern German: Venus-Striegel</note>, French: *Pique de Venus*: Italian: *Pettine de Venere*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scandix plant with a large, spherical, spiky seed head and lobed basal leaves.</image-desc>

*Scandix* <note>original: "Scandix"</note> differs from *Sandix* <note>original: "Sandice"</note>, in that *Scandix* is an herb, while *Sandix* is a mineral pigment. Mention of *Scandix* is found in the works of Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "father of botany"</note> among those plants whose stems trail along the ground. Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> classifies it among the wild vegetables. To Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and pharmacologist</note>, it is a wild vegetable, somewhat sharp, bitter, and edible.

Which plant is truly the *Scandix* today is a matter of dispute among authors: for the name *Scandix* is attributed to various species of *Venus’s Comb* <note>original: "Pectinis Veneris"</note> soon to be described, as well as to Goat's Beard, Woad, Toothpick-weed, and other herbs; but especially, the plant we depict here is presented as *Scandix*.

It heats and dries in the intense second degree <note>A reference to Galenic medicine, where plants were classified by their "humoral" qualities on a scale of 1 to 4</note>, and it is eaten both raw and cooked.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pecten Veneris showing long, needle-like seed pods arranged like a comb.</image-desc>

The common **Venus’s Comb** grows from a small and sweet root; it produces thin stems, nine inches long, furrowed, reddish near the ground, but green and furrowed higher up, divided into branches. The leaves are attached to long stalks, divided like Coriander, and endowed with a nauseating taste. The flowers very closely resemble the flowers of Myrrh-seed <note>original: "Myrrhidis"</note>, and are arranged in umbels <note>umbrella-like clusters</note>, and are white in color: these are followed by a long seed, tapering to a point, and with small beaks, or rather, as Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish botanist</note> prefers, more like thick needles: from which it is also believed to have obtained the names Shepherd’s Needle, *Acuila*, or *Acicula* <note>Latin for "little needle"</note>. Many have thought this to be the *Scandix* of the Ancients, but erroneously: for its properties, among other things, argue against it.

---

### VENUS’S COMB WITH VERY FINELY DIVIDED leaves, the Anthriscus of Casabona.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Pecten Veneris with very finely divided, feathery foliage and long seed beaks.</image-desc>

From a thin, slightly fibrous root, one (or several) thin stems emerge. The leaves at the root grow from a rather long stalk and are very fine, divided almost like Spignel <note>original: "Mei"</note>. At the ends of the stems, tiny flower clusters are attached in a very small umbel, which leave behind radiated little horns, like those of Venus’s Comb, about an inch long, but shorter and thinner than in that species; usually five where the plants are small, but where they are larger, more.

<column-break/>

### VENUS’S COMB WITH THINNER LEAVES, and fewer beaks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pecten Veneris variety with slightly broader leaf segments and fewer beaks.</image-desc>

This plant is a palm’s breadth high, with a small white, fibrous root, from which three or four trailing stems emerge: around these are leaves similar to the common *Scandix*, but thinner: the umbels are also smaller. The flowers are followed by oblong seeds, like needles; not all together as in the common Venus’s Comb, where eight are commonly observed, but in pairs, threes, or fours, and likewise smaller than those.

---

### CRETAN VENUS’S COMB.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Cretan variety of Pecten Veneris, showing dense clusters of long, upright seed beaks.</image-desc>

The upper leaves of this plant are divided in the manner of the common *Scandix*: but the lower ones are darker, slightly hairy, and less deeply cut. The stem is a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, angular, furrowed, and somewhat hairy: the umbel is small, the flowers white: and the seed is beaked, with 10, 12, or more beaks joined together: to each beak, two tips like rigid prickles are fixed.

The Cretan Venus’s Comb usually grows in fields with rich and fertile soil, and among the crops themselves: it flowers in May and June.

Its root extracts all things fixed in the body <note>likely referring to splinters or thorns</note>, and nature is believed to have shown this by the prickles on the seeds <note>A reference to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that a plant's appearance reveals its medicinal use</note>.

<column-break/>

### THE PERCHEPIER OF THE ENGLISH TO SOME, the Lesser Scandix of Tabernaemontanus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Perchepier (Parsley Piert), a small low-growing herb with fan-shaped leaves.</image-desc>

Those who have a proper understanding of the *Perchepier* of the English, says Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, botanist</note> in his *Adversaria*, consider it similar to Chervil and *Scandix*, and in no way second to them in strength. Its form is very close to the form of newly sprouted Chervil: but it is always a small herb, never higher than a span <note>about 9 inches</note>, and it breaks forth spontaneously throughout the whole year, flourishing especially in dry and trodden soil, without a main stem, with herbaceous little flowers, etc.

It springs up spontaneously in fields and cultivated lands in early Spring, and, as has been said, is endowed with the virtues and properties of Chervil. It powerfully and suddenly provokes urine <note>a diuretic</note>: it is eaten among vegetables, preserved pickled in brine, and a distilled water of great use is extracted from it.

<summary>This page describes various species of Scandix and Pecten Veneris (Shepherd's Needle), detailing their physical characteristics, historical nomenclature from ancient authorities, and medicinal uses, particularly as diuretics.</summary>
<keywords>Scandix, Venus's Comb, Shepherd's Needle, Pecten Veneris, Perchepier, Parsley Piert, botany, herbal medicine, diuretics, Dioscorides, Pliny, Theophrastus, Lobelius</keywords>

--- Page 466 ---
**IMAGES AND OUTLINES.**

**CHERVIL:** German: *Kerffel-Kraut*; Belgian: *Kernel*; French: *du Cerfeuil*; Italian: *Cerefoglio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chaerophyllum (Chervil) plant showing its taproot, bipinnate leaves, and umbel flowers.</image-desc>

It has a shining white root, about the thickness of the little finger, from which several branched, striated <note>grooved or streaked</note>, and hollow stalks arise. The leaves are similar to those of garden Parsley, but more sharply divided and not as long, being hairy on the underside. The flowers are arranged in a fixed umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster where stalks spring from a single center</note>, small and white, consisting of five heart-shaped petals and as many whitish stamens; the seed is oblong and slender, with a sweet and aromatic flavor.

It is cultivated everywhere in gardens; sown in Spring, it quickly rises into a stalk. Sown in August, it remains green throughout the entire Winter.

It warms temperately and dries moderately. Eaten, it promotes urine and dissolves obstructions; furthermore, applied externally, it disperses tumors and resolves clotted lumps of blood. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

**SWEET CICELY:** German: *Wilder Körbel*; French: *Cicutaire & Persil d'asne*; Italian: *Myrrade*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myrrhis (Sweet Cicely) plant, featuring deeply divided fern-like leaves and large umbels.</image-desc>

Sweet Cicely <note>original: "Myrrhis"</note>, as far as can be gathered from the writings of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen, was also called Myrrh, and by some *Smyrrhiza*; it has an oblong, tender, round, fragrant root that is sweet and not unpleasant as food. In its stalk, leaves, and flowers, it is very similar to Hemlock-chervil, only smaller and more slender, for which reason it is called *Cicutaria* <note>Hemlock-like</note> by some. We have shown in our great *History* that it is wrongly identified by some as Geranium, Chervil, or Angelica. From the various species of Myrrhis that are handed down, we depict here the one which has a large, long, furrowed seed; it grows spontaneously in some meadows and is commonly cultivated in gardens, where it flowers in May. *More in the Appendix.*

---

**GINGIDIUM:** German: *Strich Körffelkraut*; French: *Gingidium*; Italian: *Gingidio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gingidium plant with upright stems and dense umbels.</image-desc>

Dioscorides says that Gingidium is called *Lepidium* by some; it grows mostly in Cilicia and Syria. Furthermore, it is a small herb similar to wild Parsnip, but more slender and more bitter; it has a small, whitish, bitter root. It is eaten raw and cooked, and is ultimately beneficial to the stomach and provokes urine.

Pliny and Galen also record that it grows and is eaten mostly in Syria. However, whereas Dioscorides and Pliny make it similar to the Parsnip, Galen and Paul <note>likely Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical writer</note> compare it to Shepherd's Needle <note>original: "Scandici"</note>; this contributes little to the knowledge of this insufficiently known herb, since these two simples <note>medicinal plants</note> have nothing in common. *More on Gingidium in the Appendix, where the reader will also find an illustration.*

<column-break/>

**GREAT ALSATIAN UMBELLIFER,** with small yellowish **UMBELS.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Umbelliferous plant with distinct nodes on the stem and small umbels.</image-desc>

This plant, as far as we know, is unnamed by herbalists; we found it among the thickets between Colmar and Sulz. In height it equaled a man, with a reddish, striated, jointed, hollow stalk, firm enough, and divided into branches. At each of its nodes, stalks arise embracing the stem like a sheath, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> long, from the sides of which other shorter ones come forth, supporting leaves divided in the manner of Rock Parsley, endowed with a somewhat bitter and aromatic flavor. The umbels are small in proportion to the plant, equal to the umbels of Parsley, and consist of yellowish flowers. The seed is paired, similar to Dill, leaf-like, broad, striated, and of an aromatic, sharp, and bitter flavor. The root is woody, plowed with wrinkles, and aromatic.

---

**DOG'S BUR:** German: *Aker Kletten*; French: *Espece de Glaitteron*; Italian: *Peocchi di cane*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lappula Canaria (Bur Parsley) showing its characteristic prickly fruit (burs).</image-desc>

We shall provide the history of the common Burdock, both the Greater and Lesser, later in its proper place; however, because of the great similarity which Dog's Bur <note>original: "Canaria"</note> has with Gingidium and Caucalis, we mention it here. Furthermore, it differs from others of the same name only by its low growth; it obtained the name *Canaria* because it clings to dogs.

Its root is white, slender, and somewhat sweet; the stalks are a foot or more in height, divided into several branches—some straight, some trailing—striated, bristly, purplish, jointed, and hollow at many of the "wings" <note>leaf axils</note>. The leaves are fine-leaved like Parsnip and hairy. In the umbel are white flowers, which are succeeded by little burs that are striated and bristly. We have observed this, as well as the following plants, in various places among the cornfields and at the edges of fields. They flower in May and June.

<column-break/>

**BROAD-LEAVED DOG'S BUR, OR** Caucalis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved Lappula (Caucalis) with prominent prickly seeds.</image-desc>

The root of this is simple, white, and succulent; the stalk is a cubit high, branched, striated, and rough to the touch. The leaves are beautiful, about a span <note>approx. 9 inches</note> long, very hairy, and deeply saw-toothed; there are four or five pairs of them, with an odd leaf always closing the wing <note>the end of the leaf stalk</note>. The umbel of purplish flowers is spread out and sits upon a peculiar small fork, longer than a span. The burs are large, oblong, rough, and blackish.

It is presented in the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the 'Historia Generalis Plantarum' by Dalechamps</note> as the *Lappa boaria* of Pliny; but by Lobelius in his *Adversaria* as the second purplish *Caucalis*. It grows abundantly in the territory of Narbonne, especially around Montpellier and Nîmes, among the cornfields.

<summary>This page describes several umbelliferous plants (Chervil, Sweet Cicely, Gingidium, and various Burs), detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for digestion and swelling, and their geographical locations.</summary>
<keywords>Chervil, Sweet Cicely, Gingidium, Umbellifers, Bur Parsley, Caucalis, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, Alsace flora</keywords>

--- Page 467 ---
### ANOTHER SPECIES OF CANARY BUR-PARSLEY: By some called Maritime Bur-parsley.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lappula Canaria plant, showing a slender root system and several stems ending in small umbels.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is slender, long, and white; the stems, barely a hand-span high, are covered in a soft, grayish down and divided by very heavy joints. From these emerge branches longer than the main stem, bare, bearing "burs" <note>original: "Lappas"; referring to the prickly seed heads</note> in an umbel <note>A flower cluster where stalks spring from a common center like umbrella ribs.</note>. These are yellow, unlike those of the white Bur-parsley. The leaves are soft, hairy, and yellowish, with the fine divisions of Venus’s Comb <note>A type of wild chervil with needle-like seed pods.</note>.

We observed this in a certain sandy stretch of the Narbonne region <note>Southern France</note> and neighboring sandy plains; it is quite rare.

### ANOTHER MARITIME CHAMOMILE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamæmelum Marinum plant with spreading stems and daisy-like flowers.</image-desc>

It spreads many small stalks along the ground, a hand-span or nine inches long, and unbranched. Along these, leaves rise in order, broader, shorter, and thicker than those of common Chamomile, and not so finely cut; they are bitter and slightly acidic, with nearly the scent of Chamomile. Single flowers sit upon single joints, similar to Chamomile flowers, white and radiating, but larger, breathing out nearly the same scent. The roots are deep enough, blackish, and provided with many fibers. It blooms in April, August, and September.

In the *Adversaria* of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note>, it is called *the smallest maritime Feverfew*.

### SPANISH BUR-PARSLEY, WITH WRINKLED SEED.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis Hispanica plant with finely divided leaves and umbels of flowers/seeds.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> mentions this in Book 6, Chapter 14 of his *History* in these words: "It does not differ greatly," he says, "from the first [Greater Bur-parsley], which once grew for me from seed brought from Spain, both when I was among the Belgians and also when I lived in Vienna, Austria. It also had striated and rough stalks; but the umbels of small white flowers were smaller, and gathered as if into a rounded head. The seed was also somewhat thick, heavily striated, and not bristly."

Some label it "Foreign Bur-parsley." Otherwise, Bur-parsley grows everywhere, as Marcellus notes, especially in fallow fields before they are renewed by fresh plowing.

<column-break/>

### STINKING MARITIME CHAMOMILE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamæmelum Foetidum Marinum plant, showing a more upright growth habit and smaller flower heads.</image-desc>

The plants depicted here and in the next small table are of a different kind <note>original: "Heterogeneæ"</note> and belong to the preceding class; but a change was made while we were absent.

Furthermore, the habit of this Chamomile is not much different from the garden Chamomile. However, not only are the stems and branches striated and reddish, covered with white down, but even the leaves are very minutely divided and almost whitening. The flowers are uniform, with white star-like petals radiating at the edge, surrounding a yellow center <note>original: "umbilicum," literally 'navel'</note>.

We collected this in the coastal regions of Narbonne.

### BUR-PARSLEY: German: *Wild Peterlin*; French: *Persil sauvage*; Italian: *Petrosello salvatico*. <note>All these names translate to "Wild Parsley."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis plant with broad, serrated leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacology</note> records that Bur-parsley has a stalk nine inches high and is somewhat bristly. The leaves are similar to Fennel, hairy with many incisions; and at the top is a white, fragrant umbel. It is eaten, like garden vegetables, either raw or cooked. It also promotes the flow of urine.

Pliny mentions it in Book 2, Chapter 15, among the herbs that grow spontaneously, which most nations use for food. In Book 21, Chapter 22, he reviews its description and virtues.

Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and "Father of Botany"</note> similarly lists Bur-parsley among the garden vegetables; but what herb, what vegetable, or what "small stalk" (as Dioscorides says) Bur-parsley actually is, is not easy to learn from his writings.

### SYRIAN BUR-PARSLEY, WITH PARSNIP-LIKE LEAF, very large seed, and white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis Syriaca plant with large, distinct seed heads and feathery foliage.</image-desc>

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, Flemish physician and botanist</note> labels this *Gingidium 1* in his Latin edition; Lobelius in his *Observations* calls it *Syrian Gingidium with Parsnip leaves* <note>original: "Gingidii folia Bauciæ Syriacum"</note>; Tabernaemontanus calls it *Gingidium 1*.

Thus, distinctions of Bur-parsleys are given by location; they are also given by size, by the length and thickness of the leaves, by the shape and size of the seed, and finally by the color of the flowers, which are commonly either white or purplish. Furthermore, all species of *Canary Bur-parsley* are commonly given the name Bur-parsley; and the opinion of those who claim that Pimpinella is Bur-parsley is to be entirely rejected. Could it be Rauwolf’s *Hogweed from Syria*?

It could be called *Caucalis*, according to Lobelius, from the appearance of the seeds, which mimic oblong and hemispherical vessels <note>A play on the Greek word 'kaukis', a type of cup</note>. Moreover, we have it from the monuments of Galen <note>Prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> that *Diuco* is similar to Bur-parsley in flavor and properties.

<summary>This page describes various species of Bur-parsley (Caucalis) and Maritime Chamomile, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in Southern France and Spain, and their medicinal or culinary uses as cited by ancient authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Bur-parsley, Chamomile, botany, Narbonne, Dioscorides, Pliny, medicinal herbs, Syrian flora, Clusius, Lobelius</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<margin>Page 39</margin>

### SMALLER BUR-PARSLEY WITH BEAUTIFUL SEEDS: Tordylium & Cretan Seseli to many.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis minor plant, showing its root system, slender stalk, pinnate leaves, and umbel-shaped flower clusters.</image-desc>

It sends down a thin, woody, white root; the stalk is a foot or more in height, channeled, and hairy. The *leaves* are attached in pairs by a long footstalk <note>petiole</note>, somewhat round, saw-toothed, rough and hairy, smaller than those of the following species: those which grow at the branching of the arms are entirely similar to them, though somewhat smaller. The *flowers* are arranged in a white umbel. The *seeds* are beautiful, not very hairy, with a white, curled, or granulated fringe surrounding them.

Bellonius, Gesner, Bellus and others label this *Caucalis*: Dodonaeus (in French), the same Gesner, and the *History of Lyon* <note>Historia Generalis Plantarum</note> call it *Tordylion* and *Gordylion*. Lacuna, Lobelius, Castor, Tabernaemontanus and Gerard call it *Cretan Seseli*: Camerarius calls it the *Smaller* variety.

<column-break/>

### GREATER BUR-PARSLEY, WITH SEEDS LESS BEAU-tiful and hairy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis maior plant, featuring a more robust stem and larger, more complex leaf structures compared to the minor variety.</image-desc>

The stalk reaches a height of nearly two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note>, being hairy, channeled, hollow, and divided into branches. The *leaves* are oblong, saw-toothed, hairy, some longer, others shorter. The *umbels* are small, and the flowers are also small and white, with the outermost florets having certain larger, three-parted petals. The *seeds* are shield-shaped, like Syrian Bur-parsley but much smaller, hairy, with a reddish center and a white fringe, having an aromatic flavor.

Lobelius, the *History of Lyon*, Camerarius, and others label this *Greater Tordylium* and *Greater Cretan Seseli*.

It is cultivated in gardens and blooms in June: we ourselves have seen it growing wild near *Cormon* on the journey from Genoa to Lyon.

---

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S GREATER BUR-PARSLEY, WITH PURPLISH-white flowers: Perhaps a type of Tordylium?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caucalis variety as described by Clusius, showing broad, serrated leaves and dense flower umbels.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> thought that this Bur-parsley should also be referred to the genus of *Tordylium*; it bloomed in his garden in June and produced mature seed in July and August.

The *Smaller Bur-parsley* with beautiful seeds, mentioned previously, grows wild at Montpellier and is cultivated in gardens in various places: just as we had it blooming in July in our own gardens at Genoa and Montbéliard.

Indeed, we saw the very smallest of all Bur-parsleys near Nîmes, in the gaping crevices of rocks: the entire plant, including root and stalk, did not exceed a palm's breadth <note>about 3 inches</note>.

*More on Tordylium in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### CORIANDER; Germ. *Coriander*: French *Coriandre*: Ital. *Coriandolo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Coriandrum (Coriander) plant, showing its characteristic fine, feathery upper leaves and globular seed clusters.</image-desc>

Although Pliny says that *Coriander* is not found among wild plants, and Dioscorides mentions only one kind of *Coriannum*, and Theophrastus reckons *Coriannum* among those of which there are very few types—indeed, even Brassavola asserts that only cultivated Coriander is found, and the wild kind was unknown to Caesalpino and others among the more recent authors—nevertheless, the commentator Nicander proposes both a *Cultivated* and a *Wild* type: and three kinds of Coriander have become known to us, which we shall soon discuss in order.

We depict here the common, cultivated kind, simply called Coriander, which they also call the *Greater*. It is found everywhere in gardens, and blooms in them during the months of May, June, and July.

---

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF CORIANDER: The testiculate Coriander of C. Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Coriandrum testiculatum, showing the distinct twin-lobed (testiculate) seeds and delicate foliage.</image-desc>

The lowest leaves of this one are more finely cut, and the habit of the seed is different than that of the *Greater* and so-called *Common* kind, of which we depict a small plant here according to the image by Lobelius.

Common Coriander is provided with a sparse, thin, white, simple rootlet endowed with very few fibers. The stalk is two cubits high or more, slender, channeled, and solid. The *leaves* at first resemble Anise or Parsley, but later they approach those of Chamomile. They have the foul odor of bedbugs <note>The name Coriander comes from the Greek 'koris' for bug, referring to the smell of the unripe seeds</note>. The *umbels* of purplish-white flowers are equal to the umbels of Parsley. The seed is exactly round, channeled, divided internally by partitions, otherwise hollow, with a very pleasant, aromatic smell and taste.

<column-break/>

### WILD CORIANDER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of wild coriander (Coriandrum sylvestre), showing a more spreading habit and numerous flower umbels.</image-desc>

Its root is singular; thin and not sent down very deep. It puts forth many stalks, consisting of five angles, solid and jointed, with small branches emerging from the joints in no certain order. The *leaves* are similar to the leaves of common Coriander, but smaller. The *umbels* are filled with purplish-white flowers, just as in the other Coriander; when these have fallen, the round *seed* arises, having this peculiarity: that on each little stalk it is double, one joined to the other. The odor of the whole plant is more pleasant than that of the cultivated Coriander, but more affecting to the head <note>i.e., more intoxicating or pungent</note>.

It grows in somewhat dry places, and on the boundaries and margins of fields.

*More on Coriander in the Appendix.*

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the "Apium" (Parsley/Celery) family, following the descriptions of garden varieties. It focuses on wild, mountain, and regional species, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary Renaissance botanists like Dalechamp and Dodonaeus.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### MACEDONIAN PARSLEY: German: *Stein Eppich*; French: *Persil de Macedoine*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Macedonian Parsley plant (Apium Macedonicum) showing its taproot, ribbed stems, umbel flowers, and detailed foliage.</image-desc>

The leaves are larger than those of garden Parsley, firmer, shiny, dark green, and of a milder flavor. The stems are striated <note>ribbed or grooved</note> and covered with a hoary, downy fuzz. The umbel <note>the flower cluster</note> is white. The seed is striated, nearly equal to that of the garden and cultivated Parsley, but covered with a whitish down.

Regarding this plant, Dioscorides says: "Parsley," he says, "which is called *Petroselinum* <note>original: "Petroselinum," literally "Rock Parsley"</note>, grows in Macedonia in steep places; the seed is like Bishop’s Weed, but more fragrant, sharp, and smelling of spice." Pliny also writes that he called this genus of Parsley *Petroselinum*. Furthermore, Galen records that the Macedonian variety is the *Petroselinum* praised by everyone.

Nearly all writers following him call it Macedonian *Petroselinum*; some call it Macedonian *Apium*. Moreover, it is kept and cultivated in many gardens.

### BLACK MOUNTAIN PARSLEY: German: *Berg-Peterlin*; Cordus’s *Polychrestum*: German: *Vielgütt*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Black Mountain Parsley (Apium Montanum Nigrum) with a thick, fibrous root system and dense umbels.</image-desc>

It has leaves spread out along the ground like garden Parsley, but blacker, harder, and moderately sharp and bitter, with a somewhat aromatic and almost poisonous <note>original: "virosi," suggesting a heavy or foul medicinal scent</note> odor. They clasp the tall, manifold stem with a membranous, purplish stalk; the stem is not very thick, but solid, striated, somewhat reddish, and branched. The umbels of flowers are white, and they leave behind seeds much sharper than the leaves, which are compressed, broad, and almost circular. The root is remarkably thick, soft, hairy at the top, whitish inside and out, with a sharp and bitterish taste, releasing a milky, viscous, and resinous juice when cut.

It loves mountainous and sandy tracts: as we have frequently observed in such places at Basel, Geneva, Lyon, and elsewhere.

### DALECHAMP’S WILD PARSLEY, WITH VERY THIN LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Dalechamp's Wild Parsley (Apium Sylvestre) showing a slender stem and delicate, thin leaves.</image-desc>

The wild Parsley mentioned by Theophrastus and Dioscorides is depicted by Dalechamp in this way. It is said to have a slender, long, white, and fragrant root; a leaf very thin like garden Parsley; a stem a span high; and a tiny white flower in small umbels, which are supported and surrounded beneath by grassy sheaths, not unlike the husks of grain. The seed is very small. It grows on rough hills.

However, the Wild Parsley of Dodonaeus—of which more shortly—differs greatly from this Wild Parsley of Dalechamp. Regarding *Hipposelinum* <note>Horse-parsley</note> or the *Equapium* of the Ancients, and other matters pertaining to the history of Parsley, let the Appendix be consulted.

<column-break/>

### OREOSELINUM, OR MOUNTAIN PARSLEY: Dalechamp’s Mountain Parsley.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Mountain Parsley (Oreoselinum) featuring a large, branched root and broad umbels.</image-desc>

Theophrastus and Pliny record that *Oreoselinum* <note>original: "Oreoselinum," Greek for Mountain Parsley</note> has a leaf similar to Hemlock, a thin root, and a stem like Dill, though smaller. Dioscorides describes it differently, saying that from a thin root comes a single stem, around which are small branches and heads similar to Poppies; in these is an oblong, thin, sharp, fragrant seed, like Cumin. He adds nothing regarding the leaves.

However, Lacuna and Lonicer contend that the Mountain Parsley of the Ancients is unknown today. Nor do the characteristics of Mountain Parsley handed down by the Ancients agree very much with the Mountain Parsley of Dalechamp pictured here.

It grows in rough, rocky, stony, and sunny places; and sometimes it even springs forth from the very cracks of rocks. It is adorned with flowers, which are white, in July.

### ROCK PARSLEY, OR WHITE MOUNTAIN PARSLEY: Perhaps Cordus’s Wild Carrot with an angular stem?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Rock Parsley (Apium Petraeum) with deeply lobed leaves and a long taproot.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves nine inches long, beautifully divided into opposite wings <note>leaflets</note>, which are again subdivided into opposite segments. The stem is like Fennel, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, and full of pith. The umbel is small, woven from tiny flowers. The seeds are like garden Parsley, somewhat long, hairy, striated, bitter, and aromatic. The root is somewhat thick, white, and hairy at the top.

We have observed it in various places in the cracks of rocks: at Baden in Switzerland, on the Waterfall mountain near Basel, and elsewhere.

Furthermore, the root of Mountain Parsley is hot and dry in the third degree <note>a classification in Galenic medicine</note>: it thins, opens, and cuts <note>refers to "cutting" thick humors or phlegm</note>, promotes urine, dissolves stones, provokes the menses, clears obstructions of the liver and spleen, and aids the "Royal Disease" <note>Jaundice</note>. It provides many other uses, which is why it is named *Polychrestum* <note>meaning "of many uses"</note>.

### DODONAEUS’S WILD PARSLEY: German: *Wilder Eppich*; French: *Persil* or *Ache sauuage*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Dodonaeus's Wild Parsley (Apium Sylvestre Dodonaei) showing a tall, leafy stalk and flowering umbels.</image-desc>

The stems are two or three cubits high, striated, angular, smooth, branched, hollow, and reddish-brown at the base. From their reddish joints arise stalks nine inches or a cubit long, striated, angular, and concave in the manner of the stems; these support leaves like a Carrot, smooth, deeply cut, dark green, which yield a milky, bitter juice if broken. It bears an umbel of small flowers like *Petroselinum*, but whitish. The seed is round and flat, similar to the seed of Dill. The roots are numerous, white, and the thickness of a little finger.

Lobelius in his *Icons* and the *Hortus Lusitanicus* depict it under the name of Pliny’s *Thysselinum*; however, Cordus and Thalius call it *Olfenichium*. Could it be Pliny’s *Phellandrium*?

It grows near lakes and in boggy and damp places, and flowers in July.

<summary>This page catalogs various wild and mountain species of the Parsley family (Apium), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal properties while reconciling conflicting descriptions from classical and contemporary botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Macedonian Parsley, Mountain Parsley, Wild Parsley, Dioscorides, Pliny, Dalechamp, Dodonaeus, Polychrestum, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany, diuretics, jaundice treatments</keywords>
