<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of umbelliferous plants, moving from Sison to various species of Pimpinella (Burnet-saxifrage). The catchword from the previous page was "PIMPI-", leading into the Pimpinella section.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### SISON, SINON AND SINNON: OR THE Amomum OF THE APOTHECARIES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sison plant, showing its slender stalk, umbel flowers, and pinnate leaves with a thin taproot.</image-desc>

It produces a slender, rounded, pithy stem, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or more in height: its *leaves* are oblong, pinnate <note>feather-shaped</note>, tender, notched all around, and sometimes laciniated <note>deeply slashed</note>. The *flowers* in the umbel are small and white: followed by the *seed*, which is small, dark, furrowed, and has a somewhat sharp, aromatic taste. The *root* is slender and fibrous.

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish botanist</note> painted and drew this under the title of the true Macedonian Parsley. Lonicer also calls it the Macedonian Parsley of Dioscorides; some call it the *Apothecaries' Amomum*: Cordus, Anguillara, Gesner, and Tabernaemontanus call it the *Sison* and *Sinon* of Dioscorides: as do Camerarius and others, whose opinion we also follow.

The seed is brought from the East: however, it also grows among us in damp places, and is cultivated in several gardens.

<column-break/>

### PIMPINELLA: German: Bibernell; Belgian: Bevernell; French: Pimpinelle; Italian: Pimpinella.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pimpinella plant, featuring more robust, serrated leaves and a thicker root system compared to the Sison.</image-desc>

Pimpinella or Pipinella—also called *Bipennula* and *Pampinella*, which are thought to have been unnamed by the Ancients—are named from the rows of leaves arranged like feathers or wings <note>Latin: "pinnatim"</note>.

However, various plants are given the name of Pimpinella, such as *Caucalis, Poterium, Anagallis, Sideritis, Tragium*, and especially *Saxifraga* and *Sanguisorba*.

Furthermore, the Pimpinella called Saxifrage <note>literally "stone-breaker," used for plants thought to dissolve kidney stones</note> is threefold: *Greater, Middle*, and *Lesser*. We depict the Greater here, which has a white *root*, a finger thick, and of a burning taste: the *stems* are three cubits high, hollow, furrowed, angular, and jointed. The *leaves* resemble the fragrant umbel-bearing Sium, shining: the *little flowers* in the umbels are white: the *seed* is dark, furrowed, sharp, oblong, and aromatic. It grows in sunny meadows.

---

### MIDDLE GOATISH BURNET-SAXIFRAGE.
<note>original: "Pimpinella Saxifragia Hircina Media"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pimpinella Saxifragia Hircina Media, showing deeply serrated, almost lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It has leaves of two kinds: the lower ones indeed approaching the Lesser Saxifrage, but the upper ones more similar to the leaves of the Greater, oblong, ending in a point, and deeply notched. The *root* is long and moderately thick: the *stem* is furrowed, a cubit high, branched with several arms: the *umbels* are white and somewhat large.

The illustration, which is from our purchased collection, does not please in all respects, nor does the preceding one.

Moreover, various differences are observed in the Greater Burnet-saxifrage which that image shows. For the *leaves*, which in all types are indeed serrated and arranged in order, are sometimes dark green and shining, at other times not at all: and even the *flowers*, which are commonly white, sometimes turn reddish from purple.

<column-break/>

### LESSER GOATISH BURNET-SAXIFRAGE, with Sanguisorba leaves.
<note>original: "Pimpinella Saxifragia Hircina Minor, folijs Sanguisorba"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pimpinella Saxifragia Hircina Minor, with smaller, more rounded serrated leaflets.</image-desc>

It has a *stem* of nine inches or a cubit, stiff, solid, and divided into branches: on which there are few, and those very thin, *leaves*: for the rest, rising immediately from the root, are more numerous and broader, serrated around the edge, stiff, smooth, and of a sharp taste. The *flowers* are umbelled, like the Greater Saxifrage, white, but smaller. The *root* is long, wrinkled, simple, smaller than the Greater: and of a more vigorous taste.

It delights in rough and stony places and grows abundantly at Basel, on the way to St. Jacob; at Montbéliard around the city, on the hill toward the gallows, and elsewhere.

Furthermore, these Saxifrage Pimpinellas are called "Goatish" <note>Latin: "Hircina"</note> because they give off the smell of a goat. However, they are by no means *Tragium*, for that does not smell of a goat.

---

### SMALLEST GOATISH BURNET-SAXIFRAGE: Tragus's Crisped Pimpinella.
<note>original: "Pimpinella Saxifragia Hircina Minima: Pimpinella crispa Tragi"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the smallest variety, with very fine, feathery, or "crisped" foliage.</image-desc>

In *root, stem, flower, seed, smell*, and *taste*, it is plainly similar to the one just mentioned, differing from it only by this one name: that it has *leaflets* very minutely dissected and serrated: so much so that it can hardly be distinguished from *Carum* <note>Caraway</note>, and could scarcely be believed to be a Pimpinella, unless the root is tasted.

It grows in the same places as the Lesser: namely in stony mountains, and especially in the fissures of rocks and old walls and ruins. It prevails with the same medicinal powers as that one.

Fuchs, Turner, and Camerarius describe the Lesser Pimpinella: the same Camerarius and the *History of Lyon* call it *Lesser Burnet-saxifrage*: the same Camerarius and Gesner call it *Lesser Saxifrage*: Cordus calls it *Daucus Selinoides*: Tragus calls it *Crisped Pimpinella*. More on the Burnet-saxifrages in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### GREATER BURNET SANGUISORBA: German: Gross Welsch Pimpernell; French: Grande Pimpinelle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pimpinella Sanguisorba Maior, showing a tall plant with distinct globular flower heads rather than flat umbels.</image-desc>

In its whole appearance, this agrees with the *Lesser Burnet Sanguisorba*, of which we shall speak soon: but the *leaves*, which are nine or eleven attached to one rib, are more than twice as large, emulating the leaves of Betony, deeply serrated, smooth, and with the same smell and taste as the lesser. The *stems* indeed rise from fibrous roots to two cubits and higher. The *little flowers* come forth from an oblong *head* in an umbel <note>here referring to the cluster</note>, blood-red, chestnut-colored, four-petaled, with tips of the same color.

Clusius calls it the Pimpinella of the Italians and French, and the *Sanguisorba* of the Germans. It loves rich, muddy, and marshy places, and also grows in other gardens: it flowers in June and July.

<summary>This page details the botanical characteristics and nomenclature of Sison and various species of Pimpinella (Burnet-saxifrage), distinguishing them by their leaf structure, scent, and habitat. It highlights the "Goatish" varieties named for their scent and provides synonyms from contemporary botanists like Fuchs, Gesner, and Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>Sison, Amomum, Pimpinella, Burnet-saxifrage, Sanguisorba, botany, medicinal herbs, Basel, Montbéliard, Dodoens, Dioscorides, taxonomy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on umbelliferous plants (those with umbrella-like flower clusters) and their medicinal varieties, following the previous descriptions of herbs.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### Small Burnet Saxifrage: Germ. *Small Foreign Pimpernel*: French *Small Pimpinelle*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pimpinella plant with small serrated leaves and rounded flower heads on long stalks.</image-desc>

It is called by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> the *Small Pimpinella of the Italians and French*, and the *Blood-sorrel of the Germans*: and by some the *Small Hairy Pimpinella*.

It is found on the drier and rougher borders of fields: and in cultivated fields and open plains, as well as in rocky, rough, elevated places. It is also cultivated in gardens, and propagates itself by fallen seed, flowering in May.

It is kept in the more cultivated gardens of Ferrara, Padua, Lyon, and Basel: at Basel it grows wild near the Birs river and in the meadows: it is accustomed to break forth abundantly almost everywhere in shady places without cultivation. *Regarding its use and powers, see the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### Alexanders: Germ. *Smyrnen, Myrrh-Herb*: French *Smyrnium*: Ital. *Smyrnio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Smyrnium plant with broad, lobed leaves and umbel-shaped flower clusters.</image-desc>

Shining with a cheerful greenness, it produces bright and polished shields <note>referring to the leaf shape</note>, a foot long, fixed on a long stalk; these are divided at certain intervals into opposite wings, and these again into others, quite deeply notched and sufficiently thick: these indeed grow forth immediately from the root. For those which are beneath the branchings of the stems depart immensely from this form, being of an almost circular roundness, in the manner of "through-leafed" plants <note>perfoliate, where the stem appears to pierce the leaf</note>, pierced through by the stem, an inch and a half or two inches wide, and sometimes doubled, one placed upon the other. It has the umbels <note>flower clusters</note> of Dill or Thorough-wax, with whitish flowers. The seed is dark and somewhat round. The root is fragrant, sharp, soft, and juicy. *More in the Appendix.*

---

### Macerone (Black Lovage): Germ. *Great Smallage*: French *Great Parsley, Macero*: Ital. *Macerone*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Macerone plant with large, broad leaves and a thick, tapering root.</image-desc>

It rests upon a thick root, white inside and out, fragrant, sharp, and somewhat bitter. It puts forth stems a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, stuffed, branched, furrowed, and somewhat reddish: the leaves are like Marsh Celery, but larger and dark green. The flowers are composed in an umbel of five or six greenish-white leaflets, with as many tips of the same color. The seed is thick, black, and angular.

It grows in cemeteries and everywhere in gardens near stone walls, in shady and rich soil. It provides the same benefits as Celery: and its leaves, stems, and roots are eaten both raw and cooked. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### Silphium or Laserwort, Maspetum, Magydaris, Altith & Aniuden, Laser, Asafoetida.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Silphium plant with deeply lobed, fern-like leaves and a large umbel of flowers.</image-desc>

Silphium, according to the accounts of Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny, grows in Syria, Armenia, Media, and Libya. The root is large and thick: the stem is like Giant Fennel: the leaves are like Celery: the seed is broad and leaf-like. Some have called the stem *Silphium*, the root *Magydaris*, and the leaves *Maspeta*.

It is indeed called *Aniuden* by the Arabs, and in the writings of Serapion, the leaf of the tree is called *Asse*, and its gum is called *Altith*, and the root *Maharot*.

We depict here the Silphium or Laserwort which is found in the region of Marseille, and is usually brought from there: which Rondeletius thought agreed better with the Laserwort of the Ancients than any other of the many Giant Fennels he had seen. We saw this ourselves in Paris in the garden of Robin <note>Jean Robin, herbalist to the French kings</note>.

---

### A narrow-leafed plant similar to the Marseille Laserwort.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to Laserpitium with narrower, more delicate foliage.</image-desc>

We saw this in the same garden, and nowhere else: and we know of no mention made of it by any writers.

However, since it is very difficult to determine from the quite confused and obscure history of Silphium among the Ancients which plant today can properly be called *Laserpitium*, some have wanted common Lovage to be Silphium; others make *Angelica* the French Laserwort: by others *Masterwort* is called the Laserwort of Cesalpino, and by others Macerone is held to be Laserwort: but they all wander in great error. We have shown the Marseille Laserwort of Pena and Lobel in the preceding table.

Furthermore, Dioscorides says the juice of Silphium is the most effective, then the leaves, and lastly the stem. *More in the appendix.*

<column-break/>

### Masterwort: Germ. *Meistervourts*: French *Ostruth & Imperatoire*: Ital. *Imperatoria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Imperatoria plant with broad, serrated leaflets and a thick, fibrous root system.</image-desc>

The root is a thumb's thickness, wrinkled, and endowed with lateral fibers by which it propagates itself. It is driven obliquely through the top of the earth, with white flesh, aromatic, and vehemently sharp. The leaves are mostly joined in threes, like Macerone but sharper and rigid: each of these is divided again into three serrated segments, sometimes lightly and sometimes more deeply. The stems reach a height of a cubit or a cubit and a half, furrowed, hollow, and divided into wings: the umbel of white flowers is broad, like that of Myrrh: the seed is almost white like Dill, full, and somewhat broad.

It grows spontaneously in various mountainous places, especially in Italy and Austria: and is commonly cultivated in gardens, and flowers in June. The root is long-lived and easily endures the winter.

<summary>This page describes several umbelliferous plants including Small Burnet, Alexanders, and the mysterious Silphium (Laserwort), noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and the confusion among ancient and contemporary scholars regarding their identification. It highlights the medicinal and culinary uses of these herbs, such as Masterwort and Macerone.</summary>
<keywords>Pimpinella, Smyrnium, Macerone, Silphium, Laserpitium, Masterwort, botany, herbal medicine, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Pliny, Renaissance gardens</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of plants (Stirpium), specifically focusing on the Masterwort and Angelica families. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, blending physical description with medicinal properties and geographical origins.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### ALPINE MASTERWORT: The lesser Masterwort of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Imperatoria Alpina plant, showing its broad, serrated leaves and a tall stalk topped with an umbel of flowers. To the left, smaller details of the flower and seed are shown.</image-desc>

In all its parts it is smaller than the preceding one: in other respects it is similar to it, but with a sharper and more burning taste, and thus superior to it in all its medicinal powers. Some call it the *male Masterwort*.

Furthermore, Masterwort <note>original: "Imperatoria"</note> was so named because of the rare and excellent powers with which it is endowed <note>The name implies "Imperial" or "Commanding" power over diseases</note>: and almost everyone retains that name. Brunfels, Gesner, and Dodoens write it as *Astrantia* in Latin. Camerarius and others call it *Magistrantia*. Some call it *Astrantium, Astericium, Asteritum, Ostricium, and Osteritium*; Cordus calls it *Struthium*; Dodoens (in French) and Lonicer call it *Ostrutium*.

The root heats in the third degree and dries in the second: it dissipates wind <note>flatulence</note> of the stomach and intestines; etc. More in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### ANGELICA: German: Breast-wort, Angel-wort; Belgian: Angelica; French: Angelique; Italian: Angelica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Angelica plant, featuring large, compound leaves and a thick, ribbed stem leading to a large flowering umbel.</image-desc>

The plant is two cubits high <note>about three feet</note>, and sometimes taller: with a jointed, striated, pale, gray, reed-like stem provided with many "wings" <note>leaf sheaths</note>. It puts forth very large, soft, greenish leaves, notched around the edges, of varying shape as chance brings them, yet always oblong, but unequal with much swelling, sometimes continuous and sometimes divided. The flowers in the umbels are whitish: the seeds are yellowish, flat, broad, and membrane-like. The root is thick and long, divided into many branches, with the skin being a reddish-gray, but the pulp is white, with a sharp and bitter taste, and a very sweet aromatic scent. Indeed, an oily liquid exudes from it, fatty and of the same scent which the leaves themselves and the shoots exhale.

Angelica is distinguished into the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*, and both into the *Greater* and the *Lesser*.

---

### ANGELICA OF THE SHOPS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Angelica Officinarum, showing the thick, branched root system and the base of the plant's stem.</image-desc>

It consists of many thin, long, and black fibers from one head, in the manner of White Hellebore.

Furthermore, Domestic and Cultivated Angelica grows in the same places as the Wild; it loves the higher mountains and cold ridges. If it is cultivated in gardens, as we have observed it cultivated in various places—Florence, Lyon, Geneva, and Basel—and as we ourselves had it at Montbéliard in the Princely garden, it first comes forth with leaves like Parsley <note>original: "Petroselinaceis"</note>, and only in the second or third year does it send out a stem. It flowers in June and July.

Herbalists commonly record it as *Angelica, Cultivated Angelica, Garden Angelica, Greater Angelica, and Moderate Angelica*.

<column-break/>

### COMMON WILD ANGELICA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Angelica Sylvestris, showing the plant with its characteristic umbel and pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

Wild Angelica has many characteristics in common with the cultivated variety: so much so that it is not difficult to recognize from it, only everything in this one is smaller. But the taste is no less vigorous, though also less sweet, while the scent is equally strong. Furthermore, it is by no means *Libanotis*, as Cordus established in his Dispensatory. Moreover, it is distinguished by its place of birth into mountain, wild, and aquatic varieties.

All Wild Angelica enjoys cold, marshy, and meadow-like places. At Basel it abounds on the mountains *Montats* and *Wasserfall*; at Geneva near the Rhone; at Nuremberg around the city in marshy places, and it even grows in the shady spots of gardens. It flowers in August.

---

### CREEPING WILD ANGELICA: AND Hairy, Scentless Wild Angelica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Angelica, showing a creeping root system and smaller umbels.</image-desc>

This one has a thin, striated, reddish, hollow stem, concave at the wings: the root is thin and fibrous, creeping far and wide. The leaves are like Angelica but smaller and dark green. The umbel is also like Angelica, but smaller. The seeds are oblong, striated, joined together in pairs.

We have seen this flowering in June in the gardens of Padua, Lyon, and Geneva; at Basel by the river Birs, and elsewhere.

Caspar Bauhin mentions a Hairy Wild Angelica which was sent from Lusatia <note>A region in Eastern Germany/Poland</note> as *Podagraria* <note>Gout-weed</note>: that one, as well as the creeping variety, is less scented.

Botanists assign a heating and drying power in the third degree to Angelica: it opens, thins, disperses, and is uniquely opposed to poisons; etc.

<column-break/>

### ARCHANGELICA: German: Norwegian & Pomeranian Angelica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Archangelica plant, showing its robust structure and large flowering head.</image-desc>

It has leaves much larger than the cultivated variety, dark green, broad, spread on the ground, bluish-gray on the underside, and red at the first sprouting. The stem is concave with many wings, the height of a man, and reddish at the beginning. In the broad umbel are yellowish flowers, and a leaf-like seed, larger and rounder than cultivated Angelica. The root is deep-set and little scented. They assert it was made a resident in Belgium from Norway: so says Lobelius.

Some also record it as *Scandinavian Angelica* and *Norwegian Archangelica*; Lobelius, Dodoens, Clusius, Castor, the *History of Lyon*, and Camerarius call it *Archangelica*; Schwenckfeld calls it *Greatest Angelica*. More concerning Angelica in the Appendix.

<keywords>Masterwort, Angelica, Archangelica, botany, medicinal herbs, umbellifers, European flora, pharmacology</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### LIGUSTICUM OR LIBYSTICUM.
<note>Commonly known today as Lovage.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ligusticum plant showing a thick, branched root system, serrated leaves, and a tall stalk ending in an umbel of flowers.</image-desc>

Ligusticum, according to the report of Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, grows most abundantly in Liguria <note>A region of North-West Italy</note>, from which it also took its name: specifically on the mountain called the Apennines which borders the Alps. The inhabitants there call it "Panaces" <note>A "panacea" or all-healing herb</note> not without reason, since it is similar to the Heracleotic Panax in both root and stalk, and is endowed with equal powers. It is produced in the highest, rugged, and shady mountains: especially around ditches and trenches. Thus says Pliny: *Ligusticum*, he says, *is preserved in the mountains of Liguria: some call it Panax.* Galen <note>An influential Roman-era Greek physician</note> called it *Libysticum* by the change of a single letter.

However, the plant we depict here is labeled by some as *Ligusticum with leaves of Angelica*, and is called by Matthiolus *the second Ligusticum*.

<column-break/>

### THE SECOND LIGUSTICUM OF THE BELGIANS, WITH LEAVES almost like Wormwood, according to Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second variety of Ligusticum with more finely divided, feathery leaves and a single flowering umbel.</image-desc>

Rue-like leaves, or rather approaching the leaves of shrubby Wormwood, surround a stalk a cubit or a cubit and a half high <note>About 18 to 27 inches</note>. The umbels <note>Flower clusters</note> are equal to the umbels of Cretan Smyrnium. The seed is round and somewhat aromatic.

This not inelegant plant was first discovered by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish botanist</note> on the most pleasant hills of Turin near the currents of the River Po, and thereafter began to be kept and nourished in more cultivated gardens.

There is furthermore a certain plant called the *Greater Ligusticum*, which some label as the *Greater Masterwort with a yellow flower*.

---

### RAUWOLF’S LIGUSTICUM, WITH LEAVES of Columbine.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, lobed leaves resembling Aquilegia (columbine) and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Caspar Bauhin describes this at length in his *Phytopinax* and both there and in his *Prodromos*, he labeled it as *Broad-leaved Libanotis with a Columbine leaf*, or form.

This is how Dioscorides describes his own Ligusticum. It produces, he says, a thin stalk like Dill, jointed, around which are leaves like Melilot, but thinner and fragrant, more slender near the top, and with many incisions. At the summit is an umbel, from which hangs a black, solid, oblong seed, very close to Fennel, sharp to the taste and smelling of spice. The root is white, similar to Heracleotic Panax and fragrant. He adds that the power of the seed and root is warming and aids digestion.

<column-break/>

### THE LEVISTICUM OF THE APOTHECARIES, LIGUSTICUM in French: *Leuesche*: called *Hipposelinum* by some.
<note>This is the common garden Lovage.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Levisticum (Lovage) showing large, compound leaves and a robust flowering structure.</image-desc>

It has a stalk exceeding the height of a man, thick, jointed, hollow, and furrowed. The leaves are like Marsh Celery, a foot long or larger, divided into wings. The branches bear large umbels of yellow flowers. The seed is rather large and compressed. The root is thick and wrinkled.

It loves rich and moist places, and flowers in Summer. We have seen it in gardens, and nowhere else.

And this is that plant which Ruellius calls the *Levisticum* of the Apothecaries: and he denies, not without reason, that it is the *Ligusticum* of the Ancients.

Brunfels, Cornarius, Tragus and others also called it *Levisticum*, who by a great error confuse it with the *Ligusticum* of Dioscorides and Galen.

---

### SISER, SISAR, SISARUM: in German: *Gerlin, Gierlin*: in French: *Escheruis, Giroles*: to the Italians: *Sisaro*.
<note>Commonly known as Skirret, a root vegetable.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Siser (Skirret) plant with pinnate leaves and a cluster of elongated tuberous roots.</image-desc>

Today, the name of the *Sisar* of the Ancients is given to various plants by various people: the *Thin-leaved Parsnip* properly called *Carrot*; the *Wild Parsnip of the Greeks*; the *German Wild Parsnip*; the *Cultivated Broad-leaved German Parsnip*; *Rampion*; and finally this one which we depict here.

Dioscorides does not describe *Siser*, as if it were well known. He only says it is known: and that the cooked root is pleasing to the mouth and beneficial to the stomach, and stirs up urine, and provokes an appetite for food: to which Galen adds that it warms in the second degree. Pliny makes a double *Siler* <note>likely a typo for Siser</note> when he says: *The wild Siser is similar to the cultivated, etc.*

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER BETTER IMAGE OF THE SISER.

<image-desc>A more detailed woodcut illustration of the Siser plant, emphasizing the structure of the roots and the umbel flowers.</image-desc>

The preceding image is from our purchased stock, but this one is better.

Many roots hang from one head, glandular, thin and fragile, wrinkled, covered with a thin and pale skin, with white flesh, the thickness of a finger, some a foot long, others smaller, with a sweet, pleasing, and somewhat aromatic flavor. The stalk rises a cubit and a half high, single, jointed, and furrowed. The leaves are arranged in a wing-like pattern, like *Daucus* <note>Carrot</note>, but smaller, thinner, pointed, and notched with small teeth around the edge. The umbels of yellowish flowers turn white: producing seed like Parsley.

It is commonly cultivated in gardens, and is known by its roots rather than its seed. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various species of Ligusticum (Lovage) and Siser (Skirret), focusing on their physical characteristics, medicinal properties for digestion, and the historical confusion regarding their naming among ancient and Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Lovage, Skirret, Ligusticum, Siser, Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany, root vegetables, digestive health</keywords>

--- Page 474 ---
### HOGWEED OR SPONDYLIUM.
### Greater Spondylium: known to some as Hercules’ All-heal.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spondylium (Hogweed) plant, showing large pinnate leaves, a thick ridged stem, and a broad compound umbel of flowers. A separate detail of the seed is shown to the right.</image-desc>

Hogweed, according to the opinion of Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, <gloss>namely</gloss> has leaves somewhat similar to the Plane tree, and approaching the shape of the leaves of All-heal; the stalks, however, are a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note> and resemble Fennel. The seed at the top approaches that of Hartwort, but is broader, whiter, and has a heavy odor. The flowers are white, and the <gloss>root</gloss> is likewise white, resembling a Radish. It grows in marshy and watery places.

In place of the ancient Hogweed, some present Angelica, others Bear's Breech, of which more shortly. And since Hogweed varies by reason of its location, size, and leaf shape, the one we depict here has obtained the name *Greater Spondylium*, and is inscribed by some as *Hercules’ All-heal* <note>original: "Panax Heracleum"</note>.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE HOGWEED OR SPONDYLIUM, smooth, of Caspar Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Alpine Spondylium, similar in structure to the previous but with slightly different leaf margins and a more slender habit.</image-desc>

It has a thick <gloss>and</gloss> white root; a stalk two cubits high, jointed; leaves like those of a Fig tree, smooth, and notched along the margin. At the top of the <gloss>root</gloss> <note>likely referring to the main stem arising from the root</note> sits an umbel of white <gloss>little flowers</gloss>; the <gloss>seed</gloss> is somewhat round and flat, with a pointed tip fixed at the top.

Caspar Bauhin, the author of this description, saw it only on the <term>Wasserfall</term> <note>Waterfall</note> mountain near Basel; he also mentions a Small Alpine Hogweed and a Curled Hogweed.

Furthermore, on the authority of Dioscorides and Pliny, the seed of Hogweed has a sharp and drying power. Taken as a drink, it draws out phlegm through the bowels, and also heals those suffering from liver complaints, asthma, epilepsy, and the "royal disease" <note>Jaundice</note>. The root is beneficial for the same things, etc.

---

### SILAUS OR SILAUM TO SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Silaus plant, featuring finely divided, fern-like foliage and multiple umbels of small flowers.</image-desc>

Of Silaus, as far as we know, only Pliny makes mention, who in Book 26, Chapter 8, records that Silaus grows by gravelly and perennial streams, a cubit high, with a resemblance to Celery. It is cooked, indeed, like a sour vegetable, with great benefit to the bladder.

The plant is a cubit or a cubit and a half high, with a smooth, furrowed stalk that is hollow at the "wings" <note>the leaf axils</note>. The flowers are in umbels, whitish, which are followed by seeds joined in pairs, humped, furrowed, and with an aromatic, wine-like taste. The leaves are large, minutely divided, with incisions almost like <term>Mountain Siler</term> <note>Laserpitium siler, a mountain herb</note>, and have a sharp taste. The root is long, a finger's thickness, dark on the outside, white within, tufted near the ground, divided into several heads, and endowed with an aromatic flavor.

It grows in meadows and damp places, and is also cultivated in gardens; it flowers in June and July.

<column-break/>

### ENGLISH SAXIFRAGE, SIMILAR TO SILAUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of English Saxifrage, showing upright stems with umbels and deeply incised leaves.</image-desc>

Because of its excellent gift for breaking stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, the English have named this plant Saxifrage <note>literally "stone-breaker"</note>; it is familiar with damp places. It has leaves broader than Fennel, but smaller than Meadow Hartwort. The root is fragrant, black on the outside, white within, with the appearance of Sulphur-wort. The *flowers* in the umbels are white; the *seed* is like Fennel; the stalk is a cubit or a cubit and a half high.

Lobelius, the author of the description, calls it *English Saxifrage, with the appearance of the Meadow Hartwort of Montpellier*. In the *Flora of Lyon* it is called *Umbelliferous English Saxifrage*.

It is hot in the third degree and dry in the second: it has the power of opening, thinning, dispersing, and dissolving, which same faculties Silaus also possesses.

---

### ANTHRISCUS OF SOME, WITH ROUGH, bristly seed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Anthriscus (Chervil), showing hairy stems and small umbels of flowers, with a detailed view of the bristly seed.</image-desc>

The stalk is a cubit and a half high, hairy, rough, and jointed. The leaves are those of common Chervil, but hairy. The small umbels are whitish. The seed is equal to Coriander, and bristly like the Bur-parsley, rough, furrowed, double, blackish, and somewhat bitter. The root is white, scented, and aromatic, in the manner of the Wild Parsnip. It abounds at Montbéliard in hedges and near <term>la Crose</term>, flowering in July and producing seeds in August.

Is it the Greater <term>Drucoides</term> of Cordus? Or the <term>Gingidium</term> of Caesalpinus? Gesner in his *Gardens* calls it a small, somewhat rough kind of Carrot, growing around hedges and walls, and of no use.

<column-break/>

### A BEAUTIFUL KIND OF EXOTIC PEA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an exotic pea plant with broad leaves and a large, round seed pod or fruit shown at the base.</image-desc>

These items found at the bottom of this page and on the next were almost of a different kind and were being reserved for the Appendix. However, this gap had to be filled, which was caused by our absence from the printers. We thought this should be mentioned, lest this displacement <note>original: "Metastasis"</note> be turned into a fault against us.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of exotic legumes, specifically focusing on varieties of peas and beans from the Americas, Africa, and Asia.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SCARLET AMERICAN PEA, OR Black, called ABRUS by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a climbing plant with pinnate leaves and clusters of small pea-like pods. To the right of the plant are individual seeds, some showing a dark spot (hilum).</image-desc>

The Scarlet American Pea is smaller than our native variety, oblong and rounded in the manner of the seeds of the female Peony <note>The Peony (Paeonia) was often used as a size and shape reference in early botany</note>, shining, and wonderfully hard. It is covered by a skin that is either entirely black or two-colored, such that the area of the germ <note>The hilum or "eye" of the seed</note> is blackish, while the rest either shines with a cheerful dark luster or is stained with a more common reddish-brown color. The inner meat is remarkably hard, split in two, yellowish, and has the flavor of a legume. We also have some that are entirely black, and others of a reddish-brown color marked only with a black spot.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE SCARLET AMERICAN PEA, by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a similar leguminous plant with more detailed seed pods and larger pinnate leaves. Below the plant are three individual seeds.</image-desc>

A kind of Pea brought from the New World: called by Lobel in his *Observations and Icons* the *Scarlet American Pea*; by Caesalpinus the *female Red Sandalwood*; by Alpinus the *Red Bean*, called *Abrus*; by Camerarius in his garden, the *Indian Bean*, commonly known as the *Small Indian Peony*, noted as *Ginge* and *Abrus*; in the *History of Lyon*, the *Indian American Pea*; by C. Bauhin in his *Pinax*, the *Scarlet Indian Pea*, a type of bean which the Egyptians call *Abrus*.

According to Alpinus, they have the taste of beans, and the Egyptians are accustomed to eating them after they have been boiled in broth.

---

<column-break/>

### WHITE GUINEA PEA, OR INDIAN CHICKPEAS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing several rounded seeds (chickpeas) and a cross-section of a seed below.</image-desc>

Of these, some are equal to our native chickpeas and peas, others are larger, somewhat oblong from a rounded shape, with a smooth and shining surface of a single color, yellowish, except that the germ is white, with a small band—sometimes diagonal, sometimes straight, and now wider, now narrower—of a paler yellow. The flavor is the same as our native peas, as is the consistency.

<column-break/>

### Various species of INDIAN AND EXOTIC PEAS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of six large, oval-shaped seeds or beans, showing different orientations and surface textures.</image-desc>

The Scarlet American Pea, of which Prosper Alpinus spoke previously, is the fruit of a shrubby, leavened <note>original: "fermentosa," likely referring to the plant's vigorous growth or pulpy nature</note> tree, a climber (*Lablab*) creeping in the manner of a vine, raising itself higher and spreading itself wider. It has leaves clearly similar to those of the Tamarind, but much smaller, which move toward the Sun and close when it sets; its flowers are very close to the flowers of the Bean. He says that it produces small, round, red, hard seeds in pods, which clearly rival Coral.

But he improperly calls a "Tree" a plant which he writes creeps in the manner of a climber, and he depicts it ridiculously twisting about.

---

<column-break/>

### BRAZILIAN OR AMERICAN BEAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bean plant with large trifoliate leaves and pods. Several dark, rounded beans are shown at the base.</image-desc>

Throughout the island of Madagascar, and even in China, as reported by Linschoten, a certain kind of bean grows which is called *Conduci* by the Malays, *Saga* by the Javanese, and *Abrus* in Latin. These are very elegant, small, round, and marked with a black spot. He says they use them only for weights <note>Rosary peas were historically used as standard weights for gold and gems due to their uniform mass</note>, not for food; for they have an extremely bitter taste and are even believed to be poisonous.

<column-break/>

### Another Image of the BRAZILIAN OR AMERICAN BEAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another bean variety with broad leaves and hanging pods. Two dark seeds are illustrated at the bottom.</image-desc>

We have frequently planted exotic seeds of this kind, as well as the so-called scarlet peas, at Montbéliard in the Prince's garden; but they did not germinate, and the following year we found them intact. This is not surprising, since they are of a truly unconquerable hardness. For this reason, on account of their elegant shape and color, they are pierced with silk thread and, with small pearls placed between them, are hung from the neck like a necklace and worn on the arms in place of bracelets.

Furthermore, the items contained on this page belong to CLASS XVII, and they should be referred to that place as their proper location.

<summary>This page describes various exotic legumes, primarily the "Abrus" or Rosary Pea, noting its physical characteristics, its use as jewelry and weights, and its difficulty to cultivate in European climates.</summary>
<keywords>Abrus precatorius, Rosary Pea, American botany, Prosper Alpinus, Linschoten, Madagascar, medicinal plants, botanical illustration, seed weights</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of umbelliferous plants (those with umbrella-like flower clusters), focusing on water-parsleys and the deadly hemlock family. It maintains the structure of comparing ancient descriptions from Dioscorides and Pliny with contemporary 16th-century observations.</meta>

# PLANTS

### WATER-PARSLEY, WATER CELERY: German: *Wasser Eppich*; French: *Ache d'eau, Berle*; Italian: *Crescione*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Water-parsley plant, showing its upright stem, pinnate leaves with serrated edges, and umbel flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Water-parsley <note>original: "Sion aquaticum"</note>, according to the account of Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, is found in waters; it is a small, upright, and succulent shrub which has broad leaves, etc.

We depict here the variety called *Umbel-bearing*, which almost everyone considers to be the *Sion* of Dioscorides. Its root consists of long-haired, downward-reaching fibers; the leaves are similar to those of the German Parsnip, but less wrinkled, attached in a feathered pattern <note>term: pinnatim (pinnate) — leaves arranged like a feather on either side of a stem</note> to a long, hollow, smooth, and ribbed stalk, with other smaller leaves existing on the stem. The stems are like Fennel, ribbed, hollow, and branched. The flowers are similarly tiny, clustered in umbrellas, white, like those of Parsley, with several narrow leaflets situated at the base of the umbrella. The seed is small, fragrant, and sharp.

### GREAT BROAD-LEAVED WATER-PARSNIP, German: *Groß Wasser Pastinach*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Great Broad-leaved Water-parsnip, featuring a thicker stem, larger pinnate leaves, and a broad flowering umbel.</image-desc>

In its roots, leaves, stems, flowers, and seeds, it is similar to the "Medium" variety, except it is twice as large, and a stronger smell of bitumen <note>a mineral-like, tarry scent</note> is detected.

We found this between Worms and Oppenheim, in a place called *Alt Rhein* <note>The "Old Rhine"</note>, where the water of the Rhine flows back. We have observed the so-called "Medium" variety in various places, likewise near still waters, ponds, and ditches. But the "Umbel-bearing" kind we saw in the waters of Montpellier (where they call it *Berla*) and Padua; at Geneva between the Bridge of Arve and Lancy; and in the ditches of the city of Montbéliard.

Furthermore, all Water-parsley <note>original: "Sium"</note> dispels swelling, provokes urine, promotes menstruation, and breaks up and expels kidney stones. More on this in the *Appendix*.

### HEMLOCK: COMMON HEMLOCK: German: *Schirling*; French: *Ciguë, Cocue*; Italian: *Cicuta*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Common Hemlock, showing its characteristic finely divided, fern-like foliage and umbel flowers.</image-desc>

It is so similar to Cow Parsley <note>original: "Myrrhidi"</note> that the similarity is often dangerous to those gathering it, as they do not distinguish them accurately enough: for the root is no different, nor the stem, nor the leaf. The umbrella of flowers is similarly white, and the seed is like Anise, ribbed, and a dark green.

Thus we read in Dioscorides and Pliny that Hemlock is similar to *Cow Parsley* in its stem and leaves. But this plant differs from that one, most especially by its poisonous smell, by which it testifies to its own destructiveness.

It abounds everywhere around villages and towns, in shady and rich soils, and near ditches, mounds of fields, and the fences of meadows. It flowers in July, and is seen heavy with seed in August.

<column-break/>

### MEDIUM WATER-PARSLEY: German: *Wasser Peterlin*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Medium Water-parsley plant, showing its root system, stem, and umbel flowers.</image-desc>

Cæsalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino, an Italian botanist</note> recognizes two kinds of Umbel-bearing Water-parsley: one with a weak stem, the other with a thicker stem; he calls them *Crescione* and *Herba canilla*.

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus, a famous German herbalist</note> makes four species in the genus of Water-parsley, and names our "Umbel-bearing" one as the first and smaller kind, writing that Dioscorides and Pliny mentioned it. For us, there are three kinds of Water-parsley: the Umbel-bearing, the Medium (which we depict here), and the Great, of which we speak next.

In its stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds, this Medium Water-parsley is similar to the Umbel-bearing kind; however, each part is much larger, and the smell is less pleasant. Regarding the location and medicinal powers of this and the preceding plant, see the following sections.

### GESNER’S WATER HEMLOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Water Hemlock, showing its thick, jointed stem and spreading umbels.</image-desc>

The name "Sium" is attributed to various plants: to the aforementioned species, to the Water Dropwort, to the Fine-leaved Water Dropwort, to another Water Pimpernel of Tragus, to Whorled Mint, and to *Gesner’s Water Hemlock* <note>named after Conrad Gesner, the Swiss naturalist</note> which we depict here.

The root is a thumb’s thickness and gradually tapers, hairy with many fibers. The stem is one to two cubits <note>about 1.5 to 3 feet</note> high, thick, ribbed, smooth, jointed, and hollow. The leaves are attached to long stalks, with the division of Mountain Laserwort, but with longer and sharper segments, saw-toothed around the edges. The flowers are white, like Parsley, arranged in a wider umbrella.

It grows naturally around marshes, on the edges of swamps, and in perennial streams.

### WILD CHERVIL: German: *Wilder Körffel, Kerbel Kern*; French: *Persil d'âne* <note>literally "Donkey's Parsley"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Wild Chervil, showing its root and delicate, parsley-like foliage.</image-desc>

The root is thick, long, white, gifted with many side-roots, and has a sharp and aromatic taste. The stems are a cubit high, hollow, hairy, somewhat reddish, and channeled. The leaves are very close to those of Hemlock, but broader, shining, and fragrant. The flowers in the umbrellas are white. The seed is like Chervil or Dill.

It abounds everywhere in meadows planted with trees, and flowers in May. Many of the learned consider this to be the "Legitimate Myrrh." Furthermore, the whole plant recently called *tombaca* <note>likely a local folk name</note> perishes. It remains green in winter, with its leaves spread out upon the ground. More on these in the *Appendix*.

<summary>This page describes various species of water-parsleys and hemlocks, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe, and medicinal properties while warning of the deadly similarity between Hemlock and edible herbs.</summary>
<keywords>Water-parsley, Hemlock, Water Hemlock, Wild Chervil, Dioscorides, Pliny, Gesner, medicinal herbs, botany, poisonous plants, European flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of umbelliferous plants (those with umbrella-like flower clusters), focusing on various species of Wild Hemlock and related medicinal herbs. ### WILD HEMLOCK WITH CELERY LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cicutaria plant with finely divided, celery-like leaves and a small umbel of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

The root is small in proportion to the plant, and white. The stem is about three feet high <note>original: "bicubitalis," referring to two cubits</note>, nearly the thickness of the pinky finger, divided by long joints, hollow, and fluted with a reddish-green color; however, it is not spotted like the True Hemlock <note>The author distinguishes this from Conium maculatum, which has characteristic purple spots</note>. The leaves and flowers resemble Hemlock, but it has no scent. The seeds are paired, similar to Hemlock, and channeled.

It grows abundantly in some vegetable gardens along with Parsley <note>original: "Petroselino"</note>, of which it is considered a contaminant.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY BROAD-LEAVED WILD HEMLOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed, hairy Cicutaria plant with serrated leaflets and a developing flower head.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various places: Geneva, Zurich, and elsewhere; and we frequently encountered it on the highest ridges of the Solothurn mountains.

Is this the *Cough-remedy* <note>original: "Ptysipharmon"</note> of Cordus in his History? Or the *Second Myrrh* of Lobelius in his Adversaria? Or perhaps the *Silaus of Pliny* described by Caesalpinus, a herb growing in streams? Or his *White Alpine Wild Hemlock*? Camerarius calls it, not inaptly, *Wild Spignel with Hemlock leaves*; Gesner calls it *Water Seseli*.

<column-break/>

### FRAGRANT AND BULBOUS WILD HEMLOCK:
->Called "Peperlin" by the Austrians.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous Cicutaria plant showing a thick, tuberous root system and delicate, fern-like foliage.</image-desc>

Having found this near Entzheim in Alsace toward Mulhouse, we transplanted it to Montbéliard, where it grew for us in the garden of the Most Serene Prince <note>original: "S. P. horto," likely referring to the Duke of Württemberg's botanical garden</note>, sprouting a stem and dying back every year, and propagating itself by dropped seed. It flowers in June.

Camerarius calls this chestnut-bulbed plant *Hemlock-leaf* <note>original: "coniophyllon"</note>; Clusius calls it *Pannonian Wild Hemlock*. Clusius describes it at length and says that in early Spring, the roots with their young leaves are found for sale in the markets of Vienna, where they are eaten as a first course with oil, vinegar, and salt; for this reason, the Hungarians call it *Magyaro salata* <note>Hungarian Salad</note>.

<column-break/>

### GREAT STINKING WILD HEMLOCK.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, robust Cicutaria plant with broad, divided leaves and a thick, segmented stem.</image-desc>

The stem is the height of a man and four fingers thick. The leaves, seed, and root are far larger than those of the Peloponnesian Seseli. It is celebrated by "bedside women" <note>original: "Clinicis mulieribus," likely referring to midwives or folk healers</note> for inducing various discharges. Thus says Clusius, for whom this is *Thapsia I*.

In his Observations and Icons, Lobelius calls it *Brancion's Great Wild Hemlock*; he asks whether it is the *Thapsia of Salamanca*, commonly called *Canahria*, or rather the *Great Stinking Wild Hemlock*?

<column-break/>

### THE PHELLANDRIUM OF PLINY (ACCORDING TO SOME):
->By others called WATER HEMLOCK.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an aquatic Phellandrium plant with a dense root mass and multiple umbels of flowers.</image-desc>

It loves the water, rising above it to a height of three feet or more. The stem is a thumb's width, or sometimes even a span thick; it is fluted, hollow, marked by joints, and divided into various branches. The leaves are about nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantalia"</note>, more or less, with the division of Chervil, and are nearly smooth. The flower clusters on the branches are small in proportion to the plant, consisting of tiny white flowers with small, dark red tips in the center. The seeds are small, oblong, and fluted, possessing no hairiness or roughness. From the lowest joints, it occasionally sends down long, numerous hair-like fibers, by which it takes root at the bottom.

It delights in marshy places and is found everywhere in ditches and trenches. It flowers in June and July. More details are in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### THAPSIA WITH THE APPEARANCE OF CARROT:
French: Grey Turbith; Italian: Thassia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thapsia plant with carrot-like foliage and a thick, tapering taproot.</image-desc>

The pharmacies have considered this Carrot-like Thapsia to be the true Thapsia; but although the root is similar to it, it differs in the appearance of the leaves, which in the true Thapsia resemble Giant Fennel <note>original: "Ferulae"</note>, and it is far removed from the description given by Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>.

Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax*, calls it *Thapsia 2 with Carrot leaf*, and he doubts (as does Lobelius) whether it is the Sagapenum-bearing Fennel. He writes, however, that some use the root of this plant in place of Turbith <note>A medicinal purgative</note>. Others label it *Thapsia*, *True Thapsia*, and *Turbith of Mount Gargano*.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince.

# OF PLANTS

### BROAD-LEAVED THAPSIA WITH YELLOW FLOWERS AND BROAD SEEDS, according to Clusius: similar to the Peloponnesian Seseli of Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thapsia latifolia plant, showing broad leaves, a thick stalk, and an umbel of flowers/seeds.</image-desc>

Clusius labels this as the first Thapsia <note>original: "Thapsiam I."</note>, and he also mentions a second, third, and fourth variety. He states that this first kind, which we depict here, delights in rocky hills and is found in many high, uncultivated places in Portugal and Spain.

It blooms in August. Those who use it in place of Turbith <note>A medicinal root used as a purgative; the author warns that substituting Thapsia for it is a dangerous mistake due to Thapsia's toxicity.</note> commit a great error.

<column-break/>

### THE THAPSIA OF SOME, WITH HEMLOCK-LIKE LEAVES: to others, Peloponnesian Seseli.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thapsia variety with finer, hemlock-like foliage and a prominent root system.</image-desc>

The stalk is a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or higher, like Giant Fennel <note>original: "Ferulaceo"</note>, rounded, spongy inside, and branched with many arms. The leaves are somewhat similar to Hemlock leaves, rather thick, hairy, rough, and jagged, arranged in opposite wings. The flower cluster is broad and yellow. The seed is large, split at the ends, and oblong-round. The root is about a span and a half long <note>roughly 12 inches</note>, thick, solid, blackish on the outside and white within, with a bitter, sharp, and aromatic taste, and hairy toward the ground.

It grows in the mountains around Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausum"</note> and blooms in the month of May.

---

<column-break/>

### SESELI, OR MOUNTAIN SILER: German: *Waldt Kummel*; French: *Sermontain*; Italian: *Siler montano*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Seseli montanum, featuring deeply divided leaves and a large flowering umbel.</image-desc>

The stalk of the Mountain Siler exceeds the height of a man. The leaf stalks, a span or a span and a half long, embrace the main stem and branches like a loose sheath. The leaves themselves are divided into opposite wings; the furthest segments are usually in threes, similar to the leaves of the Bean-Trefoil <note>original: "Cytisi Tragi"</note>, oblong, somewhat broad, with a slightly blunt tip. The flower clusters are large and white. The seed is large, striped with a leafy fringe, oblong, and has a sharp, somewhat bitter flavor. The root is large, ending in a tuft at the top of the stalk, wrinkled, and a finger's breadth in thickness.

It grows abundantly on many mountains, especially in marshy places; it blooms in June and July, when the seed ripens. More details are provided alongside the following figures.

<column-break/>

### SHRUBBY ETHIOPIAN SESELI, WITH HONEYSUCKLE-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Seseli aethiopicum, showing a woodier stem and distinct leaf shapes.</image-desc>

It grows as a shrub with several branches a cubit or more in height, which are stiff, woody, covered in a blackish bark, and divided into many small twigs. Along the branches are leaves like those of Honeysuckle <note>original: "Periclymeni"</note>, but narrower, slightly pointed, shorter than Spurge Laurel, smooth, and with a taste and smell like Fennel <note>original: "Foeniculaceæ"</note>, but much milder and more pleasant. The flower cluster is beautiful. When the yellowish flowers fall, they bear an oblong, channeled seed, the size of Fennel seeds.

Belon is the authority that it is evergreen near the rocky Salo where it grows wild. We have the testimony of Dodoens and Lobelius that it is found in profusion in various rocky and coastal places in Mediterranean France <note>original: "Gallia Narbonensis"</note>, blooming in July and August.

---

<column-break/>

### THE PELOPONNESIAN SESELI OF MATTHIOLI, OR the *Cicuraria* of some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Seseli peloponnense with dense, feathery foliage and a thick root.</image-desc>

Lobelius describes this plant thus: "The entire plant," he says, "as soon as it is touched even slightly, exhales a poison." The root is thick, and in its whole appearance it somewhat resembles the scented Sweet Cicely <note>original: "Myrrhidi odoratæ"</note>, but the leaves are broader, longer, and darker. The seed is also shorter. The stalk is branched with wings, reaching a length of one and a half to two cubits.

Matthioli, Lacuna, and Lonicer label this as Peloponnesian Seseli; but who, I ask, would believe that the foul smell of this plant matches the Peloponnesian Seseli described by Dioscorides? <note>The author is questioning the accuracy of the identification based on ancient Greek texts.</note>

We have seen it at Zurich in the garden of Gesner.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE OR MOUNTAIN SESELI I of Clusius, with shining leaves and small white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Seseli alpinum, showing a basal rosette of leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It has large leaves spread on the ground, divided into many wings, green and shining on the upper side, but not at all on the underside, with the smell of Giant Fennel and a sharp taste. The stalk is a cubit and a half long, thick, striped, spongy inside, and produces knotted branches from each joint. The ends of the branches finish in large clusters of whitish flowers, with a scent almost like Elderberry. The flower is followed by a twin seed, striped and yellowish, with an aromatic and burning taste. The root is thick and black on the outside.

It grows on the ridges of the Alps where the pastures are more lush; it blooms in June and ripens its seed in August.

Furthermore, the seed of Mountain Siler heats and dries in the third degree <note>A reference to Galenic medicine, where "degrees" measured the potency of a plant's "humoral" qualities.</note>; it promotes urine and menstruation, aids digestion, and dispels gas. The root is effective for the same purposes, but less powerfully.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### II. MOUNTAIN SESELI OF HUNGARY, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Seseli plant with a thick, dark, scaly root, a tall striated stem, and large umbels of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

We consider that this plant of ours can be referred to the Mountain Seseli II of Hungary described by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational Flemish botanist</note>. He describes it thus: It rests, he says, on a root sometimes the length of a forearm, covered with a thick, wrinkled, and black bark. At the very top, it abounds in many hairy heads, from which emerge large and quite ample leaf-wings, consisting of several leaves serrated around the edges and somewhat incised, attached to a single rib but growing opposite one another. Between these emerges a stem a cubit and a half high <note>about 27 inches</note>, channeled, a thumb's thickness, jointed, and divided into several branches; smaller leaf-wings surround it at each node. The top of the stem and the ends of the branches are adorned with umbels of pale flowers, which are succeeded by seeds similar to the seeds of Mountain Siler <note>Laserwort</note>.

### OENANTHE, OR DROPWORT, of Montpellier, with Celery-like leaves.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of an Oenanthe plant showing tuberous roots hanging from long filaments and finely divided leaves resembling celery.</image-desc>

Just as with the more common *Oenanthe*, or Dropwort, so too this one has glandular roots hanging from long threads (from which they take their name <note>original: "Filipendula," meaning "hanging by a thread"</note>), propagating more abundantly than others, covered in a blackish skin, white inside, with a pleasant and sweet taste. The leaves vary greatly; at first germination they are broad, soon taking on the appearance of common Parsley, and finally the form of Hog’s Fennel. The several stems are bluish-gray, angular, channeled, a cubit or a cubit and a half tall, with many hollow wings. The flowers in the umbel are mossy, very small, turning from white to purple. The seeds are like the aforementioned Parsley, but longer and having a sort of little head.

We saw it blooming near Montpellier in June.

### WATER OENANTHE OR WATER DROPWORT: German: Water Saxifrage.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of an aquatic Oenanthe with bulbous roots and delicate, feathery foliage.</image-desc>

Several olive-shaped little bulbs hang from thin threads. The stem is a cubit to a cubit and a half in height, channeled, hollow, branched, and jointed. The lower leaves are more sparingly divided, the rest cut into longer and thinner segments. The umbels are small and white; the seed is oblong, divided as if into two points.

It loves water, and grows near ditches and streams, and in wetter meadows.

As it resembles *Sium* <note>Water Parsnip</note> in smell and taste, so also in its powers and temperament: for it is hot and dry, and provokes urine.

<column-break/>

### OENANTHE, DROPWORT: German: Red Saxifrage; French: Filipende; Italian: Filipendula.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Filipendula plant with numerous small tubers attached to the root system and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The name *Oenanthe* <note>literally "wine-flower" in Greek</note> is ambiguous for many things: for sometimes it denotes the flower of the Wild Vine; sometimes the domestic vine; sometimes the wild flowers of another; sometimes Lily of the Valley; and sometimes Dropwort, which is the subject here.

According to the authors Dioscorides and Pliny, *Oenanthe* has leaves like a Parsnip, white flowers, an upright stem a palm high, seed like Orache, and a large root having many round heads. It grows among rocks.

We have observed it in various places, in rough, mountainous, dry, and rocky areas; it also occurs in gardens in Padua, Lyon, and elsewhere, as we have seen. It is in flower during June and July.

### OENANTHE OR DROPWORT with Carrot-like leaves and a beautifully channeled stem.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of an Oenanthe with leaves resembling Staphylinus (Wild Carrot) and a distinctly striated stem.</image-desc>

The umbel of this plant is prepared with very dense, whitish, tufted flowers. It was sent to us from the Paduan garden. It may be the thin-leaved *Oenanthe* of Tabernaemontanus; the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" by Dalechamps</note> calls it the second *Oenanthe* of Matthiolus.

Furthermore, it is evident that Dropwort, and especially its root, is hot and dry, as well as opening and cleansing, and that it expels urine and stones. According to Dioscorides, the seed, stems, and leaves are drunk in wine to expel the afterbirth; the root with wine is also useful for the "dripping of urine" <note>strangury</note> and the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>. Some have written that in its qualities it comes very close to the Peony.

### SPANISH OENANTHE OF MYCONUS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Spanish Oenanthe with a basal rosette of leaves and a tall, branched flowering stem.</image-desc>

The learned Myconus, a physician of Barcelona, increased the number of types of *Oenanthe* by sending this one from Spain, which was previously very little known.

Born in mountains and rocky places, this plant spreads its leaves on the ground near the root; they are small, incised, smooth, approaching the leaves of Coriander, and hanging from long stalks. The stems are a cubit high, reddish from the bottom, surrounded by few joints, rounded, smooth, slightly channeled, and somewhat hollow. At the top of these, the flowers hang as if in an umbel, white, consisting of five small petals, mossy in the middle; when these perish, the seed matures in small vessels or pods. *History of Lyon*.

<summary>This page describes various species of Seseli and Oenanthe (Dropwort), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in France, Italy, and Spain, and their medicinal uses for urinary and reproductive health.</summary>
<keywords>Seseli, Oenanthe, Dropwort, Filipendula, Clusius, Dioscorides, Myconus, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, diuretic, jaundice</keywords>

# PLANTS

### POISONOUS WATER DROPWORT, with the appearance of Hemlock, according to Lobel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Oenanthe (Water Dropwort) showing a thick cluster of tuberous roots, bipinnate leaves, and several umbels of small flowers.</image-desc>

The roots of this plant are divided into many parts like the bulbs of an Asphodel <note>Asphodelus: a common Mediterranean lily-like plant</note>, and are almost branched, without any connecting fibers or intervals. They push forth stems two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> high, which are tender, sharp and unpleasant to the taste, and full of a milky, poisonous juice <note>original: "succóque lacteo & viroso"</note>. The leaves resemble Meadow Rue, with a foul smell, and have the appearance and color of Hemlock. The flower-umbels also resemble Hemlock, to which those who claim to have experienced its harmful effects assert it is closely related.

It grows in the streams of northern regions, and in muddy and watery places.

<column-break/>

### SAMPHIRE OR SEA FENNEL: German: *Meer Fenchel*: French: *Bassille, Feneuil marin*: Italian: *Finocchio marino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Crithmum (Rock Samphire) showing fleshy, segmented leaves and terminal umbels.</image-desc>

Samphire <term>Crithmum: from the Greek 'krithmon'</term>, according to the author Dioscorides, is a shrubby herb, leafy on all sides, reaching nearly a cubit in height. It grows in stony and maritime places. It is filled with thick, whitish leaves, similar to Purslane leaves, though wider and longer, and salty to the taste. It has white flowers and a fruit like that of the Frankincense-herb <note>Libanotis</note>, soft, fragrant, and round, which splits apart when dried, containing a seed inside like Wheat. The roots are the thickness of a finger, numbering three or four, fragrant and pleasant.

It grows in maritime and rocky places, and is frequently seen all along the coast surrounding Italy; from there we have also seen it transplanted into gardens in Montpellier, Lyon, and elsewhere. More details are in the Appendix.

---

### MATTHIOLI’S UMBELLIFEROUS SAMPHIRE: Land Samphire: German: *Suchel-kraut, acker Bacillen*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Crithmum Matthioli showing a long, creeping rhizome and upright stems with finely divided leaves and umbels.</image-desc>

This plant is troublesome due to its creeping roots; for they are very long, and even if the smallest fiber is left behind, they come back to life. They are quite thick and white. The leaves are divided into three, four, or more or fewer segments, half an inch wide and long, and saw-toothed all around. The stem is like Fennel, striped, solid, knotted, and very branched. The umbels are quite large, composed of very small white flowers. The seed is slender, somewhat long, sharp, and fragrant.

Lobel writes that this has no similarity to the Samphire of the Ancients, but he wrongly calls it *Eryngium* <note>Sea Holly</note>.

It grows in fields and blooms in June and July. It is very common near Basel between St. John’s Gate and the village of Hunningen. It heats, dries, opens <note>refers to opening blockages in the body</note>, and aids digestion.

<column-break/>

### PERFOLIATE: German: *Durchwachs*: French: *Percefeuille*: Italian: *Perfoliata*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Perfoliata (Hare's Ear) showing the stem passing through the center of the circular leaves (perfoliate).</image-desc>

It has a single root nearly a thumb’s thickness, hairy with a few fibers, with the flavor of a Rampion. The stem is a cubit or a cubit and a half high, smooth, round, striped, jointed, hollow, and divided into many "wings" <note>branches</note>, striking the nostrils with an aromatic scent when broken. The leaves are somewhat long but rounded, sea-green, smooth, and hairless; the stem or branch passes through the middle of them <note>hence the name "Perfoliata" or "through-leaf"</note>. The ends of the small branches break into several stalks, bearing three or five small pointed leaves, among which shine tiny yellow umbel-flowers, or flowers resting on individual stalks, like those of Lady's Mantle <note>Alchimilla</note>. These are followed by a dark, oblong seed, sharper at one end. It blooms in July and August. More in the following section. Other species of *Siseleos* <note>Seseli</note> were discussed previously in this same Class.

---

### PERFOLIATE WITH LONGER LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Perfoliata with more elongated leaves and spreading habit.</image-desc>

This has an annual life cycle, like the Common variety preceding it. It does not push its stems upward, but puts out branched, cubit-long stems scattered across the ground, numerous and as if interrupted by joints. The leaves, which the stem passes through, are slightly longer and more pointed than the Common variety, gifted with five or seven veins running along their length. The flowers are yellow. They are similar to "Hare's Ears" <note>a common name for Bupleurum</note>. The root is thin and slender, with many smaller roots attached.

In some places, these Perfoliates grow spontaneously in plowed fields, among the crops, and also in meadows and near the edges of fields. They are also sown in gardens and bloom in August.

<column-break/>

### GREAT LONG-LEAVED ALPINE PERFOLIATE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alpine Perfoliata showing large, broad leaves clasping the stem and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

The Alpine Perfoliate is larger and gifted with larger leaves; these are oblong, a palm's breadth or wider, which also pass through the stem, or at least clasp the stem with the "wings" of their fins. The flower is small and yellow, surrounded by round leaves. The seed is oblong and striped, larger than that of the common Perfoliate. The roots are thick and perennial. It blooms in June.

Furthermore, Perfoliate is moderately warm and a little more dry, somewhat bitter and astringent. The leaves boiled in wine, or ground into powder, are recommended for ruptures <note>hernias</note>, for those who have fallen from a height, and for the "ranices" <note>likely swellings or sores</note> of children.

<summary>This page describes various umbelliferous plants, including the toxic Water Dropwort, the coastal Samphire, and several varieties of Perfoliate (Hare's Ear), noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses for injuries and digestion.</summary>
<keywords>Water Dropwort, Samphire, Sea Fennel, Perfoliata, Hare's Ear, Lobelius, Dioscorides, medicinal herbs, botany, Basel, alpine flora</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
**Fff**

### SMALLER PERFOLIATE WITH GRASSY LEAVES. HARE’S EAR, OX-STINGER, HARE’S LITTLE EAR: The stiffer Hare’s Ear.
<note>original: "PERFOLIATA MINOR... BVPLEVRVM, BVPRESTIS, AVRICVLA LEPORIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, grass-like leaves and small umbels of flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

It has a somewhat thick root, tufted toward the earth, from which several stems sprout, ranging from a span to a foot or a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height; these are rounded and channeled. Along the stems are sharp leaves, clasping the stem with a broader base, one or two inches long and about half an inch wide; others, however, are grass-like, even longer than a span, and as wide as a stalk. The umbels consist of unequal clusters of tiny yellow flowers, protected by a rampart of round leaves.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader, lance-shaped leaves and more complex flower clusters, showing the root system.</image-desc>

Intending to set forth several varieties of Hare’s Ear, we depict here the one whose leaf is larger, thicker, stiffer, and more veined; which Dalechampius <note>Jacques Daléchamps, a 16th-century French physician and botanist</note> describes thus: "It is seen," he says, "with a long, stiff, somewhat broad leaf, ending in a narrow point at the top, almost lance-shaped, distinguished by many stripes, somewhat concave and bent inward, from which it takes the name Hare’s Ear. The stem is tall, jointed, and divided into branches in the upper part. The umbels at the summit have tiny, scattered, yellowish flowers; the seed is oblong, like Anise or Dill."

Dodoens, Lobelius, and others <note>famous Renaissance botanists</note> record this as the "other broad-leaved Bupleurum." We shall discuss *Bupleurum* and *Buprestis* <note>Ox-stinger</note> further in the Appendix.

---

### YELLOW-UMBelled HARE’S EAR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with alternating leaves clasping the stem and a terminal cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

The root is small, wrinkled, somewhat greenish, fibrous, and sharp in taste. The stem is thin, rounded, smooth, channeled, provided with frequent joints, hollow inside, one or two cubits high, with many concave branches, sometimes reddish in color, other times green. The leaves, especially those on the stems, are somewhat long and narrow, provided with several veins along their length. The flowers are like Fennel, yellow, in an umbel that is less yellow; these are succeeded by a sharp seed like Parsley.

Most authors record this as the "narrow-leaved Bupleurum."

It grows abundantly on many hills and flowers in July and August. It is plentiful around Basel near the Mill and the Birs River, and around Mount Kreutzach, and at Montbéliard near Arbehans.

<column-break/>

### A RELATIVE OF HARE’S EAR, the yellow TOOTH-WORT of Valerandus and Dalechampius.
<note>original: "AVRICVLÆ LEPORIS AFFINIS ODONTITIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy plant with many small leaves and numerous small flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rests upon a hard, woody, and whitish single root; from which several small stalks immediately rise, about nine inches or a little more in height, similar to *Bupleurum*, divided into many branches. The leaves are disordered, like Toadflax. The tiny flowers are yellow, like Perfoliate, surrounded by a rampart of oblong and sharp leaves. The seed is almost similar to the Knotgrass of Tragus.

It delights in damp places, and is abundant at Montpellier on the slopes around Castelnau.

Dalechampius wrote that if anyone rinses the mouth with a decoction of it, the torment of teeth <note>toothaches</note> is soothed.

---

### SMALLEST HARE’S EAR.

This is a small plant, a foot or a cubit high, which rises from a small, white, hard, and woody root provided with a few tiny fibers. It sends up slender, rounded stalks, branched like arms from bottom to top into many small twigs, ending in what look like small umbels. These consist of tiny, thin, and somewhat stiff leaflets; in their center, three or four channeled seeds project from very short stalks, resembling common Parsley. Each individual leaf at the bottom is pointed and endowed with four veins along its length. We have not seen the flower.

We have found it occasionally at Basel between the Birs and the Woods on the way to Augst.

<column-break/>

### INDIAN NARD: German: *Indianischer Nardus*; French: *Aspic d'outre mer*; Italian: *Spico Nardo*.
<note>This is Spikenard, a famous aromatic oil source from the Himalayas.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the fibrous, hairy root structure of Spikenard (Nardus Indica).</image-desc>

Today, only a small part of the plant retains the name "Indian Nard," which also deserves to be called a "Spike" because of its shape. It is, however, nothing other than the head of the root's foliage, gathered from the tangled fibrous filaments of withered leaves, reddish in color, bitter in taste, and with a sharp and aromatic scent, stronger than Celtic Spikenard. This "hair" is attached to a root the thickness of a finger, of a deeper red, solid but brittle. There are places where the leaves are also found, not yet torn into fibers, appearing whitish. Small hollow, channeled stems and several spikes from the same hairy root are occasionally seen. We depict the common Indian Nard here, about which we say more in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Hare's Ear" (Bupleurum), noting their physical characteristics and medicinal uses for toothaches, concluding with a description of the exotic aromatic Spikenard.</summary>
<keywords>Hare's Ear, Bupleurum, Tooth-wort, Spikenard, Nardus Indica, medicinal plants, Basel, Montpellier, botany, Renaissance science</keywords>
