### CELTIC NARD: German: *Celtischer Nardus*; French: *Nardus Gaulois*; Italian: *Nardo Celtico*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Celtic Nard, showing a small plant with fibrous roots, narrow leaves, and small flower clusters at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

Celtic Nard, as Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> notes, grows in the Ligurian Alps, but it also occurs in Istria. It is truly a tiny and short shrub, which is gathered along with its roots into hand-sized bundles; it has oblong, yellowish leaves and a yellow flower. Only the stems and roots are used, and they possess a sweetness of scent.

The same Dioscorides says it is also called *Alsungia*. Most learned men believe it was called *Saliunca* by Pliny, although it seemed otherwise to the Commentator from Siena <note>Likely referring to Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist born in Siena.</note>. The apothecary shops call it Roman Spike, Celtic Spike, and Celtic or Gallic Nard.

It grows abundantly in the Alps that divide Germany from Italy; it delights in the mountainous regions of Genoa and the barren Ligurian Alps. It flowers in August. *More on this in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### NEAPOLITAN NARD OR SALIUNCA, Mountain Nard.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Mountain Nard, featuring a thicker, more robust root system and broader, lance-shaped leaves compared to the previous specimen.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is quite thick in proportion to its size, very wrinkled, yellowish, topped with fibers, and rising in nodes. From the sides of these nodes come forth oblong, narrow leaves, somewhat resembling Plantain, narrower at the bottom and wider at the top; the whole plant resembles Valerian in its sharp taste and smell.

Some believe this to be one and the same as the "Scented Leaf" and *Malabathrum* <note>An aromatic leaf from India, often cinnamon-leaf.</note>; but it is established that they are in error, because those plants are peculiar to India.

However, Dioscorides writes that Mountain Nard, called *Thylacitis* and *Nerin*, grows in Cilicia and Syria, with leaves and stems similar to Eryngo <note>Sea Holly</note>, and black, fragrant roots. It has the same powers as the Celtic variety, according to Galen, Paulus, and Aetius <note>Authorities of ancient and Byzantine medicine.</note>.

---

### PHU: VALERIAN, WILD NARD: German: *Baldrian*; French: *Valeriane*; Italian: *Valeriana*.

<image-desc>Large woodcut of Wild Valerian (Phu), showing a tall plant with divided leaves and a large cluster of flowers at the top, with a thick, fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Whether the Great Valerian which we depict here is the first and most noble *Phu* <note>original: "Phu" - the ancient Greek name for Valerian</note> of the Ancients or not, has been doubted by Anguillara and Camerarius in his garden; and Fabio Colonna openly denies it, concluding it to be Wild Valerian. On the other hand, almost all other learned men hold the affirmative view.

It raises stems two cubits <note>About 3 feet</note> or higher, which are hollow, jointed, and provided with "wings" <note>leafy appendages along the stem</note>. Some leaves are whole, others are deeply cut in the manner of Lesser Centaury, with no remarkable smell or taste. The flowers in their cluster are sweet-smelling, turning from white to purplish. The seed flies away with a certain downy fluff. The root is a finger thick, whitish, provided with many fibers, and has an aromatic taste and smell.

It is found in high, wooded mountains and is cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST NARD-LEAVED VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut of the smallest nard-leaved Valerian, a smaller variety with narrow leaves and a single flower cluster.</image-desc>

The roots of this small herb have the fragrant scent of Celtic Nard; they are thin, coming from a slanted, hairy head, from which emerge leaves an inch long, oblong, approaching the leaves of Plantain or rather Celtic Nard. Between these rises a single, thin little stalk, about a palm's breadth high.

Is this the "Lesser Apulian Phu" of Tabernaemontanus? Or the "Alpine Rock Wild Valerian" in Clusius's *History*?

Furthermore, the root of *Phu* or Valerian is hot and dry in the second degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine regarding the intensity of a plant's "humoral" properties.</note>: it opens, thins, digests, and provokes <insert>menstruation</insert>. When drunk, it drives out wind <note>gas</note> and helps with pains in the side. It is also excellent against difficulty in urinating and asthma. It is added to drinks for internal wounds and to Antidotes, so that it may be mixed into Theriac and Mithridatium <note>Famous complex ancient "universal" cures.</note>.

---

### BROAD-LEAVED RED VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut of broad-leaved red Valerian, showing broad leaves and dense flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rests on a root about the size of a finger and is almost woody. From this rise stems a cubit and a half high, rounded, smooth, blue-grey, and hollow. At each joint are two opposite leaves, embracing the stem from a wide base and ending in a point, occasionally provided with some jagged edges; they are fleshy and pale green, with a somewhat sharp taste. The flowers hang in clusters, very crowded, pleasant, purplish, extending a little horn like a spur. The seed is downy.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Prince; and it flowered in June and July. Lobelius named it *Ocimastrum Valerianthon*; it is depicted by Dodoens in French as *Polemonium*, and called *Lychnis rubra* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED RED VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut of narrow-leaved red Valerian, similar to the previous but with significantly narrower leaves.</image-desc>

It is similar to the broad-leaved Red Valerian, especially regarding the flowers provided with a spur, which are a pleasant red and turn into down. The stem is also similar; but the leaves seen along it differ greatly, for they are almost a palm in length, but only the width of a stalk.

We found this at Annecy in Savoy, on the slope outside the gate by which one goes to Geneva, flowering in July.

It is also called *Lychnis rubra* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*.

<keywords>Celtic Nard, Valerian, Phu, Saliunca, medicinal roots, Alpine flora, Dioscorides, botanical classification, herbal medicine</keywords>

### IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### BULBOUS VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana bulbosa showing a plant with broad, lobed basal leaves, a central stalk with smaller opposite leaves, and a terminal cluster of flowers. The root system shows a distinct bulbous structure.</image-desc>

This plant, called *Bulbous Valerian* by us, has not been described by anyone else as far as we know. It first puts forth leaves that rival those of White Henbane, but are a little smaller. However, the subsequent leaves are deeply divided. The flowers are like those of the Great Valerian. The root is unique, bulbous, and smells of Nard <note>Nard or Spikenard is an aromatic essential oil used in ancient perfumes and medicine</note>. It is very similar to Mountain Nard in both form and scent; for this reason, some classify it among the species of Nard.

It is an inhabitant of the mountains of Liguria <note>A coastal region of north-western Italy</note>.

<column-break/>

### TUBEROUS VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana tuberosa featuring a tall flowering stalk with pinnate leaves and a dense terminal inflorescence. The root system consists of several elongated tubers.</image-desc>

This plant has been described by no one else, as far as we are aware, except by Imperato <note>Ferrante Imperato (1550–1625), a Neapolitan apothecary and natural historian</note>. It produces leaves very similar in appearance to the leaves of the Lesser Valerian, but thicker. The flowers are white, like the Great Valerian, and somewhat fragrant. The scent of the tuberous root resembles Nard.

It grows in the mountains of Liguria.

---

### ALPINE VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana alpina showing a plant with heart-shaped or rounded basal leaves on long petioles, and a flowering stalk with smaller, narrower leaves ending in a cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

With a long, fragrant, and slightly sweet root, it fixes itself into the crevices of rocks, deeply embedded. It puts forth several rather thick, jointed stems with a resinous, somewhat sharp taste, which are slightly reddish. The lower leaves are indeed ivy-like, wavy-edged, sometimes increased by two "wings" <note>small leaflets at the base of the main leaf</note>, and attached to long stalks; the upper leaves, however, are oblong, pointed, jagged, and sometimes cut with multiple divisions right down to the midrib. The small flowers are arranged in an umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster</note>, many of them tiny and purplish.

We saw this growing at Genesius on Mount <term>Saleya</term> <note>likely Mont Salève near Geneva</note> flowering in June; and we also encountered it during our passage through the <term>Hercynian Forest</term> <note>The ancient and dense forest region of central Germany</note>.

<column-break/>

### LESSER VALERIAN, MEADOW OR WATER VARIETY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana minor showing a plant with a creeping rhizome, basal leaves that are mostly entire and rounded, and a flowering stalk with deeply lobed, pinnate leaves.</image-desc>

To proceed in describing the remaining differences of Valerian: besides those already presented, there is a certain kind called "Wild," and it is either large or small, and both are found either in meadows or near water. We depict the Lesser one here.

It creeps with a thin root which, where it touches the ground, takes root from fibers sent down from the joints; it has a bitter taste. The stem is about nine inches high, angular, streaked, hollow, and interrupted by several joints. The flowers in the umbel turn from white to reddish. Some leaves are whole, somewhat round, small, and on a long stalk; others are in opposite pairs without a stalk, jagged at the bottom and almost feathery, while the upper part is whole and oblong, with a somewhat bitter taste. In the Great Valerian, all parts are larger.

---

### GREAT WILD WATER VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana sylvestris magna aquatica showing a robust plant with large, deeply pinnate leaves and a tall, branching inflorescence at the top.</image-desc>

The root is composed of many white fibers, aromatic in taste, which propagate themselves by creeping. The stems rise to the height of a man; they are straight, hollow like a pipe, interrupted by long spaces between the joints, streaked, and moderately hairy. The leaves are like those of the Garden Valerian, but more feathery and a deeper green, and somewhat hairy on the underside. The flowers in the umbel are similar to the garden variety, five-petaled, turning from white to purplish, which eventually turn into downy seeds <note>pappos: the fluffy part of a seed that allows it to be carried by the wind</note>.

It grows everywhere in damp places and around water, and flowers in July and August; it sometimes rises to a wonderful height. We have seen it nowhere taller than at <term>Ebrodunum</term> <note>Yverdon-les-Bains, Switzerland</note> above the mill. It also grows in groves and woods managed for timber, but it does not emerge to such great height there.

<column-break/>

### FOREIGN OR INDIAN VALERIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Valeriana peregrina showing a plant with slender stems, deeply divided (laciniate) leaves, and small clusters of flowers at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

It rests on a thin, short, white root, hairy with many fibers and having an aromatic taste. The stem is generally spread out, nine inches long, smooth, hollow, rounded, and reddish. The leaves are situated in pairs opposite each other at the branching of the "wings" <note>the leaf axils</note>, approaching the leaves of the Broad-leaved Plantain; they are tender and succulent, with an aromatic taste, the upper ones being smaller and surrounded by small teeth. The flowers are arranged as if in an umbel, odorless, a pleasant red, like the Valerian-flowered Red Campion, but without the spurs; when these fall off, oblong small vessels succeed them, in which is a rather long seed.

This grew for us at <term>Montbéliard</term> <note>A city in eastern France</note> from seed sent from Florence; it flowers in July and August.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and habitats for six varieties of Valerian, noting their physical characteristics, root scents (often compared to Nard), and specific geographic locations where they were observed.</summary>
<keywords>Valerian, botany, Liguria, Alpine flora, medicinal herbs, Nard, Montbéliard, Yverdon, plant morphology</keywords>

# THE PLANTS: GREEK VALERIAN AND SOME CALL IT CARPESIUM.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of Valeriana Graeca, showing the plant with its fibrous root system, pinnate leaves along the stem, and clusters of small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

It creeps along with a small, thin, fibrous, whitish, and distinctly bitter root: raising straight stalks two cubits <note>about three feet</note> high, which are thin, hollow, somewhat angular, and hairy. Attached to these are leaf-stalks about six inches to a foot long, crowded with leaves like those of the Wild Valerian, but not at all toothed: they are dark green, slightly hairy underneath, and arranged in a beautiful winged series on both sides. At the top of the stalk and branches, many flowers burst forth in clusters, shaped like little bells: yet they are not one continuous piece, but composed of five small petals. They have a foul odor and are mostly blue in color, though sometimes white. From their center, besides a longer violet-colored three-parted style, there usually emerge stamens of the same color with saffron-yellow tips.

By Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician and botanist</note> in his French and Latin works, it is called *Foreign Phu* <note>original: "Phu peregrinum"; 'Phu' was an ancient name for Valerian</note>. By Lobelius in his *Adversaria*, *Observations*, and *Icons*, it is called *Foreign Valerian of the Belgians and Herbalists*. By Tabernaemontanus and Gerard, it is called *Greek Valerian*: by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, *Foreign Valerian with a blue flower, and more rarely white*.

We have seen it growing spontaneously in the forests of Rhaetia <note>a Roman province in the central Alps</note>: elsewhere it is common in the gardens of France, the Low Countries, and England, and it flowers for the greater part of the Summer. However, it has no medicinal use, except that it adorns the borders of gardens.

<column-break/>

Galen <note>the influential Greek physician of the 2nd century</note> mentions Carpesium in the 7th book of *On Simple Medicines*. In these words, he says: *Carpesium* is similar to what is called *Phu*, that is, Valerian, not only in taste but also in its medicinal properties; but it is more potent. Two kinds of it are found, one named *Laeticum*, the other *Pontic*, etc.

Dodoens is the authority for the claim that Avicenna <note>the Persian polymath</note> makes Galen's Carpesium to be *Cubebs* <note>a type of pepper</note>: and Matthaeus Sylvaticus, citing Serapion and the Arabs, says that *Cubebs* are nothing other than the Carpesium of Galen. Gesner considers Galen's Carpesium to be nothing other than *Rock Phu*, which we label *Alpine Valerian*.

Scaliger and Caesalpinus would have thought that the tiny shoots of Cloves were Carpesium, had not the same Galen recorded that it grows in Pontus and Pamphylia <note>regions in modern-day Turkey</note>.

Thus, what Galen's Carpesium actually is at this time is very difficult to explain, as Mattioli and Brassavola have skillfully noted; sometimes Galen suggests substituting Carpesium for *Asarum* <note>Wild Spikenard</note>. Furthermore, Quintus, in the works of the same Galen, uses Carpesium when Cinnamon is lacking, and finally Galen himself substituted it for *Phu* in his medicines.

# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXVIII.

->WHORLED PLANTS, AND THOSE BEARING HOODED FLOWERS: TO WHICH ARE RELATED MOST AROMATIC HERBS.<-

---

**MINT: German: *Müntz*: French: *Menthe*: Italian: *Mentha*: Arabic: *Nahanaha*.**

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a Mentha plant with a tall, upright flowering spike and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Regarding the different types of Mint and the true nature of its scent <note>original: "Etymosmos," referring to the essential fragrant quality</note>, we shall treat this generally in the Appendix. Here, however, we shall deal with Mint specifically, beginning with the **Curled Whorled Mint**, which we depict here.

This variety, like the other species, possesses a creeping root as well as square-shaped stems. In this particular plant, the stems exceed two cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches; the plant stands about 3 feet tall</note> and are rigid, upright, turning purple near the ground, hairy, and joined with many side-shoots. The fragrant leaves grow from the joints of the stems and branches; they are dark green, somewhat round, wrinkled, curled, saw-toothed around the edges, and either smooth or only slightly hairy. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils in whorls <note>circles around the stem</note>, resembling Pennyroyal, but fading into a pale blue. It is known in almost every garden.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER WHORLED MINT, POINTED, not curled, with the scent of Basil.**

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a smaller Mentha variety with pointed leaves and flowers clustered in the leaf axils.</image-desc>

The distinct and very sweet scent of Basil <note>original: "Ocymi"</note> and the flavor of Lemon Balm <note>original: "Melissæ"</note> easily distinguish this from the other species of Mint. Otherwise, its triple-creeping root habit is common to the others, as are the square, hairy, cubit-high, branched stems. The leaves, however, are at first similar to medium-sized Basil and somewhat hairy; later they become sharper and grow opposite one another from the joints. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils in whorls, tinted with a dilute purple.

Its powers are the same as the preceding plant. It consists of "thin parts" <note>a Galenic medical term meaning it is easily absorbed</note>, and it warms and dries in the second degree. It thins, digests, dissolves, opens, cuts <note>breaks down thick humors</note>, and stimulates. It expels wind and slippery humors, checks vomiting, etc.

---

**HAIRY WILD FIELD MINT. German: *Wild Poley, Veld Müntz*.**

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a wild mint variety with hairy stems and leaves.</image-desc>

Its place of birth gives the **Field Mint** its name, as it grows very frequently in fields, propagating itself far and wide by creeping, with square stems that are shaggy with white down and branched. The leaves are opposite, like those of Mattioli’s Wild Basil <note>original: "Clinopodii Matthioli"</note>, lightly notched around the edges, downy, and with a pleasant scent. It has the scent of Calamint and a somewhat sharp, not unpleasant taste. The flowers are whorled, smaller than those of Water Mint <note>original: "Menthæ Sisyimbricæ"</note>, reddish in color, and fading almost to white. The root is very much a creeping type.

Some call it *Mentha strum*, others Wild Pennyroyal, and others Field Calamint.

<column-break/>

**CURLED ROUND-LEAVED SPIKED MINT.**

<image-desc>Botanical woodcut of a mint variety with rounded, crinkled leaves and flowers arranged in terminal spikes.</image-desc>

The roots of this plant propagate by creeping. The stems are square, hairy, and reddish at the lowest part. The leaves grow opposite from the joints; they are curled, wrinkled, scarcely hairy, and saw-toothed, approaching the Whorled Mint in scent and flavor. However, the arrangement of the flowers is very different, since they are arranged in spikes of one to two inches long <note>original: "unciales & sextantales"</note>; yet the appearance or color of the individual small flowers is not different at all.

It is almost entirely a garden plant and flowers in August and September.

For recurring headaches, there are those who soak linen cloths, folded three or four times, in the water of this Mint and apply them to the temples.

<summary>This page provides botanical descriptions and medicinal uses for four varieties of mint, distinguishing them by their leaf shape, scent (such as Basil-scented), and flower arrangement.</summary>
<keywords>Mint, Mentha, herbal medicine, botany, headache remedies, aromatic herbs, whorled flowers</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### CULTIVATED SPIKED WILD MINT, with round, wrinkled leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mentha (mint) plant with upright flowering spikes and rounded, textured leaves, showing the root system.</image-desc>

It is cultivated in gardens, though eventually little liked by gardeners because of its hateful creeping <note>referring to the invasive nature of mint rhizomes</note>. It has more stems than the Spiked Curled Mint, and they are blacker, hairy, and softer than those of the Whorled Curled Mint. The flowers are arranged in spikes, very small, white, and of a pleasing scent.

Some call it *Garden Sisymbrium* <note>original: "Sisymbrium hortense"</note>, others *Sisymbrium Water Mint* <note>original: "Sisymbriam Mentham aquaticam"</note>.

There is also a Smaller kind of this genus.

<column-break/>

### CULTIVATED SPIKED WILD MINT, with a rounder curled leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mint variety with more pronounced crinkled (crisped) leaves and multiple flowering spikes.</image-desc>

Just like the others, the root of this one creeps: the stems are square, hairy, and somewhat reddish. The leaves are opposite, somewhat round, saw-toothed, and downy, playing marvelously with a variety of colors on the same plant: sometimes entirely white, sometimes fading from white into a grassy green; at other times half white and the other half green; at others variously spotted with both these colors. The scent is less heavy than the common Wild Mint; the taste is better than the curled variety, sharp but not unpleasant. The spiked flowers are whitish, with a sweet scent that is not overpowering.

This is kept in the more refined gardens: it grows successfully for us at Montbéliard in the garden of J. P. <note>Likely referring to Jean Bauhin's botanical associates</note>.

---

### WILD MINT WITH ROUNDER WRINKLED LEAF, wild-growing, with a spiked flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild mint plant with broad, rugose leaves and dense flowering spikes.</image-desc>

This has stems a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, quadrangular, and hairy. The leaves are placed at intervals on opposite sides in an alternating and cross-shaped order; they are notched, wrinkled, and covered in a downy hair. The flowers are numerous, spiked, and reddish-white: a small black seed follows them. The root is fibrous with many filaments and perennial. Indeed, the whole plant has a bitter, sharp, and astringent taste; and a heavy scent, much more unpleasant than the cultivated Mint.

We have seen it growing wild in many places: at Basel near St. Jacob by the river; at Geneva everywhere at Plainpalais; at Montpellier along the waters; and at Montbéliard on the road leading to the Mill.

<column-break/>

### SPIKED MINT, WITH A LONGER, sharp, smooth, and blacker leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mint plant with elongated, pointed, and smoother leaves compared to the previous specimens.</image-desc>

Not unlike other Mints, it propagates itself by the long creeping of its roots, with fibers sent down here and there. The stems are two cubits high, somewhat reddish, and square; from their nodes, at certain intervals, twin opposite branches emerge, so that the position of the lower ones is always cross-shaped in relation to the upper ones: such is also the alternation of the leaves both on the stems and on the branches. These are indeed oblong, sharp, dark green, very slightly hairy, and saw-toothed around the edges. The whorls of very small, whitish flowers, dotted with reddish points, form the shape of a spike in a somewhat long series.

Some label it *Roman Mint* <note>original: "Mentham Romanam"</note>. Others *Saracen Mint*, others *Heart Mint* <note>original: "Cardiacam"</note>, and Gerard calls it *Cross-mint* <note>original: "Crucigetam"</note>.

It abounds in gardens in Geneva, Padua, Basel, and many other places.

---

### SPIKED WILD MINT: German: *Wilde Müntz*; French: *Menthe Chevaline*; Italian: *Menta Selvatica*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild mint variety with lanceolate leaves and tapered flowering spikes.</image-desc>

It is two cubits high, with jointed, creeping, fibrous roots. The stems are square and entirely hairy: attached to their joints are oblong, pointed leaves, saw-toothed around the edges, turning white with soft down (especially on the lower part), with a fairly pleasing scent. The flowers fade from reddish to white.

It abounds in various places everywhere around streams; but nowhere more than at Montbéliard around the city, and at Yverdon on the road leading from Grandson.

It thins <note>humors</note>, opens, and cuts <note>phlegm</note>; spread on the ground or burned, it puts snakes to flight; the juice is dropped into the ears for earworms, and whether drunk or applied as an ointment, it inhibits nocturnal pollutions, etc.

<column-break/>

### WILD MINT, WITH A TUBEROUS ROOT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mint plant characterized by a thick, tuberous root system and whorled flowers.</image-desc>

It has stems a cubit high, quadrangular, straight, surrounded by frequent nodes, and somewhat hairy. The leaves are rather long, wrinkled, surrounding each node in an equal but opposite position. The highest branches, along with the outermost stem, end in soft, whitening spikes of small leaves; and little stalks are born in a grand manner in the fashion of whorls, from which come forth small white flowers, rivaling the flowers of Catmint <note>original: "Cattariæ Menthæ"</note>, which are followed by a small, black seed. The root is thick, succulent, almost equal to a Radish, somewhat dark on the outside, swelling out here and there at the sides into many small turnip-like shapes, and furthermore endowed with rather long fibers; it is perennial.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of spiked mints and wild mints (Menthastrum), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in European cities like Basel and Geneva, and medicinal uses such as treating earworms and repelling snakes.</summary>
<keywords>Mint, Menthastrum, botanical gardens, Montbéliard, medicinal herbs, Roman Mint, tuberous roots, taxonomy</keywords>

### WATER MINT; Aquatic Mint; Italian: Sisembro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mentha aquatica plant, showing its roots, square stems, serrated leaves, and whorled flower clusters.</image-desc>

From a creeping root provided with numerous fibers, several square stems emerge which are hairy, either hollow inside or stuffed with a spongy pith, and gifted with many "wings" <note>lateral branches</note>. The leaves grow in pairs from the joints, similar to the whorled Curled Mint, yet not at all curled, although they are serrated around the edges just like that variety, ending in a blunt point. They possess the powerful scent of Pennyroyal <note>original: "Pulegij"</note> and a color ranging from blackish to reddish. The flowers grow in whorls, a dilute purplish-red in color; the four-cleft calyx is moist, with small protruding stamens of a whitish color supporting reddish tips <note>anthers</note>.

It is a lover of wetter soil and a nursling of irrigation channels and damp places. Pliny says it grows most joyfully on the walls of wells and around fishponds and pools. Dioscorides claims it comes forth in uncultivated soil. Theophrastus (Book 4, Chapter 7 of *On the Causes of Plants*) notes it is known to be cultivated.

### A HAIRY KIND OF WILD WATER MINT, with a broader spike.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mentha aquatica variety with broader flower spikes and hairy leaves.</image-desc>

It puts forth square stems, two or three cubits <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> in height, which are hairy. The leaves are like those of the pointed-leaf Spiked Mint, oblong, serrated, and turning white underneath with much downy hair; the taste is sharp and burning, and the scent is that of Water Mint. The stalk of the stems is divided into three parts, and bears as many broadish spikes (not narrow, as in the Spiked Mints and Wild Mints), and not much longer than an inch: in which are purplish flowers, divided into five parts, emerging from hairy, striped, reddish calyxes that are split into five tips. The root is creeping.

We found this in <term>Joncherey</term> <note>original: "Ioncerey"</note>, a village two miles distant from <term>Montbéliard</term> <note>original: "Montbelgardo"</note>, on the bank of a river, flowering at the beginning of September.

### CAT MINT, or NEPETA: German: Katz Müntz: French: Herbe au chat: Italian: Gattaria.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Nepeta cataria (Catnip), showing its characteristic upright growth and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

From a woody root it raises a square, hairy stem two or three cubits high, reddish near the ground but otherwise hoary <note>gray-white</note>, jointed, and hollow with many wings, these always being two and opposite each other. In this same order (though not always in equal number) the leaves spring forth almost at the joints; they are heavily scented, like those of Balm <note>Melissa</note>, serrated around the edge, pointed, and budding with a hoary down, with a burning taste. The flowers surround the nodes in whorls, like Balm, whitish, with the "lip" <note>the lower petal</note> spotted with occasional dots. Dark tips <note>anthers</note> shine out from the "gaping mouth" of the flower, sitting upon whitish filaments.

It loves damp and marshy soil: and it grows around the edges of gardens, along embankments, ditches, and roads.

<column-break/>

### HAIRIER WATER MINT, OR Hairier Sisymbrium.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very hairy variety of water mint.</image-desc>

Not only the square stems and leaves, but even the calyxes of the flowers are covered with a thick downy hair, so much so that they appear white. The leaves are an inch or an inch and a half long, somewhat round, and lightly serrated around the edge: from the hollow where the leaf meets the stem, stalks emerge supporting flowers gathered in clusters rather than spikes.

Furthermore, Water Mint <note>original: "Sisymbrium"</note> is composed of "thin parts" <note>a Galenic medical term meaning it is easily absorbed</note>, having the power to disperse, warm, and dry. It moves the urine and expels stones if drunk with wine: it restrains vomiting, hiccups, griping pains, and "dissolutions" <note>weakness or upset</note> of the stomach. The leaves are smeared on the forehead and temples for headaches, and so applied they are useful against the stings of wasps and bees, and they wipe away freckles and the blackness of the skin caused by the sun.

### MOUNTAIN WILD MINT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain mint variety, showing branched stems and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rises with a stem a cubit or more high, quadrangular, full of pith, and consisting of many nodes: from which two small branches always arise opposite each other, similarly quadrangular. Around their extremities arise oblong spikes of flowers of a pleasant scent, whitish, similar to the flowers of the Wild Mint. The leaves surround the stem and branches at each node with opposite stalks; they are similar to the leaves of Wild Mint, but green, not whitish like those, yet of the same scent and taste. The hard and woody root spreads shoots from its sides, like other plants of its kind.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> found it growing spontaneously at the roots of the Austrian Alps, flowering in August.

### SPANISH CAT MINT, OR Foreign Nepeta.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Spanish variety of Catnip, showing more elongated leaves and dense flower spikes.</image-desc>

It rises with many straight stems, square, channeled, stuffed with spongy pith, smooth, three cubits high, with many hollow wings, divided into branches opposite one another. The leaves are like Wild Mint or common Catnip, but longer, wider than a thumb, smooth, dark green above, whitening below, wrinkled, serrated around the edge, with a heavy scent. At the joints, opposite each other, flowers grow from two stalks in thick whorls somewhat mimicking a spike; they are flesh-colored, and the bottom is spotted with deep red dots. The seeds are two or three, oblong and red. The taste of the leaves is unpleasant.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Water Mint, Catnip, and Wild Mint, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses such as treating stings and stomach ailments. It cites classical authorities like Pliny and Dioscorides alongside contemporary botanists like Clusius.</summary>
<keywords>Water Mint, Catnip, Nepeta, Sisymbrium, medicinal herbs, botany, Pliny, Dioscorides, Clusius, Joncherey, Montbéliard</keywords>

# OF PLANTS

### ANOTHER SPANISH CATNIP Illustration: with narrower leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mentha Cattaria (Catnip) plant with tall, spiked flower clusters and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This variety does not differ much from the preceding one, except almost entirely in its leaves, which are narrower.

It is called Catnip <note>original: "Mentha Cattaria"</note> because of the argument of a most pleasant spectacle: for as soon as a Cat has caught sight of it and smelled it, it will embrace it and kiss it intensely. In its playfulness, now approaching and now retreating, it acts as if the plant were a hindrance to its feet; after many marvelous gestures, it greedily licks the whole thing.

It warms considerably, says Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note>, dries, thins the humors, penetrates, promotes [circulation], and possesses all the faculties of Calamint, in whose place it can even be used. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that it is of exceptional prerogative for facilitating conception and rendering the womb prolific.

### MOUNTAIN CALAMINT, WITH A LARGE FLOWER from a large calyx.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Calamintha Montana showing a detailed root system, broad serrated leaves, and larger flowers emerging from prominent calyxes.</image-desc>

The leaves are opposite, resting on half-inch stalks, an inch and a half in length, and a little less in width; they are somewhat hairy and deeply serrated around the edges. From the crook of each leaf emerges a single half-inch stalk, bearing three or four flowers on their own individual stems; these are purplish with a wide opening, fringed an inch above a long, striated calyx <note>the protective outer layer of a flower</note>, from which they protrude in length. The root is much longer than in the common variety.

This Calamint is not commonly found except on the shady and rocky slopes of the Cévennes in Narbonne <note>Southern France</note>, and in the Roman and Paduan territories. It blooms in gardens in June. More on Calamint follows below and in the Appendix.

### CALAMINT WITH SMALL HOARY LEAF AND FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Calamintha variety with smaller, more delicate leaves and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

The stems are hairy, exceeding a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height, with small opposite branches; at the top are gaping little flowers of a heavy scent, sitting upon two somewhat long stalks. The leaves are like Marjoram, but smaller, especially toward the upper parts; they are scarcely notched, or quite rarely so, almost hoary <note>grayish-white</note>, and very hairy (especially on the lower part).

Furthermore, Calamint is of a thin essence, according to Galen <note>the influential Greek physician of antiquity</note>, and is hot and dry in the third degree: it cuts through [phlegm], cleanses, etc., and the Mountain variety is more effective than the others.

Bayrus <note>Pietro Bayro, an Italian physician</note> recommends an infusion and decoction of Calamint for dyeing the hair.

<column-break/>

### CALAMINT: German: Wild Pennyroyal; French: Calament, Wild Pennyroyal; Italian: Calamento.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the common Calamintha plant with upright stems and small, paired leaves.</image-desc>

The differences among Calamints are commonly taken from their place of birth, their scent, and the size of their flowers and leaves. In the *Common* Calamint with a large flower, which we depict here, the leaves grow opposite one another along square, branched stems; they are an inch or an inch and a half long, serrated, hairy, and with a pleasant enough scent. From the middle to the very top of the branches, two stalks from the leaf axils divide into several smaller ones, upon which the flowers sit; these emerge from small, bearded, and striated cups, gaping, purplish in color, and endowed with a delightful scent.

It loves mountains, and specifically their shady and rocky slopes; from there it is also transferred into gardens, where it grows successfully and sows itself very easily. It blooms in Summer.

### CALAMINT WITH A SMALLER FLOWER, with the scent of Pennyroyal.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender Calamintha variety with very small flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

It rises high with stiff, square stems, divided into frequent branches, hairy and somewhat reddish. The leaves are opposite at intervals, cut with rare notches, hairy, with a heavy scent of Pennyroyal, and a sharp, biting taste. The flowers are clustered in whorls, small, purplish, clinging to somewhat long stalks.

It is found in fields where the crop has been harvested, or when they lie fallow; and elsewhere in sunny places exposed to the Sun, which it enjoys; it blooms in the Summer months.

To say something regarding the ambiguous names of Calamint, it should be known, as Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> notes, that the Ancients were accustomed to confuse the species and names of Calamint, Catnip, Lemon Balm, Mint, and Costmary.

### THE HERB ZATARENDI.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Zatarendi herb, featuring broad, rounded, heavily veined leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

A small herb which the Egyptians call *Zatarendi*, because it is brought there from India, according to Alpinus <note>Prospero Alpini, a Venetian physician and botanist who studied Egyptian plants</note>; it has thick, round, white leaves, full of juice, and very fragrant. The same Alpinus adds that among them it is used as a condiment, and is in greatest use for coughs and difficulties in breathing, as well as for provoking both urine and menstrual purgations.

<summary>This page describes various species of Catnip and Calamint, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses as recorded by historical authorities like Galen and Mattioli. It also introduces the Egyptian herb Zatarendi, noting its Indian origins and respiratory benefits.</summary>
<keywords>Catnip, Calamint, Mentha Cattaria, Calamintha, Zatarendi, medicinal herbs, botany, Mattioli, Lobelius, Galen, Alpinus, respiratory health, reproductive health</keywords>

### MELISSA, BEE-HERB. German: Melissenkraut; French: Melisse; Italian: Melissa.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Melissa (Lemon Balm) plant, showing its upright square stems, opposite serrated leaves, and small clusters of flowers at the leaf axils, including the root system.</image-desc>

It grows with stems a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or higher, square, almost smooth and shining, divided into many branches <note>original: "alas," literally wings</note> situated opposite one another, solid and hard. The leaves arise from the joints, opposite, hanging from inch-long stalks, rivaling Calamint, of a dark-shining green, hairy with a short down, serrated around the edges, with the scent of a citron <note>lemon</note>. From their axils, indeed, whorled flowers spring forth, whitish or reddish-white. The root is driven obliquely through the earth, woody, many-forked, rounded, fibrous, and perennial.

It is commonly and everywhere cultivated in gardens, and flowers in Summer. However, in woods, mountains, and other neglected places, it also grows spontaneously.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF FALSE MELISSA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variant of Melissa, showing a similar structure with broad, serrated leaves and flowers emerging from the upper leaf axils.</image-desc>

One Melissa is of the garden, another is wild and comes forth in neglected places; one is the Common sort, already described before, and another is Foreign, of which more soon: one has a white flower, another red, and another flesh-colored: one has darker and hairier leaves: one is true, but another is "false" <note>original: "adulterina," meaning a look-alike or non-standard variety</note>, of which we here exhibit a second image, and which Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish botanist</note> marvels to admit as the true one, while on the contrary, he determined the Common and domestic sort to be the false one: one is more fragrant, recalling the scent of a citron fruit, and another is more foul-smelling, which some, by the distinction of the scent, claim reminds the head of Bedbugs.

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> records the Common Melissa as twofold: one cultivated in gardens, and the other growing spontaneously in woods, mountains, or other neglected places.

### MOLUCCA, CONSTANTINOPLE MELISSA, with a purplish-white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Molucca balm, featuring distinctively large, cup-shaped calyxes that surround the small flowers, arranged in whorls along the stem.</image-desc>

The name was not bestowed upon this plant from the Molucca Islands, says Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> in his *Adversaria*: but the name was sent with the plant from Syria to Venice by the effort of Martinelli Sequioi.

There are, however, two kinds: the rougher and various spiny Molucca, of which more soon, and the other smooth one, which we depict here.

Both are now commonly sown in gardens: as we have had them in our own at Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard. They flower in May, June, July, and August, and the flowers are purplish-white.

Some call them Syrian Heart-herbs <note>original: "Cardiatas Syriacas"</note>, because they are believed to do much for afflictions of the heart. They are also recommended against worms.

<column-break/>

### THE "FALSE MELISSA" OF SOME; with large leaves, etc.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of "Melissa Adulterina," showing a plant with more elongated, deeply veined leaves and prominent flower spikes.</image-desc>

It rests upon a fibrous, somewhat sharp, and bitter root. The stems are square, hairy, jointed, and stuffed with much pith. The leaves are like Dead-nettle <note>original: "Galeopsis"</note>, oblong, wrinkled, hairy, born from the joints, opposite, serrated in circumference, with a slightly pleasant scent: from their axils spring flowers of a purplish-white or flesh-colored hue.

We find this plant gifted with the names of Melissa and Bee-leaf <note>original: "Melissophylli Apiastri"</note> among writers: Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse</note> labels it Pannonian Dead-nettle.

Moreover, we have observed it coming forth in various places: at Basel on Mount *Mouter*, at Geneva on the hill *la Bastie*, at Lyon *in the woods of the Good German Woman*, at Montbéliard on the hill *In chau*, and elsewhere.

### TURKISH OR MOLDAVIAN MELISSA, with a purple and white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Moldavian Dragonhead (Melissa Turcica), showing long, narrow, serrated leaves and dense whorls of flowers forming a spike-like inflorescence.</image-desc>

The scent and taste prove it to be a Melissa: and the leaves on the branched, square, reddish stems—a cubit high—are an inch and a half long, scarcely half an inch wide, serrated around the edge, situated opposite at the joints, and gifted with very thin little "beards" at the top. The flowers grow in whorls around the joints, blue or white, consisting of a two-cleft lip and a two-cleft hood with a gaping mouth, and two small wings.

It is sown in gardens, but was first brought to us from Moldavia, where it grows spontaneously by itself. We have had it in gardens at Geneva, Lyon, and Montbéliard, with purple and white flowers.

### ROUGHER MOLUCCA, WITH FOETID LEAVES, and very spiny segments of the cups.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the "rougher" Molucca balm, showing the characteristic spiny, enlarged calyxes and jagged leaves.</image-desc>

Here we shall treat the qualities and virtues of Melissa. Since, therefore, Dioscorides and Pliny are very numerous in reviewing them, and they unanimously recommend the flowers, leaves, and their juice against "strangulation of the womb" <note>hysteria</note>, and scrofula <note>original: "strumas," swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, and griping pains of the belly, and ailments of the seat <note>rectum</note>, and likewise the bites of wasps, bees, and spiders, dysentery, joint diseases, and various other afflictions: we marvel that Galen makes it similar in faculty only to Horehound <note>original: "Marrubio"</note>, and determines it to be greatly surpassed by it. The Moors <note>referring to Arabic physicians</note> please us more, in whose opinion the Moderns follow <note>original: "pedibus eunt," literally "go by foot," meaning to agree</note>: they attribute excellent faculties to Melissa. For Avicenna writes that it heats and dries in the second degree, cheers the spirit, strengthens the vital faculties, and is useful not only for the heart but also for all the remaining internal organs. Indeed, what Pliny writes—that bees delight in no flower more—daily experience proves true.

<summary>This page describes various species of Melissa (Lemon Balm) and Molucca Balm, detailing their physical characteristics, geographic origins, and medicinal uses according to classical and Arabic authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Melissa, Lemon Balm, Molucca Balm, Moldavian Dragonhead, Dioscorides, Pliny, Avicenna, medicinal herbs, botany, heart health, bee-keeping</keywords>

# OF OREGANO
## SAMPSVCHVS <note>original: "SAMPSV"; likely a reference to Sampsuchum, an ancient name for Marjoram or Oregano.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Origanus vulgare, showing a low-growing herbaceous plant with small leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips of the stems, including visible root structure.</image-desc>

### ORIGANVS or ORIGANVM: German *Wolgemuth*, French *Origan*: Italian *Origano*.

The Common Oregano <note>original: "Origanum vulgare"</note> which we depict here, puts forth thin, woody, slanted roots that are fibrous with many small hairs. The stalks are about two or three feet high <note>original: "sesquicubitales aut bicubitales"; a cubit is roughly 18 inches.</note>, hard, square-shaped, and hairy. At the nodes of these stalks, leaves grow opposite one another like those of Field Calamint, and they are hairy; from the "armpits" <note>axils</note> of these leaves grow other tiny leaves, mimicking the leaves of Marjoram. The flavor of all these is sharp and aromatic, and the scent is sweet. The tiny flowers, colored flesh-pink or white, burst forth protected by reddish leaflets as if in an umbrella <note>an umbel</note>. The seed is very small, similar to the seed of Marjoram.

It grows in uncultivated soil along roadsides, on hills, and in sunny places. It flowers in the summer months. More on this in the following section and in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Origanum Heracleoticum, showing a more upright plant with distinct, compact, cone-like flower heads (spikes) at the ends of the branches.</image-desc>

### HERACLEOTIC OREGANO OF MATTHIOLUS <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist.</note> Called Cretan Oregano by some.

The stalk is square and hairy, like the common Oregano. The leaves growing from the joints are smaller and moderately hairy, with a sharper scent and taste. The flowers are white or purplish, appearing in scaly heads that are slightly spiked and spread out almost in the manner of an umbrella.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince. Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, another major 16th-century botanist.</note> used to call it *Slender-leaved Goat-oregano* <note>original: "Tragoriganum tenuifolium"</note>; by some it is called *True Oregano*, by others *Heracleotic Oregano*, and by several others it is Pliny’s *Gallic Cunila*.

Furthermore, Common Oregano varies mildly; for sometimes it has round leaves, sometimes long and large; sometimes the flowers are spiked, and often they are not spiked.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Origanum Creticum, featuring long, slender, scaly spikes at the branch tips and small, rounded leaves.</image-desc>

### CRETAN OREGANO.

It possesses a most persistent and pleasing scent. The parts primarily brought to us are the *Cymæ* <note>the tops or young shoots</note>, which are similar to the spikes of Marjoram—some short, others long—layered like tiles with a four-fold series of small, striated, densely packed scales. The taste is very sharp and the aromatic scent is delightful. The leaves are more rarely brought to us; they are hairy, smaller than common Marjoram, and not at all round.

By Matthiolus, Laguna, and Camerarius it is called *Origanum Onites*; by Tragus it is called *Another most beautiful foreign Oregano*; by Lobelius in his *Adversaria* it is *Syrian Wild Oregano*; by Anguillara it is *White Oregano*, which is perhaps the *Cilician Hyssop* of Dioscorides.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Origanum Monspeliense, showing a plant with very dense, elongated flower spikes and small leaves.</image-desc>

### BEAUTIFUL OREGANO OF MONTPELLIER according to Camerarius.

This is very similar to the *Onites* depicted by Matthiolus, but it is not the same. It does not differ much from Common Oregano, except almost entirely in the fact that it has many beautiful, somewhat long, purple spikes. The stalk also turns entirely purple. It produces a reddish and tiny seed, like the other kinds of Oregano.

It abounds near Montpellier.

Regarding the powers <note>medicinal properties</note> of Oregano: according to the teachings of Galen, Heracleotic Oregano is more effective than *Onites*, but the wild versions of both are stronger. Indeed, all of them possess the faculty of cutting through <note>breaking up phlegm</note>, thinning, drying, and heating; they possess these qualities in the third degree <note>a measure of potency in Galenic medicine</note>. *More on their powers in the Appendix.*

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Marum Veterum, showing a plant with elongated, leafy flower spikes and small, pointed leaves.</image-desc>

### MARUM OF THE ANCIENTS, OR CORTUSUS’S MARUM. <note>Marum is often identified as Cat-thyme.</note>

Although Galen, Aetius, and Paulus passed over Marum in their lists of simple medicines, Dioscorides and Pliny nevertheless remembered it. For Pliny writes that it grows in Egypt, and Dioscorides says it is a medicinal herb with a flower similar to Oregano. However, the leaves of this one are much whiter and the flower more fragrant. It has a power similar to Watercress <note>original: "Sisymbrio"</note>, etc.

Marum is referred to by various plants: to the so-called Mastic-herb, to Marjoram, and to Heracleotic Oregano; indeed, Hermolaus in his commentary on Dioscorides seems to have determined it to be Lemon Balm.

However, the plant depicted here, which we label as Cortusus’s Marum, seems to correspond in all respects to the history of Marum in Matthiolus. Camerarius also labels it as Marum in his works on Matthiolus. Nor do we reject the opinion of Matthiolus, although it may seem otherwise to Lobelius and Apollo <note>likely a reference to a specific scholar or a poetic allusion to botanical wisdom</note>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Marum Valerandi Dourez, showing a woody-based plant with small, opposite leaves and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

### MARUM OF VALERANDUS DOUREZ, a most fragrant foreign plant.

This plant, of which we have had fragments for many years, has woody stalks covered in thick down, divided into opposite branches. The leaves grow in pairs from the joints, situated opposite each other and entirely woolly; they are equal to the leaves of cultivated Marjoram, or even a little larger, ash-colored, somewhat thick, with a fragrant scent and a lively, sharp, and aromatic taste.

We saw Cortusus’s Marum at Padua at the home of Cortusus, a shrubby plant cultivated in a pot. He used to say that cats are exceedingly delighted by this herb, and it is hardly safe from them; and that being driven by it, they pour out their genital seed <note>semen</note> all around it.

<summary>This page describes various species of Oregano and Marum (Cat-thyme), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal properties according to classical and contemporary authorities. It notably mentions the intoxicating effect of Marum on cats.</summary>
<keywords>Oregano, Marum, Cat-thyme, Origanum vulgare, Mattioli, Dioscorides, Galen, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, Montpellier, Padua</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<sig>Ggg 2</sig>

### SAMPSUCHUM, AMARACUS, & MARJORAM: Germ. Maioran, Meyran: Gall. Mariolaine: Ital. Maiorana.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Marjoram plant with small, rounded leaves and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

It is a small shrub, a palm <note>about 3 inches</note> or even a span <note>about 9 inches</note> high, hollowed with very frequent wings <note>referring to branching structures</note>, which are woody, mostly square, hairy, and slightly reddish. The leaves are positioned opposite one another, shaped like common Oregano, but much smaller, covered in a hoary down, and possessing a fragrant odor. Around the top of the stem and branches, from the axils of the leaves and at the ends of the branches, arise spikes of flowers, which are tiny, whitish, gaping, etc.

It is almost entirely a garden plant, which is sown by seed and by branch; today it everywhere adorns the hanging gardens of Adonis <note>A reference to "Adonis Gardens," small pots of quickly fading herbs used in festivals, here meaning decorative container gardening</note>.

It is commonly distinguished into the **Garden** variety, which is Noble and more fragrant, having smaller and thinner leaves; and the **Wild** variety, which is less scented, coarse, and larger, which all experts agree should be understood as *Heracleotic Oregano*. More details are in the Appendix.

### OCYMUM, OCYMUM or OZIMUM <note>Basil</note>: Germ. Basilien: Gall. Basilic: Ital. Basilico.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Basil plant with broad, ovate leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Various plants are given the name *Ocymum* <note>Basil</note> among writers: *Chamaemyrsine* <note>Ground-myrtle</note>, *Great Scrophularia*, *Savoy Hawkweed*, *Sweet Esula*, *Touch-me-not*, and *Warty Ozimastrum*.

Furthermore, various kinds of Basil are recounted by the same authors: Serapio has four—the Large, Medium, and Small, and also a certain Wild kind. Gesner mentions the Clove-scented and Lemon-scented varieties.

We depict here the **Greatest** kind, whose leaves are twice or thrice larger than the Common sort, oblong, saw-toothed with rare notches, endowed with a pale green color, or red, with a sweet scent of Lemon or Clove. The flowers are spiked, white or red.

### SMALLEST BASIL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, bushy variety of Basil with tiny leaves.</image-desc>

The plant is a palm high or a little more, bushily branching with very frequent woody twigs, through which the leaves—equal to the leaves of Wild Thyme or Marjoram—grow, ranging from oblong to round, greenish or red, with a very lively and sweet flavor of Cloves. The tiny flowers are arranged in whorls along the stalks of the branches. The root is fibrous. *Our image, which was purchased already engraved, pleases us less.* <note>A rare personal note from the author regarding the quality of the woodcut</note>

Camerarius calls the smallest Basil "white and black garden basil"; Tabernaemontanus calls it "Small Clove Basil." Others call it small, minute, dwarf, or tiny Basil; some call it Wild Basil; Amatus and Gesner call it *Ocimoides*, *Ocimastrum*, and *Acinos*, whose opinion Robert Constantius rejects.

<column-break/>

### CLINOPODIUM TO SOME, MASTICHINA of the French: FABREGUE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with whorled flower clusters (verticils) along the stem.</image-desc>

It bushes out like Marjoram: at first it sometimes grows to a height of two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> with many branching arms; through these, the leaves grow, intermediate between the leaves of Thyme and Wild Thyme, and endowed with a sharp taste. At the nodes and at the ends of the branches, white flowers spring forth from mossy whorls. The root is woody and tuberous. The scent is pleasant with a certain heaviness.

We have seen it in gardens in Paris, Lyon, and Genoa, as well as Montpellier, where they call it *Mastic*. Most label it *Mastichina* both because of the stickiness with which it becomes moist, and because of the delightful odor of Mastic <note>a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree</note>. Perhaps it is the *FABREGUE* of Olivier de Serres.

Otherwise, the *Clinopodium* of Dioscorides is a small, twiggy shrub that grows on rocks; the leaves are similar to Wild Thyme; the flowers are similar to the feet of a bed <note>original: "lecti pedibus"; the name Clinopodium literally means "bed-foot" in Greek</note>, etc.

### MEDIUM AND MORE COMMON BASIL, black.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a medium-sized Basil plant with darker foliage.</image-desc>

The plant is nine inches high, with several branches forming a stalk, square, somewhat reddish, and slightly hairy. The leaves are smaller than Pellitory, smooth, sometimes notched around the edge, sometimes not at all, rising opposite from the joints, with a fragrant odor and no outstanding taste. The flowers are whorled, arranged in a somewhat long spike, sweet-smelling, white or purplish in color, with a somewhat long, narrow lip. The root is woody, black, and fibrous.

This is common everywhere in gardens and flowers in June. We had this and the "Greatest" (mentioned before) at Montbéliard, both this one and that one with dark and white flowers; and sometimes even variegated with purple spots.

### SAINT-MAURITANIAN BASIL, BROAD, curled, greatest. Perhaps the RIHAV of the Egyptians.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, broad-leafed Basil variety with ruffled (crisped) leaf edges.</image-desc>

It grows to a cubit's height <note>about 18 inches</note>, with square stems clothed in sparse hairs, from which opposite branches fall. The leaves, on long stalks, are rounded in outline at the joints, large, curled, fringed, dark green, or spotted with an admixture of red, and of a fragrant odor. The flowers are similar to common Oregano, whorled, arranged in a spike, turning from white to reddish. The seed is black, oblong, enclosed in leafy heads.

This is the "Exotic Basil" of Colonna; the "Indian" or rather "Spanish Basil" of Camerarius. Is it perhaps the *Rihon* of the Egyptians mentioned by Prospero Alpini? We have seen it at Velunzio and Strasbourg in the more cultivated gardens. The seed was sent from India to Spain, and from there elsewhere. More about Basil in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various aromatic herbs of the Marjoram and Basil families, detailing their physical structures, scents, and the different names used by contemporary botanists across Europe and North Africa.</summary>
<keywords>Marjoram, Basil, Clinopodium, Mastichina, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, garden plants, aromatic plants, 16th-century botany</keywords>

--- Page 492 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of aromatic and medicinal herbs, following the previous discussions on savory and marjoram. The catchword "ACINO" from the previous page likely refers to a species of wild basil or thyme discussed in the preceding section.</meta>

### FRAGRANT BASIL OR BASILICUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Basil plant (Ocimum basilicum) showing its upright stems, opposite leaves, and terminal flower spikes.</image-desc>

Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a 16th-century German botanist</note> discussed it in this manner: There are, he says, three kinds of Basil, two of which are cultivated, such as those sown annually in gardens; the third is wild, most noble and beautiful, having leaves similar to Marjoram <note>original: "Amaraco"</note>, yet a little larger, with a most sweet and excellent scent, etc.

It is a very fragrant herb, says Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino, Italian physician and botanist</note>, slightly sharp in taste, delighting in Sun and Water. It is received among vegetables both raw and cooked, and also among seasonings. By the common consent of all, there are held to be three kinds distinguished by size: one broad-leaved, another thin-leaved, and a third medium. So he says. Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner</note> distinguishes between the clove-scented <note>original: "ingariophyllatum"</note> and lemon-scented <note>original: "citratum"</note> varieties in his garden writings.

### THE CUDWEED OF THE ANCIENTS: COTTONWEED: Called by some Bastard Dittany.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Gnaphalium (Cudweed), showing a woolly plant with small, clustered flower heads.</image-desc>

One uses the white and soft leaves of Cudweed <note>original: "Gnaphalii"</note> in place of flock <note>wool stuffing</note>. Furthermore, it is effectively administered in dry wine for dysentery, says Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician</note>, and he says no more.

Caesalpinus describes it thus: It is, he says, a large tuft, with more numerous twigs, taller and whiter than Horehound; the leaves are also rounder, smaller, and similar to Dittany of Crete, covered with a whiter down, with a slightly bitter taste and a faint, not unpleasant scent. It bears soft whorls among the leaves, in which the little flowers are purplish.

It differs in size, being large, smaller, or smallest; and also by location: whence one is of the garden, another of the sea, another alpine; one American, another German. *More in the Appendix.*

### THE MALE PENNYROYAL OF PLINY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pulegium mas (Pennyroyal), showing creeping stems and whorled flowers at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Pennyroyal <note>original: "Pulegium"</note>; as a commonly known herb, Dioscorides does not describe it. Pliny, since Common Pennyroyal bears a purple flower, mentions another with a white flower, and calls that one the Female, and this one the Male.

It has leaves, like the former, of Water-mint or Wild Marjoram, and they also have stems, like the former, with whorls of flowers at intervals: but white. The powers and scent are exactly the same.

Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli</note> writes that it is found on the road where one goes from Rivoli to Turin, at the edges of the fields.

Furthermore, the name *Pulegium* comes from fleas <note>Latin: "pulicibus"</note>, because its fresh flower, when burnt, puts them to flight and kills them with its scent. The Greeks call it *Blechon*, as if it were the "bleating herb," because when tasted by livestock when it is in bloom, it excites bleating in them.

<column-break/>

### DITTANY or DICTAMNUM: Germ: & Belg: Diptam: Gall. Dictam: Italian Dittamo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Dictamnus (Dittany), showing a tall flowering stalk with distinct, five-petaled flowers and pinnate leaves at the base.</image-desc>

It has hairy stems, somewhat purplish, from whose joints opposite branches arise, and from these others in the same order. The position of the leaves is also opposite, the outline almost circular, sometimes more oblong, like a vetch, covered everywhere with a somewhat greyish down <note>original: "tomento"</note>, though sometimes smooth in gardens, of a strong scent and sharp flavor. The little heads sitting at the ends of the twigs mimic a somewhat long spike, compacted like scales from leaves almost equal to Marjoram, from whose bosom they come forth: The flowers are purplish, small tubes of equal shape, with little stamens protruding from the opening, sitting in a channeled calyx. *More in the Appendix.*

### PENNYROYAL: Germ. Poley, Heart-Poley: Belg. Paleye? Gall. Pouliot: Ital. Pulegio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pulegium (Pennyroyal), showing its characteristic low-growing habit and dense flower whorls.</image-desc>

By an persistent creeping, wherever it touches the earth, it flourishes, rooted by fibers sent down from the joints of the square, hairy, nine-inch stems, shading the ground beneath it far and wide. The leaves arise from the joints, approaching the leaves of Wild Marjoram, with a scent of heavy sweetness and a burning taste. Purplish whorls of four-parted flowers crown the stems and branches in a long and spiked series at short intervals, with a pair of leaves placed beneath each one.

We depict the Common variety here; which delights in marshy places and those flooded in the winter months, or at least in uncultivated ground. It blooms in July and August, and is then to be gathered.

### NARROW-LEAVED HART'S PENNYROYAL of Montpellier, more fragrant.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pulegium cervinum (Hart's Pennyroyal), featuring narrower leaves and distinct globular flower clusters.</image-desc>

It produces frequent thin, round, reddish, jointed twigs, a foot long or more, moderately upright. Opposite leaves come out from the joints, with the scent of Savory or common Pennyroyal, and a sharp, burning, and biting taste. Globular whorls of flowers arise at the nodes below the tops of the twigs, of a pale blue color. The root is woody and whitish.

It grows spontaneously at Montpellier near *Aigremont*, and is very rare in other regions of France, nor is it found growing wild in Germany. But we have seen it in gardens at Zurich, Basel, and Lyon.

Furthermore, Pennyroyal thins <note>the humors</note> and heats vehemently: taken as a drink, it brings forth and ejects the menses, the afterbirth, and the fetus. And this variety is more pleasing and more powerful in taste, scent, and virtues than the common one.

<summary>This page describes several aromatic herbs including Basil, Cudweed, and various types of Pennyroyal and Dittany, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses, and geographical locations. It emphasizes their roles in treating digestive issues and as pest repellents, while citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Basil, Ocimum basilicum, Cudweed, Gnaphalium, Pennyroyal, Pulegium, Dittany, Dictamnus, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on aromatic herbs of the mint family, specifically Acinos, Tragoriganum, and Thyme. It maintains the encyclopedic style of comparing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny with contemporary 16th-century botanists.</meta>

# IMAGE AND OUTLINE
### ACINOS ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL: Acinos to many.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Acinos plant, showing a bushy herb with small leaves and multiple stems arising from a central root.</image-desc>

There is no *Acinos* <note>likely Wild Basil or Mother of Thyme</note> in Theophrastus. Dioscorides calls it *Acinon* and *Aconon*: and he says it is an herb with slender shoots, used for garlands, and very similar to Basil: but more hairy and sweet-smelling, usually cultivated in gardens by some. They believe this stays <note>stops</note> the bowels and the menses, etc. Pliny mentions Acinos in various places, and reads it sometimes as *Acinon*, sometimes *Achoen*, and sometimes *Arineon*. However, Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a Renaissance scholar</note> wishes to distinguish *Acinon* from *Acina*: and denotes that *Acine* is a kind of wild Basil, while *Aconon* is a thorny, short, and broad herb approaching Eryngo <note>Sea Holly</note>.

### COLUMNA’S ACINOS: To some the Clove-scented Basil of the Monks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller variety of Acinos with distinct whorls of flowers along the upper stems.</image-desc>

The Monks say they brought the seed of this plant, previously unknown to all, from Apulia to Rome, and afterwards it became known to Physicians and Pharmacists from there. Moreover, the whole plant except the root has the odor and taste of Cloves: and the older the plant, the more fragrant and sharp the leaves.

Furthermore, besides those described, various other plants are gifted with the name of Acinos: *the lesser Moonwort, Goosefoot, Wild Olive, Chaste Tree*, etc.

Moreover, it was called *Acinos* from the privative letter *a* <note>meaning "not"</note> and the verb *kineo* <note>original Greek: κινέω</note>, which is "to move" or "to stir up": because it does not move the bowels and menses at all, but stops them.

### GOAT-ORIGANUM WITH THINNER LEAVES, and a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tragoriganum plant with slender stems and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This has smaller and whiter shoots, thinner and longer leaves, somewhat hoary, of a sharp taste, and an odor not very pleasant. The flowers, as in the preceding, are born in whorls around the highest twigs, coming forth from little husks, larger, hooded, and white. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note>, the author of the description, did not observe the seed. The root is woody, hard, and many-forked. Almost everyone labels this as the second or alternative Goat-Origanum.

Clusius observed it growing spontaneously in the Valencian field. It was flowering in March. There is also found a kind of this genus which has blackish leaves, marked with points or spots.

<column-break/>

### A BEAUTIFUL SPECIES OF ACINOS: Austrian Bedstraw to Clusius: Broad-leaved to C. Bauhin.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Clinopodium variety, showing broader leaves and distinct floral clusters.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are not very unlike the leaves of common Acinos, placed two-by-two opposite each other, pointed, and notched. The flowers at the joints from the fold of the leaves are two or three together, two or three times larger than in common Acinos, tubular and purplish.

It grows on various mountains situated near the Danube, and in various other places: and it flowers in May. But we have previously observed it depicted in many uncultivated and sunny places: such as in the *plain palais* <note>a public square</note> at Geneva, on the hill near the city at Montpellier, on the journey toward the mountains at Basel, and elsewhere. It flowers in April, May, and June.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> thinks *Acynon* should be written with a *y*.

### GOAT-ORIGANUM: German: Tragodepten: French: Great Marjoram, Tragoriganum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Tragoriganum plant with dense foliage and flowering tops.</image-desc>

Called *Tragoriganum* <note>Goat-Origanum</note> by the Greeks and Latins alike, it is a shrub, according to Dioscorides, similar in both leaves and twigs to Origanum or wild Thyme. Indeed, it is found to be more beautiful in some places, with broader leaves, and very sticky. Some have a slender shoot and thin leaves, which some also call *Prasium*. The best is that which grows in Cos, Chios, Smyrna, and Crete. However, they all provide heat, stir the urine, and are beneficial to the belly, etc.

Pliny also makes Goat-Origanum similar to wild Thyme, and assigns the same powers to it. Galen writes that it binds, Celsus that it disperses. But what is the agreement between these and those? We depict Mattioli’s Goat-Origanum here.

### THYME: German: Foreign Wild Thyme: French: Thyme, Lemon Thyme, Mignotise: Italian: Thymo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thyme plant, showing its characteristic woody base and small, dense leaves.</image-desc>

Thyme is known by everyone, says Dioscorides: a small, twiggy shrub, surrounded by many narrow leaves, having at the top little heads of flowers reflecting purple. It grows mostly in stony places and places of thin soil: So he says: making only one kind of Thyme: but in the chapter on *Epithymum* <note>Dodder of Thyme</note> he mentions a mountain Thyme, distinguishing it from the other by its hardness.

To Theophrastus, whom Pliny followed, there are two kinds of Thyme, White and Black, and the more recent writers of botanical matters have the same: namely the White, which is larger and gifted with white hairy leaves, and called *Cephalotum* and Cretan; and the Black, which is less rigid and common, depicted here. More in the following pages.

<summary>This page describes various aromatic herbs including Acinos, Goat-Origanum, and Thyme, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal properties, and the differing classifications provided by ancient and Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Acinos, Clinopodium, Tragoriganum, Thyme, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Pliny, Clusius, Mattioli, botany, medicinal herbs, aromatic plants</keywords>
