<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of aromatic herbs, specifically focusing on varieties of Thyme and the parasitic Dodder plant. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, citing authorities like Dioscorides, Clusius, and Fuchs.</meta>

### CREEPING THYME OF THE PISAN GARDEN: Epithymum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping thyme plant with small leaves and clusters of flowers, showing its root system.</image-desc>

This plant branches out with several small, woody stalks, a foot or a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient measurement, roughly the length of a forearm</note> long, creeping along the ground. At intervals of an inch, these are crowded with clusters of very short branches bearing small green leaves; these are somewhat stiff, narrow, and covered around the edges with short, white, bristly hairs. The tiny flowers are reddish.

The common variety previously described, which some name *hard thyme*, grows wild everywhere around Montpellier; the stony fields of Mediterranean Spain and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> are filled with it, blooming sometimes with purple flowers and sometimes white. It is commonly cultivated in gardens and flowers in Summer. The Cretan variety grows abundantly on the island of Crete, from which it received the name Cretan. *More information in the Appendix.*

### SERPYLLVS or SERPYLLVM: German & Belgian: Quendel; French: Serpolet; Italian: Serpillo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Serpyllum (Wild Thyme) showing a dense root system and multiple stems with small leaves and flower heads.</image-desc>

The Greeks call it *Herpyllon* <note>original: Ἑρπυλλον</note>, and indeed the name—both Greek and Latin—is derived from the way it creeps <note>The Latin 'serpere' and Greek 'herpein' both mean to creep or crawl</note>. It has hard, square, reddish stems that are moderately hairy; wherever they touch the earth, they immediately strike new roots. The primary roots are woody, quite thick and numerous, dark brown, and fringed with many fibers. At each node of the branches are several leaves, broader than common Thyme, somewhat round and veined, with a sharp and aromatic taste. The flowers grow in heads like Thyme, sometimes white, but mostly purplish.

### SERPYLLVM WITH NARROW AND DOWNY leaves: And long-leaved bristly Serpyllum.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Serpyllum with longer, narrower leaves and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> says this grows alongside the common variety in Pannonia, Austria, and neighboring provinces; he describes it at length and says it flowers in June. Furthermore, in this small illustration, we show a branch of the other long-leaved, bristly Serpyllum.

Common Wild Thyme was once planted in gardens and is still kept in them today. It occurs everywhere (though rarely with white flowers) in almost all provinces of Europe; there are few bare hills, grassy fields, or overgrown roadsides where it does not flourish. It flowers mostly in the months of June and July, and sometimes even in May and August. Its scent changes according to the diversity of the location and the climate.

<column-break/>

### CASSVTA OR CVSCVTA: German: Todtern; French: Augure de Lin, Goute de Lin; Italian: Cuscuta.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Cuscuta (Dodder), a parasitic plant shown as leafless, twining stems wrapping around a host plant.</image-desc>

Always a follower of another's table, *Cassutha* or *Cuscuta* <note>Commonly known as Dodder</note> is never anything but a parasite and an unwelcome guest. Once it has seized upon herbs or shrubs, it embraces them so tightly with its very long, thread-like, reddish stems that it robs them of their vital spirit and kills them completely by stealing their nourishment. After it has climbed upward, it relies on no roots of its own, although it is by no means without them when it first breaks from the ground. The flowers grow in clusters without any order along the winding threads, appearing reddish or whitish. The subsequent seed-heads contain round seeds, equal in size to those of a Poppy.

Some call this the *Androsaces* of Dioscorides, which we, along with Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, author of a famous 1542 herbal</note>, do not approve of. *More in the Appendix.*

### LEMON-SCENTED SERPYLLVM: Called Lemon Thyme by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lemon Thyme, showing upright stems and clusters of flowers.</image-desc>

The Ancients distinguished Serpyllum into *Cultivated* and *Wild*. But many other differences have been observed by more recent authors. For one flowers with larger blooms, another smaller; one purple, another white. One has a sweet scent, another none at all. There is also a difference in the leaves, which are observed to be narrow, long, downy, etc.

Clusius illustrates this one, describing it at length and adding that it was not observed by others. He spotted it in Pannonia, mixed with the common variety and flowering with it in June. We found it again near Dornach flowering in August, with a distinctly purple flower.

### WILD SERPYLLVM, the ZYGIS of Dioscorides according to Clusius, approaching common Thyme.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild variety of Serpyllum with small, dense foliage and a woody base.</image-desc>

Dioscorides recognized one garden Serpyllum, resembling Marjoram in scent and used for garlands; and he recognized another wild type, which is also called *Zygis*. It is either creeping or upright, sending out thin, twiggy branches full of leaves similar to Rue; the flowers are sharp to the taste but with a pleasant scent; the root is useless.

Serpyllum is hot and dry in the third degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of humors used in ancient medicine</note> and consists of fine parts. It provokes the menses, stimulates urine, expels stones, and moves the waters; hence Macer <note>A reference to the medieval medical poem 'De viribus herbarum'</note> says:

> The Ancients called it Serpyllum, because it creeps
> Close to the earth: it has a fierce and drying power, etc.

Under the name of Serpyllum, various plants are denoted, such as Oregano, Watercress, Mugwort, and others.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SAVORY, CUNILA, THYMBRA: German & Belgian: Saturey: French: Sarriette: Italian: Sauoreggia.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Satureia (Savory) plant, showing its root system, thin stems, and small leaves.</image-desc>

Cultivated or garden Savory <note>original: "Satureia satiua, siue hortẽsis"</note>, which we depict here, rests upon a woody and simple root: from which rise small twigs a foot or a cubit high, rounded, reddish, somewhat hairy, and marked by distinct joints: at each of these grow leaves like those of common Hyssop, somewhat bristly, and worn away with frequent small holes (though these do not pass all the way through), with the scent of common Thyme but milder: the flavor is sharp. From the "wings" <note>the axils where the leaf meets the stem</note> of the leaves come small flowers, divided into four little segments, of a purplish-white color. The seed is small and blackish.

It is sown almost everywhere in gardens: it flowers and produces seed in the same year it grows, and then it dies. It also grows spontaneously on sunny hills and in the beds of torrents.

### FINE-LEAVED SAVORY OF ST. JULIAN according to some: True or genuine Thymbra to others.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Satureia Tenuifolia, featuring a more dense, shrub-like appearance with numerous small leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

In the rugged areas of the Tyrrhenian Sea, and the rough ground of St. Julian in Tuscany, this elegant little herb grows in great abundance: with slender twigs, a palm's breadth high, trailing and woody: the leaves are more crowded at the bottom, like Cretan Thyme, but narrower and somewhat long. At the top of the small branches is a spike of flowers turning from purple to white. In the local tongue it is called <term>Thymbra of St. Julian</term> <note>original: "Thymbra de S. Iuliano"</note>, etc. <margin>Lobel in Adversaria.</margin>

Savory <note>Satureia</note> is believed to be named from <term>Saturando</term> <note>Saturating or satisfying</note>, because it is frequently added to and cooked in foodstuffs. More on Thymbra, Cunila, and Savory in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### HARDER SAVORY, OR THYMBRA.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Satureia Durior, showing a woody stem with small, pointed leaves and clusters of flowers at the nodes.</image-desc>

Harder Savory has smaller, broader, and tougher leaves, of a paler green than the cultivated kind, numerous, on two-edged branches sprouting from a perennial woody root. From the wings of the leaves, short spikes burst forth on both sides, somewhat similar to Hyssop, with whiter flowers.

We have observed it in various gardens, flowering in Spring and Autumn. It is said, however, to grow plenteously in the mountainous and rocky regions of Narbonne and Piedmont, in certain rugged and uncultivated places.

As for the powers of Savory, it is determined to be hot and dry in the third degree; it thins, cuts <note>breaks up phlegm</note>, clears the passages: and performs everything that Thyme is capable of.

### HYSSOP: German: Ysop, Hyssop: Belgian: Ysope: French: Hyssope: Italian: Hyssopo.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hyssop, showing a robust plant with square stems, opposite leaves, and flower spikes.</image-desc>

The common spiked Hyssop which we depict here has a woody, hard root, the thickness of a finger: from which rise several stalks, square, somewhat hairy, jointed, nine inches long, and branched. The leaves grow at their nodes, placed in whorls, similar to the leaves of Lavender but half as long, with a somewhat sharp taste and a not unpleasant scent. The flowers are arranged in a long spike, mostly blue in color, or white. The seed is tiny in oblong vessels.

It is found growing wild on some rugged hills of Romagna, and not easily elsewhere. In gardens, however, it is kept in abundance, with white, red, and blue flowers. More in the following.

<column-break/>

### HYSSOP WITH A SHORT BROAD SPIKE, and blue flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a broad-spiked Hyssop variety with dense flower heads.</image-desc>

Hyssop, as noted by C. Bauhin: varies chiefly in its leaves, flowers, and scent. For sometimes it has divided leaves, and other times not. The flower is commonly blue, and sometimes white or red: and it also sometimes flowers on only one side, sometimes indeed on both. And finally, some Hyssop smells of Musk, others do not. Thus he distinguishes them. By us and by others, still other differences have been observed, as will be clear from what follows: but that species of Hyssop which we depict here is considered very rare.

<column-break/>

### GORIZIAN HYSSOP, with flowers surrounding the stalks in whorls.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hyssopum Goritiense, showing flowers arranged in whorls (verticils) around the stem.</image-desc>

Dioscorides says that the herb Hyssop is well known, and does not describe it. He makes it two-fold, the garden and the mountain variety: adding that the best is that which grows in Cilicia.

Whether indeed the Hyssop of the Greeks is the same as that of the Arabs and our common Hyssop, or not, is not without merit a matter of controversy. Fuchs, Cordus, Mattioli, and Amatus accept it as Dioscorides' Hyssop. But the negative opinion is held by the Monks, Anguillara, Turner, Lobel, Gerard, Sylvius, Clusius, Bellonius, the History of Lyon, C. Bauhin, and others: nor are their reasonings of small weight; let the learned weigh them.

<summary>This page provides detailed botanical descriptions and classifications for varieties of Savory (Satureia) and Hyssop (Hyssopus), noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and the scholarly debate regarding their identification in ancient texts.</summary>
<keywords>Savory, Hyssop, Satureia, Thymbra, botanical taxonomy, Dioscorides, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of aromatic herbs, specifically focusing on varieties of Hyssop and Stoechas (French Lavender), maintaining the encyclopedic style of the previous entries.</meta>

### MOUNTAIN HYSSOP OF MACEDONIA
According to Valerandus Dourez: Is this the *Abs, Abes*, or *Guseh* of the Arabs, mentioned by Anguillara? <note>Valerandus Dourez was a 16th-century physician; Anguillara was a famous Italian botanist. The Arabic names refer to traditional medicinal terms for similar plants.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a single stalk of Hyssopum Montanum Macedonicum, showing small, narrow leaves and clusters of flowers at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

The branch is about nine inches long <note>original: "Dodrantalis"</note>, square-shaped, woody, and bristly with a somewhat rough, hoary down; it is split into short, attached shoots. The leaves are arranged in whorls at intervals, stiff, blackish, rough, narrow, and pointed, adorned with white down along the edges. The flowers are blue, arranged in whorls at the tips of the branches emerging from the leaf axils.

### HYSSOP WITH LEAVES OF HERACLEOTIC OREGANO
according to Dalechamps.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hyssopus Origani Heracleotici, showing a more branched plant with broader, rounded leaves similar to marjoram.</image-desc>

In its scent, taste, and blue spike, this is no different from the Common Hyssop: only the leaf is similar to Marjoram or Pennyroyal, being rounder and not as elongated as the Common variety.

The *History of Plants of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugdun."</note> establishes this as the genuine Hyssop of Dioscorides according to the opinion of Dalechamps; hence it rejects that common Marjoram which Pena and Lobel assumed to be the <term>Gicçosum</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for a specific type of Hyssop</note> for the twin Hyssop.

### THE COMMONLY NAMED ARABIC STOECHAS
Another Illustration.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Stoechadis Arabicae, showing a woody base with several upright stems topped with dense, pine-cone-like flower heads.</image-desc>

Galen writes that Stoechas <note>French Lavender (Lavandula stoechas)</note> grows in many places throughout the world, but most abundantly in Crete and the Stoechades Islands located in the Iberian Sea. However, the Stoechades Islands are not situated opposite Marseille, as Dioscorides incorrectly wrote (as noted by Lobel), but are opposite Olbia, commonly called Hyères; they are two days' journey along the coast from Marseille. Not only the Stoechades Islands, but also the hills of Narbonne and the rugged tracts of Provence teem with Stoechas—indeed, so abundantly that they suffice for heating ovens.

We have records from Mattioli, Clusius, and Camerarius that it grows in certain mountains of Italy, Spain, and Portugal. Germany has it only in gardens.

<column-break/>

### MOUNTAIN HYSSOP OF CILICIA
according to some.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hyssopum Montanum Cilicium, showing a branched plant with small leaves and elongated flower spikes.</image-desc>

Fuchs labels it thus: in the *History of Plants of Lyon* it is called *Fuchs's Mountain Hyssop*; by Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* it is called *Hyssop or Mountain Hyssop of the History of Lyon*.

Furthermore, Hyssop consists of fine parts; it dries and heats in the third degree <note>A reference to the Galenic system of "humors" where medicines were graded by intensity</note>. However, the garden variety heats and dries less than the wild one; and that which bears white flowers is considered even less hot and dry. It opens obstructions, cuts through thick humors, thins viscous fluids to make them easier to cough up, promotes urine, and is quite pleasant when eaten in meat broth, etc.

### STOECHAS or STICHAS: German: Stoechas-herb;
French: *Stoechados*; Italian: *Stoechado* or *steca*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Stoechas, showing long stems with narrow leaves and distinct, tufted flower heads at the apex.</image-desc>

This is a shrub as useful as it is beautiful, with a woody, somewhat thick root, sending out woody twigs one or two cubits long <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>, divided into several branches. The leaves grow in pairs at the joints like Lavender, with other smaller, more numerous leaves emerging from the axils, hoary, with an aromatic scent and taste. Each small branch is four-angled, tapering into thickish spikes an inch or more long, layered with hairy scales in which the purple florets reside. Moreover, from the top, several small purple-violet leaves shoot out for the sake of beauty, much like those in Mattioli’s Clary Sage.

This is the *Stoechas* of Dioscorides, Pliny, Mesue, Serapion, and other Ancients; the opinion of Ruellius, who distinguishes Arabic Stoechas from the Greek Stoechas, should not be accepted.

### GREEN STOECHAS OF DALECHAMPS.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Stoechas Viridis, showing a similar structure to the previous Stoechas but with a more compact flower head and distinct leaf arrangement.</image-desc>

The whole plant shines with a pleasant greenness; the leaves are produced in pairs from the stem joints at long intervals, along with several others much shorter. A long, round head sits at the top of the stem, with two small leaves at the very summit, from which yellow flowers emerge.

It received the name *Stoechas* from the Stoechades Islands where, as mentioned, it grows. There are some, however, who think Stoechas is more correctly called *Stachun*, as if meaning "a spike."

Our first two illustrations are from Fuchs's works and correspond to those of Clusius.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, focusing on aromatic herbs of the lavender family and their medicinal relatives. It maintains the systematic descriptions of species found in Southern Europe and the Levant.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### STOECHAS WITH SERRATED AND CURLED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Stoechas plant with serrated, wavy leaves and a long flowering stalk topped with a dense spike.</image-desc>

This kind of Stoechas <note>French Lavender or topped lavender</note> is quite rare, according to the author Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, who observed it only at the summit of Calpe in Spain <note>The Rock of Gibraltar</note>. In its branches, flowers, seeds, and root, it differs in no way from the common variety; but the leaves are oblong, narrow, serrated, and curled, with a green upper surface and a whitening underside. The ends of the small branches terminate in little twigs about nine inches long, which are bare, four-sided, and hoary; these support a spike longer and more scattered than the common Stoechas, approaching the spike of the smaller Lavender, and composed of many similar membrane-like scales crowded together, with certain broader little leaves standing out at the top, of a purplish-blue color, as in the Arabian variety. More on Stoechas in the Appendix.

### FALSE NARD, COMMONLY CALLED SPICA: German: Spicanardi; French: Narde, Aspic; Italian: Spigo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Pseudo-nardus (Lavender) plant showing upright stems and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

It is named False Nard <note>original: "Pseudo-Nardus"</note> in Greek and Latin because it is not the true and genuine Nard <note>Spikenard</note>, and does not resemble it in appearance, but only in scent.

There are two kinds, Male and Female: the Male is commonly nicknamed *Spica* <note>Spike Lavender</note>, while the Female is called *Lavendula* <note>True Lavender</note>. The Male is taller and breathes out a greater scent, and is no less pleasing than Nard. It grows as a shrub with many square, hard twigs, a cubit or a cubit and a half high, rising from a woody root. The lowest leaves are indeed disordered; but the upper ones grow in pairs opposite each other at rather long intervals, hoary, a straw's breadth wide, or 3 inches long, with a nerve running through the middle, having a powerful, pleasant scent and a somewhat bitter taste. At the tips of the branches, it bears a long spike of blue flowers, which are also sometimes white.

### LAVENDER WITH MULTI-CLEFT LEAVES, hairy branches, and blue flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lavender variety with more complex, divided foliage and flowering spikes.</image-desc>

Clusius found this around the city of Malaga in Spain <note>original: "Baetica"</note>, and around Murcia; he depicts and describes it at length, and it is found nowhere else.

As for the Male Lavenders, they clothe most of the mountains and deserted fields in Spain and Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>. In the rest of France, among the Germans, and elsewhere, it is sown in gardens; and sometimes it even grows on the hills of vineyards.

Furthermore, all Lavender heats and dries in the full third degree; it opens, thins, dissolves, and aids digestion. Applied in any manner, it is beneficial for cold diseases of the head, strengthens the stomach, and frees the liver from obstruction; it helps those with spleen ailments and stimulates menstruation. The distilled water of the flowers restores lost speech, and when drunk or applied to the nostrils and arteries, it is conducive for fainting fits.

<column-break/>

### THE SECOND TRAGIUM OF DIOSCORIDES: The *Secudes* of the Arabs and Aleppines.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Tragium plant with small leaves and rounded flower heads.</image-desc>

The root is whitish, somewhat long, and slender. From it emerge woody shoots, scarcely a little finger's length; to these adhere small, somewhat long leaves, arranged in a beautiful series, opposite each other, laid out not unlike those in *Trichomanes* <note>a type of fern</note>, yet longer than those, beautifully green on top, but covered with a gray down underneath. Among the said shoots, other small stalks come forth, bare, supporting purple spiked flowers.

It grows abundantly in open places around Aleppo and the neighboring mountains, according to the testimony of Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, physician and botanist</note>, especially in those locations.

### FEMALE FALSE NARD, OR LAVENDER: German: Lauendel; French: Lauande; Italian: Leuanda.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the female Pseudo-nardus (Lavendula) with slender stems and spikes.</image-desc>

In its whole appearance, the Female, or so-called Lavender, is very close to the commonly named *Spica*, or Male False Nard; however, it is smaller, its leaves are not so white, nor endowed with such a powerful scent. The spiked florets are not dissimilar, but with a shorter and more upright spike.

It is commonly called *Lavandula* or *Lavendula* because it is sought after for baths and the washings of men <note>from the Latin 'lavare', to wash</note>, to such an extent that if mixed with them, it commends everything with the sweetness of its scent.

The flowers in this, as in the Male, are for the most part blue in color, and sometimes also white. Some call it the Lesser Lavender, just as they call the Male the Greater Lavender.

It delights in sunny and stony places, and in the months of June and July it produces its spikes and becomes pregnant with flowers.

### VERONICA: German: Ehrenpreis; French: Veronique; Italian: Veronica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Veronica plant showing its creeping habit and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Whether or not this herb was known to the ancient Greeks and Latins is not yet clearly established; some contend it is the true *Teucrium*.

However, many *species* and *differences* of it are reviewed, as will be clear from what follows, of which we depict the more common one here.

It propagates itself by occasionally sending down fibers <note>roots</note>. The thin, round, long, hairy, jointed vines are gifted with leaves growing in pairs opposite each other at every joint, which are hairy and serrated around the edge. They are similar to the leaves of a plum tree, with a bitter and sharp taste. The flowers rise in spikes, in the manner of common *Chamaedrys* <note>Germander</note>, of a diluted purplish-blue, with small flames of the same color. When these are shed, it leaves behind a seed like common Germander, enclosed in small compartments.

<summary>This page describes various species of Lavender (Stoechas, Pseudo-nardus, and Lavendula) and Veronica, detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins in Spain and the Middle East, and medicinal uses for the head, liver, and stomach.</summary>
<keywords>Lavender, Stoechas, Veronica, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Aleppo, botany, aromatherapy, distillation, Spanish flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Veronica genus, specifically focusing on the upright spiked varieties and their regional habitats.</meta>

### GREATER UPRIGHT SPARKED SPEEDWELL.
<note>Latin: Veronica spicata recta maior. Today known as Veronica spicata.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Veronica plant with a single long, dense flower spike and serrated leaves arranged oppositely along the stem, showing the fibrous root system.</image-desc>

It produces a slanted, fibrous **root**, raising an upright **stem** half a foot, a foot, a cubit <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note>, or even higher, and for the most part it is unbranched. At its nodes, **leaves** grow that are narrower and sharper than those of the common Speedwell, lightly notched, hairy, and somewhat broad at the base. The **stem** ends in a long spike very densely packed with blue flowers like those of the common Speedwell, blooming little by little—first the lower ones, then the highest—and as they fall away, long stamens remain. The **seed** is contained in flat, twin capsules.

Our illustration is taken from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of modern botany.</note>.

<column-break/>

### LESSER UPRIGHT SPIKED SPEEDWELL.
<note>Latin: Veronica spicata recta minor.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Veronica spicata, similar in structure to the "Maior" but with a shorter stature and slightly different leaf proportions.</image-desc>

This variety differs from the Greater only in its size.

It grows in uncultivated and woody places, in sunny, sandy, and rocky areas; and not infrequently near mounds, embankments, and field hedges. It is sometimes found in great abundance in felled forests, as we have often observed in the nearby forests of Montbéliard; at Geneva in the wooded parts of Mount Salève; at Lyon *in the woods of the Good German woman* <note>Original: "au bois de la bonne Allemande"</note>; and especially at Yverdon-les-Bains <note>Latin: Ebroduni Heluetiorum</note> in the mountainous areas toward *Sainte-Croix*. It blooms in June and July.

<column-break/>

### GREATER BROAD-LEAFED SPEEDWELL, with shining and non-shining leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Veronica with a thick stem and a very dense, conical flower spike.</image-desc>

It puts forth branches a cubit or more in height, provided with few offshoots but many nodes. The **leaves** growing at each node are two or three inches long and one inch wide, thick, dark green, and shining, with rare and barely visible serrated notches. At the top of the stem grow many crowded little flowers in a spike, similar in shape to the flowers of the common Speedwell, but a little paler. The **seed** in the flat vessels is small and dark. The **root** is thick and fibrous.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), an influential Flemish botanist.</note>, the author of this description, notes two varieties: one whose leaves are neither shining nor dark, and another which has longer flower spikes.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S GREATER NARROW-LEAFED SPEEDWELL.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Clusius's narrow-leafed Veronica, showing more slender leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

This differs from the one just mentioned by its green stems and narrower leaves, which closely resemble the leaves of the Blue Loosestrife <note>Latin: Lysimachia caerulea</note>, and by its seed, which is small and reddish. It varies in its leaves, which are sometimes intermediate between the two types, in its less branched stems, and in its paler spike of flowers.

These Speedwells of Clusius, both the broad-leafed and narrow-leafed types with all their species, are found in many wooded mountains of Hungary <note>Latin: Pannonia</note>, Austria, and Styria; they delight in the shade and bloom in June and July. They are also cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

### UPRIGHT SPIKED SPEEDWELL, DEEPLY SERRATED: called Blue Loosestrife by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Veronica with deeply serrated (toothed) leaves and a prominent flower spike.</image-desc>

Clusius relates that it grows wild in Hungary, Austria, and Styria, either along streams or in mountain meadows. It is also kept in gardens, but in exposed and dry places. It grows with difficulty in shady spots. It produces flowers throughout the entire summer.

Furthermore, it must be concluded that Speedwell is hot and dry, based on its bitterness combined with an astringent quality. Fuchs writes that it is wonderfully beneficial for bloody wounds and old internal ailments; that it heals the itch <note>Scabies or general skin irritation</note> and all blemishes of the skin, and even diseases of the lungs; and in short, that it is not only very useful but even essential for the most serious afflictions.

<column-break/>

### ROCK SPEEDWELL.
<note>Latin: Veronica saxatilis.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, woodier Veronica species with smaller leaves and a shorter, looser flowering head.</image-desc>

The little stalks, a span high <note>About 9 inches</note> and woody, are clothed with numerous leaves set in opposite pairs, slightly longer than the leaves of Wild Thyme, occasionally notched, smooth, and rounded at the tip. The tops of the stems are adorned with rather large blue flowers, similar to the flowers of Germander <note>Latin: Chamaedrys</note> (though few are like the common variety). The root is woody and quite long. The whole plant is very bitter.

It grows on the higher summits of mountains, as we observed at Geneva on Mount Thuiri, and Clusius observed in Styria. It blooms in July.

Furthermore, Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist.</note>, determining that Speedwell is actually the plant *Teucrium*, highly commends it for both internal and external ailments of humans and pack animals.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of upright spiked Speedwell (Veronica), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe (including the Alps and Eastern Europe), and their medicinal applications for wounds, skin conditions, and lung diseases.</summary>
<keywords>Veronica spicata, Speedwell, Clusius, Fuchs, Tragus, medicinal herbs, Hungary, Austria, Styria, botany, wound healing, mountain flora</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### FEMALE VERONICA TO SOME.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Veronica plant with small, rounded, serrated leaves and tiny flowers on thin stems.</image-desc>

Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> labels it thus in his French edition. L'Obel, however, says the present Veronica is called "Female Veronica" by Thalius. In the *Portuguese Garden* it is called Marsh Chickweed; to some it is the Thyme-leaved Veronica: it is the *Alyssum* of Dioscorides according to Colonna.

It grows in meadows, forests, mountains, hills, and at the edges of fields: it flowers and flourishes in June and July. We observed it at Lyon in flower during March, at Genoa among the corn crops in April, and at Basel, not far from the Hirmei Castle, in May.

### CHAMAEDRYS: German: Ground Oak, Germander: French: Germandrée: Italian: Quercinela.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamaedrys (Wall Germander) plant with deeply lobed, oak-like leaves and spiked flower clusters.</image-desc>

According to the testimony of Dioscorides and Pliny, the Greeks also called the *Chamaedrys* <term>Chamaedrys: literally "Ground-oak," referring to the leaf shape</term> *Chamaerops* and *Chamaeregen*; the Latins called it *Trissago* and *Trixago*, and some, due to its similarity, called it *Teucrium*.

The ancients assigned no specific species to this plant: but the moderns have recognized many. For Fuchs says there are two "males" and just as many "females": Dodoens says there are two creeping types and just as many upright types. Others distinguish between the true or legitimate type and the "bastard" type, and recognize various differences in their medicinal powers.

We depict the True Common type here, which has woody little roots provided with many fibers; the sprig is about nine inches long, hairy, and downy: upon which the leaves grow in pairs almost opposite one another at intervals, in shape and notches almost like Oak leaves, stiff, veined, hairy, and somewhat bitter. The flower is tiny and purplish.

### SPINY CHAMAEDRYS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spiny variety of Chamaedrys with small leaves and sharp thorns along the stems.</image-desc>

This plant, which Caspar Bauhin calls in his *Phytopinax* (and also in his edition of Mattioli) the *Chamaedrys or spiny plant from Bembo's garden*, we keep among our dried plants, having received it from him. Our illustration is depicted from that dried specimen.

Furthermore, *Chamaedrys* is placed in the third order of heating and drying medicines by Galen and the moderns; it heats more than it dries. It consists of "thin parts" <note>A Galenic term meaning it is easily absorbed or penetrates the body's channels</note> and, on the authority of Pliny and Dioscorides, it is a remedy for the stomach, an old cough, ruptures, convulsions, and pains in the side: it consumes the spleen <note>reduces swelling of the spleen</note>, provokes urine and menstruation: and is most effective against the venom of serpents, whether drunk or applied as an ointment.

<column-break/>

### EVERGREEN ROCK VERONICA of Pona, approaching the Chamaedrys.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rock-dwelling Veronica with small, thick leaves and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

It grows from the crevices of simple and entirely bare rock on Mount Baldo, flowering at the beginning of July, ripening its seed toward the end, and is always green.

This Rock Veronica of Pona—or as Caspar Bauhin calls it in his *Phytopinax*, the *Rock Chamaedrys of Mount Baldo*—was described by Clusius in his *History* under the title of the 6th [or 3rd Pannonian] dwarf *Teucrium*.

### CHAMAEDRYS OF MOUNT SUMANO.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain variety of Chamaedrys with elongated, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

This elegant plant, gathered on Mount Sumano, has a great similarity to Pona's Evergreen Rock Veronica.

The authority of the principal writers states that the true common *Chamaedrys* grows to maturity in any place, especially sunny ones. We have observed it in various places flowering in March, April, and May, and even in June and July. At Montpellier near Castelnau; at Basel on the mountain near Moniert; at Montbéliard near La Crotte; at Yverdon on the hill near Chamblon and in gardens, and elsewhere.

Pliny writes that it was called "The Serrated One" by some, and that the saw was invented from the pattern of its leaves.

### ALPINE RELATIVE OF THE COMMON CHAMAEDRYS: The Alpine Clinopodium of Pona.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine plant related to Chamaedrys, featuring whorled leaves and terminal flower heads.</image-desc>

The leaves are situated opposite one another along the stalks, in pairs like the *Chamaedrys*, pointed, wrinkled, hairy, and serrated around the edge: from their "wings" <note>axils</note>, along the upper part of the stalks, two also rise opposite each other from little vessels, which open themselves into two keels, each divided into as many compartments: full of small, black seed. The stalks are between four and nine inches long, firm, with many rising from a woody, blackish root divided into many heads.

We collected this in the Savoyard Alps, and we have seen to it being depicted and described from the dried specimen.

# OF PLANTS

### ALPINE GERMANDER WITH STRAWBERRY FLOWERS.
<note>original: "Chamædrys Alpina Flore Fragariæ" - likely *Dryas octopetala*, known today as Mountain Avens.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with serrated leaves and small flowers, showing the root system and a single stem with a seed head resembling a Pulsatilla.</image-desc>

It spreads tough, woody twigs across the ground, about a palm or a span <note>a "span" is roughly 9 inches</note> in length, somewhat thick and endowed with a reddish color. Along these, the leaves grow in no particular order; they are smaller than the common Germander, tougher, more wrinkled, saw-toothed, grayish-white underneath, and dark green above. On thin, hairy stalks a palm long, sit individual white flowers, like those of the Strawberry but twice as small. When these fall away, they are succeeded by a feathery head like that of the Pasque-flower <note>original: "Pulsatillæ"</note>, with an oblong, hairy seed. The base of the entire flower is supported by oblong, hairy, narrow leaves. The root creeps far and wide, thick, woody, and blackish-red.

### BROAD-LEAVED SPURIOUS GERMANDER with flowers arranged in a stalk, of a cheerful blue.
<note>original: "Chamædrys Spuria Latifolia" - likely a species of Speedwell (*Veronica*).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright plant with broad, opposite, serrated leaves and a terminal spike of small flowers.</image-desc>

It is better known than needs to be refuted that this plant, like the preceding one, is neither a *Teucrium* nor the legitimate Germander. Nevertheless, before the true Germander was well known, the name of Germander was given to these, and they were accepted in place of Germander in medicinal compositions. Furthermore, it grows in the same locations as the narrow-leaved variety.

Tragus, Lobelius, and Dodonæus <note>Famous 16th-century botanists Hieronymus Bock, Matthias de l'Obel, and Rembert Dodoens.</note> record that it is beneficial for an incipient cough, dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, a hardened spleen, strangury <note>painful urination</note>, obstructions of the internal organs, bad humors <note>original: "cacochymiæ"</note>, and the "foul colors" of young women <note>likely referring to chlorosis or anemia</note>.

### ANOTHER SPECIES OF SPURIOUS GERMANDER: The smaller Pannonian Teucrium of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with smaller, more rounded serrated leaves and a dense terminal flower spike.</image-desc>

The branches of this plant lie prostrate on the ground, a span long, along which always grow two leaves opposite each other, similar to Germander leaves, saw-toothed, and ending in a blunt point. The flowers occupy a large part of the small branches, arranged in spikes, similar to the blue flowers of the young Germander. These are followed by two-parted, compressed capsules containing reddish seed. A fibrous root lies beneath.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a primary figure in 16th-century botany.</note> identifies three species of it, namely by the color of the flowers: either a very deep blue, or a paler ashen color, or a whitish-flesh color.

It grows in drier, uncultivated fields and grassy banks, and it flowers in May.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED SPURIOUS GERMANDER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with narrow, elongated serrated leaves and a slender terminal flower spike.</image-desc>

From a single thin but long, creeping, woody, and fibrous root, it produces many twigs spread across the ground; these are rounded, thin, hairy, and likewise woody, a palm or a span in length. On these, two leaves are placed opposite each other at intervals, oblong and saw-toothed around the edges. The twigs, divided into several small branches toward the end, support flowers arranged in a spike, blue in color, which do not all open at the same time.

It grows in many places in meadows near rivers, streams, ditches, and springs, as well as in wooded areas; it flowers in June, July, and August.

### GREATEST SPURIOUS GERMANDER: Perhaps the greater Pannonian Teucrium of Clusius?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, robust plant with large, deeply serrated leaves and a prominent terminal flower spike.</image-desc>

It is of the same genus as the common Germander, but it is larger by many degrees. The leaves are long, pointed, and saw-toothed, growing in pairs along hairy stems. The branches, likewise positioned opposite one another, support a long spike of flowers similar to the common Germander but larger, followed by compressed, two-parted capsules.

It grows in grassy places on stony hills, such as on the hill of La Bastie in Geneva, and elsewhere.

Lobelius mentions a false, prostrate Germander with dark green leaves.

### SMALLER NARROW-LEAVED SPURIOUS GERMANDER: with a white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, more delicate plant with narrow leaves and a small flower spike.</image-desc>

It is more branched than the others, and its leaves are two or three times narrower than the aforementioned narrow-leaved spurious variety.

The uncultivated fields of the Rauraci <note>The region around Basel, Switzerland.</note> have it in abundance in drier spots, and it grows in various other places; sometimes it even grows spontaneously in gardens.

Furthermore, to say something in general about the etymology of *Chamædrys*: Marcellus says that *Chamædrys* is nothing other than a "low and ground-creeping oak" <note>From the Greek *chamai* (on the ground) and *drys* (oak)</note>, looking to the meaning of the word; he relates that because of its stunted height, the name *Chamærops* was given to it by some.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of "spurious" Germander (mostly Speedwells), detailing their physical structures, habitats in regions like Geneva and Basel, and their medicinal applications for internal obstructions and respiratory issues.</summary>
<keywords>Germander, Speedwell, Teucrium, Clusius, Lobelius, medicinal herbs, Geneva, Basel, botany, taxonomy</keywords>

### **Teucrium** or **Teucris**: German: *Large Germander*;
### French: *Teucrion*: Italian: *Teucrion*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Teucrium plant, showing a woody root system, serrated leaves on upright stems, and small flowers clustered at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Teucrium, according to the author Dioscorides <note>A famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, is an herb called *Chamaedrys* <note>Wall Germander</note> by others due to its similarity: presenting the appearance of a twig, etc. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> records that it was discovered by Teucer, the brother of Ajax, and takes its name from him.

It is indeed related to the Germander, but it grows as a taller shrub, with straight, woody, square, and hairy shoots. Upon these, at short intervals, are seen pairs of leaves placed opposite one another, hairy on both sides, shining with a dark green color, and serrated; they are oblong-round (especially the lower ones, for others end more in a point) and are not deeply cut around the edges; they have a pleasant scent if rubbed.

### **Boetic and Cretan Teucrium**
### of Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note>,

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Boetic and Cretan variety of Teucrium, featuring more elongated, narrower leaves and distinct floral spikes.</image-desc>

The branch of the Boetic Teucrium <note>From Boetica, a Roman province in southern Spain</note> becomes woody and is very white, square, and entirely covered in downy hair. At its joints, leaves grow in opposite positions, like the common Teucrium, dark green above and quite white and veined beneath, covered with a denser down. The *flowers* are white, emerging from the leaf axils on very short stems; they let down a long lip, and in place of a "helmet" <note>The upper hood of a flower</note>, of which they have none, they thrust out long stamens. The *calyxes* <note>The outer protective envelope of the flower</note> are white, striped, and divided into five pointed segments. It blooms in March in the coastal regions of Boetica.

Furthermore, many plants are gifted with the name of Teucrium: most species of *Germander* and *Speedwell*, as well as *Spleenwort*, *Mule's Fern*, *Hart's Tongue*, etc.

### **Scordium**: German, French & Italian: *Scordium* <note>Water Germander</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Scordium plant, showing creeping stems with small, serrated, hairy leaves and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

From hair-like roots rise stems a span high, branched, advancing joint by joint, hairy, square, and hollow. From their joints emerge opposite leaves, like Germander, somewhat long, wrinkled, serrated, soft to the touch, hairy, whitish, and with the smell of Garlic <note>The name Scordium comes from the Greek 'skordon' for garlic</note>. The *flowers* also come from the same place, all along the stem, in groups of four, very similar to Germander flowers, with a short stalk, reddish in color, with stamens of the same color; when these fall away, a tiny seed is found in small vessels.

Dioscorides mentions only one Scordium: but Pliny has two: and Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, 16th-century Italian botanist</note> also has two when he imitated him: namely the Common sort, and another with a leaf like *Wild Mint*. Others distinguish them into *Greater*, *Middle*, and *Lesser*.

<column-break/>

### **Another illustration of Teucrium.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Teucrium, showing a more sprawling habit with smaller leaves and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

The *flowers of Teucrium* spring from the upper leaf axils, several joined together, clinging to fairly long stalks, with a hairy, grayish calyx, in the shape of Germander flowers: with a longer lip hanging down, but lacking a hood, in place of which yellowish stamens emerge, which is the same color the flower possesses. The taste of the herb is somewhat bitter, with a bitterness that is not unpleasant.

It grows in stony and rough places, and loves mountains and dry, sunny spots, and it thrives successfully in gardens.

Galen <note>Prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> places it in the third order of drying medicines and the second order of heating medicines: and records that it heals the spleen.

### **Scutellaria with the appearance of Teucrium.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Scutellaria, showing an upright, square stem with opposite leaves and a terminal floral spike.</image-desc>

The plant is a cubit high, with a square, hairy stem, branched into opposite arms: and with pairs of leaves placed opposite each other, like common Teucrium. Large flowers occupy almost the entire ends of the branches in a spike, like *Hedge-nettle*, sometimes red in color, sometimes white, somewhat hairy, coming from a short, shaggy calyx. The leaves below them are small, somewhat broad, roundish, pointed, downy, and a dull red.

We saw it blooming in May in the garden at Padua.

Furthermore, Pliny reveals how it was discovered that **Teucrium** heals the spleen. *When the entrails [of a sacrificed animal], he says, were once thrown upon Teucrium, they stuck to the spleen and drained it: hence it was called "Splenion" by some. Thus they tell of pigs that eat its root, that they are found without a spleen.*

### **Downy Cretan Scorodotis:**
### **The true Scorodotis of Pliny, according to some.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Scorodotis, showing a very hairy (tomentose) plant with thick, textured leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

Regarding the *birthplaces of Scordium*: Dioscorides wrote that Scordium grows in mountainous and marshy places; Pliny says in the rich and damp plains of Pontus. From these we gather that it grows in mountains and plains, but in moist ones. It was once brought at great expense from the most remote regions: but today it is kept in many places in Germany, France, and Italy. We ourselves saw it in a nearby meadow at Montpellier, blooming in May and September: abundantly around Lyon: at Geneva in the "Bishop's Meadow": at Montbéliard between the city and the village of *Souchaut*: and also at Yverdon in those pleasant vales which lie near the Lake. However, when moved into gardens, it easily perishes.

<keywords>Teucrium, Scordium, Germander, medicinal herbs, spleen treatments, Dioscorides, Pliny, botanical geography, Montpellier, Padua garden</keywords>

### SCORODOTIS, OR SCORDIUM, WITH SAGE-LIKE LEAVES: German: *Wild Salbey* <note>Wild Sage</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scorodotis plant showing a fibrous root system, square stems, and serrated leaves resembling sage.</image-desc>

It rests upon a winding and fibrous root: from which several stems rise up, two cubits high <note>about three feet</note>, four-sided, hairy, turning purple or blackish, and filled with white pith. At the joints of these stems, leaves come out in pairs opposite one another at intervals; they are like Sage, wrinkled, dark green, rough and weathered, hairy, saw-toothed around the edges, and bitter in taste. The top of the stem is divided into several small forks, in which the flowers are arranged in a spiral, turning to one side; they are like Germander <note>original: *Chamædryos*</note>, but of a grassy, white, or pale color. From their gaping mouth, in place of a "helmet" <note>the upper petal of the flower</note>, purple-tinted stamens spring forth. The seeds are contained in the husks, dark, similar to heavy Basil <note>original: *Ocymi grauis*</note>, somewhat bitter, round, and dark.

### CHAMÆPYTIS, or MUSK IVY: German: *Erdpin* <note>Ground Pine</note>: French: *Iue muscate*: Italian: *Chamapitio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chamæpytis (Ground Pine) with narrow, needle-like leaves and a long taproot.</image-desc>

Chamæpytis is a small plant about a palm's breadth high, with a fairly long, simple, and hard little root. The small stalk is rounded, hairy, reddish near the ground, and elsewhere turning from grassy green to yellow, just like the leaves. These leaves grow in pairs opposite each other at the nodes at short intervals; they are hairy, mimicking the fingered feet of a small bird <note>original: *auriculæ* - likely referring to a bird's claw shape</note>, with the taste and smell of Pitch or Resin. From the "wings" <note>axils</note> of the leaves, yellowish flowers emerge with a wider, two-cleft lip, the upper part spotted with small red dots; these press down the pale purple stamens in place of a "helmet." Small heads follow, swelling into four little rounded mounds, containing as many three-cornered seeds. We present two images from Fuchs’s works, neither of which is satisfactory.

### ORIENTAL CHAMÆPYTIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Oriental Chamæpytis, showing a more upright growth habit and dense foliage.</image-desc>

It grows like a shrub with several shoots a palm's length long, thick, square, and covered with much white downy hair. The leaves are crowded at the nodes, about an inch long, like the Musk Ivy of Montpellier (which we will discuss shortly), downy, thick, and finely toothed at the ends, with a very bitter taste. From their axils, from the lowest branches all the way to the top, hairy little vessels break out, gaping open into four ridges.

The common yellow-flowered Chamæpytis grows in fields and grassy plains; it blooms from the month of April until September, earlier or later depending on the variety of the location.

It is abundant at Lyon, at Geneva near the Arve bridge, at Basel on the way to Tortocum, at Yverdon in the district of *Susenne* in the adjacent fields, and in various other places.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SCORDIUM WITH SAGE-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of Scordium with a more vertical growth habit and distinct leaf arrangement.</image-desc>

Lobelius, Camerarius, and others declare this to be the "second Scordium" of Pliny, but too hastily. Gesner calls it the "everlasting Stachys"; it is better judged as the *Polemonium* or *Polemonia* of Ruellius, which he says is also called *Philetaerium*, and by the Cappadocians—on account of its multitude of uses—*Chiliodynamis* <note>Greek: "thousand-powers"</note>. Most call it Wood Sage or Wild Sage; Belon calls it the "bastard and false Scorodotis," whom few follow.

It grows in woods and uncultivated places. We have seen it at Montpellier in the mountains around *Esperon*; at Lyon, *in the woods of the Good German Woman* <note>original: "au bois de la bonne Allemande"</note>, and elsewhere.

*Regarding the Etymology and Virtues, see the Appendix.*

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF CHAMÆPYTIOS, OR MUSK IVY.

<image-desc>Alternative woodcut illustration of Chamæpytis showing a denser, more spreading foliage pattern.</image-desc>

Dioscorides has three species of Chamæpytios, the third of which he calls the "Male." Pliny also has three, which were called *Chamæpytis* in Latin (and *Aiuga* by others) because of their use in abortions, and by some "Incense of the Earth" <note>original: *Thus terræ*</note>. Matthiolus and others among the more recent authors have the same number; they determine that the third species, or the "Male" of Dioscorides, fits best with the common *Iua arthritica* <note>Gout Ivy</note>. They admit that his first species, the larger and branched one, is well enough known, but they report it is uncertain what can be shown for the second. There are those who recognize a difference in the flowers, since a certain kind is found with a white flower. Dodoens adds three other "false" kinds to the three commonly accepted ones.

### CHAMÆPYTIS, OR MUSK IVY of Montpellier, with a purplish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Montpellier Chamæpytis with broader, more lobed leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

Clusius writes that this grows in rich soil by the Tagus river in Portugal, in the great kingdom of Granada, and in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>; it blooms in Summer and Autumn. Lobelius says it shrubs in the olive groves and dry fields of Narbonne and Provence, and is not easily known elsewhere. It is called "Musk-scented" by way of contradiction and irony <note>original: *per antiphrasin atque ironicè*</note>, since it has a great odor indeed, but one that is not at all pleasant. We observed it at Montpellier, in the mountains around *Castelneuf*, in very stony places, blooming in September.

Is it the "second Anthyllis" of Dioscorides (Book 3 and Book 16)? Or the "Greater Chamæpytis" of Cesalpino?

# IMAGES AND OUTLINE:

### GROUND PINE WITH UNSLIT LEAVES.
### Ground Pine 3 of Dioscorides, according to Mattioli.
<note>original: "Chamæpytis folio non laciniato." Chamæpytis comes from the Greek for "ground pine" due to its resinous scent.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ground Pine plant, showing a central stem with small, narrow leaves and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

From a fibrous root, it puts forth branches a palm-width high, spread upon the ground, with small leaves like those of the lesser savory <note>original: "se-peratui minoris," likely Satureja</note>, less fleshy, but tiny and hairy: among which are small flowers of a yellowish-white color, with a scent that is not unpleasant.

It is less well-known and encountered in few places, except in Nice in Savoy, and on the arid hills of Ligurian Genoa. However, Lobelius writes that it is kept as a green plant in Belgium.

His illustration shows it without hairs: but the one depicted in Dodonaeus, taken from Fuchs, is hairy. Lobelius labels this as the 1st Ground Pine of Dioscorides: but Dodonaeus, Mattioli, and others label it as the 3rd. More on Ground Pine in the Appendix.

### POLY-MOUNTAIN.
<note>original: "Polium." A medicinal herb of the Teucrium genus, often called Hullwort.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Polium plant with upright stems, small leaves, and rounded flower heads at the tips.</image-desc>

Dioscorides makes two kinds of Poly: the *Mountain* and *Another* which is more shrub-like, not of such a strong scent, and less effective in its powers. But many other differences of Poly are held among more recent authors, taken from their place of birth, size, strength, the color of the flowers, and other marks.

The one we depict here is entirely delicate, with slender branches creeping on the ground, nine inches long, covered in much white down, which occasionally strike roots at the nodes. Its leaves are narrow, oblong, small-toothed, and woolly: and it also has small *Heads*, likewise round and woolly: in which the flower is purple or white, or white tinged with purple.

It grows in sandy places and flowers in May and April.

### VENETIAN POLY: GOAT-WHEAT.
<note>original: "Polium Venetum: Ægipyrus."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polium Venetum, featuring tall, branching stems with clusters of flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This one has broader leaves, a less white head, but a more divided foliage. It grows abundantly in the Lido of the Venetians.

Moreover, various plants are gifted with the name of Poly, such as *Wild Thyme, Savory, Axines, Pliny's Impious-weed, Golden Cudweed, Sea Starwort, Honeysuckle Ground-pine*, and others similar: but improperly so.

However, Poly properly so-called is bitter to those who taste it, according to the author Galen, and moderately sharp: it frees all the internal organs from obstruction, and provokes urine and the menses. Spread beneath one or used as a fumigant, says Dioscorides, it puts venomous beasts to flight; applied as a poultice, it glues wounds together: a decoction of it helps those with dropsy <note>edema</note> and the royal disease <note>jaundice</note>.

Concerning *Goat-wheat* <note>original: "Ægipyro"</note>, which is considered a species of Poly, see the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### OAK OF JERUSALEM: Germ. Traubenkraut: Gall. Pymen, Pymen, Millegrain: Ital. Botry.
<note>original: "Botrys." Also known as Feather Geranium or Jerusalem Oak.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Botrys plant, showing a thick root system and stems with lobed leaves and grape-like flower clusters.</image-desc>

One kind of Botrys is cultivated, another is wild. Here we depict the wild, whorled variety, which is accustomed to grow in vineyards and on their walls, and in warm, sunny, and elevated places; sometimes it is even found in fields among the crops, as we have observed here and there in Montbéliard, and in Montpellier around Mount Esperon.

The cultivated kind has a more cheerful appearance overall, but is shorter in stature, about a palm high: with square, hairy branches, on which are the leaves of the Botrys, but woolly and of a deeper green, rising branched from the joints, with a sweet scent and a bitter taste. The *Flowers* likewise burst forth in whorls, turning purple: which are followed by fourfold blackish seeds. The root is woody, slender, and endowed with few fibers. More on Botrys in the Appendix.

### MONTPELLIER POLY: The MOUNTAIN Poly of Dioscorides: Mountain Poly, or Teuthrium to others.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polium Monspessulanum, showing a woody base with several upright stems and small, dense flower heads.</image-desc>

The leaves in this plant grow many together from the same spot at certain intervals, opposite one another; they are narrow, oblong, small-toothed, white, woolly, and of a sharp and bitter taste: along branches nine inches or a palm long, firm, round, and hoary. The root is woody, endowed with few fibers. The *Heads* are clustered, white, woolly, consisting of oblong cups from which the gaping, white flowers burst forth. Threads similar to Dodder <note>original: "Epithymo"</note> are often interwoven in its twigs.

It grows abundantly at Montpellier near the sea: and is also found elsewhere. Namely, in maritime places and on sloping hills and sandy shores. When cultivated, it is less white and puts out broader leaves. It flowers in Summer.

### BETONY or VETONY: Germ. Bethonien: Gall. Betoine: Ital. Betonica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica plant, showing a basal rosette of leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

One Betony is the *Common* kind, another is the *Rarer* kind which delights in cultivation, and grows more broadly green in gardens and is broad-leaved. And both, again, have flowers that are for the most part purple, and sometimes also white.

The *Common* kind, which we depict here, rises with numerous stems, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or more in height, square, and knotted at long intervals. Some leaves are at the joints of the stem in pairs, opposite each other; others are scattered on the ground, disordered, endowed with stalks about a palm long, fringed around the edges, wrinkled, rough, and possessed of an aromatic taste. The *Flowers* surround the joints in whorled spikes, turning purple. The *Seed* is oblong and angular. The *Root* is a thumb's thickness, hairy with frequent and long fibers.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of medicinal herbs, specifically focusing on varieties of Betony and Sage. It maintains the encyclopedic style of early modern herbals, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary botanists.</meta>

### WHITE-FLOWERED BETONY, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betony plant with a tall flowering spike and broad, serrated basal leaves.</image-desc>

Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), a German botanist</note> also mentions this plant; he, like Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), who used the name Tragus</note>, relates that it differs from the common variety only in the color of its flowers. Tragus wonders at Dioscorides—and not without reason—that although he followed the history of Betony most diligently in other respects, he nevertheless did not indicate the color of the flowers.

The reason is that this one is red <note>referring to the common variety</note>, but it grows in the same places. For both grow in meadows, mountainous woods, and in cold and shaded places; they flower in the months of May and June, and sometimes even in Autumn. Cordus writes that Betony grows in meadows, thickets, and grassy places, in almost any kind of soil. We observed it growing green in December in the public garden at Padua.

### SAGE : German: Salbey : Belgian: Sauie : French: Sauge : Italian & Spanish: Salvia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Salvia (Sage) plant showing opposite leaves and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Although Dioscorides is found to have recognized only one kind of Sage, Theophrastus described two types: *Sphacelon* and *Elelisphacon* <note>Greek names for varieties of sage</note>, which Pliny wrongly categorized as a type of wild lentil. More recent authors commonly distinguish it into Garden (or domestic) and Field (or wild) Sage. And that, in turn, into Greater and Lesser, Broad-leafed and Narrow-leafed; with curled or non-curled leaves, and likewise white, blackish, or dark purple; and into eared <note>having small lobes at the leaf base</note> or non-eared. These same authors further distinguish them by the color of the flowers: blue, white, or whitish-purple.

### LESSER NARROW-LEAFED SAGE : Cretan Gall-bearing SAGE.

The root of this is hard, woody, and divided into branches. It puts forth woody twigs of a reddish-brown color, which are surrounded by pairs of leaves always placed opposite one another; these are long and narrower than in any other kind of Sage, and somewhat notched around the edges. The middle stalk ends in a spike of purple flowers, with no small leaves intervening.

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> labels this Spanish Sage, while Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus</note> calls it Indian Sage.

The Cretan Sage, called "Gall-bearing," is entirely covered in thick down and appears white. The leaves are partly eared and partly truncated, ending in a blunt point. At the joints, sitting on a stem an inch and a half long, are round galls, similar to the little balls that usually grow on the leaves of Oaks.

<column-break/>

### BETONY-LEAFED FOXTAIL of some authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with serrated leaves similar to Betony and a fuzzy, cylindrical flower head resembling a fox's tail.</image-desc>

This is called *Mountain Foxtail* <note>original: "Alopepuros montana"</note> by herbalists, from the fruit's certain shaggy resemblance to a fox's tail.

It grows in the shaded valleys of high mountains, darkened by a frequency of trees and damp from the flow of waters.

Furthermore, the Greeks called Betony *Cestron*, and some of the Latins called it *Serratula* <note>meaning "little saw," referring to the leaf edges</note>; others called it *Vetonica*, named after its discoverers, the Vettones, a people of Spain.

Antonius Musa, the most famous physician to Augustus Caesar, wrote an entire book on its powers. Who could recount them all? It is known that in extolling the power and utility of a thing, it is common to say: *it is more useful than Betony*.

### BROAD-LEAFED SERRATED CURLED SAGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Sage plant with distinctly crinkled or "crisped" leaf margins.</image-desc>

This is kept in the more cultivated gardens in London. However, Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585)</note> writes that the common variety grows spontaneously in rough places and among rubble. In Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note> and Piedmont, it grows luxuriantly among the vines. When moved into gardens, it turns out more beautiful. It flowers in May in Montpellier and Lyon, and later in colder climates.

Furthermore, it was called *Salvia* by the Latins because it makes men "safe and sound" <note>original: "salvos et incolumes"; a play on the Latin 'salvere', to be well</note>, or because it is beneficial for fertility. We read in Aëtius that the name *Sacred Herb* <note>original: "Sacra herba"</note> was granted to it for that reason. The Greeks called it *Sphacelon* and *Elelisphacon*, from the peculiar power it possesses in healing "Sphacelus" or gangrenous parts.

### LESSER EARED SAGE : German: Klein Salbey : French: Sauge franche : Italian: Salvia minore.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Sage variety with "ears" (auricles) at the base of the leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves of this are smaller in size than the Greater Sage; however, they surpass it with a more powerful scent and a more vigorous taste, and they are very white. At the bottom of the leaves are placed two little wings <note>pinnulae</note>, sometimes one, and in some places none. Other features are common with the Greater Sage, but this one is more woody and does not multiply as easily.

In certain places in Italy and Spain, and in the territory of Marseille, it grows abundantly and spontaneously in the fields; in Germany, however, it is only kept cultivated in gardens.

Concerning the temperament and powers of Sage, see the Appendix.

<keywords>Betony, Sage, Salvia, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Antonius Musa, plant morphology, Cretan Sage, Foxtail</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of aromatic herbs, specifically focusing on Sage and Clary Sage varieties, following the previous discussions on labiate plants.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### SAGE SMELLING OF WORMWOOD.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Salvia plant with broad, textured leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

The flower is quite large, arranged in whorls <note>circles of flowers around a stem</note>, purplish or white: the leaf is truly that of the common Sage, sometimes feathered, sometimes stunted, smelling of *Wormwood* <note>original: "Absynthium"</note>. It is kept in the more cultivated gardens.

As for the common Sage, which the lack of space did not allow to be described in its own proper place, it has a hardy, woody, and perennial root: from which many shoots rise up, woody, square-stemmed, hairy, and gray-white or greenish. The leaves rival the leaves of Mint, pointed, white, greenish, or reddish-brown in color, of an excellent scent, and of a sharp taste with an aromatic bitterness. The flowers are arranged in a spike, blue, or purplish-white, with the hairy hood and split lip characteristic of the "dead-nettle" family <note>original: "lamia"</note>.

### RED-TOPPED CLARY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Horminum plant with a dense, leafy floral head and broad basal leaves.</image-desc>

This differs from the preceding only by its red "hair" <note>the colorful bracts at the top of the plant</note> and smaller flowers. Both are cultivated in gardens, as we have had in our own at Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard: it flowers in May, June, and July.

Furthermore, it is called *Horminum* from the Greek *horman* <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρμᾶν"</note>, meaning to be moved by impulse, to be carried by instinct, and to be stirred for Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, because, as Dioscorides says, it stimulates the libido. He divides it into the *Cultivated* and the *Wild*, attributing a round and dusky seed to the former, and an oblong and black seed to the latter.

Galen and Theophrastus numbered Clary among the types of grain; in Theophrastus's work, Gaza translates the name as *Geminata* <note>the doubled one</note>: while Pliny mentions *Horminum* and *Herminium*. More can be found in the *Appendix*.

### COMMON WILD CLEAR-EYE, or Wild Clary.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Gallitricum with deeply lobed, serrated leaves and a long, slender flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant sometimes rises to two cubits <note>about three feet</note>: with a square, hairy, hollow stem, divided into "wings" <note>branches</note>. The leaves are much larger than in the cultivated Clary, rough, wavy-edged, saw-toothed, and approaching the leaves of Sage, with a heavy scent. The flowers in the long spike are blue and purple, large, in the shape of Sage flowers. The seed is black. The root is woody and fragrant.

Ruellius calls it *Centrum gallinæ* <note>Hen's spur</note> or *Centrum galli* <note>Cock's spur</note>, and he rebukes the Apothecaries because they wrongly call it *Gallitricum* <note>Clear-eye</note>. Some call it *Overseas Sage* or *Roman Sage*.

It grows spontaneously in meadows, hills, level fields, and the borders of farmlands: it flowers in the month of June and is then heavy with seed.

<column-break/>

### CLARY, ORMINUM, GEMINALIS: German: Garden Scarlet; French: Hormin; Italian: Horminio.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Horminum plant with prominent bracts and opposite leaves.</image-desc>

*Horminum* <note>Clary</note> has much similarity with *Salvia* <note>Sage</note>. The stems are reddish, branched with many "wings," hairy with thick down, square, a foot or more in height. At their joints, leaves are produced in opposite pairs, but less rough, hairy, with no remarkable scent, and a bitterish taste: however, the "phalanx" <note>cluster</note> of those leaves at the ends of the branches is denser, and the "hair" <note>top bracts</note> is purple-violet. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils, partly purple and partly whitening, like Sage. The seed is oblong, dusky or black. The root is woody and fibrous. It is an annual plant.

The Clary with purple-violet hair, which we depict here, grows abundantly: Camerarius says it grows in the territory of Siena and Illyria, and all of Greece: we have seen it nowhere except in gardens.

### CLEAR-EYE, CLARY, ALL-GOOD: German: Scharlach; Italian: Sciaria; French: Oruale, Toute bonne.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Sclarea plant with large, heart-shaped, rugose leaves and a branching inflorescence.</image-desc>

Many species of *Gallitricum* <note>Clear-eye/Clary</note> are described, differing among themselves by their place of birth, size, leaf shape, and the color of the flowers and "hair."

OUR CULTIVATED VARIETY which we depict here has a square stem, two cubits high, almost the thickness of a pinky finger, stiff, hairy, full of white pith, split into opposite branches in pairs at intervals. The flowers are spiked, composed of many whorls, very similar to Sage flowers, hooded, with a color verging from blue to white. The seeds are four-fold in small striated pods, polished with a slippery stickiness, of a reddish color. The leaves are in pairs opposite each other, wrinkled, like *Ethiopis* <note>Woolly Clary</note>, but less shaggy. The root is woody. The scent of the whole plant is powerful, and the taste is bitter.

It is sown in gardens, and flowers in June and July.

### A VARIETY OF WILD CLEAR-EYE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of wild Gallitricum with a single, tall, upright flowering spike and basal foliage.</image-desc>

Cordus, Lonicer, Fuchs, Camerarius, Schwenckfeld, Thalius, L'Obel, Clusius and others contend with Ruellius that the common wild Clear-eye is actually *Horminum*. Many others, however, refer it to *Sclarea* or *Gallitricum*.

Furthermore, Clear-eye, especially the cultivated kind, is of a hot and dry temperament in the third degree, and possesses the power of loosening, thinning, and expelling. Taken in any manner, it moves the menses and stimulates fertility. If wine in which Clear-eye has been placed ferments, it is especially suited for a cold stomach; it cuts through and consumes phlegm, and assists women suffering from coldness, infertility, or "white menses" <note>leukorrhea</note>.

<summary>This page describes various species of Sage and Clary Sage (Horminum/Sclarea), detailing their physical characteristics, botanical nomenclature, and medicinal uses for digestive and reproductive health.</summary>
<keywords>Sage, Clary Sage, Horminum, Gallitricum, Sclarea, medicinal herbs, women's health, botany, Dioscorides, Renaissance medicine</keywords>
