<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the genus Gallitricum (Clary or Sage varieties), following the previous discussions of cultivated herbs. The catchword "GALLI-" from the previous page is here completed.</meta>

### EXOTIC GALLITRICUM, OR BISERMAS.
#### The Syrian "Aman" of some authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gallitricum plant with broad, textured leaves and a tall flowering stalk with small blossoms.</image-desc>

The exotic plant *Bisermas* <note>likely *Salvia hierosolymitana* or a related Eastern Clary</note> greatly resembles our cultivated Clary <note>original: "Sclaream sativam"</note> in its entire appearance: it has square stems, hairy and somewhat rough to the touch, divided into frequent branches <note>original: "alas," literally wings</note> placed in pairs opposite one another. The leaves are like those of our Clary; the first ones at the bottom are small and oblong, while those that follow are large, wrinkled, and shaggy, with the faint scent of Basil <note>original: "Ocymi"</note> and the arrangement of Clary. Likewise, the appearance and placement of the flowers are like Clary, but the color is milky-white, with the small lower lip spotted with a few little dots on the inside. The seed is similar to cultivated Gallitricum, but a little larger.

It grew for us at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi," the estate of the Duke of Württemberg where the author worked</note> in the botanical garden <note>original: "S. P. horto," likely referring to the Prince's Garden</note>; it bloomed in July, August, and September.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH GALLITRICUM, WITH SAGE-LIKE LEAVES,
#### and purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with slender, serrated leaves resembling sage and a vertical flowering spike.</image-desc>

This is very similar to the common Wild Gallitricum. The leaves grow opposite one another at the nodes of the stem, but they are much smaller and narrower, saw-toothed <note>term: serrata (edges like a saw)</note> around the edges and appearing as if nibbled, without hairs, approaching the appearance of Sage leaves. Numerous whorls <note>term: verticelli (circular arrangements of flowers around a stem)</note> of flowers form a spike; they are purple-violet and smaller than in the aforementioned Wild Gallitricum. Beneath each whorl are two short, somewhat broad leaves that are even slightly blue in color.

It grows everywhere around Vienna in Austria and in other places along roadsides and at the edges of fields and vineyards; it blooms in the height of Summer. Some call it Wild Sage <note>original: "Salviam agrestem"</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### WILD GALLITRICUM, WITH A GREEN
#### tuft.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Gallitricum with large, deeply lobed lower leaves and a branching flower head.</image-desc>

This variety exceeds the others in size, having a four-angled stem as in the other species, and leaves growing opposite at each joint. However, its topmost part does not turn purple but remains green. Although the flowers are similar in shape, they are of a paler color. The lower leaves have larger notches so that they appear somewhat jagged <note>original: "laciniata"</note>; the other characteristics agree with the rest.

It grows spontaneously here and there in coppiced woods, mountains, and the margins of fields, blooming in May and June.

<column-break/>

### GALLITRICUM WITH ROUNDER LEAVES:
#### and a large violet flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded, scalloped leaves and a prominent flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Doctor Agerius <note>Nicholas Ager (1568–1634), a French botanist and physician</note> collected this in the high meadows of the Tyrolean mountains, from whom we received it.

Furthermore, the seed of Gallitricum—and indeed the whole plant when it goes to spike—has a scent that is not unpleasant, yet it induces a heaviness in the head. Nevertheless, it is of great use among Northern peoples for the making of *Zytum* and Beer <note>original: "Cerevisiæ"</note>. Indeed, for lack of Hops, or for the sake of making a more potent drink, they add it to the boiling vats. It creates a strong liquor <note>original: "temetum"</note> by which, after draining not many cups, they become intoxicated, with a cheerfulness that is unpleasant to us—and in some, more worthy of pity than laughter. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note> notes that it stimulates lust <note>original: "Venerem stimulat," literally 'stimulates Venus'</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### GALLITRICUM WITH SMALLER FLOWERS,
#### purplish and red.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Gallitricum variety with dense foliage and small flowers.</image-desc>

With a long-lived root, this plant—related to Wild Gallitricum—lasts for many years. It is fragrant and not dissimilar in appearance, stem, leaves, and manner of growth. However, the flowers are so few that they hardly project beyond the calyx <note>term: calyx (the green outer protective layer of a flower)</note>; they are purplish and somewhat gaping, whereas in the Common variety the flowers are large and hide many stamens <note>original: "apices"</note> under a large, prominent hood <note>original: "galea"</note>.

It is cultivated in gardens and grew for us at Montbéliard in the botanical garden, blooming in May and June.

<column-break/>

### GALLITRICUM WITH TINY WHITE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a delicate Gallitricum with very small flowers and thin stems.</image-desc>

It spreads many stalks on the ground, provided with long petioles <note>term: pediculo (leaf stalks)</note>; these are quite thick and stiff, blunt, notched, covered in white hairs in groups of six, and scentless. The stems are four-angled, hairy, and divided at long intervals into opposite branches; at their origin, the leaves are also opposite and almost similar to the lower ones. The flowers, arranged in whorls at intervals, occupy the tips; they are fragrant, tiny, white, and barely project from the calyxes. The root is oblong and provided with small fibers.

It grew for us at Montbéliard in the botanical garden from seed brought from Italy, and it bloomed in June.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Gallitricum (Clary/Sage), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in Austria and Tyrol, and their use in Northern Europe as a potent additive to beer in place of hops.</summary>
<keywords>Gallitricum, Clary Sage, brewing history, beer additives, Montbéliard botanical garden, Doctor Agerius, medicinal herbs, Austrian flora, Tyrolean plants</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the Dead-nettle family and related species, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary observations from Clusius.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### A PLANT RELATED TO WILD CLARY, the broad-leaved Wild Sage of Clusius. <note>original: "Horminum sylvestre latifolium Clusio"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a flowering plant with broad, serrated leaves arranged in pairs along a square stem, ending in a spiked inflorescence of small flowers.</image-desc>

It is found, says Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note>, everywhere in the Viennese territory, along roadsides, in mountain meadows, and throughout the alpine regions of Styria and Austria. It grew for us at Montbéliard in the garden of the Most Serene Prince: it bloomed in June, July, and August, enduring the winter and propagating itself by seed.

Its flowers are bluish-purple, arranged in whorls <note>circles around the stem</note> at short intervals, forming a spike, very closely resembling the flowers of the small Dead-nettle.

### GALEOPSIS, LAMIUM, DEAD-NETTLE: German: *Taub Nessel*: French: *Ortie morte*: Italian: *Ortica morta*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Galeopsis (Dead-nettle) showing heart-shaped, serrated leaves and clusters of hooded flowers at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Galeopsis, according to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and pharmacologist</note>, is a shrub-like plant, entirely similar to the Nettle in its stem and leaves, but the leaves are smoother: and when they are rubbed, they give off a very heavy <note>foul</note> odor. The flowers are slender and purplish. It grows by hedges, and around roads and the courtyards of houses everywhere. The leaves, juice, stem, and seed have the power to dissipate hard swellings, carcinomas, scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, parotid tumors, and superficial abscesses.

Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> records the words of Dioscorides: and Paul <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> also reports the same concerning its medicinal powers, but Galen <note>the influential Roman-era Greek physician</note> makes no mention of it at all.

Furthermore, from the various differences observed in Galeopsis, we depict here the one which has an entirely yellow flower: in other respects, it is almost similar to the common variety.

### GALEOPSIS, OR THE SMALLER DEAD-NETTLE: with leaves surrounding the stem, and a purple flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a smaller variety of Dead-nettle with rounded, deeply lobed leaves that appear to clasp the stem.</image-desc>

The plant is a span and a half <note>about 12 inches</note> and sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high: with square stems, weak, sometimes upright, but more often spread on the ground. The leaves first breaking forth are provided with stalks, almost round and serrated: others on the upper parts of the stems arise in pairs, adhering immediately to the stems, surrounding the stem almost in the manner of Thorough-wax <note>Perfoliata</note>, round, hairy, deeply notched and curled, with an odor less foul than the other species. The flowers are purple, gaping, in whorls among the leaves at the nodes, emerging from long, hairy, many-cleft calyxes <note>the leaf-like base of the flower</note>. It sends down a simple root, somewhat rigid and fibrous.

It grows abundantly everywhere in fields and gardens.

<column-break/>

### AETHIOPIS: In Greek: Αἰθιοπίς: German: *Mohrenkraut*: French: *Ethiopide*: Italian: *Ethiope*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of the Aethiopis plant, featuring large, deeply lobed, woolly basal leaves and a branched flowering stalk with small blossoms.</image-desc>

Aethiopis, according to Dioscorides, has leaves similar to Mullein <note>Verbascum</note>, but very hairy and thick, in a circle around the bottom of the root: a quadrangular stem, thick and rough, similar to Wild Parsley <note>Apiastrum</note>, hollow with many wings. The seed is the size of a Vetch, paired in one pod: many roots from the same tuft, long, thick, and sticky to the taste; which when dried become black and hard, like horns.

Pliny has exactly the same descriptions, so that he seems to have transcribed them from Dioscorides. Galen passed over Aethiopis in his list of simples <note>medicinal herbs</note>: but Paul also transcribed his account from Dioscorides. Among more recent authors, some say it is unknown, others offer the plant which we depict here in its place. More in the appendix.

### ANOTHER SPECIES OF YELLOW GALEOPSIS, sticky, fragrant, of the woods.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a yellow-flowered Galeopsis with elongated, serrated leaves and distinct floral clusters.</image-desc>

It rests upon a remarkably fibrous root, from which many stems rise up, two cubits <note>approx. 3 feet</note> and higher, square, hairy, stuffed with a spongy pith, branched into wings. The leaves come out opposite from the joints, attached to long stalks, winged in the manner of Celery, but wrinkled and hairy like the Dead-nettles, although much larger, serrated around the edge, and some occasionally tinged with a deep redness along the margins. The flowers surround the branches in whorls on long spikes, hairy on the outside, smooth on the inside, with a three-parted lip, partly white-yellow and partly spotted. They sit in long, ribbed, sticky calyxes, in which the seed grows. The whole plant is sticky to the touch and fragrant.

### THE GREATEST GALEOPSIS WITH A LARGE red or purple flower.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a large-flowered Galeopsis with prominent serrated leaves and large, gaping flowers.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various forests around Zurich, Basel, Geneva, Montbéliard, and elsewhere. Moreover, the whole plant has a most foul odor, and a taste that is unpleasant and bitter.

Furthermore, various other differences of Galeopsis are recounted, taken from the color of the flowers and the shape, size, and stickiness of the leaves, and their pleasant or unpleasant odor. Thus, some have white flowers, some a spotted leaf, some a smaller leaf and flower, some a narrower leaf, etc.

Otherwise, the Dead-nettles have the same power as the stinging ones, and even in tumors and external ulcers, they are believed to be more effective. More in the Appendix.

<keywords>Dead-nettle, Galeopsis, Aethiopis, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Clusius, European flora, 16th-century botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXIX.
### CONTAINING CROWN-PLANTS <note>Latin: *Coronarias*. These are plants used for weaving garlands or crowns.</note> bearing seeds in small vessels and husks, and those closely related to them.

**CROWN BETONY, CARNATION:**
*German: Little Clove, Clove-flower; Belgian: Gillyflower; French: Carnations; Italian: Cloves.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica Coronaria (Caryophyllus) plant, showing the stem, leaves, and a single flower at the top with roots at the base.</image-desc>

There are two main types of Crown Betony: one is the wild variety and the other is the cultivated. The latter is sometimes satisfied with a single row of petals in its flowers, while at other times it is endowed with a double row.

Among the Carnations <note>Latin: *Cariophyllis*. The term refers to the clove-like scent of the flower.</note>, whether full-petaled or single, most have two narrow leaves at each joint. Some have three, which are shorter and more meager. All, however, have hard leaves, sharpened at the tip, and are of a bluish-gray or sea-green color. The stems are smooth, rounded, about a cubit <note>Approximately 18 inches.</note> high, jointed, and knotty. At their somewhat long tips, rounded husks are seen, which, when they gape open, reveal various kinds of flowers. The seed in the oblong vessels is small, black, and broad. The roots are fibrous and simple.

### RARE CROWN BETONY, WITH A full purple-red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rare variety of Betonica Coronaria with a fuller, multi-petaled flower head.</image-desc>

This very elegant and rarer species of Crown Betony puts forth straight, long, and somewhat slender stems. The leaves are sea-green or bluish-gray, channeled, quite firm, and rather narrow. The primary elegance is in the flowering: for before it emerges, it puts forth three little horns of a pale red color. Afterward follows the flower, of a medium size among the Betonies of this kind, of a diluted Phoenician red <note>A deep scarlet or purple-red.</note> color, and with a pleasant scent, as in the others.

*Clusius* <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist.</note> calls it the *Cinnabar-red full-flowered Carnation*. *Schwenckfeld* calls it the *Domestic full-flowered Carnation, the color of an Orange*. A single-flowered variety of this kind is also found. It blooms in June and July.

<column-break/>

**THE LARGEST FULL-FLOWERED CROWN BETONY,**
**variegated with small red spots: or the largest double Carnation.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, double-flowered variety of Betonica Coronaria with ruffled petals.</image-desc>

As has been said, various kinds of flowers are seen on this plant: white, purplish-white, scarlet, blackish, worm-patterned <note>Latin: *vermiculata*, referring to wavy or marbled patterns.</note>, and variegated in many ways and colors. Indeed, you may find those in which white and scarlet are so mixed that in one the white petals and in another the red petals turn out to be superior in number. Some are white, encircled with very tiny red spots, or red sprinkled with milky marks. Indeed, sometimes even from one and the same stem, various kinds of flowers arise—white, red—and sprinkled with marks partly white, partly red, and partly scarlet, etc. In the middle of the flowers, two white stamen-like tips spring forth.

### CROWN BETONY OR THE GREATER Carnation with a variegated flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-flowered Caryophyllus with distinct petal patterns and a thick stem.</image-desc>

This Betony has broad leaves and large flowers, very full and fragrant, of varying color. For they are sprinkled with many red lines and dots: some petals are half-red, some almost entirely red, some half-white, and others white altogether.

By Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, Flemish physician and botanist.</note> in his *Images*, it is called the *Double Garden Carnation, Greater and Lesser, red-striped, multi-colored, and very pleasant*. Those of Basel call them *Gentlemen's flowers* <note>German: *zuncker blumen* (Junkerblumen).</note>.

Furthermore, writers have called this "Crown Betony" or "Vetony" to distinguish it from the other Betony which the Greeks call *kestron* <note>Greek: κέστρον, referring to Stachys officinalis.</note>. Because of its scent, they call it *Cariophyllum* <note>Clove-leaf</note>. And the French, as Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, French physician and botanist.</note> thinks, call it *Ocellum* or *Oeillet* <note>Little eye</note> from the appearance of the flower.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Crown Betony or Carnation (Caryophyllus), detailing their physical characteristics, color variations, and the nomenclature used by contemporary 16th-century botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Carnation, Betonica Coronaria, Caryophyllus, botany, floriculture, Clusius, Lobelius, Ruellius, flower classification, 16th-century herbals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of "Betonica" (Betony) species, specifically focusing on the "Coronary" or "Clove-scented" varieties, which we now identify as members of the Dianthus or Pink family (Carnations).</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### WILD BETONY OR VETONY, with a simple, jagged red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica plant with serrated leaves and a single flower at the top of a long stem.</image-desc>

There are some who believe that the *Coronary Betony* or *Vetony* of the Ancients is actually the *Baccaris* <note>original: "Baccarem"; likely referring to a plant mentioned by Virgil or Dioscorides, often debated by Renaissance botanists</note>. There are others who think it is their Marsh Marigold <note>original: "Caltham palustrem"</note>, but many facts clearly speak against this. Others, according to the testimony of Dalechamps, have wanted it to be the *Iphyum* of Athenaeus, or the *Iphyum* of Theophrastus; but what do bulbous plants have to do with this Betony? To others, it is the *Herba Tunica*, but it is better judged to be the *Polemonium* of Dioscorides. Others have numbered it among the *Saxifrages* <note>Stone-breakers; plants believed to dissolve kidney stones</note>, but again with little agreement. It is therefore more likely to be as Ruellius writes, and as Cordus and Mattioli establish with him, that the *Clove-flower* <note>original: "Caryophyllum"; the Carnation or Pink</note> was unknown to the Ancients.

### CREEPING CORONARY OR CLOVE-SCENTED BETONY, red and white: according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping variety of Betonica with multiple stems and flowers, showing detailed root structure.</image-desc>

This plant has little stems about nine inches long <note>term: "Dodrantales" (nine inches or three-quarters of a foot)</note>, rounded and jointed. The leaves are oblong, narrow, hard, and pointed, with a color somewhat like bluish-gray. The flower emerges from a reddish little cup <note>the calyx</note>, consisting of five small petals, fringed, with a color of reddish-purple diluted with white; it is hairy around the center and fragrant. The seed in the cups is chaff-like and dark. The root is long, spreading out thin fibers. It is sometimes cultivated in gardens and flourishes for a long time.

### CORONARY OR CLOVE-SCENTED BETONY, with a whitish-red flower and a curled fringe.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica variety with a more robust stem and a large, fringed flower head.</image-desc>

Commonly, Coronary Betonys with full flowers <note>double flowers</note> and more elegant forms are kept in gardens; but the most beautiful are almost always kept in earthenware pots. They bloom for a very long time, indeed throughout the Summer, and even in Autumn, and sometimes in Winter, provided there is warmth from being kept in underground rooms <note>original: "hypogaeis"; likely a cellar or early greenhouse structure</note>.

It is a hardy plant and lasts for many years, provided that in the winter months it is protected from the injuries of the cold.

<column-break/>

### TREE-LIKE CORONARY BETONY OR VETONY of Crete.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody, shrub-like Betonica with thick stems and clustered leaves at the branch tips.</image-desc>

It is certainly a wonder, as was said a little before, that our Coronary Betony—so famous and so pleasant a flower, which in size, beauty, variety, scent, and every other praiseworthy quality could compete with the Rose for the leadership—was passed over in silence by the Ancients. Thus we do not owe everything to them, but many things to the diligent investigation of more recent scholars.

The *Cretan Coronary Betony* which we depict here grows like a shrub with hard, knotted, somewhat thick and fibrous stalks. You see it has bluish-gray leaves, about an inch and a half long, narrow, rigid, ending in a sharp point, and positioned closely together at the ends of the runners and shoots. The flower is purple, emerging from little cups that are prickly like a sea urchin <note>original: "echini instar"</note>.

### CORONARY OR CLOVE-SCENTED BETONY, distinguished by a purple crown.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betony with a dense, bushy habit and numerous small flowers.</image-desc>

This variety does not rise very high at all. The branches are spread out over the ground, protected by a dense crowding of leaves, and they are somewhat hard and almost woody at the bottom. Later they are divided into two or three stems, each of which supports a single, most elegant flower, divided into five parts, beautifully cut around the edge, and decorated in the middle with a lovely "little crown" <note>original: "coronallâ"</note> of a deeper purple. The scent is most sweet and pleasing.

It is cultivated in gardens and is early-blooming, surpassing the others.

### SMALLEST CORONARY OR CLOVE-SCENTED BETONY, sprinkled with golden specks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing Betonica variety with delicate foliage and flowers.</image-desc>

Clove-scented Betony plants are more frequently propagated from shoots with small leaves than from seeds. For flowers born from seed return to a wild nature and are rendered less fragrant; those which were previously "multiple" <note>double-petaled</note> become "simple" <note>single-petaled</note>. Sometimes Cloves <note>the spice</note> are inserted into the split shoots of the plants so that the flowers might attract their scent and represent their pleasant sweetness more abundantly to the nostrils. <note>A common Renaissance horticultural myth that plants could "absorb" the scent of spices placed in their stems.</note>

<summary>This page describes various species of "Coronary Betony" (modern Dianthus/Carnations), debating their identification in classical texts and detailing their cultivation, fragrance, and physical characteristics.</summary>
<keywords>Betony, Carnations, Dianthus, Clove-scented flowers, Crete, Horticulture, Renaissance Botany, Clusius, Mattioli</keywords>

--- Page 510 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of labiates (mint family), specifically focusing on Scordium and Ground-pine varieties. The catchword from the previous page, "CHAMÆ-", leads directly into the discussion of Chamæpytis.</meta>

### SCORODOTIS, OR SCORDIUM, with Sage-like leaves: German *Wild Salbey* <note>Wild Sage</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scorodotis plant, showing a central stalk with serrated, opposite leaves and small flower clusters at the nodes, ending in a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

It rests upon a flexible and fibrous root: from which several stalks rise, two cubits high <note>about three feet</note>, four-sided, hairy, purplish or blackish, and filled with white pith. At the joints, leaves come out in opposite pairs at intervals, like Sage, wrinkled, dark green, rough and weathered, hairy, saw-toothed around the edges, and bitter in taste. The top of the stalk is divided into several small forks, in which the flowers are arranged in spikes, all turning to one side, like Germander, but of a grassy, white, or pale color. From their opening, in place of a "helmet" <note>the upper petal of the flower</note>, purplish stamens spring forth. The seeds are contained in the calyxes, dark, similar to the seeds of heavy Basil, somewhat bitter, round, and dark.

### CHAMÆPYTIS, or MUSK IVY: German *Erdpin* <note>Earth-pine</note>: French *Iue moschate*: Italian *Chamapitio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chamæpytis (Iva Moschata), featuring a low-growing plant with narrow, needle-like leaves and a long, winding taproot.</image-desc>

Chamæpytis <note>Ground-pine</note> is a small plant about a palm's breadth high, with a fairly long, simple, and hard rootlet. There are three stalks, hairy, reddish near the ground, the rest turning from grassy-green to yellow, as do the leaves, which grow in opposite pairs at the nodes at short intervals; they are hairy, mimicking the shape of a small fingered foot <note>likely referring to the three-cleft leaf shape</note>, with the taste and smell of Pitch or Resin. From their "wings" <note>the leaf axils</note> emerge yellowish flowers with a wider, two-cleft lip, the upper part spotted with small red dots; these put forth pale purplish stamens in place of a "helmet." Small heads follow, swelling into four little rounded sections, containing as many three-cornered seeds. We present two images from Fuchs's works, though neither is entirely satisfactory.

### ORIENTAL CHAMÆPYTIS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Chamæpytis Orientalis, showing a denser, more upright shrub-like habit with very fine, crowded foliage.</image-desc>

It grows as a small shrub with shoots a palm's breadth long, thick, square, and covered with much white downy hair. The leaves are crowded at the nodes, about an inch long, like the Musk Ivy of Montpellier (which we will discuss shortly), downy, thick, finely toothed at the ends, and bitter to the taste. From their axils, from the lowest branches all the way to the top, hairy little vessels break out, opening into four ridges.

The common yellow-flowered Chamæpytis grows in fields and grassy plains; it blooms from the month of April until September, earlier or later depending on the variety of the location.

It is abundant at Lyon, at Geneva near the Arve bridge, at Basel on the way to Dornach, at Yverdon in the village of Sussève in the adjacent fields, and in various other places.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SCORDIUM WITH SAGE-LIKE LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alternative Scordium specimen, showing a more upright growth habit with distinct floral spikes.</image-desc>

Lobelius, Camerarius, and others declare this to be the "second Scordium" of Pliny, but too hastily; Gesner also wrongly calls it *Stachys*. It is better judged as the *Polemonion* or *Polemonia* of Ruellius, which he says is also called *Philetaria*, and by the Cappadocians—on account of its multitude of uses—*Chiliodynamis* <note>Greek: "The plant of a thousand powers"</note>. Most call it Wood Sage or Wild Sage; Bellon calls it the "bastard and false Scorodotis," whom few follow.

It grows in woods and uncultivated places. We have seen it at Montpellier in the mountains around Espérou; at Lyon, in the "Wood of the Good German Woman," and elsewhere.

Concerning the Etymology and Medicinal Virtues, see the Appendix.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF CHAMÆPYTIOS, OR MUSK IVY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Chamæpytis, showing a more branched structure with similar needle-like foliage.</image-desc>

Dioscorides has three species of Chamæpytios, the third of which he calls the "Male." Pliny also has three; according to his testimony, it was called *Aiuga* by some in Latin because of its use in abortions, and by others *Ibus terra* <note>Ground-ivy</note>. Matthiolus and others among the more recent authors have the same number, determining that the third species (or "Male") of Dioscorides agrees best with the common *Iva arthritica* <note>Gout Ivy</note>. They admit that the first species (the larger and branched one) is well enough known, but they report it is uncertain which can be shown as the second. There are those who recognize a difference in the flowers, since a certain kind is found with a white flower. Dodoens adds three other "false" kinds to the three commonly accepted ones.

### CHAMÆPYTIS, OR MUSK IVY of Montpellier, with purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Montpellier variety of Chamæpytis, showing a very bushy, leafy plant with a thick root.</image-desc>

Clusius writes that this grows in rich soil by the Tagus river in Portugal, in the kingdom of Granada, and in Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>; it blooms in Summer and Autumn. Lobelius says it grows as a shrub in the olive groves and dry fields of Narbonne and Provence, and is not easily found elsewhere. It is called "Musky" by way of antiphrasis and irony <note>meaning the name implies the opposite of the truth</note>, since it has a great odor indeed, but one that is not at all pleasant. We observed it at Montpellier, in the mountains around Castelnau, in very stony places, blooming in September.

Is this the "second Anthyllis" of Dioscorides (Book 3 and 16)? Or the "Greater Chamæpytis" of Caesalpinus?

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES:

### GROUND-PINE WITH UNDIVIDED LEAVES.
### The third Ground-pine of Dioscorides, according to Matthiolus.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamæpytis plant with small, narrow leaves and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

From a fibrous root, it produces branches a palm's breadth high <note>about 3–4 inches</note>, spread across the ground, and clothed with small leaves like those of the lesser Savory <term>Satureja</term>, though less fleshy; they are tiny and hairy. Among these are small, yellowish-white flowers, which have a not unpleasant scent.

It is less well-known and found in few places, except in the dry hills of Nice in Savoy and Genoa in Liguria. However, Lobelius writes that it can be found in the green spaces of Belgium.

This figure shows it without the pea-like pods; however, the one depicted in Dodoens, taken from Fuchs, is hairy. Lobelius identifies this as the first Ground-pine of Dioscorides, but Dodoens, Matthiolus, and others label it as the third. More concerning Ground-pine can be found in the Appendix.

### POLEY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Polium plant with small, serrated leaves and clusters of flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

Dioscorides describes two kinds of Poley: the *Mountain* variety and *Another* which is more shrub-like, with a less powerful scent and weaker medicinal properties. However, more recent authors identify many other differences in Poley, categorized by their native habitat, size, strength, flower color, and other characteristics.

The one we illustrate here is quite delicate, with thin, creeping branches about nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantalibus"</note>, covered in a white, woolly down; these branches occasionally take root at the nodes. Its leaves are narrow, long, small-toothed, and woolly. It has small, entirely woolly heads, in which the flowers are purple, white, or a purplish-white.

It grows in sandy places and flowers in March and April.

### VENETIAN POLEY: GOAT-WHEAT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polium Venetum, showing a low-growing plant with small leaves and terminal flower heads.</image-desc>

This variety has smooth leaves and a less white "mane" <note>the tufted top of the plant</note>, which is more spread out. It grows abundantly on the Lido of Venice.

Various plants are improperly given the name of Poley, such as Wild Thyme, Savory, Arines, Pliny's "Impious weed" <note>original: "Impia Plinij"</note>, Goldilocks, Tripolium, Honeysuckle, Ground-pine, and others similar to these; but they are named so incorrectly.

True Poley, however, is bitter to the taste and moderately acrid, according to Galen. For this reason, it clears obstructions from all the internal organs and promotes the flow of urine and menstruation. Dioscorides says that when used as bedding or burnt as incense, it puts venomous beasts to flight; applied as a poultice, it knits wounds together. A decoction of it helps those with dropsy <note>edema</note> and the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>.

Concerning *Ægipyrus* <note>Goat-wheat</note>, which is considered the fruit of the Poley, see the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### JERUSALEM OAK: German *Traubenkraut*: French *Pymen, Pyment, Millegrain*: Italian *Botry*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Botrys plant with deeply lobed leaves and elongated flower spikes resembling clusters of grapes.</image-desc>

There is a cultivated Jerusalem Oak <note>original: "Botrys"</note> and a wild one. We illustrate the wild, whorled variety here, which usually grows in vineyards, on stone walls, and in warm, sunny, elevated places; it is also sometimes found in fields among the crops, as we have observed frequently in Montbéliard and around Mount Esperon in Montpellier.

The cultivated variety has a more vibrant appearance but is shorter in stature—about a palm's breadth high. It has square, hairy branches with leaves like those of the common Jerusalem Oak, but they are woolly and a deeper green. These grow from the joints of the branches and have a sweet scent but a bitter taste. Purple flowers bloom from the same spots in whorls, followed by four blackish seeds. The root is woody, slender, and has few fibers. *More on Jerusalem Oak in the Appendix.*

### MONTPELLIER POLEY: The MOUNTAIN Poley of Dioscorides: Mountain Poley, or Teuthrium to others.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polium Monspessulanum, showing upright stems with narrow leaves and dense flower heads.</image-desc>

In this variety, many leaves grow together at specific intervals in opposite pairs; they are narrow, long, small-toothed, white, and woolly, with an acrid and bitter taste. They grow along branches that are nine inches or a palm's breadth long, which are firm, round, and hoary <note>grey-white</note>. The root is woody with few fibers. The heads are clustered, white, and woolly, consisting of long calyxes from which gaping, white flowers emerge. Threads similar to Dodder <term>Epithymum</term> are often found interwoven among its twigs.

It grows abundantly by the sea at Montpellier and is also found elsewhere, specifically in maritime areas, on sloping hills, and sandy shores. When cultivated, it is less white and produces broader leaves. It flowers in Summer.

### BETONY: German *Bethonien*: French *Betoine*: Italian *Betonica*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica plant with broad, serrated basal leaves and a tall flower spike.</image-desc>

There is a *Common* Betony and a *Rarer* kind that delights in cultivation, growing more vibrantly in gardens and having broad leaves. Both varieties usually have purple flowers, though they are sometimes white.

The *Common* variety, which we illustrate here, rises with numerous stalks a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or higher; these are square and have nodes at long intervals. Some leaves grow in pairs opposite each other at the joints of the stalks, while others are scattered at the base without a fixed order. These base leaves have stalks about a palm's breadth long and are fringed around the edges, wrinkled, rough, and possess an aromatic flavor. The purple flowers surround the joints in whorled spikes. The seed is long and angular. The root is as thick as a thumb and hairy with many long fibers.

<summary>This page catalogs several aromatic and medicinal herbs, including species of Ground-pine, Poley, Jerusalem Oak, and Betony, noting their physical characteristics, habitats (such as Venice and Montpellier), and medicinal uses for internal obstructions and jaundice.</summary>
<keywords>Ground-pine, Poley, Jerusalem Oak, Betony, Dioscorides, Galen, medicinal herbs, Montpellier, Venice, botany, jaundice, diuretics</keywords>

### WHITE-FLOWERED BETONY, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica plant with a long stalk, serrated leaves, and a spiked flower head at the top.</image-desc>

Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German botanist</note> also mentions this plant; he, along with Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, known as Tragus</note>, notes that it differs from the common variety only in the color of its flowers. Tragus is surprised—and not without reason—that although Dioscorides <note>The famous 1st-century Greek physician</note> described the history of Betony most diligently in other respects, he did not indicate the color of its flowers.

This white variety is rarer than the red, yet it grows in the same locations. Both are found in meadows, mountainous woods, and cold, shady places. It flowers in the months of May and June, and sometimes again in Autumn. Cordus writes that Betony grows in meadows and among shrubs and grassy places in almost any soil. We have observed it growing green in the public garden at Padua in December.

### SAGE: Germ. Salbey: Dutch. Sauie: Fr. Sauge: Ital. & Span. Salvia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Salvia (Sage) plant with broad, textured leaves and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

Although it appears Dioscorides recognized only one kind of Sage, Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" from ancient Greece</note> described two types: *Sphacelon* and *Elelisphacon* <note>original: "Sphacelon & Elelisphacon"</note>. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist</note> mistakenly categorized this as a type of wild lentil. More recent botanists commonly distinguish between the Garden (or domestic) variety and the Field (or wild) variety. They further divide these into the Larger and Smaller, the Broad-leaved and Narrow-leaved; those with curled leaves or smooth leaves; and those that are white, dark-colored, or dark purple. They also distinguish them by the presence or absence of "ears" <note>small lobes at the base of the leaf</note> and by the color of the flowers, which may be blue, white, or a whitish-purple.

### SMALL THIN-LEAVED SAGE: Gall-bearing Sage of Crete.

The root of this plant is hard, woody, and divided into branches. It produces small woody stems of a reddish-brown color, which are surrounded by pairs of leaves growing opposite one another. These leaves are longer and narrower than in any other kind of Sage, and somewhat notched <term>crenata</term> around the edges. The central stalk ends in a spike of purple flowers, with no small leaves growing in between them.

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> labels this "Spanish Sage," while Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus, a student of Bock</note> calls it "Indian Sage."

The "Gall-bearing Sage of Crete" <note>original: "Gallifera Cretica"</note> is entirely covered in a thick, white down. Its leaves are partly eared and partly truncated, ending in a blunt point. At the joints of the stems, sitting on an inch-and-a-half-long stalk, grow round galls <term>Gallæ</term>, similar to the small galls usually found on oak leaves.

<column-break/>

### BETONY-LEAVED FOXTAIL, of some authors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with leaves similar to Betony and a fuzzy, cylindrical flower head resembling a fox's tail.</image-desc>

Herb-gatherers call this "Mountain Foxtail" <note>original: "Alopecuros montana"</note> because its hairy fruit has a certain resemblance to a fox's tail.

It grows in the shady valleys of high mountains, darkened by a density of trees and kept moist by the flow of water.

Furthermore, the Greeks called Betony *Cestron* <note>original: "Cestron"</note>. Among the Latins, some called it *Serratula* <note>meaning "little saw," referring to the leaf edges</note>, while others called it *Vetonica*, named after its discoverers, the Vettones <note>an ancient people of the Iberian Peninsula</note>.

Antonius Musa, the most famous physician to Augustus Caesar, wrote an entire book on its medicinal powers. Who could list them all? It is well known that when people wish to praise the power or utility of something, they often say, "It is more useful than Betony" <note>original: "id Betonicâ esse vtilius"</note>.

### SAGE WITH BROAD, SERRATED, CURLED LEAVES.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sage variety with broad, highly textured, and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

In London, this plant is kept in the more cultivated gardens. However, Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that the common variety grows wild in rough places and among ruins. In Narbonne Gaul <note>Southern France</note> and Piedmont, it grows luxuriantly among the vines. When moved into gardens, it becomes even more beautiful. It flowers in Montpellier and Lyon in May, but later in colder climates.

The Latins called it *Salvia* because it makes humans "safe and sound" <note>from the Latin *salvus*</note>, or because it is beneficial for fertility. We read in Aëtius <note>a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> that the name "Holy Herb" <note>original: "Sacra herba"</note> was granted to it for this reason. The Greeks called it *Sphacelon* and *Elelisphacon* because of the peculiar power it possesses in healing "sphacelus" <term>Sphacelo</term> <note>the death or gangrene of body parts</note>.

### SMALL EARED SAGE: Germ. Klein Salbey: Fr. Sauge franche: Ital. Salvia minore.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Sage variety with distinct "ears" (auricles) at the base of the leaves.</image-desc>

The leaves of this plant are smaller than those of the Great Sage, but they surpass them with a more powerful scent and a more vigorous taste; they are also more whitish. At the base of the leaves are attached two small wings <note>pinnulae or auricles</note>, though sometimes only one, and occasionally none at all. In other respects, it shares characteristics with the Great Sage, but it is more woody and does not multiply as easily.

In certain places in Italy and Spain, and in the countryside around Marseille, it grows abundantly and wild in the fields. In Germany, however, it is found only as a cultivated plant in gardens.

Details regarding the temperament and medicinal strengths of Sage can be found in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various species of Betony and Sage, focusing on their physical characteristics, geographical distribution, and the origins of their names. It highlights the medicinal reputation of Sage as a "holy herb" and the historical prestige of Betony.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Salvia (Sage) family, moving from the common varieties discussed on the previous page to more specialized types like Wormwood-scented Sage and various forms of Horminum (Clary). It maintains the structure of comparing classical descriptions from Dioscorides and Theophrastus with the observations of Renaissance botanists.</meta>

### SAGE SMELLING OF WORMWOOD.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Salvia plant with broad, textured leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

The flower is quite large, arranged in whorls, and is purplish or white. The leaf is truly that of the common Sage, sometimes pinnate <note>feather-like in arrangement</note> and sometimes incomplete, smelling of Wormwood <note>original: "Absynthium"</note>. It is kept in well-tended gardens.

As for the Common Sage—which the constraints of space did not allow to be fully described in its own place—it has a vigorous, woody, and perennial root. From this root rise several shoots that are woody, square-stemmed, hairy, and either hoary-white or greenish. The leaves rival those of Mint, being pointed and colored white, green, or reddish-brown; they have an extraordinary scent and a somewhat sharp taste with an aromatic bitterness. The flowers are arranged in a spike, colored blue or purplish-white, resembling Dead-nettles <note>original: "Lamiis"</note>, with a hairy hood and a two-cleft lip.

### RED-TUFTED CLARY.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Horminum plant with a dense, leafy flowering head.</image-desc>

This plant differs from the preceding one only by its **red** tuft <note>original: "coma," referring to the leafy top of the flower spike</note> and its smaller flowers. Both types are cultivated in gardens, as we ourselves have kept them in our gardens at Lyons, Geneva, and Montbéliard. It flowers in May, June, and July.

Furthermore, <term>Horminum</term> <note>Clary</note> is named <term>from the Greek 'to rush'</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρμᾶν" (apo tou horman)</note>, meaning to be moved by impulse or carried by instinct, certainly in relation to Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, because, as Dioscorides says, it stimulates the appetite for love. He divides it into the Cultivated and the Wild varieties; to the former he attributes a round, brown seed, and to the latter an oblong, black one.

Galen and Theophrastus numbered Clary among the types of grain; in Theophrastus's works, Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Greek texts</note> translates it as *Geminalis*. Pliny mentions both *Horminum* and *Herminium*. More information can be found in the Appendix.

### COMMON WILD CLARY,
#### or Wild Sclarea.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a wild Gallitricum plant with large, serrated basal leaves and a tall stalk.</image-desc>

This plant sometimes rises to two cubits <note>about three feet</note> in height. It has a square, hairy, hollow stem divided into "wings" <note>side branches</note>. The leaves are much larger than in the cultivated Clary, appearing rough, wavy-edged, and serrated, approaching the appearance of Sage leaves, with a heavy scent. The flowers in the long spike are blue and purple, large, and shaped like Sage flowers. The seed is black. The root is woody and scented.

Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French physician and botanist</note> calls it "Hen’s-center" or "Cock’s-center" <note>original: "Centrum gallinae" / "Centrum galli"</note>, and he criticizes the Apothecaries because they wrongly call it *Gallitricum*. Some call it Overseas Sage or Roman Sage.

It grows naturally in meadows, hills, open fields, and at the edges of farmlands. It flowers and is heavy with seed in the month of June.

<column-break/>

### CLARY, ORMINUM, GEMINALIS: Germ. Garden Scarlet: Fr. Hormin: Ital. Horminio.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Horminum plant with broad leaves and a thick flowering spike.</image-desc>

Clary <note>original: "Horminum"</note> bears a great resemblance to Sage. Its stems are somewhat reddish, drawn out into many wings, bristly with thick down, square, and a foot or more in height. At their joints, leaves come forth in pairs, opposite each other, but they are less rough, hairy, with no outstanding scent, and a very bitter taste. However, on the furthest small branches, the leaves are more densely packed, forming a purple-violet tuft. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils, like those of Sage, partly purple and partly whitening. The seed is oblong, brown or black. The root is fibrous. It is an annual plant.

The purple-violet tufted Clary that we depict here is said by Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger</note> to grow abundantly in the territory of Siena, in Illyria <note>the Balkans</note>, and throughout Greece. We have seen it nowhere except in gardens.

### CLARY, SCLAREA, ALL-GOOD: Germ. Scarlet: Ital. Sciaria: Fr. Oruale, Toute bonne.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Sclarea plant with large, heart-shaped leaves and a branching inflorescence.</image-desc>

Very many species of Clary <note>original: "Gallitrici"</note> are described, differing among themselves in their place of birth, the size and shape of their leaves, and the color of their flowers and tufts.

Our Cultivated variety, which we depict here, has a square stem two cubits high, almost the thickness of one's little finger, rigid, hairy, full of white pith, and split at intervals into opposite branches in pairs. The flowers are spiked, composed of many whorls, very similar to Sage flowers, hooded, and of a blue color verging toward white. The seeds are found in sets of four in small, furrowed pods, polished with a slippery moisture, and of a reddish color. The leaves are in opposite pairs, wrinkled like those of *Aethiopis* <note>Woolly Sage</note>, but less shaggy. The root is woody. The scent of the whole plant is powerful, and the taste is bitter.

It is sown in gardens and flowers in June and July.

### A VARIETY OF WILD CLARY.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a variety of wild Gallitricum with a long, slender flowering spike.</image-desc>

Cordus, Lonicer, Fuchs, Camerarius, Schwenkfeld, Thal, Lobel, Clusius, and others contend along with Ruellius that the common Wild Clary is actually the *Horminum* of the ancients. Many others, however, refer it to *Sclarea* or *Gallitricum*.

Furthermore, Clary—especially the cultivated kind—is of a hot and dry temperament in the third degree <note>a Galenic classification of medicinal potency</note>, and possesses the power to resolve, thin out, and expel humors. Taken in any manner, it stimulates the menses and aids conception. Wine in which Clary has been steeped and allowed to ferment is especially suited for a "cold stomach"; it cuts through and consumes phlegm, and assists women suffering from "coldness," infertility, or the "white flow" <note>leukorrhea</note>.

<summary>This page details various species of Sage and Clary (Horminum/Sclarea), contrasting their physical characteristics, garden cultivation, and medicinal uses for digestive and reproductive health.</summary>
<keywords>Sage, Clary, Sclarea, Horminum, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, women's health, Galenic medicine, Dioscorides, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Salvia (Sage) family, specifically focusing on the different varieties of Gallitricum, which we know today as Clary Sage and its close relatives. The previous page discussed various forms of Sclarea and Horminum, and this page expands on those with exotic, wild, and smooth-leaved varieties, noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal or industrial uses.</meta>

### EXOTIC CLARY, CALLED BISERMAS.
-> Known to some as Syrian Aman. <-

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut of a flowering plant with broad, textured, heart-shaped leaves at the base and upright flower spikes. The plant is identified as Gallitricum Exoticum.</image-desc>

This exotic plant, Bisermas, remarkably resembles our common Clary <note>original: "Sclarea"</note> in its overall appearance. It has square, hairy stems that feel somewhat rough to the touch, divided into frequent branches <note>original: "alas," literally "wings" or side-shoots</note> positioned in opposite pairs. The lower leaves are initially small and oblong, like our Clary; those that follow are large, wrinkled, and hairy, with a scent like Basil <note>original: "Ocymum"</note>, and are arranged in the same manner as Clary. The flowers also have the placement and appearance of Clary, but their color is milky white, with the lower lip spotted with a few small droplets inside. The seed is similar to cultivated Clary, but slightly larger.

It grew for us in Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince’s garden <note>referring to the botanical gardens of the Dukes of Württemberg</note>; it flowered in July, August, and September.

### WILD CLARY, WITH A GREENISH TUFT.
-> with a greenish tuft. <-

<image-desc>A woodcut of a wild Clary plant featuring deeply notched, serrated leaves and a dense, leafy flowering head.</image-desc>

This variety exceeds the others in size. It has a four-angled stem, as in the other species, with leaves growing opposite one another at each joint. However, its uppermost part <note>original: "coma," referring to the leafy cluster or "tuft" at the top of the spike</note> does not turn purple, but remains greenish. Although the flowers are similar in shape, they are of a paler color. The lower leaves have larger notches, appearing somewhat jagged <note>original: "laciniata"</note>; its other characteristics match the common type.

It grows wild everywhere in coppiced woods, mountains, and at the edges of fields; it flowers in May and June.

### CLARY WITH SMALLER FLOWERS, PURPLISH AND RED.
-> purplish and red. <-

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Clary variety with smaller, more delicate flowers and many-branched stems.</image-desc>

With a long-lived root, this plant—related to the wild Clary—remains for many years. It is fragrant and not so dissimilar in appearance, stem, leaves, and habit of growth; however, the flowers are so small that they hardly project beyond the calyx <note>the green outer cup of the flower</note>. They are purplish and slightly gaping, whereas in the common variety the flowers are large, and with a great protruding hood <note>original: "galea"</note> they conceal many stamens.

It is cultivated in gardens, and grew for us in Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince’s garden, flowering in May and June.

<column-break/>

### SMOOTH CLARY, WITH SAGE-LIKE LEAVES,
-> and purple flowers. <-

<image-desc>A woodcut of a smooth-leaved plant resembling Sage, with long, slender spikes of whorled flowers.</image-desc>

This is very similar to the common wild Clary. The leaves grow opposite each other at the stem nodes, but they are much smaller and narrower, serrated along the edges as if nibbled around, without hairs, and approaching the appearance of Sage leaves. Frequent whorls of flowers form a spike; they are purplish-violet and smaller than those of the aforementioned wild Clary. Beneath each whorl are two short, rather broad, and even somewhat blue leaves.

It grows everywhere around Vienna in Austria and in other places along roadsides and at the margins of fields and vineyards. It flowers all summer. Some call it "Wild Sage" <note>original: "Salvia agrestis"</note>.

### CLARY WITH ROUNDER LEAVES:
-> and large violet flowers. <-

<image-desc>A botanical illustration showing a Clary plant with distinctly rounded leaves and prominent flowers.</image-desc>

Doctor Agerius <note>Nicolas Ager, a 16th-century botanist</note> collected this in the high meadows of the Tyrolean mountains, and we received it from him.

Furthermore, the seed and the oil that the whole plant breathes out (though the scent is not unpleasant) induces a heaviness in the head. Nevertheless, it is of great use among Northern peoples for the making of Ale or Beer <note>original: "Zytum" and "Cerevisia"</note>. For when Hops <note>original: "Lupulus"</note> are scarce, or for the sake of making a more potent drink, they add it to the boiling brews. It produces a reckless intoxication <note>original: "firgi temerium," likely referring to a brew's "wild frenzy"</note>, such that after draining not many cups, the drinkers become drunk. This brings about a cheerfulness that is not unpleasant, though in some, it is more worthy of pity than laughter. According to *Lobelius* <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a famous Flemish botanist</note>, it also stimulates the bowels.

### CLARY WITH TINY WHITE FLOWERS.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a low-growing Clary with many spreading leaves and small, white, whorled flowers.</image-desc>

This plant spreads many leaves on the ground, provided with long stalks; they are quite thick and somewhat stiff, with blunt teeth <note>original: "crenata"</note>, covered with white hairs along the veins, and odorless. The stems are four-angled and hairy, divided at long intervals into opposite branches. At the base of these branches are also opposite leaves, almost similar to the lower ones. The flowers, arranged in whorls, occupy the tops at intervals; they are fragrant, tiny, hardly projecting from the calyxes, and white. The root is oblong and provided with small fibers.

It grew for us in Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince’s garden from seed brought from Italy, and it flowered in June.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Gallitricum" (Clary), detailing their morphology, habitats in places like Vienna and Tyrol, and their use as a hop substitute in beer brewing, which was noted for its intoxicating effects.</summary>
<keywords>Clary Sage, Gallitricum, Bisermas, Wild Sage, beer brewing, hops substitute, Montbéliard, Vienna, Tyrol, Matthias de l'Obel, Nicolas Ager</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, moving from the true Clary Sages (Gallitricum/Horminum) into their close relatives and the "Inert" or Dead-nettles (Galeopsis/Lamium). It transitions from garden-cultivated varieties to those found in the wild across Central Europe, maintaining the focus on physical description, habitat, and medicinal virtues established on the previous page.</meta>

### A PLANT RELATED TO CLARY SAGE, BROAD-LEAVED WILD SAGE
-> according to Clusius. <-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with broad, serrated leaves and a tall, spiked inflorescence, showing the root system.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> says it is found here and there in the Viennese territory, along roads, in mountain meadows, and throughout the alpine locations of Styria and Austria. For us, it grew in Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince’s garden <note>the botanical gardens of the Dukes of Württemberg</note>; it flowered in January, July, and August, enduring the winter and propagating itself by seed.

Its flowers are blue-purple, arranged in whorls <note>circles of flowers around the stem</note> at short intervals, forming a spike, very closely resembling the flowers of the small Dead-nettle <note>original: "Lamii"</note>.

### DEAD-NETTLE, LAMIUM, OR INERT NETTLE: Germ.
-> Deaf Nettle: Gall. Dead Nettle: Ital. Dead Nettle. <-
<note>original: "Taub Nessel" (German), "Ortie morte" (French), "Ortica morta" (Italian). These names refer to plants that look like stinging nettles but do not sting.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Galeopsis plant with opposite, ovate, serrated leaves and clusters of flowers in the leaf axils.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and authority on herbal medicine</note>, the Dead-nettle is a shrubby plant, entirely similar in stem and leaves to the stinging Nettle, but the leaves are smoother; and when rubbed, they give off a very heavy odor. The flowers are delicate and purplish. It grows by hedges, along roads, and in the courtyards of houses everywhere. The leaves, juice, stem, and seed have the power to dissipate hard swellings, cancers, scrofula <note>original: "strumas," swellings of the lymph nodes</note>, parotid tumors <note>swellings near the ear</note>, and superficial abscesses <note>original: "panos"</note>.

Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> records the words of Dioscorides; Paulus <note>Paul of Aegina</note> also transmits the same concerning its virtues, though Galen <note>the influential Roman-Greek physician</note> makes very little mention of it.

Furthermore, from the various differences observed in Dead-nettles, we here depict the one with an entirely yellow flower; otherwise, it is almost similar to the common type.

### SMALLER DEAD-NETTLE OR INERT NETTLE:
-> with leaves surrounding the stem and purple flowers. <-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Galeopsis variety with rounded, deeply crenated leaves that appear to clasp the stem.</image-desc>

The plant is about a span <note>about 9 inches</note> and sometimes a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> tall: with square, weak stems, sometimes upright, but more often spread on the ground. The first leaves to sprout have stalks and are nearly round and serrated; others on the upper parts of the stems arise in pairs, adhering immediately to the stems, surrounding the stem almost in the manner of Thoroughwax <note>original: "Perfoliatæ," referring to leaves where the stem seems to grow through the center</note>, round, hairy, deeply notched and curled, with a less foul odor than the other species. The flowers are whorled at the nodes between the leaves, purple, gaping, coming out of long, hairy, multi-cleft calyxes. It sends down a simple, somewhat stiff, fibrous root.

It grows abundantly everywhere in fields and gardens.

<column-break/>

### ETHIOPIAN SAGE: in Greek Αἰθιοπὶς: Germ. Moor-herb:
-> Gall. Ethiopide: Ital. Ethiope. <-
<note>original German: "Mohrenkraut." This plant is likely Salvia aethiopis.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Aethiopis plant, featuring large, woolly, basal leaves and a branched flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Ethiopian Sage, according to Dioscorides, has leaves similar to Mullein <note>original: "Verbasco"</note>, but very hairy and thick, in a circle around the base of the root; the stem is four-angled, thick and rough, similar to Balm <note>original: "Apiastro"</note>, with many hollowed side-shoots. The seed is the size of a Bitter Vetch <note>original: "Erui"</note>, two in one seed-pod; the roots from the same clump are many, long, thick, and sticky to the taste; when dried, they become black and hard, like horns.

Pliny has exactly the same information, so much so that he appears to have transcribed it from Dioscorides. Galen passed over Ethiopian Sage in his assessment of simples <note>single-ingredient medicines</note>; but Paulus also transcribed his notes from Dioscorides. Among more recent authors, some say it is unknown, while others provide the plant we depict here for it. More in the appendix.

### ANOTHER YELLOW SPECIES OF DEAD-NETTLE,
-> sticky, fragrant, and woodland-dwelling. <-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Galeopsis species with elongated, serrated leaves and prominent floral whorls.</image-desc>

It is supported by a remarkably fibrous root, from which many stems rise, two cubits or higher, square, hairy, filled with a spongy pith, branching out into side-shoots. The leaves emerge from the joints in opposite pairs, hanging from long stalks, winged like Celery <note>original: "Apii"</note>, but wrinkled and hairy like the Dead-nettles, although much larger, serrated around the edge, and some are occasionally tinged with a faint redness along the margins. The flowers surround the branches in whorls in long spikes, hairy on the outside, smooth on the inside, with a three-part lip, partly white-yellow and partly spotted. They sit in long, striated, sticky calyxes, in which the seed grows. The entire plant is sticky and fragrant to the touch.

### GREATEST DEAD-NETTLE WITH LARGE FLOWERS,
-> red or purple. <-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Galeopsis variety with a thick root system and broad, pointed, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various forests, around the Tigerus <note>a local geographic reference, possibly near the Turgi region</note> at Basel, Geneva, Montbéliard, and elsewhere. The whole plant has an extremely foul odor and an unpleasant, bitter taste.

Furthermore, various other differences of Dead-nettle are listed, based on the color of the flowers and the shape, size, and stickiness of the leaves, as well as their pleasant or unpleasant odor. Thus, some have white flowers, some have spotted leaves, some have smaller leaves and flowers, some have narrower leaves, and so on.

Moreover, the "inert nettles" <note>Dead-nettles</note> have the same medicinal power as the fresh stinging ones, and are even believed to be more effective for treating tumors and external ulcers. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several species of wild Clary and Dead-nettles (Galeopsis and Lamium), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe, and their traditional medicinal uses for swellings and ulcers.</summary>
<keywords>Dead-nettle, Galeopsis, Ethiopian Sage, Clusius, Dioscorides, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, Alpine flora, Mullein, medicinal roots</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from the previous discussion of Dead-nettles and Clary Sages, now focusing on the Horehound family (Marrubium). The catchword "LOCVSTA" from the previous page likely refers to the "locust-like" appearance of some seed pods or a transition to Valerians, but here we begin a detailed study of White and Black Horehounds and their medicinal relatives.</meta>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### HOREHOUND: Germ. Horehound, Lungwort: Gall. Horehound: Ital. Horehound.
<note>original: "MARRVBIVM: Germ. Andorn, Lungenkraut: Gall. Marrube, Marrubin: Ital. Marobio." The name "Lungenkraut" (Lungwort) was often applied to Horehound because of its use in treating chest ailments.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Marrubium plant (Horehound) showing its fibrous root system, square stems, opposite serrated leaves, and whorled flower clusters at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> and Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> identify two types of Horehound, namely the *White* and the *Black*: Theophrastus <note>the Greek "Father of Botany"</note> also establishes two types, the *White* and the *Round*. However, more recent physicians have established four kinds: *White, Black, Water, and Field*.

Common White Horehound is depicted here, which Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Galen <note>the influential Roman-era physician</note> call *prasion* <note>original Greek: "πράσιον"</note>: but the Latins and more recent authors call it *Marrubium*: it is called *Prassium* by Anguillara and the Apothecaries, and some call it *Female Marrubium*.

It rises with square stems a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> high, covered in a gray downy fuzz, and having hollow tubes within. The *leaves, flowers, seed, and roots* are as described below.

### NARROW-LEAVED WHITE HOREHOUND. Cretan Horehound to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of white horehound with narrower, more deeply serrated leaves and similar whorled inflorescences.</image-desc>

This is whiter than the common Horehound, with square, thinner stems and branches. The leaves rise from the joints in opposite pairs; they are exceptionally white, oblong, saw-toothed, and veined. The flowers on the branches are set in whorls <note>circles around the stem</note> with two spreading leaves placed beneath them; sometimes they are arranged in the form of a spike. They are small and white, with a two-parted, leafy, upright upper lip and a hanging lower lip, emerging from whitish, ribbed calyxes <note>the protective outer part of the flower</note>.

Lobelius and Pena, the History of Lyon, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, and others call this *Cretan Horehound*.

Those already mentioned grow of their own accord in many places: on the edges of vineyards and fields, in dry and grassy plains, in city ditches, and near the ruins and rubble of buildings. They bloom in Summer.

### WATER HOREHOUND OF CERTAIN AUTHORS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of water horehound, showing more deeply lobed or laciniate leaves and smaller flower clusters.</image-desc>

The height of this plant is one or one-and-a-half cubits: the stem is rigid, square, slightly hairy, and divided into opposite branches. The leaves are always placed in pairs opposite each other, deeply saw-toothed and sometimes jagged <note>original: "laciniata"</note>, ending in a point. They are slightly hairy on the upper side and smooth underneath, attached by a very short stalk, with a bitter taste. At their base are whorled clusters of small white flowers sprinkled with red spots, hardly protruding from their slightly rough calyxes. The root is fibrous, whitish, and moderately astringent.

According to the judgment of Galen, Horehound is hot in the 2nd degree and dry in the 3rd, and is highly recommended for wasting disease <note>original: "tabe," often referring to tuberculosis</note>, jaundice, and obstructions of the internal organs.

<column-break/>

### WHITE HOREHOUND, with roundish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a white horehound variety with more rounded flower clusters and broader leaves.</image-desc>

From a fibrous and blackish root, it produces stems one or two cubits high, which are square, covered in hoary down, and hollow in many parts: at each of their joints, leaves rise in opposite pairs, likewise covered in soft hair, attached by a broadish stalk, saw-toothed around the edges, oblong, blunt, and with no remarkable scent. The flowers embrace the stem in whorls at the joints, raising a two-parted crest with a hanging lip on each side, set in white, soft, downy calyxes. The seed is roundish and slightly rough.

The whole plant, like the common variety, is pleasant and of a sweet odor, and smells somewhat of Musk, especially in the winter months. Concerning its location and powers, see below.

### BLACK HOREHOUND, OR BALLOTE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Black Horehound (Ballota nigra) with darker, broader leaves and distinct whorled flowers.</image-desc>

This is taller by half a cubit, with square, hairy, somewhat reddish stems that are hollow: at their joints, on stalks an inch-and-a-half long, grow leaves like those of Lemon Balm <note>original: "Melissae"</note>, but dark green, wrinkled, stinking, and saw-toothed around the edges, with other smaller shoots bearing leaves growing from their axils <note>the "armpit" of the leaf</note>. The flowers are like those of the Dead-nettle <note>original: "Lamii"</note>, red, crowning the stem in a whorled circle, emerging from oblong ribbed calyxes. The root is like that of the Chaste-tree <note>original: "Vitica"</note> and is fibrous.

It grows everywhere, on the edges of fields, along roads, hedges, and walls, and in shady places. It blooms in Summer.

It is called *ballote* <note>original Greek: "βαλλωτή"</note> by the Greeks and *Ballote* by the Latins: it is called *Marrubium* because of its similarity to Horehound; *Black* because of the color of its leaves; and *Stinking Prassium* because of its heavy and foul odor.

### FIELD HOREHOUND: STACHYS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Stachys (Woundwort), showing a more upright, spicate inflorescence and elongated, hairy leaves.</image-desc>

To Dioscorides, *Stachys* is a shrub similar to Horehound: bearing more leaves, but they are sparse, hairy, fragrant, and hoary. It has several stalks from one root, whiter than Horehound. It grows in mountains and rough places. It has a heating and sharp power, etc.

Galen also said that *Stachys* is a shrub similar to Horehound, sharp and bitter in taste, and that it is in the third degree of heating plants. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German physician</note> also makes it similar to Horehound.

Depicted here is the *Stachys* of Fuchs, which Guillandinus wrongly determined to be *Sphacelus* <note>Sage</note>: but Lobelius, Castor, Lonicerus, Tabernaemontanus, and most others more correctly accept it as the *Stachys* of Dioscorides.

<summary>This page describes various species of Horehound (Marrubium) and their relatives like Black Horehound (Ballota) and Stachys. It details their physical characteristics, habitats such as ruins and ditches, and their medicinal classification under the Galenic system of humors.</summary>

<keywords>White Horehound, Black Horehound, Ballota, Stachys, medicinal herbs, Galen, Dioscorides, botany, 16th-century herbal, respiratory medicine</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA."</note>

### LOCUST HERB, LOCUST FOOT: Germ. Little Rabbit’s Ear, Vine-Cress; Gall. Fat Hen, Corn-Salad, Rampion.
<note>original: "LOCVSTA HERBA, PES LOCVSTÆ: Germ. Hasen-öhrlin/ Reben Kressig; Gall. Poule grasse, G. neven-sib. Rampon."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Locusta Herba (Lamb's lettuce), showing a slender plant with small, rounded leaves arranged in pairs along the stem and clusters of tiny flowers at the top.</image-desc>

We are by no means speaking here of the Locust animal, upon which authors such as Dioscorides, Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny, and the Holy Scriptures record that the *Acridophagi* <note>a mythical "locust-eating" people</note>, a portion of the Ethiopians, the Parthians, and the Holy Precursor of Christ <note>John the Baptist</note> lived. Nor are we speaking of the hanging tufts of authors, which Dioscorides also called "Locusts." Nor of the various plants which others believe the said Holy Man lived upon in the wilderness. Rather, we speak of a particular herb known by that name today.

In height, it sometimes barely exceeds a palm’s width <note>about 3-4 inches</note>, at other times it is nine inches or larger. It is gifted with a thin root, fibrous at the bottom, with a somewhat sweet and almost tasteless flavor. The leaves are tender and delicate, half an inch, an inch, or two inches long, of a grassy color, and slightly exceeding a third of an inch in width; they are somewhat round, attached without a stalk, sometimes serrated, and of the same flavor as the root. From this root, several stems break forth, which are angular, thin, and branching. Between the small leaves of the topmost rings are several pretty little flowers together, whitish or fainting with a diluted purple, oblong, divided into five segments, embracing very thin and almost invisible tips. I have not been able to observe the seed. This image is from the Plantin collection <note>the famous printing house of Christophe Plantin</note>.

### ALYSSUM OF THE ANCIENTS AND MODERNS.
<note>original: "ALYSSVM VETERVM ET NEOTERICORVM." Alyssum, or "Madwort," was historically believed to cure rabies.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Alyssum plant, featuring upright stems with small, narrow leaves and dense clusters of small flowers at the terminal ends.</image-desc>

The opinion of authors concerning Alyssum is quite varied: its history among writers is so diverse and uncertain, and the number of plants which are eagerly presented as Alyssum is so great, that it is very difficult to assert which might be the legitimate Alyssum of the Ancients. For this reason, Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician</note> judged that these varieties should be suppressed rather than described.

Whatever the case, it is likely that it obtained its name from its property of healing the bite of a rabid dog <note>from the Greek "a-" (not) and "lyssa" (rabies)</note>. To Dioscorides, it is a small shrub, single-stemmed, having somewhat rough, round leaves, around which is the fruit, shaped like a double shield, in which the seed is somewhat broad. It grows in mountainous and rugged places.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE LOCUST HERB.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Locusta Herba, showing a more mature specimen with broader basal leaves and a branching flowering stalk.</image-desc>

We paint the green plant here, with a branch of the "White Pot-herb" of Agerius added. To Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, as well as to Lobelius, it is called the larger odorless Valerian of the fields <note>original: "Valeriana 1. siue campestris inodora maior"</note>. To the same Lobelius in his *Observations* and *Images*, it is the smallest *Phu* <note>a type of Valerian</note>. To the Latin Dodonaeus and several others, it is the White Pot-herb; to Tabernaemontanus, it is Lamb's Lettuce <note>original: "Lactuca agnina"</note>, and he makes two kinds, the first and the second.

Some also call it "Fatty" <note>original: "Pinguicula"</note>. Otherwise, it is frequent in fields, vineyards, and gardens. It is sown by some in the month of September so that it may come into use for salads in the winter months; at other times, it is usually sown in the months of January and February.

Furthermore, this herb is cooling and somewhat moistening, and in its power and temperament is not unlike Lettuce. In place of Lettuce, it is sown in the winter and early spring months, and is eaten pleasantly with oil, salt, and vinegar, like other salad herbs, among which it holds no lowly place. It is also eaten in the manner of spinach or other pot-herbs, especially by the sick, for whom it is a very grateful and sweet food.

However, it is by no means, as it seems to some, that plant which is commonly called *Rapunculus* or *Napunculus* <note>Rampion</note>, called *Rapuntzel* by the Germans, *Raiponce* by the French, and *Rapuncioli* by the Italians; for it differs from that in form and properties, as is evident from its history previously given in Class 20.

### MOTHERWORT, RUELLIUS’S WOLF’S-FOOT: Germ. Heart-cramp; Belg. Heart-cramp; Gall. Motherwort.
<note>original: "CARDIACA, LYCOPOVS RVELLII: Germ. Hertzgespan: Belg. Herteghespan: Gall. Agripaulme."</note>

Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French physician and botanist</note> describes this plant under the name of "Wolf’s Foot" thus: Wolf’s foot, he says, is an herb similar to wild Horehound, with a leaf in the likeness of a wolf’s foot, divided, of a heavy scent, with an angular and jointed stem, a spongy pith inside, and a root fibrous with many hairs. The French, he adds, call it sometimes "Wolf's Paw," sometimes "Chest-herb," and sometimes "The Hand of Saint Mary."

There are some by whom it is called the "Male Horehound"; others make it "Christ’s Palm"; others the "Alyssum" of Galen and Aetius. Very many, however, determine it to be uncertain by what name it was called by the Ancients. But because it is a ready remedy for palpitation of the heart, it has obtained the name *Cardiaca* <note>Motherwort</note> among almost everyone. Matthiolus writes that it cleanses the chest of phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>, kills worms, and that one spoonful of its powder drunk in wine wonderfully assists those suffering through a difficult labor.

Furthermore, it delights in ruins, stony places, and other uncultivated and rugged spots. It flourishes from June well into Autumn, and abounds in flowers (especially in July). We will provide the image in the Appendix.
