# IMAGES AND OUTLINES OF PLANTS
# CLASS XXIX.
### CONTAINING CROWN-PLANTS BEARING SEEDS IN VESSELS
### and small cups, and those somewhat related to them.
<note>The term "Coronarias" (Crown-plants) refers to flowers traditionally used to weave garlands, wreaths, or "crowns" for festivals.</note>

---

**THE GARLAND BETONY, OR CARNATION:**
*German: Little Nails, Nail-flowers; Flemish: Gillyflowers; French: Eyelets; Italian: Carnations.*
<note>original German: "Negelin, Negelblumen"; Flemish: "Gerofelblumen"; French: "Oeuillets"; Italian: "Garofoli." The name "Nail-flower" refers to the clove-like shape of the flower's dried bud.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica Coronaria (Caryophyllus) plant, showing the roots, long stems with nodes, narrow leaves, and several small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

There are two main types of Garland Betony: one is the wild variety, the other is the cultivated variety <note>original: "sylvestris" and "farina" (likely a transcription error for "sativa" or referring to a mealy-textured variety)</note>; and this latter kind is sometimes found with a single row of petals in its flowers, and sometimes with a double row.

Among the Carnations <note>original: "Cariophyllis"</note>, whether they are double-flowered or single, most have two narrow leaves at each joint; some have three, which are shorter and smaller. All of them, however, have stiff leaves that taper to a point at the end, and are of a bluish-gray or sea-green color. The stems are smooth, round, about a cubit <note>approx. 18 inches</note> tall, jointed, and knotty. At the tips of these long stems, one can see rounded calyxes <note>the green, cup-like base of the flower</note>, which, when they open, reveal various kinds of flowers. The seed is small, black, and broad, contained in oblong vessels. The roots are fibrous and simple.

**RARE GARLAND BETONY, WITH A FULL crimson flower.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rare variety of Betonica Coronaria with a large, dense, multi-petaled (pleno) flower head and broad leaves.</image-desc>

This very elegant and rarer species of Garland Betony sends out straight, long, rather slender stems. The leaves are sea-green or bluish-gray, channeled, fairly firm, and quite narrow. The flower possesses exceptional beauty: before it emerges, it sends forth three pale red "horns" <note>pointed buds</note>; later the flower follows, of a size medium among the Betonies of this genus, with a lighter crimson color and a pleasant scent, as in the others.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> calls it the "Full-flowered Vermilion Clove Pink." Schwenkfeld <note>Caspar Schwenkfeld, a naturalist</note> calls it the "Domestic Clove Pink with a full flower the color of an orange." A single-flowered version of this kind also exists. It blooms in June and July.

<column-break/>

**THE LARGEST FULL-FLOWERED GARLAND BETONY, variegated with little red dots: or the Greatest Double Clove Pink.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very large, full-petaled flower head (Cariophyllus multiplex) showing intricate, ruffled petals.</image-desc>

As mentioned, various types of flowers are seen in this plant: white, purplish-white, scarlet, dark, "worm-patterned" <note>original: "vermiculata," meaning marked with wavy, line-like patterns</note>, and variegated in many patterns and colors. Indeed, you may find those in which white and scarlet colors are so mixed that in one plant, the upper petals are white, and in another, they are red. Some white ones are crowned with tiny red dots, or red ones are sprinkled with milky spots. Indeed, sometimes from one and the same stem, different kinds of flowers grow: white, red, and those sprinkled with partly white and partly red or scarlet marks. In the center of the flowers, two white tips <note>the stamens</note> spring forth.

**THE LARGER GARLAND BETONY OR CARNATION with a multicolored flower.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Betonica Coronaria with two flower heads, one in full bloom and one budding, showing the characteristic jointed stems.</image-desc>

This Betony has broad leaves and large flowers, very full and fragrant, with varied colors. For they are sprinkled with many red lines and dots: some petals are half-red, some almost entirely so, some half-white, and others completely white.

In his *Images*, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> calls it the "Double Garden Clove Pink, Large and Small, red-streaked, multicolored, and very delightful." The people of Basel call them *Juncker-blumen* <note>meaning "Young Nobleman’s flowers"</note>.

Furthermore, writers have called this the "Garland Betony" or "Vetony" to distinguish it from the other Betony which the Greeks call <term>κέστρον</term> <note>original: "kestron," referring to Wood Betony or *Stachys officinalis*</note>. From its scent, however, it is called *Caryophyllus* <note>Clove Pink or Carnation</note>. And the French, as Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French botanist</note> believes, call it *Ocellum* or *Oeuillet* <note>meaning "Little Eye" or "Eyelet"</note> because of the appearance of the flower.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Garland Betony" (modern Carnations and Pinks), detailing their physical characteristics, color variations, and the different names given to them by Renaissance botanists like Clusius and Lobelius.</summary>
<keywords>Carnation, Clove Pink, Dianthus, Betonica Coronaria, botany, Renaissance herbal, floriculture, Clusius, Lobelius, plant classification</keywords>

--- Page 519 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of "Crown-plants" or Garland-flowers, specifically focusing on the various species of Carnations and Pinks, which were historically classified under the name "Betony" or "Caryophyllus." It follows the previous page’s introduction to the genus by detailing specific wild and cultivated varieties.</meta>

# IMAGES AND SKETCHES.

### WILD BETONY OR VETONY, with a simple, fringed red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Betonica sylvestris plant, showing long stems with small serrated leaves and fringed flowers at the top.</image-desc>

There is no shortage of those who believe the *Garland Betony* or *Vetony* of the Ancients to be the *Baccaris* <note>original: "Baccarem"; an ancient plant name used by Virgil and others, though its exact identity was debated by Renaissance botanists</note>. There are some who think it is their Marsh Marigold <note>original: "Caltham palustrem"</note>, but many facts clearly argue against this. Others, according to Dalechamp, have wanted it to be the *Iphyum* of Athenaeus, and others the *Iphyum* of Theophrastus; but what do those plants have in common with this Betony? To others, it is the *Tunic Herb* <note>original: "Herba Tunica," an old name for the Pink or Carnation</note>, but it is better judged to be the *Polemonium* of Dioscorides. Some have numbered it among the Saxifrages, but again with little agreement. It is more likely, as Ruellius writes—and as Cordus and Matthiolus agree—that the *Clove-pink* flower <note>original: "Caryophyllum florem"; the modern Carnation</note> was unknown to the Ancients.

### CREEPING GARLAND BETONY OR CLOVE-PINK, red and white: of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping Betonica coronaria with multiple stems and smaller, denser foliage near the base.</image-desc>

This plant has little stems about nine inches long <note>original: "Dodrantales"; a dodrans is a measure of about nine inches or three-quarters of a foot</note>, which are rounded and jointed. The leaves are oblong, narrow, hard, and pointed, with a color somewhat like bluish-gray. The flower emerges from a reddish little cup <note>term: "calyculo" (calyx), the green outer part that holds the petals</note>; it consists of five small, fringed petals of a reddish color in a dilute purple, hairy around the center, and fragrant. The seed in the small cups is chaff-like and dark. The root is long, spreading out thin fibers. It is sometimes cultivated in gardens and flourishes well into the height of Summer.

### GARLAND BETONY OR CLOVE-PINK, with a flower turning from reddish to white, with a curled fringe.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caryophylea variety with tall, straight stems and prominent fringed flowers.</image-desc>

Commonly, the double-flowered Garland Betonys and more elegant plants are kept in gardens; but the most beautiful ones are almost always preserved in earthenware pots. They bloom for a very long time—indeed, throughout the whole of Summer, and even in Autumn—and sometimes even in Winter, provided there is warmth in the cellar rooms <note>original: "hypogæis"; referring to heated indoor spaces or conservatories used to protect plants from frost</note>.

The plant is long-lived and lasts for many years, provided it is protected from the injuries of the cold during the winter months.

<column-break/>

### TREE-LIKE GARLAND BETONY from Crete.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woody, shrub-like Betonica from Crete with thicker stems and clustered flowers.</image-desc>

It is certainly a wonder, as was mentioned just a moment ago, that our Garland Betony—a flower so celebrated and so pleasant, which in its size, beauty, variety, scent, and every other praiseworthy quality might compete with the Rose for the prize of sovereignty—was passed over in silence by the Ancients. Thus, we do not owe everything to them, but much to the diligent investigation of more recent authors.

This *Cretan Garland Betony* which we depict here grows like a shrub with woody, knotted, somewhat thick and branched stalks. It has bluish-green leaves about an inch and a half long, narrow, stiff, and ending in a sharp point; these are placed closely together at the ends of the runners and shoots. The flower is purple, emerging from little cups that are prickly, like a sea urchin <note>original: "echini instar"</note>.

### GARLAND BETONY OR CLOVE-PINK, marked by a notable purple crown.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Caryophyllea with a distinct dark-centered flower and pointed leaves.</image-desc>

This variety rises very little in height. Its branches are spread across the ground, fortified by a dense crowding of leaves, and they are somewhat hard and almost woody at the bottom. Later, they are divided into two or three stems, each of which sustains a single, most elegant flower. This flower is divided into five parts, beautifully cut around the edge, and decorated in the middle with a lovely, more saturated purple "little crown." The scent is most sweet and most pleasing.

It is cultivated in gardens and is an early-bloomer <note>original: "praecox"</note>, coming before the others.

### SMALLEST GARLAND BETONY OR CLOVE-PINK, sprinkled with golden specks.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, delicate variety of Betonica with thin stems and numerous small flowers.</image-desc>

Clove-pink Betony plants are more frequently propagated by tearing off small shoots with their leaves, and more rarely from seeds. For flowers born from seed return to a wild nature and are rendered less fragrant; those which were previously double-petaled become simple. Sometimes, dried Cloves <note>term: "Caryophylli"; here referring to the spice</note> are inserted into the split shoots of the plants, so that the flowers might draw in that scent and represent their pleasant sweetness more abundantly to the nostrils. <note>This reflects a common early modern belief that a plant's fragrance could be altered by physical contact with spices during growth.</note>

<summary>This page describes various species of "Garland Betony" (Carnations and Pinks), noting their physical characteristics, garden cultivation, and the debate over whether ancient Greeks and Romans knew of them. It highlights the beauty and fragrance of these flowers, comparing them to the rose and describing specialized Cretan and "crowned" varieties.</summary>
<keywords>Carnation, Pink, Dianthus, Betonica coronaria, botanical history, Crete, flower cultivation, fragrance, Renaissance botany</keywords>

--- Page 520 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of various species of Garland Betony, known today as Pinks or Carnations (Dianthus). It moves from the wild varieties described on the previous page to more specific garden cultivars and their medicinal virtues, as observed by famous botanists like Clusius and Matthiolus.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### GARLAND BETONY, OR Smaller Creeping Clove-pink.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing flowering plant with small, five-petaled blossoms and narrow leaves, showing the root system and creeping stems.</image-desc>

The foliage of this plant is green and somewhat blackish; the flower, however, is marked with silver-colored dots.

It grows for us at Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France, then a center of botanical study</note> in the S.P. garden, and was in bloom during May and June. Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering Flemish botanist</note>, however, heard that it grows in the mountains of Moravia, not far from the district of Nikolsburg, in shady places.

Furthermore, it is a marvelous thing that Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist</note> notes: he saw at one time a stem or stalk in long-lived plants that had reached such a thickness that it equaled the girth of an average man's arm.

### GARLAND BETONY with very finely cut leaves, or the Taller Common Superb Clove-pink.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller plant with deeply fringed or laciniated petals and long, slender stems with nodes.</image-desc>

This plant has many stems, one to two cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> high, which are branched and jointed. The lower leaves are numerous, somewhat broad, nine inches <note>original: "dodrantalibus"; a measure of about 9 inches</note> long, and greenish; the upper leaves are otherwise similar to those of other Garland Betonies. The flowers are large, sitting on longer stalks, and consist of five small petals, sometimes white and sometimes purplish, which are very deeply and finely cut. They have a greenish, hairy center <note>original: "umbilico"; literally "navel"</note> and a very sweet scent. Seed pods follow that are two finger-widths long and thin, containing flat black seeds.

We have kept these in gardens at Geneva and Montbéliard. Indeed, we have seen them growing abundantly in the wooded, fenced meadows in Savoy, and Clusius attests to this as well. It blooms later than the others.

### GARLAND BETONY, with a larger, finely fringed, pale red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with large, deeply cut petals and long, thin leaves.</image-desc>

The flowers of the Garland Betony show that they possess a dry and warm quality, as Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and herbalist</note> skillfully notes, evidenced both by the fragrance of their scent and a certain bitterness in their taste. Those which shine with a purple color are more effective than the others. They are recommended, when taken as a drink, for all afflictions of the heart, for dizziness, stroke, paralysis, and convulsions. They are also preserved with sugar, not only for all the aforementioned conditions but also against poisons and the infections of venomous animals. The wild varieties are as effective for all these purposes as the garden ones, though they work a little more slowly.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST CREEPING GARLAND BETONY, with a double reddish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing plant with double flowers and a dense root system.</image-desc>

We saw this plant at Heidelberg in Sprenger’s garden, and at Speyer at the home of the noble Lord Tengnagel.

Furthermore, Camerarius writes that a variegated flower of the Garland Betony can be created if the seeds of plants of different colors are enclosed together in a writing quill <note>original: "calamo scriptorio"</note> and committed to the earth. And, as also happens with Jasmines and Roses, when one flower withers away, another similar one is produced on the same stalk.

### SUPERB GARLAND BETONY, with very finely cut leaves and a double purplish flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, multi-petaled (double) flowers and long, narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This "Superb" double variety is twofold: one is a more intense purple and appears more showy; the other is a little smaller, less purple, and has almost more white parts. Both have narrower leaves and are not as bluish-grey <note>original: "glauca"</note> as is seen in other Clove-pink flowers.

Both bloomed for us in July at Montbéliard in the S.P. garden. Our illustrator <note>original: "Pictor"</note> painted the leaves a little broader than they actually are.

### LESS-BRANCHED GARLAND BETONY, with a finely fringed white flower and emerging horns.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with fringed petals and distinct "horns" or styles emerging from the center.</image-desc>

The flowers of the Garland Betony—especially the purple ones and those that smell like aromatic cloves—strengthen the stomach, brain, heart, and liver, and are very powerful in all afflictions of these organs. Their juice is not inferior to that collected from the dye-grains called Kermes <note>original: "granis tinctoriis Kermes"; a red dye and medicine derived from scale insects</note>, and it is most conveniently administered in malignant fevers. Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany</note> writes that the same juice wears down and expels kidney stones. A distilled water is drawn from them using glass instruments for the same uses; it is mixed into juleps and medicinal washes for the heart and liver. Many people put the flowers into vinegar, which gives it a pleasant scent and is very useful for headaches when applied or inhaled.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of "Garland Betony" (Dianthus species), detailing their physical characteristics, garden locations in Europe, and their significant medicinal uses for the heart, brain, and fevers.</summary>
<keywords>Garland Betony, Clove-pink, Dianthus, medical botany, heart remedies, Montbéliard, Clusius, Camerarius, Matthiolus, Kermes, kidney stones</keywords>

# IMAGES AND SKETCH.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
Kkk

### LESS BRANCHED GARLAND BETONY,
### with a finely fringed flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with long, slender leaves and a single tall stalk topped with several fringed flowers.</image-desc>

It has flowers similar in shape and whiteness to the one immediately preceding, but they lack the inner horns <note>Likely referring to the curved styles or specific petal appendages</note>; instead of those, they have ten **small filaments** <note>original: "staminula"</note> that slightly exceed the surface of the flower itself. The **Seed-heads** <note>original: "Capitula"</note> in which the seed is contained are also longer.

We had this variety, along with the preceding one, at Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France known for its botanical gardens</note> in the S.P. garden, and they bloomed in May, June, and July.

---

### BROAD-LEAVED ROCK GARLAND BETONY
### with a double red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader leaves and a dense, multi-petaled (double) flower head.</image-desc>

This plant has broad leaves, like those found in the simple rock variety. The **Flowers** are red, or approaching purple; or, more rarely, they are white and double <note>original: "pleni," referring to flowers with extra rows of petals</note>.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous Flemish botanist</note>, in his work on the plants of Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions</note>, called it the *Double-flowered Armerium* <note>original: "Armerium pleno flore"</note>, as it consists of a double or triple texture of petals. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, in his *Images*, called it the *Multiple Red Armeria*. Tabernaemontanus called it *Carthusian Pink* <note>original: "Caryophyllum Carthusianorum"</note>. Gerard called it the *Broad-leaved Red Armeria*.

It is kept in various gardens and is of great use for removing stains of any kind from linen cloth; specifically, if the cloth is rubbed with the herb and then washed with clear water.

---

### THE MOST COMMON GARLAND BETONY,
### in French: *Armoires, Armoiries*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common flowering plant with multiple stems and clusters of small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

This plant has several stems that are straight, round, and lean; they are sometimes a span <note>about 9 inches</note> high, sometimes a foot, and even a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, and are not branched except occasionally at the top. The **Leaves** are grass-like and green, appearing in pairs at the joints, and are more numerous near the ground. The **Root** is long and quite thick, dark on the outside and white inside, with a somewhat bitter taste. The **Flowers** are sometimes solitary and sometimes several together, a pleasant red color, notched along the blunt edges, consisting of five petals, with no remarkable scent, etc.

It grows wild everywhere in mountainous and wooded areas, uncultivated fields, meadows, and dry or sandy places. It blooms in the months of June, July, and August.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAVED ROCK GARLAND BETONY,
### with the flower marked by small white dots.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad leaves and flowers marked with small spots.</image-desc>

The woody **root** sends out stems one or two cubits high, which are smooth, round, jointed, and hollow; at each of these joints are dark green, lily-like **leaves**. The **Flowers** at the ends of the stems and side-branches are sweet-smelling and joined together many at once in the form of an umbel <note>a flat-topped flower cluster</note>. Emerging from long reddish calyxes <note>the protective outer cup of the flower</note>, they consist of five petals; they are scarlet and notched, forming a circle of white and deep purple dots around the base of the petals.

Some call it the "Scarlet Herb." The Germans call it *Scharlach blumen* <note>Scarlet flowers</note> and *Carthäuser blümlim* <note>Carthusian little flower</note>. Others call it the *Armerium flower*.

---

### BROAD-LEAVED GARLAND BETONY,
### with a variegated flower, from Besançon.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with thick, gnarled roots and variegated flowers.</image-desc>

This is cultivated in gardens for the sake of its elegance and blooms in the months of June and July. Dr. Cargill, a Scotsman, sent this to us from London with this inscription: *A multi-colored Armerium flower—white, red, flesh-colored, and spotted—on the same little branch.*

---

### SCALY WILD GARLAND BETONY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild variety of the plant with scaly calyxes and thin leaves.</image-desc>

It sends out several straight **stems** that are smooth, jointed, nine inches <note>original: "dodrantales"</note> or longer; at each of these joints are two narrow, grass-like **leaves**. At the top of the stem and the tips of the branches sits a **Calyx** having white scales. It produces a small, pale red flower; as that one withers, another flower—and then several more, each wrapped in its own little calyx—grows out from beneath it. They appear in such numbers that eventually the "pregnant" main calyx, which embraces the smaller ones with its offspring, has its belly burst by the multitude of its progeny <note>This describes a "proliferous" growth habit where new flowers emerge from the center or base of older ones</note>.

Lobelius labeled this the *Proliferous Armeria*. Gerard called it *Viscaria* <note>Catchfly</note>, though mistakenly.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of the "Crowned Betony" family, which refers to the genus *Dianthus* (pinks and carnations). Following the previous page’s discussion of broad-leaved and double-flowered varieties, the text now moves to smaller, alpine, and rush-leaved species, many of which were documented by the botanists Clusius, Fuchs, and Lobelius.</meta>

### CROWNED BETONY, WHICH IS THE
### Dwarf Taurus Carnation, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flowering plant with a thick, scaly root system and several stems ending in single flowers with five petals.</image-desc>

It is supported by a somewhat long, scaly **root**, divided into several heads. From these emerge **stalks** <note>original: "pediculi"</note> of one or one-and-a-half inches in length, jointed with one or two nodes, and clothed at each joint with two grass-like leaves. These support a large, purplish **flower** composed of five small petals, emerging from a hairy, ribbed calyx an inch long, which one might not inaccurately compare to the flower of the Swiss Gentian <note>original: "Gentianellę Helveticæ"</note>.

Authors record this as the Mountain or Alpine Carnation with a long, hairy calyx.

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLEST CROWNED TAURUS
### BETONY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small plant with a fibrous root and multiple thin stems topped with small flowers.</image-desc>

The **root** of this variety is somewhat thick, multi-headed, and fibrous. The **stems** <note>original: "coliculi"</note> are numerous, a palm’s height <note>about 3 to 4 inches</note> or taller, and branched. At each joint, there are rather large, whitish-purple leaves, about an inch long. At the ends of the branches, individual, rather large whitish-purple **flowers** grow. This illustration is from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous 16th-century German physician and botanist</note>, in which the root is not very well depicted.

It is found in sandy and dry places, and under the eaves of walls. We have seen it flowering in June in Geneva, on the walls across from the Senator's house, and in the Plainpalais <note>A famous public square and district in Geneva</note>.

---

### GRASS-LIKE CROWNED BETONY:
### or the Tiny Grass Carnation.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tufted plant with grass-like leaves and thin stems bearing small flowers.</image-desc>

The **root** has many heads and is moderately thick. The **leaves** are crowded together, stiff, and shining, like those of Hyssop but smaller and sharper. The **stalks** are numerous, a palm's height, slender, jointed, and sometimes nearly bare; occasionally, however, they branch out into a few short shoots. They bear single or twin **calyces** of half an inch or nearly an inch, from which pretty, purplish flowers burst forth.

It grows in sandy and dry places.

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLEST LEAFLESS-STEMMED
### CARNATION FLOWER of Montpellier.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick root, basal leaves, and leafless stalks ending in flower heads.</image-desc>

It sends out many rush-like stems without nodes, two palms high <note>roughly 6 to 8 inches</note>, on each of which sits a single, sufficiently large flower at the summit. It consists of four small toothed scales <note>original: "calyculis liris"</note> emerging from a long calyx, and has a sweet taste. The **root** consists of many fibers—long, twisted, woody, hard, and white—around which are many grass-like leaves that wither quickly.

It flowers in April at Montpellier near Castelnau <note>A village near the city of Montpellier in southern France</note> on the mountain; and on the summit of Mount Sète <note>original: "montis Ceti"</note> in May and June.

---

### THE LESSER RUSH-LIKE CARNATION FLOWER,
### or Leafless-Stemmed.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with long, thin leaves and a single stalk topped with a globose flower head.</image-desc>

The **leaves** are like those of Flax before it blooms, and then like those of the Serpentaria <note>likely referring to *Plantago serpentina*</note>, being short, about two inches long; but once the stem has grown and it flowers, they reach 4 or 5 inches. It has a thick **root**, divided into several heads where it pushes out the leaves. The **stem** is at first a few inches, then a palm’s height, and slender. The **flower heads** resemble the head of the Sheep's Scabious; between its membranes, shiny leaflets arise, followed by the flowers, which are succeeded by seeds that also mimic those of the Scabious.

It occurs frequently in the coastal regions of England, and for that reason, the English and the Belgians use it to decorate the borders of their garden paths.

<column-break/>

### THE GREATER RUSH-LIKE CARNATION FLOWER, OR
### Leafless-Stemmed. Called Sea Moly by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger variety of the previous plant, with a thicker root and a more substantial globose flower head.</image-desc>

The **stems** of this variety are nine inches to a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> tall, straight, and without nodes; at the summit of each sits a clustered flower, much like the appearance of Chives <note>original: "Schænoprassi"</note>, of a whitish-purple color, surrounded by a valley of leafy scales. The **root** is long, woody, round, and quite thick, divided into many heads, from which a large "crop" of leaves emerges close to the ground; these are grass-like and vary in the width of the <unclear>Gladiolus-like</unclear> leaves.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes that it is called "Sea Moly" by the Belgians, and is called *Holosteum* <note>meaning "all-bone"</note> by others; some call it the Great Sea Grass.

It grows in dry and stony places, such as the locations where we have seen it in Lyon and around Paris <note>original: "Lutetiam"</note>, flowering in August.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the *Cariophyllus* (Carnation and Pink) family and related species such as the *Saxifraga* (Saxifrage) and *Lychnis* (Campion). It moves from the alpine varieties described on the previous page to "woolly" and "umbel-bearing" wild types, as well as plants commonly found in grain fields.</meta>

### WOOLLY ALL-BONE CARNATION.
<note>original: "Cariophyllvs Holosteus Tomentosus"; likely a species of *Cerastium* or Mouse-ear Chickweed, noted for its "all-bone" stems that snap easily at the joints.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with fuzzy, lanceolate leaves and small five-petaled flowers at the tips of branched stems.</image-desc>

The entire plant is covered in a soft, dense, white **felt** <note>original: "tomento"</note>, so much so that it seems to be made of nothing but wool. The **stems** <note>original: "caiculi"</note> are jointed and about nine inches long. From each node, two leaves emerge opposite one another; they are somewhat long, pointed, and covered in wool. The upper part of the stem divides into several small branches, each of which bears a white **flower**. It has the appearance of a Mouse-ear flower <note>original: "Auriculę muris"</note>, even possessing a woolly calyx. At the division of the branches, there are also very short leaves that shimmer with a silvery brightness.

We have seen this plant in Florence in the Duke’s garden, and in Rome in the garden of Corvinus, a Belgian pharmacist.

<column-break/>

### UMBEL-BEARING FIELD CARNATION.
<note>original: "Cariophyllvs Arvensis Vmbellifervs"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a fibrous root, thin stems, and flowers arranged in an umbel-like cluster at the top.</image-desc>

It has a hard, fibrous **root**. The **leaves** are shaped like rocket <note>a type of leafy green</note>, being hard, broad, and woolly. The **stems** are thin, small, round, about a span long <note>roughly 9 inches</note>, and marked by three or four joints. From these joints grow two opposite leaves, equal in size to the lower ones that emerge from the root. At the tips sit five, six, or seven **flowers**—sometimes more, sometimes fewer—supported by long stalks, and they are white. When these flowers fall away, they are followed by small, long **seed pods** <note>original: "capitula"</note> containing small seeds, which point downward toward the ground.

It is found in the fields, as we observed near Basel, outside the St. Alban’s gate <note>original: "portam Blasianam"</note>, and it grows in great abundance between Worms and Neuhausen.

---

### THE SAXIFRAGE OF THE ANCIENTS,
### known to some as *Gypsophyton* and Rock-Comfrey.
<note>The name *Saxifraga* literally means "stone-breaker," reflecting the historical belief that these plants could dissolve kidney stones.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick, woody, twisted root and small, narrow leaves on branched stems.</image-desc>

The **root** is as thick as a pinky finger and longer than a palm’s width; it is divided into many heads from which spring countless **shoots** <note>original: "stolones"</note>, some spreading and others longer and jointed. The **leaves** at the joints are paired and opposite, similar to Hyssop leaves but smaller. A single **flower** sits at the tip of each shoot, containing many stamens in the center, emerging from a whitish, half-inch-long calyx striped with green.

Among writers, the name *Saxifragia* or *Saxifraga* has been used for many different things. However, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a prominent Flemish physician and botanist</note> identifies this plant as the *Saxifragia* of the Ancients without hesitation. He records that it grows in great quantity in Italy, France, England, the Dauphiné region, and other areas.

<column-break/>

### FALSE NIGELLA, OR CORN-COCKLE.
### German: *Kornrosen*; French: *Nielle des bleds*; Italian: *Githone*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with long, narrow leaves and a single large flower at the apex of the stem.</image-desc>

It is supported by a simple, white **rootlet**. The **stem** is one or one-and-a-half cubits high <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>, round, downy, grayish-white, branched, hollow, and jointed. The **leaves** are about a palm’s length, more or less as wide as a stalk of grain, hairy, and grow in opposite pairs from the joints. The **flowers** are like those of the Rose Campion (which we discuss next), purple in color, consisting of five petals, with the surrounding parts a faded purple. These are followed by an oblong **seed vessel** <note>original: "pericarpium"</note> filled with black, reddish seeds.

It grows everywhere in the fields among the crops; it flourishes in flower during the months of May and June.
*More details are in the Appendix.*

---

### ROSE CAMPION.
### German: *Marien Röslin* <note>Mary’s Little Rose</note>; French: *Oeillets, Passeroses*; Italian: *Lychnide coronaria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lychnis plant with broad, fuzzy basal leaves and upright stems bearing flowers.</image-desc>

Out of the countless plants recorded by authors under the ancient name of *Lychnis*, we here illustrate and begin our description of the one called *Coronaria* <note>The "Crowned" or "Garland" Lychnis</note>.

Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century herbalist</note> claims there are two types: the garden and the wild. Castore Durante distinguishes between the "simply named" *Lychnis* and the "Wild Lychnis." Lobelius separates them into the Rose Campion, the Red Lychnis, and the White Lychnis—but what, I ask, is the real distinction? Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus, a student of Bock and Fuchs</note> divides them into Red and White. But why does he provide two figures for one and the same plant? Certainly, one would have sufficed for us, if it were ready and if there were space here.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE ROSE CAMPION.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing a different view or variety of the Lychnis coronaria, emphasizing the branching structure and flower buds.</image-desc>

In the Rose Campion, straight **stems** emerge from a very fibrous root; they are one to one-and-a-half cubits tall, round, covered in a grayish-white down, and divided into several "wings" <note>side branches</note>. At each joint, two opposite **leaves** grow, similar to a pair of Sage leaves or a little larger; they are oblong, blunt, somewhat thick, soft, and turning white with dense hair on both the top and bottom. The **flowers** burst forth from oblong, channeled, hairy calyxes; they have little scent and are white, red, or a mixture of red and white. They are composed of five broad petals, forming the shape of a small rose. At the base of each petal, there are two sharp, rigid tips <note>referring to the corona or "crown" at the center of the flower</note>.

<keywords>Cariophyllus, Saxifraga, Corn-cockle, Rose Campion, Lychnis coronaria, Lobelius, Matthiolus, botany, medicinal plants, Florence, Basel</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the *Lychnis* (Campion) genus, transitioning from the alpine and woolly varieties on the previous page to garden favorites like the Rose Campion and the Jerusalem Flower, as well as wild species documented by notable botanists.</meta>

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED ROSE CAMPION.
<note>original: "Lychnis coronaria flore pleno"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lychnis coronaria with double flowers, showing upright stems, lanceolate leaves, and dense, multi-petaled blooms.</image-desc>

Having explained the different types of Rose Campion <note>original: "Lychnidis coronariæ"</note>, Schwenckfeld <note>Caspar Schwenckfeld, a 16th-century Silesian physician and naturalist</note> adds one more: specifically, a white variety sprinkled with red spots. There is also another variety with multiple and double flowers, which we illustrate here. Its stem and the cups <term>calyxes</term> of the flowers differ very little from the common variety, but the red flower is seen with a dense packing of many petals; because of this complexity, it is left without seeds.

This is sown, like the common single-flowered variety, in gardens and in earthenware pots; they bloom in the months of June, July, and August. Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a renowned Italian physician and botanist</note> writes that a wild variety grows spontaneously among the Anauni <note>original: "Ananienses"; people of the Val di Non in the Italian Alps</note>.

### WILD LYCHNIS WITH NARROW LEAVES, and several at each joint: of Clusius.
<note>original: "Lychnis sylv. foliis angustis... Clusii"; Carolus Clusius was a pioneering 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Lychnis with narrow leaves arranged in whorls around the stem joints and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

It has jointed stems, thin and divided into many branches, reaching a foot or more in height. At each joint <term>node</term> there are two or three leaves, sometimes more, which are narrow and of a bluish-gray <term>cesious</term> <note>original: "cesii coloris"; a pale blue-green or gray-green</note> color. The flowers bloom at the tips of the branches, consisting of five petals with a two-pronged tip, white on the inside and somewhat purplish on the outside. The calyxes are quite short and somewhat round, containing small, round, ash-colored seeds. The root is quite thick, white, and many-forked, perishing in its second year.

### WILD LYCHNIS RELATED TO RAGGED ROBIN, or Cuckoo Flower, of the same Clusius.
<note>original: "Lychnis sylvestris Odontidi, sive Flos Cuculi, affinis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Lychnis (Ragged Robin type) with deeply laciniated or fringed flower petals and slender stems.</image-desc>

It raises a stem a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, straight and hollow, divided by long intervals between the joints, and sticky to the touch near the top. From each joint, two leaves are situated opposite each other, like the Ragged Robin <note>original: "Floris Cuculi"; literally "Flower of the Cuckoo"</note>; they are oblong, pointed, thicker, and of a deeper green. From these same joints, from almost the middle of the stem to the very top, long stalks emerging from the leaf-axils <note>original: "foliorum sinu"</note> support many crowded flowers of a beautiful purplish color, followed by reddish seeds. The root is somewhat thick and black, spreading many fibers.

It is common in mountain forests and high, grassy places. Clusius found it flowering in May in the forests near Frankfurt.

<column-break/>

### CONSTANTINOPLE LYCHNIS or Cretan Lychnis, called Jerusalem Flower by others.
<note>original: "Lychnis Constantinopolitana vel Cretica, Flos Hierosolymitanus"; known today as Lychnis chalcedonica or the Maltese Cross.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lychnis chalcedonica (Maltese Cross), showing the characteristic dense terminal cluster of flowers and opposite leaves.</image-desc>

It is rooted with numerous fibers that have a slightly sharp taste. It raises stems about a cubit high, which are round, hairy, hollow, and interrupted by frequent joints. At each joint, two leaves grow in pairs without a stalk <term>sessile</term>; they resemble those of the Wild Lychnis but are darker, stiffer, and covered in a rougher down. The flowers at the ends of the small branches form an umbel <note>a flat-topped cluster where the stalks arise from a common point</note>, with a sweet though faint scent, and a very pleasant scarlet <term>minium</term> color, consisting of five petals with purple stamens. They emerge from an oblong, hairy, greenish calyx, which later contains tiny dark seeds.

It is sown in gardens only for the sake of ornament.

### WILD LYCHNIS WHITENING WITH DOWN, with a rather large flower, of the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a woolly wild Lychnis with soft, hairy leaves and stems, and larger solitary flowers.</image-desc>

It has many stems from a single root, which are round, somewhat long, weak, trailing on the ground, and jointed. At each joint are two leaves, long, soft, and whitening with a certain down. Between these, the flowers grow alternately along the length of the branches, being flesh-colored <note>original: "incarnati"; a pale pink or peach</note>. The root is thick and fibrous.

Clusius, the author of this description, found this plant, as well as the one immediately preceding <note>referring to the previous wild variety</note>, on the edges of fields in Castile <note>Spain</note>.

### FEATHERY LYCHNIS: German: Little Plum-Fringe Rose: of Tabernamontanus.
<note>original: "Lychnis plumaria: Germ. Pflaum Margen Röslin"; likely referring to the fringed petals of a Dianthus or Lychnis species.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lychnis plumaria with feathery, deeply cut petals and slender, upright habit.</image-desc>

Tabernamontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a famous German botanist</note> says it is so named because of the small, white, round, striped balls in which the flower—similar to wool or feathers—is contained. Furthermore, he says the plant has a firm, straight stem with two leaves at the knotted joints. But this description seems very meager to us, as neither the locations, nor the blooming time, nor the flavors are noted.

Is it perhaps the Catchfly with the mossy flower <note>original: "Muscipula muscoso flore"</note>, which is mentioned shortly?

As for the powers of the *Lychnis*: Schwenckfeld said that it draws out bile through the bowels and glues together fresh wounds; he also noted that the juice of the root, when drawn into the nostrils, provokes sneezing. Matthiolus writes that it is sought after in a wonderful way by young women for the making of wreaths <term>coronas</term>.

<summary>This page describes various species of Lychnis, including garden varieties like the Rose Campion and the Maltese Cross (Jerusalem Flower), and wild species documented by Clusius and Tabernamontanus. It concludes with notes on their medicinal use for bile and wounds, and their cultural use in wreaths.</summary>
<keywords>Lychnis, Rose Campion, Maltese Cross, Jerusalem Flower, Ragged Robin, Carolus Clusius, Mattioli, Tabernamontanus, botanical illustration, medicinal herbs, garden flowers, Castile</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the *Lychnis* (Campion) genus. The previous page ended with a description of a wild variety with narrow leaves as documented by Carolus Clusius. This page expands into smaller, rigid varieties, alpine species, coastal English varieties, and the "Catchfly" group known for their sticky stems.</meta>

# IMAGES AND DESCRIPTIONS
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### SMALLEST RIGID CAMPION.
<note>original: "LYCHNIS MINIMA RIGIDA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, upright Lychnis plant with thin stems and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This is a somewhat rigid plant, usually reaching a height of nine inches <term>dodrantium</term>, and rarely as small as four inches <term>palmus</term>. It has hard, stiff, and branched little stems. The leaves are positioned in pairs opposite one another at the nodes; they are about half an inch long or shorter, very narrow, and hairy. From the leaf axils <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> grow the flower cups <term>calyxes</term>, which are half an inch long, very slender, uniform, shaggy, and rough. Within these is a purple flower, so tiny it can scarcely be seen. The root is hard and woody.

We observed this plant near Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausum," a city in southern France</note>, next to the Mill.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S CREEPING CAMPION WITH GREEN LEAVES and white flowers.
<note>original: "LYCHNIS REPENS FOLIO VIRIDI, flore albo: Clusii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lychnis plant with a creeping habit and several flower heads.</image-desc>

According to Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, a Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist</note>, who describes it at length, this plant grows at the base of the Styrian Alps <note>in modern-day Austria</note>, on the *Schnealpe* above the Neuberg Monastery, and even more abundantly in *Eisenerz*.

In Lobelius’s <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> *Illustrations of Plants*, it is called the *smallest humble exotic pink with a lovely white flower*.

Regarding the *Lychnis Erymo*, one should consult the Appendix.

---

<column-break/>

### ENGLISH SEA CAMPION.
<note>original: "LYCHNIS MARINA ANGLICANA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a coastal Lychnis with thicker leaves and distinct seed pods or flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves attached in pairs at the joints; they are somewhat thick, smooth, blue-green <term>glaucous</term>, and saw-toothed. The small stems are rounded, nine inches or more in length, smooth, and spread out across the ground. The flowers emerge from swollen, beautiful, striped pods <term>calyxes</term>; they consist of five white petals that are split in two <term>bifid</term>, with yellowish stamens.

It grows on the embankments of the Isle of Wight <note>original: "Vectis Insulæ"</note> in England, and throughout that region among Sea Cabbage. According to Lobelius, it blooms in the months of May, June, and July. It is so similar to the *White Behen* <note>White Bladder Campion</note> of the apothecaries that it can hardly be distinguished by anyone.

<column-break/>

### CUCKOO FLOWER, OR PLINY’S ODONTITIS.
<note>original: "FLOS CUCULI, ODONTITIS PLINII"</note>
**German:** *Gauckblum* <note>Cuckoo flower</note> **French:** *Fleur du Coeu* <note>Cuckoo flower</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Cuckoo Flower" with deeply fringed or lobed petals.</image-desc>

The plant called Cuckoo Flower <note>Likely *Silene flos-cuculi*, known today as Ragged Robin</note> propagates itself by a creeping, fibrous root. It raises stalks about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> or higher, which are hollow, jointed, and streaked. From these stalks, leaves grow in pairs at the joints; they are narrow, oblong, and pointed. The flowers are like those of the "Superb Pink," of a reddish or flesh color (rarely white), fringed, and appearing either as single or double blooms with ash-gray tips. They emerge from an oblong, purple, striped, and somewhat fluted cup <term>calyx</term>.

Some label it the *many-flowered aquatic Armerium*. In Venice, Camerarius and Caspar Bauhin <note>two influential 16th-century botanists</note> found it under the name *Margaritæ*. It commonly adorns meadows in May, June, July, and August, and is also transplanted into gardens. It is recommended as a treatment for poisons.

---

<column-break/>

### STICKY CATCHFLY, A SPECIES OF CAMPION.
<note>original: "MUSCIPULA VISCARIA, LYCHNIDIS species"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Catchfly" plant with clusters of flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

This plant bushes out immediately from the root with many branches that equal the main stem in height (about a cubit). These branches are jointed, solid, and round. Along them, leaves grow in pairs opposite each other; they are oblong, pointed, green, and smooth, though the lowest leaves are wider and more blunt. Reddish flowers emerge both from the ends of the branches and from the leaf axils, coming out of an oblong, striped cup. These are followed by blackish seeds. The root is woody, white, and divided into many parts.

It is cultivated in gardens and grows wild in fields with rich soil among the crops, in many places in Old Castile <note>a region in Spain</note>. Clusius, Tabernaemontanus, Caspar Bauhin, and others label it *Lychnis viscaria* or "Campion with a sticky stem" <note>the name *Muscipula* or "Fly-trap" refers to the sticky substance on the stems that traps insects</note>.

<column-break/>

### GREATER CATCHFLY, WITH A SWOLLEN, BELLY-LIKE CUP.
<note>original: "MUSCIPULA MAIOR, CALYCE TURGIDO ventrioso"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Muscipula with prominent, swollen (ventricose) calyxes.</image-desc>

This plant sends up a straight, somewhat thick, hairy, striped, and brittle stem about a cubit high. The leaves are not particularly striking, resembling those of the *Ocymoides* <note>Basil-like plants</note>, being hairy and soft. From the leaf axils rise fairly long stalks supporting flowers made of five petals split in two. These are purplish with white tips in the center. They emerge from an oblong, hairy, beautifully striped cup <term>calyx</term>, which the seed vessels distend to a great size. These vessels are swollen <term>ventricose</term> from a wide, flat base and taper to a point; they contain beautiful, compressed, striped, ash-colored seeds. The root is robust and fibrous. The entire plant is sticky to the touch.

It is cultivated in gardens and grows wild in the same locations as the preceding species.

<summary>This page describes several specialized varieties of the Lychnis genus, including the English Sea Campion, the Cuckoo Flower (Ragged Robin), and the "Muscipula" or Catchflies, noted for their sticky stems and unique seed pods.</summary>

<keywords>Campion, Lychnis, Cuckoo Flower, Ragged Robin, Catchfly, Isle of Wight, Carolus Clusius, Lobelius, botanical classification, medicinal plants, sticky stems, alpine flora</keywords>

--- Page 526 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Lychnis (Campion) and Muscipula (Catchfly) families, moving from the rigid varieties of southern France and the Alps into species known for their sticky stems and bladder-like flower cups. It transitions here into the "Basil-like" wild plants and the Polemonium.</meta>

### CATCHFLY WITH A LARGE, SWOLLEN CALYX, and similar varieties; also considered a species of Lychnis by many.
<note>original: "MVSCIPVLA MAIORI CALYCE VENTRIOSO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Muscipula plant with large, ribbed, bladder-like calyxes and opposite leaves on a jointed stem.</image-desc>

This herb bears a great resemblance to the preceding one. The root is white, somewhat thick, and endowed with few fibers. The stems are rather thick, rigid, a foot <term>pedales</term> high, purplish, and jointed <note>having nodes or "knees"</note>. At the joints, the leaves grow in pairs, clasping the stem; they are long, narrow, hairy, and whitish. At the ends of the stems are the flower cups <term>calyxes</term>, which are swollen and large—though smaller than the previous species—and within them are the seed vessels. These are divided into layers or tunics, much like a Poppy <note>original: "Papaveris modo"</note>, containing small, ash-colored seeds.

We observed this plant growing along the roadsides in Montpellier <note>a city in southern France famous for its botanical garden</note>.

### CRETAN CATCHFLY OR STICKY-PLANT, resembling Bear's Ear.
<note>original: "MVSCIPVLA SIVE VISCAGO CRETICA, Auriculæ ursi facie"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Muscipula Cretica with a basal rosette of broad leaves and a branching flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It produces fibrous roots, from the head of which it puts forth quite large leaves. These leaves approach the form of the Bear's Ear <note>original: "Auricula ursi," likely a species of Primula</note> when in bloom, though they are whiter, thicker, and denser. The stems grow to one or two cubits <note>about 1.5 to 3 feet</note> in height; they are shaggy, round, and covered in a sticky juice <term>viscago</term>. By this stickiness, flies and other tiny insects are trapped in great numbers. At the tops of the branches, it bears many flowers gathered as if in an umbrella-like cluster <term>umbel</term>, even if individuals sometimes have their own distinct nodes; they are quite small for the size of the plant, consisting of five petals, with a greenish-yellow color.

Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, 1526–1609, a Flemish botanist</note> calls this the broad-leaved wild Campion.

### WILD BASIL: German: *Wildt Basilien*: French: *Basilic sauvage*: Italian: *Basilico Salvatico*.
<note>original: "OCIMOIDES, OCIMVSTRVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ocimoides with serrated leaves and small flowers clustered at the leaf axils and stem tips.</image-desc>

Just as Wild Mint <term>Mentha-strum</term> and Wild Parsley <term>Apiastrum</term> differ from their garden counterparts primarily by the nature of their birth, so too does Wild Basil <term>Ocimoides</term> differ from Garden Basil <term>Ocimum</term>. Indeed, according to Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note>, it has leaves similar to Basil, with branches three inches <term>palmi</term> high and hairy. It has pods similar to Henbane <note>original: "Hyoscyamo"</note>, filled with black seeds like those of Black Cumin <note>original: "Melanthio"</note>. It rests upon a slender, white, and shallow root. He records nothing of the flowers. However, they cling to the tips of the small branches, consisting of five split petals, either snow-white or purple, with white stamens rising higher than the flower itself; the flower cup is hairy, channeled, and slightly swollen.

<column-break/>

### CATCHFLY WITH A MOSSY FLOWER, OR Bell-shaped Wild Basil.
<note>original: "MVSCIPVLA MVSCOSO FLORE"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Muscipula Muscoso Flore with slender stems and small, delicate flowers.</image-desc>

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> in his *Adversaria*, the *History of Lyon*, Caspar Bauhin, and others record this as the "Catchfly with a mossy flower." Cesalpinus calls it a type of "Sticky-plant" <term>Visago</term>, bearing small and somewhat pale flowers arranged in a cluster like a spike.

We observed it blooming in June in Bormio, within the Rhaetian Alps <note>original: "Burmii in Rhetia"</note>, and in July at Basel in the garden of Doctor Zuinger.

### POLEMONIUM OR JACOB'S LADDER. Gesner’s Rock Polemonium.
<note>original: "POLEMONIVM SIVE POLEMONIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Polemonium with pinnate leaves and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Polemonium—which others call *Phileterium* and the Cappadocians call *Chiliodynamin* <note>original: "a multiplici potestate," meaning "thousand-powers" in Greek</note>—has slender branches, says Dioscorides, which are feathered <term>pinnated</term> on both sides. The leaves are a little larger than Rue, approaching the leaves of Calamint. At the summit are clusters <term>corymbs</term> in which the seed is black. The root is a foot and a half long, whitish, and similar to the root of Soapwort <term>Struthium</term>. It grows in mountainous and rugged places. Pliny records almost the same details as Dioscorides. However, various plants are handed down by the Ancients as the true "Polemonium": the White Behen of the apothecaries, Rose Campion, Wild Basil, Cowherb, Valerian, Wild Mint, Dittany, and Gesner's Rock Polemonium, which we depict here. It abounds on the walls in Geneva, Zurich, and Basel; it blooms in April and May.

### UN-SHOWY WILD BASIL.
<note>original: "OCIMOIDES NON SPECIOSVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a non-showy Ocimoides with simple leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The flowers of this plant are smaller than those of the Common Wild Basil; they are white on the upper part, or even a dilute red, but on the underside, they turn pale from a faint yellow.

Furthermore, the Common Wild Basil is referred to the Wild Campions <term>Lychnides</term> by some, and to Soapwort <term>Saponaria</term> by others; let the learned examine by what right they do so.

Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, an Italian physician and botanist</note> claims it grows abundantly everywhere in Italy among the cornfields and at the edges of fields; Clusius notes it in Austria, Styria, and Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Balkans</note>. It blooms throughout the Summer and into Autumn. It lives everywhere in the hedges of Geneva; in Basel, it is found on the road to Wyhlen <note>original: "Krentzack"</note> and where one descends to the Paper Mills.

<summary>This page describes various species of "Catchfly" (Muscipula) and "Wild Basil" (Ocimoides), detailing their physical characteristics, sticky properties for trapping insects, and their various names in European languages. It also discusses the historical identification of Polemonium, citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny alongside contemporary Renaissance botanists.</summary>

->IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the plant Ocimoides Creticum, showing its stems, leaves, and flowers with a detailed root system.</image-desc>

### SMALLER RED-FLOWERED BASIL-LIKE CATCHFLY, from Crete.
<note>original: "OCIMOIDES FLORE RVBRO MINVS, Creticum." The name "Ocimoides" refers to the plant's resemblance to Basil (Ocimum).</note>

The gardener of the Grand Duke [of Tuscany] sent us the seed from Florence under that name. From it grew a plant with stems a foot <term>pedalibus</term> long, hairy, thin, and numerous, sprouting from a slender root. At the joints <note>the "nodes" or "knees" of the stem</note> of these stems, leaves were seen in pairs, oblong in shape with a blunt tip. From the axils <note>the "armpits" where the leaf meets the stem</note> of these leaves, two opposite branches sprouted, supporting long flowers at their tips, which were wrapped in a long, striped outer casing <term>tunica</term> or calyx.

As for the properties of the **Basil-like Catchfly**: Dioscorides <note>a famous 1st-century Greek physician</note> recommends its seed for the bites of venomous animals. In the judgment of both himself and Galen <note>the influential Roman-era physician</note>, the root is of no use for medical purposes.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the plant Ocimoides Lychnitidis, showing upright stems with small flowers and a creeping root system.</image-desc>

### BASIL-LIKE CAMPION with a CREEPING root.

In the judgment of Fabio Colonna <note>a noted Italian botanist of the era</note>, this plant is a middle ground between the **Basil-like Catchfly** and the **Rose Campion** <note>Lychnis coronaria</note>. It is like the **Basil-like Catchfly** because it has small leaves, which cling in pairs to each individual joint starting from the root. It is like the **Campion** <term>Lychnis</term>, however, because its leaves are hoary <note>gray-white</note>, hairy, and fleshy—no less suitable for making lamp wicks than the leaves of the true Campion <note>The name Lychnis comes from the Greek word for "lamp."</note>. He adds that it grows wild and frequently in damp places on the mountain called Saint Mary the Virgin.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the plant Saponaria, showing broad leaves and clusters of flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

### SOAPWORT, SOAP-ROOT, WOOL-PLANT: Germ. Seiffkraut, Vzeschkraut.
<note>The German names translate to "Soap-herb" and "Wash-herb," referring to its ability to create a lather.</note>

The thin little roots of **Soapwort** wander about in various tangled patterns. Several stems are attached, which are mostly upright, a cubit <term>cubitales</term> <note>about 18 inches</note> or higher, reddish, hairy, and jointed with frequent nodes. The leaves grow from these nodes in opposite pairs, like those of the **Cross Gentian**, but with a less cheerful color, a rigid texture, and a salty, nitrous taste. The flowers are arranged in an umbel <note>a flat-topped cluster</note>; they are whitish or a very pale purple, fragrant, and consist of five petals with white stamens occupying the center. They emerge from a thin, hairy calyx an inch long. The seed is plentiful, small, nearly round, compressed, and chestnut-colored.

It grows wild near rivers, mountain streams, and ponds in sunny and sandy places; it blooms throughout the entire Summer and Autumn.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Saponaria minor, showing a smaller variety of the plant with similar leaf and flower structures.</image-desc>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF SOAPWORT: The LESSER SOAPWORT of some. The CREEPING BASIL-LIKE CATCHFLY of others.

Sandy places situated to the south nourish this plant in great and beautiful abundance, such as near Geneva by the Rhone and Arve rivers, and at Yverdon <note>Ebrodunum</note> in that pleasant valley adjacent to the city called "Behind the Lake" <note>original: "derriere le Lac"</note>.

Furthermore, Rembert Dodoens <note>a Flemish physician and botanist</note> attests that **Soapwort** is hot and dry in its temperament, and endowed with a non-negligible power of cleansing. When pressed, it emits a salty juice that is capable of washing away scabies <note>a skin infestation</note> and all foulness of the skin; it also excites sneezing with great violence. It is allowed into floral crowns because of the very sweet scent and beauty of its flower. It is a matter beyond dispute that it removes greasy stains from clothes if they are washed with this herb. More regarding this plant, as well as **Soap-root** and **Wool-herb**, can be found in the Appendix.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Centaurium minus, showing a slender plant with small opposite leaves and a terminal cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

### LESSER CENTAURY: Germ. Tausendguldenkraut: Gall. Petite Centaurée: Ital. Centaurea minore.
<note>The German name translates to "Thousand-guilder-herb," highlighting its high medicinal value.</note>

It is commonly known that two main types of the plants passed down under the name of **Centaury** have been established: namely, the **Greater** and the **Lesser**. The Greater was treated in Class XXV of this *Outlines of Plants*; we shall now speak of the Lesser.

Dioscorides describes it thus: **Small Centaury**, he says, which some call *Linnaeus* <note>meaning "of the flax," or "growing in damp places"</note> because it loves moist places, is a herb similar to **St. John's Wort** or **Oregano**. It has a stem exceeding a palm's breadth in height, which is angled. The flower approaches the likeness of the **Campion** <term>Lychnis</term> flowers, specifically inclining from a scarlet color toward purple. The leaves are quite long and tiny, like those of **Rue**. The seed is like wheat. The root is small, smooth, and useless; yet [like the flowers and leaves] it is endowed with a remarkable bitterness. Pliny <note>the Roman natural historian</note> records the same details.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Centaurium minus perfoliatum, showing a variety with leaves that appear to surround the stem and yellow flowers.</image-desc>

### LESSER PERFOLIATE CENTAURY, with a yellow flower.
<note>"Perfoliate" describes leaves that surround the stem so that the stem appears to grow through them.</note>

Several differences are observed in the **Lesser Centaury**: specifically in size, for in damp places it grows a cubit high, while in dry places it is much smaller. Furthermore, it varies in the color of the flower, which for the most part is a reddish-purple, but is sometimes also white, rust-colored, or even yellow.

The common purple variety loves grassy places that have not been turned by the plow and are somewhat moist; it blooms in July and August. It is frequent near Basel, close to Lörrach, and around Dornach in the woods, as well as in the woods around Geneva. We have seen the yellow-flowered variety on the hills of Zurich, and in the wet meadows of Geneva, Montpellier, and Bologna. It possesses the same medicinal powers as the scarlet variety, about which more is found in the Appendix.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of various flowering herbs, moving from the Basil-like catchflies to the "White Behen" used by apothecaries, grassy-leaved flowering plants, and the "Cowherb" (Vaccaria), focusing on their physical descriptions, medicinal uses, and the locations where the authors observed them.</meta>

### WHITE BEHEN OF THE APOTHECARY SHOPS.
<note>original: "BEHEN ALBVM OFFICINARVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with slender, branched stems and small, opposite leaves, showing a detailed root system.</image-desc>

With a thick, white, woody root, it sends out stalks a cubit or a cubit and a half <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note> high; these are thin, rounded, smooth, and jointed, dividing into "wings" near the top. At each joint, two leaves grow opposite one another, shaped like those of a Campion <term>Lychnis</term> but entirely hairless, somewhat sharp to the taste, and obscurely bitter. The flowers emerge slightly from their husks <term>calyces</term>; they are white, or purplish-white, composed of five deep-notched petals, with purplish filaments occupying the center. The husks later contain seed pods full of Campion-like seeds.

There are two kinds: one found in the mountains, which is taller, and another found in meadows. We have seen it ourselves in Montpellier, Lyon, Geneva, and Basel, growing in woods, plowed fields, meadows, and among ruins. Concerning its medicinal powers, follow the figure on the side.

<column-break/>

### RAUWOLF’S WHITE BEHEN, with a Dock-like leaf, yellow flower, and long, flexible root.
<note>original: "BEHEN ALBVM RAVVVOLFFII, FOLIO LA-pathi, flore luteo, & radice longâ flexili." Leonhard Rauwolf was a 16th-century physician and pioneering botanist who traveled the Levant.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broader, lanceolate leaves and a thick, tapering root.</image-desc>

Rauwolf is the authority who states that this White Behen grows at the foot of Mount Lebanon; he says it is the true "Behen" of the Arabs, and that in our own age they still call it *Behen ackma* and *Behen abiad*, which is to say, "White Behen."

Furthermore, although Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician</note> believed the powers of the commonly named White Behen were unproven, Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock</note> recommends it for warm compresses and sweat-baths, by which he strives to soften hardened nerves. According to Schwenkfeld, the juice removes "hot" inflammation of the eyes <term>ophtalmiā</term> and soothes eye pain. The seed purges phlegm and is given to those with the "Comitial disease" <note>epilepsy</note>; it is even believed that if placed under sick patients without their knowledge, it can stir the bowels <note>original: "Cisim moliri," likely referring to a purgative effect or a specific humoral movement</note>.

---

### FUCHS’S GRASS, OR WHITE-FLOWER.
<note>original: "GRAMEN FVCHSII, SIVE LEVCANTHEMON." Named after the botanist Leonhart Fuchs.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a grass-like plant with small flowers and a creeping root system.</image-desc>

It creeps along with a thin and weak little root, which is jointed at the very top of the turf. The stalks are hollow, square, and vary from nine inches to a cubit in height, marked by joints. At each joint, two grass-like leaves grow, sharp and stiff. From the "axils" <note>the angles between leaf and stem</note> of these leaves, thin, hairy stalks emerge, upon which sit lovely, bright white little flowers. These are composed of five deeply cleft and streaked petals, with saffron-colored tips and a greenish husk. The flowers are followed by small vessels containing round seeds.

Some call it Eyebright <term>Euphrasia</term>, others call it White-flower Grass, others Knotted Grass, and Tabernaemontanus calls it Virgin Grass.

It grows abundantly in various places in hedges and blooms in April and May. It is powerful for cooling and drying.

<column-break/>

### AN HERB RELATED AND SIMILAR TO FUCHS’S GRASS OR WHITE-FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the previous one but with smaller leaves and more delicate stems.</image-desc>

This one blooms later, with thinner square vines and little milk-white flowers on long stalks. These flowers are composed of twelve little petals <note>original: "bis senis foliolis," twice-six</note> smaller than the previous plant, with reddish tips. The heads are smaller and oblong; the leaves are shorter, wavy-edged, and grow in pairs. The root is similarly fibrous and creeping.

By Tabernaemontanus it is called the Lesser Flowering Grass.

We observed it blooming in May in the thickets near Geneva and Zurich, and also near Masmünster. It grew of its own accord in the St. Pierre Garden at Montbéliard.

---

### COWHERB. French: The herb for cows.
<note>original: "VACCARIA: Gall. L'herbe aux vaches."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with broad, clasping leaves and terminal flower clusters.</image-desc>

It rises with a single stalk, a cubit or more high, smooth, rounded, and hollow. Near the top, it divides into opposite branches, and these into others, always in an opposing arrangement. Pairs of leaves grow opposite each other at the joints of the stem; they are a pale sea-green <term>glauco</term>, oblong, and pointed. Their bases clasp the stem so thoroughly that the stem seems to pass right through them <note>this is called a "perfoliate" leaf</note>. At the end of each branch sits a reddish flower, consisting of five petals, protruding slightly from the husk. The seed is small, black, and round. The root is woody, white, and straight, spreading fibers from its side.

Botanists call this plant *Vaccaria* <note>from "vacca," the Latin for cow</note> because cows gladly feed upon it. It varies in size, leaf width, and in the color of the flowers, which may be red or pale. It blooms in June.

<column-break/>

### HOARY CHICKWEED-LEAVED WHITLOW-GRASS.
<note>original: "PARONYCHIA ALSINEFOLIA INCANA." "Paronychia" refers to a whitlow or nail infection, which this plant was thought to cure.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, leafy plant with a dense root system.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, the *Paronychia* is a tiny shrub growing in meadows, similar to the *Peplos* <note>a type of Spurge</note>, but shorter and with larger leaves. Applied as a poultice, it is a remedy for nail infections <term>paronychiis</term> and honeycomb-like sores <term>fauis</term>.

Galen says it was named after the condition it treats, for it heals nail infections and sores. Its quality consists of "thinning parts," and it heats and dries in the third degree.

Mattioli writes that *Paronychia* also grows on the walls of old buildings and dry tree trunks, with leaves like *Peplos* or Rue, pale on the underside, or rather covered in spots in the manner of Spleenwort or Hart’s Tongue fern. We saw it blooming in June at Montpellier, near the woods on the way to Aigremont.

<keywords>White Behen, Rauwolf, Fuchs's Grass, Vaccaria, Cowherb, Paronychia, Whitlow-grass, botanical medicine, 17th-century botany, Montpellier, Lebanon</keywords>

->ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA.<-
<note>original: "Images and Outlines/Descriptions"</note>

### MOUSE-EAR, OR LITTLE MOUSE-EAR:
<note>original: "MYOSOTIS, SIVE AVRICVLA MVRIS"</note>
Germ. *Mouse-ear*: French *Mouse-ear*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myosotis (Mouse-ear) plant showing hairy leaves and small flowers with visible root structure.</image-desc>

The common Mouse-ear, which we depict here, is rooted with hair-like fibers. The little stems are between three and nine inches <term>palmares aut dodrantales</term> high, partly upright and partly lying flat; they are thin, rounded, hairy, and hollow. At each joint <term>genicula</term> grow two opposite leaves, which perfectly resemble the sharp and hairy ears of mice—from which they take their name—and have no particular taste. The little flowers are small and white in color, followed by long, shiny seed-vessels <term>loculi</term> containing many seeds.

It stays green in the fields and gardens throughout the winter, and blooms in May, June, and July.

Is this perhaps Thalius’s *Hairy Chickweed* <note>original: "Alsine hispida"</note>, which grows everywhere in damp places?

### MOUSE-EAR, OR LITTLE MOUSE-EAR
with very slender leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Myosotis with much finer, narrower leaves and more numerous flower heads.</image-desc>

It sends out many woody branches about nine inches long from a thick, hard, and perennial root; many very thin leaves are clustered around their joints. The flowers are large and white, similar to the flowers of the Mouse-ear mentioned just before.

These plants are by no means common, nor do they grow everywhere. We have observed them in the mountains around Geneva and Montbéliard, and on the hills adjacent to the Rhine, but nowhere else.

### CHICKWEED, OR HEN’S-BITE:
<note>original: "ALSINE, SIVE MORSVS GALLINÆ"</note>
Germ. *Hen-bite*: French *Chickweed*: Ital. *Little hen*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine (Chickweed) showing paired ovate leaves and small star-like flowers.</image-desc>

Dioscorides says that some call Chickweed *Myos ota* <note>Greek: "Mouse-ears"</note> because it has leaves similar to the ears of a mouse. It is called *Alsine*, however, because it loves shady groves—which the Greeks call *alsē*—and woody places.

It has small hair-like roots and delicate, hairy, reddish, jointed trailing stems that spread across the ground. The leaves are like those of Pimpernel <term>Anagallis</term>, slightly hairy, growing opposite each other from the joints; they have a bland taste. The little white flowers are smaller than those of the Star-flower. The seed is reddish, like a poppy seed.

We depict here the common Chickweed, which some call the *Greater Hippia*; others, however, wrongly confuse it with Pimpernel because of the similarity of the leaves. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a 16th-century German botanist</note> judges it, with no less of an error, to be the *Telephium* of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Serapion.

<column-break/>

### MOUSE-EAR, OR LITTLE MOUSE-EAR
with a beautiful white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myosotis variety with larger, more distinct white flowers and broader leaves.</image-desc>

This plant consists of a thin root that wanders with various creepers and takes hold of the earth again by means of fibers sent down from the joints. The stems are rounded, hairy, and jointed; at the tips of the branches, they bear lovely, milky-white flowers. These consist of five petals, notched and streaked to some depth with a green division in the middle; on the outside, five small hairy leaves support them at the base, while in the center are yellow stamens and a yellow stalk <term>stilo</term>. The leaves at the joints are almost always in pairs, hairy, about half an inch long, and tapering gradually from a wider base without a leaf-stalk <term>pediculo</term> into a sharp point.

It grows in grassy, sandy places, but is not encountered very frequently.

### MOUSE-EAR, OR LITTLE MOUSE-EAR
alpine and hairless: The smallest smooth-bulbed Lychnis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine, hairless variety of Myosotis with dense foliage at the base.</image-desc>

It rests upon roots that are somewhat hard and thick, white, and not very fibrous. There are several small stems about three inches long, thin, smooth, and reddish toward the bottom. The leaves are oblong, hairless, and pointed. The flowers stand upright and are white, with five petals that are notched along the edges, with little points in the center. The cups <term>calyces</term> are streaked and somewhat fringed at the top. The seed in the small vessels is thin.

Furthermore, Mouse-ear is dry in nature, but temperate in heat. The flowers are used to treat heart ailments <note>original: "cardiaco morbo"</note>, and a water distilled from them is used for epilepsy in children. Externally, it is highly praised for whitlows <term>paranychia</term> <note>infections around the fingernails</note> and for the relaxation of the nerves <note>original: "nervorum resolutionem," likely referring to palsy or loss of motor function</note>.

### GREAT CREEPING CHICKWEED, PERENNIAL.
<note>original: "ALSINE MAIOR REPENS, PERENNIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger, creeping variety of Alsine with elongated flower spikes.</image-desc>

Although Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen mentioned only one kind of Chickweed, more recent authors have observed several types of it, as will be clear from the following pages.

The Great Chickweed, or Hen’s-bite, which we depict here, comes up among briars, in thickets under brambles, in rough and wide spaces, and also near springs and flowing waters. It blooms in Summer and Autumn.

The common variety depicted a little earlier also loves groves and damp places, but it also thrives in gardens among vegetables and even in vineyards.

<summary>This page describes various species of Myosotis (Mouse-ear) and Alsine (Chickweed), detailing their physical characteristics, specific habitats ranging from the Alps to the Rhine, and their use in treating heart conditions, epilepsy, and nerve issues.</summary>
<keywords>Myosotis, Mouse-ear, Chickweed, Alsine, botanical taxonomy, alpine flora, heart medicine, epilepsy, whitlows, Dioscorides, Tragus, medicinal herbs</keywords>
