# OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### CHICKWEED WITH PLANTAIN-LIKE LEAVES.
<note>original: "ALSINE PLANTAGINIS FOLIO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine plantaginis folio, showing a plant with broad, ribbed leaves similar to plantain and small flowers at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

This variety is very similar to the common chickweed. The root is hairy with thread-like fibers; the small branches are of a similar shape and hairy, as are the leaves, which hang from the joints <term>ex nodis</term> on somewhat long stalks. These leaves are roundish, hairy, and blackish in color. There is, however, a notable difference in that the veins or "nerves" run lengthwise, just as they do in the Plantain <term>Plantago</term> plant. The tiny flowers are small and white, like the chickweed already described.

We have observed this plant near Lille <note>original: "Lisla"</note> in Burgundy, growing in vineyards. Is this perhaps the *Hairier and blacker Chickweed* from Gesner’s garden? Or Lobel’s *Greater Hippia*? Or Dodonaeus’s *Sea Chickweed*?

<column-break/>

### THE SMALLEST CHICKWEED.
<note>original: "ALSINE MINIMA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine minima, showing a small, delicate plant with thin stems and tiny leaves.</image-desc>

This variety is smaller in all its parts, possessing tender and hairy little branches, for the most part simple and unbranched. It has tiny leaves—smaller than those of the medium chickweed—which are blackish, slightly hairy, and rest on a very short stalk. The flower is similarly white. The seed contained in the small pods <term>pericarpis</term> is very tiny and reddish-brown.

Furthermore, among the plants given the name of "Chickweed" <note>original: "Alsine"</note>, the following are also categorized: *Stone Knee-grass* <note>original: "Polycnemum petræum"</note>, *White Stone Saxifrage*, *Smallest Shepherd's Purse*, *Woodruff* <note>original: "Asperula"</note>, *Pellitory-of-the-wall* <note>original: "Parietaria"</note>, *Chickweed-Silene* <note>original: "Cacubalum"</note>, as well as various species of *Mouse-ear* and *Pimpernel* <note>original: "Anagallidis"</note>.

<column-break/>

### THIN-LEAVED CHICKWEED.
<note>original: "ALSINE TENVIFOLIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine tenuifolia, featuring very thin, needle-like leaves and a branched root system.</image-desc>

It has numerous roots that are whitish, woody, and split into many parts. From these rise little stems about three to five inches <term>palmares & sesquipalmares</term> high, which are rounded and branched. At their joints, leaves grow in pairs; these are long and thin, like those of the smallest Pink <term>Tunica</term>. The tiny, white, star-shaped flowers cling to the ends of the branches on long stems that rise from the crook of the leaves.

It blooms in the fields of Montpellier in April.

<column-break/>

### THE MOSSY CHICKWEED OF SOME.
<note>original: "ALSINE MVSCOSA QVIBVSDAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine muscosa, showing a low-growing, moss-like plant with numerous small flowers.</image-desc>

This is a very tender and weak little plant, covering the surface of the earth like moss. It has very thin and branched stems, three to six inches <term>palmaribus aut bipalmaribus</term> long. At their joints grow leaves about an inch or an inch and a half long; they are as thin as a thread and a bright green color. The tiny flowers consist of four small petals; they are white, with the appearance and shape of Spurry <note>original: "spergulæ"</note>, and have very white tips <note>anthers</note> in the middle. Small pods follow the flowers, stuffed with seeds that are nut-brown or dark red. The root is slender, fibrous at the joints, and has no known use.

It delights in the shady and damp entrances to high mountain passes.

<column-break/>

### CLUSIUS’S HORNED CHICKWEED.
<note>original: "ALSINE CORNICVLATA CLVSII"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine corniculata clusii, showing a plant with distinct seed pods shaped like small horns.</image-desc>

This little herb is about three inches <term>palmaris</term> high, consisting of a single stem divided into several branches. The stem is jointed, tender, and slightly hairy, like common chickweed. The leaves also mimic those of the common chickweed, though they are a little longer, slightly hairy, grow opposite one another, and appear in pairs at intervals. In the hollows of the "armpits" <note>axils</note> of the plant sit tiny, whitening flowers, which are followed by parchment-like, transparent little horns <term>cornicula</term>. These are shaped like a cock's spurs and are found to be covered in a certain sticky moisture when touched. The seed within them is tiny and black. The root is useless and lives for only one year.

It is common among the grain crops in the region of Salamanca.

<column-break/>

### LONG-LEAVED CHICKWEED, growing in marshy places.
<note>original: "ALSINE LONGIFOLIA, VLIGINOSIS proueniens locis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alsine longifolia, showing elongated leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has thin, creeping little roots. The stems are a foot long, square-shaped, and firm. At their joints, the leaves grow in pairs, similar to the leaves of Hedge Hyssop <note>original: "Gratiola"</note> but smaller; they are not jagged or "saw-toothed" around the edges, they end in a point, and are smooth. The flowers sit at the ends of the branches; they are star-shaped and white, like common chickweed. The taste of the herb is sticky and bland.

It grows in the marshy areas of mountains.

<summary>This page describes six varieties of Chickweed (Alsine), detailing their physical characteristics such as leaf shape, stem height, and seed pod structure, alongside their geographical locations across Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Chickweed, Alsine, Plantain-leaved, botanical classification, Montpellier, Salamanca, Lille, marsh plants, mountain flora, Clusius</keywords>

<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
Eee 2

### STINKING CHICKWEED OF FABIO COLONNA, with greenish-white flowers like Castor or Hemp.
<note>original: "ALSINE FOETIDA FAB. COLVMNÆ, FLOSculis ex albido virentibus ricinino Cannabino"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine foetida) showing a central stalk with serrated leaves and small flower clusters, with a detailed root system at the base.</image-desc>

Fabio Colonna <note>Fabio Colonna (1567–1640) was an influential Italian botanist known for his detailed illustrations.</note> offered this as the "Alsine" described by Dioscorides, but mistakenly so, as is clear enough from its foul odor alone. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax*, names it *Chickweed with Pellitory leaves*. It is called "Good Dog-Cabbage" <note>original: "Cynocramben bona"</note> on Mount Baldo by Cerutus and Honoré Bellus, and the same by Caspar Bauhin.

It loves the same locations as Pellitory <term>Helxine</term>. Bauhin, however, received it from the island of Capri, where it grows frequently of its own accord, brought by Colonna. To us, however, it grew in the Prince's Garden <note>original: "S. P. Horto"</note> at Montbéliard. It flowers in the spring and reaches maturity in the summer.

<column-break/>

### CHICKWEED WITH SMOOTH SERRATED LEAVES.
<note>original: "ALSINE SERRATO FOLIO GLABRO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine serrato folio glabro) featuring slender, branching stems with small, pointed leaves and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

This is a dwarf plant, extending several reddish, somewhat hairy, and jointed stems from a white fibrous root. At each joint <term>genicula</term> there arise small leaves, always in opposing pairs, intersected by reddish veins; they are longer than they are wide, serrated like common Germander <term>Chamaedryos</term>, smooth, and attached by very short stalks. From the "armpits" <note>The axils where the leaf meets the stem.</note> of the stalks, very slender stems support a tiny flower enclosed by four little leaves; the flower itself consists of four blue (or more rarely, white) petals, joined at the bottom, surrounding a few stamens and a thin style. When the flowers fall away, they are succeeded by two-parted seed pods <term>foculi</term> containing round seed.

It grows everywhere in gardens, and flowers in Spring and Summer.

---

### CHICKWEED WITH HAIRIER SERRATED LEAVES, with flowers and pods clinging to the stems.
<note>original: "ALSINE SERRATO FOLIO HIRSUTIORE, FLORIBUS & loculis cauliculis adhærentibus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine serrato folio hirsutiore) showing an upright, hairy stem with densely packed leaves and small flowers along the stalk.</image-desc>

It rests upon a thin, fibrous root. It bears many stems about nine inches <term>dodrantales</term> long, some larger and some smaller, upright, slightly branched, reddish at the base, and hairy. The leaves are somewhat long, less deeply serrated, slightly hairy, and cling directly to the stems. The flowers are small, divided into four parts, purplish, and streaked. The taste of the plant is somewhat bitter.

It grows in elevated, sun-drenched, rocky, and uncultivated places, and also sometimes on walls and in drier meadows. It flowers in April and May.

Furthermore, Chickweed is useful for healing ulcers and wounds, whether they are fresh or old; it also cures Scabies <note>A contagious skin disease caused by mites.</note> and all blemishes of the skin. *More is written at the side of the following figure.*

<column-break/>

### CHICKWEED WITH OBLONG SERRATED LEAVES and a blue flower.
<note>original: "ALSINE OBLONGO FOLIO SERRATO, flore cæruleo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine oblongo folio serrato) with a thick root, broad serrated leaves, and flowering stems.</image-desc>

It puts forth angular stems, four to six inches long, hairy, quite sturdy, and branched. Along these, leaves arise alternately, half an inch to an inch long, and half an inch wide, serrated around the edge, hairy, and with a sticky taste. The flowers are small and blue, with somewhat large, hairy leaves situated beneath them; these are followed by capsules containing small seed. The root is woody, white, and divided into many parts.

We saw it near Montpellier, flowering in April and May.

This Chickweed is beneficial for a cough and ailments of the chest; it opens obstructions of the liver and spleen, cleanses the kidneys and bladder, and drives out fevers and contagious diseases.

---

### CHICKWEED WITH DEEPLY CUT LEAVES and a purple or violet flower.
<note>original: "ALSINE FOLIO PROFUNDE SECTO, flore purpureo sive violaceo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine folio profunde secto) showing sprawling stems with deeply lobed leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

Sometimes this little plant is only two or three inches tall, rarely four inches <term>palmaris</term>, with stems that are almost turned upward and hairy, upon which are opposite leaves, cut into several deep segments <term>lacinias</term>; others are entire, especially the lower ones, and somewhat fleshy. From the hollows of these <note>The leaf axils.</note>, stalks arise bearing purple flowers, which leave behind two-parted capsules; in other cases, the flowers sit directly among the leaves. The root is small and fibrous.

We found this near Geneva toward Châtelaine, among the cornfields.

<column-break/>

### A KIND OF CHICKWEED ACCORDING TO FUCHS, with hairy Ivy-like leaves and a Blue flower.
<note>original: "ALSINES GENUS FUCHSIO, FOLIO Hederulæ hirsuto: flore Cæruleo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen (Alsine genus Fuchsio) showing a plant with ivy-like hairy leaves and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

We have found this growing wild in gardens in Geneva and Montbéliard, flowering in February and March.

Caspar Bauhin says it varies in the size of its leaves (both large and small) and also in the color of the flower, which can be purplish or milk-white.

Tabernaemontanus and others call it *Ivy-leaved Chickweed*; the *Portuguese Garden* calls it the same. Dodonaeus (in French) calls it *Elatine*, and Anguillara calls it Pliny's *Lappago*.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Chickweed (Alsine), distinguishing them by their serrated leaf shapes, hairiness, and flower colors while noting their geographic locations across Europe. It also details medicinal applications for both skin conditions like scabies and internal issues like liver and spleen obstructions.</summary>

### OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### PIMPERNEL: Germ. Gauchheyl: Fr. Mouron: Ital. Anagallida.
<note>original: "ANAGALLIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Anagallis (Pimpernel) showing a small herbaceous plant with oval leaves and small five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

Pandectarius and Santes <unclear>rd</unclear>ynus are completely mistaken when they confuse Pimpernel with Mouse-ear; so too are those who call it Chickweed <term>Alsinem</term> or "Hen’s Bite" <note>original: "Morsum Gallinæ"</note>, Hippia, and Cento.

Dioscorides and Pliny distinguish it by sex and the color of the flower. To the Male, which we depict here, they attribute a scarlet <term>phœniceum</term> flower. To the Female, however, they give a blue flower, and they say it differs in no other way. These are small shrubs, says Dioscorides, spread across the ground, having small, somewhat round leaves on four-angled stems, similar to Pellitory <term>Helxine</term>, with a round fruit.

They grow in gardens, plowed fields, vineyards, and alongside paths, and they produce flowers throughout the entire summer.

<column-break/>

### BLUE FEMALE PIMPERNEL.
<note>original: "ANAGALLIS CŒRVLEA FŒMINA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the female blue pimpernel, similar in structure to the previous plant but with slightly different leaf density.</image-desc>

Except for the blue flower, it is similar to the Male in all other respects: it has a white and very fibrous root, from which arise small branches the length of a palm <term>palmares</term>, often lying flat, and square-shaped. On these, the leaves grow at the joints <note>original: "nodulos"</note>, similar to those of Chickweed <term>Alsine</term>, placed opposite one another, with a sharp, biting taste. From the "wings" (axils) of the leaves come forth long, very thin stalks, upon which sit blue flowers consisting of five radiating blue petals, with yellow tips on the stamens. A small seed-head follows, like that of Chickweed, filled with tiny round seeds.

Pimpernel is beneficial for the bites of serpents and vipers if it is crushed and applied to the wounds, or if a decoction of it is drunk. Distilled water made from it is highly praised for use during the plague.

---

### THYME-LEAVED AQUATIC PIMPERNEL: Yellow Pimpernel.
<note>original: "ANAGALLIS SERPILLIFOLIA AQVATICA: Anagallis lutea"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping aquatic plant with small rounded leaves, identified as Anagallis serpillifolia.</image-desc>

We found the Thyme-leaved aquatic Pimpernel depicted here near Lure <note>original: "Lutiam"</note>, a city of the Prince of Maubec, and also between Masmünster and Belfort <note>original: "Bessort"</note>, near a pond. It was beautifully adorned with flowers at the beginning of May. To Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist</note>, it is a kind of *Syngona*.

Furthermore, besides the scarlet and blue Pimpernels known to the Ancients, a third has become known to more recent authors: the Yellow one <note>original: "Lutea"</note>. Nearly all herbalists mention it, and we ourselves observed it in the Le Chesnois forest very near Montbéliard, and from there we transferred it into the Prince’s garden <note>original: "S.P. hortum"</note>, where it flowers all summer.

<column-break/>

### ANTHYLLIS: Germ. Fr. & Ital. Anthyllis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Anthyllis, showing a more upright plant with clustered leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Dioscorides is the authority that there are two kinds of Anthyllis: for he says one has soft leaves, otherwise very similar to the Lentil, with branches a palm high, and a thin, small root. It grows in sandy <term>fabulosis</term> (or salty, according to Cornarius) sunny places, and is somewhat salty to the taste. The other, however, has leaves and branches like Ground-pine <term>Chamæpyti</term>, with a purple flower and a root like Succory <term>Cichorii</term>, etc.

Pliny described only one, which matches the first of Dioscorides; Galen, however, agrees with him that there are two. Yet today there is very little agreement among writers concerning these plants, as some offer one kind and others offer another as the Anthyllis of the Ancients. We depict here the Lentil-leaved Sea Anthyllis with the appearance of *Peplios*, which is commonly accepted as the first kind of Dioscorides.

---

### CERTAIN SPECIES OF ANTHYLLIS.
<note>original: "ANTHYLLIDIS SPECIES QVYBVS DAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a sprawling species of Anthyllis with many small leaves and branching stems.</image-desc>

This plant is nine inches <term>dodrantalis</term> or taller, branched with frequent offshoots, and knotted at the joints where the offshoots emerge. The leaves are very small, somewhat round, and crowded together in clusters around the nodes. The shoots are woody, firm, rounded, turned back, spread on the ground, and branched in various directions. It has a single root.

Clusius calls this the "Valentian Anthyllis," saying he saw it nowhere else but in Valencia, in the ditches of the city in Spain. He denies it is the first kind of Dioscorides, which has thin branches. Lobel calls it "Sea Anthyllis of Narbonne" <note>Southern France</note> with the appearance of *Chamaesyce*. Dodoens calls it *Peplis*, Tabernaemontanus calls it *Chamaesyce*, and Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax*, calls it "Sea Anthyllis similar to Chamaesyce."

<column-break/>

### SNOWY ANTHYLLIS, Clusius’s Spanish Whitlow-grass.
<note>original: "ANTHYLLIS NIVEA, PARONYCHIA Hispanica Clusij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, dense plant with small leaves, identified as Anthyllis nivea.</image-desc>

This plant is very beautiful to look at, spread across the ground with rush-like stems nine inches <term>dodrantalibus</term> long. From their nodes, inch-long offshoots emerge alternately, laden with clustered, very dense silvery scales. The root is woody, white, somewhat thick, long, and divided into many parts.

Lobel calls it "the smallest mountain Knotgrass, snowy and silky."

We saw it in maritime areas between the Balaruc baths <note>original: "Bellelucanas thermas"</note> and Agde in Gallia Narbonensis. As for the Lentil-leaved Anthyllis with the *Peplios* appearance we depicted earlier, Lobel writes that it grows in the sandy, low-lying, and sunny fields of the southern islands of England.

More concerning Anthyllis can be found in the Appendix.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from page 454. Having previously discussed the Pimpernels (Anagallis), the author moves to plants with similar growth habits: the Moneyworts, the Elatine (Fluellen), and the Knotgrasses, focusing on their medicinal names and physical characteristics.</meta>

### MONEYWORT, or HUNDRED-ILLNESS: Germ. *Pfennigkraut*: Fr. & Ital. *Nummularia*.
<note>original: "NVMMVLARIA, seu CENTIMORBIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Moneywort plant (Lysimachia nummularia) showing creeping stems with opposite, rounded leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

It creeps along with long but thin angular shoots, upon which two opposite leaves grow from the joints at short intervals. These leaves are rounder than those of the Pimpernel <term>Anagallis</term> and somewhat curled. From their armpits <note>the "axil" or junction of leaf and stem</note> come flowers in pairs, or more rarely in threes, like those of the yellow Pimpernel and endowed with the same color. Their taste, like that of the leaves, is astringent. The flowers consist of five petals, supported by as many small green leaves of the calyx. The seed head resembles that of Chickweed <term>Alsine</term>, filled with tiny seeds.

It grows among ditches and streams and other watery places; it is also found occasionally in damp woods. It flowers from the month of May well into the Summer.

<column-break/>

### RED MONEYWORT.
<note>original: "NVMMVLARIA RVBRA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems, small opposite leaves, and flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

On somewhat long, delicate branches, small leaves grow in pairs at short intervals; they are like the leaves of Ground Spurge <term>Chamæfice</term>, almost wider than they are long, soft, and smooth. From the hollows of these leaves emerge thin, long, solitary stalks, bearing a rather large red flower, similar to the flower of the scarlet Pimpernel <note>original: "Anagallidis phœniceæ"</note>.

We saw this near Montpellier, by Mount Calcaris.

Furthermore, this plant was named *Nummularia* from the shape of its leaves, which resembles a coin <note>Latin: "nummus"</note>. It is called *Centimorbia* or *Centummorbia* <note>meaning "Hundred-illness"</note> from its miraculous power and efficacy, by which it prevails against a great many diseases and many ulcers. *More can be found in the Appendix.*

---

### ELATINE, HEN’S BITE: Germ. *Hünerbiss*: Fr. & Ital. *Elatine*.
<note>original: "ELATINE, MORSVS GALLINÆ"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing plant with small, rounded leaves and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

That which is called *Elatine* by the Greeks and Latins, and *Athir* by the Arabs, is described by Dioscorides and Pliny. It has the leaf of Pellitory <term>Helxine</term>, but smaller and rounder, and hairy; it has thin branches about nine inches <term>dodrantalibus</term> long, full of leaves. They say it grows in cornfields and cultivated ground.

Among more recent authors, however, various plants have obtained the name *Elatine*: Moneywort, Pellitory, Ground Ivy, Wild Mustard, Elaterium and Vetch, Chickweeds, and various species of Mouse-ear. How aptly or ineptly they are named is clear from a comparison of those plants with this one.

Furthermore, by common consent, two types of Elatine are established: Male and Female. We depict the Male here, which almost everyone accepts as the true and legitimate Elatine of the Ancients.

<column-break/>

### FEMALE ELATINE, WITH ANGULAR LEAVES.
<note>original: "ELATINE FOEMINA, FOLIO ANGVLOSO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with more angular, pointed leaves and spurred flowers resembling toadflax.</image-desc>

The Male, from a small, white, woody root, spreads many little stems across the ground, which rise very little or not at all from the earth; they are thin, hairy, and occasionally somewhat branched. The leaves are less rough than those of Speedwell <term>Veronica</term>, almost round, soft, and downy, with a bitter taste. From their armpits, a reddish and hairy stalk, half an inch or more in length, rises to support a flower made of small green hairy leaves. The flower is somewhat similar to Toadflax <term>Linaria</term>, with a spur and a lip of a yellowish-green color, and a dark upper fringe under which hide small, partly black tips. The seed in the small vessels is round.

The Female is more fertile, and is raised higher from the ground; it has leaves like Bindweed <term>Cissampelos</term>, and in other respects is similar to the Male.

*More can be found in the Appendix.*

---

### KNOTGRASS or HUNDRED-KNOTS: Germ. *Vveeggrass*: Fr. *Renouée, Corregiole*: Ital. *Corregiola*.
<note>original: "POLYGONVM siue CENTINODIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Knotgrass plant with many joints (nodes) and small linear leaves.</image-desc>

If you look at the force of the word, the name *Polygonum* <note>from the Greek for "many-jointed" or "many-seeded"</note> could be extended to many plants, derived from the multitude of frequent joints, or, as others prefer, seeds. However, the common Knotgrass <term>Polygonum Gramen</term> has earned this name above all others. From a hard, woody, twisted root, headed with many fibers, it sends out its shoots which are a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note>, rounded, branched, furrowed, and interrupted by very frequent joints. The leaves emerge only from the joints, in the shape of Olive leaves, tender, and with a viscous taste. Tiny flowers of a purplish-white color grow along the stem at the nodes; these are followed by blackish, three-sided seeds, rivaling those of Dock <term>Lapathum</term>.

<column-break/>

### DOUBLE NARROW-LEAVED KNOTGRASS.
<note>original: "POLYGONVM ANGVSTIFOLIVM DVPLEX"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Polygonum with very narrow, fine leaves.</image-desc>

Knotgrass is commonly distinguished into Male and Female, which species Dioscorides embraced under one heading. However, because Female Knotgrass has a great similarity in appearance and origin with the Horsetails <term>Equisetis</term>, we have decided it should be referred to their class; here we shall hand down only the history and species of the Male.

With common Male Knotgrass already described, the narrow-leaved Knotgrass which we depict here is very similar. It has a tender, white little root, producing very many branches creeping far and wide over the ground. Its leaves are also similar to those of the "Hundred-knots" <term>Centinodia</term>, but smaller and sharper, and are sometimes shorter and wider, sometimes longer and narrower.

<summary>This page catalogs several low-growing herbs including Moneywort (Nummularia), Elatine (Fluellen), and Knotgrass (Polygonum). It emphasizes their naming conventions based on physical traits—like the coin-shaped leaves of Moneywort or the many joints of Knotgrass—and their historical medicinal uses.</summary>

<keywords>Moneywort, Nummularia, Centimorbia, Elatine, Knotgrass, Polygonum, Centinodia, Dioscorides, Pliny, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, creeping plants</keywords>

->**OF PLANTS**<-
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### GREATEST SEA KNOTGRASS.
<note>original: "POLYGONYM MARINVM MAXIMVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Polygonum marinum plant, showing thick, knotted stems, small leaves, and a detailed root system.</image-desc>

It has long, woody, somewhat thick, twisted, and black roots. The shoots are sprawling, thicker than those of common Knotgrass, and are divided by more frequent and shorter joints <term>internodes</term>. It is clothed not only with larger and whiter leaves but also with transparent, thin, and whitening scales. The beautiful flowers surpass the common variety in both number and size. The seed is black and three-sided, similar to the seed of Sorrel <term>Oxalis</term>.

It grows in abundance near the Adriatic Sea and also around Narbonne <note>a city in southern France</note>.

We have represented the two varieties of narrow-leaved Knotgrass described by Tabernæmontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a 16th-century herbalist</note> in the single preceding plate.

<column-break/>

### SMALL WORM-LIKE KNOTGRASS with Wild Thyme leaves.
<note>original: "POLYGONVM PVSILLO VERMICVLATO Serpylli folio"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, spreading plant with tiny, dense leaves resembling Serpyllum.</image-desc>

This is a fairly rare plant, flourishing with long, slender, twig-like branches and stems that spread upon the ground like Wild Thyme <term>Serpyllum</term>. From the joints <term>geniculis</term> emerge leaves that are rounded and succulent, equal and similar to Stonecrop <term>Aizoon or Illecebra</term> or our own small Thyme. The root is very long, woody, and has a somewhat warm, bitter taste. According to Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note>.

It flourishes on the maritime hills of Provence <note>original: "Galloprouinciæ"</note>.

Furthermore, Knotgrass—according to the author Galen—possesses a certain astringency; it is in the second order of cooling medicines and in the third order of drying ones. It binds together bloody wounds and is a remedy for herpetic ulcers and for parts of the body suffering from inflammation or "flux" <note>an abnormal discharge of fluids</note>.

---

### POLISH COCHINEAL KNOTGRASS: AND other varieties of Sea Knotgrass.
<note>original: "POLYGONVM POLONICVM COCCIFERVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with thin stems and small clusters, likely representing the "cocciferum" variety used for dye.</image-desc>

It grows with very thin and pointed leaves, knotted whitish stems, and small white flowers at the tip among greenish scales. At its roots grows the "Grain" <term>Coccum</term> <note>refers to the kermes scale insect, which was harvested for red dye</note>, which possesses a most elegant redness recommended for dyeing fabrics crimson <note>original: "Charmesina"</note>, as Joachim Camerarius says in his *Epitome of Mattioli*. He adds that it is called *Kosmaczek* by the Poles, among whom it is found in sandy places.

Most everyone praises the "water" <note>a distilled herbal extract</note> of Knotgrass against vomiting, diarrhea, and dysentery. This is due to its effect; Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel, a French physician</note> relates that it earned the name *Sanguinaria* <note>the blood-herb</note> because if the juice is applied, either whole or crushed, to a bleeding part, the blood congeals into clots and no longer flows out.

<column-break/>

### SMALL KNOTGRASS, with WHORLED WHITE FLOWERS.
<note>original: "POLYGONVM PARVVM, FLORE ALBO verticillato"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small plant with upright stems and whorled white flowers.</image-desc>

It consists of shoots about a palm or a palm-and-a-half long <note>roughly 3 to 5 inches</note>. They are slender, somewhat rigid, jointed, and divided into other smaller branches. From these joints, which are about an inch apart, emerge two small leaves, almost like Rupturewort <term>Herniaria</term> but round like Ground Spurge <term>Chamasice</term>. Between these are tiny, whitening flowers, arranged in whorls <term>verticillatim</term> and tapering into very thin points. The small root is fibrous.

It flourishes in ditches, trenches, and the margins of fields.

Charles Estienne <note>original: "C. Stephanus"</note> writes that Knotgrass is a harmful herb for sheep, and that their bellies become bloated if they feed on it.

---

### FLAX-LEAVED PLANT RELATED TO KNOTGRASS, known to some as the smallest Allseed.
<note>original: "POLYGONO AFFINIS PLANTA LINIFOLIA, Millegrana minima"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very fine, branched plant with numerous tiny seeds or flowers.</image-desc>

From a thin root, which is singular but sometimes multi-parted, white leaves emerge that precede the stems of Flax <term>Linum</term> or Toadflax <term>Linaria</term>. But the stems, when they come forth, are spread across the ground, a palm or nine inches long, branched, and clothed with leaves placed in no particular order. These are smaller than those of Knotgrass, of a bluish-gray color, and with no evident taste. At the ends of the branches, numerous tiny flowers are crowded together in clusters; they are similar to Knotgrass flowers but smaller, purplish on the outside and white within, imitating the curved tail of a Heliotrope or a Water Scorpion-grass. The seeds are small, variegated with white and green stripes.

It grows in cultivated places.

<column-break/>

### CAMPHOR-PLANT OF MONTPELLIER: Germ. *Kamfferkraut von Monpelier*.
<note>original: "CAMPHORATA MONSPELIENSIVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright, tufted plant with needle-like leaves, identified as Camphorata.</image-desc>

It has a root almost a thumb's breadth in thickness with many heads. It sends out woody stems that are somewhat thick, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or shorter in length, branched, slightly hairy, and whitish. Along these stems, leaves are seen placed alternately; from each of these come very crowded small leaves, not exceeding a third of an inch, thin, hairy, moderately rigid, with an aromatic odor and a somewhat sharp taste.

It grows naturally in desolate and sandy places along the road to Frontignan. We ourselves have cultivated it in the princely garden at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi in S. P. horto"</note>.

<summary>This page describes various species of Knotgrass (Polygonum), detailing their physical forms, habitats (from the Adriatic to Poland), and their use in medicine as astringents or in industry as red dyes. It also introduces the aromatic Camphor-plant of Montpellier.</summary>

<page-num>455</page-num>
<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES:</header>

### RUPTUREWORT, TURKISH HERB <note>original: "HERNIARIA, HERBA TVRCA"</note>: German: Rupture-herb <note>original: "Harnkraut"</note>: French: The Turk's Herb <note>original: "l'Herbe au Turc"</note>: Italian: Thousand-seeds <note>original: "Millegrana"</note>.

It shades the ground over which it is widely spread, growing with a lush abundance of many small branches which it pours forth from a tiny little root. These branches are scattered here and there, rounded, and divided by very frequent joints <term>nodes</term>. At each of these joints, pairs of leaves face one another; they are smaller than those of Wild Thyme <note>Serpyllum</note>, of a greenish-yellow color, and sharp to the taste. In these same places, a wonderfully large number of tiny flowers break forth, composed of yellowish tips.

Some call it *Herniaria* <note>Rupturewort</note> and *Lithontribon* <note>Stone-breaker, from the Greek for "crushing stones"</note> because of its effects. Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist</note> calls it *Lesser Cancer-weed*; Clusius, Matthiolus, and Caspar Bauhin call it *Small Knotgrass*; many call it *Thousand-seeds* and *Turkish Herb*. Could it perhaps be the *Elleborine* of the Ancients?

There are, however, two kinds: the hairy and the smooth, the latter of which we depict here.

<column-break/>

### HAIRY RUPTUREWORT <note>original: "HERNIARIA HIRSUTA"</note>.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Herniaria hirsuta, showing a low-growing plant with numerous small, spreading branches and tiny leaves clustered along the stems.</image-desc>

Both types of Rupturewort grow spontaneously in various places in cultivated fields and sandy locations. We have also observed them being cultivated in gardens, such as in Zurich, Basel, and Padua; we ourselves have even grown them in the Princely garden at Montbéliard.

Regarding its powers: Clusius and Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German physician and botanist</note> report that a decoction of the herb is successfully administered for the "stone" <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>. Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, a 16th-century Italian botanist</note> attributes three remarkable faculties to it: I. The juice, when drunk, or the herb when eaten or applied as a plaster, helps against the bites of vipers. II. A plaster made from it restores a hernia <note>or "rupture"</note> in a wonderful way. III. It benefits the liver and jaundice. The powder, when sprinkled on the wounds of oxen and horses, kills the worms within them.

---

### ST. JOHN’S WORT, ASYCRON, TUTSAN, CORIS <note>original: "HYPERICVM, ASCYRON, ANDROSÆMVM, CORIS"</note>: German: St. John’s herb <note>original: "S. Iohans kraut"</note>: French: Thousand-holes <note>original: "Mille pertuis"</note>: Italian: Hyperico.

The plants handed down under the names of *Hypericum*, *Ascyrum*, *Androsaemum*, and *Coris* belong to one and the same family; yet they are distinguished by certain certain marks, as will be clear from what follows.

In the common St. John’s Wort, which we depict here, many little rods rise from a woody root that is divided in many ways and covered in box-colored bark. These rods are stiff, woody, round, reddish, divided into branches, and stand one or two cubits <note>about 1.5 to 3 feet</note> high. The leaves are like those of Marjoram, smooth, and pierced with innumerable tiny holes <note>these are actually translucent oil glands</note>. The flowers at the ends of the branches are plentiful, yellow, composed of five radiating petals, with many tips <note>stamens</note> of the same color. The seed is small, blackish-red, and oblong-round.

It is very common and widely used everywhere.

We do not show the figure here because it was not ready; the reader will find it in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### ST. JOHN’S WORT CALLED ASCYRON: German: Hard-hay <note>original: "Hartheuv"</note>: Old French: lauerette.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hypericum ascyron, featuring an upright stem with opposite, lanceolate leaves and a large, five-petaled flower at the apex.</image-desc>

From a creeping, fibrous, reddish root, it sends out stems equal to common St. John’s Wort, though they are square, reddish, and branched. The leaves also correspond in origin and size to those of common St. John’s Wort, yet they are somewhat broader and more fibrous, with no visible pores <note>holes</note>. In the flowers, there is also hardly anything different, and the seed vessels and seeds are similar. This is because in this plant, as in that one, the taste of the leaves is dry and astringent, while that of the seeds is resinous. Furthermore, both the flowers and the heads heavy with seed yield a blood-red juice. The illustration, which is from Fuchs' work <note>Leonhart Fuchs, author of a famous 1542 herbal</note>, is not satisfactory.

It is a lover of all streams and moist places.

---

### ST. JOHN’S WORT CALLED TUTSAN <note>original: "ANDROSÆMVM"</note>.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hypericum androsaemum (Tutsan), showing a woody stem with broad, oval leaves and clusters of flowers and berry-like seed pods.</image-desc>

The stem of the plant called Tutsan <note>from the French "toute-saine" or "all-heal"</note> exceeds two cubits in height. It is stiff, rounded, and downy, as are the leaves, so much so that they appear white on the underside. They are very close to the leaves of *Ascyrum*, being fibrous, but longer, and like St. John’s Wort, they are full of holes. They are placed opposite one another at the joints of the stem, from whose "arms" <term>axils</term> the small branches grow. Near the top, the stem divides into many shoots bearing flowers like common St. John's Wort, followed by similar vessels containing resinous seed. The root does not grow straight down but is provided with many fibers on the sides.

It abounds on the hills of Montpellier, Geneva, and Montbéliard; it flowers in July and August.

<column-break/>

### TRAGUS’S BEAUTIFUL ST. JOHN’S WORT <note>original: "HYPERICVM PVLCHRVM TRAGI"</note>.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Hypericum pulchrum, showing a slender, upright plant with small, heart-shaped leaves clasping the stem and a cluster of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

The plant that Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> depicts under the name "Beautiful Hypericum" rests on a woody, somewhat fertile root. The stems are nine inches <term>dodrantalibus</term> or larger, rounded, smooth, reddish in part, and branched, though not always. The leaves are in pairs from the joints, placed opposite, firmer, rounder, and smaller than in the common variety, yet pierced with no fewer frequent holes. The flowers are yellow, similar to the common flowers but few in number, hanging on short stalks, usually in opposite pairs arising from the base of the leaves.

We found it flowering in August on the summit of Mount Balos.

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### VERY ELEGANT ST. JOHN’S WORT, unbranched, broad-leaved, and not perforated <note>original: "HYPERICVM ELEGANTISSIMVM NON ramosum, folio lato, non foraminulento"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hypericum plant with a single upright stem, broad opposite leaves, and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

We have observed this plant in the woods of Basel <note>Basileæ</note>, and in Montbéliard on the hill toward Audincourt, and on the hill of La Chau, as well as on Mount Rossberg near Masevaux <note>Masmünster</note>. In Geneva, it flowered for us in the garden during June, having been brought from the nearby Mount Tuiri.

Furthermore, St. John’s Wort warms and dries; it strengthens the nervous system. It heals sciatica <note>Ischiadicis</note> and is useful for provoking menstruation and urination. A decoction, when drunk, treats Tertian and Quartan fevers <note>recurring fevers associated with malaria</note>. Some administer the distilled water against apoplexy and the "Comitial disease" <term>epilepsy</term>. It is especially useful when mixed into medicines dedicated to healing wounds.

### SMALLEST PROSTRATE ST. JOHN’S WORT <note>original: "HYPERICVM MINIMVM SVPINVM"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, low-growing Hypericum with multiple stems spreading from the base and small leaves.</image-desc>

It has long fibers for roots, hanging from a woody base. The little stems are spread across the ground, very thin, a hand-span or nine inches <term>dodrantales</term> in length, numerous, sometimes simple and sometimes divided into small branches, along which the leaves are placed in pairs opposite one another. These pairs of leaves are smooth, like those of Wild Thyme <note>Serpyllum</note>. The little flowers are like those of common St. John’s Wort, yellow, differing only in size, and fewer in number; the shape of the seed-heads is likewise not dissimilar.

It is found in the forest of Montbéliard, Le Chesnois, where it flowers in August.

### ST. JOHN’S WORT-LIKE CORIS OF CERTAIN AUTHORS, and the True Cretan Coris <note>original: "HYPERICOIDES CORIS QVORVMDAM, & Coris legitima Cretica"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a shrubby plant with thin, needle-like leaves arranged in whorls and small flowers at the branch tips.</image-desc>

This is certainly a charming little plant, with woody branches like Heath <note>Erica</note>, the size of a Thyme shrub, or rather like the Coris of Montpellier, but with thinner, upright branches, spreading into many "wings," rounded and reddish. The leaves appear at short intervals, as if at joints, in groups of three like a star <note>radiata</note>, similar to those of the Tree Heath. The tips of the stems, occasionally turning into small branches, bear rather long flowers, clearly those of a St. John's Wort—yellow, consisting of five radiating petals, with a cluster of numerous saffron-colored tips <term>stamens</term> occupying the center. Small green leaves are placed at the base of the entire flower.

We saw it flowering in May at Padua, in the garden of Bembo <note>likely the garden of Cardinal Pietro Bembo</note>.

<column-break/>

### SYRIAN AND ALEXANDRIAN ST. JOHN’S WORT <note>original: "HYPERICVM SYRIACVM ET ALEXANDRINVM"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hypericum variety with upright stems and clusters of flowers, showing detailed leaf structure.</image-desc>

Lobelius and Tabernaemontanus label it thus; but to Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax*, it is called *Hypericum 6, or the shorter-leaved variety*. And not without reason, since it produces leaves four times smaller than those of the common variety, which emerge in whorls <note>verticillatim</note> on yard-long rods. The yellow flowers are very similar to the petals of our local variety.

Some call St. John’s Wort *Chase-devil* <note>original: "Fugam Dæmonum"</note>, because it is believed to put demons to flight, in the same way that an antidote <term>Alexiterium</term> resists a poison. Others call it *Perforated* <note>Perforata</note>, because if the leaves are held up to the sun, they reveal almost innumerable pores, as if pierced with a needle, through which both our sight and the rays of the sun pass.

### WOOLLY ST. JOHN’S WORT <note>original: "HYPERICVM TOMENTOSVM"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Hypericum with fuzzy or tomentose leaves and stems, showing a decumbent growth habit.</image-desc>

The root is somewhat thick, woody, and reddish; the stems are many, roughly a hand-span or nine inches long, entirely hairy and hoary; the leaves are like common St. John's Wort, but covered in a white down <note>albicâ lanugine</note>. The flowers are yellowish, smaller, and the seed-heads are shorter.

We have such a specimen among our dried plants.

The much-celebrated Oil of St. John’s Wort <note>Oleum Hyperici</note> is prepared by surgeons in this way: They take 2 pounds <note>lb. ij</note> each of the tops of St. John’s Wort and common oil; 2 ounces <note>℥. ij</note> each of Myrrh and Gum Elemi; 3 ounces of Turpentine; 1 ounce of Aloes; and a half-ounce <note>℥. ß</note> each of Frankincense and Mastic. Let them be infused and boiled in a double boiler <term>diplomate</term> according to the rules of the art.

### PHYTEUMA OF MONTPELLIER <note>original: "PHYTEVMA MONSPELIENSIVM"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a single thick root, upright stems, and elongated, notched leaves.</image-desc>

It relies on a single root, gifted with no or very few fibers, sufficiently thick, woody, and white. It sends out several foot-long stems, split into many branches, partly upright and partly reclining. Along these are oblong leaves, blunt at the end, and occasionally notched (especially the upper ones), soft, and about four inches in length. The flowers are numerous along the branches, white, composed merely of stamens, with radiating green leaves placed beneath them. The pods are slightly swollen, a half-inch long, striped, and perforated at the top, enclosing a large quantity of black seed.

It is found especially in Montpellier, and flowers in April and May.

More on *Phyteuma* can be found in the Appendix.

### SICILIANA, CALLED BY OTHERS CICILIANA. VII.
#### Tutsan: All-heal and Ibutuani <note>original: "Androsæmos: Tota sana & Ibutuani." Tutsan comes from the French "toute-saine," meaning "all-heal," because of its traditional medicinal uses.</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tutsan plant (Hypericum androsaemum) with broad, opposite leaves and small clusters of flowers at the nodes and the top.</image-desc>

It rests upon a long, woody, perennial root. The stems are <unclear>maple-like</unclear> <note>original: "acerno"</note>, up to a cubit <term>about 18 inches</term> in height, of a different color; from the feast of St. Nicholas <note>December 6th</note>, they are winged with <unclear>feathery</unclear> membranes. The leaves are situated in pairs, opposite one another. It is not unlike the stem of Woodbine <note>Periclymeni</note> or <unclear>Samen</unclear>. The leaves are dark green above and <unclear>paler</unclear> beneath. The flowers are like those of St. John's Wort <note>Hyperici</note>, but more elevated and larger, the <unclear>color of gall</unclear> <note>yellowish</note>; they consist of five petals, with as many stamens placed between them, having <unclear>dark red</unclear> tips. The seed-heads turn black upon maturity and contain seeds similar to <unclear>melon seeds</unclear>, but they are not <unclear>leafy</unclear>.

It springs up in <unclear>damp</unclear> and shady places. We have found it in the <unclear>Jura Mountains</unclear>, at <unclear>Caye-canis</unclear>, on <unclear>Mount Valdonne</unclear>, and at <unclear>Nanterre</unclear> on <unclear>Mount Gualdo</unclear> in the garden of St. P. More information is in the <unclear>Appendix</unclear>.

### MILKWORT ACCORDING TO MANY, German: *Kreutzblümt*.
#### Lesser Milkwort <note>original: "Polygala minor." The name Polygala comes from the Greek for "much milk," as it was believed to increase milk production in livestock.</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Milkwort plant with numerous tiny leaves and a terminal flower spike.</image-desc>

With a perennial root half a palm or a palm <term>roughly 3-4 inches</term> long, woody and somewhat white or moist, it puts forth many stems—some straight, others spreading—thin, somewhat hairy and <unclear>low-growing</unclear>, reddish, and shimmering like silk with <unclear>tiny blue flowers</unclear> that do not all open at once. The leaves are scattered here and there on the ground, gradually becoming <unclear>round</unclear> as they join the stems toward the <unclear>top</unclear>, while these others are oblong and sharp.

Valerius Cordus says that some wish this to be the *Polygala* which our people call *Kreutzblümt* <note>German for "Cross-flower," referring to the flower's shape or its blooming period around Holy Cross Day</note>. But since this plant grows in summer and is distinguished by its flowers in <unclear>August</unclear>, they want the *Polygala* to be the one with white flowers, while they refer the other two kinds to *Glaux* <note>Sea-milkwort</note>.

### GREATER COMMON MILKWORT,
#### with somewhat broad leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger Milkwort variety with broader leaves and a dense spike of flowers.</image-desc>

From the same root there sometimes emerge five or six slender, crossing twigs, a foot long, flexible and yielding, with leaves arranged in no particular order, and as pleasant as the leaves of common Hyssop. The flowers are crowded together and grow in a spike; they are a delicate purple, most elegant, and not much unlike the flowers of Fumitory. These are followed by seeds in a pouch, found everywhere in lower places, containing two <unclear>dark</unclear> and somewhat long seeds. The root is somewhat thick, short, woody, fibrous, and long-lived. The whole plant has a bitter taste.

It occurs everywhere in Pannonia <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, according to Clusius, the author of this description, but it rejects cultivation.

<column-break/>

### GOAT-WEED, RUE-LIKE ST. JOHN'S WORT
#### to some, related to the Siciliana <note>original: "TRAGUM, RVTA HYPERICOIDES"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "Tragum" plant, showing woody stems and small, narrow leaves similar to Rue or St. John's Wort.</image-desc>

Dioscorides said that *Tragium* grows only in Crete, similar to the Mastic tree <note>Lentisco</note> in its leaves, seeds, and branches, yet it produces something like gum every month. He also mentions <unclear>another</unclear> among the spurious plants. Galen also says *Tragium* is like the Mastic tree; he does not know the other kind, though he mentions these things as being consistent. Pliny makes it similar sometimes to the Turpentine tree and sometimes to the Juniper. Furthermore, he rightly says it is <unclear>thickly covered</unclear>, and it is reported that if tied on for three days, it <unclear>reduces</unclear> the spleen. According to Galen's report, it is of thin parts and, in the third degree <term>a classification of medicinal potency</term>, it begins to <unclear>purge</unclear>. There are those who say it has a juice and a tear <term>sap or resin</term> with the power of <unclear>digesting</unclear> and <unclear>dissolving</unclear>. It is <unclear>applied</unclear> to hard tumors <note>scirrhos</note> and hemorrhoids; and, as Dioscorides recently stated, it breaks stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and provokes menstruation when a drachm's weight is drunk.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF MILKWORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another Milkwort variety, showing a similar growth habit but with slight variations in the foliage.</image-desc>

It is no different than what Tragum says of the flowers; the Milkworts are of various colors: for some are seen to be snowy white, others <note>original: "Berfilici"</note> reddish-purple, and others blue. Yet, as that noble author says, the leaf, the stem, and the root are the same. I am convinced this is the *Polygala* of Dioscorides, especially the one that bears white flowers; for the one that shines with purple and blue, I refer to *Glaux*.

We have seen this smaller Milkwort in the meadows of Montpellier, Geneva, and Tübingen, flowering in July and August; and near <unclear>Lörrach</unclear> <note>Laurach</note> at Basel, and on the <unclear>Mure</unclear> mountain in <unclear>August</unclear>. Clusius observed it in the drier meadows of Austria and Pannonia, distinguished by three flower colors. They also have it in gardens.

### GREATER COMMON MILKWORT,
#### with very narrow leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Milkwort with very narrow, linear leaves and a tall spike of flowers.</image-desc>

In some places it rises with stalks a foot or more high, a large part of which is bare, being clothed with leaves mostly toward the bottom; these leaves are narrower and more pointed than in the other "Hypericum-like" Milkworts. Tiny flowers are placed at the ends of the branches, of a faded color, and these are followed by two small membranous vessels, drawn away from the shining leaves.

It grows in uncultivated places of Narbonnese Gaul <note>Southern France</note>, and especially on the hills around Montpellier.

Furthermore, the Greater Milkwort varies mostly in the color of the flower, which is either white, blue, or purple. Caspar Bauhin writes that a yellow one is also found, and that he found it between Florence and Rome.

### GLAUX & GLAX, in Greek <note>original: "γλαύξ & γλάξ"</note>: German: Milk-herb; French: Milk-herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Glaux plant (Sea Milkwort), showing a central stem with small, narrow leaves arranged closely together and clusters of tiny flowers emerging from the points where the leaves meet the stem.</image-desc>

Glaux, according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>, consists of small vines about a cubit <term>roughly 18 inches</term> in height, with tough but fleshy leaves that are white underneath and green on top. Five or six small branches emerge from the earth, reaching a height of a span <term>about 9 inches</term> from the root. The flowers are a purplish-white and smaller than <unclear>amben</unclear> <note>The original likely intended "anagallide" or Pimpernel, a common point of comparison in early botany.</note>. It grows near the sea.

In Zeeland <note>A province in the Netherlands</note> and England, it is found in many coastal lagoons and valleys. It blooms in June and July.

Regarding its powers and uses: when used in foods and broths, it increases the supply of milk. For this reason, it is extremely useful for wet nurses suffering from a shortage of milk; the name itself indicates that this property should also be attributed to Milkwort <note>original: "Polygala"</note>, both the larger and smaller varieties.

### ANDROSACE: German, French, & Italian: ANDROSACE.

Clusius <note>A pioneering 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> testifies that this plant has received no other name among writers because, as Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel, a French physician and botanist</note> says, its name promises "remedies for men" <note>From the Greek 'aner' (man) and 'akos' (cure).</note>.

Dioscorides and Pliny <note>Roman naturalist</note> write that it is a white, bitter herb, without leaves, having small pods on its heads and seeds within them. It grows in the coastal regions of Syria. When drunk in wine, it stimulates the flow of urine, a fact which Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> also records.

Clusius rightly mocks Mattioli <note>An Italian physician and botanist</note> for claiming to have sent for this plant from Syria, since Austria, where Mattioli lived, would have provided it in abundance; it grows there copiously among the grain crops, flowering in April. For us in Montbéliard, it flowered in May and June. The reader will find the illustration in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPS' YELLOW ORCHID.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Orchis Lutea, featuring a single sturdy stalk with several broad, pointed leaves and a terminal spike of flowers.</image-desc>

This plant appears on the peaks of the Jura Mountains, with a round, woody, "two-tailed" <note>likely referring to twin tubers</note>, white root. The stem is quite low, about a foot high. The leaf is like <unclear>Linio Fisiineo</unclear> <note>possibly a corruption of "fistulous flax"</note>, abundant and small, withering at the very tips. It is a rare herb, and has hardly been seen anywhere other than the aforementioned location.

### LEUCAS: LEUCOGRAPHIS.

Regarding Leucas <note>From the Greek "leukos," meaning white</note>, Dioscorides reports the following: Mountain Leucas, he says, has downy leaves and is larger than the garden <note>original: "urbana"</note> or female variety, being sharper, more bitter, and having a pleasant scent. However, it is considered more effective than Savory <note>original: "satura"</note>. Both varieties, taken in wine, are helpful against the poisons of animals, especially those of the sea.

Ruellius believes it would be Mercurialis <note>Mercury herb</note> if a white line did not run through the middle of the leaf.

Mattioli records it this way: Although, he says, Hermolaus and Ruellius contend that Leucas is closely related to Mercurialis, I would not dare to make it similar to Mercurialis, as I have so far found no botanical author who represents its appearance or provides more notes on it than Dioscorides did—who certainly, in what survives, described it with no distinguishing marks at all. Furthermore, in my judgment, Marcellus Florentinus rightly thinks that this beginning of the chapter on Leucas is well-known, as indicated by the <unclear>description</unclear> <note>original: ὑπογραφή (hypographé)</note> in Dioscorides’ discourse, in which he speaks of the garden Leucas as if it had already been described.

As for LEUCOGRAPHIS <note>"White-marked"</note>, Pliny mentions it, but does not record what kind of plant it was. According to Ruellius, no description of it is found, which is very surprising, since it is said to be useful for those coughing up blood, for heart ailments, for uterine discharge in women, and for filling up ulcers. The Greek name itself confesses that the plant claimed its name from a white marking or line.

# ON THE IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS 30.
### THE ARRAY OF THE REMAINING ORNAMENTAL PLANTS.

**Poppy**: In Greek *Mēkōn* <note>original: "Μήκων"</note>: German *Poppyseed* <note>original: "Magsamen"</note>: Belgian *Poppy* <note>original: "Mancop"</note>: French *Poppy* <note>original: "Pauot"</note>: Italian *Poppy* <note>original: "Papauero"</note>: *The Common Cultivated Poppy*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Papaver plant with a single large flower head, serrated leaves, and a visible root system.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician</note>, four types of Poppy are proposed: the *Wild*, the *Cultivated*, the *Horned*, and the *Frothy* <note>likely Bladder Campion, which was often grouped with poppies due to its seed pods</note>. Pliny mentions a Cultivated type—one for sowing and another Wild; the sown type is twofold, namely the Black and the White, but he discusses them indistinctly and confusedly.

Modern authors have treated the differences among Poppies better and more clearly. From their writings, it is gathered that two general kinds of Poppy are established: the *Garden* and the *Wild*. Among these, many varieties are again recognized, primarily distinguished by the color, density, and shape of the flowers, and also by the seeds. Thus, for them, one type is *simple* while another is *double-flowered* <note>original: "Polyanthos"</note>; and both are either *white*, *purple*, *reddish*, *mixed*, or *spotted with dots*.

<margin>Marked by stripes. And another with notched flower petals, another not at all cut. And finally, one with white seed, another grey, another yellow, another black.</margin>

**Prickly Field Poppy.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a prickly poppy with spiny leaves and a distinct seed pod.</image-desc>

Of the Wild or Field Poppy, just as with the cultivated variety, there are many distinctions. Among these are especially the *Prickly* type, the *Red* (called *Rhoeas*), the *Black*, and the *Horned*, which is again subdivided into several species.

The Prickly Field Poppy, which we depict here, has jagged leaves full of sap, a palm <term>about 3 inches</term> or a palm and a half long, smooth on both sides, and soft, with milky veins on the upper side and prickly thorns on the back. The tips of the jagged sections end in sharp, yellowish spines. It has a single stem armed with threatening thorns, a span <term>about 9 inches</term> high. It supports several poppy-like, thorny heads. The flowers are those of the Horned Poppy, yellow, which are followed by seed vessels armed everywhere with prickles, oblong, channeled, and filled with large, round, black seeds.

<column-break/>

**Fringed Cultivated Poppy,**
->with purple and white flowers.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a fringed poppy with a large, multi-petaled flower and a prominent seed capsule.</image-desc>

The Poppy that is sown in gardens has a root about the thickness of a finger, full of bitter milk, as is the entire plant. The stem is one or two cubits <term>between 18 and 36 inches</term> high, divided into "wings" <note>side branches</note>, usually smooth, but sometimes also slightly hairy. The leaves are like those of Lettuce, oblong, jagged, curled, and of a sea-green color. The flowers are sometimes simple, sometimes multiple (double), fringed or not fringed, and colored white, red, flesh-colored, or variegated. These are succeeded by the "Heads" <note>seed capsules</note>, which are globular, swollen, and more or less oblong; some are the size of a fist, others the size of a walnut, covered with a star-shaped lid. They contain seeds—sometimes black, sometimes brown, sometimes white—enclosed within membrane-like partitions.

Poppies are sown in gardens in the spring, and sometimes even in the fields, and they bloom in May.

---

**Wild Poppy, Corn Poppy:** German *Field poppy* <note>original: "Kornrosen feldmagsamen"</note>: French *Wild poppy* <note>original: "Pauot sauuage"</note>: Italian *Wild poppy* <note>original: "Papauero siluatico"</note>:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common red poppy (Papaver rhoeas) showing the flower, bud, and seed capsule.</image-desc>

In its whole appearance, it expresses the nature of a poppy and must be reckoned as part of that family. It is called *Fluidum* <note>the "Flowing" or "Fleeting" poppy</note> for this reason: because the flower, distinguished by its scarlet color, drops away not long after it has unfolded itself from its green, hairy, and very short-lived covering <note>the sepals</note>, leaving behind a poppy-like head and a star-shaped center.

There are Greater and Lesser versions of this kind, and sometimes there is some difference in the leaves being more or less notched. It grows in the fields with almost every kind of grain, and not infrequently also among vegetables and along the edges of fields. In the months of May and June, it wins great favor for the fields with its charming and beautiful flowers.

### HORNED POPPY: German: Horned Poppyseed: French: Horned Poppy: Italian: Horned Poppy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Papaver corniculatum (Yellow Horned Poppy) showing its long, curved seed pods, deeply lobed leaves, and a single flower at the top.</image-desc>

The Horned Poppy <note>original: "Papaver Ceratites"</note> has pale leaves, says Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist</note>, which are hairy and similar to Mullein <note>term: "Verbasco" - a plant with soft, fuzzy leaves</note>, serrated at the edges in the manner of the wild Poppy. The stem is similar; the flower is pale; and the small seed pod is like that of Fenugreek, bent in the shape of little horns, from which it takes its name. The seed is tiny and black, like a Poppy's; the root is black and thick at the surface of the soil. It grows in coastal and rugged places: so says he. Today, however, four distinctions of the Horned Poppy are commonly recognized: for it is either *yellow*, *violet*, or *scarlet* <note>original: "phoeniceum"</note>, the last of which is twofold.

The yellow variety is depicted here, which we have observed growing abundantly of its own accord between Yverdon <note>original: "Ebrodunum"</note> and Grandson, in the sandy areas near the Lake <note>Lake Neuchâtel</note>. It blooms in May and June.

<column-break/>

### VIOLET HORNED POPPY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Papaver corniculatum violaceum (Violet Horned Poppy) showing slender stems, smaller dissected leaves, and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

The leaves of this variety are much smaller and more delicate than the others, and very finely divided; they are not pale but green. The stems are tender and slightly hairy. The flower, as in the others, consists of four petals of a purplish-blue color, very fleeting, and shaken off by the lightest breeze. These are followed by little horns only a finger’s length, usually even shorter, slender, somewhat hard, and stiffly hairy. Inside is a tiny seed, grayish-black in color. The root is thin and useless, and does not last beyond a year's span.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> bears witness that it is found in many places in Spain among the cornfields, and also in the fields of Narbonne in France. It is also sown in gardens.

---

<column-break/>

### SCARLET HORNED POPPY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Papaver corniculatum phoeniceum (Red Horned Poppy) with branched stems, serrated leaves, and seed pods.</image-desc>

It has branched stems equal to the yellow variety's stems, spread out on the ground and tender. Its leaves are smaller than those of the yellow kind, cut into deeper segments, and hairy. The flowers are also much smaller, of a scarlet color <note>original: "puniceante"</note>, with the bases of the petals <note>term: "unguibus" - literally 'claws', the narrow base of a petal</note> being a more intense red. The little horns or pods are long and bumpy, enclosing black seed. The root is somewhat thick and oblong.

There is also a type of this genus with smooth leaves and a pale flower. This differs from the hairy kind only by age: for as it grows older, the flower becomes paler and weaker, and the branches and stems become smooth.

Clusius reports that it grows in the fields of Moravia and Bohemia.

<column-break/>

### FROTHY OR HERACLEAN POPPY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Papaver spumeum (Bladder Campion) showing an upright habit, oval leaves, and inflated, bladder-like calyxes.</image-desc>

Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Pliny mention this poppy. A certain poppy, says Theophrastus, is called *Heracleum*, having a leaf similar to the Soapwort <note>original: "Struthio"</note> used for bleaching linens, a white root at the surface of the earth, and likewise white fruit.

It is unknown whether it was named after Hercules, or whether it took its name from one of the many cities named Heraclea throughout the world, near which this poppy might grow frequently or beautifully. They call it "frothy" <note>original: "spumeum"</note> because of the whiteness and rarity of the "foam" <note>likely referring to the inflated, pale seed pods</note> which are its peculiar features. Cordus and Matthiolus <note>Influential Renaissance botanists</note> maintain that this herb is unknown to more recent authors.

---

<column-break/>

### ARGEMONE ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENTS AND IN GENERAL
### Argemone with a shorter bristly head.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Argemone (Prickly Poppy) with a short, bristly seed head and deeply divided leaves.</image-desc>

Dioscorides makes the Argemone entirely similar to the wild poppy. He attributes to it a leaf like an Anemone and a scarlet flower. The head is like the Corn Poppy <note>original: "Papaver Rhoeas"</note>, and the root is round.

Thus Ruellius feels that the Argemone is assigned to the poppy family. Similarly, for Cornarius, Tragus, Robert Estienne, Matthiolus, Frischlin, and others, the Argemone is what we, along with many others, have called the *wild corn poppy*.

However, the same name is also given to the *Horned Poppy (red and violet)*, *Agrimony*, *French Marigold* <note>original: "Tagetes Indicus"</note>, *Cinquefoil*, *Hollyhock*, and *Mayweed*.

<column-break/>

### ARGEMONE WITH A LONGER
### spiny head.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Argemone with a longer, spiny seed head and finely divided foliage.</image-desc>

The division of the leaves is like the small yellow Nigella, covered with rough hairs, growing both on the stems and the rough, hairy branches. The flowers fall off very easily and are purple, much smaller than those of the corn poppy. The little heads they leave behind are shorter, bristly with crowded, soft spines, oblong, and covered by a lid with a star-shaped pebble <note>referring to the star-shaped disk on top of the poppy capsule</note>. The root is somewhat long and simple.

Matthiolus writes that Argemone grows very frequently in Tuscany <note>original: "Hetruria"</note> and especially in the territory of Siena. It received its name because, as Dioscorides reports, it heals and drives away "Argema" <note>term: "Argema" - a small white ulcer on the cornea of the eye</note>.

More on Poppies in the Appendix.

### ANEMONE, WIND HERB; German: *Wind-flower*: French: *Anemones*: Italian: *Anemone*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Anemone plant with broad, lobed leaves and a single flower, showing the root system.</image-desc>

The name Anemone was once vague and common to many plants and flowers; the entire genus was divided by the Ancients into two parts: namely, the "coronary" <note>Used for making wreaths or garlands</note> and the "medical" Anemones. It was called *Anemone Limonia* by some, *Othona* by others, and by some the *Red Poppy* or *Astragalis*, etc. But our discussion here concerns the Anemone properly so-called, the coronary kind.

It was named <term>anemone</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνεμώνη</note>, which is to say, "from the wind," because the flower, according to Pliny, never opens unless the wind is blowing.

Dioscorides and Pliny established two primary types of Anemones: the Cultivated and the Wild. Among these, they noted several species of the cultivated variety: the scarlet <note>original: "phoenicea"</note>, the white, and the purple; and likewise, several different kinds of the wild variety.

### PURPLE STAR ANEMONE: Tuberous ANEMONE with an Earth-nut root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a star-shaped Anemone with narrow petals and a bulbous root structure.</image-desc>

This is the first variety described by Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, who illustrates and describes many others, which we have recorded in our *Great History*, though here we shall only treat those known to us.

We have observed this Star Anemone blooming in April and May, both in the botanical garden at Padua and in the mountains near Bologna; and also in certain places in Germany along the Rhine.

### BROAD-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH SCARLET FLOWERS, and likewise scarlet "claws." <note>term: "claws" (unguibus) — the narrow, stalk-like base of a petal</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Anemone with a large, dark-centered flower.</image-desc>

This is variety 16 in Clusius, who describes it thus: It has, he says, a root similar to the broad-leafed Anemone with a full flower, but its leaves (many of which spring from the root) are not as large or thick as that variety, nor are they as green. The stem is about nine inches or even a foot tall, and quite slender. The color of the flower is green on the outside, while the inner part shines with a most elegant scarlet color, with similar scarlet claws; the outer part is covered in a soft down. The middle of the flower is occupied by a hairy little head <note>The central seed-bearing part</note>, surrounded by purplish filaments <note>original: "staminulis"</note> whose tips are black.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH DOUBLE YELLOW FLOWERS, Clusius’s second variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Anemone with a double layer of petals and a thick root.</image-desc>

The broad-leafed Anemone with a yellow flower (Clusius's second) is shown in the preceding plate. Its leaves are quite large, almost circular in shape, serrated around the edges, firm and tough, supported by a long stalk; they are a deep green on the upper side and purplish underneath, with a very biting taste. The root is tuberous and somewhat oblong, resembling the common Tormentil <note>A plant in the rose family used in tanning and medicine</note>, with several hanging fibers. It is black on the outside and white within, solid, and possesses an unpleasant, nauseating, and almost "strangling" <note>original: "strangulantis" — referring to an acrid, choking sensation in the throat</note> flavor.

Clusius dug this up among the brambles on certain stony hills in Portugal near the Tagus River, and later cultivated it in his garden.

### PURPLE BROAD-LEAFED BYZANTINE ANEMONE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Byzantine Anemone with broad leaves and a multi-petaled flower.</image-desc>

This is the sixth variety for Clusius, which he records as the Purple Broad-leafed Anemone. Brought from Byzantium <note>Istanbul</note>, it bloomed for him in his gardens during April and May. He mentions another broad-leafed variety with a deeper reddish-purple color; another of a violet-purple; another violet marked with white spots; another violet with silvery claws; another of a flesh-colored hue with white claws; and still many more varieties of broad-leafed Anemones, which would take too long to list here.

### SCARLET BROAD-LEAFED BYZANTINE ANEMONE; without claws.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a scarlet Byzantine Anemone with broad leaves and a prominent center.</image-desc>

The noble Lady de Heusenstein possessed this kind of Anemone (which is Clusius’s 17th variety), characterized by a simple flower and broader leaves, brought from Constantinople. In the month of April 1587, Clusius saw it heavily laden with flowers in her garden; having received a piece of it the following July, he shared it with friends in Belgium. It was similar to the ones mentioned above, only with rougher leaves, etc.

<summary>This page catalogs several varieties of Anemones, focusing on their physical descriptions, etymology (linking the name to the wind), and the various colors introduced to Europe from the Ottoman Empire.</summary>
<keywords>Anemone, Carolus Clusius, Wind-flower, botanical classification, Byzantine plants, 16th-century gardening, Padua garden, plant morphology</keywords>
