The author continues to rely heavily on the observations of Carolus Clusius.</meta>

# OF PLANTS
<page-num>466</page-num>

### BROAD-LEAFED ANEMONE, of a SCARLET-CRIMSON
### color, with small, pale claws <note>The "claws" or "vnguibus" refer to the narrow base of the petals where they attach to the center of the flower.</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Anemone with a single flower, showing the root system, leaves, and a single blossom.</image-desc>

This is the eighteenth variety in Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>, who in his *Plants of Pannonia* <note>A region covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note> titles it the *Byzantine broad-leafed Anemone with a scarlet flower*.

He observed it blooming with a single flower in the month of May in the year 1600. It bloomed quite late because that year was delayed by a preceding, very harsh winter, the likes of which had not been seen for many years.

### BROAD-LEAFED ANEMONE, WITH A FULL FLOWER
### of scarlet: Clusius’s Greater Peacock 1 and 2.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Anemone with a dense, multi-petaled (double) flower head.</image-desc>

Some title this the *Constantinople Buttercup* <note>original: "Ranunculum Constantinopolitanum"</note>, a name under which we also received it from Padua. This flower is perhaps the same as Clusius’s *Garden broad-leafed Anemone 2 with a double flower*, as well as his *Garden broad-leafed Anemone, Greater Peacock 1*, and even his *Broad-leafed Anemone, Greater Peacock 2*.

### PURPLE THIN-LEAFED ITALIAN ANEMONE,
### with rounded flower petals.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thin-leafed Anemone with rounded petals and a distinct tuberous root.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German physician and botanist</note> says it is common in Italy, around Rome and Naples, and in Tuscany. He notes that the plant is so influenced by its environment that by the fourth year, it may produce white flowers instead of purple ones. He writes that the plant is pungent, and its juice, when snuffed into the nostrils, greatly clears the brain. It bloomed for us in Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France</note> in May, in the Prince's Garden <note>original: "S.P. horto," likely referring to the garden of the Duke of Württemberg</note>.

<column-break/>

### BROAD-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH A VARIEGATED
### full flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leafed Anemone with a large, complex double flower, showing detailed leaf structure.</image-desc>

Nothing is more beautiful than the flower of this Anemone; it is as large as a great rose and luxuriant with a very dense growth of petals, almost in the manner of a Peony <note>original: "Prouniæ," likely a reference to the Provins rose or a Peony variety</note>. The petals are oblong, sharp, reddish, and streaked; the outer ones are four or five times wider, variegated with a mix of red and green. It was brought from Constantinople. However, it is a late-bloomer and very rarely reaches maturity, because it very often develops a blight before it can unfold itself. Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, an early German herbalist</note> calls it the *Greater Chalcedonian Anemone*.

### GERANIUM-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH A
### tuberous root: with a blue or white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Anemone with leaves resembling a Geranium and a prominent tuberous root.</image-desc>

The gardens of the Low Countries <note>original: "Belgici horti"</note> first obtained this from Italy. In these gardens, it blooms in Spring; the seed ripens in May or a little later. It is sown and planted using fragments of the root. In his work on Spanish plants, Clusius names it the *Thin-leafed Anemone 3*.

In his later *History*, he calls it the *Garden thin-leafed Anemone 1 with a single flower*. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> calls it the *Tuberous Geranium-leafed Anemone*, and some call it *St. Rupert’s Anemone*.

### PURPLE THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE,
### with flower petals ending in a point.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a thin-leafed Anemone with pointed petals.</image-desc>

Just as with the broad-leafed Anemones, Clusius recounts and vividly describes many species of the thin-leafed varieties, both in his Spanish history and his later *History*. From these, as we did with the broad-leafed types, we shall only record the more beautiful ones here, leaving the rest to be sought from his own writings.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### ANOTHER THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender-leaved anemone with a single large flower and a tuberous root system.</image-desc>

This plant has a large, scarlet, circular flower with white "claws" <note>The "claws" are the narrow, often pale bases of the petals where they meet the center.</note>. The root is both tuberous and fibrous.

It is said that Venus cherished Adonis with the Anemone as a mournful offspring; so it is written in Bion’s *Idyll* <note>Bion of Smyrna was a Greek poet; his "Lament for Adonis" is a famous source for this myth.</note> and mentioned by Theocritus:

> <unclear>Whoever</unclear> <unclear>comes</unclear> <unclear>here</unclear> <unclear>shares</unclear>
> <unclear>the sorrows</unclear> <unclear>of this</unclear> <unclear>fallen</unclear> <unclear>Adonis</unclear>,
> <unclear>Venus</unclear> <unclear>shed</unclear> <unclear>three</unclear> <unclear>tears</unclear> <unclear>for every</unclear> <unclear>drop</unclear> <unclear>of blood</unclear>
> <unclear>that fell</unclear>: <unclear>From the tears</unclear> <unclear>they produce</unclear> <unclear>the Anemone</unclear>:
> <unclear>But</unclear> <unclear>that blood</unclear> <unclear>creates</unclear> <unclear>the Roses</unclear>.

### THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE, WITH A FLOWER CONSISTING
->of many petals, of a flesh color.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an anemone with multiple layers of petals (a double flower) and finely divided, feathery leaves.</image-desc>

As we have stated in the general history of Anemones, it should be noted that while Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, the influential 16th-century botanist</note> observed that all their kinds usually produce single stems, they occasionally produce two or three, or even more, with more numerous or larger leaves or bracts; but they are never found with true branches.

Pliny <note>A Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History"</note> records some superstitious beliefs regarding the Anemone: he says that many people recite a prayer when the flower is first seen, and then pull it up by the root. They then <unclear>wrap it</unclear> <unclear>in a red cloth</unclear> and tie it to the finger <unclear>as a remedy</unclear> <unclear>for tertian</unclear> and <unclear>quartan</unclear> <note>Fevers that recur every three or four days, often associated with malaria.</note> fevers, and so forth.

### THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE OF THE WHITE VARIETY,
->surrounded by colored veins.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an anemone with a cup-shaped flower and a distinct, chunky root structure.</image-desc>

Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> <unclear>testifies</unclear> that all Anemones <unclear>possess</unclear> an <unclear>extractive</unclear>, <unclear>drawing</unclear>, and <unclear>opening</unclear> power; <unclear>hence</unclear> <unclear>it is easy</unclear> <unclear>to know</unclear> <unclear>how they</unclear> <unclear>may be useful</unclear>. <unclear>For</unclear> <unclear>their juice</unclear>, <unclear>introduced</unclear> <unclear>into the nostrils</unclear>, <unclear>purges the head</unclear> and <unclear>draws away</unclear> <unclear>phlegm</unclear>; it also <unclear>thins</unclear> <unclear>white spots</unclear> <note>original: "albugines," likely referring to cataracts or corneal scarring</note> in the <unclear>eyes</unclear>.

<column-break/>

### THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH A LARGE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large-flowered anemone with prominent stamens and deeply incised, fern-like foliage.</image-desc>

This plant has a very large, blood-red flower, the petals of which end almost in a point, with large white "claws."

Furthermore, according to the authors Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> and Pliny, both the cultivated and wild Anemone have a sharp <note>acrid or stinging</note> quality. For that reason, the juice of the root itself, when infused into the nostrils, is effective for purging the head. The chewed root draws out phlegm; however, when boiled in a poultice and applied, it heals eye inflammations, cleanses foul ulcers, and improves scars on the eyes. The leaves and stems, if boiled with barley water <note>original: "ptisana," a medicinal tea or gruel</note> and taken with food, provide an abundance of milk and fertility, induce labor, and stimulate menstruation. Their powers according to Galen will be discussed later.

### THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE, WITH A TURNIP-LIKE ROOT,
->with a flower of purplish-white.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an anemone with a thick, bulbous root (rapacea) and a single cup-like flower.</image-desc>

We believe this to be Tabernaemontanus’s <note>Jakob Theodor von Bergzabern, a 16th-century herbalist</note> *Anemone II*, which he labels as "Turnip-rooted" (*Rapacea*) because of the shape of the root. In Bauhin’s *Phytopinax* <note>Caspar Bauhin, a Swiss botanist who began the binomial system of classification</note>, it is listed as *Narrow-leafed Anemone I*. To what has been said before, we add here that the flower of the Anemone, though it is most beautiful, will immediately wither and fall at a slight gust of wind or the heat of the Sun; likewise, its seed easily turns into downy fluff <note>original: "pappos"</note>.

### THIN-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH A
->Many-petaled scarlet flower.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "double" anemone with many layers of petals and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Thus Anemones differ from one another not only by having broad or narrow leaves, but also by their flowers—being purple, scarlet, blood-red, flesh-colored, kermes <note>a deep red dye</note>, white, or golden, or mixed; and likewise being single or multiple <note>double-flowered</note>, large or small; and also by their claws being large or small, of various shapes, and various colors (though they are most often white). Furthermore, other distinctions are sought from their locations, whence some are called "garden" types and others "wild." These wild ones are fewer than the garden varieties, but they are more required for medical uses, and especially for the preparation of the *Ointment of Mars* <note>original: "Unguenti Martiati," a traditional green ointment used for nerves, joints, and "soldier's" injuries</note>.

<summary>This page describes various thin-leafed Anemones, detailing their botanical characteristics, the myth of their origin from Venus's tears, and their extensive medicinal uses in treating eye conditions, respiratory phlegm, and women's health.</summary>
<keywords>Anemone, Thin-leafed Anemone, Venus and Adonis, medicinal plants, Pliny the Elder, Galen, Dioscorides, botanical illustration, turnip-rooted plants, double flowers, Ointment of Mars</keywords>

### YELLOW ANEMONE WITH THE APPEARANCE OF A CROWFOOT.
<note>original: "Anemone Ranunculi Facie Lutea"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a yellow wood anemone (Anemone ranunculoides) showing the root system, stem, trifoliate leaves, and two flowers.</image-desc>

It grows with leaves almost like a Crowfoot <note>The genus *Ranunculus*</note>, but thinner, with golden flowers: the root is small, the size of a bean: thus Camerarius describes it.

Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, an Italian botanist</note> mentions a yellow four-leafed Anemone with deeply divided leaves growing in Apulia in his 11th Letter; and Rauwolff <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a German physician and botanist</note> likewise mentions a yellow one among others in his travel journal.

<column-break/>

### GREAT WHITE ANEMONE, WITH A TUBEROUS HEAD: the stem gray-white with a tooth-like down.
<note>original: "Anemone Magna Alba, Capitulo tuberoso: caule dentâ lanugine canescenti"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large white anemone with a thick, tuberous root, deeply lobed leaves, and a single large flower at the top of a hairy stem.</image-desc>

It blooms in early Spring, Summer, and even Autumn, and propagates itself widely by the root. We find it growing wild enough in somewhat shaded places, in the meadows near Frankfurt-on-the-Main, on various hills of Bohemia, in Breisgau near the Rhine, and elsewhere: we have also seen it cultivated in the illustrious garden at Montbéliard. More concerning Anemones will be found in the Appendix.

---

### THREE-LEAFED ANEMONE WITH A WHITE FLOWER.
<note>original: "Anemone Trifolia Flore Albo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wood anemone with three distinct leaflets and a single white flower.</image-desc>

Another variety also belongs here, although it differs in its leaves. Neither does this one bear leaves similar to Coriander nor to the Crowfoot: but they are joined more like a Trefoil. Indeed, they grow in threes, large, wide, pointed, and undivided except for the notched margin. The little stem is a palm-width high, upon which sits a flower that is pure white or purplish-white. It mimics the form of the Crowfoot flowers. The slanted root grows out into several shoots, not without small hairs, appearing fibrous beneath.

Dodoens, Thalius of the Harz Mountains, the *History of Lyon*, and Caspar Bauhin all record it as the "Three-leafed Anemone." Lobel calls it "Alabastrite" or "White Toothwort" in his *Observations* and *Images of Plants*.

<column-break/>

### PASQUEFLOWER Germ. <term>Küchenschelle</term> <note>German for "Kitchen-bell"</note>: Belg. <term>Osterbloem</term> <note>Dutch for "Easter flower"</note>: Gall. <term>Passefleur</term> <note>French for "Pass-flower"</note>.
<note>original: "Pulsatilla"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pulsatilla (Pasqueflower) showing the characteristic silky, hairy leaves and a nodding flower head.</image-desc>

The *Pasqueflower* deservedly claims this place for itself, due to the great similarity it shares with the Anemone: whence some have even named it *Anemone* and *Herb of the Wind*. Caesalpinus records it as the thin-leafed and <unclear>gray-white</unclear> <note>original: "canatum," likely "canum" meaning gray or hoary</note> Crowfoot: some call it the *Sardinian Herb* and *Celery of Laughter* <note>A reference to "Herba Sardoa," which was anciently said to cause a fatal convulsive grin when eaten.</note>. But these names, in the judgment of Lobel, deserve a scoff rather than an answer: nor is it even a species of Crowfoot or Anemone, as Dodoens correctly established, although it approaches both in appearance and properties.

Some maintain it is an unknown and foreign plant: but Mattioli, Clusius, Tabernaemontanus, the *History of Lyon*, Gerard, Caspar Bauhin, and almost all others record it as the *Pulsatilla*.

---

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE PASQUEFLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Pulsatilla with more finely divided foliage and a prominent flower.</image-desc>

The color of the Pasqueflower, says Dodoens, is that of a dark purple violet, sometimes whiter, and other times more rarely reddish. It is quite common among the Germans in open and stony places, and occasionally on the rocks themselves: and indeed the purple-blue flower is more frequent, which there, by their reckoning, is either more intense or paler. White ones are found in <unclear>Styria</unclear> and among the Nathonei <note>likely a reference to a specific regional people or tribe</note>; the mountains of France also provide them, and near Paris. In Faverges of the Allobroges <note>Savoy region</note>, a red flower is found instead of the white one.

Clusius distinguishes between the Early Great variety, with a larger flower and thicker leaf, and the less early one, which is smaller in every respect. We present two figures so that if anything is lacking in one, it may be supplied by the other.

<column-break/>

### PASQUEFLOWER WITH WHITE, RED, AND YELLOW FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pulsatilla specimen with a straight stem and upright flower.</image-desc>

The white-flowered Pasqueflower has leaves much larger than any of the others, and flowers of a milky whiteness; in other respects it resembles them.

The red variety differs from the common one not only in the color of the flower, but also in the shape of the leaves, which are more finely divided: finally, the ends of the flowers <note>likely referring to the petals or sepals</note>, which are sharp in the common variety, are blunt in this one.

Finally, the yellow Pasqueflower has a thick root and leaves divided in the manner of the others but with wider segments, and they are very hairy. The rest is as in the others, except for the color of the flower, which is yellow.

We have seen these Pasqueflowers in abundance on the mountains of Montpellier and Lyon: around Bonn in Germany, and elsewhere.

### BUTTERCUP <note>original: "RANVNCVLVS"</note>: German: *Hanenfuss*; French: *Bassinet, Grenouillette*; Italian: *Ranunculo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus plant showing a fibrous root system, deeply lobed leaves, and several five-petaled flowers on long stems.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> proposes four species of Buttercups, which Pliny also describes, following the account of Galen. Among more recent authors, Cordus and Cesalpinus have striven to reconcile the Buttercups of the ancients, especially Galen’s, with known plants. Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish botanist</note> derives the first two kinds from these: one being a garden variety, the others being wild. Marantha observed ten distinctions, while others noted more or fewer. Our own observations are detailed in the following pages. Here is depicted the **Spring Hedge Buttercup** <note>original: "Ranunculus phragmites vernus"</note>: the differences in this plant are primarily observed in its color, as it may be white, purple, or yellow. This Hedge Buttercup flowers in May and is an inhabitant of the woods. More on this in the following sections.

### GLOBE-FLOWER <note>original: "RANVNCVLVS FLORE GLOBOSO"</note>, called by some the *Trollius* flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Trollius (globeflower) featuring a thick rootstock, palmately lobed leaves, and a distinct spherical, multi-petaled flower head.</image-desc>

It has a black and fibrous root resembling that of Hellebore; leaves much like Monkshood <note>original: "Aconiti"</note>; and a stem a cubit and a half tall <note>about 27 inches</note>, smooth, hollow, and branched. The flowers are perhaps larger than the common Buttercup (yet of the same color); they do not merely flourish with a dense crowd of petals, but from the middle of the flower another smaller one rises, made many-layered by a numerous cluster of petals, pierced through by the lower stalk.

Matthioli, Lacuna, and Thalius number this among the Monkshoods, but incorrectly; others more rightly refer it to the Buttercups.

It grows in the Harz Mountains <note>original: "Harciniæ"</note> and the Swiss Alps; we ourselves saw it flowering in June on Mount Thuiri in the territory of Geneva.

### THIN-LEAFED MOUNTAIN BUTTERCUP, yellow.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS TENVIFOLIVS MONTANVS luteus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain Ranunculus with very fine, deeply divided leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

This is a peculiar species of Buttercup. The root consists of a dense head of thin, long, blackish fibers. From these, the leaves immediately arise individually, hanging from long stalks; they are tripartite, with each part divided by smaller incisions. The stems are several, a half-span tall <note>about 4 inches</note>, and slender; to these the leaves adhere without stalks, but divided into narrower segments than the earlier leaves. At the very top are solitary flowers—yellow, shining, and five-petaled, with tips of the same color. These are followed by a small globe, the beginning of the future seeds, as in other Buttercups.

We found this in the high parts of Mount Thuiri near Geneva.

<column-break/>

### YELLOW SPRING HEDGE BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS PHRAGMITES VERNVS luteus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spring Ranunculus with broad, lobed leaves and several open flowers.</image-desc>

Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, and others record this as the *Yellow Wood Buttercup*. To Clusius, in his work on Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/Austria</note>, it is a type of Wood Anemone, entirely yellow; however, in his later *History*, he calls it the *Yellow Wild Buttercup*, noting it differs significantly from the white and purple varieties in its leaves, and is generally lower-growing and blooms earlier.

Furthermore, the differences among Buttercups in general are taken from the root, the stem, the leaves, the flowers, the place of birth, and the season. Thus, they are categorized as having tuberous, clustered, or bulbous roots; with stems that are upright, creeping, smooth, or hairy; thin-leafed or round-leafed; with simple or double flowers; and these again can be yellow, white, or scarlet. They are further divided into garden, field, marsh, wood, or mountain varieties; and either common or exotic; and finally, spring, autumn, or winter blooming.

### UPRIGHT BUTTERCUP, NOT CREEPING, with a simple yellow flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS RECTVS, NON REPENS, flore simplici, luteo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright Ranunculus with a prominent fibrous root and multiple flowers.</image-desc>

It rises on an upright, smooth stem to a height of one and a half or two cubits <note>approx. 2.2 to 3 feet</note>. The root is fibrous and white; the leaves, on long stalks, very closely resemble Yellow Monkshood, and at the top they are sharp, slightly hairy, and sometimes marked with purple spots. The flower is yellow, followed by a prickly head of seeds.

This is very well known in the meadows of Silesia <note>modern-day Poland/Germany</note>, where entire meadows are often covered by its flowers. It is also found in the meadows of Geneva and Montbéliard. In Basel, however, it is found in the woods. It is also found with a double flower.

### GREAT VERY HAIRY BUTTERCUP, with a yellow flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MAGNVS VALDE HIRSVTVS, flore luteo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large, hairy Ranunculus with broad, deeply incised leaves and a cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has a root divided into many fine hairs. The stems are a cubit high <note>18 inches</note>, furrowed, hollow, hairy, rough, and reflecting a yellowish light, branching out like arms. Five or six leaves are attached to stalks a span or a span and a half long; they are dense, broad, and divided into deep, jagged segments, which are themselves incised again and serrated around the edges. Their color is a blackish-green, and they are downy or hairy; other leaves on the stem are smaller. The flowers at the tops of the stems are few, gifted with five pale yellow petals; these are succeeded by the seed gathered into small heads.

It grows in shaded mountain places, and especially in the "Museto" of the people of Basel.

->Catchword: BUTTERCUP-<-
<note>original: "RANVN-"</note>

<summary>This page describes various species of the Ranunculus (Buttercup) genus, including the Globeflower and several mountain and woodland varieties, noting their physical characteristics and specific locations across Europe where they were observed by the author and his contemporaries.</summary>
<keywords>Buttercup, Ranunculus, Globeflower, Trollius, botanical classification, Geneva, Basel, Silesia, medicinal plants, 16th-century botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Ranunculus genus, transitioning from the general definitions on the previous page to specific species identified by their growth habits—upright, tuberous, or creeping—and their flower structures. The translator maintains the continuity of identifying these plants through both classical descriptions and the 16th-century observations of botanists like Clusius and Lobelius.</meta>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### UPRIGHT BUTTERCUP with paler, hairy leaves.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS RECTVS FOLIIS pallidioribus, hirsutis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall, upright buttercup plant with multiple stems, deeply lobed leaves, and several small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

It is fixed in the ground by many white, fibrous roots that do not creep at all. The stems are numerous, one to one and a half feet <note>original: "pedales vel cubitales"</note> tall, soft, hollow, and hairy, divided into various small branches. At the top of these are the yellow flowers of the Buttercup, which are followed by small seed heads similar to other Buttercups. The illustration shows the form of the leaves, which are indeed hairy.

It grows abundantly around Montbéliard and Belfort <note>Cities in eastern France, near the Swiss border</note>, especially in damp and muddy places. It flowers in May, June, and July.

### BUTTERCUP WITH A VERY LARGE TUBER and a large, double flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MAXIMO TVBERE, flore magno, pleno"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup with a large, thick tuberous root system and large, multi-petaled (double) flowers.</image-desc>

This plant is a delightful pleasure to see, and easily the foremost of the Buttercups due to the lovely display of its flowers. Indeed, they grow luxuriously with a dense crowding of petals <note>original: "foliorum," referring here to the petals of a double flower</note>, but from the middle of the flower another smaller one often rises, made manifold by a numerous mass of petals, with a small stalk pushing through the lower flower. The leaves are larger, more wrinkled, and rounder than the common variety, and divided into less sharp angles. The root is tuberous and whorled, about the size of a Sowbread <note>term: Sowbread; the Cyclamen plant, known for its thick, round tuber</note>. It is cultivated in gardens, having first been brought from England.

The English many-flowered Buttercup of Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note>.

### CREEPING BUTTERCUP with a simple yellow flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS REPENS, FLORE luteo simplici"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping buttercup with runners (stolons) extending from the base and simple five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

It relies on a fibrous and whitish creeping root, from which several hollow stems arise; these are variegated with purple and green, hairy, branched, and lie flat along the ground. The leaves are dark green, marked with white spots, hairy, and divided into seven segments. The flowers are the golden yellow of the Buttercup, with saffron-colored tips. The seed head is prickly <note>original: "echinatum," literally "like a hedgehog"</note>.

This is the most common Buttercup, found everywhere in gardens as well as meadows, and along roadsides in shady and damp places. It flowers in May, June, and July.

Many name this the "Sweet Buttercup" or "Healing Frog-plant" <note>original: "Ranunculum dulcem & Batrachium salutiferum"</note> because its root lacks the sharp, stinging acrimony usually found in this genus.

<column-break/>

### GREATER TUBEROUS BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS TVBEROSVS MAIOR"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup with a distinct bulbous or tuberous base and upright stems.</image-desc>

Just as it is found among the common Buttercups, so too it has leaves similar to theirs. The golden flower and hairy stem also correspond to the common Buttercup. Beneath is a white, bulbous root, about the size of a medium bean, which is very fibrous. In the wild, the flower is simple; however, when moved into gardens, it not only multiplies its petals but often produces one flower out of another.

### PYRENEAN BUTTERCUP with longish, undivided leaves and a white flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS PYRENÆVS FOLIIS sublongis, non laciniatis, albo flore"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pyrenean buttercup with long, undivided (lanceolate) leaves and a single flower.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a central figure in 16th-century botany</note> considered this a completely new kind of Buttercup, which he first saw in the year of Christ 1565. It was cultivated and laden with flowers near the start of March in several well-tended gardens, having been brought from the Pyrenees mountains.

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Pinax* <note>A famous botanical register of the era</note>, this is the "fourth long-leaved Buttercup," or the "Mountain Buttercup with leaves like Plantain."

### CREEPING BUTTERCUP WITH A DOUBLE FLOWER.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS REPENS FLORE PLENO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a creeping buttercup similar to the previous "repens" but with dense, double flowers.</image-desc>

This one also has hollow stems, spotted and somewhat hairy, which spread over the ground; just like the preceding variety, wherever they touch the earth, they send down fibers and take root anew. The leaves are like those of the simple creeping variety, endowed with a grassy and harmless taste. The golden flower is multi-petaled; the seed head is prickly.

Most people call this the "very common manifold yellow Buttercup."

Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> relates that this plant and the one with the simple flower are not at all sharp to the taste, and therefore can be applied to the body without danger or harm. He says that the leaves, when applied to tumors arising on the body, discuss and resolve them <note>term: discuss and resolve; historical medical terms for dispersing swelling or breaking down a growth</note>; furthermore, it is believed that cattle graze on them more than others, and that they produce an abundance of milk.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Buttercups (Ranunculus), detailing their physical forms—such as upright, tuberous, and creeping—and their medicinal or agricultural uses. It highlights the distinction between "acrid" varieties and "sweet" ones used for healing or as livestock fodder.</summary>
<keywords>Ranunculus, Buttercup, Tuberous Buttercup, Creeping Buttercup, Pyrenean Buttercup, Clusius, Caspar Bauhin, Tragus, medicinal plants, botany, double flowers, horticulture</keywords>

<header>ILLUSTRATIONS AND DESCRIPTIONS</header>
<sig>Nnn 2</sig>

### LARGE HAIRY BUTTERCUP with double flowers.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MAGNVS HIRSVTVS flore pleno"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall buttercup with large, multi-petaled (double) flowers and deeply lobed, hairy leaves.</image-desc>

We cultivated this at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden, where it bloomed in April and May.

Otherwise, the name *Ranunculus* <note>meaning "little frog"</note> was bestowed upon it because it especially delights in waters where frogs live, or because frogs are frequently found among its stalks. For the same reason, it is named *Grenouillette* <note>little frog</note> by the French. They also call it *Bassinet*, because the flowers—in their shape and color—seem similar to the brass vessels <note>barbers' basins</note> in which they soften beards. Pliny writes that it was called the *Strumaea* herb, either because it cures scrofulous tumors <note>original: "strumis," swelling of the neck glands</note> or because it is seen to have a tumorous <note>knobby or tuberous</note> root. Others have called it *Apium* <note>Celery or Parsley</note> because its leaves rival those of Celery.

### MARSH BUTTERCUP WITH THE SMALLEST FLOWER.
<note>original: "RANVNC. PALVSTRIS FLORE MINIMO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh buttercup with small flowers and distinct basal leaves.</image-desc>

The hollow root of the aquatic Buttercup grows very thick and is provided with many fibers; from which many stems arise, sometimes of remarkable thickness, hollow, striated, and branched. The leaves of the Marsh-Celery <note>original: "Paludapii"</note> shine with a bright green, sometimes spotted with white dots. The flowers, the smallest among all the Buttercups, consist of five small petals, and are golden. The seed heads are oblong, thinner than in the others, and not prickly like a hedgehog <note>original: "echinata"</note> with rough seeds, but composed of smooth and minute grains packed together.

It seeks its birthplace among the rivulets of stagnant or slow-gliding waters and other similar damp and marshy places, and it blooms in June.

### PRICKLY FIELD BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS ARVENSIS ECHINATVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a field buttercup with prickly seed heads (echinate).</image-desc>

It has a stem about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note> high, somewhat hairy, a cheerful green, hollow, and divided into several branches. The leaves are cut into thin, oblong segments, very deeply incised, and hairy. The flowers are like those of the aquatic Buttercup, but smaller than in the meadow variety, and yellowish. These are followed by prickly Seed-heads <note>original: "echinata Capitula"</note>, composed of several somewhat round, compressed, and prickly burs. The root is fibrous.

At Montpellier, Lyon, Geneva, Basel, and almost everywhere, it grows in the fields among the crops.

<column-break/>

### ROUND-LEAVED SPRING BUTTERCUP of the woods.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS ROTVNDIFOLIVS VERNVS sylvestricus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a spring buttercup with rounded basal leaves and fibrous roots.</image-desc>

It rests on a fibrous root, which is not at all sharp <note>referring to the acrid, burning juice found in many buttercups</note>, from which rise several pipe-like stems, a cubit or a cubit and a half tall, branched out like arms. On each of these sits a golden Buttercup flower, followed by a "hedgehog" <note>original: "echino," the prickly seed head</note>, as is the case in common Buttercups. But the leaves play a strange trick <note>a botanical phenomenon called heterophylly</note>, with the upper ones departing greatly from the shape of the lower ones, as is clear from the Illustration.

This Buttercup is familiar to the woods, but it is also found in meadows, and is sometimes transferred into gardens.

### PRICKLY MARSH BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS PALVSTRIS ECHINATVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a marsh buttercup with prominent prickly seed heads.</image-desc>

This has a fibrous root and several stems—some a palm's width <note>about 3 inches</note> and others higher—branched with frequent arms. Upon these sit yellow flowers in the manner of the others, simple in form. These are followed by Seed-heads very similar to the heads of the field buttercup, gathered together from ten or twelve prickly, oblong, compressed seed-vessels. The leaves very much resemble those of the Maple, but they are larger and more numerous.

It enjoys damp and watery places and is often found in ditches.

### WHITE-FLOWERED BUTTERCUP, both simple and double.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS FLORE ALBO, EOQVE tum simplici tum pleno"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a white-flowered buttercup with multiple blooms on a single stem.</image-desc>

The flower of both is conspicuous for its milky whiteness; they differ from each other almost only in the number of petals in the flower.

Both abound in the plains of France, Germany, and the mountains of the Allobroges <note>the region of Savoy</note>. It is most frequent in Silesia, especially in marshy, mountainous places. Clusius also observed it frequently in the Pannonian <note>Hungarian and Austrian</note> mountains. We, however, found it on the Genevan mountains of Salève and Tivery, by the rivulets flowing down from them. It blooms in July.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Ranunculus genus, focusing on their diverse habitats (marshes, fields, and woods) and their seed structures, ranging from smooth to prickly. It also provides historical etymologies for the name "Buttercup," linking it to frogs, barbers' basins, and medicinal uses for tumors.</summary>

<keywords>Buttercup, Ranunculus, botany, etymology, Pliny, marsh plants, white buttercup, prickly seed heads, European flora, Montbéliard, medicinal herbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Ranunculus (Buttercup) genus, specifically focusing on white-flowered and alpine varieties. It maintains the previous page's reliance on the observations of Carolus Clusius and other Renaissance botanists, shifting from lowland marsh types to high-altitude specimens found in the Alps and Jura mountains.</meta>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>
<meta>catchword: BUTTER-</meta>

### LARGE WHITE-FLOWERED ALPINE BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS FLORE ALBO ALPINVS, maior"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Ranunculus plant with large, deeply lobed basal leaves and several five-petaled flowers on branched stems.</image-desc>

The shepherds and hunters of the Austrian Alps, according to Clusius, call this *Abbeiss* and *Teuffels Abbeiss*—that is, the "Devil's Bit." <note>original: "Diaboli morsum"</note>

He states that it grows abundantly in various wooded locations of the Austrian Alps and blooms in June.

### ANOTHER HAIRY WHITE MOUNTAIN BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MONTANVS ALBVS, hirsutus alius"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant similar to the first, but with more jagged leaf margins and a slightly more compact growth habit.</image-desc>

This grows in great numbers on the shaded ridges of the Jura Mountains, blooming in June and July, and ripening its seeds in August. On Mount <term>Thoiri</term> <note>Le Reculet de Thoiry, a peak in the Jura range</note> we saw one adorned with a purplish flower; it differs from the previous one in this regard, and also because the flower consists of seven petals and the entire plant is hairier.

### THE SMALLEST WHITE AND YELLOW ALPINE BUTTERCUP of Clusius.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MINIMVS ALPINVS, albus & luteus, Clusii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of two small alpine Ranunculus specimens, showing fibrous roots and small, delicate flowers.</image-desc>

He says that of all the Buttercups he has seen, these observed in the mountains of Rhaetia <note>an ancient Roman province covering parts of modern-day Switzerland and eastern Austria</note> are the smallest; white or yellow flowers sit upon the tops of their stems, not differing much from the flowers of other Buttercups, etc.

The shepherds and hunters of the Austrian Alps are accustomed to using these to drive away fevers, applying the crushed leaves to the wrist. <note>original: "carpo"</note>

<column-break/>

### ALPINE BUTTERCUP WITH WHITE, FRAGRANT NARCISSUS-LIKE FLOWERS.
<note>original: "RANVNC. ALPINVS NARCISSI FLORE albo, odorato"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus with distinct, broad-petaled flowers resembling narcissus blossoms and deeply divided leaves.</image-desc>

This is found on the higher ridges of the same Alps, but it is much shorter, more fragrant, and blooms later, according to Clusius. It is also said to be found in the mountain valleys of Silesia. <note>A region mostly in modern-day Poland</note>

Caspar Bauhin cataloged this as the "Hairy Mountain Buttercup with a Narcissus flower" in his *Phytopinax*. Schvenckfeld called it the "Hairy Narcissus-flowered Mountain Buttercup."

### BUTTERCUP WITH MEADOW-RUE LEAVES AND PURE WHITE FLOWERS.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS THALICTRI FOLIO, flore candido"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with leaves resembling Thalictrum (meadow-rue) and small white flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius classifies this among the early-blooming plants, naming it the "Early Buttercup with a Meadow-rue leaf." <note>original: "Præcocem Thalictri folio"</note> It grows in the shady forests of the Viennese countryside and blooms in May.

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF THE SMALLEST WHITE AND YELLOW ALPINE BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLI MINIMI ALPINI, ALBI & lutei, alia Icon"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another small alpine variety, showing a single stem with a flower and a cluster of basal leaves.</image-desc>

To the figures of Clusius provided earlier, we add our own here, depicted from a dried plant. Occasionally, according to Dodonaeus, flowers are found consisting of a double row of petals.

<header>IMAGES AND SKETCHES.</header>
<sig>Nnn 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Buttercup-</meta>

### WHITE-FLOWERED CRETAN BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS CRETICVS ALBO FLORE"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup plant with broad, lobed leaves and a single large, open flower at the top of a long stem.</image-desc>

The leaves are similar to those of the field or creeping garden Buttercup, divided into three or, more rarely, five leaflets; they are notched along the edges and covered with very fine hairs. The stem is round and a foot long, supporting two or three large flowers composed of six or seven petals. These flowers are white and would surpass the Wild Poppy <note>original: "Papaveris erratici"</note> in size if they were any larger. They are followed by a seed-head filled with seeds, in the manner of other Buttercups.

### ILLYRIAN BUTTERCUP, WITH
->bulbous roots, long leaves, and golden flowers.<-
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS ILLYRICVS, RADICIBVS bulbosis, foliis longis, & floribus aureis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and multiple flower buds and open blossoms on branching stems. The root system shows small bulbous tubers.</image-desc>

Caspar Bauhin records this in his *Pinax* <term>Pinax Theatri Botanici</term> <note>A landmark 1623 botanical index by Bauhin</note> as the "Narrow-leaved Buttercup with a clustered Asphodel-like root." In his *Phytopinax*, however, he calls it the "Buttercup with deeply cut, oblong, downy leaves." Some call it the Sardinian Buttercup <note>original: "Ranunculus Sardonens"</note> or the "Sardinian Herb," while almost everyone else calls it the Illyrian Buttercup. To Tabernaemontanus, Dodonaeus, and others, it is the "Second Buttercup of Dioscorides."

### ASIATIC BUTTERCUP WITH CLUSTERED
->roots, the second variety of Clusius.<-
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS ASIATICVS GRVMOSA radice 2. Clusii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup with deeply incised, jagged leaves and a large, multi-petaled flower. The roots are thick and tuberous (grumose).</image-desc>

We suspect this is the same plant as Ferrante Imperato’s Illyrian Buttercup, to which he attributes deeply cut leaves that are saw-toothed around the edges, somewhat thick and hairy, and of a pale green color with an unpleasant, biting taste. It has white flowers, though sometimes they are the color of red-lead <note>original: "minii," referring to a vibrant orange-red pigment</note>; the seeds are winged and leafy but tasteless, and the roots are tuberous.

It is commonly listed as the "Buttercup with a tuberous root and crimson flower."

<column-break/>

### PURPLE MOUNTAIN BUTTERCUP,
->with a hairy calyx, according to Felix Platter.<-
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS MONTANVS PVR PVREVS, calyce villoso, Fel. Plateri"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain buttercup with deeply divided leaves and several flowers. The calyx (the green base of the flower) appears hairy or shaggy.</image-desc>

The appearance and careful consideration of this small plant will easily show its distinctiveness from other species of Buttercups. The plant is about nine inches tall <note>original: "Dodrantalis"</note>; its leaves are dissected like fingers, some attached to long stalks at the base of the stems, others hanging from the stalks themselves. At the top sits a single purple Buttercup flower, covered by a very hairy calyx.

### TRIPOLITAN BUTTERCUP
->with a crimson flower.<-
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS TRIPOLITANVS flore phœniceo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a buttercup with a thick, fibrous root system, upright stems, and flowers with prominent centers.</image-desc>

Clusius also records this as an Asiatic Buttercup with a clustered root; he reports that it was brought from abroad and delivered from Constantinople, and that it blooms at the beginning of summer. He adds that it was distinguished by the name *Tarsholas catamer lale*, which signifies a "Full flower from Tripoli."

### CONSTANTINOPOLITAN BUTTERCUP,
->with a full, blood-red flower.<-
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS CONSTANTINOPOLITANVS, flore sanguineo, pleno"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a lush buttercup with broad, serrated leaves and a very full, "double" flower head with many layers of petals.</image-desc>

Clusius gave this the surname "of Constantinople" or "Byzantine" because he understood it was found in certain gardens near Byzantium <note>Modern-day Istanbul</note>, situated within sight of that city but across the Bosphorus. For the same reason, however, it might perhaps more rightly be called "Asiatic."

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Ranunculus family (Buttercups) and introduces Scrophularia (Figworts). It maintains the sequence from the previous page's discussion of white-flowered varieties while focusing on their medicinal properties and geographical locations.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

<meta>Catchword at bottom right: RAN N (indicating Ranunculus)</meta>

### TUBEROUS-ROOTED BUTTERCUP, with a snow-white flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS GRVMOSA RADICE, flore niueo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus plant with a cluster of tuberous roots, several deeply lobed leaves, and two large open flowers with prominent centers.</image-desc>

Here we shall treat the temperament and powers of the Buttercup.

Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> proposes several species of Buttercups, but attributes the same power to all of them: they are acrid and cause severe blistering. Thus *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> says that all Buttercups have a caustic power; if the leaves are applied to the skin, they produce pustules just like fire. And *Galen* <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> likewise established that all Buttercups possess a vehemently acrid power that causes blistering with pain. Medical practitioners and apothecaries <note>original: "Seplasiæ," referring to the famous ointment-sellers of ancient Capua</note> are well aware of their particular uses.

### GREATEST LONG-LEAVED BUTTERCUP, known as Pliny’s Tongue.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS LONGO FOLIO MAXIMVS, Lingua Plinij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Ranunculus plant with long, lance-shaped leaves and several flowers at the ends of branched stems.</image-desc>

In damp soil and marshy places, there emerges the Buttercup thought by Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, a 16th-century French botanist</note> to be the "Tongue" described by Pliny. It has a stem a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> or higher, thick, smooth, and divided here and there into branches. Along the stem and branches, leaves are produced alternately, about a foot long and barely an inch wide, somewhat thick, smooth, and pointed, with an acrid and bitter taste. The flowers sit at the ends of the small branches, having the form and color of other Buttercups. These are followed by hedgehog-like seed-heads <note>original: "Capitula erinacea"</note> the size of a walnut, with sharp prickles. The root is held firm by many fibers.

We have seen this between Worms and Oppenheim <note>Cities in Germany along the Rhine</note> in marshy places and the old ditches of the Rhine.

### RED-FLOWERED FIGWORT, of Camerarius.
<note>original: "SCROPHVLARIA FLORE RVBRO, Camerarij"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scrophularia plant with opposite, serrated leaves and a tall spike of small, dark flowers.</image-desc>

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German botanist</note> records another Figwort "without scrofulae" <note>referring to the lack of tuberous nodules on the roots</note>; he says it is similar to the common variety in its small flowers and leaves, though more elegant, and that it agrees with it in almost all other respects, propagating itself spontaneously every year.

Furthermore, Figwort is of a hot and dry nature; therefore, it dries out, thins, disperses, and cleanses, for it is bitter to the taste and composed of fine parts. For this reason, it is said to be beneficial for hard glandular tumors, which the Greeks call <term>choiradas</term> <note>original: "χοιράδας" — glandular swellings in the neck</note> and the Latins call *strumas* or *scrophulas*. Indeed, there is a common opinion that it is very effective against these ailments whether hung around the neck or otherwise carried.

<column-break/>

### LONG-LEAVED BUTTERCUP, called Spearwort.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS LONGIFOLIVS, FLAMMVLA dictus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Ranunculus (Spearwort) with narrow leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

The stem is nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantali"</note>, smooth, hollow, and knotted at the joints; it is sometimes solitary and sometimes divided into branches. The first leaves grow from long stalks and are half an inch wide; some are oblong, others somewhat round. The upper leaves grow in pairs from the joints of the stems and are occasionally serrated. The flowers are like those of the common meadow Buttercup but more compact, with a golden luster. The root is composed of whitish fibers.

It takes the name *Flammula* <note>Little Flame</note>, or "Fire Herb," from its excessively burning heat.

It grows in marshes and damp places, flowering in May and June. It is abundant at Geneva around St. Gervais, in the form depicted here.

### GRASSY BUTTERCUP with a full flower.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS GRAMINEVS PLENO flore"</note>
**German: Double-flowered Great Buttercup.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus with grass-like leaves and a very full, multi-petaled (double) flower.</image-desc>

Lobelius calls it the "Many-flowered Grassy Buttercup" in his *Images of Plants*. Tabernaemontanus calls it the "Multiple, many-flowered, or Garland Buttercup." Caspar Bauhin calls it the "Grassy Buttercup with multiple flowers" in his *Phytopinax*. The illustration is by Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note>, who applies the description to it that actually fits another plant. It is cultivated in gardens.

### GREAT YELLOW FIGWORT with large leaves.
<note>original: "SCROPHVLARIA MAGNA LVTEA amplis foliis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust Scrophularia plant with large, broad leaves and a dense floral spike.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius, a pioneering botanist</note> observed this in the more cultivated gardens of Vienna, Austria. We ourselves have kept it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Prince <note>original: "in S. P. horto"</note>, where it flowers in April and May, renewing itself from seed every year.

Furthermore, the common Figwort, which we shall discuss shortly, is generally given the title of "Greater Figwort" to distinguish it from the "Lesser," which is called *Fabaria* or *Lesser Celandine*. Whether it is truly the same as *Galeopsis* <note>Hemp-nettle</note>, as some have thought, we shall examine in the Appendix.

Moreover, the reader should know that the last two figures on this page belong to the end of the page immediately following; they were misplaced due to an error in layout during the author's absence.

It includes botanical observations from regions like the Rhine and Geneva, and notes a printing error regarding the placement of illustrations.</summary>

->IMAGES AND OUTLINES<-

### AUTUMN BUTTERCUP, with a broad, round, serrated leaf.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS AVTVMNALIS, FOLIO lato, rotundo, serrato"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus autumnalis showing a basal rosette of rounded, serrated leaves and a single flowering stalk with a bulbous base and a five-petaled flower.</image-desc>

Lobelius and Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a 16th-century herbalist</note> record this as the Portuguese Buttercup, or the Autumn Buttercup of Clusius.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, one of the most influential botanists of the Renaissance</note> states that it is common around Lisbon <note>original: "Olyssiponem"</note> among olive groves and in the fertile regions of Andalusia <note>original: "Baeticae," a Roman province in southern Spain</note>, and that it produces flowers in October and November. In Belgium, it blooms in gardens even in the middle of winter, according to the testimony of Lobelius. Clusius also writes that it is called "Monte" by some in Portugal.

### NARROW-LEAVED BULBOUS BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS ANGVSTIFOLIVS BVLBOSVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Ranunculus angustifolius bulbosus featuring long, narrow leaves and a distinct bulbous root structure with a single flower.</image-desc>

Dalechamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps, a French physician and botanist</note> judges that this plant, though not mentioned by the ancient authors, should be numbered among the Buttercups because of its taste and the form of its flowers and roots.

It is rarely encountered, except on the mountains of Our Lady of Montserrat <note>A mountain range near Barcelona</note>, where it is very common near thickets and oak groves.

Caspar Bauhin, in his *Pinax* <note>term: Pinax <gloss>an influential botanical index published in 1623</gloss></note>, records it as the "Bulbous buttercup with a grass-like leaf." In his *Phytopinax*, he calls it the "Long-leaved mountain buttercup."

### FIGWORT: German: <unclear>Braunwurtz</unclear>, <unclear>Scrophulartz</unclear>: French: *Scrofulaire*: Italian: *Scrofularia*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scrophularia plant with broad, serrated leaves and a tall inflorescence of small flowers.</image-desc>

The root grows obliquely; it is white, somewhat thick, and lumpy with irregular swellings <note>original: "strumosa," referring to lumpy growths resembling scrofula</note>. The stem is firm, upright, square, hollow, and purplish, reaching three feet in height <note>original: "bicubitalis," meaning two cubits</note> and divided into branches. The leaves are like those of the Hemp-nettle <note>original: "Galeopsis"</note>, but larger, pointed, and saw-toothed; they grow opposite one another from the joints of the stem and are dark green. Many flowers hang from hairy stalks; they resemble those of the smallest Snapdragon <note>original: "Anthirrhini"</note>, shaped like a gaping mouth, and are dark purple mixed with a pale green color. A small green style protrudes from the mouth, along with other hidden, twisting stamens tipped with ochre-colored points.

Among the various species of Figwort <note>original: "Scrophulariæ"</note>, we illustrate here the one called "The Greater." It usually grows in woods and along the edges of fields, blooming in July and August. It is common everywhere in Basel, Geneva, and Lyon.

<column-break/>

### BLISTERED PORTUGUESE BUTTERCUP.
<note>original: "RANVNCVLVS LVSITANICVS bullatus"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ranunculus lusitanicus bullatus showing broad, textured (bullate) leaves and a flowering stem.</image-desc>

This elegant kind of Buttercup was brought from Portugal through the efforts of Clusius, and was first displayed by Lobelius under the name "Portuguese Buttercup of Clusius."

In Caspar Bauhin’s *Pinax*, it is called the "Buttercup with an Asphodel root and a large flower."

### SMALLEST BUTTERCUP WITH GRASS-LIKE LEAVES.
<note>original: "RANVNCV. MINIMVS GRAMINEIS FOLIIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Ranunculus with very thin, grass-like leaves and a single small flower.</image-desc>

This is also rarely encountered. However, we have found it in several places in Provence <note>original: "Gallo-Provincia"</note> and Languedoc <note>original: "Gallia Narbonensis"</note>, and especially around Montpellier.

If it is planted in rich and moist soil, it grows out significantly and is beautiful to look at.

### GREATEST LUMPY FIGWORT.
<note>original: "SCROPHVLARIA MAXIMA STRVMOSA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Scrophularia maxima strumosa, a robust plant with large, deeply serrated leaves and a tall, branching flower spike.</image-desc>

With its square stems, it grows to a height of several cubits. Along these stems are leaves like those of the common Figwort or Betony—saw-toothed, blackish, and foul-smelling. The flowers and seed vessels approach the manner of the common Figwort; however, its root is not lumpy, but composed of countless fibers.

Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German physician and botanist</note> records it as the "Smallest Figwort"; Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, known as Tragus</note> calls it the "Greater Water-Basil"; Lobelius and Dodonaeus call it the "British Water-Plant." Could it be the *Clymenum* of Dioscorides?

It grows spontaneously in various places, along the banks of ditches and near flowing waters. We have observed a great deal of it, along with the common variety, in Basel by the river Birs, blooming in July.

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, transitioning from the buttercups (Ranunculus) discussed on previous pages to various species of Scrophularia (Figwort) and Sideritis (Ironwort). It focuses on their physical descriptions, medicinal uses for healing wounds, and the observations of notable Renaissance botanists like Clusius and Bauhin.</meta>

### INDIAN FIGWORT WITH VERY LARGE HEADS; and on the Cretan Figworts of Clusius.
<note>original: "SCROPHVLARIA INDICA CAPITVLIS MAximis; & de Creticis Clusii Scrophulariis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Scrophularia indica plant with broad, serrated leaves and a cluster of large seed pods or flower heads at the top.</image-desc>

We received certain seeds under the name of **Indian Figwort**, the figure of which we provide here. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax* <note>A landmark botanical register published in 1596</note>, calls it the sixth species of Figwort, or the Indian variety, with several joined heads, but four times larger than those in other species.

Furthermore, Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist</note> records and describes two types under the name of **Cretan Figwort**: the first, which grew at Frankfurt from seed received from Crete, under the name of **Wild Rue**; and the second, which he says has the leaf of a **Nettle**.

### THE GROUND-PALM OF PLINY TO SOME.
<note>original: "CHAMÆROPS PLINII QVIBVSDAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Chamærops plant featuring a central stalk with pairs of pointed leaves and small flowers or fruits emerging from the leaf axils.</image-desc>

It has a thick and multiple root; many stems a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>; leaves like those of the **Myrtle**, growing in pairs around the stem. The flowers are numerous, rising from the armpits of the leaves, followed by seed in oblong vessels. Thus the *History of Plants of Lyon* <note>The "Historia Generalis Plantarum" (1586) by Jacques Daléchamps</note> describes and illustrates it, though no place of origin is recorded. We frankly confess that we have not seen it; and perhaps not without reason, one might wonder with Caspar Bauhin what plant this might actually be?

### IRONWORT OF MONTPELLIER.
<note>original: "SIDERITIS MONSPESSVLANA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sideritis monspessulana, showing a plant with whorled leaves and small flowers arranged in spikes at the nodes.</image-desc>

The **Common Ironwort** illustrated previously sends up stems from a woody root that are one to two feet high, square, hairy, and of a yellowish-green color. At the joints, the leaves come out opposite one another; they are wrinkled, hairy, four to six inches long, about half an inch wide, and notched around the edges. The flowers, arranged in whorls, embrace the joints; they are helmet-shaped, yellowish-white, with the "lip" spotted with blood-red dots, emerging from hairy calyxes that end in five pointed segments. Each flower leaves behind four seeds.

In the **Montpellier** variety, which we illustrate here, the leaves are shorter, rounder, and more hairy, and the flowers are a yellowish-white.

<column-break/>

### FINE-LEAVED FIGWORT, called Dog's Rue by some.
<note>original: "SCROPHVLARIA TENVIFOLIA, RVTA Canina quibusdam dicta"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Scrophularia tenuifolia, showing a tall plant with deeply laciniated, thin leaves and small flowers on a terminal spike.</image-desc>

It has a long, simple root of moderate thickness. The stems are a cubit high, grooved, rounded, almost blackish, filled with a spongy marrow, and branched. Upon these are oblong, narrow leaves, deeply jagged <note>laciniated</note>, and heavily scented. The flowers are arranged in the same order as in the **Great Common Figwort**, but more numerous, black, and small; these are followed by seed vessels like those of the **Lesser Figwort**, pointed, and gaping open into two cavities.

Lobelius and Clusius call it **Dog's Rue**; Caesalpinus and Camerarius call it **Ironwort**. Could it be the *Herba mora* of the Italians mentioned in the *History of Lyon*?

### IRONWORT: German: *Wundkraut*; French: *Espece de Terrait*; Italian: *Sideritide*.
<note>original: "SIDERITIS: Germ. Vvundkraut: Gall. Espece de Terrait: Italis Sideritide"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sideritis species with upright stems and small flowers clustered in the upper leaf axils.</image-desc>

The Ancients distinguished plants with the notable name of **Ironwort** <note>Sideritis</note> if they recognized them as fit for "gluing" together wounds made by iron. This is based on the origin of the Greek name: namely, that <foreign language="Greek">Σιδηρῖτις</foreign> is so called <foreign language="Greek">ἀπὸ τοῦ σιδήρου</foreign>, that is, "from iron" <note>original: "Sideritis apo tou siderou"</note>. Thus the Latins called it the **Iron-Solderer** <note>original: "Ferruminatricem"</note>.

However, since there are very many plants—some quite notable and of different genera—that promise help to parts wounded by iron, we shall describe here only those which, in the opinion of both the Ancients and Moderns, seem to belong properly to this category.

### PANNONIAN IRONWORT, with dark flowers barely protruding from the seed-vessels.
<note>original: "SIDERITIS PANNONICA, FLOSCVLIS VIX ex vasculis prominentibus, fuscis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sideritis pannonica, showing a leafy plant with small flowers tucked into the leaf bases.</image-desc>

We obtained this Ironwort, never seen before, from the plants of Dr. Agerius. He said it was very common in the fields of **Pannonia** <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria</note> and Lower Austria, growing among the crops in lean and dry soil, blooming in June and July.

The **Common Ironwort**, according to Clusius, grows everywhere in France, Germany, Pannonia, and other European regions, along the drier edges of fields and cleared woods, and on sunny hills facing the midday sun. Lobelius writes that it is also found in the coastal and mountainous regions of Italy, Insubria <note>modern Milan/Lombardy</note>, and the Lido of Venice.

It usually blooms in June and July.

<summary>This page describes various species of Figwort (Scrophularia) and Ironwort (Sideritis), detailing their physical characteristics, their naming by various Renaissance botanists, and their traditional medicinal role in treating wounds caused by iron weapons.</summary>
<keywords>Figwort, Ironwort, Scrophularia, Sideritis, wound healing, Pannonia, Montpellier, Clusius, Bauhin, Lobelius, medicinal plants, botany</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of plants categorized as Ironworts (Sideritis) and Self-heals (Prunella), focusing on their physical characteristics, geographical distribution (particularly around Basel and Montbéliard), and medicinal applications for wound healing and other ailments.</meta>

### SMOOTH FIELD IRONWORT
<note>original: "SIDERITIS GLABRA ARVENSIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sideritis glabra arvensis, showing a plant with upright stems, opposite serrated leaves, and small flower clusters at the nodes.</image-desc>

This plant resembles common Ironwort, both in its square stem and in the similar placement and serration of the leaves. However, in this species, both the stem and leaves are smooth <note>original: "glabra"</note> and shine with a greenish-gold luster, and the leaves are also broader. The whorls of flowers <note>clusters of flowers encircling the stem</note>, shaped like an open mouth in a spike, have two "claws" <note>bracts or small leaf-like structures</note> beneath them. The flowers are larger, of a snowy whiteness, and are occasionally hairy, as is the calyx <note>the green outer protective layer of the flower</note>. The root is simple and slender.

We have seen it frequently in the fields around Basel, and also in Montbéliard between the villages of *Arbouans* and *Audincourt*. It blooms in July and August.

<column-break/>

### SHORT-SPIKED IRONWORT
<note>original: "SIDERITIS BREVI SPICA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Sideritis brevi spica, featuring a plant with broader, hairy leaves and dense flower spikes at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

Valerandus Dourez <note>a 16th-century physician and plant collector</note>, from whom we obtained this, titled it "Short-spiked Ironwort"; but since he sent it dried, we can say nothing of its color. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, the *History of Lyon*, and Caspar Bauhin record it as "Mountain Ironwort."

Regarding the virtues of the Ironworts, we will briefly summarize those from the Ancient and more recent authors. It dries powerfully, is somewhat fragrant with a notable astringency, possesses a pleasant taste, and is naturally suited for treating wounds. The itinerant healers <note>original: "Cursores Empirici"</note> even use these to treat intestinal hernias and white discharge <note>original: "alba menstrua," likely leukorrhea</note>. Others wash the forehead with a decoction of it for persistent headaches; still others claim that tired feet or other stiff limbs are usefully bathed in the same decoction.

---

### IRONWORT SPECIES WITH SPINY WHORLS
<note>original: "SIDERITIS GENVS SPINOSIS VERTICILLIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sideritis species with spiny whorls, showing elongated leaves and distinct prickly floral clusters.</image-desc>

We believe this plant should be numbered among the Ironworts. It has a square, hairy stem, and at each node, flowers grow in a whorl around it. These are similar to the flowers of common Ironwort—white and gaping—though they do not protrude as much. The calyxes are loose and hard, divided into five rigid, spiny segments <note>original: "lacinias"</note>, of which the uppermost is by far the largest. Furthermore, from the base to the very top of each whorl, leaves grow in opposite pairs; these are covered in hair and serrated like Germander <note>original: "Teucrii"</note>, but are somewhat longer and narrower.

It is found near the city of Rome.

More regarding Ironworts can be found in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### SELF-HEAL or BRUNELLA: Germ. Braunellin, Fr. Carpenter’s Herb, Ital. Prunella.
<note>original: "PRVNELLA siue BRVNELLA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Prunella (Self-heal), showing the characteristic square stem, ovate leaves, and a dense, cylindrical terminal flower spike.</image-desc>

We here illustrate the common small-flowered Self-heal, which occasionally takes root from the low-hanging fibers of its square, somewhat hairy, and purplish stems. The leaves are generally in pairs, opposite at the joints; they are somewhat reddish and hairy, similar to common Oregano. The flowers are arranged in whorled, hooded clusters, always with two reddish hairy leaves beneath them, forming a spike. They are blue-purplish in color, not unlike the flowers of Dead-nettle <note>original: "Lamii"</note>, emerging from a calyx that is likewise hairy and purplish.

It is found everywhere in meadows and on hills, especially near flowing water, and it blooms in Summer.

---

### TINY SELF-HEAL
<note>original: "PRVNELLA MINIMA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Prunella species, showing a more delicate habit and smaller leaves.</image-desc>

Some record this as the **Lesser Comfrey** or **Smallest Comfrey**; some as the *Polycnemon* of Dioscorides; others as the *Peristereon* of Prepositius; and Melchior Guillandinus calls it **British plant**.

It is abundant in various places around Basel, within the city, around Mount *Krentzach*, and also by the river *Birse*. We observed it blooming in Lyon and Montpellier in May; and in Montbéliard in the meadows during June, July, and August.

The common Self-heal is found everywhere in the drier meadows of various European provinces, where it grows luxuriantly and blooms in Summer.

<column-break/>

### LARGE PURPLE-FLOWERED SELF-HEAL, with fringed leaves.
<note>original: "PRVNELLA FLORE MAGNO PVRPVREO, foliis laciniatis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Prunella species with large flowers and deeply lobed (laciniate) leaves.</image-desc>

The stem is a palm’s breadth high <note>about 3-4 inches</note> and hairy. Each joint is adorned with two leaves placed opposite one another; the lower leaves rest on a one-inch stalk, while the upper ones have a proportionally smaller stalk, or none at all. They are nearly an inch and a half long, somewhat hairy, and cut into opposing segments <note>original: "lacinias"</note>. Large, purple, wide-gaping flowers emerge from between the scaly, reddish leaves of the spike.

A variety of this genus with non-fringed leaves is also found; we observed both types in Montbéliard on the hill of *Le Chau*, and between the bridge of *Vouaucourt* and *Dampierre*.

<summary>This page describes various species of Sideritis (Ironwort) and Prunella (Self-heal), detailing their physical forms, medicinal uses for healing wounds and headaches, and their specific locations in Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Ironwort, Self-heal, Sideritis, Prunella, wound healing, Basel, Montbéliard, botanical descriptions, herbal medicine</keywords>

--- Page 554 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog from the previous discussion of Ironworts, now transitioning into the various species of Self-heal (Prunella) and Middle Comfrey (Bugula/Consolida Media), detailing their physical forms, habitats, and medicinal uses for throat ailments and internal injuries.</meta>

### SMALL WHITE-FLOWERED SELF-HEAL, 
### with leaves deeply divided in the middle of the stems.
<note>original: "PRVNELLA FLORE ALBO PARVO, FO- liis in mediis caulibus profundè dissectis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Prunella plant with white flowers and deeply lobed middle leaves, showing the root system, stem, and flowering spikes.</image-desc>

This plant delights in grassy and herb-filled places, sometimes flooded by rivers, and is accustomed to blooming in May and June.

Furthermore, Brunfels <note>Otto Brunfels, a pioneer of German botany</note> judged the Self-heal <note>original: "Prunellam"</note> to be of the genus of *Solidago* <note>wound-healing plants</note>, because Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli</note> calls it both the "Apothecary's Comfrey" and "Solidago." Camerarius asserts that it was described in the book *On Powers* <note>original: "Lib. de dynam."</note> which was falsely attributed to Galen. The *Herbarium of Cuba* <note>referring to the "Hortus Sanitatis" edited by Johannes de Cuba</note> cites Hippocrates and Dioscorides regarding this plant, but neither of those ancient authors indicates what they named it. Thus, whether this plant was known to the Ancients or not is not sufficiently clear.

### MIDDLE COMFREY, MIDDLE SYMPHYTUM, 
### BUGLE: German: Gunzel; French: Middle Comfrey.
<note>original: "CONSOLIDA MEDIA, SYMPHYTVM MEDIVM, BVGVLA: Germ. Gunzel: Gall. Consyre moyenne."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Consolida Media (Bugula), showing a central flowering stalk with opposite leaves and a fibrous root.</image-desc>

More recent authors divide the types of Comfrey <note>original: "Symphytorum & Consolidarum"</note> into three main classes: Great, Middle, and Small. There are three "Great" Comfreys: the Alum (or Common Great Comfrey), the Tuberous, and the Spotted. There are likewise three "Middle" types: the Rock-dwelling, the Bugle, and the Self-heal. There are many "Small" types, such as the Daisies <note>original: "Bellides"</note>, of which many varieties are recorded. These were discussed previously in Class 16; the Great Comfreys will be discussed later in Class 21. Here, we shall deal with the Middle types.

We present two illustrations from Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs</note> here, not because we are unaware that they are of the same plant, but because they demonstrate the following variety and the playfulness of Nature.

### GENEVAN MIDDLE COMFREY.
<note>original: "CONSOLIDA MEDIA GENEVENSIS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Geneva variety of Consolida Media, featuring multiple flowering stalks rising from a single root base.</image-desc>

This variety appears different from the common one. It has multiple stems from a single root, which are hairier; the leaves are smaller and oblong, and the lower ones are more deeply notched <note>original: "crenata"</note>. The flowers are sometimes purple, sometimes reddish, and sometimes white.

In Geneva, it blooms around the Infirmary <note>original: "Nosodochiū"</note> in March and April.

The common Middle Comfrey, however, loves rocky places, and is also sometimes found in wetter meadows, sunny spots, and open paths; it is familiar to many regions of Europe. When moved to gardens, it grows luxuriantly. It blooms in May and June. The meadows of Yverdon <note>original: "Eburodunensium"</note> above the mill at the river support it in abundance.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED SELF-HEAL, 
### stiff and entire.
<note>original: "PRVNELLA FOLIO ANGVSTO, rigido, integro."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leaved Prunella with a rigid, upright habit and dense flowering heads.</image-desc>

We will record the virtues of the Self-heal <note>original: "Prunellæ"</note> in general here. Fuchs concludes from its taste that it is hot and dry. It is praised as a wash or lotion for gunshot wounds <note>original: "felopetorum [sclopetorum] vulnera"</note>. Its juice heals canker sores and ulcers of the mouth. It is universally acknowledged to be of exceptional power for extinguishing the "heat" or inflammation of the tongue, throat, and jaws (which the Germans call "the Browns" <note>original: "die Bräune", an old term for quinsy or tonsillitis</note>), if the area is rinsed and gargled with its decoction or distilled water. Practitioners also prescribe its water mixed with vinegar and rose oil to soothe violent headaches.

### ANOTHER ILLUSTRATION OF MIDDLE COMFREY.
<note>original: "CONSOLIDA MEDIA ALIA ICON"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another form of Consolida Media, showing detailed leaf structure and floral arrangement on the stalk.</image-desc>

It rises with a square, hollow, hairy, and somewhat bluish stem. The leaves are like those of the Great Water Pimpernel, somewhat serrated, born in opposite pairs at intervals. The flowers sit in the armpits <note>axils</note> of the leaves on a stalkless, short, hairy, bluish, five-parted calyx. They are mostly blue, though sometimes white or ash-colored, dividing into four fragments: two longer ones at the sides and two smaller but wider ones at the bottom. They have no "hood" <note>galea</note> like the Dead-nettle <note>original: "Lamia"</note>, and the tips and style are blue. The root is slender and fibrous, with an astringent taste.

### BLUE ALPINE MIDDLE COMFREY 
### of Caspar Bauhin.
<note>original: "CONSOLIDA MEDIA COERVLEA ALPINA Caspari Bauhini."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Alpine blue Consolida Media, showing a robust flowering spike and broad basal leaves.</image-desc>

Middle Comfrey possesses a certain warmth, but its effectiveness is clearly combined with some astringency. The Ancients did not mention it. According to the opinion of more recent authors, Self-heal and Bugle are wonderfully useful for internal ruptures, fractures, and wounds. Therefore, they are usefully given as a drink to those who have fallen from a height, and to those who have received internal wounds, which they heal miraculously. They dissolve and clear away blood clots that have hardened in the stomach or other parts. They are held in such high regard among the French that a common proverb is circulated among them: "He who has Bugle and Sanicle needs neither doctor nor surgeon."

<summary>This page describes various species of Self-heal and Middle Comfrey, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe (specifically Geneva and Yverdon), and their vital role in treating throat infections, headaches, and internal traumatic injuries.</summary>
<keywords>Self-heal, Prunella, Middle Comfrey, Bugle, medicinal herbs, wound healing, throat inflammation, Leonhart Fuchs, Caspar Bauhin, Geneva, botany, astringent</keywords>
