<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, moving from various species of Self-heal and Comfrey to other medicinal herbs used for eye ailments, fevers, and wound healing, specifically focusing on Eyebright, Coris, and Gratiola.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### EYEBRIGHT: German: Eye-service; Belgian: Eye-comfort; French: Eyebright; Italian: Eyebright.
<note>original: "EVPHRASIA: Germ. Augendienst: Belg. Oghen trost: Gall. Eufraise: Ital. Eufragia."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Euphrasia plant, showing its upright stem, small serrated leaves, and delicate flowers, with a detailed view of the root system.</image-desc>

Eyebright is commonly established as being of two kinds, the white and the purple; among these is also the *Coris* of Montpellier mentioned by Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note>.

The Eyebright is a small plant about a hand’s breadth in height, rising with thin, slightly hairy little stalks. The leaves are small and notched like those of Germander <note>a low-growing herb of the mint family</note>, but three times larger, curled, and hairy on the underside. They are placed in pairs opposite each other, and from their "wings" <note>the axils where the leaf meets the stem</note> spring beautiful little flowers, milky-white in color and painted with purple-streaked lines, sprinkled with a bit of downy fuzz. The "lip" of the flower is divided into three two-cleft segments, and the upper leaf is bent backward and divided into three parts. The root is thin and woody.

It grows in grassy places, meadows, along paths, and at the edges of fields; it blooms in the summer. More information is found in the Appendix.

### PURPLE MONTPELLIER CORIS.
<note>original: "CORIS MONSPESSVLANA PVRPVREA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Coris Monspessulana Purpurea, featuring a woody base, numerous small leaves along the stems, and clusters of flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacology</note> mentions the Coris when he says: "Coris, which some call *Hypericum* <note>St. John's Wort</note>, has leaves like Heather," etc. According to Galen <note>the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note>, Hippocrates <note>the famous Greek physician</note> called it *Coren* because of its seed, which has a resemblance to the pupil of the eye. Thus, modern writers also have their own Coris, which they label "of Montpellier," and they assert it matches the description of the Greek Coris in many details. However, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish botanist</note> refers it to the Heather class and says its nature is somewhat between *Hypericum* and *Ajuga* <note>Bugleweed</note>. Others wish it to be "Rock Comfrey." Writers distinguish two types: the purple, which we depict here, and the yellow, which follows.

### FEVERWORT, or TERZOLLA, by others called HOODED SKULLCAP: German: Fever-herb.
<note>original: "TERTIONARIA, siue TERZOLLA, ALIIS LYSImachia galericulata: Germ. Fieberkraut."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Tertionaria plant, showing square stems, opposite serrated leaves, and hooded flowers (galericulata).</image-desc>

It has short, square, somewhat stiff, jointed stems, divided into many branches. The leaves arise at the joints in opposite pairs, mimicking those of Betony but smaller, just as wrinkled, and more sparsely serrated around the edges, with a notably bitter taste. From the leaf-axils, the flowers spring forth with an upright little tube; they are a faint pale-greenish color, with the lower lip painted with darker little spots, emerging from a short, rounded calyx <note>the protective cup of the flower</note>. The thin root creeps along.

It delights in watery and marshy places, and on the banks of streams descending from mountains. It blooms in June and July. In the region of Montbéliard, it is found in the meadows of Scuchaux. Its use is for treating fevers.

<column-break/>

### GRATIOLA, or GRACE OF GOD: German, French, & Italian: Gratiola.
<note>original: "GRATIOLA, GRATIA DEI"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Gratiola plant, showing creeping roots, upright stems with opposite leaves, and tubular flowers.</image-desc>

The roots of this plant grow luxuriously, being as thick as a goose quill, creeping obliquely, white, and knotted with frequent joints from which many white fibers hang down. There are several stems, about nine inches high, reddish near the ground and greenish-white above, marked by frequent joints. At each joint, two leaves grow, smaller than those of Soapwort <note>a plant used for making soap</note> and somewhat notched around the edge. From their axils grow either little shoots with very small un-notched Hyssop-like leaves, or single, streaked, oblong flowers, partly yellow and partly white, hanging on a half-inch stalk from a five-parted calyx. These are eventually followed by a seedpod that is rounded-oblong, containing tiny seeds. More information is found in the Appendix.

### YELLOW MONTPELLIER CORIS.
<note>original: "CORIS MONSPESSVLANA LVTEA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Coris Monspessulana Lutea, showing a similar structure to the purple variety but with distinct floral arrangements.</image-desc>

Its root is simple and woody. The stem is solitary, about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, woody and round, divided into opposite, hard, woody branches. The lower leaves are similar to Hyssop leaves, but narrower, pointed, and falling off early; the upper leaves are thin, mimicking tree heather. The branches bear long spikes of gaping yellow flowers with many tips, with a small leaf situated under each flower. Sometimes the stems and leaves are entirely red.

We saw this in Montpellier on the mountain near Castelneuf in a rocky place, blooming in August.

The purple variety grows in the coastal regions of Narbonne, France.

### ROCK COMFREY.
<note>original: "SYMPHYTVM PETRÆVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Symphytum Petraeum, showing a low-growing plant with small leaves and clusters of flowers, emerging from a thick root.</image-desc>

Many plants are given the name "Rock Comfrey," such as Sanicle, Self-heal, Goldenrod, Montpellier Coris, common Hyssop, common mountain Germander, Throatwort, and some species of Comfrey, etc. Regarding the true Rock Comfrey, Dioscorides writes as follows: "Rock Comfrey," he says, "grows on rocks; it has branches similar to Oregano, with heads like Thyme. The whole plant is woody, fragrant, and sweet to the taste, and it provokes saliva. It stands on a long, yellowish root, a finger's thickness." He recommends it for lung diseases, spitting of blood, dysentery, and many other ailments. He also asserts that if it is added to meats while they are cooking, it will glue them back together <note>a common historical claim for the *Symphytum* genus, whose name comes from the Greek word "to unite"</note>.

<summary>This page describes various medicinal plants, primarily Eyebright (used for vision), Coris, Feverwort, and Gratiola, detailing their physical appearances, habitats, and historical botanical classifications.</summary>
<keywords>Eyebright, Euphrasia, Coris, Gratiola, Skullcap, Rock Comfrey, Dioscorides, medicinal herbs, botany, Renaissance science</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### YELLOW RATTLE: German: Red rattle; French: Cock’s Comb; Italian: Cock’s comb.
<note>original: "CRISTA GALLI: Germ. Reel rodel: Gall. Creste de Coq: Ital. Cresta di gallo."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with serrated leaves and hooded flowers, identified as Crista Galli (Yellow Rattle).</image-desc>

We know of no one besides Caspar Bauhin <note>a famous Swiss botanist who categorized thousands of plants</note> who has observed the six kinds or varieties of Yellow Rattle. It varies in the size and length of its leaves, the number of stems, the color of its flowers and seeds, and even in its sex. The leaves are either longer and wider, or small and narrow; the stems are more or fewer; the flowers are most often yellow, and occasionally white; the seed is either black or yellowish. Finally, it is identified as either Male or Female.

We depict here the **Female Yellow Rattle**, which has a less robust stem, narrower leaves, and much smaller flowers than the Male (which we shall describe shortly), and with tips that are less white.

It grows everywhere in fields, as well as in drier meadows, and blooms throughout the entire summer.

### MALE YELLOW RATTLE.
<note>original: "CRISTA GALLI MAS."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller, more robust version of the Crista Galli plant with larger flower heads.</image-desc>

The root is small; the stem is a foot or a foot and a half high, upright, thin, square, hollow, and divided into several branches. These branches are always surrounded by pairs of leaves placed opposite each other without stalks. The leaves are somewhat wide at the base, gradually tapering to a point, and sharply notched <term>crenated (scalloped or notched edges)</term> like a cock’s comb. Around the top of the plant, they are whiter than in the Female variety. At the top of the branches or the stem, flowers emerge from the "wings" <note>the leaf axils</note> along with a flattened, hairy, and jagged little pod. From this pod, the flowers protrude in a way that resembles a clucking and brooding hen; the upper petal forms a yellow cock’s head with a blue beak. More details appear at the side of the following figure, marked with this symbol. †

<column-break/>

### A PLANT RELATED TO YELLOW RATTLE, or Great Italian Yellow Rattle.
<note>original: "CRISTA GALLI AFFINIS PLANTA Romans, siue Crista Galli maior Italica."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to Yellow Rattle but with broader, more deeply serrated leaves.</image-desc>

We have observed this plant growing abundantly around Rome, blooming in May.

† To continue the description begun a little earlier: within that blue "beak," four hairy tips are hidden, spreading out into two jagged parts. The lower leaf (or petal) is a deeper saffron-yellow and ends in three segments, spotted with black marks. The small, leaf-like pouches, which bulge slightly, contain hairy, membrane-like, and translucent seed vessels. In these, the seed is dark, round, flattened, and curved, with a membrane-like border. It grows in the same places as the Female Yellow Rattle and blooms at the same time. These plants have no known medicinal use.

### LOUSEWORT, CALLED BY SOME YELLOW RATTLE: German: Louse-herb; French: Louse-herb.
<note>original: "PEDICVLARIS, QVIBVSDAM CRISTA GALLI: Germ. Leuskraut: Gall. l'Herbe aux poux."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pedicularis plant with finely divided, fern-like leaves and a spike of hooded flowers.</image-desc>

We depict here the Greater Lousewort of Jacques Daléchamps <note>a French physician and botanist</note>, which he described as follows: It is related to the thorny Dropwort <note>Filipendula</note>, he says, with a root that is black on the outside, tapering like a turnip, wrinkled, and somewhat forked. The stem is nearly a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, wand-like, and single. The leaves are like those of a Fern, arranged in order on a long stalk and notched along the edges; each leaf-stalk emerges alternately along the main stem. The flower is pale, clustered in a spike at the top of the stem; the seeds are finally produced in abundance, enclosed in wide, bark-like vessels, similar to those of Madwort <note>Alyssum</note>.

It grows on the summit of the "Golden Mountain" <note>Mont d'Or</note>, not far from Lyon. We also obtained specimens from Nîmes.

### LOUSEWORT, CALLED BY SOME YELLOW RATTLE, with red and white flowers.
<note>original: "PEDICVLARIS, QVIBVSDAM CRISTA GALLI, flore rubro & albo."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pedicularis variety with dense foliage and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Some believe this is the *Alectorolophon* <note>Greek for "Cock's crest"</note> mentioned by Pliny. Carolus Clusius <note>a Flemish botanist</note> asserts it is called *Fistularia* <note>Pipe-plant</note> because of the hollowness of the stem. The name *Pedicularis* (Lousewort) was earned from its effect: not because it is an enemy to lice, as some believe, but because it causes a great abundance of lice to grow on the sheep and beasts of burden that graze in the meadows where it grows.

It grows in boggy meadows and is counted among the "vices" or weeds of the fields, nor is it useful for anything. We saw it with purple and white flowers in the meadows near the Arve river in Geneva, and also in the watery meadows of Montbéliard and elsewhere, as well as in Michelfelden near Basel.

### BULBOUS LOUSEWORT.
<note>original: "PEDICVLARIS BVLBOSA."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bulbous Pedicularis with thick, fleshy roots and a dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

It puts forth many stems, a foot high and hollow; at their peaks are many flowers clustered together, hooded, and larger than those of the common Lousewort. Many leaves emerge directly from the root on stalks a palm’s length long; they are pinnate <note>resembling a feather</note> with the divisions of a Dropwort. Few leaves grow along the stems, except at the top where the flower spike begins, where they are quite numerous. The roots are many, interwoven with hair-like fibers; they start narrow and gradually swell into bulbs, though they are much smaller than the roots of Dropwort.

It grows on the peaks of the highest mountains, and occasionally also in boggy meadows.

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### ALPINE LOUSEWORT, WITH YELLOW FLOWERS, and a black root.
<note>original: "PEDICVLARIS ALPINA, FLORE LVTEO, radice nigra"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pedicularis alpina plant, showing its serrated leaves, flowering stalk, and thick, dark root system. A small detail of a single flower is shown to the right of the main stem.</image-desc>

In the *History of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugdunensis," a famous 16th-century botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps</note> it is listed under the title Alpine Dropwort. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax*, calls it the "Yellow Alpine plant similar to Water-dropwort or Dropwort."

It grows on the highest peaks of the Alps, in pastures and meadows where the abundance of hay fattens countless flocks and herds.

### CRESTED COW-WHEAT, WITH WHITE or purple FLOWERS, and a yellow throat.
<note>original: "MELAMPYRVM CRISTATVM, FLORE ALBO vel purpureo, cum rictu luteo"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Melampyrum cristatum, featuring a tall stem with opposite linear leaves and a dense, crested floral spike at the apex.</image-desc>

We have seen this between the "Wonderful Bath" <note>likely referring to a specific mineral spring or spa in Germany</note> and Nürtingen. The common variety, however, grows in all provinces in rich soil among the grain crops, flowering and ripening alongside the harvest. There are also those who grow it in gardens for the elegance of its flower.

Furthermore, Dioscorides and Pliny <note>ancient authorities on natural history</note> recorded nothing about Cow-wheat. Theophrastus treated it only briefly and confusingly, and Galen followed his example, having been found to have borrowed his information from him.

### VERVAIN or VERBENA, THE SACRED HERB. German: Iron-herb; French: Vervain; Italian: Verbena.
<note>original: "VERBENA sive VERBENACA, HERBA SACRA: Germ. Eisenkraut: Gall. Vervaine: Ital. Berbenaca."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Verbena officinalis, showing the upright habit, lobed leaves, and slender flowering spikes.</image-desc>

Dioscorides and the Greeks distinguished Verbena into the "Upright" and the "Prostrate" types. Pliny and the Romans called them "Male" and "Female," saying the latter was leafy while the former had fewer leaves.

We have observed several differences, from which we depict the "Common" variety here. It rises with several stems from a single, fibrous, and somewhat bitter root; the stems are longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, square-shaped, slightly hairy, and purplish. The leaves are mostly opposite each other and oblong, notched somewhat like oak leaves, with the bottom two notches being deeper. They are hairy on both sides, but are a deeper green on top than underneath. The tiny flowers on the spikes are five-parted and a pale purplish color.

<column-break/>

### COW-WHEAT, or COW’S WHEAT. German: Black wheat; French: Black wheat, Cow wheat; Italian: Cow-wheat.
<note>original: "MELAMPYRVM, sive TRITICVM VACCINVM: Ger. Mohrenvveitz: Gal. Blé noir, Blé de vache: It. Melapyro."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Melampyrum arvense (Purple Cow-wheat), showing the characteristic long floral bracts and upright growth habit.</image-desc>

The root is woody and a small fibrous thing. From it rises a single stem, square, hairy, purplish, and hollowed out with many "wings" <note>referring to the ridges or side-shoots along the stem</note>. The leaves are placed opposite each other at intervals; some are like Toadflax <note>original: "Linaria"</note>, others are broad and deeply lobed, rough, and dark green. Those at the top of the spike are shorter, broader, finger-like, and tinged with a bright purple. From their armpits <note>the leaf axils</note>, hooded flowers emerge, slightly hairy, with a purplish hood, a yellow lip mixed with red, a deep yellow throat, and the rest of the tube turning purplish. These are followed by two or three seeds in a swollen, oblong pod, smaller and blacker than wheat grains. More on this in the following pages.

### BLUE PELLITORY RELATED TO COW-WHEAT: Called by some the Purple-Violet Cow-wheat.
<note>original: "MELAMPYRO AFFINIS PARIETARIA Cœrulea: Melampyrum purpuro-violaceum quorundam."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a related Melampyrum species, showing a similar structure to the previous entry but with distinct leaf and flower arrangements.</image-desc>

It grows in Hungary, Bohemia, Austria, Moravia, and Germany as well, along hedges and forest edges and in shady places. Because of its remarkable elegance and variety of colors, it is planted in gardens. Some say it heals wounds and dispels bruises.

Common Cow-wheat, however, is a very pleasing food for oxen and cows and is excellent for fattening them, which is why it earned the name "Cow-wheat." But as far as we know, it has found no use in medicine and is generally neglected.

### PROSTRATE VERVAIN or VERBENA.
<note>original: "VERBENA sive VERBENACA SVPINA."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Verbena supina, showing a more prostrate or spreading growth habit compared to the upright Verbena.</image-desc>

This plant has more and thinner stems than the Common variety, and the leaves are even more deeply cut; the flower is also smaller and of a bluish-purple. In other respects, it is similar to the other.

Both types of Vervain grow everywhere along the edges of fields and roads, in city squares, and not infrequently even among ruins. They bloom in the summer months, and sometimes even into autumn.

Both plants have the same medicinal powers: they are moderately astringent and cooling, and very drying. According to Dodoens <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician and botanist</note>, many recommend a decoction or the juice for the plague, while others recommend the powder for dropsy <note>an old term for swelling or edema</note>. More in the following sections and in the Appendix.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions from page 477. After discussing Alpine Lousewort and Cow-wheat, the author moves into the Verbena family (Vervain) and then provides an extensive study of various Nettles (Urtica) and Hemp (Cannabis), including references to newly discovered species in the Americas.</meta>

OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### KNOT-FLOWERED VERVAIN, AND Ever-green Peruvian Vervain.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Verbena plant with serrated leaves and small flower clusters at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

We received this plant from Italy under the name of knot-flowered Vervain <note>original: "Verbenacæ nodifloræ"</note>. Its leaves are like those of Sweet Maudlin <note>original: "Agerati"</note>, arranged opposite each other, about an inch long and shorter, and a little more than a quarter-inch wide. The tiny blossoms, crowded together in a heap, spring from a rounded head clinging to the end of the branch.

Monardes <note>Nicolás Monardes, a Spanish physician famous for his study of medicinal plants from the New World</note> writes that Vervain grows abundantly in *Peru* and is considered by the Indians to be a most effective remedy against <term>love potions</term> <note>original: "Philtra," referring to charms or magical drafts</note>, intestinal worms, and many other ailments.

More regarding the names, various meanings, and virtues of Vervain can be found in the *Appendix*.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COMMON NETTLE: Smaller common Nettle.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common stinging nettle (Urtica) with characteristic jagged leaves and hanging flower catkins.</image-desc>

Besides the differences of the Stinging Nettle <note>original: "Vrentis Vrticæ"</note> proposed previously, there are others: some are Larger, others Smaller; some are more "Wild," which they call the females, and others less so, called the Males, which surpass the others in height.

The *larger common Nettle* described in the preceding table is very well known for its green down, which covers its square, cubit-high <note>about 18 inches</note> stems, as well as its pointed, serrated, dark green or yellowish leaves. It rests on somewhat reddish roots. It brings forth its *flowers* like clusters on small tongues from the "wings" <note>axils</note> of the leaves, resembling a gray down. The seed is extremely small.

The *Smaller* variety, which we depict here, is very similar to the Larger in all respects, but everything is simply smaller, and it stings more fiercely.

### HEMP: German: Hampf; Belgian: Kemp; French: Chanure, Cheneue; Italian: Canape.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cannabis plant showing the distinctive palmate, serrated leaves and fibrous stalks.</image-desc>

Dioscorides distinguishes Hemp into cultivated and wild; Pliny confuses the cultivated with the wild. Galen, however, makes it similar to the Nettle, not only in form but also in its properties.

More recent authors distinguish cultivated Hemp into *Male* and *Female*, or into the Fertile and the Sterile.

It is sown every year in the Spring in fields and gardens; according to Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note>, it requires soil that is rich, dunged, well-watered, and deeply worked. The Female, which we depict here, is shorter than the Male: it brings forth mossy, yellowish flowers that vanish into a fine dust, leaving no seed behind. But the Male, with no preceding flower, bears abundant seed—naked, oily, and arranged along the stems and branches. And this species is suited for the preservation of its kind; the other, however, which matures earlier, is better and more excellent for making cloth. More in the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

### NETTLE, COMMON NETTLE: German: Nessel; Belgian: Netelen; French: Ortie; Italian: Ortica.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall stinging nettle plant with opposite leaves and axillary flower clusters.</image-desc>

Two general differences of Nettles are recorded; one is harmless and can be handled without trouble: *the other* hurts the hands of those touching it, or any other bare parts of the body it hits, with the wicked biting of its leaves and a certain stinging down on its shoots. The former is called *Dead-nettle* <note>original: "Lamium"</note>, idle nettle, or <term>Galeopsis</term> <note>Hemp-nettle</note>, which was treated in the preceding Class. The latter, however, is called by the Greeks sometimes *Acalyphe* and sometimes *Cnide*, and by the Latins the *living* and *stinging nettle*. It is so common in public knowledge that everyone recognizes it very easily, not only by day but even at night, by touch alone.

Dioscorides identifies two kinds of this: one more wild and rough, with broader and darker leaves; and another not as rough.

### ROMAN NETTLE, OR THE MALE, WITH globules.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Roman Nettle (Urtica pilulifera) featuring globular seed heads.</image-desc>

This has the root of a common Nettle, but more rigid stems, endowed with stinging prickles instead of the usual green down; likewise the leaves, which are much more deeply cut than in the common variety. The seed is in stinging, rounded pouches joined in a cluster, rivaling Flax <note>original: "Lini"</note>. The entire plant sometimes exceeds the height of a man.

It is found in dense woods, and sometimes also in hedges and shady places; it flowers in April and May.

The *Common* variety, both the Larger and the Smaller, comes up in uncultivated places. It is more frequent near hedges, houses, and old walls, and sometimes even grows in neglected spots in gardens. It thrives and flowers in summer. *Regarding its powers, see the Appendix.*

### WILD HEMP: German: Vvilder Hanft, Vvilde taub Nessel, Acker Nessel.

According to Dioscorides, it produces stalks similar to Marshmallow <note>original: "Altheæ"</note>, though smaller, darker, thicker, and a cubit long. The leaves are similar to cultivated hemp, but also darker and rougher. The flowers are reddish, similar to Campions <note>original: "Lychnidi"</note>, and the seed and root are like Marshmallow. A decoction of the root, when applied, soothes inflammations, discusses <note>disperses</note> tumors, and dissipates <term>tophi</term> <note>stony deposits or gouty concretions</note> of the joints. The bark of the herb is suitable for twisting into ropes.

Pliny records this regarding Wild Hemp: *Hemp*, he says, first grew in the woods with a darker and rougher leaf; then through cultivation at home, it lost its wildness and became accustomed to the fields, etc. But he fell into a great error: when he had read in Dioscorides that Wild Hemp had stalks like Marshmallow, he carelessly attributed to Hemp what is proper to Marshmallow—namely, the ability to thicken water, etc.

Amatus writes that it grows spontaneously in plowed fields, but he does not describe it. Likewise Matthiolus, who records that it grows in wooded and level areas, does not dare to say he has seen it. Similarly Ruellius, Cordus, and Lactina mention it, but do not record what it is. Tragus and others determine that we do not have Wild Hemp, and that Dioscorides implied some species of the cultivated kind.

There are those who contend that Wild Hemp is the "Marshmallow of the Shops" <note>original: "Alceam Officinarum"</note>; others say it is a white kind of Matthiolus’s other Wild Basil <note>original: "Clinopodii"</note>; others say it is the Hollyhock with Cinquefoil leaves, and others the Yellow Rattle. However, Thomas Hariot <note>an English astronomer and translator who accompanied the 1585 Roanoke expedition</note> is the authority that Hemp grows spontaneously in *Virginia*, but differing from our cultivated kind in its leaves and stem.

<summary>This page catalogs varieties of Vervain, Nettles, and Hemp, distinguishing between cultivated and wild species while noting their physical characteristics and medicinal uses. It features a significant early mention of plants found in the Virginia colony by Thomas Hariot.</summary>

<keywords>Vervain, Nettle, Hemp, Roman Nettle, Wild Hemp, Peru, Virginia, medicinal roots, Thomas Hariot, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, botanical classification</keywords>

### FLAX, in Greek *Linon*: in German *Lein* or *Flachs*: in Dutch *Vlachs*: in French *Lin*: in Italian *Lino*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common flax plant (Linum usitatissimum) showing the slender stem, narrow leaves, and fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist</note> rightly counts Flax among those plants so well known—not only to physicians but also to farmers and all common women—that it seems entirely unnecessary to pursue their history at great length. For this reason, Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose work "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical text for 1,500 years</note> also omitted its physical description, recording only its medicinal powers and uses. The Arabs mention only the seeds, calling the plant *Bizechihitem*, or, as Serapion <note>Referring to the 12th-century physician Serapion the Younger</note> prefers, *Bezirichichen* <note>original: "Bizechihitem" and "Bezirichichen," derived from the Arabic "bazr al-kattan," meaning flaxseed</note>.

Flax is commonly divided into the Cultivated and the Wild types, of which there are again various different kinds, as will be clear from what follows. Regarding the claim written by Theophrastus <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note> that Flax degenerates and turns into <term>Darnel</term> <note>original: "Lolium," a weed often found in grain fields; it was an ancient belief that crops could "transform" into weeds</note>, our local farmers deny that they have ever seen such a thing.

### NARROW-LEAVED WILD FLAX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of narrow-leaved wild flax, showing multiple stems arising from a single root and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

There are various different kinds of Wild Flax. The one we depict here has a woody and quite thick root. It produces many stems that are tough and about a <term>cubit</term> <note>about 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> high; the leaves are streaked, very crowded, very thin, and nearly the same length as those of cultivated Flax. From somewhat long calyxes, the flowers grow in pairs at the ends of the branches; they are large and white, or almost ash-colored, with faint streaks showing through. They are so fragile <note>original: "caduci," literally "falling"</note> that they can scarcely be touched without falling off. The seed-capsules are smaller than those of cultivated Flax and are divided into four parts; within them is the seed, which is likewise similar to the cultivated type but smaller.

It grows naturally in higher grassy areas and alongside roads; it flowers in May and June.

### BROAD-LEAVED WILD FLAX, with yellow flower, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of broad-leaved wild flax with yellow flowers, showing broader lanceolate leaves and clustered floral heads.</image-desc>

This grows abundantly on the mountain overlooking the baths at Baden in Austria, in grassy places along hedges, and in many other locations. It flowers in June and July.

Clusius <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609), an influential Flemish botanist</note> also mentions a hairy, broad-leaved wild flax with a blue flower, and also a downy, broad-leaved wild flax with a white flower streaked with purple lines, which he observed in both <term>Pannonia</term> <note>An ancient province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria</note> and <term>Lusitania</term> <note>An ancient province covering modern-day Portugal</note>.

<column-break/>

### SHRUBBY WILD FLAX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of shrubby wild flax, showing a woodier, more branched base and upright stems with small leaves.</image-desc>

Numerous leaves, between the size of Thyme and <term>Fleawort</term> <note>original: "Psyllii," likely referring to Plantago psyllium</note> and somewhat whitish, adorn the branches, which are nine inches to a foot long and evergreen. The flowers are entirely snow-white, followed by little heads full of seed. The root is hard and woody.

It grows in certain deserted, sun-drenched places in Spain; it flowers in June and July, and shortly after produces seed.

### WHITE NARROW-LEAVED WILD FLAX: with purple lines in the center, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a white-flowered narrow-leaved flax, showing a dense cluster of stems and delicate flowers.</image-desc>

We saw this in Montpellier, flowering in April and September, and near Basel at Krentzach in October. Clusius observed it both in the open areas of the Madrid forest and in the grassy fields of the Vienna countryside.

The same Clusius saw a *shrubby or bush-like Flax with an entirely white flower* in certain deserted and sun-drenched places in Spain.

Among the people of Metz <note>original: "Mediomatrices," the ancient name for the people of the region around Metz, France</note>, whole fields are sown with a wild Flax that clearly resembles the cultivated kind as summer approaches; it is also sometimes found among the oat crops.

### YELLOW NARBONNE FLAX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of yellow Narbonne flax, showing a tall central stem with alternate leaves and terminal flowers.</image-desc>

Several stems a cubit high rise from a single root, dividing into branches at the top. Along these are soft, somewhat broad leaves, shorter than those of cultivated Flax and tasteless. The flowers cling to the ends of the branches; they are like those of common Flax but yellow in color and bitter to the taste. These are followed by little heads smaller than those of cultivated Flax, containing the seed.

It grows not far from the sea in meadows and grassy places in several regions, especially in <term>Gallia Narbonensis</term> <note>An ancient Roman province in what is now Southern France</note>. We saw it at Montpellier, flowering in September. Mattioli writes that it grows everywhere in the territory of Bologna and that it can be drawn out into threads for spinning.

<summary>This page describes various species of Flax (Linum), ranging from the common cultivated variety to wild, shrubby, and yellow-flowered versions found across Europe. It highlights the plant's familiarity to both physicians and common folk, while documenting specific regional varieties identified by botanists like Clusius and Mattioli.</summary>
<keywords>Flax, Linum, botany, medicinal herbs, Mattioli, Clusius, wild flax, Narbonne flax, textile plants, European flora</keywords>

--- Page 560 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Flax family, moving from the common cultivated varieties discussed previously to various wild, dwarf, and annual species identified by contemporary botanists like Clusius, Lobel, and Tragus.</meta>

### DWARF FLAX WITH WHITE OR PALE YELLOW FLOWERS, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small flax plant with thin stems, narrow leaves, and small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

It rises with a small, round stem about nine inches <note>original: "dodrantali," a Roman measurement of about 9 inches or three-quarters of a foot</note> high, or slightly more. Pairs of small leaves always clasp the stem in an opposite arrangement, much like St. John’s Wort <note>original: "Hyperico"</note>, and are nearly equal in size to the leaves of cultivated flax. The top of the stem divides into several small branches which produce tiny flowers on long stalks; these consist of five white petals with little yellow stamens inside. Small seed heads follow the flowers, not unlike the pods of common Flax but smaller, containing the seed. The root is thin and provided with several fibers.

It grows everywhere on the grassy hills of Austria and Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>; it blooms in June and July.

For information on the sowing and use of Flax, consult the Appendix.

### LOBEL’S SPARROW-WORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with many small, narrow leaves clustered along the stem and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

The leaves are crowded along a nine-inch stem, similar to Flax, green, pointed, and an inch long, becoming more sparse toward the top. The flowers are yellow and gathered in clusters on short branch-tips; these are followed by tiny, cone-shaped seed vessels, half or a third the size of common Flax pods, wrapped on all sides by sharp little leaf-like structures. They are full of slippery, dark seeds, much smaller than Flax seeds. The root is quite long, twisted, white, and woody.

### TOADFLAX: in Greek <term>Osyris</term> <note>original: Ὀσύρις</note>: in German <term>Lynkraut</term>: in French <term>Linaire, Wild Flax</term> <note>original: "Lin sauuage"</note>: in Italian <term>Linaria</term>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Linaria (toadflax) plant with dense, narrow leaves and a spiked inflorescence at the top.</image-desc>

There are very many species of the Toadflax herb, the most common of which is pictured here. It so closely mimics the common small Spurge <note>original: "Esulam," referring to plants in the Euphorbia genus</note> that before it flowers, it can only be distinguished from it by its lack of "milk" <note>Spurges produce a milky white sap or latex when broken, while Toadflax does not</note>, hence the verse:

> Spurge yields milk, while Toadflax grows without milk. <note>original: "Esula lactescit, sine Lacte Linaria crescit"</note>

However, error is also prevented by the emerging flowers of the Toadflax, which are arranged in a cluster <note>original: "thyrsum"</note>. In their back part, they sport a small spur like that of the Royal Larkspur <note>original: "Consolidæ regiæ"</note>, while the front resembles a Snapdragon <note>original: "Anthirrhinum"</note>. They are yellow in color with tips of the same hue. The seed is broad and contained in round pods. The root is woody, hard, white, and fibrous.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST FLAX WITH WHITE FLOWERS: also called Smooth Spring Chickweed by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small, delicate plant with multiple thin stems arising from a single root, topped with tiny flowers.</image-desc>

From a thin but somewhat stiff root with many tiny hair-like fibers, it sends out small stems that creep a little at first, then raise themselves a palm's breadth or higher from the ground. The stems are branched and nodding at the top, smooth, thin, jointed, and reddish near the earth. The lowest leaves are almost round, like those of the smaller Chickweed <note>original: "Alsines"</note>, while the upper leaves are a bit longer. The small flowers are bright white, composed of five petals with yellow tips inside. Small channeled pods follow, like those of Flax, in which the bright, slippery Flax-like seeds are conspicuous and oblong.

It blooms in grain fields in Spring and Summer; it is frequent in Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France</note> before the bridge.

### TRAGUS’S SPARROW-WORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems and small, pointed leaves, similar to the Passerina Lobelii but with a different branching habit.</image-desc>

The name "Sparrow’s Tongue" <note>original: "Linguæ passerinæ"</note> was given to this plant because of its pointed leaves, which mimic the tongue of the aforementioned bird. They are arranged alternately (or more rarely, opposite one another) on a stem that is nine inches or taller, straight, smooth, often simple but sometimes branched, and attached without stalks; they have a sticky taste. From the leaf axils, several pale flowers arise, yellowish-green in color, with the edges divided into four segments. The seeds are small, cone-shaped, and black, much smaller than those of Gromwell <note>original: "Lithospermi"</note>.

It grows in various places in the fields, as we have observed in Basel, and in Montbéliard between Taillecourt and Audincourt, and toward the Castle of Mathieu.

### SMALL ANNUAL YELLOW TOADFLAX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small annual Linaria with thin stems and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

This plant has several small, whitish roots. The stems are thin, numerous, and nine inches or half a foot <note>original: "sesquipalmares," literally a palm and a half</note> long. The leaves are thinner, narrower, and thicker than in common Toadflax, of a sea-green <note>original: "glauci"</note> color, growing in groups of three, four, or five at certain intervals; otherwise, they are arranged irregularly and have a slightly bitter taste. The flowers at the tips of the branches are shaped like Toadflax and are Saffron-colored, but four times smaller and without scent. These are followed by small round pods containing small, circular, flattened seeds. The root is thin and annual.

It grows alongside common Toadflax everywhere on hill slopes and along field margins; it grows happily and sturdily in these native spots and in gardens every summer.

<summary>This page describes several wild varieties of Flax and Toadflax, distinguishing them by their flowering patterns, leaf shapes, and lack of milky sap compared to similar-looking spurges. It highlights species identified by famous Renaissance botanists such as Clusius, Lobel, and Tragus.</summary>
<keywords>Dwarf Flax, Sparrow-wort, Toadflax, Linaria, Clusius, Lobel, Tragus, botanical classification, Austrian flora, Montbéliard</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Toadflax (Linaria) family, shifting from the small, white-flowered varieties found in Austria and Pannonia to various yellow and purple species, many of which were cultivated in botanical gardens like the one at Montbéliard.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.

### PANNONIAN TOADFLAX WITH YELLOW FLOWERS, smaller than the common variety.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Linaria pannonica showing a central stalk with narrow leaves, small flowers at the top, and a detailed root system.</image-desc>

It grows on the slopes of mountains, along public roads, and in places bare of grass; it blooms in June and July, and sometimes even in August.

Some contend that Toadflax <note>original: "Linaria"</note> is distinct from the plant *Osyris* <note>A plant mentioned by ancient writers, possibly a species of Toadflax or Broom-yielding plant</note>; however, Tragus, Lobelius, Fuchs, Euricius Cordus, and many other learned men maintain that they are the same plant.

The name *Urinaria* was obtained from its ability to provoke urine <note>A reference to its diuretic properties</note>; the name *Linaria*, however, comes from its leaves, which are seen to resemble the appearance of Flax <note>original: "Lini"</note>.

### THREE-LEAVED, BROAD-LEAVED TOADFLAX, with the yellow flower of common Toadflax, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Linaria trifolia featuring broader, whorled leaves in groups of three and a dense flower spike.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneer of modern botany</note> describes this as Spanish and Valentian, because he found it in shady places in Spain and the Kingdom of Valencia, and nowhere else. It blooms in July and August, and the seeds ripen in September.

Furthermore, the distilled water of Toadflax, when drunk, moves the spirits, relaxes the bowels, dispels the "Royal Disease" <note>original: "morbum regium," a historical term for jaundice</note>, and frees the liver from obstructions; the same water cleanses any ulcers if they are washed with it. The juice possesses the same powers and corrects blemishes of the face.

### A PLANT SOMEWHAT SIMILAR TO TOADFLAX, with leaves like a Daisy.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with basal rosette leaves similar to a daisy (Bellis) and a tall, flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This is placed in the Toadflax class based on the evidence of its seed vessels and upper leaves; however, in its lower leaves, it approaches the Greater Daisy <note>original: "Bellidem maiorem," likely the Ox-eye Daisy</note>. Several stems rise immediately from the root, a cubit high <note>About 18 inches</note>, smooth and round, and very branched. The small flowers emerging from the armpits of the leaves are quite tiny and only slightly open, partly blue and partly white, provided with no spur <note>original: "calcari," the nectar-holding projection at the back of the flower</note>. Other features are as in the common Toadflax.

It is produced in fields that are rough and sunny, in which places we found it between Valencia and Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunum"</note>.

<column-break/>

### LARGEST TOADFLAX WITH LAUREL LEAVES, from Dalmatia.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Linaria maxima showing large, broad leaves resembling laurel and a thick flowering stem.</image-desc>

This plant produces very large leaves, approaching the shape of Willow or Laurel, which become thinner and narrower at the tops of the stems. It has many stems, one or two cubits high, which are branched. The flowers are yellow, the size of the Large Snapdragon <note>original: "Antirrhini maioris"</note>.

It grew for us at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi," a city in eastern France</note> in the Most Serene Prince’s garden.

Furthermore, some have wished Toadflax to be "cold and humid" in temperament, but with great error, as Fuchs correctly notes; for it draws out urine, which we know from Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> is granted only to plants that are sharp and dry.

### SCENTED TOADFLAX OF MONTPELLIER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Linaria odorata with very fine, needle-like leaves and a long, slender flower spike.</image-desc>

It stands with straight and rigid stems, two cubits high, becoming reddish near the ground; these are adorned with narrow leaves, more crowded than those of common Toadflax. The very top of the stem splits into several shoots which support flowers arranged in the same order as in common Toadflax, but with a much shorter and barely visible spur; they are larger, of a very pleasant scent, and of variegated color. The white root creeps sideways.

We had this at Montbéliard in the Prince’s garden, where it bloomed in July and August.

### GREAT PURPLE TOADFLAX.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Linaria purpurea showing a tall, upright habit with numerous small flowers along the upper stem.</image-desc>

It sends out a stem a cubit and a half high from a long, black, twisted, woody root. The stem is round, smooth, firm, and divided into very long branches; it is adorned with leaves longer and broader than those of the yellow Toadflax, with no evident taste. The flowers are born in a long series along the branches, gaping forward and showing a spur at the back; they are endowed with a purple color and are much smaller than those of the yellow Toadflax. The seed is contained in small, two-cleft vessels.

It bloomed for us in the garden at Montbéliard in July.

The author also notes several varieties grown in the princely botanical garden at Montbéliard and debates their humoral qualities based on classical authorities.</summary>

->OF PLANTS<-

### SMALL PURPLE TOADFLAX.
<note>original: "LINARIA PVRPVREA PARVA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Linaria plant with multiple stems, narrow leaves, and small flowers at the tips.</image-desc>

Beneath this plant lies a twisted root with rather long fibers. It produces several stems, about a span <note>approximately 9 inches</note> or more in height, which lean toward the ground; they are branched and clothed with leaves arranged at the joints, sometimes singly, and sometimes in groups of three or four. At the ends of the branches, many flowers are clustered together; these are smaller than the common Toadflax, blue-purple in color, and endowed with long spurs. Nearly round seed vessels follow, containing somewhat long, flattened seeds.

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, the Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist</note> collected this among the rocks and precipices of the Austrian mountains. We found it between Nîmes <note>original: "Nemausum"</note> and Avignon, and also near Geneva around the Arve river. It blooms in May.

### A PLANT SIMILAR TO TOADFLAX.
<note>original: "LINARIA SIMILIS PLANTA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Linaria-like plant with upright stems and dense foliage.</image-desc>

The root is woody, quite thick, and sometimes simple, while at other times it is divided into several heads. From this root, it immediately sends out several stems, a span high or even longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, which may be branched or unbranched, and are angular. Along these stems, the glaucous <note>blue-green</note> leaves, similar to those of Flax, are joined; from the crook of these leaves at the tips of the small branches, tiny flowers emerge, followed by small seed vessels.

### THE TOADFLAX CALLED BELVIDERE BY THE ITALIANS:
#### Called the "Herb of Scholars" by some.
<note>original: "Herba studiosorum"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy plant with many vertical stems and fine leaves, identified as Belvidere.</image-desc>

It has a very fibrous root, and the plant is exceedingly twiggy and somewhat rigid, though it remains brittle. The leaves are longer than those of either Flax or the common Toadflax, more numerous, and irregularly arranged; they have a bitter taste. The tiny flowers along the stem and in the leaf-axils are herbaceous <note>greenish</note>, almost escaping notice because of their smallness, or sometimes purple; these are followed by tiny chambers containing the seed.

<column-break/>

### BLUE TOADFLAX, WITH LONG SPURS.
<note>original: "LINARIA CÆRVLEA, CALCARIBVS longis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Linaria plant with long-spurred flowers.</image-desc>

The root is twisted, white, and fibrous. It produces a single, simple stem, a foot high, which is smooth, rounded, and slender. The leaves are sometimes opposite and sometimes alternate, vocal <note>perhaps "vocalis" here implies "pronounced" or "distinct"</note>, narrow, and smooth. The flowers grow at the top of the stalk in the same order and shape as the common Toadflax, but are half the size; they have a significantly longer spur and are blue, with five narrow, long green leaves surrounding the base. The seed vessels are smaller than those of common Flax.

We discovered this near Viterbo in Italy.

### ANOTHER SIMILAR TOADFLAX of Clusius.
<note>original: "LINARIA SIMILIS ALIA Clusii"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, lanceolate leaves and a thick root system.</image-desc>

We have observed a plant similar to Toadflax in various places: Geneva, Basel, Montbéliard, and elsewhere. It blooms in May. Clusius, however, who describes it at length, records that he found it both in the mountains and grassy hills of Austria and Hungary <note>original: "Pannoniæ"</note>, and in the Madrid forest <note>referring to the park of the Château de Madrid in the Bois de Boulogne</note>, two miles from the city of Paris <note>original: "Lutetiana"</note>.

Is it perhaps the "Bastard Toadflax" <note>original: "Linaria adulterina"</note> in the *Icons and History* of Tabernaemontanus?

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE BELVIDERE TOADFLAX.
<note>original: "LINARIA BELVEDERE ALIA ICON"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a single curved branch of the Belvidere plant showing the arrangement of small leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

Some label this plant *Osyris* and distinguish it from Toadflax, because from it a <term>broom</term> <note>original Greek: "κόρημα" (korema), meaning a besom or broom</note> is composed in Italy in this age, just as it was in the century of Galen <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note>. Thus, some call it *Scoparia* <note>Broom-plant</note>, and others the "Herb of Scholars," or in German, <term>Studenten kraut</term> <note>Student's herb; historically, plants that were easy to grow or had medicinal uses for those studying</note>.

<summary>This page describes various subspecies of Linaria (Toadflax), including purple and blue varieties found across Europe, and the "Belvidere" plant, notable for its use in broom-making and its nickname as the "Herb of Scholars."</summary>
<keywords>Toadflax, Linaria, Clusius, Belvidere, Osyris, broom-making, Herb of Scholars, Viterbo, botanical geography, medicinal plants</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
**PPP 2**

### THIRD IMAGE OF THE BELVEDERE TOADFLAX.
<note>original: "LINARIA BELVEDERE ICON TERTIA"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall, slender plant with numerous small, narrow leaves and clusters of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Matthias de l'Obel <note>a Flemish physician and botanist, 1538–1616</note> states that this lovely plant—beautiful both in its physical form and its Italian name—is usually cultivated in Italy in gardens and hanging earthenware pots because of its exotic rarity. Rembert Dodoens <note>a Flemish physician and celebrated herbalist</note> is the authority for the fact that it grows wild in many parts of Greece, flourishes during the summer, and ripens its seed toward autumn. We have seen it in gardens in Lyon, Geneva, and Montbéliard; they say, however, that it occasionally grows to the height of a tree. We present three images of it here, as they had already been engraved.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COMMON SNAPDRAGON.
<note>original: "ANTIRRHINI VVLGARIS ALIA ICON"</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a flowering plant with lanceolate leaves and snapdragon-like flowers arranged along the upper stem.</image-desc>

Because the gaping mouths of the flowers resemble a lion's mouth rather than a calf's, there are those who believe this plant should be called "Lion's Bone" <note>original: "Os Leonis"</note> instead of <term>Antirrhinum</term> <note>literally "like a snout"</note>. However, Bacchanellus admits he does not know what the true Antirrhinum is. Likewise, Luigi Anguillara <note>an Italian botanist and director of the Padua botanical garden</note> did not recognize the Antirrhinum described by Dioscorides; yet he asserts that the plant described by Theophrastus and Pliny is known everywhere in Italy by the name <term>Cazzugelli</term>. In truth, all of their descriptions of Antirrhinum refer to one and the same plant.

Among more recent authors, Snapdragons are distinguished by their size and the color of their flowers: thus, they recognize the first and second types, Greater and Lesser, with flowers of white, yellow, or flesh-colored <note>pinkish-red</note>.

Our own figures, based on those of Leonhart Fuchs, are not particularly pleasing to us.

### THE NARROW-LEAVED SNAPDRAGON according to some: The Lesser Snapdragon according to others.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a smaller, more delicate variety of Antirrhinum with narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This is a quite elegant little plant with a thin, whitish root. It has rounded, hairy stems about a span <note>roughly 9 inches</note> or a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> in height. These are adorned alternately with leaves similar to those of Hyssop, often several together; the lower leaves are sometimes reddish, fleshy, and slightly pungent. The small, two-colored flowers emerge from the axils <note>the "armpits" where the leaf meets the stem</note> of the leaves; they are partly white and partly purplish, resembling the Greater Snapdragon but many times smaller. These are followed by a <term>Pericarpium</term> <note>a seed vessel or pod</note> containing the seed.

It is found almost everywhere, both at the edges of gardens and in uncultivated borderlands. It is found in great abundance at Geneva near the Rhône river toward the Castle of La Bastie, and at Montbéliard in the fields near Audincourt. It blooms in summer and autumn.

<column-break/>

### SNAPDRAGON: German: *Brackenhanupt, Kalbsnass*; French: *Mouron violet*; Italian: *Antirrhino*.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut showing a plant with broader leaves and distinct, gaping flowers resembling a calf's snout.</image-desc>

<term>Antirrhinum</term> or <term>Anarrhinum</term>, which some have also called "Wild Lychnis" <note>original: "Lychnida syluestrem"</note>, is described by Dioscorides <note>the 1st-century Greek physician</note> as a herb with a stem and leaves similar to Pimpernel <note>Anagallis</note>. It has flowers like a Stock or Wallflower <note>Leucoium</note>, though smaller and purple, and a seed resembling the nostrils of a calf.

Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> says it is called *Antirrhinon*, *Anarrhinum*, or *Lychnis agria*; it is similar to Flax, has no root, a flower like a Hyacinth, and a seed like the nostrils of a calf. Theophrastus <note>the "Father of Botany"</note> writes that this herb is useful for acquiring glory, noting it has no root, but the fruit indeed contains something like a calf's nostrils.

Thus, Dioscorides agrees with Pliny on the name, but he differs from both Pliny and Theophrastus in his physical description.

### YET ANOTHER BETTER IMAGE OF THE COMMON SNAPDRAGON.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical woodcut of a snapdragon plant with several flower spikes and leafy stems.</image-desc>

The Snapdragon scorns almost no type of soil; it descends from dry, ruined walls into more cultivated ground, and when transplanted there, it loses none of its fertility. We have seen it in abundance at Montpellier on the road leading to the Aigremont forest, and in other places. In Italy and the Narbonne region of France, it grows among olive groves. Among the Germans and Belgians, however, it is cultivated in gardens and blooms in summer; as it grew for us at Montbéliard in the Princely Garden, it bloomed in August and September.

### THE SMALLEST SNAPDRAGON.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a very small, low-growing variety of Antirrhinum with tiny leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

This entire plant is smaller than the variety called "Lesser Snapdragon." It has a small, hard, fibrous root and a stem with many hollowed-out wings; upon these are leaves not much smaller than the variety already mentioned, with a similar taste. The flower is spurred <note>literally "horned"</note> at the back and gaping at the front, colored a dilute violet. The seed pod is oblong and bulging; by means of a slightly thick internal wall, it is divided into two chambers containing many tiny, black seeds.

It grows abundantly in the fields around Basel, and also at Montbéliard in plowed fields and vineyards. It blooms in summer.

The author cross-references classical botanical descriptions from Dioscorides and Pliny with contemporary 16th-century observations.</summary>
<keywords>Snapdragon, Antirrhinum, Toadflax, Linaria Belvedere, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, botanical gardens, Montbéliard, Geneva, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the descriptions of Snapdragons and Toadflax to members of the Weld (Lutea) and Celandine (Chelidonium) families. It focuses on the plants' uses in dyeing and traditional medicine, particularly for vision and skin conditions.</meta>

# PLANTS

### THE WELD OF PLINY TO SOME.
<note>original: "LVTEA PLINII QVIBVSDAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lutea plant (Weld), showing a tall, slender stalk with narrow leaves and a spiked inflorescence at the top, with a detailed root system at the base.</image-desc>

Honorius Bellus <note>a celebrated 16th-century Italian physician and botanist</note> once sent this plant to us from Crete along with many others. He wrote that the entire herb surpasses even **Aloe** and **Colocynth** <note>a bitter cucumber-like fruit used as a purgative</note> in bitterness, and that it can be used to dye things a yellow color. He noted it was unknown to the ancients and recognized by only a few among more recent authors.

Indeed, Pliny mentions the herb *Lutea* <note>Weld or Dyer's Weed, *Reseda luteola*</note> in Book 33, and called it *Lutea*. Vitruvius <note>the Roman architect and engineer</note> in Book 7 called it *Luteum*, and Virgil wrote of it as *Lutum* in his *Bucolics*. From *Lutum* come the words "luteous" <note>yellowish-orange</note> and "lutea," just as "croceous" <note>saffron-colored</note> comes from **Crocus**. Some contend this plant is *Phyteuma*, others *Catanance*, and some believe it to be the *Reseda* of Pliny. Jean Ruel <note>French physician and botanist</note> asks if it might be the *Gaudum* or *Gaidum* of the Gauls. Its uses are described in the following sections.

<column-break/>

### THE GREAT CRETAN WELD OF H. BELLUS.
->In German: *Sterckraut*; in Belgian: *Vouwe*.<--
<note>original: "LVTEA MAXIMA CRETICA, H. BELLI"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Great Cretan Lutea, showing a robust plant with serrated leaves and a dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

The herb called *Lutea* is believed to be highly effective against poisons and venomous bites; for this reason, some call it *Theriacaria* <note>from "Theriac," a famous universal antidote</note>. The sharp flavor of the root suggests that it heats, thins, disperses, and opens the body's passages, as well as promoting urine and sweat. Daily practice testifies to how much use it has among wool dyers, especially the Belgians, as taught by Vitruvius, de l'Obel, Dodoens, and Camerarius. Woolen cloths that have not been dyed with any other color are tinted yellow by it; however, those previously dyed blue turn green.

---

### THE RESEDA OF PLINY TO SOME.
<note>original: "RESEDA PLINII QVIBVSDAM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Reseda plant, featuring a central stalk with pinnate leaves and a long, thin flowering raceme.</image-desc>

The plant recently named **Reseda** <note>Mignonette</note> has a thin but long, woody root endowed with a notable sharpness. The stems are hollow, about a cubit and a half tall <note>approx. 27 inches</note>, furrowed, slightly hairy, and branched. The leaves are deeply divided, irregular, and curly, with a vegetable-like taste. The flowers are arranged in a long spike; they are yellow and sometimes even white or greenish, with tips of the same color and a three-parted style. The seed capsules gape open at the bottom in the shape of a small pitcher, containing small black seeds.

Reseda is thought to be named from "calming" <note>original: "à sedandis"</note> pains, because it disperses swellings and inflammations.

Furthermore, it flowers in Summer and is found on walls and near grain fields.

<column-break/>

### LESSER CELANDINE.
->In German: *Feigvuarzenkraut* <note>literally "Piles-wart-herb"</note>; in French: *Petite Esclaire*; in Italian: *Favoscello*.<--
<note>original: "CHELIDONIVM MINVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lesser Celandine (Chelidonium minus), showing heart-shaped leaves and small star-like flowers with a tuberous root system.</image-desc>

There are two main types of Celandine: the *Greater*, of which we will speak soon, and the *Lesser*, which we depict here.

According to Dioscorides <note>the ancient Greek physician</note>, it is a small herb with a stemless leaf-stalk hanging from the root. The leaves are like those of **Ivy**, but much rounder, smaller, tender, and somewhat fleshy. It has many small roots emerging from the same neck, clustered together like grains of wheat; three or four of these grow longer than the rest. Some have called it "Wild Wheat." It grows near water and lakes. Writing in Sicily, Dioscorides handed down nothing regarding the flowers and seeds, parts which a later age recognized as being similar to the parts of the **Buttercup**.

---

### GREATER CELANDINE.
->In German: *Schelkraut*; in French: *Esclaire, Felougne*; in Italian: *Chelidonia maggiore*.<--
<note>original: "CHELIDONIVM MAIVS"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Greater Celandine (Chelidonium maius), showing deeply lobed leaves and small four-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

The root is thicker than the little finger, fibrous, and red or gold in color. It produces rounded, hairy stems that are tuberous near the root and at the joints. The leaves bear some resemblance to those of **Columbine** <note>Aquilegia</note>, though they are larger, longer, and more numerous, attached to the rib at intervals, usually in sixes, with a seventh leaf closing the tip. The saffron-colored flowers consist of four petals and many stamens of the same color, followed by long pods containing pale seeds, larger than those of the **Poppy**. The leaves, stems, flowers, and especially the root, pour out a thick, bitter, and very strong-smelling juice that is red or saffron-colored.

<column-break/>

### GREATER CELANDINE WITH FRINGED LEAVES,
->and likewise with cut flower petals.<--
<note>original: "CHELIDONIVM MAIVS FOLIO LACINIATO"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variety of Greater Celandine with more deeply incised or "laciniate" leaves and petals.</image-desc>

This is a variety of the common type, and is distinguished from it only by the features mentioned.

Greater Celandine grows in uncultivated places, among ruins, on old walls and stone fences, and among other "weed-like" herbs, as well as on the banks of ditches. It remains green all year and flowers from the month of April well into Summer.

Furthermore, according to Theophrastus and Dioscorides, it is believed to have obtained the name *Chelidonium* because it rises at the arrival of Swallows <note>original: "Chelidones" in Greek</note> and withers at their departure; or because, when the chicks of swallows are blinded, the mothers restore their sight by applying this herb. More information can be found in the Appendix.

<meta>The catchword "AQVI-" likely refers to the start of the next section on "Aquilegia" (Columbine) or "Aquatilis" (Aquatic plants).</meta>

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey, moving from the dyer’s weeds (Weld) and Celandines discussed on the previous page to the Columbine (Aquilegia) and Marsh Marigold (Caltha). # IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

### COLUMBINE; AQUILEGIA; AQUILINA
->In German: *Akkeley*; in French: *Ancholie*; in Italian: *Aquileia*.<--

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Aquilegia (Columbine) plant showing the roots, leaves, and nodding flowers with distinct spurs.</image-desc>

The **root** is more than a thumb’s thickness, white, and has a somewhat sweet taste. The **leaves** grow on long, stiff, hairy stalks in groups of three, resembling those of the **Greater Celandine** <note>*Chelidonium majus*</note>, though they are bluish-grey beneath and green above. The **stems** are thin, stiff, hairy, jointed, and branched. They support lovely **flowers** composed of beaked spurs which, through a remarkable craftsmanship of Nature, take the shape of a dove <note>original: "Columbam"</note> with spreading wings. In the wild variety, these are almost never any color but reddish-purple; however, in gardens, they are blue, white, red, yellowish-green, or a mixture of several of these colors. All varieties, however, have **seeds** like those of the **Larkspur** <note>original: "Consolidæ regalis"</note>; they are black and contained in the upright little horns or pods of the **Monkshood** <note>original: "Aconitorum"</note> family.

They were given the name *Aquilegia* because of the hooked tips of the flowers, which resemble the claws of an eagle <note>original: "Aquilinis unguibus"</note>.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COLUMBINE.

<image-desc>A second botanical illustration of an Aquilegia plant, showing a slightly different variety with more upright growth.</image-desc>

We present three images from the works of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous 16th-century German botanist</note>, showing the Columbine with both single and double flowers; we might have wished for better illustrations, but these had already been engraved.

Various differences are observed among Columbines, mostly in the size and color of the flower and the number of its petals. It is found as either a single or double flower; in colors of blue, white, yellow, flesh-colored, or variegated blue and purple; or white sprinkled with dark spots. Indeed, these flowers differ not only in their more abundant stature and color, but also in shape, sometimes taking on different appearances; for they are occasionally seen almost inverted, others without spurs, and so forth.

### MARSH MARIGOLD:
->In German: *Dotterblum*; in French: *Soucy de Marais*.<--

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of Caltha palustris (Marsh Marigold) showing heart-shaped leaves and five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

The **Marigold** <note>original: "Caltha Calendula"</note>, which grows in fields and inhabits gardens, was discussed in Class 16 of this Outline. Now, however, we must deal with the variety that follows water streams and marshy meadows.

The common type, which has a single flower, is similar to the **Lesser Celandine** <note>original: "Chelidoniæ minori"</note>, but it is larger in every part and has less reddish stalks. The leaves also have a deeper notch near the stalk and are marked with purple spots. There is a further difference in that the stalks of the Lesser Celandine are seen without branches. The flowers also consist of larger, rounder, and fewer petals; the roots are also different.

Valerius Cordus labels it "Marsh Celandine" and Lonicerus calls it "Chrysanthemum," but in this, he is entirely mistaken.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE COLUMBINE OR AQUILEIA.

<image-desc>A third botanical illustration of an Aquilegia, focusing on the flowering stalks.</image-desc>

It is debated whether the **Columbine** was known to the Ancients or not. Costæus and Aldrovandi contend it is the *Poison* <note>original: "Poison"</note> of Theophrastus; Cæsalpinus identifies it as his *Iasion*; Dalechampius as his *Jupiter's Flower* <note>original: "Iouis florem"</note>; and Gesner, again, as his *Leontostome* <note>meaning "Lion’s Mouth"</note>. Columella calls it the *Lion* and Dodonaeus calls it the *Lion herb*; others call it the *Aegilops* of the Greeks; Tragus calls it the *Great Centaury*, but wrongly. Some, citing Matthioli, call it *Greater Celandine*. Gesner, in his catalog of plants, calls it *Cantabrica*. Fabio Columna labels the single-flowered Columbine as the *Isopyron* <note>original Greek: "ἰσόπυρον"</note> of Dioscorides, a view which Clusius strongly approves; on the other hand, Lobelius rejects this opinion as absurd. In such a diversity of opinions, we leave the matter for the judge to decide.

### THE DEGENERATE COLUMBINE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a "degenerate" or double-flowered Aquilegia variety with many small petals.</image-desc>

The Columbine sometimes "degenerates" such that it frequently produces leaner flowers, either entirely green in color, or a faint greenish hue, or purplish-green.

Furthermore, the single-flowered Columbine flourishes in mountain meadows, specifically the blue-colored variety. In gardens, however, it is seen in various colors and also in "multiplex" <note>double-petaled</note> forms.

Regarding the **powers** of the **Columbine**: the seed, ground very finely and drunk in wine in the weight of a drachm <note>about 3.5 grams</note>, is a most excellent remedy for the "Royal Disease" <note>jaundice</note> and for difficulty in childbirth. For these same conditions, its **distilled water** is given, as well as for fainting fits <note>original: "syncopes"</note> and obstructions of the internal organs; it disperses internal abscesses, and so on.

### DOUBLE-FLOWERED MARSH MARIGOLD.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a double-flowered Marsh Marigold, showing dense, multi-layered petals.</image-desc>

It has many leaves that are almost perfectly circular, succulent, veined, and somewhat serrated around the edges. Among them rise stalks a span or a foot long or more, growing at an angle and divided into branches, which usually, in the manner of the common variety, produce two **flowers** from the top joint. These sit on inch-long stalks and are composed of a multiple layer of petals, clearly golden in color, with the five lower petals being somewhat larger. The **root** is provided with many white, relatively thick fibers.

This is found especially in England, and sometimes with a fragrant flower. It delights in water, damp places, and meadow streams; it blooms in Spring and Summer. More on the **Marigold** can be found in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes the physical characteristics, varieties, and medicinal uses of the Columbine (Aquilegia) and the Marsh Marigold (Caltha), including a discussion on their contested identification in ancient Greek and Roman texts.</summary>
<keywords>Columbine, Aquilegia, Marsh Marigold, Caltha palustris, jaundice, medicinal plants, botanical history, Leonhart Fuchs, Dioscorides, double flowers</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
<page-num>486</page-num>

### GERANIUM, STORK’S BILL: Germ. *Storchenschnabel*: Dutch *Oyenares beck*: French *Geranium, Bec de Gruë*: Ital. *Geranio*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium plant with broad, lobed leaves and long, beak-like seed pods.</image-desc>

Dioscorides identifies only two kinds of Geranium; Pliny identifies three, as does Matthiolus (having borrowed one from Pliny). Fuchs describes six, Dodoens eight, and Caspar Bauhin twenty. The ones we shall soon present have become well-known to us.

The variety called **MALLOW-LIKE** <note>original: "MALVACEVM"</note> is depicted here, which is the second kind described by Dioscorides and the "Mallow-leaved Geranium" of Pliny. It has, he says, thin, downy little stems about two spans high. The leaves are truly like those of a Mallow, and at the tops of the branches are certain small protrusions looking upward, like the heads of Cranes with their beaks.

It grows frequently everywhere in manure heaps and other rich soils. It flowers in May and September.

---

### CRANESBILL GERANIUM, with FINELY divided leaves: called "Violet Geranium" by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with finely divided, feathery leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

It rests upon a single, small root that is red both inside and out. The stems are quite branched, mostly trailing on the ground, ranging from nine inches to sometimes three feet long <note>original: "dodrantales ac interdum bicubitales"</note>; they are branched, soaked in a blood-red color, hairy, and jointed. The leaves are like those of a **Dove’s-foot** <note>original: "Pedis columbini"</note>, round but finely cut, somewhat hairy, and occasionally turning a bit reddish. The flowers are like those of **Herb Robert** <note>original: "Geranii Robertiani"</note>, though a little larger, purple, and set in a broader, less red husk. The beaked seeds are stouter than those of Herb Robert.

It grows spontaneously in the same places as the preceding variety, as well as in gardens. Some have labeled it *Geranium Robertianum* or *Cælium gruis* <note>Crane’s Heaven</note>.

---

### TUBEROUS GERANIUM

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with a thick, tuberous root system and deeply lobed leaves.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is somewhat lead-colored, tasteless, and tuberous, from which it takes the name "tuberous." The leaves, provided with a hairy stalk about a span or a span-and-a-half long <note>a "span" is roughly 9 inches</note>, are broad and divided into eight or nine parts, with each segment further finely cut; their color is a grayish-green. The flowers, held on smooth, reddish, and hairy stalks, are beautiful and purplish; when they fall away, the "Beaks" <note>the seed pods</note> follow.

It is believed to have been first brought from Constantinople to Germany, but today it is common in gardens.

Matthiolus, Anguillara, L'Obel, Camerarius, Tabernaemontanus, Gerard, and Cesalpino all maintain that this is the first Geranium of Dioscorides, with leaves like an anemone. Cesalpino calls it <term>Pæcascolum</term> <note>original: "Pæcascolum," likely a corruption of a Greek or local term</note> because in the mountains the root fulfills the role of bread and cheese.

<column-break/>

### DOVE’S-FOOT GERANIUM: with a round, highly serrated leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with rounded, serrated leaves and slender stems.</image-desc>

It is endowed with many reddish, slightly upright, jointed runners. The leaves are round like those of a Mallow, sometimes more and sometimes less deeply cut. The flowers also vary in size; they are purple and consist of five small petals like the others. When these fall off, the needles or beaks of the Herb Robert geranium follow. The root is thin but long, reddish, and has an astringent taste.

It grows along roadsides, in uncultivated fields, in cemeteries, and in gardens; it flowers throughout the entire summer.

Nearly all herbalists—excepting Euricius Cordus, Brunfels, and Camerarius—accept this as the first Geranium of Dioscorides. Some, through an error that should be rejected, believe it to be *Amomum* <note>an unrelated aromatic spice plant</note>.

---

### SILVERY ALPINE GERANIUM: "Anemone-leaved Geranium" to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an alpine Geranium with silvery, deeply divided leaves.</image-desc>

The silvery leaves, densely covered with white hairs, give this plant the name "Silvery Geranium." It grows on the cliffs of Mount Baldo, from where we obtained a dried specimen. It flowers in July.

Furthermore, the common name for all these plants is the Greek <term>γεράνιον</term> (*geranion*), which is *Geranium* in Latin. It was named Geranium from the image of a crane's head <note>Greek *geranos* means crane</note>, which is found in the highest little head of the plant with a most fitting resemblance. Thus, by more recent writers, it is called **Stork’s Bill** <note>original: "Rostrum Ciconiæ"</note> in almost all languages, after the likeness of a stork's beak.

---

### FROG-LIKE GERANIUM <note>Meadow Cranesbill, *Geranium pratense*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with large, deeply incised leaves resembling those of a Ranunculus (Batrachium).</image-desc>

The root is a thumb’s thickness, red on the outside and the color of boxwood within, provided with many fibers and a strongly astringent taste. The stems reach a cubit or a cubit and a half in height <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note>; they are thin, spongy, and slightly hairy. The flowers are showy, large, and blue, consisting of five petals streaked with purple, in the middle of which are dark purple tips <note>anthers</note>. The leaves are like those of Monkshood <note>Aconite</note>, large, wrinkled, deeply cut, and sometimes arranged almost in a circle.

It grows wild in meadows and is also cultivated in gardens; it is also occasionally found with white flowers.

Regarding what was said above, Galen omitted Geranium from his list of simple medicines. However, Paul of Aegina, following Dioscorides, records both of his types of Geranium.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Geranium (Cranesbill) genus, detailing their physical characteristics, historical classifications by ancient botanists like Dioscorides, and their common names across Europe. It highlights the distinctive beak-like shape of the seed pods which gives the genus its name.</summary>
<keywords>Geranium, Cranesbill, Stork’s-bill, Dioscorides, Tuberous Geranium, Herb Robert, Dove's-foot Geranium, botany, botanical illustration, Mount Baldo, medicinal plants</keywords>
