<page-num>487</page-num>
<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES.</header>

### WHITE CRANE’S-BILL GERANIUM: and a variety colored with white and blue.
<note>original: "GERANIVM BATRACHOIDES ALBVM". The term 'batrachoides' literally means 'frog-like', referring to the leaf shape, but it was the common name for the Meadow Cranesbill.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium plant with deeply lobed leaves and several flowers, showing the root structure at the base.</image-desc>

It grows for us at Montbéliard in the Illustrious Prince's garden, from seed brought from Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentina"</note>.

Furthermore, all Geraniums do not possess the same medicinal properties. Some, according to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note>, are of no use in medicine. The Musk-scented variety [Geranium moschatum] has the power of dispersing and warming; Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a 16th-century German physician and botanist.</note> attributes to **Herb Robert** [Geranium robertianum] an equal power of drying and binding <note>astringency</note>. Its juice and distilled water, according to Bock <note>referred to here by his Latin name, Tragus</note>, heals all kinds of ulcerations and bruises of the breasts, as well as the genitals of both men and women.

<column-break/>

### LARGEST CRANE’S-BILL GERANIUM, with the shining leaf of Aconite, according to Clusius.
<note>Clusius was a pioneering 16th-century botanist known for his work on Alpine flora.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Geranium variety with large, sharply pointed leaves and clusters of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

"It grows," says Clusius, "in the Pannonian and Styrian Alps <note>modern-day Austria and Hungary</note>, and flowers in July and August; it is also cultivated in gardens."

It varies with blue flowers, white, or variegated with blue lines; and these may be single or white.

Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano, a Renaissance polymath</note> wrote in his book *On the Wrong Use of Medicine* that the Geranium called **Dove’s-foot** <note>original: "Pedem Columbinum"</note> is a poison; but not without error: for he was perhaps mistaking it for the **Kite-foot** or **Crow-foot**, which is a type of Ranunculus [Buttercup].

---

### LONG-ROOTED, SCENTED CRANE’S-BILL GERANIUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with a thick, elongated root system and multiple flowering stems.</image-desc>

In the remarkable beauty of its flowers, it yields to no other Geranium; these scented flowers spring from a round, striped, reddish, and hairy calyx, being purple-violet in color and composed of five petals. They grow on jointed stems, ranging from nine to eighteen inches high <note>original: "dodrantalibus, cubitalibus"</note>, and are hairy. The *leaves* are divided somewhat like those of Sanicle, grayish-white from their green base, and hairy. The root is driven obliquely and is very long: as thick as a finger, fibrous, red on the outside, and offering a somewhat aromatic taste.

We have seen it at Stuttgart in the Illustrious Prince's garden.

<column-break/>

### DUSKY GERANIUM WITH REFLEXED FLOWERS.
<note>reflexed: petals that curve backward.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with broad, lobed leaves and flowers that appear to hang or reflex downwards.</image-desc>

This kind of Geranium is especially beautiful, with leaves larger than the Crane’s-bill, divided into about eight segments, slightly hairy and sprinkled with blackish spots, with somewhat broad teeth around the edges, and possessing no scent. The flower sits at the tips, purple and almost dark brown, quite large; when the flower falls, the "beaks" <note>seed pods</note> arise, being an inch long.

It is cultivated in gardens and flowers in June.

---

### GERANIUM WITH DUSKY OR DARK FLOWERS, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender Geranium with small flowers and distinct leaf patterns.</image-desc>

It is found in the Alps of Styria where the forests usually end, and it flowers in June. If planted in gardens, however, it grows most successfully and flowers in May.

It varies sometimes with jagged petals; however, in the image they are depicted as being less jagged.

<column-break/>

### LARGE GERANIUM WITH THREE-PARTED LEAVES, and purplish flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with deeply cleft, three-lobed (trifid) leaves and a robust stem.</image-desc>

This was sent to us as Mountain Geranium. It is called the *Round-leaved Anemone-Geranium* by Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax* <note>a famous botanical register of the time</note>. Could it be the *Dove’s-foot growing in the woods* of Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Caesalpino, an Italian physician and botanist</note>, etc.?

<summary>This page catalogs several species of Geranium (Cranesbills), detailing their physical characteristics, geographical origins in the Alps, and medicinal uses. The author also corrects a historical misconception by Cardanus regarding the toxicity of certain species.</summary>
<keywords>Cranesbill, Geranium Batrachoides, Herb Robert, medicinal plants, botany, Clusius, Leonhart Fuchs, Styria, garden plants, botanical classification</keywords>

The author provides specific locations where he observed these plants, including both wild settings and botanical gardens in Montbéliard, Geneva, and Basel.</meta>

<page-num>489</page-num>
<header>OF PLANTS</header>

<column-break/>

### BLOODY CRANE’S-BILL OR BLOOD-LIKE GERANIUM with a thick root and purple flower.
<note>original: "GERANIVM SANGVINEVM VEL HÆMAtodes". The name 'sanguineum' and 'haematodes' both refer to blood.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium plant with deeply lobed leaves and a thick, branching root system.</image-desc>

It grows in the mountains of Pannonia <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and Serbia</note> and Austria below Ovasum <note>referring to the region near the River Enns</note>, in mountain woods that have been cut, and in higher grassy places. It flowers in May, and usually throughout the entire following summer.

It is called *Haematodes* or *Bloody* for two reasons: first, from the blood-red color inside the root and of the flower; and second, from its wonderful power in stopping blood. Indeed, it is primarily recommended for checking blood flowing from any part of the body.

---

### BEAUTIFUL ANNUAL CRANE’S-BILL from Crete, with very long beaks.
<note>original: "GERANIVM SPECIOSVM ANN VVM LONgiſsimis roſtris, Creticum". The "beaks" are the long seed pods characteristic of this family.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with elongated seed pods (rostra) and serrated leaves.</image-desc>

It shades the ground widely with a mass of hairy, knotty little branches. It is provided with long, hairy leaves that are somewhat reddish, wavy, and serrated, with an acidic and astringent taste. The flowers are a pleasant blue, with five petals, surrounded by the five leaves of the gaping calyx <note>the protective outer part of the flower</note>. These are followed by very long "beaks."

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> writes that it grows spontaneously in the fields of Montpellier. We, however, had it at Montbéliard in the Most Serene Prince's garden, where it flowered in July and August. Herbalists commonly label it as *Cretan Geranium* and *Cadiac Geranium*, perhaps because it is abundant there or is more beautiful in that region.

---

### SHINING CRANE’S-BILL.
<note>original: "GERANIVM LVCIDVM"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Geranium with rounded, lobed leaves and thin stems.</image-desc>

It has leaves like those of the *Momordica* <note>Balsam apple</note>, or the shape of the longer-rooted Meadow Crane’s-bill, but smaller than those; they are divided into four deep segments that are almost always divided into three parts. They shine beautifully with a dark green luster and are somewhat hairy, attached to stalks a palm's-breadth long. The stems are many, shining, and reddish, divided into various branches, sometimes reaching nearly a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height. The flowers are similar and equal to those of Herb Robert. The "beaks" are short.

We observed it in abundance at Geneva on walls, as well as between Geneva and Lyon in ruins. It flowers in May.

<column-break/>

### MUSKY CRANE’S-BILL, or MUSK-NEEDLE, with a leaf like Myrrh.
<note>original: "GERANIVM MOSCHATVM, ſiue ACVS MOSCHATA, folio Myrrhidis"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Geranium with pinnate leaves resembling Myrrhis and a central taproot.</image-desc>

Writers call it *Musky Geranium* and *Musk-Needle* indiscriminately; some call it *Myrrhine*, and it is the "third Geranium of Pliny" according to the *History of Lyon* <note>referring to the 'Historia Generalis Plantarum' published in Lyon</note>.

It varies in both its size and the color of the flower: for it is either Large or small, and the flower is either white or flesh-colored.

It grows in ruins and in cultivated sandy fields, and it flowers in May. It occurs everywhere around Montpellier, and at Basel on the road that leads to Muttenz; it is also found at Geneva, at Plainpalais.

---

### HERB ROBERT: German: St. Rupert’s herb; Dutch: Robert’s herb; French: Herb Robert; Latin: Ruberia.
<note>original: "GERANIVM ROBERTIANVM". This common weed is still known by these names today.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Geranium robertianum (Herb Robert) showing its characteristic branched habit and hairy stems.</image-desc>

The root is thin and the color of boxwood. It supports stems that are nine inches to a cubit high, which are hairy, jointed, reddish, and branched. The leaves grow partly from the root and partly from the joints; they are hairy and have a reddish, hairy stalk. They are divided much like Feverfew, and are somewhat red along the edges, and sometimes entirely red. The flowers are purple, striped with a paler purple, consisting of five petals; they emerge from a hairy, dark-red, five-parted calyx, with saffron-colored tips <note>stamens</note> in the middle. These are followed by pointed "beaks" that have the seed attached.

It is found everywhere in ruins, on old walls, on felled trees, and in cold, damp, and shady places. It flowers in summer. More can be found in the Appendix.

---

### GOAT'S BEARD: Greek: *Pygonōmon*; German: *Geiss bart*; French: *Barbe de chevre*.
<note>original: "BARBA CAPRÆ". This refers to Aruncus dioicus, a tall woodland plant.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with large, serrated, compound leaves and a thick root.</image-desc>

It is endowed with a moderately thick, fibrous root, covered with a somewhat thick bark that leans toward yellow; beneath this is a woody substance with a plentiful white, tasteless pith. The stems are two or three cubits high or more, with many concave ribs, smooth, thin, and pithy. The leaves are like those of the Chestnut tree: oblong, pointed, and serrated. Several are attached to the central rib with no small leaves in between, unlike in Meadowsweet <note>Vimaria/Filipendula</note>, from which this plant and its flower differ greatly. The flowers are arranged in clusters at the angles; they are very small and white.

According to Clusius, it is found in the mountain forests of Hungary, Austria, and Styria. However, we saw it in abundance at Geneva on the hill of La Bastie, and at Basel by the Red House. More can be found in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Geranium (Crane's-bill) and the Goat's Beard plant, detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses for stopping bleeding, and the specific European locations where the author observed them.</summary>
<keywords>Bloody Crane's-bill, Herb Robert, Musky Geranium, Goat's Beard, botany, medicinal herbs, Clusius, Geneva, Basel, Montbéliard</keywords>

### MEADOW-RUE OR THALICTRUM:
### The blacker Meadow-rue, with a striated stem and seed.
<note>original: "THALICTRVM SIVE THALIETRVM: Thalictrum nigrius, caule & semine striato." Meadow-rue is not a true rue but was named for its similar leaves.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thalictrum plant with broad, lobed leaves and a cluster of small flowers at the top of a striated stem.</image-desc>

According to Pliny, Galen, and Dioscorides, with few exceptions, all the same things are said regarding Meadow-rue. Dioscorides says it has leaves like Coriander, but thicker; a stem the thickness of a wheel-spoke <note>original: "culum Rotæ"; likely a variation or error for "radium rotae" (wheel spoke), a common classical comparison for stem thickness</note>, upon which the leaves grow. It grows in flat fields.

Furthermore, various plants are given the name of Meadow-rue: it is called *Aquilegia* <note>Columbine</note> by Herold; *Potentilla* <note>Cinquefoil</note> by Ruellius; *Consolida regalis* <note>Larkspur</note> by Tragus; *Pimpinella Saxifragia minor* <note>Lesser Burnet-saxifrage</note> by Lobelius and the *History of Lyon*. It is called *German Styptic* <note>original: "Stripticum Germ."</note> by Gesner, and Pliny's *Phellandrium* <note>Water-hemlock</note> by some. But they are all in great error.

There are indeed various species and differences of Meadow-rue. Moreover, the one we depict here is abundant in the meadows of hills in many places in Germany.

### GREATER MEADOW-RUE WITH ANGULAR
### PODS, and a smooth stem, etc. of Gesner.
<note>original: "THALICTRVM MAIVS FOLLICVLIS ANGVLOsis, caule læui, &c. Gesneri."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller Thalictrum species with more delicate, divided foliage and a large, spreading inflorescence.</image-desc>

It grows to a height of a cubit and a half <note>about 27 inches</note>; it is provided with branches and swollen, polished, smooth, and hollow stems. The leaves are like Columbine, smooth, of almost the same color, scentless, and with a somewhat bitter-sharp taste. The flowers stand out like dense tufts <note>original: "Muscaria", referring to a brush or fly-whisk shape</note>; they are made of little stamens arranged in a circle, pale violet in color, with yellow tips. The roots are fibrous, multiple, thin, blackish on the outside, and white on the inside. The seed in the angular pods is thin, long, and dark.

It is abundant at Montbéliard by the Doubs river, and at Geneva on Mount Salève, and it flowers in July and August.

Furthermore, the Meadow-rues are moderately hot and dry in temperament. A decoction of the root and leaves loosens the bowels and induces vomiting, and is praised as a remedy against stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.

### MEADOWSWEET, QUEEN OF THE MEADOW:
### German: Geisbaart; French: Barbe de cheure; Italian: Ulmaria.
<note>original: "VLMARIA, REGINA PRATI". The vernacular names "Geisbaart" and "Barbe de cheure" both mean "Goat's Beard."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Ulmaria (Meadowsweet) showing pinnate leaves with a large terminal lobe and a dense cyme of flowers.</image-desc>

It has an upright stem, angular, reddish, hollow, firm, and two or three cubits high. The leaves shine with a joyful green; they are saw-toothed and somewhat shaped, with five or seven attached to the rib, and many smaller ones coming between them. The flowers are sweet-smelling, in the position and form of common Dropwort <note>original: "Filipendulæ vulgaris"</note>, consisting of five petals, whitish or verging toward yellow, with tips of the same color. The seeds are twisted and oblong. The little heads are small and pointed, composed of these twisted, oblong seeds. The root is the thickness of a finger, black on the outside, hairy with many fibers, and has a heavy scent.

It grows most joyfully by the banks of torrents and streams and in marshy meadows; it flowers in the months of June and July. There is more about this in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### MOST BEAUTIFUL GLAUCOUS MEADOW-RUE,
### with a striated seed and stem.
<note>original: "THALICTRVM SPECIOSISSIMVM GLAVCVM". "Glaucous" refers to a blue-grey or sea-green waxy coating on the leaves.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust Thalictrum with glaucous, deeply lobed leaves and a dense, upright floral spike.</image-desc>

It sometimes exceeds the height of a man; with a yellow root, slanted and fibrous, with a bitter taste. The stem is upright, single, not branched with "wings," purplish, empty inside, a finger thick, and intercepted by very long segments <note>internodes</note>. The leaves grow from the joints and embrace them with a sheath, very much resembling the leaves of the Greater Meadow-rue mentioned just before; but larger and darker, of a bluish color on both sides, with a bitter and sharp taste, and a heavy scent. Mossy flowers sit at the tops of the shoots, composed purely of yellow filaments. The seed is covered by a thin skin, not an angular pod, and is thin, long, and dark. It was formerly brought out of Spain, and is now common in gardens.

### LESSER MEADOW-RUE, OR THE SMALLER
### kind of Meadow-rue.
<note>original: "THALICTRVM MINVS, SIVE RVTA PRAtensis genus minus."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Thalictrum species with fine, rue-like leaves and a delicate flowering panicle.</image-desc>

It is very similar to the Greater Meadow-rue at first; but this has thinner stems, though they are no less rigid. The leaves are similar, somewhat thick, but smaller, arranged in the same order. The root is thin, fibrous, yellow, and creeping; the flowers are composed of radiating stamens, with smaller heads, and a color verging from dark to yellow. The seed corresponds to the seed of the larger variety.

It is usually found in flat coastal places, as well as sometimes in mountainous areas.

Clusius and Caspar Bauhin make mention of a narrow-leafed Meadow-rue; and the latter also mentions a very small, most foul-smelling Meadow-rue.

### LION’S-LEAF: in Greek, Leontopetalon;
### French: Patte de Lion.
<note>original: "LEONTOPETALVM: Græcis Λεοντοπέταλον". The name means "Lion's Petal" or "Lion's Leaf."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Leontopetalum showing broad, rounded leaves and a thick tuberous root.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, the Lion's-leaf produces a stem nine inches high, or even taller, hollow with many "wings"; at the tips of these are pods in the manner of Chickpeas, and in these are two or three minute seeds. The flowers are scarlet, similar to Anemones. The leaves are like Cabbage, but with the division of Poppy leaves. The root is black, similar to a Turnip, which has certain protrusions like knots. It grows in plowed fields and among crops. The root, drunk in wine, helps those who have been bitten by snakes, etc.

Pliny describes it in the same words. Galen writes that the use of the root is especially important, and that it has the power to disperse [humors], and is dry and hot in the third degree <note>a classification in Galenic medicine indicating a high intensity of these qualities</note>. More in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes various species of Thalictrum (Meadow-rue) and Ulmaria (Meadowsweet), noting their physical characteristics, habitats in Germany and Switzerland, and medicinal uses such as treating kidney stones. It also includes the Lion's-leaf (Leontopetalum), specifically noting its use as an antidote for snakebites.</summary>

<page-num>490</page-num>
<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### PEONY, GLYCYCIDE: Germ. Peonien blumen: French Piuoine: Ital. Peonia.
<note>original: "PÆONIA, GLYCYCIDE". Glycycide is a Greek-derived name meaning "sweet-pointed," referring to the edible nature of the seeds or root.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Peony plant (Paeonia Mas) showing its large, multi-lobed leaves and thick, tuberous root system.</image-desc>

Dioscorides and Pliny recognized only two varieties of Peony: making one the *Male* and the other the *Female*. But many others are observed by more recent authors; distinguished by location, season, size, and by their leaves and flowers. Thus, one is larger, others smaller; one earlier, another later; one has a simple flower, another a full <note>double</note> one. Furthermore, both may be deep red, flesh-colored, or whitish. One is our native variety, another is the Byzantine or exotic; one has broad leaves, another narrow, and likewise more or less curled, dissected, three-parted, or entire. Finally, some are neutral or intermediate. We depict the Male here, which is rarer than the female, and is distinguished from it by a notable difference in the leaves and the root.

### INTERMEDIATE PEONY WITH BROADER LEAVES.
<note>original: "PÆONIA PROMISCVA". Promiscua here suggests a hybrid or intermediate form.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Peony variety with broader leaves and a similar tuberous root structure.</image-desc>

This variety differs beautifully from the other species of Peony. Indeed, the leaves which cling to the lowest branches are broader than the others, and rounder; the upper part is a pale sea-green <term>glaucous: a bluish-grey or green coating</term> and hairy; the underside is a deeper green and likewise covered in hairs. The leaf is divided into three, four, or even five segments, with no fixed division, but varying randomly. The flower is not unlike the flower of the others. However, the seed pods are turned back and entirely covered with a white shagginess.

We have seen this in several gardens; however, the preceding kind is found everywhere in gardens, and it flowers in the months of May and June, multiplying itself greatly by spreading. Yet the Male Peony does not multiply itself like that one, because its solid root does not spread out wide, but descends deeply.

### FRAXINELLA, WHITE DITTANY: Germ. Weiss Diptam: French Fraxinelle: Ital. Fraxinella.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Dictamnus albus (Burning Bush) plant, showing its pinnate leaves and upright flower spike.</image-desc>

Although neither the Greeks nor the Arabs made mention of Fraxinella, its roots are nevertheless very well known to the Apothecaries by the name of White Dittany <note>original: "Dictamni albi"</note>. These are white and many-forked with various entanglements. Several stalks rise higher than a cubit and a half <note>about 27 inches</note>; they are hairy, reddish, filled with much pith, and support a long cluster <term>thyrsus: a dense, branching flower cluster</term> of very beautiful purplish flowers with yellow tips. The seed in the pods is black and shining, a little larger than the seed of Gromwell <note>original: "Milii Solis", literally 'Millet of the Sun'</note>. The leaves are like those of the Ash tree—from which it takes its name <note>Latin "Fraxinus" means Ash</note>—arranged in groups of seven, nine, or eleven.

It is found everywhere in the woody mountains and hills of Italy and Germany, in muddy and rocky soil; it flowers in June. In some places, it is grown in gardens. More is written in the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

### THE MORE COMMON FEMALE PEONY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the common female Peony (Paeonia foemina) with its characteristic flowers and roots.</image-desc>

This species of Female Peony is of common knowledge, most familiar in all gardens. It has tuberous roots <note>original: "glandulosas", acorn-shaped</note> interrupted by certain fibers, like the Asphodel, from which others are propagated anew. The stem is a cubit high, green, yet turning reddish where the leaves emerge. The leaves are variously and sharply dissected, sometimes two-parted, sometimes three-parted, at other times even entire; they are greenish above, somewhat whitish below, and a little hairy. The flowers sit at the very top, appearing singly, wide-spread, of a deep or pale red color, supported by certain keel-shaped leaves. There follow little white horns <note>seed follicles</note>, three, four, or more, hairy and hoary: in which is an elegant series of grains; first red, then dark blue, and finally black. In the center, the purplish stamens support saffron-colored tips <term>apices: the pollen-bearing anthers</term>.

### MANY-FLOWERED FEMALE PEONY.
<note>original: "POLYANTHOS", referring to double-flowered varieties.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a double-flowered Peony variety.</image-desc>

The flowers of the many-petaled Female Peony vary in color, being sometimes deep red, sometimes pale red, and occasionally even white.

Furthermore, some copies of Dioscorides claim that the Peony grows on the highest mountains: and Gesner writes that he was told the Greater Male Peony is found on the "Noble Mountain" of Switzerland <note>Mount Pilatus or similar peaks in the Alps</note>: however, we have observed it nowhere except in gardens. Truly, the greatest error is that of Tragus, who believes the Male Peony to be Fraxinella; and also those who attribute the name of Peony to Celandine <note>original: "Chelidonio"</note>, or those who determine the common Peony to be a kind of Dock <note>original: "Lapathum"</note>. More is written in the *Appendix*.

### CORTUSA, CALLED BY SOME ALPINE SANICLE: A species of Avens according to Matthiolus and Lobelius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Cortusa matthioli, showing its basal leaves and delicate flowering umbel.</image-desc>

The leaves cling to stalks that spring directly from the root, being a hand-breadth or more in width in every direction, and round in outline, though broken by rather deep notches. The stems are bare and without joints, bearing a leafy cup at the summit, from which emerge six or more stalks, half an inch long; each carries a purple flower, resembling the flowers of the Bear's Ear <note>original: "Auriculæ ursi", the Primula auricula</note>. The root is woven from numerous fibers.

Some call it Mountain Sanicle, and Lobelius calls it the *Avens of the Veronese*. However, Matthiolus, Castor, the *History of Lyon*, and Camerarius call it Cortusa: they named it *Cortusa* after the discoverer [Cortusus], who said he had seen it nowhere else but in a region of the territory of Vicenza called the Great Valley.

It serves to correct botanical misidentifications by earlier scholars and highlights the plants' physical traits and habitats.</summary>

# IMAGES AND SKETCHES.
### Qqq i
<meta>catchword: To C. Bauhin</meta>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris (Cowslip) plant showing the root system, leaves, and a single stalk with a cluster of drooping flowers.</image-desc>

**COWSLIP; German: *Key-flowers* <note>original: "Schlüsselblumen"</note>; French: *Spring-prime*; Italian: *Flower of Spring*.**

This herb obtained the name *Primula Veris* <note>literally "The little firstling of spring"</note> because it turns green and flowers at the very start of Spring. However, various names have obscured its true identity. For writers commonly call it *Primineviam*, or *Spring’s First*, *St. Peter’s Key*, *Palsy-wort*, *Joint-wort*, *Mullein-like*, *Cuckoo’s Breeches*, *Tussentanam Violet*, *White Betony*, and *Little Mullein*. <note>original: "Primineviam, Clauem S. Petri, Herbam Paralyticam & Arthriticam, Phlomidem, Brachulā Cuculi, Tussentanam Violam, Betonicam albam & Verbasculū"</note> But let the investigation of names be a secondary concern, provided the thing itself is understood.

It is not sufficiently clear what name it was given by Dioscorides, Pliny, and other ancient authors, both Greek and Latin. We shall investigate this in the Appendix.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris caulifera, showing a taller stalk with a more upright cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

### STEM-BEARING COWSLIP, with a simple flower, pale or yellow, and scentless.

This differs very little from the common variety, so we will provide this single description for both.

The root is moderately thick, uneven, reddish, and fibrous, with an aromatic scent and a slightly astringent taste. The leaves are spread across the ground, oblong, somewhat round, and wrinkled like those of Betony, but larger. In their center, a stem rises up about a hand's breadth or nine inches high [one or more], slightly hairy, rounded, and bare of leaves. At its summit are five, seven, or even more flowers, emerging from oblong calyxes <note>the green cup-like structures holding the petals</note>; they are yellow-green, gold, and fragrant, divided into five petals. These have saffron-colored tips in the center and a green style, followed by small, black seeds.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris with flowers emerging from individual pedicels at the base.</image-desc>

### COWSLIP WITH DOUBLE FLOWERS, on individual stalks.

This is also kept in more cultivated gardens, with pale or white flowers, and sometimes even simple ones.

Furthermore, Cowslips possess a drying and somewhat warming quality. The leaves, like those of the little mulleins, are effectively applied when crushed to aching joints. Since they are not unpleasant to the taste, they are eaten in pot-herbs, small cakes, and salads; they are also very useful for the head and nerves. A broth of the herb is given to drink and applied as an ointment against ruptures, dislocations, and chronic diarrhea <note>original: "lientia," referring to lientery, where food passes undigested</note>. Women who care for their beauty smear their faces with the juice expressed from the flowers, because it wonderfully clears away spots, wrinkles, and other such blemishes.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris minoris purpurascentis, showing a smaller plant with dark-shaded flowers.</image-desc>

### Another, better Illustration of the SMALLER PURPLISH COWSLIP now depicted, from Clusius.

We provide here a better image of the Smaller Purplish Cowslip, which we previously depicted from Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>. This kind of Cowslip grows naturally in boggy and damp meadows; it flowers in April and May.

For the rest, the primary differences in Cowslips are taken either from their place of birth or from the diversity of their flowers. For it is either a garden, meadow, or woodland variety; and with a flower either simple or multiple <note>double-petaled</note>, and sometimes so "proliferous" that one flower appears to be born from another. Additionally, some have a grassy or green flower, others white, others red, and others yellowish.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris caulifera with "proliferous" flowers, where one flower appears to grow out of another.</image-desc>

### STEM-BEARING COWSLIP, with multiple flowers, and the fragrant proliferous variety.

Our illustration shows both. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note>, in his *Images*, labels the proliferous Cowslip "with a twin flower, one born inside the other." Tabernaemontanus calls the proliferous Cowslip *Key-flowers with side-blossoms* <note>original: "Schlüsselblumen mit neben blümlen"</note>; but, being ignorant of the plants' nature, he separates it from the Cowslip and places it in a different chapter.

Both are kept in more cultivated gardens. The common variety described just above grows everywhere in boggy and well-watered meadows, especially in colder regions, and is also abundant in grassy mountain places. In Lyon, Geneva, and Basel, it flowers in March and April.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Primula veris with dark, fringed flowers.</image-desc>

### COWSLIP WITH DARK GREEN FRINGED FLOWERS.

Caspar Bauhin, in his *Phytopinax*, calls this the *Fourth Little Mullein, or lesser woodland variety, with a single flower, and sometimes multiple.* Lobelius, however, presents it in his *Adversaria* and *Observations* under the title placed above. Tabernaemontanus, in his *Images* and *History*, calls it the *Wild Primrose with a green flower*; Gesner, in his *Gardens*, calls it a *fragrant kind of Joint-wort with a green flower.* Clusius makes no mention of the color of green Cowslips, although he otherwise labored diligently in assigning the different varieties of Cowslips.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Cowslips and Primroses (Primula veris), detailing their physical descriptions, medicinal uses for joints and skin, and the taxonomic classifications provided by Renaissance botanists.</summary>
<keywords>Primula veris, Cowslip, Primrose, Joint-wort, Palsy-wort, Clusius, Lobelius, Caspar Bauhin, medicinal herbs, Renaissance botany</keywords>

<page-num>492</page-num>
<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### BEAR’S EAR: German: Bear Sanicle. <note>original: "Auricula Ursi," so named because the thick, rounded leaves were thought to resemble the ears of a bear.</note>
### Yellow-flowered Bear’s Ear.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Auricula Ursi plant with a cluster of bell-shaped flowers on a tall stalk and broad, rounded basal leaves.</image-desc>

Some among the more recent authors classify this beautiful plant among the Goldenrods. <note>original: "Solidaginum"</note> Fabio Columna identifies it as the *Alisma* and *Damasonium* of Dioscorides and Pliny; Charles de l'Écluse <note>original: "Clusius," a famous Flemish botanist.</note> is not much opposed to this opinion. Columna also reports that it is called *Alisma*. However, others more correctly—and especially Rembert Dodoens—consider it to belong to the Cowslips. <note>original: "Primulas Veris"</note> Clusius also states there is no doubt that this plant should be referred to the Primrose family, as they are so similar in form and temperament.

The species we depict here grows abundantly on the mountain ridges of the Austrian and Styrian Alps, and it is also cultivated in gardens; it flowers in April, and sometimes again in August.

### RED-FLOWERED BEAR’S EAR,
### with whitish spots and slightly hairy leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Auricula Ursi with serrated leaves and a cluster of flowers, labeled with the letter 'I'.</image-desc>

It has leaves that are smaller, more tender, less thick, and slightly hairy compared to the preceding kind, and they are serrated all around the edges. Among these grows a small stalk similar to the one above, bearing a few flowers in an umbel <note>a cluster of flowers where the stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs</note> which are red, yet sprinkled with whitish spots. The root is similarly fibrous, sending out new offshoots from the sides.

Clusius writes that it is found on the ridges of the Tyrol.

### NARROW-LEAVED BEAR’S EAR,
### of a reddish color.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leafed Auricula Ursi with a dense cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

This grows, says Clusius, in certain Alps of Carinthia and Upper Styria; it flowers toward the end of July—that is, when the snows on those highest ridges are melting.

Furthermore, the Bear’s Ear is cold and dry and has astringent qualities, according to the testimony of Pietro Andrea Mattioli and Dodoens. It is beneficial for intestinal ruptures <note>original: "Enterocelas"</note> and wounds of every kind, whether taken internally or applied externally. And hunters, as Clusius reports, very frequently use its root to strengthen the head, so they are not troubled by vertigo when on precipices.

<column-break/>

### REDDISH-FLOWERED BEAR’S EAR.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Auricula Ursi with large, broad leaves and a tall flowering stalk, labeled with the letter 'D'.</image-desc>

This produces a stem a palm’s breadth or more in height, bare, rounded, and whitish-green. At its summit is a leaf-like cup <note>original: "calathiscus"</note> that is almost whitish and appearing as if sprinkled with flour; from this emerge many flowers arranged in an umbel, with various half-inch stalks of the same color as the cup. These are fragrant, a pleasant reddish hue, with a yellow center inside, and divided into six heart-shaped segments. The leaves at the root are many, oblong, somewhat rounded, serrated at the edges, thick, and greener on the top than underneath; they are sprinkled on both sides with a floury white powder. The root is thick, fibrous, and white.

It grows in the same native locations as the yellow variety.

### FLESH-COLORED BEAR’S EAR,
### with leaves not at all serrated.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Auricula Ursi with smooth-edged leaves and large flowers.</image-desc>

On account of its beauty and rosy color, and because it grows among rocks, it is commonly called *Stein Röslin*—that is, the Rock Rose. <note>original: "Rosa petraea"</note>

Clusius writes that it is very common on the ridges of the Styrian Alps, and from there it is brought for sale to the Viennese market by poor women who gather herbs. <note>original: "rhizotomis mulierculis," literally "little women root-cutters."</note>

### SMALLEST BEAR’S EAR, with
### flesh-colored and snow-white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Auricula Ursi plant with tiny leaves and a few flowers.</image-desc>

The Smallest Bear’s Ear is recorded as the *Smallest Alpine Sanicle* <note>original: "Sanicula alpina minima"</note> by Clusius, Lobelius, Tabernaemontanus, Gesner, Gerard, Caspar Bauhin, and others. However, Tabernaemontanus must have been utterly ignorant of plants, as he treats the "Bear’s Ear" in three different chapters with other plants interspersed between them.

This is found on the highest ridges of the Styrian Alps.

<sig>Qq 3</sig>

### MYCONUS’S HAIRY BEAR’S EAR, blue. <note>original: "Auricula Ursi Myconi." This plant, now known as *Ramonda myconi*, was named after the Spanish physician and botanist Francisco Micón.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Myconus’s Bear’s Ear, showing a rosette of broad, hairy leaves at the base and a central flower stalk with several bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

It sends out many roots that are almost hair-like, dark in color, and which cling to rocks; they have an astringent taste. Around these roots, the leaves creep along the ground, somewhat resembling the leaves of Borage. They are slightly jagged <note>original: "laciniata"</note> around the edges, rough, wrinkled, thick, and hairy. From the middle of the leaves, two or three small stalks emerge; these are round, about nine inches <note>original: "dodrantales," a Roman measurement of about 9 inches or a "span."</note> tall, hairy, solid, juicy, and purplish. At the tips of these stalks are blue flowers made of five petals, with yellow stamens in the center.

It grows in shady, moist mountain places, and especially in the Pyrenees.

Myconus writes that a water distilled from this plant using glass instruments is very effective for breaking up stones in the kidneys and bladder.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE GROUND JASMINE. <note>original: "Chamae Iasme Alpina," likely referring to a species of Androsace or a similar alpine primrose.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Alpine Ground Jasmine, showing creeping stems with small leaves and clusters of small flowers at the tips of upright stalks.</image-desc>

It advances by creeping joint-by-joint with thin, dark little roots, spreading a "little eye" of leaves across the ground. These leaves are half an inch long, about the width of a stalk of straw, with a slightly blunt tip, and are hairy. From their center, a small stalk rises, about nine inches tall, smooth-jointed, and hairy. Its summit is adorned with an umbel <note>a cluster of flowers where the stalks spread from a common center like umbrella ribs</note> of flowers that are large for the size of the little plant. They are whitish, turning reddish through the summer, and very fragrant. Where the little flower-stems join the main stalk, there are small, green, hairy leaves underneath. Indeed, many plants hang together from a single root as if linked in a chain. It takes the name Ground Jasmine <note>original: "Chamaeiasme"</note> from the scent of Jasmine.

---

### MULLEIN. German: Wullkraut. French: White Bouillon, Good Man. Italian: Verbasco. <note>The German "Wullkraut" or "Wool-herb" refers to the plant's fuzzy texture; the French "Bouillon blanc" refers to its use in soothing infusions or "broths."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Mullein plant, featuring large, broad, fuzzy leaves and a tall, dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

The names *Verbascum* and *Verbasculum* are sometimes given to the Primrose, the Campion, the Moth Mullein, the Ethiopian Mullein, and the Ragwort, but less properly so. The true species and distinctions of Mullein are those we shall now describe.

The common kind which we depict here grows to three cubits <note>about 4.5 feet</note> or higher. From a white, woody, and quite thick root, it puts forth a similarly thick stalk, branched with many "arms," and covered in downy hair. The leaves are like those of Elecampane: broad, long, soft, and entirely covered in a greyish-white down. Some are spread across the ground, others are attached to the stalk. These vary considerably according to the plant's age—some are more wrinkled, others smoother. The stalks appear sometimes singly, sometimes in groups, and sometimes branched.

<column-break/>

### NARROW-LEAVED MULLEIN with a golden flower and thicker leaf, as described by Agetius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leaved Mullein, showing a more slender habit with elongated leaves and a flowering spike.</image-desc>

Is this the *Lychnitis* Mullein of Matthiolus? Or the narrower Mullein of Dodoens?

To continue with the description of the Common Mullein begun previously: it has many flowers joined together on a long spike <note>original: "thyrso"</note>. They are the size of a small rose, yellow, divided into five parts, with a faint but not unpleasant scent. In the middle are five tips <note>stamens</note>: two are smooth and yellow, while the rest are whitish and woolly. The seed follows in round little heads; it is tiny, like poppy seed.

It is very common along the edges of fields and plowed lands, on embankments, in ditches, and in other sandy places. It flowers from July until Autumn.

---

### THE GREATEST SOUTHERN MULLEIN, fragrant; two types, yellow and white.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large Mullein variety with very broad, textured leaves forming a dense rosette.</image-desc>

As it excels all other Mulleins in the size of its leaves, so it does in its sweet scent; though it may perhaps only be a variety of the Common Mullein. It usually produces yellow flowers, but sometimes white ones, with a very sweet scent. The leaf is very long and very wide. The root is exceedingly thick.

It is cultivated in Belgian, French, and Norman gardens; in England, Italy, and the soil of Piedmont, it is found growing wild everywhere in the fields.

Furthermore, Mullein was called <term>phlomos</term> <note>original: φλόμος</note> by the Greeks, as if it were <term>flaming</term> <note>original: φλόγινος (phloginos)</note> from the verb <term>to burn</term> <note>original: φλέγω (phlego)</note>, because its leaves and stalks were used in lamps as wicks. Some wrote *Phlomos* with an "r," calling it *Phlomon*.

<column-break/>

### Another image of the GREATEST SOUTHERN MULLEIN, white and yellow.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another large Mullein variety, showing the plant's structure from the thick root to the beginning of the flower spike.</image-desc>

Dioscorides records several kinds of Mullein. He first distinguishes it into *White* and *Black*. He then subdivides each of these into *Male* and *Female*. To these he adds a *Wild* kind of Mullein. He then adds two hairy kinds of *Phlomis*, and a third called *Lychnitis*.

Galen follows Dioscorides in describing the different types of Mullein in his eighth book on simple medicines. Pliny writes that distinguishing the kinds of Mullein is unnecessary, since they all have the same effect. Nevertheless, he distinguishes them in this manner: Mullein has two primary kinds: the White (which is understood to be the Male) and the Black (the Female). A third type is found only in the woods.

So said the Ancients regarding Mullein.

### CURLED AND SINUOUS MULLEIN. <note>original: "Verbascum Crispum et Sinuatum." Likely *Verbascum sinuatum*, known for its wavy-edged leaves.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Verbascum plant with large, wavy-edged (sinuate) basal leaves and a tall flowering spike with small blossoms.</image-desc>

The lowest leaves of this Mullein are about a span and a half long <note>A "span" or *palmus* is about 8-9 inches; a "span and a half" is roughly 12-13 inches.</note>, wavy in the manner of the Horned Poppy, and whitish. The upper leaves, however, are shorter, ending in a sharper point, almost like Ivy, and are sprinkled with a dusty coating on both sides, though they are more branch-like toward the bottom. They clasp the stem without any leaf-stalk. The flowers are small and yellow, not unlike the flowers of Moth Mullein <note>original: "Blattariae." *Verbascum blattaria*.</note>; they fall off easily and are divided into five segments, with five hairy, purplish stamens occupying the center and saffron-colored tips <note>original: "apicibus," referring to the anthers.</note>.

We have observed this species nowhere except at Montpellier <note>original: "Monspelii," a major center for botanical study in France.</note>, where it blooms everywhere in Autumn.

---

### MULLEIN WITH A SMALL WHITE FLOWER.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Verbascum plant showing a thick root system, broad leaves, and a slender flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant is found in the same habitats and is recognized as a Mullein by a form not much different from the yellow varieties. The root is similar, and the stem is hollow like the others and woolly. However, the leaves are only covered with that hoary, gray-white wool on the underside; on the upper side—unless you count the very young and tiny leaves placed near the flowers—they are hairless, dark green, and pointed. The small flowers are arranged in the leaf-axils in the manner of the Powdery Mullein; they are white in color, sitting in the same number as the petals, with hairy stamens the color of boxwood and vermilion-colored tips.

---

### WILD SAGE-LEAVED MULLEIN, Exotic, with a rounder leaf, of Lobel. <note>Named after Matthias de L’Obel (Lobelius), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Verbascum variety with rounded, sage-like leaves and a branching flower head.</image-desc>

This plant has leaves that rival those of Sage, but they are rounder, whiter, and yet less woolly; it has a woody and fibrous root. The stems and general appearance are ultimately not much different from others. It did not happen that Lobel saw the flowers described, because, as he reports, they were already withered. It enjoys the same native habitats as the *Lychnites* Mullein, which will be discussed shortly.

<column-break/>

### POWDERY MULLEIN, with a small yellow flower. <note>Likely *Verbascum pulverulentum*, the Hoary Mullein.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a "powdery" Verbascum with dense, felt-like foliage and a branched inflorescence.</image-desc>

The whole plant is covered everywhere with a very thick, whitish fine dust, though it is easily rubbed off. This coating is more abundant on the lower parts than the upper. The flowers correspond to those of the common Mullein, but they are four times smaller.

Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist.</note>, here and there in his *Commentaries* according to his custom, displays an illustration of it under the title "Second Mullein," yet without any description or note of the place where he observed it. We have often seen it blooming in June and July at Montbéliard <note>original: "Montbelgardi," a city in eastern France.</note> within the walls, from the gate called <unclear>geuirs</unclear> to the <unclear>arcti</unclear> gate.

---

### BLACK MULLEIN, with a small flower and purple tips. <note>Known today as *Verbascum nigrum*.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of "Black Mullein" with darker, more pointed leaves and a long, unbranched flowering spike.</image-desc>

The root is like that of the common Mullein, as is the stem; it is no less tall, but less hairy. The leaves are smaller, sparser, and placed alternately; they are attached to reddish stalks two or three inches long. They are foul-smelling and green, less hairy, and lightly notched around the edges. The flowers are equal in position and density to the common type, but smaller, colored with a deeper saffron, like the common Moth Mullein, with five purplish, hairy stamens. The seed is like that of the common variety.

Many people plant Black Mullein. The flower varies from a purplish-citrine to a pale yellow or even entirely white.

It grows in sandy, grassy places, blooming in Summer.

---

### WILD MULLEIN with a less pointed leaf.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild Verbascum with smaller, less pointed leaves and a compact flower cluster.</image-desc>

This plant has a woody and fibrous root; the stems are square and drawn out like rushes. The yellow flowers are notable for their feathered crests. The seeds are like those in the common variety.

It comes forth on drier and stony hills throughout Spain, Portugal, and Narbonnese Gaul <note>The southern region of France around Montpellier and Narbonne.</note>.

<page-num>495</page-num>
<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES</header>

### HOARY SYRIAN LAMP-MULLEIN, 
### with a flowering top from Jerusalem. <note>original: "Verbascum Lychnites Syriacum Incanum." *Lychnites* refers to the plant's historical use as a lamp-wick.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Verbascum plant with broad, textured leaves at the base and a tall flowering spike with small blossoms.</image-desc>

This beautiful new plant has the flowers of the Wild Lychnis <note>A group of flowering plants in the Caryophyllaceae family, such as the Rose Campion.</note>, or the Chalcedonian Lychnis, but yellow in color. The leaves are narrow, and the square stems are grey-white with a thick, downy coating; the root is woody. Many call it the broad-leaved Wild Mullein.

Regarding the powers of Mullein in general, the leaves of all types have a drying and cleansing effect. According to the testimony of Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy.</note>, a decoction of the leaves and flowers helps with ruptures, bruises, and convulsions, as well as chronic coughs. It eases toothaches when used as a mouthwash, removes burning and inflammation of the eyes, and calms the pain of hemorrhoids, resolving them if they are bathed in it several times. The yellow flowers dye the hair; the root, when worn, is believed to benefit those with the Falling Sickness <note>An old term for epilepsy.</note>.

### COMMON YELLOW MOTH-MULLEIN. <note>original: "Blattaria Vulgaris Lutea." Now known as *Verbascum blattaria*.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Blattaria plant with jagged, lanceolate leaves and a long, slender flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It raises a firm and straight stem, sometimes as tall as a man and as thick as a thumb, smooth and bushy with a very dense crowd of branches. The flowers are like those of Mullein on hairy stalks, of a reddish-yellow color, followed by black seeds. Moreover, at the base of each flower's stalk, a pointed leaf is positioned. The other leaves are like those of Mullein but narrower, dark green, and shiny on top, endowed with no downy coating, jagged around the edges, and possessing an unpleasant smell. The root is shaped like a turnip and provided with fibers.

It grows naturally along the edges of water, on muddy banks, and not far from riverbanks. It is also cultivated in gardens. It blooms from June until September.

### MOTH-MULLEIN WITH A GREEN FLOWER.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Blattaria variety with smaller, more rounded leaves and a dense flowering head.</image-desc>

It is illustrated under this title by de l'Obel <note>original: "Lobelio," referring to Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist.</note> in his *Images of Plants*. Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who categorized thousands of plants.</note> also names it the Green-flowered Moth-Mullein in his *Pinax* and *Phytopinax*. However, we have never seen it, nor has anyone else described it.

Furthermore, Moth-Mullein is found to be hot and dry, as discerned from its bitter taste. According to Bock <note>original: "Trago," referring to Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist.</note>, young girls are accustomed to gild the seed pods and place them in crowns and garlands.

<column-break/>

### MOTH-MULLEIN: German: Mottenkraut; French:
### Herbe aux Mittes; Italian: Blattaria. <note>The names in all three languages refer to the plant's supposed ability to repel moths or "blattae" (insects/cockroaches).</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Blattaria plant with broad, lobed basal leaves and a tall spike of five-petaled flowers.</image-desc>

Bock, Fuchs, and Mattioli <note>Three of the most influential "Great Herbalists" of the Renaissance.</note> say that Moth-Mullein so mimics the Mullein that it is often gathered in its place by the unskilled. However great the similarity between these plants may be, they are by no means one and the same plant; nor can we assert that our common Moth-Mullein is the *Blattaria* mentioned by Pliny.

Since there are various species of this stock, we illustrate here the Large-flowered Moth-Mullein, which Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger, a German physician and botanist.</note> relates to the Black Mullein in his edition of Mattioli, and calls the Moth-Mullein with beautiful white flowers, recently brought out of Italy. Others label it Large-flowered Moth-Mullein or Greatest Moth-Mullein.

### MOTH-MULLEIN WITH A BLUE OR
### PURPLE FLOWER.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Blattaria plant with deeply lobed leaves and a flowering stalk with distinct, open blossoms.</image-desc>

It has a thick, long, and succulent root, covered with a reddish bark and filled inside with a white pith of a sweet taste. With its leaves spread upon the ground, it resembles the Greater Fleabane <note>original: "Conyzam... maiorem."</note> of Mattioli; however, those leaves are not so hairy. The flowers and seed-heads are those of the common Moth-Mullein.

It is called the Purple Moth-Mullein by Gessner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist.</note>, de l'Obel, the *History of Lyon*, Gerard <note>John Gerard, author of the famous English herbal.</note>, and others. Camerarius refers it to the Black Mullein.

### MOTH-MULLEIN WITH A GREENISH-PURPLE
### FLOWER.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a slender Blattaria plant with small leaves and a long, thin flowering spike.</image-desc>

De l'Obel and Caspar Bauhin also mention this in the places cited; however, we would have wished these plants had been more carefully drawn by them.

It emphasizes the plant's uses for treating respiratory and inflammatory issues, as well as its historical role in folklore and repelling insects.</summary>

<page-num>796</page-num>
<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### HAIRY CRETAN MOTH-MULLEIN: Or the "Bear-plant" of some. <note>original: "Blattaria Pilosa Cretica: sive Arctos quorundam." The name *Arctos* is Greek for "bear," often used for plants with a shaggy or hairy appearance.</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with a basal rosette of serrated leaves and a tall, thin flowering stalk with small blossoms and seed pods. The roots are fibrous.</image-desc>

Giovanni Pona, in his description of Mount Baldo <note>A mountain in the Italian Alps famous for its botanical diversity.</note>, presents an illustration of this plant as the *Cretan Arctos* of Honorius Bellus, who calls it such in a letter to Carolus Clusius. However, as Pona himself remarks, it is not the "legitimate" one, since it has neither round leaves nor seeds similar to Cumin. Instead, it has serrated leaves like those of Betony or Mullein, though smaller, and the whole plant is covered in a kind of downy wool. The small stems are upright, laden with yellow flowers similar to Mullein, which are followed by small, round pods like those of the Hairy Moth-Mullein, containing tiny seeds.

It grows among rocks and atop walls.

<column-break/>

### DIOSCORIDES’ CHRYSOGONUM for some. <note>original: "Chrysogonum Dioscoridis." The name literally means "Golden-knee" or "Golden-born."</note>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with deeply lobed, oak-like leaves and a branching stem bearing small flowers. The root is a thick, dark tuber.</image-desc>

Dioscorides attributes to *Chrysogonum* leaves similar to the Oak, and says it is a dense shrub. He adds that the flower is equal to the Garland Mullein <note>original: "Verbasco coronario," likely referring to Rose Campion or a similar ornamental Mullein.</note>, and the root is equal to a Turnip, though intensely red on the inside. This root, when ground with vinegar and applied, is said to help with the bites of the shrew-spider. <note>original: "Muris aranei," literally "spider-mouse." In antiquity, the bite of a shrew was thought to be as poisonous as a spider's.</note>

Pliny does not mention *Chrysogonum*, nor does Galen, nor even the later Greek physicians. Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist.</note> reports that it is still unknown to apothecary shops and herbalists today with these words: "Unless *Chrysogonum* is brought into Italy from elsewhere, I believe it should be perpetually counted among those plants that are least known. We must search for it in the most hidden gardens of Nature where it lies concealed; for so far I have neither been able to find it, nor have I seen it discovered by others."

---

There are some, however, who wish for the plant called *Caryophyllata* <note>Wood Avens or Herb Bennet.</note> in the shops, or that called *Herba Benedicta*, to be the *Chrysogonum* of Dioscorides; others suggest Moth-Mullein (*Blattaria*), and still others Tormentil. We leave the matter to the judgment of those more skilled.

However, to Leonhard Rauwolf <note>A German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant in the 1570s.</note>, the plant we illustrate here in the last place seems to be the genuine *Chrysogonum* of Dioscorides. He describes it in his *Travels* thus: "It reaches the height of the Lion's Leaf," he says, "and is not unlike it in stem, flowers, and its round root (which is red on the inside). Yet the small stems are more slender, spreading out on the ground, and thin as a thread at the base, divided into various small branches. At the ends of these, very conspicuous yellow flowers are attached, placed in dense clusters, usually consisting of four small petals. The leaves cling to the back of the stems, in pairs on each side, and are so opposite to one another that they form the shape of a cross; they are dark green, wider at the tips, and cut like the leaves of an Oak."

The *History of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugdunensis," a massive botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps published in 1586.</note> also labels this as the *Chrysogonum* of Dioscorides in its Appendix.

---

# IMAGES AND SKETCHES OF PLANTS
## CLASS 31.
### RIBBED-LEAVED PLANTS: SUCH AS PLANTAINS, GENTIANS, Solomon’s Seals: and others somewhat similar to these.
<note>The term "Nervifoliae" refers to plants with prominent longitudinal veins or "nerves" in their leaves, a defining characteristic for this grouping.</note>

**PLANTAIN: German:** *Wegerich*; **Belgian:** *Weegbree*; **French:** *Plantain*; **Italian:** *Piantagine*.

**Greater Plantain, with a scattered panicle.**
<note>original: "Plantago Maior, panniculâ sparsâ." A panicle is a loose, branching cluster of flowers.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Plantago plant with broad, ribbed leaves at the base and several tall flower spikes with small, scattered blossoms.</image-desc>

To begin our discussion of the Plantain, we shall start with the poet Macer. <note>Aemilius Macer was a Roman poet whose work on the virtues of herbs was widely cited in Renaissance botany.</note> He says that the herb called *Plantago* in our tongue is called *Arnoglosson* by the Greeks, because its leaves are similar to a lamb's tongue. <note>original: "Arnoglosson," from the Greek "arnos" (lamb) and "glossa" (tongue).</note> There are two main forms of this Plantain: the first is called the "Greater," and the other the "Lesser," which is commonly called "Lanceolata" <note>Lanceleaf plantain</note> because its leaves rise up sharp like a lance. Dioscorides and Pliny likewise identify these two primary categories of Plantain, both of which—as will be clear from what follows—are divided into many species. We will describe the one pictured here alongside the figure that immediately follows.

<column-break/>

**COMMON GREATER PLANTAIN, with a smooth, non-notched leaf.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a common plantain with broad, oval, ribbed leaves and two dense, cylindrical flower spikes.</image-desc>

The root is as thick as a finger, fibrous on the sides, white, and in the middle, it appears as if cut off or mutilated, almost in the manner of the "Devil’s-bit." <note>original: "Morsus Diaboli." This refers to the Devil's-bit Scabious, named for its abrupt, premorse root which folklore claimed the devil bit off out of envy for its medicinal properties.</note> The leaves are quite round, wider in their middle, smooth, marked with seven distinct veins, and lie flat upon the ground; they have a harsh taste, somewhat sharp and bitter. The stalks are a foot long and flexible, bearing a "thyrsus" <note>A dense flower cluster</note> or spike of whitish, thread-like flowers [though Lobelius describes them as dark purple or blackish]. The seed is oblong, small like that of Purslane, and brown or rust-colored.

The plant pictured previously differs from this one only by its scattered spike and the irregular growth of the small, herb-like flowers that cling together in clusters like a narrow panicle.

---

**ROSE PLANTAIN.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plantain variety where the flower spike has mutated into a rose-like cluster of green bracts.</image-desc>

This plant lives for many years with a root more than an inch thick, spreading hairy and veined leaves of the broad-leaved Plantain across the ground. From among these, it raises stalks that are quite thick and hairy; at the top of these, numerous leaves—half the size of the lower ones—form an inner circle; these are very small, greenish, and shaped like a Chickweed, forming the appearance of a "rose." <note>This is a "monstrous" or mutated form of plantain where the flower parts have reverted to leaf-like bracts, creating a rose-like shape.</note>

Caesalpinus called this the *Leafy-stalked Plantain*; Dodonaeus called it *Plantain with a Rose-like spike*; Lobelius simply *Plantain*; Clusius *Common Rose Plantain*; Gerard and the Eystettensis *Spiked Rose Plantain*; and Tabernaemontanus *Multiple Plantain*.

It is cultivated in gardens.

<column-break/>

**ROSE PLANTAIN, WITH EXPANDED FLOWER, Great Sea Plantain.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plantain with a very large, flattened, rose-like head of green leaves or bracts at the top of the stalk.</image-desc>

Caspar Bauhin titles this in his *Pinax* <note>The "Pinax Theatri Botanici" (1623) was a landmark work by Bauhin that sought to organize all known plant names.</note>; Lobelius, the Eystettensis, and others call it *Simply Rose Plantain*; Gerard calls it *Exotic Plantain*. Might it be Clusius’s *Exotic Broad-leaved Plantain*?

Truly, the common broad-leaved Plantain has been known everywhere among all peoples since time immemorial. It grows abundantly in damp places, in fields, meadows, and gardens, as well as along roads and hedges. It flowers in July and produces its seed in August.

Another of this kind is found in the works of Mattioli, though perhaps only the specific location and soil make it appear different from the common smooth Greater Plantain.

<summary>This page describes various species of Plantain (Plantago), focusing on the Greater Plantain and "rose" mutations. It cites major botanical authorities to distinguish between common wild varieties and those cultivated in gardens.</summary>
<keywords>Plantain, Plantago, Arnoglosson, Greater Plantain, Rose Plantain, Macer, Dioscorides, Bauhin, botanical taxonomy, ribbed leaves</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the "Ribbed-leaved" plants (Class 31), specifically detailing the various species of Plantain (Plantago). It follows the previous page's introduction of the genus by distinguishing between hairy, narrow-leafed, and broad-leafed varieties.</meta>

### GREAT HAIRY PLANTAIN, nicknamed by some the "Middle" Plantain.
<note>original: "Plantago Maior Hirsuta, Media à nonnullis cognominata."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Great Hairy Plantain plant, showing broad, ribbed leaves at the base and several tall stalks ending in cylindrical flower spikes.</image-desc>

The fibrous, straight, and astringent root is as thick as a pinky finger. The leaves are broad and veined, turning white on both sides with a thin, soft down. The stems are straight, taller than a cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note>, round, hairy, and hollow; they carry a spike somewhat resembling a large mouse's tail, packed with a dense row of little cups. These cups unfold into four small purplish leaves, displaying stamens of the same color but with white tips.

By Tabernaemontanus it is called the Lesser Plantain of Dioscorides; by Lobel, Gerard, and others, it is called the Hoary Plantain.

The image is from our own purchased stock.

### FIVE-NERVED PLANTAIN with white hairy globes.
<note>original: "Plantago Quinquenervia cum globulis albis pilosis." This likely refers to *Plantago media* or a similar species with prominent veins and globular flower heads.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Plantago quinquenervia, featuring lanceolate leaves with five distinct veins and stalks topped with globular, hairy flower heads.</image-desc>

It spreads numerous leaves across the ground, which are five-nerved and hairy; the stalks join at the head of the root in such a way that, because of the fuzzy down, that junction is barely visible. The leaf is half an inch wide and two-sixths of a foot long. There are many stems, some upright, others lying flat, a palm or a span in length <note>A span is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, about 9 inches.</note>. They carry small heads shaggy with white down, imitating the catkins of a Willow.

The juice of the common Plantain—to continue our account of its medicinal powers—benefits bleeding gums and those coughing up blood, whether it is drunk or rubbed on. The root heals ulcers of the kidneys and bladder, and its wash soothes toothaches. The seed has a drier quality and is less cold.

### SMALLEST LANCEOLATE PLANTAIN.
<note>original: "Plantago Lanceolata Minima." A "lanceolate" leaf is shaped like the head of a lance or spear—long and narrow, tapering to a point.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Plantago lanceolata minima, showing a smaller variety with narrow, pointed leaves and slender stalks with small flower heads.</image-desc>

It is provided with a small root, which is very shaggy at the point where the leaves emerge. The leaves are as narrow as grass, two or three inches long. A short and clustered head sits at the top of a stem longer than a palm.

Herbalists commonly label this the "Lesser Narrow-leaved Plantain," for the Lanceolate Plantain is commonly distinguished into Greater and Lesser varieties.

Both, however, grow in damp and uncultivated places, and they bloom at the beginning of summer. Furthermore, it is endowed with a drier and more highly recommended quality for wound-healing potions and for treating hernias.

<column-break/>

### Another IMAGE of the GREAT HAIRY PLANTAIN, by Lobel.
<note>Mathias de l'Obel (Lobelius) was a famous Flemish physician and botanist whose woodcuts were widely reused in botanical texts.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Plantago major hirsuta, attributed to Lobelius, showing similar broad leaves and elongated flower spikes.</image-desc>

We will summarize in a few words the powers of Plantain, which Dioscorides and Pliny recite to the point of boredom. According to the authority of Galen, it is of a mixed temperature: for it has something watery and cold, and something harsh, which is earthy, and it dries in the "second degree" <note>In ancient medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a plant's primary qualities like heat or moisture.</note>. It is a wound-healing herb, curing ulcers and fistulas. It stops the flow of the bowels, dysentery, and hemorrhages of the uterus. The distilled liquor wonderfully soothes "hot" gout <note>podagra</note> at its first onset; and it is believed to be drunk usefully by those with dropsy <note>edema, or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. The juice is most usefully dropped in for earaches and bleary eyes, and it is healthy for the consumptive and those wasting away. More on this in what follows.

### LESSER LANCEOLATE PLANTAIN: German: Pointed Wegerich; French: Little Plantain, Long Plantain.
<note>original: "Plantago Minor Lanceolata." Likely *Plantago lanceolata*, the common Ribwort Plantain.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Plantago minor lanceolata, showing long, narrow leaves and tall, thin stalks with small, dark flower heads.</image-desc>

It sends down a rather long and fibrous root. The stems are equal to those of the "Greater" type, deeply furrowed, somewhat hairy, and with a flower rivaling the Greater. The leaves, however, are very different, resembling the point of a lance; they are attached to long stalks, oblong, narrow, lightly saw-toothed with rare notches, hairy, with five nerves visibly raised on the back, running the length of the leaf.

For this reason, the Greeks call it *Pentaneuron* <note>original: Πεντάνευρον; meaning "five-nerved"</note> and the Latins *Quinquenerviam*. The same people called the "Greater" broad-leafed type *Heptapleuron* <note>original: ἑπτάπλευρον; meaning "seven-ribbed"</note> and *Septenerviam*.

### SMALL BROAD-LEAVED PLANTAIN.
<note>original: "Plantago Latifolia Minor."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Plantago latifolia minor, showing a smaller plant with broad, rounded leaves and short flower stalks.</image-desc>

Tabernaemontanus made this similar in all respects to the Great Plantain; he and Gerard label it the "Small Broad-leaved Plantain."

Those things found in Dioscorides are superstitious: that three plantain roots with three cups <note>cyathis</note> of wine and an equal amount of water help "Tertian" fevers <note>malaria that recurs every third day</note>; and likewise four roots for "Quartan" fevers. He adds that there are some who use the root hung from the neck like an amulet to disperse scrofula <note>strumas; a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, often tuberculous</note>. The seed drunk in wine restrains diarrhea and the spitting of blood.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Plantain (Plantago), describing their physical characteristics, names in Greek and Latin, and their wide-ranging medicinal uses for wounds, gout, and digestive issues.</summary>
<keywords>Plantain, Plantago, botanical illustration, herbal medicine, wound-healing, Dioscorides, Galen, Lobel, Gerard, pharmacology, Greek botany, Latin nomenclature</keywords>

--- Page 579 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog of the Plantain family (Class 31), moving from the general types described on the previous page to more specific regional and structural varieties, including the "Narrow-leaved" and "Alpine" types, as well as the related genus Holosteum.</meta>

### GREAT NARROW-LEAVED PLANTAIN, leafy at the tops of the stems: and another spiked variety.
<note>original: "Plantago Angustifolia Maior, in caulium summitate foliosa: & alia spicata." This likely refers to a variety of *Plantago lanceolata* or Ribwort Plantain.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Plantago plant with long, narrow leaves and tall flower stalks, some with leaves at the top.</image-desc>

The root is woody, tasteless, and supported by thin fibers. The **leaves** are numerous at the top, long, narrow, and five-veined. There are several **stems**, which are unbranched, angular, about a cubit and a half tall <note>Approximately 27 inches.</note>, and purplish where they join the root. At the top are spikes about an inch long, in which the **tiny flowers** have somewhat long tips <note>referring to the protruding stamens</note>. Within the white **heads**, the **seeds** are somewhat long, reddish, and wrapped in a few thin husks.

### ALPINE NARROW-LEAVED PLANTAIN.
<note>original: "Plantago Angustifolia Alpina."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller alpine Plantago with a thick root and several flower spikes.</image-desc>

From a root that is somewhat thick, long, with few fibers, and widening around the head, leaves emerge that resemble those of the lance-leaf Plantain, but they are much narrower—about a third of an inch wide. They are a hand-and-a-half long <note>roughly 6 to 9 inches</note>, five-veined, slightly hairy, blackish, and somewhat firm. The **stems** are hairy at the root and equal in length to the leaves. They bear **heads** half an inch long, which are darker than those of other plantains.

### HOLOSTEUM or HOLESTEUM: German: *Hundsgrass*; French: *Holostium*; Italian: *Holostio*.
<note>Historically, "Holosteum" was used for various plants, often the "Buck's-horn Plantain" or certain grasses. Today, the name refers to Jagged Chickweed.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Holosteum plant with multiple flowering spikes and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist.</note> and Pliny, Holosteum is a small herb rising three or four fingers above the ground. Its **leaves** are very similar to Buck’s-horn <term>Coronopus</term> or Grass, and are astringent to the taste. The **root** is like a hair—thin, white, and fibrous. It grows on earthy hills. It is drunk in wine for ruptures and wounds; this is not without reason, since, if cooked together with meat, it has the power to bind and "glue" the flesh together. As Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> notes, it is endowed with a dry and astringent quality, and is therefore effective for those purposes.

According to Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneer of modern botany.</note> there are two types, the **Greater** and the **Smaller**. However, many different plants are given the name Holosteum: Pliny’s *Phalaris*, *Gramen Lagula* (Tongue-grass), *Myosuros* (Mouse-tail), Fuchs’s Grass, *Serpentina*, *Tunica*, the "smallest" *Herniaria* (Rupture-wort), and *Pilosella* (Mouse-ear).

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE SAME PLANT.
<note>original: "Eiusdem Plantae Alia Icon."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variant of the first Plantago, showing more robust flower heads.</image-desc>

This image is from Clusius, while the preceding one was from Gerard <note>John Gerard, a famous English herbalist.</note>. They differ mostly in this: in the latter image, very few small leaves sit upon the highest part of the stem.

We observed both of these in the meadow of St. Peter, which is adjacent to the garden at Montbéliard <note>A town in eastern France where the author performed much of his botanical research.</note>.

### LOBEL'S NAVEL PLANTAIN.
<note>original: "Plantago Umbilicata Lobelii." Named after Matthias de Lobel.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, wavy leaves and a thick, scaly root base.</image-desc>

In his *Adversaria* <note>A famous botanical work by Lobel and Pena.</note>, he calls this the *Mountain Navel of the Herbalists*. In Caspar Bauhin’s *Pinax* <note>A landmark botanical index.</note> it is called the *Broad-leaved or Foreign Sinuous Plantain*.

We have never seen it ourselves, nor does Lobel draw it clearly enough; for this reason, we do not include his description here.

### MONTPELIER HOLOSTEUM.
<note>original: "Holostium Monspelianum."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a bushy plant with many small flower heads and a thick root.</image-desc>

The **root** is long, thick, blackish, woody, and has several heads. The **leaves** are spread across the ground; they are entirely whitish, hairy, and woolly. Some are a palm’s length and others much smaller, not even a half-inch wide, with several veins running along their length. The **stems** are a span long <note>roughly 9 inches</note> or shorter and similarly hairy. They bear a long flower-stalk <term>thyrsus</term> several inches long, though sometimes only one. The **flowers** and **seeds** are like those of the "Hart's-horn" <note>original: "Cornu Cervino," referring to *Plantago coronopus*.</note>.

In Montpellier <note>A city in southern France famous for its medical and botanical school.</note>, it blooms in April and May, and sometimes even in Autumn, in dry olive groves and near fields. It is also cultivated in gardens. More can be found in the Appendix.
