# OF PLANTS
<note>original: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### CROWFOOT, STAR-HERB, BUCK'S-HORN, Common Crowfoot.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS, HERBA STELLA, CORNV ceruinum, Coronopus vulgaris." The name Coronopus comes from the Greek for "crow's foot," referring to the leaf shape.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Coronopus plant with long, narrow, deeply lobed leaves radiating from a central point, resembling a star or buck's horn, with several upright flowering stalks.</image-desc>

This herb is called *Raven's foot* <note>original German: "Rappen fuss"</note> by the Germans; *Stag's Horn* <note>original French: "Corne de Cerf"</note> or *Capriole* by the French; and *Coronopo* or *Star-herb* <note>original Italian: "Herba stella"</note> by the Italians. We shall discuss the opinions of the Ancient authors regarding this plant in the Appendix. Since several species and varieties of it are recognized today: the **common variety**, which we depict here, has a **thin, white root** with an astringent taste. The **leaves** are crowded together immediately from the root; they are long, narrow, hairy, veined, and divided into several side lobes like the branches of a **deer’s horn** (from which it takes its name). Among these, the **stems** rise up like those of a Plantain, supporting a head or spike that bears flowers and seeds similar to those of the Plantain.

We have observed it growing wild only around Montpellier, where it occurs everywhere; elsewhere, however, it is sown in gardens and flowers in May.

### LOBELIUS’S MARSEILLE CROWFOOT, perhaps a variety of Serpent-herb.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS MASSILIENSIS LOBELII, Serpentinæ fortè varietas."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, denser variety of Coronopus with thicker, more succulent-looking leaves and shorter flowering spikes.</image-desc>

This plant grows luxuriously with a very dense and spreading cluster of **leaves**, similar in habit and stiffness to the Small Mountain Stonecrop or the Cluster Pine, and it produces countless stalks about nine inches long <note>original: "dodrantalium"</note>. The **seed** is tiny, like that of the Plantain or the common Serpent-herb. The **root** is somewhat long, woody, and thick, with a taste that is somewhat warm and aromatic.

It grows abundantly on the hills and rocks near Marseille, toward the "Marsallino-neæ" <note>likely a local place name near Marseille</note>, appearing among the Goat's Thorn <note>Tragacanth</note>.

### RAINAUDET’S MARITIME CROWFOOT.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS MARITIMVS RAINAVDETI."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime variety of Coronopus with elongated, narrow leaves and multiple tall, slender flowering spikes.</image-desc>

The **root** is about a palm and a half long <note>roughly 6 inches</note>, thick, dark, dry, and tasteless. From it arise countless stars of radiating leaflets (as in Dalechamp’s *Phyllum*), which are more crowded together, turned backward, less than half an inch long, and narrower than Matthioli's Serpent-herb. The center of these radiating leaves is entirely hairy. From a base the width of a Lupin bean, a **small stem** emerges, an inch long, bare, hairy, and almost entirely covered by a small flower spike.

Furthermore, the leaves of the **common Crowfoot** are typically included in **salads** among the French and English after a light boiling. It is believed to benefit those with **kidney ailments** <note>nephritics</note>, not by grinding down stones, but by strengthening the kidneys. It also checks and stops the bursting of blood <note>hemorrhages</note>.

<column-break/>

### CROWFOOT CALLED SERPENTINA.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS SERPENTINA DICTA." Likely *Plantago serpentina*.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Serpentina variety, featuring long, slender, unlobed leaves and tall flowering stalks with cylindrical spikes.</image-desc>

The **root** is of remarkable thickness and length, occasionally divided into several heads. From this grows a great crop of **leaves**, as long as those of the edible Crowfoot but not even a third or fourth of their width. Among them are several **stems**, a palm’s length or higher <note>4 inches or more</note>, bare and without joints, distinguished by the flower spike typical of the Crowfoot. We kept this in our garden at Geneva, having brought it from the nearby mountains; it flowered for us in June and July.

**Matthioli** highly recommends its use against the bites and stings of **venomous serpents**, as well as for **dropsy** <note>edema</note>; others recommend it for fluxes and **toothaches**. We leave the specific method of use to be sought from his writings.

### SMALLEST SERPENTARY CROWFOOT.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS SERPENTARIA MINIMA."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a very small variety of Coronopus with a dense tuft of short, narrow leaves and several small flowering spikes.</image-desc>

This Crowfoot, the illustration of which we provide here (drawn from a dried plant we collected in the month of June at Worms <note>original: "Burmij Rhætorum"</note>), has a **thick root**. Its **stems and flowers** are like those of the Serpent-herb Crowfoot, but the **leaflets** are broader.

It grows in abundance on the high, barren mountain ridges of the Cevennes in Southern France <note>Gallia Narbonensi</note>.

Otherwise, the Crowfoot herb is **cold and dry**, clearly astringent, and approaches the Plantain in its medicinal properties. More details are provided beside the following illustration.

### OUR MARITIME CROWFOOT.
<note>original: "CORONOPVS MARITIMA NOSTRAS." Likely *Plantago maritima* or Sea Plantain.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a maritime Coronopus with thick, fleshy leaves and robust flowering spikes, showing a detailed root system.</image-desc>

The **root** is short, blackish, thick, and provided with several fibers. The **leaves** are narrower than in the common Crowfoot, but long, thicker, and more succulent—sometimes almost like rushes—measuring three to four inches long, with a **salty taste**. The **flower** is purple and spiked, as in the common variety, and its **seed** is similar to that one.

It flowers near the sea at Montpellier in the month of August; it delights in salty soil and grows abundantly on salt-marshes and shores.

We provide the reasoning behind the names Crowfoot, Buck's-horn, Sanguinaria, and Star-herb in the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Coronopus (Buck's-horn Plantain), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats ranging from Marseille to Geneva, and their medicinal uses for kidney health and snake bites.</summary>
<keywords>Buck's-horn plantain, Coronopus, Serpentina, maritime herbs, Matthioli, medicinal plants, kidney remedies, star-herb, Montpellier botany</keywords>

# ILLUSTRATIONS AND SKETCHES
<note>original Latin header: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>
<sig>Rrr 3</sig>

### MOUSE-TAIL: German: *Mouse-tail*; Flemish: *Mouse-tails*; French: *Mouse-tail*.
<note>original: "MYOSVROS: Germ. Meusf fchrvanslin: Belg. Muysensteerkens: Gall. Queue de souris."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Myosuros plant, showing its long, slender, mouse-tail-like flower spikes and basal cluster of narrow leaves with fibrous roots.</image-desc>

Herbals commonly label this plant as *Myosuron* <note>from the Greek for "mouse tail"</note> or *Mouse-tail*, and some identify it as the *Holosteum* mentioned by Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>.

It has numerous fibers for roots, from which many grass-like leaves grow, measuring three or four inches and remaining very narrow. The stems are soft, rounded, and bare, hardly exceeding the leaves in height. At the summit, they bear mossy little flowers of a herbaceous green color that open only slightly; these are succeeded by a spike two or three inches long, rounded, pointed, and compact, which skillfully mimics the appearance of a mouse’s tail.

It delights in rich fields and meadows, flowering in April.

It has a cooling effect and does not differ much in its medicinal properties from the Plantain.

<column-break/>

### ALPINUS’S THIRD SALTWORT.
<note>original: "KALI TERTIVM ALPINO." Prosper Alpinus was a famous Venetian botanist who studied Egyptian plants.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Kali Tertium, a low-growing plant with succulent-looking, curved leaves and small flower heads at the tips of the stems.</image-desc>

This plant consists of a few leaves, very close in appearance to the leaves of Bugle <note>original: "Aiugæ"</note>, but much longer. It has a single stem that is not straight, from which three or four smaller stalks rise directly upward. At the summit of each is a **Head**, prolific with five or more leaves similar to Ground-pine <note>original: "Chamæpyti"</note>; these are inclined and curved into an arc. In their center are many small flowers, similar to the blossoms of Roses. The herb is salty and has a sharp taste that stings the tongue.

It is found in Sicily, and some believe it should be referred to Dioscorides’s second species of *Anthyllis*. The Egyptians, among whom it grows, are familiar with its uses.

---

### FLEAWORT: Greek: *psyllion*; German: *Fleawort*; French: *Flea-herb*; Italian: *Psyllio*.
<note>original: "PSYLLIVM: Græcis ψύλλιον: Germ. Pfsilienkraut: Gall. Herbe aux puces: Ital. Pfilio."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Psyllium plant, characterized by its branched stems, narrow leaves, and small, rounded flower heads at the branch tips.</image-desc>

Fleawort grows with many hairy, rounded branches that spread out in various directions. Along these are messy, grass-like leaves. The top of the stem and the ends of the branches produce numerous stalks that somewhat mimic an umbrella; upon each of these sits a small, overlapping **Head**, thicker and shorter than a Plantain’s, with larger scales and similar flowers. The seed is slippery, shining, and black, resembling a flea in appearance <note>the name Psyllium comes from the Greek 'psylla', meaning flea, because of the seeds</note>. The root is woody, hard, and fibrous.

There are Greater and Lesser varieties of Fleawort, as well as Upright and Prostrate forms; there is even a certain Indian kind. It grows (according to Dioscorides) in cultivated and uncultivated fields. We depict the Greater variety here, but the root is shown doubled.

<column-break/>

### LESSER FLEAWORT: ALPINUS’S GOTNE.
<note>original: "PSYLLIVM MINVS: GOTNE ALPINI."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Psyllium Minus, showing a smaller, more compact version of the Psyllium plant with similar flowering heads.</image-desc>

Alpinus labeled this plant *Gotne rabum*, and he also mentions a white variety. However, Caspar Bauhin and other learned men have seen fit to call it **Lesser Fleawort** because of the entire plant’s resemblance to Fleawort.

Furthermore, Fleawort grows spontaneously in various places among fallow and plowed fields and sandy pits. It especially haunts sandy sea shores, though it is also occasionally sown; once planted, it easily returns for several years afterward. It is frequent in Languedoc <note>original: "Gallia Narbonensi"</note> and flowers in Spring and Autumn. We have also seen it in Genoa, and between Bologna and Florence, flowering in April. In Germany and England, it is kept only in gardens. ***Regarding its Use and Properties, see the Appendix.***

---

### DIOSCORIDES’S LION’S-FOOT, PLINY’S CEMOS: Cretan Lion’s-Foot, related to Fleawort.
<note>original: "LEONTOPODIVM DIOSCOR. CEMOS PLINII: Leontopodium Candia Psyllio affine."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Leontopodium, showing upright stems topped with woolly, star-shaped flower heads resembling a lion's paw.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, Lion's-foot is a small herb about two fingers high. It has narrow, sturdy leaves, three or four fingers in length, which are woolly. The **Heads** at the tops of the stems appear as if perforated, containing black flowers. The seed is wrapped in such thick down that it can hardly be distinguished. The root is small, black, somewhat hard, and fibrous. Pliny writes that it grows in flat fields and thin soil.

It is debated whether Dioscorides’s Lion’s-foot is the same as Pliny’s Lion’s-foot or his *Cemos*, which requires further investigation. However, the Lion’s-foot we depict here is native to Crete <note>original: "Candiæ"</note> and corresponds in all respects to the description proposed by Dioscorides. ***More in the Appendix.***

<column-break/>

### DODONÆUS’S GRASS OF PARNASSUS, called by some Liver-flower.
<note>original: "GRAMEN PARNASSI DODONÆO, QVIBVSDAM Hepaticus flos."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Gramen Parnassi (Grass of Parnassus), showing its distinct heart-shaped basal leaves and a single flower on a long stalk.</image-desc>

It has a moderately thick, fibrous root that is reddish-white. The leaves are not unlike Ivy leaves, though not angular. The stems are narrow, about half a span <note>a "palmus" or span is roughly 9 inches; "sesquipalmares" is about 13 inches</note> tall, undivided, and reddish at the lower part, usually bearing a single leaf that clasps the stem. Atop each stem sits a white flower, followed by a conical, purplish **Head** surrounded by radiating white and yellow filaments with matching tips. When this has grown to the size of a large chickpea, it opens to reveal many tiny, reddish seeds.

It grows in poor and boggy meadows that never entirely dry out. Furthermore, it strengthens the Liver and clears it of obstructions.

<summary>This page describes various low-growing herbs including Mouse-tail, Fleawort, and Grass of Parnassus, noting their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses for cooling and liver health. The text highlights the plant's visual resemblances to animal parts, such as mouse tails and fleas, which often informed their historical names.</summary>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original Latin header: "STIRPIVM"</note>

### EPIPACTIS, HELLEBORINE, DAMASONIUM.
#### Dodonaeus’s Helleborine.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with a fibrous root system, lanceolate leaves arranged alternately on the stem, and a spike of small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

*Epipactis*, which others call *Elleborine* <note>Helleborine</note> and *Borrien*, is a very small shrub, says Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician of the 1st century</note>, having very tiny leaves. Pliny <note>a Roman naturalist</note> calls it a foreign herb to Italy, counting it among the shrubs of Greece and Asia; he notes that according to Theophrastus <note>the "Father of Botany"</note>, the seed of Helleborine is mixed into a draft of Hellebore to help induce vomiting. But who can truly learn from these ancient writings what their *Epipactis* or *Elleborine* actually was? Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician</note> merely illustrates Helleborine but does not describe it; thus, various plants are mistakenly identified as Helleborine by different authors, such as Twayblade, Little Gentian, Rupture-wort, and others. We have decided here to treat the various species of Helleborine and *Damasonium* <note>a genus of water-plantains, though here applied to orchids</note> interchangeably.

### PURPLE AND YELLOW DAMASONIUM:
#### or narrow-leaved mountain Helleborine.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with narrow, elongated leaves and a terminal flower spike. The roots are thick and spreading.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> illustrates and describes this plant, which he observed flowering in the forests of Pannonia <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria</note> in June and July.

We ourselves have seen a white-to-yellowish Helleborine flowering in May on Mount Monthar in the territory of Montbéliard.

Furthermore, we saw a Helleborine or *Damasonium* with violet flowers at La Bastie on the hill of Geneva.

According to Clusius, the mountain meadows and clear-cut forests of Austria support a Helleborine with flesh-colored flowers and a narrow-leaved spiked mountain Helleborine.

The branched Helleborine, or *Alisma* of the serpent <note>original: "Alisra serpentis"</note>, is common in soft ground and especially on the shady ridges of mountains.

### A SPECIES OF DAMASONIUM CALLED BY SOME MARY’S SLIPPER: German: *Pfaffenschuch* (Priest-shoe), *Marienschuch* (Mary-shoe).

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, ribbed leaves and a large, distinctive slipper-shaped flower at the apex.</image-desc>

Some consider a plant related to Helleborine to be a species of *Damasonium*; it has leaves like Helleborine but they are wide, veined, wavy, and slightly hairy. A flower sits at the top of a foot-long stem, usually solitary, supported by four dark purple, pointed leaves arranged in a cross. These support a large, pale yellow pouch that mimics the wooden clogs of the Franciscans <note>a reference to the "slipper" shape of the orchid</note>, and it is somewhat open at the top. A seed pod follows, filled with a fine dust, as is common in Helleborines and Orchids. The root grows sideways under the earth, hairy with numerous fibers, and occasionally bears the scars of withered stems.

We observed this flowering in June in the mountains near Geneva.

<column-break/>

### ALPINE DAMASONIUM, OR HELLEBORINE, with white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a slender plant with small, white, orchid-like flowers arranged in a loose spike and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This is very similar to Dodonaeus’s Helleborine. The roots are fibrous and thin. The stem is sometimes nine inches, sometimes larger or smaller, slender, and clothed with alternating leaves like those of the Lance-leaf Plantain, sometimes narrower, sometimes wider. They are ribbed in the manner of White Hellebore. The flowers are arranged in a spike along the top of the stem, much like Orchids, emerging singly from the base of tiny leaves; they are somewhat large, milk-white, and resemble Orchid flowers. When they open, a white, shiny, short pistil appears. It supports a very bright, tender, oblong seed head.

It is found with the preceding species in shady woods and flowers in May.

### MOUNTAIN HELLEBORINE, OR ALPINE DAMASONIUM, with yellow flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, ribbed leaves and a cluster of flowers at the top, showing seed pods below.</image-desc>

The root is black, with moderate fibers descending deeply. The leaves are oblong, narrow, veined, and similar to Lance-leaf Plantain but somewhat longer and pointed. The stems are a foot high. The flower is yellow. The seeds are oblong and angular, joined in fours so that when they open in the middle, they appear like a "windowed pyramid." This structure has a black tip standing out above it, possessing a truly elegant shape similar to a lantern that is not covered or closed by horn, glass, or paper; this feature is unique to this plant.

### CHARLES TOUSSAIN’S ALISMA, WITH pale blue flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with small, star-shaped flowers and lanceolate leaves.</image-desc>

We received this beautiful plant from the distinguished pharmacist Charles Toussain, who collected it in watery places in Champagnole, Burgundy. It survived for many years when moved to a garden and flowered annually.

Furthermore, concerning the "False Damasonium," or Our Lady's Slipper (also called Priest’s Slipper), depicted in the preceding section, Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> relates: "This remarkable mask of a flower seems to have been overlooked by the ancients; some have thought it was *Alisma*. The common people of the North call it *Frauenschen* or *Papenschen*, that is, 'The Virgin's Shoe' or 'The Priest’s Slipper,' because of the shape of the flower."

<note>original: catchword "GENTIANA" (Gentian)</note>

<summary>This page describes various species of Helleborine and Damasonium (orchids), including the Lady's Slipper, noting their physical characteristics, habitats in the Alps and Central Europe, and the confusion regarding their names in ancient texts.</summary>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original Latin header: "ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA"</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentian plant with broad, ribbed leaves and a cluster of flowers at the top of the stem.</image-desc>

### GENTIAN: *German* Gentian, Bitter-root; *French* Gentienne; *Italian* Gentiana.
<note>original: "Bitterwurtz"</note>

The Ancients <note>referring to classical authors like Dioscorides and Pliny</note> recorded only one kind of Gentian; yet the Moderns <note>Renaissance botanists</note> have come to know many more, as will be clear from what follows.

We illustrate here the **Great Common Gentian**, which has leaves similar to those of the White Hellebore—many around the root, and arranged oppositely along the stalks; these leaves clasp the stems with joined stalks. They are marked with three or five veins like those of a Plantain, and are smooth, polished, and shining; by these characteristics, it is distinguished from the White Hellebore <note>which has pleated, non-shining leaves</note>. The stems are a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> or two cubits high, or even taller, growing singly and smooth. From the crotch of the upper leaves, the *Flowers* break forth, arranged in the manner of little whorls; they are individual, somewhat long, and yellow. Regarding the rest, see the notes beside its figure.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall Gentian plant with multiple whorls of flowers along the stem.</image-desc>

### GREAT GENTIAN WITH PURPLE AND WHITE FLOWERS.

Regarding the *Flowers*, to continue the description begun for the Common Gentian: there follow oblong Seed-vessels that open into two parts, containing numerous seeds, slightly reddish, approaching the seed of the Stock-gilliflower <note>original: "Leucoii"</note>, but smoother. The *Root* is thick, long, and divided into many parts, yellowish inside and out, with a remarkably bitter taste; because it is spongy, it becomes significantly wrinkled when dried.

This variety which we illustrate here differs very little in form or size from the Common kind; only the *flowers*, which are yellow in that one, are purple in this one, or milk-white marked with certain purple spots. They are not star-shaped like the common variety, but concave; yet both these and the others are entirely devoid of scent. *Concerning their season, location, and medicinal powers, see the following sections.*

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentian variety with narrower leaves and a single terminal flower bud.</image-desc>

### ENGLISH GENTIAN WITH ROLLED LEAVES, with a white-flesh colored Soapwort leaf.

Gerard <note>John Gerard, a famous English herbalist</note>, who describes this plant, calls it the "Concave Gentian"; according to his authority, it grows in a certain grove called *Sitania* in the county of Northampton in England, and it flowers in midsummer.

The common yellow Gentian grows in various places in mountain meadows and pastures; it is especially frequent on the mountains of *Suchet* and *Saincte Croix* near Embrun <note>original: "Ebrodunensium"</note>. We have seen the purple variety in the Grisons <note>original: "Rhoetorum"</note> of Switzerland; Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> found it in the Alps of Hungary <note>original: "Pannonicis"</note> and Austria <note>original: "Noricorum"</note>, and the white variety in the Alps of Styria.

Furthermore, they flower in June, and the seeds ripen in August; in that same month and September, the roots are gathered and dried in the shade.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller Gentian variety with many small flowers clustered at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

### LESSER GENTIAN, OR THE COMMON Crosswort.
<note>original: "Cruciata"</note>

The branches creep along with the root, about a span and a half or nine inches long, and are somewhat reddish. They are surrounded by frequent leaves, always two positioned oppositely—or rather, one continuous leaf enveloping the stem like a sheath at the joints—from which a segment of Gentian emerges on both sides. It is nearly six times smaller, smooth, thick, and bitter. The *Flowers* are crowded at the ends of the small branches and from the leaf axils; they are blue and divided into five parts. The *Seed* is abundant, tiny, oblong, tawny, and tasteless, contained in oblong vessels that open in two directions, wrapped in a thin, skin-like husk.

It is found on hills, mountains, uncultivated fields, and other rough places, as well as by roadsides; it is common in Germany.

---

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentian with long, pointed leaves and flowers emerging from the upper axils.</image-desc>

### GENTIAN WITH LEAVES COMMONLY BELIEVED TO BE Swallow-wort: Gentian with leaves like Silkweed.
<note>original: "Hirundinariae"</note>

This plant has a yellow root, the thickness of a finger and of a bitter taste. The stems are a cubit high, jointed, and slender; at each joint, two leaves grow opposite one another, matching the leaves of Swallow-wort <note>original: "Asclepiadis"</note> in shape and size. From their crotch, a single flower is born, large, oblong, shaped like a basket <note>original: "Calathi forma"</note>, divided into five points at the edge, and blue; there are the same number of stamens in the middle. A two-horned pod follows, which, when gaping open at maturity, reveals flat, chaff-like seeds of an ash-gray color.

According to Clusius, it grows abundantly in Hungary, Styria, and Lower Austria, at the base of mountains and on shady hills, but never on the highest and open peaks.

Some label this the "Gentian with Swallow-wort leaves."

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing Alpine Gentian with a very large, bell-shaped flower.</image-desc>

### ALPINE GENTIAN WITH A LARGE BLUE FLOWER, like a Canterbury Bell.
<note>original: "Violæ Marianæ"</note>

Clusius reports that this grows most abundantly in various Alps of Austria and Styria that are covered in snow almost year-round, flowering there in June and July. Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> observed it on the hills and slopes of Padua where vipers are commonly caught. The *History of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugdunensis," a botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps</note> states it grows in dry, snowy, windswept, and mountainous places.

Clusius notes that it, like other more beautiful Gentians, can be transplanted into gardens; however, once deprived of their native air and nourishment, they lose much of their former vigor and elegance.

<summary>This page describes various species of Gentian, including the Great Yellow Gentian, the Crosswort, and Alpine varieties. It highlights the plant's characteristic bitterness and details the differences in flower color and leaf structure across species, noting that these mountain plants often struggle when transplanted to gardens.</summary>

<keywords>Gentian, Bitter-root, Gentiana lutea, Gentiana cruciata, botanical history, Clusius, John Gerard, Alpine flora, medicinal herbs, plant morphology</keywords>

The author references the work of 16th-century botanists Leonhart Fuchs, Pietro Andrea Mattioli, Valerius Cordus, and Carolus Clusius to provide a comprehensive guide to these bitter medicinal herbs.</meta>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original Latin header: STIRPIVM</note>

### MARSH SPECIES OF GENTIAN, called the Basket Violet by some.
<note>original Latin: Gentianæ Species Palustris, Calathiana Viola</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentiana palustris plant, showing a single upright stalk with opposite leaves and bell-shaped flowers at the apex and upper leaf axils.</image-desc>

It loves the damp margins of meadows, rising with a straight, cubit-high <note>about 18 inches</note> and branched stem. Along this stem, opposite leaves grow at equal intervals, sometimes reaching a palm's length <note>about 3 inches</note> in height and the width of a stalk. They are dark green on the upper surface and paler underneath. From the axils of these leaves, starting from the middle of the stem up to the top, flowers emerge—sometimes single, sometimes in pairs or more—which are blue, five-parted, and shaped like a basket <note>original: calathi forma</note>. The roots are numerous, long, yellow, and bitter; these were not well-depicted in our illustration from Fuchs <note>referring to Leonhart Fuchs's "De Historia Stirpium," 1542</note>, which is why we have seen to it that another was drawn.

It commonly inhabits meadows situated at the roots of mountains. It blooms in August.

### LITTLE GENTIAN provided with downy fuzz on each flower segment; with a four-parted flower.
<note>original Latin: Gentianula lanugine ad singulas florum lacinias donata</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentianula plant with a branched stem, small leaves, and four-petaled flowers. The root system is fibrous.</image-desc>

We have observed this in various places within the territory of Montbéliard <note>an area in eastern France</note>, blooming toward the end of summer: near Blamont and St. Hippolyte between Vauvincourt and Dampierre above the spring; also near Basel in the meadows of Mount Monetes.

The **Common Great Gentian**, however, seeks its home in mountain meadows. Turner <note>William Turner, an English botanist</note> says it is abundant in the Alps between Germany and Italy; Mattioli <note>an Italian physician and botanist</note> says it grows on the high mountains of Trento and the Val di Non, and reports that roots an arm’s length long are dug up there. It blooms in August and September.

### CLUSIUS’S FLEETING LITTLE GENTIAN.
<note>original Latin: Gentianella Fugax Clusii</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small Gentianella plant with a cluster of basal leaves and a short flowering stalk.</image-desc>

It does not exceed nine inches <note>original: dodrantem</note> in height. The stems and branches are slender, and the leaves are even smaller. It likewise has smaller flowers, otherwise not unlike the flowers of other Gentians; these are either a pale purple or an extremely elegant blue color. The little seed pods <note>original: cornicula, "little horns"</note> are full of tiny, yellowish seeds. The root is very thin.

Is this perhaps the plant Lobel <note>Matthias de l'Obel</note> calls the *Smallest Gentian, most beautiful of all, growing on steep mountains*?

It is found in all high-altitude meadows and on mountain ridges, and it blooms in August.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THE MARSH GENTIAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Gentiana palustris, showing broader leaves and more prominent floral structures.</image-desc>

Mattioli says this plant is endowed with the same powers as the **Crosswort** <note>original: Cruciata; likely Gentiana cruciata</note>. Since the Crosswort has bitter leaves and roots, it is considered hot and dry <note>referring to the Galenic system of humors</note>. He adds that he has learned from experience that if the crushed root is applied to the belly as a plaster, the worms residing in the intestines will undoubtedly be driven out. Furthermore, ulcerated scrofula <note>strumas; swellings of the lymph nodes</note> are healed if the crushed root (newly dug) or the powder of the dried root is applied to them. In short, there are some who assert that the Crosswort Gentian can perform all the same tasks as the Common Gentian, which will be discussed in the Appendix.

### LITTLE GENTIAN CALLED HIPPION, BY CLUSIUS: *German* Blue-lung flower.
<note>original German: Blauw-lünchers blum</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gentianula (Hippion) with a low-growing habit and large, upright bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This beautiful perennial herb shades the entire turf where it grows, spreading through creeping fibers. The leaves spread along the ground and are half an inch <note>original: semiuncialib.</note> or longer, and veined. The flower stalks are an inch long and clothed with one or two pairs of leaves; upon each of these sits a single blue, five-parted flower. The seed is tiny, hard, and round.

Furthermore, it delights in high mountain ridges and blooms toward the end of Spring. It rejects all attempts at cultivation, and possesses the same medicinal powers as the Gentian. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus</note> claims it grows in the meadows between Ulm and Augsburg; we ourselves have seen it on Mount Thoiry in the Geneva region, and on Mount Braulio in Rhaetia <note>eastern Switzerland/northern Italy</note>.

### ANOTHER FLEETING LITTLE GENTIAN BY THE SAME AUTHOR.
<note>i.e., by Clusius</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another small Gentianella variety with thin stems and small flowers.</image-desc>

This one barely reaches a height of three inches, but it is provided with many branches. It has small leaves like those of the Lesser Centaury at each joint. The flowers are tiny and endowed with a most charming blue color. The little seed pods are like those in the species above, filled with black and very tiny seeds. The root is very small but gifted with numerous fibers.

Clusius says it blooms on the ridges of Mount Ötscher <note>in Austria</note> at the beginning of August. This is his *fifth* of the fleeting Gentianellas, while the preceding one was the *fourth*. We leave the rest of the species to be sought from his own writings.

<summary>This page describes several small species of Gentian and Gentianella, detailing their physical characteristics, alpine and marshy habitats, and medicinal uses for treating intestinal worms and scrofula.</summary>
<keywords>Gentian, Gentianella, Marsh Gentian, Crosswort, Hippion, medicinal herbs, mountain flora, Mattioli, Clusius, intestinal worms, scrofula</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, transitioning from Gentians to the Polygonatum genus (Solomon’s Seal) and Lily of the Valley. The author compares classical descriptions from Dioscorides and Galen with observations from modern botanists like Clusius and Mattioli.</meta>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES.
<note>original Latin header: ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA</note>

### POLYGONATUM, OR SOLOMON’S SEAL;
### German: *White-root*; French: *Seal of Solomon*.
<note>original: Germ. *Vveiss vvurtz*; Gall. *Seau de Salomon*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Polygonatum (Solomon's Seal) plant showing its characteristic arched stem, alternate leaves, hanging bell-shaped flowers, and a thick, knotted horizontal rhizome.</image-desc>

The root of the Solomon’s Seal <note>original: Polygonati</note> wanders transversely just under the surface of the soil; it is as thick as a finger, uneven and tuberous with socket-like joints <note>term: pyxidatâ commissurâ; the "scars" on the root where previous years' stems grew</note>, of a marble-white color, hairy with a dense troop of fibers, and possessing a somewhat sweet taste. The stems are one to one-and-a-half cubits high <note>about 18 to 27 inches</note> and rounded. On these, the leaves are arranged alternately, resembling those of the Lily of the Valley, veined, shining with a dark-green color on the upper side and a bluish-grey <note>original: cæsia</note> underneath. Truly from their axils <note>the angle between leaf and stem</note>, the flowers emerge on a stalk of half an inch or an inch long, which is then subdivided into short stems; they appear singly, in pairs, or in threes. They are cylindrical, whitish, with grassy-green edges divided into six segments. *More on this can be found beside the following figure and in the Appendix.*

### BRANCHED BROAD-LEAVED POLYGONATUM,
### with a rather large flower, like Lily of the Valley: *According to Clusius*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a broad-leaved, branched variety of Polygonatum with larger flowers and a similar knotted rhizome.</image-desc>

How much this differs from the remaining species of Solomon's Seal is clear from the illustration. Mattioli, however, wrongly presents this as the "Alexandrian Laurel" and even confuses it with the "Horse-tongue" <note>original: Hippoglosso; Ruscus hypoglossum</note>.

Furthermore, Dioscorides writes that the root of Solomon’s Seal is effectively applied to wounds and removes spots from the face. Galen also commends it for the same purposes; he says that Solomon’s Seal possesses a mixture of faculties and qualities, having something of an astringency, a sharpness, and a bitterness, along with a certain inexplicable unpleasantness. Thus, even today, women still wipe and beautify their faces with Solomon’s Seal, and especially with the water distilled from its roots.

### BRANCHED NARROW-LEAVED POLYGONATUM,
### *According to Clusius*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leaved, branched Polygonatum with whorled leaf arrangements and a thick rhizome.</image-desc>

It has a cubit-high <note>about 18 inches</note> stem, angular, divided into many thin branches which rise equally from each angle—sometimes four, sometimes five, according to the number of angles on the stem. The branchlets are thin, covered with long and narrow leaves, appearing equally in a circle in groups of two, three, or four; in these, the flowers, fruit, and roots are like the common Solomon’s Seal. Thalius labels this the *Lesser narrow-leaved Polygonatum*.

Moreover, Agricola writes that the water distilled from the roots of Solomon’s Seal not only cleanses the face and clears it of blemishes, but also dissolves blood that has clotted between the skin and the flesh <note>i.e., bruises</note>.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF POLYGONATUM,
### called *Ginocchietto* in Italian, BY CLUSIUS.
<note>original Italian: Ginocchietto, meaning "little knee," referring to the jointed stem</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Polygonatum, focusing on the upright stem and the distinct "knuckles" or scars on the rhizome.</image-desc>

To continue the description of the Solomon’s Seal flowers we began: saffron-colored tips <note>anthers</note> grow within them, with a whitish style hidden alongside the tips. When the flowers fall, green berries arise, which soon turn bluish-grey, similar to clusters of Ivy, or even a little larger; they are marked at the very top with three small lines <note>original: Zooulis</note>, and contain six or seven seeds, which are hard and the size of a vetch <note>a type of legume seed</note>.

Solomon’s Seal grows in woods, in shady places, and along margins; not only in mountainous areas, but also in the plains. It blooms in May and June.

Furthermore, it is called *Polygonatum* <note>from Greek: "many-kneed"</note> because the root is frequently jointed. It is called *Solomon’s Seal* because of the marks impressed upon the root which resemble a seal.

### NARROW-LEAVED POLYGONATUM.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a narrow-leaved Polygonatum with flowers hanging from the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Although Dioscorides mentioned only one Solomon’s Seal, many more are recorded both by Pliny and by more recent authors.

The white root of the one we depict here grows in a jointed fashion, no different from the broad-leaved Solomon’s Seal. The stems, which are even taller than a cubit, are also similar; but the leaves are much narrower, like the leaves of Madder <note>original: Rubia</note>, smooth, veined, and growing in star-like whorls of four or five from the joints of the stems. The herbaceous flowers are like the common Solomon’s Seal, followed by smaller berries that turn red when ripe.

It grows in mountain meadows and thickets, as we have observed on Mount Thoiry near Geneva and at the Waterfall <note>original: Vasserfall</note> near Basel. It blooms in May and June.

### LILY OF THE VALLEY: German: *May-flowers*; French: *Muguet*.
<note>original: Germ. *Meyenblüms*; Gall. *Muguet*</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lily of the Valley (Convallaria majalis) showing its broad paired leaves and one-sided raceme of bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

The root is thin, white, and fibrous, creeping just under the surface of the soil. It produces a small stem about a palm’s breadth high <note>about 3 inches</note>, which is angular. From the middle of this to the top, beautiful white flowers grow on thin, curved stalks; they tend to face one side, hanging and nodding at intervals. They are shaped like a little bell <note>original: parue nolæ effigie</note>, with the edges cut into six fringes. Six stamens, yellowish-green at the base, surround a three-sided style. The scent is most sweet, but the taste is bitter. These are followed by red, globe-shaped seed-vessels, like those of Asparagus. The leaves grow in twos or threes, are oblong, and resemble the leaves of an Orchid. The illustration from Fuchs's work does not please us much.

<summary>This page describes various species of Solomon's Seal (Polygonatum) and Lily of the Valley, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses in treating skin blemishes and wounds.</summary>
<keywords>Solomon's Seal, Polygonatum, Lily of the Valley, Convallaria majalis, medicinal herbs, cosmetics, Dioscorides, Galen, Clusius, botany, rhizomes</keywords>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original Latin header: STIRPIVM</note>

### ANOTHER BETTER IMAGE OF THE LILY OF THE VALLEY:
### Lily of the Valley of the Louvain fields, by Lobelius.
<note>original: Lilium conuallium agri Louaniensis, Lobelij. Matthias de l'Obel (Lobelius) was a Flemish physician and botanist who documented the flora of the Low Countries.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Lily of the Valley plant (Convallaria majalis) showing its broad leaves and a raceme of bell-shaped flowers, including the root system.</image-desc>

This differs from the common variety only by its pleasantly reddish color. Furthermore, the various differences of *Lily of the Valley* that are listed can easily be referred to these illustrated forms: the Great Lily of the Valley, the Broad-leaved Lily of the Valley, the Lily of the Valley with multiple rows of flowers, and so on.

Lily of the Valley grows spontaneously in woods, groves, and shady places; it is also commonly cultivated in gardens and flowers in May.

Regarding its powers and properties, Apollinaris <note>likely referring to the author of an early medieval herbal</note> and Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note> considered it to have cooling and moistening qualities. Conversely, it is established by Dodonaeus, Mattioli, and others to be of a hot and dry quality. Let those who have tasted even the first sips of Medical Philosophy be the judge. More on this plant can be found in the *Appendix*.

---

### LESSER TWO-LEAF, LESSER OPHRYS.
<note>original: BIFOLIVM MINVS, OPHRIS MINOR. Likely the Lesser Twayblade (Neottia cordata).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small orchid-like plant with two leaves and a slender spike of small flowers.</image-desc>

From a yellowish, fibrous root that smells like orchids, a simple little stem of three or four inches emerges below the leaves. To this, two leaves are attached in the manner of the common Ophrys <note>Twayblade</note>, but they are smaller, smooth, shining, and somewhat rounded. Above these, the other part of the stem towers similarly three or four inches; at its top sit small, grass-green flowers, differing from the common Ophrys flowers only in their slenderness. Small seed vessels eventually follow them.

We have seen both types of Two-leaf on Mount Salève near Geneva and on Mount *Wasserfall* near Basel. Both are of a dry and hot nature and very useful for healing wounds.

---

### WINTERGREEN: Germ. *Wintergrün*: Belg. *Wijntergroen*: Gall. *Pyrole*: Ital. *Pyrola*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Wintergreen plant (Pyrola) showing a basal rosette of rounded leaves and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

We have nothing on Wintergreen <note>original: Pyrola</note> in the records of the Ancient authors; however, Modern authors have observed several species of it. The more common one spreads five or six leaves on the ground, which are somewhat round, similar to Pear leaves <note>the name Pyrola is a diminutive of Pyrus, the pear tree</note>, thick, dark green, smooth, and with a shining upper surface, clinging to stems almost a palm's length. Between them grows a stem nine inches <note>term: dodrantalis</note> high, angular, provided with a few small and sharp leaves, and showing no branching. It bears a cluster <note>term: thyrsum</note> of lovely white flowers consisting of five petals, almost in the manner of Orchids, with many saffron-colored tips surrounding the center. Angular seed heads follow the flowers, full of tiny dust-like seeds.

<column-break/>

### OPHRYS, TWO-LEAF, ONE-LEAF:
### German: *Einblatt*, *Zweyblatt*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Ophrys or Twayblade plant with two prominent ribbed leaves and a tall flower spike.</image-desc>

Pliny enumerates Ophrys among those plants that darken the hair, and describes it as similar to a small-toothed vegetable. However, what his *Ophrys* actually is remains debated. Some think it is the *Alisma* of Dioscorides; others, the *marsh plantain*; others accept it as the *Two-leaf* or *One-leaf* of the Moderns.

Commonly, three types of Ophrys are established: *One-leafed, Two-leafed, and Three-leafed*; and the Two-leafed is again either *Greater* or *Lesser*. It could hardly be doubted that the Two-leaf is of the Orchid family, were it not for the multiple and fibrous roots; indeed, the flower and those stems are very closely related. It has only two leaves, opposite each other like broad-leaved Plantain, with one emerging from the fold of the other.

It grows in the mountains and flowers in May and June.

---

### ONE-LEAF or ONE-LEAFED OPHRYS:
### German: *Einblatt*.
<note>original: VNIFOLIVM seu OPHRIS VNIFOLIA. Now known as Maianthemum bifolium, or May Lily.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a May Lily (Maianthemum bifolium) showing its creeping rhizome, heart-shaped leaves, and small white flowers.</image-desc>

A thin, slightly sweet, white rootlet produces fibers by creeping; from this rises a stem a palm's length high, thin, provided with one or two leaves, rarely three, which are mostly veined along their length and hairy on the underside. The flowers are white, fragrant, consisting of four petals and as many two-colored stamens with a style. Berries follow, like those of Lily of the Valley, turning red when they reach maturity.

It is called One-leaf, says Caspar Bauhin, because when it first emerges, it has a single leaf; for when it acquires a stem, it has two leaves, and sometimes three.

Gesner distinguishes it into *Male* and *Female*.

It grows in the same places as the Two-leaf.

---

### SERRATED-LEAF WINTERGREEN, BY CLUSIUS.
<note>original: PYROLA FOLIO SERRATO, CLVSII. Likely Orthilia secunda, the Side-bells Wintergreen.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a serrated-leaf Wintergreen, showing the root system and a drooping raceme of flowers.</image-desc>

This second type is more delicate, with a shorter and weaker stem; its leaves are also thinner, smaller, oblong, pointed, and more sparsely notched <note>term: crenatis</note> around the edge. The flower cluster is very similar to the flowers of the previous species, but smaller. Angular seed heads follow them, putting forth a style from the center. The roots, as in the preceding and all others, creep like tubers and are thin and fibrous. However, the flowers in our illustration do not please us, as they were made after the image by Clusius while we were absent <note>a note on the production of the book, indicating the author was not present when this specific woodcut was prepared</note>.

Clusius writes that this species of Wintergreen grows very abundantly on the ridges of the Austrian Alps and Mount Jura, flowering in June and July.

<summary>This page describes various woodland plants including Lily of the Valley, Twayblades (Ophrys), and Wintergreens (Pyrola). It focuses on botanical identification, differences between species, and their medicinal qualities according to contemporary 16th-century botanists.</summary>

<keywords>Lily of the Valley, Wintergreen, Ophrys, Twayblade, Lobelius, Clusius, Bauhin, botanical classification, medicinal plants, Alpine flora</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original Latin header: ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA. "Sciagraphia" refers to a preliminary sketch or outline.</note>

Sff 2

### SHRUBBY WINTERGREEN, OF THE SAME CLUSIUS.
<note>original: PYROLA FRVTICANS, EIVSDEM CLVSII. Referring to Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius), a Flemish doctor and pioneering botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Shrubby Wintergreen, showing a woody stem with oval leaves and small bell-shaped flowers hanging from the upper branches.</image-desc>

This is sometimes found alongside the common variety. Generally, Wintergreens <note>Pyrola</note> delight in shady, mountainous, and wooded places, as well as cold regions. It flourishes with flowers in June and July and remains green throughout the year, enduring the winter and cold. Conversely, it rejects the warm recesses of gardens, urban locations, and milder parks; in those places, it grows sickly as if against its will and eventually dies.

Fuchs, Cordus, Turner, and others maintain that the Wintergreen is the *Limonium* <note>Sea-lavender</note>; but they are completely mistaken, at least in the judgment of Mattioli. It was called *Tintinnabulum* <note>Little Bell</note> by some because of the flowers' resemblance to small bells, and *Pyrola* because the appearance of the leaves approaches that of Pear <note>Pyrus</note> leaves.

### CHICKWEED WINTERGREEN, A SPECIES OF WINTERGREEN according to some.
<note>original: HERBA TRIENTALIS. Now known as Trientalis europaea.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Herba trientalis, featuring a whorl of pointed leaves at the top of a slender stem, with a single star-shaped flower emerging from the center.</image-desc>

In the *Observations* of Cordus, it is called *Herba trientalis*, with oblong leaves and a white, star-shaped flower, etc. The author of the *Gardens of Lusatia* calls it the "tiny trientalis herb with a single small stem." Thalius calls it *Alsinanthemos* <note>Chickweed-flower</note> and *Asterianthemos* <note>Star-flower</note>. To Camerarius, it is a certain peculiar species of Wintergreen, with a leaf more like an Arbutus than a Pear. Caspar Bauhin, in his *Prodromus* and *Pinax*, calls it the European Wintergreen with a Chickweed flower.

Camerarius observed this species of Wintergreen in the forests of Franconia, and especially around Gräfenthal; Thalius found it on the Brocken mountain and neighboring peaks, which are watered by perpetual moisture; others have found it elsewhere.

### MEDIUM BISTORT.
<note>original: BISTORTA MEDIA. Bistort is a member of the buckwheat family, named for its "twice-twisted" root.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Bistorta media, showing a plant with broad basal leaves, a tall flowering spike, and a thick, twisted rhizome.</image-desc>

By creeping, this plant multiplies itself greatly; it differs from the previously mentioned type by its smaller, smooth leaves and its more intensely twisted root.

Some authors in their Herbals record it as Lesser Bistort and *Dracunculus* or Lesser *Colubrina* <note>names associated with "snake-weed" due to the root shape</note>. Brunfels calls it the Male Bistort.

Bistort is commonly found in damp places and shady woods with rich and muddy soil. Mattioli reports that it grows in the mountains, as we have also seen near Geneva on Mount Thoiry, and in Switzerland on the ridges of the Jura mountains. It also grows successfully in gardens and has a perennial root.

Regarding Bistort, one may also consult the *Appendix*.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST ALPINE WINTERGREEN.
<note>original: PYROLA MINIMA ALPINA. Likely Pyrola minor or Moneses uniflora.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Pyrola minima alpina, showing a small plant with a basal rosette of rounded leaves and a single stem topped with a cluster of flowers.</image-desc>

From a creeping root, it sends out four or five leaves, nearly an inch long, round, and serrated around the edges. There is a single, bare stem, a hand-breadth high, which bears a single, rather large flower at the summit, similar to the flowers of other Wintergreens, followed by a larger angular seed-head from the middle of which a capped style protrudes.

Furthermore, Wintergreen is hot and dry in the third degree <note>a classification in Galenic medicine indicating its potency</note>. Wounds, ulcers, fistulas, and other such evils are healed by taking its decoction, juice, powder, or distilled water internally or applying them externally. Dodonaeus recommends the fresh plant, crushed and applied, or the dried powder sprinkled on, for wounds, ulcers, and burns.

### BISTORT, SERPENT-WEED: German: *Natterwurz*: French: *Bistorte*: Italian: *Bistorta*.
<note>original: BISTORTA, SERPENTINA. The names refer to the root's resemblance to a snake (Natter/Serpent).</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Bistorta serpentina, showing a tall flowering spike and large, elongated leaves with prominent veining and a contorted root.</image-desc>

Bistort takes its name from the fact that it consists of a root twisted and rolled back on itself <note>from Latin "bis" (twice) and "torta" (twisted)</note>. There are three types: Great, Medium, and Smallest.

The stems of the Great variety, which we depict here, sometimes exceed a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height; they are thin, smooth, and jointed. At their summit is a spike of flesh-colored flowers, like those of *Persicaria* <note>Knotweed</note>; each flower, when opened, consists of five small oblong petals, with tips in the center of the same color as the flower. These are followed by a reddish, three-cornered seed. The leaves are like those of the Sharp Dock <note>Lapathum acutum</note> but smaller, dark green on top and bluish-gray <note>glaucous</note> underneath, with leaf-like appendages on the stalk. The root resembles a finger joint twisted on itself; it is red and has a strongly astringent taste.

### SMALLEST BISTORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Bistorta minima, showing two small specimens with narrow leaves and short, dense flowering spikes.</image-desc>

This also has a twisted root, but it is shorter, white, and less thick. The stem is nine inches or a hand-breadth high, clothed with a few narrow, oblong, pointed leaves that have no stalk; others grow from the root with a stalk. The spike exceeds an inch in length, topped with whitish flowers. The seed is reddish, and not triangular as in the others, but round.

It shares the same native habitats as the others and flowers at the same time, namely in the months of June and July.

The powers of all the Bistorts are the same, and in summary, they all possess the same qualities as Tormentil. However, the greatest efficacy lies in the roots.

<summary>This page describes various species of Wintergreen (Pyrola) and Bistort (Bistorta), detailing their physical characteristics, preferred habitats in cold or mountainous regions, and their medicinal uses as astringents and wound healers.</summary>
<keywords>Wintergreen, Pyrola, Bistort, Natterwurz, botanical taxonomy, medicinal herbs, wound healing, Galenic degrees, Mattioli, Clusius, Bauhin</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey from the previous section. While the previous page concluded the discussion on Wintergreen (Pyrola), this page begins a new examination of Sea-lavender (Limonium) and the historically elusive plant known as Britannica. It marks the conclusion of "Class 31" in this botanical system.</meta>

**SEA-LAVENDER: German: *Meadow Chard*: French: *Limonium*: Italian: *Limonio*.**
<note>original Latin: LIMONIVM. The name comes from the Greek "leimon," meaning meadow.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Limonium plant, showing large, broad basal leaves with prominent veining and a tall, branched flowering stalk with small clusters of blossoms.</image-desc>

Pliny calls Sea-lavender "Wild Chard": and, as Dioscorides also describes, it has leaves like Chard <note>original: Beta</note>.

Among the various species of Sea-lavender that are recorded, the Greater variety which we depict here—and which the apothecaries <note>original: Seplasiæ; a term for pharmacists named after a famous perfume market in ancient Capua</note> wrongly call Red Behen, despite no evidence supporting that name—was determined by Mattioli to be the true *Limonium* of Dioscorides.

It is supported by a thick, reddish root that is astringent to the taste and divided into several heads: from which grow leaves like those of Dock <note>original: Lapathum</note>, but smaller, smoother, and of a more cheerful green. The stems are a foot long, spreading wide with many branches: along which dense, small flowers climb in a row; they are a bluish-white color, with reddish calyxes <note>the protective outer part of a flower</note>. The seed is abundant, oblong, and brownish.

<column-break/>

**SMALLER SEA-LAVENDER.**
<note>original: LIMONIVM MINVS.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the smaller Limonium variety, featuring narrower leaves and more delicate, spreading floral branches.</image-desc>

In appearance, it agrees with the Greater Sea-lavender: but the stems are shorter: the little flowers are not as blue, but lean more towards white. The leaves are also smaller and spread across the ground.

Gerard calls it "Small Sea-lavender": Cesalpino "The other tiny Sea-lavender": the History of Lyon <note>Historia Lugdunensis</note>, Lobelius in his *Adversaria*, and Durante call it "Small Sea-lavender of Narbonne": Caspar Bauhin calls it "Stone Behen," and some call it the "Smaller Tripolium."

Greater and Lesser Sea-lavender grow everywhere on Mediterranean shores especially, and they bloom in August and September. We have observed them growing in the greatest abundance on the Adriatic and Narbonese <note>Southern French</note> coasts, as well as near the salt lakes of Montpellier. Lobelius writes that it grows with difficulty from seed, and he has only seen it in grassy and wet maritime meadows. It took its name from this, as if you were to say "Meadow Herb."

---

**RARE SEA-LAVENDER, OF RAUWOLF.**
<note>original: LIMONIVM RARVM, RAVVVOLFFII. Named after Leonhard Rauwolf, a 16th-century physician and botanist who traveled the Levant.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a rare Limonium variety with deeply lobed, thistle-like leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

It has stalks a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note> and somewhat hairy: the leaves are a palm and a half long <note>about 6 inches</note>, hairy, and divided like Spleenwort <note>original: Asplenium</note>: others at the branching of the stems are narrower and not at all notched. The flowers are similar to the little flowers of Spanish Scabious, and are of a deep blue color. The root is oblong, dark on the outside and red within.

Rauwolf observed this in the damp meadows of Judea <note>modern Israel/Palestine</note>, reporting that the inhabitants use the leaves in salads.

It is clear from the astringent taste that the leaves are of a dry quality. Furthermore, we have it from the authors Dioscorides and Galen that the seed, which is also harsh to the taste, when ground and drunk with wine, is very useful for those with abdominal complaints, dysentery, coughing up blood, and for excessive menstrual flow in women.

---

**BRITANNICA: Greek: $\text{Βρετανικὴ}$ (Bretanikē).**

Dioscorides says Britannica, or Betony, is a herb with leaves like Wild Dock: but darker and hairier, and astringent in taste. It puts forth a stem that is not very large, and has a thin and short root.

Pliny and Galen also mention Britannica: Galen writes that the leaves of Britannica are astringent and help wounds knit together. Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, an Italian scholar</note>, a mimic of Pliny, records the same things he does; and finally Ruellius <note>Jean Ruel</note>, in his usual manner, repeats the words of Dioscorides, Pliny, and Hermolaus and sells them as his own: adding only that Britannica is well enough known in Italy, and is commonly called *Pistanano* there. Others point to various plants for Britannica: Bistort, Middle Comfrey, Self-heal, Betony, Cowslip <note>original: Herba paralysis</note>, Bear's Ear, Wintergreen, Smartweed, Scurvy-grass, Water-plantain, Sea-purslane, Clove Pink <note>original: Betonica coronaria</note>, Sea Holly, and others. However, in our judgment, Janus Cornarius <note>a German humanist physician</note> speaks more accurately when he writes that today it is known neither to the pharmacists nor to the botanists. Hence also Mattioli: "To me so far," he says, "not only is that name unknown, but I have not even happened to find anyone who could show me Britannica."

---

# ILLUSTRATIONS AND DELINEATIONS OF PLANTS
# CLASS 32.
### ROUND-LEAVED AND RELATED PLANTS.

**VIOLET, PURPLE VIOLET: German: Blue Violets: French: March Violet: Italian: Little Breast Violet.**
<note>original: Viola Mammula. This Italian name refers to the shape or perhaps the gentle nature of the flower.</note>

Pliny recognized three main kinds of Violets: purple, yellow, and white. Theophrastus also noted three: white, black, and "flame-colored." Hippocrates, however, mentioned only two—black and yellow—as did Nicander, who named them pale and yellow. Dioscorides also listed only two, namely white and purple, and he separated the purple violet from the white not only by chapter but by the Book in which they appeared. Following his example, we previously treated the White Violet <note>original: το λευκοϊόν (leukoion) of Theophrastus</note> in Class 21. In this section, we specifically address the Purple Violet, which is commonly called the March Violet <note>original: Viola Martia or Viola Martis</note> because it blooms most abundantly in the month of March. As will be seen from the following descriptions, it varies greatly in appearance, flower, and scent.

<column-break/>

**ANOTHER PURPLE MARCH VIOLET, with larger double flowers.**
<note>original: flore multiplicato maiore; "multiplied" refers to "double" flowers where extra petals replace reproductive parts.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Viola plant with rounded, serrated leaves and multiple stems bearing flowers.</image-desc>

Among the first gifts of Spring are the purple March Violets. Growing from fibrous roots that are sometimes divided into several heads, they send out leaves that are somewhat oblong though starting from a round shape, serrated at the edges, and attached to long stalks. Among these, other stems arising from the root each support a single flower of a purplish-blue color. These flowers possess a very sweet scent, are equipped with a spur <note>a nectar-producing projection at the back of the flower</note>, and are composed of five small petals. As the flower fades, round little heads <note>seed capsules</note> arise from other stalks at the root; these split into three "keels" <note>valves</note> and are full of small, round seeds.

It springs up frequently in shady places near thickets, walls, and the edges of fields and gardens, as well as in hedges and rich soil. It blooms mostly in March.

---

**MOUNTAIN VIOLET WITH DEEPLY CUT LEAVES.**
<note>original: Folio Multifido; "multifid" means divided into many narrow lobes.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a mountain viola with deeply lobed, multifid leaves and a single flower stalk.</image-desc>

We found this rare type of Violet on Mount Nombres in Rhaetia <note>a Roman province in the central Alps, modern-day Switzerland and Italy</note>. It grew with an almost simple stem. The leaves rested on rather long stalks arising directly from the root; they were divided into ten longish, narrow segments—each resembling a leaf of Toadflax <note>original: Linaria</note>—cut all the way to the stalk. It has a sticky taste, similar to other Violets. I was unable to observe the flower because it had already fallen.

We have also seen the March Violet, both the scented white-flowered and unscented varieties, in Geneva on the hill of *la Bastie*.

Furthermore, we kept the March Violet with smaller double flowers, very large double flowers, and various variegated colors at Montbéliard in the S. P. garden <note>likely the garden of the Prince of Württemberg-Montbéliard</note>.

<column-break/>

**YELLOW MARCH VIOLET.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a yellow marsh or mountain violet with rounded leaves and distinct floral structures.</image-desc>

The root of this variety is quite fibrous. The leaves are almost perfectly circular, hooked <note>falcata</note> at the long, thin stalk, and are smaller, more delicate, and thinner than the leaves of other Violets. The flowers sit upon stalks arising soon after the roots; they are small and yellow.

It grows abundantly in the Alps of Austria and Styria, as well as in the mountains near Geneva.

According to the judgement of all the best ancient writers, the March Violet is "cold and moist" <note>referring to the Four Humors theory of medicine</note>; however, when dried, it is less cold and less moist. Practitioners, apothecaries <note>original: Seplasiæ</note>, and wise women <note>original: mulierculæ; literally "little women," often referring to folk healers</note> are well-acquainted with its internal and external uses, as well as the methods for making *Vinegar, Oil, Conserves, Juleps, Syrups, powders*, and other preparations from it.

<summary>This page describes various species of Violets (Viola), categorizing them by color and leaf shape while citing classical authorities like Dioscorides and Pliny. It details their physical characteristics, alpine habitats, and their common medicinal preparations like syrups and oils.</summary>
<keywords>Violet, Viola Martia, March Violet, botany, Rhaetia, Geneva, medicinal herbs, double flowers, yellow violet, humors</keywords>

--- Page 590 ---
<meta>This page continues Class 32, "Round-leaved and related plants," moving from the common Purple Violet into specialized varieties and related mountain and woodland species like Butterwort, Pansies, Asarabacca, and Cyclamen.</meta>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original: STIRPIVM</note>

### GESSNER’S BUTTERWORT, the HOODED plant of the *History of Lyon*.
<note>original: Pinguicula Gesneri, Cucullata Historiae Lugdunensis. This plant is known today as *Pinguicula vulgaris* or Common Butterwort.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pinguicula plant showing a rosette of fleshy basal leaves and a single flower on a long, slender stalk, with a small fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Conrad Gessner <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss naturalist</note> calls this plant *Pinguicula* because of its leaves; five, six, or sometimes more are spread out across the surface of the ground. They are "fatty" <note>original: pinguicula; referring to the greasy feel of the leaves</note> and shining, about two inches long and an inch wide, and somewhat thick toward the edges. From among these leaves rise several stalks about a hand’s breadth or higher, each bearing a single flower at the very top. These flowers are purple-violet or white, gaping open, and equipped with a long spur; they are easily detached from the stalk.

The plant delights in very high, snowy mountains and grows forth from rocks. Shepherds use the juice of the leaves to heal both wounds and the cracks in the udders of cows.

### THREE-COLORED PANSY, WITH UPRIGHT STEMS, called "woody" by some.
<note>original: Iacea Tricolor, Surrectis Caulibus; likely a variety of *Viola tricolor* or Wild Pansy.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild pansy showing upright, branching stems, oval leaves with notched edges, and several distinct flowers.</image-desc>

We found this plant growing wild among the thickets in Montbéliard, and we have also observed it being cultivated in gardens in Esslingen and elsewhere.

The common variety comes up in many places in the fields; it also grows in gardens, often of its own accord, and is showier and more elegant than the wild kind. It first appears in early spring along with the Black Violet <note>The common sweet violet</note>, or shortly thereafter. It continues to bloom through the whole of summer, especially in the autumn, and occasionally even in winter.

Matthioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a renowned physician and botanist</note> considers it cold and moist, while others argue it is hot and dry. It is most highly recommended for treating "gatherings" in the chests of children <note>original: inthorare collectiones; likely referring to phlegm or respiratory congestion</note>, as well as the itch <note>scabies</note>, ulcers, all kinds of skin blemishes, and quinsy <note>anginas; severe throat inflammation</note> in swine. *More about this in the Appendix.*

### WALL ASARABACCA OF THE *HISTORY OF LYON*.
<note>original: Asarum Muri. This is likely a species of *Asarum* or perhaps a similar-looking wall-dwelling plant like Pellitory.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with rounded, ivy-like leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers located near the base of the stems.</image-desc>

Herbalists call this plant Wall Asarabacca because its leaves rival those of the true Asarabacca, and because it grows nowhere else but on walls. The *History of Lyon* adds some details regarding its root and leaves, but omits the flowers, seeds, taste, and its origins.

Furthermore, Dioscorides attributes a warming and diuretic <note>term: diuretic; a substance that encourages the passage of urine</note> power to Asarabacca. According to Mesuë <note>A 9th-century Persian physician</note>, the root is hot and dry in the third degree; it thins, dissolves, and opens blockages. It purges bile and phlegm through vomiting and urine, and heals Jaundice, Dropsy, and long-lasting fevers. *More on this in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### THREE-COLORED PANSY, TRINITY FLOWER. German: *Dreyfaltigkeit blumen*: French: *de la pensée*: Italian: *Iacea*.
<note>The name "Pansy" comes from the French *pensée*, meaning "thought."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a pansy plant with large, wide-petaled flowers and deeply lobed leaves at the base of the flower stalks.</image-desc>

The great beauty and variety of these flowers have led people to judge them worthy of being moved into gardens and cultivated. You may see them presenting a rare sight to the observer, with five delicate, soft petals; sometimes they are entirely purple, sometimes yellow, or variegated with blue and purple, and otherwise multicolored, sitting upon long, hollow stalks. These rise from the "wings" of the leaves <note>The axils where the leaf meets the stem</note>, which are sometimes round and sometimes oblong, notched around the edges, and growing on seven-fold, branching stems from a thin, fibrous root. The seed is small, shining, and plentiful, held in swollen, almost triangular pods.

It is commonly distinguished into the *cultivated* and the *wild* varieties, and these are again divided into the *Greater* and the *Lesser*.

### ASARABACCA: Greek: *Asaron*: German: *Haselwurtz*: French: *Cabaret, Oreillette*: Italian: *Asaro*.
<note>original: Asarum. Known as Wild Ginger.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Asarabacca (Asarum europaeum) showing its characteristic kidney-shaped, glossy leaves and small, dark flowers tucked close to the ground.</image-desc>

We shall describe Asarabacca in the words of Dioscorides: "*Asarum*," he says, "has leaves like Ivy, but much smaller and rounder. The flowers are purple, similar to the flower-buds of Henbane <note>original: Cytino Hyoscyami</note>, appearing among the leaves very close to the root; they are fragrant and contain a berry-like seed. It has stems that are angular, rough, and soft. The roots are numerous, jointed, thin, and spreading, not unlike Grass but much more slender; they are fragrant, warming, and bite the tongue sharply. It grows in shady mountains, etc."

It loves, as he says, dark and shady places, and is most often found under Hazel trees <note>German: *Haselwurtz* means "Hazel-root"</note>, as Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century botanist</note> reports. The herb is evergreen, yet it puts forth new leaves along with small flowers in the Spring.

### CYCLAMEN, SOWBREAD: German: *Schuueinbrodt*: French: *Pain de pourceau*: Italian: *Pan porcino*.
<note>Called Sowbread because the tuberous roots were famously eaten by wild boars.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyclamen plant showing the large, round, patterned leaves and flowers with petals that reflex or "turn back" upwards.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, the Cyclamen has leaves like Ivy, purple and variegated, with white spots prominently marking the upper surface. The stem is bare, about four fingers long, bearing purple flowers shaped like roses. The root is black and somewhat broad, so that it might look like a Turnip. There is also a second kind of Cyclamen, which he adds is called *Cystanthemon* or *Cystiphyllon*; it has Ivy-like leaves but smaller, with thick, jointed stems that wind themselves around neighboring trees like the tendrils of a vine. It has a white, fragrant flower, soft berries like Ivy, and a perennial root. It grows in alpine regions, etc.

Of the various species of Cyclamen, we here depict the more common one with rounder leaves and a violet flower.

<summary>This page describes various round-leaved plants including Butterwort (Pinguicula), Wild Pansy (Viola tricolor), Asarabacca (Asarum), and Cyclamen, focusing on their physical characteristics, habitats, and medicinal uses for ailments like skin ulcers and respiratory issues.</summary>

<keywords>Butterwort, Pinguicula, Wild Pansy, Viola tricolor, Asarabacca, Asarum, Cyclamen, Sowbread, Dioscorides, Conrad Gessner, medicinal herbs, mountain plants, skin treatments</keywords>
