## IMAGES AND OUTLINES
<note>original: ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA</note>

### SMALL-ROOTED CYCLAMEN
<note>Also known as Sowbread; the name Cyclamen comes from the Greek word for "circle," referring to its round tuber.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyclamen plant with a small, round tuberous root, heart-shaped leaves with patterned tops, and nodding flowers on long stems.</image-desc>

Mesue <note>A famous 8th-century Persian physician</note> mentions a smaller cyclamen with a small root, the size of a hazelnut. Matthiolus <note>A renowned 16th-century Italian doctor and botanist</note> testifies that it grows abundantly in the mountains of the Val d'Anania <note>A valley in the Trentino region of Italy</note>. Anguillara mentions a cyclamen with the smallest root of all, found on Mount San Giuliano near Lucca, and he believes it is even smaller than the root described by Mesue.

Furthermore, the more common Cyclamen grows on high mountains and in places where the brush is not too dense; it loves muddy soil, much like Asarabacca <note>original: Asarum</note>. We have observed it in abundance on Mount <term>Salève</term> <note>A mountain in the French Prealps near Geneva</note> near Geneva and in the mountains of Rhaetia <note>The Swiss Alps</note>. Clusius <note>An influential Flemish botanist</note> writes that there are no forested mountains or thickets in Pannonia <note>Western Hungary</note> and Austria that do not overflow with Cyclamen. It blooms in June and July.

<column-break/>

### LONGER-ROOTED CYCLAMEN

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyclamen variety with a more elongated, irregular tuberous root and similar nodding flowers.</image-desc>

This variety differs from the common one just described and illustrated only by the head of the root, which grows somewhat longer. Furthermore, since Dioscorides <note>The ancient Greek author of the foundational herbal "De Materia Medica"</note> proposes two types of Cyclamen, this second (or "other") type seems to correspond in every way to the first, except that it is not as sharp and burning in taste.

However, more recent authors observe various differences, taken mostly from the roots, leaves, flowers, and blooming time. Namely: by the root (larger, smaller, heart-shaped, round, or of another form); by the leaves (round, oblong, angular or not, more or less spotted); and by the flowers (which are red, white, or yellow; scented or scentless; blooming in Spring or Autumn).

---

<column-break/>

### ANGULAR-LEAVED CYCLAMEN

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cyclamen with distinctly angular, lobed leaves and several flowers.</image-desc>

This one has a circular root like the previous one. Its leaves rest on stalks a span and a half long <note>A "span" or palm was about 3 inches; these stalks are roughly 5 inches long</note>; they are thick, purple underneath, marked with whitish spots on top, and light green on the lower side. They are three-cornered, similar to ivy leaves, longer than they are wide, and rounded at the base. The flowers correspond to those of the other varieties, being turned backward <note>A characteristic of cyclamen where the petals reflex upward</note>, and white in color [at least in the dried plant].

We observed this on the ridges of the Apennine Mountains and at Besançon <note>original: Vesontii</note>, in the garden of Lord de Bellefontaine.

According to Pliny <note>An ancient Roman naturalist</note>, Cyclamen should be planted in every home, if it is true that where it is sown, harmful medicines <note>original: mala medicamenta; likely referring to poisons or sorcery</note> can do no harm.

<column-break/>

### SPRING CYCLAMEN WITH LARGE RED FLOWERS, and with white flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering Cyclamen with large blooms and a thick root system.</image-desc>

Freitag <note>A 17th-century physician</note> describes the qualities of Cyclamen more vividly than others. He says it possesses not only diverse but even contrary powers. By reason of its substance and obvious qualities, it is hot and dry in the third degree <note>A classification in Galenic medicine indicating a very potent drug</note>; and therefore it cuts, thins, resolves, wipes away, cleanses, opens obstructions of the chest and all internal organs, and unlocks the openings of the veins. *From the shape and nature of the leaves, it draws out phlegm and the fluids of those with dropsy.* Through the combined virtues of its form and temperament, it specifically cures jaundice whether used internally or externally, opens obstructions of the spleen, and is always most harmful to the fetus <note>Warning: This plant was historically known to be an abortifacient</note>. Physicians know the proper method of use. More is found in the Appendix.

---

<column-break/>

### BIRTHWORT: German: <term>Hollwurtz, Osterlucey</term> <note>meaning Hollow-root or Easter-light</note>; French: <term>Sarrazine</term>; Italian: <term>Aristolochia</term>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Aristolochia (Birthwort) plant with heart-shaped leaves and a single, tubular, curved flower.</image-desc>

Some distinguish between "False" and "True" Birthwort <note>original: Aristolochiam</note>, and now say it belongs to the genus of bulbous Fumitory. Following Dioscorides, they divide this true kind into three types: Round, Long, and Climbing <note>original: Clematitim</note>. Matthiolus makes these same true distinctions, saying this last one is quite rare and known to few, while the other two are known to almost all students of herbs. Renodaeus lists five species: Long, Round, Climbing, Saracen, and Pistolochia, all of which are so similar in stem, foliage, and flower that they can scarcely be distinguished except by the most sharp-eyed. Caspar Bauhin lists eight in his botanical works; Anguillara lists twelve. Finally, those known to us are presented here.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER BETTER IMAGE OF ROUND BIRTHWORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a different variety of Aristolochia with more prominent, rounded leaves and multiple tubular flowers.</image-desc>

Many weak shoots, a cubit long <note>about 18 inches</note>, sprout from its root. Leaves grow alternately from these, attached by very short stalks and clasping the stem closely with their "wings" <note>auricles at the base of the leaf</note>; they are the roundest of all, soft, and somewhat pale. From the leaf-axils <note>the joint between leaf and stem</note>, flowers emerge on stalks half an inch long, of a blackish-red color. There follow top-shaped, ribbed seed pods which, splitting into six parts, reveal many black seeds. The root is tuberous, round, and bitter, with long fibers hanging from the bottom.

It grows in rich soil, in wetter meadows and at the edges of fields; it blooms in May and June.

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey of the Birthwort family (Aristolochia), following the discussion of the Cyclamen species on the previous page. The text focuses on the various forms of Birthwort, valued in the Renaissance for their medicinal properties, particularly in childbirth and wound care.</meta>

# OF PLANTS
<note>original: STIRPIVM</note>

### LONG BIRTHWORT
<note>original: ARISTOLOCHIA LONGA. The name Aristolochia comes from the Greek words for "best" and "childbirth," reflecting its historical use in obstetrics.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aristolochia Longa showing a climbing vine with heart-shaped leaves and tubular flowers, with a thick, elongated tuberous root.</image-desc>

Long shoots spread across the ground, about a <term>cubit</term> <note>An ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or the length of a forearm</note> in length; they are square-shaped and sometimes quite hollow. Along these shoots grow leaves that are sickle-shaped and sharper than those of the Round Birthwort, clinging to longer stalks. From the crook of the leaves emerge long flowers, similar to the Round variety but less yellow. The fruit that grows afterward is pear-shaped and full of seeds, as was described for the Round variety. The root is as thick as a thumb or a forearm and about a foot long, with the same bitterness as the Round species.

It grows in open fields among the grain crops; it is especially frequent in <term>Narbonne Gaul</term> <note>A Roman province in what is now Southern France</note>, where it is also found in several green meadows.

### CLIMBING BIRTHWORT (Not the common kind), according to Clusius.
<note>original: ARISTOLOCHIA CLEMATITIS NON vulgaris, Clusii. Carolus Clusius was a foundational 16th-century botanist.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aristolochia Clematitis showing upright stems with heart-shaped leaves and clusters of small tubular flowers at the leaf axils.</image-desc>

Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a famous Flemish physician and botanist</note> calls it simply Climbing Birthwort; Lobelius in his *Observations* calls it the "Other Spanish Climbing Birthwort"; the *History of Lyon* <note>original: Historia Lugdunensis</note> refers to it as "Dodonaeus’s Climbing Birthwort."

Clusius writes that this kind of Birthwort grows wild around Seville <note>original: Hispalis</note> on the road to Lisbon, in many places in <term>Baetica</term> <note>A Roman province in southern Spain, modern-day Andalusia</note>, and also around Cordoba in rich soil, among thickets, brambles, and certain old Olive trees. However, the common Climbing variety is sometimes kept in gardens, where it is a nuisance to gardeners because of its creeping roots; elsewhere, it grows wild here and there in various parts of France, Spain, and both Upper and Lower Germany.

### THE OTHER MANY-ROOTED BIRTHWORT OR PISTOLOCHIA, evergreen, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aristolochia Pistolochia showing a plant with smaller, more rounded leaves and a dense, fibrous root system.</image-desc>

These "many-rooted" Birthworts <note>original: polyrrhizę Aristolochiæ</note> were unknown to Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician</note> and to the Commentator from Siena <note>A reference to Pietro Andrea Mattioli</note>.

The shoots of this illustrated variety are scattered on the ground, branched, flexible, difficult to break, and dark green in color. The flowers are long, grayish-white, or somewhat yellowish. The leaves are small, dark, and endowed with a greenness that does not wither. Other features are much the same as in the other Birthworts.

Furthermore, all Birthworts are "hot" according to Mesue <note>A famous 8th-century Persian physician</note>—at the beginning of the third degree—and "dry" in the second degree. They open obstructions, dissolve humors, and draw out thorns fixed in the flesh; they also purge phlegm and bile. However, since the Round variety is of a more delicate substance, it is more effective for all these purposes than the others.

<column-break/>

### COMMON CLIMBING BIRTHWORT
<note>original: ARISTOLOCHIA CLEMATITIS VVLGARIS</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the common Aristolochia Clematitis showing slender stems, heart-shaped leaves, and elongated tubular flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has a thin root with many hair-like fibers; it has a not unpleasant smell but a bitter taste. The little vines are a foot long, weak, grooved, and jointed like a reed. From each joint grows a single leaf, shaped like ivy and wrinkled, attached by a long stalk curved like an anchor. From the leaf-axils come long, yellow flowers, shaped like a small scoop <note>original: palæ effigiaturâ</note>, with a fuzzy channel inside. At the base of the flower sits a small round head containing semi-seated tips with a grassy scent. The fruit is pear-shaped, grooved, and the size of a walnut.

### MANY-ROOTED BIRTHWORT
<note>original: ARISTOLOCHIA POLYRRHIZOS</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Aristolochia Polyrrhizos featuring a very dense, bushy root system and stems with heart-shaped leaves.</image-desc>

This plant gets its name from its root, which is composed of many long, rush-thin rootlets of a boxwood-yellow color, all meeting at a single head. The little vines are nine inches long, slender, and branched. The leaves are similar to those of the Long Birthwort but smaller, clinging to longer stalks and somewhat more wavy along the edges. The flowers, born from the leaf-axils, are similar to the others—grassy-green, or turning blackish from a green base at the tips. The fruit is swollen and full of seeds, as mentioned for the previous kinds.

It grows in the olive groves and rocky places of Spain and Narbonne Gaul. It blooms later than the rest.

### PLANT SIMILAR TO BIRTHWORT, the "Rhasut" and "Rhumigi" of the Moors, according to Rauwolff.
<note>original: ARISTOLOCHIIS SIMILIS RHASVT & Rhumigi Maurorum, Rauuvolffii</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to Aristolochia, with pinnate-like leaf structures and a thick root.</image-desc>

Usually four whitish shoots emerge from the root, as thin as thread. Attached to the upper part of these shoots near the root are seven or eight small leaflets on each side; they are ash-colored and correspond in size and position to the leaves of the "Flowering Fern," except that the lowest ones are sometimes shaped like Small Sage. Between the lowest leaflets, which are spaced a bit further apart than the upper ones, hang flowers similar to Birthwort, though a little larger, darker in color, and on a longer stalk. The root is fixed deep in the ground, white and bitter. Thus describes Rauwolff <note>Leonhard Rauwolff, a 16th-century German physician and traveler who documented Middle Eastern plants</note>.

More on Birthwort in the Appendix.

<note>Vocabulary: Long Birthwort, Climbing Birthwort, Many-rooted Birthwort, Pistolochia, Clusius, Dodonaeus, Rauwolff, Narbonne Gaul, Spain.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the study of Birthworts to the Tussilago (Coltsfoot) and Petasites (Butterbur) families. These plants were often grouped together in early modern botany due to their similar leaf shapes and their "prolepsis"—the botanical habit of flowering before the leaves emerge.</meta>

-># IMAGES AND DESCRIPTIONS<-
<note>original: ICONES ET SCIAGRAPHIA</note>

### COLTSFOOT, FARFARA: Germ. *Hufflattich*: French *Pas d'asne*: Ital. *Farfara*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tussilago (Coltsfoot) plant showing its distinctive broad, heart-shaped leaves and a single flowering stalk with a composite flower head.</image-desc>

The leaves of Coltsfoot <note>original: Tussilago, from 'tussis' meaning cough, indicating its use as a cough remedy</note> are similar to Ivy, somewhat large, with six or seven coming from the root; they are whitish underneath but green on top, and possess many angles. The stem is the height of a <term>palm</term> <note>A measurement of about 3–4 inches</note>: the flower is a yellowish-white: and the root is thin and <unclear>bitter</unclear> <note>original: luctuaca, possibly a variant of 'lactuca' (milky) or referring to a bitter quality</note>. Thus did Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the father of pharmacology</note> describe it.

It grows naturally near springs and the banks of streams and rivers, as well as the edges of pits and ditches; it is also found in the shaded areas of gardens. The flowers are very fleeting and are visible toward the end of March—sometimes earlier, sometimes later—and they wither away along with their little stalks; afterward, the leaves are produced, which remain in their full vigor throughout the entire summer.

### BUTTERBUR: Germ. *Pestilentzwurtz*: French *Herbe aux tigneux*: Ital. *Petasite*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Petasites (Butterbur) plant featuring very large, rounded, slightly lobed leaves and a thick flowering spike.</image-desc>

The name *Petasites* comes from the great size of the leaf, which resembles a <term>petasos</term> <note>original: πέτασος; a wide-brimmed Greek sun hat</note> or a cap; for this reason, it is also called *Galerita* <note>from 'galerus', a skull-cap</note>.

We depict here the common reddish variety with the rounder leaf: it has stems about a <term>span</term> <note>original: dodrantales; approximately 9 inches</note> long, more or less, which are hollow, woolly, and clothed with narrow, pointed leaves. These stems rise into a <term>thyrsus</term> <note>A dense, tufted flower cluster</note> of purplish flowers that eventually fade into downy seeds <note>original: pappos</note>. After these fall away and the stem withers, very large leaves succeed them, which are sickle-shaped at the stalk, nearly round, and saw-toothed only at the edges; they are not angular like those of the White Butterbur. They are covered in a greyish-white down underneath, while the upper side is dark green and not entirely free of fuzz. The root is red, thick, and tastes bitter.

### MATTHIOLI’S ASARINA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Asarina, showing kidney-shaped leaves with serrated edges and small flowers on thin stems.</image-desc>

It seems to us that this plant, which grows in the mountains of Bohemia, should be joined with the Coltsfoots and Butterburs. Matthioli, Castor, Tabernaemontanus, and Gerard <note>A list of influential 16th-century botanists</note> chose to call it *Asarina*. The *History of Lyon* and Clusius call it "Matthioli’s Asarina," and Caspar Bauhin calls it "Asarina with the leaf of Asarum."

It creeps along the ground, with a leaf rounder and rougher than that of the *Asarum* <note>Wild Spikenard</note>, lightly circled and saw-toothed: the little stems are hairy: the flowers are honey-colored, like Chamomile <note>original: Anthemidis</note> but much smaller, and not without scent: and finally, the roots are thin, long, and sharp to the taste.

<column-break/>

### SMALLER ALPINE COLTSFOOT, with round leaves.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller alpine Tussilago with rounded, scalloped leaves and a single flower head on a long stalk.</image-desc>

This plant has five or six, and sometimes even twelve leaves spread upon the ground; they are thick, wrinkled, and of a circular roundness (unless they are made uneven by a slight trace of lobes). They shine with a deep green on the upper side and are covered with white down underneath, resting on somewhat long, hairy stalks. The stem is purplish, single, a palm or a <term>cubit</term> <note>usually 18 inches, but here likely referring to a smaller hand-span length</note> high, and woolly: at the top, it bears a single, large, purplish flower, somewhat similar to the flower of the common Coltsfoot, which breaks down into seeds with long, slender tufts of hair attached. The root is wrapped in fine hairs, quite thick, and has many long fibers. It flowers in July and August. More regarding Coltsfoot can be found in the Appendix.

### ANGULAR-LEAVED BUTTERBUR, with a jointed root, striped stem, and white flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Petasites variety with distinctly angular, lobed leaves and a tall flowering stalk.</image-desc>

The different varieties of Butterbur are observed in the flower, the leaves, the size, the location, and their place of birth. Hence, one kind of Butterbur has a reddish flower that is scented and larger; another is the "Female," whose flower is white, smaller, and usually scentless. One is common and familiar in our regions, while another is "Indian." One has round leaves, and another has angular leaves.

We depict here the "Female" Butterbur with the angular leaf; it is clear from the image how it differs from the "Male" pictured previously.

Furthermore, Butterbur grows in the Alps and in moist mountainous and river-side places, near the banks of rivers, and along the edges of lakes and ponds and nearby embankments. It flowers at the beginning of April. More in the Appendix.

### CACALIA or what some ancients called LEONTICE: others call it a species of Coltsfoot.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Cacalia, showing upright stems with clusters of small flowers and broad, basal leaves.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, *Cacalia* produces very large, white leaves: from the middle of these, a straight, white stem springs up, bearing a flower similar to <term>Bryony</term> <note>A climbing vine with small, greenish-white flowers</note>. It grows in the mountains. Pliny describes it a little differently but agrees with Dioscorides on its medicinal powers. Galen, however, passed over *Cacalia* in his list of simple medicines, unless it is the same as his *Cacanum*, as Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century medical writer</note> translates *Cacanum* as *Cacalia*.

Furthermore, Caspar Bauhin identifies three types of *Cacalia*: namely, the woolly, the hairy, and the smooth.

The *Cacalia* we depict here grows on mountain ridges and at the edges of forests in shady places.

<summary>This page describes various species of Coltsfoot (Tussilago) and Butterbur (Petasites), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats, and the botanical distinction between "male" and "female" varieties. It also discusses the related plant Cacalia, referencing classical authorities like Dioscorides, Pliny, and Galen.</summary>
<keywords>Coltsfoot, Butterbur, Tussilago, Petasites, Cacalia, Dioscorides, medicinal plants, Renaissance botany, Alpine flora, Bohemia</keywords>

--- Page 594 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of medicinal plants, moving from Coltsfoot and Butterbur on the previous page to the various species of Burdock and Cocklebur. These plants were grouped together in the Renaissance based on their hooked, "clinging" seed heads and their broad leaves.</meta>

### GREATER BURDOCK:
Greek <note>original: ἀρκτιον</note> *Arktion*: Germ. *Great Burdock*: Dutch *Great Burdock*: French *Burdock*: Ital. *Greater Burdock*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Personata (Greater Burdock) plant, showing large broad leaves, a thick stalk, and several prickly flower heads (burrs) at the top, with a detailed root system at the bottom.</image-desc>

It is two cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> high, and sometimes taller. It has a long, thick root, black on the outside and white on the inside, with a pleasantly sweet taste. The stems are straight, fluted, woolly, reddish, and branched. The leaves are like those of Mullein or Elecampane, but shorter and rounder; they are dark green on the upper side and covered in a greyish, woolly down underneath. The flower heads are prickly <note>original: echinata</note> and bristling with curved hooks that cling stubbornly to clothes and anything they encounter. The flowers are purplish. The seed, as Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician</note> says, is similar to small cumin.

It grows easily in rich and fertile soil, and in pits and pools after they have dried up. Burdock flourishes in June and July, becoming full with seeds in the month of October.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER BURDOCK, WITH
Hairy Heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a variant of Personata with smaller, more numerous villous (hairy) flower heads and similar broad leaves.</image-desc>

One can notice scarcely any difference between this and the more common previous one, except in the burrs, whose spines are covered in a greyish down, as if interwoven with spider webs. Otherwise, the flower of this one is also purplish, and the leaves and other parts are not dissimilar.

Furthermore, I know <note>original: scio</note> that what we call *Personata* <note>The Latin name for Burdock, from "persona," a mask, referring to the large leaves</note> is a name used not only for various species of Burdock, but also for <term>Greater Fleabane</term>, <term>Cotton Thistle</term>, <term>Bappium</term>, and <term>Coltsfoot</term>, though less correctly. Indeed, it is a remarkable error—in the judgment of Mattioli and Maranta <note>Sixteenth-century botanists</note>—to believe that Burdock is the same as the *Aparine* <note>Cleavers or Goosegrass</note> described by Dioscorides, as Brassavola did in his examination of medicinal plants.

Moreover, how *Arction* differs from *Arctium* we shall discuss in the Appendix.

---

### ARCTION WITH SOFT
hairy heads.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Arction plant, featuring deeply lobed, almost palmate leaves and soft, hairy flower heads.</image-desc>

*Arction* is depicted in this form in an ancient Manuscript of the Imperial Library, according to the author Dodonaeus.

Furthermore, the root of *Arctium* boiled in wine with the seed soothes toothaches if the liquid is held in the mouth. Burns and chilblains <note>Painful inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin caused by exposure to cold</note> are treated with the same decoction; it is also drunk in wine for sciatica and difficulty in urinating. Dioscorides attributes these powers to it, with Pliny and Galen agreeing. Galen says it consists of "fine parts" and has a drying and cleansing faculty. The juice of the herb, when drunk, wonderfully heals all snake bites and provokes urine. The root, crushed with salt, is most usefully applied to the bite of rabid dogs. Apuleius writes that those suffering from fever should be wrapped in the leaves to mitigate the fever and calm the heat. When applied to the head, they ease pain, according to the scholar from Wittenberg. The stems, emerging in early Spring, are usually eaten raw or cooked as a first course after the bark is scraped off. Maranta writes that a leaf of Great Burdock worn on the crown of the head lifts the womb upward, but if placed under the sole of the foot, it pulls it downward.

<column-break/>

### COCKLEBUR, OR LESSER BURDOCK: Germ. *Small
Burdock*: Dutch *Small Burdock*: French *Little Burdock*: Ital. *Lesser Burdock*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Xanthium (Lesser Burdock/Cocklebur), showing a central stalk with smaller, more angular leaves and clusters of oblong, prickly burrs.</image-desc>

The stem is about a cubit high, hairy, dotted with red spots, and branched. The alternate leaves sit upon stalks three inches long of the same color as the stem; they are lobed, sandy in texture, and as the name implies, yellow <note>original: Xantho, from the Greek 'xanthos' meaning yellow</note> in color. They are hairy on both sides, with a somewhat sharp and aromatic taste. Where the leaf stalks emerge, several bulb-like heads come forth together, emitting flame-colored florets. After these fall off, the burrs grow in pairs, clinging to clothes; they are oblong and end in two rigid spines or sharp points, which hide two barley-like grains in two distinct chambers. It has a single root, putting out many fibers on all sides.

It has the same birthplaces as the Great Burdock and flourishes at the same time. It is understood to be of a hot and dry temperament due to its bitter and somewhat sharp taste. According to Aetius, the fruit has the power to disperse swellings; and if applied in the proper way, it turns the hair yellow. A daily drink of the decoction consumes "lichens" <note>A term for various skin eruptions or scurvy</note> and strengthens the teeth when they are washed with it.

---

<meta>This page continues the botanical survey, moving from the burred plants of the previous section to Class 33, which focuses on the Boraginaceae family, including Borage and Bugloss. These plants were highly valued in the Renaissance for their supposed ability to "gladden the heart."</meta>

# OF THE IMAGES AND OUTLINES
# OF PLANTS
## CLASS XXXIII.
### VIPER’S BUGLOSS, BUGLOSS, HOUND’S TONGUE, HELIOTROPES: AND OTHER RELATED PLANTS.

**BORAGE, BUGLOSS: Germ. *Borage*: French *Borage*: Ital. *Borage*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Borage plant (Borrago) showing its broad, hairy leaves and flowering stems.</image-desc>

Whether the plant called *Borage* today is the *Bugloss* of the Ancients, or not, is a great controversy debated among the most approved writers, the consideration of which we refer to the Appendix.

Borage is either cultivated or wild. The cultivated kind, which we depict here, is a weak plant that lifts itself with difficulty in winter. The root is white, the thickness of a finger, and sticky when chewed. The leaves are broad, somewhat round, rough, wrinkled, and folded, spread across the ground, with very thin, sharp prickles standing out from the new shoots. The stem is bristly, cylindrical, hollow, a cubit high <note>A cubit is about 18 inches</note>, with branching arms. The flowers are lovely, star-shaped, consisting of five petals, in a sky-blue, purplish, or white color. The seed is black and furrowed. It is sown in gardens; every year it sprouts again from fallen seeds, and it does not easily leave a place it has once occupied. It flowers in summer and autumn, and in some places, such as Montpellier, throughout the whole winter, which it can manage almost everywhere. Some mistakenly call it *Corago* <note>original: Coraginem</note>, others *Porago* <note>original: Porraginem</note>.

**COMMON BUGLOSS. Germ. *Ox-tongue*: French *Bugloss*: Italian *Bugloss*.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Bugloss plant (Buglossum vulgare) with elongated, lanceolate leaves and clusters of small flowers.</image-desc>

Bugloss [also called *Buglossa* or *Buglossus*] obtained its name from the shape of an ox's tongue, which it resembles; and because it has a great power to induce cheerfulness, it was also called <term>euphrosynon <note>Greek for "mirth-maker" or "good cheer"</note></term>.

It has oblong leaves, with a thorny roughness, but smaller than in the aforementioned Borage, dark green and shiny. The stems are a cubit or a cubit and a half high, likewise rough and hairy, split into many branches. The flowers are solitary in a certain series along the branches, and crowded at the tip, half the size of Borage flowers, of a paler blue color, and sometimes white. The seeds are placed in groups of four in small vessels, oblong, wrinkled, with an almond-like flavor. The root is black on the outside, white on the inside, with a slow <note>viscous or mucilaginous</note> taste.

<column-break/>

**THIN-LEAVED WILD BORAGE.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a wild, thin-leaved Borage (Borrago sylvestris) showing a more slender habit than the garden variety.</image-desc>

It seems to differ from the cultivated variety only in its leaves, which are narrower. However, Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus, a famous 16th-century German botanist</note>, whose illustration we present here, also makes a distinction in the flower, which in the wild variety is almost always white.

Furthermore, Galen <note>An influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine medical writer</note> assign a moist and warm temperature to Borage; but many wish it to be of a moderate temperature. We have the same Galen and Paul, along with Pliny, Simeon Seth, Apuleius, Serapion, Avicenna, and Quintus Serenus as witnesses that the flowers, when cast into wine, increase cheerfulness—and daily experience is also a witness, whence the verse:

> I am called *Borage*, I always bring joy. <note>original: "Dico Borrago, gaudia semper ago." This was a popular medieval medical rhyme.</note>

For this reason, Pliny also called it <term>Euphrosynon <note>The "rejoicer"</note></term>. More in the following.

**SPANISH BUGLOSS, with Borage-like leaves and blue flowers.**

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Spanish Bugloss (Buglossum hispanicum) with broad leaves similar to Borage and small flowers.</image-desc>

Various differences are observed in Bugloss: in the leaves, which are either more lean and narrow, or thick and somewhat wide; in the flower, blue, purple, or reddish, and sometimes even white and variegated. Furthermore, there is one Greater and another Lesser; and finally, one of the garden and another of the wild. Tabernaemontanus also established a difference in sex <note>Renaissance botanists often labeled plants "male" or "female" based on robustness or color, rather than modern biological sex</note>. But he does not sufficiently distinguish the Male from the Female.

Common Bugloss grows spontaneously in fields in some places. We have seen it in Lorraine, Rhaetia <note>A region in the Alps</note>, and Alsace, and near Montpellier; otherwise, it is cultivated in gardens. It flowers in May, and from that time until the end of summer.

Concerning the powers and use of these species, see the Appendix.

<summary>This page describes the physical characteristics, varieties, and habitats of Borage and Bugloss, emphasizing their historical reputation for promoting happiness and their botanical classification by ancient and contemporary authorities.</summary>
<keywords>Borage, Bugloss, botanical classification, medicinal plants, cheerfulness, Tabernaemontanus, Galen, Pliny, European flora</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the Boraginaceae family, specifically focusing on the various species of wild borage and the group of plants known as "Anchusa" or Alkanet. The translator maintains the distinction between the "Wild Borage" of early modern botanists and the different varieties of Alkanet described by ancient authorities like Dioscorides.</meta>

# OF PLANTS

### WILD BORAGE FOR SOME, Fuchs’s Viper’s Bugloss.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with hairy stems and lanceolate leaves, showing the root system and clusters of small flowers at the top.</image-desc>

It is endowed with a root like that of a foxglove <note>original: Digitalis</note>, somewhat long, and fibrous with sparse filaments. From the head of the root, many stems emerge, ranging from nine inches to a cubit <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches</note> or even higher; these are hairy, rough, branched, and fragile. The leaves are like those of Viper’s Bugloss <note>term: Echium (Viper's Bugloss)</note>, but more bristly and wavy, with a bland taste. The flowers are purplish-violet, smaller than those of the common Bugloss, divided into five parts, and emerging from a calyx made of the same number of leaflets; it contains four seeds like those of Viper's Bugloss.

It is found repeatedly in gardens among the vegetables, as well as in grain fields. We have seen it thus in the crops at Montpellier, and also at Montbéliard near Courtfelles. It flowers in July.

<column-break/>

### ALKANET: Germ. *Ochsenzunzg* root: French *Orchanette*: Ital. *Anchusa*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a thick, branched root and upright stems bearing small flowers and narrow leaves.</image-desc>

Authors do not sufficiently agree on which plant today is properly called *Anchusa* <note>term: Anchusa (Alkanet), a plant often used for its red dye</note>. Indeed, various plants are given the name of Alkanet: the common Bugloss (both greater and smaller), common Viper’s Bugloss, *Onosma*, Hound’s-tongue, Lungwort, Amaranth, Teasel, Hyacinth, and the species of Alkanet soon to be described.

However, Dioscorides mentions three kinds of Alkanet, Pliny four, and Galen also four, agreeing with Dioscorides. Thus, Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar known for correcting errors in ancient texts</note> rightly said that the Alkanets are manifold and that the same names wander among them.

---

<column-break/>

### THE RARER AND MORE ELEGANT YELLOW ALKANET, of Lobel.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, textured leaves and clusters of bell-shaped flowers at the apex of the stems.</image-desc>

It has a root full of blood-red juice. The stem is bristly, a foot long, and thin. The leaves along the branches are shorter than those of the *Onochiles* <note>A related plant, likely another species of Alkanet</note>, yet of equal width. The flowers are clustered at the top, concave, like those of the Greater Comfrey but smaller and yellow. The seed is similar to that of Viper's Bugloss, shiny, ash-colored, marked with tiny black dots, almost triangular and pointed, shaped like the ear of a small head.

Some label this as the third Alkanet of Dioscorides and the fourth or "small" Alkanet of Galen. There is also a smaller version of this kind. They flower in June.

It was previously depicted from the works of Fuchs and our own acquired specimens.

<column-break/>

### WHITE OR PALE-FLOWERED ALKANET, of Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a dense rosette of long, narrow leaves at the base and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant has numerous leaves, a palm’s length, very narrow, and hairy with a stinging down. From their midst rises a stem a foot high, somewhat thick, firm, hairy, and divided into many branches, upon which are much shorter and bristly leaves. From rough and hairy sheaths at the ends of the branches emerge white or pale flowers, divided into five angles. Once these have fallen away, the seed is seen in the sheaths, resembling the head of a viper. The root is the thickness of a finger, covered in a black skin, which, when removed, is entirely red and stains things with a most elegant color.

It is found in various arid and dry places in Austria and Pannonia <note>An ancient province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and the Balkans</note>; it flowers in May.

---

<column-break/>

### MONTPELLIER ALKANET.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a long, twisting root and several stems bearing small leaves and flowers.</image-desc>

It has a thick and long root, woody and red. The stems are nine inches long, hairy, along which grow leaves like those of Viper’s Bugloss, covered in stiff hairs. The flowers cling to the ends of the branches, clustered, purplish, and somewhat long; these are followed by a seed that is somewhat long, ash-colored, and small.

It is very well known in the territory of Agen <note>original: Nitiobrigum agro</note>, from where the pharmacists of Montpellier and Lyon fetch it every year.

Furthermore, the root of the Alkanet has an astringent quality, and perfumers <note>original: Voguentarii</note> use it to thicken their ointments. The leaves drunk in wine stop the bowels <note>i.e., treat diarrhea</note>. Dioscorides reports these and other things, assigning various powers to it. More will be found in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### Lycopsis: Germ. *Wald Ochsen Zung*: French & Ital. *Lycopsis*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a robust plant with large, broad leaves and multiple flowering spikes.</image-desc>

*Lycopsis* <note>term: Lycopsis (Wild Bugloss or Wolf's-face)</note>, which some have also called Alkanet, as Dioscorides reports, has leaves similar to Lettuce; but they are longer, thicker, and broader, rough, and falling toward the ground around the head of the root. The stem is long, straight, and scaly, with many cubit-long, rough stems attached, upon which are small purplish flowers. The root is red and endowed with an astringent power. It grows in open fields.

Pliny reports the same things regarding *Lycopsis*, but in various places; the older Greek writers made it a relative of the Alkanet. Among more recent authors, Rauwolf and the *History of Lyon* present the plant depicted here as the *Lycopsis* of Dioscorides.

<summary>This page catalogs several species of wild borage and Alkanet (Anchusa), detailing their physical descriptions, medicinal uses as astringents, and the historical confusion among ancient authors regarding their classification. It highlights the use of Alkanet roots in dyeing and pharmacy, as well as the plant Lycopsis.</summary>
<keywords>Wild Borage, Alkanet, Anchusa, Lycopsis, medicinal herbs, botanical history, Dioscorides, red dye, astringent, Renaissance botany</keywords>

# IMAGES AND OUTLINES
->Ttt 3<-
<meta>Catchword: psilique</meta>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Echium plant (Viper's Bugloss) showing large, hairy, lanceolate leaves and a dense flowering spike.</image-desc>

<margin>
**VIPER'S BUGLOSS**: German: *Wild Ochsenzung* <note>Wild Ox-tongue</note>; French: *Buglosse sauvage* <note>Wild Bugloss</note>; Italian: *Buglossa salvatica* <note>Wild Bugloss</note>.
</margin>

Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> mentions only one kind of Viper's Bugloss <note>original: Echium</note>, which he describes as being very close to the leaves of Alkanet. However, the ancient writer Numenius and the historian Pliny record two kinds. Yet, more varieties have become known to more recent botanists.

The common variety we illustrate here is found everywhere; its stems are sometimes a cubit and a half high <note>About 27 inches</note>, bristly, and marked with black spots. They are laden with flowers from the bottom almost to the very top; these are a beautiful blue, or purplish-blue, or sometimes flesh-colored or white, with stamens and tips of the same color. The leaves are rough, hairy, long, narrow, and bland in taste. The root is long, as thick as a thumb, woody, and has no remarkable flavor.

### VIPER’S BUGLOSS WITH BRIGHT RED FLOWERS AND PALE LEAVES.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Echium variety with a more slender stalk and distinct bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

This grew for us at Montbéliard in the Georges Prefecture garden <note>referring to the botanical gardens of the Dukes of Württemberg</note> from seed sent from Florence by Casabona <note>Giuseppe Casabona, a Flemish botanist and plant collector</note> under the title *Red Alkanet of Crete*. The whole plant was paler than the common Viper's Bugloss and more branched; however, the flowers were similar in shape but of a different, beautiful red color. It flowered in July and August.

### CLUSIUS’S RED-FLOWERED VIPER’S BUGLOSS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a flowering plant with a thick, upright, bristly spike of flowers.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a highly influential 16th-century botanist</note> observed this in great abundance in the dry meadows above and below the city of Sopron in Hungary, flowering in May; it was sometimes a deep, saturated red, and other times a paler red, and he saw it nowhere else.

Nicander, in his *Theriaca* <note>A poem on venomous creatures and their cures</note>, records that this herb was discovered by a certain Alcibiades. While he was sleeping near a threshing floor, he was bitten by a viper in the outer groin; awakened from sleep, he pressed the juice from this herb and drank it, and placed the remainder upon the wound, and thus he escaped unharmed. From this, the name *Alcibiace* has remained for the plant *Echium*.

<column-break/>

### GREATER WHITE-FLOWERED VIPER'S BUGLOSS.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a tall Echium plant with a thick central stem and numerous small flowers.</image-desc>

This is larger and rougher than the preceding one, robust and upright.

Furthermore, Viper’s Bugloss loves rich and fertile soil and delights in sunny places, occurring almost everywhere along roads and paths, on walls, in abandoned fields, and at the edges of farmland. It flowers all summer and stays green throughout the winter, its leaves enduring the winter frost.

It found its name *Echion* from vipers (for a viper is called <term>Ἔχις</term> <note>Echis</note> by the Greeks), either because it bears a seed similar to a viper's head, or because it is a most excellent remedy for the bites of vipers.

### CLUSIUS’S WOOLLY WILD VIPER’S BUGLOSS, with dark flowers.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a wild Echium variety with hairy leaves and a curved flowering top.</image-desc>

He says it grows in many places near Vienna and throughout the lower parts of Austria and Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary and Austria</note>, in drier and grassy meadows at the foot of hills; it flowers in May.

Viper's Bugloss not only has a seed similar to a viper's head, but its stem is also spotted like the skin of serpents; and from the flowers, it puts forth small, divided tongues like the tongue of a serpent. From all these signs <note>This refers to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that a plant's appearance reveals its medicinal use</note>, it is gathered by a very strong argument that this herb is most excellent against the bites of vipers.

### SCORPION-GRASS THAT FOLLOWS THE SUN.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant with a distinctive coiled, scorpion-like flower head (Scorpioides).</image-desc>

From a black, fibrous root, several thin, hairy stems rise up, branched, about nine inches high. The leaves grow onto these without stalks, about an inch long and a third of a thumb wide, ending in a blunt point; they are hairy, similar to mouse-ears, with a bland taste. The sequence of flowers twists itself like the tail of a scorpion; they are very small, blue with a yellowish center, and divided into five segments.

It varies with larger or smaller flowers, white or blue.

Brunfels and Humelberg label it as the *Lesser Hound's Tongue* <note>Cynoglossa</note>. Gesner calls it *Aquatic Scorpion-grass*.

It delights in watery places, and flowers in May. <note>original: psilique</note> <note>The catchword 'psilique' is likely a fragment of a Latin word like 'palustribus' or 'pascua,' though it is unclear in this OCR</note>

<summary>This page describes various species of Echium (Viper's Bugloss), detailing their physical characteristics, their medicinal use against snake bites based on the "Doctrine of Signatures," and their geographical locations across Europe.</summary>
<keywords>Viper's Bugloss, Echium, Clusius, medicinal herbs, botany, Doctrine of Signatures, snakebite remedies, Austria, Hungary, Casabona</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the detailed catalog of the Boraginaceae family, specifically focusing on the hard-seeded Gromwell (Lithospermum), the various species of Comfrey (Symphytum), and the medicinal Lungwort (Pulmonaria). It follows the previous page’s discussion on Viper's Bugloss, maintaining the same method of reconciling classical descriptions with contemporary 16th-century observations.</meta>

->OF PLANTS<-

### GROMWELL, OR STONESEED: German: Sea Millet; French: Gromwell, Pearl-Herb; Italian: Lithospermo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Gromwell plant, showing upright stems with small leaves and clusters of flowers and seeds at the tips, with a detailed root system.</image-desc>

Pliny <note>A 1st-century Roman naturalist</note> says that this species of Gromwell <note>original: Lithospermum, from the Greek for 'stone seed'</note> is such that it can be recognized at a glance, even without a written description. Galen and Aetius <note>Ancient Greek medical authorities</note> omitted it from their list of simple medicines, but Dioscorides described it so diligently that, in the judgment of Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock, a German botanist</note>, it seems even a blind man could easily recognize it by touch alone.

The root is about the thickness of a thumb, woody, and spreading several fibers from its side. From this rise many stalks, some upright and others trailing, whitish, rough to the touch, and divided into "wings" or branches. The leaves are sometimes alternate and sometimes opposite, long, narrow, and hairy. The flowers are small, white, and five-petaled, set in long, bristly calyxes; these are followed by an ash-colored seed of invincible hardness and exceptional smoothness.

### GREATER COMFREY: German: Wall-root; French: Great Comfrey; Italian: Greater Consolidator.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Greater Comfrey (Symphytum maius), featuring large, broad, lance-shaped leaves and drooping clusters of bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Botanical writers recognize three main types of Comfrey <note>original: Symphytum, from the Greek meaning 'to grow together'</note>: *Small*, *Medium*, and *Large*. The *Small* Comfreys are the Daisies <note>original: Bellides</note>, of which many varieties are recorded. The *Medium* types are numbered as three: the Rock-comfrey, Bugle, and Self-heal. And likewise, there are three *Large* types: the White or Common, the Tuberous, and the Spotted.

We have already dealt with the Small and Medium types in Classes 16 and 30 of this *Drafting*; now we shall speak of the Large Comfrey.

Various distinctions are again proposed for it; for instance, Caspar Bauhin <note>A Swiss botanist who developed early plant classification</note> lists seven.

We distinguish them into *Large*, *Tuberous*, and *Spotted* Comfrey: about which more will be said in the following sections and in the Appendix.

### SPOTTED COMFREY, OR LUNGWORT: German: Lung-herb; French: Lung-herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Lungwort (Symphytum maculosum), showing broad leaves near the base with characteristic spotting and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

To Tragus, Cordus, Lonicer <note>Renaissance botanists</note> and others, this is the *Wild Comfrey*. Turner <note>William Turner, the 'Father of English Botany'</note> calls it Jerusalem Sage and the *Pulmonaria* of the apothecaries. Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a German physician</note> calls it the Bugloss of Theophrastus. Many call it the Lungwort of Pliny or Italian Lungwort. Caspar Bauhin in his *Phytopinax* calls it Broad-leaved Lungwort or Spotted Comfrey, and says it is found with leaves marked with white spots and also without spots; the flowers are commonly blue-green, and occasionally even white.

We have seen the variety without spots in the gardens of Lyon, Geneva, and Basel, as well as at Montbéliard on the hill across from the bridge. The variety with spotted leaves is more frequent in Italy, as we observed it in Bologna, Padua, Ferrara, and other places. It blooms in Spring.

<column-break/>

### DODONAEUS’ GREATER GROMWELL, WITH PURPLE or violet flowers, and seeds like Alkanet or Viper's Bugloss.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a larger variety of Gromwell, showing a more robust plant with curved flowering tops and a thick root.</image-desc>

Some distinguish Gromwell into *Garden*, *Wild*, and *Field* varieties; others establish various kinds of it based on appearance and strength, though they differ only in size. Caspar Bauhin, in his commentary on Mattioli, mentions the *Greater*, *Smaller*, and *Smallest*. He says the *Greater* has leaves either like an Olive or like a Reed; the *Smaller* is either broad-leaved or narrow-leaved; and finally the *Smallest*, called *Passerina* <note>Sparrow-wort</note>, he identifies as either German or Montpellier Gromwell.

Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> also mentions a variety called *Black*, which indeed has white flowers, but has black seeds like Viper's Bugloss and blackish leaves.

More on this in the Appendix.

### TUBEROUS COMFREY, OR COMFREY WITH A tuberous or bulbous root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tuberous Comfrey, highlighting the distinct knobby, bulb-like root structure and upright growth habit.</image-desc>

Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino, an Italian physician and botanist</note> describes it thus: *The Lesser Consolidator, or the second kind, has leaves like Borage, but smaller and less rough; the stalks are about nine inches or a little higher; the flower is pale, and the roots spread out sideways, containing round little tubers of a white color, soft, and of a not unpleasant taste.*

It grows not only in gardens and cultivated places but is also found growing wild in shady forest spots, under shrubs, and around hedges; it is very common under Olive trees in Italy. Anguillara <note>Luigi Anguillara, a 16th-century botanist</note> writes that it is of miraculous efficacy for consolidation <note>healing/knitting together</note> and the joining of flesh and bones.

Regarding the origins and powers of the Common variety, see the Appendix.

### NARROW-LEAVED LUNGWORT, WITH BLUE flowers, described by Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Narrow-leaved Lungwort, showing narrower leaves and a cluster of flowers at the top.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering 16th-century botanist</note> says it grows here and there through Pannonia <note>modern-day Hungary/western Balkans</note> and Lower Austria, in mountainous areas and felled forests. It shoots up in early Spring and produces a cluster of gathered flowers almost before the leaves appear, and it blooms for a very long time.

The *Common Comfrey*, however, delights in marshes, damp spots, grassy gardens, shores, and riverbanks. Once it has taken root, it cannot easily be driven out; for even the smallest portion of the root fixed in the ground immediately emerges as a plant. It blooms in the months of May, June, and July. It is abundant in the meadows of Lyon, Basel, Montbéliard, and Yverdon.

<summary>This page catalogs several species of Gromwell, Comfrey, and Lungwort, detailing their physical characteristics, their classification by Renaissance botanists, and their medicinal reputation for healing flesh and bone.</summary>
<keywords>Gromwell, Comfrey, Lungwort, botany, medicinal herbs, Lithospermum, Symphytum, Pulmonaria, Dioscorides, Pliny, Bauhin, Renaissance medicine</keywords>

### SECOND NARROW-LEAVED LUNGWORT, with a red flower and leaves like Viper's Bugloss.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Pulmonaria plant with long, narrow, lanceolate leaves and small clusters of flowers at the top of the stems.</image-desc>

In its medicinal properties, this Comfrey corresponds to the Great Common Comfrey, called <term>alum</term> <note>original: "alum"; a name occasionally used for Comfrey or related plants in early modern botany</note>. Furthermore, the root of that common variety has greater use in medicine than the herb itself. It is of a warm and moist temperament. Once cleaned, boiled in wine, and drunk, it is beneficial for overcoming ulcers of the lungs and ailments of the chest; it is also most suitable for all kinds of wounds, ruptures, and bone fractures, as daily experience attests.

Thus, surgeons are accustomed to adding it to their plasters.

A decoction of the flowers in red wine is drunk for bloody urine; the powder of the root, applied with egg white, soothes immoderate hemorrhoids.

### HOUND'S-TONGUE 1. German: *Hundszunge*; French: *Langue de chien*; Italian: *Lingua di cane*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cynoglossum (Hound's-tongue) plant, showing broad, hairy leaves and a long taproot.</image-desc>

This plant receives its name from the shape of its leaves <note>Cynoglossum literally means "dog's tongue" in Greek</note>, a name which is also bestowed upon various others, such as *Viper's Bugloss, Alkanet, Gromwell, Honeywort, Narcissus, and Plantain*.

Indeed, many species and differences of the aforementioned Hound's-tongue are described, but those known to us will soon be handed down.

We depict here the common variety, whose root is black on the outside and white within, entirely thick and fleshy <note>original: "cassa"; here implying a full or substance-heavy root</note>, with a somewhat sweet and bland taste.

The stalks are two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> high, divided into many branches, becoming hollow with age, and covered in much downy hair. The leaves are long and somewhat broad in the first year; in the second year, when it bears a stalk, they are narrow, pointed, grayish-white, soft, and downy, with a heavy scent. More on this follows at the side of the next figure.

### SMALLER HOUND'S-TONGUE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller species of Cynoglossum with more slender leaves and stems.</image-desc>

The plant we display here we have called the "Smaller Hound's-tongue," before we had noticed any mention of it made by anyone else. It has a stalk nine inches high <note>original: "dodrantali"</note>, though in cultivated soil it grows to a large cubit <note>about 18–20 inches</note>, and is branched. The leaves are much larger than the common sort, a palm's breadth long, approaching the leaves of the Small Bugloss, being bristly and heavily scented. The small reddish flowers are succeeded by seeds like burs <note>original: "Lappacea"</note>, beautiful and arranged in fours, which cling to clothing and are much smaller than the common variety.

We have seen it in the meadows of Tübingen and Geneva, and we have kept it in the garden of His Serene Highness <note>original: "S. P."; likely referencing the Prince's garden at Montbéliard</note> at Montbéliard. It blooms in August.

<column-break/>

### CREEPING DWARF COMFREY: EXOTIC WHITE LUNGWORT.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, creeping plant with rounded leaves and small flowers.</image-desc>

This is that creeping dwarf Comfrey with the appearance of Borage mentioned by Lobelius <note>Matthias de l’Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist</note> in his *Observations and Images of Plants*. He says that the Illustrious Prince of Chimay and other more skilled explorers of Belgian plants call this beautiful plant Lungwort, but with smaller leaves; the small flowers are like Borage, blue-purple; the root is dark, like Meadowsweet or Avens, entangled with fibers. It blooms in winter in hanging gardens, but in spring and autumn in others. However, we are still ignorant of what the ancients called this plant.

The same Lobelius mentions an *Exotic Lungwort with Water-Plantain leaves prostrate on the ground and white flowers, etc.*; we have not seen it.

### A SMALLER AND WHITER SPECIES OF COMMON HOUND'S-TONGUE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller, lighter variety of Cynoglossum with prominent seed pods.</image-desc>

To complete the description of the common Hound's-tongue's flowers begun previously: they are similar to the flowers of the Apothecary's Bugloss, with a dull reddish color; they are embraced by four or five hairy, grayish leaves.

These are followed by four little burs, somewhat compressed and bristly with small spines, which cling tenaciously to clothing; they are provided with a single cavity in which there is likewise a single seed.

Both species of the small common Hound's-tongue grow near hedges, in uncultivated and sandy places, in courtyards and near walls where filth of all kinds is accustomed to be thrown; it blooms in May and June.

### GREEN-LEAVED HOUND'S-TONGUE, with a small, rusty-red flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cynoglossum variety with dense foliage and small flowers.</image-desc>

We found this on a mountain near Masmunster <note>Masevaux, in the Alsace region</note>, and planted it in the garden of His Serene Highness at Montbéliard; there it bloomed in April and May, renewing itself from fallen seed. This is what Caspar Bauhin <note>A famous Swiss botanist</note> in his *Phytopinax* titled "Evergreen Hound's-tongue"; but he did so erroneously, as it is accustomed to perish.

Hound's-tongue has a cold and dry temperament and is most effective for healing degenerate and malignant ulcers.

The dry root, ground into powder and drunk in red wine, cures dysentery, and is especially useful in cases of gonorrhea <note>In this period, the term was often used for any involuntary discharge</note>. It is a <term>vulnerary</term> <note>a medicine used in healing wounds</note>, stops bleeding, and cures all kinds of ulcers and wounds.

<summary>This page catalogs various species of Lungwort and Hound's-tongue, detailing their physical characteristics, habitats in Europe, and significant medicinal uses for treating wounds, ulcers, and internal ailments.</summary>
<keywords>Lungwort, Hound's-tongue, Comfrey, botany, medicinal herbs, wound healing, Lobelius, Caspar Bauhin, Montbéliard, ulcers, dysentery</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical cataloging of the Boraginaceae family, moving from the Lungworts and Common Hound's-tongue described on the previous page to more specific regional varieties like the Cretan Hound's-tongue and related species like Honeywort and Onosma.</meta>

### THE FIRST CRETAN HOUND'S-TONGUE, with a small, pale purplish flower, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Cynoglossum plant with long, lanceolate leaves and small flowers at the top of the stems, showing the root system.</image-desc>

In his later *History*, <note>Carolus Clusius (1526–1609) was one of the most influential botanists of the Renaissance.</note> Clusius mentions two kinds of Cretan Hound's-tongue, and he depicts and describes them graphically. He observed them only in some of the more refined gardens of the Low Countries, where they had grown from seeds sent from Italy. We depict the *first* of these here.

Furthermore, for <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>original: "mariscas"; small swellings or piles</note>, the water, juice, and powder of common Hound's-tongue are very useful when applied by rinsing or sprinkling. In cases of <term>thrush</term> <note>original: "Aphthis"; mouth sores</note> and malignant ulcers of the mouth arising from the <term>Venereal disease</term> <note>original: "lue Venerea"; syphilis</note>, it is most beneficial if they are rinsed with a decoction of the root and its powder is sprinkled on: *More on this to the side of the following figure.*

### PERHAPS THE ORNAMENTAL HOUND'S-TONGUE OF PLINY; the Bur-like Viper's Bugloss to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with upright stems, narrow leaves, and small burr-like seed pods or flowers along the stalks.</image-desc>

It has stems two cubits high <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches, so about 3 feet tall</note>, which are angular, branched, and hollow; it has small, stiff, rough burs that cling to clothing and spread across the ground, unless there is something nearby for them to climb. The *leaves* grow in twos or threes, are narrow, and two inches long. *Small flowers* break out from the axils of the leaves; they are purple-violet, very small, divided into five parts, and possess short stalks. These are followed by *seeds* that are dark, shaped like sesame seeds, and a little larger. The *root* is straight, about the thickness of the little finger, and has several fibers.

The smell and taste of the whole plant are like those of Borage. We have seen it growing wild in Raetia <note>a Roman province in the central Alps</note> and have also cultivated it at Montbéliard in the garden of the Illustrious Prince.

### PERHAPS A SPECIES OF HONEYWORT OR WOAD, or the Mountain Woad of Dalechamp.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafy plant with broad, veined leaves and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

Mountain Woad, he says, is produced on the snowy peaks of mountains: with a thick, black *root* covered in many hairy fibers. It has many *leaves* around the root, supported by a long and thick stalk; they are veined and similar to <term>Woad</term> <note>original: "Glasto"; Isatis tinctoria, used for blue dye</note>, but more blunt at the top. There are many *stems*, over a foot high, on which the leaves are narrower and sharper than those mentioned above. The *flower* is abundant and shines yellow at the top of the stems; it has a somewhat oblong shape, divided into points at the top, with a thin hair projecting from the center of its hollow.

How much this "Woad" of Dalechamp differs from Honeywort, let the experts decide.

<column-break/>

### THE SECOND CRETAN HOUND'S-TONGUE of the same Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a second Cynoglossum variety, similar to the first but with broader leaves and slightly different floral arrangement.</image-desc>

This plant has flowers shorter and broader than the flowers of the preceding one, and they are of a whitish color at first, but are later adorned with many thin purplish veins.

Furthermore, the juice and distilled water of the common Hound's-tongue are known to be recommended for burns because of their obvious cooling and drying qualities, and because they are able to soothe pain and prevent a greater flow of humors. They also help with <term>alopecia</term> <note>original: "alopecis"; hair loss</note> caused by a sharp and eroding humor. Whether it is safe to use the crushed herb for the bite of a mad dog, as Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist</note> prescribes, should be considered.

### THE HONEYWORT OF THE ANCIENTS: CERINTHE to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Cerinthe plant, featuring distinctive overlapping bracts and tubular flowers.</image-desc>

Pliny recorded in Book 21, chapter 12, that <term>Honeywort</term> <note>original: "Cerinthen"</note> should be sown for the sake of beehives and bees. It is, he says, a plant with a white, curved leaf, a cubit high, with a hollow head containing a honey-like juice; bees are most greedy for its flowers. Theophrastus numbers it among the summer flowers; Columella among the gifts of Spring. Paolo Manuzio, Servius, and Virgil (in the 4th *Georgic*) call it an "ignoble grass." They call it "vile" or "ignoble" because of its abundance, since it grows everywhere.

Furthermore, four varieties of Honeywort are commonly listed: *Greater, with a multicolored flower (yellow and reddish-purple); and Lesser, with a yellow flower.*

### ONOSMA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Onosma plant, showing a basal rosette of hairy leaves and a flowering stalk.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacology</note> records this about Onosma: Onosma, he says, has oblong *leaves* similar to Alkanet <note>original: "Anchusæ"</note>, four inches long and one wide, soft and lying on the ground, without a stem, without seed, and without a flower. But it rests upon an oblong, thin, weak, reddish *root*. It grows in rough places. The leaves drunk in wine "draw out the offspring" <note>induce labor</note>; and if a pregnant woman steps over this herb, it is said to cause a miscarriage.

Pliny records almost the same things. But *Onosma*, or *Osmado*, or *Philonitin*, or *Ononin*, consists of a sharp and bitter substance, and therefore it is believed to kill and eject the fetus, as Galen writes in Book 8 of *On Simple Medicines*.

Some believe it to be a type of Wild Bugloss.

<margin>**HELIOTROPE, OR CANCER HERB**: German: *Krebsblumen* <note>Cancer-flower</note>, *Sonnenwirbel* <note>Sun-whirl</note>; French: *Tournesol*; Italian: *Girasole*.</margin>
<margin>**THE SMALLER HELIOTROPE OF SOME AUTHORS**, Pliny’s Three-seeded Heliotrope: Wartwort.</margin>

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Heliotropium plant with broad leaves and a curved, scorpion-tail-like flower spike on the left. On the right, a second botanical illustration shows a smaller variety with three-seeded fruit clusters.</image-desc>

Although there are many plants that might deservedly be called <term>Heliotropes</term> <note>original: "Heliotropia"; from the Greek "helios" (sun) and "trepein" (to turn)</note> and <term>Helioscopes</term> <note>original: "Helioscopia"; sun-viewers</note> because they always turn toward the Sun and move around with it, here we are specifically dealing with the Heliotrope of <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for centuries.</note>.

He identifies two kinds: the Greater and the Lesser. Pliny identifies the same number, though he distinguishes them differently.

By the consensus of all, the plant we illustrate here is the **Greater Heliotrope** of Dioscorides, of which he says: The Great Heliotrope has a flower in the shape of a scorpion’s tail, which is why it is named <term>Scorpiurus</term> <note>Scorpion-tail</note>; and, because it turns its leaves with the Sun, it is called Heliotrope. It has leaves like <term>Basil</term> <note>original: "Ocimi"</note>, but hairier, whiter, and larger. Three, four, or often five small branches spring from the root, with many hollow "armpits" <note>axils</note>. The flower at the tip is white or slightly yellowish, curving like a scorpion's tail. The root is thin and useless. It grows in rugged places.

However, although he records that it grows only in rugged places, it actually grows spontaneously in various other locations: in fields, along roadsides, in town squares, around the foundations of buildings, and in dry or sandy spots. It is very common in the <term>Lyonnaise</term> <note>Region around Lyon, France</note> and <term>Narbonnese</term> <note>Southern France</note> regions of Gaul, as well as in <term>Alsace</term>, where the fields are so filled with the Greater Heliotrope that they seem to have been intentionally sown with it. It abounds in the fields of **Montbéliard** above the village of *Audincourt*, as well as in certain places around **Basel**, and in **Geneva** at *la petite Grave*. It flowers in Summer and Autumn.

The **Lesser Heliotrope**, according to Dioscorides, grows in marshy areas near lakes; its leaves are very similar to those mentioned before but rounder, with seeds hanging down in a round shape like <term>warts</term> <note>original: "actocordonum Verrucarum"; likely referring to 'acrochordons' or skin tags</note>.

<term>Clusius</term> writes that it is very frequent in the territory of **Salamanca**, and <term>Lobelius</term> finds it in Narbonnese Gaul. We, however, have kept it in gardens at Lyon and Geneva. The peasants of Lunel, Narbonne, and other nearby places gather the ripe seeds in September with great profit, later selling them to **Dyers** and Surgeons.

Indeed, its powers are the same as the Greater variety: the rubbed herb effectively removes warts, <term>myrmecia</term> <note>ant-warts</note>, and <term>thymus</term> <note>wart-like growths</note>. It is also most effective against <term>carcinomas</term> <note>original: "Carcinomata"; malignant ulcers or cancers</note> and gangrenous sores; for this reason, some have called it the *Cancer Herb*. <term>Matthiolus</term> recommends the whole plant for the aforementioned conditions and for scrofulous tumors; Lobelius recommends the seed.

---

### THE THREE-SEEDED HELIOTROPE OF FUCHS, OR WARTWORT.

Galen passed over the Heliotrope in his catalog of simple medicines. However, following the example of Dioscorides, both Varro and Paulus, as well as Pliny, made it two-fold—namely, the Greater and the Lesser. Pliny labels the Lesser and smaller one as <term>Tricoccon</term> <note>Three-seeded</note>, while the Greater is called by the generic name *Heliotropium*. There are some who distinguish them into the "upright" and "creeping" varieties.

This figure of ours, which is taken from <term>Fuchs</term> <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist.</note>, did not please us; therefore, we have taken care to prepare another previously provided by Clusius. As for the one Matthiolus has, we believe it was fashioned and depicted based solely on Dioscorides' description <note>rather than from a live specimen</note>.

*For more on the Heliotrope, see the Appendix.*

<image-desc>A third botanical woodcut at the bottom left showing a smaller, upright plant with distinct three-lobed seed pods, identified in the text as Heliotropium Tricoccum.</image-desc>

## OF PLANTS
### CLASS 34.
#### MALIGNANT AND POISONOUS PLANTS.

<columns>2</columns>

**NIGHTSHADE** or **SOLATRUM**: German: *Nachtschatt*; French: *Morelle*; Italian: *Solatro*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Solanum plant (Nightshade) with broad, pointed leaves and small clusters of berries.</image-desc>

<term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 371–287 BC) and the "father of botany."</note> records only two main kinds of Nightshade (called *Vesicariarum* or "bladder-plants" by his translator <term>Gaza</term>): specifically, the Sleep-inducing and the Mad varieties. <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose work "De Materia Medica" was the standard botanical text for 1,500 years.</note> lists four: the Garden, the <term>Halicacabum</term> <note>Winter Cherry</note>, the Sleep-inducing, and the Manic. <term>Pliny</term> identifies just as many and the same types, but with less distinction. <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> only briefly touched upon the powers of Nightshade. <term>Apuleius</term> <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, author of a famous 4th-century herbal.</note> covered all kinds of Nightshade in a single chapter, but shamefully confused their names with one another. Among more recent authors, <term>Caspar Bauhin</term> <note>A Swiss botanist (1560–1624) who refined the classification of plants.</note> proposes twenty species and differences in his *Phytopinax*. As we set out our own sequence of descriptions, we shall follow in the footsteps of Dioscorides, beginning with the Garden, Sown, or Common variety illustrated here; we shall treat it more specifically in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

**COMMON WINTER CHERRY.** <note>original: "Solanum Halicacabum Vulgare"</note> German: *Iuden kirschen* <note>Literally "Jew's cherries," a common historical name for the Winter Cherry/Physalis.</note>; French: *Baguenaudes*; Italian: *Halicacabo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Solanum Halicacabum (Winter Cherry/Physalis) showing the characteristic papery husks or bladders enclosing the fruit.</image-desc>

This plant propagates itself abundantly by the fertility of its small, creeping roots. It has thin, reddish, and slightly hairy stems. These support leaves similar to the Garden Nightshade, but larger, slightly hairy, and often growing in pairs from the same spot. From the "wings" <note>axils</note> of these leaves emerge drooping, whitish **flowers**, divided into five segments with tips of the same color, on an inch-long stalk. These are followed by grassy-green **little bladders** <note>original: "utriculi"</note> which turn red as they ripen. Within each of these is a **fruit** the size, color, and shape of a cherry, with a sour and slightly bitter taste, containing flat, circular **seeds**.

It delights in shady places and grows on old walls, in vineyards, in hedges, and along the margins of fields. It flowers in Summer and ripens its fruit in Autumn.

---

**INDIAN WINTER CHERRY.** <note>original: "Solanum Halicacabum Indicum"</note> Perhaps the **Plant of Concord**, or **Flower of the Night**?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Indian variety of Solanum Halicacabum with more complex leaf structures and bladder-like fruits.</image-desc>

The stem of this Nightshade is a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> high, quite thick, and divided into many branches. Along these are leaves resembling the common Nightshade, but lobed and tapering, with veins extending from the central rib into the lobes, on a stalk of two or three inches. **Flowers** emerge from the fork of the branches and the hollows of the leaves; they are yellow and similar to the Winter Cherry. **Bladders** follow, equal to the Winter Cherry and green in color; these are filled by a large **berry** full of seeds like the Winter Cherry, though it is tasteless.

This is found only in more cultivated gardens; we had it in the <term>princely garden at Montbéliard</term> <note>original: "S.P. horto," likely referring to the gardens of the Dukes of Württemberg-Montbéliard.</note>. Some call it the "Flower of the Night" because, as if shuddering at the shadows, it closes at night, but opens when the Sun approaches.

<column-break/>

**SLEEP-INDUCING NIGHTSHADE, WHORLED.** <note>original: "Solanum Somniferum, Verticillatum"</note> Called "Whorled Nightshade" by some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Solanum Somniferum (Withania somnifera, commonly known as Ashwagandha) showing upright stems with whorled leaf arrangements and small fruits.</image-desc>

This plant reaches a height of a cubit or more, with a straight, round, and hairy stem. Along it grow alternate leaves, very close in appearance to the leaves of the <term>Priapea</term> <note>likely referring to a species of Mandrake or similar Solanaceous plant</note>, tapering gently from a rounded shape to a point, hairy, and attached by stalks shorter than an inch. From the hollows of the leaves, **flowers** arise in whorls <note>circles</note> around the stem, similar to those of the common Nightshade, pale yellow in color and composed of five petals with several tips in the center. Large **seed-vessels** follow, containing the **seed**, wrapped in hairy, fringed bladders.

<term>Clusius</term> <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering European botanist.</note> saw the Sleep-inducing Nightshade growing wild in Spain, in the citadel of the city of Malaga. We have seen it nowhere else wild; however, we had it in the princely garden at Montbéliard, and we observed it in gardens in Basel and Padua.

It provides historical context from classical authors and detailed descriptions of the Common Nightshade, the Winter Cherry (Physalis), and the Sleep-inducing Nightshade (Ashwagandha).</summary>
