### MAD NIGHTSHADE, German: *Dollkraut*; French & Italian: *Bella Dona*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a Mad Nightshade (Belladonna) plant, showing its thick root system, tall stems, large broad leaves, and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

From a thick root, it raises stalks higher than three <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note>, thicker than a thumb, and hairy; these grow thick into a tuber and branch out into many limbs arising from nearly the same point. The leaves have the form of Nightshade, but are much larger and not at all wavy at the edges; they are hairy on both sides, dark green above, and almost bristly beneath. The flowers are streaked and concave, growing from the <term>axils</term> <note>The angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem.</note> of the leaves; they are divided into five segments like little bells. On the inside, the color is a lurid purple with a variegated yellow base; on the outside, they are a reddish-green hue, somewhat hairy, with white tips. When the flowers fall, shiny berries sit upon a hairy, five-parted <term>calyx</term> <note>The leafy base that supports the flower.</note>; the plant has a foul smell.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF MAD NIGHTSHADE, OR BELLADONNA.

<image-desc>A second botanical illustration of Mad Nightshade, depicting the plant with its characteristic dark berries and broad, pointed leaves.</image-desc>

It is found around forests, near walls, the hedges of fields, and other little-cultivated or deserted places, and it loves shady spots. It blooms toward the end of May, and in August, sooner or later, it displays its ripe berries.

We have seen it growing wild in the forests of <term>Montpellier</term> and <term>Zurich</term>, blooming in May, and likewise in the shady areas around <term>Bephamp</term> by the river <term>Doubs</term> in <term>Montbéliard</term>. However, it is commonly cultivated in gardens, where its peculiar beauty overshadows its wild luxuriance. Furthermore, where it is found grazed upon in the woods, it is often a sign to hunters that deer are present. *More in the Appendix.*

### HERB PARIS; German: *Wolffs beer*; French: *Raisin de Renard*.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of Herb Paris (Paris quadrifolia), showing a single upright stem with a whorl of four leaves and a single central berry at the top.</image-desc>

It is found in the wooded areas of mountains, in the dim and shady spots of valleys and thickets, in rich and fertile soil. In April it puts forth its flower, consisting of four green leaves; in May and June, the purple berries ripen. The leaves around the top of the stem are almost always four in number, more rarely five.

Whether this herb should be numbered among the deadly plants is a matter of sharp dispute among writers. However, it is clear to all, on the testimony of <term>Gesner</term> and <term>Tragus</term> <note>Conrad Gessner and Hieronymus Bock, influential 16th-century botanists.</note>, that it has a great cooling effect. <term>Matthiolus</term> recommends it against poisons; <term>Camerarius</term> <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598).</note> writes that an oil is prepared from its berries against the great pains of witchcraft and hemorrhoids. *More in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF MAD NIGHTSHADE, OR BELLADONNA.

<image-desc>A third botanical illustration of Mad Nightshade, showing a tall specimen with detailed leaf structure and hanging flowers.</image-desc>

Camerarius, who calls it the "Greater Nightshade," says it is called <term>Bella Dona</term> <note>literally "Beautiful Lady" in Italian.</note> because women decorate their faces with its juice <note>Belladonna juice was used to dilate the pupils, which was considered a sign of beauty, or applied to the skin to create a flushed appearance.</note>. <term>Clusius</term> <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist.</note>, who labels it "Lethal Nightshade" and "Bella Dona," suspects—not without reason—that it was once thought to be the Mandrake of <term>Theophrastus</term>. [He testifies that there are two kinds: one with more pleasing leaves hanging from shorter stalks and a larger flower; the other with smaller, darker leaves supported by longer stalks and a smaller flower.]

<term>Fuchsius</term> writes that it is called "Marine" by some because it is found with difficulty on rocks not far from the sea. Matthiolus, because he did not know it, claimed it was unknown to everyone in Italy, a statement for which <term>Guillandinus</term> <note>Melchior Wieland (1520–1589), a critic of Matthiolus.</note> rightly mocks him.

### APOLLINARIS, A SPECIES OF NIGHTSHADE FROM THE APENNINES; Strychnodendros; Tree-like Nightshade.

<image-desc>A botanical illustration of a woody Solanum species, showing upright stems with small round fruit or seed pods.</image-desc>

Some relate the plant pictured here to the species of <term>Hyoscyamus</term> <note>Henbane</note>, others to Nightshade. The *History of Lyon* <note>Referring to the "Historia Generalis Plantarum" (1586) edited by Jacques Daléchamps.</note> labels it as Daléchamps' Foreign Henbane, which is also called *Apollinaris* after the philosopher Apollonius, who showed it to Plato. It is found in the shady and dense forests of the <term>Apennines</term>.

It is indeed the *Strychnodendros* <note>literally "Nightshade Tree" in Greek.</note>, a small tree three cubits high, with a slender trunk and a greyish bark; the leaves are dark green like the Spindle-tree; the flowers are like Garden Nightshade; and the fruit and seed are like those of the Winter Cherry. <term>Lobelius</term> writes that some believe it to be the *Amomum* of Pliny. It is cultivated in gardens and is not found elsewhere.

### AMERICAN POTATO, PYCNOCONVM; ORIPpauk [Openauk] of the Virginian Island root; Channos.

<image-desc>A detailed botanical illustration of a potato plant (Solanum tuberosum), showing the compound leaves, clusters of flowers, and the characteristic tuberous roots (potatoes) underground.</image-desc>

The American Potato is given a stem of two or three cubits, somewhat thick, succulent, nearly round, streaked, slightly hairy, green, spotted, and branched. The leaves are a <term>span</term> and a half long <note>A span is roughly 9 inches.</note>, and otherwise of the form and arrangement pictured here. The flowers are pale and slightly hairy, resembling the flowers of the Wild Mallow. The "apples" <note>original: "poma", referring here to the green fruit/seed pods of the potato plant.</note> are the size of a chestnut, round, dark green, and slightly hairy; inside are small, flat seeds similar to Nightshade seeds. The root is bulbous and thick, about a span long, whitish-red on the outside and pale white on the inside, and tasteless. From it, the Peruvians make a bread they call *Channos*; the inhabitants of the Island of <term>Virginia</term> call the plant *Openauk*; and today it is known in the gardens of Europeans.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Nightshade family, including Belladonna (Mad Nightshade), Herb Paris, and a very early European description of the American Potato (Solanum tuberosum).</summary>

# THE MANDRAKE PLANTS, CIRCEAN: Germ. *Alraun*; French: *Mandragore*, *Main de gloire* <note>Hand of glory</note>; Ital. *Mandragora*. THE FEMALE MANDRAKE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut illustration of a Mandrake (Mandragora) plant, showing a thick, bifurcated root resembling human legs, a cluster of large ribbed leaves emerging from the crown, and small flowers and round fruits.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist, author of "De Materia Medica."</note> assigns two kinds to the Mandrake: the Male, also called *Morion*, and the Female, which is called *Thridacias* <note>original: "Thridacias," a name derived from the Greek word for lettuce, referring to the leaf shape.</note>.

The Male, which we depict here, has a thick, long, forked root; it is hairy with fibers sprouting here and there, looking somewhat like an unstable human form. From its head emerge leaves about a <term>cubit</term> <note>Roughly 18 inches.</note> long and a <term>palm</term> <note>About 3-4 inches.</note> and a half wide, narrow at the base and the tip, endowed with a dark green color, and foul-smelling. Between these, arising also from the root—*for it produces no central stalk*—many small stems emerge, a palm long, each supporting a *flower* that is white-purplish, moderately hairy, shaped almost like a Bellflower, and of a foul odor. A round *fruit* follows, the size of a small Medlar, colored yellowish-green.

The Black Mandrake, called *Thridacias*, and which is considered the Female, has narrower leaves, says Dioscorides, and smaller than those of Lettuce; they are poisonous and heavy-smelling, spread out upon the ground. It bears fruits similar to Service-berries, pale and fragrant, in which the seeds are like those of Pears. Furthermore, it clings to quite large roots, two or three twisted together, black on the outside and white within. It bears no stalk.

Which plant might be the Mandrake of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the "Father of Botany."</note> is debated by herbalists. Indeed, Pliny and other ancient writers acknowledge the two proposed by Dioscorides, but they do not remember the third, which he adds from the opinion of others.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel, a Flemish physician and botanist.</note> writes that the male Mandrake is kept in gardens in Spain, Italy, Provence, and Gallia Narbonensis, with seeds or roots brought from Crete or the Cyclades Islands; however, in other regions, it is not so easily kept. Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician.</note> claims the Female grows copiously in Gargano and other mountains of Apulia, and Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a pioneering botanist.</note> finds it above Cadiz. We ourselves have seen both in Geneva, in the garden adjoining our house. However, following the example of many, we show only a single illustration, because they differ in little else but size, and as has been said, everything is simply smaller in the Female.

It is claimed that it obtained the name *Mandragoras* because, being impatient of the burning sun, it grows near the *mandras* <note>original: "mandras," meaning stalls or pens for cattle.</note> of the flocks and in other shady caves. *More can be found in the Appendix.*

---

### THE ARABIC EGGPLANT, MELANZANA: THE FRUIT-BEARING NIGHTSHADE.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Eggplant (Melongena), featuring large, broad leaves with wavy margins and a single large, oval fruit hanging from a stem.</image-desc>

The Eggplant was first celebrated in the books of the Arabs; some suspect this to be a certain species of the fruit-bearing Nightshades.

Various differences are found among them, as will be clear from what follows. The one depicted here fixes its fibrous roots not very deeply; it has a single stalk, a foot high, somewhat thick, firm, purplish, and hairy. The *leaves* are a palm or a palm and a half long, and almost a palm wide, slightly wavy around the edges, and hairy both above and below. The *flowers* cling to short enough stems; they are whitish or purplish, in the shape of a star. Concerning the *fruits* and *seeds*, refer to the Latin description of the next figure.

<column-break/>

### FRUIT-BEARING NIGHTSHADE WITH CURVED FRUIT.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a variety of eggplant or pepper, showing a plant with lobed leaves and a long, curved, horn-shaped fruit.</image-desc>

The *fruit* of this nightshade is about the size of an egg or a cucumber, with a shape almost oblong from a round base, and sometimes curved. It is covered in a smooth skin of yellow, grey, greenish, or purple, with a juicy and whitish pulp inside, in which are many whitish, flattened seeds, rivaling those of the <term>Siliquastrum pepper</term> <note>A reference to chili peppers or bird's eye peppers.</note>.

Some have called them *Melanzena*, or *Mala insana* <note>original: "Mala insana," literally "Mad Apples."</note>, including Hermolaus; but this was done with poor judgment, as Scaliger rightly notes, since they excite no madness when eaten.

They are also called *Poma amoris* <note>original: "Poma amoris," meaning "Love Apples."</note>, but wrongly so in the judgment of Ruellius, unless we think everything that pleases by its beauty and elegance is worthy of that name.

---

### FRUIT-BEARING NIGHTSHADE WITH SPINY FRUIT; *The Bahelschain of the Arabs and Ethiopians.*

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a Solanum variety with deeply lobed, prickly leaves and a small round fruit.</image-desc>

Rauwolf <note>Leonhard Rauwolf, a German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant.</note> observed two species of this: namely, a long one and a round one. To Camerarius, in his German History of Matthiolus, it is called a species of "Mad Apple" with very spiny leaves and stalks, and larger flowers.

These nightshades are commonly cultivated in Italy, both in gardens and in earthenware pots. Gluttons devour these fruits greedily in salads, just like cucumbers, with more pleasure than benefit; for the juice is worse than that of any melon or cucumber. Those who believe these are the *Melongenas* of the Arabs ascribe the same virtues to them. However, those who believe this is the Mandrake of Theophrastus are mistaken.

---

### THE APPLE OF JERICHO, related to the EGGPLANT.

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of a plant identified as "Pomum de Hiericho" (Apple of Jericho), showing stems with small, pointed leaves and small round fruits.</image-desc>

The Apple of Jericho of Ferrante Imperato <note>An Italian apothecary and naturalist.</note> is a plant foreign to Italy and not described by others. it produces whitish *leaves*, approaching those of the fruit-bearing nightshade, but smaller. The *stalks* and the ribs of the leaves are spiny. The flowers are blue, like the flowers of Bugloss. The *fruits* are round like an apple (in the manner of a melon); their color is green before they ripen, and yellow when mature. They have an insipid taste and very little smell.

Caspar Bauhin mentions a clustered Nightshade in the form of cherries, which some call the "Cherry of Love," in his *Physin* and *Prodromos*.

### GOLDEN APPLES: Germ. Gold Apple: French. Golden Apples, Love Apples <note>original: "Pommes d'amour"</note>: Ital. Golden Apples.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum) showing the root system, pinnate leaves, and several ribbed fruits.</image-desc>

The stem is one, two, or three <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is about 18 inches.</note> high, nearly the thickness of the little finger, hairy, and spreading its branches widely. The leaves are tender, feathered (pinnate), hairy, yellowish-green, oblong, and wavy-edged. The flowers are similar in shape to the common Nightshade <note>original: "Solatri vulgaris"</note>, turning a yellow color. These are followed by the "Apples," not much smaller than oranges, sitting close to the stem, ribbed with channels, exceptionally smooth, and colored either gold, ochre, purple, or even variegated. Inside is a plentiful seed, circular, flattened, and hairy. The root clings to the very surface of the earth, thickly covered with long fibers.

It is kept in gardens; it blooms in June and July and perfects its fruit in August. *More on this in the Appendix.*

<column-break/>

### THORN APPLE, OR THE SPINY APPLE: Germ. Prickly Apple: French. Apple of Peru.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Datura stramonium plant, showing large ovate leaves with toothed margins and a spiny seed pod (thorn apple).</image-desc>

It is taller than a cubit, with a multi-part, woody root. The leaves are attached to the stem by long stalks, large, wavy-edged, and exhaling a heavy odor. The flowers are shaped like a long trumpet or basket, large, white, with an angular rim; they hide five stamens with long tips in the center. Each flower is followed by a round "Apple" the size of a walnut still wrapped in its thick husk, bumpy and roughened with short spines. The seed is compressed and ash-colored.

It is cultivated in gardens. Indeed, the fruits and even the whole plant possess sleep-inducing <note>original: "soporiferae"</note> properties.

---

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF THORN APPLE, THE METHEL NUT, Datura the sleep-bringing herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of another variety of Stramonium with more deeply lobed leaves and a prominent spiny fruit.</image-desc>

Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a 16th-century Italian physician and botanist.</note> says that a certain plant called *Stramonium* by many should be classified among the types of Nightshade (Solanum), being so similar to Nightshade that it represents nothing else. Likewise, because of the kinship of its appearance and power, Renodæus also judges it should be placed among the Nightshades. However, Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner, a Swiss naturalist.</note> thinks it should rather be numbered among the Mandrakes; to him, as to Dodoens, Fuchs, and others, it is also called *Stramonia*. Renodæus called it *Stramonium* or more correctly *Strychnonium*; Lobelius and Gerard called it "Foreign Thorn Apple" <note>original: "Stramonium peregrinum"</note>; Cordus called it "Peruvian Henbane"; some call it "Peruvian Apple"; Guillandinus calls it "Turkish Tablet"; and Matthiolus, Castor, Acosta, Camerarius, Anguillara, Fuchs, and others call it the "Methel Nut" <note>original: "Nucem Methellam"</note>.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER SMALLER THORN APPLE, OR TATULA to some.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Datura (Tatula) with similar leaf structure and spiny fruit.</image-desc>

Two distinctions of Thorn Apple are handed down: One is the *minor* sort, which usually rises to a height of two cubits, shown previously in two figures; the other is the *major* sort, which equals and often exceeds the height of a man. The appearance of both is the same, and both bear white flowers resembling those of Bindweed <note>original: "Smilacis"</note>, and thick, spiny, burr-like "Apples": in the smaller kind they are round, but in the larger kind, which we depict here, they are pointed, and like all other parts, larger.

Camerarius calls this the largest species of Thorn Apple, and many call it Acosta's Datura; Bellonius calls it the "Turkish Tatula," the "Methel Nut of the Arabs," and the "Sleep-bringing Nightshade of the Greeks."

---

### HENBANE: Germ. Henbane <note>original: "Bilsemkraut"</note>: French. Henbane: Ital. Henbane <note>original: "Iusquiamo"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Henbane plant (Hyoscyamus niger) showing the characteristic hairy leaves and bell-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Dioscorides <note>The ancient Greek authority on medicine.</note> proposes three distinctions of Henbane: with purple, yellow, and white flowers. Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist.</note> proposes four, though he would have better said three, since his second and fourth are one and the same. More recent authors have observed even more differences.

The *Common Henbane* which we depict here easily reveals itself by its foul odor; it is found everywhere. Its leaves are like those of the White Thorn, soft, woolly, hoary, numerous, and arranged in no particular order on thick stems covered with dense down. The flowers arise in clusters in the shape of a basket, yellow but variegated with many running lines of purple; they are hairy on the outside, with purple tips and a central stalk (style) occupying the middle.

<column-break/>

### WHITE HENBANE: IN WHICH EVERYTHING IS WHITER, hairier, and smaller.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of White Henbane (Hyoscyamus albus) showing its root, leaves, and seed capsules.</image-desc>

In the Common or Black Henbane, depicted here to the side, the seed-vessel is hairy, oblong, and sits close to the stem like an acorn <note>original: "Glandis instar"</note>; its five-pointed rim contains tiny black seeds. Below is a thick, wrinkled root, dark on the outside and white inside, and less smelly than the leaves. It varies with leaves that are sometimes whole, sometimes divided, and sometimes split into sharp segments at the edges. It is the most familiar of all and grows almost everywhere along roads, in sandy places, and in uncultivated spots. It blooms in summer.

However, this *White Henbane* depicted here grows wild at the edges of sown fields and fallow lands along roads. But our image, which is from the purchased stock of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous German botanist; the author implies the illustration quality here is not to his liking.</note>, is not at all pleasing.

<keywords>Tomato, Golden Apple, Thorn Apple, Datura, Henbane, Hyoscyamus, botany, Renaissance herbal, medicinal plants, nightshades</keywords>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### SMALL WHITE HENBANE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Hyoscyamus Albus Minor plant, showing its leaves, flowers, and root system.</image-desc>

It grows frequently and wild in warmer regions; however, in colder climates, it is found only in the gardens of those who take delight in botany. Its leaves are whiter and softer than those of the Black Henbane, and they are not as jagged, but rather somewhat wavy, shorter, quite thick, and supported by a longer stalk. The flowers are white and smaller, and the <term>calyxes</term> <note>The green protective cup surrounding the base of the flower.</note> are smoother.

All varieties of Henbane have a cooling effect; they induce sleep and soothe pain. It is beneficial against sharp and hot discharges from the eyes, restrains eruptions of blood and "womanly flows" <note>Menstruation.</note>, and is applied to inflammations of the testicles and other parts.

<column-break/>

### CRETAN HENBANE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Hyoscyamus Creticus plant, featuring rounded, serrated leaves and flowering stems.</image-desc>

The leaves are almost like those of the <term>Xanthium</term> <note>Cocklebur.</note>, but smaller, nearly round in shape, with a jagged and seemingly "gnawed" edge, and a one-inch stalk. The stem reaches a height of one or one-and-a-half <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is about 18 inches.</note>, is branched, and is covered in white fuzz. The flowers cling to one-inch stalks, emerging from a long, milky, streaked calyx, with a purplish base; the seed is tiny and bumpy.

This is considered either the "Greater" or "Lesser" variety, and according to the authorities Carolus Clusius and Caspar Bauhin, it is known to the Latins as "White Henbane."

Camerarius teaches that an oil prepared from the aforementioned white variety is more effective for toothaches and earaches.

<column-break/>

### SPECIAL HENBANE, WITH PURPLISH FLOWERS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Hyoscyamus Peculiaris, showing broad leaves and a central flowering stalk.</image-desc>

This plant grew for Camerarius from an old seed; the flower is pale in color at the beginning, but quite elegant, later becoming purplish and curved. It does not open evenly like the others, but is somewhat turned back on one side. The leaves are like those of the common Henbane, but a brighter green and much smaller. The plant itself was about a cubit high.

Furthermore, the people of Poitou and Anjou <note>Regions in France.</note> strongly recommend Henbane against itching, and thus in their local tongue they call it *Herbe aux tignes* <note>Scurf-herb or Ringworm-herb.</note>. They are accustomed to sprinkling the dried <term>citinos</term> <note>original: "Citinos"; here referring to the seed capsules or husks.</note> onto hot coals and catching the rising smoke with their hands; they claim that the itching, contracted by such cold, is thereby removed.

<column-break/>

### SYRIAN HENBANE: Germ. Syrischer Bilsen: French. Hanebane de Syrie.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Hyoscyamus Syriacus plant, with jagged leaves and upright growth.</image-desc>

It is described by Clusius under the title "Foreign Henbane with a reddish flower."

Regarding the qualities of Henbane, Galen writes as follows: "Henbane," he says, "whose seed is sharp, brings on madness and deep sleep; that which has a moderately yellow seed is similar in power. Indeed, both should be avoided as they are harmful and deadly. However, the one whose seeds and flowers are white is most suitable for healing, being in a way of the third order of cooling medicines."

Remedies made from Henbane, both for arthritis and for <term>quartan fevers</term> <note>A fever where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day, often associated with malaria.</note>, we have recorded in our "Great History."

<column-break/>

### TOBACCO, NICOTIANA: Germ. & Belgians. Taback: French. Nicotiane, Herbe a la Reine: Ital. Tabaco.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Tobacco plant (Nicotiana), showing large broad leaves and flowering tops.</image-desc>

This plant has retained the name "Tobacco" among almost all nations, taken from the province called *Tabaco* in New Spain in the Indies <note>The Americas.</note>, where it not only grows in abundance but was also first discovered. The French call it *Nicotiana* and the "Queen's Herb" because Jean Nicot, once the Royal Ambassador to Portugal, first brought its seed to the Queen, the mother of the King of France. The Italians call it *Tornabona* because it was sent or brought by Tornaboni; for the same reason, it is called the "Herb of the Holy Cross" because it was brought by the Cardinal of Santa Croce, the Nuncio of the Roman Church. The Indians call it *Picietl*; the natives of Virginia call it *Uppowoc*.

<column-break/>

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF NICOTIANA, OR TOBACCO. Greater Narrow-leafed Tobacco.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a different variety of Tobacco, labeled as the "greater narrow-leafed" type.</image-desc>

Some have also called Tobacco "Antarctic Bugloss"; others "Peruvian Henbane"; some "Holy Health" and the "Panacea Herb" because of its wonderful virtues. Many call it *Petum*, although Jean de Léry reports that the Nicotiana called *Petum* is not the true *Petum* of the Brazilians, nor does it have anything in common with it.

Four species of it have been observed: the "Greater," which is either broad-leafed or narrow-leafed; the "Lesser"; and the "Smallest." We have depicted the Greater broad-leafed variety in the preceding plate; here we illustrate the "Greater narrow-leafed" type. The rest will be discussed in what follows.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Henbane (Hyoscyamus), detailing their physical characteristics and medicinal uses for pain and inflammation, and introduces the Tobacco plant (Nicotiana), explaining its various names and origins in the Americas.</summary>
<keywords>Henbane, Hyoscyamus, Cretan Henbane, Syrian Henbane, Tobacco, Nicotiana, Jean Nicot, medicinal herbs, cooling remedies, New Spain, botanical history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the botanical catalog, transitioning from the Henbanes (Hyoscyamus) described on the previous page to its relatives: the newly-imported Tobacco plants (Nicotiana) and the potent medicinal Hellebores (Veratrum and Helleborus).</meta>

527
<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES.</header>

### LESSER OR SMALLEST TOBACCO: Nicotiana or the Smallest Holy Herb.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small tobacco plant (Nicotiana) showing broad leaves, a central stalk with flowers, and a fibrous root system.</image-desc>

In addition to the previously mentioned varieties of Tobacco, a distinction in gender is also observed: the "Male" is considered the Greater broad-leafed Tobacco, while the "Female" is the Greater narrow-leafed variety. The Female is smaller than the Male in all its parts; its leaves are not pressed close to the stem as they are in the Male, but hang from fairly long stalks, and they are more pointed and less hairy.

Tobacco grows in most parts of the Indies <note>original: "Indiæ"; here referring to the Americas</note>, and it is quite common among Europeans today. The flowers appear in June and July, turning purplish, etc.; these are followed by small pods containing abundant, tiny, fresh seeds. The root is white and fibrous. The stem reaches two or three <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> or more in height; the leaves are similar to those of Elecampane in their shape and size.

<column-break/>

### PRIAPEIA: known to some as LESSER NICOTIANA: A type of Petum <note>An early name for tobacco derived from an indigenous Brazilian word.</note> smaller in every way, according to Clusius.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Priapeia or Nicotiana Minor plant, featuring smaller, more rounded leaves and distinct floral clusters.</image-desc>

Gessner, Lonicer, Dodonaeus, Camerarius, and Gerard list this plant as "Yellow Henbane"; others identify it as the second variety described by the ancient Greek physician Dioscorides. Tabernaemontanus calls it "Peruvian Henbane," while some describe it as a plant wavering between a Henbane and "Furious Nightshade" <note>likely Jimsonweed or Belladonna</note>.

It is endowed with the same medicinal powers as common Tobacco, but they are weaker. It is considered hot and dry in the second degree: thus it warms, relaxes, cleanses, and is slightly <term>astringent</term> <note>Causes the contraction of skin cells and other body tissues.</note>. It contributes greatly to the relief of chronic headaches, migraines, <term>tetanus</term> <note>referring generally to muscle spasms or "lockjaw"</note>, toothaches, wounds, hunger, thirst, and countless other ailments, for which the Appendix should be consulted.

---

<column-break/>

### HELLEBORE, VERATRUM: German: Nieszwurtz; French: Ellebore; Italian: Elleboro.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Helleborus (Veratrum album), showing a tall stalk with numerous small flowers and a thick, bulbous root with many fibers.</image-desc>

We shall deal with Hellebore according to the opinions of the Ancients in the Appendix. To them, it was of two types; however, for more recent authors, there is White and Black Hellebore. Modern botanists again distribute both of these major groups into various species. For some, the White Hellebore is categorized as either Greater or Lesser. The Black, indeed, is either the "true and legitimate" kind or the "false" kind, called <term>Pseudo-Hellebore</term>, the various differences of which will be described in their proper place.

The White Hellebore, which we depict here, delights in mountainous and rough terrain; it is found not only in warmer regions but also in colder ones. It also lives in gardens and blooms in the Summer.

<column-break/>

### Another Image of WHITE HELLEBORE OR VERATRUM.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of Veratrum Album, focusing on the ribbed, broad leaves and the structure of the flowering spike.</image-desc>

White Hellebore has fibrous, white roots gathered into a central head; the stem is one or two cubits high and rounded, crowded with leaves whose stalks wrap around the stem. The leaves themselves are similar to those of Gentian, about a foot long and nearly as wide, soft, slightly hairy, and streaked with very dense ribs. From almost the middle of the stem to the very top, it sends out flower spikes from the leaf joints <note>axils</note>, about a palm <note>roughly 3-4 inches</note> or more in length, consisting of very crowded flowers with six radiating petals that are a greenish-white color.

Furthermore, those err greatly who, as Valerius Cordus notes in his commentary on Dioscorides, confuse this Hellebore with Dittany and Solomon's Seal.

---

<column-break/>

### BLACK HELLEBORE WITH A WHITE FLOWER, and sometimes also very red.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Helleborus Niger (Black Hellebore/Christmas Rose) showing palmate leaves and large, single flowers.</image-desc>

Its leaves are green, says Dioscorides, similar to the Plane tree but smaller, very close to the leaves of Cow Parsnip, somewhat rough, darker, and cut into many divisions. The stem is rough; the flowers are a whitish-purple, clinging together in clusters. The seed is like that of Safflower. It clings to black, thin roots that grow from a head resembling an onion, which is the part used in medicine. It grows on hills and in rough, dry places. The best is sought from such lands as Anticyra <note>A Greek city famous in antiquity for its Hellebore, often used as a treatment for madness.</note>.

We have observed this Hellebore in various gardens and woods; it abounds especially in Italy on the Euganean hills. The flower is mostly white at first, then purplish, and finally turns green.

<column-break/>

### COMMON BLACK HELLEBORE: with a green or grassy flower; with a long-lasting root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of common Black Hellebore with deeply lobed leaves and nodding green flowers.</image-desc>

This plant has numerous, black, fibrous roots. Its leaves are larger than those of the wild "False" <note>original: "Adulterino"</note> variety, of a grassy green, and more tender than in the other two types; they are divided into many segments, each ending in a sharp point rather than a blunt one (unlike the white-flowered garden type), and are serrated around the edges, though not as rigid as the False variety. The flowers hang from stalks about a palm or nine inches long and are grassy-colored. Like the False Hellebore, they consist of five large petals <note>actually sepals</note> surrounding a center of many pale yellow tips <note>stamens</note>. The seed is joined to several upright "horns" <note>seed pods</note> that contain it.

The habitats assigned to the previous plant also suit this one.

<keywords>Tobacco, Nicotiana, Hellebore, Veratrum, medicinal herbs, botany, Dioscorides, Clusius, Anticyra, plant morphology</keywords>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### WILD FALSE BLACK HELLEBORE,
### also green in Winter.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Helleborus niger plant, showing its root system, stems, and distinctive palmate leaves.</image-desc>

Some call it Pliny's Nine-leaf <note>original: "Enneaphyllon Plinij"</note> because it has nine leaves. Gessner records it as Vegetius's Lungwort <note>original: "Pulmonariam Vegetij"</note>; he himself and many others also call it Consiligo <note>A historical name for several plants used to treat lung diseases in livestock.</note>.

It varies in size, which is why Tabernaemontanus distinguishes between the *Greater* and *Lesser* Helleboraster.

It grows in rough and stony places, and it blooms around Spring and in Spring itself. However, Tragus and Dodonaeus (the Frenchman), who identifies it as his first *Licogonum*, write that this species of Hellebore should not be used for the internal parts of the body as it is harmful.

The preceding variety, however, is recorded as *Garden or Domestic False Black Hellebore* by Tragus, Fuchs, and others. *Concerning its powers, see the Appendix.*

### DODONÆUS’S OX-EYE: by others called
### fine-leaved Consiligo.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Buphthalmum plant with finely divided, feathery leaves and daisy-like flowers.</image-desc>

The root of this plant is quite similar to the root of Hellebore. It produces several stems about a <term>span</term> <note>A span is approximately 9 inches or 22 centimeters.</note> long, which are striated and thin. On these are very finely divided leaves, which some call *Eranthemum* <note>original: "Spring-flower"</note>. The flowers are beautiful and yellow, with no notable scent, composed of sixteen oblong, striated, pointed petals, which are somewhat notched near the tip. In the middle, a pleasing crown of many stamens, partly grass-colored, surrounds a small head that is oblong and prickly, like those found in Buttercups. Beneath the flower itself sit five oblong green leaves.

It grows on sunny and drier hills and in grassy fields; it blooms in April and May.

### STAVESACRE, LOUSEWORT: German *Leufskraut*; French *l’herbe aux poulx*; Italian *Staphufaria*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Staphysagria plant with large, deeply lobed leaves and a tall flowering spike.</image-desc>

Stavesacre has a hairy stem, more than a <term>cubit</term> <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> high, rounded, and divided into many branches. On these, the leaves cling to long stalks; they are large and vine-like (from which the whole plant gets its name) or similar to the Castor-oil plant <note>original: "Ricini"</note> in size and finger-like division, and they are hairy. The flowers sit on frequent stalks arising from the axils of the leaves, the top of the stem, and the branches—one flower per stalk. They are blue, composed of five hairy petals, with leafy tips and stamens occupying the center. The seed is wrinkled, black, angular, and of a sharp <note>original: "vridæ," likely a typo for "acris" or "vividae"</note> quality.

It is called Lousewort <note>original: "Pedicularia"</note> because it kills lice and their eggs.

<column-break/>

### SANICLE, DIAPENSIA: German, Flemish & English *Sanickel*: French *Sanicle*: Italian *Quinquefoglio maiore*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Sanicula plant showing its basal leaves and small umbels of flowers.</image-desc>

The leaves of Sanicle are elegant, emerging from an astringent root that is black on the outside, white on the inside, and fibrous. They come out a shining green, somewhat stiff, almost round, and divided into five parts, with each segment subdivided into beautiful patterns. The stem is a cubit high, without knots, smooth, and divided at the top. It supports little flowers clustered together as if in tiny <term>umbels</term> <note>Umbrella-like flower clusters typical of the carrot family.</note>; they are white, with five petals, and are followed by little burs that stick to clothing.

It grows in shady woods and enjoys rich soil and wide, moist ground. It blooms in May and June. The leaves stay green all year and do not dread the winter cold. *More in the Appendix.*

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF DODONÆUS’S OX-EYE, OR
### fine-leaved Consiligo.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Buphthalmum plant, showing a slightly different growth habit and root structure.</image-desc>

Our images are from those we bought some time ago, and they do not please us much; therefore, we present two, so that what is lacking in one, the other may supply.

Some want this to be the Consiligo of Columella and Pliny; others call it *Dioscorides’ Lesser Sesame-like plant*; others *Ferula-like Black Hellebore*. Fuchs calls it Helleborine. Gessner and Camerarius call it Black Helleboraster; many call it *Dodonaeus’s Ox-eye*.

Mattioli testifies that it grows most abundantly in the Prague region; Camerarius says it is found around Jena in Thuringia and Vienna in Austria. To the Flemish, it is a garden plant. It blooms in April and May.

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF STAVESACRE.

<image-desc>A second woodcut illustration of the Staphisagria plant, focusing on the detail of the flowering stalk and seed pods.</image-desc>

Dioscorides describes Stavesacre thus: It has leaves, he says, like those of the wild Vine, split; straight, soft, black stalks; a flower similar to Woad <note>original: "Italidi," likely "Isatidi"</note>, and seed in green pods like a Chickpea, triangular, rough, blackish-yellow, white inside, and sharp to the taste.

Pliny calls it *Astaphisagria* and *Staphis*, Galen calls it *Astaphis agria*; in the apothecary shops, it is corruptly called *staphusariam*. Mattioli says it is very common in Dalmatia, Apulia, and Calabria; colder places, however, do not have it except in gardens.

The herb, crushed and smeared with oil, or the powder of the seed sprinkled on, removes itching, scabies, and the "louse disease" <note>Pediculosis</note>. According to Dioscorides, ten or fifteen of its heavy grains induce vomiting.

<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES</header>
<sig>Xxx</sig>

### EPIPACTIS OR HELLEBORINE OF THE ANCIENTS: Matthiolus’s Epipactis.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Epipactis plant, showing broad, ribbed leaves and a central flowering stalk with small, delicate blossoms.</image-desc>

Epipactis, according to Dioscorides, is called Helleborine <note>original: "Elleborine"</note> by others; it is a very small shrub consisting of quite tiny leaves. Pliny and Paulus say nearly the same things. Galen, however, has nothing to say regarding Epipactis. But Theophrastus mentions it in Book 9, Chapter 1, recording that Helleborine should be added to portions of White Hellebore <note>original: "Veratro albo"</note> so that they might work more effectively.

We depict Matthiolus’s Epipactis here, which some consider to be a fabrication. What he adds is truly ridiculous: that he himself does not know whether it is Helleborine, yet he asserts it is Epipactis; it is just as if he were to say it is uncertain whether it is Helleborus, but certain that it is Veratrum <note>The author is mocking Matthiolus because "Epipactis/Helleborine" and "Helleborus/Veratrum" were essentially synonymous pairs in the botanical Greek and Latin of the time.</note>.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPS’S MANY-ROOT OF PLINY.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Polyrrhizos plant, characterized by an exceptionally dense, fibrous root system and multiple thin stems with small leaves.</image-desc>

It has a manifold, black root: many narrow stems, a <term>palm</term> <note>A measurement of roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note> high: leaves like Myrtle, though a little more blunt, growing in pairs at intervals, with a pale flower: the seed is contained in oblong vessels. It delights in rough places. It obtained its name from the multitude of its roots <note>From the Greek "poly" (many) and "rhiza" (root).</note>.

It is thought to be Pliny’s Many-root <note>original: "Polyrrhizos Plinii"</note>. Caspar Bauhin asks in his *Pinax*: *Whether it is a species of Black Hellebore or Black Helleborine.* But from where, I ask, did he get that suspicion? The *History of Lyon* <note>original: "Historia Lugd." referring to the massive botanical work by Jacques Daléchamps.</note>, from which we borrow this figure and description, contains another Many-root of Dalechamps which he labels "broad-leaved," but we believe that one is actually the White Mountain Buttercup.

---

### CASTOR OIL PLANT, PALM OF CHRIST: German: *Wunderbaum;* French: *Palme de Christ;* Italian: *Girasole.*

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Ricinus plant, showing its large, palmate, star-shaped leaves and a spiked cluster of seed pods.</image-desc>

Herbalists commonly label the Castor plant <note>original: "Ricinum"</note> as the *Greater Drooping Palm of Christ*, the *Royal Grain*, and the *Greater Cataputia*. It obtained the name *Ricinus* from the similarity the seed has to the *Ricinus* <note>The Latin name for a tick.</note>, a livid and foul animal that clings to dogs, cattle, goats, and other quadrupeds, and does not fall off until it is gorged so full of blood that it bursts.

Dioscorides says it is a tree the size of a Fig tree: with leaves larger, smoother, and darker than the Plane tree: with branches and trunks that are hollow like a Reed: with seeds in rough clusters which, when stripped of their husks, resemble the tick. From these, an oil named *Cicinum* is pressed, which is foul for food but useful for lamps and medicinal plasters.

<column-break/>

### GREATER AMERICAN CASTOR PLANT, called CURCA, and the Purgative Bean of the West Indies.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of large, oval, mottled seeds (Castor beans) shown from various angles to show their marbled texture.</image-desc>

Monardes labels this the "Hell-feces" <note>original: "Fæcum infernalem"</note> of the Spaniards, and says it is a tree similar to the Castor plant in both fruit and leaves; but growing to a greater height due to the abundance of its foliage.

They say it is endowed with such a miraculous purging power that half of a single seed is enough to purge a healthy person both upwards and downwards <note>Meaning it causes both vomiting and bowel movements.</note>; and they claim it performs various other feats.

The fruit is a little larger than the common variety depicted before, and it is not spotted like that one; otherwise it is similar and black. However, the triangular pod containing the seeds is not covered with rough bumps as in the common variety.

---

### SMALL ORIENTAL CASTOR PLANT, called BENDE, and by some the PURGATIVE BEAN.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller variety of Ricinus with more delicate leaves and seed pods.</image-desc>

Furthermore, the common Castor plant (the description of which is lacking in Dioscorides) has flowers clinging in clusters on a special shoot in a long thyrsus-like <note>A dense, flower-bearing stalk.</note> series, composed of blood-red and curled stamens which spring in threes from the budding fruit. These are succeeded by prickly, three-sided vessels which enclose the oblong seeds, mimicking the tick-insect, livid and spotted on the outside, with a white inner pith. And besides the flowers, there are on the same stalk mossy, clustered, grass-colored nutlets, which finally wither away leaving no fruit. The root is simple, long, thick, hard, and white, sending out numerous fibers all around.

<column-break/>

### PURGATIVE BEANS OF THE CARTHAGINIANS: Serapion’s Dende, and the Albelmoluch of the Moors.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of several seeds and seed casings, some shown in cross-section to reveal the internal structure.</image-desc>

We present various images of these beans, both in this and in the preceding tables, taken from Imperato. Some think they should be referred to Serapion's *Dende* and the *Albelmoluch* of the Moors; Monardes, however, reports that they grow in Carthage.

Matthioli is the authority that the common Castor plant grows spontaneously in Egypt. In our regions, it is sown in gardens, not only as a spectacle but also against the harm of Moles, which they say the Castor plant puts to flight. It flowers in Summer, and in warm regions it lasts for many years and grows to a great height.

<keywords>Epipactis, Helleborine, Polyrrhizos, Ricinus, Castor oil plant, Palma Christi, purgatives, West Indies botany, medicinal seeds, moles</keywords>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### FRUIT SIMILAR TO RICINUS: ERAVVAI, POISON, THORA, ACONITUM: German: Wolfsberry <note>original: "Wolfsbeeri"</note>
### A small kind of Ricinus, brought from Guinea. French: Aconite; Italian: Aconito.

Among the exotic fruits that were brought from the East Indies, this one was also included, which in many ways resembled the common Castor oil plant <note>original: "Ricinum vulgarem"</note>; it was called the fourth type by Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational botanist.</note>.

The common Castor oil plant is hot and dry at the beginning of the third degree <note>This refers to the Galenic system of grading the "temperament" or intensity of a plant's medicinal effects.</note>. It violently expels phlegm, fluids collected in the abdomen, serous humors from the joints, and bile—as well as arthritic conditions—doing so with great natural disturbance and upset of the stomach, purging both upwards and downwards. The seed is the part most sought after for use; however, it would be a matter of professional conscience <note>original: "religio erit," implying a moral or serious hesitation due to the danger involved.</note> to administer it unless it has been properly "corrected" <note>In early pharmacy, "correcting" meant processing a toxic substance with other ingredients to make it safe for human consumption.</note>. Practitioners and pharmacists <note>original: "Seplasiæ," referring to the street of perfume and drug sellers in ancient Capua, used here for apothecaries.</note> know the method for its use and correction.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Thora plant with broad, lobed leaves and small flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

According to Dioscorides, there are two kinds of Aconite: the first is called Leopard’s-strangler <note>original: "Pardalianches"</note>, and the other is called Dog-killer <note>original: "Cynoctonon"</note> or Wolf-killer <note>original: "Lycoctonum"</note>, of which he describes three species.

We depict here the Thora with the leaf of a Cyclamen, also called Taura, Tuira, Dora, and even the "Taura of the Waldensians." Some have judged this to be the "First Aconite" of Dioscorides; Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist.</note> expresses doubt on this, while Clusius refers it to the family of the Ranunculus <note>The Buttercup family.</note>.

It is found in the Alps, in the mountains of the Allobroges [Savoy] and the Swiss, and among the Waldensians, as well as on Mount Baldo in Italy. It blooms in June, and the seed ripens in July. We ourselves observed it in abundance on Mount Jura above Lausanne.

---

### APULIAN THORA, WITH THE LEAF OF ALCHIMILLA <note>Lady’s Mantle</note>, ROUGH AND SPOTTED, described by Tabernaemontanus.

### ANTHORA OR ANTITHORA: German: Poison-heal <note>original: "Gifftheyl"</note>; French: Anthore; Italian: Anthora.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Thora Apula plant with deeply lobed, serrated leaves.</image-desc>

Commonly, two types of Thora are established, the Greater and the Lesser. The Greater variety varies in the emergence and number of its leaves; for it may be endowed with a single leaf, or two, three, four, or five at most, and these may grow either directly from the root or on the stem.

Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (c. 1522–1590), a famous German herbalist.</note> distinguishes between a Male and Female type, assigning four leaves to the latter and two large leaves to the former. Otherwise, the Thora has a single stem, a palm <note>A measurement of about 3 to 4 inches.</note> high, and rush-like. At the top of the stem sits a flower, usually solitary, similar in shape and yellow color to a Buttercup <note>original: "Ranunculi"</note>. The seed head is a rounded cluster of seeds, not unlike the Burr Buttercup <note>original: "Ranunculo echino"</note>. The root rivals the roots of the Asphodel. We observed it in abundance on Mount Jura, appearing sometimes with one leaf, sometimes with two or more.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Anthora plant, showing tall stalks with fine, divided leaves and hooded flowers.</image-desc>

The stem is a cubit <note>About 18 inches.</note> high, single, rigid, angular, and slightly hairy. The leaves grow alternately upon it, resembling Monkshood <note>original: "Napelli"</note> but more finely cut; they lack that particular luster, are whitish on the underside, possess a bitter taste, and are somewhat similar to Nigella. The flowers have a not unpleasant scent and are hooded; their "gape" <note>The opening of the flower.</note> is deeper than that of the Monkshood, except for the color, which in this plant is a pale yellowish hue. The horned seed-vessels are likewise similar. The root consists of olive-shaped bulbs, dark on the outside and white within, bitter to the taste, and fibrous.

Some call it "health-bringing Aconite"; others call it the "true Zedoary of the Arabs." Some, following Avicenna, call it "the herb like Monkshood that resists its poison." Most everyone calls it Anthora.

---

### ANOTHER IMAGE OF ANTHORA, OR ANTITHORA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Anthora plant showing the root structure and lower leaves.</image-desc>

Anthora grows in great quantities in the Rhaetian, Savoyard, and Swiss Alps, as well as in the mountains of Cisalpine Gaul and Liguria. It is also cultivated in gardens and grows easily from the roots; however, it rarely rises from seed before the third year. It blooms in July and ripens its seeds in September.

Tabernaemontanus and Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist.</note> identify two types: the Common with a yellow flower, and a rarer type with a blue or purple flower. Camerarius also observed that the shapes of the roots are not all of one kind; some have a single tuber, others have two joined together. They may be top-shaped or oblong, and sometimes triple—occasionally even mimicking the image of scorpions, as we endeavor to show in our dual illustrations.

<column-break/>

### YET ANOTHER IMAGE OF ANTHORA.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration focusing on the tuberous roots and lower stem of the Anthora plant.</image-desc>

The power of Thora is extremely destructive and poisonous, so much so that it is said to exceed the malice of Monkshood <note>original: "Napelli"</note>. Its poison is rarely fatal if swallowed; however, it is said that a wound made by a weapon dipped in its juice kills within the space of half an hour.

Yet divine providence wished to provide well for the human race with the gift of Antithora <note>The name literally means "Against Thora."</note>. For, as Matthiolus reports, the roots of Anthora are effective not only against the ingestion of Monkshood but also against all other poisons whatsoever, as well as the bites of vipers and other venomous creatures. They are helpful in all conditions of the heart, and in spotted fevers <note>original: "petechialibus," referring to fevers with purple spots, often associated with typhus.</note> and plagues. But one must take the greatest care that a species of Monkshood or Aconite is not accidentally taken instead of Antithora.

<summary>This page discusses the highly toxic Thora plant and its botanical counterpart Anthora, which was historically believed to be a powerful antidote to Aconite and other poisons. It provides detailed morphological descriptions, geographic locations in the Alps, and medicinal warnings regarding these potent members of the Ranunculaceae family.</summary>

531
<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES:</header>
<sig>Xxx 6</sig>

### WOLF-SLAYER ACONITE: German: *Wolfsbane* <note>original: "Wolfswurtz"</note>; French: *Wolf-strangler* <note>original: "Estrangle Loup"</note>; Italian: *Aconite for killing wolves* <note>original: "Aconito per amassar Lupi"</note>.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with deeply lobed leaves and a cluster of hooded flowers at the top, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This is the second Aconite of Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work was the standard botanical text for centuries.</note>, called Wolf-slayer and Dog-slayer. Although he describes three species, the one depicted here refers to the third, which he says is called "Pontic." It has leaves like the Plane tree, but longer, darker, and more frequently divided. The stem is similar to the stalk of a Fern, bare, and a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> in height. It hides its seed in oblong pods, and its root consists of several dark parts joined together in the manner of a Sea Squill.

We shall add that, by the judgment of almost all learned men, the flowers are yellow; and according to Camerarius <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist.</note>, this species is twofold: namely, a Greater and a Lesser variety, which are called "Wolfsbane" by way of excellence.

<column-break/>

### GREAT ACONITE, OR MONKSHOOD: German: *Blue Iron-hat* <note>original: "Blauw Eisenhütlein," referring to the helmet-shaped flower.</note>; French: *Napel*; Italian: *Napello*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with highly dissected, feathery leaves and a dense spike of helmet-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

It rises to a height of three cubits, the height of a man, with a smooth, purplish, rigid stem that is difficult to break. This stem divides into branches bearing a singular spike of flowers, which are blue and covered by a hood formed by the remaining four petals. These flowers are followed by roughly three little horns, similar to those of the Columbine <note>original: "Aquilegiæ Cornicula"</note>, filled with seed. The leaves are arranged alternately on various long stalks, shining with a dark green color; they are larger than the leaves of the common Wolf-slayer Aconite and deeply divided into many narrow segments. The root is the size of a small turnip <note>original: "Napi," from which the name "Napellus" or "Little Turnip" is derived.</note>, black, and produces fibers from its sides; they often have other collateral "turnips" attached. More will be said in the Appendix.

---

### ACONITE SIMILAR TO MONKSHOOD, BUT SMALLER, blue and early-blooming.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a smaller aconite plant with similar hooded flowers and palmately lobed leaves.</image-desc>

It is found on the Tauric mountain ridges <note>The Crimean Mountains.</note>, where it blooms in July. In cultivated gardens, however, it blooms much earlier—indeed, earlier than the other kinds of Wolf-slayer. It is so similar to Monkshood that it is distinguished from it only with difficulty.

More commonly, the previously described *Monkshood* grows without being sown in the Alps of Anania and Rhaetia <note>Regions in the Italian and Swiss Alps.</note>, as well as elsewhere, both in the mountains and in the plains of higher elevations. It blooms in summer, with the seeds ripening in August.

It grows wild and in great abundance at Montbéliard <note>A city in eastern France.</note>, between the Bridge of Vauiancourt and Dampierre, among the thickets. It is also kept in gardens. Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German botanist.</note> writes that three species of it are found: the Greatest, the Lesser, and a yellow-flowered variety.

<column-break/>

### BLUE WOLF-SLAYER ACONITE with large spurs.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a flowering plant with broad, lobed leaves and hooded flowers, showing the fibrous root system.</image-desc>

Cromer <note>Marcin Kromer (1512–1589), a Polish historian and geographer.</note> reported that this is found in several mountains of Silesia. We ourselves have seen it in certain Alps within the territory of Bern.

Now, the power and property of Monkshood is destructive to both man and many four-footed animals, and it kills in a short time. Let mortals therefore beware lest they pay a heavy price for the elegant beauty of the flowers by coming into contact with the roots. Furthermore, according to Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>, Monkshood is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>In Galenic medicine, the "fourth degree" was the highest level of intensity, indicating a substance that is fundamentally poisonous or life-threatening.</note>.

It is acknowledged by almost everyone that the *Napellus* of Avicenna <note>The famous Persian polymath (980–1037).</note> and the Arabs is a species of Aconite.

---

### WOLF-SLAYER ACONITE SIMILAR TO MONKSHOOD, with broader leaves and purple flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, hand-shaped leaves and a cluster of flowers at the apex.</image-desc>

This grows on the ridge of Mount Neuberg in the Duchy of Styria <note>A region in modern-day Austria.</note>, near the stables of the cows grazing there in the summer months. It blooms shortly after the common variety, specifically in July.

The common Wolf-slayer Aconite grows in the highest mountain valleys, especially in Austria, Pannonia <note>The Roman province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>, and Switzerland; it is also found in the Hercynian Forest <note>A vast ancient forest in Germany.</note>. Matthiolus <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Italian physician and botanist.</note> writes that it grows on nearly all the mountains of Italy. Thalius says it grows in mountain brushwood where the grass is most lush, and Gelenius notes it grows on the stones and rocks of mountains where they are covered with a thin layer of earth.

<column-break/>

### NODDING-HEAD WOLF-SLAYER ACONITE, the largest, with blue flowers.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a large aconite plant with nodding flower heads and broad, deeply incised leaves.</image-desc>

All kinds of Aconite are poisonous, and they do harm primarily through the juice of the root. This juice is not only a most certain poison to humans and beasts when swallowed, but even when smeared on spears and arrows, it inflicts lethal wounds. Indeed, according to Paré <note>Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), a pioneering French surgeon.</note>, it kills mice by its scent alone. As Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of Natural History.</note> reports in Book 27, Chapter 2, if the root is touched to the genitals of female animals, it brings death on that very day. And perhaps this was the poison with which, as the same Pliny testifies, Casserius killed sleeping beasts <note>note: This passage likely refers to historical accounts of poisoning mentioned in Pliny's encyclopedic work.</note>. Writers place its quality as hot and dry in the fourth degree, which is why when chewed it burns the tongue and throat. More on this in the following pages.

<summary>This page provides a detailed botanical and geographical survey of various Aconite species (Monkshood and Wolfsbane), emphasizing their distinct physical characteristics and their extreme toxicity to both humans and animals.</summary>
<keywords>Aconite, Monkshood, Wolfsbane, toxicology, botany, poisonous plants, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, herbal medicine, Alpine flora</keywords>

<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### WOLFSBANE ACONITE WITH LARKSPUR FLOWERS, according to Dodoens. <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585) was a Flemish physician and one of the most influential botanists of the Renaissance.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall flowering plant with deeply lobed leaves and a spike of hooded flowers, showing the root system.</image-desc>

This plant rises with tall stems like those of Monkshood <note>original: "Napelli"</note>. Its leaves are similarly divided into various and very frequent deep incisions. The flowers are arranged along the upper parts of the stems as if in a long, composite spike; in their reddish and darker purple color, they mimic the "Royal Flower" <note>A common name for the Larkspur or Delphinium.</note>, having almost the same shape. *The pods and the seed are like those of the larger yellow Wolfsbane. The roots are oblong and thick, with a few fibers clinging to them.*

Here we shall note a thing that seems a wonder—and not mistakenly so—to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was a primary source for Renaissance scholars.</note>: namely, that Aconite acts as an adversary to the stings of Scorpions. He says that it fights with the scorpion's venom alone, as if it had found an equal match within the body. This is the only such battle; when the plant finds the venom in the viscera, it is a marvel that, although both are deadly on their own, the two poisons die together within the man, so that the man survives.

<column-break/>

### WOLFSBANE ACONITE WITH VERY LARGE FLOWERS, of a bluish-purple color.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant similar to the previous one but with larger, more distinct hooded flowers and a thick, fibrous root.</image-desc>

Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering botanist who helped create one of Europe's first botanical gardens.</note> says that this grows wild on *Judenberg*, the highest mountain in all of Styria <note>A region in modern-day Austria.</note>, and blooms in August. We kept it at Montbéliard in the Saint-Pantaléon garden, where it bloomed alongside the preceding variety toward the end of July.

When Aconite is consumed, however, the head is greatly disturbed, followed by heaviness, vertigo, convulsions of the muscles at the temples, delirium, tremors, involuntary tears, redness of the eyes, pain in the sides, heaviness of the chest, difficulty breathing, a biting sensation around the hairs <note>This likely refers to "formication," a sensation like insects crawling on the skin, or perhaps goosebumps.</note>, copious gas in the intestines, swelling of the entire body, and finally—unless its malicious power is most effectively broken—it brings death.

---

<column-break/>

### BLUE-FLOWERED WOLFSBANE ACONITE, with a taller helmet and a bulbous root.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Aconite plant with a distinct bulbous root and tall, helmet-shaped flowers.</image-desc>

Besides the fibers by which it is occasionally rooted in the earth, it bears cone-shaped bulbs from whose base other fibers emerge. The leaves are produced alternately along the stem and are of moderate size; they are cut into five deep segments, which are again more lightly subdivided, and they possess a shining green color and are slightly hairy. The hooded flowers are sparse and raise a long helmet <note>The 'galea' or helmet is the characteristic upper sepal of the Aconite flower that gives it the name Monkshood.</note>, blue in color.

Furthermore, the power of Aconite is so malignant that unless help is given immediately, it kills a person suddenly, and indeed within the space of a single day; hence Pliny writes that Aconite is the swiftest of all poisons. Nevertheless, some maintain that Monkshood <note>original: "Napellum"</note> is even more harmful, and the Indians <note>Likely referring to the peoples of the East Indies or Americas, known for using plant-based arrow poisons.</note> have plants that are even more poisonous.

<column-break/>

### CLUSTERED ACONITE; CLUSTERED MONKSHOOD; called Herb Christopher by some. Could it be Pliny’s Actaea?

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with broad, compound leaves and a cluster (raceme) of small flowers/berries.</image-desc>

The herb called Herb Christopher <note>original: "Christophoriana," now known as Actaea spicata or Baneberry.</note> has a somewhat thick root that is black on the outside and gifted with fibers. The stems are a cubit and a half high <note>About 27 inches.</note>, incised, thin, rounded, and jointed. The leaves are large, oblong, sharp, and shining, and are deeply cut in many ways. The flowers are arranged in clusters, white, and composed of five falling petals; inside these are white stamens, sometimes with a greenish tip. These are succeeded by berries that are oblong and turn black when ripe, clinging together in the manner of a grape cluster.

It occurs in many places in Germany, and around the Rhine and Meuse rivers, especially in mountainous woods, and it blooms in May.

When Aconite has been consumed, vomiting must be induced above all else, and then its evils must be countered with alexipharmics <note>Historical term for antidotes or remedies used to neutralize poison.</note>.

---

<column-break/>

### SPURGE, OR WOLF’S MILK: Germ. *Wolfs Milch*: Gall. *Tithymale*, *Milk-weed* <note>original: "Herbe à laict"</note>: Ital. *Tithymalo*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a Tithymalus (Spurge) plant with characteristic umbel-like flowering tops and milky sap indicated by the stem structure.</image-desc>

Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "Father of Botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note> lists only three types of Spurge. But according to the authorities Dioscorides, Pliny, Galen, and Apuleius, there are seven: *Characias* (Male Spurge), *Myrtites* (Female Spurge), *Paralius* (Sea Spurge), *Helioscopius* (Sun-turning Spurge), *Cyparissias* (Cypress Spurge), *Dendroides* (Tree Spurge), and *Platyphyllos* (Broad-leaved Spurge). Even more species and differences of Spurges are described today, as will be clear from what follows.

Here we depict the Cypress Spurge, which often nourishes hedges and the edges of meadows, and sometimes even grows in fields among the stubble after the grain has been reaped; some also keep it in gardens. It varies significantly according to the season, which is why writers vary not a little in their descriptions of it.

<column-break/>

### SMALLEST NARROW-LEAVED ANNUAL SPURGE; Little Spurge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, slender annual spurge with narrow leaves.</image-desc>

This is a small plant, about a palm or half-palm in height <note>A "palm" was roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note>, with a thin black rootlet three or four inches long. The stems and branches are packed with small leaves about half an inch or a third of an inch long and half a stem wide; they are crowded, pointing upwards, and swollen with milk <note>The caustic, milky latex characteristic of the Euphorbia genus.</note>. The small flowers are greenish, and the seed-pod is three-cornered, like that of the Cypress Spurge, but many times smaller.

Lobelius <note>Matthias de l'Obel (1538–1616), a Flemish physician and botanist for whom the Lobelia flower is named.</note> found it quite often in the grain fields of Gallo-Belgium and England during the summer; Tragus <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a German physician and one of the "fathers of German botany."</note> found it in fields after the harvest in the autumn.

Furthermore, from the sap with which both this and all other varieties swell, the common name "Milk-herb" <note>original: "Herba lactaria"</note> has been given to all Spurges.

<sig>Xxx 3</sig>

### APIOS OR ISCHAS. <note>The name "Apios" comes from the Greek word for a pear, referring to the shape of the root.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a plant with a large, tuberous, pear-shaped root and several stems with small leaves.</image-desc>

The identification of the *Apios* is easily made from its root, which, because it is oblong, swollen, and shaped like a pear <note>original: "Pyri modum turbinata"</note>, gave the plant its name. You might rightly compare it to the root of a Turnip. From the head of the root, several small branches emerge, shorter than a palm’s width; these are clothed with quite frequent leaves like those of the Round Spurge or *Peplus*, but smaller, gradually widening from a narrow base and rounded at the tips.

Tabernaemontanus, Castor, Dodoens, Lacuna, Clusius, and others record it as the "Tuberous Spurge" and "Spurge with a tuberous root." Matthiolus, Anguillara, and Dodoens (in his French edition), Lacuna, and the *History of Lyon* call it "Apion." Gesner and Lobel call it the "True Apion."

<column-break/>

### THE OTHER APIOS OR ISCHAS, OF CLUSIUS.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a similar plant to the first, but with a more elongated, branched tuberous root system.</image-desc>

Our previous illustration comes from folk practitioners <note>original: "ex empiricis"</note>, and is not satisfactory in all respects. Therefore, we include here another from Clusius, which he titles the "Second Apion." Caspar Bauhin calls it the "Tuberous Spurge with an oblong root."

It is also called *Ischas* <note>original Greek: "ἰσχάς"</note>, meaning a "dried fig," because the root resembles a dried fig; from this shape, it also obtained the name <term>Chamaebalanus</term> <note>original Greek: "χαμαιβαλάνυ," meaning "ground-chestnut" or "earth-nut."</note>.

According to Pliny <note>A famous Roman naturalist and author.</note>, the *Apios* grows in mountainous and rugged places, and also in grassy areas. Furthermore, the upper part of the root, when taken, draws out bile and phlegm through vomiting, while the lower part purges through the bowels. If the whole root is taken, it purges by both means.

---

<column-break/>

### GROUND SPURGE OF DIOSCORIDES AND PLINY. <note>Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the foundation of botany for 1,500 years.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a low-growing, creeping plant with small, paired oval leaves and tiny flowers.</image-desc>

It has a slender little root, about a palm’s length, gifted with several very thin fibers. The branches are a foot long, subdivided into "wings" (side-shoots), reddish, slightly hairy, and trailing along the ground. To these branches are attached leaves in opposite pairs at the joints; they are nearly round, reddish on the side facing the ground and green on top, usually with a purple spot in the middle. Tiny purple flowers spring out between the leaves where the branches divide; the three-celled seed pods <note>original: "Pericarpia tricocca," a hallmark of the Spurge family.</note> hide beneath the leaves.

Pliny and Dioscorides write that it grows in dry, neglected, and stony places. Lobel writes that it appears nowhere in Germany, but is found in great abundance in the dry and sandy regions of Southern France <note>original: "Galliæ Narbonensis."</note>.

<column-break/>

### SUN-LOOKING SPURGE, OR THE SUN-FOLLOWER: Known to some as the Common Spurge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an upright plant with a terminal umbel of flowers and rounded leaves.</image-desc>

This plant has a short and usually single stem, moderately hairy. The leaves are like those of Purslane, though less round, yellowish-green, sometimes notched around the edges and other times not. The shoots born from the top of the stem form a sort of "umbel" <note>A flat-topped flower cluster where stalks radiate from a central point like umbrella ribs.</note> supporting tiny, grass-like flowers. These are shield-shaped, with the appearance of Myrtle Spurge. The seed is in three-cornered pods. The root is single and fibrous.

It obtained the name *Helioscopios* <note>From the Greek for "Sun-watcher."</note> because it turns its heads with the Sun. Furthermore, it is familiar to all nations, growing on hills, uncultivated fields, ruins, and around town walls; it is even a troublesome weed in gardens.

---

<column-break/>

### PEPLOS OR ROUND SPURGE: AND OF PEPLIS: Ruellius’s "Morning Watch." <note>Jean Ruel (Ruellius) was a French physician who translated Dioscorides into Latin.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a small, leafy plant with numerous small, rounded leaves and delicate stems.</image-desc>

For *Peplos* and *Peplis*, we provide only one illustration, and perhaps not without reason, since they resemble one another in both name and appearance. They are gathered, stored, preserved, and administered in one and the same way, and are endowed with the same medicinal powers.

They seem to differ, however, in that *Peplis* seeks its origins on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea; it is rarely found in Northern regions except in gardens, nor is it found on the shores of the Ocean. *Peplos*, however, grows everywhere in Germany and France around hedges, the edges of gardens, and in vineyards.

Nevertheless, writers describe and depict them separately, and each is distinguished into "Greater" and "Lesser" varieties, which we also allow.

<column-break/>

### PITYUSA: THE LARGER SPURGE: Fuchs’s Broad-leaved Spurge, and the Spotted-leaved Spurge. <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566) was a German physician whose botanical woodcuts set a new standard for accuracy.</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a tall plant with narrow leaves and a large, spreading floral umbel at the top.</image-desc>

Some contend that the Broad-leaved Spurge of Fuchs, which we depict here along with the *Pityusa* and the "Greater Spurge," is the same plant. Lobel, however, doubts whether this is true. It appears that Fuchs depicted the plant as it first emerges, before the umbel has become branched.

Two types are observed: the *Greater* and the *Lesser*, the latter of which has hairy leaves.

It grows in fields, around thickets, and on the sandy banks of rivers. It blooms in August and September; when it first comes forth in early Spring, the leaves are seen to be sprinkled with blood-red spots.

The *Peplos*, which we just discussed, obtained its name from the way its branches spread around to form a "veil" <note>original: "velum," from the Greek "peplos" meaning a robe or cloak.</note> that covers the ground.

<summary>This page describes various species of the Spurge family (Euphorbiaceae), detailing their physical characteristics, medicinal uses as purgatives, and their habitats across Europe. It highlights the naming conventions derived from the plants' appearances, such as the pear-shaped root of the Apios and the sun-tracking habit of the Helioscopios.</summary>
