<header>OF PLANTS</header>

### WOODLAND SPURGE RETAINING ITS
### leaves all year: Tree-like Spurge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus sylvaticus, showing a tall plant with a woody stem, narrow leaves, and umbel-like flowering tops with small seed capsules.</image-desc>

This plant abounds here in Spain, France, Switzerland, and the rest of Germany, in shady and wooded places; it flowers in early Spring. In Geneva, it is abundant around Mount Salève and the Arve bridge; likewise in Basel near Krentzach, Dornach, and Muttenz.

Cordus and Gesner, in his *Horti*, call this Tree-like Spurge <note>original: "Tithymalum dendroidem"</note>. Dioscorides describes Tree-like Spurge thus: It grows on rocks, he says, and the foliage is at the top, spreading into a thick head of hair, pregnant with milky sap, with reddish branches, and leaves around it like those of the Myrtle, but thinner; its seed is like that of the *Characias* <note>original: "semine Characiæ"</note>.

<column-break/>

### ALMOND-LIKE SPURGE, OR
### Characias, that is, the Stake-Spurge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus amygdaloides, featuring a robust plant with broader, oblong leaves and dense clusters of flowers at the apex of the stems.</image-desc>

The "Male Spurge" is called *Characias* <note>This name derives from the Greek for "stake," referring to its upright, sturdy stems</note>, says Dioscorides. Some call it "Tufted" <note>original: "Comatus"</note>, and others "Almond-like" <note>original: "Amygdaloides"</note> from the shape of its leaves; others call it *Gobios*. Furthermore, its stems reach a height of over a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term> and are reddish. The leaves around the branches are like those of the Olive, but longer. The root is thick and woody. At the tips of the stems hangs a tuft of rush-like twigs, beneath which are certain hollows similar to basins or small troughs; and in these is the seed.

It abounds in Montpellier in rocky places, and, according to Clusius, in the rough and mountainous parts of Spain, though it is rarely found growing wild elsewhere.

---

### WARTY SPURGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus verrucosus, showing a plant with multiple stems arising from a central root, with small rounded leaves and distinct warty seed capsules.</image-desc>

Many thin roots of this plant eventually join into one, about a finger's thickness, woody and a foot long, with the bark black on the outside and white on the inside. There are many branches, bright and resistant to breaking, thin and reddish, a foot long. They support leaves attached alternately, more than an inch long and nearly half an inch wide, covered with a thin down—though more so on the underside than the top—and sometimes turning red. The flowers turn yellow in an umbel <term>umbel: a flower cluster where stalks of nearly equal length spring from a common center, like the ribs of an umbrella</term>. These are succeeded by small round heads, roughened with a crinkled texture like a mass of tiny grains of sand, or like warts <note>original: "verrucarum instar"</note>. When these are mature and open, they are divided into three parts, containing three seeds.

It grows in dry and sandy places.

<column-break/>

### DALECHAMPS' SERRATED SPURGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus serratus, depicting a plant with serrated or notched leaf margins and small flower clusters.</image-desc>

This plant is endowed with a stem a cubit high, along which grow inch-long leaves; some are wider than the stalk, others less wide, and most are not pointed but somewhat round, notched with small teeth <note>original: "crenata"</note> around the edge. The mossy yellow flowers sit in the hollow of the cups. The seed heads are rather large, three-sided, on thin stalks, nearly equal in size to those of the Myrtle-like Spurge.

In our illustration, the serrations <note>original: "serraturę"</note> are not well represented, and the leaves are painted as being too sharp.

It is frequent in the territory of Narbonne, and is rarely found elsewhere.

---

### MYRTLE-LIKE SPURGE, or MYRTLE-SPURGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus myrsinites, showing a low-growing plant with thick, fleshy, pointed leaves arranged densely around the stems.</image-desc>

With branches a span <note>original: "dodrantalibus," about 9 inches</note> long and somewhat thick, it mostly spreads across the ground. These branches are surrounded in a certain order by leaves like those of the Myrtle, which are somewhat fleshy, possessed of a glaucous <term>glaucous: a pale bluish-green or greyish-green color, often with a waxy coating</term> color, and ending in a point. The ends of the branches branch out into shoots arising from the same point, passing through round, box-shaped leaves arranged in an umbel. Among these leaves sit flowers of a grass-green color. The seed vessels are three-sided.

It received the name *Myrtites* or *Myrsinites* from the resemblance of its leaves to the Myrtle. It grows of its own accord in several mountainous places in Italy; however, we have seen it nowhere except in gardens.

One might judge that Matthiolus and Lacuna never actually saw it, as they depict it so ridiculously, even in the judgment of Lobelius.

<column-break/>

### SEA SPURGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of Tithymalus paralias (Sea Spurge), showing a plant with many upright, densely leafy stems and small terminal umbels.</image-desc>

It grows in maritime areas, says Dioscorides, with reddish branches a palm's width high, with five or six emerging from the root. The leaves are like those of Flax—narrow, small, and oblong—arranged in certain rows. The head at the top is circular, in which the seed shines out with various colors like a Bitter Vetch seed; the flower is white, etc.

It grows not only on the maritime coasts of Italy and Spain, but also in Holland, Zeeland, and the rest of Lower Germany, in uncultivated, dry, and very high places. When transplanted into gardens, its leaves become more sparse.

<summary>This page describes several varieties of Spurge (Tithymalus), detailing their physical characteristics, habitats across Europe (from Switzerland to the Dutch coast), and the accuracy of botanical illustrations by contemporary authors.</summary>
<keywords>Tree Spurge, Almond-like Spurge, Warty Spurge, Serrated Spurge, Myrtle Spurge, Sea Spurge, Dioscorides, botanical illustration, European flora, medicinal plants</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on various species of Spurge (Tithymalus), the author now examines the Alypum—a woody, shrub-like relative—and other leafless or garden varieties, concluding with a detailed investigation into the identity of the medicinal root known as Turpeth.</meta>

<header>IMAGES AND OUTLINES.</header>

### ALYPUM OF MATTIOLI, related to Spurge.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Alypum plant, showing a woody stem with small, dense leaves and flower clusters at the tips of the branches.</image-desc>

Alypum <note>original: "Alypum," a plant often called "fruticose globe-daisy" or "herb-terrible" for its purging effects</note>, according to Dioscorides, is a shrubby herb, somewhat reddish, with slender branches and thin leaves. It bears a soft, smooth, and abundant flower, and has a root like a Beet, thin and filled with acrid juice. It grows in coastal regions, especially in Libya. The seed expels "black bile" <note>In ancient medicine, one of the four humors; excess was thought to cause melancholy</note>, but it can cause ulcers in the intestines. So says he.

Dalechamp shows how much Coldenberg was mistaken when he claimed, in his commentary on Valerius Cordus's *Dispensatory*, that Mattioli had skillfully depicted the herb known today as Alypum.

We received the plant whose figure we show here from Stuttgart, sent by Doctor Schwaitz.

<column-break/>

### ALYPUM TO SOME, OR RARE SPURGE, with a purple flower.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a taller variety of Alypum or Esula, featuring elongated leaves and drooping flower clusters at the terminal ends of the stalks.</image-desc>

It produces stalks longer than a cubit and a half <note>about 27 inches or 70 cm</note>, with frequent and long branches. Along these are leaves like those of the Mastick tree <note>Lentiscus</note> or Licorice: oblong, blunt at the tip, smooth, and marked with many evident diagonal veins stretching to the edges. They are arranged in pairs at modest intervals on short stems. The flowers hang from the tips of the branches, gathered in a cluster; they are individual, oblong, shaped like a small nose, and purplish in color. The root is very long and quite thick. Like the Spurges <note>original: "Tithymalorum," refers to the genus Euphorbia</note>, it pours out an acrid and burning milk from all its parts.

It is found nowhere else but on the shores and islands of the Adriatic Gulf, and on the small island of Lio. Is this perhaps the "Turbith" of the ancients?

---

### LEAFLESS SPURGE.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a leafless Tithymalus, showing upright, naked stems emerging from a central root system.</image-desc>

The stems are straight and naked, like those of Spanish Broom or Gorse, or certainly provided with very few leaves. Around the middle of Spring and Autumn, it bears pale flowers at the summit, which soon fall away and leave the stalks naked for the rest of the year. The seed lies hidden within the Autumn flowers.

This plant is quite common in the coastal regions of Africa; it does not grow easily among us. A white milk drips abundantly from it, which has a very sharp and almost caustic <note>burning or corrosive</note> taste.

The Ethiopians use this plant when dried and reduced to powder as a seasoning, just as we use Pepper. Some believe this is the plant called *Xabre* and *Camarranum* by the Persian physician Rhazes. More on the Spurges can be found in the Appendix.

<column-break/>

### LATHYRUS OR LESSER CAPER-SPURGE: German: *Springkraut*; French: *Espurge*; Italian: *Lathyri*, *Cacapuzza*.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the Lathyrus plant, showing a central stalk with symmetrical, pointed leaves and flowering structures at the top.</image-desc>

Because Lathyrus <note>original: "Lathyris," likely Euphorbia lathyris</note> swells with milky sap and possesses almost the same powers as the *Esula* <note>another name for purgative spurges</note>, it is grouped by many in the Spurge family. According to Dioscorides, it is called the "un-angled" Spurge <note>original Greek: "aponnyllis"</note>.

Once sown in gardens, it propagates itself every year by seed, remaining green even in Winter; it does not bear fruit in its first year. It is found on the borders of fields in England and France, and is very common among the people of Milan <note>original: "Insubres"</note>, and also along the Rhine, springing up in various places. It flowers in Summer, and the seeds ripen in August and September. Depending on whether it is older or younger, it has wider or narrower leaves, which is why Tabernaemontanus provides two different figures for it. More in the Appendix.

---

### CONCERNING TURPETH, OR TURBITH.

What kind of plant Turpeth <note>A potent purgative root used in medieval medicine</note> belongs to is a matter of great controversy among botanical writers. Mesue calls it a milky, fennel-like plant. Serapio and Avicenna, although it is not recommended by any scent nor seems acrid to the taste, nevertheless thought it was *Tripolium* <note>Sea Starwort</note>. Actuarius sometimes says the root is *Peplus* <note>Petty Spurge</note>, and other times the *Alypum* of Dioscorides. Brassavola thinks it is the root of the Myrtle-leafed Spurge; but those who do not know how much Myrtle leaves differ from Fennel leaves should consult those skilled in herbal matters. Fuchs wanted it to be the root of *Thapsia* <note>Deadly Carrot</note>, but *Thapsia* does not swell with milky sap, which is a trait attributed to Turpeth. Some believed it to be the root of Antioch Scammony. Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a Portuguese physician in India</note> holds tenaciously to a different opinion, stating the plant has a root that is neither large nor long; a stem that spreads across the ground like Ivy, the thickness of a finger and two or three palms long; with leaves and flowers like Marshmallow, the flowers being white and sometimes reddish. Thus, what the true Turbith is remains uncertain. Be that as it may, there is no apothecary shop <note>original: "Officina"</note> where Turbith cannot be found marked with the signs that Mesue attributes to the best kind: namely, gummy, white, hollow, reed-like, with a gray and smooth bark, easy to break, etc. According to the same Mesue, there is a garden variety and a wild variety, and both may be large or small, white, yellow, or black.

Furthermore, it is established as hot and dry in the "third degree" <note>A classification of a medicine's potency in Galenic medicine</note> and serves various uses. Regarding this, Fallopius says: "Turbith has no less power than Scammony. But because its juice is not in use as the juice of Scammony is, but rather the root is used, it therefore seems to have less power than Scammony. However, if juice is compared to juice, and root to root, surely Turbith has no less power than Scammony." For this reason, some claim *Turbith* is named from the Latin *turbando* <note>"disturbing," referring to the stomach</note>. But they are deceived, because it is called *Turbith* by the Arabs, as if it were *Turpethum*, taking the name from the more recent Greeks, and especially from Actuarius, who calls this medicine by the name Turpethum.
